## Volume front matter

### Series title page

**The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reissue of all the extant monuments of Catholic tradition during the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully compared with one another and with several manuscript codices, corrected with the greatest diligence; continually illuminated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by others possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers commented on the individual texts of each book of Scripture, and in which places of their works they did so.**

**An edition most carefully prepared and easily preferable to all others, if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the corrections, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the extremely convenient format of the volumes and its consistent similarity throughout the entire work, the low price, and especially this collection, which is the first single, systematic, and chronological gathering in our library of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, collected from works relating to every period, place, language, and form.**

**Second series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Prepared by J.-P. Migne, editor of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning. Patrology has been printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. The Latin edition is sold for twelve hundred francs; the Greek-Latin edition for thirteen hundred. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter are presented in it in Latin translation only.

# Continuation of Hincmar’s works

[Column 0009]

## Letters

### First letter of the bishops of the dioceses of Rheims and Rouen to Louis, king of Germany

[Note: Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims; Immo, bishop of Noyon; Ermenfroi, bishop of Beauvais; Hincmar, bishop of Laon.]

[Note: This letter is attributed to Hincmar of Rheims.]

*(From the Acts of the provincial Council of Rheims, vol. I, p. 247.)*

To the lord Louis, glorious king, the bishops of the diocese of Rheims and of Rouen who were able to be present.

### I. They explain why they could not come to the assembly at Rheims

We each received a letter from Your Lordship in which you ordered us to meet you at Rheims on the seventh day before the Kalends of December, so that there you might discuss with us and with your other faithful servants the restoration of holy Church and the condition and salvation of the Christian people. But we could not attend that meeting, both because of the difficulty and shortness of the time and because of the unsuitable location; and, what is more grievous, because of the confusion caused by the tumult that had arisen.

Moreover, the divine laws—which you announced to us that you and your brothers would observe—plainly establish that just as archbishops may not act without their fellow bishops, so fellow bishops may not act without the consent or command of the archbishops, except in matters pertaining to their own parishes. In so short a time we were unable to receive letters from the archbishops concerning the assembly.

Therefore let Your Sublimity know that our humility did not despise your command. But, as was said long ago, “Whoever commands what is impossible makes himself contemptible.”

### II. They complain that he has not hitherto obeyed their admonitions and counsels

The discussion concerning the restoration of holy Church and the condition and salvation of the Christian people—which you now say you wish to hold with us—could have taken place more justly and reasonably if you had been willing, with heavenly regard, to obey our counsels—or rather, divine counsels and admonitions and exhortations. For we did not write, command, or say things of our own, but what we found in the sacred writings under the guidance of charity, which is God, and what we recognize as implanted in nature.

Furthermore, what has been done or is being done contrary to what we wrote, commanded, and said is recognized even by the less wise as the sickness and vice of the natural law. Accordingly, let every prudent person come to his senses and understand how greatly God is offended when one sins knowingly against matters so great and so clear.

Hence it is written: “Let them descend alive into hell” (Psalm 54), that is, “Let them fall into sin knowingly.”

These things occur by God’s permission, deservedly, because of the suffering world and our common sins—those of shepherds and flocks alike—and because of the transgressions of king and kingdom, as it is written: “He made a way for his indignation through the sending of evil angels” (Psalm 77).

Nevertheless, as Truth bears witness, neither will the rod of the Lord’s fury be without the vengeance of punishment. Thus we read, thus we have heard, thus we have seen, and certainly thus we shall soon see. For although we are sinners, we are repentant and place firm confidence in divine mercy; and, with the Holy Spirit carrying out the sacred ministry, we have undertaken that ministry—for without him we do not minister sacred things. We know that Truth has truly said to us: “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10).

### III. They have frequently urged him to enter into concord with his brother

Although Your Lordship knows better from which writings, commands, and sayings we speak, it is nevertheless not out of place for us to recall them to your memory.

First, through Hildegarius, the venerable bishop, by writings and spoken words; second, through Aeneas, the honorable bishop, by letters and words; again through Aeneas by word of mouth; then through Hincmar of Rheims and Wenilo of Rouen. Again, through these same men, together with others whom you yourself summoned, you heard sufficiently what was appropriate for your salvation, when—as we had previously requested—we asked that your brother and all his faithful servants come before you and your faithful servants, at a suitable place and time, so that we might come to an accounting before you and your faithful servants, at a suitable place and time, and, with God’s help, whatever had been badly done might be corrected by your counsel and assistance.

[Note: Hildegaire, bishop of Meaux.]

[Note: Aeneas, bishop of Paris.]

Because you did not heed any of these words, we greatly fear what is said: “If they have kept my word, they will also keep yours” (John 15), together with the other threats uttered by the Lord. And if those words have not been heard, it may also be thought that these words—which you say you wish to seek and hear from us—will not be heard either.

Some people think that just as the Lord, when he sought figs on the fig tree which he cursed, although, as the Gospel testifies, it was not the season for figs, wished to signify something else, so also in this hastily arranged and unsuitable assembly, apart from Your Lordship’s sincerity—about whose purity we wish to presume nothing contrary—something else may perhaps be understood.

And since blessed Peter admonishes every bishop to be ready to give satisfaction to everyone who asks him for an account, we now give Your Lordship, in accordance with the circumstances, our faithful counsel.

### IV. He should consider why he has entered his brother’s kingdom and whether he wishes to endure what he has done

First of all, examine at the very root of your heart your arrival in this kingdom, and weigh it on the scales of justice before the eyes of the Lord, to whom, according to the Psalmist, human thought makes confession. Return to your heart, whatever your advisers, counselors, and flatterers may say to you; question your conscience about whatever you can find and say in accusation or commendation of your arrival; and judge whether you are willing to endure such things as you are doing.

Place before the eyes of your mind that hour which you know you will in no way be able to escape, when your soul departs from the body—when it will leave behind the whole world, every power, all riches, and the body itself; when, without the help of wife and children and without the consolation and company of retainers and vassals, it will go forth naked and desolate; and when it will leave unfinished whatever it has thought and planned, as Scripture says: “On that day all their thoughts will perish” (Psalm 145).

It will see all its sins and feel them, seeing the devils binding and constricting it. Whatever it thought, spoke, and did in this world against charity and the faith that was owed, and did not amend through worthy fruits of repentance, it will always have before its eyes. It will wish to escape, but will not be able.

For it is certain that, when all human beings leave the body, devils come to them—to the just as well as to sinners. They came even to Christ, in whom they found nothing belonging to them, as it is written: “The prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14).

And believe us truly, O king—would that you were always good and Christian!—that hour is not far away; indeed, it is very near—nearer than you may think. Therefore do not let these things you see deceive you.

In the time of your father we saw certain things begun and done by some men which, in this present time, we see being carried out by those who now accomplish them, and which will be completed by others. When the hour of your departure comes, just as they now laugh when through you they obtain what they want, at the hour of their own desire, so they will laugh at the hour of your departure and seek how, through another, to keep what they obtained through you. It may even be that some will seek this during your lifetime.

But unless they perform worthy repentance, they too will come miserably to the hour of their departure, as did those who deserted your father together with your brother. For just as those men, while organizing seditions against paternal reverence, so these men, while stirring you up against brotherly affection, have attempted to put forward the name of peace, the condition of the Church, and the salvation and unity of the people. But poison lay hidden beneath the honey.

What the Psalmist said has been fulfilled in those men and is being fulfilled in these: “They speak peace with their neighbor, but evil is in their hearts” (Psalm 27), together with what follows. Those men received in this world what is known, and in the other world they received what will be more fully revealed at the judgment.

Seeing their end, these men ought to have feared their own actions; and they will do so, if the Lord, who regards the humble and protects the little ones, has looked upon them. Thus, when the pestilent man is scourged, as it is written, the simple person will become wiser. They will understand, because the Lord will not reject his people, nor forget them forever: “Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I will arise,” says the Lord (Psalm 11).

Otherwise, just as he then said to those men, so now the Lord says to these: “I have been silent; shall I always be silent? I will cry out like a woman in labor” (Isaiah 42).

“My hour has not yet come, but your hour is here, and the power of darkness.” And indeed, on this your day, what belongs to your peace! But now these things are hidden from your eyes, because days will come upon you.

We beg you, my lord, to ask for yourself, in a place where you can properly attend, to read Saint Gregory’s homily on the Gospel reading: “When Jesus saw the city, he wept over it.”

We beseech you, my lord, also to keep before the eyes of your mind that day when, together with all human beings, your soul will receive back its own body and you will come before the face of the eternal Judge in the presence of all angels and human beings. On that day, as Saint Paul says, the Lord will judge each person—not through another’s testimony, but through each person’s hidden thoughts, which will accuse or even defend him—when each will receive according to what he did in the body, whether good or evil.

Then our words, which we have written, will not be despised by those who now disregard them. Without a doubt, they will be repeated as testimony at that dread judgment itself. None of those men will then help you, since none will be able to help himself, when those who do such things as we hear, perceive, and grieve over—if they persist in such conduct—go into eternal fire, while the just, who suffer injustice, go into eternal life.

### V. Concerning the things cruelly and impiously done along his route, so that he may prohibit and restrain them

We have heard that such great and cruel, abominable things are being done throughout the parishes through which you pass; some things we perceive, others we fear to perceive, and we grieve with those who have perceived and are perceiving them. These things surpass the calamity and misery which we suffer from the pagans, because they are being carried out by Christians against Christians, by parents against parents, by a Christian king against a Christian king, and by brother against brother, contrary to every divine and human law.

Against these things the Church, afflicted by pagans, cries out: “They have added to the pain of my wounds” (Psalm 68). And we, together with all who suffer, say: “We hoped for peace, and it did not come; we sought good, and behold, disturbance” (Jeremiah 14).

Therefore prohibit, restrain, and calm such things, for your palace ought to be sacred, not sacrilegious. A king’s palace is so called because of the rational people who inhabit it, not because of senseless walls or enclosures.

A king is so called from ruling: he ought to rule himself under God, and the good together with God, with purity of heart, truthfulness of speech, and steadfastness; and he ought to correct the wicked in their wickedness and direct them toward uprightness.

If you have come to correct what has been badly done, you ought not to inflict things worse than those we have seen being done by Christians against Christians. If you have come to make peace, you must obtain peace peacefully from the author of peace. If you have come to drive out discord and restore charity, you must display the charity which Christ taught through Paul.

For he says: “Charity is not ambitious, does not act wrongly, does not seek its own; it does not rejoice over iniquity, but rejoices with the truth” (1 Corinthians 13). It comes from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith; it works through love, not through power or unlawful greed. Without this charity, as it is written, even if someone were to hand over his body to be burned, it would profit him nothing.

The Lord gave this charity to all as a sign, so that they might know whether someone is a Christian and whether he will enter the kingdom of God: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 10). For those who at the beginning of the faith were called disciples are now called Christians.

This is also the wedding garment. Whoever does not have it will, at the future judgment, be cast out from the wedding feast of the heavenly banquet into the outer darkness and into eternal fire, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

### VI. He should turn his arms against the pagans instead, and should not allow those fleeing from them to be harassed by his own people

Let charity itself kindle you against the pagans, so that those who were not then moved by compassion to go with us against them—although they held and still hold great honors in this kingdom—may now, whatever their intention, free holy Church from their domination through your arrangement, and rescue from unlawful tribute the kingdom that is being redeemed from them.

Those who flee from the face of the pagans should also find, when they come into the regions over which you rule, a tranquil refuge, not such plunder that neither the inhabitants can live nor the fugitives receive assistance.

For now, because our sins demand it, what was once spoken through the prophet is being fulfilled: “He who flees from the face of the lion will fall upon the bear; and when he enters the house and leans his hand against the wall, the serpent will bite him. And when they have escaped iron weapons, they will fall upon a bronze bow” (Amos 5). Everywhere, alas, the wretched find affliction.

### VII. He should preserve the privileges and immunities of the churches, not trouble their rulers, and not permit their possessions to be seized

If, as you have written to us, you seek to restore the Church of God, preserve intact the privileges owed to bishops and to the churches entrusted to them, as they have been divinely established.

Take care to preserve their charters, immunities, and honor, as your grandfather and father preserved them. Likewise preserve what your brother, our lord—who received a portion of the kingdom both through your father’s donation and through mutual agreements with you and with your faithful servants—did for the worship and honor of the churches.

Honor the rulers and shepherds of the churches as fathers and vicars of Christ, as Holy Scripture commands: “Sanctify the priests of God, and humble your head before the great” (Ecclesiasticus 7).

Obey their spiritual counsels, Scripture again saying: “Ask your fathers, and they will declare it to you; your elders, and they will tell you” (Deuteronomy 31). And again: “Ask my priests about my law” (Haggai 2). The Lord also says through the prophet Malachi: “The lips of the priest will guard knowledge, and they will seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Malachi 2).

Do not disturb them at unsuitable or inconvenient times. Let them carry out, for the salvation of the people, the sacred ministry to which they have been ordained. Do not harass those subject to them in domestic matters, and do not permit them to be dishonored or oppressed.

Take pains to ensure that priests retain the appropriate honor and the due rights established by the canons and by the capitularies of your grandfather and father.

Arrange that bishops have the peaceful liberty to travel through their parishes, preach, confirm, and correct.

Entrust to the public official—that is, the count’s minister—the duty of accompanying them when they order it, and of bringing free men accused of incest to the bishop’s court if, after the priests’ admonition, they refuse to come to the bishop.

If a bishop sends to you for any ecclesiastical necessity, let his own messenger come to you, through whom he may obtain whatever he reasonably requests. Establish an appropriate office for this purpose in your palace, just as the count of the palace has an office for public cases.

Permit provincial synods with the bishops, and particular synods with the priests, to be held peacefully at the times established by the sacred rules.

[Note: It appears that Louis of Germany had forbidden the bishops to hold councils.]

Do not tolerate the plundering or tearing away from churches of ecclesiastical property and resources, which are the vows of the faithful, the redemption-price of sinners, and the stipends of the servants and handmaids of God. Rather, resist and defend them firmly, as a Christian king and foster-son of the Church.

The successors of the apostles ordained that free men serving the churches should possess, under the direction of the churches’ rulers, portions of those things consecrated to God, so that, since the vows of the faithful had grown and the sins of the faithful had increased, the kingdom’s military force might be enlarged through ecclesiastical administration to resist the wickedness of evil men. Thus the churches themselves would have defense and peace, and Christendom would enjoy tranquility.

Therefore, just as the goods and resources from which clerics live are under the protection of consecrated immunity, so too are those from which vassals are to perform military service; and both kinds ought to be protected by royal authority for the use of the churches.

But Charles, the prince, father of King Pippin, who first among all the kings and princes of the Franks separated and divided the property of the churches from them, has been condemned to eternal ruin above all for this one reason.

For Saint Eucherius, bishop of Orléans, who rests in the monastery of Saint-Trond, while engaged in prayer was carried away into the other world. Among the things which the Lord showed him, he saw Charles being tormented in the lowest hell.

When Eucherius asked, the angel who was guiding him replied that, by the judgment of the saints—who will judge with the Lord at the future judgment—he had been assigned, in soul and body, to everlasting punishments even before that judgment, because he had seized and divided their property. He was receiving punishment together with his own sins because of the sins of all who had given their property and resources, for the honor and love of the Lord, to holy places, for the lamps of divine worship and the support of Christ’s servants and the poor, for the redemption of their souls.

When Eucherius returned to himself, he summoned Saint Boniface and Fulrad, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Denis and chief chaplain of King Pippin. He told them these things and gave them a sign: they were to go to his tomb, and if they did not find his body there, they were to believe that what he had said was true.

They went to the monastery mentioned above, where Charles’s body had been buried, and opened his tomb. Suddenly a dragon appeared to come out, and the entire interior of the tomb was found blackened, as though it had been burned.

We ourselves saw men who survived until our time and who had been present at this event; they truthfully testified to us by word of mouth what they had heard and seen.

[Note: Despite the testimony of the bishops at the Council of Quierzy, this supposed vision of Saint Eucherius must be regarded as a fable.]

When his son Pippin learned of this, he caused a synod to be assembled at Liptina. George by name, legate of the Apostolic See, presided over it together with Saint Boniface. We possess the synod itself, and Pippin did everything he could to restore to the churches the ecclesiastical property which his father had taken.

[Note: The Council of Lestines was held by order of Carloman, mayor of the palace, in 743. Hincmar claims that George, legate of the Holy See, attended it with Saint Boniface; this is an error, for George was sent to Gaul only after that bishop’s death.]

Since Pippin could not restore all the property to the churches, because of the conflict he was waging with Waifar, prince of Aquitaine, he asked the bishops to make leases of it. He decreed that ninths and tenths should be given for the repair of roofs, and twelve denarii from each household to the church from which the property had been granted as a benefice, as long as the property itself should return to the Church. This is recorded in the book of the kings’ capitularies.

Accordingly, the lord Charles the emperor, while still bearing the royal name, issued an edict that neither he nor his sons nor his successors should attempt to undertake such an action. He confirmed it with his own hand; we possess the complete document, and anyone who has that book and wishes to read it can find an excerpt of the relevant chapter in his *Book of Capitularies*.

We also possess this account in written records, and some among us heard the lord Emperor Louis, your father, report it orally.

The sacred canons, dictated by the Holy Spirit, count those who plunder ecclesiastical resources and unlawfully appropriate church property as like Judas, the betrayer of Christ. The saints who reign with God in heaven and shine with miracles on earth exclude such men by divine judgment, as murderers of the poor, from the thresholds of the Church and from the heavenly kingdom.

Concerning such sacrilegious men, the prophecy of the Psalm says: “They said, ‘Let us take possession of the sanctuary of God as an inheritance.’ My God, make them like a wheel, and like straw before the face of the wind. As fire burns the forest and as flame burns the mountains, so pursue them in your storm and trouble them in your anger. Fill their faces with shame” (Psalm 82).

### VIII. He should restore to religious persons the monasteries granted to laymen by Charles

Restore to their rightful privilege the monasteries and other religious and distinguished dwellings of canons, monks, and holy women which your ancestors established long ago under religious discipline, appointing male and female superiors over them.

This includes those monasteries established when your ancestors held the primacy of the kingdom, and even when Saint Remigius, with the Lord’s help, converted the Franks to the faith and baptized them together with their king.

Your brother, our lord, partly through youth, partly through weakness, partly through the crafty suggestions of others, and partly through the necessity created by threats—for the petitioners said that unless he gave them those sacred places they would defect from him, and that he would eventually lose the kingdom through you, as now appears, or through your brother—entrusted them to such persons as you know. Restore them to their rightful privilege.

Your brother had already corrected part of what he had done wrongly, both through divine inspiration, through priestly rebuke, and after being admonished by the Apostolic See. He often asked, sighing, how he might correct what still remained uncorrected.

Far be it from you, who have come here for the restoration of holy Church, either to worsen what he corrected, so that as he offended, you too may offend, or to leave uncorrected what he was not yet able to correct. You often admonished your brothers about such matters, as we ourselves also testify, and in every public announcement you made together you argued the point most readily.

Likewise, near Teudonis villa, at the place called the Judgment, you accepted with your brothers the capitularies which we possess, and at Marsna you confirmed them with your own hand in a written charter.

If someone has acted contrary to this, you will not therefore be exempt if—God is witness—you fail to take care to observe what you agreed and confirmed.

For no one is helped by condemning another’s evil unless he himself avoids it. Paul demonstrates this when he says: “Do you think, O man, that you will escape God’s judgment while doing the same things that you judge?” (Romans 2).

### IX. The rulers of the monasteries should diligently ensure that God’s servants and handmaids live according to their order

Firmly and earnestly command the rulers of the monasteries to which you entrust monasteries to take careful and diligent measures so that, according to the order, habit, and sex for which the inhabitants were appointed, the servants and handmaids of the Lord may live according to their proper discipline.

Let them have the necessary provisions for food, clothing, and everything else; and let the superiors of the religious houses provide them with dwellings and servants as appropriate, in accordance with their religious habit and manner of life. Let them in no way neglect the reception of guests and the poor.

Nor should unsuitable persons or things inconsistent with religious life be introduced into the monasteries. We do not say this because we are unaware that religious superiors must undertake the necessary provision and care in these matters.

### X. The hostels for pilgrims should be administered by their superiors for the purpose for which they were established, with the bishops’ counsel

Maintain the hostels for pilgrims, such as those of the Scots, and those which were built and established in the time of your royal predecessors, so that they remain devoted to the purpose for which they were founded and are organized and supervised by God-fearing superiors, lest they be dissipated.

Also command the rulers of monasteries and xenodochia—that is, hospitals—to be subject to their proper bishops, as canonical authority teaches and as the capitularies of your grandfather and father command, and to govern the monasteries and hospitals entrusted to them according to the bishops’ counsel. For the bishops will strive to provide them with paternal care in accordance with their ministry.

Since you have often, together with your brothers, granted to everyone in every order the law and justice appropriate to them through frequent public declarations, let men and women of ecclesiastical and religious life, as well as pilgrims and the poor—in whom Christ is especially received—always perceive that your grant of protection is present to them.

### XI. That it is fitting for the king to order his life so as to be an example to everyone
And since, as you have written to us, you wish to inquire into the condition and welfare of the Christian people, begin first with yourselves, who ought to correct others, as it is written: “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke 4); and the hand that tends to cleanse the filth of others must itself be clean of filth. What you ought to correct in others, let no one rightly be able to reproach in you. For over as many people as you are placed in authority at the summit of the kingdom, to that many people’s conduct you ought to minister; and, like a lamp placed upon a lampstand in a house, display examples of goodness, [Col. 0018A] because everyone’s eyes ought to be fixed upon you. If you destroy those whom, through you and from you, ought to have been built up for good by your bad example, you will necessarily be tortured in the future age by punishments as great as theirs.

Therefore, since you are king and are called lord, you ought always, with your heart raised up, to look toward Him from whom—as King of kings and Lord of lords—you borrow the name of king and lord. And just as He orders the world in equity, and, as is said in the Book of Wisdom, appointed humanity for this purpose, so that humanity might likewise do the same, imitate Him if you wish to reign with Him. For whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk as He walked, and He says: “Be perfect, you also, just as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matthew 5).

And if you should say, “How can I be [Col. 0018B] perfect,” when another Scripture says, “If anyone does not stumble in speech, he is a perfect man,” one does not fall away from perfection if one does not sin through the malicious desire to sin: “For the righteous man falls seven times and rises again, but the wicked fall into evil” (Proverbs 16). And: “When the righteous man has fallen, he will not be shattered, because the Lord supports him with His hand” (Psalm 36).

However anyone may sin—whether by the will of desire or by the necessity of weakness—no one can judge him better than his own conscience, which cannot remain hidden from the eyes of its examiner. Therefore you ought to live, judge, and act even in secret as though you were always in public. For often someone will praise you with his words while severely reproving you in his heart; often, too, he will judge among others as blameworthy the very things he has praised to you and in you.

[Col. 0018C] If, as we say, with the Lord’s help you are able to live, judge, and act in this way; if private affection does not spur you on; if desire for glory, wealth, possessions, and power does not inflame you; if you do not believe another person’s tongue more than your own conscience; if the moth of flattery does not gnaw at you; if envy of another’s happiness does not burn you; if neglect of the soul and love of the flesh do not trouble you; if you believe that Christ the King died not for Himself—that is, not from His own need—but for us, so that we who were dead might live; and if you strive more to live for others, in the interests of their salvation, than for yourselves in the pursuit of your own desires; if you know that you will die, and believe that you will render an account to the Lord for your own deeds; and if you believe that you will possess, without end or any alteration, whatever you have deservedly received, [Col. 0018D]

## XII. How he ought to govern his household, what he ought to render to God and to his subjects, and what sort of ministers he ought to appoint for the palace and the commonwealth

Nourish, govern, and order your household in such a way that, when the people of the kingdom come to you, they may see in you and in your household how they ought to nourish, order, and govern themselves and their household—with such humility and chastity, and with such sobriety, justice, and devotion. For, as a certain wise man said, “The household will be kept according to the character of its master.”

For this reason the king’s household is called a school—that is, a discipline. It is called not merely because its members are scholars, that is, disciplined and well-corrected, as others are, but rather because the household itself is called a school, which is interpreted as discipline or correction: it should correct others by its dress, manner of walking, speech, conduct, and restraint from every kind of vanity.

And you, like a stake that has not been firmly driven in, will fall, and those who hang upon you will slip, unless you are firmly supported in the Lord of hosts. Therefore, just as the Lord taught those placed under authority, on the occasion of the tempter’s question, to render “to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s,” so you, who are under God and over human beings, must render to God the things that are God’s; and, like an equitable Caesar, render to subjects the things that belong to subjects.

Render to God pure and undefiled faith and the most sincere worship: in priests; in the privileges of churches; in holy places; in ecclesiastical and religious men and women; in the defense [Col. 0019B] of the Church and of Christianity; in equity and justice for the Christian people; and in the raising up, tranquillity, and consolation of all who are in need, as we have already said. Pay Him His daily due in daily prayer and in just and continual almsgiving. Offer Him your devotion in sacred offerings and in tears poured out according to the greatness and multitude of your daily sins.

Render to your subjects judgment with mercy and justice with equity. Strive to exalt the humble and those who fear God, and to defeat and humble the proud. Strive to be loved by the good more than feared. See to it that the wicked, if not for God’s sake, at least through fear of you, dread doing evil. Among you, let a deceitful tongue, a hand full of gifts, or undue service have no greater force than truth, equity, and sincerity, knowing what is written: “The one who shakes his hands free from every gift will dwell on high” (Isaiah 33).

From this it must consequently be understood—and not something else. For a gift from the tongue is favor; a gift from the hand is a donation; a gift from service is undue subjection.

Appoint ministers of the palace who know, love, and fear God; who take the greatest care that all who come to the palace in need, and all through whose lands you travel, should run joyfully to see you, marveling at you as a father and consoler—not, as we do not wish to say, flee from you groaning and cursing.

Appoint counts and ministers of the commonwealth who do not love gifts, who hate greed, who detest pride, who do not oppress or dishonor the peasants [Note: [Col. 0019D] Peasants.], who in no way devastate their fields, vineyards, meadows, or woods; who do not plunder or seize their livestock, whether cattle, young pigs, or whatever belongs to them [Note: [Col. 0020D] “Friskingas”: young pigs.], and who in no way take away their property by violence or malicious schemes; who, with the counsel of their bishops, do what belongs to God and accords with Christianity.

Let them hold assemblies not to acquire profit, but so that God’s churches, widows, orphans, and the people may have justice; and let them strive more to recall litigants to concord, with justice preserved, than to allow themselves to obtain some profit from the matter. If they cannot reconcile them, then, as is right, let them take great care to have a just judgment issued, knowing that it is written: “I will show you, human being, what is good”—that is, “to do judgment and justice, and to walk carefully with your God” (Micah 6). That means: let what pleases Him please you, and do it; let what displeases Him displease you, and do not do it.

But if through weakness you do something wrong, do not persist stubbornly or obstinately in your evil deed. Instead, immediately withdraw your foot from it as from hot iron, and direct it onto the path of the will of the Lord your God. And since it is written, “There are ways that seem good to human beings, but they lead to destruction” (Proverbs 16), do what Scripture commands you, whoever you are: “Ask about the good way, and walk in it” (Jeremiah 6). For, as it is said in the Gospel: “Broad is the way that leads to destruction, and many go by it; narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life, and few find it” (Matthew 7).

Therefore, whoever you are, listen to the prophet and pray with the prophet: “Teach me Your law, Lord, the way of Your statutes, and I shall always seek it” (Psalm 118). And: “Lead me in the path of Your commandments; remove from me the way of iniquity, and have mercy on me according to Your law” (ibid.). For, as the prophet Jeremiah says: “A person’s way is not his own, nor does it belong to a man to walk and direct his steps” (Jeremiah 10); rather, “the steps of a man are directed by the Lord, and He wills his way” (Psalm 36).

The counts themselves should likewise appoint, as far as they can, ministers like themselves—God-fearing and lovers of justice—who, when they see their elders kind and approachable toward their peasants, may themselves strive, according to their ability, to imitate them in [Col. 0020C] every goodness and justice.

## XIII. That he should strive to recall to the peace of the Church those who have been excommunicated on account of these uprisings

Recall also to the path of the laws and of justice those worldly men of power who, amid these uprisings, have rejected the yoke of the law and the justice of equity, and have committed such and so great deeds that they have deserved ecclesiastical and episcopal excommunication. Command or compel them to come humbly, as they must, to their bishops. Persuade them, and command them by royal authority, either to make due and necessary satisfaction humbly to the Church against which they have sinned, or humbly and truthfully to excuse themselves, so that through the episcopal ministry they may be able to be absolved by the Lord.

[Col. 0020D] And if perhaps you, or any others who have been infected and condemned through association and fellowship with them, are involved, let each person who recognizes this make penance. For, as sacred authority bears witness, one who is damnably burdened by external sins will not be able to be absolved from his own sins. As the holy prophet David demonstrates while praying to God, saying: “Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults, and spare Your servant from those of others” (Psalm 18).

## XIV. How judges of the royal estates are to be appointed

Finally, appoint judges of the royal estates who are not greedy, who do not love avarice, and who neither practice usury themselves nor lend royal or personal money at interest, and do not allow usury to be practiced by their subjects. You above all your ministers ought to hate and flee all these things.

Let the judges not oppress the royal serfs, nor demand from them more than they were accustomed to render in your father’s time. Let them not afflict them with compulsory labor at an unsuitable time, nor condemn the tenants through deceit, malicious schemes, or inappropriate petitions. For if, through such or similar actions, you have a weight of silver or gold in your treasury, the greater and heavier weight will be the burden of sin that you have in your conscience and soul.

Let them build up your estates with moderate expenditures, so that what is necessary for respectability may be present without burdening the household. Let them work and cultivate the lands and vineyards in due season with appropriate care; let them preserve and distribute what has been produced with faithful discretion; let them provide suitable and necessary nourishment. Let them guard the woods, so that they may have pastures; let them protect and cultivate the meadows, so that they may have fodder.

Thus it will not be necessary for you, on every pretext and at the urging of anyone, to travel around the estates of bishops, abbots, abbesses, or counts, demanding reception expenses greater than reason permits [Note: [Col. 0021D] Reception expenses.], and burdening poor ecclesiastical persons and the tenants of your faithful with carts and transport horses exacted contrary to obligation [Note: [Col. 0022D] “Carts and transport horses”: carts and horses for carrying out labor.], thereby piling upon your soul the sin of resources unjustly consumed.

Do not strive to demand from counts or faithful men, concerning what they receive from free men, more than the law and custom required in your father’s time. Rather, ensure that you have enough to live sufficiently and honorably with your household court, to receive embassies coming to your palace, and, as it is written, to give from just labor to those suffering need. For a king ought to be generous, but he ought not to seek what he may give from injustice or wrongdoing.

The judges of the estates, however, should restrain the tenants so that they do not oppress ecclesiastical people, poorer free men, or the slaves of others under the pretext of royal privilege, nor devastate woods or anything else belonging to others in their vicinity.

For a just king, who ought to love justice, must not have impious and unjust ministers and tenants; rather, he ought to display in himself and in his own people the proper example for imitation by all. For if he himself loves God, all good people will love him; and if he himself fears God, all wicked people will fear him. Let the king and his ministers do good through love of God, and teach everyone to do good; let them flee evil through fear of God, and let everyone learn from them to flee evil.

Appoint throughout the kingdom such envoys as know how the counts and the other ministers of the commonwealth render justice and judgment to the people; and just as they are placed over the counts, so let them surpass them in knowledge, justice, and truth.

## XV. That the kingdom’s synod of bishops should be awaited, at which they may deliberate what action is necessary; how much reverence is owed to kings, and that bishops are not to be compelled to swear oaths

[Col. 0022A]

Because you have indicated in your letters that you wished to discuss with us the restoration of the holy Church and the condition and welfare of the Christian people, we have taken care to respond to your lordship in writing. We were unable to come into your presence because of the severity of the weather, the unsuitability of the season, and the approaching feast of the Nativity of our Lord.

In the meantime, carry out those things which you are able to carry out with your faithful without our bodily presence. When the appropriate time designated by the sacred canons arrives—when, because of the pagan invasions and the exceedingly wretched confusion caused by the uprising, plundering, and robbery that have arisen, it is permitted us, with the lords and brothers and fellow-provincial archbishops and fellow-bishops, by the Lord’s favor, to celebrate a synod—we shall strive to discuss with them what remains to be done, as with teachers and fathers, and to give due counsel to your lordship.

And if God has determined to unite and prosper the stability and welfare of the Church and the kingdom in your hand, we shall strive, under the service of your righteous rule, to carry out whatever we see, together with our archbishops and fellow-bishops, to accord more fully with the divine dispositions.

For God is able to turn a less good beginning into a perfectly good course of action; for Him, what people customarily judge impossible is known to be possible.

If your wisdom considers it appropriate to speak and deliberate with the neighboring king and his faithful, while the lord of this part of the kingdom, namely our lord your brother, is absent, it is all the more necessary for us to await the canonical time, so that we may speak with our brothers and fellow-provincial archbishops and bishops, since the general cause of the entire Cisalpine Church is at stake.

Above all, it is necessary for us to speak with those archbishops and bishops who, by the agreement and will of the people of this kingdom, anointed our lord, your brother, king with sacred chrism according to divine tradition, and whom the holy apostolic see, our mother, endeavored in its apostolic letters to honor and confirm as king.

Read the Books of Kings, and you will find with what reverence the holy Samuel, whose place in the Church we, although unworthy, occupy, considered it right to treat Saul, rejected and cast off by the Lord. And consider how highly holy David, chosen and anointed by the Lord in Saul’s place, valued laying hands upon the Lord’s Anointed. Saul was not only from another lineage but from another tribe; David knew that Saul had been rejected and that he himself had been chosen by the Lord. Yet David had done Saul no injury, but had provided him with the greatest assistance and devoted service.

He did not attempt either to take the kingdom from him by war or to steal it from him by a cunning scheme. Although he had many persuaders and helpers for this purpose, he allowed none of them to undertake such a plot, even though he had very often endured many persecutions and dangers near death from Saul.

Moreover, you know well what he commanded concerning the man who, although falsely, announced that he had laid hands upon the Lord’s Anointed in order to gain favor with Saul. For if anyone is unaware of this, we tell him that David ordered him to be killed by the sword.

Likewise, whoever disloyally and insolently lays hands upon any anointed one of the Lord despises the Lord, Christ of the anointed ones, and beyond doubt perishes in his soul through the punishment of the spiritual sword.

We say these things not to seek inappropriate exaggerations against your lordship, but to demonstrate more clearly, in accordance with the character of our ministry, what—apart from the faith and beneficence that are owed—we must revere in your brother.

We ought and wish to believe you to be such that you neither desire to obtain an increase of the kingdom at the expense of your soul, nor that we should, with such dishonor, accept you into the assistance of ecclesiastical rule and governance, so as to be without priestly office. We would be deprived of that office if, against God and the authority of reason, we committed ourselves and our churches to you.

Indeed, the churches entrusted to us by God are not such benefices, nor the property of such a king, that he may give or take them away at his pleasure and without deliberation, since everything that belongs to the Church has been consecrated to God. Therefore, whoever defrauds or takes anything from the Church is known, according to Holy Scripture, to commit sacrilege.

And we bishops, consecrated to the Lord, are not the sort of people who ought, like secular men, to commend ourselves to anyone in vassalage, or to commit ourselves and our churches to anyone for defense and assistance in ecclesiastical governance, or in any way to make the oath which the authority of the Gospel and the apostles forbids us to make.

For it is abominable that a hand anointed with holy chrism—the hand that, through prayer and the sign of the cross, consecrates from bread and wine mixed with water the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood—should, whatever it may have done before ordination, in any way take a secular oath after episcopal ordination.

And it is wicked that the tongue of a bishop, which by God’s grace has become a key of heaven, should, like that of any secular person, swear over sacred things in the name of the Lord and by invocation of the saints—unless, perhaps, which God forbid, a scandal should arise against him in his own Church; in that case he should act with such moderation as the rulers of the Church, instructed by the Lord, have established in synodal council.

And if oaths have at any time been demanded from or made by bishops contrary to God and the ecclesiastical regulations dictated by the Holy Spirit and confirmed by Christ’s blood, the pages of Holy Scripture declare them invalid; and those who demand or make them require the remedy of saving penance [Note: [Col. 0023D] See the Council of Pontyon, in the year 876, where Hincmar swore an oath of fidelity to the king.].

Therefore, my lord, wait patiently, as a Christian prince and son of the Church, and honor the rulers of the holy Church, so that He may honor you who said to us: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever rejects you rejects me” (Luke 10). And: “Those who honor me I will honor, but those who despise me will be held of no account” (1 Samuel 2). And: “Whoever touches you touches the apple of my eye” (Zechariah 2). And in the psalm: “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not act wickedly against my prophets” (Psalm 104). For: “Those who act wickedly shall be destroyed, but those who wait for the Lord shall inherit the earth” (Psalm 36)—that is, the kingdom of God.

And when the time and place arrive, as we said above, we shall speak with our fellow-bishops; and whatever we see to accord with the Lord’s just dispositions, we shall certainly do.

There is no reasonable cause that ought to spur you on against what we request. For we are not the sort of people who, once we have known the Lord’s will, would wish or ought in any way to resist it, or to stir up, begin, or maintain quarrels, dissensions, or uprisings—which the common people call *werras*. The Lord appointed us as preachers and followers of peace; He commanded us to lament and care for our sins, those entrusted to us, and the whole people, and ordered us to wage war against vices and keep peace with our brothers.

We desire and seek peace and quiet, not quarrels and wars. For, as the Apostle says: “Our weapons are not carnal but spiritual, and powerful” (2 Corinthians 10). With these weapons our feet are shod for the preparation of the gospel of peace; we are clothed with the breastplate of justice and the helmet of salvation, our loins are girded with truth, and we have the shield of faith and the sword of the Holy Spirit. For “our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the principalities and powers, against the rulers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.”

We do not serve an earthly king, but a heavenly one, for the salvation both of ourselves and of the earthly king and of the whole people entrusted to us. Our duty is to harm no one, to act disloyally toward no one, and to wish to benefit everyone.

Finally, my lord king, do not listen, against God and against your own soul, to those who may say to you: “King, do not concern yourself with what those traitors and lowborn men report to you. Do what we tell you, for your parents held the kingdom together with our parents, not with the parents of those others.”

But we beseech your lordship: consider instead, if you are a Christian king—as you have given thanks to God, believe in Him, and wish to reign through Him—through whom, as it is written, “kings reign” (Proverbs 8), and to whom belongs the kingdom, indeed the earth and its fullness. For the same God, coming in the flesh—He alone who could become both king and priest—and ascending into heaven, established His kingdom, that is, His Church, to be governed between pontifical authority and royal power. He did not choose the wealthy and noble for this purpose, but the poor and fishermen. And, as it is written: “He chose the base and despised things of the world in order to confound the strong” (1 Corinthians 1).

It may be that such men say these things to you—if perhaps those who fear God less than is necessary have said them—men whose parents the devil, who according to Scripture “is king over all the sons of pride” (Job 41), has disturbed the kingdom of Christ, which is the Church, and whom he now holds in his own kingdom, that is, in hell, and will hold there with himself forever.

Know for certain, however, that with our parents—that is, with the apostles—Christ, the King of kings, acquired, enlarged, and governed His kingdom, that is, the Church. And through us and with us—may we not say this to our own judgment—the same Lord Jesus Christ daily acquires, increases, and governs that Church, that is, His kingdom, as was said by the Lord to the Church through the prophet: “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you” (Psalm 44)—that is, in place of the apostles He created bishops for you, to govern and teach you.

With this Church entrusted to us by God, Christian king and lord, as you commanded in your letters, we shall strive through fasts, prayers, and litanies to knock upon and awaken the supreme governor, the Lord, who is sleeping in the ship of the holy Church as it tosses upon this sea—that is, this shipwrecking age—because of our common sins, and to pray to Him for you. May He, in His ineffable mercy, awaken as quickly as possible and command the winds and the sea—that is, the devil’s temptations and the disturbances of worldly people—so that some measure of tranquillity may return through the grace and mercy of the same Lord Jesus Christ. To Him belongs, and to Him be, power, honor, glory, and dominion, for ever and ever. Amen.

# LETTER II. TO POPE NICHOLAS

Concerning the vacancy of the see of Cambrai, and the union of Baldwin and Judith; and concerning the deposition of Rothad and the heresy of Gottschalk.

(From Sirmond.)

[Col. 0025C]

To the uniquely and singularly revered Father of the Fathers and most reverend Pope NICHOLAS, honored with the highest veneration: HINCMAR, undeservedly but in name bishop of Rheims, and servant of the people of God.

In your letter, addressed through Bishop Odo to the bishops in the kingdom of Lothair concerning the prejudice inflicted upon the Church of Cambrai, I reread your authority, in which you inquire through whose neglect that same Church had remained without a pastor for more than ten months.

Therefore, lest I incur your apostolate’s anger as negligent, I report to your authority that, after letters had been sent to Lothair, to the bishops of his kingdom, and to Hilduin, who irregularly occupies that same Church, the prejudice has continued to the present—indeed, even before you sent those letters. I have repeatedly admonished King Lothair, both through envoys and letters, as far as I could, and continued to do so until he replied to me in a royal letter that Hilduin had sent his own legate to your authority and that he ought to make no other disposition concerning the aforesaid Church than what he had already done until he received your reply on the matter.

Baldwin likewise, in the month of October that has just passed, on the fifth day before the Kalends of November, sent me through two of his men a letter from your authority. It contained instructions that I should read the same letter to my fellow-bishops of the province and that we should receive Judith, to present her to her father and mother, provided that we understood that our aforesaid most excellent king intended immediately to fulfill what he had promised to report to your apostolate, in writing and orally through your envoys, concerning her.

But if we could discover that their minds were bent on postponing this, we were not to receive her at all. Otherwise—that is, if we acted differently—we would in no way be able to enjoy your grace and communion.

I received this letter of your authority reverently, as was proper, reread it to our fellow-bishops, and, as you commanded, intervened collectively on behalf of the aforesaid Judith with her father and mother as far as we could. We strove to present her to the eyes of her father and mother.

After this, because it had seemed right to us according to the sacred regulations, as we understand them—for we do not think that one can be absolved without worthy fruits of penance when we see that one is bound by the bond of anathema according to the sacred regulations—we wished them first to make satisfaction, according to ecclesiastical tradition, to the Church which they had injured, and only then to arrange for the fulfillment of what the laws of the world prescribe.

But because they wished to regard your letters—which issued no command on this matter and indeed indicated that no postponement should be made in their union—as sufficient for themselves, and because, without your authority, to which they had appealed, they ought not to have been compelled unless they submitted in some other way, I reported to them from another letter of your holiness that you had not dissolved the ecclesiastical laws, but had sent petitions on behalf of one who could be punished according to worldly laws, so that he might have an opportunity to do penance for what he had committed against the divine laws.

Thus also our Savior, who wishes all human beings to be saved and wishes no one to perish, interceded with the Father upon the cross, in the right of a priest, for His persecutors. In those among them who believed after His Passion and, pierced with remorse, did penance, He effectively obtained it from the Father, with whom He grants all things.

Following His example, you, the vicar of the apostles, to whose threshold they fled, and supreme pontiff of the Catholic and apostolic Church, asked that the sin committed against a human king and against the laws of the world be pardoned, so that what had been committed against the King of heaven and earth and against the laws of the heavenly kingdom might be given an interval for removal through penance.

On the other hand, the worldly men—and even some of those who had previously opposed such a union—protected themselves with this defense as they understood it, but stripped themselves bare of salvation, as the truth stands. They refused to depart from the wording of this latest letter of yours, which, they claimed, demonstrated that their union ought to take place without postponement.

When I said to them that, for no earthly power, ought I to abandon what I understood from the ecclesiastical regulations—especially since our lord King Charles, your son, was doing this with me, or rather with God—some of them, as though offering me advice, gave me counsel in which I shall use not my own words but theirs. Your gentleness, as an example and teacher of God’s discipline, mild, humble of heart, and patient, will bear with them calmly.

They said that, since not secular but ecclesiastical piety commanded me in this matter, I should withdraw somewhat from the conspiracy of those resisting, lest some rival of ours should suggest to your holiness that they had acted in contempt of your holy apostolate and the apostolic see, and thereby stir your gentle disposition toward me against me; and lest they should obtain some excommunication—just as had been done in the case of Rothad, although that did not reach me except insofar as Bishop Odo, and later Luido, reported it—before we had been able to send your authority a complete account of the proceedings or before you had learned through your envoys how the matter had been conducted.

This was especially so because your letter of authority was read to say that, if we acted otherwise than it instructed, we would in no way be able to enjoy your grace and communion.

When I replied that you had inserted this in your letter so that the woman might not be deceived by us, not so that she would fail to make satisfaction to the Church, they answered: why did I wish to understand your letter otherwise than you had chosen to compose it, when I could plainly discern its meaning from those you had sent me previously?

Therefore, remembering your earlier letters sent to me and to the bishops of the kingdom of your son, our lord Charles, and also considering what your gentleness had recently commanded me in the letter delivered by Luido—for these matters were being debated at Auxerre after Luido’s arrival—I avoided open contention in this matter by concealing it, caught between fear of the earlier letters and hope of the later letter, which showed me a milder course. I concealed my concession by postponing it, as it were, to another time, awaiting the disposition of this case, which is now pending, so that from the matter of Rothad I might learn how I ought henceforth to act in such circumstances.

Thus, while we prohibited them nothing concerning the ecclesiastical ministry, but nevertheless withdrew our presence from this affair as far as we could, Baldwin and Judith endeavored to carry out the secular laws which they had chosen.

Our lord the king, your son, likewise did not wish to attend this betrothal and union. But, having sent ministers of the commonwealth, as he had promised you, he permitted them to be joined to one another in marriage according to the laws of the world, and granted Baldwin his honors solely at your request.

Finally, in order obediently to hear the letter of your authority to which you summoned me—the letter sent through Bishop Odo to all the bishops of the kingdom of our lord, the glorious King Charles, concerning Rothad—I assembled with all the bishops, just as your holiness commanded in the letters addressed to my unworthiness.

Together with those venerable bishops, and to the extent that it depended upon me, I immediately took care, before the synod was dissolved, to fulfill your command concerning Rothad, lest any delay in carrying out your order should intervene, whether because of the pagan invasion or for any other reason. Your holiness will learn this fully from the letters of our lord the king’s envoys, from our own envoys, and from our letters.

But because an intervening circumstance—which the envoys themselves will report to you—prevented them, immediately after we had issued the letters and appointed our representatives, from going with Rothad into your presence, they were delayed longer than we wished.

Meanwhile, Luido, the envoy of our lord the king, returning from your holiness, brought your apostolic letters to our lord the king, your son, at the city of Auxerre on the day before the Kalends of December.

His son and namesake, Charles, had offended his father’s mind in certain matters and, because of this, had delayed coming into his presence for a time at the urging of certain people. He asked his father through his envoys to send my unworthiness, together with some other faithful men, to lead him to his father’s feet, so that through our intervention he might find his father more favorably disposed.

Our lord the king had ordered my humble person to go there into his service. As soon as I arrived, he gave me your letters to read. In them, although your exalted dignity, in accordance with your gracious favor, treated my humility kindly without any claim of merit on my part, and although your wisdom deigned to praise writings produced by my foolishness beyond what I know and understand, nevertheless, I seem to see that my many words are growing burdensome to you.

Therefore, may your holiness graciously accept what blessed Augustine did not hesitate boldly to say about his own many words to the Lord of lords, when he wished to excuse himself before Him. Among other things, he writes: “To speak much is not excessive, provided that it is necessary” (Book XV of *The Trinity*, at the end).

[Col. 0028C] Therefore, most holy lord and most reverend Father, bear with equanimity a little of my foolishness; and also support me if I again write something about Rothad’s case, already sufficiently well known to you, as though repeating it. Since it pleases you—whom all good things please—we are sending our representatives, not as accusers to engage in conflict, but as men accused by Rothad and by our neighbors, who either do not fully and truthfully know the case or do not wish to know it. We judged it necessary humbly to inform your supreme authority of this—not in contempt of the Apostolic See, to which Rothad appealed according to the canons of Sardica, but because he appealed to the judgment of the elected judges on specified charges, in accordance with the Carthaginian and African canons and the decrees of blessed Gregory.

[Col. 0028D] For far be it from us to esteem the privilege of the first and supreme see, that of the holy Roman Church’s pontiff, so lightly that we should bring before your supreme authority, to weary it, controversies and quarrels both of the higher and of the lower order—matters which the canons of Nicaea and of the other holy councils, as well as the decrees of Innocent and of the other pontiffs of the holy Roman See, prescribe should be settled in provincial synods by the metropolitans.

But if a case should arise concerning bishops for which we do not possess definite and explicit judgments in the sacred rules, and which therefore cannot be decided in a provincial or regional examination, then we must have recourse concerning it to the divine oracle—that is, to the Apostolic See.

If, moreover, in a major case an appeal has not been made by the provincial bishop to the judgment of elected judges, and that bishop has been judged in some matter—that is, deposed from his rank in a regional synod—and thinks that he has a good case, and the deposed man appeals and takes refuge with the bishop of the Roman Church, wishing to be heard: if he should judge it right that the examination be renewed, those who examined the case after the episcopal judgment must write to that supreme pontiff, and, according to the seventh chapter of the Council of Sardica, the examination shall be renewed at his direction.

But in the case of a metropolitan established according to the sacred rules, who by ancient custom receives the pallium from the Apostolic See—as Leo writes to Anastasius, which the Council of Nicaea also indicates, and the other pontiffs of the Roman See demonstrate in their decrees from the sacred canons—the judgment of that pontiff must be awaited even before the trial.

For he is the one who, according to the prophet Ezekiel, dwells in the treasury that faces the southern way and keeps watch over the temple’s guardposts (Ezek. 40:45). We metropolitans, in comparison with him, are like those who serve in the ministry of the altar that is before the face of the temple, where the flesh is burned. We labor to settle the controversies of carnal persons in provincial synods, and we take care to refer major matters and matters concerning the great to the examination of the pontiff of the supreme see after judgment.

[Col. 0029A] For we have under his authority men serving alongside us, and we say to one, “Go,” and he goes, and to another, “Come,” and he comes. For, as Leo says (Letter 82, to Anastasius):

> “Even among the most blessed apostles, although there was equality in the likeness of their honor, there was nevertheless a certain distinction of authority; and although the election of all was equal, to one nevertheless it was granted to preside over the others. From this model also arose the distinction among bishops, and provision was made by a great ordering that no one should claim everything for himself, but that in each province there should be individual men whose judgment would have first place among the brethren, and through whom the care of the universal Church would converge upon the one see of blessed Peter, so that nothing anywhere would dissent from its head. Therefore, he who knows that he has been placed over certain persons ought not to take it ill that someone has been placed over him; but the obedience that he demands, he himself should also render.”

Rothad has labored more to demand this from his own people than to render it to the sacred rules, although even the holy angels are read to obey their superiors in heaven. And thus he reached the point that he deserved to be deposed. For many years I took care, through benefits bestowed, admonitions, and entreaties, through myself, my fellow bishops, and all the associates I could enlist, to admonish him to obey the sacred rules.

Many times also, through metropolitan letters and on the authority of the Apostolic See, I took care to impress threats upon him, and I strove to show him from the reading of Catholic writers how grievously he was giving offense. To this he replied that I knew how to do nothing else except show him my little books all day long.

[Col. 0029B] Hence I was reproved by many people, and very frequently, for knowingly carrying for so long, against the will of God and sacred authority, an incorrigible man useless to the sacred ministry. I, however, although he very often strove, as though deliberately, to provoke both the king, his fellow bishops and neighbors, and even me—though he was unable to do so—knew it most dangerous for a priest to have disturbed and precipitous anger, to pronounce a precipitous judgment, and to add to the cruelty of persecutions. I therefore bore him for a long time, not without fear for the danger to the souls entrusted to him, despite the dissimilarity of his conduct, the defiance of the disobedient, and the arrows of wicked tongues.

When I ought no longer to bear him, I brought him before a council of many bishops, so that at least he might listen to them. He preferred not to listen to their counsel but to demand judgment against me.

[Col. 0029C] In order to satisfy his request, so that he might at least feel shame and withdraw from the folly he had begun, I bound myself to judgment, as I have already more fully reported to your holiness in other letters. Necessity compels me to repeat this for the satisfaction of your authority, so that you may know that I did nothing against him with an inimical intention, but out of divine zeal, as far as I can discern within my conscience.

These things are also known to our lord the king, to the bishops of his kingdom, and to very many ecclesiastical and secular men.

After his deposition, I obtained that our lord the king and the bishops should agree to give him a very good abbey, and that all of us should serve him as a father from our own resources, so that he, who had always led his life in luxury, would not be broken.

[Col. 0029D] The only condition was that he should not strive to be seditious and troublesome to the Church over which he had presided. At first he agreed to this.

But, as those who claim to know this report, certain bishops of Lothar’s kingdom, moved against us by bitter zeal because we had not followed their counsels concerning Waldrada, and also, as some say, certain men from Germany, at the persuasion of their king Louis—for I had not acted with him as Rothad had acted in the expulsion of his brother from the kingdom—persuaded Rothad not to abandon the stirring up of sedition, while they themselves would obtain from you that he be restored.

Now, as you commanded, we have obtained from our lord the king, your son, that he be brought to your presence and judgment, trusting that the Lord will deign to inspire your heart with whatever will be more pleasing to Him in this matter.

Since your most gracious dignity deigned to write through Luidon to me, your servant, instructing me, together with a complete college of brethren and according to the procedure described there, relying on your apostolic censure, to strive to restore him decently to his former office, let your most reverend, most beloved, and sweetest fatherhood know that I have been unable to do this for the reasons contained below.

[Col. 0030A] Namely, when Rothad had already been entrusted, together with letters to be delivered to your authority, to those who were to bring him into your presence, it was impossible for me to convene the complete college of the brethren. For, as I wrote above, I was far removed from our diocese, serving your son, our king. Moreover, he could not be regularly restored without the judgment of those who had taken part in his deposition and to whom you had written about it; and the bishops of other provinces, being occupied with many matters, could not be assembled by my summons.

The bishops of the province of Rheims also hastened from the very synod at which we heard the letter of your holiness to return to their sees, because they had to resist the Normans.

The few bishops who were with me in the service of your son, our king, after I reread to them your gracious recommendation concerning Rothad, replied that they did not know that he possessed such a life, understanding, or devotion to the sacred ministry as would allow them to dare to involve themselves in this matter. This was especially so because the man who had formerly shown some reverence concerning his deposition, and had always been disobedient to the sacred rules, to royal dignity, and to metropolitan privilege, ought now to rage more unrestrainedly, as a harmful example to many and a scandal to many well-disposed persons, and to live more carelessly and perniciously, serving his own desires with freedom.

[Col. 0030B] As for what your goodness of spirit, considering not the beastly but the human disposition of the man, wrote, saying:

> “Perhaps he will recognize his offense and of his own accord choose to remain in the judgment by which he was judged. If he does this, action should be taken with King Charles, your most beloved son, so that in his generosity he may graciously bestow upon him suitable benefits, by which he may adequately support himself and his household and live honorably,”

let your dignity know that he is not of such moderation. For he could never be recalled from what he had begun.

I, your servant, also reflected on these matters in my heart and, consulting your most faithful son, my lord the glorious king, considered it fitting to write to your most wise authority in this case.

[Col. 0030C] Although, relying on your letters of authority, sent through Luidon to my insignificance—the letters you mentioned in the epistle that you sent to your son, our lord the king, and which I reread to him—I might have obtained from him that he order his messengers, who had undertaken to bring Rothad into your presence, to wait and not undertake the journey to Rome until an opportune time had arrived for convening the bishops of our regions, there was no reasonable way for it to be made known to others why Rothad’s transfer was being delayed before your letter of authority had been read to the bishops.

It could have happened that those who, by divine mercy, his kindness, and the devotion of his love, honor me, and who think that I am something although I am nothing, might, upon learning that this had happened through my intercession, take offense at me, as though I were causing your recommendation to be despised or neglected—although, within the days fixed by you in the letter sent through Bishop Odo, I had done everything I could to hasten obedience to your command.

And if, whenever they came together, I were to speak with the bishops who know, and know that I know along with them, Rothad’s negligence and longstanding uselessness in the sacred ministry concerning his restoration, they would all denounce me and judge me utterly mad.

[Col. 0030D] If we also promised Rothad that we would obtain benefits for him so that he might submit—which he would not do with a view to his salvation—almost everyone in these provinces knows that, according to the Carthaginian and African canons and the decrees of blessed Gregory, he had submitted himself to the judgment of the elected judges.

More than five hundred men of various ranks were present when the golden chalice with jewels was taken from a lodging-house keeper and tavern woman by the king’s messenger, being recovered from his pledge, and was brought to the synod. They also know that silver crowns were taken back from the Jew to whom he had given them; that ecclesiastical goods which he had concealed and secretly entrusted were recovered from him and restored to the Church; and that silver vessels, which for a long time had hung in the church and were of no small weight, were recovered.

[Col. 0031A] There were also other things which his predecessors and forebears, and other faithful people, had offered to that Church for the remedy of their souls, but which he had given away at his own pleasure without the consent of the metropolitan and fellow bishops, and without the consent of the steward, priests, and deacons of his Church.

Yet blessed Gregory frequently writes in his letters, on the basis of the sacred canons, that whatever a bishop acquires after his ordination to the episcopate belongs entirely to the Church in which he was ordained. Hence it is clear that he himself ought not to dispose of those things without the steward and without the knowledge of the clergy.

[Col. 0031B] All the inhabitants and people of the city who came together with the king and bishops to the synod also know this. They saw him coming, as though to a spectacle, as far as the door of the synod, and returning sorrowful like a madman (maestum ut maniacum; the supplied reading is uncertain). They know how, scorning the great kindness of the king and the brethren, he withdrew harder than a stone, with the king and bishops weeping, after being judged on specific charges for which the sacred canons had prescribed explicit judgments.
