They would think that we—who judged him according to the sacred canons as we understood them, and afterward, as those canons themselves prescribe, arranged through our fellow bishop who had taken part in that judgment first to report our judgment concerning him, and now, as you commanded, took care to send that same judgment with our letters and representatives to the Apostolic See, which confirms that the paternal canons must be observed and demonstrates through its own observance that they have been confirmed and must be observed—doubted the justice and equitable balance of your authority, and therefore promised him a benefice in order to induce his submission, and thus might rightly mark us as mad.

[Col. 0031C] Even if it could happen—which is not believed possible from that first and holy See and from your supreme apostolate—that such a man, known and restored by you, should be named restored to his rank, we would thereafter have no danger to our consciences concerning the souls entrusted to us by you.

Since everyone in these regions knows how negligent he has been, how contemptuous of the sacred canons, how long and patiently and kindly he was tolerated, and how reluctantly he was judged according to the sacred rules as we understood them because he refused to correct himself, we could feel no shame concerning his restoration if it were carried out through the piety of your supreme pontificate. For all of us, old and young, know that our Churches are subject to the Roman Church, and that we bishops are subject in primacy to the Roman pontiff. Therefore, while preserving the faith that has always flourished in the Church and, with the Lord’s cooperation, will flourish, we must obey your apostolic authority.

[Col. 0031D] For it is written to us, along with all others, that Jesus was subject to his parents (Luke 2:51). It is likewise written to us: “Obey your leaders and submit to them” (Heb. 12:17); and: “Do nothing through rivalry or empty glory” (Phil. 2:3); and: “If anyone wishes to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor does the Church of God” (1 Cor. 11:16).

For this reason, after speaking with your most faithful son, my lord the glorious king, I repeated to him what I have often impressed upon him and what he gladly accepted and desires to fulfill: just as “the earth is the Lord’s and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it,” and the kingdom belongs to Him and He gives it to whomever He wills, so He founded His Church upon the foundation of the apostolic rock. Before His Passion and after His Resurrection, He entrusted that Church, with special care and singular privilege, to blessed Peter and, in him, to Peter’s vicars.

Whoever honors Peter’s see and the pontiff of that see honors Him who said, “Whoever receives anyone whom I send receives me” (Matt. 10:40); and he will be honored by Him who says: “Those who honor me I will honor, and those who despise me will be held in low esteem” (1 Sam. 2:30).

[Col. 0032A] Therefore, since many people know the character of Rothad’s complaint, while some speak differently about it, and since everyone generally knows that your authority ordered him to be sent with our representatives for judgment before you, it is right and just that whenever the Roman pontiff orders any bishop to come to him in Rome, that bishop should make every effort to come to him, provided illness or some more serious necessity or impossibility, as the sacred canons specify, does not detain him.

This is all the more true of one whom the pontiff indicates must be brought into his presence because he has cried out to him in such a complaint, in whatever manner. Whoever sees or hears that the king and bishops promptly obey and honor the supreme pontiff of the Apostolic See will themselves obey their subjects all the more promptly and humbly.

For, as blessed Gregory says, just as when the head is suffering the limbs subject to it are vigorous in vain, so when the head is crowned with glory and honor—that is, honored and adorned—its subject limbs will shine with its honor and beauty.

[Col. 0032B] Rothad could not have been better satisfied in any way than by going into your presence and having it shown to him, through the subscriptions of so many bishops who do not wish to lie to God or to you, and through the allegations of so many representatives of those bishops, that he by no means has a good case.

Therefore he ought to attribute to himself, and not to you, the fact that he has wearied himself and many others without a good cause.

[Col. 0032C] Accordingly, your most discerning piety, which knows how to prescribe compassion toward one’s neighbor and rectitude toward vices, sufficiently warned him in your apostolic letters. He is recognized, among his other foolishnesses, as possessing such hardness that, although for so many years and in so many cases he repeatedly resisted the sacred canons, the decrees of the pontiffs of the holy Roman See, the privilege of his metropolis, and synodal judgments, without any regard for fear or divine love and without any human shame, and although he had been tolerated for so many years, he scorned to withdraw from his folly.

Nevertheless, after being repeatedly entreated by the king and bishops, he could be brought to the point of subscribing that henceforth he would obey the sacred canons and the decrees of the pontiffs of the holy Roman See, and, according to them, the privilege of his metropolis; for without observing these things none of us can be a bishop. In this way he would have enjoyed fraternal peace in all respects.

[Col. 0032D] But afterward, of his own accord, in the written profession by which he appealed to the judgment of the elected judges, he sent to the synod an impudent claim that he had observed these things—although everyone who knew the facts recognized it as a lie—and thus appealed to the judgment, while refusing, lest he be judged, to subscribe that he would observe these things.

The reason he refused to subscribe, as those who heard it from him later told us, and as we ourselves understood, was that he did not want to be defeated. Rather, if the king and bishops persisted in our judgment, he would go to Rome before being defeated, and when he arrived there, he would subscribe to these things by your command, once he had been absolved by you against our wishes.

[Col. 0033A] He did not understand—or rather, he was unable to understand, for his wickedness had blinded him—that your authority most wisely understood why the Lord, speaking from heaven to Paul when Paul said, “What do you command me to do, Lord?” did not explain to him everything that he had to do, but directed him to Ananias, from whom he was to hear and receive what he had to do (Acts 9:6).

So also the angel sent Cornelius to Peter’s teaching and obedience after announcing to him that his prayer had been heard (Acts 10:5). Although Cornelius had been baptized, so to speak, by the Holy Spirit before baptism, blessed Peter commanded him to be baptized with the baptism of the One who baptizes in the Holy Spirit, in whom the hearts of believers are purified by faith.

[Col. 0033B] When a question was consequently raised against him even by his own, though faithful, subordinates as to why he had entered among the Gentiles, that same prince of the apostles, filled with the grace of the highest gifts and supported by the power of innumerable miracles, answered the complaint not from authority but from reason. He explained the matter in order, with the gentleness with which he said to the aforementioned Cornelius, who wished to worship him: “See that you do not do this; for I myself am also a human being, just as you are” (ibid., v. 26).

For if, as Gregory says, he had spoken something from his authority in the complaint of the faithful, he would certainly not have been a teacher of gentleness. Therefore, he calmed them by a humble explanation, humbly rendered an account in the matter in which he was reproached, and also brought forward witnesses, saying: “These six brothers also came with me” (Acts 11:12).

[Col. 0033C] Following his humble authority, his most gentle power, and his most upright preaching—“not as domineering over the clergy, but becoming examples to the flock” (1 Pet. 5:3)—blessed Gelasius says in his decrees to all bishops concerning ecclesiastical institutions (Letter 6, to all bishops):

> “Since we desire to presume that we may do nothing against the reverence due to the rules that bring salvation, and since the Apostolic See, with the Lord’s favor, strives with devout and faithful purpose to preserve all that has been established by the paternal canons, it is sufficiently unworthy for anyone, whether among the pontiffs or among the succeeding ranks, to reject this observance, which he sees the See of blessed Peter both follow and teach. It is entirely fitting that the body of the Church should agree with itself in this observance, which it sees flourishing there where the Lord established the primacy over the whole Church.”

[Col. 0033D] Concerning Barnabas and Saul, he truthfully says that Paul the apostle was not from human beings or through a human being, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father. After they had for a long time enjoyed the company of the apostles, the Holy Spirit said—not to the apostles themselves, but, according to the faith of sacred history, to the prophets and teachers who were ministering to the Lord in Antioch—“Set apart Barnabas and Saul for the work of the ministry to which I have taken them.” Then, after fasting and praying and laying hands upon them, they sent them away (Acts 13:2).

They, indeed, sent by the Holy Spirit, departed as apostles who had been called. In the following year—that is, the fourteenth after the Lord’s Passion—although the One who worked through Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision also worked through Paul among the Gentiles, nevertheless, according to the agreement of James, Cephas, and John, Paul received, together with Barnabas, the ministry among the Gentiles.

[Col. 0034A] The same Paul wrote to the Corinthians concerning the incestuous man, when their rulers were negligent: “When you are assembled, and my spirit is present, I have handed such a man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord” (1 Cor. 5:4).

The rulers of the Corinthians handed him over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh; and Paul, once he had learned of his conduct, restored him by his own authority together with them. When his repentance became known, they restored him by their authority together with Paul. “To whom you have forgiven anything,” he says, “I also forgive; for if I have forgiven anything, I have forgiven it for your sake in the person of Christ” (2 Cor. 2:10).

[Col. 0034B] Hence blessed Gregory says (Morals, Book 33, chapter 8):

> “I do not dissent from your good action; let what you have done be mine. As though we should dare to say to him: Why do you so cautiously join yourself to the disciples? Why do you confirm either yourself through their actions or them through yours with such attentive care?—‘So that we may not be deceived by Satan,’ he says (ibid., v. 11). For we are not ignorant of his thoughts—that is, lest he turn to an evil end what the mind has begun well.”

And Innocent says:

> “This apostolic kindness was declared toward the Corinthians, so that in one spirit the good may always follow without distinction the judgment that was both imposed and withdrawn.”

And Leo, drawing from the Apostle (Leo, Letter 88, to Anastasius), says:

> “Let no one seek what is his own, but what belongs to another” (1 Cor. 10:24); and: “Let each person please his neighbor for his good, for edification” (Rom. 15:2). “For the bond of our unity cannot be firm unless the tie of charity binds us to inseparable solidity. For just as in one body we have many members, although all the members do not have the same function, so we are one body in Christ, but individually members of one another. The connection of the whole body produces one health and one beauty. This connection of the whole body requires unanimity, but it especially demands concord among priests. Although they have a common order, their dignity is not common to all.”

[Col. 0034C] These matters were carried out concerning the persons mentioned above, and taught by those already mentioned, with a deeper understanding, so that it might be recognized how inferiors ought to obey superiors, superiors provide for inferiors, and the order established by God be preserved by all and in all.

Hence the supreme shepherd of the Church teaches: “If anyone ministers, let him do so as from the strength that God supplies, so that God may be honored in all things” (1 Pet. 4:11)—the God who entrusted His affairs to His servants, and to each according to his own ability. So also it is written concerning the Holy Spirit, who distributes gifts to each as He wills.

[Col. 0034D] And therefore, according to the Council of Sardica (canon 7), the supreme pontiff of the first and holy Roman See, when a deposed provincial bishop appeals and takes refuge with him, crying out concerning the renewal of his examination, does not immediately restore him by the singular privilege and authority of his office. Rather, he sends him back to the province where the case occurred, and where, according to the Carthaginian canons and the provisions of Roman law, the case can be carefully investigated and the truth discovered without difficulty by producing witnesses.

Alternatively, he deigns to write to neighboring bishops, or sends someone from his own side who, possessing his authority, judges in person together with the bishops and carefully investigates and decides the case; or he deigns to believe that the bishops are sufficient to bring the matter to an end.

[Col. 0035A] Innocent also (Letter 1, to Victricius) commands that if controversies or disputes arise among clergy, whether of higher or lower rank, the bishops of that province should be assembled according to the Council of Nicaea and the quarrel brought to an end.

Boniface writes concerning Maximus (Letter 2, to the bishops of Gaul) that he should be compelled to come to the province, present himself there before the constituted judgment, and that whatever the bishops of the province should decide concerning him, once it had been reported to Boniface, should be confirmed by his authority.

Thus, as the same Boniface writes to Hilary (Letter 3), each province should always await the ordering of its metropolitan in all matters, as it is written in the Council of Nicaea: just as at Alexandria, and since the bishop of the city of Rome follows the same practice, so also at Antioch and in the other provinces the privileges belonging to their Churches should be preserved.

[Col. 0035B] Hence it was rightly decided that councils should be held twice each year in every province, so that when all the bishops of the province were assembled together, such questions might be discussed jointly.

I say these things not, God forbid, to prejudice in any way the power of the supreme Apostolic See and of your holy apostolate, which I am ready, as is right, to obey in all things. Rather, I think that I offer the highest obedience to your authority when I humbly disclose what I think, either for the purpose of proving or of correcting it, to the wisdom of your teaching, and strive to inform you of Rothad’s conduct, lest, through my negligence, you remain unaware of what I know about him, so that your authority may decide more certainly whatever pleases you concerning him.

[Col. 0035C] If you now decide that your judgment concerning his deposition should remain in force, we know the kindness, moderation, and piety of your son, our lord King Charles: whatever your aforesaid son commands concerning him, insofar as he can reasonably fulfill it, he will obey without any reconsideration.

Our fellow bishops will also contribute to him most generously from the resources of their Churches. As for my insignificance, just as I have never wished to seek repayment of evil for the contempt and insults inflicted upon me by him, so whatever kindness I am able to show, I shall gladly take care to bestow even more abundantly than I have ever done.

[Col. 0035D] But if, without any satisfaction for such a long contempt of the sacred canons, the decrees of the Apostolic See, the privilege of his own metropolis, and the synodal judgments—things which he neither obeyed nor wished to profess or subscribe that he would henceforth obey—and without a profession or subscription of his correction and obedience before his brethren, whose canonical admonitions he had repeatedly despised, although this is read repeatedly in the letters of Leo and Gregory, it should please your piety to restore him, I shall bear it with an even mind, as is fitting for the pontiff of the first See, the mother and teacher of all Churches, and the father and teacher of all bishops, to render a regular judgment.

[Col. 0036A] Nevertheless, I believe that your most diligent discernment will take into account the contempt and defiance of subjects toward their superiors, and the freedom to offend the sacred canons with impunity—things which, as some think, could thereby acquire harmful strength in our regions.

This is especially so since it is perfectly well known to your most wise authority that the Council of Sardica, in its seventh chapter, demonstrates how the execution of the restoration or continued deposition of a deposed bishop who cries out to the Apostolic See should be carried out by that See, with the judges who rendered the judgment suffering no harm.

[Col. 0036B] Innocent and Boniface, and indeed Leo in his decrees, and Gregory even more clearly in his letters, demonstrate the same, following the decrees of the Council of Carthage—or rather, of the Apostolic See, which presided over that council through its representatives—namely, that when an appeal has been made from ecclesiastical judges to other ecclesiastical judges where there is greater authority, it should not harm those whose judgment has been set aside, provided they cannot be convicted either of having judged with an inimical intention or of having been corrupted by some desire or favor.

Our conscience bears witness to this, and it is recognized to have become known to all who were present: we preferred to preserve him rather than judge him, if we had not feared being condemned together with him, for neglecting the sacred canons, by the judgment of those through whom, under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, those canons were promulgated.

[Col. 0036C] Therefore, corrupted by no inimical intention and by no desire or favor, we carried out the canonical judgments against him, grieving over his incorrigible folly and irreversible obstinacy. We did not dare suspend those judgments from him any longer.

Your wise and supreme authority will also attend, in making its decision, to the Apostle’s teaching: “The sins of some people are manifest, going before them to judgment; but those of others follow after” (1 Tim. 5:24).

[Col. 0036D] As blessed Ambrose explains this (Apology of David, chapter 6), it is as though the sins were placed in a balance and examined in judgment: whether good works, weighed more heavily, precede and deserve reward, showing that evil deeds should be mercifully forgiven as slight; or whether evil deeds, weighed more heavily, precede, so that they deserve the judgment of condemnation and suffocate the few good deeds.

We too, according to our limited ability, weighed in Rothad not only what was useful but also what was harmful, together with his actions. Like a fruitless fig tree uselessly occupying rational soil for a long time, and even after many periods of time and many admonitions failing to receive, as it were, the baskets of richness placed before it, but remaining barren, we judged that he should be cut down—not without grief of heart.

And since these matters stand thus, I confidently trust without hesitation that what follows without any interruption in the aforesaid chapter of the Council of Carthage would by no means escape the notice of your governance:

“Indeed,” it says (African Council, canon 89), “if judges have been chosen by agreement of the parties, even though they are fewer in number than was prescribed, it is not permitted to appeal.”

That prescribed number, demonstrated in the preceding twelfth chapter, and the agreement of the parties having been sought, is clearly shown to have been complete in the adjudication of Rothad. But if, for whatever more reasonable cause—and one still unknown to us—your supreme authority should choose to oppose their judgment, since it is my duty to entrust myself to you through obedience and not to examine your judgments, I shall endure it; nor shall I resist your regular restoration of him, if it should happen to appear that this ought to be done in his case. Your authority will determine how that same victor, as is his custom and as one who has obtained his wish, should thereafter act regarding the bishops. I shall regard it as a great blessing if at last I may be able to breathe freely after the long and numerous [Col. 0039A] troubles which I have suffered from him and on his account, and if I may never again be compelled to labor uselessly against his disturbances.

Moreover, since our judgments are despised and treated as worthless not only by ecclesiastical persons but much more even by secular ones—who say these things and bring forward matters which I ought not to ascribe to your authority—I take care not in any respect to move the disposition of your sweetness, which I most earnestly desire to avoid. If any persons in our province, whose complaint might reach you after his restoration, should hereafter commit certain offenses of greater importance, as certain matters are more frequently committed than in former times, I shall endeavor to admonish them, lest God condemn me for silence; and if they wish to correct themselves, I shall rejoice with them. If not, I shall appeal them to your judgment. If they wish to go, your holy wisdom will take care to decide what it sees to be best in the matter. If they do not wish to go, they will do what they judge useful for themselves.

Would that the judgment of Saint Ambrose might free me from divine condemnation in this matter, for he says: “If someone does not have the authority to cast out one whom he knows to be guilty, or is unable to prove him guilty, he is free from blame.” Thus, I think, because I am occupied with many matters and constrained by the length and difficulty of my journey, I cannot refer everything to the Apostolic See before the complaint of insolent persons reaches you. Weighed down by illness and already near the end of my life, thanks be to God, I shall be able to take precautions so that the disposition of your holiness may not be moved against me by anyone, and so that no excommunication may be threatened against me. And although I know, according to the Apostle’s Gospel, that the Lord “will render to each according to his works” (Rom. 2:6), while conscience bears witness to them, and their thoughts accuse or even defend one another on the day when he will judge the hidden things of human beings; and although, as Leo says, “if anything through our service—that is, our priestly service—is fulfilled in good order and with a grateful disposition, let us not doubt that it has been given to us through the Holy Spirit, while whatever is otherwise cannot be valid”—nevertheless, in every way, insofar as he grants it, from whom comes every good gift and every perfect gift, I shall strive to take care that the final day, which is uncertain to me and may come suddenly, does not find me, God forbid, in any manner excluded from communion with the Apostolic See.

For there will indeed be—although later than is necessary, since I, a grave sinner, am long held confined in the grievous prison of the body and deservedly afflicted in many ways, while the most provident Lord so provides—a time and a person in the Church of Reims when and in which that Church will possess, restored by Apostolic authority, the privilege granted to it and preserved from ancient custom. That Church has never had a primate other than the Roman pontiff, except for the period when its bishop Rigobert was violently expelled by the tyrant Milo without any fault on his part, and, while the see was vacant during the reign of Prince Charles, it was entrusted for some time to Boniface, a legate of the Apostolic See, just as the Church [Col. 0040A] of Trier was.

Between the Churches of Reims and Trier—for these two provinces alone belong to the Belgian region—there has always been this distinction, as we find in ecclesiastical records and discover to have been maintained by the most ancient custom: according to the sacred rules, the same bishop was regarded as first, not by the location but by the dignity of his rank, who had previously been ordained in the metropolitan church of either of these Churches.

It will be necessary for me to conduct myself in such a way that hereafter I do not again receive so many letters from your authority threatening excommunications and containing rebukes—letters such as we read in the writings of Apostolic men should be sent only rarely and under great necessity—as I have frequently received in these times, deserving them through my sins. If this pleases your holiness, you will not need to undertake such action against me hereafter, until your Apostolic command should find me disobedient in some matter against the sacred rules, which God forbid.

For whoever understands why the Lord praises the centurion’s faith in the Gospel when he says, “Say the word, and my servant will be healed” (Matt. 8:8), recognizes how operative the word of a bishop is—indeed, as in Paul, where Christ speaks in him—and how much more operative is the word of the pontiff of the Apostolic See, and how his command must be obeyed, without any need for an added expression of wonder. We bishops must impress this upon those who know it and make it known to those who do not, being debtors to the wise and the foolish alike. If hereafter the words of wicked men prevail against us, as they boastfully claim they will, there will be no need for us to labor greatly over provincial synods, in which we have hitherto labored; for each person will have his own law and his own hope.

I gratefully received what your sublimity wrote to my humility: that at first you had been moved to investigate Rothad’s case by the concern with which you are bound to all your brothers. I understood from this that we, whatever sort of metropolitans we may be, must be counted among your brothers. Therefore, just as your discretion must take care that subject bishops are not irregularly condemned by metropolitans, so likewise it must take care that metropolitans are not irregularly despised by their subject bishops.

Secondly, I gratefully received what you wrote with the utmost clarity: since Rothad is known to have appealed to the Apostolic See, and since you do not wish it to appear that during your lifetime you have calmly tolerated any diminution of the privileges of your Church, this too must rightly be accepted by us all and most diligently preserved. I have wished and still wish, for my part, that it be preserved, and, with the Lord’s favor, I shall remain steadfast in this devotion, knowing that the privilege of the metropolitan see of Reims, which divine favor has appointed me to serve, remains within the supreme privilege of the holy Roman See; and that it is itself a privilege of the Roman See if, by its authority, it causes the privilege of a see subject to it to remain in force and endeavors to confirm it.

Regarding what you brought forward third in your letter, [Col. 0041A] I did not presume to write anything else except that Rothad’s case differs in almost every respect from the cases about which you wrote.

Regarding what your Apostolic kindness finally deigned to write to my unworthiness—that I should consider these matters with you, approve what you decide concerning Rothad, and not suppose that you have acted in any way to my injury—I return immense thanks to your holy Apostolate with all the strength of my heart, with every plea and with due submissive humility. I reply with complete sincerity of mind that, just as you deigned to write to me, so I believe in every respect.

And because you have secured, as is fitting and as we all desire, the privilege of your supreme pontificate—a privilege which none of us had contradicted—I desire to see Rothad brought into your presence as you commanded, in order that you may grant him pardon, [Col. 0041B] and I trust that I shall see this, since nothing else is required except what I have shown above: what the sacred rules command, what I must request, and what you must grant.

I ask, then, that compassion be shown to Rothad by your authority in such a way that ecclesiastical rigor is not dissolved; and that ecclesiastical rigor be preserved in such a way that due mercy and necessary provision are not denied him. Thus neither should others be provoked by his example to transgress, nor should those to whom the moderation of ecclesiastical discipline has been entrusted in these regions, so distant from the Apostolic See, see here—God forbid—a reason for negligence or laxity, or claim that they may take from this an occasion for transgressing the boundaries established by the Fathers, which, as we understand, we believe we have hitherto preserved.

You will see what would be best to do in the matter; and we must see, in accordance with your judgment, what God wills. For the divine judgments cannot be unjust: they will be pronounced by justice from the firmness of the confession of the apostolic rock, against which the gates of hell—that is, evil suggestions or actions—will not prevail.

The letter which your authority solemnly commanded me to send to Rothad was sent to him by our lord the king, your son, through his abbot as soon as it reached him. Rodulfus too, the uncle of that same son of yours, our lord the king, returning from Louis, king of Germany, on the third day before the Ides of the month of December just past, sent his man, named Rodulfus, to me. I was then hurrying very late in the evening from our king’s court to our lodgings on the Loire, near the border of the kingdom of Aquitaine. He conveyed the message that the aforesaid King Louis had entrusted one of Rothad’s men, together with letters from your holiness, to his protection and pledged faith, so that he might bring him with those same bishops into the presence of our lord King Charles without inflicting any harm upon him.

That man is accused before our lord the king of having defrauded the Church of property and treasure, and, after committing perjury in the matter, of having fled and gone to King Louis. Therefore Rodulfus asked me to assist him before our lord the king, so that, since he had received the man under his protection, he would suffer no harm. I replied that he should keep the man with him so that he would meanwhile suffer no harm, until I returned to the court, and that I would do what I could to assist him in the matter. But I neither saw the man then nor afterward, nor did I hear where he had gone with the bishops.

I have therefore taken care to write this to your holiness so that, if any of our ill-wishers should, as is their custom, wish to suggest something sinister to you from this matter, you may know what the truth is and not allow your disposition toward me to be moved against me.

Finally, the account which I rendered before the chosen judges—before whom Rothad had summoned me by a written appeal to the judgment of the chosen—those venerable bishops are sending to your authority. As for the acts compiled by Rothad after his excommunication in the provincial synod, which we have heard reached you through our neighbors to our detriment, the bishops of the province of Reims have taken care, through our common envoys, to make known to your holiness what they know.

Likewise, after some material concerning the promotion of that lord Hincmar to the episcopate—partly noted above, which we have not thought necessary to repeat here—when the aforesaid Ebo had died, our Church and diocese, according to the ancient custom it has also observed concerning those bishops who did not remain in the same Church in the episcopate until their death, began, as an act of piety, to recite his name among the sacred mysteries in the catalogue of bishops, and continues to do so to this day.

I did not presume to prohibit this without the authority of the Apostolic See, lest I scandalize the devout by appearing to envy the salvation of a brother, especially of a soul resting in the Lord. He was not anathematized for departing from the soundness of the Catholic faith, but, provoked by his own conscience, he was first condemned by himself and afterward by a synod and also by the Apostolic See. Blessed Pope Celestine says that “it is impious that religious souls should suffer such things, since, when those who are our members are afflicted, it is fitting that we too should be afflicted.”

But now, in the letters of your holiness which the deacon Engelvinus brought to us, we find that we are not to receive Teotgaudus and Guntharius into the catalogue of bishops. Therefore, as we have already stated—and you yourself know it better—may your Apostolic authority deign to write back to me concerning the decree of the Council of Antioch regarding one who, after condemnation, presumes to exercise the episcopal ministry according to the preceding custom, which Ebo unquestionably did. Should I be permitted to name that same Ebo among the bishops in the sacred diptychs of our Church, or ought I to prohibit his being named thereafter in the catalogue of bishops? Thus, supported by your authority, I may make clear, without ambiguity, what you determine must be observed in this matter in our Church.

Furthermore, Luido told me that he had discussed with you the condemnation and confinement of Gothescalc. Since I had already heard from others that reports about him had reached your holiness, I sent to your authority, through Bishop Odo, a written roll containing certain passages from the words and opinions of Catholic teachers, explaining how I understand the matter in opposition to that pestilent man’s view; but I was not deemed worthy to receive any reply concerning it.

Nevertheless, in order that I might render an account of it, certain bishops—who had no concern for him, since, as they themselves clearly revealed, neither charity moved them to do so nor authority compelled them—summoned me to the assembly recently held at Metz, which you forbade to be called a synod, as I understand. They summoned me irregularly by a layman’s letter on the fourth day before the assembly was to convene, while I was more than eighty miles away from the city and Gothescalc more than a hundred miles away, and I had received no prior notice.

I therefore now bring this briefly to the attention of your holiness, because, before I attained the episcopal order, as his abbot and the monks among whom he had lived testify, he was a monk in habit but savage in mind in the monastery of the metropolitan Church of Reims, in the diocese of Soissons, called Orbais. He was impatient of quiet, delighted in novel expressions, and singular among his companions for a harmful instability. From all the things that he knew had then been perversely believed in these regions, he selected certain chapters for himself, so that he might become known through the novelty of his expressions, corrupt the minds of the simple and deceived, usurp the name of teacher, and draw disciples after him. He also sought improperly—since he could not do so legitimately—to preside through an appearance of religious life and learning over those who, itching in their ears for teachers, strive to heap up teachers for themselves according to their desires.

He was ordained a presbyter contrary to the rules by the chorepiscopus of Reims who then held that office. He then irregularly left the monastery, traveled through many regions, and, as a very evil sower, scattered destructive seeds. At last, when a synod was held in the city of Mainz, he presented a booklet containing his error to Archbishop Rabanus. He was condemned by all the bishops of Germany and sent with synodal letters to the metropolitan Church of Reims, over which, by the Lord’s authority, I was then presiding.

Afterward he was heard by the bishops of the provinces of Belgica, Reims, and Gaul and was found to be a heretic. Because he refused to repent of his perversity, and so that he might not harm others when he himself refused to be of benefit to them, he was confined under monastic custody by the judgment of the bishops of those provinces. This was done in our diocese because Rothad, in whose diocese he belonged, did not know how to resist him, and because we feared that, being a lover of novelties, he might learn to think perversely, since he had refused to learn to teach what was right. It was also done lest Gothescalc, living a common life with others, make them share in his error. The Apostle teaches: “Avoid a heretical person after the first and second correction, knowing that such a one is perverted and condemned by his own judgment” (Titus 3:10).

As Pope Leo says concerning Eutyches, when he saw that the opinion of his foolishness displeased Catholic ears, he ought to have withdrawn from his position and not so stirred up the leaders of the Church that he deserved to receive a sentence of condemnation. If he should wish to remain in his opinion, no one will be able to release him from that condemnation. But if he had wished to repent and return to Catholic understanding, I was and am always ready, since the venerable bishops judged that he should be received into the communion of the Catholic Church. Accordingly, I order that the things necessary for the body be supplied to him.

If, however, your Catholic wisdom wishes to know what he appears to say against the Catholic faith from the ancient Predestinarian heresy—which first arose in Africa and afterward in Gaul around the same time as the Nestorian heresy, and which, in the time of Pope Celestine, was refuted by his authority and through the efforts of Saint Prosper—we shall indicate a few points to you by number, though not by weight, in outline.

He says what the ancient Predestinarians also said: that just as God predestined some to eternal life, so he predestined others to eternal death.

He says what the ancient Predestinarians also said: that God does not wish all human beings to be saved, but only those who are saved; and that he wishes all those to be saved whom he himself wills to save. Consequently, whoever is not saved is entirely outside his will to be saved. For if not all whom God wishes to be saved are saved, then he has not done everything that he willed; and if he wills what he cannot accomplish, he is not omnipotent but weak. Yet he is omnipotent who has done whatever he willed, as Scripture says: “All that the Lord willed, he did in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses” (Ps. 134:6); and again: “In your will, Lord, all things have been placed, and there is no one who can resist your will; if you have decreed to save us, we shall immediately be delivered” (Esther 13:9).

He says what the ancient Predestinarians also said: that our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ was not crucified and died for the redemption of the whole world—that is, for the salvation and redemption of all human beings—but only for those who are saved.

In another form of expression, with a different tradition but the same error, he says what the ancient Predestinarians also said when explaining the sentence of the Apostle Peter, “denying the one who bought them” (2 Pet. 2:1): “He bought them through the sacrament of baptism, but he did not undergo the cross for them, nor suffer death, nor shed his blood.” That the reception of baptism is called redemption, however, the teacher of the nations clearly affirms: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (Eph. 4:30).

But that redemption which is proper and particular to all the elect alone, which the merciful Redeemer bestowed upon them alone when he was crucified, redeemed, delivered, and cleansed from sins all the elect alike—those born and those yet to be born, the living and the dead—both from former times and from the present. They, entirely and solely, are the world for which the Lord suffered, as he himself said: “The bread which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John 6:52).

And elsewhere that same Gothescalcus writes:

“Far be it from me even to wish to dream of such a thing, much less to whisper it even once: that the ancient serpent could seize and carry away into everlasting destruction any one of those for whose redemption so precious a blood—the blood of our Lord’s Son—was poured out to God the Father. Amen.”

And again, speaking to God:

“It is therefore plainly and clearly evident that no one is lost to you who has been redeemed by the blood of your cross.”

What the ancient Predestinarians did not say, he says more boldly and therefore more perniciously: that the Deity of the Holy Trinity is threefold.

There are also other things which he and many others in these regions say, which appear to us contrary to the sound faith. When your authority learns of these through someone other than one so insignificant as I am, you may perhaps attend to them more carefully and take pains to teach us as soon as possible what must be feared in the matter. The need for this will soon arise. For although their hearts boil with the madness of a perverse understanding, they do not dare, during the reign of our orthodox king, your son and our lord Charles, to speak openly of the perverse opinions they hold.

Thus we plainly see fulfilled what is written: “Gathering the waters of the sea as in a wineskin” (Ps. 32:7). The water of the sea has been gathered as in a wineskin because the bitter knowledge of heretics confines within the heart whatever perversity the kingdom of your son, our lord Charles, presently harbors, and does not dare to speak openly. They also secretly gnaw at my insignificance with a dog’s tooth. Yet, with the Lord’s help, I shall easily endure it. For only a little time remains to me; and if, by God’s permission, they receive power among the sons of the Church to afflict me bodily, they will, with the help of divine grace, exercise my patience.

Even if they merely oppose me by holding evil opinions, they will exercise whatever small measure of knowledge I possess; and, so that enemies too may be loved according to the Lord’s command, they will exercise goodwill. But if your authority writes to me that I should release the aforesaid Gothescalcus from custody and either grant him permission to come to you, so that you may examine his teaching yourselves, or grant him permission to go to anyone specifically named, I shall in no way resist your commands. For, as you yourselves know better, just as no one may be ordained unattached, so neither may a monk, or anyone placed under a rule, be released from his place in accordance with the sacred rules in order to be entrusted to a particular person and sent to a particular place, except with the consent of the one to whom he is known to belong.

I ask only that I have your authority, so that I may not appear, through my presumption, to disregard the judgment of so many bishops. It is not that I take pleasure in the small hardship of confinement which he stubbornly endures justly; rather, I grieve over the faithlessness from which he cannot be recalled. If your authority should deem him fit to be entrusted to anyone, it should also make provision in the commendation that the person to whom he is entrusted be Catholic and possess ecclesiastical gravity, vigor, and knowledge of the Scriptures. For he is able to recite from memory throughout the entire day, without any pause for breath, not only passages of Scripture violently twisted to his own meaning but also mutilated statements of Catholic teachers.

Thus he was accustomed to lead into admiration of himself not only the ignorant but also the half-educated and unwary, and those who possessed zeal for God but not according to knowledge, drawing them over to his own opinion. He desires to appear not merely as the teacher of his own teachers; and he takes very careful pains to entrap those who converse with him in argument. If he cannot overcome them by the truth, he will make every effort to affirm invincibly under oath that those speaking with him said things which perhaps they did not say, so that he himself may be proved truthful and those who contradict him and teach against his doctrine may be proved liars.

## LETTER III. TO THE BISHOPS OF THE SYNOD OF SOISSONS

Concerning Vulfadus and his colleagues, whose judgment Pope Nicholas had ordered to be renewed in this synod.

*(In Sirmond.)*

[Col. 0046B]

HINCMAR, bishop of Reims, to Remigius, Wenilo, and the other archbishops and bishops summoned by the authority of Lord Pope Nicholas to the synod to which he ordered my insignificance to come together with our fellow bishops, in this city of Soissons, for the case of Vulfadus and his colleagues.

[Col. 0046C] If it should seem good to you to examine and investigate carefully, through whatever persons may be appropriate for learning the facts, and in accordance with the tenor of the letters of the apostolic lord, everything that was done concerning the aforementioned brothers, so that you may carry out without contradiction whatever proves to be just and pious in their case, as that same apostolic lord wrote both to your fraternity and to my humility, I will receive this devotedly and gladly. And if you should judge that the brief response which follows is sufficient, so far as depends on me, for the apostolic writings, perhaps it will not be unwelcome that I report as concisely as possible what pertains to the matter.

Namely, the sons of the Church of Rheims from the company of Vulfadus, ordained by Ebo after his deposition, were not first suspended and afterward expelled by my judgment, nor by the bishops of the province of Rheims alone, so that by my decision, or by a decision shared only with them, they might be able to receive a more lenient or another sentence, in accordance with the canons of Nicaea and Antioch (Council of Nicaea, canon 5; Council of Antioch, canon 4). Rather, after being suspended, and in due course judged by a synod of bishops of five provinces, to which they had appealed, according to the decrees of Innocent [Col. 0046D] addressed to Rufus and Eusebius, after consideration of what he wrote to Marcianus, and according to the decrees of Zosimus, Innocent’s successor, addressed to Patroclus, bishop of Arles, and to the Church of Marseille (Innocent, letters 21 and 22; Zosimus, letters 6, 11, and 12), as well as to several other Churches, concerning those whom Proculus—conscious of his own conduct and, having issued letters for his own abdication, removed from the priesthood by a document of his profession and subscription—ordained—and according to the sacred canons and the decrees of Leo and the other pontiffs of the Roman See, which I have omitted to insert here both for the sake of brevity and because they are very well known to you—they were judged and expelled from the ecclesiastical orders. Pope Leo had already given judgment against them, saying (letter 1, to the bishops of Campania):

“We command that all decretal constitutions, both those of blessed memory Innocent and those of all our predecessors, which have been promulgated concerning ecclesiastical orders and the discipline of the canons, be so observed by your charity that, if anyone should violate them, he must know that thereafter pardon will be denied him.” [Col. 0047A]

In that matter, since, as the sacred rules declare, a complete and canonical synod of the bishops of five provinces had been held, and since the sons of the Church entrusted to me had appealed to neighboring bishops concerning their case—and since the canons of the province of Africa of this kind (Council of Africa, canon 92) command neighboring bishops to hear such men and, having been appointed between them and their own bishop, to settle the complaint—I did not judge Vulfadus and his colleagues. I neither expelled them from the ecclesiastical orders before the people nor signed together with their judges, as those who were present know, and as the episcopal acts themselves, supported by the unimpaired subscriptions of those by whom they were carried out, plainly show.

Therefore, at the command of those same bishops, I was merely the bearer, namely, of conveying to the apostolic See the case of the Church entrusted to me, as they had settled it. These proceedings were confirmed by the privilege of the apostolic lord Benedict, with an anathema attached, so that no question might ever arise from them at any time. Finally, they were strengthened by the confirmation of Pope Nicholas, just as Benedict, pontiff of holy memory, had confirmed them, with the command and judgment of the Roman See preserved in all things, and under a terrible anathema: whoever, great or small, should presume by rash endeavor to act against this apostolic decree of his would be bound by the chain of anathema. You can read these matters here in full, and you can inspect their seals intact, together with the writings and subscriptions uncorrupted.

And because the apostolic See, as we read in the decrees of its pontiffs, very carefully preserves its own rights in this matter and guards those of others—or rather, makes them its own—so that every question referred to it may receive an end through its judgment and the decision of its confirmation, the confirmations and subscriptions of these two most illustrious lights have removed every suspicion of complaint from our regions and minds.

Now, however, since that same lord and father of ours, Pope Nicholas, has decreed in his letters that the judgment in this matter be reopened by you, I heed the Apostle’s admonition: “Obey your leaders and be subject to them” (Hebrews 13:17). Whatever he decides or shall decide concerning these brothers by the privilege of the apostolic See, as is fitting for my submission, I obey and shall obey, just as until now I have preserved what was established by the authority of the lord Benedict and by his own.

And since the Apostle likewise says, “Let all of you say the same thing, and let there be no divisions among you” (1 Corinthians 1:11), just as I have preserved until the present what the predecessors of some of you, together with certain of you, regularly settled concerning these same brothers, so also, whatever you shall canonically settle concerning them according to the tenor of the letters of the apostolic lord, while the earlier constitutions remain in force, as Gelasius says (Decree, chapter 2), out of reverence due to them, and while the privilege of the apostolic See’s judgment and jurisdiction is preserved in every respect, I shall agree to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, carefully observing your regular decisions.

I do not begrudge the happiness of these brothers in question, or of any others, nor do I hasten to harm them by any malice. I have desired, and do desire; I have sought, and do seek, their sound and regular status. I grieved greatly, and still grieve, over their expulsion, because no one suffers greater loss from their expulsion than I do. As the apostolic lord deigned to write to me, if I had expelled them from those same ranks solely by my own judgment and that of the co-bishops of the province of Rheims, I would hasten, judging what was just and pious, to restore them to their orders with the consent and judgment of those co-bishops, without reconsideration.

But, in accordance with his most discerning words, because I did not expel them, a clear conscience did not permit me to be moved to this. I fear to do it on my own authority, since they were expelled by you, or by your predecessors—the bishops of the five provinces—whom they sought as judges with my consent and who were chosen according to the sacred canons, the case having been settled with the consent of the parties.

For this reason I have in no way presumed to usurp the work of others in restoring them. As you know, the sacred rules even decree, by a comparable rule of excuse, that those expelled by some are not to be received by others, and still less restored, but are to await the investigations and judgments of the same council of bishops or of a greater one.

And because Leo says (letter 95, to Rusticus of Narbonne) that in matters which are doubtful or obscure we must recognize as worthy of following whatever is found to be contrary neither to the evangelical precepts nor to the decrees of the saints, and because the lord and father of ours, Pope Nicholas, as it seems to me, wrote to you that he does not consider the measures established concerning the aforementioned men to be violated unless perhaps they should be found contrary to the sacred laws, I await, with a simple and sincere intention of heart, that the sacred rules may plainly show my sluggish understanding whether what our brothers and co-bishops settled, and what has until now been observed, ought henceforth to be observed as consonant with the rules, or whether their settlement, once found contrary to the sacred laws, ought to be rejected.

I also await a clearer explanation than I am able to understand from his sacred letters: whether we can, without prejudice to the rules and the apostolic See, and without common danger to ourselves, dissolve or alter the privileges of confirmation under anathema granted by the lord Benedict and that same lord Nicholas concerning this same decision—unless perhaps he himself should see fit to dissolve and alter them by his singular authority—since he wrote to us that their full force and firmness had been reserved to the discretion of the power of the apostolic See.

For Celestine says (letter 3): “What dignity will be preserved by us if the standard of decretal constitutions is broken at the pleasure of certain people and permission is granted to the populace?” Nor should we greatly disregard what Pope Leo wrote concerning himself to Leo Augustus (letter 84): “If I destroy these things and build them again, I make myself a transgressor and subject myself to those conditions of punishment which not only the authority of Marcianus of blessed memory but also my own confession has confirmed.”

You yourselves know better what has been decreed by the Holy Spirit through the councils of the province of Africa, and by the wisdom of God—by which, as it is written, the founders of laws establish what is just—concerning those conditions of punishment. If such a great pope and pontiff of the first See, understanding this about himself, cautiously refused to subject himself to these legal conditions, this plainly shows how much we, who are subject to them, ought cautiously to fear being subjected to those same conditions of punishment.

Nor is it hidden from your wisdom, taught by God, what Saint Gregory says to the patrician Theoctista concerning contempt for an anathema pronounced duly under necessity—how much more under deliberation—which is contained in the aforementioned privileges (book 9, letter 79). Symmachus also says (letter 1, to Aeonius) that this belongs to the very holy Catholic religion, whose entire authority is weakened unless everything once regularly established by the priests of the Lord remains perpetual; and that this could happen in another way if a successor did not grant firmness to the acts of his predecessor, and, by strengthening what had been done, make valid what he himself had done.

And Gelasius says (letter 11, to the Germans):

“Our fathers, namely our Catholic and learned pontiffs, whatever they once decreed, after assembling together, for the sake of faith, truth, Catholic and apostolic communion, according to the course of the Scriptures and the tradition of the ancestors, desired thereafter to remain unimpaired and firm. Nor did they permit what had been established in this same matter to be reconsidered through any recent presumption. They perceived with the greatest wisdom that, if anyone were permitted to repeat salutary decrees, no stable ecclesiastical constitution would remain at all against the various errors, and every complete settlement would always be disturbed by the return of the same frenzies.” [Col. 0049C]

I therefore present these matters, received from divinely inspired writings or made evident for knowledge of the case, not, God forbid, to oppose in any respect the apostolic decrees of the lord pope, nor to resist your regular decisions. Rather, I present them so that, just as I have hitherto obeyed what was settled concerning their expulsion, so in their restoration—of which you have been appointed arbiters by the apostolic lord—if you find that it ought to be carried out canonically and that it has been so done, I may, so far as depends on me, not dangerously oppose the sacred rules mentioned above, or the episcopal and apostolic confirmations issued concerning them.

Nor shall I knowingly deviate, even by a “transverse fingernail,” as the saying goes, from the commands contained in the apostolic letters, with the Lord’s favor; nor shall I wander through ignorance in any matter. I wish clearly to learn, by the course of those same rules, how I ought to follow without danger the regular decision of you, whose responsibility it is, by delegation of the apostolic See, to settle this matter.

For this above all is why a bishop comes to a synod: that he may either learn, teach, be corrected, or correct. And since Celestine says (Decree 20, to the bishops throughout Apulia, and elsewhere) that no priest may be permitted to be ignorant of his canons or to do anything contrary to the rules of the Fathers, it is necessary that you decide these matters here, so that they may not return to dispute, so that no occasion for subsequent presumption may arise, and so that it may not be necessary in our times or those of our successors to dissolve them.

“How great,” says Symmachus (letter 1, to Aeonius), “will reverence for the vicars of the blessed Apostle Peter be judged to be, if what they prescribe in the priesthood is dissolved when those same men have passed away?” For, as he himself says, what touches the injury of the whole cannot be firm only in part.

## LETTER IV. TO THE SAME SYNOD OF SUESSONS

Concerning Ebo of Rheims: that, having been lawfully expelled from the episcopate and afterward not legitimately restored, he could not ordain clergy; and that those whom he had ordained, suspended in the synod of Meaux and deprived of their rank in that of Soissons, had been so treated.

*(In Sirmond.)*

Hincmarus, bishop of Rheims, to the holy synod convened by the authority of the lord Pope Nicholas.

### CHAPTER I. Concerning Ebo

Some people speak about Ebo without knowing his case, or without wishing to know or hear it. I will enter into no dispute with anyone through contentiousness, since the apostolic lord did not write to me that I should undertake this matter, since I was never Ebo’s adversary during his lifetime, since after his death I am not his detractor, and since I was not an invader of his See, which, after he had departed this life in the priesthood according to the rules, I, the fourth after those who had held it, having been canonically elected and ordained in it, received to govern.

But reason dictates that I may lawfully state the truth, which I ought not to deny to anyone who asks. For Ebo himself, according to the sacred rules and ecclesiastical tradition, and according to the decrees of the pontiffs of the Roman See—Zosimus, John, and Gregory—as is repeatedly read in their constitutions, deposed himself in a synod through a document of his profession, dictated and subscribed in his own hand, with the moderation which Pope Leo the Great decreed for all the bishops throughout Samnium, Picenum, and Tuscany (letter 86). He stripped himself of the episcopal ministry, and according to his profession and subscription received the judgment of deposition from forty-three bishops.

This is clearly shown by the document itself which he presented to the synod and by the synodal record that we possess. For, as Gelasius says, a certain person is summoned to judgment so that he may either confess the charges brought against him or be convicted by them. Ebo was convicted both by an action known to almost the whole world and by his own voice and subscribed profession, by which he condemned himself.

Afterward, without any regular restoration, he usurped the same episcopal ministry of which he had deprived himself, contrary to the sacred canons. Finally, coming to Rome under Pope Sergius, he was condemned by a strict sentence, as the acts of that pope himself show, to remain in lay communion only.

Although the metropolitan Church of Rheims, in which he had been ordained, remained without a pastor for ten years after his deposition, and although he lived almost seventeen years after his condemnation, until the end of his life, he neither canonically reclaimed the same See from which he had regularly deprived himself nor obtained it. Nor did he present to any synod, to the princes of the earth, or to the peoples who knew that he had been condemned, any document of his canonical restoration according to the sacred rules.

If anyone wishes to say that he was regularly restored by the consent of the bishops or of the apostolic See, as Saint Gelasius says in his decretal letter concerning Acacius (in the book On the Bond of Anathema)—whom his accomplices and supporters pretended had been restored—let him show by whom and where that consent of restoration was enacted: whether it was celebrated according to the rules of the Church, whether it proceeded from the tradition of the Fathers, whether it was promulgated according to the custom of the ancestors, whether it was brought forth after suitable examination, whether it was referred to the first See, whose concern it was, concerning the sentence by which he was held bound, according to the rules of the Church, and whether the same authority that bound him also released him.

If these things were not done, since he was not lawfully released by pontiffs and ecclesiastical laws, no secular power could absolve him at all outside the course of the Church. Nor ought anyone to have communicated with him after his deposition as though he had been restored, in that particular matter from which he had been excommunicated by himself, by the council of bishops, and, moreover, by the apostolic See, without canonical letters of his restoration, prepared by those who restored him according to custom, as the sacred canons and the decrees of Pope Felix demonstrate (Felix, Roman synod, letter 59).

Therefore, as Leo writes to Theodore, what he did not receive while remaining in the body he cannot obtain after being stripped of the flesh. Hence we must hold concerning him what Gelasius says concerning Acacius (On the Book of Anathema):

“Such is he as he was declared, such as he was bound; such he remained until the end; such he did not cease to be. Thus he is today such as he was declared; he cannot now be other than he is. Therefore, while remaining such, he will never be released.”

It is clear that, having eaten the fruit of his own way and being filled with his own counsels, as Innocent teaches, I cannot find how one who became a participant with the condemned could receive honor. He left his remains to his little ones. Moreover, every question concerning him is excluded by the ecclesiastical and secular laws approved by the Church, since he was condemned in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 835, in the thirteenth indiction, on the fourth day before the Nones of March; more than thirty years have now passed since that time.

### CHAPTER II

But it is said that until the end of his life he carried out the episcopal ministry in all ecclesiastical functions. Sound-minded people do not accept this presumption as an example. For in both the old and the new priesthood this is an ancient device of the devil. Many have presumed to do this: Bonosus, against whose disease Innocent acted; Proculus, against whom Zosimus labored at length; and Acacius, whom Felix deposed, while Gelasius, following the sacred canons and the decrees of his predecessors, destroyed and extinguished him together with his presumption and usurpation.

There were also many others who adopted this presumptuous position and consented to those who passed into it. In our own age we have heard of some and have even seen others who did this. But, as Scripture warns, we must not follow the crowd into wrongdoing. As Innocent says when speaking of Bonosus (decree 56):

“Whenever sin is committed by peoples or by a crowd, because punishment cannot be inflicted upon everyone on account of their number, it usually passes unpunished. I therefore say that earlier matters should be left to God’s judgment, and that henceforth the greatest care must be taken to prevent them.”

And concerning what is inconsistent with the sacred Scriptures and the decrees of the saints, it is likewise read in the decrees of the apostolic See that, even if all the priests and the whole world should consent, condemnation involves those who consent; consent does not absolve transgression. For a crime is not diminished but increased when a private offense becomes general. [Col. 0052A]

God demonstrated this, for he destroyed the sinful world by a universal flood. The sacred Council of Nicaea also says (canon 9) that the Catholic Church defends whatever is irreprehensible. For if it were permitted with impunity that those who had either not received sacred orders at all, or had received them contrary to the rules, or had been regularly forbidden to exercise the ministry of sacred orders, should usurp authority to minister in those orders or to confer them, every ecclesiastical order and vigor would not merely waver or be confused but would be utterly destroyed.

### CHAPTER III

Finally, because Ebo ministered in the province of Mainz, this is known to be contrary to every authority. For the canons of Antioch established a rule concerning a vacant bishopric and a vacant Church (canons 16, 17, and 18), and also concerning one who receives the laying-on of hands for the episcopate and refuses to minister, as well as one who, after being ordained, does not go through any fault of his own to the parish for which he was ordained. None of these rules applies to Ebo.

The Sardican canons (canon 21) plainly show what must be observed concerning those suffering unjust force, those expelled for discipline and Catholic confession or in defense of the truth, and those seeking to escape dangers. But this rule does not absolve Ebo either. For priests, almost the whole world, and even the apostolic See itself had deeply lamented that the pious Emperor Louis, attacked by false accusations, sold through a certain betrayal for honors accepted thereafter under oath, and expelled from the empire and from the very entrance of the Church through Ebo’s efforts, was nevertheless found innocent of the charges and restored with complete justice; and the whole world rejoiced with gladness, while it cried out together with him for the expulsion of Ebo, who had irreverently laid his hand upon the Lord’s anointed, as upon one guilty of treason.

Nor was Ebo driven out by enemies, after losing his own province through necessity, with the city in which he had been ordained captured, so that he might be incardinated elsewhere, as we find in the decrees of blessed Gregory and of other pontiffs of the Roman See. Nor is there any canonical document showing that he was unjustly and contrary to the sacred rules expelled and then, according to the Sardican canons (canon 3), restored to his own See by command of the apostolic See after the judgment had been reopened.

Therefore he ought immediately to have been excluded, by judicial authority through the governor of the province, from the very parish where he was staying, after being brought to trial there, according to the African council; nor ought he to have been defended either by the Churches over which he had presided or by any person.

It is therefore clear that, having been justly expelled, he presumed upon things that were not his. We need not examine his merits and actions, since he has the one whom he has as witness and judge of his conscience and work. For, as Leo says (letter 84, to Leo Augustus), to seek what has been revealed, to reconsider what has been completed, and to overturn what has been settled—what else is this than failing to give thanks for the grace received and extending the wicked desires of deadly greed toward the food of the forbidden tree?

### CHAPTER IV. Concerning my own ordination

Although perhaps some secretly disparage my ordination—I do not hear them do so openly—I will enter into no dispute against anyone on this account, since, as the Apostle says, “A testament is confirmed over the dead” (Hebrews 9:17).

For when Folco had held the Church of Rheims for nearly nine years without any regular protest from Ebo, and after him Noto had held the same See for almost a year and a half, likewise without any reclamation by Ebo, I was sought under Pope Sergius at a synod of many archbishops and bishops held at Beauvais in the diocese of Rheims, by the clergy and people of that metropolitan Church and also by the bishops of the same province. I was presented by my then archbishop and my own bishop, as well as by the co-bishops of that province, according to the Council of Laodicea (canon 12), with the consent of my abbot and of the brothers of the monastery in which I lived, to the bishops of the province of Rheims, and to the clergy and people of that metropolitan Church, by canonical letters.

With a canonical decree, in the presence or with the consent of all the suffragans of that metropolitan Church, and by my metropolitan, who had presented me to them, I was ordained in that same Church, with everyone acclaiming and without anyone’s contradiction or reclamation, canonically and according to the decrees of the pontiffs of the Roman See.

My ordination was confirmed not only by the subscriptions of the bishops of the province of Rheims—namely, my ordainers—in accordance with the African council, but also by the hands of nearly all the bishops of Gaul, as well as those of Neustria and Aquitaine. A subscribed letter was unanimously sent to the aforementioned Pope Sergius. It was also approved by an edict of the lord King Charles, confirmed by his own hand and strengthened by his seal.

All these documents were sent to Pope Leo, who had succeeded Sergius before I could make my way to him. They were accompanied by a letter from the lord Emperor Lothair to that same Pope Leo, in which he wrote how much effort he had exerted with Pope Sergius for Ebo’s restoration and how he had been able to obtain nothing. Pope Leo repeatedly approved my ordination by his favor, by the use of the pallium, by the privilege of the apostolic See, and by several of his apostolic letters, namely, as occupying the place of a pastor who had died in the priesthood. [Col. 0054A]

Benedict, of holy memory both in grace and in name, and the lord and father of ours, Pope Nicholas, also strengthened my ordination by their privileges. The sacred rules demonstrate that both my election in an episcopal council, before my ordination, and my subsequent ordination were carried out canonically—not in response to anyone’s question, but against the detractors of whisperers and secret murmurers, so that every iniquity might close its mouth.

There is also this reason why I have decided not to enter into any dispute against anyone on this matter: the lord pope has not written to me in his apostolic letters that I must give an account of it to anyone through a legal inquiry.

I do not say this out of lack of confidence, as though I would fail in the proofs of documents for these matters. In whatever right anyone dares to act, I too dare. But I also follow, according to my ability, Leo’s words to Leo Augustus (letter 84), where he says that concerning matters settled at Nicaea and Chalcedon, as God willed, “we dare not undertake any discussion, as though those things were doubtful or weak which such authority, through the Holy Spirit, established.”

If so great a pope of so great a See said that he did not dare to undertake such a discussion, how could I, such a very little man, dare to enter into any contest concerning what the authority of so many councils and of so many pontiffs of the apostolic See approved and established regarding my ordination, an ordination of whatever servant of the people of God, as the most certain records declare, as though it were a doubtful or weak matter?

### CHAPTER V

Concerning these brothers of ours, about whom the apostolic lord recently wrote to us jointly: if the brief response I have given does not suffice for you in relation to the apostolic writings, here you have the episcopal acts and the privileges of the lord Benedict and the lord Nicholas. They show you by what reasoning and in what order, by what authority, by whom, where, and when the actions concerning these men were carried out.

After examining all these matters, decide according to the most discerning and regular command of the lord and father of ours, the apostolic pope, whatever you find to be just and pious, according to the sacred canons, and, so far as depends on me, carry it out without any contradiction. For, as I wrote to you in the preceding document, I will contradict neither his apostolic commands nor your regular decisions.

### CHAPTER VI

Moreover, if it should seem necessary to your gracious will—not for any contention or against anyone’s questioning, but for fuller knowledge of the matter—for me to disclose to your fraternity more extensively the regular deposition of Ebo, his lack of any canonical restoration, the manner in which my ordination was celebrated, the reason why our brothers and co-bishops suspended in the synod of Meaux the sons of the Church of Rheims now in question, and the source from which the synod of Soissons determined that they ought not to remain in their ecclesiastical ranks, together with the reasoning, order, and authority that were there demonstrated and undertaken by the care of my humility, I will not refuse to reveal it, lest by keeping silent I offend by failing to speak the truth at the proper time.

Only let your minds not be wearied by an account that is tedious and perhaps, if it is known to you, unnecessary, so that the truth may be demonstrated by me in such a way that the charity of your unanimity toward me may be preserved. I desire to benefit not only our brothers but also our enemies without detriment to ourselves. I do not answer the apostolic commands with any obstinacy, nor do I prepare to stretch out my intention or hands against your fraternal admonitions and regular decisions, provided—and I know that you too wish and strive for this—that the order of the rules and the privilege of the apostolic See remain intact, and that our common danger may be avoided.

After this document had been shown to the synod, the episcopal acts of the synod of Soissons were presented through the hands of Hincmarus, bishop of Laon; the acts of the synod of the province of Bourges through the hands of Raginelmus, bishop of Tournai; the privilege of the lord Benedict through the hands of Erchanradus, bishop of Châlons; and the privilege of the lord Nicholas through the hands of Hodo, bishop of Beauvais. [Col. 0055B]

After all this, the following document was delivered: it explained how, while the earlier constitutions remained in force, as Gelasius says, out of reverence due to them, and while the privileges of the apostolic See were preserved, the brothers in question might, by the indulgence and authority of the lord pope, be received and advanced in their orders without contradiction, with the preservation also of those who had subscribed the synod in which the brothers had been expelled.

By then all the bishops who had taken part in Ebo’s deposition had passed away except Rothadus. Likewise, those who were said to have communicated with that excommunicated man had died, and others had been substituted in their places, through whom, so to speak, countless men had been ordained. The only concern was that, henceforth, the scandals that might arise from this should be avoided by the authority and foresight of the apostolic lord.

## LETTER V. TO THE BISHOPS OF THE SYNOD OF SUESSONS

That what has once been established or judged in councils ought not to be changed without necessity.

*(In Sirmond.)*

Hincmarus, bishop of Rheims, to Remigius, Wenilo, and the other archbishops and bishops, convened by the authority of the lord Pope Nicholas in this city of Soissons for the case of Vulfadus and his colleagues, to which synod he also commanded my humility to come with our co-bishops.

We read, as blessed Innocent writes (letter 2, to Exuperius), that concerning certain matters the earlier observance was stricter, while the later one, mercy intervening, was more accommodating. And Saint Leo says (letter 95, to Rusticus) that, just as there are certain things which cannot be overturned by any reasoning, so there are many things which ought to be moderated either because of consideration for ages or because of the necessity of circumstances.

Thus, concerning a certain right of indulgence, he says: “We do not establish a rule in this matter, but we judge what is more tolerable.”

And the eloquent Gelasius says (letter 6):

“While the earlier constitutions remain in force out of reverence due to them, they ought regularly to be observed whenever no pressing necessity of circumstances or times demands otherwise.” [Col. 0056A]

Here, without doubt, our God and ruler must be proclaimed to all Christian peoples: he is spoken of as dwelling in the heights of ecclesiastical dignities, and in whose virtue hearts must be placed in good works, with the ranks duly distributed. No one should now think that anything has been diminished for him, since nothing is lost from the perfection of each rank; and, by retaining appropriately what has been bestowed through heavenly dispensation, God grants that he be made known to us as ruler and that he be acknowledged as such.

Even if something is granted because of the length of time, it is compensated by the vigor added in conduct, provided that what would have required care at a more advanced age is now contained in the purpose of one’s life. This is on condition that those matters do not stealthily intrude under any pretext, for if any one of them should clearly be found to exist, it rightly proves the person to be unworthy of the clerical insignia.
