And although matters which, if the integrity of the others is assured, cannot by themselves cause harm must sometimes be tolerated, nevertheless those matters must be guarded against with the greatest care which cannot be admitted without obvious disfigurement.

The African council, reconsidering the veiling of virgins (canon 93), decreed that the constitution of the earlier council should remain in force where no pressing necessity demands otherwise. It also decreed that a later council does not offend the earlier one when, for definite reasons, it changes what had been established, nor does a later council oppose an earlier one when no necessity presses it to change that earlier decision (canon 35).

The council also decreed concerning the Donatists that, with the consent of the brothers and co-bishops, and especially of the apostolic See by which the matter had been settled, they should be received into their honors according to the will and counsel of each Catholic bishop who governs the Church in the same place, if this should seem beneficial to Christian peace, just as it is evident that this was done in the earlier periods of that division. The examples of many, indeed nearly all, the African Churches in which such an error arose bear witness to this.

This was not so that the council held overseas concerning this matter should be dissolved, but so that it should remain in force concerning those who wished to pass in this way to the Catholic Church, while no restoration of unity was to be procured through them.

But wherever Catholic unity should appear capable of being wholly achieved or assisted through them, with the evident gain of their brothers’ souls, the fact that the overseas council established something against their honors should not harm them, although salvation was closed to no one.

[Col. 0056D] Therefore, while the enactments remain in force, without prejudice to the rules and to the Apostolic See, and without any discrimination on the part of the judges, those whom not only the authority of the Council of Carthage defends from every blemish—if the sentence against them is rescinded, since it cannot be proved that those who judged them did so with hostile intent or were corrupted by some desire or favor—but whom that same council, as well as the Council of Antioch and the decrees of the Roman pontiffs Innocent, Zosimus, and Leo, commend: through these authorities they confirmed their judgments, by which our brothers and fellow bishops, at the Council of Soissons, passed ecclesiastical sentence against the sons of the Church of Rheims who had been ordained by Ebo after his deposition. I did not judge them there, nor did I subscribe with their judges.

[Col. 0057A] Let the authority of the privileges of lord Benedict and of our lord and father, Pope Nicholas, also remain—as it ought and must—if it pleases him to whom all good things are pleasing that, out of mercy and by way of indulgence, the judgment contained in the privilege of his predecessor Benedict and in his own privilege, which he himself confirmed, concerning these brothers should be altered, where it is written that the command and judgment of the Roman See in all things are preserved. Let the decree then be confirmed in another form and let it be commanded that we observe it, in accordance with the moderation of Innocent, who says that the earlier observance is the harsher, but the later, because mercy has intervened, the more lenient (Epistle 2, to Exuperius). And if your fraternity—who judged these same brothers, or whose predecessors judged them—should agree, with unanimous benevolence founded upon justice and piety, and should consent and decree accordingly, as the sacred and mystical Council of Nicaea decreed concerning the Novatians (canon 8), and as it decreed by indulgence in its letter to all the bishops established throughout Egypt, Libya, and Pentapolis concerning the condemned Meletius, with a merciful judgment, although by a careful and truthful assessment he deserved no pardon, and concerning those whom he ordained after his condemnation—whom it calls Meletians—

[Col. 0057B] For, as we read in a true and acceptable history, Meletius, bishop of an Egyptian city under Peter, archbishop of Alexandria, who received martyrdom under the emperor Diocletian, was deposed both for many other reasons and especially because, during the persecution, he denied the faith and sacrificed. Thus, although condemned, he acquired many followers and became the heresiarch of those who to this day in Egypt are called Meletians after him, without possessing any satisfaction of justice that could explain why he remained separated from the Church. He indeed said that he had suffered injustice, and he spoke against and disparaged Peter. But Peter died after attaining the palm of martyrdom in the persecution; Meletius, however, carried his slanders against Achillas, who succeeded Peter in the episcopate, and again against Alexander, who is known to have been ordained after Achillas.

Meanwhile the Arian controversy arose, and Meletius, together with his followers, defended Arius, having conspired with him against the bishop. Concerning this Meletius and his accomplices, the aforesaid sacred council, in the aforementioned letter, decreed the following for the restoration of peace and unity:

[Col. 0057C] “It pleased us,” it says (the letter of the Council of Nicaea to the Egyptians), “that Meletius, by a merciful judgment, although by a careful and truthful assessment he deserved no pardon, should indeed remain in his own city, but should in no way possess any power either to elect or to ordain, whether in the province or in any city, and should possess merely the bare name. Those, however, who were appointed by him are to retain the honor and ministry conferred by the mystical ordination, yet they are to be in every respect subordinate to all those consecrated in the individual parishes and churches by our beloved fellow minister Alexander. They are to have no power to elect persons of their own choosing, to put their names forward, or in any way to do anything contrary to the will of the Catholic Church’s bishop Alexander.

[Col. 0058A] “For, by the grace of God and your prayers, they are found in no schism, but remain without blemish in the Catholic and Apostolic Church. It is therefore right that they should have the power both to elect anyone and to present the names of those worthy of the clergy, and freely to do everything according to the law and ordinances of the Church. If one of them should happen to die while in the Church, then those who have recently been appointed are to be promoted to the honor of the deceased, but only if they appear worthy and the people elect them, with the bishop of the great city of Alexandria agreeing and confirming the decision.

[Col. 0058B] “This, then, was granted to all the others; but in the case of Meletius the same provisions were by no means approved, because of his former insubordination and because of his insolent and wanton disposition, lest any authority or power be granted to a man who might again foment the same acts of insubordination.”

Pope Anastasius the Younger, writing to the emperor Anastasius concerning those ordained by the condemned Acacius, says in a single letter that they are to be received in their orders. Although some say that this same letter does not agree with the sacred canons and the decrees of Innocent, Zosimus, Leo, and Gelasius, this is because Anastasius writes in that letter an ambiguous sentence: “and he baptized catholically, not canonically.” Acacius, though condemned, ordained neither priests nor deacons according to the sacred rules or according to the custom of the Catholic Church. For, as Gelasius says, even Catholic laymen who have been baptized can sometimes baptize catholically, and even criminals—

[Col. 0058C] —still sitting upon the cathedra, like the scribes and Pharisees, and like Judas, by virtue of the ministerial dignity entrusted to him among the apostles, which he had not yet lost by an openly pronounced judgment, can perform, in the exercise of his office, the acts that are to be performed in that ministry.

There are other matters that could be set down here, were it not clearly known that other enactments and decrees of the saints oppose them; for, as Daniel says, “Many shall pass to and fro, and knowledge shall be increased” (Daniel 12:4). It is found that decrees concerning such matters were made otherwise. And therefore it is enough to have set down these examples, which seem rather to follow the mercy of indulgence than to impose the severity of justice.

[Col. 0058D] These things being so, insofar as depends upon me, I am concerned to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, in harmony with the benevolence of the Apostolic See and with the agreement pleasing to your fraternity, without opposing the canonical status of these brothers. As I stated at the beginning of the preceding memorandum delivered to you, I have both desired and do desire, sought and do seek, their healthy and canonical status; and I have grieved and do grieve over their deposition, because no one suffers a greater loss from their deposition than I do.

I have written these things according to the modest capacity of my little intellect, showing my disposition of mind toward the brothers, while the ancient enactments remain, as Gelasius says, on account of their own reverence, and while in every respect the privilege of the judgment and right of the Apostolic See is reserved. I do not prejudice your judgment, or that of anyone else which is more reasonable, more binding, or of greater authority; if such a judgment is shown to me, I am prepared to follow it without any contradiction.

[Col. 0059A] Nevertheless, in every respect, if your unanimous agreement concerning the status of these men is given and confirmed by the lord pope, this condition must be preserved—a condition which we ask the Apostolic See, for the sake of ecclesiastical vigor, to have observed by all, and which your fraternity must take care to enforce: that, on this pretext, those who either have never received authority to minister in the sacred orders, or have received it contrary to the rules, or whose ministry has been canonically prohibited, should not usurp authority in those orders. For if this were permitted with impunity, the whole ecclesiastical order and vigor would not merely waver but would be utterly thrown into confusion.

There are other matters besides these, concerning which the supreme authority of the Apostolic Lord will prudently provide; and under his guidance your diligent discernment will consider them here, matters that my humility will show you in another document, lest further abuses arise in the Church on this pretext. Your prudence will contemplate these matters more clearly, as well as others that the narrowness of my understanding cannot reach; and the pre-eminent wisdom of the Apostolic Lord will much more carefully both see what must be provided and impose a remedy upon the present and a safeguard upon the future.

## EPISTLE VI. TO THE BISHOPS OF THE COUNCIL OF SOISSONS

Concerning Vulfadus, who presumed to usurp the Church of Langres when it had been deprived of its shepherd, and who declared in a written statement of satisfaction that he would never again aspire to the administration of ecclesiastical grades.

(From the same source.)

[Col. 0059C]

HINCMAR, bishop of Rheims, to Remigius, Wenilo, and the other archbishops and bishops summoned to the city of Soissons by the authority of lord Pope Nicholas, who ordered even my unworthiness to come with our fellow bishops to the council, convened for the case of Vulfadus and his associates.

I say this unwillingly, and I do not dare suppress it altogether, lest those who know these matters perhaps accuse me of having concealed the truth by some artifice; and lest, if this case, having been decided by synodal judgment in accordance with the ancient constitution, should in any way be obstructed without a definitive synodal sentence, it should be charged against our beloved brother Vulfadus as the result of some renewed hostility.

This same beloved brother of ours, after everything concerning the judgment against him and his associates had been decided by a synod of bishops from five provinces, and confirmed by the authority of the Apostolic See with the imposition of an anathema, presumed—without a hearing or the counsel of the episcopal council of the priests who judged him, without the authority of the Roman pontiff who confirmed those judgments, and without consulting the Church of Rheims—to usurp, outside its province, the Church of Langres, which had been deprived of its shepherd, under the title of a bishop-elect, in order to be ordained there as bishop.

He had been baptized and tonsured as a cleric in the province of Rheims, and for many years had publicly read the sacred Scriptures in its Church. According to the decree of the African council, chapter 58, after a person has once read in one Church, he ought not to be received unadvisedly by another Church, as the same council clearly demonstrates in chapter 21. Vulfadus also appropriated for his own use and that of his associates the resources of the Church, which, according to the Council of Chalcedon (canon 25), ought to have been kept by the steward for the future bishop.

The council itself decreed that those who dared, after the decision of this great and universal synod, to perpetrate any of the prohibited acts should withdraw from such an office (canon 12). The Council of Antioch likewise decreed concerning condemned persons who presumed to undertake anything in the ministry that they should in no way be permitted to hope for restoration in another synod.

[Col. 0060B] Having been recalled from this presumption by synodal authority, whose constitution we possess, and, at the Lord’s command, “If your brother sins, rebuke him, and if he repents, forgive him,” he earned the right to receive communion through a written statement of satisfaction confirmed by his own hand—a communion from which he had been regularly deprived according to the canons of Nicaea and Chalcedon and the decrees of Gelasius—as the same statement, now before us, shows.

In it, under oath by the Holy Trinity, one Godhead, he professed that he would never and nowhere again aspire to the forbidden presumption or to the administration of ecclesiastical grades, nor knowingly or willingly undertake any other such rash act by which the peace of the Church might be disturbed or the tranquility of the priesthood troubled.

He presented this statement before the bishops Pardulus of Laon, Guntbert of Évreux, Aeneas of Paris, the king, and many others—before us, his judges appointed by the synod. Blessed Gregory decreed that those returning from schism should profess under oath and subscribe that they would never return to the schism to which they had returned.

[Col. 0060C] And according to the tradition of Pope Leo, who wrote to Januarius, bishop, he says (Epistle 3): “It is most salutary and wholly filled with the benefit of spiritual medicine that, whether priests, deacons, or clerics of any order who wish to appear corrected, they should first acknowledge without ambiguity that their error has been condemned by them; so that, once their perverse opinions have been condemned and long since put to death, no occasion for aspiring may remain, and no member of the Church may be violated by association with such men, once their own profession has in every respect begun to oppose them.”

And in his letter to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, concerning one who had gone astray from ecclesiastical discipline, he says (Epistle 12): “If he grieves faithfully and beneficially, and, although late, recognizes how rightly episcopal authority was exercised, or if, for the fullness of satisfaction, he condemns by living voice and present subscription everything that he had wrongly thought, then no degree of mercy toward one who has been corrected will be blameworthy. For our Lord, the true and good Shepherd, who laid down his life for his sheep and came to save souls, not to destroy them, wishes us to be imitators of his compassion, so that justice may restrain sinners, but mercy may not reject those who have turned back.”

[Col. 0061A] He also wrote to Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, concerning the presbyter Atticus (Epistle 82), that, with all doubt removed, he should profess that he would in every respect observe the definition of the Council of Chalcedon concerning the faith, which the authority of the Apostolic See had also confirmed, adding his own handwritten subscription, which was to be read in the Church in the presence of the people.

It is therefore established that those who deviate contemptuously from ecclesiastical tradition must be received in this manner; for, as Hilary says (Epistle 2), one sins no less against the sanctions of holy traditions than one rushes into an insult against the Lord himself.

Concerning such persons, if they deviate from their profession or subscription, the Council of Carthage says (Council of Carthage II, canon 13): “If anyone,” it says, “in any respect acts against his own profession or subscription, he shall deprive himself of his honor.”

[Col. 0061B] And Saint Gregory, writing to Maximus, bishop of Salona, concerning the deacon Andrew, says (Epistle 125, Book VII) that judgment ought not to be demanded concerning a case which he himself judged.

But because the synodal decision of the bishops, as well as the authority of lord Pope Benedict of the Apostolic See, had been disregarded through an unwarranted presumption, when an opportunity arose I sent, through our venerable brother and fellow bishop Odo, a copy of lord Benedict’s privilege, under guarantee of faith, to the authority of lord Pope Nicholas, and asked that what his predecessor had confirmed should be strengthened by him.

This was not done, God forbid, as an insult to the Apostolic See, as though its judgment were still being called into question, or as though what had once been confirmed by it through the authority of Pope Benedict were insufficient—confirmed precisely so that no dispute concerning it should ever arise and so that the presumptuous aspirations of those improperly seeking office should be utterly and permanently suppressed.

[Col. 0061C] Rather, because reckless presumption demanded that the constitution be renewed, it was done so that, if obstinacy chose to persist, the offender might understand that after so many prohibitions he could not attempt with impunity what had been definitively decided.

I have considered it necessary to bring these matters to your attention—not out of malice, but lest they be thought to have been concealed through cunning—you who must examine canonically, in due order, everything that has been done concerning our aforesaid brother Vulfadus and his associates, according to the command of our lord pope, investigate it more precisely, and, if anything is found to accord with justice and piety, complete their restoration, lest something appear to have been omitted which it is necessary for you to know and concerning which it is appropriate for you to give a decision.

## EPISTLE VII. TO POPE NICHOLAS

Sent through Egilo together with the acts of the Council of Soissons in the year 866.

(From the same source.)

Lord Nicholas, most holy and most reverend Father of Fathers, pope of the first and supreme Apostolic See and of the universal Church:

HINCMAR, bishop of Rheims and the most devoted servant of your most holy fatherhood, sends greetings.

On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the fourteenth indiction, in accordance with your apostolic command, I hastened to meet the brothers and fellow bishops of the province of Rheims at the city of Soissons, where archbishops and bishops were gathering there at your order. I also urged our beloved brother Vulfadus to come.

I brought with me those of our brothers from his company who live under our care. As you deigned to write to me, I would have hastened to restore them, by the consent and judgment of the fellow bishops of the province of Rheims, to their orders without hesitation, if I had deposed them from those same grades by my own judgment alone.

[Col. 0062B] But since they were deposed by the decision of a synod of bishops from five provinces, whose judgment they had sought with my consent—and, as your wisdom knows better, the sacred canons decree, even to the point of a similar punishment of excommunication, that those deposed by some are not to be received by others, and especially are not to be restored, but must await the decisions and judgments of the same bishops or of a greater council—I did not presume to usurp the work of others in restoring those whom I had not suspended from office by my own judgment.

At the aforesaid synod of bishops from five provinces, I not only did not judge or depose them; I did not even subscribe with their judges, because the sons of the Church entrusted to me appealed to neighboring bishops concerning their case, in accordance with the Sardican canons. The canons of the province of Africa likewise command that neighboring bishops hear such cases and, being called in by them, settle the complaint between them and their own bishop.

[Col. 0062C] Therefore I humbly beseech you not to regard it as disobedience on my part that I did not restore them immediately. Fearing to act on my own authority alone at the council to which, as you commanded, I obediently came, I sought to comply with what our brothers and fellow bishops—devoted sons of your most holy fatherhood and supported by your authority—decreed concerning their restoration, in accordance with what the mystical Council of Nicaea, writing to the diocese of the Church of Alexandria, established by a merciful judgment concerning those ordained by Meletius, the condemned bishop: namely, that those confirmed by the mystical ordination should retain their honor and ministry, and that any one of them should be advanced to the honor of the deceased bishop in the Church if he appeared worthy and the people elected him, with the consent of the Alexandrian bishop under whose care that diocese was governed.

This resembles, in a certain manner, what the African council decreed concerning the Donatists. I do not present these matters to you as though they were unknown, but repeat them as matters well known, so that, while the enactments of the sacred canons and of the Apostolic See remain in force, I may readily agree to them, carefully preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, and obey.

[Col. 0062D] And because the synod, through this venerable Archbishop Egilo, who was present at its proceedings, sent a letter from all of us who were able to be present, speaking with him orally as well: “If you extend a hand to them, we shall likewise extend one with you,” it was unnecessary for Vulfadus and his associates to appeal to the Apostolic See on account of disagreement among the judges, since everyone in that synod unanimously held the same view.

For this reason I did not send such an envoy—one who, representing my person to you, would answer the allegations of anyone holding a different opinion, although now there are none, and would bring back your decision. For whatever, verbally and in writing, you command me through this religious archbishop to follow and observe, I shall strive to obey and preserve to the best of my knowledge and ability, just as until now I have preserved what had been established and confirmed concerning this matter.

Nor did I omit to send my subordinate with this venerable archbishop out of disobedience. Rather, I understood your authoritative letter to say that only if, while we were disputing or perhaps deciding different things, the aforesaid deposed men should appeal to the Apostolic See and ask to be condemned or absolved by its special judgment, and if neither I nor Vulfadus or his associates could come to you personally, then, immediately after the council convened by your authority on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September of this present fourteenth indiction had been completed, we were to send our representatives to deliberate and conclude this matter, presenting our persons to you, with neither side making any excuse, to the see of blessed Peter.

[Col. 0063A] Therefore I beg that I may deserve to receive your decision in writing, which I am prepared to observe most earnestly, as is fitting.

As for the complete account of everything reported, examined, and discovered in the council, which you ordered to be sent to your discernment, so that whatever appears salutary might be strengthened, if anything remains in the synodal letter that ought to be explained, this venerable and religious archbishop, your most devoted son in holiness and our unanimous brother and fellow priest, Egilo, will be able to disclose it fully and faithfully to your Apostolic authority, and to report it as he learned it by sight and hearing and discussed it in his episcopal capacity.

[Col. 0063C] Concerning the aforementioned brothers of ours, sons of the Church of Rheims, ordained by Ebo after his deposition, there are no more than nine of them among canons and monks, townsmen and parishioners, together with Vulfadus among us. Your most holy fatherhood wrote to me concerning them that, whenever they should wish to submit the cause of their deposition to examination, none of them should suffer my displeasure, and none should be subjected to any disadvantage through my intervention in carrying out what they had undertaken.

How I acted toward them before and after this, our brothers and fellow bishops, together with him, will be able to explain sufficiently to your graciousness. I have both desired and do desire their healthy and distinctive status; I have both sought and do seek it; I have grieved over their deposition, and I rejoice in their established condition.

Concerning Queen Teutberga, about whom you asked that a report be sent to your eminence from my humility: since I did not see Lothair or Teutberga herself after the venerable bishop Arsenius, legate of the holy Roman Church, departed from the palace at Attigny of the glorious lord King Charles, I cannot send you a reliable account of what would be salutary.

[Col. 0064A] In another hand:

May almighty God deign to preserve your holiness, for the instruction and correction of his holy Church, in his fitting service through many years, most holy and most reverend Father of Fathers in the Lord.

Given on the Kalends of September, in the fourteenth indiction.

## EPISTLE VIII. TO EGILO, ARCHBISHOP OF SENS

He instructs him, as he travels to Rome, concerning what took place at the council in the case of Vulfadus and how he should conduct himself in the City.

(From the same source.)

HINCMAR, bishop of Rheims in name but not in merit, and servant of the people of God, sends abundant greetings in the Savior to the most holy and most reverend Egilo, archbishop, my dearest, unanimous, and most faithful friend.

You can judge from your own mind how great is the confidence with which I rely upon your affection. For I hold you in my mind no otherwise than as another self, except for my sins. Therefore, just as I trust in you and concerning you, and just as I wish to be in every respect with you and for you, so you should be toward me in all things.

In addition, I am sending to your affection the copy of the letter of the Apostolic Lord to lord Charles, which you did not request, as well as the copy of the letter sent to me, as you requested. You already possess the copy of the letter sent in identical form through the archbishops of this kingdom; you must not go without it.

[Col. 0064C] I am also sending you the capitula containing a summary of all the letters that the Apostolic Lord sent to all of us concerning this case. It will be necessary for you to know these capitula thoroughly and to remember what is contained piecemeal in those letters, so that, if those whom you know should wish, as is their custom, to wrap up and obscure their statements, you will possess the truth with which you can answer them.

As for the documents that I presented at the council, concerning which you asked me to determine whether you needed to carry them, it did not seem to me that you had any need of them. Rather, it seems to me that, if they were shown to the Apostolic Lord or to the Romans, they might create some doubt for the Apostolic Lord, as though there had been disputes among us concerning Vulfadus’s restoration, and, together with your embassy, the acts of the council and my letter might become suspect. This could cause some impediment and delay to what our senior wishes soon to obtain concerning Vulfadus himself.

[Col. 0064D] And I think that some people would not be displeased if an opportunity arose that made it necessary for him to turn to them, and, as I have already been instructed, the Apostolic Lord and the Romans are becoming increasingly annoyed at reading so much.

In the document that I first gave, there is nothing other than this: that I did not suspend these same brothers from office, nor judge them, nor depose them from their ecclesiastical grades, nor subscribe with their judges; rather, the synod of bishops from five provinces did so, and whatever you should find to have been canonically determined concerning the matter, I would follow without hesitation according to the tenor of the Apostolic Lord’s letters. Thus both the synod and I give an account in our letters to the Apostolic Lord of why I did not restore them.

[Col. 0065A] I gave the second document because, as you know, Vulfadus did not think that I was willing to yield to him. Although not in my presence, I had nevertheless heard from others that he sometimes said that Ebo had not been regularly deposed, and at other times that he had been regularly restored. Therefore I demonstrated that Ebo had been regularly deposed and had not been regularly restored.

He was condemned in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 835, on the fourth day before the Nones of March; and although he lived in the flesh for seventeen years afterward, he neither reclaimed nor obtained his see regularly in a synod, nor did he show any synod, during his lifetime, a regular canonical restoration made either by the Apostolic See or by a synod, in accordance with the canons and decrees of the Roman See.

Moreover, every question concerning him has already been excluded by ecclesiastical and human laws for thirty years and more. For, as Leo writes to Theodore (Epistle 59, near the middle), “What he did not receive while remaining in the body, he cannot obtain after being stripped of the flesh.”

[Col. 0065B] I possess considerably more concerning his deposition than I showed at the council, just as was reread in the document itself at the council, where I demonstrated that I had been canonically elected and canonically ordained.

In these matters, as you know, the king and everyone else agreed, knowing that I did not wish to persist harshly against Vulfadus, who sometimes even said that he was not my cleric, pressing, as you know, to obtain a grade by any means whatsoever.

I would have sent these documents to you not for you to display but to have, if our notary had been able to undertake transcribing them despite his illness.

Afterward, the synod to which I did not subscribe was produced. In it, those very men who had taken part in Ebo’s condemnation proved before the king, by words, writings, and authoritative documents, how Ebo had been canonically deposed by himself, in accordance with the decrees of Zosimus, Leo, John, and Gregory, through a written profession signed by his own hand, and by forty-three bishops in accordance with his profession and subscription; and how he had not been canonically restored. For this reason, according to the decrees of Innocent, who, writing to Martianus, the Naxitan bishop (Epistle 28), ordered that those whom Bonosus had ordained before his condemnation should be received in their orders, whereas, writing afterward to Rufus [Col. 0065D], Eusebius, and the other bishops of Macedonia (Epistle 27), he did not permit those whom Bonosus had ordained after his condemnation to be received into ecclesiastical orders; and according to the decrees of Zosimus to Aurelius and to all the bishops established throughout Africa and the other provinces (Epistle 6), and to the Church of Marseille and Patroclus, bishop of Arles, concerning those whom Proculus ordained after his condemnation—he who, having signed his profession in a written declaration, deposed himself in the synod—and according to the decrees of Leo and the sacred canons, these brothers were judged to remain deposed because they had communicated with an excommunicated man.

The synod of the bishops of the province of Bourges was also produced, subscribed by their hands and presided over by [Col. 0066A] Rodulfus. In it, those who had taken part and had heard from Aiulfus, who had been one of Ebo’s judges, established that the same Ebo had been canonically deposed. Then the privileges of Lord Benedict and Lord Nicholas were produced; by their subscriptions they had confirmed both Ebo’s deposition and these men’s removal.

If it should be too lengthy for you to recount all this, you can briefly say what you must hold firmly and well, because you know what certain men are like. I ask that you not be displeased that I instruct you to hold such things firmly, as though I considered myself wiser than you. I say this out of charity, and I would wish such instructions from you if I had the sort of mission that you have.

The words that you and [Col. 0066B] your people must hold firmly, if anyone among them should be questioned concerning this matter, are these:

“According to the tenor of the letters of the apostolic lord, as they are written in them, after canonically examining in due order everything that was done in the case of these brothers, you found Ebo justly and canonically deposed but not canonically restored; and you found that these brothers were judged not by me but by a synod of bishops from five provinces, according to the sacred canons and the decrees of Innocent, Zosimus, and Leo, as is contained in the synodal letter.

“And because the apostolic lord’s letters state that what has been established must not be dissolved unless it is found contrary to the sacred laws, the synod, recognizing in those same letters his benevolence toward these brothers, found the authority of the Council of Nicaea concerning those ordained by Meletius [Col. 0066C], formerly a condemned bishop. The bishops unanimously communicate this authority to him in their synodal letter, so that, with the ancient arrangements remaining in place—as Gelasius says—out of reverence for their antiquity, and with the privileges of the Apostolic See preserved, as well as the security of those who subscribed to the synod in which the brothers in question were removed, these brothers may, through his indulgence and authority, be received and advanced in their orders without contradiction, since all the bishops who took part in Ebo’s deposition have now departed this life except Rothadus alone.

“Moreover, those bishops who were said to have communicated with Ebo after his deposition have also now departed to divine judgment. Others have been substituted in their places, and through them, so to speak, innumerable men have been ordained; yet none of these brothers’ restoration is opposed by anyone.”

[Col. 0066D] Nevertheless, if it would not burden you, I would very much like you to report to the apostolic lord the whole fullness of what I have written above concerning Ebo’s deposition and these men’s judgment. I entrust this to your wisdom, in which I place greater confidence than if I were to send the writings themselves.

There is also this consideration: if I were to send writings through you and you were to carry them—apart from the synodal letter and my letter agreeing with that letter—you know what we are like. It might happen that some people would take offense against us on that account. I avoided this as much as I could at the synod itself, where, as was demonstrated, I did not judge these brothers, nor did I subscribe to that synod.

There were canonical authorities and decrees of the [Col. 0067A] Roman See’s pontiffs by which those bishops themselves judged these brothers. Those who subscribed to the synod, even if I remained silent, were necessarily obliged either to establish what they judged and subscribed to, or, by acting against their own profession and subscription, to deprive themselves of their honor according to the Council of Carthage. You yourselves saw and heard what the privileges of the Apostolic See granted by the two pontiffs were, and what they confirmed concerning the judgment of those bishops.

Nevertheless, so that no scandal might arise, I followed the example of the Lord, who said to Peter: “We do not owe the tax, but lest we scandalize them”—that is, those who demanded the tax—“give a stater from the fish’s mouth for me and for you” (Matthew 17:26). Avoiding scandal and prejudice against the Apostolic See, so that not we but its authority, if it wishes, may [Col. 0067B] dissolve and alter its own sentence, which it bound and confirmed, I deemed it necessary to preserve the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace, both in this matter and as there: namely, that I send no writing and that you carry nothing else except what has been agreed upon by the king, the bishops, and us.

Let us proceed simply, for, as Scripture says: “Whoever walks simply walks confidently” (Proverbs 10:9).

But if you see an opportunity, you should open this matter to the apostolic lord, because many are already saying that, if those things which were then confirmed there were not firm, neither will these things now being done be firm. Nothing that the bishops and the Apostolic See decree is now firm; they care neither about our judgments nor about excommunication. Nor will the priests degraded by us abandon their ministry because of our judgment, since nothing that we do is [Col. 0067C] firm. Rather, just as the king wishes, and as hatred, favor, greed, or fear moves us, so our judgments and those of the Apostolic See proceed.

You must also remind the apostolic lord how Guntharius acted concerning his own excommunication and the confirmation made by his own hand. Therefore provision must be made in such matters, because people are now more inclined and willing to sin with impunity than to accept and observe canonical discipline.

If the apostolic lord asks you for the authorities explaining how these men were judged deserving of removal, you may, if it seems right to you, answer him as follows: the bishops unanimously directed their efforts toward restoring these brothers; for that reason they sent him the authority they had found. Since their purpose was not [Col. 0067D] that the brothers should remain deposed, they omitted sending him the authorities of the sacred canons and the decrees of Innocent, Zosimus, and Leo mentioned above, which are known to him.

As for their restoration, if Vulfadus were not involved in the matter, the Church could well have endured without it; counting canons and monks, urban and parish clergy, together with Vulfadus, they are no more than nine.

I say this as it seems to me, out of a charitable affection. Your prudence, thanks be to God, will be sufficient for this and for many other matters.

I also ask that, regarding what the apostolic lord wrote to me about Pharaoh’s hardness, as you read in the letter sent to me, you explain to him in due order how kindly I treated these same brothers both before and [Col. 0068A] afterward, as I proved in their presence at the synod, lest he think me to be the sort of man my rivals portray me to be.

Also obtain copies of the synodal letter and of my letter, so that, if anyone wishes to say anything about them after you have delivered them to the apostolic lord, you may have copies and know them well.

Likewise, take care to read the letters that the apostolic lord will order to be written concerning this matter before they are sent here, lest their scribes, as they are said to do, be able to insert some deception into them.

And do not forget to make the apostolic lord aware that the letter of Pope Leo IV concerning the complaint of these brothers—which he mentions in his letters—was not known in these Cisalpine regions except through the letters he recently sent. Ask [Col. 0068B] one of your people who is a mindful man to remind you often, since you will be occupied, so that you do not forget to obtain the records of the pontiffs from the beginning of the records of Pope Sergius, in which Ebo is found to have been condemned, up to the present year of this pontificate; for we in these regions have great need of them. If you do not possess the records of the other pontiffs, you can obtain them through me or through Fulcricus.

Concerning all these matters that I entrust to your affection—how they please or displease you, as far as you wish and are permitted, and how the things I send arrive safely to you—send me a written reply through this messenger of ours.

In conclusion, I write to you what the holy apostle Peter said to Apollinaris when he sent him to preach [Col. 0068C] at Ravenna: “May my Lord Jesus Christ send his angel before you, to guard your ways before you, and grant what you ask.”

## EPISTLE IX. TO THE SAME EGILO, ARCHBISHOP

Concerning Gottschalk and his assertions, and concerning Bishop Prudentius, so that he may make a report to the pontiff.

*(In the same collection.)*

To my dearest and most faithful friend, abundant greeting in Christ.

In another letter I wrote so much to you so that you might have the order, fullness, and truth of what was done at the synod, because the apostolic lord, as you will read in the letter directed to you, ordered that everything [Col. 0068D] done there be reported to him in a full and faithful account. Your mind, however, occupied with a sudden and difficult journey, may perhaps not have been able to attend to everything, although the synodal letter contains a sufficient account of it. Nor was I able to discuss with you in person the other matters about which I am writing. I ask you to ensure that these matters, as well as those that follow, do not come into the hands of such people as might derive scandal from them.

After that letter had been written, I was informed that from our cell called Altumvillare our monk Guntbertus had fled with books, clothing, horses, and other things he was able to steal. He had often been canonically corrected for his negligence. Because he had often joined himself secretly to Gottschalk, had given him letters [Col. 0069A], and had received letters from him, he was sent, according to the rule, to confinement for graver offenses; and he is said to have been corrupted by Gottschalk’s perverse teaching.

As I have been told, he wishes to carry Gottschalk’s complaint to the apostolic lord, seeing how the accusations against me that reach him from these regions run their course. He has also heard that the apostolic lord wrote to Lord King Charles about me, saying that he ought not, and is not able, always to shield me from such things, so that I should take care lest I eventually incur what I do not desire, while this brother and others freely devise or do whatever they wish.

For I do not know in what matters the apostolic lord says that he has so often shielded me. If he means Rothadus, it was not my authority alone but that of the bishops of the realm of our [Col. 0069B] lord Charles, to whom Rothadus appealed against me, that deposed him, as their subscriptions demonstrate.

If he means those who were ordained, as you have now seen and heard demonstrated, I did not judge or depose them, nor did I subscribe with their judges.

If he means Gottschalk, concerning whom, as well as concerning the aforesaid ordained men, I gave a written account when questioned in writing by Arsenius: I received Gottschalk, who had been condemned by two synods, into custody at the bishops’ command after he had been judged, so that he would not harm others by his perverse teaching, since he was unwilling to benefit himself.

I also reported to the apostolic lord by letter what his teaching was and asked whether he wished me to give Gottschalk permission to go to him, or whether I should entrust him to someone else at his command, lest I dissolve without authority the [Col. 0069C] decision of two synods.

If it pleases him to hear Gottschalk himself, let him order it, and I will release him to go to him. For if the king does not send him, I do not have enough guards to escort him.

If it also pleases him that someone else receive him, and that either a synod or some bishop hear his teaching, let him follow it if it is good, and let those who hear him refute it if it is wicked. Those to whom he entrusts him will do with him what they see accords with the sacred rules, just as those who thought they understood the sacred rules did with him. It makes no difference to me.

Nevertheless, if anyone asks you about his teaching, you may answer that it is as follows, as both his words and writings demonstrate:

1. He says that the deity of the Holy Trinity is threefold [Col. 0069D], just as there are three persons of the Holy Trinity.

2. He says that God’s predestination is so twofold that, just as God predestined some to eternal life, so he predestined others to eternal death.

3. He says that God does not wish all human beings to be saved, but only those who are saved; and that all are saved whom he himself wishes to save. Consequently, whoever is not saved is entirely outside his will to be saved.

4. He says that our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ was not crucified and died for the redemption of the whole world—that is, for the salvation and redemption of all human beings—but only for those who are saved.

5. Explaining the apostle Peter’s statement about those who deny the Lord who bought them, he says: “He bought them through the sacrament of [Col. 0070A] Baptism, but he did not undergo the cross for them, nor endure death, nor shed his blood.”

More extensive statements are found in his writings, which I am sending to you on another sheet, so that, if it seems appropriate to you, you may show it to the apostolic lord as something sent to you by me—not for you to display to him on my behalf, but for you to keep.

He says other things as well that seem to me harmful and contrary to the Catholic faith. If the matter reaches this point, wise and Catholic men will prove it.

For one so fiercely and seriously attacked, it is enough for me to sit in the corner of the roof and not join battle in disputes with a contentious woman in a common house; and it is enough for my soul to be my spoil.

For the same Gottschalk—either because the time has now come when what the [Col. 0070B] apostle Paul foretold about the last times will arrive, or because of envy toward me, as though it were a personal matter for me that I guard him at the bishops’ command—is said to have many supporters. Among them he had Lord Prudentius, as Prudentius’s own writings testify, writings that can be produced by many who possess them.

The same Lord Prudentius, in the Annals of the Deeds of Our Kings that he composed, inserted, in order to confirm his opinion, the following statement under the record for the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 859:

“Pope Nicholas of Rome faithfully confirms and Catholicly decrees concerning the grace of God and free choice, concerning the truth of twofold predestination, and concerning Christ’s blood, that it was poured out for all believers.”

We have heard this from no one else, nor have we read it anywhere else. Since the record in which these things were written has now come into the hands [Col. 0070C] of many, you must report this matter to the apostolic lord in such a way that no scandal may arise in the Church, as though he himself—God forbid—held such views as Gottschalk.

I ask that nothing be said to him on my behalf, because he is said to have his mind stirred against me, with many writing to him against me and disparaging me. I do not want him to turn the scandal against me on account of something for which I bear no guilt.

The king himself possesses the Annal that I have mentioned. It is the very book that, in your presence, in the church where he commended you to us, I returned to him after he had lent it to me.

Finally, I could have written more to you about Gottschalk—how harmful he is, and how much more dangerous he will be to many if he is released from that custody—for he certainly says and does things [Col. 0070D] by which he is clearly recognized as either possessed by a demon or manic; and you know that mania is not ordinarily found without a demon.

If anyone asks you about his custody, you may truthfully answer him as follows:

“Whatever the brothers have in food and drink is supplied to him every day without any negligence. Clothing is offered to him in sufficient quantity, if he wishes to accept it. He is given enough wood to make a fire. In the dwelling where he lives he has a heated room and a privy. Baths are not denied him; but after entering that same dwelling he not only refused to wash his body, but also his hands and face.

“Previously, as those among whom he lived testify, he was extremely filthy, and he still [Col. 0071] remains as filthy as he can. And know that great revulsion will be stirred up in this Church if he is ordered to come to the synod or is released from that custody.”

I do not say this on my own behalf, for I have no concern in the matter except for others; but you will prove that I am speaking truthfully. For such men will arise as are still hidden.

## EPISTLE X. TO THE SAME EGILO, ARCHBISHOP

A fuller exposition of Gottschalk’s same teaching, which he promised in the preceding letter.

*(In the same collection.)*

HINCMAR, bishop of Rheims in name but not in merit, and servant of the people of God, to the most holy and most reverend Egilo, archbishop.

If anyone asks you about Gottschalk’s teaching, concerning which I have already written certain things to you, you may answer the questioner that it is as follows, as both his words and writings demonstrate:

1. He says that the deity of the Holy Trinity is threefold, just as there are three persons of the Holy Trinity.

2. He says that God’s predestination is so twofold that, just as God predestined some to eternal life, so he predestined others to eternal death.

3. He says that God does not wish all human beings to be saved, but only those who are saved; and that all are saved whom he himself wishes to save. Consequently, whoever is not saved is entirely outside his will to be saved.

“Whatever the Lord willed,” says Scripture, “he did in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses” (Psalm 134:6), etc.; and: “All things, Lord, have been placed in your will, and there is no one who can resist your will” (Esther 13:9). Therefore he does not wish all to be saved, but only those who are saved, because if he wishes something he cannot accomplish, he is not omnipotent.

4. He says that our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ was not crucified for the redemption of the whole world—that is, not for the salvation and redemption of all human beings—but only for those who are saved.

5. Explaining the apostle Peter’s statement about the Lord who bought those who deny him (2 Peter 2:1), he says: “He bought them through the sacrament of Baptism, but he did not undergo the cross for them, nor endured blood [the text reads *sanguinem*, “blood”; the parallel in Epistle IX above has *mortem*, “death”], nor shed blood.”

More extensive statements are found in his writings. From these deadly propositions every Catholic and educated person can see what destructive consequences proceed.

1. From this teaching, by the devil’s invention when he said to Adam, “You shall be like gods” (Genesis 3:5), a plurality of gods is introduced: for if the Deity is threefold, there will be three gods.

Unity in the Trinity is fulfilled not by the same person but by the same essence—that is, by the deity, which is the Trinity’s unity. Thus, in the Law, the Lord says: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deuteronomy 6:4). In the Gospel: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). And the seraphim sing [Col. 0072]: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth” (Isaiah 6:3).

David also sings: “May God, our God, bless us; may God bless us, and may all the ends of the earth fear him” (Psalm 66:8). Paul confesses: “From him, and through him, and in him are all things. To him be glory” (Romans 11:36).

When God is said to be one; when believers are commanded to be baptized in the name, not in the names; when the seraphim sing “Holy” three times and confess one Lord God of Sabaoth; when David names God three times and prays that one God be feared by all the ends of the earth; and when Paul glorifies one God after confessing the Trinity—the one deity of the three persons of the Holy Trinity, which is the Trinity’s unity, is demonstrated.

Consequently, insofar as this most pernicious heresy is concerned—namely, the mother of idolatry, slain by the sword of God’s word at the mystical Council of Nicaea and recently revived by this man—the faith in which we were baptized, by which one believes in the heart unto righteousness and confesses with the mouth unto salvation, is overturned.

2. This perverse teaching makes clear that the works of free choice, whether good or evil, have no value for merit, but that in both life and death everything is accomplished by God’s predestination.

By this teaching the merit of condemnation is taken away from the reprobate, and the merit of salvation from the just. Consequently, those who cannot be just are not justly condemned, nor are these others justly rewarded, since they cannot be anything other than just.

Therefore merit acquires nothing for the unjust, and grace accomplishes nothing in the elect. In both groups, destruction and salvation arise not from the judgment of one’s own actions but from the prior determination of the Lord’s will, and everything is attributed to God’s workmanship.

For the creature cannot say to the one who fashioned it, “Why did you make me like this?” Therefore no one will be condemned by free choice, and no one will sing forever of the Lord’s mercies on account of grace.

If free choice did not exist—as this blind man, groping at midday, fails to see—how would the world, lost as the whole of Adam in the mass of perdition, be justly judged, together with its own added sins? And again, if God’s grace did not exist, how would the world, chosen from that same mass of perdition—that is, selected by grace—be saved?

The psalm says: “Mercy and truth have met each other; justice and peace have kissed” (Psalm 84:11). Mercy is that by which the elect are saved; truth is that by which those left behind are abandoned in the mass of perdition. Justice is that by which the reprobate are not taken up; peace is that by which those who are made good by grace are brought from one and the same mass of perdition.

Hence Paul says: “The wages of sin is death, but the grace of God is eternal life” (Romans 6:23).

3. By wrongly interpreting Scripture—“Whatever the Lord willed, he did in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses” (Psalm 134:6), and “All things, Lord, have been placed in your will, and there is no one who can resist your will” (Esther 13:9)—he asserts that God is unjust because he inflicts wrath upon those who cannot be saved against his predestination and will [Col. 0073A], and upon those who were sold into slavery through another’s sin, namely that of the first parent, for whom no redemption was given.

Either not understanding, or knowingly and falsely interpreting from Scripture what was rightly and truly said, he makes God unjust in avoiding the claim that God is weak. Using himself as the worst teacher, he disdains learning from another how he ought to understand these matters, because there are certain things which, as Paul teaches, the omnipotent God is said not to be able to do: “God remains faithful; he cannot deny himself” (2 Timothy 2:13).

He also cannot be changed, lie, be deceived, sin, become miserable, be defeated, or die. If he could do such things, or could wish to do them, he would not be omnipotent.

It would now take too long to write about this. If this fool had sound understanding in these matters [Col. 0073B], he would not err in this opinion. While he disdains becoming a disciple of truth, he would, if permitted, wish to become a teacher of error.

4. Moreover, although the Lord speaks of himself through the great Peter: “The Lord is not slow concerning his promises, but deals patiently for your sake, not wishing any to perish but all to return to repentance” (2 Peter 3:9). and through the divine Paul: “He wishes all human beings to be saved, who gave himself as a redemption for all” (1 Timothy 2:4, 6); and: “By the grace of God he tasted death for everyone” (Hebrews 2:9); and: “If one died for all, then all died, and Christ died for all” (2 Corinthians 5:14).

and through the prophet, with an oath for the sake of unbelievers: “As I live, says the Lord [Col. 0073C], I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live.”

and in the entire Catholic Church—which, by apostolic tradition, petitions him on behalf of all human beings and thereby establishes for us, through the law of prayer, the law of what we are to believe—Gottschalk teaches that Truth is a liar.

When Christ says of the devil, “He is a liar from the beginning, and the father of lies” (John 8:44), if Christ himself is a liar according to this man’s teaching, he is shown by his own words—something impious to say—to be like him, that is, like the devil, a liar.

But God is truthful and Gottschalk is a liar. For Christ, the one and same Sun of righteousness, received the cause of all in order to restore the life of all. From there righteousness flows to all, where he assumed the whole of human nature, not its guilt. He arose for all, came for all, and [Col. 0073D] suffered for all, and wishes all to be saved—for he suffered for all—yet he is not seen by all, and not all are saved.

“For the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.” This does not pertain to the guilt of the light but to that of the darkness. The light came into the world, saying: “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me will not walk in darkness but will have the light of life” (John 8:12). But people loved the darkness more than the light, for their works were evil.

And when the darkness comprehends the light, the light itself says through the Apostle: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5:3).

That some, by following the light, are saved is the gift of the one who saves; that some, remaining in darkness [Col. 0074A], perish is the merit of those who perish.

For all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth. That the guilty person is condemned is the blameless justice of God; that the guilty person is justified is God’s ineffable grace.

The redemption of the human race has been offered to all, but it gives salvation to believers. “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life; but whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John 3).

The Lord also showed this when he handed over the sacraments of his Passion to his disciples and apostles, saying: “This is my body, which will be handed over for you” (Luke 22:19); and: “This is my blood, which will be poured out for you and for many” (ibid.). Both forms are found in the Gospel.

Among those to whom he handed these things [Col. 0074B] was Judas, who held the portion of the reprobate, just as the other disciples bore the portion of the elect. He said not “for all” but “for many,” because not all were going to believe.

The pouring out of Christ’s blood—the just one for the unjust—was so abundant as a price that, if the whole company of captives believed in its redeemer, no one would remain held by the devil’s chains.

Those who do not believe acquire condemnation for themselves.

For just as the Incarnation, preaching, and miracles of Christ are salvation and honor for believers but a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense for unbelievers, so also is his death. Those who read the Scriptures find this stated many times and in many places, and it can be seen in the nature of created things, through which, as Paul says, God’s invisible attributes may be known (Romans 1:20).

The one and [Col. 0074C] same sun hardens mud and melts wax. Likewise, our Creator, Redeemer, and Savior does not assist the just by one intention and condemn the unjust by another. Rather, by one and the same power of his singular nature, always like itself, he orders unlike things by one predestination of his own, which is always directed toward the good.

His predestination is twofold in the same way as there is one Holy Spirit and two gifts of that same Spirit, one charity and its two commandments: one predestination of God, pertaining either to the gift of grace or to the recompense of justice.

God is not therefore to be thought to have predestined the reprobate to punishment, God forbid, just as he is believed to have predestined the elect to glory and prepared everlasting glory for them. Rather, by his predestination—just as the prophet sings to him, “Mercy and truth shall go before your face” (Psalm 88:15)—things belonging to the gift of grace are bestowed [Col. 0074D] through mercy, while things rendered by the recompense of justice are assigned to the truth of just judgment.

For the Lord is good and just in all things. It is good when what is owed is repaid, and it is just when what is not owed is given without anyone’s being defrauded, as it is written: “He has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills” (Romans 9:18).

God has mercy by freely imparting mercy and removing wickedness. He hardens, however, not by imparting wickedness but by justly withholding mercy; thus he is said to have hardened Pharaoh’s heart—that is, not to have softened it through grace—and to have handed certain people over to a reprobate mind—that is, according to the recompense of justice, not [Col. 0075A] to have freed them from a reprobate mind through grace.

Many other statements of this kind are found in Scripture.

### 5.

And He who spoke through the prophets, as the Spirit of God says through the apostles and evangelists: “There is one God, one faith, and one baptism” (Ephesians 4:5). In this baptism the sanctification of the Spirit is effected through the sprinkling of Christ’s blood, by which we have been redeemed from the futile manner of life handed down by our fathers (1 Peter 2). For the blood of that same Jesus Christ, the Son of God, cleanses us from every sin (1 John 1:7). Jesus Christ came through water and blood—not through water alone, but through water and blood. And it is the Spirit who bears witness that Christ is truth, because there are three who bear witness: the Spirit, the water, and the blood; and the three are one (1 John 5:6).

[Col. 0075B]

The Spirit, certainly, of sanctification; the blood of redemption; and the water of baptism: these three are one and remain indivisible, and none of them is separated from its connection with the others. By this faith the Catholic Church lives and advances, cleansed by the washing of water in the word. For the one saving baptism celebrated in that same Catholic Church is neither water without the word nor the word without water; rather, when the word is added to the element, it becomes a sacrament. Sanctified by the Spirit who in the beginning was borne over the waters, this sacrament was disclosed when one of the soldiers opened Christ’s side on the cross with a lance, and immediately there came forth from the hidden mystery of divine humanity and human divinity—namely, blood and water. From this the people of the Church of believers are watered by the washing, and their hearts are purified by the faith given through the Spirit. [Col. 0075C]

They are saved through hope, because “the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5); in whom believers were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise.

And again, as the same Apostle says: “In whom we were sealed for the day of redemption” (Ephesians 4:30)—that is, in the same sacrament of baptism, in which there is no distinction among those reborn. The Apostle says: “All of us who were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death” (Romans 6:3); and: “All of you who were baptized in Christ have put on Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek; there is neither slave nor free; there is neither male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:27).

[Col. 0075D]

For those whom sex distinguishes in the body, or age distinguishes in time, Grace, the mother, gives them all birth into one infancy from the immaculate womb of the divine font. The person reborn from water and the Spirit becomes not only spiritual but also, invisibly, spirit, and through the grace of adoption becomes God’s son, although visibly, to those who see, there appears flesh and a human son.

Against all this, the truth of that one and the same baptism is emptied by this most deadly doctrine, which leaves believers no hope of salvation, nor any one from whom believers can hope for salvation. It makes God unjust, deceitful, and a respecter of persons, and leaves Him so. You know that these and other blasphemies of the same man can easily be refuted by the authority of Scripture and by the tradition of Catholics who, with the Lord speaking in them—He whose face is wisdom and understanding, and who teaches human beings knowledge—have made crooked things straight and rough roads level.

[Col. 0076A]

Therefore, what Celestine wrote concerning and against such men must not be passed over casually (Letter 8, to the bishops of Gaul):

> “The matter rightly concerns us if we favor error by our silence. Therefore, let such men be corrected; let it not be free for them to speak as they please. If matters stand thus, let novelty cease to assail antiquity; let disturbance cease to trouble the peace of the Churches.”

Otherwise, as Leo says, the faults of those in lower orders should be attributed to no one more than to negligent and careless rulers, who often allow a pestilence to grow unchecked while pretending not to apply the necessary remedy.

[Col. 0076B]

I could have written much to you about these matters, and also about the other most destructive statements of this extremely insolent man, if I had been permitted, and I had previously intended to write to you from here. But because, just as my messenger was on the point of setting out—the messenger whom I was sending to you—I was informed that our monk, wearing only the habit, an associate of that same Gottschalk, had fled into the regions of Italy to which you are going, taking with him whatever he had been able to steal from the monastery, I considered it necessary to summon a notary and send you, in this brief and hurried speech, whatever my mind prompted my mouth to utter. Thus, if perhaps that poisonous man has sown in those regions some of the tares of his teacher, and you are questioned about them by certain people, you may have a firm response that you can give them. I also wished to prevent my messenger, detained on account of many matters, from being forced to delay so long that he would have to follow you farther.

## LETTER XI. TO POPE NICHOLAS

He responds to his reprimanding letter, clearing himself of arrogance and deceit, of the charges brought in the case of Ebo and Vulfad, and also concerning the privilege of Pope Benedict, the Acts of the Synod of Soissons, and the excessive use of the pallium.

*(In the same work.)*

[Col. 0076C]

To the most holy and most reverend Father of the Fathers, Nicholas, pope of the first and highest apostolic see and of the universal Church, Hincmar, bishop of Reims and the most devoted servant of your most holy fatherhood.

[Col. 0076D]

On the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June of the present fifteenth indiction, having been summoned by our lord, your most devoted son, the glorious King Charles, to meet him as he was going to the city of Metz for a conference with his brother, the glorious King Louis, and having been taken there with him, I came to his palace called Salmontiacus, in the diocese of Laon. In accordance with his command, I brought with me our brothers from Vulfad’s group. There our brothers and fellow priests, Rothad, bishop of Soissons, and Hincmar, bishop of Laon, also assembled, and our aforementioned beloved brother Vulfad was present as well. There, before the same lord king and our aforesaid brothers, I received from Egilo, the venerable archbishop of Sens, letters from your most holy fatherhood and pre-eminent authority.

[Col. 0077A]

When these letters had been read there, as well as the letters addressed generally to the bishops who had been assembled by your authority in the synod at Soissons, I found in them such and so great a rebuke inflicted upon my unworthiness by your dignity as my sins deserve. Therefore, if I were bodily present before you, I would without hesitation or delay strive to carry out what the Holy Spirit commands through the mouth of blessed Benedict in the Rule dictated by him:

> “If any brother, for whatever, even the slightest, reason, is rebuked by his prior, or if in any way, even slightly, he perceives that the mind of any prior is angry or disturbed against him, however mildly, let him immediately, without delay, lie prostrate on the ground before his feet, making satisfaction, until that disturbance is healed by a blessing.”

[Col. 0077B]

Since I cannot fulfill this bodily at the feet of your holiness, wherever I am I fulfill it in mind and spirit, with the proper devotion of the mind. Blessed Gregory, the predecessor of your holiness, urges this when he says in his exposition of the Gospel passage, “If you bring your gift to the altar” (Matthew 5:23), and so forth:

> “We ought in our minds to go to our neighbor, however far away and separated from us, and submit our spirit to him, appeasing him with humility and goodwill. Then, clearly, our Creator, when He sees such peace in our mind, will release us from sin, because He will accept the gift in place of the fault.”

[Col. 0077C]

And because I understood that the year’s time which I found granted to my humility in the letters sent to me concerning the case of Brother Vulfad and his associates had been conceded through the movement of your benevolence, I did not allow myself to endure any further delay. After returning from the journey mentioned above, now, consequently, in the month of July that is approaching in this present fifteenth indiction, our lord king is going with the army gathered from his entire kingdom against the Bretons and the Northmen allied with them, just as our other brothers and fellow priests are going with him according to the burdensome custom of our regions. I too, as far as I am able, exhausted by illness, am going with the men of the Church entrusted to me. I hastened, as quickly as I could, to send these letters of my humility to the feet of your holiness by such means as I could, since, because of the plots of princes hostile to me—men whom I dare not openly please according to their wishes—I was unable to do so openly.

[Col. 0077D]

After the letters expressing your authority mentioned above, the decree of your command concerning the restoration of our aforesaid brothers was read in the place mentioned. We gladly embraced what you had decreed, and what the aforesaid venerable Archbishop Egilo imposed upon me concerning this matter at your command, I strove to carry out without hesitation. Consequently, I do not wish hereafter to repeat anything concerning this matter except as it was defined by your authority, just as I shall explain more fully in the course of these painful pages of mine what your anger toward me has brought about. As it is written, in the words of one speaking from sorrow: “If I speak, my pain will not cease; and if I remain silent, it will not depart from me” (Job 16:7).

[Col. 0078A]

For I know that unless my Maker saw much rust in me, He would not so often, through the authority of the apostolic see and the faction of certain people stirred up against my insignificance, hold me so harshly in this fire of purification—and would that He might cleanse me by it. Thus, at the beginning of my ordination, the lord Lothair of blessed memory exerted himself with Sergius, and afterward with his successor Leo, on account of the dispute over the kingdom that he had with his brother, the lord Charles, whose service I faithfully supported. Later, by God’s inspiration, he did penance and, sending letters to the apostolic see, endeavored to correct what he had done wrong. The fact that through these events the most serene tranquility of your holiness has so often and so greatly been stirred against my unworthiness ought not to be charged against me, nor ought I to be troubled by unjust suspicions.

[Col. 0078B]

There are, however, two things that I firmly believe, and a third that I recognize in my mind. First, that the disturbance of your spirit toward my humility proceeds not from your own impulses but from the suggestions of others. And if what I hear that certain people have said to you about me were true, you would not merely be rightly moved in this way against me; rather, your zeal for rectitude would kindle you to incomparably greater severity than that with which you are moved.

But thanks be to Him by whose grace I am what I am: my conscience bears witness to me that, although I am a sinner in other matters, nevertheless, in those matters for which I hear that I have been denounced before your authority, I am not such in the sight of God as I am portrayed in human ears.

[Col. 0078C]

For arrogance toward the apostolic see, the mother and teacher of all the Churches, had already been charged against me before Sergius and Leo, of holy memory. Yet, with the Lord’s cooperation, wherever circumstances allowed me, I demonstrated by the service I owed them that I had always been faithful and devoted, humble and submissive, in all things and everywhere toward the apostolic see and its rulers. Now, however, in addition to arrogance—which I have avoided as far as I could from my earliest age—I seem to be charged before your holy and most prudent simplicity with deceit and cruelty.

After I had sensibly understood that the Holy Spirit had spoken, and that the holy Church of God had invoked curses, concerning those who speak with duplicity of heart: “May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips” (Psalm 11:4); and, “Let deceitful lips become mute” (Psalm 30:19); and that the Lord abhors a deceitful man no less than a man of bloodshed (Psalm 5:7), I took care to flee and execrate deceit and cruelty as though from the face of a serpent (Ecclesiasticus 21:2), knowing that the merciful are blessed and that judgment without mercy awaits the one who does not show mercy.

[Col. 0078D]

Concerning these vices, neither the Church entrusted to me in these regions nor the neighboring Churches have hitherto complained against me; nor are they complaining now. Hence it may be understood that if those who falsely spread these things about me had perceived in me even the appearance of other crimes—though I confess that this would not be an excuse for excuses in sins—they certainly would not have kept silent about them before you.

But blessed be the Lord, who has not yet delivered me into the grasp of their teeth—those who have often attacked me from my youth and have not prevailed against me—while the Lord protects me. He has rescued me from many tribulations, and in Him I hope that He will rescue me still.

[Col. 0079A]

These things, most holy lord and Father, I earnestly beg with all contrition of spirit and with as much humility as I can muster: weighing the great grief of heart with which they have been spoken, do not receive them with disdain, and do not allow anyone to persuade you that I have written my submission to your authority deceitfully.

Do not understand what I have now dared, relying upon the clemency of your benevolence, to write to your dignity as though, having received your rebukes harshly, I wished with a rebellious heart to resist them, to undo what you have written with an irreverent face or an uplifted neck of heart, or in any way or in the slightest degree to oppose your apostolic commands or decisions. Rather, as a servant to his lord and a son to his father, I desire in all things to satisfy and obey your apostolic authority.

[Col. 0079B]

As for Ebo, about whom your sublimity wrote to my humility, much is recorded both in the accounts of kings and in the acts of bishops who have already gone before us to the Lord but who still live with us in their monuments and subscriptions. Many such records are preserved among us and among others in our regions, and I do not doubt that many are also kept in the archives of the holy and supreme Roman see.

Therefore, lest I seem to disparage a dead man for my own sake, or wish to revive reprehensible acts of one who has been buried, it seems more reasonable for us to remain silent about why and how his deposition occurred, rather than to speak of it fully and in order, on the basis of the acts concerning it preserved among us.

[Col. 0079C]

Nor do I wish, presume, or dare to raise any dispute or offer any opposition concerning his deposition, whatever it may have been, against your manifold wisdom, which surpasses our sense and understanding, or against your supreme authority, which towers above our submission. This is especially so since both he himself and those who judged him thirty-three full years ago—he having neither cried out nor resisted but rather, as far as could be seen by those present, having willingly acquiesced—are undoubtedly now in the place where each person, under so great a Judge, before whose eyes all things are naked and open, cannot lose the quality of his merit.

[Col. 0079D]

Nevertheless, to recall a few matters from their acts in order to bring the facts to your attention: after Hildemann, bishop of the Church of Beauvais, had been freed through regular satisfaction from the accusations by which he had been denounced, Ebo—who long before, together with other archbishops and bishops, had issued in his own hand the petition concerning the restoration of the emperor Louis which we possess, with an addition by the archbishop—at that same synod, following the tradition of the apostolic see, acted as the decrees of Zosimus concerning Proculus, of John concerning Contumeliosus, and of Gregory concerning Paul show.
