And just as Gregory wrote on many occasions concerning a bishop unable through bodily illness to rise to episcopal ministry, saying that if he wished, he could in this way—that is, by submitting a petition—remove himself from the episcopate, so Ebo, by letters given for his abdication of the priesthood, voluntarily removed himself from it.

[Col. 0080A]

As Pope Alexander demonstrates in his decrees, fear, force, or fraud—which he suffered from no one—could not make him innocent or excusable. Nor, as Gregory shows concerning Pompeius, could violence or affliction, which he suffered from no one, do so. Nor could an appeal to the apostolic see, which he did not make while present at the trial, benefit him. For no one compelled him, nor did anyone even request it; rather, of his own accord, conscious of the crimes of which he had been partly accused at the synod and for which, unless he had sought a place to obtain counsel with certain bishops, he would likewise have been accused—and of which he could not clear himself—he submitted to the synod, without any opposition, a petition signed in his own hand and confirmed by his own confession.

He did this according to the counsel of those same bishops, who followed the African Council, lest the dignity of the priesthood be polluted because of the Church’s disgrace and the insolent abuse of secular people, and according to the moderation that blessed Leo prescribed to all the bishops throughout Campania, Samnium, and the other provinces.

[Col. 0080B]

The African canons say that the testimony even of a bishop lying about himself must be believed to such an extent that he loses the episcopate, just as the Lord also shows in the Gospel, saying: “Out of your own mouth I judge you” (Luke 19:22); and: “By your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned” (Matthew 12:37). The prophet David likewise said to Saul, who had lied that he had killed him: “Your blood be upon your own head, for your mouth has spoken against you” (2 Samuel 1:16).

[Col. 0080C]

And Saint Gregory, concerning Andrew, says:

> “Judgment ought not to be demanded concerning a case that he himself judged. For if he confessed the truth about himself—as it is written in the petition of his profession, which we possess, a copy of which, together with a copy of the synodal record, was sent to Pope Leo of holy memory—in that petition he rendered himself unworthy of pontifical ministry because of his offenses and decreed that another should be consecrated in his place without canonical repetition, then, as a criminal convicted by his own testimony, he ought to cease from pontifical ministry and, in accordance with the decrees of Leo and Gregory, seek private withdrawal in order to obtain God’s mercy.”

[Col. 0080D]

But if he had spoken falsely about himself, then, as a false witness against himself, he ought to have been rejected, since the Lord forbids this: “You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor” (Exodus 20:16). If this was not permitted against one’s neighbor, much less was it permitted against oneself.

Therefore, as his judges said, they justly and reasonably rendered him, together with himself, unworthy of pontifical ministry.

Of those who at that time bore the name of bishop in these Cisalpine regions, as far as we are able to discover, no one is alive in the body except Rothad alone. Nevertheless, there are still many who know that he had previously abandoned his Church and province, while no one was bringing an accusation against him, contrary to the sacred rules, and who afterward learned the manner of his deposition. The Apostle says that a testament is confirmed over the dead (Hebrews 7:9).

[Col. 0081A]

Indeed, among those who ordained me in his place, none survive except the aforesaid Rothad and Erpoinus. Yet in these provinces—namely, those of Reims, Trier, Cologne, Mainz, Lyon, Arles, Narbonne, Rouen, Tours, Sens, Bourges, and Bordeaux—it would not easily be possible to find many bishops, priests, or deacons who were either not ordained by those who were present at Ebo’s deposition, some of whom ordained me and were themselves ordained by them; or who did not subscribe in agreement at my ordination; or who were not ordained either by me or by them—those whom, by God’s grace, I ordained.

[Col. 0081B]

After ten years had passed since the same Ebo had been deposed, as the bishops of the Cisalpine regions stated, and had remained so without regular restoration or appeal; and after one year had passed since he received from Pope Sergius the sentence of which your authority most rightly explained the meaning to us, as though it were an oracle of divine law, in the synodal letter sent through Egilo, I was requested and elected at a synod in the city of Beauvais, in the province of Reims, by the clergy and people of Reims, the metropolitan city, and also by the bishops of that province.

With the canonical decree and the presence and unanimous consent of all the suffragans of that metropolitan see, while everyone acclaimed and no one protested or contradicted, I was regularly ordained in that same Church. This is shown by the letters concerning my ordination sent to Pope Leo of holy memory and by the written records of ecclesiastical tradition preserved in the Church of Reims.

Among other things, those bishops—my ordainers—declared that they had followed the authority of the African Council, which ordered a bishop to be ordained for a Church that had long been left without one because of the flight of Equitius.

[Col. 0081C]

They also followed the decrees of Pope Damasus, sent to Bishop Paulinus from the synod assembled in the city of Rome (Letter 3), concerning bishops who still remained in their status but had migrated contrary to the rules:

> “Those who have migrated from one Church to another we hold separated from our communion for as long as it takes them to return to the cities in which they were first established. But if, when one has migrated elsewhere, another has been ordained in the place of the living man, let the one who abandoned his city remain without the dignity of the priesthood until his successor rests in the Lord.”

[Col. 0081D]

For my part, the sacred canons of the Council of Carthage decree that clerics or deacons who, for the needs of the Churches, do not obey their bishops when the latter wish to promote them to greater honor in their own Church, are not even to minister in the rank from which they refused to depart.

Saint Gregory also approves this in his letter to the bishops of Gaul, saying (Book 7, Letter 110, indiction 11):

> “Just as one who, when invited, refuses, and when sought, withdraws, is to be admitted to the sacred altars, so undoubtedly one who seeks office voluntarily or thrusts himself forward importunately is to be rejected.”

I bowed the neck of my mind and body to obedience to my bishops and ordainers, because, guided by devotion—as it seemed to me at the time—I did not dare to act otherwise.

[Col. 0082A]

I had been educated from the earliest beginnings of infancy in the monastery, under the canonical habit, and had been brought from there to the palace of the lord Emperor Louis, where I remained for a considerable time. When the brothers in the monastery of Saint-Denis, where I had been raised, turned to the regular life and habit, I returned to that monastery, fleeing the world, and lived there for a long time without hope or desire of the episcopate or of any other position of authority.

Afterward I was taken from there and, serving in the familiar duties of the aforesaid emperor and in the assemblies of bishops, solely out of the obedience imposed upon me, I returned after several years to the peace of the monastery. From there, because my sins demanded it, the cable of my anchor was broken—the cable by which I had negligently bound myself in harbor—and, persuaded by the exhortations of those whom I found it easier to believe than myself, under the pretext of the salvation of many, I was cast most dangerously into the storms of the great and spacious sea.

[Col. 0082B]

A year after my ordination had passed when, as I have said, Emperor Lothair, moved against me because of his brother, demanded letters from Pope Sergius to reopen the council concerning Ebo’s deposition, as later became known to me, as though there were disagreement in the Church of Reims concerning my ordination. This was in no way established.

Therefore, the same apostolic lord sent letters to the lord Charles, ordering him to send Gunthold, archbishop of Rouen, together with the other bishops of his kingdom whom the aforesaid Gunthold would choose for this purpose, to meet the envoys of the emperor at Trier in order to investigate this matter, and to have me come to that synod.

[Col. 0082C]

He also sent Gunthold a letter on the matter, instructing him that, when the same lord pope sent his envoys into the emperor’s service after the day of the holy Resurrection, he should go with the bishops to the place mentioned in order to decide this case.

He also sent me a letter on the matter, instructing me to come to the same council.

We, however, waited for those envoys until the appointed time, and they did not come. Therefore, by the authority of the letters of Pope Sergius, with the assent of our lord King Charles and with the consent of the archbishops and other bishops of his kingdom, Gunthold convoked a synod.

Through Erpoinus, bishop of the province of Reims, he sent Ebo letters, a copy of which we possess, summoning him on the authority of the aforesaid pope so that, according to the pope’s instruction, he might settle this case according to the rules and take care to refer the decision in the matter to the apostolic see in accordance with the sacred regulations.

[Col. 0082D]

But the same Ebo, conscious of his guilt, did not wish to come, nor did he make any effort to be absolved at the apostolic see, from which he had received a sentence of condemnation, although he had the opportunity to go there. For he had remained for a long time in Italy and possessed property acquired from the resources of the Church of Reims; he had obtained the abbey of Saint Columba from Lothair, and in these regions as well he had acquired another abbey. He held these until he refused to carry out the embassy to Greece entrusted to him by Lothair. Because of this he lost the honors he had received from the aforesaid emperor and, through the clemency of King Louis of Germany, obtained safe-conduct in the province of Mainz.

[Col. 0083A]

During his lifetime he showed no synod any canonical document concerning his restoration or absolution by the apostolic see, as the rules require. Without documentary testimony or letters concerning his restoration, he ought not to have ministered or been received into sacred ministry, as Pope Felix decreed. He was consistently excluded by himself and by the metropolitans of many provinces together with their fellow bishops, while he was present at the judgment and did not appeal to the apostolic see.

[Col. 0083B]

This was especially so because for so many years, even after receiving the sentence from the apostolic see, he did not assert his innocence, which he could not demonstrate. Moreover, before a regular hearing, or before his restoration had been issued, confirmed, and displayed by the apostolic see, he presumed to exercise episcopal ministry by an imperial edict of Emperor Lothair, which we possess. As Gelasius demonstrates in his letters concerning the condemnation of Acacius, this was manifestly opposed to the sacred canons. You yourselves know better what and how many judgments he incurred.

For even if, as we have said, letters were sent from the apostolic see at the demand of Emperor Lothair in order that a synod might be convened for this matter, when a legate of that see should come into these regions, nevertheless, just as the same Ebo did not attend any synod, nor even the one that Gunthold convened on the authority of the letters of Pope Sergius, so no envoy sent by the apostolic see to convene a synod concerning this matter came into these regions.

[Col. 0083C]

This is demonstrated by the letter of the emperor himself, as well as by the letter of the bishops of the provinces of Belgica, Gaul, Neustria, and Aquitaine, sent together with the letters of the lord King Charles to Pope Leo of holy memory—letters which we believe are preserved in the Roman archives.

Thus the aforesaid Ebo, without any restoration or appeal of his see at any synod or before the apostolic see, by which it had been decreed that he should not even receive communion among the clergy, remained in that condition until his death. This was after the letters of Pope Sergius had been sent for the convening of a synod concerning the matter, when he sent his envoys into these regions, and after the synod had been convened by the authority of those letters, to which, as we have said, he did not come when summoned.

[Col. 0083D]

Clearly, as the letters of your authority mentioned above demonstrate, he was regarded by the apostolic see and by Pope Sergius as others knew him to be regarded: namely, as the episcopal book shows, deprived of his dignity on account of his crimes and expelled from the Church, and therefore, before the examination of the synodal inquiry—which by God’s judgment he did not reach—not received in accordance with the sacred Nicene canons.

Therefore, what, as Leo writes, he did not receive while remaining in the body, he will not be able to obtain after being stripped of the flesh. Saint Gelasius says the same about Acacius, who, condemned by the apostolic see and not restored, died even though Pope Anastasius, as we read in the episcopal book, wished to receive him:

> “He was declared to be such as he was marked, never to be released; he remained such until the end; he did not cease to be such. Thus he is today what he was and was declared to be; he can no longer cease to be such. Therefore, by remaining such, he is never to be released.”

[Col. 0084A]

Concerning our beloved brother Vulfad and his associates, about whom your supreme authority wrote to my humility whatever seemed good to it, I have presumed to write nothing else to your holiness except that I receive your rebukes not negligently but diligently, and that I obediently hear and obey your commands.

Since the graciousness of your excellent authority ought to be sufficient for them, it will also be abundantly sufficient for me if, having received the satisfaction of my humility, you deign to believe that I have written to you simply and sincerely.

[Col. 0084B]

I acted according to the command of my ordainers, who, before two full months had passed after my ordination, commanded me at a synod held in the city of Meaux—at a time when I still did not know that Ebo had ordained certain people in the Church of Reims—not to permit those men to minister with me until the matter had been examined more carefully.

Through Pardulus, then a deacon of the Church of Reims who had attended the synod, they conveyed this same command to those brothers, in accordance with the decree of the Council of Carthage that, once bishops or clerics have been ordained, the decisions of councils should first be impressed upon their ears by their ordainers, so that they may not afterward regret having done anything against the statutes of a council.

[Col. 0084C]

Because later canons require deference to earlier ones, after the synod held at Soissons, I do not deny that I sent to the apostolic see, to Pope Leo, their letters—of which we possess a copy and which I believe can be found in the Roman archives—together with my letters written at their request and with my other petitions, for the confirmation of their acts. They were not compelled to attend the synod, and I did not write or subscribe to those acts, as I also demonstrated at the synod assembled by your authority.

In those acts I did not silently approve the true prosecution of the aforesaid brothers against me. Therefore, by common consent and according to the canons as we understood them, I requested judges. I saw that their judgment had to be followed until I should receive a contrary decision from a greater authority.

[Col. 0084D]

After I received Pope Leo’s letter of excuse explaining why he had not confirmed those same acts, he said, among other things:

> “We shall explain to your charity the reasons why we have suspended this matter until now. The first reason is this: just as the synod mentioned by the bishops was beneficially discussed or brought to rest, so you ought to have sent the statutes of your synod through some of them, so that the doubt might be entirely uprooted.”

He did not know that we metropolitans in these regions do not have the power, without the consent or command of the king, either to go anywhere ourselves or to send our fellow bishops farther away.

The same pontiff added in his apostolic letters:

> “Another matter, contrary to the desire of your wish, in no way permitted us to accomplish this, because legates of the apostolic see were not present there, nor was an imperial letter presented to us of such a kind that it could specifically indicate what you had sent to be sought. [Col. 0085A]

The fourth reason is this: those whom your charity asserts were deposed by the authority of the synod have appealed to the apostolic see by their own letters, and they wish to be heard again in our apostolic presence; and if they are found guilty, they do not refuse to submit to canonical discipline.”

And after I received these letters of the lord Pope Leo, as I learned, the lord Lothar, at the request of a certain bishop of his kingdom who is still alive, instructed the aforesaid lord pope, through Peter, bishop of Arezzo, not to confirm the episcopal proceedings concerning those same clerics. When I reported this to our brothers and fellow bishops, at their request I obtained from Emperor Lothar, through my messengers and with his spontaneous generosity, a letter concerning the matter, in which, among other things, it is written:

> “But in order to carry out and obtain our requests, we have appointed the venerable and most beloved Peter, bishop of Spoleto, as executor in our name by word of mouth; and we have also notified in writing the other Peter, likewise a venerable and most beloved bishop of Arezzo, and have similarly notified your other faithful men and ours concerning the matter,”

and so forth.

Thus, together with this letter and the emperor’s embassy, I sent my messengers with letters to Rome through the aforesaid venerable bishop. On the way, however, news arrived of the death of Pope Leo. When we reached Rome with the aforesaid letters, and with the intervention of the bishops mentioned above, the lord Benedict, in name and grace, sent me the privilege concerning the matter, as you know.

I have never heard that a synod for the clerics so often mentioned was convened—or ordered to be convened—by apostolic authority, either by Peter of Spoleto or by anyone else in these regions, neither by report nor in fact, as you can also learn through others in these parts. I have heard only of the synod which was convened last year by your authoritative command, at which I most readily agreed to their restoration according to the tradition of our forefathers.

After I had subsequently received your authoritative letters concerning this matter, I desired that restoration to be salutary and canonical. For that reason, I greatly wished them to be restored by the very men who had deprived them, or by no smaller a number, together with my consent. Therefore I waited for the synod and desired that the matter be more fully confirmed by the Apostolic See under your authority, since the supreme authority and confirmation of the privileges of the Apostolic See had been reserved to its judgment, as your letter addressed to us states. We also wrote this by common consent in the synodal letter whose copy we possess and which was addressed to your holy authority.

In that letter we made no mention whatever of any deposition of Ebo. Moreover, I inserted the following in the letter of my insignificance, with a simple mind:

> “Because, when the venerable archbishop Egilo, who was present at the proceedings, sent, through him, a letter from all of us who were able to be present, while speaking with him in person: ‘For if you extend your hand to them, we shall likewise extend ours with you’; and again, after a little further on: ‘Whatever you command me through this religious archbishop, by word and writing, concerning what I must follow and observe, I shall strive, insofar as I know and am able, to obey and preserve.’”

I did not send that letter sealed—for I confess this truthfully to you—for the synod had not sealed the letter it sent. It judged it inappropriate that, since the archbishop who had been summoned to that synod by your apostolic letters and had attended it was being sent to you, a sealed letter should be entrusted as though to someone untrustworthy. I did not presume to do myself what the synod had not done, lest I cause scandal to anyone.

Therefore, let your holiness, filled with that charity which believes all things, truly believe me: simply and without any deceit, after I learned your disposition concerning the matter, I consented from a willing mind to the restoration of the aforesaid brothers, and simply and without any deceit I wrote what I sent to your holiness. From that consent I have never afterward in any way departed, except as I wrote to you in the aforesaid letters: that in all things the judgment and legal privilege of the Apostolic See were reserved, and that the decision and confirmation of your awaited discernment and authority remained intact.

Now, however, having received the decision concerning their restoration—which, as was proper and as order required, was preceded by your supreme authority and which your perfection strengthened by its subsequent synodal confirmation—I never have intended, planned, wished, or sought thereafter, at any time or place, to devise, remove, stir up, or foment any complaint against anyone. Nor, after receiving your letter concerning this matter through your kindness, have I contemplated removing anything from my synodal consent, then or thereafter, against that decision and your confirmation, now and forever.

For although they were marked by no personal crime, and, not knowing that Ebo had been condemned, they entered upon ordination—not improperly, as they themselves say, and as no one contradicts—but obeyed as elected and summoned, just as you wrote to the lord King Charles with the excellence of your wisdom: if they had refused to obey one who wished to promote them to a higher rank, everyone would have reproved them as insolently resistant and condemned them as contumacious toward the sacred canons. You likewise made this clear in the letter addressed to the bishops who, by God’s grace and your decree, assembled at the city of Soissons:

> “Whatever Ebo may have been, and whatever he may have suffered, he caused no offense at all to those whom he ordained, since they exhibited nothing but humility and obedience.”

For the most blessed Leo, writing to the Mauri, gives the following instruction concerning a certain Maximus (Letter 91, near the end):

> “As for Maximus, although he was ordained reprehensibly, nevertheless, if he is no longer a Donatist and is alien from the spirit of schismatic perversity, we do not exclude him from the episcopal dignity which, in whatever manner, he obtained.”

Anastasius, likewise a prelate of that Apostolic See, writing to the emperor Anastasius (in his single letter), demonstrates with the clearest reasoning that those who administer good things while themselves being evil harm only themselves and do not defile the sacraments of the Church.

To this devout understanding, as we read in their decrees with the addition of certain conditions, what blessed Augustine wrote can, in a certain respect, seem not unsuitably applicable. Pope Anastasius adopted some of Augustine’s sense and words in the aforesaid letter:

> “If, he says, extreme necessity should compel someone, when he has found no Catholic through whom he might receive it, and if he preserves Catholic peace in his heart, and receives through someone outside Catholic unity what he would have received within that very Catholic unity, then, should he immediately depart this life, we reckon him as nothing other than a Catholic. But if he is delivered from bodily death, and returns bodily to the Catholic congregation, from which he had never departed in heart, we not only do not condemn what he did, but praise it with the greatest confidence and truth, because he believed that God was present in his heart, where he preserved unity.”

Finally, I sent a copy of the privilege of blessed memory, Benedict, without any mutilation, addition, or alteration, through our venerable brother and fellow bishop Odo, to your most holy fatherhood. Concerning this you may, if you please, read again in the letter sent to you by me through him, where it is written, among other things:

> “I would send, I said, the authentic charter of the privilege itself, which my predecessor, the lord Benedict of blessed memory, sent to me by his authority; but I feared that some misfortune might befall me on the way because of it, leaving me deprived of the protection which I possess against the attacks of those rising up against me. Your dignity, however, can request a copy of it from the archives of the holy Roman Church, according to custom, and can clearly ascertain whether it is so. In it, if it pleases your holiness, it is necessary for you to add certain things which this brother and son of ours, knowing our necessities, will suggest to your holiness. For, as Saint Augustine says, new kinds of illnesses require new experiments in remedies. But concerning the synod held at Soissons, where—through the faction of one of our clerics, who, frightened by his own negligence, had fled from us—something was inserted under a certain doubt, this brother and son of ours, who attended that synod and still subscribed in the name of an abbot, can tell you the truth of the matter.”

These are my words in the letter addressed to your holy fatherhood. For if I had erased what is placed there, if it were true, I would have written superfluously that something had been inserted there under a certain doubt. And if I had added, altered, or removed anything, I would not have dared to write that you should request a copy of it from the archives of the holy Roman Church and ascertain whether it was so.

But if, in whatever way, on whatever occasion, and by whomever, something else was reported to you, nevertheless I sent you, through our aforesaid venerable fellow bishop, a copy of that privilege exactly as it stands. If it is not burdensome for you to compare with it, while retaining the copy preserved in the Roman archives, you will find the truth.

I also displayed to the synod convened by your authority the actual volume of the privilege, not merely a copy, together with the privilege of your holiness. I showed the uncorrupted writings and seals, and had it read in full before your son, the lord King Charles, with all the bishops and those who attended the synod listening. Accordingly, in the letter of the synod addressed to your authority, the following is written, among other things:

> “We would hasten to restore them to their orders, were it not that due reverence had to be shown to the privileges of the holy Roman See, which our revered brother Hincmar, archbishop, produced before our unanimity. Those privileges established certain provisions concerning these men, and their complete, perfect, and undiminished force, as is clear and just, has been reserved to the judgment of the authority of the Apostolic See.”

The synod would not have written this to you if I had not displayed the privileges to them in their entirety.

Concerning what your most kind and holy fatherhood deigned to write to me—that I should not think I had exaggerated anything that was entrusted to me, since I know that the wounds of one who loves are better than the deceitful kisses of one who hates—and lest I seem to have risen too immoderately in defense or exaltation of my privileges, so as to appear in any way rashly to have touched the rights of the Apostolic See, I truthfully confess that this thought never entered my heart. Ever since I was able to know myself, I have been, according to my knowledge and ability, faithful, devoted, humble, and submissive both to the Apostolic See and to its rulers; and, with the Lord’s help, I shall remain so.

I did not seek the privileges of the Apostolic See because what the sacred canons and the decrees of the bishops of the Roman See grant to each metropolitan see was insufficient for me. Nor did I specifically seek, nor do I seek, to have anything else or anything more generously granted to me than what has anciently been conferred upon the Church of Reims.

I sought them because not only my diocese but also my parish is divided between two kingdoms under two kings, and the property entrusted to me appears to lie under the power of many princes, from whom our Church can receive little or no benefit. Since the ancient constitutions are now regarded by some as almost worthless, I thought that, frightened by these new decrees, worldly and unspiritual men might act with greater reverence toward the Church entrusted to my unworthiness.

As for these privileges, I do not claim their defense for myself; nor is there anything else from which I can become inflated or exalted. Even if I were righteous, I would not lift my head, saturated as I am with affliction and misery.

Finally, concerning the pallium, which in my presumption I have used at times not fixed, and otherwise than the custom established for other metropolitans, and about which you wrote that information had been conveyed to the ears of your holiness against my unworthiness, I truthfully confess to your authority—and, if it pleases you, you will be able to learn this from others in these regions—that, except on the day of the Lord’s Nativity and on the day of his holy Resurrection, I scarcely use that same pallium throughout the entire year.

For, because of my sins, I have become one of those of whom it is written, “The burdens of the world have made them wretched.” I am rarely permitted to be in my see on the appointed festivals on which metropolitans are allowed to use the pallium, because of the many occupations and necessities of the Church and the kingdom. And unless I am in that see on the appointed festivals, I not only do not use that pallium as often as has been permitted to me, but scarcely ever or never use it.

I sought nothing from the Apostolic See concerning its use except what my predecessors and those before them were accustomed to do when ordaining a bishop. I do not think that the use of the pallium belongs to my personal dignity; rather, I recognize it as belonging to the character of the metropolitan see.

Although there are many holy bishops who do not use that same pallium, I know that if I use the pallium without the virtues which blessed Gregory explains that the pallium signifies, and if its use demonstrates in the eyes of men that the metropolitan see of Reims is more eminent than the other sees of the province, it nevertheless does not make me greater in the eyes of the Lord.

I truthfully confess to your holy fatherhood that, if I had not been ordained a bishop, I would not have sought the use of the pallium. For I know that, without episcopal ordination, I could by God’s grace have acquired eternal life through right faith and good works.

If, in this world, I had known then what I know now, I would not have undertaken the episcopal order if I could have avoided it. But even now my soul is sufficient spoil for me. For, afflicted by many illnesses, weighed down by age, and exhausted by injuries, I am already being consumed, and the time of my dissolution is near.

Therefore, although I may be portrayed by my Transalpine friends in the Roman regions as something else, I must strive toward another goal and think of other things than applauding or in any way serving pomp and display—least of all in ecclesiastical ministry.

I have written these things to your most illustrious holiness and most renowned wisdom not to provoke any controversy or contumacious resistance, God forbid, but encouraged by the truthful judgment of your—indeed, divine—authority, which you deigned to write to me, saying that truth liberates whereas falsehood destroys. In humility I have laid before you this account of the truth.

Finally, I ask that your dignity send an answer to my service concerning our brothers, the sons of the Church of Reims, who have been restored by your authority to their orders. For the venerable archbishop Egilo, by your authority, instructed them to minister in their own ranks and not presume to ascend to higher ones. I ask whether I ought to promote them to higher ranks if our fellow bishops and fellow ministers should elect them. I do not wish to injure their minds through my negligence, and I desire by every means to avoid acting against your command and disposition, since I wish to obey in all things the decrees of the Apostolic See.

May almighty God deign to preserve your sincerity for many years in his fitting service, for the instruction and correction of his holy Church, most holy and reverend lord, Father of Fathers in the Lord.

## LETTER XII. TO POPE NICHOLAS

Of the same subject as the preceding letter, and composed for the most part in the same words.

(From the same source.)

[Col. 0090A]

To the most holy and reverend Father of Fathers, Nicholas, pope of the first and supreme Apostolic See and of the universal Church: Hincmar, bishop of Reims and most devoted servant of your most holy fatherhood.

I received a letter from your most holy fatherhood and pre-eminent authority on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the fifteenth indiction, from Egilo, the venerable archbishop of Sens. In it, and also in a letter addressed generally to the bishops who had been present the previous year at the synod convened by your authority at Soissons, I found such great and severe reproaches directed by your dignity against my unworthiness as my sins deserve.

To answer all of them would be presumptuous for my humility and plainly inappropriate to your sublimity, especially since, after many other things, you deigned to write to me words that encouraged my weakness:

> “Do not think that we have exaggerated these things to the detriment of your holiness or dignity, since you know that the wounds of one who loves are better than the deceitful kisses of one who hates.”

Furthermore, because, on account of the many, great, and almost continuous attacks of pagans and false Christians which we suffer, and because the bishops of our regions had previously been continuously occupied with their labors, it was not possible for us to meet together so that the letter of your holiness, sent to us collectively, might be read again collectively. As you commanded, everything written concerning this matter—whether previously and now by you, or by us—and whatever my humility and those deposed clerics had submitted or reported to the Apostolic See was to be arranged in a single volume, in the order in which it had been sent, and forwarded with the greatest care to the Apostolic See, while copies were retained for us as appropriate.

Now, having obtained a little respite from the attacks of the pagans in one part of the kingdom, but laboring under the groans of other anxieties and still fearing more serious dangers that threaten, our brothers and fellow bishops, your most devoted sons, are faithfully undertaking what you commanded: concerning Ebo’s deposition and his restoration; concerning the advancement of the brother Vulfad and his colleagues; concerning the renewed rejection of the aforesaid Ebo and his migration to another Church; and also concerning what they have learned about my ordination.

My humble service has presented to them, to be appended to, submitted with, and conveyed together with what they have collected and are sending to your authority, the account written with all humility and purity concerning what your dignity deigned to write to my unworthiness, in accordance with your command.

Concerning our beloved brother Vulfad and his colleagues, about whom the supreme authority of your dignity wrote to me whatever it pleased, I do not presume to write anything else to your holiness except that I receive your reproaches not negligently but diligently, and obediently heed your commands.

Since the kindness of your eminent authority ought to suffice for them, and will abundantly suffice for me if you deign to accept the satisfaction of my humility and believe that I have written to you about this simply and truthfully, I shall say the following.

According to the commands of those who ordained me and who had taken part in Ebo’s deposition, and who, before two full months had passed after my ordination, instructed me at the synod held at the city of Meaux—at that time I was still unaware that Ebo had ordained anyone in the Church of Reims—I acted so as not to permit those whom he had ordained to minister with me until a more careful examination could be made.

They also communicated this very instruction to the same brothers through Pardulus, then a deacon of the Church of Reims, who had attended the synod. The Council of Carthage had decreed that, before ordained bishops or clerics undertook their ministry, the decisions of councils should first be impressed upon their minds by those who ordained them, lest they later regret having done anything contrary to the statutes of a council.

When Pardulus returned with me from that synod to Reims, he reported to the same brothers who were with us and about whom the matter concerned what the bishops had commanded me. He instructed them to observe the order that they should not minister in the ranks which they had received from Ebo after his deposition, until a more careful examination could be made.

The brother Vulfad was not yet with me. But after several months had passed—if I reckon correctly, before nearly a year had been completed—he came to me from another province. He was received with kindness and generosity and treated honorably, until, at his own request, I commended him to our lord King Charles.

Ebo died in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 851, in the sixteenth indiction, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April. Since our aforesaid brothers who had been ordained by him and were with me, after approximately eight years of suspension from office—that is, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 853—asked me to do so, I permitted those same brothers to go to the synod and ordered that the necessary assistance be provided to those who needed it, so that they could go to that council without difficulty.

There I neither judged nor deposed them, nor did I subscribe with their judges, as those who were present know and as the episcopal proceedings themselves demonstrate. I displayed those authentic proceedings, with the subscriptions of the bishops who subscribed to them but without my subscription, at the synod held the previous year at Soissons by your authority.

And since later canons command that precedence be given to earlier ones, when those same bishops instructed me to do so, I do not deny that I sent myself, together with their letters—of which we possess a copy and which I believe can be found in the Roman archives—and with my letters written at their request, and with my other petitions to the lord Pope Leo to confirm their proceedings. I did not write those proceedings myself.

In those proceedings I did not silently confirm the true prosecution of the aforesaid brothers against me. Therefore, by common consent and according to the canons as we understood them, I requested judges, whose judgment I saw should be followed until I received a different decision from a greater authority concerning the matter.

After receiving the lord Pope Leo’s letter of explanation, and so forth, as above, through the end of the letter.

## LETTER XIII. TO THE MONKS OF THE MONASTERY OF ALTOVILLARE

That, if Gothescalc repents before his death, they should show him spiritual and bodily kindness.

(From the same source.)

At the appropriate time, insofar as I was able, I told you under what condition you should show Gothescalc both spiritual and bodily kindness if, before his soul departs from his body, he should come to his senses. But lest anything be lacking to you in any act of grace, I send you ecclesiastical authority concerning the matter, drawn from the words of orthodox writers.

Leo says concerning such a case (Letter 12, to Flavian) that, if a person grieves faithfully and profitably, and recognizes, even at a late hour, how rightly episcopal authority was moved against him, or if, for the fullness of satisfaction, he condemns everything that he wrongly thought, either by spoken words or by an appropriate sign, reconciliation and communion should not be denied him, as Celestine, Leo, and the sacred canons have decreed.

If he dies in this confession and communion, provide him, as to the other brothers, with common burial, the rite of burial, and prayer after death. For our Lord, the true and good shepherd, who laid down his life for his sheep and came to save human souls, not to destroy them, wishes us to be imitators of his mercy, so that justice may restrain sinners but mercy may not reject those who have turned back.

But if he remains obstinate until death, we must hold concerning him what Saint Leo says of those deprived of communion and dying in that condition (Letter 95, to Rusticus):

> “Their case,” he says, “must be reserved for God’s judgment, in whose hand it lay that the death of such people should not be postponed until the remedy of communion. But we, who did not communicate with them while they were alive, cannot communicate with them when they are dead.”

And again (Letter 59, to Theodore):

> “If one of those for whom we entreat the Lord, seized by some obstacle, falls away from the present gift of forgiveness and ends his temporal life by the human condition before reaching the appointed remedies, he cannot obtain, after being stripped of his body, what he did not receive while remaining in the body. Nor is it necessary for us to examine the merits and deeds of those who have died in this way, since the Lord our God, whose judgments cannot be comprehended, has reserved to his justice what priestly ministry was unable to accomplish.”

The holy apostle John also says: “There is sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it” (1 John 5:16).

“Sin,” Gregory says (Morals 16.28), “is unto death, because the pardon of a sin that is not corrected in this life is sought in vain after death.”

Sin is said to extend even to hell when it is not corrected before the end of the present life through correction and repentance. It is by no means permitted that the memory of such people—namely, those who persevere in sin until death—be celebrated amid the sacred mysteries of the altar, in which prayer is offered for those who preceded us with the sign of faith and sleep in the sleep of peace, resting in Christ.

According to Catholic teachers, those who sleep in the sleep of peace are those who have not been separated from the unity and fellowship of the Church of Christ by heresies, schisms, or mortal sins. Even if they were once involved in such things, they were healed through repentance and reconciled through the prayer of the Church, to which it was said in Peter, “Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16:19), and were joined to the mystery of redemption. They therefore died in peace, through the mercy of him who does not desire the death of a sinner, but that he should turn and live.

Nor are the souls of the pious dead separated from the Church, which now reigns with Christ over the living and the dead. For this reason, as the Apostle says, Christ died so that he might rule over both the living and the dead (Romans 14:9). Elsewhere he says:

> “For God has not appointed us to wrath, but to the acquisition of salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us, so that, whether we are awake or asleep, we may live together with him” (1 Thessalonians 5:9–10).

Those resting in Christ are the ones of whom the Apostle says, “And the dead who are in Christ will rise first” (1 Thessalonians 4:16), and of whom it is likewise written, “Blessed is the one who has a share in the first resurrection; the second death shall not harm him” (Revelation 20:6).

Therefore Judas the priest, as we read in the Book of Maccabees (2 Maccabees 12:46), sent offerings to Jerusalem for those who had received their death in piety.

But if, as I stated above, he dies while remaining in his obstinacy, then, as we have learned from the authority of blessed Gregory and the sacred canons, he ought not to be carried to burial with psalms and hymns or buried in the common cemetery of the brothers. Nevertheless, the humane treatment of private burial, as I told you, must not be denied him.

## LETTER XIV. TO ODO, BISHOP OF BEAUVAIS

Concerning the objections of the Greeks, sent into Gaul by Pope Nicholas, so that responses might be made to them.

(From the same source.)

[Col. 0093D]

Hincmar, bishop of Reims, sends greetings to his beloved brother and venerable bishop Odo.

The Apostolic Lord sent a letter jointly to us and to the other bishops of the kingdom of our lord Charles. It states that the Greeks are attempting to criticize both the Roman Church in particular and, in general, the whole Church that uses the Latin language, because we fast on Saturdays and say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, whereas they confess that he proceeds from the Father alone.

Moreover, they say that we abominate marriage because we prohibit priests from taking wives. They also attempt to accuse us because we forbid those same priests to anoint the foreheads of the baptized with chrism, although they falsely suppose that we make this chrism from river water.

They further attempt to criticize us because, according to their custom, we do not abstain from eating meat for eight weeks before Easter and from eating cheese and eggs for seven weeks.

They also falsely claim, as is indicated by other writings of theirs, that on Easter we bless and offer a lamb upon the altar together with the Lord’s body, following the custom of the Jews.

They even strive to criticize us because our clerics do not refuse to shave their beards, and because among us a deacon is ordained bishop without having received the office of the priesthood. Yet they themselves did not fear promoting to the height of the episcopate, by imperial favor and power, the man whom they call their patriarch, taking him suddenly from the laity, tonsuring him, making him a monk, and advancing him by a leap, as they suppose.

What is more serious and more insane still, they attempted to demand from our envoys, contrary to every rule and beyond every custom, a written confession of faith, if they wished to be received by them, in which both these articles and those who held them would be anathematized. They also shamelessly demanded canonical letters from those envoys to the man whom they call their ecumenical patriarch.

Photius himself, the invader of the Church of Constantinople, calls himself in his writings archbishop and universal patriarch. The emperors of the Greeks also refused to receive the legates of the Apostolic See with the letters with which they ought to have been received, in the reverence due to them.

Therefore, let each of you who possesses the rights of a metropolitan, together with the brothers and fellow bishops subject to him, undertake careful consideration of these matters. Let him diligently investigate what must be opposed to their envious slanders, and strive with the greatest zeal to discover it. Let him not think it unimportant to send what he has found to us promptly, and let him send to our episcopate writings inspired by your divinely given wisdom, rebuking and vigorously striking down the great madness of those emperors.

When we receive them, we shall be able to send them again, together with our other customary writings, to refute the folly of those people as well. Therefore, dearest brother, following the Apostolic Lord’s recommendation, study what we can suitably write back to them from the testimony of Scripture and the tradition of our forefathers, and collect it into one body. Then, when we come together with the Lord’s help, we shall read individually, through our common effort, what each of us has found and arrange what must be written by us to the same lord pope.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of January, in the first indiction.

## LETTER XV. TO KING CHARLES

Concerning Hincmar of Laon.

(Acts of the provincial Church of Reims.)

To the glorious lord King Charles: Hincmar, in name but not in merit bishop of Reims, and servant of the people of God.

Behold, lord, as this beloved brother, our venerable co-bishop Odo, and your envoys can say more fully in words, and as my insignificance has indicated to your lordship in this little letter [Col. 0095A], the case brought against the same Hincmar, after Bishop Hincmar had been restored to the ecclesiastical possessions and resources of which he had been stripped, has been heard, examined, and settled according to canonical procedure in the province and at a suitable place by judges chosen with the consent of both parties, without any diminution of your power and with an increase of your honor, as the Spirit of God says through the Psalmist: “The king loves judgment” (Psalm 98). This is so insofar as the episcopal ministry was concerned, although that bishop was not restored in full. The case of the contumacious parties, however, awaits another conclusion.

Therefore, since something that did not happen in your youth—when the human spirit is unstable and usually inclined to seize what is not due, though the Lord guarded you—must not now be stolen from you in your mature age, and you must not allow yourself to be persuaded to infringe, however slightly, or overturn the ecclesiastical laws, by anyone whatsoever. “Knowing,” as the emperors Constantine and Constans say in the edict of their law by which they grant immunity to the Church and to its ministers, “that the commonwealth ought to be maintained more by religious observances than by offices, bodily labor, and sweat.”

And as you often recall, blessed Gregory wrote to Brunichild, queen of the Franks: “Do what belongs to God, and God will do what belongs to you.” He prefaced this statement with these words: “We trust,” he says, “that he will arrange your affairs with his mercy all the more favorably, the more he sees you concerned for his cause.”

For formerly, as the emperors Honorius and Theodosius write in the law given to the Church—to use their words—“An unfortunate usurper had decreed that clerics should indiscriminately be brought before secular judges; rejecting the tyrant’s usurpation, we reserve them for episcopal judgment. For it is not right that ministers of the divine gift should be subjected to the arbitrariness of temporal powers.” This law was afterward preserved by your successors and predecessors, the kings, for the Church and its ministers—unless perhaps, through the excesses of princes or the negligence of bishops, it was violated in some way for a time. Whatever required correction or renewal by statute was restored by them to a settled condition, or confirmed in its settled condition.

Thus, in the capitularies of your grandfather and father, in the first book of the Capitularies, you have what you can easily reread in the little booklets [Col. 0095D] recently presented to you at Pistes and afterward, for convenience, collected by me in a roll [Note: [Col. 0095D] This concerns the first memorandum presented to Charles the Bald. See above among the minor works.] and given to your lordship [Note: [Col. 0095D] Second memorandum to the king. See there.]. It may happen that something of this sort was for a short time secretly taken from a prince before you and was then corrected by the eternal law.

Thus Julian and afterward the emperor Maurice decreed that someone who had once been enrolled in the earthly military service could not be received into a monastery and serve as a soldier for Christ unless he had either completed his military service or had been rejected because of bodily infirmity. The religious emperors and Saint Gregory destroyed this practice by apostolic authority, with the general consent of the bishops, through ecclesiastical rigor and the religion that restrains the Christian commonwealth, as is shown in his letters sent to the emperor Maurice himself and to numerous archbishops.

The same thing was secretly taken from your grandfather, the emperor Charles of blessed memory, as we have learned from the tradition, words, and writings of our forebears. In the first book of the Capitularies, chapter 112, this is demonstrated concerning free men not being converted to the service of God without their permission. The Church and the commonwealth did not consent to this, and afterward corrected it, as is shown in the same book, chapter 134.

Likewise, with regard to the division of ecclesiastical possessions, certain incongruous measures were secretly imposed upon that same grandfather of yours; he corrected them by an oral declaration and by signing an edict, as is clearly shown in the aforesaid first book of the Capitularies, chapter 74. Therefore no sane person has regarded, regards, or will regard a prejudice temporarily extorted or usurped as the judgment of the law.

Furthermore, in the second book of the Capitularies, chapter 13, it is stated:

> “If such a case should arise in any province or county as concerns either the dishonor of the kingdom or a common loss, and which cannot be corrected without our authority, do not allow it to remain hidden from us for long, since, with God’s help, we ought to correct everything. Whatever up to now, in matters pertaining to the peace and justice of the whole people, to the honor of the kingdom, and to the common good, has been neglected either by us or by you, we ought, with God’s help, to strive to have corrected from now on through our joint effort.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0096D] Capitulary of the year 813, chapter 13.]

In the fourth book, chapter 24, it is also written:

> “If anyone, compelled by some necessity, commits homicide, let the count in whose jurisdiction it was perpetrated compel him both to pay the composition and to settle the feud by oath. If one party wishes to consent to this—whether the person who committed the homicide or the person who is to receive the composition—let him cause the party who is contumacious to come before us, so that we may send him into exile for whatever period seems good to us, until he is corrected there, so that he may no longer dare to disobey his count and no greater harm may arise from it.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0096D] Capitulary of the year 819, chapter 13.]

Why, then, do I write these things to you, who know them well? I openly show the reason: I do not dare remain silent before you. It is now more than four years since Luido unwillingly committed homicide in our parish, whereupon your nephew Lothar, in his kingdom and without regard to any person, fulfilled the royal duty.

Now, at Pistes and from there to Basivus, I endeavored to bring that same Luido so that he might be reconciled with your lordship’s men, as I heard had been agreed between you and your nephew. According to your recommendation, the case proceeded by lawful judgment to the point at which your men were not to swear the feud. They then sought, on your recommendation, a course by which, once judgment had been rendered, the leude might be redeemed for them and your men might swear the feud. If they wished to bring any other charge against Luido, they were to summon him before his own mallus on whatever matters they wished, and he himself was to render justice. Luido himself humbly offered this.

Afterward, however, you are not unaware of what was done there. I know, nevertheless, that it was not handled according to what the Capitularies prescribe. Nor was as much carried out there in your palace as the capitulary requires, namely, what every count ought to do in his county by authority. For this reason I did not then wish to trouble you because of the presence of the men from Aquitaine.

Now, since those men of yours possess both property and a benefice in your kingdom and in my parish, and since Boso also holds your benefice in our diocese, let your wisdom consider how the matter ought to be handled according to the ministry entrusted to you by God and according to your honor, lest this case remain unfinished on your part any longer and, if greater harm should result, you incur danger to your soul—which may the Lord avert.

Whether you wish those men of yours to come with your envoy into our parish, where they possess property and a benefice and where the case itself ought to be corrected; or whether, if they do not come, what they hold in your kingdom should be placed under ban; or whether something else should be done about it—this will be for your wisdom to decide.

But because I no longer dare to delay this case, if in the meantime I receive from you or from them nothing else that accords with reason and authority, then, on the day of the feast of Saint Remigius, if my life is spared, with the Lord’s help, when the place for my sermon comes amid the solemn celebration of the Mass, before the most sacred body of him who truly is a bishop, by the authority of God, of the holy apostles, and of that apostle of the Franks himself—in whom the Lord says to us also, unworthy though we are, as sons born to our fathers, “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven” (John 20)—I shall take care to excommunicate from the whole fellowship of Christendom those who refuse to return to peace, as the sacred canons prescribe, together with anyone who in any way consents to them, until they arrange to return, with due satisfaction, to the peace that Christ showed and taught.

I shall also announce by letter to kings, bishops, and everyone whom I can that they have been excommunicated, as the canons prescribe, so that those who do not communicate with the excommunicated may likewise be regarded as excommunicated themselves.

For we must not treat lightly the judgment of blessed Gregory, in which, agreeing with the Apostle, he says especially concerning those who possess authority: “Whoever does not correct what must be cut away commits it.”

Finally, I have heard some people reproach us bishops and say that we want to chatter through the Scriptures all day long. May your religious devotion not allow such words to be whispered into your ears.

The Apostle, filled with the Spirit, says: “Whatever was written was written for our instruction; it was written for our sake” (Romans 15). And the Lord says to the prophet: “What you hear, announce to them from me” (Jeremiah 3). “From me,” he says—that is, what I speak in the Scriptures—not from yourself, that is, from your animal and carnal understanding.

And Saint Leo says that the sacred canons were established by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world.

Regarding the laws by which the Church is governed and Christendom regulated, the wisdom of Christ the Lord says: “I, Wisdom, dwell in counsel; through me kings reign, and lawgivers decree what is just” (Proverbs 8). Lawgivers did and do establish laws not by bare speech but in writing, and they confirmed and confirm them by subscription.

The kings who preserve these laws are not those of whom God says—as it is written, “He makes a hypocrite reign because of the sins of the people” (Job 34)—“They have made kings, but not through me; they have appointed princes, and I knew it not” (Hosea 8). Rather, they are those kings who establish and preserve them, of whom the Lord also says, as we have already stated, “Through me kings reign.” In reference to what sort of kings these are, the Apostle commands, “Fear the Lord,” and says: “Honor the king and obey the king as supreme” (1 Peter 2)—that is, the king who obeys the commands of the King of kings and keeps his judgments.

Otherwise, as Saint Peter says: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5). For this reason his fellow Apostle says: “There is no authority except from God”; and, “Whoever resists authority resists what God has appointed” (Romans 13). For nothing happens in the world except what God either mercifully brings about or justly permits to happen.

When kings reign from him, therefore, it is his mercy that the peoples entrusted to them may be saved. But when they appear to reign not from him, but by the permission of his just judgment, it is the vengeance of the sinful people and an accumulation of punishment for the ruler.

The faithful do not resist authority, whether conferred by God or permitted by God, since, in Peter’s words, they “humble themselves under the hand of God” (1 Peter 5), give thanks for good princes, and groan yet rejoice concerning those whom God has permitted to reign for their purification, as it is written: “The daughters of Judah rejoiced in all your judgments, O Lord” (Psalm 96).

Thus they do not resist God’s ordinance—he who knows not how to do evil but how to order things. They do, however, resist the wicked deeds and commands of the wicked. Hence it is written: “The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven deeply” (Ecclesiastes 12), because they do not stroke faults but prick them; and, for the Lord’s sake, they patiently endure the evils inflicted upon them by wicked rulers.

Therefore, those who disparage us by saying that we want to speak through Scripture all day long—if, as the Truth says with its truthful mouth, they will give an account on the day of judgment for every idle word (Matthew 12)—should consider what they will endure for this criminal word of disparagement and murmuring against us.

We do not say to them, with holy Moses, “Your murmuring is not against us but against the Lord. What are we?” (Exodus 16). Rather, with the Apostle we impress upon them: “Do not murmur, as some of them murmured and perished by serpents” (1 Corinthians 10).

Those who are annoyed at reading or writing what has been written or is being written should know that they will not be judged for ignorance; rather, they will be condemned for the contempt by which they do not wish to know, read, or hear. They belong to the company of those concerning whom the Lord says: “He refused to understand so as to do good; he devised iniquity upon his bed” (Psalm 35). For he does not say, “He was unable to understand,” but “He refused to understand,” plainly declaring the guilt of contempt; and each contemptuous person will pay the punishment deserved for that contempt. . . .

## LETTER XVI. TO THE CLERICS OF THE PALACE

*That they restrain the depredations of their men.*

*(In Sirmond.)*

Hincmar, bishop of Rheims, to our brothers—the priests, deacons, subdeacons, and other clerics residing in the palace of our lord the king and our lady the queen, and to their faithful servants who minister to ecclesiastical affairs.

I hear concerning your men that they commit many evils in my parish—namely, acts of robbery and plundering, fornication, and adultery. I also hear concerning you that you consent to those robberies, since you live from them and feed your men and horses from their proceeds.

Therefore it is to be feared that the Lord may say of you through the prophet: “As is the people, so is the priest” (Isaiah 24:2).

I ought not to have to labor long in admonishing you, since by both your office and your instruction you are such people that you know and ought to know that you must not only abstain from evil yourselves, but also turn others away from evil and admonish them to do good.

Nevertheless, because of the ministry imposed upon me, I admonish you with the Apostle Paul and adjure you in Christ and through Christ, who spoke through Paul, “to show yourselves as ministers of God, so that our ministry may not be blamed” (2 Corinthians 6:3–4).

And since you have begun the Lenten fast, keep before your eyes what the Lord Jesus said at Easter—that is, at his passage from this world to the Father—when, in handing his body and blood to his disciples, he spoke of the betraying disciple: “Behold, the hand of the one who betrays me is with me at the table; but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed” (Luke 22:21).

You celebrate this Easter every day: priests by offering the sacrifice, deacons by ministering, subdeacons by serving, and the other clerics by responding “Amen”—with your mouths full of plunder and your hearts full of iniquity.

Have you forgotten what is written in the Gospel: “After the morsel, Satan entered into Judas” (John 13:27)? That is, he whom Satan had earlier entered in order to persuade him to betray the Lord then entered him completely, taking possession of him; as it is written: “Satan entered into Judas, who was called Iscariot” (Luke 22:3); and again: “The devil had already put it into the heart of Judas to betray the Lord” (John 13:2); and afterward it was said: “After the morsel, Satan entered into him.”

For when the holy bread entered a belly full of iniquity, the ancient enemy, called the devil and Satan, entered the cruel and impious mind. You yourselves know better what end that communion reached for him, since he received it in order to deceive and conceal his evil conscience.

For he too, as you yourselves read in the Scriptures, after Judas’s example betrays the Son of Man—not indeed to sinful Jews, but nevertheless to sinners, namely Christ’s own members, who presume to violate that immeasurable body of the Lord.

And woe to the man who approaches the Lord’s table wickedly; who, with treachery hidden in his mind and with his inmost parts polluted by plunder or some other crime, does not fear to participate in the mysteries of Christ.

Woe, I say, to that priest; woe to that deacon; woe to that subdeacon; woe to that cleric; woe to that man concerning whom Jesus—who, while sacrifice is being offered at the most holy altars, is undoubtedly present, about to consecrate the gifts set before him, with the heavenly ministers standing by—must complain in the words he spoke about Judas at the disciples’ supper: “Behold,” he said, “the hand of the one who betrays me is with me at the table” (Luke 22:21).

And woe to the person of whom the Apostle Paul says—as we read, as though by a special privilege, in the account of the Lord’s Supper when these things were handed down: “Whoever eats this bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord” (1 Corinthians 11:29).

Yet he approaches the Lord’s table without reverence and fear concerning his sins, just as he gladly approaches when his companion feeds him at a full table from his plunder.

And what the same Apostle says—“That is why many among you are weak and infirm, and many sleep” (ibid., 30), that is, die—is shown in the bodily illnesses and deaths of certain people as an example of what occurs in the soul through the spiritual illnesses and deaths of all who approach without reverence.

With what face does a priest approach to offer sacrifice, and a deacon to minister at the holy altar, so as to make the Lord favorable on behalf of others’ sins, when they not only fail to make satisfaction to him for their past sins but also provoke him to anger by daily and recent sins?

And with what confidence does anyone send such an intercessor to God on his behalf, ministering at the altar, when he daily gives serious offense to God? If he were to send that man to his own equal, who was angry with the intercessor himself, he would arouse the other more to anger than to reconciliation.

You celebrate this Easter, which the Lord then enacted in the new mystery, every day, whenever you celebrate Mass, just as he then said in his apostles to all the bishops, priests, and other faithful who were celebrating and standing by at this terrible sacrament: “Whenever you do this, you shall do it in remembrance of me” (2 Corinthians 11:25).

Consider what kind of people you are when you approach with the Lord to celebrate the Lord’s Passion, you who are defiled by such miseries—if indeed you consent to your men, as I have heard.

Therefore, unless you correct yourselves, I shall without doubt deprive all who belong to my diocese of office and communion until the synod. Those who do not belong to my diocese I shall excommunicate from my parish and diocese, and I shall command them by divine authority to return to their own bishops, who are to correct and judge them.

To ensure that this need not be done, brothers and sons, correct yourselves and your men, and admonish others. For just as your sin is greater than that of the people when you sin, so you will have greater glory before God if you guard yourselves and your men and admonish others.

Know that he who turns one sinner back from the error of his way—consider what follows from this, and how much more if you strive to provide salvation for yourselves and your men, for whom you will have to give an account.

You will also be more beloved and more honored by our lord the king; when the occasion arises, he will more securely place you over the churches; and, by God’s will and with the favor of our lord himself, we shall be able to ordain you with greater confidence and affection.

## LETTER XVII. TO THE PRIESTS OF THE DIOCESE OF RHEIMS

*That they announce excommunication to those who do not desist from depredations after being admonished.*

*(In the same source.)*

[Col. 0101B]

Hincmar, bishop of Rheims, to all the priests residing in our parish.

As I have often told you, priests are spiritual physicians, and sick people are sinners. Although we are sinners, nevertheless by God’s gracious favor we have undertaken the office of healing sinners, just as bodily physicians who are often themselves sick commonly heal the sick through their medical expertise.

When a familiar illness comes upon someone, they apply familiar medicine; but when an unfamiliar illness arises in a sick person, physicians devise an unfamiliar remedy through their experience of medicine.

Therefore, brothers, whenever any of you celebrates Mass, until this misery that we suffer in our parish has ceased—for these are people who come to church not for salvation but from habit, and who customarily stand at Mass only until the Gospel, at which you ought to have preached these things, and then leave—read this admonition of ours, from beginning to end, immediately after the Apostle, that is, after the Epistle, together with the words of the prophet or Apostle, because—would that we not say this to our own judgment—we too are God’s apostles, that is, God’s messengers.

Since I cannot announce this in person to those who commit such great evils in our parish, may the word of God sent through us to them—whose proclamation cannot be bound by any infirmity—announce their salvation to them.

Pray for them and for all of us, that they may repent of the devil’s snares, by which they are held captive for his will; that God may grant us patience to endure what we suffer; that he may free us from the evils we endure because of our sins; and that he may give peace in our days.

Our admonition to them is as follows.

I beg all of you, in the love of God, carrying his embassy, through Christ who was crucified for you, and through the Holy Spirit by whom you were sanctified in baptism—you who belong to my parish, as well as those of you who have come and continue to come into this parish from other parishes—to abstain from these depredations and fornications and from the other crimes that plunge those who commit them into hell, and to make a pure confession and worthy penance for the evils you have committed in my parish.

The Apostle Paul lists these evils for you and for all Christians, saying: “Do not be deceived: neither those who serve idols, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor those who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor the rapacious shall possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6:9), if any people die in this life with even one of these sins upon them.

Again the same Apostle Paul says: “If anyone is called a brother”—that is, if anyone is called a Christian—“and is a fornicator, or greedy, or serves idols, or is a drunkard, or a reviler, or rapacious, with such a person a true Christian must not even eat” (1 Corinthians 5:11).

And again he says: “Not only those who do such things, but also those who consent to those who do them, are worthy of death” (Romans 1:32).

For, as the holy Apostle John demonstrates, whoever consents to someone doing such evils—that is, if he can correct him, or can forbid him to do them, or, if he cannot correct such a person, can separate himself from his fellowship and does not do so—shares in and becomes a participant in his wicked deeds (2 John 11).

Therefore, brothers and sons, consider how great a misery comes upon us from pagans and from other evil Christians. Every day most of those who commit these evils depart from this world into torments without end, dead because of the misdeeds they committed in a short time.

Fearing God’s judgment, withdraw yourselves from this robbery and from the other evil deeds.

Especially at this time, when you ought to repent of and make satisfaction to God for the other sins that, as frail human beings, you commit throughout the year, so that you may receive the communion of the Lord’s body and blood on the most holy day of our redemption not for judgment but for salvation.

For if anyone full of these sins approaches that holy communion, he will undoubtedly receive his own destruction, as Judas did. He betrayed the Lord, was strangled by the noose with which he hanged himself, burst open in the middle, and went into hell with his entrails poured out.

For just as Judas handed the Lord over to the Jews, so this sinner, receiving the body and blood of Christ, hands it over for condemnation to his own sinful members.

And concerning what Judas suffered in soul and body alike, the Lord awaits many for repentance, so that they may not suffer in the body. But all who receive this communion wickedly suffer in soul and will perish eternally unless, through repentance, they are freed by God’s grace.

Regarding these things I am saying, it may happen that the devil, the enemy of human salvation, puts into your hearts—when you hear that there is such danger in receiving this holy communion if you refuse to withdraw from your iniquities—that you say: “If it is dangerous for us to communicate, as this bishop says, we shall abstain from that communion, since we are not withdrawing from our evil deeds.”

Therefore hear again, whoever the devil whispers such things to.

For just as the Lord said concerning baptism that no one can be saved unless he is born again of water and the Holy Spirit (John 3:5), so concerning this holy communion he said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54).

And just as he said, “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark 16:16)—that is, if he keeps what he promised in baptism by renouncing the devil and his works, believing in God with the faith that works through love, which means remaining in faith and good works; and if he sins after baptism, correcting what he has done badly through confession and worthy penance, forgiving those who have sinned against him, and devoting himself to good works—so also concerning this holy communion he said:

“Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6:57); and, “If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever, and I will raise him up on the last day” (ibid., 52, 55).

Therefore, all Christians, pay attention: without this communion you can receive neither the remission of sins, nor liberation from hell, nor admission to the kingdom of God.

Those who receive this communion with hatred and a heart full of iniquity, as I have said, and with the intention of sinning, will receive judgment and condemnation for themselves.

Therefore no other counsel remains for anyone who wishes to be saved except to cease from iniquities, repent of them, offer God confession of past sins, and make a declaration that thereafter he will cease from sins as far as God grants him help, devote himself to good works, and, trusting in God’s mercy, receive the communion of the Lord’s body and blood with a clean body, a pure conscience, and a contrite heart.

Then it will not be for his condemnation but for the remission of all his sins and for strength, so that he may resist the devil and reach the kingdom of God.

For just as the person who clings to a prostitute becomes one body with her, so the person who worthily receives this communion is one spirit with the Lord (1 Corinthians 6:16). In that person God dwells, and he dwells in God. In such a person, in whom God dwells and who dwells in God, sin and the devil, the author and instigator of sin, will not have a condemnable place.

If he perseveres in this way, after death he will be in refreshment, and after the resurrection he will reign forever with Christ in the company of the holy angels.

Do not suppose that I say these things merely to terrify you and not in truth. God is my witness that, just as I received them from the mouth of God through the Scriptures, so I have written them here for your salvation and correction.

And know that unless you correct yourselves and abandon these evils, I shall excommunicate all who commit these evils in my parish. I shall command the priests knowingly to give communion to no one who, after this admonition has been read, commits these evils in my parish; nor to anyone who voluntarily associates with one who commits them or consents to someone doing these evils.

And to all who approach communion, every priest shall announce that whoever has not ceased from these evils after this admonition is not to approach communion, knowing that he will receive condemnation.

By the word of God I shall command that no priest coming from another parish celebrate Mass in my parish for those who have not corrected themselves of these evils. This I beg of you in the love of Christ.

Let no one despise this, saying: “What if this bishop has ordered such things?” Let him know for certain that, whatever sort of person I may be, God is truthful and almighty, and he said to us: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven” (Matthew 18:18).
