And if anyone says, “I shall go to another parish on those days,” let that person know—he is not mocking a man but God, and is deceiving himself—that if, while excommunicated, he goes to another parish to receive communion, he will face an even greater judgment before God, because he thinks he can escape the one who is everywhere. By his word, not by my human power but according to the divine ministry, I shall excommunicate him.

And do not be angry, beloved brothers and sons, because I admonish you with fatherly affection. Correct yourselves, attending to God’s threat addressed both to me and to you.

For the Lord says to everyone who has undertaken the priestly office: “If you announce his iniquity to the wicked man, and that wicked man turns from his wickedness, he shall live, and you will have saved your soul. But if you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked man, and that impious man does not turn from his wickedness, the wicked man shall die in his iniquity, but I will require his blood from your hand” (Ezekiel 3:39).

Therefore, brothers and sons, pay attention. Almighty God is the one who has said these things; he made us, and he redeemed us. Before his judgment we shall all stand, and there we priests, princes, and elders—who ought to admonish and correct you—shall be judged for our sins and yours.

You too will be judged, not only for the sins you committed and did not repent of, but also for the admonitions and corrections that you despised.

May almighty God, who speaks these things through me in your ears, speak them himself in your hearts.

## LETTER XVIII. TO THE PRIESTS OF THE PARISH OF RHEIMS

*Concerning baptism.*

*(Acts of the provincial Church of Rheims.)*

[Col. 0104D]

Hincmar, bishop and servant of the people of God, to our beloved brothers, the fellow priests of this parish of Rheims.

Desiring that, by God’s grace, you may be enriched in every understanding, teaching, and perfection of works, I have taken care to excerpt briefly for each of you and for all of you together, from the breadth of the fullness of the holy Scriptures and the teaching of the catholic fathers, certain matters concerning the administration of holy baptism, because of the ministry imposed upon my insignificance, and to set them before your knowledge.

Thus, according to sacred Scripture, you may understand everything that you do in the holy ministry, and so that, in plain speech, you may have no difficulty understanding it, nor, in reading and committing it to memory at length, any weariness.

The Lord Jesus Christ, our Creator and Redeemer, says in the Gospel: “Unless someone is reborn of water and the Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3). Therefore he commanded his disciples, saying: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you” (Matt. 28). In these very few words he set forth the order of the whole sacred preaching: twice he said “teach,” and once “baptize.” First of all he commanded that the Catholic faith be taught; then, after the faith had been received, he ordered baptism in the name of the Holy Trinity. Thereafter he commanded that the person imbued with faith and cleansed by holy baptism be instructed in the evangelical commandments [Col. 0105B]. First the faith must be taught, and thus the sacraments of baptism must be received; afterward the evangelical commandments must be handed down. But if any one of these three is lacking, the hearer will not be able to possess the salvation of his soul.

This order of catechizing—that is, instructing adult men—must everywhere be firmly retained. To the more fragile age, however, the devout mother Church has granted that the one who is bound by another’s sin of paternal transgression may be released, in the mystery of baptism, through another’s renunciation and profession of faith. And if this were not so, how many infants would perish, from whose number the heavenly Jerusalem is daily built? For baptism without faith is of no benefit, as the Apostle says: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11). We read, indeed, that there is a distinction between “impossible” and “difficult.” What is difficult can, although scarcely, nevertheless be done; what is impossible, however, [Col. 0105C] cannot be done at all by human frailty. Therefore, when the apostles were astonished and asked who among the rich could be saved, the Lord himself answered in the Gospel: “With human beings this is impossible; but with God all things are possible” (Matt. 19).

A person possessing rational understanding must therefore be taught and drawn by preaching of many kinds, so that he may recognize the truth of the sacred faith. Above all, the mercy of almighty God must be implored for him, because the tongue of the teacher is useless if divine grace does not imbue the hearer’s heart, as Truth himself says: “No one can come to me unless my Father has drawn him” (John 6). And so that you may understand that the holy Trinity works equally in the salvation of humanity, [Col. 0105D] the Lord himself also says in the Gospel: “No one can come to the Father except through me” (John 14). Likewise concerning the Holy Spirit he says: “Unless someone is reborn of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3).

For what the priest visibly performs in the body through water in baptism, the Holy Spirit invisibly performs in the soul through faith. There are three visible and three invisible elements in the sacrament of baptism. The visible are the priest, the body, and the water; the invisible are the spirit, the soul, and faith. Those three visible elements accomplish nothing outwardly if these three invisible elements do not operate. The priest washes the body with water; the Holy Spirit justifies the soul through faith. This is what the Apostle says: “For we are God’s fellow workers” (1 Cor. 3). [Col. 0106A] A human being cooperates with the Holy Spirit in the salvation of another human being; but the person who is to be baptized must also cooperate with both in his own salvation: that is, he must humbly present his body to the Holy Spirit and the priest for the mystery of the sacred washing, and voluntarily offer his soul for receiving the Catholic faith.

So that you may understand the force of this most sacred rite according to the understanding of the holy Fathers and the ecclesiastical statutes, I shall set forth these same sacraments to your charity by a Catholic interpretation. For we believe that no one may doubt that everything done in them has been established with great holiness and venerable significance.

I. First, the pagan becomes a catechumen—that is, an instructed person—by approaching baptism, that is, the holy dipping, according to the prescribed order; and he renounces the evil spirit [Col. 0106B] and all his destructive pomp.

II. He receives the laying on of hands and the cross on his forehead in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit; and he is breathed upon in the face, so that, once the devil has been driven away, an entrance may be prepared for Christ our God.

III. He is exorcised—that is, the evil spirit is adjured—so that it may depart and withdraw, giving place to God.

IV. The catechumen receives salt, so that his rotten and fluid sins may be cleansed by the salt of wisdom, a divine gift.

V. Then the faith of the Apostles’ Creed and the Lord’s Prayer are handed over to him, so that the empty house, abandoned by its former inhabitant, may be adorned by faith and prepared as a dwelling for God. You have their exposition—that is, of the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer—in the scrutiny that takes place at the opening of the ears [Col. 0106C], as we believe is known to you. For what is called symbolum in Greek is interpreted in Latin as “indication,” “sign,” or “collation.” It is an “indication,” because by it the integrity of the faith is indicated. It is a “sign,” because, when it is rightly retained and understood, the faithful are distinguished from the unfaithful by it. It is a “collation,” because in it the holy Apostles brought together the whole integrity of the faith. What all the Apostles retained in their hearts with equal sincerity of faith, they confessed with their mouths; and, bringing together their individual statements, they issued the symbolum—that is, the collation of the whole faith. For, as they were about to depart from one another into the provinces of the whole world, they established together the rule of the preaching that was to come, lest, departing locally from one another, they should preach anything different or discordant.

The Lord’s Prayer, which all Christians [Col. 0106D] must necessarily recite frequently with a sincere heart, is so called because, when the Apostles asked our Lord Jesus Christ to show them how they ought to pray, he composed this prayer for them, as the holy Gospels teach, and commanded them to pray in this way.

VI. Then the scrutinies are performed—that is, examinations or investigations—according to the custom known to you, so that it may be examined repeatedly how firmly, after the renunciation of Satan, the sacred words of the faith that has been delivered have been deeply fixed in the heart. As you know, seven scrutinies are held on the appointed days in holy Lent, according to the form of the sevenfold Spirit.

VII. Next the priest, in consecrating him, touches the candidate’s nostrils and ears with saliva and says: “Ephphatha,” which means “Be opened” [Col. 0107A] (Matt. 7), and what follows. Among the other beginnings of consecration, the priest touches the nostrils and ears of the person being consecrated with the saliva of his mouth and says: “Ephphatha,” which means “Be opened.” Humanity became deaf to hearing the word of life after, in fear, it heard the deadly words of the serpent against God; and the deafness that the first human being earned by sinning was contracted by everyone generated from him through the transmission of male seed.

Through the saliva of the priest’s mouth, the taste with which the person being initiated is to receive heavenly wisdom is signified, because saliva descends from the head, in which all the human senses are located. The Apostle says: “The head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. 11). The divinity, assuming humanity, made a kind of eye-salve from the conjunction of two substances in the one person of the Son of God, by which the human race, [Col. 0107B] born blind from its first parents, might be illuminated.

It is not without reason that the ears and nostrils are touched with spittle: the one who, by spitting, touched the tongue of the mute, made clay with spittle, and opened the eyes of one born blind now, through the ministry of priests, grants spiritual hearing to those who are to be baptized, gives them the ability to speak rightly—that is, to confess the true faith—and opens their nostrils so that they may receive the good fragrance of Christ.

The touching of the nostrils signifies that, having rejected harmful pleasures, the person should always embrace only the fragrance of Christ, of whom the Apostle says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place” (2 Cor. 2). It also signifies that he should remember, according to the example of blessed Job, that, so long as breath remains in him and the spirit of God is in his nostrils, he must not speak iniquity with his lips or devise falsehood with his tongue.

Moreover, [Col. 0107C] the touching of the ears signifies that, having abandoned the hearing of a wicked tongue, he should hear the words of Christ and do them, like the prudent man who built his house upon rock. Incorporated into the Church, which is the body of Christ, he says with the Psalmist: “Sacrifice and offering, namely, the ancient ceremonies, you did not desire; but you perfected ears for me, so that I might proclaim all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion” (Ps. 39); and: “My vows are upon me, O God; I shall render praises to you” (Ps. 55).

We also read that in certain regions there is a custom that the lips of the person being consecrated are touched with the priest’s saliva, on the authority of the holy Gospel. For after the Lord put his fingers into the ears of the deaf and mute man, he touched his tongue with spittle and added: “Ephphatha,” [Col. 0107D] which means “Be opened.” Immediately his ears were opened, the bond of his tongue was released, and he spoke rightly.

In certain regions others touch the ears and nostrils of catechumens with holy oil, because no one can recognize the sacraments of faith through the grace of the Holy Spirit, which is signified by oil, unless he hears the preacher, as the Apostle says: “Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (Rom. 10). The nostrils are likewise sanctified by a similar touch, so that those who come to baptism may be admonished to preserve the sacrament of so great a mystery inviolate and whole through the grace of the Holy Spirit until death. So long as they draw the breath of this life through their nostrils, they are not to depart from the worship and service of Christ our Lord.

[Col. 0108A] But just as the custom of our regions is not to be condemned by them, so neither should the custom of those regions be wholly rejected by us, since it does not appear to be contrary to the faith. In the solidity of one faith, diverse custom in certain matters is not usually harmful. Thus the sacraments of the Old and New Testaments, although they differ according to the circumstances of the times, nevertheless agree in one and the same faith, because what we have learned was accomplished through the Apostles, the Fathers of the Old Testament had learned through the prophets was to come as the dispensation of Christ.

VIII. After this, the priest calls the person being consecrated by name and asks him whether he renounces Satan and all his works, and what follows. After his response, he anoints him with exorcised oil on the chest and [Col. 0108B] between the shoulders, saying: “And I anoint you with the oil of salvation in Christ Jesus our Lord unto eternal life.”

The chest is thoroughly anointed with oil so that, by the sign of the holy cross, entry may be closed to the devil. He is also marked between the shoulders so that he may be protected on every side. Likewise, the anointing of the chest and the space between the shoulders signifies firmness of faith and perseverance in good works.

The person being baptized is also marked on the chest and between the shoulders with holy oil, so that he may be anointed with that holy oil—namely, with the anointing of the Spirit—of which the Apostle says: “His anointing teaches you about everything” (1 John 2). Protected in front and behind against all circumstances, whether favorable or adverse, he is to be watchful.

The person being baptized renounces the devil—that is, he resists him—as the Apostle Peter commands, saying: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (1 Pet. 5). [Col. 0108C] To renounce means to repudiate, despise, reject, oppose, deny, abandon, or whatever else may express this meaning in the present context. Although the sense of the verb *nuntio* (“announce”) is clear when it is used without a prefix, with a prefix it sometimes does not depart far from its meaning, as in *nuntio* and *renuntio*; but at other times it turns into another sense, as in: “So therefore, every one of you who does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14). In explaining this saying in a homily on the Gospel, blessed Gregory showed that *renuntiare* must be understood as “to deny.”

Finally, after the renunciation of Satan, the person being baptized is asked whether he renounces all his works. What the works of Satan are, the divine Apostle Paul, in whom Christ speaks, demonstrates when he writes to the Corinthians: “If any brother is a fornicator, or greedy, or serving idols, or abusive, or drunk, or rapacious, with such a one not even to eat” (1 Cor. 5). And again: “Do you not know that the unrighteous will not possess the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor men who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor the abusive, nor the rapacious will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 4).

And to the Galatians: “The works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, uncleanness, lust, service of idols, sorceries, enmities, quarrels, jealousies, angers, strife, dissensions, sects, envy, [Col. 0109A] murders, drunkenness, carousings, and things like these, which I foretell to you, as I foretold them, because those who do such things will not obtain the kingdom of God” (Gal. 3)—unless, before they depart from the body, they cover these things by the appropriate fruits of repentance and take care to cleanse them through devoted prayers, almsgiving, fasts, tears, and offerings of the saving sacrifice.

The person being baptized therefore renounces all the pomps of the devil—that is, spiritual vices—such as ambition, arrogance, vainglory, ostentation, and other things of this sort that proceed from the fountain of pride. For *pompa* properly means a public display accompanied by great ambition. *Ambitio* is called *phantasia* in Greek; by this name the elaborate apparatus and pomp of royal office are signified. And on this condition, after the renunciation, as we have said, he is anointed with holy oil.

IX. And thus, after the font has been consecrated with solemn words, while the person being baptized stands beside the font and his sponsor assists, the priest asks him whether he believes in God the almighty Father, and what follows, according to custom. When he has answered according to ecclesiastical custom—after the threefold renunciation mentioned above of the devil, his pomps, and his works, and after the threefold confession of the true faith, since no one can be cleansed except by a threefold renunciation and a threefold confession—he is baptized by three immersions in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

Thus, just as the inner person, who was created in the image of the holy Trinity, is recalled to that same image through the invocation of the holy Trinity, so the one who fell into death by the threefold degree of sin—that is, by thought, speech, and action—may, having been raised three times from the font, rise again through grace to life.

And just as the inner person is to be reformed in the faith of the holy Trinity according to the image of his Creator, so the outer person must be washed by three immersions, so that what the Spirit invisibly works in the soul, the priest may visibly imitate in the water. For original sin was committed in three ways: through pleasure, consent, and action. Likewise, every sin is effected either by thought, speech, or action. Therefore a threefold washing appears appropriate to the threefold kind of sins—either because of original sin, which brings infants to perdition, or because of those sins that are added in people of more advanced age by will, word, or deed.

And because, according to holy [Col. 0109D] Scripture, there is one God, one faith, and one baptism, the person being baptized is immersed three times in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, so that the Trinity may appear as one sacrament. He is not baptized in the names of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, but in one name, which is understood to be “God,” according to the Apostle.

Thus there is one God, one faith, and one baptism; but there are two covenants that are made in baptism, which sponsors must carefully explain and impress upon those entrusted to them when they reach an age capable of understanding. One of these covenants is that by which the baptized person renounces the devil, all his works, and all his pomps; the other is that by which each baptized person professes that he believes in the Father, and in the Son, and in the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0110A] The faithful must preserve these with unwavering mental attention, and, so that they may be kept undefiled, must always seek the help of the one by whose grace they have been reborn in baptism.

EPISTLE XIX. TO KING LOUIS III, SON OF THE STAMMERER. That he permit a free episcopal election to take place in the Church of Beauvais.

(In Sirmond.)

To the glorious lord King Louis, Hincmar, bishop and servant of the people of God.

CHAPTER I

We bishops who assembled in the name of Christ at the shrine of Saint Macra did so not out of any improper desire, but for the honor and salvation of the holy Church, of you, and of the kingdom entrusted to you, as the writings that we sent to you through our fellow priests demonstrate. Having reread the presumption of the clergy and people of the Church of Beauvais, who presented to us at the synod a person unsuitable according to the sacred rules, together with a decree confirmed by the hands of each of them—as had already happened when they elected a certain Fromold, and, after he was rejected because of his foolishness and wickedness, Odo was elected there from the neighboring parish with a canonical decree—we reread the sacred canons before everyone who was present and, according to those same sacred laws, appointed by name our beloved brothers and venerable fellow bishops. Through them we sent letters to your lordship, containing, among other things, the following:

“So that, as the sacred laws and rules command, you may deign to grant the archbishops and bishops of the neighboring dioceses the right of election, so that, from wherever they may be, the bishops may, according to the regular form of election, elect a man who will be useful to the holy Church, beneficial to the kingdom, and a faithful and devoted co-worker with you; and, with the consent of the clergy and people, may bring him to you, so that, in accordance with your ministry, you may entrust to his administration the property and resources of the Church that the Lord has commended to you for its defense and protection, and, with your consent and letters, may send him to the metropolitan bishop and the fellow bishops of his diocese, who ought to ordain him, so that he may be advanced to the holy priesthood without the stain of scandal.” And the other matters that follow there.

CHAPTER II

In these words there is no improper desire of anyone, nothing contrary to the will of the Lord, nothing contrary to your honor, and nothing opposed to the salvation of the kingdom entrusted to you. Rather, they contain the full order by which one elected for the merit of his life and the teaching of his wisdom ought to be regularly ordained by the metropolitan and the fellow bishops of the province, according to the holy and great Council of Nicaea, where, among other things, it is written (canon 6):

“It is generally clear,” it says, “that if anyone has been made a bishop contrary to the judgment of the metropolitan, the great synod has determined that he cannot be a bishop; but the confirmation of what is done in each province is to be attributed to the metropolitan bishop.”

And concerning this mystical Synod of Nicaea, the Apostolic See bears witness (Leo, Epistle 56, to Anatolius): “Because it has been consecrated by such a great divine privilege, whatever is done contrary to its constitution is entirely void of authority, whether ecclesiastical judgments are celebrated by fewer or by more bishops.”

You must therefore observe without hesitation, as holy Pope Leo wrote to Emperor Leo (Epistle 81), that royal power has been granted to you not merely for governing the world, but especially for protecting the Church, so that by suppressing wicked attempts you may defend what has been rightly established and restore true peace to what has been disturbed. This too you ought to desire, seek, and preserve, as your predecessors, emperors and kings, did.

Nor ought you to try to bend the inflexible will of God—who, even when he changes a judgment, does not change his purpose—to your human and fragile will. This cannot be done. Rather, you must subject your will to God’s will, just as Christ gave himself as an example for us and for all Christians to follow, speaking from his human nature and saying: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me” (John 5:30; 6:38); and: “Let it be not as I will, but as you will, Father” (Matt. 26:39).

For if your human will should persistently disagree with the divine will—may the Lord not permit this—the words of the Apostles must be spoken in the episcopal ministry: “We must obey God rather than human beings” (Acts 5:29); and: “Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, judge for yourselves. For we cannot fail to speak of what we have seen and heard” (Acts 4:19).

CHAPTER III

For if what I have heard some people say is true—namely, that when you grant the election requested of you, the bishops, clergy, and people ought to elect the man whom you want and whom you command to be elected—then this is not an election according to divine law, but an extortion by human power. If it is so, as I have heard some people say, that evil spirit who deceived our first parents through the serpent in paradise and drove them out from there is hissing these things into your ears through such flatterers. For nothing of this kind is contained in the Scriptures of either the Old or the New Testament; nor is it found in the sayings of the Catholic Fathers or in the sacred canons; nor is it written or decreed in the laws promulgated by Christian emperors and kings. Such statements have been vomited forth by hell.

For Christ, speaking through the Apostle, commands that one be elected “who is able to exhort in sound doctrine and to refute those who contradict” (Titus 1:9). And if anyone speaks against this, he speaks iniquity against the Lord and is counted by the Holy Spirit among blasphemers.

Thus your ancestor Charles and your great-grandfather Louis, emperors, understood the matter. Therefore, in the first book of their Capitularies, they promulgated the following (chapter 84, on electing bishops):

“Not ignorant of the sacred canons,” they say, “so that the holy Church may more freely enjoy its honor in the name of God, we give our assent to the ecclesiastical order, namely, that bishops be elected through the election of the clergy and people, according to the provisions of the canons, from their own diocese, with personal preference and acceptance of gifts removed, on account of the merit of their life and the gift of wisdom, so that they may be able to benefit their subjects everywhere by example and word.”

It should certainly be noted that it says, “Let them be elected according to the provisions of the canons,” so that they may be able to benefit their subjects everywhere by example and word.

The sacred canons also say [Col. 0112A] (Celestine, Decrees 18): “First, those clerics of each Church must be rejected, so that men from other Churches may be preferred on the basis of merit.” And again: “Let bishops be advanced to ecclesiastical authority by the judgment of the metropolitans and of those bishops who are in the surrounding regions—namely, those who have been tested for a long time both in the word of faith and in the example of upright conduct.”

It must therefore be considered how this imperial capitulary [Col. 0112B] agrees with the sacred rules and the laws of the ancient emperors. It shows that, just as the laws and rules say, in the election of a bishop the king’s role is assent, not choice; election, like ordination, belongs to the bishops’ execution.

CHAPTER IV

There are people who say, as I have heard, that the ecclesiastical property of the bishoprics is in your power, so that you may give it to whomever you wish. If this is so, that evil spirit who, as was stated above, destroyed our first parents is whispering your destruction into your ears.

For the Holy Spirit, through those who reign with Christ in heaven and shine forth on earth through miracles, has spoken and caused the following to reach us in writing:

“Ecclesiastical property and resources are called offerings because they are offered to the Lord [Col. 0112C]; they are the vows of the faithful, the prices of sins, and the patrimonies of the poor. If anyone seizes them, he is guilty of the condemnation of Ananias and Sapphira, and such a person ought to be handed over to Satan, so that his spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord.”

The aforesaid glorious emperors Charles and Louis inserted this in the first book of their Capitularies, saying (chapter 83):

“Since, according to the tradition of the holy Fathers, we know that the property of the Church is the vows of the faithful, the prices of sins, and the patrimonies of the poor, we desire, with God’s assistance, not only to preserve what is possessed by each person, but also to contribute much more. Nevertheless, so that we might wholly remove from the clergy the suspicion long ago conceived concerning the division of Church property, we decree that, neither in our time nor in that of our sons—or, by God’s dispensation, in the time of our successors [Col. 0112D] who may wish to imitate the will or example of us or our ancestors—shall it suffer any division or loss whatsoever.”

You too ought to preserve this if you wish to reign happily, since you are still inferior in power, age, and wisdom to those who both preserved these principles and promulgated them for preservation.

CHAPTER V

Remember, I ask you, your profession, which you promised on the day of your consecration, as we have learned from those who were present, and to which you subscribed with your own hand and offered upon the altar before the Lord in the presence of all the bishops who attended. Have it carefully reread before you and your faithful [Col. 0113A], by whose counsel and assistance you ought to govern the holy Church and the kingdom entrusted to you. And if, through ignorance or the suggestion of others, you have deviated from it in any respect, do not neglect to make satisfaction to the Lord for this.

And pay attention to what you wrote in the letter addressed to me and reread at the synod, as is fitting for you. For it is written there:

“Let us join together, so that I, as king, and you, as God’s priest, may be able to fulfill worthily the ministry of our offices, both in divine and in human matters.”

Thus, by devotion and action, show that Christ, from whom every legitimate episcopate took its beginning and from whom every principate received its advancement, is the author of your government and the protector of your highness.

Through him I beseech you in my episcopal ministry: do not attempt in your time [Col. 0113B] to introduce such things into the holy Church as the great emperors and your predecessors did not presume to introduce in their own times.

And since the episcopal ministry is not carried out without the Holy Spirit, do not consider it a light matter to grieve the Holy Spirit in bishops, when the Lord threatens terribly, saying: “Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the depths of the sea” (Matt. 18:6). And the Apostle says: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God” (Eph. 4:30).

The same Apostle also says that “Christ dwells in our hearts through faith” (Eph. 3:17). Though now seated at the right hand of the Father, he thundered from heaven to Saul, saying: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). [Col. 0113C] He thereby demonstrated that Christ is persecuted and scandalized in his members, and received in his members, just as he promises that he will say to the elect in judgment: “As long as you did it to one of the least of mine, you did it to me” (Matt. 25:40). The Holy Spirit is grieved in those in whom he dwells, as we showed above from the Apostle’s words.

And since the time has already passed beyond which the sacred canons, created by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, decree that the ordinations of bishops are not to be delayed—and since the synod held at the shrine of Saint Macra defined this according to the laws and rules—let your lordship consent to the election of the bishops who were designated at the synod, with your consent, for carrying out this matter, as is written in the letter sent to you by that synod [Col. 0113D]. Do not delay in hastening the matter, as we urged you, so that the Church itself may not remain long without a pastor contrary to the promulgation of the Holy Spirit, and so that you may not, God forbid, incur no small danger.

For since the sacred canons say that a council is complete when the metropolitan bishop is present with his suffragans (Council of Antioch, canon 16), what metropolitans have decreed with bishops of various provinces according to the sacred laws and rules must be held all the more valid.

For six hundred and thirty and more bishops, whose names are written in heaven and whose names we have written in our books, assembled in the city of Chalcedon in the name of Christ at the shrine of Saint Euphemia and established the following [Col. 0114A] (canon 25): episcopal ordinations are not to be delayed beyond three months; and, with a judgment confirmed by decree, the holy synod decreed that those who dared, after the definition of this great and universal synod, to perpetrate anything among the prohibited acts should withdraw from their own rank.

And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them.” And: “If two of you on earth agree about any matter, it will be done.” And: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven” (Matt. 18:18–20). If he will deign to be present where two or three are gathered, how much more where so many holy Fathers have assembled and irrefragably decreed that these things must be observed?

CHAPTER VI

Concerning what I reread in your letters on the day before the Nones [Col. 0114B] of the past month of May, delivered by a cleric named Teutbert: that you wished voluntarily to submit yourself to the counsels of my insignificance; that, according to whatever I should advise, you would act and arrange matters in ecclesiastical and secular affairs; that you wished to subject yourselves to my trust; and that, according to the counsel given by me, you would order the laws of your kingdom—I write back to your lordship that you should strive in all things to place the will of the Lord before your own will.

You can learn his will through the holy Scriptures; through those who now reign with him in heaven and shine forth on earth through miracles; and through the sacred laws promulgated by Christian emperors and kings, as he himself says: “Through me kings reign, and lawmakers decree what is just” (Prov. 8:15). You can also recognize it through the writings sent to you by us from the synod [Col. 0114C] held at the shrine of Saint Macra and through our fellow priests.

But I grieve deeply and fear greatly because, if I may say so with your permission, insofar as it appears in this matter under discussion, you are more intent on following your own will than divine authority, and the greed of those who thrust themselves forward unseasonably than the usefulness of the holy Church; and the favor of the flattery of those of whom the Apostle says that they “do not know what they are saying or about what they are making assertions” (1 Tim. 1:7), rather than your own salvation.

You wrote that the votes of everyone residing in the Church of Beauvais agree upon Odacrus. It is not surprising if fools and wicked people, blinded by greed, act in this way so often. They were not corrected by the rejection of their wicked election [Col. 0114D] of Fromold, nor by the rejection of Rodulf, nor by the election among themselves of Honoratus, who was still unsuitable to the sacred episcopal order in the teaching of the faith. They lost the election, as was shown to them in the synod, and through the sacred rules it was made clear that the election belonged no longer to them but to the bishops; that their election was not to precede but to follow; that they ought not to withdraw from it; and now, contrary to the rules and laws, they have presumed to hold an election without a visitor.

Therefore that prophetic saying must be referred to this same people: “You have acquired the forehead of a prostitute; you do not know how to be ashamed” (Jer. 3:3). And the Apostle James rebukes such clergy and laypeople alike, saying: “Adulterers, do you not know that friendship with this world is enmity with God?” (Jas. 4:4). He rightly calls them adulterers, rebuking those who, [Col. 0115A] having abandoned the love of heavenly wisdom—which says, “Keep my laws” (Lev. 18 and 20)—have turned instead toward the embrace of worldly friendship.

Therefore they deserve to be corrected by excommunication rather than to be heard while corrupted by their own desires.

But perhaps the matter is not as it has been reported to you. To your lordship I point out what has been written, under the dictation of the Holy Spirit, in the Decrees of the Apostolic See:

“Even if all the priests and the world should assent to error, the condemnation involves those who consent; agreement does not absolve them from the condemnation of transgression. For the crime is not diminished but increased when what was private becomes general. God made this clear when he destroyed the sinful world by a universal flood.”

## CHAPTER VII

You wrote that, just as I have always been useful and devoted to your predecessors, the kings, in every matter concerning the kingdom, so I should be faithful and devoted to you. This I have observed until now, and I desire to continue observing it. But you must preserve for the holy Church, its rulers, and me what they preserved; and, in return for the devoted fidelity that I showed you, together with your other faithful subjects, in your election—not without great labor—for the advancement of the rule which, now bearing that name, the Lord has also granted you to possess in power, do not repay me evil for good by urging—though the Lord does not assist you in this—to make me in my old age turn aside from the sacred rules, something I have never done either through greed or love or fear, so that I should justly fall from the episcopal office which, by God’s grace, I have held for thirty-six years until now.

For I have not forgotten the Savior’s saying: “For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but loses himself and suffers the loss of his soul? Or what exchange can a man give for his soul?” (Luke 9:15; Matthew 16:25). And the sacred canons, decreed by the Holy Spirit, say (Council of Carthage II, canon 13): “If anyone,” they say, “acts in any matter contrary to his profession or subscription, he will deprive himself of his honor.”

And if I should agree with you that, contrary to divine and human laws, and contrary to your own profession and mine—which was made publicly before many bishops restraining you in synod—you should act, I would destroy myself and would not save you, since the Apostle says: “Not only those who do such things, but also those who consent to those who do them, are worthy of death” (Romans 1:32). And, as it is written in ecclesiastical and secular laws: “Those who do evil and those who consent to evil are held by an equal judicial penalty; nor is he considered free from the crime who, although he himself did not commit it, nevertheless admits those who commit it into his fellowship and alliance.”

## CHAPTER VIII

You wrote that, through my will and ministry, you might be able to grant the bishopric of the Church of Beauvais to my beloved son and your faithful servant Odacer. If you are concerned for him, do not do this in any way, lest, if you do, and he should presume to invade that bishopric and the Church, vacant of its shepherd, contrary to the sacred rules of the Church, it should happen—as the sacred laws and rules require, though I do not wish it—that thereafter he be unable to exercise ecclesiastical ministry in the diocese of Rheims, either during my life or after my bodily death.

## CHAPTER IX

Concerning what you wrote: if I obey your will, which is contrary to the ecclesiastical rules, you would take care to honor in every respect those whom you know to be dearer and more familiar to me, provided only that I agree with you in this request of yours: I answer you not in my own words but in the words of the sacred canons. According to those canons, for the needy, for those connected with me, and for others, as they command, I shall approach your royal power with petitions for the increase of your salvation and the honor of your authority, as long as the Lord commands me to remain in the body.

Yet, as Saint Pope Innocent says: “I gladly hear that you are concerned for your salvation; but I do not gladly admit anything against the head.” And Saint Gregory, explaining the Gospel’s saying (Homily 37 on the Gospels), “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:26), says:

“Since whoever now desires eternal things must, in the cause of God which he undertakes, become outside father, outside mother, outside wife, outside children, outside relatives, and outside himself, so that he may know God more truly, inasmuch as he recognizes no one in God’s cause.”

Therefore, in this episcopal ministry I do not acknowledge a blood relative, nor a friend familiar to my heart, with carnal affection. Instead, I heed the Lord’s sentence, who says: “He who does not enter the sheepfold through the door, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber” (John 10:1). Thus I choose no one, acknowledge no one, and receive no one except him who approaches this episcopal ministry through the keys of the Church, with life and conduct and Catholic knowledge and teaching, and who knows and does what the sacred ministry requires.

And since God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation whoever fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him (Acts 10:34), in this matter I accept no one’s person, just as the holy prophet describes the just man: “He shakes his hands free from every gift” (Isaiah 33:15). For he did not say merely “from a gift,” but added “from every gift”: from the gift of the hands, from the gift of the tongue, and from the gift of service, as I have already written to you—if only you had wished to store it in your mind.

## CHAPTER X

Finally, you must carefully and attentively keep your lordship, dear to me, before the eyes of your mind, because, as I have already written to you, those who are ordained contrary to the sacred canons, and those who ordain them, are heretics, as Saint Gregory and the other Catholic teachers and rulers of the holy Church frequently demonstrate in their books.

Saint Peter first condemned this heresy in Simon Magus with an eternal anathema (Acts 8). Moreover, the great and holy Council of Chalcedon commands that mediators of this kind—not of ordination but of disorder—if they are clerics, be deprived of their proper rank; but if they are laymen or monks, they are to be anathematized without any exception or regard for any person (canon 2).

Therefore I urge your lordship to beware of such mediation or intervention. Do not incur eternal danger for the sake of temporal favor toward anyone. And let my beloved son, your faithful servant, for whom you are laboring, not forget what I remember having written, among other things, in the letter sent to you, to your chaplains: the canonical sentence which says:

“Just as the one who, when invited, refuses, and, when sought, withdraws, is to be brought to the sacred altars, so the one who seeks office voluntarily or thrusts himself forward importunately is undoubtedly to be rejected.”

What has been stated above, therefore, is not my wording, nor something devised by me, but words spoken by Christ, through the apostles and his saints, under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, let those who cannot bear to hear these things, or who disdain to obey them, fear the Lord, who says what we all recently heard read in church on the fifteenth day before Holy Easter:

“He who is of God hears the words of God. The reason you do not hear is that you are not of God” (John 8:47).

Hence Saint Gregory says (Homily 18 on the Gospels):

“If he who is of God hears the words of God, and whoever is not of him cannot hear his words, let each person ask himself whether he perceives the words of God in the ear of his heart, and he will understand from whom he comes.”

And Saint Paul the Apostle, through whom Christ himself spoke, says: “Do not participate in the unfruitful works of darkness; rather, rebuke them” (Ephesians 5:11). Again the same Apostle says: “If anyone does not obey our word in this letter, take note of him, and do not associate with him, so that he may be put to shame” (2 Thessalonians 3:14).

Therefore the sacred canons have decreed that those who associate with excommunicated persons are themselves excommunicated. These things Christ from heaven, and his holy apostles, and his saints who now reign with him in heaven, thunder forth. And we, though sinners, bishops on earth, vicars of Christ, and successors of the apostles on earth, pursue them by his power and divine ministry, desiring to imitate what we sing of the holy man: “He contended for the law of his God unto death, for he was founded upon the firm rock.” “The rock,” says the Apostle, “was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4).

Let the bishops, clergy, and people of the Church of Beauvais therefore meet in the peace of Christ, as was established according to the sacred canons, with your free consent, as befits royal ministry; and let the election be carried out and the ordination proceed according to the lawful and regular form.

# LETTER XX. TO THE SAME KING LOUIS III

## Concerning Odacer, the invader of the Church of Beauvais

*(In the same collection.)*

To the glorious lord Louis, king, Hincmar, bishop and servant of the people of God.

From the letters bearing your seal below, which the cleric Warinus delivered to me on the Ides of this present month of June on your behalf, I had not resolved to reply to each point, since I had already answered you sufficiently concerning your earlier commands and letters. Nevertheless, because in these letters also you asked me to reply, although they disagree among themselves so that the middle differs from the beginning and the end from the middle—as an ancient poet says of a certain monster:

“Lion at the beginning, dragon at the end, and in the middle the chimaera itself”—

I shall, with the Lord’s help, though wearied by your messages and letters, reply to you concerning certain passages about the Church of Beauvais, according to the proverb which I once read in the books of the ancients: “The weary ox plants its foot more firmly.”

### I

Concerning what is written in the place in your earlier letters delivered to me: “A father ought in no way to reject the just request of a beloved son”: my insignificance approves this, and so does the Lord, who says to his disciples: “Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you” (John 16:23).

For the name of the Lord Jesus is interpreted as “savior,” and that request is just which pertains to true salvation. Since the Lord does not reject such a request, neither should any Christian reject it. But if anyone asks for something contrary to true salvation, he will hear from the Apostle James: “You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly” (James 4:3).

### II

Concerning what follows there: “Kindly favor our request and will, and fulfill our desire for the present”: I reply that you should wish and desire what the Lord wishes, to whom the Psalmist says: “Lord, all my desire is before you” (Psalm 37:10). I shall safely favor your will, and, insofar as I can, I shall take care to fulfill your desire.

But you must attend to what Scripture says to every person who wishes to please the Lord: “Do not follow your desires”—that is, your blameworthy desires—“and turn away from your will,” namely, your carnal will (Ecclesiasticus 18:30); and: “There are ways that seem right to men, but their end plunges down to the depths of hell” (Proverbs 16:25).

### III

Concerning what follows there about Odacer, I have already answered you sufficiently in the preceding letters.

### IV

Concerning what follows immediately: “Because my messenger, the monk Altramnus, reported to you on my behalf that I wish to do nothing else in this matter except what you, Abbot Hugh, Count Theodoric, and your other faithful men should decide”: I know that this command did not proceed from me, nor did the brother himself claim that he had said such things to me.

I send him back to you, so that before your faithful men he may either admit that he said this or truthfully deny that he conveyed such a message to you on my behalf. Hence I think that, just as there was an error in the name, so there was also an error in the message. For this brother of ours, returning from you to me, conveyed to me on your behalf that he should kiss my foot and ask me to honor you by granting the bishopric of the Church of Beauvais to Odacer.

I replied that, as I knew would be better, more honorable, and more beneficial, I had taken care to honor you in this matter. I urged you, just as you professed on the day of your consecration, to honor God in the governance of the kingdom according to the custom of your predecessors, by consenting to him and preserving for the holy Church and its rulers the laws of him who said: “Those who honor me I will honor” (1 Samuel 2:30), as is written in the letters I sent to you through him.

He also told me what you had said concerning the will of Abbot Hugh, and how moderately Count Theodoric had answered your question about it.

### V

In what is written at the beginning of the letter which the aforesaid cleric delivered to me after the letters mentioned above—“If I do not consent to you in the ordination of Odacer, know for certain that I do not wish to treat your honor kindly, nor do I wish to consent to your rightful dignity and the privileges of your predecessors, but to resist your will in everything”—your writer lied both in meaning and in wording.

### VI

Concerning the honor of your predecessors, the emperors and kings, and how they decreed and preserved the privileges of the holy Church, its rulers, and its ministers, I have already taken care to write to you sufficiently in other letters. If those letters have not benefited you, neither will further ones.

### VII

Concerning what follows there: “How you would vindicate your honor to the utmost of your power against one equal to you; how much more ought you to despise him—namely, me—who, entrusted to your authority, strive to cast down your honor lest it prevail in strength”: whoever persuaded you to write this to me, however insignificant a minister of Christ I may be, did not know the Lord or his Scriptures well.

For, as has already become known to you from the divinely inspired Scriptures, there are two principal powers by which this world is governed: the sacred authority of pontiffs and royal power. The burden of priests is so much greater because they will render an account before the divine judgment even for the kings themselves. Pontiffs can ordain kings, but kings cannot consecrate pontiffs.

And God said to the pontiffs: “He who hears you hears me, and he who rejects you”—that is, despises and scorns you—“rejects me” (Luke 10:16); and: “Those who despise me shall be dishonored” (1 Samuel 2:30).

You therefore ought not to have written so shamelessly to a pontiff, however insignificant, saying that he was entrusted to your authority. For, as the Lord said to his apostles, of whom I am the least by merit but their successor by office: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15:16), so I too, according to my measure, can say with humble heart and voice: “You did not choose me to preside over the Church; rather, I, together with my colleagues and the other faithful of God and of your forebears, chose you to govern the kingdom, on the condition that you observe the laws owed to them.”

### VIII

Concerning what follows there:

“From this act—that is, because you entrusted the Church of Beauvais, vacant of its shepherd, to Odacer—you will do nothing more beyond what you have done until you have communicated the matter to your brother and your kinsmen, the kings; and, by their commands or authority together with your own, all the archbishops and bishops from their kingdoms and yours are summoned, so that the matter may then be authoritatively defined, with the dignity of your honor fully upheld”:

See to it that, because of this unlawful act, you do not suffer canonical sentences, either in this age or in the future. For we do not fear rendering an account before the archbishops and bishops for what we have done, because we have no other evangelical or apostolic writings, nor any other canons or decrees of the pontiffs of the Roman See, nor any other sacred laws by which the Catholic Church is governed together with the holy canons, than those which they have.

For with them, and also in the synod of the lord pope, we have already given a defensible account concerning the holy Scriptures, the sacred rules, and the laws.

### IX

You commanded that you would do nothing further concerning that unlawful act beyond what you have done. If you do not do so, the Lord will do it when it pleases him.

The Emperor Louis did not live as many years as his father Charles; your grandfather Charles did not live as many years as his father; your father did not live as many years as his father. And when you stand in the place where your grandfather and father stood at Compiègne, lower your eyes to where your father lies. If you do not know, ask where your grandfather died and where he lies.

Do not let your heart be lifted up before him who died for you and for all of us, and rose from the dead and now dies no more. Be certain that you will die, though you do not know on what day or at what hour. Therefore it is necessary for you and for all of us to be ready, according to the Lord’s summons, because we do not know at what hour our end will come.

Do not let your heart be exalted against him in whose hand our life and days rest. You will soon fail, but the holy Church with its rulers under Christ, its ruler, will remain according to his promise, like the full moon forever (Psalm 88:38).

### X

Concerning what follows there: “Moreover, if necessity arises, we shall do what is right”: as I understand it, you wished to write this to instill fear in me, so that, although unwilling, I might obey your command.

I therefore answer: “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man can do to me” (Psalm 117:6). And: “The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?” (Psalm 26:1).

Another Scripture says: “Lots are cast into the lap, but they are directed by the Lord” (Proverbs 16:33). And the Lord himself said to the governor before whom he stood: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above” (John 19:11). And the former highest archangel could not seize even one little sheep belonging to Job, God’s servant, unless the Lord permitted it.

Would that the Lord, through you or through whomever he pleases, would lead me from this prison—namely, this weak and aged body—to the one whom, by the gift of his grace, I desire with all my heart to see: not through my merits, which are nothing but evil, but through his undeserved mercy and gratuitous grace.

But concerning what you said—“Moreover, if it is necessary, you will do what is right”—I embrace what you promise: you will do what is right toward me. It is therefore right, as Scripture shows, that “by the very things through which anyone sins, by those things he should also be tormented” (Wisdom 11:17).

Because I consented to your election against the will, threats, and suggestions of many, I wish and rejoice that, if I sinned in that matter, then, with the Lord permitting it, I should receive retribution here through you and not in the future through the Lord, just as we read concerning Saint Paschasius, who, through ignorance, consented to someone’s election.

### XI

And since you are so greatly concerned about the ordination of Odacer, inform me of the appointed time when the bishops of the diocese of Rheims, as well as the venerable bishops and our beloved brothers who were sent to you with letters from the synod held at the shrine of Saint Macra, may assemble at the same place.

Then, if life and ability permit, I shall have myself carried there to meet them. Let your Odacer come with his electors, whether they are members of the palace or of the Church of Beauvais. If you wish, come there yourself, or send your representatives.

The Lord says: “He who does not enter the sheepfold through the door, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber” (John 10:1); and: “He who enters through the door into the sheepfold, to him the gatekeeper opens” (ibid., 3). “I am the door,” he says; “if anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (ibid., 9).

See, then—or hear through your representatives—whether the gatekeeper will open the door of his sheepfold to your Odacer, so that he may enter securely, that the sheep may hear his voice, and that he may not be a hired man but a shepherd, and that the Church of Beauvais may not groan under a hired man.

Let it be known to us, and let Odacer himself know with certainty, that if he does not come to us but chooses to remain in the obstinacy of his transgression, then, since the Apostle says that “the word of God is not bound” (2 Timothy 2:9)—the word of the Lord, which is living and effective and sharper than any two-edged sword (Hebrews 4:12)—we shall go to him wherever he may be in the province of Rheims.

What the sacred canons judge concerning a contemptuous person and an invader of the Church contrary to the laws and rules, we shall endeavor to carry out against him insofar as it pertains to us, so that he may never, nowhere in the province of Rheims, minister in an ecclesiastical rank. And all who thereafter associate with him in this matter shall, according to the sacred canons composed by the Spirit of the Lord and confirmed by the blood of Christ, be excommunicated until satisfaction has been made to the Church.

Moreover, whoever incites you in this matter against authority, reason, and his own salvation will bear judgment, whoever he may be, as the Apostle says (Galatians 5:10).

The Apostle Paul, compelled by necessity, wrote to the Corinthians: “I have become a fool; you compelled me” (2 Corinthians 12:11). And he who does not hide my groaning knows with what great sorrow, because you compelled me, I have written these things to you.

Know with complete certainty that, with the Lord’s help, neither any terror nor any blandishments, from anyone or from any persons, will make me deviate from the sacred laws and rules in this matter under discussion.

# LETTER XXI OF THE COUNCIL OF TUSIACUM TO THE INVADERS OF CHURCH PROPERTY AND THE PLUNDERERS OF THE POOR

## How and when church property came to be consecrated to the Lord, and how great the danger of plundering the poor is

*[Note: Our Hincmar wrote this letter.]*

*(In Labbe, Councils, volume VIII.)*

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 860, in the ninth indiction, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of November, a holy synod was assembled at the estate of Tusiacum in the parish of Toul, consisting of bishops from fourteen provinces—namely, those of Lyon, Rouen, Tours, Sens, Vienne, Arles, Besançon, Mainz, Cologne, Trier, Rheims, Bourges, Bordeaux, and Narbonne.

To all the faithful of God and sons of the holy Church to whom this notice of the divine constitution may come, it wishes peace and salvation in the Lord.

Almighty God, supreme and true, one and alone—the Father, that is, and the Son, who is his consubstantial Word, and the Holy Spirit of them both, coeternal and coequal with both—the undivided and inseparable Trinity, who alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen or can see, who is contained neither by a finite nor by an infinite extent of place, and is altered neither by a finite nor by an infinite succession of time—for in his substance, by which he is God, there is nothing that is shorter in part than in the whole—who is without beginning and remains without end, living in unchangeable eternity: he created all things together, from which times would proceed, places be filled, and the ages revolve through the temporal and local movements of things.

Among these things he created some spiritual and some bodily, visible and invisible. He formed matter which no other, and no one else, but he himself entirely instituted as formless and formable, so that it preceded its formation not in time but in origin. Scripture bears witness: “He who lives forever created all things together” (Ecclesiasticus 18). And: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Genesis 1), and all his works, which are very good, those in heaven and those on earth.

He also created two rational creatures from among these creatures of his: the angelic and the human, endowed with the gift of his image and likeness and possessing free choice. Thus, just as he himself is good and voluntary not by necessity but by nature, so those rational creatures might be good not under compulsion of necessity but by nature and likewise voluntarily.

For if they had been such that, by the judgment of free will, they could neither avoid evil nor do good, they would be more like stones and other insensible and irrational things than like God, and they would rightly lack his recompense; nor would there be any basis on which God could reward them according to the quality of their will and action.

He is good because he wills, not because he is compelled; and he possesses the will to be good, not accidentally, but essentially, so as to be both good and omnipotent. According to the opinion of some, this does not conflict with what the Apostle says: “He cannot deny himself” (1 Timothy 2).

Moreover, he can neither sin nor die. Yet the angel and man, who were able to sin, are read to have been endowed with the dignity of his image and likeness. For likeness is one thing and the mark of likeness another; to be an image is one thing, and to be made according to an image another.

Only the consubstantial Son is essentially the image of the invisible Father, the radiance and figure of God the Father’s substance. In this respect, it belongs even more to the Almighty’s omnipotence that he can do nothing other than will what is good, and nothing other than be good and omnipotent. He cannot deny himself, sin, die, change, be deceived, become wretched, or be overcome. Far be it that the Almighty should be able to do such things.

But because he does not will them, he cannot do them; indeed, he cannot will them. Justice cannot will what is unjust, wisdom cannot will what is foolish, and truth cannot will what is false. Thus truth not only shows that the Almighty is not less than omnipotent because he cannot do these things; truth also compels us to conclude that one who could do them would not be omnipotent.

God is willing whatever he is. He is therefore willingly eternal, unchangeable, truthful, blessed, and unconquerable. If, then, what he does not will could exist, he would not be omnipotent. But he is omnipotent; therefore he can do whatever he wills. Consequently, what he does not will to exist cannot exist, and he is called Almighty because he can do whatever he wills.

Of him the Psalm also says: “In heaven and on earth he has done whatever he desired” (Psalm 134). For nothing occurs in heaven or on earth unless he either mercifully does it or justly permits it to occur.

He wills all human beings to be saved and wills no one to perish. Yet the just Lord, loving justice and not willing iniquity, does not wish forcibly to remove from those whom he made in his image and likeness the free choice of their will, even after the fall of the first man. He is ready to repay them according to their merit, as Scripture shows: “Who is the man,” it says, “who desires life?” (Psalm 33.)

And as though the man answered, “I do,” the Lord says: “Turn away from evil and do good” (ibid.). Conversely, the one who wishes to be saved says: “I will sacrifice to you willingly” (Psalm 53), and: “I will confess to him according to my will” (Psalm 27).

Of him it is written: “He will not deprive those who walk in innocence of good things” (Psalm 83). But so that those who walk may walk and persevere in innocence, grace heals and assists their free choice, as the Apostle testifies: “The grace of God was not empty in me, but I labored more abundantly than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God with me” (1 Corinthians 15).

By these and other sayings of Scripture it is shown that, after the fall of the first man, a free will remains in man for willing good, beginning good, completing it, and persevering in good: liberated by grace, healed from corruption by grace, preceded and assisted by grace, and to be crowned by grace.

But the man who falls away from good and advances in evil, after the fall of the first man, has free choice—free with respect to righteousness, but enslaved to sin. Those who, by this will, distance themselves from God, who wishes to gather the children of Jerusalem while they are unwilling, will perish.

Thus, because God’s grace is present, the world is saved; and because free choice exists in man, the world will be judged.

From these rational creatures—the angelic and the human—he placed angels in heavenly glory to know him and praise him forever. Therefore a certain part of the angels, intoxicated with pride, fell through free choice; these are called devils. Through their own fault they became such that they no longer will or can be good in merit.

Those who remained by free choice in the will of the Creator, however, received as a gift, through his grace and the recompense of justice, what the Creator—whose mark of likeness they are—possesses essentially: that they neither will nor are able to be evil.

God the maker formed man bodily from the clay of the earth. He breathed into him a soul which he had created, through an operation of his power incomprehensible to us, in character and eternity according to his image and likeness; in this soul—namely, the inner man—he dwells in us through faith.

Although our outward man is corrupted, we are renewed by putting on the new man, who was created according to God in righteousness, holiness, and truth. And he made this first man a living soul—[the source reads *ventem*, apparently an OCR or textual error; the intended sense is “living”]—that is, he made him a rational soul and a life-giving flesh, subsisting in two substances and from two substances, namely spirit and clay, in the unity of one person.

He placed him in the paradise of delights which he had planted from the beginning, so that he might work it or work in it, just as he had commanded him, and guard it so that he would not commit what and in the manner he had forbidden him.

From his side he fashioned a woman while he slept in the sleep of the body. Hence he said: “The two shall be one flesh” (Genesis 2). Therefore they are no longer two but one flesh. According to his foreknowledge, by which he knows all things even before they occur, he thus demonstrated by a true sign that, without the transmission of a man’s seed, he himself would come into the flesh from a woman in order to redeem the man whom he had formed in the flesh.

He who fashioned him from dust, and without the transmission of seed made a man from a man, also fashions human beings from seed. He who, by the death of the body, died on the cross for all who were debtors to death—alone among the dead free from the debt of death, the Son of God predestined in power according to the Spirit of sanctification—became the head, light, and example of all the predestined.

Born of a woman, and made under obedience to the law although he owed nothing to the law, he came to redeem those who were destined to be under the law of sin and death, so that we might receive the adoption of sons which we were destined to lose in Adam.

For those who would wish to believe in him—whether they had preceded his coming in the flesh or would be like them, since “we believe that we shall be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they were” (Acts 15)—he was to build the Church with his side opened by a lance. From that side he brought forth water and blood, by which the Church is now watered by font and cup: that is, it is cleansed by the water of baptism and, through faith, incorporated into him by drinking the blood of redemption, justified by the Spirit of sanctification.

“This is a great mystery in Christ and in the Church” (Ephesians 5). By the same Holy Spirit, from the womb of the undefiled divine font, the Church regenerates those born to her, by whom Christ was also born from the undefiled Virgin.

The same first man—for Eve herself is Adam—was created so that, having been made by the Creator, he might rule over creation, order the world in justice and equity, and judge judgment with an upright heart, if he had remained in the law of life and discipline which he had received, with free choice; that is, if he had persevered in the will of the Creator so as not to sin.

Then neither he nor mortals would have died, nor would he have generated children subject to death and hell. But, as a reward for this perseverance and in recompense for justice, he would have received as a gift, just as the holy angels did, what the Creator—according to whose image and likeness he was created—possesses essentially: that he would neither will to sin nor be able thereafter to fall.

But the devil envied him, because an earthly man was destined to ascend through due obedience to the place from which the angelic spirit had fallen through pride. The man believed the devil, who persuaded him with lies, more than he obeyed the will of his Creator. Abusing his free choice, he abandoned God; and, justly abandoned by God, he sinned and fell.

Through willing evil he lost the power to do good, although by the power to do good he could have overcome the will to do evil. Thus the mass of the entire human race became a mass of perdition. If no one were rescued from it for salvation, God’s justice would be beyond reproach. But because many are saved, God’s grace is ineffable.

From the very beginning of the world, beginning with righteous Abel, he sent forth through patriarchs, teachers of the law, prophets, and righteous men heralds of human salvation to the world, languishing in its weakness and wasting away in the darkness of its sins, proclaiming salvation through words and signs and offering consolation until the light of the world himself should come.

At last he himself, who is always one and everywhere one with the Father and the Holy Spirit in the essence of his majesty, for us human beings and for our salvation, conceived through the working of that same Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary—that is, from the substance of virginal maternal flesh—came to us through the presence of assumed flesh.

In two natures and from two substances, namely divinity and humanity, he was true God in every respect and true man, subsisting in the unity of one person with a rational soul and human flesh. Through deeds and words he invited believers in him to another age: namely, to eternal glory, which the holy angels possess in heaven, and which the first man had been created to obtain.

Since we cannot reach it except by the way taught to us by him of whom it is written, “It was necessary for Christ to suffer these things and to enter into his glory” (Luke 24:26), he is the guide and teacher of this journey: through the labors and sufferings which we earned in our first parent, we earn the kingdom of God, because “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Romans 8:18).

And as we contend in the arena of this struggle, we cannot endure without provisions for the journey.

The primitive Church—that is, the faithful at the beginning of the Church’s birth—sold everything they possessed and brought the price of their possessions to the apostles’ feet. They taught that a rational human being ought not to be subjected to wealth, but ought to rule over it, and use it for passing needs rather than love it as a means of attaining eternity. From that price distributions were made to each according to his need.

[Col. 0126B]

When, however, by God’s grace, the number of believers began to increase, the income from the proceeds was insufficient for their support, since not everyone contributed to this purpose and they could not be compelled to do so, and they could not be compelled to abstain entirely from marriage and worldly activities lest the world perish, until all who are to be saved—that is, all the predestined, as it is written, the children of God who were scattered—namely, scattered throughout the mass of the whole human race condemned to destruction by reason of its abandonment, and chosen from it before the world was made by God’s predestination, to whom nothing past has passed away and nothing future has yet happened—should be gathered together in one, namely, into the fullness of the heavenly and eternal Church, to which as many of the saved and incorporated human beings will ascend as there remained chosen angels in the place from which the devil and his followers fell, so that one flock of one shepherd, filled with the perpetual vision and perfect knowledge of the undivided Trinity—which is the life not only of human beings but also of angels—may rejoice without end in glorious fellowship:

[Col. 0126C]

The same Lord and teacher of salvation, through his saints, in whom and with whom he spoke, and through whom he governed his Church and continues to govern it to this day by their merits and prayers, established that believers should no longer sell their possessions and estates in their entirety, but should consecrate portions of those possessions to the Lord. Therefore, those who adhere, as it were, in a special way to the same Lord of lords, and who live as ministers of the word, of the gifts of eternal salvation, and as mediators between God and human beings through the continual work of intercession, are to live; and all necessities without which human frailty cannot subsist are to be supplied to them as alms from those who have consecrated those possessions to the Lord.

[Col. 0126D]

Thus, while Christ’s poor and the ministers of the Church subsist in the present world from these resources, the donors of the possessions, through their faithful almsgiving, are cleansed from sin—as also in baptism—by being turned completely away from evil, persevering in right faith and good works, and are made sharers in heaven with Christ, to whom they had devoted them, as he himself says in the Gospel: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11); and again: “Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me. Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25).

[Col. 0127A]

Therefore, just as those who have consecrated themselves, their wealth, and their possessions to the Lord with faithful devotion are called and made heirs of God and fellow heirs of Christ by the prophets and apostles and by the Lord himself, so also such possessions and resources, consecrated to the Lord in his churches and for the particular uses of his servants, are called, in a special sense, God’s inheritance on account of Christ’s faithful, who are nourished by them and from them, since the whole world and its fullness belong to him.

For just as, when the whole house of Israel was called the Lord’s inheritance, the tribe of Levi nevertheless—like a tithe still chosen by God in Abraham’s loins—was called the Lord’s special inheritance, portion, or allotment, together with tithes and firstfruits, cities and suburbs, villages, possessions, and all resources; so also these people, who are called *eleroi*—that is, “the lot” or “the portion” of the Lord—together with all the churches belonging to them, that is, the divine folds, are called and exist as Christ’s special inheritance, although all believers and future believers, both from the circumcision and those from the uncircumcision, are called Christ’s inheritance. The Prophet says: “O God, the nations have entered into your inheritance” (Psalm 78); and: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Psalm 2).

[Col. 0127B]

Whoever unlawfully misuses anything belonging to these is, without any doubt, punished by that curse and held liable to it—the curse that both the heavenly and the entire earthly Church continually sings to the Lord:

[Col. 0127C]

“They said, ‘Let us take possession of God’s sanctuary as an inheritance.’ My God, set them like a wheel, and like straw before the face of the wind. As fire burns the forest, and as flame consumes the mountains, so pursue them in your storm, and in your anger trouble them. Fill their faces with disgrace, so that they may seek your name, O Lord. Let them be ashamed and troubled forever and ever; let them be confounded and perish, and let them know that your name is Lord, that you alone are the Most High in all the earth” (Psalm 82).

The holy Pope Anacletus, ordained presbyter by the blessed apostle Peter himself and later made his successor as bishop in the Roman see, judged together with the priests of the whole world:

“Whoever takes anything from father or mother is a participant in homicide. Our father is undoubtedly God, who created us; but our mother is the Church, which spiritually regenerated us in baptism. Therefore, whoever steals, takes away, or defrauds Christ’s money and the Church’s money is a homicide, and as a homicide will be reckoned before the sight of the just Judge. Whoever steals his neighbor’s money commits iniquity; but whoever takes away the Church’s property commits sacrilege and must be judged as a sacrilegious person.”

[Col. 0127D]

Likewise, the holy Pope and martyr Urbanus said:

“Church goods and resources are called offerings because they are offered to the Lord; they are the vows of the faithful, the prices of sins, and the patrimonies of the poor. If anyone steals them, he is guilty of the condemnation of Ananias and Sapphira, and such a person ought to be handed over to Satan, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord” (1 Corinthians 5).

Likewise, the holy Pope Lucius said:
