“We expel and condemn, by apostolic authority, as anathematized from the thresholds of the holy Church, those who steal Church property and resources, and we judge them to be sacrilegious—[Col. 0128A] not only them, but also all who consent to them, because not only those who commit an act are judged guilty, but also those who consent to its perpetrators. Equal punishment embraces both those who act and those who consent. Those whose office is to prevent, restrain, and correct such things cannot be free from this punishment if they do not take care to correct them.”

And Saint Gregory, in a letter to the subdeacon Sabinus, says:

“It is sacrilege and contrary to the laws if anyone attempts, through the efforts of his perverse will, to retain for his own advantage anything that has been left to venerable places.”

And Saint Augustine, in his sermon on the holy Gospel of John, says:

“Judas is the sacrilegious thief of sacred and Lordly treasuries; and whoever steals or snatches anything from the Church is compared with the ruined Judas.”

[Col. 0128B]

Likewise, in the sacred canons dictated by the Holy Spirit and confirmed by Christ’s decree, it is written (Council of Toledo I, canon 11):

“If anyone among the powerful has stripped a cleric, or any poor person, or a religious person, and the bishop has sent to him ordering him to hear the case, but he has refused, let written communications immediately pass in turn through all the bishops of the province, and through as many as can be reached, so that he may be regarded as excommunicated until he hears the case and restores what belongs to another.”

And it is written likewise (Council of Agde, canon 4):

“Clerics and laypeople who have presumed to retain offerings of their parents, whether given during life or left by testament, or who have thought that what they themselves gave to churches or monasteries ought to be taken away, shall, as the holy synod has decreed, be excluded from the churches as murderers of the poor until they restore them.”

[Col. 0128C]

Therefore all the more powerful—each in his own rank and dignity—must be extremely careful not to presume to take Church property for themselves to their own condemnation, nor to weary or afflict the churches of God and the places of the saints with unusual customs. They must know that, as we have stated above, Church property consists of the vows of the faithful, the patrimonies of the poor, and the prices of sins; and that they belong to Christ’s protection and defense. Christ entrusted them to the rulers and leading men of the earth for protection and preservation, not for affliction, usurpation, or presumption.

[Col. 0128D]

For whatever pretext of usefulness or necessity anyone may put forward, he sees the hearts of all, knows human thoughts, rewards actions, and will in no way leave even thoughts unrewarded. Therefore everyone who wishes to be saved, to be freed from eternal death, and to attain eternal life must listen with the most attentive ear of the heart to what the Holy Spirit has spoken through those to whom the Lord said:

“Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28);

“It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10);

“Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 18);

“Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John 20);

“Whoever hears you hears me; and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10).

For those who shine with miracles in heaven and on earth, who live with us even to this day and will live with our successors forever, say that their reward is with the Lord:

“If anyone wishes to receive or give the Church’s offerings outside the Church, without the knowledge of the bishop or of the person to whom such duties have been entrusted, and does not wish to act with his advice, let him be anathema” (Council of Gangra, canon 7).

“Anathema” is interpreted in the Roman language as “alienation,” because everyone who does such a thing, as long as he remains in those sins, [Col. 0129B] even if we bishops—who, in the apostles and with the apostles, received the power of binding and loosing, not by our own merit but by divine grace—are sometimes slow, sometimes ignorant of the divine meaning, sometimes unaware of what is being done, and sometimes unable to correct what has been done as expediency requires, and thus fail to carry out or even neglect what has been decreed, so that we do not separate such a person, by excommunicating him, from the Church and the fellowship of the faithful, is nevertheless already excommunicated and condemned in advance by the sacred canons, until he abandons that sin and, through ecclesiastical satisfaction and priestly reconciliation, receives the Lord’s grace and the fellowship of the faithful.

[Col. 0129A]

Whoever, entangled in his sins and such crimes, ends this life before the necessary satisfaction will in no way be able to have communion and fellowship with the elect in the kingdom of God; nor will he ever be able to escape the punishments of hell and the fellowship of demons.

[Col. 0129C]

But perhaps there are people who, disregarding privileges concerning places and things dedicated to God and confirmed by the hands of the saints, lighten for themselves—as they wish, not because they are able—the excommunications imposed by the saints of the Lord upon usurpers of Church property and resources, saying that they are not bound by the condemnation inflicted for this offense, that is, by the bond of anathema.

[Col. 0129D]

Saint Gregory says of such people in a letter to the patrician Theoctista:

“They themselves are witnesses against themselves that they are not Christians, since they think that the bonds of the holy Church can be loosed by futile efforts. Therefore they do not consider the absolution of the holy Church, which she grants to the faithful, to be true if they do not consider her bonds effective. There is no need to dispute at length against them, because they must be utterly despised and anathematized; and by the very means through which they think they deceive the truth, they are truly bound in their sins.”

If, therefore, there are people who, under the Christian name, dare either to preach such things or silently to retain them within themselves, I, together with all Catholic bishops and the entire Church, anathematize them, because they think and speak contrary to the truth.

Robberies and plunderings, which in these kingdoms are now so commonly practiced by almost everyone that they are treated as though they were not sins, or as though they were light sins, were placed by the holy apostle Paul—through whom Christ spoke, and who, before paying the debt of death, was caught up to the third heaven and to paradise, where he learned the Lord’s secret words—among mortal crimes. He says:

[Col. 0130A]

“Do you not know that the unjust will not possess the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor men who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor robbers will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6).

And again he says:

“If anyone is a fornicator, or greedy, or serves idols, or is a reviler, or a drunkard, or a robber, with such a person do not even take food” (1 Corinthians 5);

that is, a disciple of Christ, a Christian, may not take food before satisfaction—that is, correction and amendment, and worthy repentance—not with such a human being but with such a devil.

[Col. 0130B]

The holy apostle John, Christ’s chosen and beloved disciple, who reclined upon his breast at the supper, even forbids greeting such a person:

“Do not even say ‘Hail’ to him, and do not receive him into your house. For whoever says to him, ‘Hail,’ shares in his evil works” (2 John 10).

Likewise Saint Paul says to every Christian:

“Do not share in the sins of others” (1 Timothy 5).

And the Lord, when he comes to judge the living and the dead, when at his coming all human beings will rise with their bodies and render an account of their own deeds, promises in the Gospel that he will say to those who, although they could have redeemed their sins through alms, refused to do so:

“Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25).

Therefore robbers must consider where those who steal what belongs to others will go, if those who did not give alms will go into hell.

Again, through the prophet Isaiah the Lord says to robbers:

[Col. 0130C]

“The plunder of the poor is in your house” (Isaiah 3);

and:

“The widow’s tears descend upon her cheek, and her cry against the one who causes them to flow rises from her cheek to heaven before God; and the Lord will not delight in them” (Sirach 35)—that is, in the widow’s tears. He is the father of orphans and defender of widows, and he complains against the judges, saying:

“The widow’s cause does not come before them” (Isaiah 1).

Therefore robbers must know in whose house—whether of the body or of the dwelling—the poor person’s plunder is found, because the Holy Spirit does not dwell in that house, but an evil spirit does.

[Col. 0130D]

And if such a person approaches communion of the body and blood of Christ before worthy satisfaction, he is not cleansed from sin through that communion, but is possessed more fully by the devil, like Judas, when, full of robbery, iniquity, greed, and desire, he presumed to receive communion at the Lord Savior’s hand during the Lord’s Supper.

Perhaps there will be people who, when they hear this, will say: “We will not receive communion.” But they must know that just as the Lord said:

“Unless someone is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3),

so also he said:

“Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6).

And just as he said:

“Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark 16),

so also he said:

“Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him; and I will raise him up on the last day, and he will not die forever” (John 6).

[Col. 0131A]

Therefore no other refuge of salvation remains except that whoever wishes to be saved should turn away from these evils and from other mortal crimes, be reconciled to God through repentance, and receive the life-giving mysteries, so that he may be able to live forever.

For it profits no one to be called a Christian if he does not perform Christ’s works, which Christ himself commanded. Indeed, a Christian who, under Christ’s name, worships the devil’s idols is called a Christian all the more to his own judgment.

For Truth itself, who is God, declares that whoever serves mammon—for this is the name given to the demon appointed over riches—serves the devil or worships the devil’s idols. Whoever serves lust serves the desire of the flesh as a god; therefore it is written:

“Their glory is in their shame” (Philippians 3),

that is, in the genital members, which are commonly called the shameful parts.

[Col. 0131B]

For Scripture called God “glory,” when it says of the Jews:

“They exchanged their glory for the likeness of a calf that eats grass” (Psalm 106).

And concerning those who boast when they overcome chastity by their own lust and stain the beds of others, the Apostle says the same as above:

“Their glory is in their shame, who set their minds on earthly things” (Philippians 3).

And elsewhere Scripture says:

“They rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things” (Proverbs 2).

Against this he commands that whoever boasts should boast in the Lord (1 Corinthians 1).

Whoever serves greed worships idols, as Paul says:

“Greed, which is the service of idols” (Colossians 3).

Whoever serves gluttony and drunkenness worships the belly as a god; therefore he also says:

“Their god is the belly” (Philippians 3).

[Col. 0131C]

The Apostle calls these things so, not with reference to the dignity of those who rule, but to the wretchedness of those who serve.

Whoever unjustly oppresses his brother—that is, a Christian—through power, or administers justice in exchange for receiving gifts, imitates the devil and sells justice, which is Christ, and is thus like Judas.

Whoever perverts the truth out of envy, or conceals the truth, or speaks it for gifts, imitates the devil and is like Judas. The same is to be understood of the other vices. Whoever serves any vice is subject to the devil who has authority over that same vice, and will be tormented with him without end unless he has previously repented worthily.

[Col. 0131D]

And lest the rulers of the earth, or any Christians, say: “God gave stricter commands to bishops, presbyters, and monks; we, who are laypeople and secular persons, cannot attend to all these things,” let them hear what the Lord says in the Gospel:

“Whoever is of God hears God’s words. The reason you do not hear is that you are not of God” (John 8).

And it is certain that whoever is not of God belongs to the devil’s party.

What will it profit a person if he possesses even the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul? Or what exchange will a person give for his soul?

Therefore, whoever he may be, let every person hear the Lord saying to him through the prophet:

“I will show you, O man, what is good: to do judgment and justice, and to walk attentively with your God” (Micah 6).

[Col. 0132A]

Brothers and sons, we direct these commands from the Lord to you, whatever rank or dignity each Christian may occupy. The Lord says concerning all human beings to every bishop:

“But you, hearing, shall announce to them from me” (Ezekiel 33).

He says “from me,” not “from you.” Therefore receive these things as the Lord’s commands. You cannot resist his power, and you ought not to resist his will and command, if you do not wish your own enemies to obstruct your salvation.

We can neither be silent nor dare to remain silent about such matters before you, for the Lord says through the prophet that, if we do not announce them to you, he will require your blood from our hand. And before the Lord in heaven we will be degraded by those Fathers and predecessors whose place we occupy on earth if we do not carry out what they established by rules inspired by God.

[Col. 0132B]

Therefore, if you do not correct yourselves as soon as possible in those matters about which you are being admonished, we, together with the bishop of the apostolic see and the entire unanimity of the priests, will separate you from the fellowship of Christ and of his faithful—those in heaven and us on earth. Do not compel us to do this; for Christ’s sake and for your salvation we earnestly implore you.

But if you strive to obey the Lord’s commands, you will work for your salvation, both present and future, and you will be our glory and crown before God. For we will render an account to him concerning you on the day of judgment, just as you will undoubtedly render an account concerning yourselves and concerning all those entrusted to you.

Therefore strive with the greatest diligence to be separated from the company of the wicked on that dreadful day. This will happen if now you separate yourselves from diabolical and evil works and from perverse people, defending against the devil, vices, and sins the honor that belongs to you as human beings made in God’s image.

[Col. 0132C]

For this purpose, as it is written, every human being was made: to fear God and keep his commandments. For his sake God became human, and he lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit forever and ever.

## LETTER XXII. TO RODULFUS OF BOURGES AND FROTARIUS OF BORDEAUX, METROPOLITANS OF AQUITAINE

**Concerning the marriage of Stephanus and the daughter of Count Regimundus**

[Col. 0132D]

HINCMARUS, archbishop of Rheims in name but not in merit, and servant of God’s people, sends the fullest greeting in the Savior to the most reverend archbishop of Bourges and dearest brother Rodulfus, and to his brother Frotarius, honorable archbishop of Bordeaux, together with all the venerable bishops of your provinces.

Recently, at a synod of bishops of fourteen provinces—namely, those of Lyon, Rouen, Tours, Sens, Vienne, Arles, Besançon, Mainz, Cologne, Trier, Rheims, Bourges, Bordeaux, and Narbonne—held at the village of Tusiacum in the parish of Toul in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 860, in the ninth indiction, in the month of November, letters were brought forward presenting Count Regimundus’s complaint against Stephanus.

[Col. 0133A]

The complaint stated that Regimundus had legally given his daughter to the aforementioned Stephanus for marriage, but that he did not make use of her as his wife because, as he confessed, he had once engaged in carnal intercourse with a relative of the same girl. He did not wish to indicate with whom this had occurred or how closely related she was to the girl.

This was the substance of the letter, if I recall it correctly, though I do not retain its exact words, as it was read out at the synod. Although such an accusation did not deserve to receive a synodal response, since no one can regularly accuse another in writing while absent, and since, if he had legally given his daughter in marriage to another, he had released her from his authority, he could not, on account of this matter—about which it might perhaps be unclear whether it was true or not, or which might be interpreted differently from what had been stated—canonically accuse the man to whom he had given her.

[Col. 0133B]

For this reason, if necessity requires it, the wife ought to bring an accusation or complaint against her husband; the father, however, ought to seek advice on her behalf and to act sufficiently for her, by persuading or advising her husband’s correction in whatever ways he can.

But since this matter had been debated by many people for approximately three years, and since both men were noble and illustrious, powerful according to the dignity of the world, and since, if they continued to disagree with each other over this matter, the Church might suffer the greatest scandal and the kingdom the greatest injury, and since Stephanus was then engaged in the service of the lord king, it seemed good to the synod to summon him and to learn from him what he had to say about these matters.

When he was summoned and these things had been reported, after some objections in his reply, he asked that he be permitted to speak only with the bishops. When the others had withdrawn, he disclosed to the bishops what seemed appropriate to him.

[Col. 0133C]

Among other things, the bishops said that, since Regimundus’s letters concerned matters of such a kind, matters discussed by almost everyone throughout many kingdoms, they could neither give him secret counsel nor issue a private judgment. Therefore he himself said that he wished what had been kept within him concerning this matter to become known to everyone, and wished to obtain necessary counsel and have a salutary judgment issued for him. Nevertheless, he first wished the synod patiently to hear his statement, and only then to give him counsel and pronounce judgment.

[Col. 0133D]

And to introduce him as speaking:

“According to what commonly happens in the fragile age of youth,” Stephanus said, “I had intercourse with a certain young woman. But when the time came for me to seek a legitimate marriage according to the custom of my predecessors, with the consent of my parents and friends, I legally asked Regimundus, a noble man, for his daughter, suitable to my birth, as my wife, and, having obtained her, legally betrothed her.

[Col. 0134A]

“Coming to my senses and knowing what I had done, I went to my confessor and sought his advice. Since the young woman with whom I had engaged in carnal intercourse was a relative of this girl, and since I had heard that persons related to one another from the fourth degree onward could not be joined in marriage, I asked whether I could join this girl, who had been betrothed to me, to myself in marriage while secretly remaining under penance, without eternal condemnation for either her or me.

“He showed me a book which, as I hope, he called the canons, and read before me that, for as long as the proximity of affinity could be reckoned, neither I nor any Christian could licitly be joined to his female relative, or to a woman whom his relative had possessed, or to two female relatives; and that, as long as we remained in such incest, neither she nor I could perform fruitful penance. Nor could such incest be healed except by our separation from one another.

[Col. 0134B]

“In the meantime, discord arose between my lord, my senior, the king, and my youth, to such an extent that I could not securely remain in that kingdom. Therefore, constrained on both sides, I could neither break off the betrothal nor dare to take the same betrothed woman as my wife, lest, in addition to the disagreement with my senior, the disagreement of Regimundus himself and of her noble parents should be added, and so either he would drive me completely from the kingdom or, if I wished to remain in the kingdom, I would perish.

“For this reason I avoided taking my betrothed as my wife through two royal assemblies. At last, however, compelled by necessity, because my life was in danger, I endowed her and received her with the honor of a public wedding. But, lest I destroy her, who was still uncorrupted, together with myself, and acquire an even greater destruction for myself, I resolved to preserve her untouched until now.

[Col. 0134C]

“And since the truth of the matter is in every respect as I have stated, and since I have done this neither by deceit, hatred, contempt for anyone, nor love of another woman, but only as I have just narrated to you with God as my witness, I will demonstrate its truth to you myself, through my parents and friends, or through my faithful men, by an oath or by any other suitable means you prefer. And if you wish and ask it, I will send as many of my servants as you determine to judgment concerning this matter. Whatever counsel you give me concerning it according to God, for my salvation, and according to the world, for suitable honor, the reconciliation of Regimundus, and the safety and honor of the girl herself, I am prepared to obey in every respect in which I am able.”

[Col. 0134D]

After hearing him, the synod ordered him to withdraw. Then, after each person had spoken as seemed appropriate to him, it was decreed that you, the archbishops of the same province, together with your fellow bishops, should convene a synod at a suitable place and time in that kingdom, and that a public assembly should be held in which the prince would be present with the leading men of the land. This was so that, God forbid, when these illustrious men gathered from both sides with the assistance of their parents and friends, a seditious tumult might arise through the devil’s activity.

The king, together with the noble men, should arrange to pacify this matter between the noble men. You, however, should strive to settle it by episcopal authority and canonical definition, and bring it to its proper and salutary conclusion.

When Stephanus was recalled, this condition was proposed to him, and he accepted it most gratefully.

[Col. 0135A]

As for the manner and order of the decision in this matter, since the poverty of my small understanding attempted, as the synod instructed, to suggest what it thought about it, the holy unanimity was pleased by common consent that the matter should be committed to writing and transmitted to your wisdom as it had then been accepted in council.

For this reason I have not done so as though the following matters were necessary for you, who already know them, nor as though I were arrogantly asserting the authority of special knowledge or boasting of the audacity of a decision. Rather, as the servant of the Church and of all of you—that is, the servant of the servants of the Lord and minister of the Lord’s people—I have endeavored, with devoted obedience, to gather these things as I was able, though not as I ought, and to transmit what I gathered to you.

In these matters I have not wished to set out anything concerning civil judgment, whose judges we bishops ought not to be, but have briefly attempted to note, as far as memory permits, what is known to belong to ecclesiastical definition.

[Col. 0135B]

Saint Gregory demonstrates the order of judgment concerning persons who have not confessed voluntarily or been openly convicted—for no one can otherwise be regularly judged, as Pope Leo decrees—in his *Commonitorium* to John the Defender, saying:

“First, so that judgment may proceed in an orderly manner, there must be different accusers and different witnesses. Next, the nature of the case must be examined, to determine whether it is worthy of exile or condemnation. In the presence of the accused, testimony must be given against him under oath and inserted into the written record of the proceedings. The accused must have the opportunity to respond and defend himself.

“It is also necessary to inquire carefully into the persons of the accusers and witnesses: what their status and reputation are; whether they are poor; whether perhaps they hold any enmity against the accused; and whether they have given testimony from hearsay or have expressly testified that they know the matter personally. The sentence decided in the presence of the parties must be read out in writing, and thus everything must be solemnly confirmed.”

[Col. 0135C]

But in a manifest case known to many, or in a case confessed in such a way as this—provided, however, that the girl says that it happened as Stephanus professes, since we often hear among men and women that what one says the other frequently denies—witnesses are not to be sought. Saint Ambrose says this in his letter to the Corinthians, explaining the Apostle’s judgment concerning the fornicator:

“It is not the judge’s place to condemn without an accuser, because the Lord did not cast out Judas, although he was a thief, since he had not been accused. Once this deed was known, he ought to have been expelled from the gathering of the brethren, for everyone knew his crime and did not denounce it. He publicly kept his stepmother in the place of a wife; in this matter there was no need for witnesses, nor could the crime be concealed by any evasion.”

And shortly afterward:

“Absent in bodily presence but present by the authority of the Spirit, who is nowhere absent, I have already judged, as though present, the man who committed this act.”

[Col. 0135D]

Therefore Stephanus must bring the girl to the synod, and the girl’s father must come, and the girl must be questioned whether what Stephanus says is true: that he has preserved her untouched until now.

And since we have heard concerning the other woman that, wishing to be freed from her husband, she has already, as is reported, been persuaded to say certain things about herself that were not true, the freedom due to her must be granted, and the danger must be pointed out to her, lest, because she has been persuaded, she confess a falsehood as the truth.

[Col. 0136A]

And if she says that it happened as Stephanus states, then, if necessary, credence consonant with reason and authority should be given to an oath concerning the matter, or, if necessity so demands, satisfaction must be sought by judgment through a suitable person, so that it may be established that Stephanus withdrew from carnal intercourse with this girl neither through deceit nor for any other reason, but for the reason that he himself indicated to the synod—namely, because he had carnally lain with a woman related to his betrothed by blood and close kinship of the flesh.

For this is what holy Pope Leo and blessed Gregory clearly decree must be done under oath, whether by a presbyter or by anyone at all, man or woman, noble or lowborn, in a doubtful case, as anyone who wishes to read may discover. Among other things, the younger blessed Gregory says in the letter sent through the presbyter Denuald [Col. 0136B] to Boniface, bishop of Mainz:

“In a case,” he says, “in which there are no certain witnesses to establish the truth of the accusation brought forward, an oath shall be required, and let the accused produce as witness to the purity of his innocence Him to whom everything is naked and open; let him have as the witness of his conscience the one whom he will also have as judge.”

This purgation by oath is extremely customary both in ecclesiastical and in secular laws, and it is established that it arose from the truth of the faith even in the earliest centuries. A judicial proceeding, however, is ordinarily conducted only for the concord of peace and charity between equals; it is conducted by subjects for the satisfaction of superiors, and in this case it cannot be demanded with authority unless it is undertaken by agreement.

Having learned the truth from this, since we have been told that Stephen is required to name the woman and demonstrate a definite relationship of affinity, because of intercourse with whom he cannot safely join himself in carnal union to this girl, we have thought it fitting to set down here what apostolic authority has decreed on this matter and the Catholic Church maintains—since something contrary to ecclesiastical reason and authority and to the custom of Christian devotion is being demanded from him, if indeed it is being demanded.

“Leo sends greetings to all the bishops throughout Campania, Samnium, Picenum, and all the provinces. I am moved by great indignation and afflicted by profound sorrow because I have discovered that some of you have forgotten the apostolic tradition and are devoted to the pursuit of their own error.”

And a little later:

“Concerning the penance that is demanded from the faithful: a written public declaration concerning the kind of each individual sin should not be published, since it is sufficient for the guilt of consciences to be disclosed to priests alone by secret confession. Although that fullness of faith appears praiseworthy which, out of fear of God, is not ashamed to blush before human beings, nevertheless, because not everyone’s sins are of such a kind that those seeking penance are unafraid to make them public, let the objectionable custom be removed, lest many be kept away from the remedies of penance while they either blush or fear that their deeds will be disclosed to their enemies, who might strike them under the force of the laws. That confession is sufficient which is first offered to God and then also to the priest, who approaches as a sinner on behalf of the sins of those doing penance. More people can then be summoned to penance if the penitent’s conscience is not made public to the ears of the people.”

And since both the Old and the New Law teach how marriage ought to be contracted—the Lord giving command through Moses and the Gospel demonstrating it—Matthew says: “When Mary the mother of Jesus had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together” (Matt. I), that is, before they came together in the celebration of the wedding, as he likewise showed in the wedding that he deigned to sanctify by his presence and to illuminate by the miracle performed there.

Holy Evaristus, fourth bishop of the Roman See after blessed Peter, and holy Siricius, and blessed Leo, together with all the other teachers, also set forth these matters. We avoid placing them all here because of their number and length.

[Col. 0137B] We have thought it necessary to say only this: lawful marriages are contracted between equals when a woman, sought from the parents whose concern it is, legally betrothed, endowed, and honored by a public wedding, is joined to a man in the bond of marriage, and from two they become one body and one flesh, as it is written: “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. II); “they are no longer two, but one flesh.” And: “What God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matt. XIX).

Concerning this union, the great Pope Leo writes to the bishop of Narbonne:

“Not every woman joined to a man is the man’s wife, just as not every son is his father’s heir. The marriage bond is lawful among freeborn persons and among equals.”

And a little later:

“Since, therefore, the partnership of marriage was established from the beginning in such a way that, besides the union of the sexes, it contained within itself the sacrament of Christ and the Church, there is no doubt that a woman does not belong to marriage when it is shown that the nuptial mystery was absent.”

We can also demonstrate the converse from this: not every wedding produces conjugal union when the mingling of the sexes does not follow, just as a person is not always the son and heir of the one whose heir he is known to be. Nor do weddings contain within themselves the sacrament of Christ and the Church, as blessed Augustine says, if they do not use one another nuptially—that is, if the mingling of the sexes does not follow them.

Nor can that woman belong to marriage with whom it is shown that there was no mingling of the sexes, just as there is no doubt that a woman does not belong to marriage when it is shown that the nuptial mystery was absent.

The aforesaid Leo demonstrates this by saying:

“Since, therefore, the partnership of marriage was established from the beginning in such a way that, besides the union of the sexes, it contained within itself the sacrament of Christ and the Church.”

And again the same writer says:

“Therefore, when someone gives his daughter in marriage to a man who has a concubine, this must not be understood as though he had given her to a married man—unless, perhaps, that woman appears to have been made freeborn, legally endowed, and honorably joined in a public wedding. Women joined to men by paternal decision are without guilt if the women whom those men possessed were not in marriage.”

By these statements he plainly shows that the true lawful conjugal union exists when it is made between freeborn persons and between equals, when a woman joined to a man by paternal decision has been legally endowed and honorably joined in a public wedding, and when they are united by the mingling of the sexes. Then weddings contain within themselves the sacrament of Christ and the Church, and the woman is known to belong to marriage when both the mingling of the sexes and the nuptial mystery are shown to have been present.

Concerning this mystery the Apostle Paul says to the Ephesians:

“He who loves his wife loves himself. For no one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the Church; because we are members of his body, of his flesh and of his bones. Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh. This mystery is great; but I speak concerning Christ and the Church” (Eph. V).

From this holy Ambrose indicates that the sacrament of the mystery is great in the unity of man and woman. He not only reveals this, but also demands another cause that does not conflict with the mystery mentioned, one which he knows pertains to the advancement of the human race—that is, to the Church and the Savior. Thus, just as a man clings to his wife after leaving his parents, so the Church, after abandoning every error, should cling to and be subject to her head, who is Christ.

Since there is one nature in man and woman, the man is therefore instructed to love the woman as though she were himself. By natural reason the woman is a portion of the man’s body; and thus the man loves himself in the woman. If he commits fornication, he sins against himself, because the two are one flesh. They do not, therefore, divide the substance of the person so that number arises among the persons of the nature; rather, they exist in the unity of one nature.

And holy Augustine says in his book On Marriage and Concupiscence:

“Certainly, not only fertility, whose fruit is offspring, nor only chastity, whose bond is fidelity, but also a certain sacrament of marriage is commended to married believers. Hence the Apostle says: ‘Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the Church’ (Eph. V). Beyond doubt, the reality of this sacrament is that male and female joined in marriage remain inseparably united as long as they live; nor is it lawful, except for the cause of fornication, for one spouse to be separated from the other. This is preserved in Christ and in the Church, so that the living may remain with the living forever, separated by no divorce, in the city of our Lord, on his holy mountain—that is, in the Catholic Church.”

And holy Gregory says in his letter to the patrician Theoctista [Col. 0138D]:

“For Truth itself says: ‘What the Lord has joined, let no human being separate’ (Matt. XIX). It also says: ‘It is not lawful to dismiss a wife except for the cause of fornication.’ For we know that it is written: ‘The two shall be one flesh’ (Gen. II). If, then, husband and wife are one flesh, and the husband dismisses his wife for the sake of religion, or the woman her husband, who remains in this world or perhaps goes over to illicit things, what kind of conversion is this, in which one and the same flesh passes over to continence in one part while in the other it remains in pollution? But if both agree to lead a continent life, who would dare to condemn this, when it is certain that the almighty Lord, who has permitted lesser things, has not prohibited greater ones?”

And a little later:

“If the wife does not follow the continence that the husband desires, or the husband refuses the continence that the wife desires, it is not lawful to divide the marriage, because it is written: ‘The woman does not have authority over her own body, but the man; likewise, the man does not have authority over his own body, but the woman’ (I Cor. VI).”

And in his letter to Adrian, bishop of Palermo:

“For, except for the cause of fornication, divine law in no way permits a husband to leave his wife, because after the union of marriage has made man and woman one body, it cannot be converted in one part while remaining in the world in the other.”

And holy Augustine says in his book On the Good of Marriage:

“For this reason marriages exist: so that concupiscence, reduced to a lawful bond, might not flow about deformed and disordered, possessing from itself an uncontrollable weakness of the flesh, but from marriage an indissoluble partnership of fidelity; from itself an immoderate impulse toward intercourse, but from marriage the proper measure for chaste procreation.

“Married persons therefore owe one another not only the fidelity of mingling with a person of the other sex for the sake of begetting children, which is the first partnership of the human race in this mortal life, but also a mutual service, as it were, for bearing one another’s weakness and avoiding illicit intercourse. Thus, even if perpetual continence pleases one of them, neither can practice it without the consent of the other.

“For this reason the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the man, and likewise the man does not have authority over his own body, but the woman: so that, whether he or she seeks it from marriage or from the spouse not for the procreation of children but because of weakness and lack of self-control, they may not deny one another, lest through this they fall into damnable corruptions, when Satan tempts either both of them or one of them because of lack of self-control.”

And again in the same book:

“That marriages are contracted for the sake of procreation is testified by the Apostle when he says: ‘I desire younger women to marry.’ And as though he were asked, ‘For what purpose?’ he immediately added: ‘To bear children and to be mothers of families’ (I Tim. V). The statement ‘The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the man; likewise, the man does not have authority over his own body, but the woman’ (I Cor. VI) pertains to the fidelity of chastity; the statement ‘A wife should not depart from her husband; but if she does depart, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband’ (I Cor. VII), and ‘Let the husband not dismiss his wife,’ pertains to the sanctity of the sacrament. All these are good things for which marriage is good: offspring, fidelity, and sacrament.”

[Col. 0139D] And in his book On Marriage and Concupiscence:

“Yet in marriage let the goods proper to marriage be loved: offspring, fidelity, and sacrament. Offspring, however, not merely so that children may be born, but also so that they may be reborn; for a person is born for punishment unless reborn for life.

“Fidelity, moreover, not of the kind even unbelievers possess among themselves when they jealously guard the flesh—for what husband, however impious, wants an adulterous wife, or what wife, however impious, wants an adulterous husband? This is indeed a natural good in marriage, but it is nevertheless carnal. A Christian spouse ought to fear the adulterer for the adulterous spouse, not for himself or herself, and ought to hope from Christ for whatever reward is due to the spouse.

“But the sacrament is something which even separated and adulterous spouses do not lose; they ought to preserve it together in harmony and chastity. For it alone is what even a sterile marriage retains under the laws of devotion, after the hope of fertility for which it was joined has been lost.

“Let the person who wishes to praise marriage praise these nuptial goods in marriage.”

And in his Literal Commentary on Genesis:

“What is good in marriage, and that marriage is good, can never be sin. This good is threefold: fidelity, offspring, and sacrament. In fidelity, care is taken that intercourse does not take place with another man or woman outside the marital bond. In offspring, care is taken that the child be received lovingly, nourished kindly, and religiously educated. In the sacrament, care is taken that the marriage not be separated, and that neither the dismissed husband nor the dismissed wife be joined to another, not even for the sake of offspring. This is, as it were, the rule of marriage, by which either the beauty of nature is made fruitful or the depravity of lack of self-control is governed.”

Now let us compare with what the holy teachers say about marriage the marriage of Stephen, in which there was not love of offspring but the necessity of avoiding exile or death; in which there was not the fidelity of preserving conjugal chastity but the serious fear of incurring deadly incest; in which there was not the sacrament of incorporation into Christ and the Church but a covering placed over disgrace; and in which everything that was done was a fiction of pretense, not the truth.

Although that wedding was celebrated between freeborn persons and equals, preceded by betrothal and endowment according to paternal decision, even if the mingling of the sexes had subsequently followed it, it could not obtain a legitimate conjugal union or establish a valid marriage. Rather, everything would have become void, because, without separation on account of the crime of incest—which cannot possess the sacrament of Christ and the Church—the wounds inflicted upon the persons who had intercourse could not have been healed in them by the medicine of penance, as the subsequent judgments of orthodox teachers and masters of the Church will demonstrate.

Therefore such a wedding is neither mystical nor lawful in the eyes of God.

For if, through the sexual intercourse of Stephen and the girl—who was not lawfully taken before God but rather carried off—a single body were made from the two, it would not be according to the good of marriage but according to the evil of incest. Because of Stephen’s incest they would become one body, as it is written: “He who joins himself to a prostitute becomes one body” (I Cor. VI).

Thus the girl, previously free from incest, would through intercourse joined to Stephen become the flesh of an incestuous man; and Stephen, joined to her, would be not only a fornicator as before but also, after joining with her, would become incestuous, since he had intercourse with his relative.

For this reason, by the sounder counsel, and for the girl’s welfare—she who had not yet been injured—he prudently preserved her untouched and guarded himself more carefully before God from committing a graver offense, according as the circumstances required. For, as the sacred canons say, such a marriage, or rather adultery, could not be healed without separation if they were to mingle carnally.

Hence it is written there (Council of Epaon, canon 30):

“We reserve absolutely no forgiveness for incestuous unions, unless they have healed the adultery by separation. We do not count incestuous persons under any name of marriage, and it is even fatal to designate them as such.”

And Saint Gregory, in his letter to Felix, bishop of Sicily, whom he had heard to be perversely interpreting the counsel that blessed Gregory had given to Augustine, bishop of the English, concerning indulgence toward pagans from the fourth generation and thereafter, so that they might not withdraw from the faith, writes back to the same Felix:

“We decree that each person shall observe his own lineage, among those who have been faithfully instructed and now stand unshaken, planted with a firm root, through the seventh generation; and, as long as they recognize themselves as related by affinity, they shall not enter into such a partnership of union. Nor is it or will it be lawful for any Christian to take in marriage a woman whom someone had as a wife from his own blood relationship, or whom he had stained by any illicit pollution, because such intercourse is incestuous and abominable to the Lord and to all the faithful. We have long ago read that the holy fathers established that incestuous persons are not to be counted under any name of marriage.”

Nor do we leave unmentioned in this matter of concern that incestuous persons must be separated from the thresholds of the holy Church until they are reconciled to that same holy Catholic Church through the satisfaction expressed in the prayers of priests.

And in the canonical edict issued before the body of blessed Peter:

“If anyone takes as wife a woman from his own kinship, or one whom his kinsman had, let him be anathema.”

And all replied a third time: “Let him be anathema.”

There is no doubt that Stephen’s marriage ought to have been subject to this anathema if he had intercourse with this woman, since he confesses that he had intercourse with her relative.

Again it is written in the canons (Council of Lleida, canon 4):

“Concerning those who stain themselves with the pollution of incest, it has been decided that, as long as they persist in that detestable and illicit cohabitation of the flesh, they shall be admitted in the Church only up to the Mass of the catechumens; and with such persons no Christian ought even to take food, as the Apostle commanded.”

We could have gathered many more statements from the canons if, with incest intervening—something Stephen avoided—it had been necessary for him to separate himself from his wife on that account.

But now, lest incest be added to the pretense of marriage, since those who were not seen to have been joined lawfully in divine justice ought to be separated lawfully and reasonably both before divine eyes and before human eyes, let us offer the testimonies of the holy Fathers that most clearly pertain to the case.

Holy Ambrose says in his commentary on the First Epistle to the Corinthians:

“For a brother or sister is not subject to bondage in such matters; that is, a person does not owe the respect due to marriage to one who has recoiled from the author of marriage. For a marriage that exists without devotion to the Lord is not valid.”

And holy Jerome, in the third book of his commentary on Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians:

“Therefore, just as the Church is subject to Christ, so let the wife be subject to her husband. The husband and wife are bound to the same order as Christ and the Church, who possess authority and subjection. But care must be taken that, just as there is a holy union in Christ and the Church, so there may be a holy union in the woman.

“Just as not every gathering of heretics can be called the Church of Christ, nor is Christ their head, so not every marriage that is not joined to her husband according to Christ’s commands can properly be called marriage, but rather adultery.”

Concerning such matters the sacred canons define:

“Those who are prohibited from an illicit union shall indeed have the freedom to enter a better marriage.”

And in the synod held at Liptina in the year 743, under the rule of Prince Carloman, presided over by Bishop George, John the sacellarius, and holy Boniface, by command of Pope Zacharias, it is stated that if a man cannot render the marital debt to a woman who has been betrothed, endowed, and brought to him in a public wedding, according to the Apostle, and this has become clear either by the confession of both parties or by some certain proof, they are to be separated, and the woman, if she cannot remain continent, may lawfully marry another man.

For, according to the definition of holy Pope Leo and the tradition of the teachers demonstrated above, there is no doubt that a woman does not belong to marriage when the sacrament of Christ and the Church—that is, the nuptial mystery—is not shown to have existed in the union of the sexes.

Much more, therefore, in the case at issue, once the marriage has been separated, it will be lawful for her to enter another legitimate union, since it was not impotence of the flesh but reverence of the mind that prevented her from contracting intercourse with him.

In a conjugal union in which, through betrothal, endowment, and the sacrament of marriage—that is, through the unity of the body—the mystery of Christ and the Church is shown to have existed, the marriage cannot be dissolved except by bodily death, as evangelical and apostolic authority and the chorus of all Catholic teachers testify.

And blessed Augustine says in his book On Adulterous Marriages:

“For if, whether because of an intolerable and prolonged illness the husband cannot perform intercourse or the woman endure it, or because of sterility, or because of religious continence, or for any other reason except the cause of fornication, a husband and wife who have been legally joined by carnal union cannot be separated.”

Therefore, when the disciples heard this law from the Lord, they said: “If this is the situation of a man with his wife, it is not expedient to marry” (Matt. XIX). Yet the Lord did not on this account change his judgment.

For this reason Leo also wrote to Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, that if, through military disaster and extremely severe attacks by enemies, certain marriages had been divided so that, after the husbands had been carried off into captivity, their wives remained abandoned, and those women thought their husbands had been killed or believed they would never be freed from the power of their enemies, and, compelled by their solitude, had entered the embraces of other husbands, then, because it is written by the Lord, “A woman is joined to a man,” and “What God has joined, let no human being separate” (ibid.), if the husbands returned, or the captured wives returned, the lawful marriage bonds were to be restored.

The person who had assumed the position of a husband or wife who was no longer thought to be alive was not, however, to be judged as an intruder; rather, what necessity had brought about was to be judged blameless, and what fidelity demanded was to be restored.

But women or men captivated by the affection of their later husbands or wives, and unwilling to return to the love of their former spouses, he decreed were to be deprived of communion.

Since ecclesiastical regulations also pronounce a judgment concerning those who violate the fidelity of betrothal, it seems to us—not speaking according to authority, but offering advice, if this should seem right to you—that, if Stephen had broken the fidelity of the betrothal, he would according to civil law have been judged liable to pay a fine for that betrothal.

After the girl had received the betrothal endowment, which, if she had joined herself carnally, she ought to have earned for herself, it appears that the offense by which she ought not to retain that same endowment was committed not by the girl but by Stephen. Let her therefore have, in place of the fine for the broken betrothal, the endowment given to her by Stephen; let her be restored to her father with that same endowment, and let her marry, with her parents’ counsel, whomever she wishes, provided that it be in the Lord. Let there be peace between her parents and Stephen.

And lest someone, wishing cleverly to oppose what we have said, should ask: “If the endowment remains, and the betrothal and the celebrated wedding are not denied, how can it be that Stephen does not remain the husband and she the wife? Or how will he be able to join himself to another woman, and she to another man, without adultery?”—especially since blessed Augustine says in the aforementioned book On the Good of Marriage:

“If an ordination of clergy is carried out for the gathering of a people, even if the gathering of the people does not follow, nevertheless the sacrament of ordination remains in those who have been ordained; and if someone is removed from his office because of some fault, he will not lack the sacrament of the Lord once it has been imposed, although he remains subject to judgment.”

So also, while the betrothal, endowment, and wedding remain, the conjugal bond will remain, and neither of them will be able to join another without adultery unless the death of one of them intervenes.

Let anyone who has attempted to raise this objection hear that, concerning possession of the girl’s endowment, we spoke only for the sake of reconciling her parents and Stephen, and that we designated it as a fine for the broken betrothal. If her parents prefer to demand that fine after the endowment has been dissolved, or if both parties prefer to waive it, or both prefer to reclaim it, let them decide for themselves, provided that the matter accords with the civil laws and with their reconciliation.

For our part, we answer the person who perhaps cunningly asks this question: blessed Augustine made the comparison with ordination not concerning an imaginary union of man and woman but concerning a union incorporated through the mingling of the sexes, as he says immediately before:

“The boys will follow the Lamb, singing a new song, as it is written in the Apocalypse, those who have not defiled themselves with women, and for no other reason than that they remained virgins. Nor should they therefore consider themselves better than the holy fathers of old, who used marriages, so to speak, in a nuptial manner.

“For the use of marriage is such that, if anything is done in it through the mingling of the flesh beyond the necessity of begetting children, although it may be done venially, it is nevertheless a pollution.”

And a little later:

“The good of marriage, therefore, among all nations and human beings, consists in the matter of begetting children and in fidelity of chastity; but, as it pertains to the people of God, also in the sanctity of the sacrament, by which it is unlawful even for someone who has departed after a divorce to marry another while his or her spouse lives—not even for the sake of bearing children. Although this is the sole cause for which marriages are contracted, the marital bond is not dissolved when the thing for which they are contracted does not follow, except by the death of the spouse.”

Immediately afterward he added the comparison with the ordination of clergy for the gathering of a people. In the same sense he says in his book On Marriage and Concupiscence:

“Thus, even among the living, something conjugal remains which can be removed neither by separation nor by union with another. It remains, however, for the liability of the crime, not as the bond of the covenant—just as the soul of an apostate, which departs from the marriage of Christ, does not lose, even after faith has been lost, the sacrament of faith that it received through the washing of regeneration. It would certainly be restored to the one returning if it had lost it when departing.”

Earlier in the same book he says concerning the sacrament of marriage:

“For this reason the sacrament of marriage in our time has been reduced to one husband and one wife, so that no one may be ordained as a minister of the Church unless he is the husband of one wife. Those who understood this more carefully judged that even a man who had possessed another woman while a catechumen or pagan ought not to be ordained. For the issue is the sacrament, not the sin.

“For all sins are forgiven in baptism. But the one who said, ‘If you take a wife, you have not sinned’; ‘If a virgin marries, she does not sin’; and ‘Let her do what she wishes; she does not sin if she marries’ (I Cor. VII), clearly declared that marriage is no sin.

“Because of the holiness of the sacrament, however, just as a woman, even if she had been violated while a catechumen, may after baptism be consecrated as a virgin of God, so it has not seemed unreasonable that a man who exceeded the single number of wives had not committed some sin but had lost a certain sacred norm, necessary not for the merit of a good life but for the sign of ecclesiastical ordination.”

And if someone should attempt to oppose what we have said with the following argument, let him say whether, if Stephen is overtaken by death and the girl remains untouched as she has remained until now, and she does not wish to marry—since a catechumen who has been violated cannot after baptism be consecrated as a virgin of God—she will be able to be consecrated by the bishop as a sacred virgin, when he ought to consecrate under the profession of virginity only a virgin, or one in a legitimate conjugal union; just as a man cannot become bishop who, besides a virgin, has taken one wife.

Let him also say whether, if she remains a virgin after Stephen’s death and cannot remain continent, and chooses to marry rather than to remain continent, she will be able to be joined to Stephen’s brother.

If he cannot contradict these points, either let him fail in his question or let our solution satisfy him.

Let him recognize that, while Stephen is alive, the girl may, as reason and authority demonstrate, either be consecrated if she chooses or married if she prefers. Let him also know that, as we have shown from a tradition greater than ours, because of such a betrothal, endowment, and wedding as this was, there is no marriage, since the union of the sexes was absent, together with the sacrament of fidelity joined to the hope of offspring.

This sacrament operates most fully in every salutary action, and also in this matter, in which through the nuptial mystery husband and wife become one flesh. Yet it operates more powerfully in baptism, through which, by the sacrament of faith, not only does the whole Church in general become the body of Christ and his fullness, as the Apostle says, but each individual believer, incorporated into Christ, becomes a member of him.

Hence Saint Bede says in a homily on the Gospel:

“For the person who is baptized appears to descend into the font; he appears to be immersed in the waters; he appears to rise from the waters. But the devotion of the faithful alone knows that the sinner descends into the font and rises purified. To the eyes of the foolish, however, such a person appears to leave the font as he entered it, and everything that is being done seems to be a mere game.”

In this betrothal, endowment, and wedding, everything was likewise pretense, not truth. Therefore, just as holy Leo decrees concerning those who received only the form of baptism without the power of sanctification that they should be strengthened by episcopal confirmation, so this, not the reality of marriage but an image of union, should be dissolved by ecclesiastical action and healed in the person who requires ecclesiastical medicine.

Moreover, if what we have set down is not at all sufficient for the diligent or the curious, we shall undertake to add still more.

For blessed Augustine says in his book On Marriage and Concupiscence:

“‘A man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh’ (Gen. II), which the Apostle calls a great sacrament in Christ and the Church (Eph. V). What is great in Christ and the Church is small in each individual husband and wife, but is nevertheless the sacrament of an inseparable union.”

Therefore those who have been lawfully and nuptially joined cannot be separated except for the cause of fornication; and those separated for the cause of fornication ought either to remain unmarried or to be reconciled to one another, as evangelical and apostolic authority teaches and the African synod defined:

“It has been decided,” it says, “that, according to evangelical and apostolic discipline, neither the man dismissed by his wife nor the woman dismissed by her husband shall be joined to another; but let them remain so, or let them be reconciled to one another. If they despise this, let them be reduced to penance.”

And since a wife cannot and ought not to leave her husband, nor a husband his wife, except for the cause of fornication, blessed Augustine says on the basis of this evangelical and apostolic teaching in the first book of On Adulterous Marriages, addressed to Pollentius:

“Who is there who would say that, if a woman leaves a husband who is not committing fornication, she should remain unmarried, when she is absolutely not permitted to leave except a husband who is committing fornication?”

And again:

“The Lord the Teacher made this the sole exception, the cause of fornication, when he spoke of dismissing a wife; and he made it understood that the same rule must also be observed by the husband, since not only does the woman not have authority over her own body, but the man does, and likewise the man does not have authority over his own body, but the woman (I Cor. VII).

“Therefore they cannot separate even for the sake of continence unless by mutual consent. Thus, if a husband is converted against his wife’s will and is tonsured, or if a wife is converted without her husband’s consent and takes the veil, holy Gregory commands in his letter to Secundus, bishop of Taormina, and in his letter to Adrian, bishop of Palermo, that the woman be restored to the husband or the husband to the woman.

“But if they permit themselves to change their way of life by mutual consent, and one of them afterward withdraws from it, that person is ordered to follow the other in his or her conversion.

“When a husband or wife separates from the other because of fornication, they will, because of the sacrament of the nuptial union, either remain unmarried until one of them dies or strive to be reconciled to one another. Reconciliation must take place after the penance and priestly reconciliation of the one who sinned, so that the sinner may first be restored to the sacrament of the Church and afterward to the nuptial mystery.”

And therefore Saint Augustine says in the second book *On Adulterous Marriages*:

“Thus a wife may lawfully be dismissed on account of fornication, but the bond of chastity remains; because of this, the man who takes the dismissed woman in marriage—even for this reason of fornication—is guilty of adultery. For just as, when the sacrament of regeneration remains in a person, one excommunicated as guilty of some crime does not lose that sacrament, even if he is never reconciled to the Lord, so, when the bond of the marriage covenant remains in her, a wife dismissed on account of fornication does not lose that bond, even if she is never reconciled to her husband. She will lose it, however, if her husband has died; but the excommunicated person guilty of any crime will never lose the sacrament of regeneration, even if unreconciled, because God never dies.

“It remains, therefore, that if we wish to understand the matter according to the Apostle, we must not say that the husband is to be counted as dead because he is an adulterer, and that for this reason it is lawful for his wife to marry another. Although adultery is a death—not of the body, but, what is worse, of the soul—the Apostle was not speaking of that death when he said, ‘But if her husband is dead, let her marry whom she wishes’ (I Cor. VII), but only of that by which one departs from the body.

“And again, in the same work:

“‘For this bond is not dissolved even when, through repudiation, a husband is separated from a chaste wife; much less is it dissolved if, without being separated, she commits adultery. Accordingly, nothing dissolves it except the death of the spouse—not the spouse who falls into adultery, but the spouse who departs from the body. Therefore, if a woman withdraws from an adulterous husband and does not wish to be reconciled to him, let her remain unmarried; and if a husband dismisses an adulterous wife and does not wish to receive her, even after she has done penance, let him preserve continence—not, indeed, from the desire to choose a greater good, but at least from the necessity of avoiding a destructive evil.’”

Saint Augustine, the most eloquent teacher, argues this matter at greater length in the books mentioned above, as anyone who reads them intelligently will be unable not to know.

But in the first book *On Marriage and Concupiscence* he also says that by the washing of regeneration [Col. 0147A] and the word of sanctification all the evils of regenerated human beings are entirely cleansed and healed—not only the sins that are all forgiven in baptism, but also those later contracted through human ignorance or weakness—not so that baptism is repeated as often as one sins, but because, through the baptism once given, the faithful obtain forgiveness not only of sins committed previously but also of any committed afterward. For what benefit would penance before baptism provide if baptism did not follow, or penance afterward if baptism did not precede it?

And in his letter to Boniface he writes:

“No remnant of any past sin remains unforgiven in baptism, provided that baptism itself is not held in vain outside, but is either given within, or, if given outside, one does not remain outside with it. And whatever faults are contracted through human weakness by those who live here after receiving baptism, of whatever kind they may be, are forgiven because of that washing.”

From this it is plainly demonstrated that, just as the sacrament of baptism, once received—by which every believer is incorporated into Christ within the unity of the Catholic Church—is afterward never lost for any intervening cause, so the marriage bond, lawfully and nuptially celebrated, remains indissolubly joined, even if it appears to have been separated on account of fornication or for any other reason.

If a marriage separated on account of fornication is reunited after penance, it is nevertheless not thereby repeated, because it remains one. But if the spouses are unable to remain in penitential continence, which is more appropriate for penitents, then, through a medicinal reconciliation by mutual consent after ecclesiastical reconciliation, it may be considered healed by indulgence: just as baptism is not repeated as often as one sins, but, through the medicine of penance and ecclesiastical reconciliation, is believed not to be repeated but to be restored by divine grace.

It is said to be restored, although it was not lost, in the same way that the mind and body are said to be restored through receiving the Eucharist, and the spirit of our mind is read to be renewed through fitting satisfaction. And just as sins committed through human ignorance or weakness before or after baptism are forgiven, for those who are worthy, through the gift of baptism together with the fruits of penance, so the good of marriage protects against counting as crimes those acts which the Apostle grants by way of concession [Col. 0147D]—namely, those which, under the impulse of concupiscence, are granted only to married persons—provided that intercourse takes place naturally between those lawfully married.

We say “naturally” because it is read of Onan (Gen. XXXVIII) that, when he did not have natural intercourse with his wife, he died, struck down by the Lord.

Accordingly, blessed Augustine argues sufficiently in his book *On the Good of Marriage*, in *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, and in his other books. There also, among other things, he says:

“What the apostles command married people is proper to marriage: namely, that the husband render the marital debt to his wife and the wife to her husband, that they beget children, and that they be mothers of families. What they permit venially, or what hinders prayer, is not imposed by marriage, but is borne by it.”

And just as good works do not benefit a person toward eternal salvation without the sacrament of baptism—and baptism is not true, because it is not the one baptism according to Scripture, that is, the unique baptism within the unity of Catholic faith, if it has not been celebrated Catholicly—so there cannot be a lawful and true marriage in which it is taught that there is no nuptial mystery, or which is not taught to have been joined nuptially.

Therefore the Lord, as the histories relate, called John away when he wished to marry—not after the marriage had been celebrated, but from marriage, and before the union of the flesh—he who came not to abolish the law but to fulfill it. Concerning John’s future wife: if the Lord had not recalled him not only before the union of the flesh but also before the completion of the wedding ceremony, then, just as it is not recorded of blessed Peter’s wife, who persevered most chastely, whether she remained continent or perhaps chose to marry another according to the ancient law, so that she might leave offspring in Israel, this would not have remained within her discretion if, after a lawful wedding, they had been joined in a nuptial union.

Nor would it have been lawful for John, according to the teaching of the Gospel, if he had taken a woman who had been betrothed, endowed, and honored by public marriage, to leave her even before the union of the flesh, unless he had chosen by consent to remain continent, but instead to take another.

In the same way, it is not lawful for Stephen to leave this woman whom he betrothed, endowed, and honored with a public marriage—although he was not sent to her [the reading is uncertain]—and to take another, with or without penance, unless incestuous evil could have occurred in intercourse with this woman. Rather, either Stephen should remain continent with her by mutual consent, or, if he could not remain continent, he should remain joined to her in marriage.

But if, without incest, they had been joined in the proper order, they could not be separated except by mutual consent for the sake of continence; or, if separated on account of fornication, they ought either to remain unmarried or to be reconciled to one another. If, however, they had been joined in incest, their adultery ought to be healed through their separation and penance, according to canonical authority.

Sacred authority likewise shows that these matters agree with one another when it says concerning Mary and Joseph: “Before they came together” (Matt. I)—that is, before they properly celebrated the solemnities of marriage. For by the expression “came together” it indicates not intercourse itself but marriage, which ordinarily precedes the time of intercourse, when she who had previously been betrothed began to be a wife.

And shortly afterward: “He wished to dismiss her secretly” (ibid.). When Joseph saw that his betrothed had conceived, although he knew well that she had not been touched by any man, and since he was just and wished to act justly in all things, he judged it best neither to disclose this to others nor to take her as his wife, but, secretly changing his intention concerning the marriage, to allow her to remain in the condition of a betrothed woman, as she was.

But if he had dismissed her secretly and had not taken her as his wife, and she had given birth while still betrothed, very few would have believed her to be a virgin; they would much more likely have judged her a prostitute, and she would have been stoned by the Jews as though she were an adulteress.

[Col. 0149A] Therefore the sacred canons, in the chapter where they legislate concerning parents who violate the faith of betrothals, most prudently decreed that the following should be added (Council of Elvira, canon 54):

“Nevertheless, if the betrothed man or woman is found to have committed a serious crime, the parents shall be excused; for the judgment of punishment which the parents should have endured because of the broken pledge shall now fall upon those who deserved it.”

And, to return to the order of the example above, Joseph’s decision is suddenly changed into a better decision for this reason: namely, that, in preserving Mary’s reputation, he himself might take her as his wife after celebrating the marriage, but might keep the chaste woman perpetually chaste, as follows:

“While he was considering these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying: Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary your wife” (Matt. I).

Concerning this kind of marriage, Siricius wrote to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona, saying (chapter 4):

“You have inquired concerning the violation of marriage, whether one man may take in marriage a girl betrothed to another. We absolutely forbid this from happening, because that blessing which the priest imposes upon those about to marry is, among the faithful, like a form of sacrilege if it is violated by any transgression.”

And in the Council of Ancyra (canon 10):

“It has been decided that betrothed girls who are afterward abducted by others are to be rescued and returned to those to whom they had previously been betrothed, even if it is established that force was inflicted upon them by their abductors.”

Those women, who according to the order described above have become not merely betrothed women but almost wives, even if they have been violated by force, are to be returned to their betrothed men just as separated spouses are to be reunited—whether they were separated on account of fornication or were separated without mutual consent. Those separated on account of fornication will either remain unmarried or be mutually reconciled by consent.

Concerning those who have been married but remain unmarried—that is, concerning marriages in which the pledge of betrothal, the priestly blessing, the confirmation of the dowry, and the mystery of Christ and the Church are directed toward the perfection of completion, but are not completed by the union of the flesh—and concerning the good decision, as we said of Joseph, which is changed into a better decision so that perpetual continence may be maintained, it is again written:

“Joseph rose from sleep and did as the angel of the Lord had commanded him, and he took his wife, and he did not know her” (Matt. I).

He took her in the name of wife because of the necessary circumstances then pressing upon them; and he did not know her for marital intercourse, but both remained continent.

Paul demonstrates in his First Epistle to the Corinthians that this may lawfully be done, and Augustine demonstrates the same in the first book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, saying:

“But if they agree to abstain perpetually, by mutual consent, from the use of carnal desire, far be it from us to say that the marital bond between them is broken. Rather, it will be stronger, insofar as they have entered into agreements with one another that are to be observed with greater affection and harmony—not through voluntary bodily unions, but through the voluntary affections of their souls. For the angel did not falsely say to Joseph: ‘Do not fear to take Mary your wife,’ and the rest, which he explains at greater length in the same work.”

Having been instructed by these testimonies of sacred authority, we hold that all who take as wives freeborn women who have been betrothed, endowed, and honored by public marriage—or who have thereby been made freeborn—must either remain in perpetual continence or, unless this incestuous crime or some other prohibition prevents it, a prohibition which does not admit within itself or between them the sacrament of Christ and the Church, must marry nuptially if they cannot remain continent by mutual consent. They must be separated only on account of fornication.

Those who are separated must either remain unmarried or, if they cannot remain continent, be reconciled after penance. But when, as in Stephen’s marriage, danger has arisen that one danger must be avoided by means of another, the lesser danger must be chosen in order to avoid the greater danger, as Saint Gregory teaches in the books of the *Moralia*. Yet the danger that is chosen must not itself be neglected; rather, every effort must be made before the mercy of almighty God to ensure that, through worthy fruits of penance—namely, pious works and abundant tears—it may not remain an eternal danger but may be moderated by a saving remedy or wholly escaped.

We have thought it necessary to insert these matters because we have heard certain people—even some who claimed to be teachers—arguing obstinately, as though from the words of blessed Ambrose and Saint Augustine, which they had considered insufficiently carefully, that a man who was not committing fornication and had separated from a fornicator woman could take another wife while the former was alive, and that a woman who had left her husband on account of fornication could not be reconciled to him.

They also held that a woman who had withdrawn not on account of fornication but for any other reason ought either to be reconciled or to remain unmarried. They failed to notice that in this way they were interpreting the Apostle’s words in an adulterous sense, just as those men did against whom blessed Augustine formerly composed these books, and as the African synod, which we cited above, defined—when it cut out the Coelestians and also shook out the very marrow of the Pelagians.

Nor is this surprising. They had been infected with a perverse doctrine, just like the modern Predestinarians, who strive to revive the heresy of the ancient Predestinarians as though it had been compiled from the words of Saint Augustine. Blessed Pope Celestine broke their heads and crushed and shattered the crown of those walking in their sins, in his decretal letter to Venerius and the other Gallican bishops; and blessed Augustine did the same in his books *On Rebuke and Grace*, *On the Predestination of the Saints*, and *On the Gift of Perseverance*.
