Saint Prosper also, by delegation from the apostolic see, dissolved their arguments with Catholic understanding and the eloquent teaching of perfect and most evident reasoning, in his responses to the objections of the Gauls, the Vincentians, and the Massilians, and likewise in his books *On the Calling of the Nations*. We would set out here the words of those same authors from which unskilled teachers have gathered such foolish notions, if we were not avoiding the attempt to untie one knot by tying another.

We have also thought it necessary to add that, from these judgments of the saints, we may understand that marriages which intercourse does not follow for certain reasons can be dissolved, and that women may be permitted, because of incontinent desire, to turn to other men.

But careful investigation and reasonable discernment must first be applied in such cases: whether this impossibility of intercourse is something natural in the men—for there are eunuchs, as it is written, who were born that way from their mother’s womb—or whether this impediment has happened to them through the operation of the devil, as often occurs.

If it has happened through sorceresses (33 q. 1) and witches, secretly but never unjustly or nowhere unjustly, by the permission of the Lord’s hidden judgment and through the devil’s activity, those to whom such things happen must be exhorted to make a pure confession of all their sins to God and to the priest, with contrite heart and humbled spirit [Col. 0151B], and to satisfy the Lord with abundant tears, generous almsgiving, prayers, and fasts. By his judgment, according to their deserts, they unwillingly deserved to be deprived of that blessing which the Lord gave to our first parents in paradise before sin and by which, even after sin, he did not wish the human race to be deprived altogether.

Through exorcisms and the other offices of ecclesiastical medicine, the ministers of the Church should endeavor, insofar as the Lord permits, to heal such persons—the Lord who healed Abimelech and his household through Abraham’s prayers (Gen. XX). If they perhaps cannot be healed, they may be separated.

But after one of them has sought another marriage, while those to whom they have been joined are still living, they will not be able to be reconciled to their former spouses whom they left, even if the ability to have intercourse has been restored to them.

Let us understand that incestuous marriages, because of the crime of incest—which, as we said before and say again, cannot possess the sacrament of Christ and the Church—must not remain, but that the crime must be healed through separation and penance.

Let us recognize that Stephen’s marriage, which is under discussion, must be dissolved by every means so that incest may not be admitted. And let us hold, taught by the authority of Truth, that marriages possessing the nuptial mystery can be dissolved for no other reason than fornication alone.

For even if married couples vow continence by mutual consent, they will remain joined in the Lord all the more firmly insofar as they are joined more spiritually. No pretense can intervene before the eyes of him who is known to be the searcher of hearts and reins, whether in their union or in their undivided separation.

Therefore Stephen could have done penance for the fornication secretly, unless compelled by necessity to make it public. But because, although compelled by necessity, he introduced the fault of pretense into the sacred nuptial mystery, like one who did not fear to sow weeds over wheat, and because after such a marriage—before it was legally dissolved, although it appeared to have been begun almost legally—he is said to have used a concubine, thereby destroying others through his wicked example, he should, in proportion to his fault and with pious modesty, since he showed reverence to God by not joining incest to fornication, receive regular penance from his own bishop according to the bishop’s judgment, as the canons decree [Col. 0152A].

He should complete that penance with worthy fruits, so that he who presumed through his own negligence to scandalize the Church and many sons of the Church may make satisfaction to the Church, its rulers, and its sons. After satisfaction, if he cannot remain continent, he should await the intercourse of his lawful wife, according to the judgment of Pope Leo the Great in his letter to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne, and according to the decrees of the holy Council of Toledo (Decretal, chapter 25; Council of Toledo VI, canon 8), so that he may not again incur the crime of fornication.

In this matter, however, speaking with that most holy Father, we do not establish a rule but assess what is more tolerable. For according to true understanding, nothing is more fitting for one who is doing penance than persevering chastity of both mind and body. To prevent us from laying a snare for him, we extend the hand of a remedy; we do not impose a command to act.

Since Saint Siricius also took care to set down certain matters concerning the blessing of brides in his decrees, the sacred canons make the known rulings concerning them, and we have said certain things on that basis and would say many more if we heard that a priestly blessing had been given to the marriage of which we speak according to ecclesiastical custom.

But since the requisite faith was lacking in those persons, the priestly blessing had no place—especially since it is written:

“Into whatever house you enter, first say: Peace to this house. And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him; but if not, your peace will return to you” (Luke X).

And Peter says of the Lord and the faithful: “Purifying their hearts by faith” (Acts XV). It is also written: “All his works are from faith,” and again: “Whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. XIV).

Where sin remains, there is no place for a blessing before suitable satisfaction. For, as blessed Gregory says, prayer is of no benefit where the action is wicked.

After all this, if Regimund does not wish to receive his daughter, or if she decides to remain in her own freedom, it must be indicated to them that, if she consents to any act of fornication, whatever is perpetrated will pertain to him or to her, but not to Stephen.

You also, holy bishops, must suggest, declare, and command to Regimund and Stephen, and to their parents and friends, by divine mandate, that they maintain peace among themselves—the peace which the Lord commanded, and without which they will not be able to see him except for judgment. The princes of the land, together with the leading men, must take care that scandals and seditions do not arise in the Church and in the kingdom on this account.

Whoever among them refuses to obey this must, according to the evangelical command, become as a pagan and a publican. According to the Apostle, the one who does not obey must be marked, so that no one associates with him. Whoever does not accept this teaching of peace should receive no greeting, so that no one shares in his sins; and, as the canons decree, his offering should not even be received in the sanctuary.

Whoever refuses to return to peace must remain excommunicated for as long as he refuses to return to peace, and must hasten as quickly as possible to return to charity, which covers a multitude of sins.

It is also written in the canons that from a council two or three judges are to be chosen and sent to determine each matter that must be examined and decided by ecclesiastical judgment, and that can be defined elsewhere more reasonably and suitably than in that same council. Whoever is proved, through contumacy, unwilling to obey the judges, once this has been established before the bishop of the first see, must be sent letters ordering that no one communicate with him until he obeys.

For this reason the holy synod has endeavored to choose you, who are the bishops of the principal sees of the Aquitanian kingdom, together with your fellow bishops, the princes, and the leading men of that land, to decide this case. Whoever delays obeying your decision will not be able to escape without danger to himself and the imposition of excommunication [Col. 0153B].

I have endeavored to gather these matters concerning evangelical truth, apostolic and canonical authority, and the teaching and tradition of Catholics, as the holy synod commanded, according to the modest measure of my little intellect.

No one should become angry with me on account of them, as I have heard certain people do, because I have not composed these words according to my own judgment, nor presumed to claim for myself what is not mine, nor tried to write in this case by establishing or commanding something that is not mine. I have prejudiced no sound judgment, dishonored no authority, and sought to compel no one to obey.

Rather, following blessed Leo, who wrote to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne, I admonish your most beloved and most reverend fraternity that, just as there are certain matters which cannot be overturned by any reasoning, so there are many matters which ought to be tempered either in consideration of the ages involved or because of the necessities of circumstances. This condition must always be preserved: that in matters which are doubtful or obscure, we know to follow what is found to be neither contrary to the evangelical commands nor opposed to the decrees of the saints.

## LETTER XXIII. TO CHARLES THE EMPEROR

*On the authority of the Life of Saint Dionysius translated by Anastasius.*

*(In Mabillon, Analecta, p. 212.)*

To the glorious lord Charles, Emperor Augustus, Hincmar, bishop of Rheims in name, though not in merit, and servant of the people of God [Col. 0153D].

Having read the Passion of blessed Dionysius, dictated in Greek by Methodius, who had been sent from Rome to Constantinople, and written in Latin by Anastasius, skilled in both languages and learned in every field, librarian of the apostolic see—as he himself relates in his preface—I recognized that what is written there agrees with what I had read in my youth, namely, by whom and how the events of the martyrdom of blessed Dionysius and his companions came to the knowledge of the Romans and from there to that of the Greeks.

For when, by God’s arrangement, you were born in the palace at Frankfurt, the episcopate of the city of Meaux was entrusted to Hubert, the palace precentor. There, because of the advanced age and prolonged illness of Bishop Hildegar, he found certain matters relating to learning and religion, as well as buildings and everything else necessary, neglected.

For this reason he obtained from his associate Bodo, a cleric of my lord and foster father Hilduin, abbot and chief of the clerics of the sacred palace, one of Bodo’s own relatives, a cleric named Wandelmar, who had learned singing exceptionally well from the teacher Teugarius at the monastery of Saint Dionysius, to instruct his clerics. He gave him the little abbey of Saint Sanctinus as a benefice.

That same Wandelmar, in the place entrusted to him, found some very worn little booklets, in which what had been written was almost erased, concerning the life and deeds of blessed Sanctinus. Because of our acquaintance, and because he thought me a little scholar [the reading is uncertain], he entrusted them to me so that I might draw out what they appeared to contain and clearly transcribe it onto new parchment.

I diligently carried this out and returned the corrected text to him for further correction. But since Wandelmar died long ago, even before Hubert’s death, and since, as I heard, that place remained neglected, and later the Northmen were in the same city and burned some things in a fire while plundering and carrying off others, I do not know whether those little booklets or copies of them can still be found in that city.

Therefore I thought that I should offer you the copy which I retained, for your devout and worthy study, so that, if any remnants remain of those who denied that our lord and father, our patron Dionysius, was the Areopagite, baptized by the blessed apostle Paul, ordained bishop of the Athenians, and sent into Gaul by Saint Clement, they may also recognize as established in this copy what had been said before our time on the basis of Greek testimony, the assertion of the Roman see, and Gallican witness.

For truth, when more frequently examined, shines forth more brightly into the light.

## LETTER XXIV. TO THE ASSEMBLY OF BISHOPS

*Reply to the inquiry of Gunthar, archbishop of Cologne, concerning the wife of Boso, who had left her husband.*

*(In Sirmond, from an old manuscript of the Thuana Library.)*

Hincmar, bishop of Rheims in name, though not in merit, and servant of the people of God, to the sacred assembly [Col. 0154D].

Someone proposed certain questions to blessed Ambrose, and he invited the questioner to the church on the following day to answer them. Beginning his discourse there (*On the Incarnation of the Lord*), he said:

“‘I have come to pay the debt owed to my creditor.’ But I too was unable to respond at that time to Lord Gunthar’s question, which had been put to me the previous day, for three reasons: first, because we were already preparing to depart at once; and second, because many wise men are present in the assembly, some striving to put forward arguments and others to resolve them. Sometimes, compelled by necessity, I am forced to confuse my words by speaking with such speed rather than uttering them properly, before another snatches the thought from my very lips, that my mouth is not even able to express what my shaken memory supplies.

“Moreover, as it is written, ‘He who presses the breasts forcefully extracts butter, and he who milks violently draws blood’ (Prov. XXX), I feared that if I answered rashly and too hastily I might fall into a carnal understanding, because my heart had abandoned me, occupied with other matters, and the clear light of my small understanding was neither within me nor with me.

“Therefore I postponed my answer until perhaps, according to the prophet (Ezek. III), a hand might be sent to feed me with a scroll of understanding. That hand is sent as often as divine grace reveals to us what we previously did not know. Accordingly, let us set forth Lord Gunthar’s proposal and give the answer according to the capacity of our understanding, from the abundance of divine grace.”

“If,” he said, “Boso’s wife comes to us and publicly confesses, saying: ‘It is my fault; I committed adultery against my husband. Therefore, terrified by fear of death, I have fled to you, who are God’s representative, so that you may save me for God and free me from the bodily death that threatens me from my husband’s side’—should I impose public penance upon her, which she would perform in my parish, where she has taken refuge, separated from her husband? Or should I return her to that same husband under the condition that he in no way kill her, but keep her in marriage after her penance? If he kills her, let him know that he will be punished by ecclesiastical condemnation, since it is a crime for anyone in public penance to be killed by anyone.”

We answer:

That woman was born, baptized, raised, and brought to adulthood in your parish or in someone else’s; she was endowed with an inheritance of property. Boso, born not merely in another parish but in another province, and brought through every stage of growth to mature manhood, living under the care of another bishop, obtained her from those whose concern it was, according to divine and human law. He betrothed her, endowed her, honored her with a public marriage, joined her to himself in the marital union, and made one body and one flesh with her, as it is written:

“The two shall be one flesh; therefore they are no longer two but one flesh” (Gen. II; Matt. XIX);

and:

“What God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matt. XIX).

This is so unless perhaps they remain perpetually continent by mutual consent, in which case they are joined all the more closely insofar as they are joined more spiritually; or unless they separate for a time in order to devote themselves to prayer and then return again to the same union, lest they be tempted by Satan because of their lack of continence (I Cor. VII); or unless they separate on account of fornication, in which case they must either remain thus—that is, unmarried and separated—or be mutually reconciled.

How will you be able to separate the lower part of that man’s body, who lives under another bishop’s care, and hold it under penance, when it cannot devote itself continually to prayer without the consent of the superior part? For “the woman does not have authority over her own body, but the husband; and likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife” (ibid.).

The husband must render the marital debt to his wife, and the wife to her husband, so that they may not be tempted by Satan because of their lack of continence. Whoever among them does not do this, unless he dismisses the other by consent for God’s sake, makes his partner—or rather, the part of his own body—commit adultery.

If you impose penance upon this woman, who is a part of her husband’s body but belongs to another diocese, without the consent of her bishop and husband, you act against ecclesiastical regulations and, as Pope Leo teaches, you are deprived of the fellowship of honor.

And again: if you lay the hand of penance upon this woman, and she follows her head—her head being the husband—into another province, under the care of another prelate, who will take responsibility for her penance? Who will attend to her tears and confession so that she may be reconciled, according to the canons, when he has not heard them? Who will lay a hand upon her for reconciliation, when the sacred rules decree that no bishop may receive for reconciliation someone placed under the hand of another priest, nor receive someone who has been reconciled without the letters or consent of the one who reconciled him?

And how will you judge—or rather, condemn through a penitential judgment—a part of the body, indeed a person, belonging to another bishop and parish, when it is written, as Saint Gregory explained this passage in his decrees:

“If you pass through your friend’s grainfield, you may pluck the ears with your hands and eat, but you must not put in a sickle” (Deut. XXIII)—that is, you may hasten to bring people of another parish into the body of Christ, which is the Church, by the word of preaching and the example of good works, but you are not permitted to put in the sickle of judgment or reap with the sickle of judgment, that is, to cut into or cut off—while taking care not to trample upon your simpler brother, lest you fall into ruin and the devil’s snare, namely, vainglory.

And since, as Boso himself says, he brings no crime against this woman, who is his flesh, but only a considerable negligence—because she withdrew herself from his service and, insofar as it depended on her, made him commit adultery by unjustly leaving him and remaining for about three years in other kingdoms, persisting so stubbornly in disobedience to his commands that she did not return to him even after being summoned over so long a period—he is prepared, at the order of the apostolic lord, to grant her indulgence.

It remains, therefore, that the king in whose kingdom she lives should, according to the written agreement of our kings, have her brought into the presence of her husband. And you, the bishop in whose parish she resides, since this is not the king’s responsibility, should, as Saint Gregory commands concerning those who flee to the Church, if necessity requires, seek and obtain from her husband a guarantee that she will be treated equitably. After this, an official of the state should restore the wife who fled to her husband.

If that husband breaks his pledge and proves disobedient to the apostolic admonitions, the bishop whose care he belongs to should exercise canonical judgment against him accordingly.

But if she escapes unharmed after confessing or being legally convicted of adultery, that same bishop should subject her to penance according to ecclesiastical law, since it is known to be established and customary even under secular laws that the evils committed in a particular place are corrected in the places where they are legally proven to have been committed.

Beyond this, I see nothing to be done except either to carry out the apostolic lord’s admonitions or to incur judgment.

Concerning the oath, since he has fled, as it were, for refuge to ecclesiastical mercy, because he sought your assistance—that is, episcopal assistance—which you require against impunity, even by the lawful deprivation of limb or life if the nature of the deed so demands—you must carefully consider, beyond what Saint Gregory decreed should also be required for those who have fled to sacred sanctuaries, namely, an assurance that equity will be observed, lest you appear or be said to wish to confuse and destroy not only the condition, order, and vigor of the Church but also those of the whole world, and to resist the teaching of the apostle and of apostolic men. For they not only observed and handed down for observance the laws promulgated by Christian kings, but also sought that laws be promulgated, as is repeatedly found in the canons of the Council of Carthage, the African Council, and other councils, and in the decrees of the apostolic see.

Accordingly, Saint Gregory composed an entire set of instructions for John the Defender and for others concerning legal edicts; and Saint Gelasius wrote to the emperor Anastasius (Letter 10, near the beginning):

> “For if, as far as the order of public discipline is concerned, the prelates of religion themselves obey your laws, recognizing that the imperial authority has been conferred upon you by heavenly disposition, so that they may not appear, even in worldly matters, to oppose an enacted judgment, with what disposition, I ask, is it fitting and proper for you to obey those who have been appointed to administer venerable mysteries?”

And Saint Leo, writing to Turibius, bishop of Astorga (Letter 4, near the beginning), says:

> “With good reason our fathers, in whose time this detestable heresy broke forth, labored insistently throughout the whole world so that the impious madness might be driven from the universal Church. For even the rulers of the world so detested this sacrilegious insanity that they struck down its author, together with many of his disciples, by the sword of the public laws. They saw that every concern for morality would be removed, every marital bond dissolved, and divine and human law alike overturned, if people of this kind were anywhere permitted to live while maintaining such a profession. This strictness long benefited ecclesiastical leniency. Although leniency, content with priestly judgment, avoids bloody punishments, it is nevertheless supported by the severe constitutions of Christian rulers, since those who fear bodily judgment sometimes have recourse to a spiritual remedy. But after a hostile incursion occupied many provinces, and the storms of war blocked the execution of the laws; after communication among the priests of God became difficult and assemblies began to be rare, secret treachery found freedom amid the public disorder, and was encouraged toward the subversion of many minds by those evils by which it ought to have been corrected.”

[Col. 0158A] Read Book XVI of Roman law; read the decrees of Damasus; go through the letters of Leo and of the other pontiffs sent from various councils to the emperors; examine the edicts of the Augusti promulgated concerning heretics at the petition of the pontiffs; search the chapters of our Caesars, and you will find how much the severity of the laws has benefited and continues to benefit not only ecclesiastical leniency but also the desired peace and cultivated tranquility of all Christendom.

For Wisdom—namely, Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God—says: “Through me kings reign, and those who establish laws decree what is just” (Prov. VIII); and the Apostle says: “The law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy, just, and good” (Rom. VII, 12). Hence Ambrose says:

> “That the commandment is to be understood as law is attested by the evangelical word. For he says: ‘If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments’ (Matt. XIX). And again the Apostle says: ‘The law was established because of transgressions’ (Gal. III, 19). And: ‘The law is not established for the righteous, but for the unrighteous and disobedient, the ungodly and sinners, the wicked, the defiled, those who kill fathers and mothers, murderers, fornicators, those who have intercourse with males, kidnappers, liars, and whatever else is contrary to sound teaching’ (I Tim. I, 9).”

And again:

> “For those who rule are not a terror to good works but to evil ones” (Rom. XIII, 3).

Hence Ambrose says:

> “By ‘those who rule’ he means those kings who are created for correcting life and preventing wrongdoing. They bear the image of God, so that the others may be subject to one.”

And again the Apostle says: “Do you wish not to fear the authority? Do what is good, and you will receive praise from it” (ibid.). Here the same teacher says:

> “Praise arises from authority when someone is found innocent. For he is God’s minister to you for good. It is clear that rulers were therefore appointed so that evil might not be done. But if you do evil, be afraid. For he does not carry the sword without cause: that is, he threatens so that, if he is despised, he may punish. For he is God’s minister, an avenger in wrath against the one who does evil. Since God has established a future judgment and wishes no one to perish, he appointed rulers for this age, placing fear before human beings as though they were pedagogues, teaching them what they should observe so that they might not fall into the punishment of the future judgment. Therefore be subject, not only because of wrath—that is, present vengeance—but also because of conscience. He rightly says that they ought to be subject not only because of wrath, that is, present vengeance, which produces punishment, but also because of the future judgment; for if they escape here, punishment awaits them there, where they will be punished while conscience itself accuses them.”

And Saint Cyprian says in the ninth degree of abuses:

> “Because a king ought to be not an unrighteous man but a corrector of the unrighteous.”

And there, among other things:

> “He ought to restrain thefts, punish adulteries, remove the impious from the land, not allow parricides and perjurers to live, and not allow his own sons to act impiously.”

And blessed John Chrysostom, in the sixteenth homily on the evangelist Matthew, says:

> “You have heard, the Lord says, that it was said to the ancients: ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth’ (Matt. V). He did not enact this law so that we might in turn gouge out one another’s eyes, but so that, through the fear by which we fear suffering such a thing from another, we too might take care not to commit anything of the kind; so that even those who, through the goodness of their will, were unwilling to cease from cruelty might at least be compelled by fear to spare the eyes of their neighbors. But if it is called cruel to restrain a murderer and an adulterer, let that also be called cruel. Yet these are altogether the words of fools and of those driven mad by extreme frenzy. For I am so far from fearing to say that these things are cruel that I would prove even their opposites to be unjust; and common reason itself certainly recognizes this.

> “You say that because he commanded an eye to be taken for an eye, he was cruel. I, however, answer that unless he had issued this command, then among very many people there truly would have been the very condition which you falsely complain that he possessed. Let us finally imagine in speech that every law had been dissolved, that no one feared punishment for such deeds, and that all the wicked were entirely permitted to use their own ways—adulterers, murderers, thieves, perjurers, and parricides. Would not, under such permission, all things alike be engulfed in one confusion of wickedness? Would not cities, marketplaces, houses, seas, and the whole world have been filled with a thousand crimes and slaughters? For if, while laws rule and threats and terror remain in force, wicked desires are nevertheless scarcely restrained, what method could have curbed wickedness if this protection too had been absent? What plague would not have rushed upon human life?

> “Nor is only this cruel—namely, permitting the wicked to do whatever they wish. There is another thing no less so: neglecting and despising the one who has been injured and afflicted undeservedly. Tell me: if someone gathered fierce and always-wicked men together, armed them with swords, and ordered them to go throughout the whole city stabbing everyone they met, what could be more savage than this? But if another person bound and forcibly restrained those who had been armed by him, and freed from those unjust hands the people who were to be killed, what could be found more humane than this?

> “Transfer these examples also to the laws. The law that commanded an eye to be gouged out for an eye, instilling in sinners the fear of executioners, is found to resemble the one who restrained those armed men whom I mentioned. But the one who decreed no punishment at all for the wrongdoer, and thus seems to you to have armed wickedness, imitating the one who equipped those criminal swords and thereby unleashed the destruction of the whole city—do you see how those commandments are not only free of all cruelty but are also commandments of the greatest mercy?”

And whoever wishes to read the letters of blessed Gregory will likewise find in them very frequently that evil-doers and the unrighteous are punished by appropriate vengeance.

Therefore, dearest brother, understand that to act or demand anything contrary to these principles is not only to confuse the rights of mercy, but also to bring the troubles of detraction upon priestly innocence and purity, and to inflict the blasphemies of disparagement. For slanderers will say: “Paul says: ‘Not only those who do these things, but also those who approve of those who do them, are worthy of death’ (Rom. I, 32); yet this man does not permit the unrighteous to be restrained.” Hence the Lord also says through the Psalmist to a priest such as this:

> “Why do you recount my righteous acts and take up my covenant in your mouth? You hate discipline; you ran with the thief, and you placed your portion with adulterers” (Ps. XLIX, 16–18).

For he would not foster the wicked if he loved what is good; but, loving the Lord and hating vice, he would do what belonged to him and would not attack what had been decreed by God through those who establish laws and decree what is just.

And wicked women and perverse men will say: “Let us do what we wish and approach the church or the bishop, and we shall remain unpunished.” Thus our ministry will be discredited and we shall become contemptible, since we despise the legal justice established by the Lord for the unrighteous—for every just law has no crime in it, lest it be unjust, and yet it punishes the criminal, so that it may truly be just.

On the other hand, some will boast: “Scripture says: ‘Do not be excessively righteous.’ ‘Blessed are the merciful’ (Eccles. VII; Matt. V). And: ‘Judgment without mercy awaits the one who has shown no mercy’ (Jas. II, 13); and: ‘Mercy triumphs over judgment’ (ibid.); and the Lord said to the adulterous woman: ‘Neither will I condemn you; go, and from now on do not sin’ (John VIII, 11). And you, priest—upon whom should you bestow mercy if not upon the wretched? Yet, by withholding mercy, you close the inward parts of mercy against him, although you are exempt from punishment in his regard?”

To guard carefully and prudently against the disparagement of both sides in relation to those who serve the sacred mysteries, blessed Gregory writes to Leontius, former consul:

> “Your Glory ought to remember that he never accepted my letters on behalf of anyone except so that you might provide your protection while doing justice; for it is shameful to defend something that has not first been established as just. I love people because of justice, but I do not set justice aside because of people.”

And to Romanus the Defender (Book VII, Letter 24, indiction 2):

> “Whether you receive ecclesiastical patronages or my letters have not even been sent, you ought to provide protection with such moderation that those involved in public thefts may not appear to be unjustly defended by us, lest through the boldness of indiscriminate defense we in any way transfer the reputation of evil-doers onto ourselves. Rather, as befits the Church, help those whom you can by admonishing them and offering a word of intercession, so that you may both bring them aid and not stain the reputation of the holy Church.”

He also writes to John, bishop of the city of Caralis, concerning those who have fled to the precincts of the church and even to the sanctuaries themselves:

> “If those concerning whom there is a dispute should perhaps flee to the church, the case ought to be arranged in such a way that neither they themselves suffer violence nor those who are said to have been oppressed suffer loss. Therefore let it be your concern that they promise under oath to those concerned that the law and justice will be observed; and let them be admonished in every way to leave and render an account of their actions.”

These matters, lords and brothers, I have laid before you at your hearing, having been asked by our aforesaid venerable fellow priest to do so. If they do not seem sufficient to him in answer to his question, he can read more on this subject in the pages of the saints and find more extensive discussions by my poor self in the answers to questions on which I have been consulted by others, in the twenty-second and twenty-eighth [responses].

Since I made mention above of the agreement of our kings, I have taken care to append here what was established there concerning these matters (Capitularies of Charles the Bald, title 8, chapter 4):

> “And because the peace and tranquility of the kingdom are commonly disturbed by vagabonds and by irreverent men acting according to tyrannical custom, we wish that whenever such a person comes to any one of us, so that he may not evade an account and justice concerning what he has done, none of us receive or retain him for any other purpose than to bring him to a proper reckoning and due correction. And if he evades a proper reckoning, let us all together pursue him into whatever kingdom he has entered, until either he is brought to account or is removed from the kingdom.

> “The same is to be done with one who is accused or excommunicated by any bishop for a capital and public crime, or who, after committing a crime before excommunication, changes his kingdom and the rule of his king so as not to undertake the due penance or lawfully complete the penance he has undertaken; or who, while fleeing, takes with him an incestuous female relative, a nun, a woman abducted by force, or an adulteress whom he was not permitted to keep there. When such a man’s bishop, whose responsibility he is, has informed us, he must be diligently sought, so that he may not find a place in the kingdom of any one of us in which to remain or hide, and infect God’s faithful and ours with his disease. Instead, he must be restrained by us or through the ministers of the state, so that, together with the diabolical spoil he has taken with him, he may return to his own bishop and undertake due penance for whatever public crime he has committed, or be compelled lawfully to complete the penance he has undertaken.”

## LETTER XXV. TO HILDEGARIUS, BISHOP OF MEAUX  
### Concerning the Judgment of Cold Water

*(In the same author, from a manuscript of Saint-Remi of Reims.)*

HINCMAR, bishop of Reims and servant of the people of God, sends greetings to his beloved brother and venerable bishop HILDEGARIUS.

[Col. 0161D] While we were conversing and asking one another about various matters, the subject arose of the judgment by cold water, concerning which you said that the venerable archbishop of Mainz, Rabanus, had written certain things, and you wished to ask what I thought of his writings. Accordingly, among other matters I replied to you that I had once written, in answer to questions from our brothers and fellow bishops from the kingdom of the younger Lothair, and you earnestly requested that extracts from my writings be taken and sent to you.

Since it is written, “Give to everyone who asks of you, and do not turn away from the one who wishes to borrow from you” (Matt. V, 42), I send to your affection what you requested, excerpts from my inadequate answers to the questions of those aforementioned brothers of ours. Whether these things are probable, or ought to be rejected on the authority and basis of reason, I leave to the judgment of the Catholic reader.

When speaking of the judgment that will occur through fire at his second coming, the Lord recalled the judgment that first took place through water: “As it happened in the days of Noah, so will it be in the days of the Son of Man” (Matt. XXIV, 37). And, referring to the fact that he judged Sodom through fire, he likewise says: “So it was in the days of Lot” (Luke XVII, 28).

The ingenuity of Christianity, standing between judgments already carried out and judgments still to come, established and frequently practiced from ancient times the judgment that takes place through water—a judgment that had occurred under Noah in the ark of faith, delivering the innocent and condemning the guilty.

But concerning the fiery water, as happened under Lot through fire and will happen at the coming of the Son of Man, Peter bears witness, saying:

> “The heavens existed long ago, and the earth was formed out of water and through water by the word of God; through these the world that then existed, flooded with water, perished. But the heavens and earth that now exist have been stored up by the same word, reserved for fire on the day of judgment and the destruction of ungodly people” (II Pet. III, 5).

He plainly teaches that the heavens destined to perish by fire are none other than those that perished through water—that is, these empty and cloudy expanses of the windy air. For it is not to be believed that the water of the Flood, which rose only fifteen cubits above the mountain peaks, reached beyond the boundaries of the air and the ether. Wherever it was able to reach, there also, according to the aforementioned statement of blessed Peter, the fire of judgment will reach.

But since it is written, “Heaven and earth will pass away” (Matt. XXIV, 35), and again, “The earth stands forever” (Eccles. I, 4), we must understand that heaven and earth pass away in the appearance they now possess, while nevertheless continuing without end in their essence. “The form of this world is passing away” (I Cor. VII, 31), and, he says, “there will be a new heaven and a new earth.” These will not be created as something different, but these same things will be renewed. They will pass away and remain, because they will be cleansed of the form they now possess and will be preserved forever in their own nature. Hence it is written: “You will change them, and they will be changed” (Ps. CI, 27).

Therefore, the making of fiery water for investigating two judgments joined together into one—namely, the judgment that has already taken place through water and that which will take place through fire—is believed to have been handed down to the Church by authority. Although they differ according to the variation of times, they are one in the mystery of their operation: in them the saints are delivered unharmed, while the reprobate are punished and condemned.

The Church, which was signified by the ark of the Flood, also decreed that the Holy Spirit be breathed upon baptismal water by the breath of the priest. This is the Spirit who, at the very beginning of the world, “was borne over the waters.” Thus the nature of the waters might even then conceive the power of sanctification; and, where the rust of all sins is melted away, lighted candles, kindled with consecrated light, are to be kept immersed until the consecration of the same font is completed.

This is done through him who, washing away through the waters the crimes of the guilty world, signified the pattern of regeneration in the very outpouring of the Flood, so that, through the mystery of one and the same element, there might be both an end to vices and an origin of virtues; and through him who will come to judge the living and the dead, and the age by fire.

For in the same baptism in which, as a sign, the prophet Moses placed wood in the spring of Marah and it was sweetened (Exod. XV, 25), and in which the cross of Christ’s blood is proclaimed by the Lord’s priest, three things are one—not by nature but in the mystery of their operation: the blood of redemption, the spirit of sanctification, and the water of washing.

There, when the unclean spirit has been driven out and exorcised, he departs from the person; judgment is made upon the world, and the ruler of the world is cast out. The one who did not stand in the truth—the liar and father of lies—is separated from the truth of nature, which was created in the image of God and, reborn from water and the Holy Spirit, is restored to its origin. By faith it is cleansed inwardly and outwardly and is proved innocent of every fabrication of falsehood and of all wickedness.

But if anyone, whether by the judgment of cold water alone or by that of any fiery element, should decide, in unwavering faith—which is “the evidence of things not seen”—that it suffices him to invoke the author and governor of the elements, whom all the elements perceive when he is faithfully invoked, it makes no difference. Thus, just as in baptism, cold water is consecrated: in the Flood, the innocent were raised with the ark to heaven, while the guilty perished; and the Sodomites were punished by fire.

In the Book of Numbers, a woman who had committed adultery is said to have drunk cold water into which the Lord commanded curses to be washed, and her thigh putrefied (Num. V, 27). The apostle John escaped unharmed from a cauldron of boiling oil. And whoever chooses fiery water should understand that, when the terrible Judge comes to future judgment, storm and fire will accompany him, as it is written: “Fire will burn before him, and a mighty storm around him” (Ps. XLIX, 3), so that the storm may test those whom the fire will consume.

And that future fire will be passable for the saints, who will be caught up in clouds to meet the Lord in the air, while it will inflame his enemies all around.

Since the question of judgment for purification by boiling or cold water has arisen, let us state what certain men of keen intelligence add vigilantly. It is plainly established, they say, that in fiery water the guilty are boiled, while the innocent are freed without being cooked. For righteous Lot escaped unburned from the Sodomite fire. And the future fire that will precede the terrible Judge will be harmless to the saints but will burn the wicked, as once happened with the Babylonian furnace, which did not touch the youths at all, nor grieve them or cause them any distress, but, burning their bonds, consumed the Chaldean servants of the king whom it found tending the furnace that they had kindled (Dan. III, 48, 50).

But in the judgment of cold water it does not seem to some that the matter is consistent: the innocent are submerged, while the guilty float upon the water, even though in the judgment of the Flood the innocent were raised with the ark and the guilty perished by submersion.

The Egyptians pursuing the Hebrews through the Red Sea, when the Lord looked upon them in the morning watch through the pillar of fire and cloud, were submerged like lead in mighty waters, and not one of them survived (Exod. XIV, 24). The children of Israel, standing on the shore, saw the Egyptians dead.

Nor could the earth bear unbelievers and sinners when it opened and swallowed Dathan and covered the assembly of Abiron (Num. XVI, 32). And the instability of the water supported Peter, who trusted in faith as he walked upon it; but when he doubted in faith, it swallowed him, already almost submerged, until Christ’s right hand raised him up (Matt. XIV, 29).

The Catholic Fathers, expounding the statement of Peter’s Epistle (I Pet. III, 20) concerning the figure of baptism in the ark of the Flood, say that heretics and evil Christians are plunged into hell by the very waters by which orthodox and righteous people are lifted up to the heavenly kingdoms.

But we must bear in mind, as blessed Gregory says (Homily 26 on the Gospels):

> “If divine action can be comprehended by reason, it is not marvelous; nor does faith have merit when human reason supplies proof. And when the Apostle Paul says, ‘Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen’ (Hebr. XI, 1), it is plainly clear that faith is the evidence of things that cannot appear. For things that appear no longer require faith but recognition.”

Yet these very works of our Redeemer, which cannot at all be comprehended from themselves, must be weighed in light of another work of his, so that more marvelous deeds may give faith to marvelous things. For this reason the Lord deigned to explain certain matters from the Scriptures by himself, so that we might know to seek the meanings of things even in those matters which he himself did not wish to explain.

Therefore let those who demand human reason as proof in divine judgments and in the signs of miracles receive this answer: the ark that contained the righteous, by which the Church of the faithful was signified, and the faith of the Holy Trinity, built through the incarnation of Jesus Christ; and all those of whom the Lord said:

> “The end of all flesh has come before me, for the earth is filled with iniquity because of them, and I will destroy them with the earth” (Gen. VI, 13).

Although they were covered by the overflowing water, not all were submerged: the innocent were delivered and the guilty punished, as it is written:

> “Noah entered, and his sons, his wife, and the wives of his sons with him into the ark, because of the waters of the Flood” (Gen. VII, 7).

And shortly afterward:

> “All the fountains of the great abyss burst forth, and the floodgates of heaven were opened, and rain fell upon the earth for forty days and forty nights” (ibid., 11).

And again:

> “The waters increased and lifted the ark high above the earth” (ibid., 17).

And shortly afterward:

> “All flesh that moved upon the earth was consumed. Only Noah remained, and those who were with him in the ark” (ibid., 21, 23).

And again shortly afterward:

> “The fountains of the abyss and the floodgates of heaven were closed” (Gen. VIII, 2).

One cloud became dark for the Egyptians and luminous for the Hebrews, as it is written again:

> “Then the angel of God, who went before the camp of Israel, moved behind them; and the pillar of cloud, which had been in front of them, likewise moved and stood behind them, between the camp of the Egyptians and the camp of Israel. It was a dark cloud, yet it illuminated the night, so that they could not approach one another throughout the whole night” (Exod. XIV, 19).

And one and the same staff, stretched over the waters that stood like a wall on the right and left, led the children of Israel across, as it is written, “through overwhelming water” (Wis. X, 18), and enveloped the Egyptians in the midst of the waves, so that not one of those whom the Israelites saw dead upon the shore of the sea survived (Exod. XIV, 28).

The Lord had looked upon them, as we said, in the morning watch through the pillar of fire and cloud. He spread the cloud as a protection for his own and the fire to give them light by night (Ps. CIV, 39)—namely, Christ, who is the pillar of light, driving away the darkness of unbelief and pouring the light of truth and spiritual grace into human affections—and through the pillar of cloud, the Holy Spirit.

In this baptism the type of baptism was already displayed, just as it had been in the Flood.

Let us add further that Elijah invoked the name of the Lord his God, and fire descended from heaven (IV Kings I, 10). Under Elisha, salt or wood cast into water also effected a change (IV Kings I, 21); and Elisha invoked the name of the Lord, and the iron of the axe was raised to its wooden handle and floated upon the water (IV Kings VI, 7). For iron is heavier in substance than the fluidity of water. We therefore perceive that grace is greater than nature.

Let the explanation of blessed Ambrose concerning all these matters suffice, so that it may be gathered why, in the judgment of cold water, one person is submerged and another lifted up. For in his book On the Sacraments, or Mysteries (Book II, chapter 6), he says:

> “Nevertheless, lest the fraud or snares of the devil should prevail in this world, baptism was devised. Concerning this baptism, hear what Scripture says—or rather, what the Son of God says: because the Pharisees, who refused to be baptized with the baptism of John, rejected the counsel of God (Luke VII, 30). Therefore baptism is the counsel of God.”

And shortly afterward:

> “When you are submerged, that sentence is annulled: ‘You are earth, and to earth you shall go’ (Gen. III, 19). The sentence has been fulfilled; there is now a place for heavenly benefit and remedy. Water therefore comes from the earth, but the condition of our life did not permit us to be covered by earth and to rise again from the earth. Moreover, it is not earth that washes, but water washes. Therefore the font is like a tomb.”

Furthermore, as the Apostle says, “Every Scripture inspired by God is useful for teaching, for refutation, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness, so that the man of God may be perfect, equipped for every good work” (II Tim. III, 16).

And as we read in the sayings of the Catholic Fathers, the divine word is a pearl that can be pierced from every side. Whoever brings forward testimonies from Scripture for the instruction of the faithful—even if he explains them differently from the way they were understood by those through whom they were uttered—is not a fabricator of falsehood, provided the understanding of the elders is preserved. Therefore, from their words I shall say what, by conjecture, I suspect I can carve out according to the smallness of my intellect.

The holy Apostle teaches (I Cor. X) that the Red Sea, through which our fathers passed under the leadership of Moses, was a baptism reddened by the blood of Christ. Moses himself prefigured Christ the leader, who through baptism led us out of Egyptian slavery into the promised land—namely, from the slavery of sin and the dominion of death into the freedom of the glory of the children of God and into the kingdom of eternal life.

The rock that followed the people through the desert likewise prefigured Christ, who follows us in the wilderness of this age through his mysteries. Hence the same Apostle says concerning baptism:

> “All who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death. Therefore we were buried with him through baptism into death” (Rom. VI, 3).

John Chrysostom says:

> “What does ‘we were baptized into his death’ mean? That we too should die as he did. For the cross is baptism. Therefore what the cross and tomb were for Christ, baptism has become for us, although not in the same respects. That is why he did not say, ‘Planted together with death,’ but ‘with the likeness of death’ (Rom. VI, 5). He died and was buried in the flesh; we, in both respects, die to sin.”

From these words it seems possible to infer that one who has been buried with Christ through baptism into death, and freed through that same baptism from death, may return through sin to the same slavery and death. “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. XVIII, 4). Let him be planted in the likeness of death in water, so that either, being proved guilty, he may be compelled, willingly or unwillingly—for good things are often bestowed upon the unwilling—to confess, and through confession accompanied by amendment and correction may again be freed from the death of the sin he has committed; or, being shown innocent by God’s judgment, he may not be held by us among the accused, though planted in the likeness of death in water.

For the sea, as was shown above, signifying baptism, retains nothing dead within itself; as it is written, it cast the dead Egyptians upon the shore (Exod. XIV, 31). Therefore the dead Egyptian—that is, the person subject to sin—as long as he remains in the death of his sin by denying it, is not received or retained by water sanctified through the invocation of the truth, which is Christ.

But let him come forth, bound with the bands of his iniquities, from the hiding places of an evil conscience by confessing; and through confession of the truth he will be buried in the water, as though planted in the likeness of the death of the truest truth, and freed by that same truth.

The man who is to be examined is to be bound with a rope and lowered into the water [Col. 0166D], because, as it is written, “Everyone is bound by the ropes of his sins” (Prov. 5:22). He appears to be bound for two reasons: namely, so that he may not be able to commit any fraud in the judgment, and so that, if the water receives him as innocent, he may be able to be drawn back in time lest he perish in the water. For we read that Lazarus, dead for four days—by whom anyone buried beneath the weight of crimes is signified—was buried bound with wrappings, and that he came forth from the tomb still bound with those same wrappings when the Lord called him, and was unbound by the disciples at his command (John 6:39).

Thus the person being examined is lowered into the water bound for judgment; he is drawn back bound; and he is either immediately acquitted by the judgment of the arbiters once purged, or, remaining bound until his purification, is examined by judgment [Col. 0167A]. Again, in sacred history we read that Elijah came to the Jordan with his disciple Elisha and, wrapping his cloak, struck the waters, which divided, and both crossed over. Afterwards Elisha lifted up Elijah’s cloak, which had fallen from him, and, coming to the Jordan, struck the waters and, having invoked the God of Elijah, divided them and crossed over (2 Kings 2).

The flow of our mortality is rightly expressed by the Jordan, because *Jordan* is also interpreted in Latin as “the descent of them,” namely, of Christians. As Gregory says (Moralia, book 33, chapter 6), “Since the author of our redemption deigned to be baptized in the river Jordan, the multitude of those who are held within the sacrament of baptism is rightly expressed by the name Jordan.” Hence it is written in Job concerning the ancient enemy of the human race: “And he trusts that the Jordan will flow into his mouth” (Job 40:18) [Col. 0167B], because, after he carried away unbelievers from the beginning of the world, he presumes that he can still receive believers as well. For by the mouth of his poisonous persuasion he daily devours those in whom an evil life is at variance with the confession of faith.

Thus, as though the water were struck and divided by Elijah’s wrapped cloak, and a passage were prepared through it, this happens when such persons, as we have already said on the basis of Saint Gregory’s words, are bound and lowered into the water. The water is, as it were, divided when it receives some and shows them to be innocent, or rejects others and demonstrates that they are guilty. A passage is prepared when some are judged to be transferred from the crimes attributed to them among the innocent, or when others, by a declared judgment, are assigned among the guilty because of their denial.

For when both the person thought to be guilty and the person who actually is guilty is lowered into the water for examination, the Lord is invoked by those who lower him, according to a certain form of baptism, so that the truth being sought may be revealed and that he may deign to illumine the darkness of our ignorance, lest we unjustly condemn an innocent person, or lest a guilty person escape punishment in some way through his denial or through diabolical fraud [Col. 0167C].

The person himself who is lowered into the water for examination confirms the invocation of those invoking the Lord by his answer and declaration, in a manner according to the form preceding baptism. In baptism, either the sponsor speaks on behalf of the person who is another’s—that is, who has been lost through original sin—and is saved through another’s faith; or an adult confesses sins, whether contracted or committed, renouncing the devil and all his works and pomps. In response to the priest’s question, so that the water may receive the person whose uncleanness is no longer hidden by denial but has been made public by confession, and so that he may be buried with Christ and his sins be submerged, according to Scripture, “into the depths of the sea,” like the Egyptians in the Red Sea, he responds concerning the confession of his faith.

As Saint Ambrose says in his book *On the Sacraments* (book 2, chapter 7):

> “You were asked: ‘Do you believe in God the almighty Father?’ You said: ‘I believe,’ and you were immersed—that is, you were buried. Again you were asked: ‘Do you believe in our Lord Jesus Christ and in his cross?’ You said: ‘I believe,’ and you were immersed. Therefore you were also buried with Christ. For whoever is buried with Christ rises with Christ. A third time you were asked: [Col. 0168A] ‘Do you also believe in the Holy Spirit?’ You said: ‘I believe,’ and you were immersed a third time, so that the threefold confession might absolve the repeated fall of your former life. Finally, to give you an example, Saint Peter the Apostle, after he appears to have fallen during the Lord’s Passion through the weakness of human condition—he who had previously denied him—was later asked three times by Christ whether he loved Christ, in order to erase and undo that fall. Then he says: ‘Lord, you know that I love you’ (John 21:15). He said it three times, so that he might be absolved three times.”

So also, when a person found guilty in the judgment is perhaps suspected of several matters, he is to be examined again and again until he is found to have been proved by a confession of amendment. For this purpose let us also take up the words of Saint Ambrose, who says:

> “Finally, to give you an example, Saint Peter the Apostle, after he appears to have fallen during the Lord’s Passion through the weakness of human condition—he who had previously denied him—was later asked three times by Christ whether he loved Christ, in order to erase and undo that fall. Then he says: ‘Lord, you know that I love you.’ He said it three times, so that he might be absolved three times.”

And since, as we showed above, baptism is a judgment by divine authority—for this reason *Jordan*, signifying baptism, is interpreted as “the stream of judgment,” by which the prince of this world—the liar and father of falsehood—is cast out—and since baptism is the counsel of God, the counsel of a divine man led them to discover the judgment of cold water for investigating unknown matters.

In this judgment of cold water, when the truth, which is God, is invoked, the person who desires to conceal the truth by his lie cannot be submerged in the waters over which the voice of the Lord’s majesty thundered. For the pure nature of water does not recognize as pure the human nature that has been cleansed through baptismal water from every fabrication of falsehood and then infected again by a lie; therefore it does not receive it but rejects it as alien.

Just as in baptism the unclean spirit—that is, the prince of this world—is cast out from a human being, so also the person who has been repossessed through sin by the devil, the prince of this world, is rejected from the water sanctified by the invocation of the divine name, together with the seven other spirits more wicked than himself, as it is written (Matt. 12:45): “When he has gone out from a person, he returns to him who is vacant,” or rather empty, when he finds the person unoccupied by good works.

The water does not regard such a person as natural, as one who has been born again from water and the Spirit and cleansed—not by the putting off of bodily filth, but by the questioning and confession of a good conscience toward God. Rather, it regards him as the sort of person concerning whom it is written in Leviticus:

> “Every person of your offspring who approaches the holy things, which the children of Israel have consecrated and offered to the Lord, and in whom there is uncleanness, shall perish before the Lord” (Lev. 22:3).

It does not say, “In whom there was uncleanness.” His uncleanness is in him, because he conceals the truth by a lie. Therefore, concerning the priestly lineage, it says: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. 2:9); and in the Apocalypse: “You have made us a kingdom for God and priests” (Rev. 5:10). When such a person approaches the things consecrated to the Lord, so long as his uncleanness is in him, he will not be able to be immersed in the waters sanctified by the invocation of God, so that he may perish as innocent; rather, he will be shown to be destined to perish [Col. 0169A].

The Apostle says: “Cleanse out the old leaven, so that you may be a new lump, just as you are unleavened” (1 Cor. 5:7). It is as though he plainly said: “Purge by an oath or by the judgment of God the person who has been accused of a crime but whom you cannot establish according to judicial procedure with suitable witnesses, lest, while the accursed thing remains in your midst, it be said to you: ‘There is an accursed thing in your midst, O Israel; you cannot stand before your enemies’” (Josh. 7:13).

Again the Apostle says: “Do not participate in the unfruitful works of darkness” (Eph. 5:11). Hence Augustine says (*On the Words of the Lord*, sermon 18):

> “‘Do not participate’ means ‘do not consent.’ And because it would be little not to consent if negligence of discipline followed, he adds, ‘but rather reprove them.’ In two ways an evil person does not defile you: if you do not consent, and if you reprove him.”

Therefore the sinner is to be reproved. If he denies his guilt and cannot be proved according to judicial procedure, he is to be examined, so that once proved he may be made manifest and, once rejected, may not be able to remain hidden. When discovered, he must confess and repent. He will then no longer be held by the rope of his sins, by which he was bound, so that he may not be submerged and washed in saving water poured out with tears, and may be submerged like the Egyptians and those who had been corrupted by carnal corruption before the Lord, “like lead in mighty waters.” According to the prophet, “Let his iniquities be cast into the depths of the sea” (Mic. 7:19), because previously he could not be submerged with his lie so as to be washed until, by confession, he had cast it from himself into the depths and emerged cleansed.

Before confession he was pressed down by the water like Elisha’s iron (2 Kings 6:7), until, at the confession of the divine name, he returned to the wood. Likewise, the person who denies his sin is pressed down by an anxious conscience under the weight of sin until, proclaiming his sinfulness to the Lord, in whose wood of the cross, as Ambrose says, the weakness of all human beings is lifted up.

This is the flood, which is also baptism, by which all sins are washed away, while the mind and grace of the righteous alone are restored to life, having long before died through the denial of sin.

Let the devout reader read the book of the *Dialogues* of blessed Gregory (book 2, chapters 23, 24, 3, 28, 7, 6), and he will find that nuns who had not been corrected and who had been excommunicated by Saint Benedict because of their refusal of correction came out of their graves through the Church at the time of communion after death, because they did not communicate; but after reconciliation they remained in their graves. He will also find that the body of a boy-monk could not be held by the earth because he did not have Benedict’s grace; that a glass vessel was shattered by the sign of the cross made by Benedict; that another glass vessel, thrown at his command into a huge precipice strewn with masses of rock because of disobedience, was preserved unharmed; that his disciple Maurus walked upon the waters of a lake; and that iron from the depths of the lake was recalled into its handle by him, after the manner of Elisha.

Likewise, as is contained in the divine books (2 Macc. 1:20), sacred fire that had been hidden was found, after many years had passed, changed into thick water; and when that same water was poured over the sacrifice that had been offered, it was consumed by divine power in fire [Col. 0170A]. Gideon’s sacrifice also, with the broth poured over it—whose abundance ordinarily extinguishes fire—was consumed through angelic agency, with fire even licking the rock (Judg. 6:19). Thus, within the mystery of one and the same element, the end of vices and the beginning of virtues are brought about by the operation of the Holy Spirit in the water of sacred baptism.

The careful reader should consider these things and will not be surprised that, in the judgment of cold water, the innocent are received by the water while the guilty are not received, just as the guilty are cooked in hot water while the innocent are preserved uncooked. For Christ, the heavenly medicine of the Father and the true physician of human salvation, when invoked by his faithful—as bodily physicians also commonly do under his inspiration—heals opposites with opposites: hot things with cold, and cold things with hot.

In the ancient Church, which is more commonly called the Synagogue, among the people involved in one and the same rebellion, some were covered when the earth swallowed them, while others were consumed by devouring fire above the earth (Num. 16:30, 35). While the innocent flesh of the Savior is washed in cold waters, the fiery sword once opposed to the guilty in paradise is extinguished.

Likewise, by the arrangement of the Creator and Ruler of the elements, one and the same sun hardens mud and melts wax. Let these things be said because the unstable element, when a person is submerged, receives some in accordance with the faith of those who believe, while it does not receive others; and, through the heat of that same element, some are cooked while others escape uncooked.

Nor should it be passed over that we read in the capitularies of the emperors (Additional Book 4, chapter 80) that the judgment of cold water had been forbidden [Col. 0170C], but not in those synodal documents that we have received from particular synods. Some foolishly say that it had been forbidden for this reason: because the person who is immersed in water in the name of the Lord is, as it were, rebaptized. But we do not find this written there at all.

Nor are we unaware that blessed Ambrose speaks of several baptisms, that is, he records several proclamations concerning baptism. The sacred canons prohibit rebaptizations as things to be avoided by all. Yet scarcely anyone among the faithful enters water for washing without the sign of the cross or the invocation of the divine name, while the Apostle commands: “Do everything in the name of the Lord” (1 Cor. 10:31); and no one thinks that he is being baptized by that baptism through which he was reborn from water and the Spirit.

For the word, the work of God, and all the divine sacraments are manna, which, as it is written, “had every delight and sweetness of every taste” (Wis. 16:2). Just as manna was once made according to the desire of those who received it, so these things become, according to the devotion of believers, occasions for manifestations.

The Lord’s incarnation, for example, is “for the fall and resurrection of many”; his cross is foolishness to those who are perishing but the power of God for salvation to those who believe; and his preaching is to some “the aroma of death unto death,” and to others “the aroma of life unto life.” Likewise, according to the testimony of Catholic teachers, the sacrament of baptism, which is consecrated by solemn words, is mockery to unbelievers but redemption to the faithful.

If, however, it is performed outside the Lord’s institution and the apostolic tradition [Col. 0171A], it is a washing of bodily filth, not a cleansing of sins. Thus Saint Augustine says concerning the consecration of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ in his book *Against Faustus* (book 20, chapter 13):

> “Bread and the cup become for us what they were not born as, not by any arbitrary consecration but by a definite one. Therefore, what is not so made, although it is bread and a cup, is nourishment for refreshment, not the sacrament of religion.”

The sacraments of the altar themselves are life to those who approach them devoutly, but judgment to the undevout. Thus bread strengthens the life of the strong but kills little children; a gentle hiss calms horses but incites puppies; the sun melts wax but hardens mud; to healthy eyes it is light, but to diseased eyes darkness. Just as poison is death to a human being but life to a serpent, so this judgment is, to those who firmly and rightly believe, a manifestation of the truth, but to those who hesitate and doubt it is recognized as an error that entangles them.

For, as Paul says, “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Heb. 11:1). It is therefore clear, as blessed Gregory explains (Homily 26), that faith is evidence of those things that cannot appear. For things that appear no longer possess faith but recognition.

So in this divine judgment, once those matters about which we had previously doubted have been shown by divine manifestation—things that we cannot see with bodily eyes—we ought, contemplating them with the eyes of faith, to give them our assent. Thus Thomas, who had previously doubted, touched the Lord and saw one thing but believed another: divinity could not be seen by mortal humanity. He saw a human being and confessed him as God, saying: “My Lord and my God” (John 20:28). By seeing, therefore, he believed; while recognizing him as a true human being, he proclaimed him to be the God whom he could not see.

So also, because we cannot see with bodily eyes the truth of the matter about which we doubt, we ought, believing the divine manifestation, to praise the truth, which is God, by proclaiming it, when we see fulfilled what the Apostle says: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts” (1 Cor. 4:5).

The Lord is indeed coming now for the illumination of our darkness, so that we may know the truth through the manifestation of this judgment; he will come in the future judgment to reveal the counsels of hearts [Col. 0171D].

We say these things not in order to blame anyone—for it is not written there why this judgment ought not to be performed, but merely that it should not be performed—nor do we strive to defend our own views as though they had been advanced more wisely than what others have been or may be able to discover from the teachings of the saints. “For each person abounds in his own understanding.” Let everyone take care only that he does not depart from the Catholic faith and the tradition of the apostolic see.

As for the views we humbly express, we are prepared, if someone should show us something more appropriate, to yield without contention to sound understanding, and most gladly not only to agree but even to learn.

## LETTER XXVI. TO HILDEBOLD, BISHOP OF SOISSONS

He absolves him, detained by illness, by reconciling him in his absence according to the request contained in his letter of confession.

*(In the same author, from the manuscript of Saint Remigius of Rheims.)*

[Col. 0172A]

HINCMAR, bishop of Rheims in name, not by merit, and servant of the people of God, asks from God health of mind and body for his dearest son and venerable brother HILDEBOLD.

When our brothers and fellow bishops Hodo and Rainelmus, as well as Willebertus, Adalbern, and Gerold, and the newly ordained Hadebert, were with me at Rheims, I reread the confession of your humble and sincere mind [Col. 0172B] and requested that the Lord’s mercy be implored throughout our entire diocese for the salvation of your soul and body.

And because I knew that our brother Hodo was going to you, I did not think it necessary to send you a letter, since he himself, both by our common agreement and by his episcopal ministry, could personally carry out what ought to be done for a sick brother.

But since, sending your priest to me, you returned to me that brief confession of yours and asked me to send you a letter of absolution, I gratefully received your devotion. For I know that you attend not to good merits in me—since there are none—but to the power of the ministry unworthily entrusted to me.

Therefore, in the words of Saint Leo, I send the exercise of the ministry of my unworthiness and your faith [Col. 0172C] to Jesus, the High Priest of our confession. For that same holy Leo says that in the Church of God, which is the body of Christ, neither priesthoods are valid nor sacrifices true in any other way unless the true Pontiff reconciles us in the reality of our nature and the true blood of the immaculate Lamb cleanses us.

Although he is established at the right hand of the Father, in the same flesh that he assumed from the Virgin he still carries out the sacrament of reconciliation, as the Apostle says: “Christ Jesus, who died for us—indeed, who was also raised, who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us” (Rom. 8:34). With him we can neither set a limit to mercy nor define its times; with him true confession suffers no delay in forgiveness. The Spirit of God says through the prophet: “When you have turned and groaned, you will be saved”; and elsewhere: “Declare your iniquities first, so that you may be justified”; and again: “For with the Lord there is mercy, and with him abundant redemption” (Ps. 130:7).

Saint Ambrose also says: “Blessed is the person who, even at the stroke of death, turns away from vices. Blessed are those whose sins are covered” (Ps. 32:1), because it is written: “Cease from evil and do good, and dwell for ever and ever” (Ps. 37:27). Therefore, whoever ceases from sins and turns toward better things will have the forgiveness of former sins, whether that person has confessed them through the disposition of repentance or has turned away from them through the resolve to amend.

Therefore, just as the principal judgment establishes that “we all offend in many things,” for which we groan [Col. 0173A], so the principal judgment consoles us: if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just—indeed, Jesus Christ, our creator, redeemer, and savior, whom we have as a just advocate before the Father and who is the propitiation for our sins and intercedes for us—so that, when we faithfully confess, he forgives us our sins and cleanses us from all iniquity.

Encouraged by these divine judgments, our brother and fellow priest Hildebold, through the ecclesiastical power of apostolic authority that our Lord Jesus Christ handed over to his disciples and apostles, saying, “Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven” (John 20:22–23), and that through those same apostles he gave to their successors, whose place we unworthy men occupy—not by merit, but by name and by the assumption of office—may he, by his grace and omnipotence and through the power of the Holy Spirit, who is the forgiveness of all sins, forgive you all your sins, free you from every evil, preserve you in every good, and lead you to eternal life and to fellowship with the holy priests. Amen.

And because, dearest brother, you know that I am prevented by such an illness from going to you in body, I go to you in spirit and devotion. What I would do bodily for you, I do in spirit, and through our fellow ministers and fellow priests I ask that it be done bodily for you [Col. 0173C].

Following the example of our predecessors, I send with my own hand, through the hand of this priest, consecrated oil, so that by this service of mine, at his mention, you may receive, by the grace of the Holy Spirit—which is the forgiveness of all sins—the remission of all your offenses and fellowship with the holy bishops.

Finally, as though in excess of what is necessary, since I do not doubt that you have already done these things, I remind your good devotion that, in addition to this general confession, you should strive to confess specifically and individually to God and to the priest whatever you recognize yourself to have committed from the beginning of your life up to the present time. While you confess and mourn each stain of your error individually, cleanse yourself at the same time through tears for all your deeds.

Hence the prophet says: “My eyes have poured out divisions of waters” (Ps. 119:136). We pour out divided water from our eyes when, in confession, we offer tears apportioned to each individual sin. A single confession made once to the priest concerning each individual sin is sufficient, provided that after this confession and the amendment advised by the priest the sins are not repeated [Col. 0173D].

Nevertheless, each day, in prayer, each individual sin must be confessed to God individually, with groaning or tears, so that the person confessing to the Lord may be able to say with the Psalmist: “Wash me yet more from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin. For I know my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (Ps. 51:3–4).

If something should creep in again among those sins erased through worthy fruits of repentance, one must return to the divine counsel given through blessed John: “Remember from where you have fallen, and do penance, and do the first works” (Rev. 2:5).

But it must be understood that good works cleanse and free us from guilt only when we mourn and renounce the evils we have committed. For the person who always wishes to sin and, as though always doing good, should know that good works mingled with evil deeds do not redeem the soul when they do not restrain it from vices.

“God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart” (Ps. 51:19). Whoever mourns sins but does not abandon them does indeed crush the heart but refuses to humble it; whoever has already abandoned sins but does not mourn them does humble the heart but refuses to crush it.

According to the exhortation of the Apostle James (chapter 5:16), daily and lighter sins ought to be confessed each day to one another among equals.
