These sins should be believed to be cleansed through their daily prayer together with daily pious actions, if, with a kind disposition of mind, one truthfully says in the Lord’s Prayer: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Luke 11:4).

Dearest brother, do not make yourself secure by neglecting daily communion of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ; rather, arm yourself with it every day. Through this communion of his sacraments, may you become one with him, in whom, when the prince of this world came, he found nothing belonging to him, and who, faithful in all his words and holy in all his works, said: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6:57). Thus protected from every enemy, may you come safely into the presence of your creator, redeemer, and savior.

## LETTER XXVII. TO POPE ADRIAN

He responds to what the pontiff had commanded concerning the kingdom of Lothair and the case of Hincmar’s nephew.

*(In the same author, from the Paris edition.)*

To the most holy and most reverend Father of Fathers, ADRIAN, pope of the apostolic primatial see and of the universal Church, HINCMAR, bishop of Rheims in name, not by merit, and servant of the people of God.

Your Excellency recently sent me, through your legates, a letter filled, as seemed good to you, with many and great reprimands, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the fourth indiction. Concerning these matters, to use the words of a man schooled by afflictions, insofar as human judgment is concerned: “I will not answer a man who is like me, nor one who could be heard with me in judgment; nor is there anyone who can argue both sides and place his hand upon us both” (Job 9:31–32); and again: “If I speak, my pain will not be silent; and if I keep silent, it will not depart from me” (Job 16:7).

Therefore I must answer briefly and humbly, not equally concerning everything, but concerning certain matters among those you wrote, about which I do not dare to remain silent. You wrote that I ought to remember whether a letter had ever gone unanswered, or whether a suitable reply concerning the matters at issue had ever been referred to the apostolic see, as you plainly establish that I did through contempt for you when recently, through men sent into the regions of Gaul, you addressed letters both to me and to others and received no reply from there.

I humbly submit that I have never departed through contempt from the commands of the apostolic see. In your letter, which you sent through the legates mentioned—namely, the venerable bishops Paul and Leo—you wrote to my lowliness what I should do about the matter, but you did not write that I should send you a reply about it. Nevertheless, I replied to those same legates in words that, to the best of my ability, I would carry out your command.

I did thereafter as much as I could and as much as I was able to see ought to be done. What I saw that I could not do, I took care to refer, through my discussion of the matter, to your authority [Col. 0175B], so that you might also be informed. I knew the outcome of the matter and the certainty of its effects when you sent me the aforementioned letter of reprimand.

I was preparing to explain how, on the very day when the venerable bishops Paul and Leo delivered your authoritative letters to me, I read them to the king, the bishops, and the leading men of the kingdoms who were present, both from the kingdom previously held by Lord Charles and from the kingdom once held by King Lothair, and took care to admonish them to observe them accordingly.

To the bishops of the kingdom previously held by Lord Charles, I delivered and transmitted the letter addressed generally to them. From there I reread the same letter to the bishops from the former kingdom of Lothair who had assembled at Attigny at the command of Lord King Charles. I also gave the following document to the aforesaid Lord King Charles, to the bishops of his kingdom, to the bishops of the former kingdom of Lothair, to the bishops of Louis’s kingdom, and to Louis himself, king of Germany, after the oaths had been sworn between the kings without me [Col. 0175C].

In it I proclaimed your authoritative command in such a way that, in view of the dangers I had mentioned—since I could not avert them or completely and simultaneously remove all those dangers—I might refer the matter to your authority and, if they did not resist, seek counsel for them or for myself. That document, which I read and delivered to the kings, bishops, and leading men of the kingdoms, is as follows:

> “The apostolic lord Adrian, as is known to many, has deigned to inform my lowliness by letters that I have in my hands. Among other things, by the authority of his ministry he commanded the kings, prelates, and leading men of the kingdoms in these regions of Gaul that no mortal should invade, disturb, or attempt to draw to himself either the former kingdom of King Lothair—which by hereditary right belongs to Lord Emperor Louis, his spiritual son, and will return to him after the death of Lothair—or the people dwelling in it.
>
> “If anyone should presume to do so, he will not only be weakened through the ministry of his authority, but, bound by the chains of anathema and deprived of the name of Christian, will be placed altogether with the devil. And if any one of us bishops should either avoid, by silence, the author of such wicked audacity or consent to it by failing to resist, let him know that he must be judged no longer by the name of shepherd but of hireling; and since the sheep will no longer pertain to him, consequently pastoral dignities will no longer pertain to him.
>
> “What is contained in the letters sent to the bishops and leading men of the former kingdom of Lothair, you yourselves know better, since you have read them. I have also heard that similar letters were sent to our lord Charles, to the bishops and leading men of his kingdom, and likewise to the glorious Lord King Louis, to the bishops and leading men of his kingdom. You who are from his kingdom know this more certainly.
>
> “The apostolic lord has also specially instructed me, a lowly bishop of Rheims, in his authority to admonish, persuade, and prohibit both kings and the other ministers of God and of the world in his place, so that they may restrain and repress the vice of desire or greed, may not take what belongs to others, and may not invade the former kingdom of Lothair or the people dwelling in it.
>
> “I also hear from many people, and from many sources, that it has been spread among our princes, namely, the glorious lords and kings, and confirmed by mutual oaths, that an equal division of that kingdom should be made among those who claim to be heirs of the kingdom itself. If that agreement had not been made, as many affirm, sedition would already have arisen among the peoples subject to them. And if the agreement is not carried out, battles and seditions will arise among them, as they have already arisen since the death of Lord Emperor Louis, and from this there will result great slaughter of the people and destruction of souls, which afterwards cannot be corrected.
>
> “Therefore, amid such great dangers—the danger of neglecting the command of the apostolic lord; of judging that the pact confirmed by oaths in the name of the Lord and his saints between our kings should be dissolved; of making light of the seditions and battles of peoples; and of saying that the leaders of the churches and noble men, attacked by pagans from many regions and existing without a king or prince, except one whom each may choose according to his own convenience after Lothair’s death, should not, or as necessity demands may not, have the freedom to choose a ruler who will defend and govern the holy Church, them, and the Christian people established in that kingdom—I, without the general unanimity of the bishops of Lord Charles’s kingdom, to whom the apostolic lord sent his letter concerning the kingdom of Lothair, which I delivered to them as I was commanded, dare not, insofar as it depends on me, consent to any decision concerning the matters I have mentioned.
>
> “In all things I reserve the privilege of the judgment of the lord pope, whose authority, if anything in these proceedings needs correction, will correct it with fatherly admonition and will be able to strengthen whatever ought to be established.”

Concerning what you wrote to me, saying:

> “Who knows better than you that the sons of the former Emperor Louis, meeting together, divided the kingdom among themselves and promised one another by oath that none of them would usurp or in any way invade the kingdom of another brother? And then King Charles, disregarding his oaths, invaded the kingdom that, after the death of Emperor Lothair, is owed to his son, the most serene emperor, and violated the faith that was due?”

I will reply with the humility owed to your reverence. Even if I knew that matters were as you write, since King Charles himself does not admit that they are so, nor does he appear to have been convicted of the matter by either a legal or a canonical judgment, and since, with many testifying, he asserts that this part of the kingdom was handed over to him by his father, Louis Augustus, with the consent both of the bishops and of all the other nobles of the empire, and was publicly confirmed by an oath from his brother Lothair, I would nevertheless consider it necessary to follow what the African Council says in the judgment cited above (canon 100): “Let the bishop be more careful not to say of anyone what he cannot prove by other evidence” [Col. 0177B].

Therefore Saint Augustine, who is recorded as having taken part in that council, and who, under the teaching of the blessed Celestine, was regarded by the Apostolic See as the best among teachers on account of his life, merits, and great learning, says in his book *On Penance* (Homily 50, chapter 3):

> “Many good Christians remain silent and endure the sins of others that they know, because they are often deprived of evidence and cannot prove before ecclesiastical judges what they themselves know. For although certain things may be true, a judge ought not readily to believe them unless they are demonstrated by reliable indications. We, however, cannot exclude anyone from communion—although this exclusion is not yet mortal but medicinal—unless that person has either confessed voluntarily or has been named and convicted in some secular or ecclesiastical judgment. For who would dare assume both roles for himself, so as to be at once another’s accuser and judge? The Apostle Paul also appears briefly to have intimated this rule in his Epistle to the Corinthians. After mentioning certain such crimes, he provided from them a model of ecclesiastical judgment for all similar cases, saying: ‘I wrote to you in my letter not to associate with fornicators,’ and so forth (1 Cor. 5:9); and later: ‘If anyone bearing the name of brother is a fornicator or a robber, with such a one do not even take food. For what have I to do with judging those who are outside? Do you not judge those who are within? But those who are outside God will judge. Remove the evil person from among yourselves’ (ibid., 11–13). By these words he sufficiently shows that the wicked are not to be removed from the communion of the Church rashly or arbitrarily, but through judgment; and if they cannot be removed through judgment, they should rather be tolerated, lest, perversely avoiding the wicked, someone himself depart from the Church and bind to Gehenna those whom he appears to flee.

“And again: ‘If anyone bearing the name of brother is a fornicator or a robber,’ and so forth. By this naming, he says, the Apostle intended the kind that occurs when a sentence is pronounced against someone with judicial procedure and integrity. For if naming were sufficient, many innocent people would have to be condemned, since a crime is often falsely alleged against someone. He did not wish a person to be judged by another according to the arbitrary judgment of suspicion, or even through an extraordinary judgment usurped for the occasion, but rather according to the law of God and the order of the Church, whether he had confessed voluntarily or had been accused and convicted.”

[Col. 0177D]

For there are laws, canons, and decrees of the Apostolic See promulgated from those same canons, which make clear how, by whom, and where a person ought to be accused or judged. Concerning these, Saint Augustine says in his book *On True Religion* (chapter 31):

> “In these temporal laws, although men judge concerning them when they establish them, once they have been established and confirmed, it is not lawful for a judge to judge the laws themselves, but only according to them.”

And Saint Gelasius, in his decrees to the Eastern bishops, says:

> “For this reason a particular person is summoned to judgment, so that he may either confess what is charged or be defeated by the charges.”

And again (2 Kings 12):

> “The prophet Nathan openly and publicly declared before King David that the offense had been committed; he did not conceal the offense itself, and, once it had been corrected by confession, he consequently absolved him.”

And Saint Boniface decreed long before:

> “And when the accused is present, if he has confidence, let him answer the charges.”

It therefore did not seem to me that I ought to rise up to judge one who has neither confessed nor been named and convicted in some secular or ecclesiastical judgment. Nor did I dare assume both roles, so as to be myself his accuser and his judge.

Concerning what Your Holiness wrote to my insignificance—that because I remained silent and did not rise up, at least lightly, against such a crime, I appear not only to be an accomplice but also, what is worse, the author of this tyranny—I say, with the pardon and peace of Your Sublimity, that the person who perhaps suggested this to you, to my injury and reproach, on the basis of an opinion rather than knowledge, ought to have remembered sufficiently the gravity of your authority and what is written: “I diligently investigated the case that I did not know” (Job 29:16).

And, as the blessed Gregory says (*Moralia* XIX, chapter 14):

> “Although all things are naked and open before the eyes of the Lord, he did not wish to judge the evils of Sodom merely on hearsay, when he said: ‘I will go down and see whether they have done altogether according to the outcry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know’ (Gen. 18:21). Why, then, does the almighty Lord, who knows all things, appear to doubt before proof, unless to set before us an example of seriousness, so that we do not presume to believe the evils of men before proving them?”

For, to confess truthfully to Your Favor, I have never been, from my very cradle until now, the author, accomplice, or consenting party to any tyranny. The person who reported such things about me to you will not, with the Lord’s help, be able to prove them. And because I did not remain silent, and in announcing or carrying out what was commanded to me by Your Authority I was not sluggish or negligent, so far as I knew and was able, I have shown this both in earlier writings and by word of mouth before your envoys.

[Col. 0178D]

Concerning what you say—that I am higher than the other bishops of King Charles’s kingdom in honor and dignity—I submit that I know myself to be inferior to the others in knowledge and merits, and not superior to the other metropolitans in the dignity and honor of my see. For, as Innocent and Boniface, together with the other pontiffs of the Holy Roman See, say in their decrees promulgated from the sacred canons, each province ought to be content with its own metropolitan.

Concerning what you wrote: that if King Charles himself should prefer to persist in the obstinate faithlessness of his resistance after my summons rather than repent in accordance with your admonitions, I should separate myself from his communion and association, and, according to the Apostle, “not even say ‘Hail’ to him” (2 John 10), and that, if I wish to share in your communion, I should avoid his presence in every way—I say with great sorrow of heart and groaning that many men of both ecclesiastical and secular rank who had gathered from various kingdoms to the city of Rheims, and who could not fail to know of the command delivered to me there by you, reproachfully said and continue to say to my insignificance:

> “Such an instruction has never before been sent from that See to any of your predecessors, although in their times there were battles and seditions among kings bound to one another by oaths, between fathers and sons, and among brothers.”

I also count it among my sins that, by this threat of your intention, I have been singled out and attacked by Your Authority, whereas you merely admonished, rebuked, reproved, and instructed the other bishops of his kingdom—my fellow bishops and fellow priests—and did not threaten them, as you wished to threaten me, with exclusion from participation in your communion. Nor did you threaten those who, as some say, once invited our king into Lotharius’s kingdom out of their own necessity and obtained honors from that kingdom; nor those who, unlike me, did not announce your command and the interdict concerning that kingdom to kings and the leading men of the kingdoms, and did not oppose those advancing from the other side, as I did. I, for my part, attempted to carry out your order as best I could, and have gained no profit, not even so much as a foot's breadth in possessions, but only impediments and losses, while many possessions belonging to the Church entrusted to me have been held for a long time in that same kingdom.

[Col. 0179C]

Certain people also say, to increase the accusation against our lord King Charles, that no bishop in this kingdom received from your predecessor such an instruction or threat on behalf of Lotharius—notwithstanding the certain knowledge of many people and the testimony of children born from that affair—that public adultery had been identified and denounced before the Apostolic See, and that not only part of my diocese but also part of my parish lay within that portion of the kingdom.

Nor, they say, is it recorded that the pontiffs of the Apostolic See, or other bishops of great authority and holiness, withdrew from the presence, greeting, or conversation of heretical, schismatic, or tyrannical emperors or kings—such as Constantius the Arian, the apostate Julian, and the tyrant Maximus—when place, reason, and circumstance demanded their presence.

And if, while other bishops communicate with our king, I withdraw from his communion or presence, they say, according to the African Council (canon 100), that so long as I do not communicate with him, the bishops should not communicate with me.

This is especially so since the king himself denies that he is a perjurer; disavows that he has invaded another’s kingdom, one not belonging to him; affirms that he is not a tyrant; and declares that he is neither a heretic nor a schismatic—persons whom the Apostle has commanded no one even to greet. Rather, by confessing the true faith and embracing ecclesiastical peace, he demonstrates that he is Catholic and wishes to remain and continue in ecclesiastical peace. He also says that, according to the laws and canons, he does not refuse, when present in judgment, either to answer the charges or to be convicted by them.

And, they say, setting aside the royal person, we have not heard that he has been accused, voluntarily confessed, or openly and legally and regularly convicted in these regions, according to ecclesiastical rules and public laws, as though he were some commoner or free-born man.

But in books they place before the eyes of readers the well-known account of how his great-grandfather Pippin, when Stephen sought his help and came into Gaul for the liberation of the Roman Church, was anointed king, while the Roman Church still remained under the name—but not the aid—of the defense of the Greek emperor; and how that same Pippin, not through apostolic excommunication but by hostile force, crushed Aistulf, a Christian king whatever sort of king he may have been, subdued Italy, and obtained the rights of Saint Peter.

Likewise they recount what his grandfather Charles did in the time of Adrian and Desiderius, king of the Lombards; how he received the Roman patriciate; how, in the time of Pope Leo, he acquired the title of emperor; what he did in Italy and how much he did for the Roman Church; how Stephen came to Belgium and consecrated his father as emperor by crowning him at Rheims; how Gregory, having been carried away, came into Francia with his father Lotharius despite his father’s opposition; how thereafter there was no peace in Francia as before; and how that pope did not return to Rome with such honor as was fitting and as his predecessors had done.

They enumerate how much this man, invited into the kingdom that Lotharius had possessed by bishops and by a people who had no king and were being attacked by pagans and rebels, set in order from disorder. And they say that secular writing declares that every kingdom of this world is sought through wars, extended through victories, and obtained not through excommunications by the Apostles or bishops. They also put forward the divine Scripture as saying:

> “The kingdom belongs to the Lord; through him kings reign, and he gives it to whomever he wishes” (Ps. 21:29; Prov. 8:15; Dan. 4:29),

through the ministry of angels and men.

When we oppose to them the words of the blessed Apostle James, who says, “From where do wars and disputes arise among you? Is it not from this—from your desires, which wage war in your members? You desire and wage war, and you do not have, because you do not ask” (James 4:1–2), they reply:

[Col. 0180D]

“Therefore, since the kingdom belongs to the Lord and through him kings reign, you ought to ask him for the kingdom—you who dispute and wage war for temporal glory. For if you asked the Lord with pious intention, he himself would grant you what is necessary for temporal use and the heavenly goods to be enjoyed forever.

“And when we wish to remind them that power was given by Christ to holy Peter, the first of the Apostles, and in him to his successors, and also to the Apostles and in them to the bishops, the pontifical power of binding and loosing, they respond:

“‘Then defend the kingdom against the Northmen and other attackers by your prayers alone, and do not seek our defense. And if you wish to have our help for defense, just as we wish to have assistance from your prayers, do not seek our ruin. Ask the lord apostolic that, since a king and a bishop cannot be one and the same, and since his predecessors arranged the ecclesiastical order, which is their responsibility, and not the commonwealth, which belongs to kings, he should not command us to have a king who cannot help us in these distant regions against the sudden and frequent attacks of pagans. Let him not command us Franks to serve, because his predecessors did not impose this yoke upon our predecessors, and we cannot bear it. We hear that it is written in the holy books that we must fight unto death for our liberty and inheritance.

“‘And if any bishop excommunicates a Christian contrary to the law, he takes away from himself the power of binding, but he cannot take away anyone’s eternal life, unless that person’s own sins take it away. Nor is it fitting for one bishop to say that a Christian who is not incorrigible should be deprived, in the name of Christianity, not for his own crimes but in order to take away or acquire a temporal kingdom for someone, and that he should be placed with the devil—the one whom Christ came to redeem from the devil’s power by his death and blood, and who taught Christians to lay down their lives for their brothers.

“‘Therefore, if the lord apostolic wishes to seek peace, let him seek peace in such a way that he does not stir up strife. For we do not believe that we cannot otherwise reach the kingdom of God if we do not have as our earthly king the man whom he himself commends.

“‘And concerning the oaths and perjuries, the tyranny about which you have written, the guarantees made between our kings, and the seditions that arose on account of that kingdom and would have led to the destruction of many had those guarantees not been carried out—we say things that it is not fitting for us to communicate to your Authority.’”

Therefore I do not see how I can avoid, without danger to my soul and without harm to the Church entrusted to me, the association or presence of that king, in whose kingdom my parish and province lie, and of those who live with him. For the blessed Augustine says in the aforementioned book *On Penance*:

> “The Apostle says in the Epistle: ‘I wrote to you not to associate with fornicators’—certainly not with the fornicators of this world, or with the greedy, robbers, or idolaters; otherwise you would have had to leave this world (1 Cor. 5:9). For people living in this world cannot live except with such persons, nor can they win them for Christ if they avoid their conversation and table fellowship.”

Thus also, when the Lord ate with tax collectors and sinners, he said:

> “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I have not come to call the righteous but sinners” (Mark 2:17).

And shortly afterward:

> “By this he sufficiently shows that the wicked are not to be removed from the communion of the Church rashly or arbitrarily, but through judgment; and if they cannot be removed through judgment, they should rather be tolerated, lest, perversely avoiding the wicked, someone himself depart from the Church and bind to Gehenna those whom he appears to flee. For examples of this are also set before us in Scripture: in the harvest, so that the chaff may be endured until the final winnowing fan (Matt. 3), and in the net, where the good fish are tolerated together with the bad until the separation that will take place on the shore, that is, at the end of the age (Luke 5).”

And again, the same author, explaining Paul’s judgment:

> “A wicked person does not defile you in two ways: if you do not consent and if you rebuke him—that is, do not communicate with him and do not consent. One communicates with him when one joins fellowship of will and approval to his deed. Therefore, warning us, the Apostle says: ‘Do not participate in the unfruitful works of darkness’ (Eph. 5:11). And because it would be little merely not to consent if negligence in discipline followed, he adds: ‘But rather rebuke them’ (ibid.). See how he embraces both: ‘Do not participate, but rather rebuke.’ What does ‘do not participate’ mean? Do not consent, do not praise, do not approve. What does ‘but rather rebuke’ mean? Reprove, correct, restrain.”

This I have very often done, in accordance with your command, in words and in writing.

And in his letter to the Donatists (Augustine’s Letter 152), the same most diligent teacher says:

> “Whoever lives well in this Church is not prejudiced by the sins of others, because each person will bear his own burden in it, as the Apostle says: ‘Whoever eats the body of Christ unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself’ (1 Cor. 11:29). When he says ‘eats judgment upon himself,’ he sufficiently shows that he does not eat judgment upon another but upon himself, because the communion of the wicked does not defile anyone through participation in the sacraments, but through consent to their deeds. For if no one consents to them in their evil deeds, the wicked person bears his own cause and his own person and does not prejudice another, who has no share in the crime through consent to the evil deed.”

And in the first book *On Baptism* (chapter 17), he says:

> “The spiritual, or those who are advancing toward this through pious zeal, do not go outside, because even when they appear to be expelled by some perversity or necessity of men, they prove all the more that they remain within, since they in no way rise up against the Church but are rooted upon the solid rock of unity by the strongest force of charity. For this is what is signified by the statement concerning Abraham’s sacrifice: ‘But he did not divide the birds.’”

[Col. 0182D]

Therefore, since I do not separate myself from the solid rock of the unity of the Catholic and Apostolic Church, and since, as you know from my writings and also from your present envoys, I resisted the king and the leading men of the kingdoms so firmly, at your command, that before those same envoys he threatened me, saying that if I remained in my position I could sing at the altar of my church, but would have no authority over its possessions or people, I ought not to be separated from your communion because of the factions of others, with whose dark works, so far as it depends on me, I do not share in anything.

The Lord says: “Whoever sins against me, I will erase him from my book” (Ezek. 14:9); and: “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. 18:20). But, as you know well, and as the blessed Gregory says, even among sinners their circumstances must be weighed, and then the power of binding and loosing must be exercised. This power, as Leo says, passed to the other Apostles and to all the leaders of the Church; but it is entrusted uniquely to Peter because Peter’s form is set before all the rulers of the Church. Peter’s privilege therefore remains wherever judgment is rendered according to his equity; nor is there excessive severity or leniency where nothing is bound and nothing loosed except what blessed Peter has bound or loosed.

Your envoys can also inform you how our brother and priest Odo, bishop of Beauvais, labored with me to obey your commands. Other threats have also been hurled against us, which I do not yet wish to disclose. I know that, if the Lord allows them, they will take care to demonstrate in action, without reconsideration, what they have already threatened in deliberation.

And, as it seems to me from experience, because of my interdict—or because of the sword of the human tongue—unless someone else obstructs them, your king or the leading men of his kingdom will not desist from carrying out, as far as they can, what they have begun. I do not know how I can avoid the presence, communion, or association of that king and of those among whom I live, since the king and those dwelling with me frequently gather with him not only in my parish but also in my city. They remain there as long as it pleases the king, with so great a multitude from both the kingdom he formerly possessed and the kingdom that Lotharius possessed, as well as from other kingdoms flocking to him, as your envoys have seen. I endure this in my city as often as he wishes.

I cannot abandon the church and people entrusted to me, nor flee elsewhere like a hireling; nor do I have anywhere outside his kingdom to which I can flee. Having received him with royal ceremony, I serve him and those obedient to him from the resources of the Church, as he commands and for as long as he commands, so that I may live quietly with those entrusted to me, according to the circumstances of the time. For he says that his predecessors possessed this authority, and that he will not surrender it because of anyone’s interdict.

[Col. 0183D]

All the matters stated above and below I set forth neither to accuse nor to excuse myself in defense of the aforementioned king; he is of age and should speak for himself. Nor do I set them forth to resist Your Authority or contradict Your command, but to seek advice about how we bishops—and I above all, against whom you have directed so great a threat—ought to conduct ourselves toward our king.

For the blessed Augustine, explaining the Apostle’s teaching, says:

> “The apostolic doctrine—that every soul should be subject to the higher powers, and that all things should be rendered to all, tribute to whom tribute, tax to whom tax, and so forth—commands us, while preserving the worship of our Lord, to render to the rulers of human society what is due, since the Lord himself, in order to provide us an example of this sacred teaching, did not disdain to pay tribute for the human head with which he was clothed. Christian slaves and faithful good servants are also commanded to serve their temporal masters calmly and faithfully. They will judge those masters if they find them wicked to the end, or reign with them if those masters too have been converted to the true God.

“Everyone, however, is commanded to serve human and earthly authorities until, after the appointed time, the Church is freed from the confusion of this age, as from Babylonian captivity, and restored to Jerusalem. On account of this captivity, if even earthly kings, abandoning the idols for which they persecuted Christians, come to know and worship the one true God and Christ the Lord, the Apostle Paul commands the Church to pray for them, although they were persecuting the Church, so that we may lead a secure and tranquil life in all piety and chastity (1 Tim. 2:2). Likewise, that people who had been led into Babylon were commanded through Jeremiah to pray for the king of Babylon. And the blessed Peter says: ‘Be subject to every human institution for the Lord’s sake, whether to the king as supreme’ (1 Pet. 2:13); and again: ‘Fear God, honor the king’ (ibid., 17).

“‘Every human institution,’ says that most perceptive teacher, means every human dignity, every person, and every principality to which divine arrangement has wished you to be subject.”

For this is what he means by “for the Lord’s sake”: “There is no authority except from God, and whoever resists authority resists what God has appointed” (Rom. 13:1–2).

And again Saint Augustine, in his sermon on the Gospel of John (sermon 6), says:

> “Clear laws are read in which the emperors commanded that those who usurp for themselves the name Christian outside the communion of the Catholic Church, and who do not wish to worship the author of peace in peace, should dare to possess nothing in the name of the Church. But they say: ‘What have we to do with the emperor?’ Yet I have already said that this concerns human law. Nevertheless, the Apostle wished kings to be served and kings to be honored, and he said: ‘Revere the king.’ Do not say: ‘What have I to do with the king?’ Do not claim your possessions when you have renounced the very human laws by which possessions are held.”

And if they possess their possessions through the laws of kings, they cannot, as subjects of the king, fail to render service concerning ecclesiastical possessions, just as my predecessors rendered such service to their predecessors.

[Col. 0184D]

Therefore, most reverend lord and father, advise our subjection according to the privilege of your See, so that you do not command us, at anyone’s suggestion, to do things from which such a scandal might arise between episcopal authority and royal power, between the Church and the commonwealth, that afterward it could not easily be settled without harm to religion or injury to ecclesiastical property, from which the servants and maidservants of God ought to be nourished and ecclesiastical affairs maintained. For, as Abraham said to the Lord: “Far be this from you, Lord; shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?” (Gen. 18:25).

Receive this most humble expression of my submission with that kindness with which the chief of the Apostles not only accepted the rebuke of his lesser apostle concerning his dissimulation, but also took care to answer and appease the question of his inferiors as to why he had entered among the uncircumcised.

The general letter that you directed to the bishops of the kingdom of our lord Charles I sent as quickly as I could to the metropolitans of his kingdom, so that they too might transmit it through their fellow bishops, in order that, knowing your command, they might strive to carry it out.

Finally, last year Your Authority sent me a letter through the envoy of our fellow bishop Hincmar, commanding me to excommunicate with my mouth a Northman who had invaded the possessions of the Church of Laon. But, as is evident, that Northman did not invade the possessions of that Church in many of these regions where the laws and canons command that cases which have arisen be brought to trial and settled. Some of those possessions the same Bishop Hincmar granted to our lord King Charles, without the consent of myself, his fellow bishops, or his fellow ministers, so that the Northman might hold them as a benefice, as many people know and as he admits in writings sent to our lord king and to me.

Those possessions our lord king recently restored to the Church of Laon; the aforesaid bishop also gave certain other possessions as a benefice to the son of the Northman, who had been entrusted to him, and that son holds them as received from the bishop.

[Col. 0185C]

Moreover, if it pleases Your Authority, when matters of this kind and similar cases come before you and you are asked to issue a command concerning them, add the qualification, ‘if it is as it has been reported to you,’ so that your command, being weighed more soundly, may be carried out justly and reasonably.

And if any metropolitan, in accordance with the sacred canons, is obliged to review an excommunication imposed by a provincial bishop when a complaint concerning it comes to me, then, if it is agreeable to your kindly mind, I ought not to be ordered to excommunicate that parishioner in obedience to the provincial bishop.

You also sent me another letter concerning the business of Hincmar, saying:

> “Your fraternity is plainly astonishing: why does it abuse the ministry of episcopal jurisdiction in those regions? It is said that the charity of many is growing cold as wickedness increases. For Hincmar, your nephew and namesake, and in any case a venerable bishop, as we have heard, suffers no small losses in his Church, but, with you, so to speak, growing lukewarm, he has been unable to find any consolation.”

I therefore humbly write back to Your Authority that, as it is written, I judge according to what I hear, and you wrote according to what you heard. But whoever reported these things to Your Holiness in words or letters told you a lie. I labored greatly on his behalf, both with the king and with others. For many years, as is known to many people, I have endured much from him, and I fear that he may fall under the scriptural judgments which say:

> “The one who is hard of mind will fall; for every arrogant person is an abomination to the Lord” (Prov. 28:14; 16:5);

and:

> “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled” (Matt. 23:12).

And just as what you wrote to me on his behalf was falsely reported, so too someone told you that I had prohibited or dissuaded him from going to Rome. That person likewise told you a lie, as many people in these regions know, and I can demonstrate this by the letters I have often sent to him.

[Col. 0186A]

Concerning what Your Sublimity wrote back to my weakness, instructing me to send that same Hincmar and three other bishops, representing all the bishops of the kingdom of our lord Charles, to a synod at Rome, Your Authority should know that I have no power to send either the aforesaid Hincmar or any bishop of the diocese of Rheims—not to mention bishops of other provinces—to Rome or anywhere else on my recommendation unless our lord king has ordered them to do so. Nor can I myself go beyond the boundaries of his kingdom without his knowledge, as I told the envoys of Your Holiness in the presence of the venerable Bishop Odo and the religious priest and abbot Ansegis, who know the facts of our case.

The letter that you wrote to our lord King Charles and ordered me to deliver on Hincmar’s behalf—commanding me to insist that it be reread before him and that he fulfill what you requested—Brother Hincmar neither gave nor sent to me. Instead, as I heard, he obtained from Archbishop Remigius and Archbishop Harduin of other provinces that it be delivered to the king.

May almighty God deign to preserve Your Holiness for many years, for the honor of the Holy See and the correction of his holy Church, in his fitting service, most holy and most reverend lord, Father of Fathers in the Lord.

## LETTER XXVIII. TO POPE ADRIAN, IN THE NAME OF KING CHARLES THE BALD

See among the letters of Charles the Bald, *Patrologia*, volume CXXIV, column 881.

## LETTER XXIX. TO ADVENTIUS, BISHOP OF METZ

The order in which the metropolitan and diocesan bishops ought to be consecrated.

In Sirmond, from a manuscript of Saint Lawrence of Liège.

[Col. 0186D]

HINCMAR, bishop of Rheims, sends greetings to the glorious pontiff, Lord Adventius.

As you commanded, I am sending you the consecration rite of a bishop and a copy of the decree, which ought to be written on a large parchment so that the confirmations of the clergy and of the envoys of the individual monasteries, as well as of the principal priests of the parish and of the people, may be written there. If the same elected candidate is still in the grade of deacon, he ought to be ordained priest at the canonical time.

On the Saturday preceding the Sunday on which the elected candidate is to be ordained, the bishops of the diocese ought to assemble at the principal church of the metropolis. The decree must be read publicly before everyone, and the bishops must ask whether the votes of all, as contained therein, agree upon the same elected candidate.

After their response, the bishops must ask whether they believe or know that the virtues contained therein are present in the same elected candidate. After receiving their response, the bishops must ask whether anyone present wishes to say anything against the same elected candidate or to raise an objection contrary to his episcopal ordination, so that he may come forward and speak, mindful of his communion.

If anyone raises an objection against him, you have in the canons what must be done concerning it. But if all are unanimous in his election, praises must be offered to God by everyone, and the same elected candidate must be examined by the bishops according to the chapter of the Council of Carthage, which makes clear what kind of man ought to be ordained bishop.

If he believes accordingly and professes the Catholic faith in simple words, as it is written there, the same elected candidate must then be admonished to commend himself to the Lord during that night, according to apostolic tradition.

[Col. 0187B]

On Sunday, however, the bishops of the diocese, together with the clergy and the people, shall assemble early at the place where, according to custom, the metropolitan bishop is ordinarily ordained. Once everything has been prepared, with the bishops and ecclesiastical ministers in sacred vestments, and with the bishops standing beside the altar, the same elected candidate, dressed in pontifical vestments, shall be led out of the sacristy by the senior clerics of that metropolitan church [Col. 0187C] and placed at the very end, behind the bishops.

The diocesan bishop who is to pour the consecration over him shall begin the Introit of the Mass and proceed according to custom. When the Introit is finished, “Kyrie eleison” (“Lord, have mercy”) shall be said, with the same bishop continuing with “Gloria in excelsis Deo” (“Glory to God in the highest”). After “Gloria in excelsis Deo,” he shall say the following prayer, which is the first in the scroll of consecration.

Immediately after that prayer has been completed, before the Apostle is read, he shall admonish the clergy and people to pray for the elected candidate being ordained and for his ordainers. He shall take the elected candidate by his right hand through the candidate’s own hand; the litany shall begin, and both the bishop with the elected candidate and the other bishops who are present [Col. 0187D] shall bow before the altar until the litany has been briefly completed according to the time available.

When the clergy begin to say “Agnus Dei” (“Lamb of God”), the bishops shall rise. The bishop who is to perform the consecration shall take the four Gospels and open them in the middle. With the elected candidate bowed before the altar, he shall place the Gospels over his neck and nape. Two bishops shall hold the Gospels over him, one on each side. The consecrator and all the bishops shall hold their right hands over the head of the man being ordained, and the consecrator shall say:

“Let us pray. Be favorable, O Lord, to our supplications,” and the rest.

When the prayer has been completed and all have answered, “Amen,” the consecrator shall say: “The Lord be with you. Lift up your hearts. Let us give thanks [Col. 0188A] to our Lord God.” When the choir has responded to each phrase, he shall begin the consecration by singing: “It is truly worthy and just,” up to “eternal God.” Then, as the consecration itself proceeds, the bishops shall continually keep their right hands over the head of the man being ordained.

When they have come to the places where crosses have been marked, the consecrator shall take the vessel of chrism in his left hand and, with his right thumb, singing what is written there, shall make a cross with chrism at each of those places on the crown of the person being consecrated.

When the consecration has been completed and all have answered, “Amen,” the Gospels shall be removed from his neck by the bishops. The consecrator shall place a ring on the finger of his right hand next to the little finger, explaining why the ring is given to him. For it is a sign of faith, so that, for those who hear him, he may mark what is to be marked, and for whom, from the divine mysteries; and may open what is to be opened [Col. 0188B] and for whom.

Then he shall give him the staff of holy governance, and shall give peace to the man whom he has ordained. In due order, the ordained man shall kiss the bishops, and a seat shall be placed beside the one who ordained him. The metropolitan bishop shall sit there; otherwise, if he were not a metropolitan, he ought to sit in the order of his consecration.

Then the Apostle shall be read from the Epistle to Timothy, concerning what sort of man a bishop ought to be. When the Mass has been completed, the ordained metropolitan bishop shall be led or carried to the cathedra of the principal church, while the clerics sing what is appropriate for this action.

When he arrives there, he shall take his seat in the principal cathedra and charge the ecclesiastical ministers that each one, in his own order, may minister to him and to the Church entrusted to him [Col. 0188C].

From there he shall proceed to the sacristy. When the Introit of the Mass has begun, he shall prostrate himself according to custom; after greeting the altar, he shall ascend to his seat and remain there until “Gloria in excelsis Deo” begins in its proper place, from the steps of the seat. After he has given the prayer, he shall sit in his seat, with the bishops and priests sitting with him.

When the Mass has been completed, the bishop who ordained him shall have letters bearing his own signature, which the sacred canons command the ordained man to receive from his ordainers, specifying the day and the consul. Before the ordained man departs from the altar, they shall place those same letters upon the altar; from there they shall take them and give them to the man whom they have ordained. When everything has thus been completed, let the Lord be blessed.

Furthermore, when a provincial bishop is ordained, the canonical letters are to be signed by the metropolitan and the other bishops [Col. 0188D] while the Apostle is being read and the gradual response and Alleluia are being sung. Immediately after the Mass has ended, the bishops shall give them to the ordained provincial bishop before the altar, while the archbishop and the other bishops go to their own places. The newly ordained man, however, shall celebrate Mass wherever a suitable place is available.

Concerning all these matters that you commanded me, and also concerning those that you did not command me, so that, as the saying goes, I might have done more than was required, I have written back to you how we conduct the ordination of a bishop and how the proceedings took place in my own case. As for the decree and the episcopal consecration mentioned there, I did not possess them; nevertheless, I understand that you may be able to obtain them.

# LETTER XXX. TO THE BISHOPS

## On the right of metropolitans, when the primacy of Ansegisus was being discussed

*(In the same author, from the Mainz edition of Jean Busaeus.)*

[Col. 0189A]

### I

We reverently receive, insofar as lies within our power and without prejudging the judgments of our brothers and fellow bishops who are absent, to whom this writing of theirs is being sent, the decrees of our lord, the most holy and most reverend apostolic father, Pope John, promulgated from the sacred canons—just as his holy predecessors and forebears promulgated them from those same sacred canons, composed by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world. We receive them while preserving the right of each metropolitan [Col. 0189B], just as the mystical Council of Nicaea decreed that it must be observed inviolably, saying (canon 6):

“Let the ancient custom prevail throughout Egypt, Libya, and the Pentapolis, so that the bishop of Alexandria has authority over all these places, since a similar custom also exists for the bishop of the city of Rome. Likewise, in Antioch and in the other provinces, let the privileges belonging to their Churches be preserved. The metropolitan bishop, however, shall be granted authority over the affairs conducted in each province.”

### II

The blessed Innocent explains the decrees of the holy and great Council of Nicaea in this way to Alexander, bishop of Antioch, saying (Letter 20):

“Accordingly, when we examine the authority of the Council of Nicaea, which expresses the single mind of all the priests throughout the world, we recognize that what it decreed concerning the Church of Antioch must be preserved by all the faithful—not to say by all priests—since we recognize that the aforesaid Church has been established over its own diocese, not over any other province.” [Col. 0189C]

Pope Boniface, writing to Hilary, bishop of Narbonne (Letter 3), says:

“It is fitting that we be diligent guardians of the sanctions of our fathers. No one, indeed, can be unaware of the constitution of the Council of Nicaea, which gives this command, to use its own words: ‘In each province, each metropolitan must have his own jurisdiction, and no one may have two provinces subject to him.’ Since they judged that this must be observed, for it cannot be believed otherwise, the Holy Spirit suggesting it to them.”

And a little later [Col. 0189D]:

“We say this so that your Charity may understand that we observe the precepts of the canons so carefully that our own constitution likewise determines that each province must always await the action of its metropolitan in all matters.”

### III

The holy synod of the bishops of the province of Africa, writing to Pope Saint Celestine (at the end of the African synod), says:

“The decrees of Nicaea most explicitly entrusted both the lower-ranking clergy and the bishops themselves to their metropolitans. For they provided with the utmost prudence and justice that every matter should be concluded in the place where it arose, and that no province would lack the grace of the Holy Spirit by which equity might be both wisely perceived and most steadfastly maintained by the priests of Christ—especially since each person has been granted the right, if he has been offended by the judgment of those who heard the case, to appeal to the council of his own province or even to a universal council.” [Col. 0190A]

Accordingly, Saint Celestine, recalling the decrees of the aforementioned Boniface for their firm establishment, decreed that each province ought to be content with its own metropolitan, saying (To the Bishops of Gaul, chapter 4):

“First, in accordance with the decrees of the canons, each province must be content with its own metropolitan, as is contained in the decree sent by our predecessor to the bishop of Narbonne. No priest should be given an opportunity for usurpation to the injury of another. Let each person be content with the boundaries granted to him; let no one presume anything in another’s province.”

The same pope likewise says (To the Bishops of Apulia, chapter 1) [Col. 0190B]:

“No priest may be permitted to be ignorant of his canons, nor to do anything that could oppose the regulations of the Fathers. For what matter worthy of preservation will remain among us if the standard of decretal constitutions is broken at the whim of certain persons, with permission granted to the populace?”

And Saint Leo says to Theodore, bishop of Fréjus (Letter 92):

“The proper order of your concern ought to have been that you first confer with your metropolitan about the matter that seemed to require investigation. If your Beloved did not know something, and he himself was also unaware of it, you ought to have asked to be instructed together, because in cases that concern the general observance of all the priests of the Lord, nothing ought to be investigated without the primates.”

### IV

Since the holy Roman Church, to which the care of all the Churches was entrusted in blessed Peter, chief of the apostles [Col. 0190C], has several metropolitans in its particular diocese, as Saint Leo demonstrates in his letter to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica (Letter 88), and since the Church of Alexandria likewise has several in its diocese, while the See of Antioch also has certain metropolitans in its diocese, as Saint Innocent writes to Alexander, bishop of that same see (Letter 20), we likewise find in ecclesiastical histories and synodal acts that the rights of those same metropolitans—whom the holy Roman Church entrusted to its vicars—were decreed to be preserved according to the sacred canons of Nicaea.

Thus blessed Leo writes to the same Anastasius (Letter 88):

“Accordingly, in accordance with the canons of the holy Fathers, composed by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, we have decreed that the metropolitan bishops of the individual provinces, whose care is entrusted to your Fraternity by delegation from us, shall retain unimpaired the right of the dignity conferred upon them from ancient times, so that they depart from the established regulations neither through negligence nor through presumption.” [Col. 0190D]

It must therefore be considered that, just as we read in the letters of blessed Gregory from the Register, the apostolic see commanded that the rights of the metropolitans of its own particular diocese—those to whom it delegated its functions because of distance—be preserved according to the sacred canons of Nicaea. The same is said in the letter of the aforementioned Leo to the aforesaid Anastasius (the same Letter, earlier):

“If the metropolitan had done anything serious and intolerable, our judgment was to be awaited, so that you would decide nothing beforehand until you had learned what pleased us. For we entrusted our functions to your Charity in such a way that you were called to share in our concern, not to possess the fullness of our authority.”

### V

[Col. 0191A]

The rights of those metropolitans—who are also frequently called primates in the sacred canons, and who, in place of deceased archbishops and metropolitans, prevail in being ordained by the bishops of each province without inquiry of another primate; who, by the law of ancient custom, are accustomed to be distinguished by the pallium from the apostolic see, to which the care and precedence of all the Churches has been conferred in the primacy of Saint Peter; and who, in place of deceased bishops and without the consultation or permission of another primate, can ordain bishops in their own province [Col. 0191B]—must in every respect be preserved according to those same sacred canons of Nicaea.

Those canons decreed inviolably that, just as the Church of Alexandria has its privileges, since a similar custom also exists for the bishop of the city of Rome, so likewise at Antioch and in the other provinces the privileges belonging to their Churches should be preserved.

Concerning these sacred canons, the aforementioned Saint Leo says repeatedly to Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople (Letter 56):

“After the consecration of the bishop of Antioch, which you claimed for yourself contrary to canonical rule, I grieve that your Affection also fell into this error: you attempted to violate the most sacred constitutions of the canons of Nicaea, as though this moment had conveniently offered itself to you, when the See of Alexandria had lost the privilege of the second rank of honor [Col. 0191C] and the Church of Antioch had lost the distinction of the third dignity, so that, with these places subjected to your jurisdiction, all metropolitan bishops might be deprived of their proper honor.

“By these unheard-of excesses, never previously attempted, you have so advanced that you draw into an opportunity for ambition a holy synod convened through the zeal of a most Christian ruler solely to extinguish heresy and confirm the Catholic faith; and you compel it to grant you its acquiescence, as though what the multitude had illicitly desired could not be rejected.”

### VI

[Col. 0191D]

Consonant statements are found in other decrees of the apostolic see:

“Even if all priests and the whole world should consent, the condemnation involves those who consent; consent does not absolve the transgression. For the crime is not diminished but increased when what was private becomes general. God demonstrated this, for he destroyed the sinful world by a universal flood.”

Saint Leo likewise says to the aforementioned Anatolius (in the same letter, after the preceding passage):

“That condition of the canons of Nicaea, ordered through the truly Holy Spirit, can never be dissolved in any respect. Let no synodal councils flatter themselves because of the size of their gathering, nor let any number of priests, however much greater, dare to compare or prefer itself to those three hundred and eighteen bishops, since the Council of Nicaea was consecrated by such a great privilege from God that, whether ecclesiastical judgments are celebrated by fewer or by more persons, whatever differs from the constitution of those bishops is altogether devoid of authority.” [Col. 0192A]

And shortly afterward:

“Those holy and venerable Fathers who, in the city of Nicaea, after the sacrilegious Arius had been condemned together with his impiety, established laws of the ecclesiastical canons that would endure to the end of the world, and who live among us throughout the whole world in their constitutions—if anything anywhere is presumed differently from what they established, it is canceled without delay. Thus what was generally instituted for perpetual benefit must not be altered by any association, nor must what was established for the common good be diverted to private advantage.

“While the boundaries established by the Fathers remain, let no one reach into another’s jurisdiction. Within his own proper and legitimate limits, let each person exercise himself, as he is able, in the breadth of charity.”

[Col. 0192B]

For sees are one thing, and those who preside over them another; and each person’s integrity is a great honor to him.

### VII

The same pope, writing to the Council of Chalcedon, says (Letter 65):

“I admonish your Holiness to observe the statutes of the holy Fathers, fixed by inviolable decrees in the Council of Nicaea, so that the rights of the Churches remain as they were ordered by those one hundred and eighteen Fathers inspired by God. Let wicked ambition covet nothing belonging to another, nor let anyone seek his own increase through another’s diminution.

“However much the arrogance of vanity may equip itself with forced flatteries, and however much it may judge its desires strengthened by the name of councils, whatever differs from the canons of the aforementioned Fathers will be weak and void. [Col. 0192C] Your Holiness will be able to learn from reading my writings, by which I repelled the efforts of the bishop of Constantinople, how reverently the apostolic see makes use of their regulations; and, with the help of our Lord, you will see that I am a guardian both of the Catholic faith and of the traditions of the Fathers.”

And to the Emperor Marcian (Letter 57):

“The privileges of the Churches established by the canons of the holy Fathers and fixed by the decrees of the venerable Council of Nicaea cannot be shaken by any wickedness or altered by any innovation. In faithfully carrying out this work, with the help of Christ, I must show myself a steadfast servant, because a stewardship has been entrusted to me. It would be reckoned to my guilt if the rules of the sanctions of the Fathers, composed in the Council of Nicaea under the instruction of the Spirit of God for the governance of the whole Church, were violated with my connivance—God forbid—or if the will of one brother were more important to me than the common good of the entire household of the Lord.” [Col. 0192D]

### VIII

And to Pulcheria Augusta (Letter 58):

“Against the statutes of the canons of the Fathers, founded long ago in the city of Nicaea by spiritual decrees, no one is permitted to dare anything, so that if anyone wishes to decree something different, he diminishes himself rather than corrupting those statutes.

“If all pontiffs preserve them inviolate, as they ought, there will be peaceful unity and firm concord throughout all the Churches: there will be no disagreements about their boundaries, no disputes about ordinations, no uncertainties about privileges, and no conflicts over usurpation of another’s rights [Col. 0193A]. Rather, the rational unanimity of character and duties required by the law of charity will be preserved.

“He will truly be great who is free from all ambition, for the Lord says: ‘Whoever wishes to become great among you shall be your servant; and whoever wishes to be first among you shall be your slave. Just as the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve’ (Matthew 20; Mark 10).

“Yet these things were then being impressed upon those who wished to grow from insignificance and pass from the lowest rank to the highest.”

And to Maximus, bishop of Antioch (Letter 66):

“So great is my reverence for the canons of Nicaea that I have neither permitted nor will I endure that anything established by the holy Fathers be violated by any innovation. For although the merits of prelates are sometimes different [Col. 0193B], the rights of the sees remain. Rivals may perhaps cause them some disturbance, but they cannot diminish their dignity.

“For the present, it is enough to declare generally that if anything contrary to the statutes of the canons of Nicaea has been attempted by anyone in any synod, or appears to have been extorted for a time, it can inflict no prejudice upon inviolable decrees. It will be easier to dissolve an agreement of whatever kind than to corrupt, in any respect, the regulations of the aforementioned canons.”

For the tranquility of universal peace cannot otherwise be preserved unless the reverence due to the canons is maintained inviolate. Whatever, apart from the particular cases of synodal councils, is brought before episcopal judgment may have some basis for adjudication if nothing concerning it has been defined by the holy Fathers at Nicaea. For whatever disagrees with their regulations and constitution can never obtain the consent of the apostolic see.

### IX

[Col. 0193C]

Saint Pope Hilary says to the bishops Leontius, Veranus, and Victorius, among other things, in the following passage (Letter 4):

“We entrust to your Charity the investigation of the attached complaint in such a way that nothing contrary to the venerable canons, and nothing contrary to the judgment of my predecessor of holy memory, may stand, whatever may be shown to have been surreptitiously obtained from us.

“For we do not wish, dearest brothers, that the privileges of the Churches, which must always be preserved, be confused; nor do we permit one priest to possess jurisdiction in another’s province. For by this the sanctions of the holy traditions are violated no less than the Lord himself is injured, since the expectation of the fruit of our ministry [Col. 0193D] is placed not in the extent of territories but in the acquisition of souls.”

The same pope also says to the bishops of various provinces (Letter 10):

“We have sent this to all your Charity, now also through our brother and fellow bishop Antony. Instructed by it, let the common concern of all take care that no brother, intending to burst into another’s injury, transgress the boundaries established by the venerable Fathers.”

Concerning these boundaries, the Council of Antioch, highly praised in the great Council of Chalcedon, says in its thirteenth canon (Council of Antioch, canon 13):

“No bishop from another province shall dare to cross over into another [Col. 0194A] and ordain anyone for the advancement of ministry in its Churches, even if some appear to give their consent, unless he comes when summoned by letters from both the metropolitan and the other bishops who are with him, and then proceeds to the ordination.

“But if, without being summoned by anyone, he hastens there in a disorderly manner to settle certain ordinations and ecclesiastical arrangements that do not concern him, let the things he has done be invalid, and let him himself undergo punishment for his disordered movement and irrational audacity, already condemned for this by the holy council.”

Consonant with this, the twenty-second canon says, whose conclusion is as follows:

“If he cannot ordain, he shall in no way judge.”

### X

[Col. 0194B]

Hence Saint Gelasius, in his decrees to all the bishops concerning ecclesiastical institutions (Letter 6), says:

“Since we hold that nothing may rashly be permitted to us contrary to the reverence due to salutary regulations, and since the apostolic see, superior to all these matters by the Lord’s favor, strives with pious and devoted purpose to preserve what has been established by the canons of the Fathers, it is wholly unworthy that anyone, whether a pontiff or of the succeeding orders, should reject this observance, which he sees the See of blessed Peter both follow and teach. It is entirely fitting that the whole body of the Church agree in this observance, which it sees flourishing where the Lord established the primacy of the whole Church.”

Above all, our people must heed the statements of these two heroes, Leo and Gelasius, lest disciples presume that something is permitted to them which their teachers did not wish to be permitted. If the cedars tremble at the loud sound of such thunder, what ought to be done by the boards?

Leo says (Letter 56, to Anatolius):

“The condition of the canons of Nicaea, ordered through the truly Holy Spirit, cannot be dissolved in any respect.”

No person is exempted from this statement, whatever power or dignity he may possess.

Gelasius likewise says (Letter 6):

“Since we hold that nothing may rashly be permitted to us contrary to the reverence due to salutary regulations, it is wholly unworthy that anyone should reject this observance, which he sees the See of blessed Peter both follow and teach.”

[Col. 0194D]

Accordingly Saint Augustine, earlier in time but later in position, received by all the pontiffs of the apostolic see in his own time and after his death—and indeed by the entire Catholic Church—as one of its most highly received teachers, says in his book *On True Religion* (chapter 21):

“The spiritual person judges all things, but he himself is judged by no one—that is, by no human being, but only by the law itself according to which he judges all things. For this too has been said with complete truth: ‘We must all be presented before the tribunal of Christ.’

“Thus he judges all things because he is above all things when he is with God. He is with God when he understands with complete purity and loves with complete charity what he understands. In this way, insofar as he is able, he himself also becomes the law according to which he judges all things, and concerning which no one can judge.

“It is similar with temporal laws. Although human beings judge those laws when they establish them, once they have been established and confirmed, it is not permissible for a judge to judge them, but only according to them. Nevertheless, the maker of temporal laws, if he is a good and wise man, consults that eternal law itself, concerning which no soul has been given the right to judge, so that according to its unchanging rules he may discern what must be commanded or forbidden for a particular time.

“It is therefore lawful for pure souls to know the eternal law, but not lawful to judge it.”

### XI

[Col. 0195A]

The blessed Gelasius also confirms this opinion in his decrees to the bishops established throughout Dardania, saying (Letter 2, at the beginning):

“We trust that no one who is now truly a Christian is unaware that, of every synodal constitution approved by the agreement of the universal Church, no see ought to execute it more than the first see. For that see confirms every synod both by its own authority and preserves it through continuous moderation, in accordance with the primacy which blessed Peter the apostle received from the voice of the Lord, and which the Church, following after him, has both always held and continues to hold.” [Col. 0195B]

Pope Symmachus says to Caesarius, bishop of Arles (Letter 11):

“It is reasonable that the holy Church of Arles enjoy its own privileges, and what antiquity has granted and the authority of the Fathers has strengthened must not be violated by a new presumption. This must nevertheless be observed in such a way that the privileges acquired over time by the other Churches do not totter, because what injures the whole cannot be firm in only one part.

“Since the things granted to the individual Churches by the constitutions of the Fathers remain, we decree that your Fraternity’s diligence should watch over matters that have arisen concerning religion both in the provinces of Gaul [Col. 0195C] and in those of Spain.”

And a little later:

“Accordingly, as we said above, let the benefits that have long been preserved be maintained in each Church.”

Hence Saint Hormisdas wrote in a letter to the blessed Remigius, bishop of Reims, saying:

“To our most beloved brother Remigius, Hormisdas.

“Receiving, with the full rejoicing of your Fraternity, the communications by which the tangible evidence of your true well-being, supported by spiritual offices and soundness, has gladdened us, we have considered it fitting to disclose in words this joy that we carry in our minds.

“For you display the proofs of a supreme pontiff, since you both do deeds worthy of proclamation and do not delay in making them known. We have therefore taken the privilege of our own judgment from this fact, when we learned that you had done what we earnestly command others to do: in provinces separated by such great distance, you strive to apply both the strength of the apostolic see and careful observance of the regulations of the Fathers.

“We therefore entrust to you our functions throughout the entire kingdom of our beloved spiritual son Clovis. Recently, with the assistance of heavenly grace, you converted him with his whole people to the faith—through many miracles comparable to those of the apostolic age, accompanying your saving preaching—and consecrated him through the gift of sacred baptism. This is done while the privileges that antiquity decreed for the metropolitans remain intact.

“By the authority of this present document we entrust these functions to you, increasing through this participation the dignity of your ministry and relieving our own watchfulness by means of this distribution of responsibility. [Col. 0196A]

“Although you do not need to be instructed about each individual matter, since we have already found that you preserve everything with exceptional discernment, it is nevertheless more agreeable when a path is shown to those who are about to travel and the form of the task imposed is displayed to those who must labor.

“We therefore command that the rules of the Fathers and the decrees defined by the most holy councils be observed by all. In these matters we show your vigilance; in these matters we show our care and the exhortations of brotherly encouragement. When these things are guarded with the reverence they deserve, the safeguard of holy observance leaves no room for guilt.

“There the lawful and the unlawful have been prescribed; there is the prohibited thing toward which no one may dare to aspire; there is what has been permitted and what a mind desirous of pleasing God ought to undertake.

“Whenever the cause of the whole religion calls for a council, let all the brothers assemble at your summons. If the concern of a particular matter troubles any of them, restrain the quarrels that have arisen among them by examining and deciding their disputes according to the sacred law.

“Whatever is established there for faith and truth, commanded through prudent administration, or confirmed by the authority of our person, must all reach our knowledge through a report supported by an informed account. In this way both our spirit enjoys the charity of the duty entrusted and yours enjoys the security of the duty received.

“May God preserve you safe, dearest brother.”

[Col. 0196B]

### XII

Saint Gregory, in his letter to Virgilius, bishop of Arles (Book IV, Letter 52), says:

“We entrust to your Fraternity, with God as author, our functions in the Churches that are under the rule of our most excellent son Childebert, according to ancient custom [Col. 0196C]. Since the proper honor of each metropolitan is preserved according to ancient custom, we have also sent the pallium.”

And in his letter to Dominicus, archbishop of Carthage (Book XI, Letter 39):

“Concerning the privileges of the Churches, about which your Fraternity writes, let it hold this without hesitation: just as we defend our own rights, so we preserve the rights of each individual Church. I neither grant anyone, with favoring grace, more than he deserves, nor, prompted by ambition, take away from anyone what belongs to him by right. Rather, I wish to honor my brothers in all things and strive to raise each one through honor, provided that there is nothing that one may lawfully set against another.”

And to Natalis, bishop of Salona (the same book, Letter 37):

“You say that what was handed down and preserved by my predecessors must be maintained in our own time. Far be it from me to violate in any Church the statutes of our elders toward my fellow priests, because I do myself an injury if I disturb the rights of my brothers.”

### XIII

Thus, as has been shown above, the canons of the councils that followed the sacred Council of Nicaea established the ancient right that must be preserved for each metropolitan.

The canons of Antioch did so, saying (canon 9):

“It is fitting that the bishops of each region know that the metropolitan bishop has charge of the whole province. Therefore all who appear to have business should come from every direction to the metropolis,” and the rest.

The canons of Constantinople decreed (canon 2) that matters belonging to each province should be administered by the synod of that province itself, as is clearly established by the decree of the Council of Nicaea.

The universal Council of Chalcedon says (canon 1):

“We have decreed that the regulations of the holy Fathers established in each council up to the present shall retain their proper force.”

The same council likewise says (canon 19):

“The holy synod decreed, according to the canons of the Fathers, that twice each year the bishops of every province should assemble for this purpose at the place approved by the metropolitan bishop, so that individual matters, if any should perhaps have arisen, may be corrected.”

### XIV

In the same way, the holy councils of the province of Africa decreed that what was established at the Council of Nicaea should be preserved in every respect, and that those ordained later should not dare to place themselves before those ordained earlier.

Accordingly, among other passages, Aurelius says the following (chapter 53):

“It would not have been appropriate for us to repeat these matters unless perhaps there were certain inconsiderate minds that provoked our thoughts to establish them. But this is a common concern, which our brother and fellow priest Valentinus brought forward: each one of us should recognize the rank assigned to him by God, and those who come later should defer to those who came earlier and presume to do nothing without consulting them.

“Therefore I say, insofar as my limited understanding retains it, that those who think they may presume something while disregarding their elders ought properly to be restrained by every council.

“Xantippus, bishop of the first see of Numidia, said: ‘The entire assembly of the brothers has heard the statement of our brother and fellow priest Aurelius. What do they answer to this?’

“Datianus, bishop, said: ‘The judgment of our elders shall be committed to our agreement, so that what is preserved in the records of former councils of the Church of Carthage may, by our agreement, remain fully firm among all.’

“All the bishops said: ‘This order has been preserved both by the Fathers and by our elders, and, with God’s favor, it shall be preserved by us, while the right of the primacy of Numidia and Mauretania is also safeguarded.’”

### XV

And likewise the sacred canons (Council of Milevis, canon 14):

> “It has been decided that all who henceforth are ordained throughout the African provinces shall receive letters from their ordainers, written by their hand and stating the consul and the day, so that no dispute may arise concerning those who are later or earlier.”

Hence Pelagius, predecessor [Col. 0197D] of Saint Gregory, writes to Childebert, king of the Franks, concerning Sapaudus, archbishop of Arles (Pelagius I, letter 11), rebuking him—as we may use his own words—because, at the request of a bishop ordained by Sapaudus, he had ordered Sapaudus to appear for judgment before the bishop of the next city, although this is permitted by no ecclesiastical law or principle; thus, when Sapaudus complained that the precedence of his own see had been trampled upon, the usurper must be condemned for unlawful presumption.

And Saint Gregory decreed that it should be observed with the greatest vigilance that later men not put themselves before earlier ones, and that no metropolitan presume to exercise any jurisdiction in another metropolitan’s province without consulting him. Writing to Augustine, bishop of the Angles, he says (question 9): [Col. 0198A]

> “As for the bishops of Gaul, we grant you no authority, because from the ancient times of my predecessors the bishop of Arles has received the pallium, and we certainly ought not to deprive him of the authority he has received.”

And somewhat later:
