> “You yourself will not be able to judge the bishops of Gaul by your own authority. Rather, by persuasion, kindness, and by showing them good works worthy of imitation, reform the minds of the wicked toward the pursuit of holiness, because it is written in the Law: ‘When passing through another’s harvest, you must not put in your sickle, but you may pluck the ears with your hand and eat’ (Deut. 23:25). You cannot put the sickle of judgment into a harvest that appears to have been entrusted to another; but through the effect of good works strip the Lord’s grain of the chaff of its vices and, by admonishing and persuading, convert it into the body of the Church, as though by chewing it. Whatever must be done by authority should be dealt with through the aforementioned bishop of Arles, so that what the ancient institution of the Fathers established may not be neglected.” [Col. 0198B]

### XVI

What he said concerning this one Gallican primate, who had received the pallium from the apostolic see, must certainly be understood also of the other primates of Gaul, Belgium, and Germany. Among them, just as among the other bishops, this regular principle is observed: whoever was ordained first is regarded as senior. Saint Gregory himself clearly demonstrates this in another letter to the aforementioned Augustine. [Col. 0198C]

Concerning these primates, the same sacred canons state that whenever any bishop is accused, the accuser must bring the case before the primate of that province. Those who think an appeal should be made must appeal to the primates of their own provinces, just as has often been established concerning bishops. A bishop who does not appear at a synod is ordered to give an account of the reason for his absence to his own primate. If the bishops among whom a case has arisen belong to different provinces, the primate in whose province the disputed place is situated must appoint the judges; and the case is ordered to be concluded by episcopal judges, whether those whom the primates appoint or those whom the neighboring parties, in agreement with one another, choose.

### XVII

The order and prerogative of seniority must be preserved not only among bishops, according to the sacred canons and the decrees of the pontiffs of the Roman see, but also among presbyters. [Col. 0198D] Thus Saint Leo, in his decretal letter to Dorus, bishop of Benevento, promulgated on the basis of those same sacred canons, says in the relevant passage (letter 6):

> “If the ambition of a claimant, or the uninformed zeal of his supporters, demanded something that custom had never known—namely, that a beginner should be preferred to the experienced and a newcomer to the old—it was your diligence and instruction that should have restrained the desires of those who were making an unjust request by reasonable authority, lest one whom you were hastily advancing to priestly honor should begin to injure those with whom he was associated, and make himself their inferior, since in him not the virtue of humility but the vice of arrogance would be strengthened.
>
> “For you could not have been unaware that the Lord said: ‘Whoever humbles himself will be exalted, but whoever exalts himself will be humbled.’ [Col. 0199A] He also said: ‘Whoever wishes to become great among you shall be your servant, and whoever wishes to be first among you shall be your slave’ (Mark 10:43). Yet you seek to grow from smallness and to be greater through honor. Both things are disordered; both are contrary to proper sequence. The fruit of all labor is removed, and the entire measure of merit is emptied, if someone achieves as much dignity as he has obtained flattery, so that the desire for prominence diminishes not only the proud man but also the one who connives at it.
>
> “But if, as is asserted, the first and second presbyters were so eager that Epicarpius should be preferred to them that they asked for his honor at the cost of their own disgrace, even this should not have been granted to them when they were bringing themselves down by their own judgment. You should more properly have opposed such a wretched desire than yielded to it.
>
> “Yet a shameful and cowardly submission could not prejudice those who were conscious of their own rectitude and who did not make God’s grace void, so that, by exchanging their ranks of precedence with one another by whatever arrangement, they would diminish the dignity of those who followed them, and the man whom they had placed before themselves though last would take precedence over the rest. [Col. 0199B]
>
> “Therefore, although the aforementioned presbyters, who have declared themselves unworthy of the order of their own honor, would deserve even to be deprived of the priesthood, nevertheless, so that mercy may be shown to them for the sake of the apostolic see, they are to be regarded as the last among all the presbyters of the Church. And, as a judgment upon themselves, they will be lower even than the man whom they preferred to themselves by their own decision, while all the other presbyters remain in the order assigned to each by the time of his ordination.
>
> “No one except the two aforementioned men is to suffer the injury of diminished dignity. This disgrace is to fall only upon those who chose to become inferior to a man newly and prematurely ordained, so that they may recognize as applying to themselves the evangelical saying: ‘With the judgment with which you judge, you will be judged; and with the measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you’ (Matt. 7:2).
>
> “But Paul is to retain his own order, from which he did not yield with praiseworthy firmness, and no further presumption is to be made to anyone’s injury.” [Col. 0199C]

### XVIII

We have thought it necessary to recall these matters concerning the preservation of the rights of each metropolitan, and concerning the principle that later men must not put themselves before their predecessors, but that each must strive to preserve the order entrusted to him by God. [Col. 0199D] These matters were established irrefragably by the Nicene canons, composed by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, by the other sacred canons, and by the foresight and authority of the pontiffs of the apostolic see, who promulgated them on the basis of those same canons—for the memory of those who know them and perhaps for the information of those who do not.

This delegation of the office of the apostolic see in the Cisalpine provinces arose for the eradication of the Simoniacal heresy and for cutting off the presumption by which powerful laymen were suddenly tonsured and ordained bishops, as we read in the letters of the pontiffs of the apostolic see, especially those of blessed Gregory. The privileges of the metropolitans of the individual provinces were preserved firmly according to the sacred regulations. [Col. 0200A]

This delegation was issued during the reigns of the emperors Theodosius and Honorius, under Pope Zosimus, for seven provinces: Viennensis, Lugdunensis, First and Second Narbonensis, Alpina, Novempopulana, and Second Aquitania. It required the honored men or possessors, judges, and bishops of those provinces to assemble at the city of Arles—also called Constantina—for a civil or ecclesiastical council, from the Ides of August on any intervening day until the Ides of September. If the judges and metropolitans of Novempopulana and Second Aquitania, which were more distant provinces, were unavoidably detained, they were to send representatives according to custom, as is found in the edict of the aforementioned emperors and in the letters of the pontiffs of the apostolic see. [Col. 0200B]

Then this primacy was entrusted to the city of Vienne throughout the aforementioned provinces, and from there the bishop of Arles assumed this responsibility.

### XIX

Finally, during the reign of Clovis, when the entire people had recently been converted to the faith through the holy preaching of blessed Remigius, with the Lord cooperating and confirming the word by accompanying signs, blessed Hormisdas entrusted his powers to that same holy Remigius, bishop of Rheims—Durocortorum, the ancient metropolis—which in earlier times had twelve cities under it: namely, Soissons, Châlons, Vermandois, Arras, Cambrai, Tournai, Senlis, Beauvais, Amiens, Thérouanne—that is, Ponticum—Boulogne, and Laon-Clavatus. [Col. 0200C]

In this last fortress, from his own diocese, the same Saint Remigius, supported by the authority of the African canons and of the apostolic see, established a bishop. Hormisdas entrusted Remigius with authority over the Belgic and certain Gallican provinces, so that he might restore to their proper condition the churches of God that the Franks, still pagans, had devastated and burned while plundering everything, and so that he might correct whatever had been wrongly done. The privilege of the Church of Arles remained in force in the provinces that had been assigned to it from ancient times.

### XX

Later, in the time of blessed Gregory, when King Childebert requested it, Virgilius, bishop of Arles, received this delegation from the same blessed Gregory in Childebert’s kingdom, just as his predecessors had held it in the aforementioned provinces (book 4, letter 52). [Col. 0200D]

Finally, in the time of Charles the prince, when, because of the discord and contest over the principate between him and Raganfred, and because of the frequent wars—civil, indeed more than civil, since they were internecine and murderous—in the German, Belgic, and Gallican provinces, almost every form of Christian religion had been abolished, so that in the few places where bishops remained, bishoprics had been given to laymen and their property divided, a certain Milo, a tonsured cleric but a layman irreligious in character, dress, and conduct, usurped the bishoprics of Rheims and Trier simultaneously and ruined them for many years.

Many people, especially in the eastern regions, were already worshiping idols and remaining without baptism. Therefore Gregory II and also Gregory III sent Winfrid, surnamed Boniface, a legate of the apostolic see, ordained first a presbyter and afterward a bishop, to restore the Christian religion. [Col. 0201A]

To him, who labored for twenty-five years in that same preaching without a fixed episcopal see, his successor, Pope Zachary, wrote and confirmed the following among other things in a privilege addressed to him (letter 14):

> “Since God has increased your preaching, you have wished us to confirm for you and your successors an episcopal Church, at the request of our aforementioned sons, the Franks. Therefore, by the authority of blessed Peter the apostle, we decree that the aforementioned Church of Mainz be confirmed for you and your successors as a metropolitan church for all time, having under it these five cities: namely, Tongeren, Cologne, Worms, Speyer, and Utrecht, as well as the peoples of Germany whom your fraternity has caused to recognize the light of Christ through your preaching. [Col. 0201B]
>
> “Having defined these matters, through this document of our confirmation we order that they be preserved in your Church for all time as its confirmation.”

The sacred canons of the province of Africa likewise decreed (canon 86) that those whom a bishop, with the assistance of divine grace, is able to win to Catholic unity should belong to him.

### XXI

Concerning the primacy in other provinces as well, Pope Zachary wrote to the same Boniface as follows (letter 8):

> “Since you have asked whether you ought to have the right of preaching in the province of Bavaria, which you received as a concession from our predecessor, we, with God’s help, do not diminish what our predecessor bestowed upon you but increase it. And not only in Bavaria, but throughout the entire province of Gaul, for as long as divine majesty commands you to preside, exercise on our behalf the preaching entrusted to you, and strive spiritually to reform according to the rule of righteousness whatever you find contrary to the Christian religion or to the institutions of the canons.” [Col. 0201C]

### XXII

When Ebbo, formerly bishop of Rheims, condemned himself in writing, by his own signature, and orally before a synod of forty-four bishops because of his crimes, and declared himself alienated from priestly ministry—and when Pope Sergius later condemned him, as is also recorded in his acts—after the death of the lord Emperor Louis, when a dispute over the kingdom arose among his sons, Ebbo, who had been condemned, first betook himself to Lothar and then to Louis. [Col. 0201D]

Because those kings could not prevail by force, through the merits of the saints, with the Lord’s assistance and that of our lord Charles, they began by intrigues—both at the apostolic see and among whatever bishops they could influence, and everywhere they were able—to cast the snares they had prepared around the bishop of Rheims. Many people began to usurp the possessions of the Church of Rheims that lay in different kingdoms.

Pope Benedict, by grace and in title, in a privilege granted to the bishop of Rheims who now serves that same Church by the authority of blessed Peter and of that apostolic see itself, according to the sacred canons and the decrees of his predecessors and forebears, says in the relevant passage: [Col. 0202A]

> “Among other things, we decree this: no one subject to the rules of your diocese and Church may, while despising you, dare or be able with impunity to seek or await judgment elsewhere, as has been established by the traditions of the holy Fathers and the promulgations of the canons. In all things, the right of our apostolic see remains intact, as the sacred canons have ordained from Christ himself.
>
> “Rather, let all, whether in authority or in due subordination, observe the order handed down by ecclesiastical regulations, obey, and strive diligently to comply.”

### XXIII

In this decree he also followed the decree of blessed Innocent, who wrote to Victricius, bishop of Rouen, and who says (Innocent I, letter 1): [Col. 0202B]

> “If any cases or disputes should arise among clerics, whether of a higher or a lower order, it has been decided that judgment should be concluded according to the Council of Nicaea, with the bishops of that province assembled.
>
> “No one may, without prejudice to the Roman Church—for reverence toward it must be preserved in every case—abandon those priests who by divine will govern the Churches of God in that province and flee to other provinces. If anyone should presume to do so, let everyone judge him both removed from clerical office and guilty of wrongdoing.
>
> “If more serious cases are brought forward, they are to be referred to the apostolic see after episcopal judgment, as the synod has established and venerable custom requires.”

This is the special reverence that, as he says here, must be reserved for the apostolic see: reverence toward it must be preserved in every matter, as the synod has established and ancient custom requires. [Col. 0202C] The canons demonstrate this in their third, fourth, and seventh chapters.

### XXIV

Concerning these matters, Saint Gelasius likewise says in the memorandum given to Faustus against the Eastern bishops (letter 3):

> “Let them see, then, whether they have other canons by which to carry out their absurdities. But these canons, which are called sacred, ecclesiastical, and legitimate, cannot summon the apostolic see to judgment.” [Col. 0202D]

And somewhat earlier:

> “These are the very canons that wished appeals from the whole Church to be brought before the examination of this see, while they decreed that no appeal should be made from it at all.”

And so forth.

Whoever carefully rereads from beginning to end the aforementioned letter of Saint Innocent to Victricius, archbishop of Rouen—promulgated from the sacred canons, and from which we have placed here the substance of his preceding decree—will find that it also concerns the privileges of the individual metropolitans, that is, the primacies of the provinces, which Saint Boniface established for the Gallican bishops and for Hilary, bishop of Narbonne. [Col. 0203A]

These provisions are that no metropolitan should have two metropolitan cities and two provinces subject to him; rather, each province should always await the direction of its own metropolitan in every matter. In major cases, each metropolitan should refer matters from his own province to the apostolic see after episcopal judgment, so that whatever each metropolitan has decided with his suffragan bishops, once it has been reported to the apostolic see, may be confirmed by its authority, as is fitting and necessary, or corrected.

### XXV

Whoever attentively reviews that same letter will also find that blessed Innocent decreed that what is written in it must be observed by all the primates of the provinces and by all the bishops.

Likewise, the aforementioned privilege of Pope Benedict decrees:

> “We further promulgate and establish that you, whom we recognize as the primate of that province, may never be stripped of the right entrusted to you—whether by force or by any other means—against the canonical and apostolic decrees or the ecclesiastical judgments committed to you; nor may you be condemned by anyone before a hearing before the Roman pontiff. [Col. 0203B]
>
> “This embraces the entire order of judgment: if you are to be judged, you are to be summoned within the boundaries of your province, making lawful and regular use of your right, before the judgment of chosen judges or of his vicar, when he has been specially deputed for this purpose, on the basis of established causes for which persons of rank may lawfully and regularly be accused before canonical judges.
>
> “The canonical and legal form must be observed concerning days and postponements, and in examining the persons of the accusers and witnesses—whether they should or should not be admitted to accusation or testimony. Only after he has been lawfully and regularly convicted or has confessed is the primate of the province of Rheims to be reserved for the judgment of the apostolic pope.” [Col. 0203C]

Thus Saint Leo wrote to Anastasius, the bishop to whom he had entrusted his powers, concerning a metropolitan (letter 88):

> “Even if he had done something serious and intolerable, our judgment should have been awaited, so that you would decide nothing beforehand until you had learned what pleased us.”

Hence the aforementioned privilege continues:

> “But if, when summoned, you wish to appeal to this holy see, we command by the authority of the apostolic pope—indeed by that of blessed Peter the apostle—that you be reserved for his judgment, and that you be subjected to no one’s jurisdiction or judgment, except the authority of the pontiffs of the Roman see.” [Col. 0203D]

### XXVI

In this sentence of the canonical privilege of the lord Benedict, let anyone take heed who might wish to go beyond his proper measure and choose to belong not among those to whom the Lord says, “Behold, I send you” (Matt. 10), but among those of whom the Lord says, “They themselves went, and I did not send them” (John 23).

For it is commanded, by the authority of blessed Peter the apostle, with the prohibition of anathema, that the primate of the province of Rheims be reserved for the judgment of the apostolic pope; and he is not permitted to submit to anyone’s jurisdiction or judgment except the authority of the pontiffs of the Roman see.

If any of our number does not presume against these provisions, but obeys the Apostle, who says, “Do nothing through rivalry or empty glory” (Phil. 2), and seeks charitably, as brother from brother, the things that make for peace and love, he will hear with the Apostle: [Col. 0204A]

> “Although I was free from all, yet for you in particular I made myself the servant of all of you” (1 Cor. 9).

“For we do not preach ourselves, but Jesus Christ our Lord, and ourselves as your servants through Jesus” (2 Cor. 4), while the condition of the privilege granted in the name and by the grace of Benedict remains intact.

But if he does not cease extending his finger and speaking what is unprofitable, he will hear with the Apostle:

> “Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls before his own master. And he will stand, for God is able to make him stand” (Rom. 14:4);

and:

> “It is of very little concern to me that I should be judged by you” (1 Cor. 4:3).

Otherwise, what has been built in the aforementioned privilege by canonical and apostolic authority might be destroyed by my consent. As the great Pope Leo said to the Emperor Leo, when he was being asked to approve something that it was not lawful for him to approve (letter 84):

> “If I destroy what I have built, I make myself a transgressor and subject myself to those conditions of punishment which not only the authority of the emperor Marcian of blessed memory but also I myself confirmed by my consent; for, as he says elsewhere, just as one sins by giving evil advice, so also one sins by giving evil consent.” [Col. 0204B]

The same privilege continues.

### XXVII

> “We also wish and decree that no one from the province or diocese subject to your metropolitan Church and to you presume, with contempt, in any way to tear away the right owed according to ecclesiastical constitutions to the primacy of your Church and to you, or stubbornly to inflict any violence upon you or your Church against these canonical provisions and the decrees of the Roman pontiffs. We prohibit this under threat of anathema, by the authority of our apostolic see and of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. We wish your fraternity to remain well in Christ, now and always.” [Col. 0204C]

No one who knows the sacred canons and the decrees of the pontiffs of the Roman see, as well as the venerable laws, doubts how greatly this constitution agrees with the sacred canons of Nicaea, Antioch, Chalcedon, Sardica, and the synods of the province of Africa, as well as with the decrees of the pontiffs of the apostolic see and the sacred laws.

For it is written: “Do not follow your desires” (Ecclus. 18); and: “Do not seek what is too high for you” (Ecclus. 3). Blessed Hormisdas also writes:

> “Exaltation always brings danger to salvation; by it the devil himself, its inventor, was deprived of angelic power.” [Col. 0204D]

This has sufficiently and abundantly served—and continues to serve and will always suffice—the aforementioned man serving the Church of Rheims, to which the sacred canons and the decrees of the pontiffs of the Roman see have assigned those rights that belong to each metropolitan.

### XXVIII

We have thought it appropriate to recall these matters concerning the privilege of the lord Benedict only to avoid excessive length, since enough about it is found in the sacred canons and in the decrees of his predecessors. This privilege is known to be preserved in the archive of the holy Roman Church; it was displayed at the synod at Soissons and, if necessary, can still be displayed.

We do not say this in order—God forbid—to resist the canonical and apostolic commands of our lord and father, Pope John. Indeed, both before and after these privileges were granted, at the command of the apostolic see, at the command of the lord King Charles, now, by God’s grace, Emperor Augustus, and also at the invitation of our brothers and fellow bishops, following the apostolic rule that says, “Through love serve one another,” and “Submit to one another in the fear of Christ” (Gal. 5), we have striven to assemble in synods in different places and provinces, and, insofar as the Lord grants us the ability, we shall continue to strive to do so. [Col. 0205A]

As has been said—and must often be said, because it is not irrelevant to repeat frequently in words what must always be retained in the heart—if fraternal charity invites us, and especially if the command of the apostolic see and the instruction of our lord Charles, Emperor Augustus, should decide to summon us to a synod according to the regulations, we shall attend, while preserving the right of the privilege of the lord Benedict, for matters that perhaps could not be settled by provincial examination, especially in a matter of faith or of universal religion, as we read in the letters of the pontiffs of the apostolic see and in the letters of the emperors. [Col. 0205B]

For we find in ecclesiastical histories and in the letters of the pontiffs of the apostolic see that general synods were summoned by imperial authority.

### XXIX

Saint Gregory also frequently urged the kings of the Franks to summon synods in the Gallican and Belgic provinces.

But since, as Leo warned (letter 56 to Anatolius), the mind greedy for power neither abstains from what is forbidden nor rejoices in what is permitted, and since it is difficult for the desire of the wicked not to strive to seek something beyond its measure, let no one of us, forgetting the Apostle’s command—indeed, the command of the Lord through the Apostle, who says, “In everything we commend ourselves as God’s ministers, giving no one any cause for offense, so that our ministry may not be blamed” (2 Cor. 6)—stubbornly rise up through wickedness or flattery against the aforementioned privileges and incur the danger of the threatened condemnation. [Col. 0205C]

Pope Zosimus decreed in the same terms to Aurelius, to all the bishops established throughout Africa, to all the bishops established throughout Gaul and the seven provinces, and to all the bishops established throughout Spain (letter 6):

> “When anyone acts against the statutes of the Fathers, an injury is inflicted not only upon the foresight and judgment of those who established provisions destined to live forever, but in a certain sense upon faith itself and Catholic discipline.” [Col. 0205D]

As we showed above, Saint Hilary the pope says (letter 11):

> “One sins no less against the enactments of the holy traditions than one rushes into an injury against the Lord himself.”

And Saint Pope Symmachus says to Caesarius, bishop of Arles (letter 1):

> “Since, in the likeness of the Trinity, whose power is one and indivisible, the priesthood is one through its various bishops, how is it fitting that the statutes of earlier men should be violated by those who come after them? Furthermore, if such a diversity of judgments should arise, we believe that it concerns the very holy Catholic religion, whose entire authority is weakened unless all things once established by the priests of the Lord are perpetual.
>
> “How else could this occur, unless a successor fails to grant firmness to the acts of his predecessor and, by strengthening what has been done, makes his own acts valid? For how great will be the reverence shown to the vicars of blessed Peter the apostle if what they prescribe in the priesthood is dissolved when they themselves have passed away?” [Col. 0206A]

And Saint Pope Leo established in his decrees (letter 1):

> “Our admonition therefore declares that if any of the brethren has acted, or attempts to act, against these provisions, and dares to admit what has been forbidden, he must know that he is to be removed from his office and will not share in our communion, since he refused to be a partner in discipline.
>
> “To ensure that nothing may be thought to have been omitted by us, we command that all decretal provisions—those of Innocent of blessed memory as well as those of all our predecessors, which have been promulgated concerning ecclesiastical orders and the discipline of the canons—be observed by your devotion in such a way that anyone who violates them may know that forgiveness will henceforth be denied him.” [Col. 0206B]

Since in the Law and in the Gospel the valid judgment of two or three witnesses is confirmed, let every sensible person consider with what zeal a unanimous judgment must be maintained by these four authorities concerning the preservation of the privileges established by our predecessors—especially since each of us can acquire a reward of blessed recompense through faithful reverence and preservation, and must take the greatest care not to incur danger by transgression.

### XXX

Finally, we have decided briefly to recall that when the holy and venerable Boniface was preaching the word of the Lord in Frisia, and was crowned with martyrdom in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 754, and when the depravity of the Simoniacal heresy, the presumption of neophytes, and other matters had been dealt with according to the circumstances and needs of the times, the Cisalpine provinces remained, during the reigns of King Pippin and of the emperors Charles and Louis, for approximately twenty-three years—indeed, ninety years—without this primicerius or primate delegated by the apostolic see. [Col. 0206C]

With the rights of each metropolitan preserved, and with the favor of the apostolic see and the arrangement of their rulers, the venerable bishops carried out whatever needed to be done according to the sacred canons and the decrees of the pontiffs of that same holy see. They acted by the authority of the sacred canons and the decrees of the pontiffs of the Roman see.

### XXXI

Meanwhile Drogo, bishop of Metz, raised by the distinction of royal descent, obtained this precedence in the Cisalpine regions on a certain occasion, during the reign of the Emperor Lothar, from Pope Sergius. [Col. 0206D] But what he sought with desire he did not obtain in fact; and what he could not secure through effective exercise, because those concerned did not consent, he endured with the greatest patience, as was fitting for him, lest by generating scandal among his brothers and fellow priests he introduce schism into the holy Church.

Every one of us ought to have imitated a man of such great nobility and dignity, so as not improperly to seek what he did not possess—especially one who endured, without contention, not being able to exercise what he had obtained.

For we read that the presumption of the wicked is shown to be condemnable not only by its own crookedness but also by comparison with upright rulers. Scripture says: “Virtue, when proved, rebukes the foolish” (Wis. 2). [Col. 0207A]

How greatly we must avoid generating fraternal scandal—so that, if one of us should perhaps suffer from this disease, we do not cause scandal to our brothers through the rapacity of our exalted position—the Lord’s judgment demonstrates when he says to Peter that, in order to avoid scandal, he should pay the tax demanded for him and for himself, although they were not obligated to pay it.

### XXXII

And since, as is known, thirty years, according to the public laws and, as Pope Gelasius demonstrates, according to ecclesiastical constitution, remove human claims from litigation—and since Justinian’s law, together with the decree of blessed Gregory promulgated from that same law, establishes forty years for disputes between venerable churches, monasteries, and religious places—if the superstitious desire of our ambitious minds could bear it, one would not trouble the Apostolic See or imperial ears, without any new necessity, over this unwarranted presumption, since the peace of the bishops of the Cisalpine provinces could remain undisturbed, without the scandal and expense of this agitation, after so long a time.

For if each of us had preferred to follow in every respect, as we ought, the pastoral rule of blessed Gregory, we would in no way overstep the bounds of our measure, and we would avoid desiring what the city of any one of us had never deserved. We must indeed fear and beware of what blessed Gregory wrote from Rome in his letter to John, bishop of Constantinople, and says from heaven to anyone among us who seeks higher things (Book II, Letter 38):

> “Consider, I beg you, that in this rash presumption the peace of the whole Church is disturbed, and resistance is offered to the grace poured out commonly upon all. In this matter you will be able to grow only insofar as you set limits for yourself; and you will become greater in proportion as you restrain yourself from the usurpation of that proud and foolish title, and you will advance only insofar as you do not seek to arrogate to yourself anything by disparaging your brothers.
>
> “Whom, I ask, is this exceedingly perverse title proposed for imitation, except him who, having despised the legions of angels established in fellowship with him, attempted to break through to the summit of singularity, so that he might appear to be subject to no one and alone preside over all? He also said: ‘I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will exalt my throne; I will sit upon the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the North. I will ascend above the height of the clouds; I will be like the Most High’ (Isa. XIII, 14).
>
> “For what are your brothers, all the bishops of the universal Church, except the stars of heaven? Their life and speech shine amid the sins and errors of human beings as among the darkness of night. When, by the title of your exaltation, you desire to place yourself above them and to trample upon their name in comparison with your own, what else do you say than: ‘I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will exalt my throne’?
>
> “Are not all the bishops clouds, who rain through the words of their preaching and flash with the light of good works? When your Fraternity despises them and attempts to press them beneath itself, what else does it say than what the ancient enemy says: ‘I will ascend above the height of the clouds’?
>
> “Pestilence and the sword rage throughout the world; nations rise against nations; the earth is shaken; the world with its inhabitants is swallowed up as the earth opens; for everything that was foretold is happening. The king of pride is near, and—what may not be said without horror—an army of priests has been prepared for him, because those who were appointed to provide the leadership of humility are serving the neck of arrogance.
>
> “But in this matter, even if our tongue does not at all speak against it, the power of him who specially opposes the vice of pride raises itself against arrogance in punishment. For it is written: ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble’ (Jas. IV, 6). Again it is said: ‘He who exalts his heart is unclean before God’; and against the proud man it is written: ‘Why are you proud, earth and ashes?’ (Ecclus. X). Again Truth itself says: ‘Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled’ (Luke XIV, 11).
>
> “And in order to lead us back to the way of life through humility, it deigned to demonstrate in itself what it admonishes us to do, saying: ‘Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart’ (Matt. XI, 29).
>
> “Has it then escaped your mind what Truth says: ‘Whoever scandalizes one of these little ones who believe in me, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and he be sunk into the depths of the sea’ (Matt. XVIII, 6)? Yet if we neglect to consider this, the heavenly judgments will keep watch against the swelling of so great an arrogance.”

### XXXIII

Since matters stand thus, and since, as Saint Leo says (Letter 56), whenever a general assembly of priests has been convened because of pressing circumstances, it is difficult for the ambition of wicked men not to attempt to desire something beyond measure—as we often read also to have happened in universal synods—if anything has been imposed or decreed in this assembly of our humility through the favor of two or three and the silence of a few, through the arrogance of imperial power, against the foregoing decrees of the sacred canons and of the pontiffs of the Apostolic See promulgated from those same sacred canons, and against the ancient privileges of the individual metropolitans, privileges that are also to be preserved by the sacred laws by which, together with the venerable canons, the holy Church is governed; if anything has been introduced or decreed by an immature and inconsiderate command, then—with the Lord forbidding a grove to be planted beside his temple, that is, forbidding the purity and radiance of ecclesiastical humility to be overshadowed and disfigured by the form of earthly rule—according to the decrees of the mystical Council of Nicaea it is said:

> “If two or three, because of their own disputes, offer opposition, let the judgment of the majority prevail. But if, as we have said, two or three have perhaps conspired through flattery—not in their hearts, but in word or silence—our whole body, with God as its author, does not consent; rather, with heart and mouth, it most steadfastly rejects it. The judgment of the majority has obtained, obtains, and, with the Lord’s assistance, will always retain its due force and authority.”

For, as the aforementioned Saint Leo wrote to Maximus, bishop of Antioch (Letter 66):

> “If anything has been attempted by anyone in any synod against the provisions of the Nicene canons, or appears for a time to have been extorted, it can inflict no prejudice upon inviolable decrees. It will be easier for an agreement of any kind to be dissolved than for the rules of the aforesaid canons to be corrupted in any respect.”

### XXXIV

Regarding the fact that a certain brother appeared to exult as though something had been granted to him by imperial edict—although it was not granted to him, but, as we learned by hearing the text, was sent concerning him to us by the Apostolic See, to whom it had not been granted—the same Saint Leo wrote to Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople (Letter 54):

> “The order of secular things is one thing, and the order of divine things another; and apart from that rock which the Lord established as the foundation, no structure will be stable. He loses what is his own who covets what is not his due.”

And as Gelasius says, one never finds that the pontiffs have judged anything except the Church; nor is it the business of human laws to pronounce judgment in such matters without the bishops principally constituted by the Church. Christian rulers customarily obey the decrees of the Church and do not place their own authority above them; the prince is accustomed to subject his head to the bishops, not to judge their heads.

### XXXV

In the law of Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius, the following was decreed concerning bishops:

> “They have their own judges, and have nothing in common with the public laws, so far as concerns ecclesiastical cases, which ought to be decided by episcopal authority.”

We do not say this—as God forbid—in resistance to authority and therefore to God’s ordinance, but rather in obedience to it. For just as the Lord commanded that what belongs to Caesar be rendered to Caesar, and what belongs to God to God (Matt. XXII), so we obediently render to the emperor the services owed to him, and render to the priestly order what belongs to the priesthood, as the aforementioned holy Pope Gelasius distinguished and decreed in his letter to the Emperor Anastasius (Letter 10):

> “There are two powers, august Emperor, by which this world is principally governed: the sacred authority of the pontiffs and royal power. The burden of the priests is all the heavier because they will render an account before the divine tribunal even for the kings themselves.
>
> “For you know, most merciful son, that although by your dignity you preside over the human race, nevertheless, in matters divine, you dutifully bow your neck to the rulers, and from them you await the causes of your salvation. In receiving the heavenly sacraments and arranging them as is proper, you recognize that you ought to be subject to them, rather than preside over them, by the order of religion.
>
> “Know, therefore, that in these matters you depend upon their judgment, and do not wish them to be reduced to your will. For if, insofar as it concerns the order of public discipline, the priests of religion themselves obey your laws, recognizing that the empire has been conferred upon you by heavenly disposition, lest they appear to oppose the sentence even in human affairs, with what devotion, I ask, is it fitting that you obey those who have been appointed over the administration of the venerable mysteries?
>
> “Accordingly, just as a serious danger rests upon pontiffs if they remain silent about what is fitting for the worship of God, so—God forbid—a considerable danger rests upon those who, although they ought to obey, hold obedience in contempt.”

## LETTER XXXI. TO A CERTAIN BISHOP

**On the transfers of bishops, against Actard of Nantes**

*(From the same author, from a manuscript of Verdun.)*

The servant of Christ and of his servants sends greetings to his beloved brother and venerable bishop.

Regarding the matters about which your prudence inquires of my insignificance, and concerning which you immediately and urgently request that I answer briefly and earnestly what I think, I respond obediently to your request, since I have nothing to refuse you—and indeed ought not to refuse you—for Scripture says: “He who withholds grain is cursed among the peoples, but blessing is upon the head of those who sell it” (Prov. XI, 26). That is: he who hides the word of knowledge will hear from the Lord: “Wicked and lazy servant, why did you not give my money to the bankers, so that when I came I might at least have received what was mine with interest?” (Luke XIX, 23).

“Blessing is upon the head of those who sell,” because he who gives his fellow servants their measure of grain at the proper time will hear from the Lord: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much” (Matt. XXV, 21). And a certain Catholic teacher says: “He does not cleanse himself of the stain of envy who refuses to impart to another what he understands.”

Therefore, since for the present you do not permit me to answer you more fully and at greater length, I reply briefly and in outline, beginning from the origin of this matter, to the questions you have asked.

### I

The Apostle shows for what purpose the Son of God took the form of a servant, saying: “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned. This is a faithful saying and worthy of all acceptance: Jesus Christ came into this world to save sinners. For all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. V, 12).

### II

He himself makes clear why the apostles were ordained by him, saying: “Behold, I send you. Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you” (Luke X, 3; Matt. XXVIII, 19). “Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V, 16).

### III

In the Church, bishops occupy the place of these apostles. The Psalmist, inspired by the Holy Spirit, foretold of them as though addressing face to face the Church founded by the apostles:

> “Instead of your fathers, sons have been born to you” (Ps. XLIV, 17).

They are ordained individually according to apostolic tradition, one in each city. As the Apostle writes to Titus:

> “For this reason I left you in Crete, that you might correct what remains to be corrected and appoint presbyters in every city” (Titus I, 5),

that is, bishops, as he demonstrates shortly afterward:

> “A bishop must be blameless” (ibid., 7).

For *bishop* is the name of an office, just as *presbyter* is the name of an age—not bodily age, but age of wisdom and an unblemished life. As it is said by a certain wise man:

> “Old age is honorable, not because of long duration, nor reckoned by number of years. The understanding of a human being is gray hair, and an unblemished life is the age of old age” (Wis. IV, 8).

Thus the Lord says to Moses:

> “Gather for me seventy men from the elders of Israel, whom you know to be elders of the people” (Num. XI, 16).

What else but old age of heart is required in these men, when those are commanded to be chosen who are known to be elders? If bodily age were sought in them, they could be recognized by as many as could see them. But when it says, “whom you know to be elders of the people,” it is perfectly clear that, as Saint Gregory says, old age of mind, not of body, is shown to be the thing to be chosen.

Hence Paul also writes to Timothy:

> “Let no one despise your youth, but be an example to the faithful in word, in conduct, in charity, in faith, and in chastity” (1 Tim. IV, 12).

The apostolic authority established this tradition—that bishops should be ordained individually in each city—as Saint Clement, successor of blessed Peter the Apostle, promulgated from Peter’s own tradition. Saint Anacletus, likewise ordained presbyter by blessed Peter the Apostle and afterward bishop of the Roman See, demonstrates this in his letter, while the Holy Spirit teaches through the Prophet:

> “God has spoken in his sanctuary; I will rejoice and divide Shechem, and I will measure out the valley of tents” (Ps. LIX, 8).

Hence Saint Basil says:

> “Now I will call this chief and, as it were, private inheritance of the people into division, and I will make it common with all the others. But when the testament has been divided among all, and all its usefulness has begun to be common to everyone, with God providing something better for all of us, then also the valley of tents will be measured out—that is, the entire world, which is called the valley of tents because of the bodily dwelling places here. As though divided and measured by lot, it will be distinguished in its individual places by the parishes and settlements of the Churches of God.
>
> “Then also he who makes peace through his blood among the things on earth and in heaven, and who, having broken down the middle wall of the enclosure, makes both one, will gather the things that have been divided into the unity of faith.”

### IV

Bishops are ordained individually in individual cities—not for the power of temporal honors, not for villages and possessions, nor for abundance of wealth. Yet bishops, once they have undertaken the ministry, ought justly and reasonably to preserve, enlarge, and administer such resources according to the rules and laws promulgated by the Holy Spirit, since they are in truth sanctuaries dedicated and consecrated to God: the offerings of the faithful, the payments for sins, and the patrimonies of the poor. Rather, bishops are ordained for gaining souls and saving human beings.

As the Apostle says:

> “Every high priest taken from among human beings is appointed on behalf of human beings in matters relating to God, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins, being able to have compassion on the ignorant and those who err, since he himself is surrounded by weakness; and because of this he ought to offer for sins, both for the people and for himself” (Heb. V, 1).

Again the same Apostle says:

> “If anyone desires the office of bishop, he desires a good work” (1 Tim. III, 1).

Saint Gregory says of this:

> “He himself bears witness that he does not desire the office of bishop who seeks through it not the ministry of good works but the glory of honor. For he does not truly love the sacred office at all—and does not understand it—who, longing for the summit of government, secretly feeds upon the subjection of others, rejoices in his own praise, lifts his heart toward honor, and exults in an abundance of possessions.
>
> “Thus worldly gain is sought under the appearance of that honor by which the gains of the world ought to have been destroyed; and when the mind considers seizing the summit of humility in order to become exalted, it transforms inwardly what it pursues outwardly” (Pastoral Rule I, 8).

The same author says elsewhere concerning the Lord’s words, “As the Father sent me, so I send you” (John XX, 21):

> “The Father sent the Son, whom he appointed to become incarnate for the redemption of the human race. He willed him to come into the world for suffering, yet he loved the Son whom he sent to suffering. The Lord, likewise, sends the chosen apostles into the world not for the joys of the world, but for sufferings, just as he himself was sent.
>
> “Thus it is said: ‘As the Father sent me, so I send you’; that is, I love you with the same charity with which the Father loves me when he sends me amid the scandals of persecutors, since he caused me to come to endure sufferings.”

### V

Once bishops have been ordained individually in individual cities, not for worldly glory but amid the scandals of persecutors, they are not permitted to change the cities in which they were canonically ordained, nor to be transferred from city to city for earthly greed or ambition for glory, as Saint Gregory explains in his homily on the prophet Ezekiel (Homily 5):

> “His throne was a flame of fire, and its wheels were burning fire” (Dan. VII, 9). “For those who are guardians of souls and have undertaken the burdens of feeding the flock are not permitted to change places. But because, being placed in one location, they carry within themselves the presence of the Divinity and burn, the throne of God is called a flame of fire.
>
> “Those, however, who run about in preaching out of love for the Lord are his burning wheels, because when they run through various places out of desire for him, they themselves burn and kindle others.”

Thus blessed Paul, appointed apostle of the nations, filled, so to speak, the whole world with the Gospel of Christ. Christ’s wheel did not preside over only one city, but evangelized many cities through his presence, as sacred history relates, and confirmed them through his letters.

Hence the sacred canons of the African council also decreed that rebaptism, reordination, and the transfer of bishops should not be permitted. If any bishop should pass from the city in which he was ordained to another city and seize it, unless he voluntarily or after admonition returns to his own city, it should be lawful to approach the ruler of the province against him, so that by judicial authority he may immediately be excluded in accordance with the statutes of the most glorious emperors.

We must also gather how great a crime such a transfer is, since it is joined to and compared with rebaptism and reordination. Anyone who wishes to read about the gravity of the sacrilege of rebaptism will be able to find it in the sacred canons and the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, and especially in the letter of Pope Felix to all bishops established throughout the various provinces.

Regarding reordination, Saint Gregory says in his letter to John of Ravenna (Book II, Letter 33):

> “What you say—that one who has been ordained should be ordained again—is exceedingly ridiculous and foreign to the judgment of your intelligence, unless perhaps the example that is being brought forward is one for which the person alleged to have done such a thing must also be judged. Let such a way of thinking be far from your Fraternity.
>
> “For just as someone who has been baptized once ought not to be baptized again, so one who has been consecrated once cannot be consecrated again in the same order.”

Regarding those who come into the clerical order through ignorance or through the dissimulation of those ordaining them, and regarding presbyters promoted without examination, the sacred Council of Nicaea and the decrees of Gelasius promulgated from that same council clearly show what must be done.

### VI

If a definite necessity or benefit should require that a bishop be transferred from the city in which he was ordained to another city, it must be made perfectly clear by synodal decision or by the consent of the Apostolic See that he is being transferred from the city in which he was ordained to another city for the sake of the faith, not for temporal advantage; for the gain of souls, not for profit from temporal possessions; not because of his own fault, but because of the rejection of others; because of the necessity of persecution, not because of the heat of ambition or the presumption of his own will.

Nor should anyone, as the Apostle says, take the honor upon himself, but only one who is called by God, as Aaron was (Heb. V, 4). Likewise, Christ did not glorify himself to become high priest, but was appointed by the one who said to him:

> “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX, 4).

For it is one thing to change, and another to be changed, just as it is one thing to minister and another to be ministered to. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel:

> “I did not come to be ministered to, but to minister” (Matt. XX, 28).

Therefore, as we read in the decrees of the Apostolic See, he does not change his see who does not change his mind—that is, who does not change the intention with which he ought to undertake the episcopate—in order to pass from city to city through greed and ambition.

### VII

To bring forward a few examples from among many, blessed Peter, for the sake of the faith, after ordaining a bishop in Antioch in his place, came to Rome in pursuit of Simon Magus. There he exercised the apostolate and episcopate for twenty-five years.

Augustine, sent by blessed Pope Gregory to the English as Christ’s wheel for the sake of the faith, after that people had accepted the faith through his preaching, was ordained bishop by the bishop of Arles at the command of blessed Gregory. Then, after receiving the pallium from the same blessed Gregory in the royal city of that people, he was established as archbishop. Yet afterward he did not change his see, as anyone who reads blessed Gregory’s letter will be able to discover.

To pass over examples from earlier times: in the time of Prince Charles, when ecclesiastical order and the Christian religion had almost been abolished in these Cisalpine regions, Winfrid, also called Boniface, was ordained bishop at Rome by the third Pope Gregory and sent to these regions for the gain of souls.

When, through his preaching and the example of his holy conduct, ecclesiastical order and religion began to be restored there, he sat for some time in the city of Agrippina, Cologne. When necessity and benefit arose, he was transferred to the city of Mainz and was canonically established there as archbishop. Yet afterward he did not change his see, as a diligent reader can learn from the letters of the pontiffs of the Apostolic See.

### VIII

Regarding one who, not through his own fault but through the rejection of others, is transferred to another city in which he was not ordained, the canons of Antioch say (Canon 18):

> “If a bishop has been ordained and has not at all gone to the parish for which he was appointed, not through his own fault, but because either the people avoid him or some other cause—not, however, caused by his fault—has intervened, he shall share both in honor and in ministry, provided that he causes no disturbance to the affairs of the Church in the place where he is known to minister. He must also observe whatever the completed synod of the province has decreed in judgment.”

The Council of Ancyra likewise decreed concerning those who had been promoted to the episcopate but were not received (Canon 17):

> “If any bishops have been ordained but not received by the parish for which they had been designated, and wish to seize other parishes and use force against their bishops by stirring up seditions against them, it has been decided that they should be removed.
>
> “But if they wish to remain as presbyters, in the place where they had formerly been, they should not be deprived of their proper dignity. If, however, they stir up seditions against the bishops established there, the honor of the presbyterate should also be taken away from such men, and they should become notorious by condemnation.”

The Antiochene canon says that the sacred rules command that no one be given as bishop to unwilling people; the consent and desire of the clergy, the people, and the order must be sought, and the one whom the clergy and people have unanimously requested must be placed over all, lest a city either despise or hate an unwanted bishop and become less religious than it ought to be because it was not permitted to have the one it wanted.

### IX

Regarding one who, because of the necessity of persecution, passes from the city in which he was ordained to another city, the Sardican canons say (Canon 21):

> “If any bishop has suffered violence and has been unjustly expelled for discipline and Catholic confession, or for the defense of truth, and, fleeing danger, has come innocent and devout to another city, he must not be forbidden to remain as long as he is either able to return or receives a remedy for his injury. For it is harsh that one suffering persecution should not be received; indeed, generous kindness must be shown to him.”

Hence Saint Gregory writes to all the bishops throughout Illyricum (Book I, Letter 43):

> “You ought willingly to receive our brothers and fellow bishops, whom captivity and the distress of various necessities oppress, so that they may be comforted and live together with you through ecclesiastical support. This is not, indeed, so that their dignity may be divided through participation in the episcopal throne, but so that, according to your ability, they may receive from the Church sufficient provisions for their sustenance.
>
> “In this way we show that we love our neighbor in God and God in our neighbor. We grant them no authority whatsoever in your Churches, but we earnestly exhort you to keep them sustained by your consolations.”

These final words of the letter agree with the chapter cited above from the Council of Sardica.

### X

The persecution for which a bishop may or must pass from one city to another must also be carefully considered. The Sardican canons demonstrate this (Canon 21):

> “If any bishop has suffered violence and has been unjustly expelled for discipline and Catholic confession, or for the defense of truth, and, fleeing danger, has come innocent and devout to another city—for heretics, schismatics, or criminals commonly persecute Catholics—”

Saint Augustine also explains this in his letter to Bishop Honoratus (Letter 180):

> “It remains that we, whose ministry is so necessary to whatever small people of God remains where we are that it would not be right for them to remain without it, should say to the Lord: ‘Be for us a God of protection and a fortified place’ (Ps. XXX, 3).
>
> “But, as you write, this counsel is not sufficient for you, lest we attempt to act against the Lord’s command or example, where he teaches that we must flee from city to city. For we remember the words: ‘When they persecute you in this city, flee into another’ (Matt. X, 23).
>
> “Who, however, could believe that the Lord wished this to happen in such a way that the flocks he purchased with his own blood should be abandoned when the ministry necessary to them is absent, without which they cannot live? Did he himself do this when, carried by his parents into Egypt, he fled as an infant, before he had gathered the Churches that we could say were abandoned by him?
>
> “Or when the Apostle Paul, so that the enemy would not seize him, was lowered in a basket through a window in the wall and escaped his hands (2 Cor. XI, 33), was the Church that was there deprived of the ministry necessary to it? Was what had to be done not fulfilled by other brothers established there? The Apostle did this with their consent, in order to preserve himself for the Church, since that persecutor was seeking him personally.
>
> “Let the servants of Christ, ministers of his word and sacrament, do what he commanded or permitted. Let them flee from city to city when one of them is specially sought by persecutors, so that the Church may not be abandoned by others who are not sought in the same way; rather, let them provide nourishment to their fellow servants, whom they know cannot otherwise live.
>
> “But when the danger is common to all—that is, to bishops and clergy—those who need others must not be abandoned by those whom they need. Therefore either let all move to fortified places, or let those who have the necessity of remaining not be abandoned by those through whom their ecclesiastical need must be supplied, so that they may either live together or endure together whatever the master of the household wishes them to suffer.
>
> “If it should happen that some suffer less and others more, or that all suffer equally, it becomes clear which of them suffer for the others: namely, those who, although they could escape such evils by fleeing, preferred to remain so as not to abandon the need of the others.
>
> “Here above all the charity commended by the Apostle John is proved, when he says: ‘As Christ laid down his life for us, so we also ought to lay down our lives for our brothers’ (1 John III, 16). For those who flee—or who cannot flee because they are bound by their own necessities—if they are captured and suffer, do not suffer for their brothers. But those who suffer for this reason, that they do not wish to abandon the brothers who need them for Christian salvation, unquestionably lay down their lives for their brothers.”

And a little later:

> “Why do they think that the command must be obeyed without distinction when they read that one must flee from city to city, while they do not abhor the hired servant who sees the wolf coming and flees because he has no concern for the sheep?””

And shortly afterward:

> “The Apostle fled when he himself was being specifically sought by the persecutor, while others who did not have a similar necessity remained there; far be it from them to abandon the ministry of the Church.”

So also Saint Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, fled when the Emperor Constantius desired to seize him personally.

And somewhat earlier Augustine says:

> “For no one says that ministers ought to remain where there are no longer any people who need to be ministered to.”

And hence St. Gregory, in the thirty-first book of the *Moralia* (chapter 14):

> “It is pleasing to contemplate that horse, roused by the spurs of its rider against armed enemies, and to consider how great a fervor had inflamed Paul when at Ephesus the flame of zeal carried him away to break into the crowds in the theater. For it is written: ‘They were filled with anger, and cried out, saying, “Great is Diana of the Ephesians.” And the city was filled with confusion, and they rushed with one accord into the theater’ (Acts XIX, 28), having seized Gaius and Aristarchus, his Macedonian companions. And immediately afterward it is added: ‘But when Paul wished to enter among the people, the disciples did not permit him. Some of the Asiarchs also, who were his friends, sent to him, begging him not to give himself up in the theater’ (ibid., 30). [Col. 0216D] From these words we certainly recognize with what force he would have rushed against the opposing ranks, had the reins of charity not held him back through his friends and disciples.
>
> “But if we ought to confront enemies, voluntarily seek battle, and always abandon ourselves to the course of our fervor, what is the meaning of the confession of that same outstanding preacher, who says: ‘The governor under King Aretas guarded the city of the Damascenes in order to seize me, and through a window I was let down in a basket by the wall, and so I escaped his hands’ (II Cor. XI, 33)? What does it mean that this horse at one moment voluntarily attacks armed ranks, and at another, as though frightened, hides himself from armed enemies, except that we must learn from his skillful virtue both steadfastly to seek battle with adversaries at times and prudently to avoid it at others?
>
> “[Col. 0217A] For it is necessary that in everything we do we weigh, on the scales of the mind, on one side the burden and on the other the fruit of our labor. When the burden outweighs the fruit, anyone may harmlessly avoid the labor, provided that he exercises himself in other matters in which the weight of labor is surpassed by the gain of fruits. But when the measure of labor is either equaled or outweighed by the quantity of fruits that follows, labor cannot be avoided without grave guilt.
>
> “Thus the holy preacher, seeing that the minds of those persecuting him at Damascus were exceedingly obstinate, did not wish to engage their opposition, because he saw that he, whom he knew would benefit many, might be exhausted and might benefit either no one there or only a few. He therefore sought withdrawal from the contest and preserved himself for other battles, in which he would fight more successfully. It was not virtue that was lacking in the place, but a place for virtue. And therefore the strongest soldier sought the open field of battle instead of the confinement of a siege.
>
> “[Col. 0217B] But when he saw that many necks of adversaries were to be brought under the yoke of their own King, he did not fear to enter the battle even at the cost of death. Thus, when he was going to Jerusalem and the disciples were trying to prevent his foretold passion, he bears witness concerning himself, saying: ‘For I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus. For I do not hold my life more precious than myself’ (Acts XXI, 13). For the outstanding preacher, scorning the powers of this world, fears no sound of threats.
>
> “[Col. 0217C] Let us look at another horse of God: how he devours the earth, how no terror of the crowd touches him. It is written: ‘But some Jews came from Antioch and Iconium, and having persuaded the crowds, they stoned Paul and dragged him outside the city, supposing him to be dead. But when the disciples surrounded him, he rose and entered the city; and on the following day he departed with Barnabas for Derbe. And after they had evangelized that city and taught many, they returned to Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch, strengthening the souls of the disciples’ (Acts XIV, 17).
>
> “[Col. 0217D] Let us therefore consider what threats could restrain this horse, when death itself cannot prevent him from his purpose. Behold, he is overwhelmed with stones, yet is not removed from speaking the truth. He can be killed, but he cannot be overcome. He is thrown outside the city as though extinguished, but on the following day the preacher is found unharmed within the city. O how great is the steadfastness present in this man! O how victorious is punishment! O how sovereign is endurance! He is provoked to action by being driven back; he is raised up to preach salvation by blows; punishment renews him so that he may repel the weariness of labor.”

The same blessed Gregory also writes in his letter to Bishop Agnellus (Book XI, Indiction 11, Letter 13):

> “Since, therefore, because of the calamity of enemy hostility, no one is permitted to dwell either in the city or in your Church, for this reason, by our authority, we appoint you cardinal priest of the Church of Terracina.”

And in his letter to Bishop John (Book XI, Indiction 10, Letter 25):

> “[Col. 0218A] Since we have deemed it necessary to appoint you, John, bishop of the city of Lisbon, which has been captured by enemies, cardinal priest in the Church of Squillace, so that, both in view of the future reward, you may fulfill the care of souls once undertaken, and, although you have been driven from your Church by the threatening enemy, you may govern another Church that is without a pastor. This arrangement is to stand, however, so that if it should happen that the city is freed from its enemies and, with the Lord’s protection, restored to its former condition, you may return to the Church in which you were previously ordained. But if the aforesaid city continues to be oppressed by the calamity of captivity, you are to remain in the Church in which we have incardinated you.”

### XI

By these authorities, Actard, bishop of Nantes, who had first been expelled from his city by Nominoy, duke of the Bretons, was restored to his see by the lord King Charles. After that Breton duke had been driven out, the king, with the advice of the bishops, ordered [Col. 0218B] the man whom that same tyrant had irregularly installed in the see of Nantes to be exiled to the monastery of Saint Martin, and Actard to be restored to his see.

Later, when the same Actard had been expelled from his city by the tyrant Salomon, the council’s consent allowed him to reside for some time in the vacant Church of Morini, until, at the request of the clergy and people of the province of Tours, and with the agreement of the bishops, he returned to his own province and was incardinated by the pontiff of the Apostolic See in the vacant metropolitan church.

Actard ought not to have changed his see if he could remain there, or if there were someone else who could be regularly ordained in the Church of Tours with equal or perhaps greater benefit. For Celestine says (Letter 1, to the bishops of the province of Vienne, etc.):

> “[Col. 0218C] Then let another be chosen from another church if, among the clergy of the very city in which the bishop is to be ordained, no one worthy—which we do not believe can happen—can be found. For those men must first be rejected, so that some from foreign churches may deservedly be preferred. Let each person enjoy the fruit of his service in the church in which he has passed his entire life through all its offices. Let no one intrude upon another’s stipend, nor dare to claim for himself the reward owed to another.”

### XII

But in undertaking to hold both sees simultaneously, namely Tours and Nantes, the same Actard appears to have acted against the Council of Chalcedon (canon X), which decreed:

> “[Col. 0218D] It is not permitted for a cleric to be enrolled simultaneously in the churches of two cities: both in the one in which he was initially ordained and in the one to which he has fled, as though it were the more important, out of a desire for empty glory. Those who do this are to be recalled to their own church, in which they were first ordained, and there alone are they to minister. If someone has already been transferred from one church to another, he is in no way to share in the possessions of the former church, or of the martyr-shrines dependent upon it, or of its poorhouses or hospices. Those who dare, after the definition of this great and universal synod, to perpetrate anything of what has been prohibited are decreed by the holy synod to withdraw from their own rank.”

### XIII

[Col. 0219A] But certain people, contrary to this chapter of the great and universal synod, strive to fortify themselves, as though by the words of blessed Gregory, so that they may be able to hold two sees simultaneously—even though no Christian is permitted to have two wives at once, or a wife and a concubine at once. They should carefully distinguish the words of that same blessed Gregory in his letter to Bishop Bacundus, in which he speaks not of cities far distant from one another, but of neighboring cities, deprived both of clergy and people and desolated in their possessions and resources:

> “The necessity of the time,” he says (Book I, Letter 8), “presses us, and the diminution of persons requires that we come to the aid of deserted churches with a salutary and prudent arrangement. And therefore, since we have learned that the Church of Minturnae has been utterly deprived of both clergy and people through desolation, and since we foresee that your petition concerning it—that it should be joined to the Church of Formiae, in which the body of blessed Erasmus the martyr rests and over which your fraternity [Col. 0219B] presides—is pious and most just, we have judged it necessary, taking thought both for the desolation of that place and for the poverty of your church, that the revenues of the aforesaid Church of Minturnae, or whatever by ancient or modern right or privilege could or can in any manner belong to it, should, by the authority of this our decree, pass into the right and power of your church.”

In these words everyone should note that he says the necessity of the time presses and that the diminution of persons requires aid to be given to deserted churches; and he judges it necessary to provide both for the desolation of the place and for the poverty of the church.

[Col. 0219C] Some also wish, through an invention of the recent age, to usurp the presumption that they may change their sees—not for reasons of usefulness, but under the supposedly protective veil of necessity, when in reality out of the ambition of desire. They cite cases in which certain bishops were transferred from city to city, and even from lesser to greater sees, before definite decisions of the sacred canons had been established; but it is dangerous to transgress those decisions.

As the holy Pope Hilary writes to Leontius and the other bishops (Letter 11):

> “For the sanctions of the sacred traditions are violated no less than an assault is made against the Lord himself.”

And Saint Celestine says (Letter 11):

> “Let no priest be permitted to be ignorant of his canons, nor to do anything that could oppose the rules of the Fathers. For what worthy matter will be preserved by us if the norm of decretal ordinances is broken, through the license of some people, and permission is granted to the populace according to anyone’s inclination?”

And Saint Leo says (Letter 1):

> “[Col. 0219D] Our admonition declares that if any of the brethren attempts to come against these constitutions and dares to admit what has been prohibited, he should know that he is to be removed from his office and will not be a sharer in our communion—he who did not wish to be a partner in discipline.”

And Saint Gelasius (Letter 6, to all the bishops):

> “Since we desire to presume that nothing is permitted to us against the reverence due to salutary rules, and since the Apostolic See, with the Lord’s favor, earnestly strives to preserve, with pious and devoted purpose, everything established in these matters by the canons of the Fathers, it is exceedingly unworthy for anyone—whether among the bishops or among the ranks that follow them—to reject this observance, which he sees the See of blessed Peter both follow and [Col. 0220A] teach. It is entirely fitting that the whole body of the Church should agree with itself in this observance, which it sees flourishing where the Lord placed the principate of the whole Church.”

And again the same author says:

> “[Col. 0220B] Our Fathers, namely Catholic and learned pontiffs, whatever they once established, after assembling, for the faith, for truth, for Catholic and apostolic communion, according to the course of Scripture and the tradition of the ancestors, wished thereafter to remain unshaken and firm. They did not permit what had once been established in this same matter to be reconsidered by any new presumption, wisely recognizing that, if anyone were permitted to reopen salutary decrees, no established ordinance of the Church would remain stable against every error, and every complete definition would continually be disturbed by the return of the same madnesses.”

Symmachus says (Letter 1, to Aeonius):

> “It belongs to the very sacred Catholic religion, whose entire authority is undermined unless everything once regularly established by the priests of the Lord remains perpetual. How else could this happen, unless a successor grants firmness to the acts of his predecessor and, by strengthening what was done, makes his own acts valid?”

And again the same author (in the same letter):

> “How great will be judged the reverence shown to the vicars of the blessed apostle Peter if what they prescribe in the priesthood is dissolved when they themselves pass away?”

And again:

> “[Col. 0220C] What touches the injury of the whole body cannot be firm in part; and what was presented as though for confirmation, but rather for destruction, rests upon the preceding invention.”

Hence the holy Fathers of Nicaea say in their second chapter (canon 11):

> “Since many things have been done either out of necessity or because people were otherwise compelled, contrary to ecclesiastical rule…”

[Col. 0220D] And holy Pope Leo, in the forty-fourth chapter of his *Decretals*, says that what necessity has imposed should be omitted and judged without blame.

Anyone who reads these chapters plainly recognizes how far this pernicious permission is from the reason and authority of the proposed defense. For the proceedings of that second chapter of the Council of Nicaea, which had previously been wrongly carried out, prohibited with a grave threat that no one should thereafter presume such a thing. And Leo’s forty-third chapter is wholly unrelated to this argument, as the thirty-eighth chapter of his decrees to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica, itself clearly demonstrates.

Regarding matters done out of necessity and appearing rather to be usurpations, Saint Innocent, in his decrees to Rufus, Eusebius, and the other bishops, says (Letter 27):

> “Let your affection therefore recognize that such things have gone far enough, and observe that what necessity, as you say, compelled cannot be presumed upon in churches already established in peace.”

And shortly afterward:

> “I say, therefore, that what preceded must be left to God’s judgment, and that henceforth the greatest care must be taken to prevent such things.”

[Col. 0221A] Those who devised these practices should therefore have seen with the eyes both of mind and body the judgment of Paul, who says: “For we are not like the many, adulterating the word of God” (II Cor. II, 17).

> “An adulterer,” says blessed Gregory (*Moralia*, XVI, chapter 25), “in carnal intercourse seeks not offspring but pleasure; and every perverse person who serves empty glory is rightly said to adulterate the word of God, because through sacred speech he desires not to beget children for God but to display his own knowledge. Whoever is drawn to speak by a lust for glory devotes himself more to pleasure than to procreation.”

Likewise, anyone who changes his church for the sake of wealth, abundant resources, and earthly possessions is rightly called an adulterer and will be counted among adulterers.

[Col. 0221B] For to abandon the bishop of the city in which the count resides, where clerics and lay nobles—and also common people and rural laborers, and even Jews, as is said—live, and where they dwell in the parish under the Christian name; to abandon its bishopric out of desire or the ardor of ambition; to seize another vacant see; and to retain both that see and the one in which he was ordained, and in which he can live without danger of death—this is not merely disgraceful but dangerous and pernicious.

The sacred canons even decree concerning a vacant bishop who rushes into a vacant church (Council of Antioch, canon 14):

> “If any bishop, while vacant, rushes into a vacant church and seizes its see without a complete and perfect council, he must be deposed, even if the entire people whom he has seized should choose to have him. A perfect council is one in which the metropolitan bishop is present.”

Concerning one who irrationally and irregularly abandons the city in which he was ordained and transfers to another, the Council of Sardica says (canon 1):

> “[Col. 0221C] A bad custom no less than a pernicious abuse must be utterly eradicated, so that no bishop may be permitted to pass from his own city to another city.
