For the reason why he attempts this is obvious, since no bishop has ever been found who passed from a greater city to a lesser one. Hence it is clear that they are inflamed by greed, serve ambition, and seek to exercise domination. If this is acceptable to all, let such wickedness be punished more severely and more strictly, so that one who is such may not even have lay communion.”

In this chapter, the greater and lesser city must be considered not only by name but also by possessions. Likewise, greed concerns not only money and property but also elevation.

[Col. 0221D] In the case of the metropolitan, greed is present when exaltation above measure is sought. In the matter of possessions—namely, abundance of goods and resources—there is the greed that the Apostle calls the service of idols.

Following this chapter, holy Pope Leo decreed (Letter 88, to Anastasius of Thessalonica):

> “[Col. 0222A] If any bishop, despising the modesty of his own city, has sought the administration of a more celebrated place and has transferred himself by any means to a greater people, let him indeed be driven from the foreign chair, but let him also lose his own, so that he may preside neither over those whom he desired through greed nor over those whom he despised through pride. Let each person therefore be content with his own boundaries, and let no one seek to be increased beyond the measure of his lawful right.”

The Council of Sardica also says (canon 11):

> “Even if someone should prove so rash as perhaps to claim in excuse that he received letters from the people, when it is clear that a few could have been corrupted by payment and reward—those who have no sincere faith—so that they might cry out in the church and appear to demand that man as bishop, I judge that such deceptions must altogether be condemned, so that such a man may not even receive lay communion at the end.”

Since one metropolitan bishop cannot regularly preside over two metropolitan sees, holy Pope Boniface makes this clear by the authority of the Council of Nicaea, writing to Hilary, bishop of Narbonne (Letter 8):

> “[Col. 0222B] No one, I think, is unaware of the constitution of the Nicene synod, which commands as follows, in its very words: that each province ought properly to have a single metropolitan, and that no one may have two provinces subject to him. Since this must not be believed otherwise, they judged, under the prompting of the Holy Spirit, that this should be observed.”

And after some further remarks:

> “We say this so that your charity may understand that we observe the precepts of the canons so carefully that our own constitution likewise determines that each province should always await, in every matter, the arrangement of its metropolitan.”

[Col. 0222C] Augustine says that the experience of many diseases compels us to discover remedies for many illnesses. And because, as Daniel says, “Many shall pass to and fro, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Dan. 12, 4), certain things are permitted according to the diversity of times, the variety of illnesses, and the health of human beings.

Thus new foods were granted by a fresh permission for the use of Noah and his sons; later they were prohibited to the Jewish people through Moses; and again they have been permitted to us, so that what was forbidden to the Jews in animals is forbidden to us in conduct, just as the Lord says in the Gospel: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients: but I say to you” (Matt. V, 21).

Therefore, although it was once permitted, out of necessity or usefulness, for bishops to transfer from churches to churches before the sacred rules were established, afterward it was, is, and will be so unlawful to usurp such transfers against those same sacred rules that Saint Gregory Nazianzen, a most learned, most Catholic, and most eloquent man, venerable for the merit of his life and the teaching of his wisdom, who among the Greeks is called “the Theologian,” acted as follows.

[Col. 0222D] As we read in ecclesiastical histories, he was transferred from the small city of Nazianzus to Constantinople for the sake of the faith by the decree of many bishops. He governed Constantinople with outstanding distinction for twelve years, gloriously freed it from the Arian heresy, and by his expositions revived in that royal city the doctrine of the Council of Nicaea, which had seemed already dead.

Recognizing that the bishops were murmuring because he had been transferred contrary to the canons from one city to another, and wishing to avoid—or rather remove—fraternal scandal, lest he appear to introduce schism into the Church, he followed the Apostle’s admonition: “In all things let us show ourselves as God’s ministers, giving no one any occasion of offense, so that our ministry may not be blamed” (II Cor. VI, 4).

[Col. 0223A] When the emperor Theodosius arrived at Constantinople, Gregory peacefully obtained permission and thereafter declined to remain in that same city. He followed the Lord’s saying to Peter, that those who did not owe the tax should nevertheless pay it when the tax was demanded, so that scandal might be avoided.

The Lord says:

> “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that an ass’s millstone be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the depths of the sea” (Matt. XVIII, 6).

By the ass’s millstone, as Saint Gregory explains in his *Pastoral Rule* (Part I, chapter 2),

> “the round of secular life and its labor is signified, and by the depth of the sea final damnation is designated. Whoever, therefore, having been led to the appearance of holiness, destroys others either by word or by example would assuredly have been better off if earthly actions under an outward appearance had constrained him to death, rather than sacred offices displaying him as an example of guilt for others to imitate. For, certainly, if he fell alone, the punishment of hell would torment him in a somewhat more tolerable manner.”

And again (Part III, chapter 5):

> “[Col. 0223B] Superiors must know that if they ever commit perverse acts, they are worthy of as many deaths as examples of destruction they transmit to their subjects. Hence they must guard themselves from guilt all the more carefully, the more their evil deeds cause not only themselves to die.”

But if someone should say, “I am not invading the Church to which I am transferring with the consent of many bishops and the people,” let him carefully consider, as blessed Gregory of Nazianzus also considered, what has been established by the sacred canons, as we stated above. To depart from those canons through contempt is to fall into schism, [Col. 0223C] as holy Pope Hilary plainly shows (Letter 11):

> “The sanctions of the sacred traditions are violated no less than an assault is made against the Lord himself.”

By this judgment blessed Pope Hilary denounced heretics and schismatics alike: schismatics in saying that the sanctions of the sacred traditions are violated no less, and heretics in saying that an assault is made against the Lord himself.

> “For heretics,” as Saint Gregory demonstrates from the judgment of the apostle Paul, who says, “If I hand over my body to be burned, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (I Cor. XIII, 3) (*Moralia*, XVIII, chapter 14), “think wrongly about God; schismatics hold correct views about the Creator, but do not maintain unity with their brethren in the observance of the sacred traditions. The former are divided by error of faith, the latter by the perpetration of schism. [Col. 0223D]
>
> “Thus, in the very first part of the Decalogue, the guilt of both parties is restrained, when the divine voice says: ‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength’ (Deut. VI, 5), and immediately adds: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ Whoever thinks perversely about God plainly does not love God; but whoever thinks correctly about God while being divided from the unity of the holy Church clearly does not love his neighbor, whom he refuses to have as his companion.
>
> “Therefore, whoever is divided from this unity of Mother Church—whether through heresy, by thinking perversely about God, or through the error of schism, by failing to love his neighbor—is deprived of this grace of charity, concerning which Paul says what we quoted above: ‘If I hand over my body to be burned, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing.’ It is as though he were saying openly: ‘Outside its proper place of smelting, fire applied to me afflicts me with torment; it does not purify me.’”

[Col. 0224A] Gold has a proper place in which it is smelted: that is, the unity of the Catholic Church. Within it, baptism, good works, and even martyrdom are beneficial; outside it, neither baptism, nor good works, nor even martyrdom is profitable.

That heretics and schismatics are related is also shown in the solemn prayers of the Friday before Easter.

> “Therefore,” as Saint Celestine writes (Letter 8, at the end), “let the law of believing establish the law of praying.”

How grave a sin schism is, Saint Augustine demonstrates in the second book *On Baptism* (chapter 6), saying:

> “[Col. 0224B] Let us bring forth the divine balance from the Holy Scriptures, as from the Lord’s treasures, and weigh upon it what is more serious. Rather, let us not weigh it ourselves, but recognize what has been weighed by the Lord, at the time when the Lord showed that former sins were to be avoided through fresh examples of punishment: an idol was fashioned and worshiped; a prophetic book was burned in the anger of the contemptuous king; and schism was attempted. Idolatry was punished by the sword; the burning of the book by slaughter in war and foreign captivity; schism by the earth’s opening, with its authors buried alive and the rest consumed by heavenly fire. Who, then, would doubt that the act more severely punished was the more wicked?”

[Col. 0224C] Hence it is also written in the decrees of the Apostolic See:

> “For just as the Lord foretold that the righteous would go into eternal life, so the wicked would be condemned to eternal destruction; and just as the blessedness of the righteous cannot end, so neither will the torments of the wicked end.”

These statements concern heretics and schismatics.

Since everything the Church now does is mystically a type of future things, if they taste the heavenly bread—that is, divine sweetness—then participation in hell is the condemnation of heretics and schismatics through communion in the body and blood of Christ.

Whoever therefore assents to a schismatic cannot deny that he is himself a schismatic. Even if all priests and the whole world give their assent, condemnation encompasses those who consent; consent does not absolve transgression. The crime is not diminished but increased when what was private becomes general. God, who destroyed the sinful world by a universal flood, demonstrated this.

> “[Col. 0224D] And just as,” Gelasius writes (Letter 10, to Anastasius), “when a communicator in perversity has been received, perversity itself cannot fail to be approved along with him, so perversity cannot be rejected when its accomplice and follower is admitted, since the Apostle says that not only those who do what ought not to be done are judged guilty, but also those who consent to those who do them” (Rom. I, 32).

Public laws bind accomplices to crimes and receivers of robbers with the same judicial penalty. Nor is someone considered free of wrongdoing who, although he did not commit it himself, nevertheless received those who committed it into familiarity and alliance.

Let us therefore hear how the Lord also calls those who, contrary to the sacred canons established by the Spirit of God, leap into the sheepfold of the sheep—that is, seize the governance of the Church rather than attain it:

> “[Col. 0225A] The one who does not enter by the door into the sheepfold of the sheep, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber” (John X, 1).

Of such people he says through the prophet:

> “They have reigned, but not from me; they have become princes, and I did not know them” (Hos. VIII, 4).

Gregory says of them (*Pastoral Rule*, Part I, chapter 1):

> “They reign from themselves and not by the choice of the supreme ruler who, inflamed by their own desire, seize the summit of government rather than attain it. Yet the inner Judge both promotes them and does not know them, because those whom he tolerates by permitting them, he certainly ignores by the judgment of rejection.”

Those who favor such men should therefore fear the judgment of Paul, cited above by blessed Gelasius in this sense:

> “Not only those who do such things, but also those who consent to those who do them, are worthy of death” (Rom. I, 32).

[Col. 0225B] For, as Leo says, in promoting such men one does not provide for the people but harms them; one does not offer governance but increases danger.

### XIV

You wrote that the bishop in question says, in order to make excuses for his sins, that there are ecclesiastical ministers in the metropolitan city in which he had been ordained who can provide for the needs of the needy, but that he himself does not possess sufficient goods and resources to subsist honorably there. In trying to excuse himself on this account, he appears rather to accuse himself and to brand himself with the mark of desire and ambition, since he seems to seek earthly possessions more than gains of souls.

[Col. 0225C] He ought to have kept in mind what the Spirit said to Paul: that he should not leave the city in which he had a large people, but should preach steadfastly. For what does he know whether many of those pagans who live in that same city have been predestined by God to life, and might have been converted through the preaching of his mouth and conduct? And where there are Christians, they might be saved if he remained there, even if necessity compelled him to remain there in such a condition, just as Paul said that he had remained among the Corinthians:

> “I was among you in weakness, fear, and much trembling” (I Cor. II, 3).

Let him therefore read the fourteenth homily of blessed Gregory on the Gospel reading, “I am the good shepherd” (John XI, 14), and he will find how and how far he has departed from authority and from his own order.

[Col. 0225D] He has also caused scandal in the Church, just as certain bishops in times long past introduced scandal into the Church for the sake of their own rest and pleasures, appointing chorepiscopi and permitting them to perform what belongs to the highest pontiffs. The Apostolic See has often condemned these men and cut them off with the apostolic sword, as anyone who wishes to examine their decretal letters will find.

Among them, Pope Damasus speaks of such bishops (Letter 5, to the bishops of Numidia):

> “Those bishops,” he says, “who presume to do such things appear to me like prostitutes who, as soon as they give birth, hand their infants over to other nurses to be raised, so that they may more quickly satisfy their lust. So these men hand over their infants—that is, the peoples entrusted to them—to others to be raised, so that they may satisfy their own lusts: that is, so that they may devote themselves according to their own pleasure to secular concerns and do more freely whatever each of them wishes.”

[Col. 0226A] And other statements, which the reader will be able to find in their proper places.

It is also contained in the letter of blessed Pope Nicholas, sent to certain bishops of the province of Belgium, that the Greeks raged against him because he, like his predecessors, commanded priests to abstain from their wives. They wished to establish by canons that it should be lawful for them to have wives.

But we modern and Gallican bishops are attempting to make new canons so that what is more serious than carnal intercourse—spiritual adultery—may be permitted to us: either to have two wives, that is, two sees, simultaneously; or to keep a wife and a concubine at the same time; or, while the wife is alive, though weakened—that is, while our Church has been diminished by persecution in its goods and possessions—to transfer ourselves to another union.

[Col. 0226B] Just as a man has no authority over his own body, but the woman does, so long as his wife, though weakened, remains alive, so a bishop has no authority to abandon his Church, namely his people, and invade or usurp another, so long as, as Saint Augustine says (Letter 180, to Honoratus), fellow servants remain in it for whom he may provide food and whom he knows cannot otherwise live.

If he does this, he commits adultery all the more seriously because he commits spiritual adultery, and makes his own people commit adultery, if while the other remains alive and he remains secure in his priesthood he joins himself to another. For a woman has no authority over her own body, but the man does, so long as her husband lives; and he makes the people whom he has invaded commit adultery with him, as blessed Innocent shows in his decrees, speaking about the separation of husband and wife. This ought rightly to be understood and followed concerning the spiritual union of the bishop and the Church in which he was first ordained.

> “[Col. 0226C] Your affection,” he says (Letter 11, to Exuperius), “has inquired about those who, after a divorce had intervened, have joined themselves to another marriage. It is clear that they are adulterers on both sides. Those who, while their husband or wife is alive, although the marriage may appear to have been dissolved, have hastened to another union cannot fail to be regarded as adulterers. Indeed, even the persons to whom such people have been joined appear themselves to have committed adultery, according to what we read in the Gospel: ‘Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery; and likewise whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery’ (Matt. V, 21). Therefore all are to be excluded from the communion of the faithful.”

[Col. 0226D] But if the bishop’s wife—that is, his church and parish—has been desolated by any oppression of persecution, namely has slipped from the land so that no one remains in it who needs to be served, the bishop may lawfully transfer to another vacant church, as has been demonstrated above by the words of blessed Augustine and Gregory.

And the people deprived of their bishop—that is, vacant—may regularly receive a bishop deprived of his priesthood by death or regularly vacant, just as the Apostle says concerning a woman:

> “When her husband has died, she may marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord” (I Cor. VII, 39).

[Col. 0227A] For holy Leo, one of the foremost ornaments of the Roman See, explaining the Apostle’s judgment concerning man and woman, clearly shows what he wished to be understood by this union:

> “This is a great sacrament; but I speak of Christ and the Church” (Eph. V, 32).

There are indeed two: God and man, Christ and the Church. The Church came forth from the flesh of the Bridegroom and, from the blood and water flowing from the side of the Crucified One, received the sacrament of redemption and regeneration.

And elsewhere the same saint says:

> “Therefore, since the partnership of marriage was established from the beginning in such a way that, beyond the union of the sexes, it contained within itself the sacrament of Christ and the Church, let no one, then, commit fornication by abandoning, through an improper desire, the wife lawfully and spiritually allotted to him in marriage; rather, let him love and cherish her, just as [Col. 0227B] Christ does the Church. Nor, after abandoning her own shepherd who remains in faith and good works—the shepherd whom, by God’s ordering, she received as her lawful portion—let the Church commit fornication; rather, let her remain in that calling to which she was called, as sacred Scripture and ecclesiastical traditions have prescribed.
>
> “For if, because the Apostle permits it, a man of one wife is commanded to be admitted to the priesthood so that he may cherish and protect with chaste assistance the wife whom he had before the priesthood, and must not leave her abandoned, much less may a priest abandon or neglect a Church left without a shepherd, either for the sake of a subsequently imposed Church or together with such a Church; and least of all may he commit adultery with another Church while still joined to that one. And just as he must not adulterate the word of God, so neither must he adulterate his own Church.
>
> “For unless the lawful union of husband and wife [Col. 0227C] pertained to the mystery of the bishop and the Church joined to him, the great Council of Chalcedon would not call a Church widowed by the death of her bishop ‘widowed’; nor would it command that her revenues be reserved with the steward for the future bishop, and that they not be seized or destroyed by anyone else, whether the bishop of that city were living or dead. Those who presume to do so ought to fear the sentence of that same holy and universal Council, which, by its threat, decrees as follows (canon 10):

> “‘The holy Synod has decreed that those who have dared, after the definition of this great and universal Synod, to perpetrate anything among the things that have been prohibited, must withdraw from their own rank.’”

And concerning those who transgress what has been established, it says in the same connection (canon 27):

> “If they are clerics, let them fall from their own rank; [Col. 0227D] but if they are laymen, let them be anathematized.”

Thus, too, the canons of other councils and the pontiffs of the apostolic see have repeatedly decreed concerning those who presume upon the goods and resources of others. Those who believe the Lord’s unanswerable judgment do not treat these matters lightly—the judgment in which he says through Peter, and through all the apostles, and in them through their successors: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven” (Matt. 16:19).

For just as Peter answered on behalf of all the apostles when Christ questioned them, so Christ spoke these words through Peter to the apostles and to all their successors. This privilege remains with them, and from them judgment is rendered according to the equity of the apostles, as Saints Leo and Gregory clearly demonstrate. Hence Saint Gregory also says:

> [Col. 0228A] “They are not Christians who imagine that they can dissolve the bonds of the holy Church by empty efforts. Consequently, they do not consider the absolution of the holy Church, which she grants to the faithful, to be genuine if they do not consider her bonds valid. There is no need to argue at length against them, for they must be utterly despised and anathematized. In the very matter by which they think they are deceiving the truth, they are truly entangled in their sins. Both I and all Catholic bishops, and the whole Church, anathematize them, because they hold and speak opinions contrary to the truth.”

We have inserted these remarks about reserving the goods and resources of a widowed Church with the future bishop through the steward so that the bishop in question may consider the matter at stake. For if no Christian is permitted to presume upon such goods, much less may a bishop, without endangering his office and damaging his soul, usurp the goods and resources of a Church that he has invaded. [Col. 0228B]

Just as the count of the city, a secular man, and other secular persons—those of greater and lesser power—have the means to remain in their metropolitan city, and his ecclesiastical fellow ministers are able to live there, so he too, unless greed and ambition were driving him away, could remain there, either by the work of his hands, or from the tithes of the faithful and the contributions of the priests, or, if he could manage in no other way, by paying a rent, as the patriarch does at Jerusalem and as religious and faithful men do at Córdoba and in other cities throughout Spain. There he could remain and give his fellow servants their measure of wheat at the proper time—that is, impart the word of preaching—and perform those ministries that can be supplied only by bishops to ecclesiastical ministers and congregations. [Col. 0228C]

These include the ordination of ecclesiastical ministers; the preparation of the sacred chrism; the consecration of exorcised oil and of oil consecrated for the anointing of the sick; the confirmation and signing of the baptized; the laying on of hands and the reconciliation of public penitents; the veiling of virgins; and other matters that it is unnecessary to enumerate individually. These things can regularly be performed only by bishops, and one bishop cannot perform them at suitable times in both cities, so far apart from one another—indeed, he neither can nor ought to do so, nor do the rules permit it.

Even if he can perform these functions in his metropolitan city from time to time, it is thereby proved that he can remain there and carry out the duties that belong to him toward his subjects. Let him read [Col. 0228D] the Second Epistle of the Apostle Paul to the Corinthians, and he will see with what difficulty and labor he carried out the ministry of preaching. Besides the hardships he endured in prisons, he suffered beatings beyond measure, frequent dangers of death, lashes, stonings, shipwrecks, and repeated hardships on journeys; dangers from rivers, dangers from robbers, dangers from his own people, dangers from the Gentiles, dangers in the city, dangers in the wilderness, dangers at sea, dangers from false brothers; labor and toil, many vigils, hunger and thirst, frequent fasts, cold and nakedness; and, apart from these external things, the daily pressure of responsibility, the care of all the Churches (2 Cor. 11:25–28).

He also labored with his own hands [Col. 0229A] to provide what was necessary for himself and his companions, so as not to burden anyone. He will find himself excluded from the succession of the one whose example he refuses to follow, and bound by the judgment of those who now reign with God in heaven and who, inspired by the Holy Spirit, promulgated the sacred canons through that same Holy Spirit. These canons decree that such a man is not to be regarded as a bishop in that place, as we have written above, nor deemed worthy even of lay communion. Saint Leo, pontiff of the apostolic see, clearly decrees this repeatedly in his letters (Letter 1, at the end):

> “Our admonition declares that if any of the brethren comes or attempts to come against these established provisions, and dares to admit what has been prohibited, he must know that he is to be removed from his office and will not be a sharer in our communion—he who was unwilling to be a partner in discipline. [Col. 0229B] Lest anything be thought to have been omitted by us, we command that all decretal constitutions, both those of blessed memory, Innocent, and those of all our predecessors, which have been promulgated concerning ecclesiastical orders and the discipline of the canons, must be observed by your devotion. If anyone commits such an offense against them, let him know that forgiveness will thereafter be denied him.”

## XV.

Why could not a religious man, a bishop, and one living in continence, without wife or children, live in his own city as a secular count, who has a wife and children and lives even among pagans—especially since he possesses other estates and abbeys through the generosity of our lord the king, from which he can obtain the resources sufficient to serve God and carry out his ministry among the people entrusted to him?

“But there are some,” says Gregory (Homily 14 on the Gospels), “who, because they love earthly substance more than the sheep, rightly lose the name of shepherd. Concerning them it is immediately added: ‘But the hired man, and he who is not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, sees the wolf coming, abandons the sheep, and flees’ (John 10:12).

“He is called not a shepherd but a hired man who feeds the Lord’s sheep not out of intimate love but for temporal wages. For the hired man holds the shepherd’s place, but does not seek the profit of souls; he longs for earthly advantages, rejoices in the honor of authority, is nourished by temporal gains, and delights in the reverence shown him by men. These are the hired man’s wages: that, for the very labor he undertakes in governing, he find here what he seeks, and in the future be excluded from the inheritance of the flock.” (The same work, after some intervening material.)

> “The wolf also seizes and scatters the sheep. The wolf comes and the hired man flees, because the evil spirit tears apart the minds of the faithful in temptation, while the one who holds the shepherd’s place does not exercise watchful care. Souls perish, and he rejoices in earthly advantages.”

Therefore, since, as blessed Gelasius says (Letter 10, to Anastasius), “there are two powers by which this world is principally governed, the sacred authority of pontiffs and royal power,” bishops and princes of the earth should follow the counsel—or rather the command—of the Apostle, who urges:

> “Do not participate in the unfruitful works of darkness; rather, rebuke them” [Col. 0230A] (Eph. 5:11).

Hence Saint Augustine says:

> “The evil person does not defile you in either of two ways if you do not consent and if you rebuke him: that is, do not participate and do not consent.”

Participation occurs when one joins to another’s deed a partnership of will or approval. Thus the Apostle warns us: “Do not participate in the unfruitful works of darkness.” And because merely refusing consent would be insufficient if negligence of discipline followed, he adds: “Rather, rebuke them.”

What does “Do not participate” mean? Do not consent, do not praise, do not approve. What does “rather, rebuke them” mean? Reprove, correct, restrain.

The African Council also expressly commands that those who neglect to win for Catholic unity the places belonging to their own cathedra are to be summoned by diligent neighboring bishops, so that they may not delay in undertaking this work, as the careful reader will find in its proper place, with the clearest definition.

It is entirely certain that this man has exchanged his own city, where many remain in need of episcopal ministry, for another that is quieter and wealthier, and has allowed another to be ordained in his place. Since, as we have shown above, he cannot preside over two metropolitan cities, he has done this not for the gain of souls but for temporal advancement, to his own spiritual detriment. For, as Leo says, that honor will not be considered legitimate which has been conferred contrary to the precepts of divine law.

The decretal judgment of the holy Pope Simplicius strikes such supporters and ordainers. He says:

> “He deserves to lose his privilege who abuses the power entrusted to him.” [Col. 0230C]

So far as time and my duties have allowed, and as the Lord has granted me to bring these matters to mind, I have taken care to answer you, dearest brother, concerning the things you had asked. If anything here displeases anyone, let him be angry not with me but with himself, since he cannot be angry with the divine words except to his own harm.

While he is still on the way—that is, in this life—let him quickly come to terms with his adversary, lest his adversary hand him over to the judge, the judge to the officer, and the officer cast him into prison. Amen, I say to you, he will not come out from there until he has paid the last farthing.

Even those with only a little knowledge of Scripture know that in this passage our adversary is called the word of God, because it commands things contrary to the evil deeds we commit. [Col. 0230D] If we do not come to terms with it, by God’s just judgment we shall be handed over through the officer to prison, and we shall not come out until we have paid the last farthing—that is, until we have paid even for the smallest sin.

## LETTER XXXII. TO POPE JOHN, IN THE NAME OF EMPEROR CHARLES II

Concerning the judgments and appeals of bishops and priests.

(Printed in the same author, from the Mainz edition of John Busaeus.)

To the most holy and most reverend Father JOHN, supreme pontiff and universal pope, CHARLES, by the grace of God emperor Augustus and your spiritual son.

### I.

Before the Transalpine provinces, because of the frequent seditions and wars, had fully acquired knowledge and observance of the sacred laws and rules—as afterward, through the increasing zeal of our forebears, they acquired them by God’s grace from this holy see—our grandfather of glorious memory, Charles, emperor Augustus, for a long time inquired through distinguished men of exceptional authority and wisdom how priests defamed by accusations of crimes ought to be judged or clear themselves.

He discovered the procedure that he left to posterity for observance in the edicts of his imperial authority, which we have written in another document. From that time until our own, these provisions have been observed in the Transalpine regions and, whenever necessity required, put into effect.

### II.

In the days of our lord and father, the emperor Louis of pious memory, when the execution of these provisions had begun somewhat to grow lukewarm, a reminder was given concerning the matter to Pope Eugenius. For this reason, when that universal pope summoned a synod, he took care, among other general decrees, to promulgate provisions that Leo IV later decreed were to be observed in the time of our brother Lothair and our nephew Louis. We believe that these provisions are preserved in the synodal acts and in the archive of this holy Roman Church, and we possess them as a venerable sanction sent from this holy see to our predecessors.

But when, not many years ago, our nephew Louis, emperor of Italy, was stirred up against us by certain persons, letters were sent to us as if with the authority and in the name of this apostolic see. Their inconsistent wording showed that they had not been sent by this holy and most discerning see.

### III.

And since evil people are more often made known by evil deeds than by good ones, an opportunity arose for the priests of the Transalpine regions who had been regularly deposed from the priestly order by their bishops for certain crimes and subjected to penance to begin coming here without the permission or knowledge of their primates and bishops, and to take back letters that do not conform to the rules.

The bishops of that region suppose that these letters were produced not by apostolic command but, as also happens in public administration, through the supposedly pious compassion of various officials on account of the many affairs of complainants.

Therefore, because, as Saint Augustine says (Letter 50, to Count Boniface), “the experience of many illnesses compels us to discover many remedies,” we have set aside, for the sake of brevity, the chapters of our imperial predecessors’ sacred laws that agree with ecclesiastical rules. We have thought it necessary to disclose to your most holy fatherhood and supreme authority how we understand the rules concerning the honor and proper status of bishops, and concerning appeal—if necessity and reason should require it in the case of their deposition—and also concerning the appeal of priests; and we have learned that the rulers of the Transalpine Churches understand them in the same way.

Thus our sound understanding, as we believe it to be, may be confirmed by the authority of this holy see, from which it took the beginning of faith and religion and from which it daily receives increase, thanks to God. And if anything evil is growing in the Lord’s field, may it be cut away by the sickle of your decree. If, through anyone’s negligence or presumption, there has been a departure from the established rules, may the diligence of your authority restore the order.

### IV.

Just as Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God, distinguished the order and dignity of the apostles and the seventy disciples during his bodily presence, as the reading of the holy Gospel clearly shows, so that same one through whom kings reign and lawgivers decree what is just distinguished, through the sacred laws and canons established by his Spirit and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, the order and dignity of bishops—who hold the place of the apostles in the Church—and of priests—who are appointed in the place of the seventy disciples—in administration and honor, just as in the Old Testament he distinguished between the high priests and priests of a lower order.

Therefore all must honor and venerate those sons born in place of fathers—that is, bishops ordained in place of the apostles—because of the dignity of their order and the honor of him who said to the apostles:

> “I will no longer call you servants, but my friends” (John 15:15);

and:

> “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16);

and concerning them:

> “Go, announce to my brothers” (Matt. 28:10).

There are also other things that the text of sacred Scripture proclaims concerning the honor due to them.

### V.

Even if some of them are poor in temporal possessions—and perhaps rich in merit—but are certainly exalted in sacred rank, they must not be despised by anyone possessing either ecclesiastical or secular power, nor in any way placed below the powerful of this world. The Apostle James commands everyone:

> “Do not hold the faith of our glorious Lord Jesus Christ with partiality” (James 2:1),

because those who are richer in worldly terms are not therefore better in God’s judgment.

“Has not God,” he says, “chosen the poor of this world, rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom which he promised to those who love him?” (James 2:5.) And Paul says:

> “God chose the base and despised things of the world,” and so forth (1 Cor. 1:28).

Saint Gregory, in his letter to the emperor Maurice (Book IV, Letter 31), says:

> “May our Lord not quickly become indignant with priests because of earthly power; rather, with excellent discernment, because of the one whose servants they are, let him rule them in such a way that he also renders them their due reverence. For in the divine utterances priests are sometimes called gods and sometimes angels.
>
> “Through Moses, concerning one who is to be brought to an oath, it is said: ‘Bring him before the gods’—that is, before the priests. Again it is written: ‘You shall not revile the gods’ (Exod. 22:8)—that is, the priests. And the prophet says: ‘The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts’ (Mal. 2:7).”

Why, then, should it seem surprising if your piety deigns to honor those whom God himself, granting them honor in his utterance, calls either angels or gods?

Ecclesiastical history also testifies that when written accusations against bishops were presented to the emperor Constantine of pious memory, he burned the documents he had received, saying:

> “You are gods, established by the true God. Go and examine your cases among yourselves, for it is not fitting that we should judge gods.”

In this statement, pious lord, he showed greater humility toward himself than reverence toward them. Before him, pagan rulers had governed the state. They did not know the true God, but worshiped gods of wood and stone; nevertheless, they granted the greatest honor to their priests. Why, then, should it seem surprising if a Christian emperor deigns to honor the priests of the true God, when pagan rulers, as we have said, knew how to honor priests who served gods of wood and stone?

The same most holy, eloquent, discerning, and truly humble man in the sight of God, writing to John, bishop of Syracuse, concerning the bishop of Constantinople, says among other things (Book VII, Letter 64, indiction 11):

> “As for his saying that he wishes to subject himself to the apostolic see, if any fault is found in bishops, I do not know which bishop is not subject to him. But when fault does not demand it, all are equal according to the law of humility.”

### VI.

After Constantine, each of the Christian emperors—our predecessors and forebears—established laws concerning the honor and privilege of bishops.

Therefore, most holy Father, since, as Saint Gelasius says (Letter 10, to Anastasius), “there are two powers by which this world is principally governed, the sacred authority of pontiffs and royal power,” to which appeal may be made and from which no one is permitted to appeal, let us weigh our judgments under the eyes of God, the strict and most equitable judge, who judges without partiality.

Even if there are often among negligent or sluggish brothers matters that ought to be addressed with greater authority, “correction must nevertheless be applied,” as Saint Leo says (Letter 88, to Anastasius), “in such a way that love is always preserved; benevolence should accomplish more toward those being corrected than severity, exhortation more than agitation, and charity more than power.”

Let us honor bishops who remain in their proper status with the reverence due to them, and by showing them the fitting honor that belongs to them, let us offer others an example of reverence toward the priestly order. For if we despise the sacred order in their persons—persons who, like a mirror placed before the eyes of all subject to us, serve as an example to be imitated—we shall be judged by the strict Judge, namely the supreme pontiff and King of kings, for all the faults for which our conduct may, God forbid, have supplied examples of wrongdoing.

As blessed Gregory also thunders terribly in the *Pastoral Rule* (Part I, chapter 5):

> “Those in authority must know that if they ever commit wrongdoing, they are liable to as many deaths as the examples of perdition they transmit to their subjects. Therefore they must guard themselves from fault with all the greater caution because, through the evil things they do, they do not die alone [Col. 0234A] but become liable for the souls of others whom they have destroyed by their evil examples.
>
> “Conversely, for however many they have won for the Lord by word or example, or through correction by those to whom the power of correction has been given—for good things are often imposed upon unwilling people, as the master of the household says to his servant, that is, to the company of those in authority, ‘Go out quickly into the roads and hedges, and compel them to enter, so that my house may be filled’ (Luke 14:23)—they will receive a crown of glory for so many.
>
> “The Apostle bears witness: ‘Whoever converts a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins’ (James 5:20).”

### VII.

Moreover, since there is no person on earth who does good and does not sin, and even those who adhered to heavenly teaching were not without sin, as John says:

> “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8),

and the Apostle James says:

> “We all offend in many things” (James 3:2),

and, as Scripture shows, wickedness was found even among the angels (Job 4:18), if necessity, after careful weighing and examination, compels bishops to be judged by bishops, or priests to be deposed from ecclesiastical rank by bishops, sacred authority has distinguished discretion both in honor and administration and in judgment and appeal.

It has decreed that if the necessity and weight of a lawful and canonical accusation require it, a bishop must be judged by his episcopal judges—those by whom, together with the primate of the province, he could regularly have been ordained according to the Nicene and Antiochene canons and the decrees of the pontiffs of the Roman see. The bishops of that region are to be assembled together with the provincial primate according to the Sardican canons, and the bishop is to be judged canonically by the established number of twelve bishops according to the Carthaginian canons, if more cannot be assembled.

### VIII.

> “And if that accused and judged bishop, after the bishops of the same region have assembled and deposed him from his rank, appeals to the apostolic see, takes refuge with the bishop of the Roman Church, and wishes to be heard by him after judgment, then, according to the Sardican canons (Council of Sardica, canon 7), and the decrees of Innocent to Victricius, of Boniface to the Gallican bishops, and of Leo to Anastasius, those who examined the case must write to the Roman pontiff.
>
> “If he judges that the case ought to be reopened, let it be reopened, and let him appoint judges. But if he determines that the case is such that the proceedings already conducted should not be disturbed, whatever he decrees shall be confirmed.
>
> “If he considers it right that the examination be renewed, let him graciously write to those bishops who are in a neighboring and nearby province, so that they may investigate the matter with complete diligence and decide it according to the truth.
>
> “But if the one who requests that his case be heard again moves the Roman bishop by his petition to send a priest from his own side, it shall be within the bishop’s power to decide what he wishes and what he considers appropriate. If he decrees that men should be sent to judge together with the bishops who are present, possessing the authority of the one by whom they were sent, the matter shall remain within his discretion.
>
> “If, however, he believes that the bishops are sufficient to bring the case to an end, he shall do what he judges by the wisest counsel.
>
> “Meanwhile, no other bishop is to be ordained to the cathedra of the deposed bishop after his appeal until his case has been determined in the judgment of the Roman bishop.”

### IX.

This provision concerning appeal to the apostolic see does not conflict with the sacred and mystical Council of Nicaea, concerning which Pope Leo the Great wrote to Anatolius (Letter 56):

> “That decree of the Nicene canons, established by the truly Holy Spirit, can never be dissolved in any respect. Let no synodal councils flatter themselves because of the size of their assemblies, and let no number of priests, however much greater, dare to compare itself with or place itself above those three hundred and eighteen bishops. The Council of Nicaea was consecrated by so great a privilege from God that, whether ecclesiastical judgments are held by fewer or by more, whatever differs from the constitution of those bishops is entirely devoid of authority.”

Concerning this privilege, blessed Ambrose also says (*On the Faith*, Book I, chapter 9):

> “The three hundred and eighteen bishops did not come together in council through human effort or by any arrangement. Rather, so that the Lord Jesus might prove himself present in their council by the sign of his passion and name, the cross is represented by the three hundred, and the name of Jesus by the eighteen priests.”

Hilary says the same (*On the Synods*, at the end):

> “For me also that very number is holy, in which Abraham, victor over impious kings, is blessed by him who is the pattern of the eternal priesthood.”

And again blessed Pope Leo writes to Anatolius (Letter 56, after the foregoing):

> “Those holy and venerable Fathers who, in the city of Nicaea, after condemning the sacrilegious Arius together with his impiety, established laws of ecclesiastical canons that would remain until the end of the world, live among us throughout the entire world in their constitutions. If anything is presumed anywhere contrary to what they established, it is cancelled without hesitation.”

### X.

That holy and mystical Council prescribes the following (canon 5):

> “Concerning those who are deprived of communion: whether they belong to the clergy or the laity, a canonical sentence pronounced by the bishops throughout each province shall have effect, so that those who are rejected are not received by others. Inquiry must nevertheless be made to ensure that the person does not appear to have been excluded from the congregation through faintheartedness, contentiousness, or any other fault of the bishop.
>
> “Therefore, so that this may be investigated more suitably, it has seemed good that councils be held twice each year in every province, so that when all the bishops of the province are assembled together, such questions may be examined in common. Thus those who have clearly sinned against their own bishop may reasonably be considered excommunicated by all until either the common body or the bishop sees fit to issue a more humane sentence concerning them.”

### XI.

The Sardican canons do not overturn the constitution of this holy synod (chapter 7). They prescribe that the case of a bishop judged in a provincial synod be concluded through the Roman pontiff’s representative or at his discretion, and by the determination or judgment of the bishops who judged him together with the bishops of a neighboring and nearby province, so that, whether the sentence is maintained or changed, there may be a common decision in accordance with the Nicene canons.

Concerning these sacred Nicene canons, the African Council wrote to holy Pope Celestine (chapter 105):

> “They provided most prudently and justly that all cases should be concluded in their own places, where they arose, and that no province should lack the grace of the Holy Spirit, by which equity may be discerned wisely and held most firmly by the priests of Christ.”

### XII.

Blessed Innocent, in his letter to Victricius, bishop of Rouen, explains in one chapter, with skill and clarity, two chapters of the great Council of Nicaea—namely, the chapter concerning those who are deprived of communion [Col. 0236B] from the clergy, and the other concerning the preservation of the privileges of the Churches in each province—as well as the chapter of the Council of Sardica concerning the appeal of bishops to the apostolic see. He says (Innocent, Letter 1):

> “If any cases or disputes arise among clerics, whether of higher or lower rank, it has been decided that, according to the Council of Nicaea, the judgment must be concluded after all the bishops of the same province have assembled. No one may, without prejudice to the Roman Church—for reverence toward it must be preserved in every case—abandon those priests who, by divine will, govern the Church of God in that province and hasten to other provinces.
>
> “If anyone should presume to do so, let him be judged by all to have been removed from the clerical office and guilty of injury. But if more serious cases arise, they are to be referred to the apostolic see after episcopal judgment, as the synod has established and pious custom requires.”

When he says that, according to the Council of Nicaea, judgment concerning cases that have arisen must be concluded after the bishops of the same province have assembled, he explains the chapter of the Council of Nicaea concerning excommunicated persons. When he prohibits anyone of the ecclesiastical order from hastening to other provinces, he explains another chapter of the Council of Nicaea, which commands that each province preserve the privileges of its own Churches—yet without prejudice to the Roman Church.

Thus, if more serious cases arise, one of which is the appeal of a judged bishop, they are to be referred to the apostolic see, as the synod—indeed, the Council of Sardica—has established and ancient custom requires, after episcopal judgment. This means that either, according to the aforementioned seventh chapter of the Council of Sardica, the case of the appealing bishop is to be settled in the province where it arose, or the judgment of the provincial bishops is to be confirmed by the authority of the apostolic see according to the decrees of Boniface, and, as Leo wrote, strengthened by the sentence of that same see.

Since Saint Innocent invoked not the Nicene but the Sardican synod as authority for the appeal of a bishop to the apostolic see, anyone who reads both synods understands this clearly.

### XIII.

The sacred laws and rules command that priests and other clerics of lower rank be accused nowhere except before their own bishops. Their case must be heard by those bishops, as the canons of the province of Africa decree, and they must be judged with the priests or clerics of their own parish, as Saint Gregory established.

If some of them should complain about the judgments of their own bishops, and it becomes necessary to determine to whom they may appeal, the appeal of priests and deacons to neighboring and nearby bishops is set out in the seventeenth chapter of the Council of Sardica, in the memorandum sent by Pope Zosimus through Bishop Faustinus and the priests Philip and Asellus to the Council of Carthage. It reads as follows.

Bishop Hosius said (chapter 17):

> “I must not remain silent about what still troubles me. If some bishop, perhaps being angry—although he ought not to be—should quickly and harshly become enraged against his priest or deacon and wish to expel him from the Church, provision must be made lest an innocent man be condemned or lose communion.
>
> “Therefore, let the one who has been rejected have the power to appeal to the neighboring bishops, so that his case may be heard and examined with greater care; for it is not right to deny a hearing to one who asks for it.
>
> “Let the bishop who rejected him, whether justly or unjustly, patiently accept the examination of the case, so that his sentence may either be approved by many or corrected.
>
> “Nevertheless, before everything has been carefully and faithfully examined, no one may presume, before the investigation, to restore to communion the man who had been separated from communion.
>
> “If those who assemble to hear the case perceive clerical arrogance and pride—for it is not fitting that a bishop should suffer injury or insult—let them correct the clerics with harsher words, so that they obey the bishop who gives an honorable command.
>
> “For just as the bishop ought to show his clerics a sincere love of charity, so in turn the ministers ought to show their bishop unstained obedience.”

## XIV

Nor does this chapter of the Council of Sardica appear to dissent from the chapter of the Council of Nicaea, which decreed more explicitly and clearly than the Council of Sardica concerning those who are deprived of communion by their own bishop, as we set out above, and concerning the privileges of the individual metropolitans, saying (canon 6):

> “Let the ancient custom be observed throughout Egypt, Libya, and the Pentapolis, so that the bishop of Alexandria shall have authority over all these, since a similar custom also belongs to the bishop of the city of Rome. Likewise, in Antioch and in the other provinces, let the privileges belonging to their Churches be preserved.”

The Synod of Antioch explains this, saying (canon 9):

> “It is fitting that the bishops of each region should know that the metropolitan bishop has charge of the whole province. Therefore all who appear to have business should come from every direction to the metropolis.”

And the Council of Constantinople, saying (canon 1):

> “Let the synod of each province administer the matters belonging to that province, as it is established that the Council of Nicaea decreed.”

## XV

Hence Innocent wrote to Alexander, bishop of Antioch (letter 30):

> “Reviewing the authority of the Synod of Nicaea, which expresses the one mind of all priests throughout the world, we recognize that it judged it necessary for all the faithful—indeed, I should say, for all priests—to observe what it established concerning the Church of Antioch: that this Church was constituted over the aforesaid diocese, not over any other province.”

And Pope Boniface wrote to Hilary of Narbonne (letter 111):

> “The constitution of the Synod of Nicaea is unknown to no one. It commands—and let us state its very words—that each metropolitan is to possess jurisdiction in his own province, and that no one is to have two provinces subject to him. Since it is impossible to believe otherwise, they judged, under the prompting of the Holy Spirit, that this should be observed. We say this so that Your Charity may understand how carefully we observe the precepts of the canons: our own constitution likewise decrees that each province must always await the direction of its metropolitan in all matters.”

In agreement with this, Celestine writes (letter 11, concerning Vienne and Narbonne):

> “According to the decrees of the canons, let each province be content with its own metropolitan, as the constitution sent by our predecessor to the bishop of Narbonne establishes. No opportunity for usurpation should be granted to any priest by injuring another. Let each person be content with the boundaries granted to him; let no one presume anything in another’s province.”

And Leo writes to Bishop Maximus (letter 66):

> “Although the merits of prelates are sometimes different, the rights of the sees nevertheless remain.”

[Col. 0238C]

## XVI

The Council of Antioch, favorably commended by the great Council of Chalcedon in its twelfth session, following the decrees of the Council of Nicaea, says (canon 6):

> “If anyone has been deprived of communion by his own bishop, let him not be received by others before he has been reconciled with his own bishop, or, having come to the synod assembled for this purpose, has made satisfaction on his own behalf and persuaded the council to accept another sentence. Let this definition also remain in force concerning laymen, presbyters, deacons, and all who are shown to be subject to a rule.”

Speaking about councils in chapter 20, it says:

> “Let presbyters, deacons, and all who consider themselves injured be present at the councils themselves, and let them submit to the examination of the synod. Let no one be permitted to hold councils privately, except those to whom metropolitan rights appear to have been entrusted.”

And in chapter 16:

> “That council is complete at which the metropolitan bishop has been present.”

## XVII

The sacred Carthaginian canons clearly show in chapter 20 and chapter 28 by whom, and in what manner, presbyters or deacons who appeal are to be judged. As to where a case should be heard between accusers and accused, the Council of Carthage established the following (canon 30):

> “Let the accused person or the accuser choose for himself a place near the place from which the accused comes, so that it will not be difficult to produce witnesses and the case may be concluded there.”

Hence the laws say:

> “The investigation of crimes must be conducted where the crime was committed. For elsewhere the accused party in a criminal case is forbidden to be heard.”

And again:

> “If anyone brings a charge against an adversary, whether by a claim for recovery or by an accusation of crime, let the province in which the person charged resides exercise its jurisdiction, and let him not suppose that his adversary may be dragged elsewhere or to a more distant place.”

If the person charged has considered the judge suspect, he is permitted to appeal—ecclesiastical persons to neighboring bishops, as the canons of Sardica and Carthage, as we have stated, decreed, or to provincial councils, as the sacred canons of Nicaea and Antioch established, and as the African Council showed in its letter to Pope Celestine (chapter 105):

> “It is granted to everyone, if he has been offended by the judgment of those who have heard the case, to appeal to the council of his province, or even to a universal council. Unless perhaps someone believes that God can inspire justice in the examination of any single person, while denying it to innumerable priests gathered in council; or how will that overseas judgment itself—which is the same as a transalpine judgment—be valid, when the necessary persons among the witnesses cannot be brought to it, whether because of their sex, the weakness of old age, or many other obstacles that may arise?”

## XVIII

A regular appeal cannot be made from judges—whether those whom the primates appoint according to the African canons, or those whom the primates themselves, by common agreement, delegate from among their neighbors—in order to bring a case to an end elsewhere.

Saint Gregory, in his letter to the Gallican bishops (Book XI, letter 110), says:

> “We do not leave unaddressed, in this part of our concern, what the foresight of the Fathers established for the sake of usefulness concerning the holding of councils throughout the parishes. Therefore, so that there may be no disagreement among brothers and no fuel for discord between superiors and subjects, the priests must come together as one, so that disputes concerning matters that arise may be settled and there may be a salutary exchange concerning ecclesiastical observance. Thus, while past matters are corrected through this process and a rule for the future is adopted, the almighty Lord may everywhere be praised in the concord of the brothers. Know that his presence is with you if you observe these things, for it is written: ‘Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them’ (Matthew 18). If he deigns to be present where two or three are gathered, how much less will he be absent where more priests have assembled?

> “It is indeed not unknown that the rules have established that a council of the Fathers should be held twice a year. But lest some necessity prevent this from being fulfilled, we nevertheless decree that it be assembled once, without any excuse, so that, while the council is awaited, nothing evil and nothing unlawful may be presumed. For often, even if not out of love of justice, fear of examination will nevertheless restrain a person from doing what everyone knows may incur the displeasure of judgment.”

## XIX

These provisions, concerning the appeal of bishops from the churches of Transalpine regions to this apostolic see, and concerning the appeal of presbyters and deacons—if they should complain about the judgments of their bishops—to the synods of their fellow provincials, as well as concerning their regular adjudication in those same synods, have been observed by the Transalpine Churches and their rulers from the apostolic see, from times reaching back beyond the longest span of human memory down to our own days; they were followed and carried out by their predecessors and earlier forebears.

But if these provisions have not been observed by them, nor followed and carried out by them, it is of no benefit for them, according to the sacred canons and the decrees of the Roman pontiffs’ see, to hold the synods of their bishops’ fellow provincials concerning presbyters accused of manifest crimes. Rather, each presbyter will freely do whatever he wishes, and, if he is reproved for it, he will come to Rome.

## XX

Since the bishops of the Transalpine regions cannot regularly send messengers for each presbyter who has been judged, nor write out the records of the proceedings, nor bring here the necessary witnesses—whether because of their sex, the weakness of old age, or many other impediments—anyone who lies will be able confidently to assert his innocence, since there will be no one able to refute his falsehoods.

Therefore, as we stated above, the legislators and framers of the canons wisely and justly saw that every case should be concluded in the places where it arose, judged with the utmost discretion through explicit regular judgments, and preserved after judgment.

This applies especially to the introduction of women in violation of the rules. For this reason, presbyters regularly judged by the bishops of the Transalpine regions come to this holy Roman see without the knowledge of their bishops, bring here letters contradicting their judgments, and command them—or their fellow ministers—to come to this see to lodge complaints against them. We read that nothing of this kind was decreed by any ancient law or rule of the Fathers.

## XXI

We believe that these letters, being contrary to the sacred rules, as we mentioned in the preface to this little work, were not sent with apostolic authority but were compiled through the cunning of various persons. For the apostolic see cannot be contrary or divergent from itself.

Concerning this, Pope Gelasius says (letter 11 to Dardanus):

> “We are confident that no one who is now truly a Christian is unaware that, of all the sees, the first ought most diligently to carry out the constitution of every council approved by the assent of the universal Church. That first see both confirms each council by its authority and guards it through continuous moderation, on account of its primacy, which the blessed apostle Peter received by the Lord’s word and which the Church, following thereafter, has both always held and continues to hold.”

And again (letter 1):

> “Since we desire that nothing rash be permitted to us against the reverence due to salutary rules, and since, with the Lord’s favor, the apostolic see piously and devoutly strives to preserve what has been established by the canons of the Fathers, it is most unworthy for any bishop or member of a subordinate order to reject this observance, which he sees the see of blessed Peter both follow and teach. It is entirely fitting that the whole body of the Church should agree in this observance, which it sees flourishing where the Lord established the primacy of the whole Church.”

It may happen that those who are in the neighboring parishes of this holy Roman Church, and who, according to the sacred rules, usually come here for the laying on of hands and for synods, may themselves come together for a complaint against their presbyters before the aforesaid examination, as the sacred canons and laws command. They should be invited to come to the primate of each province, to whom those who appear to have business should assemble, or to the synod, so that those who consider themselves injured may be heard in a place where it will not be difficult to produce witnesses.

For the Transalpine peoples, however, and for others who live in similarly distant regions, the apostolic see and the promulgators of the sacred canons, with the Holy Spirit speaking through them, have most carefully established what is possible for each province, consistent with authority, and conducive to the peace of the Church, to be maintained and carried out.

[Col. 0241B]

## XXII

We also read—although very rarely—that the apostolic see has commanded certain persons from more distant parishes of the special diocese of the Roman pontiff, to whose care the universal Church belongs, to be summoned on account of obstinate disputes.

But concerning the Transalpine regions, whose decreed privileges must be preserved, we do not read that anything of this kind was commanded by the apostolic see with regard to appeals by presbyters and deacons.

Nevertheless, concerning ecclesiastical privileges, we read in the letters of blessed Gregory to Dominicus, bishop of Carthage (Book XI, letter 39):

> “Let Your Fraternity retain this without hesitation: just as we defend our own rights, so we preserve the rights belonging to each individual Church. By Christ’s grace, I do not grant to anyone more than he deserves, nor, driven by ambition, will I take away from anyone what belongs to him by right. Rather, I desire to honor my brothers in every way, and I strive to advance them in honor, provided that there is nothing that one may lawfully oppose to another.”

And elsewhere he says the same in this connection (Book XI, letter 37):

> “As for what you say—that what was handed down and preserved by my predecessors ought to be maintained in your time—far be it from me to violate in any Church the statutes of my elder fellow priests. I do myself an injury if I disturb the rights of my brothers.”

## XXIII

Finally, besides the ancient constitutions of the rules and laws, we have at hand the synodal chapters decreed by the apostolic pontiffs: by Eugene, in the thirteenth year of the reign of our lord and father Louis; in the tenth year of the reign of our brother Lothar, in the month of November; by Leo IV, in the thirty-seventh year of Lothar; and in the fifth year of our nephew Louis, in the month of December.

These decrees command:

> “If any priest—that is, a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or even subdeacon—is suspected of the crime of fornication with any woman, and, after a first, second, and third admonition by the metropolitan, another bishop, or the person to whom he appears subject, is found talking with her or associating with her in any manner, he is to be judged canonically.”

Therefore every bishop must attend to such a matter carefully and diligently, lest the Church of Christ be defiled by its own ministers. Since he is not permitted to have a wife of his own, he must especially abstain from every woman.

And again:

> “If a priest, or anyone else advanced into an ecclesiastical order, is found in a crime for which he ought to be removed, after deposition he is to be placed, through the bishop’s provision, in a suitable location, where he may mourn his sins and commit them no further.”

Thus the great Pope Leo, long before this constitution, decreed by the authority of sacred Scripture to Hilary of Narbonne (letter 95, to Rusticus of Narbonne):

> “Let fallen presbyters or deacons seek private withdrawal in order to obtain the mercy of God, so that, if their satisfaction is worthy, it may also be fruitful.”

## XXIV

Since these matters stand thus, your pontifical authority and our imperial power must not give merely superficial attention to what our predecessors established concerning the observance of sacred laws and holy rules. From their many enactments we have judged it appropriate to set forth here a few in number, though not few in weight.

Concerning the laws, Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius decreed, saying (Book II of the Theodosian Code, *On the Constitutions of Princes*):

> “We do not permit anyone either to be ignorant of the constitutions of our serenity, considered after long deliberation, or to disregard them.”
>
> **Interpretation:** “No one may be ignorant of the laws or despise what has been established.”

Saint Celestine says something similar concerning the sacred canons (letter 3):

> “No priest may be permitted to be ignorant of his canons, or to do anything that could conflict with the rules of the Fathers. For what matter worthy of preservation will remain among us if the norm of the decretal constitutions is broken at the discretion of some people and permission is granted to the populace?”

For, as Pope Hilary says (letter 11, to Leontius):

> “One sins no less against the sanctions of the sacred traditions than one rushes into an affront to the Lord himself, when the expectation of the fruit of our ministry is placed not in the breadth of territories but in the acquisition of souls.”

And again, concerning the laws of the aforesaid emperors (Book III of the Theodosian Code, same title):

> “All constitutions do not bring accusation against the past, but impose a rule upon the future.”
>
> **Interpretation:** “All laws do not condemn what was done in an earlier time, but establish what must be observed in the future.”

## XXV

Hence Pope Symmachus writes (letter 1, to Aeonius):

> “Since, in the likeness of the Trinity, whose power is one and indivisible, the priesthood is one through different bishops, how is it fitting for the statutes of earlier persons to be violated by those who come later? Moreover, if such a variety of judgments should arise, we believe that it would affect the holy Catholic religion itself, whose entire authority is undermined unless all things once regularly established by the priests of the Lord remain perpetual.

> “This could happen in another way if a successor did not grant firmness to the acts of his predecessor, and, by strengthening what has been done, make his own acts valid. For how great would be the reverence shown to the vicars of the blessed apostle Peter if the commands they issue in the priesthood were dissolved when those very men passed away?”

Let us therefore preserve these things in our own time, all the more gratefully because they will be more advantageous both to the Church and to the empire; and, by preserving what has been done legally and regularly, let us make valid what we ourselves have done legally and regularly.

## XXVI

We also consider it necessary to bring to your supreme authority the matter of restraining the inconsiderateness of certain bishops, so that, by instructing others through a general decree, you may make them cautious.

Their judgments ought to be mature and carefully weighed; therefore they must not be hasty in pronouncing sentences, nor act easily or indiscriminately, nor proceed in any other way than according to the path of the sacred Scriptures, the tradition of the Fathers, and manifest offenses. They must not, because of personal injuries, movements of their own spirit, or anger, separate anyone from communion in the body and blood of the Lord our God Jesus Christ, in which, after the one baptism, the reconciliation and supreme salvation of humankind especially consist.

For, as Saint Gregory says, “the anger of a priest” (Homily 17 on the Gospels):

> “Must in no way be hasty and disturbed, but should rather be feared because of the gravity of his counsel. Nor should they rashly judge matters not investigated, or believe statements made casually without proof. They should weigh the deeds of our Creator, to whom all things are naked and open; yet, as sacred history teaches, he did not wish to judge the evils of Sodom beforehand, but first examined them, instructing us not to presume to believe human evils before we have proved them.”

## XXVII

Let the teachings of the holy pontiffs of the Roman see—Leo and Gregory—therefore guide the pronouncement of a judicial sentence.

Leo says (Sermon 3, on the anniversary of his assumption):

> “Christ says to the most blessed Peter: ‘I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven.’ The right of this power certainly passed also to the other apostles, and the constitution of this decree came to all the rulers of the Church. Yet it is not without reason that what is announced to all is entrusted to one alone. For this is believed to have been given uniquely to Peter because Peter’s form is placed before all the rulers of the Church.

> “Peter’s privilege therefore remains wherever judgment is rendered according to his equity. Neither excessive severity nor excessive leniency exists where nothing is bound and nothing is loosed except what blessed Peter has bound or loosed.”

From this it is clearly understood, upon careful consideration, that Peter’s privilege is not present in judging when judgment is not rendered according to his equity. It is therefore prejudice, not judgment, because it has not been pronounced according to right—that is, according to the law of justice.

Saint Gregory likewise says (Homily 26 on Ezekiel):

> “It often happens that one who does not know how to govern his own life becomes a judge of another’s life, either condemning the undeserving or, while himself bound, loosing others, since he follows the impulses of his own will rather than the merits of the cases. Thus he deprives himself of the power of binding and loosing, because he exercises it according to his own desires and not according to the conduct of his subjects.

> “Those who follow either their own hatred or their own favor in the cases of their subjects cannot judge their subjects worthily. Therefore it is rightly said through the prophet: ‘They put to death souls that should not die, and they kept alive souls that should not live’ (Ezekiel 13). He puts to death one who should not die when he condemns the righteous; and he tries to give life to one who will not live when he attempts to absolve the guilty from punishment. The cases must therefore be weighed, and only then must the power of binding and loosing be exercised.”

## XXVIII

This most blessed teacher, filled with the Holy Spirit, shows repeatedly in his writings that a bishop who does not follow the judgment of a judge in binding and loosing deprives himself not only of the power of binding and loosing but also of the kingdom of God, if he pronounces the curse of binding not according to a judicial decision of justice but out of the spite of vengeance, as Paul bears witness when he says: “Nor will revilers possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6).

Sacred Scripture, however, mentions a curse in two ways: one that it approves and another that it condemns. A curse is pronounced in one manner by the judgment of justice and in another by the spite of vengeance. Holy men, when they pronounce a sentence of the curse of excommunication in binding someone, do not allow it to burst forth from a desire for spiteful retaliation, but from an examination of justice.

Within themselves they perceive the subtle judgment of God, and they recognize that the evils arising outwardly must be struck by the curse of binding through excommunication. They do not sin in that curse of binding and excommunication because they do not depart from the inward judgment.

Against the curse of excommunication produced by the spite of vengeance, we are warned by the voice of the preaching Paul, who says: “Bless, and do not curse” (Romans 12:14), because “revilers will not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6:10).

[Col. 0244C]

For if anyone, perhaps not out of malice but through carelessness of speech, hurls a word of cursing at his neighbor, then before the strict Judge, from whom an account of every idle word is required on the day of judgment, that utterance is condemnable if it is not free from malice, and it is punishable if it lacks the goodness of usefulness.

One must therefore consider with the greatest seriousness how severe a punishment should be imposed upon an excommunication hurled by a bishop against his neighbor through unjust binding—an excommunication that ought rather to be called a curse—since the bishop’s speech is always commanded to be seasoned with salt, that is, with wisdom (Colossians 4:6).

## XXIX

Let us therefore follow the rulers of the holy Church, whose backs are anvils beneath the minds of sinful people, as the Psalmist says: “Sinners forged upon my back” (Psalm 128:3), concerning separation from communion and reconciliation in the sacraments of Christ: the sacred Council of Nicaea; the canons of the province of Africa; the decrees of Siricius, Innocent, and Leo; and Leo’s own letter to Theodore, bishop of Fréjus (letter 59).

Let them not deprive of communion in the body and blood of Christ anyone whom they have deprived of ecclesiastical rank because of manifestly serious offenses, just as the canons have prescribed. For this is the straight way, as Scripture says, so that the upright may walk in it and fools may not go astray in it (Isaiah 35:8).

As for those who excommunicate unjustly, and those who are unjustly excommunicated, your wisdom cannot be unaware of what the law of Justinian also decrees.

# LETTER XXXIII. TO THE BISHOPS OF THE DIOCESE OF RHEIMS AND TO ALL RULERS AND FAITHFUL OF THE CHURCH

Against Odacrus, whose excommunication it announces.
