*(From the Acts of the provincial Church of Rheims.)*

[Col. 0245A]

HINCMAR, bishop and servant of the people of God, together with our venerable fellow bishops of the diocese of Rheims, to all rulers and faithful of the holy Church to whose knowledge the following matters may come:

So that, knowing by whom, in what manner, how often, and for what offenses Odacrus—the invader of the Church of Beauvais, our metropolitan’s suffragan—has been excommunicated, they may guard themselves against his harmful communion, lest, as it is written, those who touch pitch be defiled by it, and lest a diseased sheep, unless separated as quickly as possible from the healthy flock, infect many with its disease.

## I

Long before, it was foretold by God through the Psalmist: “I will measure out the valley of the tents” (Psalm 107). This means, as Catholic teachers explain, the whole world, which is called the valley of tents because it is the dwelling place of bodies. We read that it was measured even before Christ shone upon the world through the Incarnation, and we possess that measurement.

Afterward, as he himself likewise commanded—“Distribute his houses” (Psalm 47)—we recognize the houses of the universal Church, spread throughout the whole world and divided among the parishes entrusted with their care; and we possess this division as well.

Therefore the sacred canons, created by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, decree, saying (Council of Antioch, A.D. 341, canon 9):

> “It is fitting that the bishops of each region should know that the metropolitan bishop has charge of the whole province,”

and the other provisions that follow there.

And Saint Pope Boniface, explaining the sixth chapter of the mystical Synod of Nicaea, through which the Holy Spirit spoke, says:

> “Each province must always await the direction of its metropolitan in all matters.”

## II

For us human beings and for our salvation, the mediator between God and humanity, the man Christ Jesus, said to humanity:

> “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matthew 15),

and again he says:

> “I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice, and there will be one flock and one shepherd” (John 10).

He was designating the holy Church, formed from circumcision and uncircumcision under the one true shepherd, who laid down his life for his sheep, and united in him as the cornerstone.

Concerning the fold of this holy Church, he likewise says:

> “Whoever does not enter the sheepfold through the gate, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber” (John 10).

The sacred canons plainly show how and in what order a person ought to approach and be advanced to the guardianship of this holy fold, that is, to the governance of the holy Church.

Namely, with the assistance of an appointed intermediary, a bishop is to be elected for a church deprived of its bishop, by the clergy and the people according to the apostolic and canonical form. The future bishop must be unable to oppose the sacred canons. Then, with the decree confirmed by the hands of all, he is to be brought, through the intermediary himself, to the metropolitan and the other provincial bishops for ordination.

Thus, by the common, reasonable decree of all, approved according to ecclesiastical rule, he is to be ordained in accordance with the fourth and sixth chapters of the mystical Synod of Nicaea and the twenty-fourth chapter of the Council of Antioch, just as Saint Gregory repeatedly decrees in his register.

Odacrus, however, the invader of the widowed Church of Beauvais through foreign powers, despised and trampled upon these sacred canons, treating them as nothing. For more than a year now he has usurped the church, held captive by his tyrannical devastation, contrary to the great Council of Chalcedon of six hundred and thirty or more bishops, which commands that the ordinations of bishops be celebrated within three months (Council of Chalcedon, canon 25).

He neither reverenced divine judgment nor considered the magnitude of the danger: on the immediately preceding day of the Lord’s Supper, many people, because of public crimes, were placed in public penance by Bishop Odo—a matter that may be done only by a bishop—and remained mourning without reconciliation and holy communion.

How many were left without canonical baptism and episcopal confirmation? How many children of rural parishes may have perished without baptism during so long a period while the presbyters of those parishes were dead? How many men and women departed from this world without reconciliation, the anointing with holy oil, and holy communion, and without the solemn commendation of their souls through prayers?

Against his prolonged usurpation, beyond the period established by the aforesaid great council, the saints of God—through whom the Holy Spirit decreed what was defined there and who now reign with Christ in heaven—cry out terribly. The holy synod decreed that those who dared, after the definition of this great and universal synod, to commit any of the prohibited acts must withdraw from their own rank.

Saint Gregory, writing to the Gallican bishops concerning such an impostor (Book VII, letter 110), says:

> “Since he attends to the title and not the office, he desires vainly not to be a priest but merely to be called one. If this is permitted, what else is being done by it except that there is no examination of conduct, no concern for morals, and no investigation of life? If this matter is weighed by a correct and balanced examination, then, while he wickedly hastens to seize a position of usefulness for empty glory, he is for that very reason unworthy, because he seeks the honor.
>
> “Just as one who, though invited, refuses, and when sought, withdraws, ought to be brought to the sacred altars, so one who seeks office of his own accord or thrusts himself forward importunately must unquestionably be rejected. For one who strives in this way to climb to higher things does nothing except diminish by growing and descend inwardly into the depths while ascending outwardly.”

## III

The same holy and great council decreed (Council of Chalcedon, canon 25):

> “Let the revenues of a church deprived of its bishop be preserved intact by the steward of that church.”

The aforesaid invader Odacrus dared to usurp these revenues without any reverence for divine law.

Therefore, together with other presumptuous persons of this kind, he is struck down by the same holy and great council. It decreed that those who dared, after the definition of this great and universal synod, to commit any of the prohibited acts must withdraw from their own rank.

IV. Odacrus, abandoning ecclesiastical judgment and the definition of the sacred canons, and invading by secular power the goods and properties of the Church of Beauvais—which according to the sacred rules are called offerings, because they are offered to the Lord, and are the vows of the faithful, the prices of sins, and the patrimonies of the poor—cast upon himself the sentence of condemnation. For, as Pope Saint Leo defined together with the Roman synod (Epistle 96):

> “Whoever, being placed under a rule, abandons ecclesiastical judgment, flees to the protection of laymen, seeks their judgments, and, passing over the priest of his own church, comes to the adjudication of secular men, is ordered to be expelled from the sacred thresholds—that is, from the entrances of the church—and to be barred from the heavenly altar—that is, to be separated from the body and blood of Christ.”

And the sacred canons define (Council of Antioch, canon 2):

> “If anyone subject to the rule of the Church approaches the emperor without the counsel and letters of the bishops of the province, and especially of the metropolitan, he ought to be rejected and cast out, not only from communion but also from the honor of which he appears to be a participant.”

And Pope Saint Hilary says in his decrees:

> “One transgresses no less against the sanctions of the sacred traditions than one rushes into an injury against the Lord himself.”

Therefore, as a schismatic, severing himself from the unity of the Church through contempt for the sacred canons—which were established by the Holy Spirit and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world—although perhaps he believes as Catholics do, with the same worship and the same rite, he nevertheless remains in the evil division of condemnation through his greed.

How great an evil the division of schism is, Saint Augustine demonstrates from the sacred Scriptures in his book *On Baptism*, as follows:

> “Let us not bring deceitful scales on which we weigh what we wish, and as we wish, saying according to our own judgment, ‘This is heavy; this is light.’ Rather, let us bring the divine scale from the holy Scriptures, as from the Lord’s treasuries, and on it weigh what is heavier—or rather, let us not weigh it ourselves, but recognize what has been weighed by the Lord. At that time, when the Lord showed through recent examples of punishment that former offenses were to be avoided, an idol was made and worshipped, a prophetic book was burned in the wrath of a contemptuous king, and schism was attempted: idolatry was punished by the sword, the burning of the book by slaughter in war and foreign captivity, and schism by the opening of the earth, its authors being buried alive and the rest consumed by heavenly fire. Who, then, would doubt that the deed more severely punished was the more wicked?”

If we carefully consider these three grave offenses, which were not punished lightly, in the authority of the holy Scriptures, we find them in this tyrannical invasion by Odacrus of the church left without a pastor. For the Apostle says: “Avarice, which is the service of idols” (Colossians 3). And blessed Gregory, speaking of the Lord’s temptation in a homily on the Gospel, and invoking another saying of the aforementioned Apostle, shows that avarice concerns not only money but also elevation.

Odacrus, the invader of the church left without a pastor, because according to the path of the sacred canons he did not deserve, under God’s judgment, to attain the advancement of episcopal rank so as to possess the goods and properties of that church, first obtained the goods and property of the vacant church through secular power, so that by some sort of leap he might reach the height of episcopal title; and he desired, not to be a priest, but merely to be called one in vain. [Col. 0248B]

He did not consider that the offices of authority were so distinguished by Christ himself, the supreme pontiff and King of kings, that spiritual action should remain separate from carnal incursions; that those serving God should by no means entangle themselves in secular affairs; and, conversely, that those entangled in secular business should not appear to preside over divine matters.

Secular men were to submit to the judgment of priests, not priests to bend them to their will; priests were to examine the judgments of secular men, whereas secular men were not to trouble the judgments of priests. The divinely inspired writings plainly demonstrate this, and the great Emperor Constantine showed it at the Council of Nicaea by submitting himself to their judgments.

Since these things are so, Odacrus is shown to be an idolater through his avarice for elevation and possession, in his invasion of the vacant church. Through Moses it is said of the Lord: “In his right hand was a fiery law” (Deuteronomy 33). Gregory says:

> “On the left are the reprobate, who are also to be placed on the left; the elect, however, are called the right hand of God. Therefore, in the right hand of God there is a fiery law, because the elect do not hear the heavenly commandments with a cold heart, but burn toward them with the flames of inward love.”

And the Apostle says: “Our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12); and the Lord says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke 12). The Lord casts fire upon the earth when he sets aflame the hearts of carnal people, breathed upon by the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit, therefore, is fire.

And the sacred canons, as we read, were established by the Holy Spirit. Odacrus, inflamed by the torches of his greed, when he seized the church lacking a pastor not through spiritual ecclesiastical tradition but through the carnal power of the world, attempted, so far as lay in him, to extinguish the Holy Spirit by whom the canons were established, while Scripture cries out: “Do not extinguish the Spirit” (1 Thessalonians 5). By his contrivance he also attempted, as though by fire, to burn away the authority of the sacred canons, so that it would not remain powerful in his church.

Since he has been excommunicated from the unity of the Catholic Church because of his offenses—as we have shown and shall further show—and since he does not follow the sacred canons consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, as is made clear by the sacred judgments written above, he cannot be denied to be a schismatic, as Saint Augustine demonstrates in his exposition of the Gospel according to John:

> “We possess the Holy Spirit if we love the Church; and we love it if we remain in its structure and charity.”

And in the letter of the council to the Donatists:

> “Whoever has been separated from the Catholic Church, however commendably he may think he lives, will not have life because of this one crime: that he has been severed from the unity of Christ; rather, the wrath of God remains upon him. But whoever has lived well in this Church is not harmed by the sins of others, for ‘each person will bear his own burden in it’ (Galatians 5), as the Apostle says. And whoever eats the body of Christ unworthily in it ‘eats and drinks judgment upon himself’ (1 Corinthians 11). When he says ‘eats judgment upon himself,’ he sufficiently shows that he does not eat judgment upon another but upon himself, because the communion of the wicked does not defile anyone through participation in the sacraments, but through consent to their deeds. For if someone does not consent to them in their evil deeds, the wicked person bears his own cause and his own person; he does not prejudice another whom he does not have as a partner in the consent to an evil work or in the crime.”

Those who, from whatever station or order, favor his schism should attend to and weigh the definition of the Apostolic See, which it inserted into its decrees:

> “Whoever assents to the leader of a schism cannot be denied to be a schismatic. Even if all the priests and the whole world should assent, condemnation envelops those who consent; their agreement does not absolve them from transgression. For the crime is not diminished but increased when what was private becomes general. God showed this in the case of all humanity, when he destroyed the sinful world by a universal flood.”

Yet this man, as his supporters boast and his accomplices in his presumption applaud him, does not set God before his eyes. He persuades himself that he may hold and usurp the goods and properties of the church that he invaded, even if he should be unable to attain the episcopal title. To increase his condemnation, they take examples from certain churches that remained vacant for a long time under certain rulers, believing that their own conduct is fortified, as blessed Gregory shows, by something like hides taken from the dead, while they defend their wickedness by the wickedness of others.

Because they observe that such things have occurred, they think that they may licitly do them; yet it is plainly shown that this is schism, contrary to ecclesiastical tradition and the constitution of the sacred canons. Saint Gregory rebukes this in a homily on the Gospel, saying:

> “There are some who, because they love earthly substance more than the sheep, deservedly lose the name of shepherd, since they feed the Lord’s sheep not out of inward love but for temporal wages. For he is a hireling who holds the place of a shepherd but does not seek the profits of souls; he longs for earthly advantages, rejoices in the honor of pre-eminence, feeds on temporal gains, delights in the reverence shown him by men, and, because he labors in government, finds here what he seeks, while remaining forever alien from the inheritance of the flock.”

V. Since schism and heresy are related—as the solemn prayers of the universal Church on Good Friday also openly demonstrate—we shall endeavor, with truth consenting, to show that he is not free from the condemnation of the Simoniac heresy.

The Lord says in the Gospel concerning the bestowal of sacred orders: “You received without payment; give without payment” (Matthew 10). Blessed Gregory says:

> “He knew in advance that some would turn this very gift of the Spirit they had received toward commercial use, and divert the signs of miracles to the service of avarice. Thus Simon Magus, seeing miracles performed through the laying on of hands, wished to obtain the gift of the Holy Spirit with money, evidently so that he might sell at a worse price what he had wrongly purchased. Therefore the prophet aptly described the righteous man when he said: ‘He who shakes his hands free from every gift’ (Isaiah 33). For he does not say ‘he who shakes his hands free from a gift,’ but added ‘from every gift,’ because one kind of gift comes from service, another from the hand, and another from the tongue. A gift from service is undue submission; a gift from the hand is money; a gift from the tongue is favor. Therefore, he who confers sacred orders shakes his hands free from every gift when, in divine matters, he seeks not only no money but also no human favor.”

For this reason the Lord drives sellers and buyers from the temple, condemning either those who confer the laying on of hands for a payment or those who strive to buy the gift of the Spirit. The sellers in the temple are those who grant for a price what is lawfully due to certain people. The buyers in the temple are those who purchase sin by giving a reward to their patrons.

This is why the sacred canons condemn the Simoniac heresy and order that those who seek a price for conferring orders be deprived of the priesthood. And since the Simoniac heresy first arose against the holy Church, why should it not be apparent that the one whom he advances by ordaining him for a price is thereby made a heretic? For the sacred canons irrefragably condemn those who ordain and those who are ordained for a payment, as well as the intermediaries, as the reader may find in the second chapter of the great Council of Chalcedon.

We have learned, not from uncertain report, that the aforementioned Odacrus offered not only money but also property through persons who were not unknown, in order to receive episcopal rank. And Saint Augustine says in his book *On the Usefulness of Believing*:

> “He is a heretic who, for the sake of some temporal advantage, and especially for the sake of glory, authority, or pre-eminence, either generates or follows false and novel opinions. But he who believes such a man is a person deceived by a certain semblance of piety.”

VI. In the privilege of the Church of Beauvais, we, the bishops of four provinces—namely, Rheims, Rouen, Tours, and Sens—following the examples of our predecessors, subscribed with the consent of our lord Charles, decreeing by canonical and episcopal authority:

> “No secular power shall presume to exercise authority over the goods of the bishopric of the Church of Beauvais. If any king, priest, judge, or secular person, knowing the text of this constitution, should attempt to act against it, let him know that he will stand guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed. And unless he either restores what he has wrongly taken from it or mourns through worthy repentance the unlawful acts he has committed, let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God the Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ, and be subjected to strict punishment at the eternal judgment.”

And in this constitution we believe that the presence of the Lord was with us, according to his promise, in which he says: “Where two or three have been gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them” (Matthew 18). If he deigns to be present where two or three have gathered in his name, how much more will he not be absent where many priests, following or consenting to his authority, assemble?

Those who have succeeded in the seats of those who have already departed to the Lord, as Saint Siricius demonstrates in his decrees, ought to succeed to their labors and concerns, and with the greatest effort defend what their predecessors had regularly established. For, as Pope Symmachus says:

> “Since, in the likeness of the Trinity, whose power is one and undivided, the priesthood is one through various bishops, how can it be fitting for earlier decrees to be violated by those who follow? Moreover, if such a diversity of judgments should occur, we believe that it concerns the very holy Catholic religion, whose entire authority is weakened unless all things once established by the priests of the Lord remain perpetual. How else could this be maintained, unless a successor grants firmness to the acts of his predecessor and, by strengthening what has been done, makes what he himself does valid? For how great will reverence be judged to be owed to the vicars of the blessed Apostle Peter if what they command in the priesthood is dissolved when they themselves pass away?”

VII. In the privilege which our lord Pope Nicholas granted to the Church of Beauvais during the time of Odo, bishop of that church, it is written at the relevant point:

> “Therefore, no king, no judge, and no one supported by the dignity of any secular power shall have authority over, or the power to dominate, receive, or remove, any goods, estates, fields, or serfs, or anything else that has been bestowed upon the monasteries described there, except the bishop of Beauvais who shall at that time preside over that church. Whatever in gold or silver, in any kind of property, or in the whole substance of their resources has been assigned to those monasteries today, or may be bestowed in future times, shall be subject to the distribution and administration of the bishop of Beauvais; nor shall any other power have any right or dominion over them, except insofar as divine authority, law, and justice permit . . . . . . . . . let him go with his eyes to everlasting fire.”

Therefore the sentence of blessed Gregory, which he placed in a letter to the regions of the Greeks against the four chapters of those who held erroneous opinions, must be impressed upon him and his accomplices. Those men, anathematized along with other pernicious persons, persuaded themselves that they were not held by the bond of anathema. Gregory says:

> “They themselves are witnesses that they are not Christians: they think that they can dissolve the bonds of the holy Church by empty efforts, and therefore they do not truly believe in the absolution of the holy Church which it grants to the faithful, if they do not believe that its bonds have force. There is no need to dispute at length against them, since in every respect they are to be despised and anathematized. By the very means through which they think they deceive the truth, they are truly bound in their sins. I, together with all Catholic bishops and the whole Church, anathematize them, because they think and speak contrary to the truth.”

VIII. Finally, the sacred canons of Nicaea decree concerning those deprived of communion, whether from the clergy or from the lay order (Council of Nicaea, A.D. 325, canon 5):

> “Let a canonical sentence prevail among the bishops of each province, so that those who are rejected by some may not be received by others.”

Concerning the privilege of this great council, Saint Hilary and blessed Ambrose write wonderfully. But Pope Leo the Great also says (Epistle 106, to Anatolius, chapters 2 and 4):

> “The Council of Nicaea has been consecrated by such a privilege divinely granted that, whether ecclesiastical judgments are celebrated by fewer or by more persons, whatever differs from its constitution is utterly void of authority.”

And again (Epistle 53):

> “Those holy and venerable Fathers who, after condemning the sacrilegious Arius with his impiety in the city of Nicaea, established laws of the ecclesiastical canons that would endure to the end of the world, live among us throughout the whole world in their constitutions. If anyone anywhere presumes to act otherwise than they decreed, it is annulled without hesitation.”

And again, in the same man’s decretal letter (Epistle 12, to the bishops of Africa, chapter 2):

> “The command of the blessed Apostle Paul, sent through the Spirit of God, instructs the whole number of Christ’s priests in the person of Timothy. Accordingly, it is said to each of us: ‘Lay hands hastily on no one, nor share in the sins of others’ (1 Timothy 5).”

And shortly afterward:

> “What is it to share in the sins of others except to make such an ordination as is the man who did not deserve to be ordained? For just as the person who makes a sound judgment in choosing a priest obtains the fruit of a good work for himself, so he inflicts serious harm upon himself who admits an unworthy man into his own college. Therefore, what is contained in the general regulations must not be omitted in anyone’s case, nor should that honor be considered legitimate which has been conferred contrary to the commands of divine law.”

And again:

> “We resist those placed outside the Church to no purpose if we are wounded by those within it, in the persons whom they deceive. For we must remember the Gospel command, prescribed by Truth itself: if an eye, foot, or right hand causes us to stumble, it is to be removed from the body, because it is better to lack these members in the Church than to go with them into eternal punishments.”

This utterly destructive tolerance must be cast away from priestly firmness: by sparing the sins of others, it does not spare itself, as once happened with the priest Eli. By tolerating his sons’ offenses, he deserved to experience the sentence of divine justice with them, because through sluggish indulgence he neglected to punish sinners.

Therefore, according to the command of Leviticus—in which the priest is ordered to inspect the stones of leprous houses, and whatever among them cannot be purified is to be counted among the unclean, removed from the order of clean stones, and cast out from the heavenly building, namely, the holy Church, as unworthy, while another who is worthy is placed in his position by divine judgment—the aforementioned Odacrus, who is not a cleric of the province of Rheims, presumed, contrary to the sacred laws and rules, to invade a suffragan church of our metropolitan church while it was vacant of a pastor.

He sacrilegiously usurped the revenues of the widowed church, which the great Council of Chalcedon orders to be preserved intact under the care of the steward of that church. He has been excommunicated by the defined judgment of that council, by the excommunication of the bishops of four provinces, and moreover by that of our lord Pope Nicholas, pontiff of the Apostolic See, through evangelical, apostolic, and canonical authority, so that he may never, anywhere in the province of the Church of Rheims, minister in an ecclesiastical rank.

If thereafter he presumes to remain in the obstinacy of his invasion, he shall never, anywhere in the province of Rheims, communicate with any Christian, nor receive the body and blood of Christ, except perhaps, according to the mystical Council of Nicaea (canon 13), if placed at the point of death, he receives the viaticum of sacred communion.

## LETTER XXXIV. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF CAMBRAI  
### Concerning the Purification of Hunold and of a Priest of Bad Reputation

*(In Sirmond, from a manuscript of Saint Lawrence of Liège.)*

[Col. 0253C]

Hincmar, bishop of Rheims and servant of the people of God, sends greetings in the Savior to his beloved brother and venerable fellow bishop John.

This priest, named Hunold, told me that he had certain priests with him with whom he wished to purge his reputation by oath concerning a certain woman. Because he refused to undergo judicial examination, so that those priests might swear with him more securely, the priestly ministry was forbidden to him.

Therefore we inform your affection how, by the authority of our predecessors, we observe the practice in our diocese. As Saint Gregory decreed, inquiry is made concerning a priest of bad reputation by means of suitable witnesses, so that those who know the matter may neither speak falsely nor conceal the truth; apart from the accusers, six witnesses are to swear.

After this oath, we do not question whether the priest had sexual relations with any woman, because the canons do not contain this requirement, but concerning his visiting and frequenting women, and living with women, contrary to the prohibition of the sacred canons—conduct from which an evil suspicion and a reputation unbecoming a priest arose.

After their testimony, a seventh witness, if the condition or standing of the person permits it, comes forward for judgment: namely, that the six have spoken the truth about this matter under oath. For many have already been discovered among us who, having been hired for money, committed perjury.

If in this manner the priest is convicted of unbecoming cohabitation with a woman contrary to the laws and canons, he is deposed, as the sacred rules prescribe. Accusers and witnesses, however, are accepted for accusing or testifying in such matters according to the African Council, in accordance with the persons whom the public laws admit for accusation and testimony in the assembly or court.

But if a bad reputation about a priest has arisen throughout the diocese from mere appearance, and there are no lawful accusers or witnesses, then, so that the hearts of the weak may not be struck by the priest’s bad reputation contrary to the Apostle, and so that our ministry may not be blamed, while priests who feel more secure may not fall more freely into sin, he is to purge his reputation, according to the decrees of our predecessors, together with the priests whom we have named to him as neighbors and whom we know would not wish to commit perjury under oath.

If he cannot have the priests whom we have named to him for the purging of his reputation, and he hires others to swear with him, because we have learned by experience that some have conspired with one another so that, having been mutually regarded as trustworthy, they might swear in one another’s purgation, then, just as the priests full of wicked intent conspired against Susanna, before a trustworthy envoy sent to us, the priests who offer to swear together with the disgraced priest in his purgation are to undergo the judge’s examination through the advocate of the disgraced priest, so that they do not destroy themselves before God by their oath, as we have already found certain persons here to have been convicted of this.

The invocation over the person who submits to judgment is as follows: that the priest did not have with that woman such visiting, frequenting, and cohabitation contrary to the sacred canons as would justly give rise to an evil suspicion and a reputation unbecoming a priest.

For just as corrupt priests, at the devil’s urging, contrive to have women in their houses—whether from their inherited property, their natural holdings, or property they have purchased—who wash their clothes, make garments for them, and sometimes even take charge of the keys to their possessions, and thus live with them improperly, so, as Saint Augustine says, they are driven to seek new experiments in medicines for various kinds of disease, because, although they do not care to obey the prohibition of the canons and laws, they fear to depart from them because of the severity of the penalty.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the seventh indiction.

## LETTER XXXV. TO ALL THE FAITHFUL  
### The Deposition of the Priest Godbald, Convicted Concerning a Woman

*(In the same author, from an old manuscript of Saint Lawrence of Liège.)*

[Col. 0254D]

Hincmar, bishop and servant of the people of God.

Let it be known to all rectors, ministers, and sons of the holy Church of God to whom this letter may come that Godbald, formerly a priest of our diocese, was accused concerning a certain woman named Doda, and the accusation was established by suitable witnesses. When summoned to judgment according to the sacred canons, he was convicted by his own conscience in that very judgment and fled.

Therefore, according to the sacred canons established by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, he has been deprived of every priestly office. Blessed Pope Boniface teaches this (Epistle 11):

> “If he neglects to appear, let him not gain a postponement of the sentence by reason of his absence. For it is manifest that a person confesses himself guilty who does not use the opportunity granted him, and repeatedly assigned to him, to purge himself. It makes no difference whether everything that has been said is proved in his presence, since his very absence, repeatedly procured for the purpose of confession, is also established.”

Given from the synod held in the metropolitan church of Rheims, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER XXXVI. TO ALL THE FAITHFUL  
### The Excommunication of Fulcher and Hardoisa for Incestuous Marriage

*(In the same author, from an old manuscript of Saint Lawrence of Liège.)*

[Col. 0255B]

Hincmar, bishop and servant of the people of God.

Let it be known to all rectors, ministers, and sons of the holy Church of God to whom this letter may come that Fulcher and Hardoisa, related by blood, have been joined not in marriage but in incestuous carnal intercourse, contrary to the commands of the law, the prophetic statements, the evangelical, apostolic, and canonical rule, and also human laws. This has been established by suitable and truthful witnesses, after the kinship of both parties was reckoned.

Because they refused to obey divine and human laws by separating themselves from this incest according to the sacred canons, they have been cast out from the sacred communion of the body and blood of Christ and from every society of Christians, until, with the Lord looking favorably upon them, they are separated by repentance from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive, and turn away from this incest.

Blessed Gregory decrees this (the Younger Gregory, canons 8 and 9):

> “If anyone takes his cousin in marriage, let him be anathema”; and all answered three times: “Let him be anathema.”

And again:

> “If anyone takes a wife from his own kin, or one whom his kinsman had as a wife, let him be anathema”; and all answered three times: “Let him be anathema.”

You, brothers and sons, who have not learned letters, should know what *anathema* means in our language: alienation. Thus such people are alienated from Christ, from whom Christians are named, and from the society and communion of Christians, until they separate themselves from that unlawful union and, through repentance and priestly ministry, are reconciled to Christ and to the holy Church—that is, to Christians.

Divine laws decree that every Christian must observe his lineage up to the seventh generation, and for as long as the parties recognize themselves as related by affinity, so that no one may take a spouse from his own blood relation, or one whom someone from his own blood relation had as a spouse, or whom anyone has defiled by any unlawful pollution; for such intercourse is incestuous and abominable to God and to all people.

They command that incestuous persons be separated from the thresholds of the holy Church until, through satisfaction and the prayers of priests, they are canonically reconciled to that same holy Church, as we have stated above.

If they wish to separate themselves from this incest in which they lie ruined—for, as the sacred laws say, incest is counted under no designation of marriage—then, if they are unable to remain continent, after repentance and reconciliation, by which the unlawful union is forbidden, they shall have the freedom to enter a better marriage.

As long as they remain in that unlawful union, no Christian may communicate with them in any way, since no Christian is permitted even to share ordinary food with such people. Therefore, brothers and sons—in short, all Christians—separate yourselves from all communion with them, lest, God forbid, by communicating with them you perish together with them.

Nor is it surprising that this principle is observed among human beings, since you also know that it is observed among animals: those that appear to have mange are separated from the healthy, lest the others be condemned or perish through their disease.

And since the Lord says: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezekiel 33:21), if, before separating themselves from this incest, either of them should fall ill and thereby come into despair of his temporal life, then, if he should repent from the heart even at that time, confess before God, a priest, and faithful people, and provide sureties that, if he recovers from that illness, he will not return thereafter to that incestuous union, let him make a pure confession of this incest together with his other sins, be reconciled by the priest, be anointed with holy oil, and receive communion of the body and blood of Christ.

But if either of them remains obstinate in this way until death, and dies without reconciliation and communion of the body and blood of Christ, let him be buried without psalms, hymns, or prayers, and not with other Christians. For, as we read written under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, those with whom we did not communicate while they lived, we cannot communicate with when they are dead.

Given from the synod held in the metropolitan church of Rheims, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER XXXVII. TO ENGILGARIUS, AN ILLUSTRIOUS MAN  
### He Rebukes Him Because He Had Improperly Forced His Man to Swear

*(In the same author, from Flodoard, Book III, chapter 26.)*

Hincmar, bishop, sends greetings to Engilgarius.

It has come to us that you irrationally and improperly forced your man Ratramn to swear a dangerous oath. Although he owes you service, both you and he ought nevertheless to be under our care with regard to your salvation.

Therefore I inform you that I am greatly surprised that you did not understand that it is a more serious danger to send another into perjury by persuasion or intimidation than if you yourself alone committed perjury. For in your own case you would commit one perjury—or rather, murder in place of perjury—but when you cause another to swear falsely, you destroy both yourself and him.

Accordingly, we command that, if the matter is as it has reached us, you abstain from the church and altar until you come to us and either offer a worthy explanation for such carelessness or accept a worthy penance.

## LETTER XXXVIII. TO ANASTASIUS, ABBOT  
### Sent to Rome After He Had Received the Pope’s Rebuking Letter

*(In the same author, from a manuscript of the church of Laon.)*

Hincmar, bishop of Rheims, sends abundant greetings in the Savior to his most holy and most faithful brother Anastasius, venerable abbot.

Pressed by many illnesses and anxieties, I write a few words to one to whom I owe much, whom I love greatly, and in whom I place great confidence. Moreover, the letter of the lord apostolic, sent to us through Egilo, the venerable archbishop, in reply to our writings, expressed certain matters differently from the way in which we had written to his Holiness and authority. Yet I am certain that he wrote back to us in no other way than as he found in the writings presented to him on our behalf. Nevertheless, since we possess the authentic copies of those same writings sent by us, we find that concerning certain matters we did not write as we read them in his written reply.

Therefore, if in these writings also—those sent from the synod at Troyes under the seals of five bishops and with the consent of all who were present—anything should be sent by anyone differently (which we do not believe will happen), or anything contrary to them should be transmitted, here our venerable brother and fellow bishop Actard has obtained authentic copies of the writings of that synod, which, if necessary, he will be able to show to the lord apostolic. When these are perhaps compared with the documents sent to Pope Leo by the bishops of the provinces on this side of the Alps, by the Emperor Lothar, and also by King Charles—on whose exemplar copies, as I suppose, the bishops who sent this material based their compilation—they will be found not to differ in meaning, although some of those who were not present at the proceedings wrote more mildly than those who, having taken part in them, wrote accounts to be sent to Pope Sergius and sent to Leo.

They likewise did not include in their writings anything about the restoration of Ebo by the edict of the Emperor Lothar, because the bishops whose names are recorded there, without their subscriptions, stated that they had not participated in that restoration, whatever its character, just as Rothad has now said in the synod at Troyes. This is also so because they read that Sergius, after that same restoration, pronounced a sentence of condemnation against him, as the episcopal codex and the letters of the lord apostolic sent to us through Egilo demonstrate.

Nor is anything said in the aforesaid writings about the document of transfer to another diocese granted by Pope Gregory to the aforementioned Ebo, because it had never previously been seen in these regions of ours—except now, when our beloved brother Vulfad showed it to us at Troyes. Whether it was issued by Gregory, whose successor was Sergius, or not, will, we believe, be ascertainable from the archive of the holy Roman See.

The bishops who ordained me, the suffragans of the province of Rheims, repeatedly, both in various places and in the synod, professed that they had not communicated with Ebo in those matters for which he had been excommunicated. The only exception was our brother Rothad, as some think, because of zeal against me—the man who condemned that same Ebo, chose me, and ordained me with the other bishops. Rothad is also said to claim that certain bishops received rings and staffs from the aforementioned Ebo, although a certain Gallican synod called Toletan says:

> “If a bishop, presbyter, or deacon, unjustly expelled from his rank, is found innocent in a second synod, he cannot be what he formerly was unless he recovers the rank he lost; for before the altar, from the hand of the bishops, if he is a bishop, he receives the stole, the ring, and the staff, and so the text proceeds concerning the remaining ranks.”

It is therefore clear that Ebo, having been deposed, ought, according to this constitution, to have received the ring and staff from the bishops, not to have given them to bishops.

And because Scripture says, “Beware of your sons, and be attentive to your household” (Ecclesiasticus 32:28), and “Let each person guard himself from his neighbor and place no trust in any of his brothers,” and “A man’s enemies are those of his own household” (Micah 7:6), I would have sent through my messenger copies of the writings recently produced at the synod at Troyes, lest perhaps some matter should be fabricated in them against me by my friends, whose attacks I endure, if I were able to do so securely, because of the agitation against me of certain princes whom I dare not please according to their wishes—as this venerable brother and fellow priest of ours, mentioned above, can tell you in person.

Concerning this dearest and most faithful brother, a venerable and prudent bishop, I ask your unquestionable charity to commend him to the lord apostolic, to our father Arsenius, and to your other associates, and to assist his needs and reasonable requests to the best of your ability.

And because, when I came to the synod at Troyes, I did not expect him to go from the synod to Rome with the synodal embassy, I did not bring with me gifts of such kind or quality that I could send them suitably to the lord apostolic, to our dearest father Arsenius, and to you. After the synod, remaining ill in a small estate of our Church near our city, I could not return before his departure, lest I fail entirely to visit you with even the smallest blessing. As a remembrance of our humble self, I therefore send you through him a *crusna* made of various furs, together with a cloth of varied colors, with which [lacuna]. Very little else is missing.

## LETTER XXXIX. TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF BEAUVAIS

Concerning the elevation of a bishop.

(From the Acts of the provincial Church of Rheims.)

Hincmar, bishop of the holy metropolitan Church of Rheims and servant of the people of God, to the clergy and people residing in the diocese of Beauvais.

Since your beloved and venerable fellow brother and priest, namely your father and shepherd Odo, has died, and our lord the king has granted you, with his customary kindness, a canonical election, you must hasten to deliberate as soon as possible about choosing and appointing a shepherd, teacher, and ruler for yourselves. With the Lord’s help, our wishes must be brought together as one, after the appointed fasts and the supplications of the litanies. Having entreated him from whom every good gift and every perfect gift comes, and who makes people of one mind dwell in a house, may you therefore unite in a regular election with the efforts of this venerable brother and fellow bishop of ours [Note: Hadebert, bishop of Senlis], whom, according to canonical institution, we have appointed as visitor of the Church which is fostered by our love and care, so that you may not grieve at remaining deprived of a shepherd any longer.

Concerning the election of the bishop whom we are to consecrate, because of the ministry entrusted to us and the care of the entire province delegated to us according to the canons of the mystical Council of Nicaea, we strive to make known to your fraternity the authority promulgated by God.

First, no decree is to be drawn up without the presence of the visitor, whose testimony can establish the unanimity of the clergy and citizens. Next, from your own Church—whether it be in the city or in the monasteries—choose from among the deacons or presbyters a man trained in these disciplines and conforming to the apostolic model, to be consecrated bishop for you, with the Lord as author and supporter, just as the Apostle Paul portrays Titus and Timothy when he discusses the choosing and appointing of a bishop.

If—God forbid—no one among the clergy of your city and diocese should be found worthy or suitable for the high priesthood, although we do not believe this will happen, then arrange to choose someone from another church of our diocese. According to the African Council (canon 22), permission has been granted us, without anyone’s opposition, to ordain anyone canonically elected and requested. Choose someone who can rightly preside over you and benefit you by the excellence of his life and the teaching of his knowledge, and who cannot in any way conflict with the sacred canons, especially the chapter of the Council of Carthage:

> “What sort of person ought to be ordained bishop.”

He must likewise not conflict, insofar as human frailty permits and you are able to observe, with the decrees of the Fathers—namely, Siricius, Innocent, Celestine, Leo, Gelasius, and Gregory.

If you should prefer to choose someone known to you who is useful and beneficial from the diocese of another archbishop or from the parish of another bishop, you must obtain, with the consent of the bishop concerned, both his canonical letters and his approval of the request, and bring that man to us through your visitor for examination. If he is found suitable according to the sacred canons, he may be ordained bishop for you.

Above all, beware in the election of your pontiff of the evil of the simoniacal heresy. Do not attempt to elect anyone in return for a gift or an illicit promise, or because of anyone’s favor, familiarity, or kinship. Do not elect someone whom no dignity of birth or character supports, or who is held bound by an inherited status or by any other condition. Do not elect any layman who is a neophyte—that is, newly tonsured and without discipline—or who has not advanced to the ecclesiastical ranks at the prescribed times.

We specify this particularly because, when the canons say, “No one from among the laity is to be ordained,” they show that this was not established concerning every layman. For people cannot be born clerics rather than made clerics; instead, categories have been identified whose members cannot reach the clerical state. These include anyone who, while a believer, has served in the army; anyone who, while a believer, has practiced law—that is, acted as an advocate; anyone who, while a believer, has administered public affairs; any man who was formerly a slave; anyone who has performed public penance for criminal offenses; anyone who has been married twice, or has been the husband of a widow; or anyone who has known a concubine or mistress.

Likewise, beware electing an illiterate person, one corrupted by the plague of any heresy, or one who has suffered the loss of any limb; a cleric engaged in commerce, or occupied with dishonorable and shameful profits; one entangled in or notorious for dreadful crimes; or one ensnared by demons or similar afflictions. Instead, choose for the house of God a worthy, faithful, and prudent minister and steward.

Let him be decently adorned inwardly and outwardly, so that by a religious way of life he may display to you a pattern of living, and by sound doctrine, amid the darkness of this world and its tribulations, may be able to reveal the light of the path by which one proceeds without stumbling to the harbor of eternal salvation. If—God forbid—barbarian aggression should occur, let him know how to bring you aid through prudence, be capable of doing so through courage, and provide counsel through temperance. Let him administer outward matters without abandoning inward ones; let him serve inward matters without wholly neglecting outward ones. Let him be “ambidextrous,” devoting his mind to contemplation while intent upon the duties of the active life, so that, as a faithful and prudent servant, he may properly distribute to his fellow servants their measure of grain at the appointed time—that is, the measure of the word of faith. Let him foresee what is necessary and timely not only in preaching and by the example of his conduct, but in all things necessary for salvation and life.

Bring such a man, insofar as the Lord grants it and with his cooperation, together with your visitor—namely, our fellow brother—and with the canonical decree, to be examined by the solicitude of our humility. For, as was said long ago, it is not easy to dismiss the one to whom a charge is about to be entrusted.

Finally, I want you to know in advance that if you knowingly bring us a person who deviates from the sacred canons, you will not only fail to obtain a pontiff from him; you will also incur judgment for an illicit election as despisers of the canons. If your unsuitable election is reasonably rejected by our judgment and that of our fellow bishops, we shall strive, according to the canons of Laodicea, to choose someone who cannot consent to your vicious desires.

For just as the Lord says to those who ask rightly, “Ask, and you will receive” (Matthew 7), so through the Apostle he rebukes those who ask wrongly, saying, “You ask, and you do not receive, because you ask wrongly” (James 4). Ask God, brothers, to grant you a shepherd according to his own heart. If, in his election, you strive to consider temporal advantages no more than spiritual ones, he will endeavor, as the author and co-worker of good works and pious endeavors, to join the grace of his election to your election—he who does not see only the face as man does, but searches the hearts and kidneys of each person.

To him be honor and glory, power and dominion, forever and ever. Amen.

## LETTER XL. Fragment

TO KING CHARLES THE BALD.

What sort of judges he ought to appoint to settle cases between ecclesiastics and secular persons.

(From Sirmond.)

The royal solicitude, established by God—King of kings and most equitable Judge—to judge judgment with uprightness of heart, must carefully and diligently strive to choose and appoint, together with the bishops, such judges to settle a case between ecclesiastics and secular persons as are religious and fear God. They must not accept a person in judgment for the reward of a gift, or because of favor, kinship, or friendship, or out of obedience to an improper subjection, or hatred of the opposing party. Instead, without contention or rancor, they must judge a just judgment, as Truth itself says, not according to appearance but according to justice.

This must not take place in a public courtroom, but in private, because bishops ought or can regularly be judged neither in the court of kings nor in the praetorium of judges, and not except by bishops—either in a synod or in a private place—by the judgment of primates or of judges appointed by them or chosen by themselves.

We have learned that the ancient emperors, your predecessors and forefathers, resolved that the aforesaid laws, both public and ecclesiastical, should be observed by bishops and ecclesiastical men in their proper times and manner. Your most beloved and gracious lordship also promised at Quierzy, both verbally and by subscription, that you would observe them. There, with the advice and counsel of your faithful men, both bishops and laymen, you enacted this chapter and subscribed to it, saying:

> “To the extent that I know and reasonably can, with the Lord’s help, I will honor and protect each of you according to his rank and person, and I will preserve you honored and protected without any deceit, condemnation, or deception. I will preserve for each person the law and justice appropriate to him. To anyone who needs it and reasonably requests it, I will show reasonable mercy, as a faithful king ought to honor and protect his faithful subjects according to justice, preserve for each person the law and justice appropriate to each rank, and grant reasonable mercy to those in need who reasonably request it. For no person, insofar as human frailty permits, will I deviate from this through partiality, malice, or anyone’s improper urging, to the extent that God grants me understanding and ability. And if, through frailty, I should be led astray against this, when I recognize it I will willingly strive to correct it.”

We, your faithful men—the bishops and the others of the lay order who were present—also enacted this chapter with you and each subscribed to it, professing:

> “To the extent that I know and can, with the Lord’s help, without any deceit or seduction, by counsel and assistance, according to my ministry and my person, I will be your faithful helper, so that you may hold and govern, with due honor and strength, the power which God has granted you in the royal name and kingdom, according to his will and for the salvation of you and your faithful people.”

## LETTER XLI. Fragment

TO LOUIS, KING OF GERMANY.

On behalf of Bertulf, archbishop of Trier.

(From the same source, from Flodoard, book III, chapter 25.)

Just as a grave danger rests upon pontiffs if they remain silent concerning what is appropriate for the worship of the Divinity, so—God forbid—a considerable danger threatens royal power if, when it ought to obey, it refuses what is announced to it by the priests from the divine voice. For the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever is from God hears the words of God.”

But if someone less devoted to you has suggested that we appointed a metropolitan pontiff in that same city in contempt of you or against your fidelity, the truth is rather that we appointed him according to the sacred canons, with the unanimous consent of us all. For, as it is written, just as God is not confined by the narrowness of a place, so his word is not bound. Our Redeemer and Savior also praised the meaning expressed by the centurion: “Say the word, and my servant will be healed” (Matthew 8:8)—that is, what you say here will be done there.

He speaks to us today, though unworthy, in his disciples: “The Spirit of your Father speaks in you,” and he fills the whole world. We beg you, do not believe anyone who gives wicked counsel. Know with certainty that we did not appoint a pontiff in that metropolitan Church either in contempt of you or against your fidelity. Rather, considering, as you know better, how long and through how many periods that Church has been desolate and deprived, and how greatly matters contrary to God’s will have increased, not only in that diocese but in the whole province belonging to it—and since the suffragan bishops can do nothing canonically without their primate except what pertains to their own dioceses—we found there a regular expedient and canonically ordained a pontiff. The suffragans of that metropolitan see could and ought to have done this under the divine laws if they had been numerous enough to ordain a pontiff regularly by themselves; he cannot regularly be ordained by fewer than three.

He then continues, bringing forward the authorities of the holy Fathers by which they supported what they had done. He proceeds:

And because there were not so many suffragan bishops in that province that they could regularly appoint a metropolitan, and because the Churches of Rheims and Trier are regarded as neighboring and sister Churches, both by authority and by ancient custom, under the condition that whichever of their bishops was ordained first should also be regarded as first in the synod, and that they should support and strengthen one another by mutual counsel and assistance, the bishops of the province of Trier sought from the primate of the province of Rheims the support of their ordination according to the sacred rules, just as the holy canons of Sardica say (chapter 5):

> “If it should happen in a province in which there had been many bishops that only one bishop should remain, and the people should assemble, the bishops of the neighboring province ought first to approach the bishop who remains in that province and show him that the people are asking for a ruler. It is just that they themselves should come and, together with him, ordain a bishop. But if, when letters have been received, the assembly should remain silent and dissemble, and should send no reply, the people must be satisfied, so that bishops may come from the neighboring province and ordain a bishop.”

From this it is properly concluded that if the province of Trier had only one bishop or none at all, the bishops of the province of Rheims would be obliged to ordain a bishop at the request of the clergy and people of the Church of Trier.

All of us whose names your glorious self reads at the beginning of this letter have therefore, by unanimous vote and consent, regularly appointed our brother and fellow priest Bertulf, as stated above, pontiff of that Church. We can demonstrate this from the sacred rules and from the proceedings of his ordination, and, if necessary, we shall demonstrate it.

Accordingly, we defend and shall perpetually defend his ordination and the administration of ecclesiastical affairs and possessions, just as the sacred canons prescribe, just as we defend our own order. For if he is not a bishop, neither ought we to be called bishops. If anyone wishes to say anything sinister against his ordination, let him come forward and speak—yet let him remember his own communion. For either he himself will not share communion with the ecclesiastical and episcopal order, or we shall not share in the episcopal ministry.

Therefore, in the words of blessed Leo, once addressing the Emperor Theodosius:

> “Most Christian, venerable, and dearest king, we address you together with our fellow priests. Showing reverence for your clemency through the service of sincere love, and desiring that you please God in all things—to whom we and the Churches entrusted to us offer prayers for you—we beg you, lest before the tribunal of the Lord we be judged guilty of silence, before the inseparable Trinity of one Divinity, which is injured by such an act, since it is itself the guardian and author of your kingdom, and before the holy angels of Christ, to order and preserve the Church of Trier, together with its pontiff, in the status, freedom, and privilege in which your ancestors and predecessors preserved it, and also in which your brother and nephew Lothar—father and son—canonically preserved it. Thus you may receive merit for this before God and before blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, in whose honor that Church has been consecrated, and may acquire us as greater debtors to you in our prayers and other required services.”

For unless we postponed this out of reverence for you, we would already have had judgment pronounced on earth against the invader of that Church, as the six hundred and thirty bishops decreed concerning such a matter in the great Council of Chalcedon; they also threaten it from heaven and will pronounce it in divine judgment to eternal condemnation unless he performs worthy penance.

And other matters from the authorities of the sacred canons.

After these words it is added:

Therefore your religious and most beloved lordship must know with complete certainty that as long as this brother of ours, Bertulf, the bishop ordained by us in the Church of Trier, lives in this mortal body, no other bishop will be ordained in that Church—unless he himself, which God forbid, should oppose the sacred rules and be deposed by those same sacred rules.

That same presumptuous apostate monk Walto, from a monastery in the diocese of Trier, will never be able to be bishop in the Church of Trier, which he disastrously usurped and injured, now that the judgment of the Holy Spirit has been pronounced against him.

And if, as we have said, we did not postpone this out of reverence for you, we would decree not only through the sacred canons that he should never and nowhere presume to approach the ecclesiastical ranks, but, placing him under anathema, we would decree according to the sacred rules that he be confined in prison. If he persists in his obstinacy, we shall decree this in every respect, without reconsideration.

We earnestly beg the Lord, through whom kings reign and from whom and through whom the sacred episcopate took its beginning, to make you free and exempt from the aforementioned threats of the sacred canons. We beseech his clemency to grant you the will and the ability to accomplish, according to his good pleasure, what he has commanded, so that you may deserve to receive the eternal joys which he promises to those who love him.

## LETTER XLII. Fragment

TO WILIGIS AND THE OTHER MONKS OF SAINT-DENIS.

That no price should be demanded for a tithe.

(From the same source, from Flodoard, book III, chapter 25.)

Far be it, brothers, that other ecclesiastical and religious men should hear that the monks of the monastery of Saint-Denis are seeking to sell a tithe, so that with the price itself they may purchase hell. Much more, however, let it be far from us that laymen should hear this—something which no one in my diocese, even if involved in public crimes, dares to do. For if anyone should attempt this in another monastery rather than ours, how much more boldly would he presume to do it? I would excommunicate him from every communion in my diocese, and so forth.

## LETTER XLIII. Fragment

TO COUNT TEUDULF.

That he must not presume to sell a church for a price.

(From the same source, from Flodoard, book III, chapter 26.)

Know therefore that if any cleric gives you even a single denarius for that church, or for any other church in my diocese, either personally or through an intermediary, he will not be ordained in it by me.

If you wish to have a presbyter there, I will seek for you a cleric of such character as is suitable for the sacred ministry; I will give him the church, and then I will ordain him, provided he satisfies me that he has given no price for it.

If you do not wish to act in this way, I will arrange for the people there to have the service they require until I ordain a presbyter there. If you cause him any impediment contrary to divine and human laws, and this becomes known, the presbyter will remain there, while you and all who agree with you will be separated from all Christian fellowship until satisfaction is made.

I command and admonish you concerning these matters, dear son, because I desire you to be safe and honored, and I wish to regard you among the sons of the Church as a son. If you force me to make you, as the Lord says in the Gospel, “as a pagan and a tax collector,” you must reckon that against yourself, not against me.

After I dictated this letter, I was told that you expelled the matricularii appointed by my minister from that poor-roll (*matricula*), installed Bonarius there, and received a donkey as the price for that *matricula*.

If this is true, you have not merely acted criminally, because, contrary to all laws, you, a layman, usurped an ecclesiastical ministry, and sold the almsgiving—that is, the mercy shown to the poor—and thereby God, who is the mercy of the wretched, like Judas the traitor. You also acted most shamefully in this matter: from the poverty on which beggars ought to live, you, a count and an honored counselor of the king, accepted a donkey as the price. Everyone who hears this can judge how you act justly and rightly in other matters for the love and fear of God and out of reverence for your office, when you seek shameful profit without any embarrassment from such misery.

## LETTER XLIV. Fragment

TO IRMINGARD, AUGUSTA, WIFE OF THE EMPEROR LOTHAR.

Concerning the false accusation of disloyalty brought against him before Lothar.

(From the same source, from Flodoard, book III, chapter 27.)

I know that many things contrary to me were said to him. But if he wishes, he can learn that they are not true. Nevertheless, I do not dare rebuke him, because he is my lord, nor do I apply to his person what is read in Scripture: “Whoever willingly listens to words of falsehood will also have wicked ministers” (Proverbs 29:12)—namely, those who willingly speak impious things to him about pious persons.

The man who told him, on my behalf, what you instructed me to say, spoke differently from the truth and wrongly interpreted words that had been well meant. If he had wished to learn the truth, and someone had come to me from him so that he might learn the truth from me, I would have most willingly satisfied his mind—just as the man who came and reproached me, an unworthy priest of Christ the Lord.

Concerning my own messenger, whom your most gracious lordship instructed me to send to him to affirm that I do not wish to discuss anything concerning his disloyalty, you know how many falsehoods are now circulating throughout this age, how much sincerity ought to be found in a priest, and how faithfully I rightly wish to preserve my loyalty to my lord. Therefore, lest evil interpreters interpret good things evilly, I still cannot do this.

Nevertheless, if my lord Lothar wishes to believe it, he can know truthfully that I am disloyal not only to him but to no human being in the world. If he wishes to believe, let him believe. If not, when he, among princes, and I, among bishops, come before the King of kings and the Bishop of bishops, he will then learn the complete truth about this matter without anyone’s judgment, and so forth.

## LETTER XLV. Fragment

TO ROTRUD AND THE OTHER SISTERS OF THE MONASTERY OF THE HOLY CROSS AND SAINT RADEGUND.

On the election of the abbess of that monastery.

(From the same source, from Flodoard, book III, chapter 27.)

Therefore, sisters, love above all; in private conversations and in your public assembly, forgive and utterly cast out from your hearts all injuries and causes of scandal that have arisen among you until now, so that none of you may seek vengeance against a sister, whether because of a word, an action, or some slight, either from God or in this world.

For, as the Lord declares, whatever you offer him without concord will not please him. Whether you pray, offer sacrifice, or afflict yourselves, without this concord of charity nothing will be pleasing to God, because, as the Apostle says: “Even if I hand over my body to be burned, but do not have charity, I am nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:3).

You know that the rule which you have professed, because of the thorns of scandal that customarily arise in a monastery, commands the prior to pray the Lord’s Prayer at the morning and evening offices so that everyone may hear it, in order that, fearing the agreement expressed in the words “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors,” we may drive all resentment from our hearts.

After you have done this first, lest, God forbid, the regular election perish from your monastery because of your discord, unite yourselves in God’s will and in the unanimity of regular devotion, and for your own salvation—both present and eternal—with the concord of charity, which is the mother of all virtues; with humility, which is the guardian of those virtues; and with true obedience, which is the ladder by which heaven is reached.

Agree among yourselves in a salutary election, restore yourselves to the regular norm, bind yourselves to it, and preserve yourselves in it. Otherwise, as you yourselves know best, you cannot possibly be saved.

Guard your minds from restless movements just as you guard your tongues from provocative words of anger that harm both you and others. The Apostle testifies: “Let all shouting and indignation be removed from you, together with all malice, and let no evil speech proceed from your mouth” (Ephesians 4:30–31).

Do not, as people commonly do, first moved by grief and afterward exhilarated by some joy as though victorious because they have obtained what they desired, let any one of you say concerning anyone anything improper. Otherwise you will lose before God the merit of your patience through useless speech.

If anyone should try, by some provocation, to incite any one of you to utter anything improper against anyone, so that he might find a way to seize upon it and reasonably condemn her, leave neither the devil nor a clever person any opportunity to do so in any manner.

Instead, conduct yourselves in such a way that, decently adorned inwardly and outwardly, you may be able to send worthy and acceptable prayers into the ears of the Lord both for yourselves and for your elder and lady, and not only for your friends but also for your enemies.

## LETTER XLVI. TO AENEAS, BISHOP OF PARIS

On the ordination of Berno, an acolyte of Paris.

(From the Acts of the provincial Church of Rheims.)

Our brothers from the monastery of Saint-Denis, with the permission of the lord abbot Louis, entrusted to me a certain young man named Berno, to educate and instruct him. Your fraternity ordained him an acolyte.

Therefore, since we do not wish him to remain for a long time in our Church without your permission, we ask your affection to prepare canonical letters for us concerning him, so that we may be able regularly to ordain him in our Church.

## LETTER XLVII. TO KING CHARLES

That he permit the clergy and people of Senlis to elect a new bishop, and designate a visitor to preside over the election.

(From Labbe, *Councils*, volume VIII, page 1866.)

May salvation and life always be granted to the glorious lord King Charles.

On the seventh day before the Ides of June, at about the second hour, three clerics and two laymen of the Church of Senlis came to my lowliness, informing me that, with our brother and fellow priest Erpoinus dead, that same Church was left without a shepherd; they also brought the petition of both the clergy and the people of that Church, asking that a pastor be assigned to them according to the sacred regulations. I asked them whether they had any word of agreement from the clergy and people of that Church concerning some specifically designated person [f., “from the party” of the clergy and people]. They replied that they brought no other request on behalf of their companions than that I should endeavor, through your customary mercy, to obtain for them a free and regular election, so that, according to the sacred regulations, with a canonical visitor appointed, he whom all must obey might be elected by all the members of that Church.

Although, as has been stated, I had learned from our brother and fellow presbyter Hildebold that your priest Erpoinus had died on the eighth day before the Ides of June, I nevertheless had not previously decided to suggest anything about the matter to your lordship or to make a request on behalf of that Church before receiving its envoys according to regular custom. For, as Leo says in his Decrees (chapter 49):

> “If, in any of the degrees of the Church, it must be carefully and wisely ensured that nothing in the house of the Lord be disordered or out of place, how much more must we labor lest there be error in the election of him who is placed above all? For the condition and order of the entire household of the Lord will totter if what is required in the body is lacking in the head. Where is that command of blessed Paul the apostle, sent forth through the Spirit of God, by which, in the person of Timothy, the whole number of Christ’s priests is instructed, and therefore each of us is told: ‘Lay hands hastily on no one, neither share in the sins of others’ (1 Tim. 5)?”

Therefore, your religious wisdom will weigh with the greatest discernment these two statements of blessed Leo, among others, in which he says that nothing in the house of the Lord should be disordered or out of place. If that same holy and wise man had not expressed them so plainly, your intellectual subtlety would have sufficiently elucidated them.

For this reason, most reverend and most merciful lord, may your lordship deign to inform me by letter whom you wish from among our fellow bishops, so that I may send him the canonical letters according to custom. Acting as visitor, he is to conduct a canonical election in that Church and, either in person or by his letters delivered through his vicar, report that election to me, together with the canonical decree confirmed by the hands of each member, so that through me the election may reach your lordship’s judgment.

And because, as we have already stated from Leo’s words, authority permits nothing in the house of God to be disordered or out of place, once we have learned of the unanimous agreement of the clergy and people in a regular election, or of the consent of your lordship, we shall send letters of metropolitan authority concerning the election of a definite person to the fellow bishops of the diocese of Rheims, designating a definite day and place [Col. 0268C] at which and to which they are either to assemble for the ordination of the elected man or to transmit, through a presbyter or deacon acting in their place, letters of their consent.

## LETTER XLVIII. TO HEDENULPHUS, BISHOP OF LAON  
### That he should act as visitor in the election of the bishop of Cambrai

*(In Labbe, in the same place.)*

HINCMAR, bishop of the holy metropolitan Church of Rheims and servant of the people of God, sends greetings to his beloved brother and venerable fellow bishop HEDENULPHUS.

Since our beloved brother and venerable fellow priest John, of the Church of Cambrai, has died, I exhort and admonish your affection, dearest brother, that, having undertaken the office of visitor of that Church by delegation from our metropolitan humility, you hasten to proceed to that Church as quickly as possible, and make haste publicly to admonish the clergy and people of the Church by continual exhortations, so that, setting aside private interest, they may with one and the same agreement seek and elect for themselves such a priest as can be found worthy of so great a ministry and in no way rejected by the venerable canons.

I am sending your affection the form of the election—how and what sort of man they ought to elect—and let your diligence have it read publicly before everyone, so that no one may be able to excuse himself on the ground of ignorance. This election is not to be conducted only by the clerics of the city: representatives from all the monasteries of that parish and from the presbyters of the rural parishes must also attend, bringing with them the unanimous votes of those dwelling with them. Noble laymen and citizens must also be present, since he must be elected by all, and all must obey him.

If, after your affection has transmitted to them the form of the election sent by us, you find them all in agreement concerning any regular person, admonish them to draw up a canonical decree and have it confirmed individually by the hands of all. Then, with the canonical decree and with as many persons as can sufficiently bear witness on behalf of all concerning the elected man, when I have instructed them to do so, let them arrange to bring that elected man to us.

## LETTER XLIX. TO HADEBERTUS, BISHOP OF SENLIS  
### That he should act as visitor in the election of the bishop of Beauvais

*(In Labbe, in the same place.)*

[Col. 0269B]

It is the same as the preceding letter, with only this difference: at the beginning a mention of royal consent has been added in the following form: “In the office of visitor, with the consent of our lord King Louis, of our humility,” and so forth.

At the end, after the words mentioned above have been omitted, instead of “when I have instructed them,” it continues somewhat farther in this manner:

> “Arrange to bring the elected man with you to us, so that he may be examined. Your affection, dearest brother, must watch over this election with vigilant care, especially since it will be necessary for you to lay hands with us upon the man who is to be ordained—he who should carefully observe the command of blessed Paul the apostle, sent forth through the Spirit of God, by which, in the person of Timothy, the whole number of Christ’s priests is instructed; therefore each of us is told: ‘Lay hands hastily on no one, neither share in the sins of others’ (1 Tim. 5:22),” and so forth.

## LETTER L. TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF CAMBRAI  
### That they should conduct a canonical election with the visitor appointed for them

*(In Labbe, in the same place.)*

HINCMAR, bishop of the holy metropolitan Church of Rheims and servant of the people of God, to the clergy and people residing in the diocese of Cambrai.

[Col. 0269D]
