Since our beloved and venerable fellow brother and fellow priest, your father and shepherd, John, has died, it is necessary that, with our votes brought together into one through the Lord, you hasten as soon as possible to deliberate, according to the ecclesiastical regulations, about choosing and appointing a shepherd and teacher for yourselves, after undertaking fasts and supplications of the litanies. Having entreated him from whom every good gift and every perfect gift comes, and who makes people dwell together in unity in a house, unite yourselves harmoniously in a regular election, together with the efforts of this venerable brother and fellow bishop of ours, whom we have appointed, according to canonical institution, to the office of visitor in the Church by whose love and strength you are sustained.

Choose for yourselves as future shepherd such a man as may be able to preside over you and benefit you by the merit of his life and the teaching of his knowledge, and who does not conflict with the sacred canons. Concerning his election, take care to draw up a canonical decree by unanimous vote and to confirm it individually by the hands of all of you in the presence of this visitor of yours.

## LETTER LI. OF THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF LAON TO HINCMAR, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS  
### Concerning the ordination of Hedenulphus

*(From the Acts of the provincial Church of Rheims.)*

To the most reverend and most holy lord HINCMAR, archbishop, and to the other holy fathers and bishops of our diocese, the clergy of Laon, together with the peoples of the entire parish and the bishops joined to them, sends eternal salvation and peace in the Lord Jesus Christ.

We recall that it has been established by canonical regulations and apostolic institutions that, whenever any city has been deprived of the ministry of pontifical dignity and left vacant without its own shepherd, its people must approach the metropolitan pontiff with a decree of election confirmed by the hands of each petitioner and humbly petition him concerning the substitution of a shepherd in the place of the one who has died. Thus the city, deprived of pastoral care, may recover its own bishop, and the man who is to be ordained may approach with greater favor. For he whom all must obey must also be elected by all, lest the city either despise or hate a bishop whom it did not desire, and become less religious than it ought because it was not permitted to have the man it wished. Those who are to ordain him, however, will be able to lay hands upon him more readily and freely when they see toward whom the votes of all incline most harmoniously.

Therefore, approaching your fatherhood with the decree of our election, confirmed by the hands of each of us, we implore, beseech, and ask that Hedenulphus, a son of our Church, promoted in our Church through the merits of his service up to the priestly burden, approved as suitable in life, conduct, and holy way of life, whom, with your permission and with the favor of the most Christian emperor Charles, we have elected with equal agreement, harmonious devotion, and unanimous will, be consecrated through your hands and those of the other holy bishops of your diocese, and be appointed for us and for our Church as teacher and pontiff.

We are confident, with the cooperation of Christ’s grace, that we have elected as our shepherd a man who corresponds to the apostolic form in which blessed Paul demonstrates what a bishop ought to be adorned with, and who does not conflict with the sacred canons. We pray that your holy fatherhood may now and always prosper in Christ.

Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, in the basilica of holy Mary, Mother of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the year of the Incarnation of that same Lord Jesus Christ 876, in the thirty-sixth year of the reign of our lord Charles the emperor, and the first year of his empire, in the ninth indiction.

## LETTER LII. TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF LAON  
### Concerning the ordination of Henedulphus, bishop of Laon

*(From the Acts of the provincial Church of Rheims.)*

[Col. 0271A]

HINCMAR, bishop of the holy metropolitan Church of Rheims, to the clergy, order, and people residing in the holy Church of Laon: peace and salvation in the Lord.

As blessed Pope Innocent teaches, we ought to follow what the Roman Church preserves, since there is no doubt that we received the beginning of sacred institution from it. Therefore, by the testimony and words of blessed Gregory, we endeavor to address you, making known that we have brought no delay to your reasonable desires, since we have ordained for you our already brother and fellow bishop Hedenulphus, in the presence, or with the consent and letters, of the fellow bishops of the entire province entrusted to us, according to the sacred canons, as priest, shepherd, and ruler.

By these letters—which the sacred canons command those who have first been ordained, instructed in the decisions of the councils so that they may not regret having done anything contrary to those statutes, to receive from their ordainers, written by their hands—we have given him, according to ecclesiastical tradition, the following instructions: he must never presume to perform unlawful ordinations; he must not permit a bigamist, or one who, if the matter concerns married men, has not taken a virgin as his wife; nor an illiterate man, one physically deformed in any part of his body, one who has publicly performed penance, one subject to the court or to any other condition, or one marked by infamy, to approach the sacred orders.

If he should happen to find anyone of this kind, he must not dare to promote him, out of regard for divine judgment. He must not solicit, receive, or ordain in the Church entrusted to him a cleric from another bishop without the will and consent of that cleric’s own bishop, contrary to the sacred regulations. Nor must he presume in any way to admit to sacred orders those whose faith has not been proven.

In the ordination of presbyters, deacons, and the other ministers of the ecclesiastical order, he must, as far as human weakness allows, present hands pure in heart and body from every form of unlawful payment—that is, from the hand, the tongue, or an improper service—according to what the Lord commands through the prophet. He must not kill both the giver and the receiver of the gift with one and the same sword, nor, having polluted his hands with an unlawful gift, suppose that he is conferring a blessing upon others, when he has already been subjected to his own iniquity and remains captive to his own ambition.

He must not compel those whom he ordains to make an improper oath to him contrary to the sacred regulations. But just as the Lord, foreknowing that some would turn the gift of the Holy Spirit they had received toward commercial use, commanded, saying, “Freely you have received, freely give” (Matt. 10), so, freely—that is, without any sale or purchase, or even any gift promised or hoped for—he received it, insofar as depended upon us, through the ministry of our lowliness. Let him also confer it freely upon his fellow ministers, knowing from the Gospel what our Redeemer did himself: namely, that when he entered the Temple, he overturned the seats of those selling doves.

For to sell doves is to receive temporal profit from the Holy Spirit, whom almighty God, consubstantial with himself, grants to human beings through the laying on of hands. Whoever presumes to do this overturns his own seat before God the Judge; and by promoting those whom he ordains for a price, he causes them also to become simoniacal heretics along with himself. Instead of a blessing, they receive the curse justly inflicted by blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, upon Simon Magus, who wished to buy the gift of the Holy Spirit for a price; together with him and through him, they receive the judgment of that same Holy Spirit, by whom they are not blessed but cursed.

And since, as we have learned, certain men, pursuing shameful profits by various devices—something wholly unbecoming to ministers of the altar—have, when presbyters died, demanded *exenia* in order to obtain the resources of churches which they had learned were left widowed; and have not conferred ecclesiastical ranks before the same *exenia* had been paid to them; and have rashly attended synods so that, through the agency of their ministers, they might receive denarii in various ways as though for *eulogies*; and, what is unspeakable, have even devised ways to obtain profit from the distribution of the sacred chrism or from the consecration of churches; and since we must seek the salutary remedies of medicine against these deadly kinds of disease, just as we have forbidden him to receive anything for the laying on of hands, so also we forbid him to receive anything from this cunning and wickedly contrived collection of the simoniacal heresy.

We admonish him to heed the Lord’s threat through the prophet: “Lest my indignation go forth like fire and burn, with no one to extinguish it, because of the wickedness of your practices” (Jer. 21:12). Again, in anger, he says: “I will visit upon you according to the fruit of your practices” (ibid., 14).

We also admonish him in the words of blessed Gregory, and forbid him, whenever he goes out through his parish to confirm infants, to burden the priests beyond measure or to exceed the amount of the contribution with which his predecessors, who carried out this duty well, mercifully, reasonably, and in accordance with the sacred constitutions, were suitably content.

As for chapels anciently subject to churches, he must not demand an equal contribution from them as from the principal churches. Rather, the principal church, together with its dependent chapels, must provide the contribution that is due and has been customary from ancient times. He must not subject principal churches to other churches as though they were chapels, since, according to the sacred canons, bishops are not permitted rashly to confuse and divide a parish established from ancient times.

He must not make presbyters prepare lodging provisions for his friends or his men. Nor must he, as though for the reception of a king, an embassy, or the adornment of his church, accept—or rather extort—money, horses, boars, *friskingas*, riding horses for some journey, or anything else, under the pretext of requesting assistance. From the verb “to take” (*accipere*) birds that seize other birds are called hawks (*accipitres*). Bishops ought not to seize their subjects like hawks, but should cherish them like a hen her chicks, and should care for each of the weak like a skilled physician, with suitable medicine and at the suitable time. Those whom they cannot cure they should either patiently tolerate or, in accordance with the rules, sustain until correction, removing them from the healthy body.

He must understand the rule concerning the fourth part of the Church’s revenues according to the custom of other regions, exactly as it is written, and must not interpret it perversely and consequently plunder, contrary to the sacred regulations, what belongs to the presbyters in these regions. Therefore, if any burdens have been imposed upon them, let him moderate them, since he will provide for himself both in the present life and in the life to come if he strives to preserve without burden those entrusted to him.

As ministers—that is, archpresbyters and archdeacons—he must appoint, insofar as he is able with the Lord’s inspiration and cooperation, men who hate avarice, do not love gifts, and do not pursue recompense; men who will accept no gift for ordaining clerics or reconciling penitents, nor strive to corrupt him by that very gift.

Let them not afflict presbyters with provisions and improper *exenia*. As we said above concerning the bishop, they must not, under various requests that they may provide assistance to them, plunder what belongs to the presbyters and from which those presbyters ought to live, receive guests, and maintain their churches, by any kind of collusion. Nor must they accept any profit in order to spare them investigation into their ministry or to suppress or cover their infamy.

If he finds ministers engaging in such acts, he must not allow them to remain in the ministry and must rebuke them with canonical condemnation. He himself must not establish rewards for appointing ecclesiastical officials—namely, the steward, that is, the dispenser of the Church’s resources, the archpresbyters, and the archdeacons—in whom he ought to choose sincerity of faith, upright conduct, and a religious life. For, having obtained their ecclesiastical service improperly, they will take gifts from their subjects and undertake to sell that service even more wickedly.

He must accept no price for any judgment contrary to the sacred laws, or against an innocent person and contrary to the truth. Nor must he, insofar as he knows and is able, deviate from righteous judgment out of hatred, favor, envy, or anger, since the Lord says: “You shall not do what is unjust, nor judge unjustly. Judge your neighbor justly, and execute what is just with justice” (Lev. 19). For the one who executes what is just with justice seeks justice itself in asserting justice.

Finally, concerning the baptism of infants or burial, in obedience to the decrees of blessed Gregory, he must not allow anyone in his parish to seek payment for land granted to corruption, or wish to make profit from another’s grief. But if someone has permitted a person to be buried in a place entrusted to him, and that person’s nearest relatives or heirs wish voluntarily to offer something for lights or as alms for the deceased, he must not forbid its acceptance. But he must prohibit anything from being requested or demanded, lest the Church be called—God forbid—very irreligious or venal, or lest priestly religion appear to rejoice in human deaths if it strives in any way to seek profit from their corpses.

He must himself abstain from all avarice, usury, and shameful profit according to the sacred canons; he must cause the ministers of the Church to abstain from them and urge laymen also to abstain. He must diligently and carefully guard himself and the ecclesiastical ministers entrusted to him, lest they become, contrary to the sacred canons, tenants or administrators of other people’s possessions.

They must not seek their livelihood through shameful business or dishonorable profit. Nor must they undertake secular business under their care. They must not, despising the ministry of God, run about through the houses of secular people, nor, out of avarice, undertake the management of the interests of estates for the sake of favor, honor, or money, or the defense of other people’s wills; nor must they serve as guarantors.

He must also cause himself and his fellow ministers to abstain, according to the sacred regulations, from improper and forbidden intimacy and cohabitation with women, and from taverns. He must also heed what blessed Job says: “If my land cries out against me, and its furrows weep with it, if I have eaten its fruits without payment” (Job 30:38).

Concerning this, blessed Gregory says in his *Moralia on Job* (book 22, chapter 15):

> “Everyone who presides, if he exercises perversity against his subjects, is opposed by the cry of the earth, and its furrows weep, because against his injustice the uneducated people indeed break out in voices of murmuring, while all the perfect afflict themselves with tears because of his wicked deed. To eat the fruits of the earth without payment is to receive expenses from the Church but not to provide it with the due price of preaching. Concerning this preaching, it is said in an authoritative voice: ‘You ought to have put my money with the bankers, and when I came I would have received what was mine with interest’ (Matt. 25:27). Therefore, he eats the fruits of the earth without payment who receives ecclesiastical benefits for the use of his body but does not provide the people with the ministry of exhortation. He demands what is owed to his body but does not provide what is owed to the hearts of his subjects.”

Therefore, a bishop must not demand redemption or payment from the contributions of presbyters and silently consume ecclesiastical provisions. And when the Lord commands preachers, as they enter the houses of those to whom they preach peace, to eat and drink what is found with them, a bishop traveling through his parish to preach and confirm must not demand excessive payments in spices or anything else from presbyters who do not possess them. He must not demand such things as he may not receive in his own house, serving pleasure rather than necessity, sparing his own resources and growing rich from what he has excessively received and sold. He must not preach in order to receive provisions; rather, he must receive provisions in order to be able to preach.

Nor must he compel churches situated on the estates of free lords and co-heirs to be handed over to his church. Rather, according to the synodal and imperial capitularies, which the Church proves to be canonical, he must strive to ensure that they have, by the authority of the king, the immunities of their endowments like the other churches, and that they themselves remain in the possession of those same free men.

With the Lord’s cooperation, he must present himself in all things in such a way that he does not bring the sacred ministry into disrepute. According to apostolic teaching, he must also have a good testimony from those who are outside. For when a man’s life is despised, it remains that his preaching too will be scorned; and when a shepherd walks over precipices, it usually happens that the flock follows him to the cliff.

We also prohibit him from excommunicating any minister of the ecclesiastical order, under the pretext of shameful profit, in order to seize something from him after he has been absolved. For, as Saint Augustine demonstrates when explaining the apostle Paul’s statement, “Remove the evil person from among you” (1 Cor. 5), the wicked are not to be removed from communion with the Church rashly or arbitrarily, but by judgment.

Much greater care must be taken that the ministers of the Church not be deprived of their office without regular judgment. Therefore, as blessed Gregory teaches, if anything concerning any cleric reaches his ears that could justly offend him, he must not readily believe it, nor let an unknown matter inflame him to vengeance, remembering what is written: “I investigated most diligently the case that I did not know” (Job 29:16).

In the presence of the elders of his Church, he must diligently strive by every means to investigate the truth. Then, if the nature of the matter requires it, let canonical strictness strike the guilt of the offender, according to the procedure established by the sacred regulations.

To sum everything up briefly, he must not himself do anything contumaciously through contempt, nor, insofar as depends upon him, permit anything to be done in his parish that is hostile to evangelical truth, apostolic tradition, or the sacred regulations. If such a thing should happen, let him strive to correct it as far as he can by reproving, beseeching, and rebuking, according to what he sees to be expedient for each person, following the tradition of his predecessors.

Let him strive to follow everywhere the pastoral rule of blessed Gregory in mind, speech, and action, insofar as the Lord has granted him knowledge and ability. Let him strive to preserve, enlarge, increase, and administer the ministry, adornment, patrimony, revenues, and resources of the Church according to the divinely promulgated laws that prescribe their arrangement. Let him exercise canonical care over the monasteries situated in his parish, and, insofar as depends upon him, preserve their due privileges and their ancient and regular custom. Let him also diligently conduct the ordinations of presbyters and the sacrament of holy baptism according to ecclesiastical tradition.

Although, by the inspiration of divine grace, he may possess abundant learning, nevertheless, in fulfillment of the duty of our office, we shall endeavor to give him from the treasury of the holy metropolitan Church of Rheims instruction concerning how, with the Lord’s cooperation, he ought to conduct himself in integrity of morals and devotion to learning.

We admonish him humbly, diligently, and obediently to have recourse to that same metropolis, as to a mother, so that he may drink salutary teaching from her catholic breasts, knowing that the care of the entire province has been entrusted to the metropolitan by the sacred canons. Let him not usurp more than has been granted to him by the sacred regulations, since we are bound to one another by so great a bond of charity and humility to the saving commandments that the divine command says to him: “Ask your father, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will declare it to you” (Deut. 32:7); and says to us: “They have appointed you ruler; do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of them” (Ecclus. 32:1); and: “He who is greatest among you shall be your servant” (Matt. 23:11).

That means serving those who obey by offering paternal instruction, and correcting those who disobey with the regular correction of charity, which is the greater duty. We ought to make use of the salutary counsels of your brothers and fellow priests, and they ought to obey paternal and regular admonitions.

Therefore, both these and the other salutary commands must be observed, and you ought to obey them with devoted minds and serve them obediently, so that the body of the Church may become irreproachable and peaceful, through Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with God the almighty Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

Hincmar, bishop of the holy metropolitan Church of Rheims and servant of the people of God, and, by the favor of God, ordainer of the venerable brother Hedenulphus in the holy Church of Laon, have subscribed these canonical letters, publicly given both to the ordained man and to his electors, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 877, in the thirty-seventh year of the reign of our lord Charles the emperor, and in the second year of his empire.

Odo, bishop of Beauvais, have subscribed.  
Raginelmus, bishop of Noyon, have subscribed.  
John, bishop of the Church of Cambrai, have subscribed.  
Willebertus, humble bishop of Châlons, have subscribed.  
Hildeboldus, bishop of the Church of Soissons, have subscribed.  
Geroldus, bishop of the Church of Amiens, have subscribed.  
Hadebertus, bishop of the Church of Senlis, have subscribed.

## LETTER LIII. TO FRANCO, BISHOP OF TONGEREN  
### He commends a certain brother

*(In the same place.)*

[Col. 0276D]

To the most reverend and most holy brother FRANCO, bishop of the Church of Tongeren, HINCMAR, bishop of the holy metropolitan Church of Rheims, wishes present and everlasting salvation.

Let your beloved charity know that this brother, named Flodulfus, has come to our lowliness for this reason: he was nurtured and educated in our place. Therefore we are sending you this letter, so that your charity may receive him more willingly.

Since from now onward he desires to receive the ecclesiastical degrees under your rule and to serve God, know that he is endowed with good morals, knowledgeable in letters, receptive in intelligence, and desirous of submitting to your rule, dwelling in your parish, and willingly obeying your admonitions and ordinances all the days of his life.

And so that this little letter might be received more willingly by your affection and believed with greater certainty, we have sealed it with the impression of our seal, bearing the image of blessed Remigius the pontiff. May almighty God deign to preserve you through many cycles of years. Amen.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of May, in the thirteenth year of our episcopate.

## LETTER LIV. TO THE SAME  
### He commends the presbyter Gisebrindus by a formal letter

*(In the same place.)*

[Col. 0277B]

Let it be known to your highness and to all men that your diocese has given us permission, and that the presbyter whom I ordained in the city of Rheims, named Gisebrindus, may exercise the priestly ministry wherever he wishes, if your sacred will is present, and that of other good men wherever he himself sees it suitable.

For this reason, at the request of the aforesaid presbyter, we have sent these letters to you, so that you may also give him your consent and permission to exercise the ministry of the presbyterate. And so that you may know this more certainly, we have composed a formal letter for him according to canonical authority and have given it to him, marking upon it in Greek letters Η. Χ. Υ.

We mark my name with the first letter, H; your name with the second letter, Ο; the letter of my city with the third, M; and that of your city with the fourth, F.

We wish that your domain may prosper and flourish forever, venerable one.

H. T. P. X. H. O. M. F. Y. II. CCCC. XL. DC. XC. III. LX. DCC. VIII.

## LETTER LV. TO THE BISHOPS OF THE PROVINCE OF LYON  
### Concerning the excommunication of Carloman and his accomplices

*(From Sirmond.)*

HINCMAR, bishop of Rheims and servant of the people of God, together with our venerable fellow priests of the diocese of Rheims, sends greetings to REMIGIUS, most reverend archbishop of Lyon, and to the venerable bishops of his diocese.

Carloman, son in the flesh of our lord, the glorious King Charles, regenerated by the Holy Spirit in the diocese of Reims and offered by his father at the sacred altar, to be dedicated to the devout duties of divine service and tonsured as a cleric; but in the diocese of Sens, and in the parish of Meaux, advanced by Hildegarius, the devout bishop of that city, through each grade up to the order of the diaconate—recently, after his father had bestowed upon him very many gifts of kindness and beneficence, he fled and gathered around himself very many sons of Belial. These committed unheard-of evils in our times in the parishes of the diocese of Reims: robberies and depredations, murders and adulteries, [Col. 0278A] violations of churches, and very many other shameful acts and crimes that can be perpetrated through diabolical instigation and human cruelty.

Our lord King Charles, devoutly and mercifully, and likewise his accomplices, he earnestly endeavored to recall four times, as you can read again in the command that he had sent to them. But I also, Hincmar, bishop of Reims, addressing him and his satellites personally, face to face, three times, and afterward for the fourth time through our fellow minister, together with certain colleagues and co-bishops of ours, having caused him and his accomplices to be publicly admonished, set before them, insofar as the Lord granted me, both the sweetness of the heavenly kingdom and the terror of eternal torments. I showed how gravely he himself had offended God by injuring his father, the holy Church, [Col. 0278B] and the whole of Christianity, and by consenting to and favoring the robbers whom he had gathered. I demonstrated how kindly both ecclesiastical piety and paternal affection ought to receive him if he abandoned the evils he had begun and returned to his father; I made known what clemency was being offered to those who were with him; and I impressed upon them that, if he neglected or despised these things and if he and his accomplices chose to persist obstinately in the undertaking of their apostasy, then, after this fourth summons, according to the Lord’s command, we would have to regard them as pagans and publicans. By episcopal authority, with the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, and according to the sacred canons—established by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world—and likewise according to the decrees of the apostolic see, they were, as true apostates, to be cut off by every means from the body and blood of the Lord and from the unity of the body of the Church, that is, from the fellowship of all Christ’s faithful.

Neither the threatened punishments terrified him and some of his men, nor did the promised sweetness attract them. Therefore—what we say with tears and announce with groaning—we separate from the body and blood of the Lord and from the fellowship and company of Christians, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit, those of his accomplices who belong to the diocese of Reims, have been entrusted to our care, and have committed in our parishes such great and such serious crimes as we have stated above. They were repeatedly admonished to repent of their evil undertakings and to return, so that they might make satisfaction, to the bosom of the pious mother Church; but they refused, and, what is unspeakable, grew worse. For, as the Apostle says, such persons will not possess the kingdom of God, and he forbids us even to eat with such people. By episcopal authority, after the fifth day before the Ides of March of the present fourth indiction, unless they correct themselves beforehand, we separate them—until perhaps God, regarding them, may, according to that same Apostle, grant them repentance so that they may recover to do his will from the snares of the devil, by which they are held captive, and may make satisfaction to the Church whom they have injured through worthy fruits of repentance. This is on the condition that, according to the form of the mystical Council of Nicaea and the canons of the province of Africa, and likewise according to the decrees of the pontiffs of the apostolic see—Siricius, Innocent, Celestine, and Leo—wherever they may be, the final penitence and communion of the necessary viaticum are not denied to those who request them. [Col. 0279A]

But those who do not belong to the diocese of Reims and are not specially entrusted to our care, yet have committed the aforementioned evils in our parishes, we have decreed to be excommunicated from those same parishes after the fifth day before the Ides of March of the present fourth indiction, unless they correct themselves beforehand. They are to have no participation there, either in ecclesiastical communion or in the fellowship of the faithful of Christ entrusted to us, because Christ has no partnership with Belial, [Col. 0280A] nor should the faithful share a portion with the unbeliever, until, with the counsel and judgment of those concerned, they make satisfaction to God and the holy Church. And because the good Shepherd, essentially and supremely good, who laid down his life for his sheep, wills that no one perish and came to seek and save what had perished, he has shown us the way we should follow and the pattern to which we should conform. We decree that, if by chance in the parishes prescribed above any of them should be overtaken by imminent and urgent death [lacuna].

[Col. 0279]

MINOR WORKS AND LETTERS OF HINCMAR, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS, RELATING TO THE CASE OF HINCMAR OF LAON.

LETTER OF HINCMAR OF REIMS TO HINCMAR OF LAON. Concerning Nivinus and his brother Bertric, whom he had expelled from the diocese of Reims as notorious for crimes.

(Printed by Sirmond from a Laon manuscript.)

[Col. 0279B]

HINCMAR, bishop of Reims, to HINCMAR, our fellow bishop, greeting.

Nivinus has been notoriously accused in my diocese of a sacrilegious outrage involving a certain nun, dedicated to God in a monastery from childhood and veiled by a priest: namely, that he first secretly violated her, then caused her to be furtively taken from the very enclosure of the monastery, kept her for some time in my diocese, with many people knowing it, and finally secretly carried her off into another province. [Col. 0279C] Accordingly, with the counsel and consent of our clergy and noble laymen, I granted him lawful and canonical time for reflection, either to confess the offence or to clear himself of the accusation against his reputation; but he was willing neither to confess his sin nor lawfully to clear himself of the accusation. Therefore, since he is not of my province, I excommunicated him from my diocese until he should either confess or clear himself of the charges.

But now I hear from many that you are receiving from him, as the price for property of his own, property in another province, and that you are giving him, as the reward of shameful gain, in benefice, ecclesiastical property and resources which, at your episcopal ordination, you received without price in order to govern and dispense them canonically. This is more than sufficiently contrary to the authority of the holy Scriptures and opposed to the decrees of the sacred canons; and, if it is so—as is widely reported by many people, even publicly in public assemblies—you understand, if you are of sound mind, how great a danger and loss you incur thereby, and how great a reproach you bring upon the priestly ministry. [Col. 0279D] [Col. 0280B]

I also repeatedly and canonically rebuked Bertric, Nivinus's brother, for adulteries and other incestuous defilements; though unreformed, he was tolerated for a long time and allowed time in the hope that he would restrain himself from his wickedness. But since I could not restrain him from his iniquities, because he is not of my province, I canonically ordered him, with his people, to leave my diocese. I have taken care to make these things known to you, as the sacred canons prescribe. Given on the Ides of February, in the present third indiction.

LETTER OF HINCMAR OF LAON TO HINCMAR OF REIMS. He clears Nivinus and himself in his affair, and censures Hincmar of Reims.

(See Patrology, vol. CXXIV, col. 979.)

LETTER OF HINCMAR OF REIMS TO HINCMAR OF LAON. He intercedes for the priest Hadulf.

(From the Acts of the ecclesiastical province of Reims.)

[Col. 0280C]

HINCMAR, bishop of Reims, to HINCMAR, beloved brother and our venerable fellow bishop, greeting.

Brother Clarentius, our fellow priest, came to me from you and told me that you had entrusted to our fellow priest Brother Hadulf a mission to Bishop Witgarius in the city of Augsburg, concerning a book of Paterius and other matters that pleased you, from which mission he did not excuse himself. Afterwards, however, you heard that he wished to go to other regions, [Col. 0280D] and you sent for him, commanding him through your cleric, by divine and episcopal authority, to return to you; and you sent your men to bring him back to you if he would not return. When he came into your presence, he did not answer you as humbly as he ought to have done, [Col. 0281A] or as pleased you; and you asked him to go to Laon and wait there until you came thither and could settle accounts with him before the brethren.

The same Hadulf went into the church at Anisy, where you too were staying, and threw himself down in prayer before the altar. But you sent after him Brother Clarentius and your deacon with him, and ordered them to forbid Hadulf, by divine and episcopal authority, to communicate in your diocese; and Hadulf put his fingers into his ears and went on his way. Subsequently the aforesaid Hadulf came to me and told me, as Clarentius had done, about the mission laid upon him and his return to you; but about the defiant answer he did not tell the same story. He also declared that, before I told him of it, he had not heard of the excommunication imposed by you. He wished to go to Laon, and sent his man ahead there together with your envoys; but the doors of the church and the gate of the cloister were shut against him, and afterwards he was unable to obtain anything of what he had in his residence there. [Col. 0281B]

He now asks me to intercede with you so that he may be permitted to communicate in your diocese, to have in full his place and residence and the things which he had served for under you, and to serve you canonically in peace. And if this should seem burdensome to you, let him at least have communion in your diocese and be allowed, under religious discipline, to live wherever he can find a place suitable for himself, and let him be faithful to you. Therefore, since your prudence knows how holy are the days at hand, in which peace especially ought to be sought, peace ought to be given to those seeking it, peace and pardon ought to be granted even to those not seeking it, every bond of impiety ought to be loosed, oppressive burdens released, and harsh commands bent down, send me without delay, by your letter and through one of our common ministers, word from the canonical practice of the Church of Laon as to what pleases you concerning Brother Hadulf himself: whether he may have communion in your diocese, and in full, with your peace, his place, residence, and the things which he had served for under you, and may live canonically with you; or whether, communion in your diocese having been granted him, he may, with your permission, live under religious discipline wherever he can find a suitable place, and wherever he can devoutly render you the fidelity which he owes you. Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April, [Col. 0281C] in the third indiction. [Col. 0281D]

LETTER OF HINCMAR OF LAON TO HINCMAR OF REIMS. He permits Hadulf, in order to regain Hincmar's favour, the place of his former residence; he does not yet grant him communion.

(See Patrology, vol. CXXIV, col. 985.)

LETTER OF THE SAME TO THE SAME. Concerning the ordination of an elderly cleric, his own detention in prison, and his appeal to the apostolic see.

(See the place cited above, same column.)

COLLECTION FROM THE LETTERS OF THE ROMAN PONTIFFS. Sent by Hincmar of Laon to Hincmar of Reims at the estate of Gundulf through Archbishop Wenilo.

(See Patrology, vol. CXXIV, col. 1001.)

A TREATISE OF FIFTY-FIVE CHAPTERS AGAINST HINCMAR OF LAON.

(Printed by Sirmond.)

TABLE OF CHAPTERS.

The opening of the letter shows what he commanded me and what I answered him, and how foolish his command was, when he said [Col. 0282B] that I had suggested to him that he excommunicate his own diocese; and he did not observe how he had ensnared himself.

CHAP. I. An account is given concerning the chapel about which he wrote to me.

CHAP. II. Concerning his acquisition, contrary to the canons, of the administration of the palace and an abbey; concerning his failure to come when summoned to an episcopal ordination, and the answer he gave when rebuked for it; and concerning the irregular excommunication of Amalbert.

CHAP. III. Concerning the irregular excommunication directed against parishioners of various bishops.

CHAP. IV. Concerning his command that I should burn the writings sent to him and to his diocese for dissolving his unlawful excommunication.

CHAP. V. Concerning his reported boast that he can resist me and dares despise me; and that, because two of my judgments have been annulled by the apostolic see, he need not answer me.

CHAP. VI. Concerning his reported habit of saying that I ought to be deposed because, in his diocese, I loosed what he had bound.

CHAP. VII. Concerning his seeking to clear himself of charges brought against him, not by ecclesiastical but by secular procedure.

[Col. 0282C] CHAP. VIII. Concerning letters sent by the apostolic lord to the lord king and to me on behalf of his complaint.

CHAP. IX. Concerning a monk excommunicated by him.

CHAP. X. Concerning the compilation from letters of the apostolic see sent to me in little quires, and concerning the public pronouncement and a chapter of Pope Leo.

CHAP. XI. That a fuller treatment of holy orders and canonical discipline must be given from the words and thought of the orthodox.

CHAP. XII. What orders exist in heaven, in the Church, and in the earthly commonwealth.

CHAP. XIII. That although the order is common to all bishops, their dignity is not common to all.

CHAP. XIV. That in the commonwealth also, after the pattern of the heavenly host, there are diverse orders.

CHAP. XV. Concerning the fatherhoods and dwellings established by God in heaven, after whose pattern fatherhoods and dwellings have been divinely apportioned in the Church and in the commonwealth.

CHAP. XVI. Concerning the established metropolitan see of the province of Reims and the fortress-town of Laon; and that, although three bishops preside over the three principal sees, they are nevertheless the one see of Peter. Also concerning the letter sent by Hormisdas to Saint Remigius, and how Saint Remigius, when ordaining a bishop in the fortress-town of Laon, caused him to sit in the lower seat of his metropolitan see and to be counted among its sees. [Col. 0282D]

CHAP. XVII. Concerning the rebellion of lesser priests against their superiors in both the Old and the New Testament; concerning metropolitans, archbishops, primates, and patriarchs; concerning the apostolic see; concerning the Church of Constantinople rebelling against the apostolic see and usurping for itself the name of universality; and what Pope Saint Gregory, writing to various persons, decreed concerning that name.

CHAP. XVIII. That one who has a cataract in his eye—that is, arrogance in his mind—cannot see lowly things; and how men of unsound mind have erred through lack of discernment in the holy Scriptures.

CHAP. XIX. That likewise men, madly misunderstanding the enactments of holy traditions and delighting in novel expressions, have on various pretexts separated themselves from the Church.

CHAP. XX. How he should beware of taking offence in the interpretation of Scripture and sacred canons, and how ecclesiastical teaching has expanded over time. [Col. 0283] Also concerning letters of pontiffs of the apostolic see, given before the holy councils to various persons for the consolation of various persons; and that, just as in public laws some provisions have been repealed, some altered, and others added, so also some things later were repealed or altered among decrees of Catholics issued according to time, reason, and necessity. Also concerning certain forms of canons; concerning what Saint Augustine wrote to Boniface on penance; concerning the diversity of the enactments in the aforesaid letters from which he made his compilation; concerning the six general synods and the name of universality; concerning what the apostolic see thought of the Gallican canons; concerning the privilege and keys of the kingdom of heaven entrusted to Blessed Peter and, in him, to the whole Church of the elect; concerning the letters of Julius and Felix and the Council of Sardica; and whence arose the opinion that more than twenty chapters were enacted at the Council of Nicaea.

CHAP. XXI. Why successors of the ancient pontiffs of the apostolic see did not employ certain matters found written in their letters, while certain matters set down in their decrees were adopted by councils among the sacred canons; and that only the twenty chapters which we possess were enacted at the Council of Nicaea.

CHAP. XXII. Concerning the four chapters mentioned by Blessed Gregory in his letter to the patrician Theoctista, some of which this brother of ours, committing a fraud, has wrongly interpreted, just as others are read to have done formerly, for which they were refuted and deposed in a general synod.

CHAP. XXIII. That the apostolic see does not accept part of the ninth chapter, together with its recapitulation in chapter 17, as Pope Saint Leo shows.

CHAP. XXIV. That some have attempted to revive and restore what the apostolic see rejected from it, alleging that the Synod of Chalcedon must either be held valid in its entirety or judged invalid in its entirety; that the apostolic see accepts the faith of the Council of Constantinople held in the time of Pope Damasus and Emperor Gratian, but does not accept that council's canons; that it accepts the canons of the Council of Chalcedon except for that one chapter recapitulated in chapter 17; concerning the canons called Apostolic; concerning the rulings said to have been collected from Greek and Latin canons, Roman synods, and decrees of Roman bishops and rulers by Pope Adrian and given to Angelram, bishop of Metz; concerning Isidore's preface in the book of letters; and concerning this brother's assertion that I alone do not understand the canons, his rebuke of me because I say that I knew the canons before he was born, and the fact that he might seek matters more necessary than such things as will not benefit his purpose. Also concerning the schedule which I sent him at Gundulf's estate through Lord Wenilo; concerning his statement, “If anyone has presumed to speak against the decrees of the Roman pontiffs”; and concerning the fact that, as he himself said, he exercised me by his compilation in a perverse order, and I was compelled, tracing its winding paths, to unfold it by a thousand routes, as the saying goes.

CHAP. XXV. Daniel's saying is explained: “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Dan. XII). Also concerning what Blessed Gelasius says in the Catalogue in which he set out which books are received by the Catholic Church, and the distinction he makes between holy councils and the aforesaid letters of the pontiffs of the apostolic see given to various persons for the consolation of various persons; concerning what the Apostle says of the old law and its ceremonies; concerning what Saint Augustine says from Cyprian's words about custom, and the distinction he demonstrates in the books On Baptism between epistolary discussion, by which the apostolic letters now in question were composed, and a regional or plenary council; between earlier and later councils; and between sacred Scripture and councils of bishops; concerning the mystical Synod of Nicaea; and concerning what Blessed Augustine says about councils in his other books.

CHAP. XXVI. An addition by way of supererogation sets forth what Blessed Augustine says to Januarius concerning councils, and what is said concerning this in Justinian's edict on the Fifth Synod; what Blessed Hilary says of the Synod of Antioch; that nothing in the Council of Nicaea has been repealed or altered by Catholics; what pontiffs of the apostolic see decreed concerning metropolitan and suffragan bishops; what Blessed Ambrose and Hilary say concerning the privilege of the Council of Nicaea; and what Leo wrote on this subject in many places.

CHAP. XXVII. Concerning this brother's statement, in the metrical title of his compilation:

“A response is not rightly to be demanded from one in bonds.”

Also concerning his message sent to me through our fellow ministers whom I had sent to him, that he ought not to answer concerning the matters laid before him; and what the sacred canons and the apostolic see decreed concerning a suffragan's obedience to his metropolitan.

[Col. 0284] CHAP. XXVIII. Concerning the irregular excommunication inflicted by this brother of ours upon ecclesiastical ministers of his diocese; who ought equally to be excommunicated by a bishop; and that, as there are two sins, two kinds of sinners, and two comings of the Lord, one hidden and the other manifest, so there are two judgments, one hidden and the other manifest, and two judicial orders, and how these two orders are to be carried out.

CHAP. XXIX. What the sacred canons say concerning those excommunicated by individual provincial bishops for causes unknown to the primate of the province and the other bishops: no one ought, before examination, presume to admit them to communion; and how one must act toward those whose causes are manifest and known to many, but who are irregularly excommunicated.

CHAP. XXX. By what reason and authority, through the sacred rules, he loosed what this brother of ours irregularly bound in his diocese; that his excommunications were not ecclesiastical bindings but curses issued by his agitated mind, contrary to evangelical truth and the apostolic and sacred rules; whom the sacred canons do not forbid others to receive when excommunicated, and whom they forbid to be received; what Blessed Gregory decreed concerning episcopal binding; what the sacred canons say on this matter; what the laws accepted by the Church determine concerning one who has unjustly excommunicated; and what the apostolic see has promulgated from these same laws.

CHAP. XXXI. Concerning his forbidding the baptism of little children who are often in danger at the crisis of death.

CHAP. XXXII. Concerning his ordering that penance be denied and that the gift of viaticum not be afforded to the dying, contrary to the Nicene and African canons and the decrees of Siricius, Innocent, Celestine, and Leo; concerning the chapter of Celestine in which he omitted something; and concerning what Saint Gregory said in an anathema against anyone who, contrary to the sacred Council of Nicaea and the other venerable councils, binds persons whom those councils loose and looses those whom they bind. The sacred Council of Nicaea says (can. 13): “That, generally, the grace of communion is not to be denied to anyone whatsoever who is at the point of departure and asks for it.” Blessed Gregory says (book I, epistle 24): “Whoever thinks otherwise, let him be anathema.”

CHAP. XXXIII. Concerning his ordering burial to be denied to the dead, as is contained in the petition presented to me by the Church of Laon.

CHAP. XXXIV. Because, in certain and manifest cases which are in no respect doubtful or obscure to us, and concerning which we have definitive judgments promulgated by the holy Fathers that can be overturned on no grounds, I ought not to wait for a synodal consultation or the counsel or consent of the fellow bishops of our province; nor ought I to depart from the established rules through negligence or presumption, nor even trouble the apostolic see by consulting it on the matter. Rather, according to those definitive judgments which have been established, I ought to decree and to bind or loose.

CHAP. XXXV. That all of us primates of provinces, established by the Lord and confirmed by apostolic authority, and likewise all Catholic bishops, concerning certain and manifest matters for which we have explicit definitive judgments to be kept incontrovertibly and inviolably, decree and judge in accordance with the sacred canons and decrees of the pontiffs of the Roman see; and that the apostolic see and the Catholic Church founded upon the foundation of the apostles, as it coordinates in ordinations, so also canonically decrees with us in decreeing and judges with us in judging. That, laws having been established, judgment must be made not about them but according to them. That by his irregular subscription this brother of ours cannot bind what was regularly loosed according to the sacred canons and decrees of the pontiffs of the Roman see. Also concerning matters which he sent in his compilations from Lucius and various predecessors and earlier predecessors of his who lived before the sacred Council of Nicaea; his misunderstanding of the proposition that no metropolitan should hear certain cases without the application of all the other bishops of the province; the distinction between a hearing and hearing or audience; between naming and naming together with examination; and again between examination and recognition; what it means to sell doves; and how grave is the danger of receiving any gift for the laying on of hands by which the Holy Spirit is received.

CHAP. XXXVI. Concerning the necessity which compels me to repeat that, if I had refused to correct what he wrongly did, I should have departed through negligence from the established rules from which he himself departed through presumption; concerning the chapters of Pope Leo; concerning the character of his irregular subscription, about which necessity compelled me to set down, point by point, from sacred Scripture and the tradition of the elders, what should be thought; and that, contrary to Blessed Hilary's teaching, he demanded the letter where the meaning did not endanger conscience, and caused them to subscribe to what it is not salutary to confess, provided that what is known to have been subscribed by him and his accomplices is in any respect contrary to the sacred Council of Nicaea, the decrees of the pontiffs of the Roman see made after the Council of Nicaea, and the sacred canons promulgated from them. [Col. 0285]

CHAP. XXXVII. He is warned not to be wise in his own eyes, contrary to the Prophet and the Apostle; and concerning discernment in maintaining peace.

CHAP. XXXVIII. He is warned to understand the words of sacred Scripture and the sacred rules as proceeding from the Holy Spirit by whom sacred Scripture too was composed.

CHAP. XXXIX. He is admonished and entreated to remove pain from me, danger from himself, and from us both the reproach inflicted by many.

CHAP. XL. Concerning his assertion that whatever has been done against him concerning his own men and men sent by the king to Laon, and concerning the fact that the king commended him, was accomplished at my instigation, counsel, and consent.

CHAP. XLI. That if I acknowledged myself guilty in this matter, since confession is the first hope of salvation and love follows it, I would not fail to seek the healing medicine of pardon, not from human but from divine fear and brotherly love.

CHAP. XLII. Concerning the removal from us both of the reproach inflicted by many.

CHAP. XLIII. Concerning my hearing that he is defaming me before many, saying that I am accustomed to mutilate the sacred Scriptures and bend them to my own interpretation—an act which I can now show that he has committed four times. Also concerning the letter sent by me to him about two men excommunicated from my diocese, because they were from another province and disdained to make satisfaction in my diocese for matters laid to their charge. Concerning his addition, after quotations from Anacletus, Victor, Callistus, and Eleutherus, who before the Council of Nicaea, as Gelasius says, sent their letters to various persons for certain consolations: “Behold, Father, which canons are to be received, venerated, and observed, and what the pontiffs of the apostolic see have thought concerning canons.” Concerning what he set down about the proscription, according to the laws, of an accuser against an accused person; the distinction between admonition and judgment upon an accusation; and between my statement, “if it is so, as is widely reported by many, even publicly in public assemblies,” and what the apostolic see thought concerning the petition presented. Also concerning a hearing without petition or accusation; an accusation of a bishop or cleric of any rank; the rule that no one is to accuse by mandate; and before whom a bishop must be accused. That the often-mentioned letters, given by the apostolic see for the consolation of various persons, are to be received with reverence, although he calls them canons; that councils instituted by the holy Fathers are to be kept and received with authority; that he inserts into his sayings obscure words and scraps collected from every quarter through glosses for display; concerning the instruction which he sent ironically through Bertric; concerning his charge against me that he knew and understood, had often heard me, and had received and maintained false reports as true; that I willingly hear lying words and readily lend my ear to his detractors for advantage; and that I often admonished him secretly by word and writing, as I do also in this chapter by the testimonies of the saints.

CHAP. XLIV. How he can return to the sweetness of paternal love once bestowed upon him by me; and that one who presumes to overthrow the orders and distinctions of bishops, the sacred canons, the decrees of the pontiffs of the Roman see, and also the laws approved and observed by the Church, strives to cut himself off from the universal Church.

CHAP. XLV. He is admonished to remember with how much kindness he was received by the lord king in the first days when he came to the episcopate; how much sweetness he enjoyed from me; with what unanimity he lived with our brethren and fellow bishops; with how much love he was honoured by the palace officials and the other people of this land; and with what reverence of affection he was venerated by those entrusted to him and also by our people, among whom, with whom, and by whom he had been reared—he who is now a song to all the day long. And concerning his assertion that he will not agree with me that the apostolic see should not possess its authority.

CHAP. XLVI. Concerning his reported vain boast that, in whatever he has undertaken against the king, against me, against any of his own people, clerical or lay, who acted against his will, or against his neighbours who rose up against him, he has always won for the most part and will overcome what remains.

CHAP. XLVII. Since he will not deign to call himself defeated, and will receive what has been written for his instruction and correction not for edification but for contention, [Col. 0286] I have set before him from the words of Blessed Gregory three things: sin, the cause of sin, and the punishment of sin, which, even if he wishes to deny it, prove that he committed it. Three further things are also set before him from the words of Blessed Augustine, so that, as it is written, he may see, know, reflect, and understand together. Also concerning the distinction which Blessed Augustine shows in the books On Baptism between an idol made and worshipped, the burning of the prophetic book by the wrath of a contemptuous king, and an attempted schism; concerning what he inserted in his perverse subscription: “If any persons, unwilling to become sharers in this discipline otherwise, are not to be held participants in our communion”; that true bonds, as true sacraments, exist only in Catholic unity undivided by heresies or schisms; that spiritual persons are not divided from the Church even unjustly by others unless they divide themselves; and what the sacred canons say concerning priests, deacons, and bishops who divide themselves from the Church. That, as is shown in the thief converted on the cross, suffering sometimes fulfils the place of baptism; concerning Cornelius and his household receiving the Spirit before baptism; concerning John's baptism; and that in the thief salvation is complete because through mercy that which was bodily lacking through necessity was spiritually present to him, just as it is to little children when others answer for them, though it does not have equal force when someone can answer for himself. That little children are not deprived of participation in and benefit of Christ's body and blood, even if, before they eat that bread and drink that cup, they depart this world while established in the unity of Christ's body. And concerning what Blessed Ambrose says about Valentinian, who died without bodily baptism.

CHAP. XLVIII. He is warned to consider carefully from these matters what he should think concerning little children who died without baptism by his command, and those who died without the gift of viaticum by his order; what the sacred rules say about this; what Saint Augustine says concerning those who love their own judgment too much, or through envy of their betters proceed as far as the sacrilege of cutting off communion and establishing schism or heresy; and the fine praise of Blessed Cyprian, who, although he held a different opinion on baptism than he should have done, nevertheless did not through obstinacy separate himself from the unity of the Church. That primacy exists only in holy conduct and a good life; that in heresy or schism nothing can be bound or loosed; that the Holy Spirit, said to be given by laying on of hands only in the Catholic Church, was understood by our elders to mean charity—a charity which one who separates himself from the unity of the Catholic Church does not possess; that communion of Christ's body and blood is the sign of unity; that one who assents to a schismatic cannot be denied to be a schismatic, and, if he tastes the heavenly bread, eats judgment to himself; and that after a revelation has been made, one who persists in his error sins knowingly and deliberately, without the excuse of ignorance. There follows the counsel of the orthodox concerning how he himself, and those led astray or enticed by him, may correct what they have done wrongly.

CHAP. XLIX. He is warned not to neglect the talent of understanding which the Lord freely gave him.

CHAP. L. Concerning what some say: that he cannot bear patiently to be told by anyone that someone has bestowed some good upon him without his merit.

CHAP. LI. Concerning what many say: that he burdens clerics and laymen entrusted to him with many exactions on various pretexts; therefore, from the words of the saints, he is warned, if it is true, to repent of such things and beware of them in future.

## Chapter 52

Concerning the fact that many accuse him of being carried away by pride, boasting of empty glory, and being overcome by arrogance. He is therefore admonished to correct himself and, since he has been placed as an example of humility, not to provide an occasion for detraction. He is also admonished concerning the report that he boasts before many of the strength and agility of his body; and because he frequently and willingly tends to speak about battles and—as it is said in the language of our people—about vassal-service matters, and irreverently to relate what he would do if he had been a layman. He also speaks and acts in other ways that do not befit him, without telling me.

## Chapter 53

And since many reproach him for disorderly bodily movements, he is admonished from the words of the saints how he should avoid them.

## Chapter 54

He is admonished not to allow himself to be deceived by the flower of youth, bodily health, and the enticements of the world, always keeping before the eyes of his mind what the Holy Spirit says here.

## Chapter 55

In conclusion of all these matters, he is told that blessed Elijah, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to Elisha, who was to be filled with the same Holy Spirit: “What was mine I have done for you.” This conclusion of the letter ends with a prayer: “May we obtain by divine grace”—that is, by grace freely given—“what we are unable to obtain by our merits.”

# Metrical Title of the Compilation Fabricated by Hincmar, Bishop of Laon, for Lord King Charles

[Col. 0287A]

This *pitatiolus* [a word of uncertain sense] plainly and fittingly brings forth

that the Apostolic See should be freely appealed to,

and that the one appealing should not be constrained by any chains,

nor should a response rightly be demanded from one bound.

It distinguishes the archbishop’s authority and limits

from those of his fellow bishops, as a sober man should.

May peace, life, and power belong to pious King Charles,

who, seeing these things, may approve them because of his probity.

If it is stolen from him by any human efforts,

he rejects it by cancelling it, when the truth of the matter returns.

[Col. 0287B]

Thus his mind, so fervent in love of truth,

does not allow what ought rightly to be frustrated to stand.

For gentle wisdom preserves his spirit strong,

which piety, above all else, redeems as its own.

O how happy is the king, a strong lover of virtues,

whom the piety of goodness alone so greatly surpasses!

But he, knowing you, Christ, as God, freely loves you;

he rejects what you reject and establishes what you establish.

Entrusting himself to you, he reveres your words;

now and forever, protect what is yours.

# Response

Concerning this title, young priest Hincmar,

it is fitting that I answer you with equal skill.

Do not be excessively wise in your own eyes, for that blinds a person.

[Col. 0287C]

Infer from the genuine forms that these inventions of yours are false,

as the very opening of your poem clearly shows them to be

of a defective grammatical gender.

For the ancients used *pitatiolus* as a neuter word,

and this sickly head shows that the rest is equally disordered.

You have compiled, for varying times and occasions,

compositions drawn from the pronouncements of the Apostolic See,

setting such things in your judgment above established councils;

from you the good and life-giving Spirit, their interpreter, is absent.

You flee from the counterfeit heart which sound discipline

does not govern, and from the things your desires simultaneously vomit forth.

Hence what the wise man once said suits you:

“A fat belly does not possess a subtle mind.”

And a mind swollen and distended with self-regard

cannot see the harmful deeds that it nevertheless itself commits.

[Col. 0287D]

Thus he always hastens to proclaim others guilty,

and thinks himself clean if he stains those who are pure.

But a contrite heart, an offering pleasing to the Lord,

attributes all evils to itself and all good things to God.

You flee from blame, yet nonetheless add blame,

attacking the innocent and thereby revealing your own guilt.

Swollen in conduct and deeds, as in body and heart,

you are said to be excessively flighty in movement and speech.

You were unable to rupture your mother’s womb

while she carried you within her, but now you desire to tear it apart.

You are a child born in piety, forgetful of the parent’s gifts,

who made you, once nurtured, sacred through honor.

The king, not—as you say—stolen away by any human efforts,

has not rejected concerning you what he knows well.

[Col. 0288A]

He has often tested how fixed your praise is—

this praise of yours, which changes with time and speech alike.

Yet a prudent man does not say everything at once,

for he keeps the proper times distinct in his mind.

And recognizing that you do not wish to abandon the leopard’s skin,

he allows you to fall by your own misfortunes.

You heap together certain things that strongly contradict you,

and which wound you all the more, though you think them pleasing to you.

Many matters appear to have been omitted by you from your studies;

because you despise them, you keep silent about them through fraud and deceit.

In your impurity you falsified certain things,

not fearing to introduce errors, because purity does not please you.

For the sacred decrees of the canons plainly bring forth,

and the laws of the Apostolic See confirm,

that the metropolitan is to have charge of the region,

so that he may preside over it, skillful in speech and discerning in action.

[Col. 0288B]

All legal matters are to come to him,

with everyone seeking his judgment; he himself stands foremost.

Under whose governance the whole province is established,

so that he may always fit it to the holy laws.

In obscure and doubtful matters he is to seek what is certain,

and, with the counsel of the brothers, determine what must be observed.

The Scriptures, nevertheless, and the sayings of the saints,

have established enduring laws; let them bring no burdensome offense.

Since every bishop of the region is subject to him,

he should be humble toward the humble and strict toward the strict.

Remaining gentle in heart, let him be fervent in zeal,

and carefully preserve what the canons prescribe;

distinguishing ages, causes, persons, times, actions,

and places, let him weigh together what must be done.

[Col. 0288C]

In all things the brothers should always await

his moderation, as the holy rule teaches.

So that, made one in Christ, father and brothers

through the bonds of charity, they may create no schisms.

For the angelic orders are preeminent in heaven’s height,

arranged in an ordered hierarchy beneath one another;

from this arises the definite distinction among priests,

and a varied order governs the peoples of the world.

You bear many members throughout your whole body,

and you see them serving their proper functions.

Therefore, with the pomp that deceives the proud mind,

bring yourself low beneath the life-giving commands of the Lord,

whose fearful words you do not hesitate to set aside,

and, swollen with pride, even desire to empty them of force.

Beyond doubt, an evil spirit suggests all this to you

[Col. 0288D]

and constantly supplies whatever belongs to him.

He is the ruler of those whom blind pride conquers,

who have been willingly made his offspring.

Finally, concerning what you say has been properly and fittingly brought forth—

that the Apostolic See should be freely appealed to—

who is ignorant of what you confess that you know?

Or are the things of God known only to you?

Indeed, the sacred canons, the Roman decrees,

and the laws proclaim it, and it is clear to everyone,

how, when, where, by whom, and concerning what matters

the See itself may be appealed to, not through fickle frivolity,

and who, and on behalf of whom, has appealed to that See

and should not be bound by any human being.

[Col. 0289A]

And who, and on behalf of whom, once stripped of his own possessions,

should not give a response when summoned—

the holy rule itself plainly indicates to you

how the proper order in these matters can be established.

If you knew the laws honored by the path of the canons,

you would clearly understand all that plainly lies open;

and you would perceive that these things are known to you,

unless, being full of a great eye-film, it dulled your sight.

While you attribute these things to yourself and boast arrogantly that you know them,

a dark night lies in the eye of your heart.

For this reason you are forbidden to offer bread to the Lord,

and even to touch the rights of the ministry.

You bear this from the proud author who fell from the light,

who sees everything lofty, indeed, but sees it lethally.

This is the one who prompts you to marvel at what you yourself accomplish—

[Col. 0289B]

something not marvelous but rather pitiable,

and detestable according to the true order of things,

not to be affirmed at all as something unlawful.

For this reason alone you seem to proclaim so loudly

the secure avenues to the Apostolic See,

so that you may freely carry out whatever you greatly desire.

Yet not everything is permitted that you may perhaps desire.

Rather, you are all the more certain of this because you yourself do not wish

to be subject to anyone, as the rule of justice demands.

Thus you imitate him who willingly desired to be subject to no one,

falling miserably through every evil;

who, having already become such through his own vice,

fears no one and afterwards fears no evil.

You follow him also in this, since you are unwilling to repent of anything

[Col. 0289C]

that you began wickedly, even when it pleases you too late,

just as he himself could not repent after he had exalted himself

above all things and, first of all, had miserably fallen to the depths.

But if you should perhaps conquer the stubborn dispositions

to which you cling so firmly by deliberate resolve,

you will immediately be able securely to hold fast to the truth,

by which you are yourself now overcome, even against your will.

And, being double-minded and inconsistent as you proceed through everything,

you soothe royal hearts with an appeasing tongue.

By despising him [the king], you know that you repeatedly injure yourself,

not obeying the command of apostolic law,

nor what the holy canons, the public laws,

and what the See itself establishes.

Namely, that every province must always everywhere

be subject to its own metropolitan See.

[Col. 0289D]

Whether you wish it or not, this will remain firm forever;

thus the Holy Spirit truly established it,

as I, your metropolitan bishop of Rheims,

sent to you written in a small document.

The whole world follows, venerates, and honors it,

and you cannot reject it, even if you should wickedly wish to.

In reversed verses, young priest Hincmar,

take back what has been returned to you, drawn from your sacred sources,

taking sevenfold within your own bosom, poet,

as justice demands, from the hands of the Lord.

# Hincmar, Bishop of the Holy Metropolitan Church of Rheims, to Hincmar, Our Fellow Bishop of Laon: Greeting

## Preface

[Col. 0290A]

Recently, when some time had passed, as is known to you and to many others, we were at Gundulfi’s estate in the service of our lord king, together with many archbishops and bishops and his other faithful servants. Since our fellow priests and venerable archbishops and bishops—just as others senior to you in rank, superior in the dignity of their order, and older in age—had made me [your metropolitan], and since you especially ought to have done so, you refused to approach my lowliness and give me the kiss of peace. You did not even deign to speak a single word with me. I do not say that you gave a great spectacle, but rather a wretched one, to many.

Therefore, concerning this matter, the venerable Archbishop Wenilo, as he told me, spoke with you and asked why you did not maintain the peace due to me and why you declined to offer the reverence due in obedience. He received from you the answer that, if I would burn before the others the writings concerning your excommunication of your parish, which I had sent to you and which you had there with you, and declare them annulled, confessing that I had acted contrary to reason, then you would wish to be at peace with me.

He also said that you had sent me word that I had suggested to you what you had done concerning that excommunication. For you have a certain estate in my parish; and because you had asked the people of that estate to give their tithe to the church to which they ought to have given it, I had excommunicated them. You also had written down how many children had died without baptism and how many people from there had died without communion—matters which you did not wish to bring publicly against me, lest I afterward reproach you that, if you knew other evils concerning me, you would mention those as well.

I therefore immediately sent you word through him that you could bring against me whatever you wished, concerning that matter or any others that seemed appropriate to you, but that you should not speak falsely about this case. I possess a document perversely compiled by you, and still more perversely interpreted after you had compiled it, which I received through Hadulf, your archpriest. I also possess the proceedings concerning what you yourself did regarding that church, as well as what and how I did concerning it, written out in a true account. Whenever you wished, I could show them either to certain brothers and our fellow priests or, if you preferred, in a synod.

But in this confession of yours, in which you said that I had suggested to you what you did concerning that excommunication, I considered three matters.

First, if a case were to be heard between you and the clerics of the Church of Laon concerning the petition they presented to me, and concerning whether the matters contained in it rested upon truth, it ought to admit no question after it had been confirmed by the testimony of your own confession.

Second, by suppressing in silence the good things that I suggested to you and caused to be suggested to you, while imputing to me that I had wrongly advised you concerning the excommunication you had carried out,

[Col. 0291A]

you confessed yourself guilty, because you knowingly acted wrongly. Consequently, according to the decrees of Pope Hilary, you yourself ought to undo your act contrary to the rules; and if you refused, metropolitan authority ought to annihilate it.

Third, so that you might entangle me with yourself—if, as can happen to an unprepared mind, I had immediately rejected these false accusations against me and, unprepared and angered, had failed to answer, allowing you to boast that I had somehow admitted the matter—you deliberately sought to throw around yourself the snare of such a confession. Repaying good with evil, you resolved openly and shamelessly to attack me, not by pretending peace with a kiss, as once did the chief of the traitors, while lacking peace in your heart, but by drawing the sword of your tongue. You sought, as though I had been betrayed as your patron, benefactor, and ordainer,

[Col. 0291B]

to suspend yourself in the snare of such a confession concerning such great impieties.

But blessed be the Lord, who, according to his promise, by which he said, “You shall be hidden from the scourge of the tongue” (Job 5:21), helped me by freeing my soul from lying lips and a deceitful tongue, and consoled me. I immediately rejected the weapon of falsehood by answering it with the shield of truth.

I say this, pierced by grief of spirit, not driven by the bitterness of resentment, knowing that many false accusations were brought against our head and Savior, and that false witnesses were produced against him. For we read that mortal and heinous crimes were falsely laid against the Roman pontiffs Damasus, Sixtus, and Leo III, and also against the bishops of other distinguished churches—namely Athanasius of Alexandria, John of Constantinople, and Caecilian of Carthage—men illustrious in the holiness of their faith, conduct, and learning, as well as against very many other venerable bishops. These accusations were brought by envious men who wished to obtain their positions and the reputation of their good name, but who strove without possessing their merit; and the charges were carried as far as ecclesiastical judgments and public hearings.

[Col. 0291C]

There are indeed men of this viperous wickedness who, although their own minds are first gnawed by envy, nevertheless think that they can conceal their own iniquities if they take care to stain others with infamy by any means. Those holy men endured their accusations with the greatest patience and, with the Lord’s help, overcame them with the greatest steadfastness.

Looking to the outcome of their conduct, as it is written (Hebrews 13:7), I must imitate their faith. Experience has taught me—and I have experienced this completely in your case against me—that a madman often gives no one a greater slap than the physician who wishes to cure him.

I was also greatly astonished at where you had your senses when you said of a man of such authority, wisdom, and religious seriousness as Lord Wenilo—and caused the matter to reach the knowledge of many bishops—that you would not be able to prove what you had said in a regular court, especially since you had confessed yourself guilty of this very matter. By confessing that you had done things which, even if you did not confess them, you could not deny having perpetrated, you were unable to see that you had entangled yourself.

For the laws approved by the Church say (Theodosian Code, concerning accusations, book 19):

[Col. 0292A]

“Certainly, those who have confessed their crimes during an inquiry are not to be believed by a judge if they wish to speak about others, because it has been established by law and legal enactment that a guilty person, by voluntary confession, does not make another guilty; nor should credence be given concerning another to one who has confessed himself to be a criminal.”

And again (in the same work, book 12):

“One must not believe against others the confession of those who are accused of crimes, unless they have first proved themselves innocent, because the confession of a guilty person against anyone whatsoever is dangerous and must not be admitted.”

And the canons say (Council of Africa, canons 96–97):

“Those whom the public laws do not admit to accusing public crimes are not to be admitted to an accusation.
