And whenever many crimes are brought against clerics by their accusers, if they have been unable to prove one of those charges—the one with which they first dealt—they are not to be admitted to the others.”

And again the canons say (Council of Carthage, canon 18):

“When bishops or clerics are to be ordained, the decisions of the councils should first be impressed upon their ears by those ordaining them, so that they may not afterward regret having done anything contrary to the council’s statutes.”

These were impressed upon you by me when you were ordained. Among them were those matters by which, in this unlawful excommunication and in your contempt for obedience, you resisted the admonitions given to you—not once or twice, but even a third time—from Scripture and the sacred rules, urging you to correct it. For it is written:

“Obedience is better than sacrifices, and to listen than to offer the fat of rams; for rebellion is like the sin of divination, and refusal to submit is like the crime of idolatry” (1 Kings 15:22).

[Col. 0292C]

But before the Church of Rheims, in which you were nurtured, and before the Church of Laon that was to be entrusted to you, and before the bishops who were present, as well as before the representatives of those bishops who were absent in bodily presence, after your confession of faith you personally affirmed that you would observe what had been impressed upon you—especially the obedience that you were regularly to show to your metropolis and to your metropolitan.

When, before the altar of Saint Mary and in the presence of all who were there, I placed in your hands the book of the sacred canons and the pastoral rule of blessed Gregory, adjuring you to preserve in living, teaching, and judging as far as God granted you knowledge and ability what was written there, you confirmed by your agreement that you would observe those books, which you had received under divine testimony and that of the faithful Church mentioned above.

[Col. 0292D]

Therefore the sacred canons say (Second Council of Carthage, chapter 13):

“If anyone in any respect acts contrary to his profession or subscription, he shall deprive himself of his honor.”

And holy Pope Leo writes to the Emperor Leo (Letter 84, through Philoxenus), concerning his agreement with the laws and what would follow if he acted against it:

“I submit myself,” he says, “to those conditions of punishment which not only the authority of the emperor Marcian, of blessed memory, but also I myself have confirmed by my agreement.”

And the canons of Carthage say (First Council of Carthage, canon 14):

“We ought to observe whatever has been set forth above, whether done or said, and whatever has been written by other councils, which is found to accord with the law. But if anyone transgresses and violates the statutes, or thinks that they should be treated as nothing, if he is a layman, let him be deprived of communion; if a cleric, of his honor. All said: ‘It is pleasing; it is pleasing.’”

# Chapter One  
## Concerning the Chapel Situated at Attola’s Estate

As for the case of the chapel about which you sent me word, the matter stands as follows. For although that chapel, situated for a long time at Attola’s estate, had been subject to the church in the village of Juviniaca, as I shall show below, your provost Bertharius—according to what many people said, and what the outcome of the matter also made clear—came to that same chapel at your command. He forbade the tithe to be given to the priest of our parish, to whom it had been entrusted and who had been ordained to it already thirty years earlier; and, as seemed right to him, he ordered that same tithe to be divided.

Moreover, he shut off that priest’s storehouse and placed in it, without the priest’s permission, grain gathered from demesne lands, removing all authority over it from the priest before any case concerning the matter had come to me or to my assistant. Even if you had any claim concerning it, the African canons say (canon 87):

[Col. 0293B]

“Bishops who think that certain churches or parishes belong to their see, if they do not reclaim them by having their cases heard before bishops acting as judges but, while another party resists, rush in upon them—whether the congregations wish it or not—shall suffer loss in their case,” and so forth, as follows there.

When our brother and fellow priest Ausoldus, to whom the portion of our parish in which that chapel stands has been delegated, heard what had been done there, he repeatedly sent to Bertharius, but was unable to obtain any settlement consistent with the rules. Therefore, since I was not then in the parish of Rheims, he ordered that Mass not be celebrated in that chapel until the people of the estate gave their tithe to their priest according to the ancient custom. If they wished to hear Mass, however, they were to go to the church in the village of Juviniaca.

No one was denied baptism or communion. And, as far as I was able to discover the truth, what you reported to me—that some children had died without baptism and some without the provision of the Eucharist for the journey—was not true. For even if something of the kind had been true, since I often passed through that area and those same people frequently came to me for confirmation and preaching, some complaint would undoubtedly have reached me.

After you sent me the matters stated above through the aforementioned venerable archbishop, I also took care to inquire diligently whether anything was true in them, and I found in every respect that what you had reported to me was false.

That chapel itself, in the village called Attola’s Estate, does not possess from the authority of the Church of Saint Mary of Laon—apart from the small burial court and the little dwelling of the chapel’s *mansellus*, together with its garden—anything except two and a half *bunnuaria* of arable land, which Attola, bishop of Laon, is said to have donated to that church, from the portion of his property that belonged to him. It also has four and a half *bunnuaria* of other land, which Frankish people living in that village on their own properties gave for a burial place at the chapel. In total, therefore, it has seven *bunnuaria* of arable land.

It has nothing of vineyard, nothing of meadow, nothing at all of pastureland, and no serf. In that same little estate there are nine free tenants (*mansi ingenuiles*) belonging to the Church of Saint Mary of Laon and eleven servile tenants (*mansi serviles*).

[Col. 0294A]

That chapel had for a long time been united to the church situated in the village of Juviniaca and subject to that parish, because the two are contiguous, without any intervening forest, water, marsh, distance, or any other obstacle. In the time of the lords whose names are written below—apart from those whom we cannot mention, who held both villages by royal benefice—namely, in the time of Count Remegaud, Count Bertmund, Bernard, Odo, Gibuin, Rothard, Godefrid, Angelbold, and Frederic, the following priests held both churches jointly, in addition to those whom we cannot mention: Priest Tetgrimmus, Priest Ermenricus, and again Priest Ermenricus.

In the church situated in the village of Juviniaca, together with the aforementioned chapel, Ebo ordained the priest who still holds them, named Ermenricus, when Count Bertmund held both villages jointly by benefice from Emperor Louis. This took place in the fourth year before Ebo’s deposition. Ebo was deposed in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 835.

[Col. 0294C]

During the time of the aforementioned lords who succeeded Bertmund in that village, Ermenricus held that chapel together with the church, until Bishop Pardulus obtained from this lord Charles that the estate be restored to the Church of Laon. Ermenricus himself, as long as Pardulus lived, held the chapel subject to his Church without any disturbance.

This was also regularly confirmed by the priests whose names we possess. Among them, a certain priest Ratramnus, now ninety years old, testified that, ever since he had possessed the understanding by which he could know such things, he had always seen the priest of the village of Juviniaca hold, together with that church, the chapel of Attola’s Estate.

This was also lawfully confirmed by the Franks living in that village, by the neighbors living around it, and by the tenants whose names we possess; it was further established in the presence of your agents.

But as some of your men say, that the chapel itself is older than the church in the village of Juviniaca—even if that were true, its antiquity would aid it only if it had continued from its antiquity down to modern times. For Arras, Vermandois, and Boulogne, from whose territory you are native, were older sees with their own bishops in the province of Rheims than the fortress of Laon was counted among the sees, in which you were ordained bishop.

But since, over a long period, through the occurrence of definite events and necessities—as we read also concerning many cities in certain provinces—those sees became subject to other cities and lost their privilege, which they did not recover, while the fortress of Laon grew strong, it is not permitted, according to the laws, the sacred canons, and the decrees of the pontiffs of the Roman See, to appeal on this ground or to resist it, because the passage of time excludes such a claim.

# Chapter Two  
## Concerning the Administration of the Palace and the Abbacy Obtained Contrary to the Canons; His Failure to Come When Summoned to the Synod; and the Irregular Excommunication of Amalbert

Nor did the chapel suffer any disturbance during your time, until you stirred yourself up against me because I dared to rebuke you. Contrary to the sacred rules of Antioch (Council of Antioch, canon 9), which prescribe:

[Col. 0295B]

“Do not act apart from me, according to the ancient rule established by our fathers, except in matters pertaining to your own parish and to the possessions subject to it,”

you nevertheless obtained, without my knowledge or that of our fellow bishops, an administrative office at the palace of our lord king. And, disregarding what I had read to you there from the sacred rules, you afterward regained that same administration of the palace, contrary to my canonical prohibition and contrary to the canons of Sardica (Council of Sardica, canon 8), which openly rebuke bishops who reject and despise the salutary counsels of their archbishop, and who bring to the court many and various cases that do not benefit the Church, seek secular dignities and offices, and stir up scandals.

The same canon states (ibid., canon 2):

“Whoever has or receives petitions should send them through his deacon, because the person of the minister is not liable to envy, and whatever he obtains—namely, concerning the cases of the poor, widows, and orphans, and concerning necessities or benefits for his Church—he will be able to report more quickly.

“It also seems appropriate that the bishops of every province should send petitions to that brother and fellow bishop who resides in the metropolitan city; he should then send both his deacon and the petitions, granting letters of recommendation in like manner to the brothers and fellow bishops who at that time reside in the regions and cities in which the fortunate and blessed Augustus governs the commonwealth.

“If a bishop has friends at the palace and wishes to obtain something that is nevertheless honorable, he is not forbidden to ask through his deacon and to inform those whom he knows can, through benevolent intercession, grant his request in his absence.”

The same canon also states (ibid., canon 11):

“We ourselves know that, very often, because of the shamelessness of a few, the religious name of the priesthood has been reproached. Therefore, if anyone, striving against the judgment of all, wishes to please ambition rather than God, he must know that, once he has rendered an account of his cases, he will lose his honor and dignity.

“And shortly afterward: If, as your Holiness has mentioned above, he goes to the court because of desires and ambitions, neither should his letters be subscribed nor should he be received into communion. If this pleases you, this constitution must be confirmed by the judgment of all.”

And all said: “It is honorable and pleasing to us that this constitution be observed.”

Moreover, together with that administration of the palace, you persisted in obtaining the governance of a monastery in a third province without my consent or that of the bishop in whose parish the monastery was situated, contrary to the sacred canons of Antioch, which say that even a metropolitan may not do what you, a provincial bishop, presumed to do.

[Col. 0296A]

They state (Council of Antioch, canon 13):

“No bishop from another province shall dare to cross into another province and ordain anyone in the churches for advancement in ministry, even if some appear to give their consent, unless he comes after being summoned by letters from both the metropolitan and the other bishops who are with him, and then proceeds to the act of ordination.

“But if, with no one summoning him, he should hasten in an irregular manner to arrange certain ordinations or ecclesiastical affairs not pertaining to him, whatever he does shall indeed be invalid; he himself, however, shall suffer punishment for his disorderly movement and irrational audacity, already condemned for this by the holy Council.”

Understand this carefully: just as it was not permitted for you to ordain anyone irregularly in that monastery, so it was not permitted for you rashly to settle any ecclesiastical matters that did not pertain to you.

Concerning the affairs irregularly conducted by you there, proceedings were submitted to me by those whose interest was involved, just as I tried to make known to you with fatherly affection. But because the principal authority had been greatly stirred up against you by your exaggerations, I omitted to proceed further in the matter, so as not to add to the pain of your wounds, hoping and carefully working toward your future caution and correction.

[Col. 0296B]

I offered a reasonable excuse for not pursuing the matter further: those proceedings had not been drawn up with both parties present, but had been prepared from one side only. Therefore, according to the laws and rules, I could not conduct an inquiry on their basis or issue a synodal judgment.

You also went repeatedly and irregularly, whenever it pleased you, to the monastery irregularly obtained in a third province, without my permission, contrary to the decrees of Pope Hilary, which say:

[Col. 0296C]

“We could not pass over that matter which must be attended to with the greatest care: no one should dare to proceed to any province without the letters of his metropolitan. This must also be observed in every kind of clerical office throughout the individual churches.”

And Saint Gregory writes to Vincent and the other bishops (Book VII, Indiction 11, Letter 8):

[Col. 0296D]

“We exhort your Fraternity that, if necessity should compel any one of you to travel somewhere far away for his own affairs, he must seek permission from his metropolitan according to the rule handed down by the holy Fathers, and must not presume in any respect to set him aside—except, which we do not wish, if it should happen that you have some case against that same metropolitan, so that for this reason you seek the judgment of the Apostolic See.

“For those who hasten to seek permission, you know, are permitted by the canons, also through the institution of the ancient Fathers, to have it.”

In that same monastery situated in the third province, to which, as I said, you went irregularly, without my permission, whenever it pleased you, you remained for a considerable time contrary to the Sardican canons (canons 14 and 15). Although summoned once and again by canonical letters to the ordination of a bishop in the church of Cambrai, in our province, which had been deprived of its shepherd—and for which, at my urging, the apostolic see had labored not a little—you neither came yourself nor sent me a deputy in your place, as the sacred rule commands. Accordingly, Pope Symmachus promulgated to Aeonius from the sacred canons that, if any bishop, having been summoned by the metropolitan pontiff in accordance with the canonical definition, should refuse to obey, he should know that he was to be cut off by ecclesiastical discipline—which we do not desire.

Concerning a representative to be sent in your place, together with a tractoria and a reasonable explanation, if you were unable to come, the sacred canons of Nicaea say (Council of Nicaea, canon 4):

> “Since it is most fitting that a bishop should be ordained by all the bishops who are in the province. But if this should be difficult, either because of pressing necessity or because of the length of the journey, then at least three must meet for this very purpose, while those who are absent likewise decide and give their consent in writing; then the ordination shall take place. The confirmation of what is done in each province, however, shall be assigned to the metropolitan bishop.”

And the Antiochene canons (Council of Antioch, canon 19), explaining the decision of the Council of Nicaea, say:

> “A bishop shall in no way be ordained without a synod and the presence of the metropolitan. Once this has been established in every respect, it is better that all the priests of the same province should be present together, whom the metropolitan bishop ought to summon,”

and so forth—matters which, like those preceding, agree with the Nicene canons.

And since the Antiochene canons, explaining, as we have said, the decision of the Council of Nicaea, call this gathering of bishops a synod and say that it is a complete council when the metropolitan bishop has taken part in it, you, having been regularly summoned, neglected either to come or to send in your place someone bearing your consent. This ought not to pass you by, since the canons of the province of Africa decreed (Council of Africa, canon 43):

> “A bishop who has been summoned to a synod by his primate shall attend appropriately. But if he has been unable to attend, unless he has given an account of the reason for his impediment to his primate, he is to be content with communion in his own church.”

(Ibid., canon 20.)

> “As for one who is not in agreement with the metropolitan church and with the council of priests, but, puffed up, separates himself from this fellowship and thinks that he ought to devote himself to his own people, and sometimes, when summoned to a council, refuses to come: concerning such a man, not only is the diocese not to be preserved for him, but, even if someone from his own church has [lacuna] shown him improper support, every effort must be made so that he may also be rejected by public authority and removed from that chief see itself.”

Since, then, once and again, while the rest of our fellow bishops were gathering for the ordination in accordance with the sacred rules and, though absent, were giving their consent in writing, you, having been regularly summoned once and again, refused either to come or to send your regular consent, we ordained, in accordance with the aforesaid sacred canons, the man regularly elected to the aforementioned church of Cambrai, together with those who had assembled or had consented in writing.

> “If,” they say (Council of Nicaea, canon 6), “two or three, because of their own contentiousness, oppose a common decree of all which is reasonable and has been approved according to the ecclesiastical rule, let the decision of the majority prevail”—

especially since we had heard neither your objection, nor had we been deemed worthy to receive your consent.

Therefore, because you had caused our brothers no small scandal, I took with me our brother Odo, the venerable bishop of the church of Beauvais, and, rebuking you, told you how great a guilt you had incurred in this matter. But I could receive from you no other acknowledgment or satisfaction, although I showed you that the rules were not a little angry with you on this account, except that you replied, full of indignation: “We are not yet,” you said, “at that point.” After this and other corrections, delivered to you by me in letters and words, you remained—and remain to this day—in the same contumacy, in which previously, contrary to the rules, you excommunicated my parishioner Amalbert on a cause that was unlawful for you: namely, because his wife, whom he had lawfully married in your parish and brought into mine, accused him before you by your command, after she had been with him for many years, alleging that he was unable to have intercourse with her, although the laws define:

> “Neither may an accuser bring an accusation through another, nor may a defendant be defended through another, unless a patron accuses an ungrateful freedman, or the absence of the defendant is being represented.”

And again:

> “Judges must take special care that in every case the sentence which has been deliberated be read out when the parties are equally present, so that those by whom the case was pleaded may know fully what sentence has been pronounced.”

And the rules say (Council of Africa, canon 96):

> “Those whom the public laws do not admit shall not be admitted to make an accusation.”

The irrational excommunication which you imposed is also demonstrated by the written statement that you gave me concerning it: a statement contrary to reason and authority, unsupported by truth, and fabricated by you. Therefore I advised you a third time to change the sentence you had pronounced contrary to the rules, as the Council of Antioch decreed (Council of Antioch, canon 13):

> “If a bishop, without being summoned, should hasten in disorderly fashion to settle certain ordinations or ecclesiastical matters that do not belong to him, those things which he does shall indeed be null; but he himself shall suffer punishment for his disorderly movement and irrational audacity, having already been condemned for this by the holy council.”

For you were not the metropolitan, so that the care of the whole province belonged to you.

But I could not obtain from you what would have been honorable for you and what the rules command, until, restraining you for the sake of preserving peace and charity, I arranged a meeting at the boundary of our parishes. There certain of our fellow bishops, many members of the clergy and the laity, and men both noble and of ordinary condition assembled. There, after the case had been conducted by you irrationally and dishonorably, it was decided regularly and lawfully; and you brought the greatest embarrassment not only upon me and upon our fellow bishops and brothers, but also upon very many well-mannered laymen, through your shameful words, disordered conduct, and uncontrolled shouting, contrary to the good name which the Apostle commands a bishop to possess (1 Timothy 3). Alas, I am ashamed to write about that disgraceful and unseemly episode of a bishop, which has become known to far too many.

## CHAPTER III. On the excommunication attempted against the parishioners of other bishops

Yet these excesses were not enough for you to commit, unless you added others to them as well. I speak of them not for your condemnation—God forbid—unless you yourself, by persevering in contumacy, force that outcome, but for your correction, as I do also in what follows.

For when the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, says:

> “What credit is it if, when you sin and are struck, you endure it? But if, when you do good and suffer, you endure patiently, this is grace before God” (1 Peter 2:20),

because of your injuries you dared, without the consent either of myself or of those to whose care they belonged, to anathematize and exclude from the fellowship of all Christians my parishioners and those of other primates and bishops of various provinces—people who had neither confessed nor been convicted of any crime committed in your parish or anywhere else. By this you scandalized many and brought the greatest scandal not only upon the Church but also upon the king and the kingdom, since the law forbids:

> “When you pass through another man’s harvest, you shall not put in your sickle; rather, you shall pluck the ears with your hand and eat” (Deuteronomy 23:25).

The blessed Gregory says:

> “You cannot put the sickle of judgment into a field which appears to have been entrusted to another; but through the effect of good works strip the Lord’s grain of the chaff of its vices, and by admonishing and persuading convert it, as though by chewing it, into the body of the Church” (Book XII, letter 32, to Augustine’s ninth question).

The laws of the world as well, which the Church approves, the sacred canons, and the decrees of the pontiffs of the holy Roman see set forth certain and established judgments concerning those who stubbornly act against them in contumacy, as you have done.

## CHAPTER IV. On his demand that the writings issued against him be burned

There are also the other matters which you commanded me through the aforesaid venerable Archbishop Wenilo: namely, that if I would burn, in the presence of others, the writings which I had sent to you and to the church entrusted to you concerning the excommunication you had attempted against your parish, and which you had there with you, and declare them void, and acknowledge that I had acted contrary to reason and authority, you would be willing to be at peace with me.

After considering this in my heart, I could not sufficiently wonder how and from where such thoughts had come to you, so that you could give me such instructions. For the devil, when he spoke to our first parents and also to our Redeemer and Savior, tempted them not through humiliation but through greed for advancement and eminence.

You, surpassing, if it may be said, the devil’s malignity, and forgetting that it is written, “Those who act maliciously shall be exterminated” (Psalm 36:9), attempted to tempt me, in extreme folly, through humiliation, although you knew that what I had sent to you and to the church entrusted to you in those writings had been composed from evangelical truth, from apostolic and prophetic authority, from canonical authority, and also from the constitution of the apostolic see, as that holy see had received it through the tradition of the blessed apostles.

Saint Jerome proves from the authority of the holy Scriptures that ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ. And the Apostle says, “If anyone is ignorant, he shall be ignored.” Gregory says plainly that those who do not know the things of the Lord are not known by the Lord; and we read that those who betray and burn the holy Scriptures are to be counted among sacrilegious persons.

If, therefore, I were to burn those things which I had written from the Gospel, from the apostles and prophets, and also from the sacred rules composed by the Spirit of God, without any admixture of heresy or schism—namely, the measure of wheat, pure from the chaff and weeds destined for burning—which I had brought forth in due season from the Lord’s granary for you and for the church entrusted to you and subject to my care; and if I were to deny what is true, I would undoubtedly deny that I knew and believed in Christ, who was foretold and revealed in those writings, through which we came to know Christ, and who himself spoke those words.

And if I were to burn and repudiate the sacred canons and the decrees of the Catholic Church, I would unquestionably not only depose myself from the episcopate, but also make myself divided from and alien to the Catholic Church—that is, a schismatic and anathematized man—by public and ecclesiastical laws, as Saint Pope Leo also says of himself in writing to Emperor Leo (letter 84):

> “If, according to the Apostle (Galatians 2:18), I build again the things which I destroyed, I make myself a transgressor, and subject myself to the conditions of punishment which not only the authority of the blessed Emperor Marcian of sacred memory but also I, by my own assent, have confirmed.”

Therefore, although you judged me—weak, fragile, and feeble, as I truly am—to be so easily overcome that I could be drawn or enticed to do these things by threats or the seductive blandishments of promises, you nevertheless, as a bishop, ought not to have doubted that what is promised by the truthful mouth of him who perfects strength in weakness is true:

> “The Lord shall give the word to those who proclaim the Gospel with great power” (Psalm 67:12).

Nevertheless, because, as we read, “there is no delay in learning when the Holy Spirit is present as teacher,” and because he himself inspires the words, “I will give you a mouth and wisdom which all your adversaries shall be unable to resist or contradict” (Luke 21:15), the Lord, not through my merit but through his grace, suddenly caused me to recall that it is written:

> “A time for silence, and a time for speaking” (Ecclesiastes 3:7).

And because I foresaw that you could not calmly endure being reproved or accused by anyone, and because I did not dare to alter the words of authentic Scripture, lest you mark me as its falsifier, I was compelled—with pardon for priestly reverence—to say:

> “Do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you become like him; answer a fool according to his folly, lest he appear wise to himself” (Proverbs 26:4–5).

Thus I postponed giving you then the answer I could have given.

Concerning the matters you had commanded me, I immediately sent you this reply: I had heard from our brothers, to whom you had shown them, that you had collected certain materials against me and against those same writings, that you had also subscribed to a certain document, and that you had caused the canons of the church of Laon, and afterward the priests of your parish, to subscribe against me and against those same writings.

I had also heard you say that you had taken apart, piece by piece, the writings which I had sent to you and to the church of Laon concerning the aforesaid excommunication imposed by you, and had shown them, in accordance with the path of the holy Scriptures and the tradition of the elders, to possess no authority or reason.

I therefore proposed that, before so many and such distinguished brothers and fellow bishops as were present there—whom and how many of them you might choose—the writings which I had sent to you and to the church of Laon for the reason stated above should be displayed. You would also bring into our midst what you had collected, those writings to which you had subscribed and had caused others to subscribe, and those writings by which you claimed to have dismantled the texts sent to you by me. They would be read in order, and whatever the aforesaid brothers and fellow bishops might then find and decree justly and reasonably, in accordance with sacred authority and the Catholic faith, and whatever might be agreed between us, I would willingly follow.

I would not deny you the peace which I held toward you in my heart and, if you wished, would also offer you outwardly and accept from you when offered to me; and I would show you sincere affection as a brother and son.

When this reply of mine was to be conveyed to you, the same venerable Archbishop Wenilo asked the glorious Bishop Adventius, who had heard my reply together with him, to go. The same venerable bishop gladly did so. After your common conversation, the venerable Archbishop Wenilo brought me, on your behalf, certain small booklets which you had given him in my presence, bearing verses addressed to our lord King Charles. He told me that you had replied to him that you did not have with you the other writings I was requesting and therefore would not send them to me.

When I came to our lodging that evening, I read through those little booklets very quickly. The next day I replied to you about them in a brief note, which I sent to you through the aforesaid venerable Archbishop Wenilo, through whom you had sent me the same booklets.

You had refused to offer them in accordance with the authority and custom by which a provincial bishop ought and normally does present such matters to his archbishop, and, as some thought, you had shown disdain for doing so.

I therefore necessarily decided not to deliver the aforesaid note to you myself, but to send it through the man by whom you had sent me the aforementioned booklets, lest, if you refused to receive the note from my hand, applause should perhaps be aroused among the ill-disposed, if any were present, and grief inflicted upon the well-disposed, who were present in great number.

I then waited until now for you to send me those writings which you had instructed me you did not have with you at that time. But since you have not sent them to this day, I judged it fitting to request that you send them to me. For this reason I present these letters, humble as they are, to your fraternity, asking that you yourself give me those writings and not delay any longer, so that, after examining them, while preserving faith and authority, we may together follow what is recognized as suitable to Catholic and fraternal peace and affection, following the Apostle who says:

> “Pursue peace and holiness, without which no one shall see God” (John 3:20).

You yourself, brother, know that he speaks the truth when he says:

> “Everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works be exposed. But whoever does the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be made manifest, because they have been done in God” (Hebrews 12:14).

Therefore, just as—although not according to the rules—you showed me what you had collected from the letters of the pontiffs of the apostolic see, to which I replied briefly, though I would have replied at greater length if necessary, so also show me the document to which you subscribed and caused others to subscribe, and those writings by which you say that you dismantled the writings sent by me to you and to your church, so that, when they come to the light, it may be manifest whether they have been done in God.

As for what I wrote to you and to the church entrusted to you concerning the aforesaid excommunication imposed by you, I first sent those writings to you which I did not write from myself, knowing the saying:

> “He who speaks from himself seeks his own glory” (John 7:18).

But I do not deny that I wrote and sent to you and to the church entrusted to you, through myself, from evangelical truth, apostolic and prophetic authority, the authority of the apostolic see, and the constitutions of the holy councils, those writings of which the Lord says:

> “You, hearing, shall announce to them from me” (Ezekiel 33:7).

Therefore:

> “I have not hidden his justice in my heart; I have declared his truth and his salvation” (Psalm 39:11).

I have not hidden his mercy and his truth from the great assembly, lest he distance his mercies from me; rather, may his mercy and truth receive me.

But because, as a human being ignorant of the divine understanding in many matters, I may err—although I do not believe that I have yet done so in this case—if you show me, in accordance with the path of the holy Scriptures and the tradition of the Catholic Fathers, the reason and authority which I ought to follow in this matter, I do not refuse to give the proper assent. I do not refuse to be corrected even by my inferiors and to follow their good words, because the Lord often reveals what is better to a younger man, and the Apostle says:

> “If something is revealed to another who is sitting, let the first be silent” (1 Corinthians 14:30).

I hold as venerable and worthy of imitation with all devotion what I read that the blessed Gregory said (Book VII, indiction 11, letter 2):

> “I am prepared to imitate in goodness even my inferiors, whom I prohibit from unlawful acts. For he is a fool who considers himself first in such a way that he disdains learning the good things he sees.”

## CHAPTER V. On the two judgments of Hincmar which he claimed had been rescinded by the apostolic see

Finally, I was told that you boast among many people that you can resist me and dare to despise me, as we read of a young man filled with the wind of vanity who burned the temple of Diana at Ephesus and, when asked why he had done it, replied that, since he could not become known through good deeds, he would at least become known through evil ones.

To this boast of yours I reply in the words of the Apostle:

> “Brother, your boasting is not good” (1 Corinthians 5:6).

For what can a human being supported by temporal power not do, so far as the higher power permits him, if he does not fear God and does not respect human beings? We too can do something, but would that we might always be able to do so in God, who strengthens us.

And since there is no power except from God, we must distinguish within power what God grants us in mercy and what he permits in anger, so that we may humbly carry out what is granted with fear and trembling, and not abuse what is permitted to our destruction. Let the one who boasts in power boast in the Lord, as in other matters, and according to the saying of the wise man (Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, Book III, meter 5):

> “If he wishes to be powerful,
>
> let him tame his fierce passions”—

for blessed are the meek, since they shall possess the earth, namely, the inheritance of eternity.

If you boast that you can resist me, beware: in resisting me contrary to the sacred rules, you resist the ordinance of God, who, through the sacred canons composed by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, placed me over you and subjected you to me.

And if you boast that you dare to despise me, beware: you imitate the one who, through his own fault, became such that he feared no one, and who will operate especially in that son of perdition called Antichrist. “And now,” the Apostle John says, “there are many antichrists” (1 John 2:18); and again it is written:

> “Those who belong to his party imitate him” (Wisdom 2:25).

Therefore, if you boast that you swell up against me and, in your swelling, despise me, and by this resist the ordinance of God—since heaven is opened, through God’s hidden or manifest working, to the humble, to those who speak for the truth, and to those who resist people who rise up against the truth, as we read concerning the blessed Stephen (Acts 7)—then to the proud, whom God resists, to those who resist God’s ordinance, and to those who swell up against their superiors, hell is opened, through God’s hidden or manifest working, as we read concerning Korah, Dathan, and Abiram (Numbers 16), whom hell swallowed when the earth opened beneath their feet.

Your madness—for that is what many call it—is also flying through the mouths of many, who say that, as though you were out of your mind, you declare that if I summon you before a synod concerning some matter, you will not answer me if you do not wish to do so, because two of my judgments have already been annulled by the apostolic see.

I therefore judged it fitting to reply to you briefly, more by indicating than by giving a full account, until either you say this to me yourself in synod or commit in writing what you are said to mutter in private—a step which I do not think you will dare to make known. For, as Scripture says:

> “Judgments are prepared for mockers, and blows for the bodies of fools” (Proverbs 19:29).

I have ready here judicial sentences which, like hammers, strike the folly of your dullness, if reason should require that they be brought forward. Again, as it is written:

> “Like a thorn in the hand of a drunkard, so is a proverb in the mouth of a fool” (Proverbs 26:9).

For just as a drunkard carrying a thorn in his hand wounds himself first, so you, if you say these things, falsely attack not only me but also very many bishops of many provinces—and, as you do not deny, because you cannot deny it, yourself as a participant in every respect in our judgment—without seeing the noose by which you strangle yourself. For our judgment could be changed canonically by a judge of greater authority, but could not otherwise be annulled, if you confess that you judged together with us, contrary to the rules, with hostile intent or through some desire or favor, as the African Council decreed (canon 91) concerning a bishop who falsely claimed that he had admitted to communion those whom it was established, with his knowledge, he had not admitted:

> “Let him also lose the episcopate.”

But because I am humble and discerning in my own eyes, and know that it is written, “A time for silence, and a time for speaking” (Ecclesiastes 3:7), I boast in the Lord, saying, “The Lord has given me a learned tongue, that I may know how to speak a word in season,” I reply to you briefly: the apostolic see did not annul our judgment, which had been carried out according to the rules. Rather, when Rothad fled to it and humbly made his request—since our legates, who had examined his case, had not come with letters, as the canons command, having been prevented from crossing the gates, before he and many others made their representations—the apostolic see, as it judged in its most wise counsel, extended to him the kindness of consolation.

> “Since all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth,” Pope Leo says, “we are compelled, in accordance with the piety of the apostolic see, to temper our judgment in such a way that, after weighing the measure of offenses—which plainly are not all of one kind—we define some as tolerable in some fashion and cut off others completely. The remission of sin does not grant permission to sin, nor shall we allow what could in some way be conceded to be committed with impunity.”

And our unanimity, as is proper and as the rules command, reverently and humbly accepted the decree of the apostolic see, whose authority was preeminent. For, as Innocent writes, reverence must be preserved toward it in every case; and when greater cases have been brought before it, they must, as the synod established and ancient custom requires, be referred after episcopal judgment—as Boniface, writing to the Gauls, and Leo, writing to Anastasius and to the bishops of the Moors, also decreed—without any contention or resistance, since both the synod so established and ancient custom so requires.

For the sacred and mystical Council of Nicaea, to which all antiquity yielded in synodal decrees, and which no Catholic posterity dared to shake either in its definition of the faith or in its promulgation of laws, judged, under the prompting of the Holy Spirit (canon 6):

> “In accordance with the ancient custom, let the bishop of Alexandria have authority over all his own churches, since the bishop of Rome likewise has a similar custom. Likewise, in Antioch and in the other provinces, let the privileges belonging to their churches be preserved.”

Following this, the holy canons and the pontiffs of the Roman see promulgated in their decrees (Celestine, letter 2, chapter 4; Boniface, letter 3; Council of Carthage, canon 19; Boniface, letter 2; Innocent, decretal letter, chapter 10):

> “Let each province be content with its own metropolitan, and let no opportunity for usurpation be granted to any priest through injury to another. Let each person be content with the boundaries assigned to him; let no one presume anything in another’s province, but let each province always await the direction of its own metropolitan in all matters. And whenever one of the bishops is accused, let the accuser bring the accusation to the primate of that province; and let the accused, regularly summoned by letter on the appointed day, answer the charges in person if he has confidence. If any cases or disputes arise among clergy, whether of higher or lower rank, let the quarrel be settled after the bishops of the same province have assembled. Nor may anyone, abandoning those priests who by divine will govern the Church of God in the same province, rush off to other provinces.”

Inspired by the same Holy Spirit, through whom the foregoing decrees were issued by different mouths and at different times, the venerable Council of Sardica established (Council of Sardica, canon 3):

> “If, in any province, one bishop has a lawsuit against another bishop, neither of the two shall summon a bishop from another province to act as judge. But if a bishop has been judged in some case and thinks that he has a good case so that the council should be renewed, let the memory of the holy apostle Peter be honored, to whom Christ, because of the strength of his most solid faith, gave the name Peter from the word ‘rock,’ saying: ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock’—that is, upon the right faith which you confessed when the Father revealed it to you—‘I will build my Church, and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven’ (Matthew 16:18–19); and again: ‘When you have turned again, strengthen your brothers’ (Luke 22:32), that is, ‘Feed my sheep’ (John 21:26). Let it be written by those who examined the case to the Roman bishop; and if he judges that the judgment ought to be renewed, let it be renewed and let him appoint judges. But if he determines that the case is such that the proceedings already conducted ought not to be reopened, what he decrees shall be confirmed. And when a bishop has been deposed by the judgment of those bishops who dwell in neighboring places, and he has appealed, declaring that his case ought to be heard in the city of Rome, another bishop shall absolutely not be ordained in his see after the appeal of the man who appears to have been deposed, unless the case has been determined by the judgment of the Roman bishop.”

The Council of Sardica rightly and with complete reason judged that, since according to the sacred Nicene canons each province ought to be content with its own metropolitan, and no opportunity for usurpation against another’s injury is granted to any priest, no one should presume anything in another’s province, but each province should always await the direction of its metropolitan in all matters. Thus, lest any bishop judged in a provincial court be condemned while innocent, if it should be necessary for him to appeal to the apostolic see of the blessed Peter, he may take refuge with his appeal in the successor of Peter, so that he may render a merciful and just judgment concerning the judgments of the provincial metropolitan sees and of the bishops.

For in Peter’s primacy he himself bears the burdens of all, and Christ Jesus, the mediator between God and human beings, exalted the Roman see above all sees by the authority of his primacy, honored Alexandria, confirmed Antioch, and decreed that the privileges of their churches should be preserved and strengthened throughout the other provinces.

The same council explains the procedure for carrying out judgment concerning an appealing bishop, saying:

> “It was agreed that if a bishop has been accused, and the bishops of that region, assembled together, have judged him and removed him from his rank, if the man who has been removed appeals and flees to the bishop of the Roman Church and wishes to be heard, if he judges it just that the examination be renewed, let him deign to write to the bishops who are in the neighboring and nearby province, so that they may investigate everything most diligently and determine the matter according to the faith of truth.
>
> “But if the man who asks that his case be heard again should move the Roman bishop by his request to send a presbyter from his own side, it shall be within the power of the bishop to decide what he wishes and what he judges appropriate. If he determines that men should be sent to sit in judgment with the bishops who are present, possessing the authority of the one by whom they were sent, that shall be at his discretion. But if he believes that the bishops are sufficient to bring the case to an end, he shall do what he judges in his most wise counsel.”

Read the letter of that same Council of Sardica to all bishops everywhere, and you will find that Athanasius of Alexandria and Paul of Constantinople, as well as others, were absolved and restored in that synod by the authority of the apostolic see.

Read the decretal letter of Leo to the bishops established throughout Caesarean Mauritania (letter 91), and you will find that Lupicinus was ordered to be heard in the province according to the tenor of this synod, once an account had been given of why he had deserved communion before his hearing.

You will also find that, without prejudice to the statutes of the apostolic see or to the decrees of his predecessors and of his own see, Donatus of Salicina, converted and having submitted a written profession of faith, presided over the Lord’s flock; and that Maximus, improperly ordained from the laity, was likewise not rejected from the episcopal dignity which he had acquired by whatever means, after he too had submitted a written profession.

Finally, you will find that the case of Aggar and Tiberianus, who were said to have been ordained amid tumults and seditions, was entrusted to the judgment of the provincial bishops, and that orders were given for their decisions to be referred to the apostolic see. If any cases should arise relating to the condition of the churches or to the concord of priests, they were to be debated in the province in the fear of the Lord, and a full report of everything settled and to be settled was to be sent to the apostolic see, so that whatever had been determined justly and reasonably according to ecclesiastical custom might be strengthened by its judgment.

You will also find a decree concerning another Maximus by Saint Boniface (Boniface I, letter 2):

> “The judgment ought to take place within the province, and a synod ought to be assembled, so that, if he wishes to be present, he may answer the charges in person if he has confidence; but if he should neglect to be present, he should not gain a postponement of the sentence through his absence. Whatever the provincial bishops should decide ought to be decreed concerning him, they should refer to the apostolic see, so that it might be confirmed by its authority.”

In the decrees of Innocent as well (Innocent I, epistle 27, at the end), you will find Photinus restored—who was said to have gained access to the apostolic see by means of a false report and to have obtained this through intrigues—because the case had returned to a salutary outcome. Likewise, we read that Misenus, condemned by Pope Felix (Felix III, epistle 4), not through secret misrepresentation but according to due process, was absolved by blessed Gelasius after he had presented a written statement of repentance (at the Roman synod [Col. 0307B]).

Furthermore, in the register of blessed Gregory, in his letter to Maximus, you will find him stating in unambiguous wording that an ordination performed by excommunicated persons upon an excommunicated person can in no way be valid. And in his letter to Columbus (Book I, epistle 33), after a petition had been presented to him by the deacons of the Church of Pudentiana, he ordered that a universal council be assembled in the province of Numidia with his representative, and that Bishop Maximian, regularly convicted, be deposed; and that, if the accusers deserved punishment for their own fault, they should not be spared because they had wearied themselves by traveling to Rome.

And in his letter to John of Syracuse (Book VII, indiction 11, epistle 62), he orders that Lucillus, bishop of the city of Melitina, be deposed after three or four fellow bishops had been summoned with him, so that, in their presence, the truth having been established, the deposition might take place. He orders that another be elected in his place [Col. 0307C], because, as blessed Gregory himself writes to the Neapolitans (Book XI, epistle 3), “The canonical rules have established that, when a shepherd has died or been removed, the Church should not remain deprived of a priest for long.”

And in his letter to Natalis, archbishop of Salona, as well as in his letter to Antoninus the subdeacon (Book XI, indiction 11, epistles 8 and 9), you have the following: Florence, a bishop accused by certain persons in criminal matters, had been removed from the office of his dignity—not lawfully but by force—without any canonical proofs having been sought and without the judgment of a priestly council having been rendered. Since no one can be removed from the rank of the episcopate except by the concordant judgment of priests on just grounds, the same Bishop Florence was to be brought out of the exile into which he had been confined, and his case was to be examined by episcopal deliberation [Col. 0307D]. If he should be convicted by canonical proof of the matters of which he had been accused, he was unquestionably to be punished with canonical retribution, and the sentence of the aforesaid archbishop against him was to retain its proper force. But if he had been acquitted by general judgment, he was thereafter to be subject to no prejudice, and his possessions were to be restored to him.

And in his letter to John, archbishop of Justiniana Prima (Book X, epistle 33), concerning Paul, bishop of the city of Diada, you will find that, because after his deposition he had dared to speak shamelessly and with a perverse mind about the episcopate and had again presumed to aspire to it, he was to be confined in a monastery until the day of his death, deprived of communion in the Lord’s body and blood and restored only the provision of viaticum [Col. 0308A].

Read also the decrees of Gelasius, and you will find him recalling decisions established long before his own time concerning Athanasius, John of Constantinople, and Flavian, showing that the same first see acted in their cases, just as we find in the most reliable documents concerning many others.

Read also how Athanasius, at the synod of Jerusalem and likewise at the Alexandrian synod, reread the authority for his absolution and restoration as having been received from the apostolic see and carried out at the Sardican synod; and how he sought the unanimity of the brotherhood, just as was done in our synod concerning our brother and fellow priest at issue here.

For, as we read concerning our Redeemer in the prophet Ezekiel (Ezek. [Col. 0308B] 47), the apostolic see, holding a measuring line in its hand, in view of the divine arrangement admits one within the measure of the elect through mercy and leaves another outside through judgment. Thus our Redeemer, while drawing some away from their iniquities and abandoning others in their iniquity, pulls the measuring line from one side and draws it back from another; he leads here the one whom he withdraws elsewhere, because in that same see the Lord, presiding as though upon his throne, examines the deeds of some and wonderfully dispenses all things from his see.

But just as we embraced the eminence of that apostolic see, so the apostolic see itself repaid us with the authority of the sacred canons in writing and displayed the kindness of fatherhood toward us, as the Council of Carthage decreed (Council of Carthage, canon 15) [Col. 0308C]:

“It was resolved,” it says, “that when an appeal has been made from ecclesiastical judges to other ecclesiastical judges where there is greater authority, it should not harm those whose judgment has been overturned, if they could not be proved either to have judged with an inimical spirit or to have been corrupted by some desire or favor. Certainly, if the judges were chosen by agreement of the parties, even if they were fewer in number than the established requirement mentioned in the preceding chapter, no appeal shall be permitted.”

Therefore, since the kindness of the apostolic see found that we had not judged with an inimical spirit or been corrupted by any desire or favor, and did not decide to be angry with us, and since—as we jointly informed Pope Nicholas of holy memory in our letters—the one who had been ordained in place of our brother died because of this judgment, the apostolic see extended the hand of its authority to him when he fled to it, undertook to carry out what it had judged with its most wise counsel, and ordered us to preserve what had been carried out. Our humility obediently received its command, as was fitting [Col. 0308D].

For who, desiring to have peace with Christ, who is our peace and who broke down the dividing wall and made both one (Eph. 2), would not embrace what the Apostle says: “Being eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4:3)? You improperly inserted this rightly spoken apostolic statement into a certain presumptuous subscription of yours.

What son of the Catholic Church would not most earnestly desire the correction and restoration of a brother, and grieve over his downfall? Who would not rejoice with all the depths of his heart over every Christian [Col. 0309A], and especially over a colleague in the ministry, at these most kindly evangelical words spoken by the mouth of the most merciful Lord: “My son, you ought also to rejoice, because your brother was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found” (Luke 15:32)?

And what he says to the one who has been healed: “Behold, you have been made well; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5:14); and: “Go to your house, and announce how great things the Lord has done for you” (Mark 5:19).

As for the other matter, concerning what you are said to say—that my judgment in the case of Wulfadus and his colleagues was annulled by the apostolic see—what Solomon says may be understood: “He who speaks what he knows declares justice; but he who lies is a deceitful witness” (Prov. 12:17). And again: “A dart, a sword, and a sharp arrow is a man who bears false witness against his neighbor” (Prov. 25:18) [Col. 0309B].

And as the Apostle shows, “For those who do not receive the truth of charity, God sends them”—that is, as a retribution of justice—“an operation of error, so that they may believe the lie, so that all may be judged who did not believe the truth but consented to iniquity” (2 Thess. 2:10).

You ought neither to have deceived nor to have been capable of being deceived concerning what you heard with your ears, handled with your hands, and saw by reading with your eyes—not, however, with those ears or those eyes of which the Lord says to the prophet: “Hear with your ears, and see with your eyes” (Ezek. 44:5).

For I was not a judge in the matter at issue; I was not numbered among the judges; I did not sit in the place of a judge; I did not conclude the judgment concerning it; and I did not subscribe with the judges or with the others who agreed with them.

But since the apostolic see did not wish to hold me accountable for it together with those who judged and subscribed to that judgment [Col. 0309C], and since, at the urging of certain persons, it wished me to agree unanimously with what seemed good to it and what the bishops of our regions and the ruler of the land desired, I consented according to the authority of the sacred Council of Nicaea and the canons of the province of Africa, which made certain decisions in accordance with the urgency of the time.

The Apostle urged us “all to say the same thing, and that there be no schisms among us” (1 Cor. 1:10). He showed what he had commanded, saying again even to his inferiors: “If you have forgiven anything to anyone, I also forgive it; and what I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, I have done for your sake in the person of Christ, so that we may not be outwitted by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his schemes” (2 Cor. 2:10–11)—he who often persuades one person to show mercy where another becomes angry.

Against these schemes of the devil we must pursue peace [Col. 0309D] and holiness, without which no one will see God.

I also endeavored to pursue this, according to my limited ability, in the present matter, as you could have perceived if your heart had not been fattened by another kind of nourishment, concerning which the saint says: “Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness” (Ps. 62). For the synodal letter jointly sent by us from here, entirely sincere in every respect, did not reach the reading of the apostolic see for the purpose of weakening my position and confirming that of the other, as is clearly shown by the letters written to us by the apostolic see concerning this matter, just as it was reread in the presence of the king and of us at the synod [Col. 0310A].

Nevertheless, I did not wish to raise any question or initiate any dispute over it, nor do I ever wish to dispute matters that we unanimously agreed upon in the synod and that the apostolic see defined, because the letters of Pope Nicholas, of good memory, which were sent through my messenger after he learned the truth about the matter, were more than sufficient for me.

He also sent me other synodal letters, which you heard, through the same messenger. Concerning the collections that he had ordered, these had been presented not to me, as he had commanded, but to the king, as suited you for your display; nevertheless, I did not take offense at them, and you obeyed as was your custom.

Furthermore, concerning what took place against me after the synod of Troyes, at which I gave an account of things I had not seized—indeed, of matters that did not concern me—and left them to those whose interest they involved, I discharged my responsibility.

Likewise, the letters of Pope Adrian, sent through the venerable Bishop Actard [Col. 0310B] concerning what was done against me after that synod, wiped away every cloud of anguish from my mind with the handkerchief of his great kindness, so that I willingly wish to follow what the Apostle advises: “Do nothing through contention or vain glory” (Phil. 2:3); and: “Let us not become desirous of vain glory, provoking one another, envying one another” (Gal. 5:26); and what is likewise written: “You shall not seek revenge, nor remember the wrong done by your fellow citizens” (Lev. 19:18).

And from the deepest recesses of my heart I wish to say to the Lord: “The daughters of Judah rejoiced in all your judgments, O Lord, and let there be peace within the strength of Jerusalem,” which strength, as Augustine explains (on Psalm 121), is charity. To the holy city—namely, the holy Church—it was said: “Let there be peace within your strength, and abundance within your towers” [Col. 0310C] (Ps. 121:7).

With the attentive eye of the mind, devoutly considering what Leo says concerning such conduct (epistle 91, to the bishops throughout Caesarean Mauretania):

“It remains,” he says, “that with harmonious obedience you receive salutary exhortations, doing nothing through contention, but united in every effort of devotion, serving the divine and apostolic constitutions, and allowing the pious decrees of the canons to be violated in nothing. For what we have now relaxed after careful consideration of particular cases must henceforth be preserved according to the ancient rules, lest we be punished hereafter with just retribution for what we have granted for a time in pious leniency.”

And so forth.

## CHAPTER VI. On his claim that Hincmar ought to be degraded

[Col. 0310D] It has also been reported to me that you often say to many people that, since matters which you bound in your parish have been loosed without your consent—or rather, since matters which you ordered contrary to the rules have been ordered according to the rules—you will be able to do and obtain this, and will do and obtain it: that I should not sing Mass, and that, if I sing it, you will not sing it.

I would answer you more gently if I had not read that the Lord was angry with Eli because he had rebuked his sons more mildly than he ought (1 Sam. 3). Therefore, if you really say this, I answer you with what is written concerning Moab: “We have heard of the pride of Moab: he is exceedingly proud; his pride and his arrogance exceed his strength” (Isa. 16:6).

And if you threaten that you can degrade me, you claim for yourself more than you can do; hence, in this matter, your pride and arrogance exceed your strength [Col. 0311A]. For you can more quickly make it so that you do not sing Mass than make it so that I become degraded. Indeed, you can make it so that you do not sing Mass, but you cannot make it so that I am degraded.

For you are not my superior, but, whether you wish it or not, subject to me in the dignity of the order; and, in the character of the order, you belong to the company of those whom the sacred canons do not permit to hold councils among themselves, and concerning whom the great Synod of Chalcedon says (canon 19):

“The holy synod decreed, in accordance with the canons of the Fathers, that bishops should assemble twice each year in every province at the place approved by the metropolitan bishop, in order to correct whatever matters may perhaps have arisen” [Col. 0311B].

And so forth.

I must summon you to a synod; you cannot regularly summon me to a synod. If, when summoned by me to a synod, you do not come, or do not send me through your fellow minister a proper excuse, called a *tractoria*, explaining the reasons for your inability or necessity that prevented you from coming to the synod, I have both the power and the duty to judge you. You, for this or any other cause, do not prevail by your own authority to judge me.

And if you are to be accused, your accuser must bring the accusation against you to me, the primate of the province. No one, however, can regularly accuse me before you for judgment. It is not your role to judge me or to appoint judges for me, because, just as it is written that “the lesser is blessed by the greater” (Heb. 7:7), so also he is judged by the greater.

Therefore the sacred canons and decrees of the apostolic see do not permit me to be subjected unwillingly to the judgment of the bishop of a neighboring city [Col. 0311C]. And if anyone complains about my judgment, the rules clearly show how and by whom it ought to be reconsidered.

I, however, must provide you with judges—either those chosen by agreement or even those appointed by me—if the case requires it. I must and may choose a place anywhere in my entire province for summoning a synod or celebrating an ordination, and if I summon you there, you must attend.

It is not your role to choose the place for summoning a synod or celebrating an ordination, nor to summon me wherever you may decide.

If, in the province of Reims, anyone has been made a bishop by any number of bishops of this province, against my judgment, then, as the mystical Council of Nicaea defined (chapter 6), he ought not to be a bishop [Col. 0311D].

But if, by the common decree of the other bishops—a decree reasonably established and approved according to ecclesiastical rule—you or two other associates of yours with you should oppose the decision because of your own ordinances, my judgment, together with that of the majority for the ordination of the bishop, shall prevail. The authority of what is done, whether concerning ordinations or other ecclesiastical matters in the province of Reims, shall be granted to me, not to you.

If a bishop in that province should die, I, not you, shall appoint a visitor for the Church left widowed. I shall order an election to be held in accordance with the canonical decree; and if the votes of those electing should be divided into factions, it shall be mine, not yours, to choose the person who is to be supported by greater efforts and merits for ordination [Col. 0312A]. It is mine, not yours, to examine the person to be ordained.

It is your role, together with the others, to ordain a bishop with me and, after me, to subscribe in your place to the canonical letters which the person ordained is ordered to receive from his ordainers.

You must not subscribe, without my knowledge or judgment, to any new matter that concerns the general observance of the Lord’s priests. The sacred rules order you, if I command you, to subscribe to my decree or report, with the faith preserved; I am not required to subscribe to your decree or report.

For you must not, apart from me, subscribe to any decree or report—whether yours or anyone else’s—concerning matters that do not pertain to your parish. Nor may you subscribe even concerning your own parish except in matters involving the affairs and possessions which you are to govern and administer with the knowledge of the priests and deacons of your Church [Col. 0312B], or concerning their exchange with the consent of the clergy.

Those judged or to be judged by your judgment may appeal to me, and if necessity requires it, they must appeal to me; but no one will appeal from my judgment to your judgment.

You are ordered to consult me concerning the sale or disposal of the affairs of your Church; I am not ordered to seek your advice in such a matter.

If you excommunicate a priest, deacon, or anyone else, and refuse patiently to allow the matter to be examined by neighboring bishops, so that your sentence may either be confirmed by the majority or corrected, and if, before the synod, you do not wish to pronounce a more merciful sentence in his case, then, once the bishops of the province have been assembled, we may and must, together with them, if it seems reasonable to us, alter your sentence and pronounce another, even if you do not wish it [Col. 0312C].

You also fail to understand properly what I found in your collections—or rather, compilations: that I may not come to your parish unless invited by you, and that I may correct whatever needs correction there. This notion of your perverse understanding, as well as many sacred councils, canonical rulings, and decrees of the apostolic see, rebuke, refute, and reject.

If a case has arisen in my province, it must either be concluded in a complete council—“A complete council,” says the canon (Council of Antioch, canon 16), “is one at which the metropolitan bishop is present”—or by episcopal judges, whether those whom I provide to the parties who seek them or those whom the parties themselves choose from among neighboring bishops by agreement.

The care of the entire province has been entrusted to me [Col. 0312D]. Therefore, all throughout the province who appear to have ecclesiastical business must come together to me from every direction, and I must regularly define their cases, including those from your parish.

You, however, must be content to govern your parish according to the reverence due to each person and to exercise care over every possession under your authority, so that you ordain priests and deacons rather than disorder them, and so that your judgment encompasses individual matters, not matters general to the province.

Nor is it lawful for you, if you have a dispute with any brother bishop, to summon a bishop from another province as an investigator; nor is it lawful for you, to settle a quarrel, to hurry off to other provinces without me.

But if necessary, for resolving an ambiguity in my province, I have the power to summon judges from a neighboring province if I decide to do so. And if you are disputing a case with a bishop of another province, and the case lies in my province to be concluded, I must provide judges who will regularly conclude that case. None of these matters belongs to your episcopal office [Col. 0313A].

Concerning doubtful and obscure matters about which we do not have a definite determination, should such matters arise, and concerning matters that cannot be settled without the judgment of many bishops, I must seek counsel with the bishops of the province, among whom you are numbered, as to how they may be settled so that they are found to be contrary neither to evangelical commands nor to the decrees of the saints (Leo, epistle 92).

In cases concerning the general observance of the Lord’s priests, you are permitted to do nothing apart from me [Col. 0313B]; indeed, you are not able to carry anything out. If you are uncertain about something in doubtful or obscure cases, you must ask me. If I do not know, I must inquire of others—or, if necessary, of the apostolic see—and explain the matter to you.

You, however, must not inquire of the apostolic see concerning general cases without me before first taking care to consult me about them. And if, compelled by necessity, you must travel somewhere farther for your own affairs, you must request permission from me according to the rule laid down by the holy Fathers. You cannot regularly travel to any province, or send your fellow minister farther to the court, without my letters, nor may you presume to put me second in any matter—except if you have some case against me [Col. 0313C], so that for this reason you may regularly seek the judgment of the apostolic see, as the Sardican canons show, and as Innocent, in his letter to Victricius, and Gregory and the other Roman pontiffs recall in their decrees; the imperial laws, which the ecclesiastical rules approve, also clearly demonstrate this.

For such business I need neither your permission nor letters from your individuality.

Finally, concerning the matters about which we possess certain and manifest judgments, to be held without alteration, inviolably and irrefutably, according to the course of Scripture, the holy councils, and the apostolic see: if you act against them, I ought not to await a provincial or general council, or the consultation or counsel of our fellow bishops. I must immediately correct, according to the judgments of our orthodox forefathers, whatever you have admitted contrary to their definition [Col. 0313D], because, as blessed Gelasius shows, in these matters I shall be not the author of a new constitution but the executor of an ancient one.

## CHAPTER VII. On his seeking to be cleared by secular counsel

Against the ancient constitutions, not only have you, as I stated above, repeatedly hurried away from the province of Reims, without regular permission and in disorderly fashion, for certain affairs as it seemed good to you; afterward, without the counsel or consent of me and our fellow bishops, having joined a secular rather than an ecclesiastical retinue [Col. 0314A], you proceeded to another province.

And if you suffered violence from anyone, so that you left that place irregularly or under compulsion, you made no complaint to me about it, as the rules prescribe. Instead, before you knew what I would do concerning the matter or what I might be able to obtain, you sent a complaint to the apostolic see without my knowledge, just as you have already done on another occasion, although the rules prescribe (Gregory, Book VII, indiction 2, epistle 8):

“Let no bishop presume to put his metropolitan second in any matter, except if he has some case against him, so that for this reason he may seek the judgment of the apostolic see, which has been permitted by the institution of the canons of the ancient Fathers.”

Indeed, before you received a reply from there, abandoning ecclesiastical judgment and the public judgment—namely, that of the chief authority presiding over the commonwealth—you sought to be cleared of the matters brought against you, as became clear through the intervention of certain secular persons and through the outcome of the affair [Col. 0314B].

For although I sent messengers and letters to you twice, and certain of your associates had the opportunity to speak with you and did speak with you, you neither sought the assistance of me or our fellow bishops nor wished to make use of our counsel. You acted as you had already done on other occasions, when we labored for you in words and writings before our lord the king and calmed his agitation against you, which you had aroused without cause and irrationally.

You therefore scorned to seek ecclesiastical judgment and refused to make use of episcopal counsel, as the rules prescribe. Nor did you afterward offer any satisfaction concerning the matter to the Church or to the ecclesiastical rules [Col. 0314C].

Rather, as it is written of the woman who wipes her mouth and says, “I have done no evil” (Prov. 30:20), so, whether failing to understand or stubbornly pretending not to understand, you persist to this day in your untamed contumacy.

You also put me aside and left behind the common fellow bishops of my province—namely, those who are both my fellow bishops and yours—and in another province chose to make use of the counsel of bishops from other provinces rather than ours, contrary to the rules, even though I was then in the vicinity of the place where our lord the king was staying and some of our fellow bishops were living with him.

Thus, without the judgment or knowledge of me and the bishops of my province, you passed by the place where I was, so close to you that you could have seen me if you had wished—for I saw you—and, passing through there without any necessity, more quickly than episcopal gravity permits, you returned irregularly to your see [Col. 0314D].

You did this before rendering an account to episcopal examination of the reason why you had irregularly or voluntarily departed from your parish and the province of Reims, or why, in any matter, you had been alleged to have been carried away by force by anyone.

“Therefore,” says Saint Gelasius (chapter 20), “every person is summoned to judgment, so that either he may confess the charges or be convicted by the charges.”

And the canons of Antioch say: “Let all who consider themselves injured be present at the councils, and let them undergo the examination of the synod.”

You ought, therefore, to have sought a synod concerning the new matter—whether undertaken by you or inflicted upon you—so that you might undergo synodal examination either concerning any charge or concerning the injury done to you [Col. 0315A]. Instead, returning rashly to your see, you subscribed to a decree contrary to the sacred canons and the constitutions of the pontiffs of the Roman see, and you compelled the clergy of your Church to subscribe to it.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the letters of the pope written concerning his complaint

You also arranged for the letters sent by the apostolic lord to the lord king and to me, through your messengers, concerning your complaint, to be delivered—not to me according to the command of the lord pope, so that I might carry out his orders—but through archbishops of other and even distant regions, to the lord king and to me in my parish, where we were staying [Col. 0315B].

And when the lord king, concerning the matters over which you accused him before the apostolic see—as he discovered in the letter of the apostolic lord addressed to him—lodged a complaint before me, the primate of the province of Reims, because you had accused him rashly and irregularly, contrary to reason and truth, even after he had received an oath from you, which your accusation is said to contradict, you preferred, without the counsel or judgment of me or our fellow bishops and in another province, to offer satisfaction to that chief authority in the manner that then seemed good to you.
