Yet it is well known what the sacred rules say concerning a cleric of any order who, whether in a criminal or civil case, abandons ecclesiastical judgment and wishes to clear himself before a public tribunal, or who, to settle a quarrel, presumes to hurry off to other provinces, abandoning those priests who, by divine will, govern the Church of God in the same province [Col. 0315C].

You could not have been ignorant of these things, since, when you lodged your complaint with me about certain matters inflicted upon you by the lord king and by various others, you read sufficiently in the written statement that I, together with our venerable fellow bishops, presented to the lord king at Pîtres what both the ecclesiastical rules and the public laws said concerning those same matters inflicted upon you. From this we obtained what seemed to us sufficient for you at that time.

For when that same chief authority, and indeed the entire administration of his kingdom, was aroused against you at the palace of Verberie because of your insolence, I again presented there the written statement that you read [Col. 0315D].

## CHAPTER IX. On the monk excommunicated by the bishop of Laon

When the lord king summoned a certain monk and priest, a religious man among his own attendants from the venerable monastery of Saint-Denis, to the monastery situated at Laon, for instruction in learning and religion—not for irregular supervision—and you rashly excommunicated him out of the hostility you harbored against the king, I was ordered by the lord king, together with our brother and fellow bishop Odo, to admonish you to change your unreasonable sentence.

But I was unable to obtain anything from you in the matter. Therefore the lord king sent other bishops, including bishops from other regions, to you concerning this same matter; you obeyed their admonitions, thereby showing that you do not deign to obey your metropolitan in me [Col. 0316A], although, according to the custom of our Church, you professed and subscribed, with a profession and subscription of faith, that you would regularly obey the privilege of the metropolitan see of Reims.

And if any dispute should arise between you and someone else, whether of a higher or lower order, it ought to have been settled by the counsel and judgment of me and our fellow bishops. Likewise, concerning the person excommunicated by you, whether in your parish or from your parish, if you had not previously been willing to change your sentence on your own initiative or at the counsel of neighboring bishops, it ought, according to the sacred rules, to have been confirmed or changed by the counsel or judgment of me and our fellow bishops.

I defer setting out here the judgments that the sacred rules pronounce in definitive sentences concerning such excesses, because, as Pope Simplicius says (epistle 16):

“We do not wish to exaggerate what has been done, lest we be compelled to judge what is just” [Col. 0316B].

## CHAPTER X. On the compilation from the letters of the apostolic see sent in small booklets, and on the verb *promulgo*, and on a chapter of Pope Leo
But I cannot pass over in silence what you recently did against the sacred rules: namely, your subscription to the detestable decree and your compilation of certain statements from the letters of the pontiffs of the apostolic see—which, as I mentioned above, you sent to me—against the privilege of your metropolitan see, wishing to defend by them what you were not permitted to do against the determinations of the Holy Spirit.

Attend, therefore, carefully and intelligently to what blessed Leo says to all the bishops established throughout the provinces [Col. 0316C] concerning the letters of all his predecessors (Epistle 1, at the end):

> “We command that all the decretal constitutions—both those of blessed memory, Innocent, and those of all our predecessors—which have been promulgated concerning ecclesiastical orders and the disciplines of the canons, be so carefully observed by Your Love that, if anyone should despise them, he should know that henceforth pardon will be denied him.”

Observe that he says those things must be observed which have been promulgated by his predecessors concerning ecclesiastical orders and the disciplines of the canons.

Therefore, since the new wine and the weighing of words are still boiling forth from your new wineskin of grammatical art, let us first examine the verb *promulgo*, from which, by derivation through conjugation, *promulgatum* is formed; from its plural number [Col. 0316D] Leo here wrote *promulgata*. Since the old cloths were also sought with which Jeremiah, having been lowered into the pit, might be drawn out more safely and gently (Jer. XXXVIII), because he had spoken in the name of the Lord, we must seek the authority and teaching of the ancients, by which we may more securely escape the snare that you have placed around all of us metropolitans.

And so that you may believe more certainly what we shall say concerning this word as well, consult the books of the ancients, and likewise that former copy of mine, received from your nephew Anselm and lent to you by me, but later retained by you, just as you retained certain other books lent to you by me. You will find that the ancients said *promulgo*, *promo vulgo*, that is, “I bring forth publicly,” or “I first publish among the people.” You will also find that this word *promulgo* was formed, according to the rule of grammatical art, as some have thought, from the two altered forms *promo* and *vulgo*, and, as others have thought, from two complete forms, namely the preposition *pro* and *vulgo*, just as with *produco*. From this simple verb *vulgo* are formed *divulgo* and related words.

Thus Cicero, explaining the meaning of the words, says:

> “*Proditum*: handed down to memory; *provulgatum*: published; *provulgavit*: he exposed, he disclosed, he uttered, he declared, he related, he narrated, he announced, he indicated, he spoke, he made a statement, he discussed, he debated, he treated, he held a conversation, he delivered a speech, he began.”

Concerning the past tense of this simple verb, Nonius Marcellus, in the book he entitled *On the Proper Meaning of Words*, says:

> “*Vulgavit*, honorably used: he held as common and cheap, and as though he gave it to the people.”

Concerning the compound verb *promulgo*, Paul, in his *Glosses*, says as follows:

> “Laws are said to be *promulgated* when they are published among the people.”

The compound therefore has this meaning: *promulgare* is to bring forth among the people, to give, to make known, and to publish. The gloss says:

> “*Promulgavit*, as though he first gave it to the people: he brought forth and extended it.”

The meaning of the simple verb, namely *vulgo*, *vulgas*, Saint Jerome used in the sense of “to make manifest”; and from this he shows that an edition is called *vulgata*, that is, known and manifest to everyone.

The meaning of this compound verb is also demonstrated by the Gospel of Luke, which says:

> “And all these words were being spread abroad throughout all the hill country of Judaea” (Luke I, 65).

Following blessed Ambrose, Bede explained the meaning of *divulgabantur* in this passage as follows:

> “Because, becoming known through report, it became known.”

Isidore too, as he himself says on the authority of Tullius, explained it by saying [Col. 0317C]:

> “*Promulgatum est*: it was brought forth publicly, as when a law is said to have been promulgated; and *promulgatum*, properly speaking, is something made known to everyone and communicated to the whole people.”

Placidus, adding one further word, says that the rest are similar:

> “*Promulgatum*, he says, is something brought forth publicly or established, as when a law is said to have been promulgated; and *promulgatum* means something made known to everyone and communicated to the whole people.”

Moreover, the ancient glosses explained this word in the following ways:

> “*Promulgans*: extending; *promulgare*: to publish; *promulgat*: he brings forth; *promulgat*: he increases, enlarges, brings forth, proclaims, announces; *promulgata*: brought forth, drawn out, produced, propagated, disclosed.”

And this, as Priscian says concerning the authorities who have explained verbs, is shown by usage itself, which is stronger than everything.

The interpreters of words wished the difference in meaning between *divulgata* and *provulgata*, or *promulgata*, to be this: *divulgata* is said simply of things disclosed so that they may become known to everyone; but *provulgata* or *promulgata* is understood of things brought forth both for the preservation of decrees and for the knowledge of everyone, so that they may preserve them without opposition.

Hence blessed Gregory, explaining the Lord’s statement to Job, “Will you bind the rhinoceros to your ploughing with your cord?” (Job XXXIX, 10), says:

> “Often, I remember, I have seen that when this rhinoceros had roused itself to strike with great violence, and, as though it had raised its horn, threatened the smallest beasts—subjecting them to immense terrors and assigning them to the exile and condemnation of death—suddenly, when the sign of the cross had been impressed upon its forehead, it extinguished in itself the whole fire of its fury, laid aside its threats, and, because it could not proceed against those who had been deliberately chosen, recognized that it had been bound. And it not only tames its own anger, but also hastens to implant in the minds of those subject to it everything that is right; and, so that all may venerate the holy Church from the depths of their thoughts, it demonstrates this by the example of its own humility” (Moral Works, Book XXXI, chapter 3).

And a little later:

> “To dissolve the hardness of such people, the holy Church sometimes seeks the assistance of this rhinoceros—that is, of an earthly ruler—because she is not sufficient by her own power, so that he himself may crush the clods lying upon the ground, which the humility of the Churches bears like the level places of valleys. This rhinoceros therefore presses and crushes these clods with its foot, because the religious authority of the ruler dissolves, by its power, the hardness of wicked and powerful men, which ecclesiastical humility is unable to resist. Since this is accomplished by divine power alone, so that the heights of an earthly kingdom may incline themselves toward the advancement of the heavenly kingdom, it is rightly said here: ‘Or will he break the clods of the valleys behind you?’” [Col. 0318B]

And shortly afterward, in the same work, chapter 4:

> “Who, at the beginning of the Church’s birth, would have believed that, while that untamed earthly principate raged against her with so many threats and torments, this rhinoceros would return seed to God—that is, would repay by its works the word of preaching it had received? Who could then have believed that it would gather his threshing floor for the weak? For behold, now, on behalf of the Church, he promulgates laws who earlier raged against her through various torments. Behold, he leads whatever peoples he is able to capture toward the grace of faith by persuasion, and he reveals eternal life to those whose present life he preserves after their capture” [Col. 0318C].

Behold what the ancients thought concerning the origin of the word and the proper meaning of its sense. Let us now examine the precise meaning of blessed Leo’s words. He commanded that all the decretal constitutions—both those of blessed memory, Innocent, and those of all his predecessors—which had been promulgated concerning ecclesiastical orders and the disciplines of the canons, should be observed.

First, then, we must know that it is one thing to promulgate sacred orders and the disciplines of the canons, and another to promulgate concerning sacred orders and the disciplines of the canons, just as it is one thing to promulgate laws and another to promulgate concerning laws.

To promulgate laws is to establish laws; to promulgate concerning laws is to derive judgments from them, to judge according to them, and to make their observance and judgments known to everyone [Col. 0318D], as Saint Augustine shows in his book *On True Religion* (chapter 31), saying:

> “It is lawful for pure minds to know the eternal law, but it is not lawful for them to judge it. He himself becomes the law according to which he judges all things, and concerning which no one can judge—just as with these temporal laws. Although human beings judge concerning them when they establish them, nevertheless, once they have been established and confirmed, it is not lawful for a judge to judge the laws themselves, but only according to them. The author of temporal laws, however, if he is a good and wise man, consults that eternal law itself, concerning which no soul has been granted the right to judge, so that according to its unchanging rules he may discern what ought to be commanded or forbidden for a particular time.”

And in the book of the *Confessions*:

> “Therefore spiritual people—whether those who preside or those who obey—judge spiritually” [Col. 0319A].

To promulgate sacred orders, however, is to establish them by the Lord. “They shall call upon me,” he says, “and I shall bless them” (Num. VI, 17)—that is, the bishops.

Through bishops, just as through apostles ordained by the Lord, Matthias was ordained an apostle (Acts I, 26). And through the prophets and teachers—who were also bishops and apostles—at Antioch, when the Holy Spirit commanded and said, “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work of the ministry to which I have chosen them” (Acts XIII, 2), Barnabas and Saul themselves were ordained.

Through Aaron, whom the Lord ordained by means of Moses, and through Aaron’s son Eleazar, the remaining lesser priests were ordained. And sacred history says:

> “Moses gathered seventy men from the elders of Israel and caused them to stand around the tabernacle. Then the Lord descended in the cloud and spoke to him, taking away from the spirit that was in Moses”—not by removing it, but by propagating or promulgating it among others—“and giving it to the seventy men” (Num. XI, 24) [Col. 0319B].

That spirit is also called Moses’ spirit, just as Elijah’s spirit is named, in the same manner of speech by which we also ask the Lord in prayer, “Give us this day our daily bread” (Luke XI, 3). For that bread is God’s, and so is the spirit, from whom we receive it as a gift from the giver; and, through receiving it, it truly becomes ours, since we receive it from him.

And when, as the history says, the spirit had rested upon them, “they prophesied, and afterward they did not cease” (Num. XI, 25).

Just as Moses, in order to obtain what he sought, set the fathers before the Lord—upon whom forgetfulness does not fall, yet who nevertheless says, “I will remember my covenant” (Gen. IX, 15)—saying, “Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, your servants, to whom you swore” (Exod. XXXII, 3), that is, to whom you spoke by a firm promise, so bishops, in the ordination of priests, recall that he himself may carry out what belongs to him through their ministry, namely, the ministry of the bishops. They say:

> “Thus, in the wilderness, you propagated the spirit of Moses through the minds of seventy wise men. Using them as assistants among the people, he easily governed innumerable multitudes. Thus also, in Eleazar and Ithamar, the sons of Aaron, you poured forth the abundance of their father’s fullness, so that the ministry of priests might be sufficient for the saving sacrifices and the mysteries of the more frequent office. By this providence, Lord, you added companions in the faith to the apostles, the teachers of your Son, through whom they filled the whole world with successive preachers” [Col. 0319C].

These bishops and priests, at the beginning of the Church’s birth and for a considerable period thereafter, were called by one name in their several offices, as is made clear in Peter’s letter, in John’s letters, and in Paul’s letters, and as Jerome demonstrates from the authority of the Scriptures in his letter to the priest Evagrius (Epistle 85).

The remaining ecclesiastical orders are also promulgated through those whom the Lord has appointed for this purpose, with the Lord carrying out through their ministry what belongs to him.

To promulgate concerning sacred orders is to make known who and how many they are, what sort they are and in what manner, by whom and when they are to be ordained, and how and to what extent each ought to minister in the several degrees [Col. 0320A]. It also includes how each may be advanced from the doorkeeper’s office up to the highest priesthood.

What has been promulgated concerning these matters by the pontiffs of the Roman see is known to be perfectly familiar to everyone trained in ecclesiastical doctrine. Since you raise no question about it, I consider it superfluous to discuss it.

Since, as I said above concerning laws and sacred orders, it is one thing to promulgate laws and sacred orders, and another—as I have shown—to promulgate concerning laws and sacred orders, it must likewise be shown that it is one thing to promulgate the sacred canons, and another to promulgate the decretal constitutions established concerning the disciplines of the sacred canons.

What the canons are, whose disciplines blessed Pope Leo commands to be so carefully preserved that anyone who violates them should know that henceforth pardon will be denied him—this same blessed Innocent, mentioned by Leo, plainly demonstrates in a discipline decreed from those very sacred canons, in his letter to Victricius, bishop of Rouen (Epistle 1):

> “If any causes or disputes should arise among clerics, whether of a higher or a lower order, then, according to the Council of Nicaea, the dispute is to be settled after the bishops of that province have been gathered together,”

and so forth.

And there, a little later:

> “But if greater causes should have been brought forward, they are to be referred to the apostolic see, as the council—namely, the Council of Sardica—has established, and as ancient custom requires, after episcopal judgment.”

And to Alexander, bishop of Antioch (Epistle 20):

> “Reviewing the authority of the Council of Nicaea, which expresses the one mind of all the priests throughout the world, we recognize that what it decreed concerning the Church of Antioch must be observed by all the faithful—not to say by all priests—namely, that the aforesaid Church was established over its own diocese, not over any other province.”

From this he promulgated concerning the ordination of metropolitans, several of whom that Church itself has subject to it, just as the bishop of Alexandria has them by ancient custom, and the bishop of Thessalonica by delegation from the apostolic see.

And to the bishops of Macedonia (Epistle 27, toward the middle), from the same sacred canons established at Nicaea, he promulgated that Novatians coming to the Church were to be received into their orders by the laying on of hands. He also plainly refuted the opinion of those who, lest scandal arise in the Church, said that Anisius should be followed in receiving the Bonosians ordained by Bonosus after his condemnation [Col. 0320D].

From the aforementioned Nicene canons he also promulgated that the Paulianists coming to the Church were to be baptized, whereas others baptized by heretics in the name of the Holy Trinity were not to be baptized.

Zosimus likewise sent to all the bishops established throughout Gaul and the seven provinces the disciplines decreed and promulgated from these sources.

Boniface too says the following to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne, in this matter (Epistle 3, to Hilary):

> “No one, I think, is unaware of the constitution of the Council of Nicaea, which commands—as we shall set down its very words—that in each province there should properly be one metropolitan, and that no one should have two provinces subject to him. Because it must not be believed otherwise, they judged, under the prompting of the Holy Spirit, that it should be observed.”

And a little later:

> “We say this so that Your Charity may understand how carefully we observe the commands of the canons: our own constitution likewise determines that each province should await the direction of its metropolitan in all matters.”

Celestine writes to all the bishops established throughout the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne (Epistle 1), and similarly to all the bishops established throughout Apulia and Calabria (Epistle 2):

> “No priest is permitted to be ignorant of his canons, nor to do anything that could oppose the rules of the Fathers. For what worthy thing would be preserved by us if the standard of the decretal constitutions were broken by the license granted to the people according to someone’s desire?” [Col. 0321B]

And not only did these predecessors of his, whose decretal constitutions concerning the disciplines of the sacred canons they promulgated, elevate those same sacred canons to authority in the manner I have described; Damasus also ordered those returning to the Church to subscribe to the observance of the sacred Nicene canons just as to the faith, in his letter to Paulinus (Epistle 4).

Moreover, the successors of blessed Leo—to name some of the many: Hilary, Simplicius, Felix, Gelasius, Symmachus, Hormisdas, and blessed Gregory—invoke as authority those same sacred canons, as well as the other councils which the Catholic Church receives, preserves, and venerates, and which the apostolic see taught must be observed, in their decrees promulgated from those councils’ disciplines.

They commanded that, in each sacred order and in each dignity of the sacred orders, all should strive to hold, preserve, and follow the canonical rule; that no one should presume to depart from their constitutions; that no one should be able with impunity to oppose those same sacred canons; and that no one should follow his own judgment in judging others.

Rather, without turning aside to the right or to the left, they should proceed along the straight path of those canons. Each person, just as those revered canons decreed, should respectfully render to his superiors the obedience that he demands from his inferiors. And just as they do not wish to bear a heavy burden themselves, so they must not dare to impose an unbearable weight upon others.

Nor should anyone establish concerning obscure or doubtful matters anything that is found to be contrary to the evangelical commands or opposed to the decrees of the saints. Each person should preserve, through those same sacred canons, the measure and order decreed for him by God.

The same blessed Leo, writing to Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople (Epistle 58), recalls the sacred canons whose disciplines he promulgated in his decretal constitutions as follows:

> “Those holy and venerable Fathers who, after the sacrilegious Arius and his impiety had been condemned in the city of Nicaea, established laws of the ecclesiastical canons that would remain to the end of the world, live among us throughout the whole world in their constitutions; and if anything is attempted anywhere otherwise than they decreed, it is annulled without hesitation” [Col. 0322A].

Again, the same man to the same recipient, a little earlier:

> “That ordinance of the Nicene canons, established truly through the Holy Spirit, can never be dissolved in any respect. Let no synodal councils flatter themselves because their assembly has increased, nor let any number of priests, however much larger, dare to compare itself with or place itself above those three hundred and eighteen bishops. The Council of Nicaea was consecrated by so great a divine privilege that, whether ecclesiastical judgments are celebrated by fewer or by more persons, whatever differs from their constitution is entirely devoid of authority.”

Again, the same man to Maximus, bishop of Antioch (Epistle 66):

> “Whatever, apart from the particular cases of synodal councils, is brought before episcopal examination may have some basis for judgment, provided that nothing concerning it has been defined by the holy Fathers at Nicaea. For whatever disagrees with their rules and constitution can never obtain the consent of the apostolic see” [Col. 0322B].

The Council of Chalcedon also says (canon 1):

> “We have decreed that the rules of the holy Fathers, established in each council up to the present, shall retain their proper force.”

And again Leo says to Anastasius (Epistle 88):

> “According to the canons of the holy Fathers, established by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, we decree that the bishops who are metropolitans of the individual provinces, and whose care has been entrusted to Your Fraternity by delegation from us, shall possess unimpaired the right of the dignity anciently entrusted to them, so that they may depart from the prescribed rules neither through negligence nor through presumption” [Col. 0322C].

Since you do not need anyone to explain to you what you ought to understand by the phrase “the prescribed rules,” examine the books of the canons. You will see that all those councils which we received from the ancients for observance were celebrated before the Council of Chalcedon, which decreed that the rules of the holy Fathers established in each council up to that time should retain their proper force. From all of these Leo commands the metropolitan bishops of the individual provinces not to depart through negligence or presumption.

For this reason Gelasius, in his general decree to all bishops concerning ecclesiastical institutions, says (Epistle 6):

> “Since we desire that we ourselves may rashly be permitted to do nothing against the reverence due to the saving rules, and since the apostolic see, with the Lord’s favor, diligently strives to maintain with pious and devoted purpose all that has been established by the canons of the Fathers, it is utterly unworthy for anyone, whether among the bishops or among the subsequent orders, to reject this observance, which he sees the see of blessed Peter both follow and teach. It is entirely fitting that the whole body of the Church should agree with itself in this observance, which it sees prevailing there where the Lord placed the principate of the whole Church.”

Saint Gregory too, writing to the bishops of Gaul, says among other things and together with other matters:

> “Let everything that is contrary to the sacred canons, as we have said above, be strictly condemned with the imposition of an anathema.”

Blessed Gregory repeatedly decrees in his decretal letters that the rules established by the councils must be observed and that no one may deviate from them in any respect.

Blessed Hormisdas likewise wrote to Saint Remigius, entrusting him with the responsibilities of the apostolic see, and said among other things:

> “We command that the rules of the Fathers and the decrees defined by the most holy councils be observed by everyone. In these matters we show your vigilance; in these matters we show your care and the exhortations of fraternal admonition. When these things are guarded with as much reverence as is fitting, no obstacle to holy observance leaves room for guilt. There what is lawful and unlawful is written down; there is forbidden that toward which no one should dare aspire; there is granted what a mind pleasing to God ought to undertake” [Col. 0323A].

Apply your understanding to these things, brother; submit your mind to them; accommodate your spirit to them; subject your intelligence to them, and you will not err or drift through your empty conjectures, by which you have been, as it were, fed by wind and, rather, swollen with inflation, while you devote yourself to your compilations—compilations that will contribute nothing to what you intend, and indeed will do you very great harm.

What, asks blessed Leo, is more unjust than to think impiously and not to believe wiser and more learned men? But those who, when hindered by some obscurity from knowing the truth, turn not to the prophetic voices, not to the apostolic writings, nor to the evangelical authorities, but to themselves, fall into this folly. They become teachers of error because they were not disciples of the truth.

Do you hear that the venerable Fathers established laws that would remain to the end of the age? Do you hear that whatever differs from their rules will be entirely invalid? Do you hear that the sacred canons were established by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, and that no one is permitted to deviate from them through negligence or presumption? Do you hear that even the apostolic see itself does not rashly desire to claim that anything against those same canons is permitted to it? Do you hear that everything contrary to the sacred canons is to be strictly condemned with the imposition of an anathema? Do you hear that what is lawful and unlawful is written there, that what no one should dare to seek is forbidden there, and that what a mind pleasing to God ought to undertake is granted there? And yet you strive to devise evasions so that you may be subject to no one, although you cannot preside over everyone.

Hear also what blessed Augustine, together with other orthodox teachers, the highly renowned man in all Catholic knowledge and doctrine, thought concerning these canons of the sacred councils. Writing to Januarius, he says (Epistle 118):

> “Those things which we observe as having been handed down, not written, but which are nevertheless observed throughout the whole world, are understood to have been commended and established for preservation either by the apostles themselves or by plenary councils, whose authority in the Church is most salutary. Therefore I consider that all such practices as are contained neither in the authority of the holy Scriptures, nor found established by the councils of bishops, nor strengthened by the custom of the universal Church, but which vary innumerably according to the differing customs of different places, so that the reasons which people followed in establishing them can scarcely, or perhaps never, be found—where the opportunity is given—ought without hesitation to be cut away” [Col. 0324A].

Pope Damasus, from whose letter you inserted certain passages into your commentaries, without understanding—or wishing to understand—what he himself said, and what you say or concerning which you make assertions, wrote, as we stated above, through Vitalis to Paulinus, bishop of Antioch. He commands those who repent and return to the Catholic Church to profess and confirm by their own subscription the observance of the canons, just as they profess the integrity of the faith. Among other things he says (Epistle 4):

> “Whoever wishes to subscribe to this letter must first have subscribed to the ecclesiastical canons, which you know very well, and to the faith of Nicaea. Such a person you must receive without any ambiguity—not because you could not propose these very things which we have written to those who are returning, but because our agreement gives you a free example in receiving them” [Col. 0324B].

Saint Leo also writes to Ravennius, bishop of Arles (Epistle 94):

> “Your Love is not ignorant of the ecclesiastical laws, so that you contain all the rights of your power within their rules and measures. For this reason it is said that the law is not established for the just (1 Tim. I, 9): because he fulfills the standard of its precept by the judgment of his will, since the true love of what is right possesses within itself both the apostolic authorities and the canonical sanctions. As their devoted follower and diligent executor, you will doubtless rejoice in the company of those who deserved to hear, for the profit of the talents entrusted to them, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant,’ and so forth” [Col. 0324C].

Saint Gregory likewise wrote to Quiriacus and the other Catholic bishops in Ireland, saying (Book IX, indiction 4, Epistle 61):

> “All who return from the perverse error of Nestorius must, before the holy assembly of Your Fraternity, anathematize Nestorius himself with all his followers, together with the other heresies; they must promise to receive and venerate the venerable councils received by the universal Church; and, without any doubt, Your Holiness should receive them into your assembly, preserving their proper orders.”

For this reason Saint Gelasius, in his letter to the bishops established throughout Dardania (Epistle 11, at the beginning), says:

> “We trust that no one who is now truly a Christian is ignorant that, among all the sees, none ought to carry out the constitution of any council whose approval has been given by the universal Church more than the first see, which both confirms each council by its authority and preserves it through continuous governance, in accordance with the principate which blessed Peter the apostle received from the Lord’s voice and which the Church, following after him, has both always held and continues to hold” [Col. 0324D].

## CHAPTER XI. That a fuller discussion of the sacred orders and the disciplines of the canons is to be given from the words and opinions of the orthodox.

I believe these things might be sufficient for one who is not high-minded but agrees with the humble. Yet because I do not believe that they ought to be sufficient for you, I shall not say “more perfectly” or “more fully,” since, as was said long before our time, perfection does not receive increase, nor does fullness receive addition. Nevertheless, I have judged it worthwhile to set forth here, at greater length, certain matters concerning the aforementioned sacred orders and the disciplines of the canons, drawn from the words and opinions of orthodox teachers, in order to repress the swelling of your understanding and dispel the darkness of your compilations.

The holy Church, which blessed Paul the apostle calls the Jerusalem above, our mother, the city that remains, and the building from God, a house not made with hands, consists of angels and human beings.

Part of it, enjoying the fellowship of the angels in distinct orders, already reigns with God in heaven; another part, still journeying on earth in distinct orders, sighs for the heavenly fellowship, where, according to the Apostle, there is a tabernacle not made with hands and not of this creation (Heb. IX, 11).

After its pattern, the tabernacle was made through Moses, concerning which the Lord said to him:

> “Make everything according to what was shown to you on the mountain.”

In that heavenly and true tabernacle, which God established and not man, within the interior of the veil—that is, into heaven itself—the high priest and eternal pontiff of our confession, possessing an everlasting priesthood, the great priest according to the order of Melchizedek, entered once for all through his own blood, having obtained eternal redemption. He sits at the right hand of the Father—that is, in the glory of the Father’s majesty—and intercedes for us, not by voice but by mercy (Heb. III, VII, IX; Rom. VIII).

The same one, King of kings and Lord of lords (Rev. IX), through whom kings reign and lawgivers decree what is just (Prov. VIII), governs the heavenly and earthly principate—that is, the entire commonwealth—and arranges and directs all its forces, both heavenly and spiritual and earthly and temporal, in distinct orders. Presiding over the heavenly and worldly court, he administers everything in wondrous order through the ministry of angels and human beings, according to the variety and suitability of times; and whatever is fitting for each particular time or person he determines either by hidden inspiration, by clearer illumination, or by revealed command.

## CHAPTER XII. What the orders are in heaven, in the Church, and in the earthly commonwealth.

Since we read that sacred orders were arranged by God in heaven and on earth, in the Old Testament and in the New, from whom, according to the Apostle, every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named (Eph. III, 15), our holy teachers plainly show what the orders—that is, the fatherhoods—are in heaven, in the Church, and in the earthly commonwealth. They draw waters from the fountains of the Savior, that is, they drink the teaching of knowledge from the holy Scriptures.

Thus blessed Dionysius the Areopagite, an ancient and venerable Father, as he learned from the apostle Paul—who, caught up to the third heaven, saw heavenly secrets—wrote two books, one concerning the angelic principate and the other concerning the ecclesiastical principate.

Blessed Gregory also discusses these matters in the books of his *Moral Works*, and at greater length in his homily on the Gospel passage, “The tax collectors and sinners were drawing near to Jesus” (Luke XV, 11), which the reader will find in its proper place. More briefly, he explains it in a letter to the bishops of Gaul, in which he says:

> “For this purpose the providence of the divine disposition established different degrees and distinct orders, so that, while inferiors showed reverence to their superiors and superiors extended love to their inferiors, a single harmony might be woven from diversity, and the administration of each might properly perform its office. The whole could not subsist by any other arrangement unless an order of such great difference preserved it. Since a creature cannot be governed or live in one and the same equality, the pattern of the heavenly armies instructs us. For while there are angels and archangels, it is clear that they are equal in nature but, as you know, differ from one another in power and order. If, then, among those who are without sin this distinction is established, who among human beings would reject submitting willingly to this arrangement? From this peace and charity mutually embrace one another, and the steadfast sincerity of harmony remains in reciprocal and God-pleasing love, because each office is then beneficially fulfilled when there is a superior to whom one may have recourse” [Col. 0326B].

## CHAPTER XIII. That, although the order is general to all bishops, the dignity is not common to all.

We also read that the orders of ministers in the Church of the ancient [Col. 0326C] people, which is more commonly called the Synagogue, were established by God through Moses. Sacred history shows what kind of persons these orders were, how and when they were to be ordained, and when, how, and to what extent they were to minister in each office. But even now, in the Church, which is called the kingdom of heaven, we read and understand that ministers of the Lord have been distinctly arranged, in the likeness of the heavenly orders, by divine institution and apostolic tradition. What they are, how they are to be ordained, by whom, and how each is to minister in his office, as we mentioned above, is shown to us by the clearest reading; there is no need now to discuss each point separately.

Concerning only the order at issue, and insofar as it pertains to the matter under discussion, blessed Leo, as I recently wrote to you among other things in the aforementioned memorandum, learned as though by apostolic tradition that it had been decreed, and wrote to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica (Epistle 84):

> “Although,” he says, “the order is general among all priests, the dignity is not common to all, because even among the most blessed apostles there was a certain distinction of authority amid their equality of honor; and although the election of all was equal, nevertheless one was given precedence over the others. From this model also arose the distinction among bishops, and provision was made by a great ordinance lest everyone claim everything for himself, but that in each province there should be one whose decision would have first place among the brethren; and again, that certain men established in the greater cities should undertake a broader responsibility, through whom the care of the universal Church would converge upon the one See of Peter, and nothing anywhere would dissent from its head.

> “Therefore, whoever knows that he has been placed over some should not take it badly that someone has been placed over him; rather, he too should render the obedience that he requires.”

For if, as we read, one angel says to another, “Run and speak” (Zech. II, 4), and an angel obeys an angel, a human being ought not to disdain obeying a human being—especially since the disobedience of our first parent was the cause of the destruction of the human race, while the obedience of our Savior, who became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on the cross, is the restoration of human salvation. The proud devil brought the proud human being into death; the humble Christ led the obedient human being back to life. [Col. 0327B] For just as the former, lifted up, fell and cast down the one who consented to him, so the latter, humbled, rose and raised up the one who believed.

## CHAPTER XIV. That in the commonwealth also there are different orders in the likeness of the heavenly host

That angels are also placed over nations, Catholic teachers demonstrate from the words of the angel through the prophet Daniel:

> “I came because of your words. But the prince of the kingdom of Persia resisted me for twenty-one days; and behold, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me” (Dan. X).

And shortly afterward:

> “Now I shall return to fight against the prince of Persia. When I was going out, the prince of the Greeks appeared, coming” (ibid.).

“Whom else,” says blessed Gregory (*Moralia*, book XVII, chapter 8), “does he call the princes of the nations except angels? For certain ministries of the angels have been placed over the administration of each nation, whenever the conduct of those subject to them merits the assistance of the spirits set over them against one another; and the spirits who preside are reported to come against one another.

“That angel who was speaking to Daniel is recognized as having been placed over the captives of the Israelite people who were in Persia; Michael, however, is found to have been placed over those of the same people who had remained in the land of Judaea. Hence, shortly afterward, the same angel says to Daniel: ‘There is no one who helps me in all these matters except Michael, your prince’; concerning him he says: ‘And behold, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me.’ Since he is said not to be present with him but to come to his aid, it is clearly recognized that he was placed over that people which was being held captive in another region.

“What, then, does it mean for the angel to say, ‘I came because of your words, but the prince of the kingdom of Persia resisted me,’ except that he is announcing to his subjects the works he has performed?”

Blessed Jerome says corresponding things, which anyone who wishes may read more fully in their proper places. In accordance with this model, orders in the world have also been distinguished by God’s ordinance, as the Apostle shows when he says:

> “Be subject to every human creature for God’s sake, whether to the king as pre-eminent, or to governors as sent by him” (1 Peter II, 13).

“It is clear,” says blessed Gregory (*Moralia*, book XXI, chapter 10), “that nature brought forth all human beings equal, but by the varying order of merits, guilt has placed some below others. This very diversity, which arose from vice, is administered by divine judgment, so that, since no human being is able to stand equally on his own, one is ruled by another.”

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning fatherhoods and dwelling-places in heaven, in the Church, and in the commonwealth

Since, through distinct orders, fatherhoods and dwelling-places have been established by God in heaven, concerning which Daniel says, “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him” (Dan. VII)—to whom the number of the elect among human beings is also joined—and since ministering is one thing and standing before him another, so, in the likeness of this heavenly arrangement, not only the divisions of ecclesiastical dwelling-places but also those of earthly ones exist as dispositions established by God, just as they existed among the ancient people, as the Pentateuch demonstrates in the division of the Promised Land among the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel.

Thus Paul, speaking in the Synagogue at Antioch, said: “The God of the people of Israel chose our fathers” (Acts XIII, 17); and shortly afterward: “Having destroyed seven nations in the land of Canaan, he distributed their land to them by lot” (ibid., 19). “He cast out the nations from before them,” says the Psalm, “and divided their land among them by lot, with the measuring-line of distribution” (Ps. LXXVII). And blessed John says in the Apocalypse that he heard the number of those sealed from each tribe: twelve thousand (Apoc. VII).

By this defined number, as Catholic teachers explain, the countless multitude of the whole Church is signified—she who has been brought forth from the patriarchs, whether by descent of the flesh or by imitation of faith. “If you are Christ’s,” he says, “then you are Abraham’s offspring” (Gal. III, 29).

For the increase of perfection, it also pertains that twelve should itself be multiplied twelvefold and brought to the total of a thousand, which is the solid square number ten, signifying the stable life of the Church. For this reason the Church is so often represented by the number twelve, because she stands in the faith of the Holy Trinity through the four-square world. Three groups of four make a *duodecimpondium* [a twelve-unit weight]. Finally, the apostles, chosen to preach the same faith to the world, are twelve, thereby figuratively expressing the mystery of their work. They were sent to preach throughout the four-square world the faith of the Holy Trinity, and the Lord Jesus Christ, incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, and him crucified, as contained in the Creed. By this sign of the cross, the faithful are shown to have been marked both figuratively through Ezekiel (Ezek. IX) and in visible reality through John (Apoc. VII).

For the very figure of the cross signifies the Lord’s kingdom extended everywhere, and the universal sovereignty of the faith represented by that sign, as the old couplet proves:

> Behold the square world, divided into ordered parts,  
> that you may prove the whole to be held by the sign of faith.

Nor was the Lord’s name, the tetragrammaton, written on the forehead of the high priest without reason, except because this is the sign on the foreheads of the faithful, concerning which the Psalm for the winepresses sings:

> “O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth!”  

and so forth, until it says, “that you may destroy the enemy and the defender” (Ps. VIII).

Blessed Basil, in his homily on Psalm LIX, also demonstrates that the dwelling-places of parishes and regions, formerly foretold by the Holy Spirit through the prophet before Christ’s incarnation, were destined after the Ascension into heaven to be measured out by that same Holy Spirit through holy men of God. He explains the verse:

> “I will measure out the valley of tents.”

“This,” he says, “which was once a special and, as it were, private people—namely, the Israelite inheritance of the people—I will summon to distribution and make common with all the others. But when the testament has been divided among all, and its benefit has begun to be common to everyone, then also ‘the valley of tents’ will be measured out—that is, the whole world, which is called the valley of tents because of the dwelling-places of bodies. It will be divided and measured out, as though by lot, and distributed in each place among the parishes and dwelling-places of the Churches of God.

“Then also he who makes peace through the blood of his cross will gather into the unity of faith the things that have been divided, whether those on earth or those in heaven; and, by dissolving the dividing wall, he made both one.”

Hence it is written again:

> “Distribute her houses”—that is, those of the universal Church—“among the parishes of the watchmen by preaching, so that you may recount it to the next generation: for this is our God, and he will rule us forever” (Ps. XLVII).

In accordance with this model, and according to the constitution of Anacletus, Pope Dionysius established and ordered definite boundaries for rural parishes; the Council of Chalcedon also issued known decrees concerning these matters.

Concerning the division of provinces and the privileges of cities, which the gentiles established in the likeness of the twelve tribes of the Israelite people and which were later confirmed by apostolic constitution, Saint Clement wrote in his first letter to James, bishop of Jerusalem, who is also called the brother of the Lord. You did not wish to insert this in your compilation, any more than the preceding words of Leo, lest it be found in them that you ought in any way to be subject to anyone except the pontiff of the Apostolic See. You foolishly thought that if you did not place these things in your little document, others would have no books in which they could read them.

But who is ignorant of what you know? Before you were formed in the womb, we knew these things; and before you came forth from the womb, we had read them very often—and we understood the sacred Scriptures and holy canons more discerningly than you do.

For blessed Clement says, among other things, in the aforementioned letter (Epistle 2, near the middle):

> “Blessed Peter ordered that in those cities where formerly, among the gentiles, their chief flamens and chief teachers of the law had been established, primates of bishops or patriarchs should be appointed. They were to handle the judgments of the other bishops and the greater affairs whenever necessary in matters of faith, and, in accordance with the Lord’s will and as the holy apostles had established, to decide them, so that no one might be unjustly endangered.

> “In those cities, however, where formerly among the aforementioned gentiles there were their chief flamens, whom they nevertheless held to be inferior to the primates just mentioned, he ordered archbishops to be instituted. They were not, however, to enjoy the name of primates, but of archbishops. He taught that the judgments of bishops, as mentioned above, and the greater affairs of the Churches, if the bishops themselves appealed, or had any fear, or regarded these or others as suspect, were to be transferred to the primates or patriarchs already mentioned, lest anyone innocent should perish.

> “In each of the remaining cities he ordered one bishop, not two or three or more, to be appointed. They were not to possess the name of primates, archbishops, or metropolitans, since they did not govern mother-cities, but were to enjoy only the title of bishops, because even among the apostles the institution was not equal, but one presided over all.

> “He nevertheless established this precaution: that bishops should not be instituted in villages, fortresses, or small cities, lest their name become insignificant. Thus, he said that the Lord taught that bishops should stand in the place of the apostles, and he indicated that presbyters ought to occupy the place of the remaining disciples.”

And Saint Anacletus, Clement’s successor, ordained presbyter by the blessed apostle Peter, says in his first letter to all bishops and the other faithful (Epistle 1, near the end):

> “The holy apostles, at the Savior’s command, decreed that the privileges of Churches and priests should remain inviolate and untouched throughout the ages. We confirm the laws of the Church by apostolic authority, [Col. 0330C] and remove foreign judgments.

> “Therefore, when the Lord makes mention of Lot, he speaks through Moses, saying: ‘You entered as a resident alien; are you now acting as a judge?’ (Gen. XIX.) Each province, according both to ecclesiastical and secular laws, ought to have its own just, not unjust, judges, and not outsiders, unless the authority of this Apostolic See should decree otherwise. Thus, whoever has a case may be judged before his own judges, and may not cross over to foreigners, driven by the arrogance of wandering about and despising his own homeland.

> “Rather, the matter should be brought before the twelve judges of that province, before whose judgment all the cases of the cities are referred. If it is an ecclesiastical matter, it should be brought before the bishops, with the intervention of the primate if the case is major, but before the metropolitan if it is minor. If it is a secular matter, it should be brought before men of the same order, though under the judgment of the bishops, since the Apostle wished the cases of private Christians to be brought especially before the Churches and settled there by priestly judgment.”

And in his second letter to the bishops established in Italy he says:

> “The provinces were divided, for the most part, long before Christ’s coming; afterward the division itself was renewed by the apostles and by our predecessor, blessed Clement. At the head of the provinces, where formerly the chief teachers of secular law and the highest judicial authority were found—those to whom the people dwelling throughout the other cities appealed whenever necessity required, when they could not or were not permitted to flee to the courts of emperors or kings because of their oppressions or injustices, and whom they appealed to whenever necessary, as their law commanded—there too they ordered patriarchs or primates of our own to be appointed and established in the cities or places. These hold one form, although their names differ, according to divine and ecclesiastical law.

> “To them bishops were to flee and appeal if necessary; they alone were to enjoy the name of primates, and no others. The remaining metropolitan cities, which had lesser judges, although they were greater than the counts, were to have their own metropolitans, who were justly to obey the primates mentioned above, just as had formerly been ordered in secular law. They were not to enjoy the name of primates, but either of metropolitans or archbishops.

> “Although each metropolis has its own province and ought to have its own metropolitan bishops, just as it formerly had secular metropolitan judges, nevertheless the provinces were ordered then and now to have primates, as stated above. After the Apostolic See, the most important affairs are to come before them, so that those who need it may there be relieved and justly restored, and those who are unjustly oppressed may be rightly reformed and supported. The cases of bishops and the judgments of the greatest affairs are to be settled with the utmost justice, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See.”

And in his third letter:

> “Concerning the primates, dearest brothers, about whom some of you have consulted me—whether they ought to exist or not—we cannot at all withhold from you what we have hitherto known to have been established concerning them by the blessed apostle Peter, by the other apostles, and by our blessed predecessor and holy martyr Clement. Who could refuse their brothers’ questions and deny them clarification or assistance?

> “The order of priests, brothers, is twofold, and as the Lord established it, it ought to be disturbed by no one. You know that the apostles were chosen and appointed by the Lord, and afterward dispersed through the various provinces to preach. When the harvest began to increase, he saw that the laborers were few and ordered seventy disciples to be chosen to assist them.

> “The bishops of the Lord occupy the place of the apostles, and the presbyters the place of the seventy disciples. Bishops ought not to be appointed in fortresses or small cities; rather, presbyters ought to be ordained and placed by bishops throughout fortresses, small cities, and villages, one in each of their proper titles.

> “A bishop ought not to be ordained by one bishop but by several; and, as has been said, he is not to be assigned and named to a small city, lest the name of bishop become insignificant, but to an honorable city. A presbyter, however, is to be placed over any kind of place, or over a church established there, and is to remain in it for the days of his life.

> “Beyond these two orders of priests, neither have we received any others from God, nor did the apostles teach them. The order of bishops is one, although those who hold the chief cities are primates, and in certain places are called patriarchs by some.

> “Those who have been established in a metropolis by blessed Peter, at the Lord’s command, by our aforementioned predecessor Saint Clement, or by us, cannot all be primates or patriarchs. Rather, those cities which in former and ancient times held primacy may enjoy the name of archbishops, patriarchs, or primates. The remaining metropolises are to use the names of archbishops or metropolitans, and not of patriarchs or primates, since secular laws also contain these same distinctions among their rulers.

> “The other chief cities, which we are sending to you written out in a certain volume, received their primate preachers from the holy apostles, from blessed Clement, or from us.

> “But this most holy Roman and Apostolic Church obtained its primacy not from others but from the Lord himself, our Savior, just as he said to the blessed apostle Peter: ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.’

And shortly afterward:

> “The first See, therefore, by heavenly favor, is that of the Roman Church, which, as has been mentioned, the most blessed Peter and Paul consecrated by their martyrdom. The second See, at Alexandria, was consecrated in the name of blessed Peter by Mark, his disciple and evangelist, because, sent by Peter, he first preached the word of truth in Egypt and received a glorious martyrdom; the venerable Abilius succeeded him.

> “The third See, at Antioch—that is, the honorable See of the blessed apostle Peter—is so called because he lived there before coming to Rome and appointed Ignatius bishop there, and because there the name “Christians” first arose for the new people.

> “As for the remaining Sees, to avoid making the letter too long, we have sent them to you written out in a certain volume. For this reason the blessed apostles also established among themselves that the bishops of each people should know who among them was first, so that the greater part of their concern might belong to him.

> “For there was also a certain distinction among the blessed apostles. Although all were apostles, the Lord granted to Peter—and they themselves desired the same among themselves—that he should preside over all the other apostles and hold Cephas, that is, the head and beginning of the apostolate. They handed down this same arrangement to be maintained by their successors and the other apostles.

> “Nor was this established only in the New Testament; it also existed in the Old. Hence it is written: ‘Moses and Aaron among his priests’ (Ps. XVII)—that is, they were first among them.”

Then the holy Council of Nicaea decreed with fewer words, but with no less authority (canon 6), that:

> “The ancient custom—that is, the custom established among the gentiles and later confirmed by apostolic constitution—shall be preserved, so that the bishop of Alexandria shall have authority over all those subject to him, since the bishop of the city of Rome has a similar custom. Likewise, the privileges of the Churches in Antioch and the other provinces shall be preserved.”

Leaving these matters aside—and also what Zephyrinus decreed (Epistle 1), namely, that any bishop who was accused should be judged by twelve bishops—you turned to Callistus and Lucius, and did not wish to mention what Stephen, who came after them, established. He says (Epistle 2):

> “No man of the aforementioned order, namely, the episcopal order, may be accused, nor ought he to answer his accusers, before he has been regularly summoned by his primate and has received the opportunity to defend himself and to investigate the charges, so that he may clear himself of the accusations.

> “No metropolitan or other bishop is to be called a primate except those who hold the chief Sees and whose cities the ancient primates judged to be primary. The others who have obtained metropolitan cities are to be called not primates or archbishops, but metropolitans.

> “For the cities and places over which primates ought to preside were established not only in recent times but also many ages before Christ’s coming; even the gentiles appealed to their primates in those cities concerning their greater affairs. In those cities, after Christ’s coming, the apostles and their successors placed patriarchs or primates, to whom the affairs of bishops—and, after the Apostolic See, the greater cases—are to be referred, with the authority of the Apostolic See preserved in every respect.

> “Although, because the Apostle forbade it, accusations ought not to be brought among Christians, if accusations cannot be prevented, the accusations against bishops must be brought by their accusers before the primates mentioned above. Nevertheless, bishops should strive to urge divided brothers toward peace rather than judgment.

> “A bishop must not otherwise be heard or judged except in the presence of all his provincial bishops and by all the provincial bishops. In their absence he neither ought nor can be judged.”

Then, while explaining many things from many sources which seemed to support your position but in fact are shown to refute it, you passed over Pelagius, the predecessor of Saint Gregory; and, so far as you were able, you alienated from its meaning a statement of his successor, blessed Gregory, to the patrician Theoctista, corrupting it with words foreign to blessed Gregory.

For Pelagius himself says to the bishops who, by an unjust summons of John to a synod at Constantinople, resolved that he should be called “universal” (Pelagius II, Epistle 1, near the end):

> “For the rest, brothers, concerning the matter of the province, about which you formerly wished to consult the Apostolic See, it seems to us that our holy predecessors dealt with it sufficiently. But since you have now thought it appropriate to question our mediocrity again about the same matter, know that a province is properly one that has ten or eleven cities, one king, and an equal number of lesser powers under him, as well as one bishop and ten or eleven other suffragan bishops as judges. All cases of bishops, the other priests, and the cities are to be referred to their judgment, so that all of them may decide them justly and with one accord, unless those who are to be judged appeal to a greater authority.

> “Therefore, each province ought not to be degraded or dishonored, but should have within itself its own priestly judges and individual bishops, according to their respective orders. Whoever has a case should be judged by his own judges, not by outsiders—that is, by the just judges of his own province and not by foreigners—unless, as has already been stated, the person to be judged appeals.

> “If questions arise in any province, and disagreement begins to develop among the bishops of that province, so that the dissenting parties cannot reach agreement, the matter should then be referred to a greater See. If it cannot there be readily and justly discerned, it should be decided canonically and justly wherever a synod has been regularly assembled.

> “But greater and more difficult questions, as the holy Synod established and blessed custom requires, must always be referred to the Apostolic See.”

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning the metropolis of Rheims and the fortress of Laon; and that the three primary Sees were one See of Peter. The letter of Hormisdas to Saint Remigius

[Col. 0334B]

See, brother, whether the province subject from ancient times to the metropolis of Rheims is indeed a fixed one. This metropolis had eleven cities under it even before blessed Remigius, by the authority of the African Council, ordained as bishop in the fortress where you too were ordained bishop as a suffragan of your metropolis—and as an opponent of that dignity and authority. From a small-town bishop, as the saying goes, you have grown into a great one in your own estimation.

According to the ancient historian Eutropius, that place was founded by the praetor Marcobrius; from its origin in paganism it possessed neither the name nor the status of a city or provincial See. After blessed Sixtus, sent by Sixtus, pontiff of the Roman See, was the first bishop dispatched to the metropolitan Church of Rheims, it retained a municipal status in Christianity for fifteen archiepiscopal terms, over the course of many years, within the parish of Rheims, just as did the other municipalities that still exist there today. The volume that Anacletus says he sent to the bishops who questioned him about the privileges of the Sees plainly demonstrates this. You can read it yourself in the same brief, where, after the cities subject to the metropolis of Rheims have been listed, you will find no mention whatsoever of the fortress in which you were ordained bishop.

For many years also, during the time of that same blessed Remigius—who, as the truthful histories of our people show, spent seventy-four years and more in the episcopate, and, distinguished by many remarkable virtues, ordained a bishop there in his old age—he sufficiently endowed that bishopric with ecclesiastical property [Col. 0334D] (for, according to the sacred rules, whatever property and bondservants a bishop acquires in the course of his episcopate, as well as those that previously belonged to the Church, are regarded as ecclesiastical).

Therefore, just as we specifically read that the Sees of the Churches of Rome, Alexandria, and Antioch are called Sees, although there are many other Sees of the apostles—for example, that of James at Jerusalem and that of John at Ephesus, where Timothy, the disciple of blessed Paul, also sat, as well as many other principal cities, since they too are Sees—or rather, although they are separated by the distances of their lands, they are one See of the great Peter, chief of the apostles—so, in its own measure, the metropolis of Rheims and the parish of Laon are, in particular, one See among the other provincial Sees of the province of Rheims. For blessed Remigius caused the same See of Laon to sit as a subordinate seat within the metropolitan See of Rheims; he cut it off from his own parish, but not from the province of the diocese.

That the Sees of Alexandria and Antioch, like the Roman See, are Sees of blessed Peter, Leo demonstrates in his letter to Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria (Epistle 7):

> “Since the most blessed Peter received the primacy of the apostolate from the Lord, and the Roman Church remains in his institutions, it is impious to believe that his holy disciple Mark, who first governed the Church of Alexandria, established the decrees of his traditions according to other rules. Without doubt, from the same source of grace there was one Spirit in the disciple and in the teacher, and the disciple could not hand down anything other than what he had received from the one who ordained him.

> “Therefore, we do not permit ourselves, while confessing that we are one body and one faith, to differ in any respect, or that the institutions of the teacher should appear to be one thing and those of the disciple another.”

And Saint Gregory says to Eulogius, bishop of Alexandria (book VIII, Epistle 42):

> “The minister of truth, follower of Peter and preacher of the holy Church, knows that you were able to say those things which ought to resound from the See of the apostle Peter through the mouth of a teacher.”

And again the same man says to him:

> “Let there be praise for him; let there be glory on high, by whose gift the voice of Mark still cries from the See of Peter.”

Concerning the Church of Antioch, Saint Innocent says to Alexander, bishop of Antioch (Epistle 20):

> “Thus, as we review the authority of the Council of Nicaea—which expresses the mind of all the priests throughout the world—we see that it judged it necessary for all the faithful, not to say all priests, to preserve what it decreed concerning the Church of Antioch. We recognize that the said Church was established over its own diocese and not over any other province.

> “From this we understand that this privilege was attributed to it not so much because of the magnificence of the city as because it is shown to be the first See of the first apostle: there the Christian religion received its name; there the most celebrated gathering of the apostles deserved to take place; and it would not yield to the See of the city of Rome except that Rome received its privilege in passing, whereas Antioch rejoices in having received and completed it within itself.”

And Leo says to Maximus, bishop of Antioch (Epistle 66):

> “Your Holiness ought with your whole heart to consider over which Church the Lord wished you to preside, and to remember the teaching which the most blessed Peter, chief of all the apostles, founded throughout the whole world by a uniform proclamation, but by a special teaching in the cities of Antioch and Rome. Thus, recognizing him as pre-eminent in the dwelling-place of his glorification, you should understand that he requires the institutions he handed down, just as he received them from the very truth he confessed.

> “Do not in any way allow the Gospel to be opposed by wicked heretics in the Eastern Churches, especially in those which the canons of the holy Fathers at Nicaea assigned to the See of Antioch.”

And after a little:

> “For it is fitting that you should share with the Apostolic See in this concern, and acknowledge, for the confidence to act, the privileges of the third See, which are diminished by no one’s ambition. For my reverence for the canons of Nicaea is so great that I have neither permitted nor will I permit those things established by the holy Fathers to be violated by any innovation.

> “Although the merits of prelates are sometimes different, the rights of the Sees nevertheless remain. Rivals may perhaps bring some disturbance against them, but they cannot diminish their dignity.”

And Saint Gregory to Anastasius, bishop of Antioch (Book VII, Letter 3):

“Behold, in your holy old age your Blessedness is laboring under many tribulations; but consider whose see you occupy. Is it not that of him to whom the voice of Truth said: ‘When you have grown old, another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go’? (John 21).”

And again to the same man (Book IV, Letter 37):

“Amen. Grace. I have placed these words, taken from your writings, in my letters so that your Blessedness may know concerning Saint Ignatius that he is not yours alone, but ours also. For just as we hold in common his teacher, the chief of the apostles, so none of us possesses privately the disciple of that same chief.”

For when blessed Peter was setting out for Rome, he ordained this Ignatius bishop at Antioch in his place. And although blessed Peter had previously occupied the see at Antioch before he came to Rome, from where he sent Mark to Alexandria, Antioch is nevertheless called not the second but the third see, and the Alexandrian Church the second see, because of the privilege of the Gospel, which Saint Mark the evangelist received and wrote down from Peter’s mouth, and which he preached in Alexandria, founding the Alexandrian people, together with the cities subject to that great city, upon the foundation of the true faith.

Thus Saint Gregory also writes, among other things, to Eulogius, bishop of Alexandria (Book V, Letter 60):

“There is something that binds us to the Alexandrian Church with a certain special bond and compels us, by a particular kind of law, to be more ready in its love. For, as it is clear to all, just as blessed Mark the evangelist was sent to Alexandria by the holy apostle Peter, his teacher, so we are bound by the unity of this teacher and disciple, so that I appear to preside over the see of the disciple because of the teacher, while you preside over the see of the teacher because of the disciple. We are also bound to this unity of hearts by the merits of your Holiness, since we recognize that you salutarily follow the institutions of its founder and perceive that you always turn yourselves with complete devotion toward the bosom of your teacher, from which the preaching of salvation arose there.”

And again, that those three sees—namely, the Roman, Alexandrian, and Antiochene—are one see of Peter, he writes to the same Eulogius, bishop of Alexandria (Book VI, Letter 37):

“Your most gracious Holiness spoke at length in your letters about the chair of the holy chief of the apostles, Peter, saying that he himself continues to sit in it to this day in his successors. I recognize that I am unworthy not only to be counted among those who preside, but even among those who stand; nevertheless, I gladly accepted everything that was said because the one who holds Peter’s chair spoke to me about Peter’s chair. Although a special honor in no way pleases me, I nevertheless rejoiced greatly because, in granting me what you did, most holy brother, you gave it to yourselves.

“For who does not know that the holy Church was established upon the steadfastness of the chief of the apostles, who drew firmness of mind from his name, so that he was called Peter from the rock? To him the voice of Truth says: ‘I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven’ (Matthew 16); and again: ‘And you, when you have returned, strengthen your brothers’ (Luke 22); and again: ‘Simon, son of John, do you love me? Feed my sheep’ (John 21).

“Thus, although there are many apostles, nevertheless, because of that primacy, the sole see of the chief of the apostles has prevailed in authority, and it is one in three places. He himself exalted the see in which he also deigned to rest and to end his life while presiding. He himself adorned the see to which he sent his evangelist disciple. He himself strengthened the see in which he sat for seven years, although he was later to depart.

“Therefore, since the see is one and the same, and since by divine authority three bishops now preside over it, whatever good I hear about you I attribute to myself; if you believe anything good about me, attribute it to your own merits, because in him we are one who said: ‘That they all may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they also may be one in us’ (John 17).”

If, then, brother, forgetting the benefits I have bestowed upon you and mindful of none of them, you do not fear rebelling against me, nevertheless fear rebelling against blessed Remigius, who, as you have just heard, continues to sit in his successors, whatever sort they may be. Since by divine authority you reside in the see that belongs to him, and since through the benevolence of that same blessed Remigius it has been counted among the sees, which previously it had not been, you ought to attribute to yourself whatever good you hear about me, who sit in his see; for whatever good I hear about you, I attribute to myself, and whatever unfavorable report I hear about you, I attribute not only to your sins but also to mine, since by the laying on of my hands I recognize that, by God’s judgment, you reside in that see.

Therefore cease from the wickedness of mind that you have undertaken, and assume humility of mind together with the strength of holy obedience, so that in him we may be one who said: “That they all may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they also may be one in us.”

For, as you have heard from the words of the apostolic see, although the bishops of these Churches—namely, the Alexandrian and Antiochene—recognize that they occupy the sees of blessed Peter, as the Roman pontiffs also attest, they nevertheless do not deny that these sees are subject to the Roman see, nor do they in any way disdain to be subject to the Roman pontiff. Nor have your predecessors and forebears disdained to be subject to the bishops of Rheims and, when they came into the parish itself, humbly and graciously to serve the Church of Rheims in matters belonging to the Church of Rheims, the metropolitan church, from which the bishopric of Laon had been enriched.

This has been so since blessed Remigius not only appointed Saint Genebaud bishop in the castle of Laon, but also—according to ancient tradition and the memorial of his confinement, by which he confined him according to the rules because of his notorious offense—restored him after suitable satisfaction. In the same way your predecessors Simeon and Pardulus, whom you succeeded, behaved toward me up to the time of your elevation. The Church of Rheims nurtured you from what I may call your very cradle with sweet kindness, washed and stripped away the clothing of your infancy, brought you to manhood, and raised you to the episcopate.

Concerning you it now says through the mouths of those who serve it, with sighs and groans: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us.”

And observing how the bishops of the cities of its province—whom it did not nurture but regularly ordained—render to it the services of kindness, humility, and obedience, it says:

“The people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me. But a foreign son lied to me; a foreign son grew old” (Psalm 17),

that is, because what he does belongs to the old man, and he limps from his paths, along which he ought to run in humility and obedience according to the Lord’s commandments. And, taking up the Lord’s lament from Isaiah, it says: “I nourished and exalted a son, but he himself despises me” (Isaiah 1).

Although you perhaps neither reflect upon nor fear this, you may nevertheless be certain that Saint Remigius will demand before the Lord from you the obedience owed to his successors and to your superiors—the obedience that he instituted when, in the same castle in which you were ordained, he consecrated a bishop, just as we read in the words of blessed Leo to Maximus, bishop of Antioch:

“I appointed blessed Peter, pre-eminent in the dwelling of his glorification, to demand the institutions that he handed down at Antioch.”

Nevertheless, whether you wish it or not, Saint Hormisdas the pope will show you that the primate of this province is the bishop ordained in the see of blessed Remigius at the metropolitan city of Rheims. For in a letter addressed to him he says:

“To Remigius, our most beloved brother, Hormisdas.

“Receiving the greetings of your fraternity, full of brotherly joy, by which you gladdened us with the evidence of your genuine salvation, and learning that your bodily health is supported by spiritual offices, we have judged it fitting to disclose in words this joy that we bear in our minds. For you perform the examples of the supreme pontiff when you do things worthy of praise and do not delay making them known.
