“We therefore took a prerogative from the judgment of our own choice when we learned that you had done what we most insistently command others to do: that, in provinces separated by such great distances, you strive to apply both the vigor of the apostolic see and careful observance of the rules of the Fathers.

“Accordingly, we entrust to you our responsibilities throughout the entire kingdom of our beloved and spiritual son Clovis, whom recently, with heavenly grace assisting, you converted to the faith together with his whole people, accompanying your salutary preaching with many miracles of signs comparable to those of the apostles, and consecrated through the gift of sacred baptism—without prejudice to the privileges that antiquity decreed for metropolitans. By this present authority we increase the dignity of your ministry through participation in this service and lighten our own watchfulness by the remedy of such an arrangement.

“Although you do not need instruction concerning individual matters, since we have already proved that you preserve everything with exceptional care, it is nevertheless more pleasing when a path is shown to those who are to travel and the form of the assigned work is displayed to those who must labor.

“Therefore we command that the paternal rules and the decrees defined by the most holy councils be observed by all. In these matters we show your vigilance; in these matters, your care and the admonitions of brotherly exhortation. When these are guarded with all the reverence that is fitting, no obstacle to holy observance leaves room for guilt. There what is lawful and unlawful has been written down; there is what is forbidden, which no one should dare to pursue; there is what has been granted, which a mind wishing to please God ought to undertake.

“Whenever the cause of religion demands a universal council, let all the brothers assemble when summoned by you. And if the particular concern of any of them presses upon them, restrain the quarrels that have arisen among them, determining the disputes after examination according to sacred law. Whatever is there established for the faith and truth, commanded by prudent administration, or confirmed by the authority of our person, let it all reach our knowledge through an informed report bearing its testimony. Thus our mind will enjoy the charity of the duty entrusted, and yours the security of what has been received.

“May God keep you safe, dearest brother.”

Pope Adrian likewise granted such privileges of his authority to Tilpin, our predecessor, and to the Church entrusted to him, as the documents we possess demonstrate. My insignificance has neither deserved, sought, desired, nor requested these privileges, although the authority of Leo IV and the authority in the name and grace of Benedict have conferred upon me privileges that I did not seek, because what has been granted to each metropolitan through the sacred canons is sufficient for me.

Therefore, just as it is generally fitting for all bishops to beseech the Lord for the Roman pontiff, the special vicar of Peter—as ecclesiastical tradition also demonstrates, concerning which Coelestine says [after Letter 8]:

“Let us consider the mysteries of priestly supplications, which, handed down by the apostles, are celebrated uniformly throughout the world and in every Catholic Church, so that the law of praying may establish the law of believing”—

and just as all ought to obey him, as is known to have been decreed from evangelical and apostolic authority, the tradition of our forebears, and ancient custom, so it is fitting that all the co-bishops of the province who are ordained by the primate of their metropolitan church should obey him according to the sacred rules and pray to the Lord for him, since the safety of the one who presides is the salvation of those subject to him.

It was also fitting that you should show more watchful care in these matters, since the metropolitan church of Rheims, having nurtured you in the manner I have described, ordained you as bishop in the seat of its own see. I present this not on my own authority but from the meaning of Scripture, following the teaching of blessed Leo (Sermon 3, on the anniversary of his accession):

“When his passion was approaching, which was to disturb the steadfastness of the disciples, the Lord said: ‘Simon, behold, Satan has demanded to sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail; and you, when you have returned, strengthen your brothers’ (Luke 22:31–32). And to all the apostles: ‘Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation’ (Matthew 26:41).

“The danger arising from the temptation of fear was common to all the apostles, and they equally needed the help of divine protection, because the devil desired to harass them all and overthrow them all. Yet the Lord undertakes a special care for Peter, so that he specifically prays for Peter’s faith, as though the standing of the others would be more secure if the mind of the chief had not been conquered. In Peter, therefore, the strength of all is fortified, and divine grace arranges its help in such a way that the firmness granted to Peter through Christ is conferred through Peter upon the apostles.”

Since, then, through the primate of the province, the grace of the Holy Spirit and the episcopal order are bestowed upon you, the co-bishops of the province, by prayers and the laying on of hands at your ordination, it is judged right that, with the Roman pope presiding, you should return to him the devotion of prayer and the affection of obedience. We read that this was done in those times when iniquity had not yet grown so abundant and charity had not yet grown cold, as is happening in our days.

Read, surely, Leo’s letter to Anastasius, and you will find that the bishops of his province came to Rome with Atticus, their metropolitan, without any postponement being granted, not deterred by fear of the highest among worldly powers, by the violence of winter, by a harsh road full of dangers, or by impassable snows. They came with such labor and peril that some of those who accompanied the bishop collapsed, and later complained to him in a tearful account about the unworthy affliction he had endured.

How would you act if you saw your metropolitan in such need—you who strive with every exertion you can muster to diminish the authority anciently attributed to your metropolitan church through the sacred rules and thereby to take away the rights owed to all metropolitans?

For just as the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “And if I am not an apostle to others, yet surely I am to you; for you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 9), and even if I were perhaps not a primate to others, I ought nevertheless to have been a primate to you and in your own eyes; for you are the seal of my primacy, since without consulting another primate, but with the consent of the co-bishops of the province of Rheims, I was able to ordain you bishop.

At that time you eagerly and ardently desired me to be primate of the entire province, merely so that you might be able to be bishop in even a single little town. And, if I had wished and authority and reason had permitted it, you, greedy for honor and power, would even have consented to become a rural bishop, who in Greek is called a chorepiscopus—that is, a “country bishop”—as is now apparent, since you abuse the ministry and authority of humility in the vanity of greed and pride.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the rebellion of lesser priests against their superiors, and on the see of Constantinople resisting the apostolic see

Since these things are so, I am not surprised that I was able to provoke you to such a degree that you swelled up against me and refused, according to the divine ordering, to be subject—though he who refused to be subject to his Creator was miserably cast down from heaven with his accomplices into this darkened air, to be tortured by eternal punishments.

For even in the Old Testament we read that priests of lesser dignity rose up against their superiors: Korah, namely, with his accomplices. Therefore they received the punishment they deserved from the Lord, as the venerable history relates (Numbers 16).

Likewise, in the New Testament we read of seditions arising among the sacred orders: first, deacons rising up against presbyters, and then presbyters and chorepiscopi against bishops. We therefore need not now extend our discourse at length on matters that we know have been settled by the sacred canons.

Let us speak only of the episcopal order, which the fire of greed and the seizure of high rank was able to inflame to such a degree, as it is written: “Open your doors, Lebanon, and let fire consume your cedars” (Zechariah 11), that some did not fear resisting God’s ordering; and when they could not obtain that they should not be subject to those set over them, they even established heresies and schisms and cast themselves out from the unity of the Church, as we can demonstrate by many proofs.

We also frequently find in the sacred canons bishops rebelling against their metropolitans or archbishops—for these two names designate the dignity of this excellence—and likewise metropolitans or archbishops against primates or patriarchs, who under these two names exercise one primatial office.

Certain archbishops or metropolitan primates of provinces are also frequently found in the sacred canons. These are those who, in place of deceased archbishops or metropolitans, prevail in being ordained by the bishops of each province without consulting another primate; who, according to the law of ancient custom, are accustomed to be marked by the pallium from the apostolic see; and who, in place of deceased bishops, can each ordain bishops in his own province without the consultation or permission of another primate.

Saint Gregory clearly shows this when writing to Augustine, bishop of the Angles (Book XII, Letter 31, Question 9):

“We grant you no authority over the bishops of Gaul, because from the ancient times of my predecessors the bishop of Arles has received the pallium, and we ought by no means to deprive him of the authority he has received.”

And a little later:

“You will not be able to judge the bishops of Gaul by your own authority. Instead, by persuasion, by kindness, and by showing them your good works as examples to imitate, reform the minds of the wicked toward the pursuit of holiness. For it is written in the Law: ‘When passing through another person’s harvest, you must not put in the sickle, but you may crush the ears with your hand and eat them.’ You cannot put the sickle of judgment into a field that appears to have been entrusted to another; but through the effect of good works, strip the Lord’s grain of the chaff of its vices and, by admonishing and persuading, convert it into the body of the Church as though by chewing it. When action must be taken by authority, let the matter be handled with the aforesaid bishop of Arles, so that what the ancient institution of the Fathers has established may not be disregarded.”

What he said concerning this one Gallican primate, who had received the pallium from the apostolic see, must certainly also be understood concerning the other primates of Gaul, Belgium, and Germany. Among them, as among the other bishops, this regular condition is observed: that whoever was ordained first is regarded as first, as the same Saint Gregory plainly shows in his letter to the aforementioned Augustine.

Concerning these primates, the councils of the African province say (Council of Carthage, canon 19):

“Whoever among the bishops is accused should have the accuser bring the case to the primate of that province.”

And again:

“Those who think an appeal should be made shall appeal to the primates of their provinces, just as has often been established concerning bishops.”

And again (African Council, canon 92):

“But if they think an appeal should be made from them—that is, from the neighboring bishops—they shall appeal only to the African councils or to the primates of their provinces.”

And again (Council of Carthage, canon 17):

“That each province, because of its great distance, should have its own primate. It has been decided that Mauritania Sitifensis, as it requested a primate from the province of Numidia, from whose assembly it is separated, should have its own primate. It was permitted to have one because of the distance, with the consent of all the primates of the African provinces or of all the bishops.”

A bishop who has not attended the synod is also ordered to give an account of the reason for his absence to his own primate. That primate must appoint judges in whose province the place has been designated, and the cases are to be concluded by episcopal judges, whether those whom the primates appoint or those whom neighboring bishops, seeking agreement among themselves, choose by common consent.

“And bishops” (Council of Carthage, canon 23) “must not travel across the sea unless they have consulted the bishop of the first see of their respective province.”

Saint Zosimus also wrote to all the bishops established throughout Gaul and the seven provinces (Letter 5):

“Whoever, having disregarded the formal letter of his metropolitan—whether he is a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or of any lower rank—comes to him must know that he cannot be received at all.”

Pope Hilary likewise says in his decrees to the five provinces (Letter 8):

“We could not pass over this matter either, since it must be guarded with more diligent concern: that no bishops should dare to travel to any province without letters from their metropolitans. This too must be observed in every kind of clerical office throughout the individual Churches.”

And Saint Gregory writes to Vincent and the other bishops (Book VII, Letter 8, Indiction 11):

“We exhort your fraternity that, if necessity should compel any of you to travel somewhere farther away for your own affairs, you must seek permission from your metropolitan according to the rule handed down by the holy Fathers, and you must not presume to disregard him in anything—except if, which we do not wish, it should happen that you have some case against that same metropolitan, so that for this reason those who hasten to seek permission may have recourse to the judgment of the apostolic see. You know that this has been permitted by the canons and by the institution of the ancient Fathers.”

It is clear that he is speaking of the Sardican canons, which Innocent also mentions in his letter to Victricius, and concerning which blessed Gregory repeatedly wrote in his letters to the Gallican bishops and to others.

The Roman laws promulgated by the emperor Justinian, which the Church approves, also make provision concerning the departure of bishops without the authority of their metropolitan. I have added here, insofar as I thought appropriate, a portion of the constitution in the following form:

“Bishops must not be permitted to leave their own Churches and enter foreign provinces. But if they do so for some necessary reason, let them produce either letters from their patriarch or from their metropolitan,”

and so forth.

According to the Sardican canons (canon 9):

“From any province, bishops who wish to travel farther away must send their requests to that brother and co-bishop who resides in the metropolitan city.”

Concerning these primates and metropolitans, the Council of Nicaea says (canon 4):

“It is especially fitting that a bishop be ordained by all the bishops who are in the province. But if this is difficult, either because of pressing necessity or because of the length of the journey, nevertheless three bishops must by all means assemble for the same purpose, with all the others likewise giving their decision and consenting in writing; then the ordination shall take place. The confirmation of what is done in each province shall be entrusted to the metropolitan bishop.”

And (canon 6):

“It is generally clear that if anyone has been made a bishop contrary to the judgment of the metropolitan, the great synod has decreed that he ought not to be a bishop.”

For this reason Innocent writes to Victricius (Letter 1):

“First, that no one should dare to ordain a bishop without the knowledge of the metropolitan.”

And Leo writes to Bishop Theodore (Letter 59):

“The order of your concern ought to have been this: that you confer with your metropolitan concerning the matter that appeared to require investigation. For in cases that concern the general observance of all the priests of the Lord, nothing ought to be accomplished without the chief men.”

Within this order of metropolitans, archbishops, and primates, the sacred canons recognize a certain succession of honor. Concerning this, the mystical Council of Nicaea decreed (canon 5) that the bishop of Aelia—that is, Jerusalem—should be honored. Since, through the grace of the mysteries of the Lord God, our King and Priest Jesus Christ, the holy city deserved to be called by that name, its bishop should also possess a corresponding succession of honor.

For, says the Council of Nicaea, custom and ancient tradition have established that the bishop of Aelia should be honored and should have a corresponding rank of honor, without prejudice to the proper dignity of the metropolitan.

By this decree the bishop of that city also deserved to be counted among the patriarchs and primates, without prejudice to the proper dignity of the metropolitan. In the same way, the city of Constantinople—which was formerly called Lygos or Byzantium and was suffragan to Heraclea—was decreed, by imperial sanction and with the consent of the apostolic see and the general synod, to be counted equally among the patriarchs or primates, without prejudice to the proper dignity of its metropolitan.

Saint Gregory also shows that this succession of honor, without prejudice to metropolitan dignity, is to be preserved. When Syagrius, bishop of Autun, requested the pallium, he granted it for the distinction and honor of his Church, saying (Book VII, Letter 112, Indiction 11):

“Lest we appear in any way to have granted you the munificence of this garment in isolation, we have also judged it fitting to grant this: that, with the place and honor of its metropolitan preserved in every respect, the city of Autun, over which almighty God has willed you to preside, should stand after the Church of Lyons and should claim for itself this place and order through the indulgence of our authority. We decree that the other bishops retain their proper places among themselves for sitting in council, signing, or any other matter, according to the time of their ordination, and claim for themselves the precedence of their respective ranks, because the order of reason wholly admonishes us that, when we grant certain privileges together with the use of the pallium, we ought to grant them in accordance with that order.”

The Greeks call those who have obtained such privileges, whether through an imperial pragmatic constitution or through the granting of the pallium by the apostolic see, “second metropolitans.” We find mention of them in the acts of the Council of Chalcedon, in the canons of that same synod, and in the decrees of Innocent.

From these and other sacred canons, and from the decrees of the Roman see, it is clear that these metropolitans are each the primates of their respective provinces. According to the ancient custom mentioned above and apostolic tradition, and in accordance with the sacred canons of Nicaea, they are able to summon synods, ordain bishops, be ordained by the co-bishops of their province without consulting any other primate, and regularly arrange matters throughout their own provinces.

The canons of Antioch also make their privilege clear (canon 9), saying that responsibility for the entire province belongs to the metropolitan bishop, who, to resolve a controversy that has arisen among the bishops of his province, ought to summon other judges from a neighboring province.

Those archbishops or metropolitans, however, who cannot carry out these matters without consulting the primate are regarded only as archbishops or metropolitans, as we find in the acts of the Council of Chalcedon, in the canons of that same synod, in the decrees of Innocent, and in Leo’s letter to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica.

For Innocent says to Alexander, bishop of Antioch (Letter 20):

“Reviewing the authority of the Council of Nicaea, which expresses the one mind of all the priests throughout the world, we recognize that it judged it necessary for all the faithful—not to say, all priests—to preserve the established order concerning the Church of Antioch, since we recognize that the aforesaid Church has been established over its own diocese, not over any other province.”

And a little later:

“Therefore, dearest brother, we think that, just as you ordain the metropolitans by your singular authority, so you should not allow the others to be made bishops without your permission and knowledge. In these matters you will properly observe the following arrangement: that you direct those who are far away to be ordained by letters issued to those who now ordain them solely according to their own judgment; but the neighboring bishops, if you think it appropriate, you should bring to receive the laying on of hands of your grace, since those over whom you have the greatest responsibility ought especially to merit your judgment.”

And Leo, writing to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica (Letter 88), clearly shows what precedence the primate of the metropolitans ought to possess by delegation from the apostolic see. He says:

“Regarding the person to be consecrated as bishop and the consent of the clergy and people, the metropolitan bishop should report to your fraternity, and he should inform you of what has been approved in the province, so that your authority also may confirm the ordination when it is properly celebrated.

“When the metropolitan has died and another is to be substituted in his place, the provincial bishops must assemble in the metropolitan city, so that, after the will of all the clergy and all the citizens has been examined, the best man may be chosen from among the presbyters or deacons of that Church. The provincial priests must report his name to your knowledge, and they will fulfill the wishes of those who petition when they learn that what pleased them has also pleased you.”

And again:

“We wish you to be most restrained in summoning bishops, lest you appear to glory in the injuries of your brothers under the pretext of greater diligence. Therefore, if some greater cause arises for which it is reasonable and necessary to summon a brotherly assembly, it should be sufficient for two bishops from each province, whom the metropolitans judge should be sent, to come to your fraternity, so that the bishops do not remain away more than fifteen days beyond the appointed time of the council.”

We find in the acts of the Council of Chalcedon that these metropolitans rose up against their primates; the same synod rightly rebuked them and restrained them by its authority.

We also read that patriarchs or primates, who perform the office of one primacy under these two names, have exalted themselves not only against the third and second sees, but even against the first and apostolic See—so much so that the bishop of the city of Constantinople, formerly a suffragan of Heraclea, presumed to ordain a bishop against the regulations of the third See and obtained from the synod and imperial authority that he be preferred to the second See, contrary to the regulations. And because a mind greedy for power cannot be content with the limits granted to it, it went so far as to have itself [Col. 0345D] called “universal” against the first and apostolic See, as we read again in the letters of Pope Leo the Great, of blessed Gregory, and recently of Nicholas. You will find in its proper place how the presumption of this profane title—that is, the seizure of eminence—was rejected by blessed Leo, together with the Constantinopolitan bishop’s arrogance in usurping an unwarranted title of address, since the complexity of your compilation requires that his words be set out elsewhere.

And what blessed Gregory thought and decreed concerning this same title, I have decided to set down here, as the place permits. The reader will be able to find his words at greater length and more fully in those same letters, from which I have excerpted certain passages here. For in his letter to John himself, bishop of Constantinople, who was striving to be called the universal bishop (Book IV, indiction 13, [Col. 0346A] letter 38), he says:

“I ask, I entreat, and with as much gentleness as I can I beseech you, that your Fraternity contradict all those who flatter you and confer upon you the name of error, and that you not consent to be called by a foolish and proud title.”

And again:

“Consider, I beg you, that in this rash presumption the peace of the whole Church is disturbed, and the grace commonly poured out upon all is opposed.”

And again:

“Who, I ask, is proposed for imitation in this so perverse title, except the one who, scorning the legions of angels established together with him, attempted to burst forth to the summit of singularity, so that he might appear to be subject to no one and alone to preside over all?”

And again:

“Certainly Peter, prince of the apostles, a member of the holy and universal Church; Paul, Andrew, and John—what are they other than the heads of individual peoples? Yet under one Head all are members. And, to bind everything briefly within a short compass of speech, the holy ones before the Law, the holy ones under the Law, and the holy ones under grace—all these, perfecting the body of the Lord, have been constituted among the members of the Church, and no one ever wished to be called universal. Therefore let Your Holiness recognize how greatly she swells within herself who desires to be called by the name which no one who was truly holy ever presumed to bear.

“Did not, as your Fraternity knows, at the holy and venerable Council of Chalcedon the bishops of this apostolic See, which by God’s ordering I serve, receive the title ‘universal’ as an honor offered to them? Yet no one ever wished to be called by such a title; no one seized this rash name for himself, lest, if he appropriated for himself the glory of singularity in the rank of the episcopate, he might appear to have denied it to all his brothers.”

And again:

“What, then, dearest brother, will you say to the Judge who comes at that fearful examination, you who desire to be called not only Father but also universal Father in the world? Behold: by this wicked title of elevation the Church is divided, and the hearts of all the brothers are provoked to scandal.”

And in his letter to the deacon Sabinianus, serving as representative in Constantinople (Book IV, indiction 13, letter 39):

“He has gone so far”—namely, John, bishop of Constantinople—“as to send here, under the pretext of the presbyter John, records in which he called himself, almost throughout every line, the ecumenical patriarch.”

And a little later:

“For to consent to this wicked title is nothing other than to lose the faith. Therefore, as I have already written to you in previous letters, do not presume ever to proceed together with him.”

And to the empress Constantina (Book IV, indiction 13, letter 34):

“When the same brother of mine calls himself bishop universal with new presumption and pride, so that, even during the time of my predecessor of holy memory, he had himself recorded in a synod under this proud title—although all the acts of that synod were annulled when the apostolic See opposed them—the most serene Lord suggests something grievous to me: that He did not correct the man who is proud, but rather sought to make me turn aside from my purpose, although in this matter I defend, by the virtue of humility and rectitude, the ordinances of the Gospels and the canons. In this matter the aforesaid brother [Col. 0347A] and fellow priest acts against the evangelical judgment, against blessed Peter the apostle, against all the Churches, and against the ordinances of the canons.”

And shortly afterward:

“Yet it is exceedingly grievous that it should be patiently endured for so long that the aforesaid brother and my fellow bishop, scorning everyone, should strive to be called the sole bishop. But in this pride of his, what else is indicated except that the times of Antichrist are already near?”

And in his letter to Eulogius of Alexandria and Anastasius of Antioch, bishops of equal rank (Book IV, indiction 13, letter 36):

“As your revered Holiness knows, at the holy Council of Chalcedon this title of universality was offered to the pontiff of the apostolic See, which by God’s ordering I serve. But none of my predecessors ever consented to use this most profane title, because, plainly, if one patriarch is called universal, the name of patriarch is taken away from the others. But far be it—far be it—from the mind of any Christian to seize for himself something by which he might appear, even in the smallest degree, to diminish the honor of his brothers.

“Since, then, we do not wish to accept the honor offered to us, consider how shameful it is that anyone should have wished to usurp it violently for himself. Therefore let Your Holiness never call anyone universal in your letters, lest, while offering another an honor that is not due, you deprive him of what is due to himself.”

And again:

“For if this is freely permitted to be said, the honor of all the patriarchs is denied; and if perhaps the one who is called universal perishes in error, no bishop at all is then found to remain in the state of truth. Therefore I exhort you to preserve the Churches steadfastly and without prejudice, as you received them, and to let this temptation of diabolical usurpation attribute nothing to itself in you. Stand firm; stand secure; and never presume either to give or to receive writings containing the falsity of the universal title. Prohibit all the bishops subject to your care from the defilement of this flattery. Let the whole Church recognize you as patriarchs, not only in good works but also in the authority of truth.

“If anything adverse should follow, we must show, by remaining united even unto death, that we do not specially love anything of our own at the cost of the common good. Let us say with Paul: ‘For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain’ (Philippians I). Let us hear what the first of all shepherds says: ‘If you suffer for righteousness, you will be blessed’ (I Peter III). Believe me: the honor which we have accepted for preaching the truth, if necessity demands it, we relinquish more securely for that same truth than we retain it. But pray for me, as is fitting for your dearest blessedness, that I may demonstrate by my works what I dare to say to you.”

And again, in his letter to Eulogius, bishop of Alexandria (Book VII, indiction 1, letter 4):

“Your Blessedness has also taken pains to indicate that you no longer write to certain persons with proud titles, which have sprung from the root of vanity; yet you write to me saying: ‘As you commanded.’ I beg you to remove the word ‘command’ from my hearing, because I know who I am and who you are. In rank, you are my brothers; in character, my fathers. I therefore did not command, but merely took care to indicate what seemed useful.

“Yet I do not find that Your Blessedness has wished to hold fully to what I brought to your memory. For I said that you ought not to write anything of this kind either to me or to anyone else; and behold, in the preface of the letter which you directed to me—the very person who prohibited it—you took care to imprint the word of a proud title, calling me universal pope.

“I ask that your most gentle Holiness do this no longer, because what is taken away from you is being offered to another beyond what reason requires. For I do not seek to prosper through words but through conduct; nor do I count as honor something in which I recognize that my brothers lose their honor. My honor is the honor of the universal Church; my honor is the steadfast strength of my brothers. I am truly honored when the honor due to each person is denied to none.

“For if Your Holiness calls me universal pope, you deny that you are what you confess me to be—the universal one. But far be this from us. Let the words which inflate vanity and wound charity withdraw. Your Holiness knows that this was offered at the holy Council of Chalcedon and afterward by the Fathers who followed, that is, by my predecessors. Yet none of them ever wished to use this title, so that, while they loved the honor of all priests in this world, they might preserve their own before almighty God.”

And in his letter to various archbishops of equal rank (Book VII, indiction 2, letter 69):

“Let your Fraternity know that John, formerly bishop of the city of Constantinople, against God and against the peace of the Church, in contempt and injury to all priests, exceeded the limits of his modesty and restraint, and unlawfully usurped for himself in a synod the proud and pestilential title ‘ecumenical,’ that is, ‘universal.’

“When Pelagius, our predecessor of blessed memory, recognized this, he completely annulled the entire record of that synod, except for what had been enacted there concerning the case of Gregory, bishop of Antioch, of venerable memory. He rebuked John with the strictest reprimand, so that he might restrain himself from this new and rash name of superstition; indeed, he prohibited his own deacon from proceeding with him unless he corrected so great a sacrilege.

“Following the zeal for rectitude which he displayed in every respect, we too, with God’s protection, preserve his ordinances without opposition, because it is fitting that the one who awaits the tribunal of the eternal Judge in order to render an account of the same place should walk with unhindered steps along the straight path of his predecessor.”

And a little later:

“I exhort and advise that none of you ever receive this name, none consent to it, none subscribe to it, none admit it where it has been written, or append his signature to it. Rather, as befits ministers of almighty God, let each of you keep himself whole and undefiled by such a poisonous infection, and not provide a place within himself for the crafty ambusher, since this is done both to the injury and division of the whole Church and, as we have said, in contempt of all of you. For if one is universal, as he supposes, it remains that you are not bishops.”

And after a little more:

“For if anyone—which we do not believe—should in any respect disregard this present writing, let him know that he has been separated from the peace of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. Therefore let your Fraternity act so that, when the Shepherd of shepherds comes in judgment, he may not be able to hold you guilty concerning the place of governance which you received.”

And in his letter to Cyriacus, bishop of Constantinople and successor to Bishop John (Book VI, indiction 15, letter 4):

“In this we embrace you from the depths of our hearts; in this we recognize you as priests: if, rejecting the vanity of words, you hold the place of holiness with holy humility. Behold, we have been scandalized by the title of that wicked name, and we retain no small complaints in our mind and express them in our speech.

“Your Fraternity knows that the Truth says: ‘If you offer your gift at the altar, and so forth’ (Matthew V). In this matter it must be considered that, although every fault is erased by an offering, so great is the evil of scandal generated in another’s heart that the Lord does not accept from the one who has sinned even that sacrifice which ordinarily removes sin. Therefore take care to wipe away quickly the scandal in our heart, so that almighty God may be able to regard the sacrifice of your offering as acceptable.”

And again, in another letter to the same man (Book VI, indiction 15, letter 28):

“You ought first to show me and all the brothers the beauty of that charity in you by hastening to remove the word of pride through which grave scandal is generated in the Churches, fulfilling in every respect what is written: ‘Be zealous to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace’ (Ephesians IV). And again: ‘Give no occasion to the adversary for the sake of reproach’ (I Timothy V).

“Then the charity displayed is truly genuine, if no division arises among us through the swelling of pride. For I call Jesus as witness upon my soul that, from first to last, I wish to give no human being occasion for scandal. I desire all to be great and honorable, provided that their honor does not detract from the honor of almighty God. For whoever desires to be honored against God is not honorable to me.”

And shortly afterward:

“Since the enemy of almighty God, Antichrist, is near, I earnestly desire that he find nothing of his own, not only in the conduct but not even in the title of priests. Therefore let those things which have been introduced in a new manner be removed in the same order in which they were introduced, and peace in the Lord will remain unimpaired among us. For what sweetness or charity will there be among us if we comfort one another with our words but sting one another by our actions?”

And in his letter to the emperor Maurice Augustus (Book VI, indiction 15, letter 30):

“I took care to admonish that same brother and fellow priest of mine”—namely, Cyriacus, bishop of Constantinople—“that, if he desires to have peace and concord with everyone, he should restrain himself from the designation of that foolish title. Concerning this matter, Your Imperial Piety instructed me in your commands that scandal ought not to be generated among us on account of the designation of a frivolous name.

“But I ask that Imperial Piety consider that some things are exceedingly frivolous and harmless, while others are extremely harmful. Surely, when the coming Antichrist declares himself to be God, will that be very frivolous? Yet it will be exceedingly destructive. If we consider the length of the utterance, there are two syllables; but if we consider the weight of its iniquity, it is utter ruin.

“I confidently say that whoever calls himself universal priest, or desires to be called so, in his exaltation goes before Antichrist, because through pride he places himself above the others and is led into error by no lesser pride. For just as that perverse one wishes to appear God over human beings, so whoever this person is who desires to be called the sole priest wishes to appear priest over the other priests.

“But since the Truth says, ‘Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled’ (Luke XIV), I know that every kind of exaltation is broken the more quickly the more greatly it is inflated. Therefore let Your Piety command those who have fallen in pride and swelling not to generate scandal through the designation of a frivolous name. For I, a sinner who by God’s authority hold to humility, do not need to be admonished to humility.”

And in his letter to Anastasius, bishop of Antioch (Book VI, letter 24):

“In receiving the synodical letter of our brother and fellow priest Cyriacus, it was not fitting for me to delay on account of the profane title, lest I disturb the unity of the holy Church. Yet I took care to admonish him concerning that same superstitious and proud title, saying that he could not have peace with us unless he corrected the exaltation expressed by the aforesaid word, which the first apostate invented.

“Nevertheless, you must not say that this matter is nothing. For if we bear it with equanimity, we corrupt the faith of the whole Church. You know how many—not only heretics but even founders of heresies—have gone forth from the Church of Constantinople. And, to say nothing of the injury to your honor, if one bishop is called universal, the whole Church collapses; if one is the whole, it falls. But far be this folly; far be this frivolity from my ears.

“Yet I trust in the almighty Lord that what He has promised He will soon fulfill: ‘Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled.’”

## CHAPTER XVIII. How people of unsound mind erred through lack of discernment in the Holy Scriptures

Pay intelligent attention, brother, to this evangelical judgment and store it firmly in your mind; and also to that saying of blessed Gregory which, as you read shortly before, he appended to this evangelical judgment: “I know that every kind of exaltation is broken the more quickly the more greatly it is inflated.”

Recognize, therefore, your measure and limit, decreed for you by God through the sacred canons, and be humble in your own eyes, remembering what the Lord said to Saul: “When you were little in your own eyes, did I not make you head over Israel?” (I Samuel XIII). “Now, because you are great in your own sight, I have rejected you, so that you may not be king.”

And cease attempting to revive those ancient and dead ashes of men who rebelled against their prelates, long ago buried by the sacred canons. But I fear that you will not be able to see what is true and humble, having a white spot in your eye—that is, arrogance in your mind. Hence the Lord says to Moses: “Whoever has a white spot in his eye shall not offer bread to his God, nor approach his ministry” (Leviticus XXI).

For this reason I impress upon you the judgment of blessed Augustine addressed to Julian, a young bishop who, thinking wrongly through pride, had been separated from the Catholic Church—one which you have already read in another work, though I wish you had not neglected it:

“When you have overcome the contentiousness by which you are held, then you will be able to hold the truth by which you are overcome. If, having abandoned that contentiousness, you do not hold this truth, you will not be able to possess discernment in the Holy Scriptures and in the sacred rules. So it was also with those who did not wish to understand them with discernment, and therefore some of them erred by failing to distinguish the words of those same Scriptures.

“For example, when the Lord says, ‘I and the Father are one’ (John X), Arius did not wish to understand ‘one’ as referring to unity of substance, while Sabellius did not refer ‘are’ to the distinct properties of the persons; and for this reason both erred.

“Likewise, in the unity of one and the same person subsisting from two and in two substances—that is, natures, namely divinity and humanity—our Lord Jesus Christ also said, ‘The Father is greater than I’ (John XIV). Arius attributed this not to the humanity but to the divinity, and therefore ended an unworthy life by a worthy death.

“Some of them, moreover, by wrongly interpreting those same Scriptures, did what blessed Peter said concerning the letters of blessed Paul: ‘In them are certain things difficult to understand, which the ignorant and unstable distort, as they do the other Scriptures, to their own destruction’ (II Peter III).

“The things difficult to understand in Paul’s letters, which he says are distorted by the ignorant and unstable, are especially those in which he speaks of the grace of God that justifies the ungodly—that is, which makes the unjust just. For Paul himself says: ‘Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more’ (Romans V). The ignorant and unstable, failing to understand this, thought that he was saying: ‘Let us do evil so that good may come.’

“But far be it from Paul to teach his hearers to do evil in order to obtain good, since his whole purpose is to restrain everyone he can from evil and call them to do good. When he says, ‘Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more,’ he commends the gift of grace all the more strongly. Grace is accustomed to forgive great sins in converts and lesser sins as well; and the greater the sins someone committed before conversion, the greater is the indulgence of the grace that pardons him when he is converted.”

Some of them also erased certain passages from the Scriptures, passages by which they feared they would be refuted. Thus it is established that the Arians erased from the Gospel what the Savior says: “For God is spirit” (John IV), because they did not wish to believe that the Holy Spirit was God almighty.

Some also erased from John’s Letter: “And every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not from God” (I John IV), lest they should be refuted by the authority of blessed John. Hence Nestorius revealed that he did not know that this sentence had been inserted in authoritative copies, and therefore he did not fear to “dissolve” Jesus, saying that the blessed virgin Mary was the mother not of God but only of a human being. In this way he made one person human and another divine, neither believing in one Christ in the Word, flesh, and soul, but separately proclaiming one Son of God and another son of man.

Some, indeed, falsified the Scriptures themselves by illicit alterations, as did Macedonius, bishop of Constantinople. He is reported to have been expelled from the city by the emperor Anastasius because he falsified the Gospels, altering the passage of the Apostle which says, “He was manifested in the flesh, justified in the spirit” (I Timothy III), through the relationship of the Greek letters Ο and Θ, changing it in this way.

Where the text had ὃς, that is, the one-syllable Greek form ΟΣ, he changed the letter Ο into Θ and made ΘΣ—that is, so that it would read, “God appeared through the flesh.” For this reason he was expelled as a Nestorian.

And there are many other passages in the Scriptures from which those who misunderstood them took scandal for themselves. Because they did not wish to become disciples of the truth, they became teachers of error.

Thus, from what the Apostle says, “The mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (I Timothy II), Photinus drew support for the authority of his heresy. And from the Letter to the Philippians, “found in appearance as a man” (Chapter II), Marcion confessed that Christ had an imaginary body rather than a body.

The heretics called Agnoites likewise brought forward for confirmation of their error what is said: “But concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven nor the Son, except the Father alone” (Matthew XXIV).

And from what is written in Genesis—that the day began after the night (Genesis I)—heretics said that darkness was coeternal with God, who dwells in inaccessible light.

And from what is said there, “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (ibid.), the devil first taught the human being idolatry, saying: “You will be like gods” (Genesis III).

And because Methuselah’s years exceed the time before the Flood, they said that not merely eight souls were preserved.

And when God heard the cries of Sodom, whose sins were already full, they said that He descended as though ignorant of the cry, in order to see whether the sins were complete.

And they said that no one knew Moses’ tomb—not even those who buried him knew that he had been buried.

And they said that the Law was its own enemy in its differing commands; that the Lord could not have sent the Holy Spirit, of whom He Himself is read to have been born; that He had not denounced death by the sword to those who use the sword, although He commanded that the sword with which He was to suffer be bought; that He did not descend to the underworld, although He entered paradise with the thief; and that the apostles are found guilty because, although they were commanded to baptize in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, they baptized only in the name of Jesus.

They raised objections from what is said: “I am God, creating evils” (Isaiah XLV), and: “He made all things, and behold, they were very good” (Genesis I).

There are many other matters which it would now be lengthy and unnecessary for us to enumerate. From these, the senseless and wicked, through their exceedingly dark interpretations of wise and holy sayings, have contrived their own destruction.

## CHAPTER XIX. How those who misunderstood the decrees of sacred traditions erred

And because, as Pope Hilary says, “One sins no less against the decrees of sacred traditions than one rushes forward in injury against the Lord Himself,” certain people took scandal from ecclesiastical regulations and founded heresies and schisms.

Thus Meletius was deposed by a synod of the bishops of Egypt. The Meletians were named after him, namely those whom he ordained after his deposition. The Council of Nicaea received them into their ranks conditionally, out of necessity, lest, remaining with the Arians with whom they had been associated, they should attack the Catholic Church more fiercely.

The aforesaid synod likewise received the Novatians conditionally. This heresy took its beginning from Novatus, a presbyter of the Roman Church at that time, who afterward, contrary to the regulations, was made a bishop by his associates.

Novatus separated himself from communion with the Roman Church because Cornelius, the bishop, had received into communion the faithful who had sacrificed during the persecution under Decius, having altered the exceedingly harsh judgment of the episcopal council—a judgment which Innocent recalls in his decrees.

The emperor Constantine summoned to the Council of Nicaea Acesius, the bishop of those Novatians. Acesius agreed concerning the doctrine of the faith and the celebration of Easter, but refused to receive penitents back into penance. The remarkable emperor said to him:

“Set up a ladder, O Acesius, and if you can, climb alone into heaven” (Book II of the Tripartite History, chapter 13).

From this condescension toward the Novatians and Meletians, arising from necessity, it came about that those whom Bonosus had ordained before his condemnation were received in their ranks. Anisius, together with certain colleagues, also decreed that those who had passed from the Catholic Church to heresy and had been ordained by the condemned Bonosus should be received in their orders, lest they remain with that same Bonosus and a considerable scandal arise for the Catholic Church. Saint Innocent dissolved and rejected this decision.

And because the same council commanded that the heretical Paulianists who came to the Church should be baptized, some also said that other heretics ought to be baptized. This the apostolic See and the plenary councils wholly rejected, as the decrees of the Roman pontiffs demonstrate and as Saint Augustine has shown in extensive books, both in his words and in his arguments.

I could have brought forward other matters of this kind, but I wish to avoid prolixity.

## CHAPTER XX. How, in the ancient letters of the apostolic See, as in laws, certain provisions were afterward abrogated or altered; concerning the six general synods, the seventh among the Greeks, the Frankish synod, and the letters of Pope Julius and Felix

[Col. 0353D]

Therefore, lest you take scandal through indiscreet understanding from the things you have gathered to strengthen your position, you must observe that, just as certain matters concerning the sacraments of human salvation—which, from the beginning of the world until the coming of the Lord and Savior, existed in different forms according to the variation of times, yet continually returned to the unity of one faith—are handed down to be understood spiritually, while some were altered, some entirely abolished, and some remain as they were decreed, so there was no period of the world devoid of holy teachers.

Whether through words, examples, or writings, they demonstrated the way of life to mortals according to the variation of times. Hence there are many things not only in the canons and decrees of the Roman pontiffs, but also in the holy Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments, inspired by the same Spirit by whom the sacred canons were promulgated, which seem to be contrary to one another but are not contrary. Rather, they were or are arranged according to the times, circumstances, and character of the cases.

Thus Solomon says together: “Do not answer a fool according to his folly” (Proverbs XXVI), and: “Answer a fool according to his folly” (ibid.).

And the Lord says through the prophet: “I do not desire the death of the sinner” (Ezekiel XXXIII); yet concerning the sons of Eli it is read that they could not listen to their father, because God wished to kill them (I Samuel II).

And in the Gospel: “A good man brings forth good things from the good treasure of his heart” (Matthew XII); and: “No one is good except God alone” (Luke XVIII).

And: “The Son of Man came to seek and save what had perished” (Luke XIX), while He says: “I was sent only to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel” (Matthew XV).

And again He says to His disciples: “Do not go on the way of the Gentiles” (Matthew X); and likewise: “Go, teach all nations” (Matthew XXVIII).

And: “God tempts no one” (James I); and: “The Lord your God is testing you” (Deuteronomy I).

And Paul says: “If I were pleasing human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Galatians I); and likewise: “Just as I please everyone in all things” (I Corinthians X).

And again: “I was wishing to be accursed from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh” (Romans IX); and likewise: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ?” and the rest (Romans VIII).

For the one Spirit is both single and manifold, stable and mobile, as it is written in the Book of Wisdom (Chapter VII). Through the human instrument most closely joined to Him, He does not produce everything simultaneously and at once.

Even for the holy disciples themselves, who clung continually to divine teaching—for no human being suddenly becomes perfect—faith and knowledge increased through the progression of time. They too said: “Lord, increase our faith” (Luke XVII). And the Lord said to them: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when that Spirit of truth comes, He will teach you all truth” (John XVI).

But after the law of nature there was also given a written law suited to the hardness of the people, which was established because of transgressions [Col. 0354D]. This was followed by the law of the Gospel, later in time but earlier in grace, which was extended progressively through the ages by the apostles and their successors. For, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles (chapter 15), at first those who believed from the circumcision received the sacraments of the Gospel in such a way that they did not withdraw from the legal ceremonies; and when the question arose whether Gentile believers ought to observe the ceremonies of the Law, they received from the apostles only three provisions to be observed.

Then the pontiffs of the apostolic see, before the establishment of the sacred councils, although not differing from one another in faith, nevertheless, in a different style, issued judgments concerning bishops in letters addressed to various people for various emerging causes, taking into consideration [Col. 0355A] the status of the persons, the necessity of the circumstances, and the suitability of the times. Thus Anacletus, in his letter to all the bishops established in Italy, says (Letter 2): “The Lord,” he says, “reserved for himself the removal of high priests, although he granted their election to good priests and spiritual peoples”—which he had written differently in the preceding letter.

The Tripartite History also reports that the emperor Constantine said something of this kind at the Council of Nicaea: “Nevertheless, the Council of Nicaea did not for that reason fail to decree” (canon 2): “If anyone,” it says, “does anything beyond these provisions, raising himself up as though against the great council, he himself shall be placed in danger of the dignity of the clergy.” In this decree, when it says “if anyone,” it excludes no one, whether from the higher or the lower order, as it plainly shows elsewhere also [Col. 0355B].

Moreover, Constantine himself, and after him other orthodox emperors, did not hesitate to promulgate laws concerning bishops. After Anacletus also, certain pontiffs before the Council of Nicaea, and Julius and certain others after the Council of Nicaea, ordered that episcopal judgments, before a definitive ruling, be referred to the apostolic see.

Innocent, however, and his successors, after judgments concerning specific matters had been more explicitly decreed by the sacred councils and the pontiffs of the Roman see, ordered that doubtful or obscure cases be referred for judgment beforehand, but that certain and already-decreed matters—since both ecclesiastical and public laws command that one who has confessed or been convicted be judged without delay or reconsideration—be referred after episcopal judgment, in accordance with the Sardican canons, with the testimony of the official records, to the apostolic see [Col. 0355C]. We find that their decrees prevailed in ecclesiastical practice even from the time of our forefathers.

Yet just as, among public laws, some have been abrogated, some altered, and some even added, so likewise certain decrees issued by Catholics according to the time, circumstances, and necessity were later abrogated or altered. Innocent demonstrates this when he says: “With regard to these matters,” he says, “the earlier observance is stricter, while the later, with mercy intervening, is more lenient,” and so forth.

The canons of the province of Africa also defined differently from the original decree matters concerning the veiling of virgins, children baptized by the Donatists, and dioceses. Saint Gelasius likewise says: “While the ancient constitutions remain in place because of the reverence due to them, they are properly to be observed whenever no pressing difficulty arising from circumstances or times makes this impossible,” and so forth.

[Col. 0355D] Long before this, Innocent said to the Macedonian bishops, who excused what they had done by pleading the necessity of the times (Letter 27): “Therefore, whatever necessity has discovered as a remedy must, when the necessity has ceased, likewise cease, since what was pressing: for one thing is the lawful order, and another is the usurpation which present circumstances compel for the time being. And observe that what, as you say, necessity commanded cannot presume to continue now that the churches have been established in peace.”

Leo, writing to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne (Letter 95, preface), says: “Just as there are certain matters which cannot be overturned for any reason, so there are some which ought to be moderated either because of consideration for age or because of the necessity of circumstances [Col. 0356A], provided that this condition is always preserved: in matters which are doubtful or obscure, we must recognize that what should be followed is that which is found to be neither contrary to the commands of the Gospel nor opposed to the decrees of the holy Fathers.”

Saint Paul also demonstrates these various forms individually when he says to the Corinthians: “This I say by way of concession, not by way of command” (1 Corinthians 7), and so forth. “To the married I give this command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not leave her husband,” and what follows (ibid.).

The African Council likewise says in one canon concerning the Donatists (canon 35): “For the peace and benefit of the Church, so that, from among the Donatists themselves, any clerics who, having corrected their judgment, wish to pass over to Catholic unity may, according to the will and counsel of each Catholic bishop who governs the Church in that place, be received in their offices if this appears beneficial to Christian peace [Col. 0356B], just as it is evident that this was done in the earlier periods of the same division—not so that the council held in the transmarine regions concerning this matter should be dissolved, but so that it should remain in force with respect to those who wish to pass over to the Catholic faith in such a way that no compensation for unity is obtained through them,” and so forth, as it continues there.

Leo also sets forth both these forms concerning one and the same matter in a single chapter addressed to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne (Letter 95, chapter 1), saying: “No reason permits those to be counted among the bishops who were neither elected by the clergy, nor sought by the people [Col. 0356C], nor consecrated by the bishops of the province with the metropolitan’s judgment. Since a dispute about an improperly assumed dignity often arises from this, who could doubt that what is not shown to have been conferred ought by no means to be granted to them? If, however, certain clerics were ordained by these pseudo-bishops in churches that belonged to their proper bishops, and their ordination was carried out with the consent and judgment of the presiding authorities, it may be considered valid, so that they may remain in those churches; otherwise, the consecration must be regarded as void, since it was founded neither upon the proper place nor fortified by authority.”

Again, in the same letter to the same man (chapter 10): “If a man who was still in adolescence, under the pressure either of fear of death or of the danger of captivity, performed penance, and afterward, fearing a relapse into youthful [Col. 0356D] incontinence, chose marital union lest he incur the crime of fornication, he appears to have done something pardonable, provided that he had no relations whatsoever with anyone except his wife. Yet we do not establish a rule in this matter; we judge only what is more tolerable. For according to true understanding, nothing is more fitting for one who has performed penance than persevering chastity of mind and body.”

And in his letter to Theodore, bishop of Fréjus (Letter 59): “So that in a time of necessity and in the urgency of imminent danger, assistance through penance and immediate reconciliation may be denied to no one who seeks it, even if, having lost the use of speech, they ask for it by signs indicating sound understanding; or if they are unable to signify this in the presence of a priest, the testimony of the faithful standing around them ought to benefit them, so that they may obtain together both the benefits of penance and of reconciliation, while the rule of the ancestral canons concerning those who have departed from faith in God by apostasy remains preserved” [Col. 0357A].

Some of those whose letters you have collected also said that the fallen and penitents ought to remain in their orders. Later, however, those who followed them established otherwise on the basis of the sacred canons. Hence blessed Augustine wrote to Boniface, saying (Letter 50): “For the rule established in the Church—that no one, after doing penance for some crime, should receive clerical office, return to clerical office, or remain in clerical office—was made not out of despair of forgiveness, but out of the strictness of discipline. [Col. 0357B] Otherwise an argument would be made against the keys given to the Church, concerning which it was said: ‘Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven.’ But lest perhaps, when their crimes had been exposed, their minds should swell with hope of ecclesiastical honor and they should perform penance arrogantly, it was decided with the utmost severity that, after performing penance for a damnable crime, no one should be a cleric, so that, through despair of temporal elevation, the stronger and truer medicine of humility might be provided.

“For holy David also performed penance for deadly crimes, and nevertheless remained in his honor (2 Samuel 12). And blessed Peter, when he shed exceedingly bitter tears, certainly repented of having denied the Lord, yet he remained an apostle (Matthew 26). But the diligence of those who came later should not therefore be considered superfluous, since, where nothing was taken away from salvation, they added something to humility, by which salvation might be more securely protected [Col. 0357C]. I believe that they had learned from the pretended penances of some people, undertaken through an affected desire for positions of honor and power. For the experience of many diseases compels the invention of many remedies.

“Yet in such cases, where, through serious divisions caused by dissension, it is not the danger of this or that individual that is at issue but the slaughter of whole peoples lies before us, something must be taken away from strictness, so that sincere charity may come to the aid of healing greater evils.”

In this way the Catholic Church has been accustomed to aid multitudes perishing through schisms and heresies. Gelasius discussed this discernment admirably in one of his letters, as did blessed Gregory in his letters and in other writings of his.

Yet the ancient pontiffs judged one way concerning the translation of bishops [Col. 0357D], while the episcopal councils judged another, and the pontiffs of the Roman see who followed them decreed what was to be observed on the basis of these judgments.

It is also written in the aforementioned letters that accusations against bishops should not be received, and in those same letters it is explained how they are to be received and that bishops cannot be accused by their own sheep. In the constitutions of Saint Sylvester it says: “No layman shall dare to bring a charge against a cleric, nor a presbyter against a bishop, nor a deacon against a presbyter”; and it is established by him again how many persons may bring an accusation.

The canons of the province of Africa, together with the legates of the apostolic see, order that only those accusers or witnesses be excluded from accusing clerics or testifying against clerics whom the public laws do not admit to accuse or testify concerning public crimes [Col. 0358A]. The Council of Nicaea ordered that a neophyte bishop who had been challenged by two or three witnesses should abstain from the clergy if some such offense against the soul were found in his case. The Apostle likewise commands that an accusation against a presbyter not be received except on the testimony of two or three witnesses.

Moreover, according to the aforementioned canons of the province of Africa, all those to whom the right of accusation is denied are not denied the permission to bring accusations in their own cases (canon 96). And the decrees of the apostolic see that we possess established rules concerning the purgation of those who have been accused but not convicted, or who have confessed.

Some also say that what Sylvester established concerning the accused and witnesses, as it is read in the *Episcopal Book*, must be upheld authoritatively because Gelasius, in his catalogue of books to be received, says that the *Acts* of that man are to be read [Col. 0358B]. But the account of his *Acts* is one thing: in them, by the authority of Scripture and the power of miracles, he overcame the Jews who denied Jesus Christ as the true God, and they are said to be worthy of reading. The constitutions attributed to him in the *Episcopal Book* are another thing. The universal Church has not preserved these, any more than certain other constitutions of other pontiffs found in the same book, as universally observed from earlier times. Yet it accepts and preserves some of those constitutions, just as it accepts and preserves some of the statements in the letters under discussion.

It is also written in those same letters that a synod ought not or cannot be convened without the command or consent of the Roman pontiff. Yet the sacred canons of Nicaea say (canon 5): “It was deemed good that councils should be held twice each year in every province, so that, when all the bishops of the province have been gathered together, such questions may be examined jointly by all” [Col. 0358C].

The Council of Chalcedon likewise says (canon 19): “The holy synod decreed, in accordance with the canons of the Fathers, that bishops should meet twice each year in every province, wherever the metropolitan bishop approves, so that each matter which may perhaps have arisen may be corrected.”

The canons of Antioch and of the province of Africa agree with these provisions (Council of Antioch, canon 20; Council of Africa, canon 62). Innocent, writing to Victricius, says: “If any cases or disputes should arise among clerics, whether of the higher or of the lower order, so that, according to the Council of Nicaea, the bishops of the same province may be assembled and the quarrel brought to an end, this is plainly demonstrated” [Col. 0358D].

Leo wrote to Anastasius: “Concerning episcopal councils,” he says, “we prescribe nothing other than what the holy Fathers beneficially established: namely, that two assemblies should be held each year, in which judgment may be given concerning all the complaints that customarily arise among the various orders of the Church.”

Saint Gregory wrote to the Gallican bishops (Book 7, indiction 2, Letter 112, at the end): “Nor do we neglect this part of our concern: the foresight of the Fathers established that councils should be held throughout the parishes for the sake of usefulness. Therefore, so that no disagreement may arise among brothers and no causes of discord may exist between superiors and subjects, it is necessary for priests to meet together, so that disputes concerning matters that arise may be discussed and a beneficial exchange may take place concerning ecclesiastical observance” [Col. 0359A].

Therefore metropolitan bishops and the primates of the provinces do not convene synods without the authority of the apostolic see, “so that,” as blessed Gregory says, “through this, past matters may be corrected and future matters may receive a rule, and the almighty Lord may everywhere be praised through the concord of the brothers. If we observe these things, we know that his presence is with us, because it is written: ‘Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them’ (Matthew 18). If, therefore, he deigns to be present where two or three are gathered, how much more will he not be absent where very many priests have assembled?”

It is therefore clear that the apostolic see said this concerning the general cause of the faith. Although there are many Catholic councils, only six synods are specifically called general or universal, because they were convened for a general matter pertaining to all Christians. As a rule, these could not and cannot be assembled without a special command of the apostolic see [Col. 0359B].

Of these universal synods, most fully received by the Catholic Church, the first was assembled at Nicaea against Arius, consisting of 318 Fathers, in the time of Pope Sylvester and under the emperor Constantine. The second was held at Constantinople, consisting of 101 Fathers, against Macedonius and Eudoxius, in the time of Pope Damasus and the emperor Gratian, when Nectarius was ordained bishop of that city. The third was held at Ephesus, consisting of 200 Fathers, against Nestorius, bishop of the imperial city, under the great emperor Theodosius and Pope Celestine. The fourth was held at Chalcedon, consisting of 630 Fathers, under Pope Leo and in the time of the emperor Marcian, against Eutyches, that most impious leader of the monks. The fifth was likewise held at Constantinople, in the time of Pope Vigilius and under the emperor Justinian, against Theodore and all the heretics.

The sixth was likewise held at Constantinople under Pope Agatho. At the request of the most devout emperors Constantine, Heraclius, and Tiberius, he sent his legates to the imperial city; among them was John, then a deacon of the Roman Church and not long afterward its bishop, for the purpose of bringing about the union of the holy Churches of God. They were received with the greatest kindness by Constantine, the most reverent defender of the Catholic faith, and were ordered, with disputations set aside, to seek the true faith through peaceful discussion. They were given from the Constantinopolitan library all the books of the ancient Fathers that they requested [Col. 0359D].

There were also 150 bishops present, with George presiding as patriarch of the imperial city and Macarius of Antioch. Those who asserted one will and one operation in Christ were convicted of having falsified numerous statements of the Catholic Fathers. When the conflict had ended, George was corrected, while Macarius and his followers, together with his predecessors Cyrus, Sergius, Honorius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter, were anathematized. The abbot Theophanius of Cilicia was made bishop of Antioch in his place.

Such grace accompanied the legates of Catholic peace that John, bishop of Porto, who was one of them, celebrated the public Mass in Latin on the Sunday of the octave of Easter in the church of Hagia Sophia before the emperor and the patriarch [Col. 0360A].

The seventh, called universal among the Greeks, was the false synod concerning images, which some said should be broken and others worshiped, although neither side defined the matter with sound understanding. Not long before our own times, a great number of bishops held this synod at Constantinople without the authority of the apostolic see and sent it to Rome; the Roman pope then sent it on to Francia.

Therefore, in the time of the emperor Charlemagne, by command of the apostolic see, a general synod was held in Francia, convened by that emperor. In accordance with the course of Scripture and the tradition of the ancestors, that false Greek synod was destroyed and utterly rejected. A considerable volume concerning its destruction, which I read as a young man in the palace, was sent by the same emperor to Rome through certain bishops [Col. 0360B].

In the fourth book of that volume (chapter 28), the following is written concerning the name “universal”:

“‘Universality’ (*universitas*) derives its name from ‘one’ (*unus*), because what is multiplied is turned toward one. For a multitude of units, gathered by being turned into one, becomes a universality. Just as the universal Church is the Church which in Greek is called Catholic, so everything that has not departed from its unity can likewise be called Catholic.

“For every Christian doctrine, or any constitution or tradition, ought to be such as to agree with the universal Church. This the heretics by no means observed: confined to certain regions in various parts of the world, they established certain conventicles by which they separated both themselves and many others from communion with ecclesiastical unity [Col. 0360C].

“Therefore, when the bishops of two or three provinces meet together, if, fortified by the institution of the ancient canons, they establish some teaching or doctrine that nevertheless does not differ from the doctrines of the ancient Fathers, what they do is Catholic and may perhaps be called universal. For although it was not carried out by the bishops of the whole world, it nevertheless does not differ from the faith and tradition of all; and we know that this has often been done in many parts of the world when certain necessities have arisen. For many councils have been held whose decisions strengthen and confirm the holy Church.

“But if the bishops of two or three provinces meet together and, wishing to establish something new [Col. 0360D], form conventicles that do not share the mind of the Church of the whole world but differ from it in some respect, what they do is not Catholic and therefore cannot be called universal.

“Everything that is ecclesiastical is Catholic, and everything that is Catholic is universal. Everything that is universal, however, is free from profane novelties of expression. Therefore everything that is ecclesiastical is free from profane novelties of expression. If this synod had been free from novelties of expression and had been content with the doctrines of the ancient Fathers, it could have been called universal. But it is not content with the doctrines of the ancient Fathers; therefore it cannot be called universal.

“We would certainly not hesitate to profess that same synod to be universal [Col. 0361A], unless we perceived that it opposed the doctrines of the universal Church.”

It is also clear from this matter, as I said, that synods are called universal and general when more bishops than were gathered in some of the aforementioned synods assemble by command of the apostolic see and imperial convocation. Such was the Sardican Synod, at which more than 300 bishops from the western regions assembled. In the African synods held together with the legates of the apostolic see, more than 200 bishops were sometimes gathered. Nevertheless, these are not counted among the universal councils, although it is clear that they are Catholic and most fully received by the apostolic see and the universal Church.

Hence Saint Gregory, in a synodical letter to Cyriacus, bishop of Constantinople [Col. 0361B], concerning Eudoxius (Book 6, indiction 15, Letter 4, at the end), says: “If anyone truly condemns him on the authority of the Catholic Fathers, we certainly follow his judgment. But if, in your synodical letter, you wished to condemn by name also those who are condemned outside the holy synods in the writings of the Fathers, your Fraternity has named too few in your letter; but if you mean those whom the general synods reject, you have added this one beyond the rest.”

We read in the African Council (canon 62): “A universal council is to be held only out of necessity. It was decided that there should no longer be an annual necessity for burdening the brothers; and whenever the common cause—that is, the cause of all Africa—demands it, whenever letters concerning this matter are sent to this see from any quarter, a synod is to be convened in those provinces where circumstances indicate that it is practicable. Causes that are not common are to be judged in their own provinces.”

Pope Leo wrote to Maximus of Antioch [Col. 0361C]: “Whatever,” he says, “is brought before the episcopal judgment for particular reasons connected with synodal councils may have some basis for adjudication, provided that nothing concerning it has been defined by the holy Fathers at Nicaea. For what disagrees with their rules and constitution can never obtain the consent of the apostolic see.”

The Council of Antioch says (canon 16): “That council is complete in which the metropolitan bishop has been present.”

Pope Zosimus wrote to Aurelius and all the bishops established throughout Africa [Col. 0361D], and also to all the bishops established throughout Gaul and the seven provinces, and to all the bishops established throughout Spain. Among other things, writing equally to all, he approved the provincial synod of the Gallican bishops in these words:

“Lazarus,” he says, “who had previously been condemned in the Council of Turin by the judgments of very distinguished bishops as a slanderer, after he had attacked the life of the innocent bishop Brictius with false accusations, afterward obtained the priesthood improperly from Proculus, who, among the others, had agreed in the synod to his condemnation. But, conscious of his own life, he afterward voluntarily removed himself from office by letters of resignation.”
