The Sardican canons also, in their fourteenth chapter, although without designating it by name, appealed to the constitution of the Council of Elvira (canon 21), which had been enacted at the same time, under the emperor Constantine and during the consulship of Paulinus and Julian, in the same period in which the Council of Nicaea was held, as Hosius related [Col. 0362A]. The apostolic see likewise embraced, through Innocent and Celestine, the decree of the Council of Carthage as though it were its own constitution.

Thus universal synods are specifically convened by the authority of the apostolic see, and likewise provincial canonical synods are convened by metropolitan bishops and the primates of the provinces by decree of the apostolic see. This is in accordance with what the holy and universal Church holds concerning the keys of the kingdom of heaven—that is, the power of binding and loosing—which were given especially to Saint Peter and at the same time conferred upon all the apostles, and through them upon Catholic bishops.

Hence blessed Leo says, among other things, in his sermon for his own anniversary [Col. 0362B]:

“What is said to the most blessed Peter—‘I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven’ (Matthew 16)—certainly passed also to the other apostles as a share in this power, and the ordering of this decree flowed on to all the leaders of the Church; yet it is not without reason that what is announced to all is entrusted to one. For this is entrusted individually to Peter because Peter’s form is set before all the rulers of the Church.

“Therefore Peter’s privilege remains wherever judgment is issued according to his equity. Neither excessive severity nor excessive leniency exists where nothing is bound and nothing loosed except what blessed Peter has bound or loosed.”

Since, as Augustine and the other teachers explain, Peter confessed the King of heaven with greater devotion than the others [Col. 0362C] and followed him with true love, he was rightly granted the gift of the keys of the heavenly kingdom above the others, so that it might be evident to all that no one can enter the kingdom of heaven without that confession and faith.

By the keys of the kingdom of heaven, however, he names the very knowledge and power of discernment by which he was to receive the worthy into the kingdom and exclude the unworthy from it. Hence he immediately adds: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven.”

Although this power of loosing and binding appears to have been given by the Lord to Peter alone, it must nevertheless be recognized beyond any doubt that it is also given to the other apostles. The Lord himself bears witness to this: after the triumph of his passion and resurrection, he appeared to them, breathed upon them, and said to them all: “Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained” (John 20) [Col. 0362D].

Even now the same office is entrusted to the bishops and presbyters throughout the whole Church: when the causes of sinners have been recognized, they should, moved by compassion for those whom they see to be humble and truly penitent, absolve them from fear of eternal death; but those whom they recognize as persisting in the sins they have committed they should declare subject to everlasting punishments.

For elsewhere the Lord commands concerning a brother who has been corrected once, twice, and three times but has not repented, saying: “If he does not listen even to the Church, let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector” (Matthew 18). And lest anyone should consider it a trivial matter to be condemned by the judgment of the Church, he immediately added in a terrifying manner: “Amen, I say to you: whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven” [Col. 0363A].

Authority to bind and loose is therefore given to the whole Church of the elect, according to the measure of their faults or penance. But blessed Peter, who confessed Christ with true faith and followed him with true love, specifically received the keys of the kingdom of heaven and the primacy of judicial power, so that all believers throughout the world might understand that whoever in any way separates himself from the unity of that faith or fellowship can neither be loosed from the bonds of sins nor enter through the gate of the heavenly kingdom.

And because, to avoid lengthening the letter, I could show you point by point, if time and leisure permitted and I did not fear wearying my readers, that precisely those things you have collected which you think most strongly support your case refute you, I shall reply specifically only to certain of the things you have collected—especially concerning the letters of Julius and Felix, as though they had been composed from the canons of the Council of Nicaea [Col. 0363B].

This was before the Council of Sardica, which Athanasius is said to have attended in the eighteenth year of his episcopate, when he returned to Alexandria from the western regions, where he had been in exile, bringing with him letters from Constans. According to the testimony of chronicles and ecclesiastical letters, this took place in the eleventh year after the death of Constantine, the father of the emperors Constantius and Constans, during the consulship of Rufus and Eusebius and in the sixteenth year of Pope Julius, who succeeded Mark, the successor of Sylvester. During the time of Sylvester, the holy Council of Nicaea had been held, presided over in his place by Hosius, bishop of Cordova, and by Victor and Vincentius, presbyters of the city of Rome [Col. 0363C].

Approximately twenty-three years after the Council of Nicaea, the Council of Antioch was held, and the letter of Julius is recognized as having been composed around the same period. It contains many canons collected in a different form; if they had been taken from one council, they would not differ in this way. If the matter of appeals had already been established at the Council of Nicaea, as it was established at the Council of Sardica, there would have been no need for it to be established again in this council. Rather, as we read in other councils, it would have been written that the provisions established at the Council of Nicaea were to be observed by all.

Felix’s letter, however, depends upon Julius’s letter. For this is the custom of the pontiffs of the apostolic see: they insert in their own letters the words of their predecessors as though they were their own, as anyone who has read them understands [Col. 0363D].

Moreover, regarding the statement in the letter written in the name of Athanasius and the Egyptian bishops to Mark, the successor of Sylvester, that there had been eighty canons—namely, forty issued by the Greeks in the Greek language and likewise forty issued by the Latins in the Latin language—and that the 318 bishops had reduced them to seventy canons: if the canons omitted from the letter of Julius are counted, and if those found in Felix’s letter are also counted, more than seventy will be found, and they will differ from one another. Furthermore, those canons which antiquity preserved from the Council of Nicaea and which the Church still holds and venerates are not mentioned, much less counted, in those letters [Col. 0364A].

As for what the most reverend Julius says in his letter:

“We have not inserted more concerning these matters—that is, the canons of the Council of Nicaea—lest we should seem to empty or cheapen the aforesaid synod, or make the letter lengthy and tedious for readers and hearers. But if anyone wishes to know more extensive and fuller information about these matters, he will be able to find in the sacred archive of the Church of our see both these things and those we have mentioned. The very Divinity bears witness that I speak the truth, and no one ought to contradict it: for unless the see itself had possessed the things it sent, it could not possibly have sent them; and since it possessed more, it is plainly established that this is true [Col. 0364B]. For it is certain that the provisions established by the sacred Council of Nicaea are preserved in the Roman archive, and the pontiffs of that holy see have promulgated their decrees concerning them and have left them to their successors to be held and observed.”

There was also, among our forefathers, a not unfounded opinion that Hosius had previously reported some of the canons of the Council of Nicaea that he himself had brought forward in a different form from that in which they were later found. At Sirmium, contrary to the faith of the Council of Nicaea, to which he had subscribed, he dared to issue and present a sacrilegious profession and subscription, as ecclesiastical histories testify concerning him, and as Saint Hilary says in his book *On Synods*:

“At Sirmium,” he says, “through Hosius, forgetful of his own deeds and words, a doctrine of impiety that was new and yet long since festering broke forth. But I say nothing about him, who was preserved for this reason: so that human judgment might not remain ignorant of what kind of man he had previously been” [Col. 0364C].

On the testimony of this blessed Hilary, therefore, in his book *On Synods*, and also concerning Hosius, we ought to place our faith in him. In the aforementioned book *On Synods* he says:

“Having long ago been regenerated and having remained for some time in the episcopate, I never heard the Nicene faith except while I was in exile. Yet the Gospels and the apostles made known to me the meaning of *homoousios* (‘of the same substance’) and *homoiousios* (‘of similar substance’). During those times, when the councils—namely, the Councils of Nicaea, Antioch, Sardica, and certain others held afterward—were celebrated, that same holy and Catholic teacher lived in the flesh; he was a true reporter concerning them and left in his writings what we ought to believe.”

The false opinion that arose from the writings of certain people must therefore be rejected: namely, that the Council of Nicaea was held in the time of Julius. For it is established that the same holy synod was held in the 636th year after Alexander, under the emperor Constantine, on the eighteenth day of the month Desius according to the Greeks, which is the tenth day before the Kalends of July, during the consulship of Paulinus and Julian, in the time of Pope Sylvester, as truthful chronicles and ecclesiastical histories testify.

Julius, however, the successor of Mark, who had succeeded Sylvester, held a synod at Rome under the emperors Constantius and Constans, in the fourth year, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, in the sixth indiction, during the consulship of Felicianus and Maximianus. He confirmed that same Council of Nicaea by the authority of the apostolic see, just as his predecessor Sylvester had done through his legates.

He also strengthened, with the authority of the most venerable antiquity, and with the ancient tradition of the ancestors, the canons established in that council, so that they were to be held with inviolable force [Col. 0365A].

## CHAPTER XXI. That only twenty canons were established at the Council of Nicaea.

And for what reason certain things found written in the letters of the ancient Roman pontiffs were not used by their successors, although they are of very great value for instruction; why, on the other hand, certain things set down in their decrees were adopted by councils and are found among the sacred canons; and from what source the opinion arose that more chapters were decreed at the Council of Nicaea than are found in the canon—for we have learned this from letters conveying the succession of ancient authorities [Col. 0365B]—I shall write to you in part, without fearing that you will bring accusations against me, as you have already done concerning what I wrote about Stephen, perverting the meaning of my words and shortening my writings in the letter you gave me concerning Amalbert, wishing to convict me by my own words and twist me according to the crookedness of your judgment. If I learn that you have made the same accusations, I shall necessarily have to write back about them and waste time on such uselessness; but if I do not learn of them, you may perhaps lead those who believe you in some way to disparage me.

I shall speak, then, from the words of the ancients concerning what we have learned about the chapters of the Council of Nicaea, so that, if you delight in fighting, you may wage battle with them, while I may rest. The *Tripartite History* (book II, chapter 7) records that Athanasius said as follows:

> “When the bishops came together at the Council of Nicaea, they drew up twenty regulations concerning ecclesiastical conduct.” [Col. 0365C]

And again:

> “Your patience remembers that a council was held in the city of Nicaea, to which I myself also appropriately offered the devotion of my conscience.”

Again, the same History states:

> “The synod, wishing to correct the life of human beings and of those dwelling in the Church, established laws which we call canons.”

The tenth book of Rufinus’s *Ecclesiastical History*, which is listed in the catalogue of the apostolic see among the books to be received, plainly shows that, after the confession of faith, only twenty-two chapters of canons, together with the decree concerning the Paschal solemnity, were enacted at that council. The two chapters established there beyond the twenty are included among us within the other twenty chapters. Thus the same book states:

> “After establishing definite statutes concerning each of the several ecclesiastical observances, the council was dissolved.” [Col. 0365D]

And after the chapters had been set out in order and numbered:

> “Therefore,” he says, “when they had decreed concerning these matters as the reverence due to the divine laws required, and had also handed down to the churches an ancient canon concerning the observance of Easter, by which no further variation would arise, once everything had been properly arranged, the peace and faith of the churches in the regions of East and West were preserved as one and the same.”

Subject to the authority of the apostolic see—which, by its primacy received from the Lord’s mouth, establishes what will benefit the Church and confirms what has been established by preserving it—the words of this historian are also supported by the Council of Carthage, which says:

> “Copies of the faith and the statutes of the Council of Nicaea, which were brought to our council through Caecilian, bishop of Carthage of blessed memory, who was present there, as well as the statutes which the Fathers established here by following those copies, or which we now establish by common deliberation, shall remain inserted in these ecclesiastical acts.” [Col. 0366A]

That Caecilian was present at the Council of Nicaea is testified by his subscription, and is affirmed by ecclesiastical histories and chronicles, in which it is written:

> “In the third year after the Council of Nicaea, during the consulship of Januarius and Justus, Donatus is recognized as the one from whom arose throughout Africa the Donatists. They first created a schism because Caecilian, bishop of the church of Carthage, had been ordained against their will, bringing against him unproved accusations, especially that he had been ordained by traditors of the divine Scriptures. But after their fabricated case had been brought to an end, they passed through obstinate discord into heresy.” [Col. 0366B]

There is also the letter of Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, whose predecessor Alexander presided, through the intervention of Emperor Constantine, together with the legates of the apostolic see—namely Hosius, bishop of Corduba, and Vincent and Victor, Roman presbyters. It was sent through Innocent the presbyter, together with the complete text of that council. Likewise, there is the letter of Atticus, bishop of Constantinople, also sent to the Council of Carthage through Marcellus the subdeacon, with the complete text of that council; the words of Faustinus, bishop and legate of the apostolic see, spoken at the Council of Carthage; and the letter of the council itself, honorably sent, as was fitting, to Pope Celestine.

There is also the twelfth session of the Council of Chalcedon, in which the ninety-fifth rule is recorded, concerning a vacant bishopric; and shortly afterward Leontius read from the same codex the ninety-sixth rule, concerning those who, when called to the episcopate, avoid it. If anyone numbers these rules consecutively, counting the twenty chapters of the Council of Nicaea from the beginning, through the councils that follow in order, he will find that in the Council of Antioch they occupy the places corresponding to the numbers mentioned above.

It is therefore clear that no more than the twenty chapters that we possess were established at the Council of Nicaea. The long periods of many ages, extending from ancient custom, during which only these twenty chapters of that council were received, also make the testimony of the aforementioned historian indisputably trustworthy.

## CHAPTER XXII  
### Concerning the four chapters mentioned by blessed Gregory in his letter to the patrician Theoctista

[Col. 0366D]

You also improperly inserted in your compilation what concerns anathema, taking words from the holy Gregory addressed to the patrician Theoctista. You presented things well and reasonably said as though they were badly understood, and you tried to interpret them not according to the meaning in which blessed Gregory set them down in that letter.

Among the Greeks, who delight in novelty of expression, four heretical chapters were found, concerning which Saint Gregory wrote to the patrician Theoctista. The first was that, under the pretext of religion, marriages could be dissolved even without the consent of both parties, contrary to the Lord’s saying: “What God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matthew 19).

The second was that baptism did not completely remove sins, although the Lord says: “The one who has bathed does not need to wash, except his feet, but is entirely clean” (John 13).

The third was that if someone performed penance for his iniquities for three years, he might afterward live perversely, although it is written: “The one who is baptized by a dead person and again touches him—what benefit is there in his washing?” (Sirach 34). He is therefore baptized by a dead person and again touches him who laments the evil deeds he remembers committing but, after his tears, entangles himself in the same deeds again.

The fourth is the one which you did not set down according to its meaning: that if certain people, reproached for having thought contrary to the Catholic Church, when compelled said that they anathematized themselves, they were in no way held by the bond of anathema. Concerning these blessed Gregory says:

> “For they are themselves witnesses against themselves that they are not Christians, since they think that by empty efforts they can sever the bonds of the holy Church; and consequently they do not consider the absolution which the holy Church grants to the faithful to be genuine, if they do not consider its binding power valid.”

Accordingly, in the writings of the orthodox we read that among those who assembled at the holy Council of Nicaea, subscribed to the definition or creed of the faith set forth by it, afterward apostatized from that subscription, and then returned to the universal Church through a Catholic subscription, some were received—as we also read concerning other synods and in the letters of Leo and Gregory.

It is therefore evident that the bonds or releases of the holy Church are not those performed against the holy Church, nor those performed by people who, while holding opinions contrary to the Catholic doctrines of the Church, bind or release things contrary to that holy Church. For the holy Church says:

> “I have not sat with the council of vanity, and with those who act wickedly I shall not enter. I have hated the assembly of evildoers, and I shall not sit with the impious. I shall wash my hands among the innocent” (Psalm 25:6).

Finally, in the very words of blessed Gregory, in which he says, “If there are some who say that one who anathematized himself under compulsion of necessity is not held by the bond of anathema,” you inserted your own words, adding also: “or has presumed against those things prohibited under anathema.”

But where he said:

> “If, then, there are some who, under the Christian name, dare either to preach these chapters of error which we have mentioned or to keep them silently within themselves,” [Col. 0367D]

you mutilated and perverted the passage, saying:

> “If, then, there are some who, under the Christian name, dare to preach these things,”

not fearing the judgment pronounced by the holy Sixth Council in its twelfth session, in these words:

> “Macarius, hardened in the doctrines of impiety, who not only by turbulent overthrow was corrupting the entire people beloved by Christ, dwelling in this city protected by God, and falsifying the testimonies of holy and approved Fathers, cutting out some things, adding others, and sending them astray according to his own judgment; and who, through the petitions presented by him, and through letters sent from sunrise to sunset by him and by the people whom he dispatched, was disturbing everyone and separating them from the true faith; having been justly and reasonably stripped of the episcopal office, the divine rule henceforth in no way allows him to sit again in the teacher’s chair, lest by this he cause the understanding of his own heresy, already greatly rekindled, to grow still more, and lest, as it is written, the last state of that man become worse than the first.” [Col. 0368A]

Macedonius, bishop of Constantinople, as I said above, is likewise recorded as having been expelled by the emperor Anastasius because he had falsified the Gospels, especially the Apostle’s statement, “He was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit” (1 Timothy 3), and had perverted it so that it read: “God appeared through the flesh.”

The apostle Paul rebukes such people when he says of himself and his companions:

> “For we are not,” he says, “like the many who adulterate the word of God” (2 Corinthians 2).

“Adulterating the word of God,” blessed Gregory says, “means either thinking differently about it than it is, or seeking from it not spiritual fruits but adulterous offspring of human praise.”

For this reason Gelasius wrote to the bishops established throughout Dardania in his decrees (letter 11, at the beginning):

> “Our predecessors necessarily took care that, against each heresy, whatever a synod had once promulgated for the sake of the faith, communion, and Catholic and apostolic truth would not afterward be allowed to be mutilated by new reconsiderations, lest an opportunity be given to wicked people to assault what had been established as a remedy. Instead, after condemning the author of any madness together with the error itself, they judged it sufficient that whoever at any time became a participant in that error should be bound by the principal sentence of its condemnation, since anyone could plainly be recognized either by his profession or by his communion.”

And a little later:

> “For the very same error, once condemned together with its author, carries its own curse and punishment in anyone who becomes a participant in its wicked communion.”

You, therefore, who have falsified these words of blessed Gregory, should consider what blessed Gelasius says and place before the eyes of your mind the fact that Macarius and Macedonius were removed from the priesthood—even before human eyes—by synodal judgment and imperial authority. Hasten to make satisfaction to the terrible one who deliberates concerning the children of human beings.

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### That the apostolic see does not receive part of the ninth chapter of Chalcedon, as blessed Pope Leo demonstrates

[Col. 0368D]

You appended to your compilation the following sentence of the Council of Chalcedon, expounded by someone who found something to say about it:

> “If a cleric has a case against his own bishop or against another, let him be judged before the synod of the province. But if a bishop or cleric has a complaint against the metropolitan of the same province, let him appeal to the primate of the diocese or to the see of the royal city of Constantinople, and let him be judged before him.”

This was also recapitulated in the seventeenth chapter.

Read the acts of the Council of Chalcedon, and the *Brief Account of the Two Heresies of the Nestorians and Eutychians*, compiled by Saint Liberatus, archdeacon of the Church of Carthage in the sixth region; read also the letters of Saint Pope Leo. You will find that this is the ninth chapter of that council. At its end it says:

> “Let him appeal to the primate of the diocese or to the see of the royal city of Constantinople, and let him be judged before him.”

You will also find that what was agreed concerning the division of the diocese between the bishops of Antioch and Jerusalem was not received by the apostolic see.

Nor did the apostolic see receive that chapter of the Council of Constantinople in which the synod itself established that Constantinople should be preferred to the second and third sees and, after the Roman pontiff, should hold primacy. Constantinople obtained this also through an imperial enactment, and the Council of Chalcedon, in the absence of the legates of the apostolic see, renewed it by confirmation, although certain persons did not consent. Later, when those same legates of the apostolic see protested the injury and prejudice done to the sacred canons and to the privilege of the apostolic and first see, the synod, with the emperor’s support, persisted in its decision.

For at that time Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, acted before the synod (Leo, letter 53, to Anatolius) and before the emperor. Taking the condemnation of Dioscorus, bishop of the second see of Alexandria, as an opportunity, he employed this stratagem: the mind greedy for power neither abstains from what is forbidden nor rejoices in what is granted. Since, at the Constantinopolitan synod of 150 bishops, Nectarius had secured the provision that Constantinople, placed before the second and third sees, should hold primacy after the Roman pontiff, Anatolius arranged that this chapter, inserted among other necessary matters, concerning appeals of bishops and clerics to the see of the royal city of Constantinople, should deprive the apostolic see of the provision of the Council of Sardica concerning appeals by clerics to neighboring bishops and appeals by bishops from a regional council to the apostolic see, and should cause this authority to be attributed to himself. Thus, as soon became clear, he might more freely usurp the primacy of the apostolic see against the sacred canons and ancient custom and might be called—and become—universal.

Therefore Saint Leo, writing to Maximus, bishop of Antioch, concerning what had been obtained at the synodal gathering, says (letter 65):

> “Now, in general, it is sufficient to declare that if anything has been attempted by anyone in any synod against the statutes of the canons of Nicaea, or appears for a time to have been extorted, it can inflict no prejudice upon inviolable decrees; and it will be easier to dissolve agreements of whatever kind than to corrupt in any respect the rules of the aforementioned canons. Ambition never fails to seek opportunities for stealth; and whenever, for reasons arising in the meantime, a general assembly of bishops has been held, it is difficult for the greed of the wicked not to try to desire something beyond measure.

> “The same occurred in the case of the Council of Ephesus, which struck down the impious Nestorius together with his doctrine. Juvenal, bishop, thought that he could obtain the primacy of the province of Palestine and dared to support his insolence by forged writings. Cyril, bishop of Alexandria of holy memory, rightly horrified by this, informed me in his writings of what the aforementioned greed had dared to do and earnestly requested that no assent be given to unlawful efforts. Since you sent us copies of the letter of Cyril of holy memory, know that we sought it in our archives and found it to be authentic.

> “This, however, is the particular principle of my decision: however large a number of bishops may decree something through the deception of certain persons, if it is found to be contrary to the constitutions of the three hundred and eighteen, it must be annulled in consideration of justice. For the tranquility of universal peace cannot otherwise be preserved unless the reverence due to the canons remains undefiled.

> “If it is alleged that anything was done by those brothers whom I sent in my place to the holy synod beyond what concerned the case of the faith, it will have absolutely no validity, because they were sent from the apostolic see for this one purpose: that, after the heresies had been cut away, they should be defenders of the Catholic faith.

> “Whatever is brought before the episcopal judgment beyond the specific matters of synodal councils may have some basis for judgment, provided that nothing concerning it has been defined by the holy Fathers at Nicaea. For whatever disagrees with their rules and constitution can never obtain the consent of the apostolic see.” [Col. 0370B]

And to Pulcheria Augusta he says (letter 58):

> “My brother and fellow bishop Anatolius, insufficiently considering how, through the favor of your piety and the assent of my support, he obtained the priesthood of the Church of Constantinople, has rejoiced less in what he acquired than he has been inflamed beyond the measure of his honor by the desire for excessive things. He believes that this unrestrained ambition can be advanced by the fact that certain people are said to have offered him their consent through an extorted subscription. Yet the opposition of my brother bishops and fellow bishops, acting in my place, faithfully and commendably met and frustrated these efforts.

> “For against the statutes of the paternal canons, founded many ages ago in the city of Nicaea upon spiritual decrees, no one is permitted to dare anything. If anyone wishes to decree something different, he diminishes himself rather than corrupting those statutes.

> “If all pontiffs preserve them undefiled, as they ought, there will be peaceful peace and firm concord throughout all the churches; there will be no dissensions concerning the measure of honors, no disputes concerning ordinations, no uncertainties concerning privileges, and no conflicts concerning the usurpation of what belongs to another. Rather, the order of charity, conduct, and duties will be preserved according to equal justice, and the truly great person will be the one free from all ambition, as the Lord says: ‘Whoever wishes to become greater among you shall be your servant. And whoever wishes to be first among you shall be your slave, just as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve’” (Matthew 20).

> “These things, however, were then being impressed upon those who wished to rise from a low position and pass from the lowest places to the highest. But what more does the bishop of the Church of Constantinople desire than what he has attained? Or what will satisfy him if the magnificence and splendor of so great a city are not enough?

> “It is exceedingly proud and immoderate to extend oneself beyond one’s own boundaries, to trample upon antiquity, to seek to seize another’s right, and, so that the dignity of one person may increase, to attack the primacies of so many metropolitans; to bring a war of new disturbance against peaceful provinces, long arranged by the moderation of the holy Council of Nicaea; and, so that the decrees of venerable Fathers may be dissolved, to produce the consent of certain bishops, although the succession of so many years has denied it effect.

> “For it is said that nearly sixty years have passed since this agreement, by which the aforementioned bishop thinks he is assisted, vainly wishing that it should benefit him. Even if someone dared to desire such a thing, no one could obtain it.” [Col. 0371B]

Because Anatolius wished to arrogate to himself the appeal of clerics from the Council of Sardica to neighboring bishops, and the appeal of bishops to the apostolic see, and wished both to be called and to be universal, while the legates of the apostolic see protested at the synod, the same blessed Leo wrote to the emperor Marcian, saying (letter 57):

> “I speak before a Christian, truly religious, and truly orthodox ruler. Bishop Anatolius greatly diminishes his own merit if he desires to grow by an unlawful increase. Let the city of Constantinople have, as we wish, its own glory, and, with the right hand of God protecting it, enjoy for a long time the rule of your clemency. Yet the order of secular affairs is one thing and that of divine affairs another. Apart from that rock which the Lord wonderfully established as the foundation, no construction will be stable. Whoever covets what is not owed to him loses what is his own.

> “Let it be enough for the aforementioned man that, through the aid of your piety and the assent of my favor, he obtained the bishopric of so great a city. Let him not disdain the royal city, which he cannot make an apostolic see, nor hope in any way that he can be enlarged through the offenses of others.

> “For the privileges of the churches, established by the canons of the holy Fathers and fixed by the decrees of the venerable Council of Nicaea, can be shaken by no wickedness and violated by no novelty. In faithfully carrying out this work with Christ’s help, I must show myself a persevering servant, because a stewardship has been entrusted to me. It will be charged to my account if the rules of the paternal sanctions, established at the Council of Nicaea for the governance of the whole Church under the instruction of the Spirit of God, should be violated with my connivance—God forbid—and if the will of one brother becomes more important to me than the common welfare of the entire household of the Lord.

> “Therefore, knowing that your glorious clemency is devoted to ecclesiastical concord and gives pious assent to those things that contribute to peaceful unity, I ask and earnestly beseech you to withhold all assent of your piety from wicked attempts contrary to Christian unity and peace, and salutarily to restrain the harmful ambition of my brother Anatolius, should he persist. Let him not, in desiring things hostile to your glory and your times, wish to become greater than his predecessors. Let him be free to shine with whatever virtues he can, but he will share in them only if he chooses to be adorned by charity rather than distended by ambition.

> “He ought never to have received this conception of wicked desire within the secret recesses of his heart. But when the brothers and fellow bishops who were present in my place opposed him, he should at least, in response to their contradiction, have ceased from his unlawful desire. Your piety’s letters and his own writings also make clear that the legates of the apostolic see, as was fitting, resisted with the most just opposition, so that the presumption would be all the more inexcusable, since it did not restrain itself even when rebuked.

> “Therefore, since it is appropriate to your faith and glory that, just as heresy was destroyed through your agency, so every ambition should also be blunted, do what is both Christian and royal: let the aforementioned bishop spare the Fathers, provide for peace, and not suppose himself permitted—without any precedent—to do what he presumed against the statutes of the canons: to ordain a bishop for the Church of Antioch. We refrained from revising this only out of love for the restoration of the faith and devotion to peace.

> “Let him therefore refrain from injuring the ecclesiastical rules and avoid unlawful excesses, lest, while attempting things hostile to peace, he cut himself off from the universal Church. I desire to love him acting irreproachably rather than see him persist in this presumption, which could separate him from everyone.”

When Anatolius saw that he could in no way obtain what he wanted, either through himself or through the emperor, and consequently withdrew from the matter, the same holy Leo demonstrates this by writing to Anatolius himself (letter 77):

> “If your Dilection had possessed, with firm and unchangeable purpose, a concern for the common grace, nothing would have arisen to cause you any anxiety. Reason did not allow me to despise the affection of one whom I had helped, out of love for peace and zeal for restoring the Catholic faith, at the very beginning of his episcopate. I desired to have in ecclesiastical affairs such a companion that, in you, I would not lack anything of the spiritual and abundant teaching of your holy predecessors: neither John, nor the authority of Atticus, nor the diligence of Proclus, nor the faith of blessed Flavian. I wished to use your efforts in such a way that no one would dare either to oppose the Catholic faith or to contradict the rules of the venerable Fathers of Nicaea.

> “But since, as you acknowledge, attempts were made against the canons which would cause the greatest scandal to all the churches, what more suitable and moderate thing could I have done than first to admonish you, with brotherly feeling and by a letter, to withdraw from this intention? When you did not reply to that letter, you yourself separated yourself from sharing my conversation.

> “Finally, I remained silent thereafter, but through frequent letters I urged the most merciful emperor, guardian of the faith, to ensure, for the peace of the churches—which you recognize to be especially beneficial to you—that the things now done by your Dilection might be fulfilled. I give him inexpressible thanks because, according to the instruction of the Holy Spirit, whose power fills him, he deigns to pursue priestly concord, knowing that the prayers of those who supplicate will benefit him more abundantly if the servants of one Lord are in no way divided from the unity of true peace.” [Col. 0373A]

And a little later:

> “The fault which, as you assert, you incurred through another’s urging you to increase his power, your charity would have washed away more effectively and sincerely if you had not transferred to the advice of the clerics alone what could not have been attempted without your will. For just as one sins through evil persuasion, so one also sins through evil consent.

> “But it is pleasing to me, dearest brother, that your Dilection professes displeasure at what ought not even then to have pleased you. Your profession of affection and the testimony of the Christian ruler are sufficient for your return to the common grace; and the correction does not seem late when such a venerable advocate has joined it.

> “Let the desire for an ungranted right, which caused dissension, be utterly cast away. Let the limits established by the most provident decrees of the holy Fathers be sufficient, so that the dignity of all priests may remain peaceful in its merits and ancient privileges.

> “Let the affection of the Lord’s charity be renewed and remain in you. I have often urged your Dilection toward this love together with our brother and fellow bishop Julian, who has always desired the common grace. Through his diligence your anxieties will be relieved and the Catholic faith strengthened.

> “Above all, I exhort and admonish you in fraternal charity to preserve those decrees of the canons of Nicaea which concern the glory and protection of the priestly office and preserve the peace of the universal Church. For charity will remain inviolate among the priests of the Lord if, with equal zeal, the things established by the holy Fathers are observed.”

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### Concerning the same Chalcedonian canon, the canons of the apostles, the judgments given to Angilramn, and the letters of the pontiffs collected by Isidore

[Col. 0373C]

But since certain people have again tried to revive and restore these matters, alleging that the Council of Chalcedon must either be accepted in its entirety as valid or judged wholly annulled, blessed Gelasius explains the matter, destroys their empty opinions and objections, and shows in his decrees what must be upheld, saying (*Book on the Bonds of Anathema*):

> “Lest, as they commonly do, the Greeks should say that, if the Council of Chalcedon is admitted, everything which appears to have been drawn up there must necessarily stand; that either the whole council must be admitted, or, if it is to be rejected in part, it cannot stand as valid in its entirety. Let them therefore understand that, according to the holy Scriptures and the tradition of our forebears, according to the canons and rules of the Church, for the sake of the common faith and catholic and apostolic truth—for which this matter was commissioned and confirmed by the apostolic see—it is to be admitted without hesitation by the whole Church. But the other matters which were brought forward there—or rather, aired there—through incompetent presumption, which the apostolic see in no way commissioned to be carried out, which were immediately contradicted by the representatives of the apostolic see, which the apostolic see, even when the emperor Marcian requested it, in no way approved, and which Anatolius, then bishop of the Church of Constantinople, did not deny had been placed within the authority of the bishop of the apostolic see, the apostolic see therefore did not receive, as has been said, because matters proved contrary to the privileges of the universal Church cannot stand on any grounds.

> “For what difference does it make that in the holy books—which we certainly venerate and follow—certain people’s profanities are said to be present and their crimes are narrated? Are these things therefore to be venerated or followed by us equally, simply because they are contained in those holy and venerable books? The holy Peter, first of the apostles, judging that the grace of the New Testament should be preached in such a way that he did not depart from the institutions of the old law, is read to have acted in a certain manner by way of pretence among Jews and Gentiles. Are those actions of his therefore to be followed—actions which his fellow apostle rightly rebuked, and which he himself subsequently avoided—and are they to be accepted together with those things which, as the first apostle, he preached for the sake of salvation? Is his sound teaching therefore to be rejected together with those human additions, or is that former weakness of understanding to be accepted together with his perfected teaching?

> “Are many things pertaining to the truth not also found in the books of the heretics themselves? Is the truth therefore to be rejected because their books, in which wickedness is present, are rejected? Or are their wicked books therefore to be accepted because the truth inserted there is not denied? The Apostle says: ‘Test everything; hold fast what is good’ (1 Thess. 5). We know that the Apostle also included certain things from pagan books. Are all the things which were brought forward alongside these therefore likewise to be accepted? The same apostle says that many preachers proclaim Christ in different ways; where Christ is preached, he says, Christ must be accepted by whatever means. Yet he does not thereby fail to warn us to avoid the practice by which Christ was not rightly preached. He himself complains of wicked workers, teaching that some of their actions must be rejected and others followed. These and similar examples instruct us, and divine testimonies confirm, that we must not indiscriminately accept everything said by anyone or written anywhere, but must retain what is good and reject what is harmful.”

And again:

> “What the apostolic see confirmed obtained authority; what it rejected could not possess validity, and it alone rescinded what the synodal assembly had presumed to usurp contrary to order.”

And again:

> “They oppose us with the canons, saying that the Eastern bishops, while not knowing what they are saying, act against the very canons by which they themselves are shown to be acting, because they refuse to obey the first see when it gives sound and righteous counsel. The canons themselves are what wished the appeal of the whole Church to be brought before the judgment of this see.”

And again the same writer:

> “Let them see, then, whether they have other canons by which to carry out their foolishness. For these canons, which are celebrated as sacred, ecclesiastical, and legitimate, cannot even summon the apostolic see to judgment,” and so forth.

Likewise the same writer:

> “Whether they wish it or not, the ancient constitutions of the canons are confirmed by the judgment of that very see, namely, the apostolic see. Yet religious and perfect men, in accordance with the canons, strive to take away the power granted to the apostolic see and contend to usurp it for themselves contrary to the canons. O teachers and guardians of the canons!”

And a little later:

> “As far as religion is concerned, the entire burden of judgment is owed, according to the canons, only to the apostolic see.”

And again:

> “The authority of the apostolic see—that it has been placed before the universal Church throughout all Christian ages—is confirmed both by the sequence of the fathers’ canons and by manifold tradition.”

And again:

> “The canons wished appeals from every part of the world to be made to that see, while no one was permitted to appeal from it.”

Blessed Gregory likewise suffered the same things from John, and after him from Cyriacus, the bishops of Constantinople, as Leo had suffered from Anatolius concerning the aforementioned Constantinopolitan canons. Writing in the same manner to Eulogius, bishop of Alexandria, and Anastasius, bishop of Antioch, he says among other things in his letters (*Book VI, Letter 31*):

> “The canons of the Council of Constantinople condemn the Eudoxians, but they do not at all say who their author Eudoxius was. The Roman Church has neither retained nor accepted those same canons, or the acts of that synod, up to the present; but it accepted that synod insofar as it defined something against Macedonius. As for the remaining heresies mentioned there, it rejects them as having already been condemned by other fathers. Concerning the Eudoxians, it has so far recognized nothing.”

And since the same blessed Gregory often says in his letters that he receives the four synods just as he receives the four Gospels, he clearly demonstrates that he receives the Council of Constantinople in the same manner as he stated above: namely, that the apostolic see accepts what was defined there concerning the faith against heretics, but does not at all accept the canons or acts of that synod insofar as they stand against the Nicene canons, as was shown above.

But that the apostolic see accepts the canons of the Council of Chalcedon, apart from that one chapter—recapitulated in Chapter XVII—which was established contrary to the Nicene canons, the same blessed Gregory clearly demonstrates in his letter to Secundinus and in the seventeenth homily on the Gospel:

> “Who,” he says, “are those in the temple of God today who sell doves, except those who receive a price in the Church for the laying on of hands, through which laying on of hands the Holy Spirit is given from heaven? The dove is therefore sold because the laying on of hands, through which the Holy Spirit is received, is offered for a price. But our Redeemer overturns the seats of those who sell doves because he destroys the priesthood of such traffickers. Hence it is that the sacred canons condemn the heresy of simony and order that those who seek payment for conferring orders be deprived of the priesthood. The seat of those who sell doves is therefore overturned when those who sell spiritual grace are deprived of the priesthood either in the sight of human beings or in the sight of God.”

No synod, indeed, decreed judgment on this matter except the Council of Chalcedon, although a decree concerning it is also found in the canons called apostolic. These were not established by the authority of episcopal councils; rather, from the earliest times they were entrusted individually to the minds of apostolic men by tradition, being set down partly in words, partly in substance, and scattered through various letters of certain people according to the nature of the cases, persons, and times. From these materials, before bishops began freely to celebrate councils, they were collected by various devout men.

Among them some matters are acceptable, while others are not to be observed. Some of them were occasionally adopted in councils, and we read that some were also adopted by great men of pre-eminent authority in their own works, just as material from the apocrypha was adopted, because certain passages are useful for instruction. Therefore, as we have learned from the tradition of our forebears, they are placed separately, before the councils, in books of canons for instruction and because of their widespread reputation. In certain manuscripts the sacred and universal Council of Nicaea is placed before the regional councils held before it, because of the authority of its greatness.

For the same canons called apostolic are not believed to have been written by the apostles. For, as we read in sacred history and have received in writing from the teachers of the Church, the first synod of the apostles was held at Jerusalem concerning the election of a twelfth apostle in place of Judas; the second, concerning the election of seven deacons; the third, concerning circumcision, so that it might not be imposed upon believers from the Gentiles; the fourth, concerning those who believed from among the Jews at that time, so that they would not be prohibited, when necessity required it, from being initiated even through the legal ceremonies—namely, to avoid the scandal of those who thought that they had condemned the Mosaic decrees as though they were doctrines of idolatry. That they had previously been accustomed to do this is demonstrated especially by the circumcision of Timothy.

Our fathers, however, report that the fifth synod of the apostles was held when the foretold time of fulfillment arrived, so that their sound might go out into all the earth and their words to the ends of the world, and so that, according to the Lord’s command, the Gospel might be preached throughout the whole world by the apostles, to whom he said: “Go, teach all nations” (Matt. 22).

Then, as the universal Church maintains, they composed the Creed, each one contributing a separate statement, as Leo also demonstrates to the empress Pulcheria (*Letter 15, at the end*):

> “For,” he says, “that brief and perfect confession of the catholic Creed, which is marked by the twelve statements of the twelve apostles, is furnished with such heavenly protection that all the opinions of the heretics can be cut down by its sword alone. If Eutyches had wished to embrace the fullness of this Creed with a pure and simple heart, he would in no way have deviated from the decrees of the most sacred Council of Nicaea, and he would have understood that the holy fathers established this: that against the apostolic faith, which is one and indivisible, no intellect and no eloquence should raise itself.”

After this, no synod is recorded as having been celebrated by the apostles, who were scattered by advancing throughout the whole earth to sow the word of faith.

Blessed Gelasius too, in the catalogue in which he listed the books received by the Catholic Church, after distinctly mentioning the authentic Scriptures, the Councils of Nicaea, Constantinople, and Ephesus, the Council of Chalcedon, and the other councils instituted by the holy fathers, together with the works of orthodox writers, the decretal letters of the bishops of the apostolic see, and other writings, was completely silent about these canons of the apostles; nor did he place them among the apocrypha.

Therefore, in reading them, one must observe the caution previously taught by that same holy Gelasius:

> “When these writings,” he says, “come into the hands of Catholics, the statement of the blessed apostle Paul must precede them: ‘Test everything; hold fast what is good’ (1 Thess. 5).”

The same applies to those chapters said to have been written in Latin and Greek from Roman laws, collected in various ways from the aforementioned letters, and brought by the diligence of Hosius to the Council of Nicaea, though only those matters which we hold to have been established there were decreed for observance.

Consequently, the same Hosius later recited certain matters at the Council of Sardica. The Catholic Church accepts them because they were confirmed by that council together with the representatives of the apostolic see. At that synod, which was presided over by representatives of the apostolic see—Hosius, bishop of Córdoba; Vincentius of Capua; and Calepodius of Naples—there were nearly three hundred bishops from the western regions and sixty-six from the eastern regions, under the emperor Constantius, when Rufus and Eusebius were consuls. When the eastern Arians withdrew from the council in flight, the western Catholics who remained devoted themselves to carrying out the matters that then had to be undertaken.

Recall when I told you these and many other things from the tradition of ancient history, when you were my dearest son; and recall where you could also have read these matters concerning the canons of the apostles and the chapters recited at the aforementioned councils through the diligence of Hosius, if you did not neglect them. Yet you refused to accept these things and contended against the authority of the ancients, who confirm by truthful testimony that the sacred Council of Nicaea had no more chapters than those which the Catholic Church, from ancient custom, holds and venerates.

You did this if you were unwilling to heed the Apostle when he says: “If anyone wishes to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor has the Church of God” (1 Cor. 11).

As for me, I shall not take up again the boxing gloves already laid aside for this matter, since what the apostolic see and the Catholic Church teach is sufficient for me.

And as for what you added in your commentaries—that there is no primate of a diocese except the vicar of the first apostle—you have read sufficiently above what the sacred canons and the decrees of the bishops of the Roman see understood and decreed concerning the primates of provinces.

As for the judgments said to have been collected from Greek and Latin canons, Roman synods, and the decrees of Roman bishops and rulers by Pope Adrian and given to Engelramnus, bishop of Metz, when his own case was being conducted—some of which you inserted into your commentaries—their mutual incompatibility, their difference from the sacred canons, and their disagreement in certain matters from ecclesiastical judgments are clearly demonstrated, as I shall set out here some examples from among many.

> “It has been decreed,” they say (*chapters 57, 73), “that either the tongue of an informer be cut out or, once convicted, his head be severed. A judge investigating a criminal must not pronounce a capital sentence before either the accused himself confesses or he is convicted by innocent witnesses. The witnesses, moreover, must be free from every disrepute, have wives and children, and altogether preach Christ. No one is to accept the testimony of a cleric against a layman.”

No one is unaware how foreign these provisions are to the sacred canons and how hostile they are to ecclesiastical judgments. Anyone can clearly recognize, from the several examples presented here out of many, how in certain respects they are opposed to you and to your recent actions, for which you are being reproved.

> “It has been decreed,” they say (*chapter 22), “that no bishop presume to judge or condemn any cleric unless, once accused, he has legitimate accusers present and is given an opportunity to defend himself for the clearing of the charges.”

And a little later:

> “Nor should the judge wish to forestall the litigants with his sentence, except when, after everything has been completed, they have nothing further to propose in the matter; and the action must be debated until the truth of the case is reached,”

and so forth.

> “Let the judges of the Church beware” (*chapter 53), “lest they pronounce a sentence in the absence of the person whose case is being debated, because it will be invalid; indeed, they will give cause for the matter to be brought before a synod as an offense.”

You acted against these judgments when you dared to issue excommunications contrary to God and his commandments, for which I rebuked you in writing.

The same judgments also state (*chapter 27*):

> “There are some who condemn people without investigation, by tyrannical power rather than canonical authority; and just as they exalt certain people through the favor of partiality, so they humble others, moved by hatred and envy, and condemn them on the light breeze of opinion, although they do not approve their crimes. Therefore, by common decree we establish that whenever any bishop is accused, his case is heard with all the bishops of the same province assembled, so that he is not judged or condemned secretly; for he cannot be judged first by others except by those by whom he could have been ordained. If it is done otherwise, it will have no force.”

A fine achievement! You labored so much to be subject to no one except the bishop of the apostolic see, and so that no one could judge you except the apostolic see—when these very judgments which you brought forward in defense of your protection speak against you, because you are subject to those by whom you could have been ordained and can be judged by them.

Wonderful—or rather pitiable—is your remarkable, indeed miserable, wisdom, because you could not or would not see these things in the very judgments themselves, although you read that the holy living creatures shown to Ezekiel were full of eyes before and behind, while the arrogant Pharisee had no eye in that place where, boastingly enumerating his good deeds, he preferred himself to the publican.

From this it may also be understood of you what Solomon says: “A man is known by his instruction; but the empty and senseless man will be exposed to contempt” (Prov. 12).

And Seneca, almost a Christian and familiar with the apostle Paul, says:

> “One must see to it that the things by which admiration is sought do not become ridiculous and hateful.”

Solomon says likewise:

> “As if you wished to adorn an earthen vessel with filthy silver, so are swollen lips joined to a most wicked heart” (Prov. 26).

And Cato:

> “He hears what he does not want who persists in saying what he wants.

> “The ulcer spreads which foolish silences conceal.

> “Remove the wicked witnesses, and we shall bear our own evils more lightly.”

Hence Solomon says again:

> “Drive out the scoffer, and strife will go out with him; causes and insults will cease” (Prov. 22).

But if you collected from the aforementioned judgments and frequently cited letters the things that seemed useful to you by cutting them apart, rearranging them, and putting them out of order because you perhaps thought that no one besides you possessed those judgments or the letters themselves, and therefore believed that you could freely collect such things, this is astonishing. For this land is full of the very judgments themselves, just as it is full of the book of letters collected by Isidore, which Riculfus, bishop of Mainz, diligently obtained after it had been brought from Spain, as he also obtained the royal chapters, and by which he caused these regions to be filled.

In its preface Isidore himself says of the canons of the apostles that some call them apocryphal, while many accept them; that the holy fathers strengthened their statements by synodal authority and placed them among the canonical constitutions. This is true of certain of their statements, as you can read elsewhere in this work.

He also established a distinction between the letters he collected and the sacred canons from the words of blessed Gelasius, into which he inserted his own words as well. Concerning the Council of Nicaea, however, the matter is not as he wrote it, as is confirmed by many testimonies of authorities. And concerning Easter, what he brought forward from the letter of Theophilus—anyone who has read ecclesiastical histories will find in that same council a letter concerning Easter, composed together with the chapters established there.

I could set out at greater length certain matters concerning the statements of that Isidore, and also concerning the letter of Damasus which he placed beneath his preface and before his collection. But since the authority and exposition of the apostolic see—of Leo, Gelasius, and the other Roman bishops after Damasus—provide more than enough for the matters required here, I considered it superfluous to bring forward unnecessary material, lest you charge me with that poetic saying:

> “Are you perhaps carrying wood into the forest, traveler?”

You say, as I have heard, “I am not the only one who understands the canons,” and you speak the truth. I accept this statement entirely—not because it is yours, but because it is true.

And I say: “You are not the only one who understands the canons well,” and I speak the truth. Receive this statement, then, not because it is mine, but because it is true.

And if you think that you know what you have not learned, I say that the only person who knew what he had not learned from a human being was that man of whom the Jews, in their amazement, said: “How does this man know letters, when he has not been taught?” (John 7).

For this reason he was able, through uneducated men and fishermen, to teach orators and to subject emperors to himself.

And since I say that he alone was the man who knew what he had not learned from a human being, you will consider the case of Paul, who says that he did not learn from a human being but through a revelation of Jesus Christ. Paul himself did not deny that Christ was human when he said that he knew nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified (1 Cor. 2). For Jesus is God and man; since divinity could not be crucified, it was the man who was crucified.

You reproach me because I say that, before you were born, I knew the canons, boasting that you should be allowed to know what I know, since you learned after me what I learned before you.

But Paul did not speak from your heart. Reading the statement spoken by Moses, “Ask your father, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will say to you” (Deut. 32), he boasts that he learned the law at the feet of Gamaliel (Acts 22).

Knowing that, when he was proud, he was struck down from heaven by the Lord, and that although he was destined to become a preacher, he did not immediately hear what he was to preach after seeing it, he was instead told while lying there: “Enter the city, and you will be told what you must do” (Acts 9).

The Lord wished him to learn this from Ananias, although he could have taught him immediately and in an instant through revelation. Then he went to Jerusalem to visit Peter (Gal. 1). After fourteen years he again went up to Jerusalem according to a revelation (Gal. 2) and compared with his predecessors, the apostles, the Gospel which he preached among the Gentiles, privately with those who seemed to be more distinguished, lest he should be running or should have run in vain.

I say these things without ignoring that it was said of certain people: “In the ancient is wisdom” (Job 12); and of others: “The wisdom of a man is his gray hair.” Likewise, of some it is to be understood: “The younger they are, the more perceptive they are”; but of others: “The younger they are, the more obstinate they are.”

Of such people Paul says: “The time will come when they will not endure sound teaching, but according to their own desires they will heap up teachers for themselves” (2 Tim. 4), and so forth.

And since we know where, for how long, from whom, and what and how much you learned—you who were not taught in the school of Daniel, concerning whom it is said, “Are you wiser than Daniel?” (Ezek. 28)—while you continue digging up such matters contained in your commentaries, which do not serve your purpose, it would be more useful—or rather, since these things are useless to you, it would truly be useful—to seek those things which you ought to carry for your own salvation and that of those entrusted to you.

You should learn, namely, how you ought to understand from the sacred rules that some people are ordered to remain in the church until the Mass of the Catechumens, while others are joined to the celebration of the sacred mysteries only by prayer within the church of the faithful, but are excluded from the banquet of the Lord’s table.

Leo says (*Letter 91, chapter 4*):

> “For those who, in a time of necessity and under the pressure of impending danger, seek the protection of penance and immediately thereafter reconciliation, neither satisfaction is to be forbidden nor reconciliation denied.”

Innocent says (*Letter 1, chapter 19*):

> “Women who are spiritually married to Christ and veiled by a priest, if afterward they marry publicly or corrupt themselves secretly, are not to be admitted to perform penance unless the man to whom they had joined themselves has departed from the world.”

Celestine says (*Letter 1, chapter 2*):

> “No one is to be denied final penance.”

For when it is said “no one,” no exception is made.

And Leo, as I stated above (*Letter 91, chapter 4*):

> “To those who implore it,” he says, “satisfaction is not to be forbidden, nor reconciliation denied.”

We also read that heretics and schismatics returning to the unity of ecclesiastical faith and peace are to be received into their orders through the laying on of the bishop’s hands. But presbyters or deacons convicted of some grave offense, for which it is necessary to remove them from ministry, are not to have hands laid upon them as penitents.

We must therefore understand why hands are laid upon returning heretics and schismatics, while hands are not laid upon fallen deacons or presbyters for reconciliation. Concerning these, Leo says:

> “For such fallen persons, a private withdrawal is to be sought in order to obtain God’s mercy; if their satisfaction is worthy, it is also fruitful.”

The same Leo says:

> “If anyone has committed an offense against the sacred rules, let him know that forgiveness will thereafter be denied him.”

And Saint Gregory, the other Roman bishops, and the sacred canons say that those who have fallen while in an order ought not to be restored, just as public penitents ought not to be promoted to an ecclesiastical order.

How, then, can penance be fruitful if penitents of this kind cannot be restored to their ranks, provided that their penance is worthy? For what good is it to sow wheat and not gather its fruit? Or to build a house and not dwell in it? “Will one who falls not rise again?” (Amos 5.)

We read that clerics of certain heretics whose baptism is judged valid are received in their orders, while we read that others are not to be received. We also read that certain heretics or schismatics are received by some with an anointing of chrism, by others through the laying on of hands without anointing with chrism, by others without the laying on of hands but with a profession and subscription together, and by others through profession alone.

Again, we read in the sacred canons (*Council of Arles II, canon 25*):

> “Those who, after making a holy profession of religion, apostatize and return to the world, and afterward do not seek the remedies of penance, are absolutely not to receive communion without penance.”

And:

> “Penitents who, while ill, have received the Eucharist as viaticum must not believe themselves absolved without the laying on of hands, if they survive.”

We also read that, just as there is one baptism, so there ought to be one penance, which is nevertheless performed publicly.

There are many people in our parishes who, after penance and reconciliation through the laying on of hands, and after communion, fall again—not only once, but a second and third time. What are we to do concerning them, since, as I stated above, they will not receive communion without penance? Or how will those who receive the Eucharist and die in this condition be absolved, when they would not have been absolved without the laying on of hands if they had survived?

And we read in the sacred canons (*Council of Vaison, canon 2*):

> “The offering of those who, after receiving penance and living in a good course of life through satisfactory contrition, are unexpectedly overtaken without communion by death in the fields or on journeys is to be received; and their funerals and subsequent memory are to be honored with ecclesiastical devotion.”

Leo says (*Letter 92 to Rusticus of Narbonne, chapter 8*):

> “The case of such people must be reserved to God’s judgment, in whose hand it lay that their death should be delayed until the remedy of communion. But we, who did not communicate with them while they were alive, cannot communicate with them when they are dead.”

We must also learn from the sacred canons how the distinct ranks of penitents mentioned in the canons are to perform penance according to the ranks established for them; how many there are and who they are; and how we ought to observe these distinctions toward penitents in the Church, lest we act contrary to the sacred rules.

If you attend carefully to some of these matters in this little work and wish to recall what I remember having already said to you, when you seemed to possess the willingness to learn and to wish to learn what ought to be taught, you will be able to understand them.

There are also many other matters which I could enumerate for you here. But I think that, especially when sowing among thorns, it would be a long undertaking for me and fruitless for you, because I hear and see that your will and desire eagerly tend toward things which, like hay, quickly wither, and which, like garden vegetables, soon fall away (Ps. 39).

Concerning these things it is written again:

> “They have slept their sleep, and all the men of wealth found nothing in their hands. At your rebuke, O God of Jacob, those who mounted horses fell into slumber” (Ps. 75).

Gregory says:

> “Those who have trusted in the honor of the present life have closed the eyes of their mind to the light of truth in the death of the soul. Temporal love and honor will then vanish like smoke, unless you turn away from them in time; when the activity has passed, guilt will remain for you.”

For this reason you ought to have embraced with complete devotion those things which would begin to benefit you here and would benefit you still more in the age that always endures, when, as the Apostle says, “what is perfect comes, and what is partial will be brought to an end” (1 Cor. 13). Then, if you were questioned today or tomorrow, you would be able to give true and salutary answers.

But because you have used yourself as your worst teacher, you disdain to know what you do not know. When questioned about it, you will either pretend to answer while hesitating or strive perversely to teach uncertain things.

Finally, concerning what you placed at the end of your little document:

> “The decretal letters,” you say, “which were established by the holy bishops of the first see of the Roman Church, by whose authority and decree all synods and holy councils are strengthened and receive stability—why do you say that you do not possess or observe them, unless it is because they contradict your arrangement?”

I wonder why you did not see that you were plainly rebuked and reproved, when you entirely omitted the matters which I gave you on a small sheet at Gundulf’s estate and placed above in this work, and which you certainly possess—unless, as you yourself wrote in your little document from the words of another, it is because they contradict your arrangement, that is, your will and your intention.

Accordingly, what is written can rightly be applied to you: “By your words I judge you” (Luke 19), just as you yourself wrote:

> “Behold, it is shown most clearly here that if anyone presumes to speak against the decrees of the Roman bishops, he will rightly be accused of rashness.”

Therefore read that aforementioned sheet and the decrees of the Roman bishops written above and promulgated from the sacred canons, and you will find that you speak against the decrees of the Roman bishops.

And when you dictate so carefully on another occasion, take greater care to polish your language, lest you dictate ungrammatically against your own grammar, as you did here when you said:

> “If anyone presumes to speak against the decrees of the Roman bishops.”

For we simple and uneducated people, if we happened to speak on this matter, would say either “to speak against the decrees of the Roman bishops” or “to speak abusively against the decrees of the Roman bishops.” For “to speak against the decrees of the Roman bishops” and “to speak abusively against the decrees of the Roman bishops” mean the same thing, as the author of the following line—an authority whose falsification must not be despised—says:

> “It makes answer in seven measures with distinctions of sound.”

Hence your Servius, explaining “he speaks against the measures,” expressed praise of the strings, which he says spoke through words. For *obloqui* means nothing other than to speak against someone who is speaking.

Accordingly, if you wish to repay me in kind and, seeking criticisms in my words, find some, I—already scorning the applause of boasting boys, who seek to be understood more than admired in their words while preserving the meaning—will say with Paul: “Even if unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge” (2 Cor. 11:6).

But you, a new grammarian who, like a leafy and dense tree adorned with the foliage of words, ought to walk about decked with verbal ornaments, puffing up your inventions with grandiloquent rhythms and spewing grammatical froth from inflated cheeks into every wind, will not be permitted to say this.

At the conclusion of your little document you wrote:

> “These matters,” you say, “I excerpted briefly and, joining them together here and there according to the nature of the case, interweaving and combining them indiscriminately, with an order now inverted and now arranged, and also gradually connected, I adopted.”

Let your prudence, and the patience of any other reader, pardon me, then, if, compelled by necessity, I have tried to describe rather than complete this little work in a hurried and frequently repetitive manner, not in a direct path or ordered discourse.

For, since your compilations are confused and set down, as you yourself said, in an inverted order, never remaining in the same condition, I could not respond otherwise than by trying—like a schoolboy whom I learned from hearing and reading in the book entitled *Cynegeticon* by Aurelius of Carthage—to explain your winding paths by running here and there, retracing even backward tracks, and following the twists of your trail, just as hunters pursue the lairs of wild beasts.

I shall still need to do this both in explaining the reasoning behind what you began and in showing the causal action concerning what you committed, for which I wrote to you and to the Church entrusted to you, against which you irregularly subscribed and caused others to subscribe, and also when I approach your new subscription—or rather, your new presumption—

> “...a thousand paths, and sorrowful labors,

> swift wanderings, battles in the open country, and domestic quarrels with an honest heart,”

which I am compelled to undertake.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the authority and distinction of the councils and letters of the bishops of the apostolic see

[Col. 0384A]

For the rest, when Daniel says, “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be increased” (Dan. XII), the Lord demonstrates this to Moses by saying, “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, and I did not disclose my name, Adonai, to them” (Exod. VI). Much later, David says: “I have understood more than my elders, and I have understood more than all my teachers” (Ps. CXVIII). The apostles saw and heard what many ancient righteous men, desiring it, neither saw nor heard.

This is shown by blessed Gelasius, filled with the spirit of wisdom and knowledge, who, after listing the authentic Scriptures in his catalogue of the books received by the Catholic Church, and after mentioning the [Col. 0384B] Nicene, Constantinopolitan, Ephesian, and also Chalcedonian synods, added:

> “And if there are any councils instituted by the holy Fathers, we decree that, after the authority of these four, they are both to be safeguarded and received.”

After also naming the works of orthodox authors, he added:

> “Likewise, we decree that the works and treatises of all orthodox Fathers who in no respect departed from communion with the holy Roman Church, nor separated themselves from its faith or preaching, but by the grace of God remained participants in its communion until the final day of their lives, are to be read.”

Then he says:

> “Likewise, the decretal letters which the most blessed popes, at various times, sent from the city of Rome for the consolation of various Fathers [Col. 0384C] are to be received with reverence.”

And, speaking jointly of the passions of the martyrs, the lives of the saints, the deeds of blessed Silvester, and, from Scripture, the discovery of the Lord’s Cross and the discovery of the head of blessed John the Baptist, he added most carefully and judiciously:

> “But when these writings have come into the hands of Catholics, let the judgment of the blessed apostle Paul precede them: ‘Test everything; hold fast what is good’” (I Thess. V).

He also intimated that discernment must be maintained even regarding the apocrypha:

> “Of these, some are altogether to be rejected; others, however, are to be counted among the apocrypha because of the accusations of heretics, but are not to be entirely abhorred, since we read that Catholic men have taken testimonies from them in their own works, just as blessed Jude the apostle also did in [Col. 0384D] his epistle.”

A distinction must therefore be noted, from the words of blessed Gelasius, between synodal councils and the letters of apostolic men. These letters, he says, were issued at various times, before the councils were held, for the consolation of various Fathers, and are to be received with reverence.
