But if there are councils instituted by the holy Fathers after the authority of the four councils, he decreed that they are to be safeguarded and observed.

Accordingly, the same man says in his decrees (Gelasius, Letter 3, to the Dardani):

> “Our Catholic and learned Fathers and bishops, whenever any heresy arose, at whatever time, after assembling once, sanctioned whatever they established for the faith, for truth, for Catholic and apostolic communion, according to the course of Scripture and the preaching of [Col. 0385A] their predecessors. They wished it thereafter to remain unshaken and firm, and they did not permit what had been established in the same matter to be reconsidered through any recent presumption.”

No one experienced in ecclesiastical doctrine is unaware of how great the difference is between those councils which he decreed must be safeguarded and received, and which the Catholic Fathers wished thereafter to remain unshaken and firm, and those letters which were issued at various times for the consolation of various people, which he says are to be received with reverence.

For if we begin to wish to hold and safeguard certain things contained in some of those letters, we shall begin to act against many others of those letters. Again, if we begin to hold and safeguard other things against which we had acted, [Col. 0385B] we shall act against what we previously wished to preserve. We shall depart from the sacred councils which must perpetually be received, held, safeguarded, and followed by us. We shall also most disastrously depart from the custom which the Catholic Church has maintained since our Fathers assembled in the holy Council of Nicaea. They still live with us in their constitutions, as Leo says (Letter 51, or 53, to Anatolius). Holding nothing certain, we shall fall into the sect of the Genethliaci, that is, the Mathematicians, who defined everything as uncertain.

Indeed, blessed Gelasius shows that these same letters are not only in some respects contrary to the sacred canons, but also differ among themselves, when he says that they were issued at various times for the consolation of various Fathers. [Col. 0385C]

And perhaps you will say against me: “Then you slander the apostolic see in its holy bishops, on the ground that they judged wrongly and did not decree that these things should be held.”

To this I answer you as the Apostle answered those who opposed one another and said, “Is the law then against the promises of God?” (Gal. III, 21): “By no means. The law indeed is holy, and the commandment is holy, righteous, and good” (Rom. VII, 12), but appropriate to its own persons and times. “It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom God had made the promise, and it was ordained through angels by a mediator” (Gal. III, 19).

I therefore say, together with blessed Gelasius, that the letters of the holy and apostolic men, issued by the apostolic see at various times for the consolation of various Fathers, as blessed Gelasius also says, [Col. 0385D] and ordained by those same priests of the Lord who are also called angels according to Scripture, are to be received with reverence. They were appropriate to their own times, until our Fathers, assembling together in the sacred councils, established laws destined to remain until the end of the age, as the bishops of that same apostolic see testify, with the Holy Spirit prompting them—for otherwise we must not believe.

And just as the Apostle says of the law, “If there had been a law able to give life, then righteousness would indeed be by the law” (Gal. III, 21), so, with due reverence for the apostolic see, I say that if the things contained in those letters, although appropriate to their own times, could in subsequent [Col. 0386A] times all be safeguarded together exactly as they are contained in them, and if it were appropriate that they be preserved and held, then our Fathers—namely, the Catholic and learned bishops—would not have established in the sacred councils laws destined to remain until the end of the age.

I therefore say, together with blessed Gelasius, that those letters are to be received with reverence. When they are read, the apostolic judgment which Gelasius himself prescribes must precede them: “Test everything; hold fast what is good” (I Thess. V).

I say this not because I claim that some things in them are not good, but because they are not in every respect consonant with the sacred canons and the councils of the Fathers. As the Apostle says: “The law indeed is good and holy, and the commandment is holy, righteous, and good” (Rom. VII, 12)—but in its own times.

And concerning the Jews, to whom that law itself had been given, [Col. 0386B] the Lord says: “I gave them commandments that were not good” (Ezek. XX)—that is, certain commandments which were to be changed at the time of revealed grace. For “law” is spoken of allegorically, as the Apostle interprets it concerning Abraham’s two sons.

He says:

> “Our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (Gal. IV, 24; I Cor. X, 4).

The law is understood in the Decalogue as that which was not changed. The law is also spoken of in the ceremonies and legal sacrifices, which the Apostle calls shadows of things to come (Col. II); and, as I briefly indicated much earlier, these are now preserved spiritually in the Church.

What was being done among that [Col. 0386C] Jewish people they did not understand, nor do they understand it now. For it was said of them: “As long as Moses is read, a veil lies over their hearts” (II Cor. III). There the veil is a figure, but the figure has been removed and the truth appears.

Hear the Apostle concerning when the veil was removed:

> “When you turn to the Lord,” he says, “the veil shall be taken away” (ibid.).

Therefore, our sins and wickedness having been pardoned through that evening sacrifice, when Christ stretched out his hands on the cross so that it might be said, “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight; the lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Ps. CXL)—as we know that the Lord hung upon the cross toward evening—he himself is the priest, himself the victim, himself the offerer, and himself the offering.

He is the priest who has now entered within [Col. 0386D] the inner veil. Alone among those who have borne flesh, he intercedes there for us. As a figure of this, in that first people and in that first temple, one priest entered the Holy of Holies. All the people stood outside, and he who alone entered within the veil offered sacrifice for the people standing outside.

Our sins and wickedness having therefore been pardoned through that evening sacrifice, we pass to the Lord, and the veil is removed. For this reason, when the Lord was crucified, the veil of the temple was torn.

Thus we neither circumcise the flesh of the foreskin according to the rite of the Mosaic law, nor abstain from the meats which that same law calls unclean. We do not observe their Sabbaths, new moons, and feast days in a carnal manner. We do not sacrifice animal [Col. 0387A] victims to God, nor celebrate Passover in the same manner with a lamb and unleavened bread. If there were any other ancient sacraments, all of which, as I have said, the Apostle calls shadows of things to come (Col. II), they signified things that were to be revealed in their own time. We receive those things now that they have been revealed, so that, once the shadow has been removed, we may enjoy their naked light.

For, by putting off the old man, we too are circumcised in the stripping away of the body of the flesh. The foods which they avoid in animals, we avoid in our conduct. We present our bodies as a living, holy, acceptable sacrifice to God (Rom. XII), and we intelligently pour out our souls to him in holy desires in place of blood. We are cleansed from every iniquity by the blood of Christ, like that of an immaculate lamb.

Because of the likeness of sinful flesh, he is also represented by a goat in the ancient [Col. 0387B] sacrifices. Nor does one who recognizes in him the greatest victim deny that he is the bull upon the horns of the cross.

When we find rest in him, we truly keep the Sabbath. The observance of the new moon is the sanctification of a new life. Our Passover is Christ, and our unleavened bread is the sincerity of truth without the leaven of antiquity.

Because of this newness of life, the first month among the months of the year was assigned to this celebration, for it is itself called the month of new things. Since the third period has now appeared in the whole course of the world’s history, the Lord’s resurrection lasts three days.

The first period is before the law, the second under the law, and the third under grace, where there is now the manifestation of the mystery formerly hidden in prophetic allegory. This too is signified by the lunar number.

Because [Col. 0387C] the number seven usually appears mystically in Scripture as signifying a certain perfection, Passover is celebrated in the third week of the moon—that is, on the day which falls from the fourteenth to the twenty-first.

Whatever else was foreshadowed for the ancient people by signs has its fulfillment in this one, “whose kingdom shall have no end” (Matt. V). In him everything had to be fulfilled who came not to abolish the law and the prophets, but to fulfill them.

Therefore, he did not nullify those ancient signs of realities by condemning them, but changed them by fulfilling them, so that the things announcing that Christ had already come would be different from those which foretold that he was to come.

Likewise, in the letters of those apostolic men, it is shown that certain things among the gentiles had also been significant before the Lord’s coming: for example, the provinces and privileges of cities, the chief priests and chief flamines, [Col. 0387D] which, in the likeness of the Mosaic law, the gentiles established long before, both in their legislation and in each of their distinctions, as I showed above; also in the division of tribes and settlements, privileges, and the precedence of individual orders.

As Clement and Anacletus show, these things are still preserved in the Church today through apostolic tradition: in the division of regions and parishes, in the privileges of sees, and in the precedence of bishops, metropolitans, and primates.

This true apostolic tradition has also been sufficiently confirmed by reason and ancient custom. Augustine says plainly [Col. 0388A] (On Baptism, against the Donatists, Book IV, chapter 5):

> “It is indeed true that reason and truth must be preferred to custom; but when truth supports custom, nothing ought to be held more firmly.”

Finally, certain things, as they are read as having been handed down by the apostles in those same letters, or are found to have been taken from Roman laws, are maintained as confirmed by the authority of plenary councils. Some of these, however, were changed in councils.

Moreover, some of the things established in regional councils were changed by the authority of plenary councils, or are held thereafter to be preserved irrevocably, as Catholic teachers and masters of the Church demonstrate. I have shown part of this above from their statements.

Apart from what I have included in this work from the words of blessed Augustine, he says in his books On Baptism—first [Col. 0388B] demonstrating that there is a difference between the exchange of letters in which these letters of the apostolic men under discussion were composed, and a regional or plenary council:

> “I see,” he says (On Baptism, Book III, chapter 2), “what may still be asked of me: namely, that I should respond to those plausible arguments by which either Agrippinus previously, or Cyprian himself, or those who agreed with them in Africa, or perhaps some people from distant overseas regions, were moved—not by any plenary council, or at least regional council, but by an exchange of letters—to think that this ought to be done. The ancient custom of the Church did not have it, and afterward the Catholic world rejected it with the strongest firmness of agreement, so that whatever had begun to creep into the minds of some through such discussions might be healed by the more powerful truth arising from the salvation of [Col. 0388C] unity and by universal medicine.”

He likewise shows the difference between regional and plenary councils in this way:

> “It is safe for us not to be drawn by any rashness into a judgment concerning matters which were begun in no Catholic regional council and concluded in no plenary council. But it is safe to affirm with the judgment of our voice whatever has been strengthened by the agreement of the universal Church under the governance of the Lord our God and Savior Jesus Christ.”

He also shows the difference between the authentic Scriptures and regional and plenary councils:

> “Who does not know that the Catholic holy Scripture, both of the Old and of the New Testament, is contained within its own definite limits, and that it is placed before all later writings of bishops in such a way that there can be no question or dispute at all concerning it—whether what is written in it is true or right? [Col. 0388D]

> “But the letters of bishops which were written, or are being written, after the canon was confirmed may be criticized if something in them has perhaps deviated from the truth—by the speech of someone more learned and more skilled in that matter, by the weightier authority of other bishops, by the prudence of learned men, and by councils.

> “The councils themselves, which are held in the various regions or provinces, must without hesitation yield to the authority of plenary councils, which are held from the entire Christian world. And the earlier plenary councils themselves may often be corrected by [Col. 0389A] later ones, when some experience of events reveals what had been hidden and makes known what had remained concealed—without any arrogance of sacrilegious pride, without any swollen-necked haughtiness, and without any contentiousness of jealous envy, but with holy humility, Catholic peace, and Christian charity.”

And again (ibid., chapter 9):

> “Let these people therefore consider one thing which is apparent to all. If the authority of Cyprian is to be followed, it ought to be followed more in preserving unity than in changing the custom of the Church.

> “But if we attend to his council, we must place above it the later council of the universal Church, of which he rejoiced to be a member and repeatedly urged the others to imitate him in retaining themselves within the structure of the whole body.

> “For later councils are placed before earlier ones by those who come afterward, and the [Col. 0389B] whole is always rightly placed before its parts. Cyprian was not the universality of the holy Catholic Church, but remained within its universality. He never abandoned its root; rather, in that root he was made fruitful—and, in order that he might be more fruitful, he was pruned by the heavenly cultivator.”

These are the things blessed Augustine said about other councils.

As for the sacred and mystical Council of Nicaea, however, as I showed above from the words of Leo and others, nothing has ever been altered by anyone—whether by a bishop of the apostolic see, by a plenary council, and certainly not by a regional council—unless it is wholly invalid.

As holy Gelasius also says in his decrees:

> “It is not unknown to us,” he says (Letter 11 to the Dardani), “that during the storm of the Arian persecution, after peace had been restored [Col. 0389C] and many bishops had recovered from exile, they organized troubled churches throughout particular provinces, assembling their brothers with them. Yet they did not do so in order to alter anything which that Council of Nicaea had defined concerning the faith and Catholic communion, nor to strike anyone with a new condemnation because of his fall. Rather, following the tenor of its decree, they judged him condemned unless he repented; and consequently, unless he corrected himself, he would undoubtedly be subject to condemnation.”

Receive, then, with reverence, as Gelasius says, those letters from which you have compiled your compositions; and preserve inviolate the sacred councils, as Gelasius decreed, and as the other Catholic—that is, learned—bishops decreed.

They also decreed similarly concerning the images of the saints. They condemned those who, as blessed Gregory demonstrates in his letters to Secundinus and to Serenus, bishop of [Col. 0389D] Massilia, said that the images ought to be broken under the pretext that they should not be worshiped. They praised those who established that the images should neither be worshiped nor broken, but should be placed solely for the instruction of the minds of the ignorant.

For in worship one must humbly prostrate oneself before the omnipotent holy Trinity alone. If anyone wishes to make and possess images of God and the saints for instruction, he must not in any way be prohibited.

And since it is written, “As faces are reflected in water, so the hearts of human beings are manifest to the prudent” (Prov. XXVII); and, “Deep water is the word from a man’s mouth” (Prov. XVIII); and, “Let your fountains flow out” (Prov. V), from the words of [Col. 0390A] the saints, as though from their images, we can come to know them—that is, their hearts and their pronouncements—and discern what each one issued for the consolation or instruction of certain people, according to the character of the times and actions, and what they commonly and unanimously decreed in the sacred councils to be observed and received universally and perpetually as authoritative.

Therefore, with this discernment, as I prefaced from the words of blessed Gelasius, receive for instruction those letters which the most blessed popes, at various times, issued from the city of Rome for the consolation of various Fathers, reading them with reverence; and preserve inviolate the sacred councils which the apostolic see and the whole Church follow.

And, just as the Lord confirms through the law in the Gospel, “Every [Col. 0390B] word shall be established on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Matt. XVIII), because this is not burdensome for me but necessary for you, I shall repeat to you what blessed Augustine says to Januarius concerning the sacred councils:

> “I therefore consider that all such things as are contained neither in the authority of the sacred Scriptures, nor found to have been established in councils of bishops, nor strengthened by the custom of the universal Church, but vary innumerably according to the different practices of different places, so that the reasons which people followed in establishing them can scarcely—or perhaps never—be discovered, ought, wherever the opportunity is given, to be cut away without any hesitation.”

You may judge how the words of blessed Augustine please you. For my small self, however, it appears safer and more salutary to follow the sacred councils with him and to impress upon all who are willing to hear me that, after abandoning the sacred councils, they should not follow those things which he considers ought to be cut away, [Col. 0390C] rather than follow the things which you propose as having been cut away and dissected. For, being diverse among themselves, they show that they cannot be preserved and followed by everyone and in every respect.

“In this matter,” says Innocent to Decentius, bishop of Eugubium, “the priests of the Lord must follow what the Roman Church observes. There is no doubt that they received their beginning from it, lest, while they strive after foreign assertions, they appear to omit the source of the institutions.”

What it is that the Roman Church observes, and what the priests of the Lord must follow, Gelasius demonstrates (Letter 11 to the Dardani):

> “We are confident,” he says, “that no one who is now truly a Christian is ignorant that, among the constitutions of each synod [Col. 0390D] which the agreement of the universal Church has approved, no see ought to carry them out more than the first see. It confirms each synod by its authority and preserves it through continuous moderation, on account of its primacy, which blessed Peter the apostle received by the Lord’s voice, and which, with the Church following, he has both always held and still holds.”

Behold: according to the law and the Gospel, you have the fullness of witnesses testifying that the councils are to be followed unshakenly, and that one must not pursue foreign assertions. The Apostle likewise commands: “Do not be led away by various and strange doctrines” (Heb. XIII).

I call those assertions foreign together with Innocent because, from the time when sacred councils began to be held in the Catholic Church, [Col. 0391A] the things which had partly prevailed in their own time flowed out of ecclesiastical usage, except insofar as the sacred councils judged that something should be taken from them. Until recently, they began to revive through you, insofar as it lies within your power, so that you might freely pass over to the desire of your heart, to which you willingly aspire, and might be restrained or judged by no one according to the rules. But the teachers and masters of the Church do not share your judgment, nor do they agree with you.

## CHAPTER XXVI

### On the Same Distinction Again, and on Plenary Councils and the Prerogative of the Council of Nicaea

Therefore, as though by way of a superabundant addition, I add what blessed Augustine likewise says to Januarius (Letter 118):

> “First, I want you to hold this as the central point [Col. 0391B] of the present discussion: our Lord Jesus Christ, as he speaks in the Gospel, has subjected us to his gentle yoke and light burden.

> “Accordingly, he bound together the society of the new people by very few sacraments, easy to observe, and outstanding in their significance: such as baptism consecrated in the name of the Trinity, participation in his body and blood, and whatever else is commended in the canonical Scriptures—except those things which, in keeping with the inclination of the hearts of that people and the prophetic period, burdened the servitude of the ancient people, and which are also read in the five books of Moses.

> “Those things which we safeguard, although not written but handed down, and which are observed throughout the whole world, are understood either to have been commended and established by the apostles themselves or by plenary councils, whose authority in the Church is [Col. 0391C] most salutary. Such are the annual celebrations of the Lord’s passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven, and of the coming of the Holy Spirit from heaven, and whatever else of this kind is observed by the universal Church wherever it is spread.”

And in the edict of the emperor Justinian concerning the confession of the true faith and the refutation of the heresies opposed to the Catholic Church of God—dictated by the fifth synod and confirmed by the same emperor—it is written:

> “Those who investigate the truth must also attend to this: perhaps, in councils, certain things are said by some of those assembled there out of favor, opposition, or ignorance. No one, however, attends to what is said by some as a faction; only those things are considered which are defined by all in common [Col. 0391D] agreement. For if anyone wished to attend to such contradictions according to those individual statements, every synod would be found to destroy itself.”

Understanding this distinction more wisely than you do, the Council of Antioch—which holy Hilary, living in the flesh at the time when it was held, demonstrates in his letter to the emperor Constantius and in his book On Synods to have been Catholic, and which the Council of Chalcedon confirms—knew that, after the times of certain men from whose letters you collected some passages and deceitfully omitted others, the Council of Nicaea had been held.

The Council of Nicaea (canon 6), to which nothing contrary was added by subsequent holy councils, just as nothing was abolished, mutilated, or altered by it, although certain ineffectual people attempted to do so, [Col. 0392A] established that the privileges of the metropolitan churches should be preserved in each province, so that the metropolitan would have authority over all those committed to him.

It decreed, saying (Council of Antioch, canon 6):

> “It is fitting that the bishops of every region know that the metropolitan bishop has responsibility for the whole province. For this reason, all who appear to have business should converge from every direction upon the metropolis.”

And again (canon 13):

> “No bishop from another province shall dare to cross into another province and ordain anyone for promotion to ecclesiastical ministry, even if some appear to give their consent, unless he comes after being summoned by letters from both the metropolitan and the other bishops who are with him, and proceeds to the act of [Col. 0392B] ordination.”

This clearly concerns any metropolitan, so that he may not presume, without being summoned or called, to enter the province of another metropolitan and undertake what is not his. It does not concern your metropolitan entering your parish, which is subject to him.

Accordingly, Innocent writes to Alexander, bishop of Antioch (Letter 20):

> “As we review the authority of the Council of Nicaea, which expresses the mind of all the priests throughout the world as one, we recognize that what it decreed concerning the church of Antioch must be observed by all the faithful—not to say by all priests—because we recognize that the aforesaid church was established over its own diocese, not over any other province.”

And Pope Boniface writes to Hilary, bishop of Narbonne (Letter 3):

> “The decree of the Council of [Col. 0392C] Nicaea is unknown to no one. It commands—and we shall set down the very words—that the individual metropolitans ought to have jurisdiction in each province, and that no one can have two provinces subject to him. Since it is impossible to believe otherwise, they judged, with the Holy Spirit prompting them, that this must be observed.”

A little later he adds:

> “We say this so that your Charity may understand that we preserve the precepts of the canons so carefully that our own constitution likewise determines that each province must always await the direction of its metropolitan in all matters.”

Coelestine says the same:

> “According to the decrees of the canons, each province should be content with its own metropolitan, as the constitutions contained in the letter of our predecessor to the bishop of Narbonne establish. No place must be granted to the usurpation by which one priest injures another. Let each person be content with the limits granted to him; let no one presume to do anything in another’s [Col. 0392D] province” (Letter 1).

For this reason, the African council writes to Pope Coelestine, saying (after the African Council):

> “The decrees of Nicaea most clearly committed both the lower-ranking clergy and the bishops themselves to their metropolitans. For they saw with the greatest wisdom and justice that whatever matters arise in their own places should be settled there, and that no province would lack the grace of the Holy Spirit by which equity might be both wisely discerned and steadfastly maintained by the priests of Christ.”

And Leo writes to Anatolius (Letter 56):

> “That ordinance of the Nicene canons, established truly through the Holy Spirit, can never be dissolved in any respect. [Col. 0393A] Let no synodal councils flatter themselves because of the increase of their assembly, nor let any number of priests, however much larger, dare either to compare itself with those three hundred and eighteen bishops or to place itself above them. The Council of Nicaea has been consecrated with so great a divine privilege that, whether ecclesiastical judgments are held by fewer or by more, whatever differs from the constitution of those bishops is utterly devoid of authority.”

Blessed Ambrose also speaks of this privilege (On the Faith, Book I, chapter 9):

> “The three hundred and eighteen bishops did not come together for the council through human industry or by any arrangement, but so that, in their number, through the sign of his passion and name, the Lord Jesus might prove himself present at the council: the cross is represented by the three hundred, and the name of Jesus by the [Col. 0393B] eighteen priests.”

Hilary says:

> “That very number is holy to me, in which Abraham, victor over impious kings, is blessed by him who is the likeness of the eternal priesthood.”

And again blessed Pope Leo says to Anatolius (Letter 36):

> “Those holy and venerable Fathers who, after the sacrilegious Arius had been condemned together with his impiety in the city of Nicaea, established laws of ecclesiastical canons destined to remain until the end of the world, and who live among us throughout the entire world in their constitutions: if anything is presumed anywhere contrary to what they established, it is canceled without hesitation.”

For this reason holy Leo says to Pulcheria Augusta:

> “No one is permitted to dare anything against the statutes of the ancestral [Col. 0393C] canons, which many years ago were founded in the city of Nicaea upon spiritual decrees. If anyone wishes to decree something different, he diminishes himself rather than corrupting them.
>
> “If these statutes are preserved undefiled by all bishops, as they ought to be, there will be tranquil peace and firm concord throughout all the churches; there will be no disagreements concerning the measure of honors, no disputes concerning ordinations, no uncertainties concerning privileges, and no struggles over the usurpation of what belongs to another. Rather, an orderly arrangement of conduct and duties will be preserved according to the equal law of charity, and the truly great man will be the one who is free from all ambition.”

## CHAPTER XXVII

### On the Canons and Judgments Wrongly Understood and Usurped by Him

[Col. 0393D]

Therefore, when you attempt to assert, from the words of Callistus and others—which do not support you in your compilations—that I cannot enter your parish in order to determine anything there, you understand the matter wrongly.

From these and other canonical constitutions you will find that each metropolitan must observe this rule in the province of another metropolitan—the very rule which you perversely claim for yourself concerning your parish, which is subject to the metropolitan see of Rheims.

Accordingly, I do not arrogate to my own person the things I set out above, but ascribe them to the dignity of the metropolitan see. For, as blessed Leo says:

> “Although the merits of bishops are sometimes different, the rights of the sees nevertheless remain. Rivals may perhaps inflict some disturbance upon them, but they cannot [Col. 0394A] diminish their dignity.”

Nor, with a meaning consonant with the sacred canons, did you write in the metrical heading of your compilation, which was to be presented to the lord king:

A response could not rightly be demanded from a man in chains; and through my fellow ministers sent to you, you sent back word to me that I should not compel you to respond so long as you were in custody and your clerics were absent. Accordingly, I then replied to you in writing, and now I show you that, as I said, you do not correctly understand the sacred regulations when you used what you said about not responding in your own defense, since the holy Pope Hilary asserts (Roman Council, canon 4):

> “We,” he says, “do not wish to exercise the severity of punishment in any matter; but whoever has offended in the affairs of God through obstinacy or contempt, or has himself been unwilling to abolish what he wrongly did, will find in himself whatever he has failed to cut away in another.”

For what you did could not and cannot in any way be reckoned among doubtful or obscure matters according to Leo’s decrees, so that you might thereby have grounds for defending yourself. Once restored to your own position and regularly summoned to the synod, you ought to have responded, as both you and anyone else who reads this little work can recognize from the sacred regulations cited both earlier and later. Therefore I was eager to write to you so that you might take care to abolish what you had done wrong in the affairs of God through obstinacy or contempt, and what you had committed improperly; and so that you yourself might undo your action, by which you had badly disturbed the order, just as the same Hilary commands concerning one who has acted improperly. Thus you would not require the severity of punishment to be exercised against you by those whose responsibility it is, and I would not find in myself something which I had failed to cut away in you. For, as the same man says (in the same council, canon 1):

> “No one may, without danger to his own standing, rashly violate either the divine constitutions or the decrees of the apostolic see. For we, who administer the offices of the highest priesthood, will be answerable for the guilt of such transgressions if we are found negligent in the affairs of God, since we remember how the Lord threatens the negligence of priests, which we must fear. Indeed, the one who enjoys the higher honor commits the greater offense, and the loftiness of dignities makes the vices of sinners more serious.”

I therefore wrote to you according to Leo’s decrees, exhorting you to take care to receive salutary counsel, and that, doing nothing through contention but united in every effort of devotion, we should obey the divine and apostolic constitutions and in no respect permit the most provident decrees of the canons to be violated.

But you, devising plans that you will not be able to establish, wish to cloak your disobedience—rather than correct what you have improperly done—and the unrestrained freedom you desire, by improperly interpreting, according to your own understanding, though not a correct one, the matter of appeal and of not being compelled to answer concerning your unjust judgments, so that you may not be subject to the metropolitan. Yet just as the canons of the province of Africa clearly show from whom it is not permitted to appeal, so the Sardican canons plainly show when, where, for what matters, and how an appeal by a bishop to the apostolic see must be made and carried out. Innocent, Boniface, and Leo likewise decree the same; and their laws, agreeing with the regulations, also state for whom and in what matters an appellant ought not to be constrained.

Consider, therefore, appropriately what the same blessed Leo wrote to Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, when he was exalting himself beyond his proper measure, saying (Letter 56):

> “A Catholic man, and especially a priest of the Lord, ought to be entangled in no error, just as he ought not to be corrupted by any desire. For holy Scripture says: ‘Do not follow your lusts, and restrain yourself from your will’ (Ecclus. XVIII). One must resist the many enticements and vanities of this world, so that the integrity of true self-restraint may be preserved; its first blemish is pride, the beginning of transgression and the origin of sin. For a mind greedy for power neither abstains from what is forbidden nor rejoices in what is permitted, while, as it advances along a disordered and perverse path, faults increase—faults that had been tolerated out of a desire to restore the faith and from love of concord.”

Therefore turn the eyes of your mind away from your perverse advances, and make straight the steps of your intention and your actions, so that we who now lament over you may rejoice in you in the Lord.

And consider what the blessed Gregory wrote to Felix, bishop in Serdica (Book IV, Letter 10):

> “You yourself do not doubt, as is evident from your own subjects, how obedience or reverence ought to be shown to superiors. In this matter it is greatly beneficial if humility, which deserves praise, preserves without compulsion whatever the rigor of discipline imposes. It has come to our attention, therefore, that your Fraternity disdains to obey our brother John, bishop of First Justiniana, according to the established custom, and was unwilling to subscribe either to his decree or to his report in accordance with custom. If this is so, we are saddened, because you offer a manifest indication of pride; and how especially blameworthy this is in a priest is expressed by the admonition of divine mercy. Therefore we exhort you, having laid aside the swelling of your mind, not to cease showing yourself humble and obedient to the aforesaid brother and our fellow bishop, so that God may rejoice in the concord of your Fraternity and others may take from you an example of goodness. For if—as we do not believe—it should happen that you persist in pride, know that the sacred canons will impose upon your obstinacy strict and canonical correction of discipline. You do well, therefore, to present yourself voluntarily, through salutary reflection, as one whom canonical coercion would compel you to be. For after this our admonition, it will not again be permitted you, at your own will and against custom, to remain disobedient to your superiors; nor should you suppose that we will overlook or postpone the ecclesiastical punishment of such great indiscipline.”

And again the same Saint Gregory wrote to Vincent and the other bishops (Book VII, indiction 11, Letter 8):

> “We exhort your Fraternity that, if necessity anywhere compels any one of you to travel farther on your own affairs, you must seek permission from your metropolitan, according to the rule established by the holy Fathers, and presume in no respect to disregard him—except if, as we do not wish, you should happen to have some case against that same metropolitan, so that on this account you seek the judgment of the apostolic see. For you know that the canons, by the institution of the ancient Fathers, have permitted those who hasten to seek permission to do so.”

It is indeed clear which canons decreed that this permission should be sought by bishops from metropolitans: namely, the council of Antioch, favorably confirmed by the synod of Chalcedon. The Sardican canons also say (canon 9):

> “Let the bishops of every province send petitions to that brother and fellow bishop of ours who resides in the metropolis, so that he may send his deacon and the petitions, granting letters of commendation, and so forth.”

Concerning seeking the judgment of the apostolic see against a metropolitan, if a bishop should have need of it, the same Sardican canons also decreed this, as Innocent plainly shows in his letter to Victricius, bishop of Rouen; and Pope Hilary says (Letter 8 to the Metropolitans of Gaul):

> “We could not pass over that matter which must be guarded with especially diligent care: that no bishops should dare to travel to any province without the letters of their metropolitans. This must likewise be observed in every kind of clerical office throughout the individual churches.”

And Saint Leo says to Theodore, bishop of Fréjus (Letter 59):

> “The order of your concern ought to have been this: that you should confer with your metropolitan about what seemed to require investigation; and if your Beloved did not know what he was seeking, you should together ask to be instructed. For in matters that concern the general observance of all the priests of the Lord, nothing ought to be investigated without the primates.”

And Symmachus says to Caesarius, bishop of Arles (Letter 5):

> “If any bishop, having been summoned by a metropolitan pontiff according to the definition of the canons, should refuse to obey, let him know that he is to be cut down—something we do not wish—by ecclesiastical discipline.”

The canons of the province of Africa say (canon 43):

> “Let a bishop summoned by his primate duly appear at the synod. But if he cannot appear, unless he has given an account of the reason for his impediment to his primate, he must be content with remaining outside the communion of his Church.”

And canon 20 says:

> “Whoever is not in agreement with the metropolitan church and with the fellowship of the priesthood, but, puffed up and separated from this fellowship, thinks that he ought to devote himself to his own people and sometimes, when summoned, refuses to come to the council: concerning such a man, not only must his diocese not be preserved, but every effort must be made concerning his own church, which has wickedly favored him, so that by public authority he too may be rejected and removed from that principal see.”

And canon 190 of Carthage says:

> “If an accused person has refused to come to give an account and has been excommunicated by his primate, during the time in which he does not communicate, he must not communicate even in his own church or parish.”

And the holy Pope Hilary writes to Leontius and the other bishops (Letter 2):

> “For one sins no less against the sanctions of the holy traditions than when one rushes into an injury against the Lord himself.”

And Dioscorus was condemned at the synod of Chalcedon, as is demonstrated both in the acts of that council and in Justinian’s edict concerning the Fifth Synod—not because he had sinned against the faith, but solely on account of ecclesiastical order, because he had rebelled against his archbishop in opposition to the sacred canons.

Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, was condemned by Pope Felix for violating the Council of Nicaea, as the same Felix wrote to him, saying (Letter 4):

> “You are found liable for many transgressions, and you have repeatedly been involved in an insult to the venerable Council of Nicaea.”

Examine these matters with the eye of your mind, and take the greatest care lest, God forbid, you incur them.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Concerning those unjustly excommunicated by him: who must be excommunicated, how they must be excommunicated, and what order must be observed in ecclesiastical judgments

Since the blessed apostle Peter says, “If, while doing good, you patiently endure, this is grace before God” (1 Peter II), and since the cause of your injuries is contained in the petition delivered to me by the Church of Laon, you excommunicated the presbyters, deacons, and other clerics who had not been accused, had not confessed, and had not been convicted, removing them from every ecclesiastical office; and you prohibited anyone from celebrating the sacred offices of the Mass in your parish.

Yet the sacred canons permit no one to be removed from office unless he has either confessed voluntarily, been regularly convicted, or, having been regularly summoned to judgment to give an account, has refused to appear. This is written in chapter 19 of the Council of Carthage concerning bishops, and in chapter 20 concerning presbyters, deacons, and the other clerics.

> “If,” they say (canon 20), “presbyters or deacons have been accused, their own bishop, with the lawful number of fellow bishops from neighboring places whom the accused have requested from him—namely, six in the case of a presbyter and three in the case of a deacon—shall investigate their cases, preserving the same procedure concerning days and postponements, removal from communion, and examination of the persons of the accusers and the accused.”

That is, just as had been defined concerning bishops in the preceding chapter. The cases of the other clerics, however, the bishop of the place alone shall hear and conclude.

And again (canon 28):

> “Presbyters, deacons, or other lower clerics, if in cases affecting them they have complained about the judgments of their bishops, shall be heard by neighboring bishops with the consent of their own bishop, and those bishops shall decide between them; or they may appeal to the primates of their provinces, as has often been established concerning bishops.”

And according to the canons of Antioch (canon 9):

> “Let all who appear to have business to conduct come from every direction to the metropolis.”

And canon 20 says:

> “Let presbyters, deacons, and all who consider themselves injured be present at canonical councils and submit to the examination of the synod. No one, however, may hold councils on his own authority except those to whom metropolitan rights appear to have been entrusted.”

Hence Saint Augustine, the most celebrated teacher and one most highly accepted by the apostolic see, who was present at the Council of Carthage—at which the matters we have set out above were confirmed by apostolic authority—and who knew most fully the intention with which that synod established the chapter, says among other things in his letter to the clergy and people of Hippo (Letter 137):

> “Recently it was established in a council of bishops that no cleric who has not yet been convicted ought to be suspended from communion unless he has failed to present himself for the examination of his case.”

The same council demonstrates what this presentation means (Council of Carthage, canon 19), namely:

> “That the accused person himself, summoned by letter to state his case on the appointed day before the judges who have been chosen, should appear; or that he should prove some genuine reasons of necessity by which it is clear that he was unable to appear.”

It must be observed that it says “was unable,” and does not say “was unwilling.” The same is said concerning the accuser:

> “So that the opportunity to conduct his case may not be taken away from him if he proves that he was unable to appear on the appointed day.”

And again concerning the accused, if he should be unwilling to appear at the annual general council, it says:

> “But if the accused or the accuser wished to appear but was unable to do so, the synod wished either of them to be excusable.”

For the African synod clearly shows this, saying (canon 46):

> “If, within a year after excommunication, he has neglected to clear his case while still remaining under excommunication.”

Hence the Council of Carthage says (canon 19):

> “Whoever among the bishops is accused, let the accuser bring the case before the primate of that province; and let the person against whom the charge is brought not be suspended from communion unless, summoned by letter to state his case before the judges chosen on the appointed day, he has entirely failed to appear.”

This judgment clearly shows that an accuser cannot accuse unless he has been present at the accusation; yet he can accuse an absent person. And one who cannot be accused except through the presence of the accuser can be judged in his absence—or rather, he has already been judged by those who enacted this rule, if, having been summoned by letter to judgment, he has failed to appear as prescribed, or has not proved some genuine reasons of necessity by which it is clear that he was unable to appear.

The following chapter demonstrates the same concerning a presbyter or deacon as concerning a bishop. Hence Boniface wrote to the seven provinces, saying concerning Maximus (Letter 2):

> “If he wishes to be present, let him answer the charges in person, if he has confidence. If he neglects to be present, let him not gain a postponement of the sentence through his absence. For it is clear that the one who does not use the opportunity to clear himself when judgment has been granted and repeatedly assigned confesses the crime.”

The laws state who ought not to be admitted as an accuser:

> “Certainly, those who have confessed their own crimes during an investigation, if they wish to speak concerning others, are not to be believed by the judge, because it has been established by law and statutes that an accused person cannot make another accused person by voluntary confession, nor can belief be placed in one who has confessed himself to be a criminal concerning another person.”

And again:

> “The confession of those who are accused of crimes is not to be believed against others unless they have first proved themselves innocent, because a confession by an accused person against anyone whatever is dangerous and must not be admitted.”

The African council also declares:

> “Whoever,” it says (canons 96–97), “after having been excommunicated, while still remaining under that excommunication, whether cleric or layman, wishes to accuse; and all slaves or personal freedmen, must not be admitted to an accusation, nor all those whom the public laws do not admit to the accusation of public crimes; likewise, all those stained by marks of infamy, that is, actors or persons subject to disgraceful occupations; heretics also, whether pagans or Jews. Nevertheless, to all those to whom accusation is denied, permission to make accusations in their own cases must not be denied.”

Canon 98 says:

> “Whenever many crimes are charged against clerics by accusers, and the accuser has been unable to prove one of them, the one with which he first dealt, he must no longer be admitted concerning the others. Witnesses who, by order, are not admitted to give testimony because they are not admitted to accusation must likewise not be admitted, nor those whom the accuser himself has produced from his own household. Witnesses under fourteen years of age must not be admitted to give testimony.”

Saint Augustine says:

> “Although some things may be true,” he says, “they are nevertheless not easily to be believed by a judge unless they are demonstrated by certain indications.”

He practiced what he taught when, in giving an account and writing to Xantippus, the primate of his province, he showed that he himself had judged one of his presbyters, Abundantius. He says of him (Letter 236):

> “I bring to your Prudence’s attention that a certain Abundantius had been ordained presbyter in the estate of Straboniana, which belonged to our pastoral care. Since he was not walking in the ways of the servants of God, he began not to enjoy a good reputation. Alarmed by this, yet unwilling to believe anything rashly, I became decidedly more concerned and took pains to see whether I could somehow arrive at certain indications of his evil conduct. First, I discovered that he had diverted the money of a certain peasant which had been entrusted to him from the sale of wine, so that he could give no plausible account of it. Then he was convicted and confessed that, on the day of the Lord’s Nativity fast, when the church of Gippita, like the others, was also fasting, he had said farewell to his fellow presbyter of Gippita at about the fifth hour as though he were going to his church; but, having no cleric with him, he had remained at the same estate, and at the house of a woman of bad reputation had both lunched and dined, had spent the night in the same house, and could not deny it. For what he denied, I left to God; what he was not permitted to conceal, I judged. I feared entrusting the church to him, especially a church situated amid the raging attacks of heretics. I had to make these matters known to your Prudence especially, lest some deception should creep upon you.”

For this man of God knew the canons and did not disdain, according to those same sacred canons, to be subject to his primate, who was inferior in knowledge and perhaps in merit but superior in rank, obeying the Apostle’s command: “Obey your superiors in the Lord” (Hebrews XIII).

As to where a case ought to be conducted between accusers and accused, the Council of Carthage established the following (canon 30):

> “Let the accused or the accuser choose for himself, in the place from which the accused comes, a nearby location where it will not be difficult to produce witnesses and where the case may be concluded.”

Hence the laws say:

> “The investigation of crimes must be conducted where the crime was committed; for elsewhere the accused person is forbidden to be heard.”

And again:

> “If anyone has proceeded against an adversary either by a claim or by an accusation of crime, let him bring his action in the province in which the person proceeded against resides, and let him not suppose that his adversary should be dragged elsewhere or farther away to judgment. If the person against whom proceedings have been brought considers the judge suspect, he is permitted to appeal.”

The Council of Carthage says (canon 15):

> “If an appeal has been made from any ecclesiastical judges to other ecclesiastical judges where there is greater authority, it must not prejudice those whose sentence has been set aside, if they could not be convicted either of having judged with hostile intent or of having been corrupted by some desire or favor. But if judges have been chosen by agreement of the parties, even if they are fewer in number than has been established, no appeal is permitted.”

The laws and sacred canons show how a sentence must be concluded: either in a synod or through judges, whether judges appointed by the primates whom the petitioners approached, or judges whom the parties themselves selected from among their neighbors by mutual agreement.

> “The appointed judges who are bishops,” as the African council says (canon 88), “must be appointed by the primate in whose province the case is being conducted. But if, by common agreement, the petitioners choose neighboring judges, let either one be chosen or three; and if they choose three, let them follow either the opinion of all or that of two.”

The Council of Chalcedon says (canon 9):

> “If a cleric has a case against another cleric, let him not abandon his own bishop and run to secular courts; but let the action first be heard before his own bishop, or certainly, with that bishop’s advice, let them hold judgment before those whom both parties have chosen. If anyone acts otherwise, he shall be subject to canonical correction.”

And Saint Innocent writes to Bishop Victricius:

> “If,” he says (Letter 1), “any cases or disputes arise among clerics, whether of higher or lower rank, let the dispute be settled according to the Council of Nicaea by assembling the bishops of that province. No one may—without prejudice, however, to the Roman Church, to which reverence must be preserved in all cases—abandon those priests who, by divine will, govern the Church of God in that province and rush to other provinces. If anyone should presume to do so, let him be judged by all both removed from the clerical office and guilty of injury. But if greater cases should arise, let them be referred to the apostolic see, as the synod established and ancient custom requires, after episcopal judgment.”

And since there are two sins and two kinds of sins—for a person sins either against God or against another person—and two advents of the Lord, who came to save sinners—for all have sinned and lack the glory of God (Romans III)—one hidden and the other manifest: one of which it is written, “He shall descend like rain upon a fleece” (Psalm LXXI), and the other of which it is written, “God will come manifestly” (Psalm XLIX); one of which it is said, “The Son of Man came not to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him” (John III), and the other when he will come to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire—so there are two judgments, one hidden and the other manifest, and two judicial procedures.

One of these is the procedure of which the Apostle says, “If anyone is named a fornicator” (1 Corinthians V), and so forth. Augustine, in his book *On Penance* (chapter 3), wishes this “naming” to be understood as that which is made against someone when a sentence is issued through judicial procedure and with integrity. For he did not wish a person to be judged by another according to the arbitrary suspicion of an individual or through an extraordinary judgment usurped without authority, but rather according to the law of God and the order of the Church, whether the person had confessed voluntarily or had been accused and convicted. For if accusation alone is sufficient, many innocent people must be condemned, since a crime is often falsely alleged against someone.

The blessed Gregory explains how this judicial procedure must be carried out in his instruction to John the defensor, who was going to Spain (Book XI, indiction 6, Letter 52):

> “Namely, there should be different accusers and witnesses; then the nature of the cases must be examined; testimony alleged in writing must be given under oath in the presence of the accused; the accused must have an opportunity to respond and defend himself; and the examination of the persons who accuse and testify must be conducted according to the rules.”

The Lord also indicates this form of judicial procedure when, in raising the girl who lay dead in the house, as though in a disclosure of a case not known to everyone, he took with him certain of his disciples as witnesses, as well as the girl’s father and mother (Luke VIII).

The other form of judicial procedure concerns matters that are not known only to a few, like deeds still concealed in a chamber which require witnesses in order to be believed to have been committed, but are recognized to have been brought to the knowledge of many, like one already carried outside the city gate amid a large accompanying crowd (Luke VII).

Concerning this form of judicial procedure the Apostle says:

> “Though absent in body, but present in spirit, I have already judged, as though present, the one who has done this, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ: when you are assembled, and my spirit is with you, with the power of our Lord Jesus, to deliver such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh” (1 Corinthians V);

and shortly above:

> “So that the one who has done this deed may be removed from among you” (ibid.).

Hence Ambrose says that, “once his deed was known, the sinner had to be expelled from the fellowship of the brethren.” For everyone knew his crime; in this matter there was no need of witnesses, nor could the crime be concealed by any evasion.

Concerning the perpetrator of manifest crimes, even if he cannot be brought to judgment, Pope Boniface, issuing a decree to the seven provinces, says concerning Maximus, who even avoided being summoned and was entirely unwilling to appear (Letter 2):

> “No one doubts that the guilty person flees judgment in the same way that the innocent person seeks acquittal. But the crafty quibbling of those who think that schemes for conducting litigation are counsels will never acquire the name of innocence. Anyone who thinks that he can flee judgment by delays confesses everything. For it makes no difference whether everything that has been said is proved in the present examination, since his repeated absence, procured for this very purpose, is itself established as a confession. If he has neglected to appear, let him not gain a postponement of the sentence through his absence.”

Coelestine likewise judged Daniel, formerly a bishop of Gaul, in this way (Letter 1):

> “And since no one is to be judged either too hastily or out of due order—that is, without warning or summons—the law speaks concerning the summons of a perpetrator of manifest crimes of this kind: Whoever has been summoned by the authority of a judge three times, or has been called to the judge by three edicts, or has been summoned once by a peremptory notice, that is, one which extinguishes the case, and has been unwilling to present himself before the judge by whom he was notified, may be judged as contumacious; indeed, whenever judgment has been rendered against a contumacious person, the case cannot be reopened even through appeal.”

Coelestine, writing to Nestorius, and the synod of Ephesus, decreeing concerning the same matter, as well as the blessed Gregory in his letter to John, confirm this judgment concerning the three summonses by the authority of the Gospel.

Concerning a peremptory written summons, the African council demonstrates the rule in the case of Cresconius (canon 15):

> “If, after being summoned, he refuses to repent, then, through his contempt and contumacy, he must immediately be excluded by judicial authority.”

And again the blessed Gregory, writing to Maximus, the presumptuous bishop of Salona, concerning a sentence against a contumacious person, says (Book V, Letter 3):

> “We exhort you to hasten to come to us, setting aside every excuse, so that, justice having been preserved, we may, with Christ revealing the truth, investigate and conclude according to canonical institutions the matters of which you are accused. Act in such a way that you no longer cause further delays in coming, lest your very absence assign you greater liability for the things alleged, and lest this matter compel us to pass against you, not only on account of the alleged crimes which you avoid purging, but also on account of the guilt of disobedience, a harsher judgment from the council, namely, as against a contumacious person.”

The African council, at the suggestion or request of Bishop Maurentius, after the written petition presented by Placentinus had been read, says (canon 67):

> “A sentence should indeed have been imposed by the holy council, according to the measure appropriate to priests, against contumacious bishops who had been ordered by their primate to appear at the council but had not come. But, preserving ecclesiastical gentleness, judges chosen by the council were appointed, and letters were sent to the primate of those same bishops.”

The ecclesiastical and public laws show how, after everything has been examined and fully ascertained, a sentence must be issued regularly and legally:

> “Judges must take special care that in every case the sentence which has been deliberated be read out in the presence of the parties together, so that those by whom the case was argued may know in full what sentence has been pronounced.”

And again:

> “Whatever has been ordered in a case in the presence of the parties shall have the fullest force and cannot be changed.”

And again:

> “Matters decided in the absence of one party do not possess the force of things judged.”

The following rule was also set forth by Saint Gregory in his instruction to John the defensor, who was going to Spain, from chapter 16 of the laws of the *Novella* concerning witnesses, and he declared it canonical:

> “We have also frequently learned this: certain persons enter and bring complaints before local defensores, or before the distinguished judges of the provinces, or—as commonly happens here—before the distinguished master of the census, as though they had suffered something from another contrary to the laws, or were enduring some other injustice, or had been damaged, and they wish to produce witnesses. But lest it afterward be objected to them that the proceedings were conducted on the evidence of one party, the person against whom the complaint is made must also be summoned by the judge or defensor, while he is in the same city where the testimony is being given, so that he may come and hear the witnesses. If he is unwilling to come, but has contemptuously refused, so that the testimony given by one party against the other might thereby be useless, we decree that such testimony shall have the same validity as if it had not been given by one party alone but had also been taken in his presence. For if he has refused and has been unwilling to come and hear what is being reported, although he is plainly available and cannot claim that he was unable to come because of some unavoidable necessity, the testimony shall stand exactly as if he had appeared; his contempt shall bring him no advantage, and the testimony shall be considered to have been taken in the presence of both parties.”

“Behold,” says Saint Gregory, “the adversary must always be warned to come to hear the witnesses; otherwise it is necessary that what has been done contrary to the laws should have no force.”

The many laws show what sort of witnesses, and of what reputation, are to be admitted to give testimony. They are almost unknown to no one; they also establish the following rule:

> “Even the most worthless witnesses must not be believed without a physical examination.”

And again, in Book VI, Title XIX, among other provisions, it is prescribed:

> “If a sentence has been delivered without writing, it does not even deserve to bear the name of a sentence.”

We read many times that this legal decree was observed both in the Passion of the Lord, when they placed above his head the written charge stating his case, and in the passions of the martyrs, when they were judged. We also read that, by the authority of Pope Leo, several legates of the apostolic see condemned in writing Dioscorus at the Council of Chalcedon, Felix condemned Acacius, Pope Silverius condemned Vigilius, and other pontiffs of the Roman see condemned those who were unwilling to repent.

## CHAPTER XXIX. What the canons establish concerning those excommunicated irregularly
See, brother, whether you followed these sacred laws when you generally excommunicated the priests and deacons of your parish from ecclesiastical office, although it is most certain and well known both to us and to everyone in this province of Rheims that they had neither been accused, nor confessed, nor convicted of any crime [Col. 0404A]. Since it is certain that you did not judge according to these rules, and since you were not elected judge in this judgment by agreement of the parties, they ought to have appealed from you, an ecclesiastical judge, to me, an ecclesiastical judge of greater authority, just as they did; and by me your unjust sentence has been duly rescinded.

The Council of Carthage decreed, saying: “If an appeal has been made from any ecclesiastical judges to other ecclesiastical judges where there is greater authority, it must not harm those whose sentence has been rescinded, provided that it cannot be proved that they judged with a hostile mind, or were corrupted by some desire, favor, or other influence,” and so forth. Whether this ruling applies to you, reason itself demonstrates.

Now let us see what the sacred canons say concerning those who are excommunicated by individual provincial bishops [Col. 0404B] for cases unknown to the primate of the province and the other bishops.

“Concerning those,” say the Nicene canons (canon 5), “who are deprived of communion, whether from the clergy or from the order of the laity, by bishops throughout each province, let the regular judgment prevail, so that those who are expelled may not be received by others. Let inquiry also be made to ensure that it does not appear that someone has been excluded from the congregation through the bishop’s pusillanimity, contentiousness, or any other fault. Therefore, so that this may be investigated more suitably, it has been well decided that councils be held twice each year in every province, so that when all the bishops of the province have assembled together, such questions may be examined communally; and thus those who have plainly sinned against their own bishop may reasonably be regarded as excommunicated by all [Col. 0404C], until either the community or the bishop sees fit to issue a more humane sentence in such cases.”

And the Council of Antioch (canon 6): “If anyone has been deprived of communion by his own bishop, he must not be received by others before he has been reconciled to his bishop, or, at least, has appeared at the synod that is convened, made satisfaction on his own behalf, and persuaded the council to accept another sentence. This definition is to remain in force concerning laymen, priests, deacons, and all who are shown to be subject to the rule.”

And the Council of Carthage, which in its twentieth chapter had said that a prescribed number of bishops, united with their own bishop, should settle the cases of priests and deacons, while the bishop alone should hear and conclude the complaints of the other clergy, says in its twenty-eighth chapter [Col. 0404D]:

“Let priests, deacons, and other inferior clergy, if they have complaints in their cases concerning the judgments of their bishops, be heard by neighboring bishops with the consent of their own bishop, and let those bishops, having been called in by them, decide between them. But if they should think that an appeal must also be made from those bishops, let them not appeal to courts overseas, but to the primates of their own provinces, as has often likewise been established concerning bishops. Those, however, who think that an appeal should be made overseas are to be received into communion by no one within Africa.”

The African Council defined the same things in its ninety-second chapter.

Because of the distances involved, these canons command appeals to be made to neighboring bishops, priests, deacons, and the other clergy [Col. 0405A], as the same canons clearly demonstrate in the chapter concerning the visitation of the provinces at the time of the council, and also where the Council of Carthage says (canon 17): “Let each province, because of the distance, have its own primate.”

For this reason Mauretania Sitifensis requested a primate from the province of Numidia, from whose assembly it had been separated, so that it might have its own primate; and, with the consent of all the primates of the African provinces—or of all the bishops because of the distance—it was permitted to have one.

Therefore, in every province that has a primate, all who appear to have cases to bring must, according to the canons of Antioch, assemble at the metropolitan see. For, as the African Council writes to Pope Celestine (canon 9):

“The decrees of Nicaea most expressly entrusted both clergy of inferior rank [Col. 0405B] and the bishops themselves to their metropolitans. For they wisely and justly judged that whatever cases arise in their own places should be settled there, and that no province would lack the grace of the Holy Spirit, by which equity might both be perceived wisely and be held with the utmost firmness by Christ’s priests—especially since everyone has been granted the right, if offended by the judgment of those who heard the case, to appeal to the council of his province or even to a universal council.”

Innocent likewise decreed this to Victricius from the Nicene canons; and Boniface, drawing on them, says to Hilary, bishop of Narbonne (Letter 1): “Let your Charity observe how carefully we preserve the precepts of the canons, so that our own constitution also determines that each province should always await the decision of its metropolitan in all matters” [Col. 0405C]. Celestine and other pontiffs of the Roman See likewise decreed this.

The Sardican canons also, because of the aforementioned distances from the primates, permitted appeals to neighboring bishops, just as did the canons of the African provinces, as is demonstrated in those same Sardican canons. Hosius recalls the importunities of the African bishops, whom he says he knew to disregard and scorn the salutary counsels of his most holy brother and fellow bishop, Gratian.

Thus it is written in the aforementioned Council of Sardica (canon 17):

“Bishop Hosius said: I must not remain silent about what still troubles me. If some bishop, perhaps in anger—which ought not to happen—is quickly and harshly provoked against his own priest or deacon and wishes to expel him from the Church, care must be taken lest an innocent man be condemned or lose communion. Therefore, let the one who has been rejected have the power to appeal to neighboring bishops, so that his case may be heard and examined more carefully, because it is not right to deny a hearing to one who asks for it. Let that bishop who rejected him, whether justly or unjustly, patiently accept that the matter be examined, so that his sentence may either be approved by many or corrected. Nevertheless, before everything has been carefully and faithfully investigated, no one should presume, before the inquiry, to join to communion the one who had been separated from communion.”

We must carefully observe what the sacred [Col. 0406A] canons say with such discrimination: that no one should presume, before the inquiry, to join to communion the one who had been separated from communion.

For, as Saint Leo writes to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne (Letter 95, in the preface): “In matters that are doubtful or obscure, let us know that we must follow what is found to be neither contrary to the evangelical precepts nor opposed to the decrees of the saints.” And again: “Because we wish the judgments of priests to be mature, we can define nothing in matters unknown in prejudice against either party before we have truthfully heard everything that was done.” And elsewhere it is said excellently: “He is not a just mediator who, in uncertain matters, hears one side in such a way that he reserves nothing for the other.”

And Saint Gregory says: “The anger of a priest must in no way be rash and disturbed, but should rather be moderated by the gravity of deliberation.” And again he says (Moralia, Book XIX, chapter 14):

“We must never be rash in delivering a sentence, nor judge matters not yet examined heedlessly, lest any evil things we hear move us, lest we believe random statements without proof. We would certainly fear committing such a thing if we considered more closely the deeds of our Creator. Although everything is naked and open to his eyes, he did not wish to judge the evils of Sodom merely on hearsay, for he says: ‘I will go down and see whether they have acted altogether according to the outcry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know’ (Gen. XVIII, 21). Why, then, does the almighty Lord, who knows all things, seem to doubt before proof, unless to set before us an example of gravity [Col. 0406C], so that we do not presume to believe human evils before proving them?”

Concerning manifest matters known by many, he continues immediately:

“Behold, he descended through angels to learn of the evils, and at once struck the criminals. Yet he who is patient, he who is gentle, he of whom it is written, ‘But you, O Lord, judge with tranquillity’ (Wis. XII, 18), he of whom it is again written, ‘The Lord is patient, but he repays’ (Ecclus. V, 4)—when he found them involved in so great a crime, as though he had set patience aside, did not wish to await the day of the final judgment for vengeance, but anticipated the day of judgment by striking them with the fire of judgment. Behold, he believed the evil only with difficulty when he heard it, yet he struck without delay when, by recognizing the truth, he discovered it: so that he might give us an example that greater crimes should be believed only slowly when heard, but punished more quickly when truly recognized.”

And he who received all judgment from the Father, and who, in his spiritual and secular commonwealth, appointed ministers to judge on his behalf, as Scripture says, and commanded them also to minister with him in judgment, saying, “If anyone serves me, let him follow me” (John XII, 26)—that is, let him imitate me—in this ministry the same one who is the way, the truth, and the life shows judges, through sacred reading, the manner of judging those who would accuse the people of Sodom.

“The outcry of Sodom,” he says, “has come to me” (Gen. XVIII, 20)—that is, their sins, not only great but also persistently manifest, call me to judgment. He then indicates who would be witnesses to their accusation [Col. 0407A], saying: “I will go down and see whether they have altogether acted according to the outcry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know” (Gen. XXI, as printed).

Thus the Lord, who knows all things, as we have shown above from the words of Saint Gregory and as other Catholic teachers explain, sets before us the manner of judging: we should not judge what is not manifest, but what is manifest we should judge without delay or hesitation, as has been shown above from the words of blessed Ambrose, explaining the apostolic sentence:

“Once the deed is known,” he says, “the Apostle declares that the sinner must be expelled from the fellowship of the brethren. For everyone knew his crime; in this matter there was no need of witnesses, nor could the crime be concealed by any evasion.”

## CHAPTER XXX. How illegitimate excommunications can be rescinded, and concerning those who excommunicate unjustly

[Col. 0407B]

Supported and strengthened by these sentences of the holy Scriptures, the sacred canons, and the decrees of the pontiffs of the Roman See—and, as I shall continue to show, by metropolitan authority—I have decreed that the execrable and destructive act you hurled against those who had neither been accused, nor confessed, nor convicted, nor even admonished by you according to the Lord’s command was null and void and without effect: it was not excommunication but your curse.

As it was known not only to me but also to nearly everyone in the province of Rheims, they were innocent of the matters for which you excommunicated them. Yet, because of your fury alone and on account of the injury done to you, so many were driven from the sacred office, sacred communion, and fellowship of the Catholic Church [Col. 0407C], to the destruction of many.

This is especially so since the sacred rules command that baptism be denied to no one placed in imminent danger of death, that no one asking for final penance and communion as viaticum be prevented from receiving it, and that the mercy of burial be denied to no one. In your parish, no one in danger of death could be baptized by those whose duty it was, no one could be reconciled through the grace of communion, and no one could be buried with the proper commendation if the ministers of the Church had been deprived of the offices of their ministries.

Your bonds, therefore, were not the bindings of the holy Church but your curses.

Thus blessed Gregory, responding to Peter, who asked, “Do we consider it very serious if, perhaps, we curse someone driven by anger?” [Col. 0407D] says in the Book of Dialogues (Book III, Dialogue 15):

“Consider how grave is the fault that separates from the kingdom of life, since Paul says: ‘Nor will the revilers possess the kingdom of God’ (1 Cor. VI, 10).”

When the same Peter asked, “What if a man, not perhaps out of malice but through carelessness of the tongue, hurls a word of cursing against his neighbor?” he replied:

“If idle speech is reprehended before the strict Judge, Peter, how much more harmful speech? Consider, then, how condemnable is the person who is not free from malice, if even speech that is without the usefulness of goodness is subject to punishment.”

And in the Book of Moralia (Book IV, chapter 6):

“It must be known that [Col. 0408A] Holy Scripture mentions cursing in two ways: one which it approves and another which it condemns. A curse is uttered in one way by the judgment of justice and in another by the jealousy of vengeance. Against a curse drawn from the jealousy of vengeance we are warned by the voice of Paul preaching, who says: ‘Bless, and do not curse’ (Rom. XII, 14); and again: ‘Nor will revilers possess the kingdom of God’ (1 Cor. VI, 10).
