For holy men, when they pronounce a sentence of cursing, do not let it burst forth from a desire for vengeance, but from an examination of justice. Within themselves they see God’s subtle judgment and recognize that the evils arising outwardly must be struck by a curse; and they do not sin in cursing insofar as they do not diverge from the inward judgment.”

But you diverged from the judgment of justice in your curses, since you [Col. 0408B] pronounced them not by the judgment of justice but through the jealousy of vengeance and because of the injuries done to you. You did not see that the sacred canons do not forbid those irregularly cursed by you from being regularly received by another bishop; indeed, they indicate all the more that they ought to be absolved by the one who presides over you.

For it is written in the Council of Carthage. Augustine, bishop and legate of the province of Numidia, said (canon 9):

“May you deign to establish that if any persons have been expelled from the Church on account of their crimes, and have been received into communion either by some bishop or by some priest, the one who received them should also be held liable to an equal guilt with them, if they have avoided the regular judgment of their own bishop.”

And again (canon 29):

“Anyone who has been excommunicated for his own negligence, whether bishop or any other cleric, and who during the time of his excommunication [Col. 0408C] presumes to receive communion before a hearing, is judged to have pronounced the sentence of condemnation upon himself.”

Do you understand what you hear? Do you understand what you read? These sacred canons forbid others to receive those who have been expelled from the Church deservedly for their crimes, who avoid the regular judgment of their own bishop, who have been excommunicated for their own negligence, and who presume to receive communion during the time of their excommunication before a hearing.

But the clerics of Laon were not excommunicated by you for their own negligence; they did not avoid regular judgment; and they did not presume, contrary to the rules, to receive communion before a hearing and inquiry.

The rule concerning who should be excommunicated, and how, has been clearly set before us by the Lord, who says: “If your brother sins [Col. 0408D] against you,” and so forth, until it says, “Let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector.” “Amen, I say to you, whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven” (Matt. XVIII).

By this rule, this regular judgment, and canonical procedure, those who have been medicinally separated from the communion of the Church until they convert and return to penance are known to have received a sentence ratified by God: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven” (ibid.).

The sacred canons likewise command that those cast out or excommunicated by their own bishops—or, if it is doubtful whether they were cast out or excommunicated in this manner, those concerning whom such a question exists—not be received by others in the meantime, if their cases cannot first be settled by neighboring bishops or by judges chosen or appointed for the purpose [Col. 0409A], until they are examined in a provincial synod which the metropolitan bishop has approved and those cast out receive the sentence commonly reached in accordance with the rules.

The Nicene canons clearly demonstrate this when they say (canon 5):

“Those who are cast out must not be received by others. Let inquiry also be made to ensure that they do not appear to have been excluded from the congregation through pusillanimity, contentiousness, or any other fault of the bishop.”

It is clear that they command doubtful or obscure matters to be investigated, not matters that are certain or manifest.

And the Council of Antioch (canon 6):

“One deprived of communion by his own bishop,” it says, “must not be received by others until he has been reconciled with his own bishop, or has appeared at the synod that is convened, made satisfaction on his own behalf, and persuaded the council to accept another sentence” [Col. 0409B].

And the Sardican canons (canon 17):

“Let that bishop,” they say, “who rejected him, whether justly or unjustly, patiently accept that the matter be examined, so that his sentence may either be approved by many or corrected.”

That is, after an investigation has been made concerning what was previously doubtful and obscure, a sentence reasonably pronounced may be approved, or one irrationally delivered may be corrected.

This could in some way have been patiently observed in the case of one, two, or three persons—or even ten, twenty, or thirty—and in matters that were doubtful or obscure. But when, as everyone knows most clearly, three hundred, four hundred, or five hundred had been expelled without any reason or fault on their part, against all authority, through your fury alone and because of the injuries done to you [Col. 0409C], what Christian could have thought that such people should be kept until examination, as though this were a matter of doubtful and obscure cases involving no danger?

Especially since they had not sinned in your injuries but had grieved over them, while God utterly detests this kind of repayment, when evils are repaid for good (Ps. XXXIV).

Therefore, not before an inquiry, as the Sardican canons command (canon 17), but after a manifest investigation, I regularly restored the clerics whom you had cursed to communion.

And if what you did had possessed any reason or authority, wherever the slaughter and danger of so many peoples [Col. 0409D] were impending, something ought nevertheless to have been taken away from severity, as blessed Augustine demonstrates, so that charity, which covers a multitude of sins, might assist in healing greater evils.

And if you had hurled your curses only against those who were the authors or perpetrators of the injuries done to you, perhaps they could have been tolerated by others until a synodal assembly demonstrated to you that you had acted contrary to reason. Blessed Peter the Apostle teaches:

“This is grace: if, because of conscience toward God, anyone endures sorrows while suffering unjustly. For what credit is there if, when you sin and are struck, you endure it? But if, when you do good and suffer, you endure it, this is grace before God. For you were called to this, because Christ also suffered for us, leaving you an example so that you might follow his footsteps. He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth. When he was cursed, he did not curse in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but entrusted himself to the one who judges unjustly” (1 Pet. II) [Col. 0410A].

And Paul says: “Bless, and do not curse,” not repaying evil for evil or cursing for cursing (Rom. XII).

For this reason the Truth itself says: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you. Pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matt. V).

“Virtue,” says Gregory (Homily 35 on the Gospels), “is to endure adversity before human beings, but virtue before God is to love; for God accepts only that sacrifice which the flame of charity kindles before his eyes upon the altar of good works.”

And the Lord calls blessed those who suffer persecution for justice’s sake [Col. 0410B] (Matt. V), not for wickedness—unless, perhaps, through that very persecution they are converted to correction and attain the blessedness of purification.

But if anything had been done against you by anyone contrary to divine or human laws, you ought to have made it known to me and patiently waited for some period of time, until I could deal with it together with our brothers and fellow bishops, as I had in fact done, rather than avenge your troubles through the destruction of others.

And if, seeking excuses for resistance, you should prefer to defend your pernicious deed rather than acknowledge and correct it, and should wish to object to me what Innocent wrote to the bishops of Macedonia (Letter 29, near the end):

“But, as often happens, whenever a people or [Col. 0410C] crowd sins, because punishment cannot be exacted against everyone on account of their number, it is customary to let the matter pass unavenged. Therefore, I say that the earlier matters should be left to God’s judgment, while for the future the greatest care must be taken to prevent such things”—

I reply to you that you should have directed these curses either against the people or against the sinful crowd, and not against an innocent people and crowd. For you are commanded to curse no one, even one who sins against you, and still less one who does not sin against you.

Concerning episcopal binding—which we must regard as a matter of great fear, caution, and observance—Saint Gregory says in his twenty-sixth homily on the Gospel:

“Often, in binding and loosing those subject to him, a shepherd follows the impulse of his own will rather than the merits of the cases. Thus it happens that the one who exercises this power of binding and loosing according to his own desires, [Col. 0410D] and not according to the conduct of his subjects, deprives himself of that power. Hence the prophet rightly says: ‘They put to death souls that should not die, and they made alive souls that should not live’ (Ezek. XIII). He puts to death one who should not die when he condemns the righteous; and he attempts to make alive one who will not live when he strives to absolve the guilty from punishment.”

It often happens, therefore, that he either condemns those who do not deserve it or, himself bound, releases others.

What I did in absolving those whom you had cursed is therefore not a new act but an ordinance of the ancient rules. As Gelasius says concerning his predecessor: “I am not the author of a new constitution but the executor of an old one.”

The Carthaginian canons clearly demonstrate this when they say (canon 5):

“New proposals, whether obscure [Col. 0411A] or hidden under a general category, will receive their form after examination by us. But concerning matters that divine Scripture has clearly sanctioned, judgment must not be postponed; rather, it must be carried out. Therefore, what is censured in laymen ought much more to be condemned beforehand in clerics. All said, ‘No one acts against the prophets, no one acts against the Gospel, without danger.’”

And shortly afterward:

“We ought to preserve the remaining matters, whether deeds or words, set out above or recorded in other councils, which are found to be in accordance with the law. But if anyone transgresses and violates the statutes, or considers them worthless, then, if he is a layman, let him be deprived of communion; if he is a cleric, let him be deprived of his honor. All said, ‘It is approved, it is approved.’”

After this synod, the Council of Chalcedon, which was held afterward, says (canon 1):

“We have decreed that the rules established by the holy Fathers in each council up to the present retain their proper force” [Col. 0411B].

And again, somewhat later (canon 10):

“As for those who dare, after the definition of this great and universal synod, to perpetrate anything among the things that have been prohibited, the holy synod has decreed that they must withdraw from their own rank.”

And if you wish to object to me here concerning what I said above about a chapter of this synod not received by the apostolic see, I refer you [Col. 0411C] to read what I said earlier and to see how much I stated: namely, that the apostolic see does not receive the chapter concerning this matter, which says: “If a bishop or cleric has a complaint against the metropolitan bishop of the same province, let him seek the see of the royal city of Constantinople and be judged there.”

I further remind you that this same council did not prohibit but granted the right to seek the see of Constantinople. In the chapter under discussion, however, it said: “Those who dare to perpetrate anything among the things that have been prohibited.”

Since it is therefore clear that you judged in these matters with a hostile mind and were corrupted by the desire to prevail, according to the Carthaginian canons your rescinded sentence works against you.

And since, in the rolls that you sent to the lord king and to me through fellow ministers of your Church, you repeatedly and in various ways set out, to confirm your sentences, not only sacred canons and the decrees of the pontiffs of the apostolic see but also legal judgments of Catholic emperors, I shall set before you a legal judgment of the Catholic emperor Justinian, which the Catholic Church approves and observes.

In Constitution 118, chapter [Col. 0411D] 441, he decreed:

“Let no bishop and no priest excommunicate anyone before the case has been proved for which the ecclesiastical canons command this to be done. If anyone excommunicates someone contrary to these provisions, let the one who has been excommunicated return to the grace of holy communion by the authority of a greater priest; but let the one who excommunicated him illegitimately abstain from holy communion for as long a period as the greater priest determines, so that he may justly suffer what he unjustly did.”

For this reason Saint Gregory wrote to John, a bishop who was excommunicating unjustly, among other things:

“First annulling and reducing to nothing the decrees of the sentence you pronounced, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we decree that you be deprived of holy communion for thirty days and that you implore from our almighty God, with the greatest penance and tears, pardon for so great an offense. But if we learn that you have fulfilled this sentence of ours with insufficient seriousness, know that, with the Lord’s help, not only your injustice but also the contumacy of your fraternity will be punished more severely” [Col. 0412A].

And elsewhere (Book II, Indiction 11, Letter 7):

“If at any time, on any occasion, or through any deception you attempt to act contrary to what we have established, know that you are deprived of holy communion. We decree that you may not receive it, except at the final moment of your life, unless by the permission granted by the Roman pontiff. For we sanction this in accordance with the definition of the holy Fathers: whoever does not know how to obey the sacred canons is not worthy either to minister at the sacred altars or to receive communion” [Col. 0412B].

## CHAPTER XXXI. Concerning his prohibition against baptizing infants, who are often endangered by the peril of death

Finally, as the petition delivered to me by the Church of Laon states, because of your injuries you prohibited the baptism of infants who are often endangered by the peril of death.

In this matter you and Pelagius have become, as an excellent poet says for the most part:

> Equal in error, although pursuing different paths.

Pelagius taught that infants newly born from their mothers’ wombs [Col. 0412C] should not be baptized for the remission of sins, because they had inherited nothing from Adam that needed to be cleansed by the washing of regeneration. He strove to show that we had been redeemed by Christ in vain, contradicting the Apostle, who says: “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and thus death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. V).

But although you knew the truth of what the Lord says—“Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John III)—you ordered that infants in your parish, even those placed in danger of death, not be baptized, so that they might not be saved, although it is written: “The Son of Man did not come to destroy souls but to save them” (Luke IX).

You also acted contrary to the decrees of Siricius, Leo, Gelasius, and the African Council, as I have already commanded you in writing not once but twice [Col. 0412D].

Since I have now sent those decrees to you in full in writing, I shall briefly recall certain points from them.

Concerning the baptism of infants who are known not yet to have been baptized, whenever necessity requires it, an ecclesiastical rule was issued through blessed Siricius, whose rule concludes as follows (Letter 1 to Himerius):

“Now let all priests hold to the rule stated above who do not wish to be torn away from the solidity of the apostolic rock upon which Christ built the universal Church.”

And Saint Leo:

“In the peril of death, in the danger of siege, in the distress of persecution, and in fear of shipwreck, he decreed that at no time should this unique protection of true salvation be denied to anyone.”

The African Council, and likewise the same Saint Leo (Letter 92 to Rusticus), commanded:

“Even those infants concerning whom no completely certain witnesses are found who can testify without doubt that they were baptized, and who because of their age are themselves unable to give a satisfactory answer concerning the sacraments entrusted to them, must be baptized without any scruple” [Col. 0413A].

And Saint Gelasius (Ivo, Part I, chapter 252) shows:

“Even if extreme necessity should compel it, such persons ought to be baptized by Christian laymen.”

## CHAPTER XXXII. Concerning his prohibition against giving penance and viaticum to the dying
In the chapter in which you forbade the granting of final penance and the provision of the viaticum to the dying [Col. 0413B], contrary to the Nicene and African canons and to the decrees of Siricius, Innocent, Celestine, and Leo, you have shown yourself to be a follower of the heretic Novatian—although by a different route, yet with no different danger—as Innocent and the other Catholic teachers demonstrate. For the Novatians teach that those who have fallen should not be received into penance and communion. Yet you knew that, according to the Nicene canons, penance and the grace of communion must not at any time be denied to one who asks for them; nevertheless, because of your injuries, you ordered—as is contained in the petition presented to me by the Church of Laon—that penance and the grace of communion should be denied even to those placed at the point of death, so that, with our Savior permitting it, they might not be rescued from eternal destruction.

Yet Truth itself says of itself: “The Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost; he did not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Luke 19), while many saints and teachers of the Catholic Church protest aloud that the aid of regeneration, penance, and holy communion must in no way be denied to anyone placed in danger of death who asks for it. Therefore I have undertaken to write to you in full what the holy Nicene canons, Saint Siricius, Saint Innocent, Saint Celestine, and Saint Leo decreed. I have also appended the judgment that Saint Leo pronounced against those who despise these things, and I have charged you to observe it.

For he says (Epistle 1):

> “So that nothing may perhaps be thought to have been omitted by us, we command that all the decretal constitutions both of Innocent, of blessed memory, and of all our predecessors, which have been promulgated concerning ecclesiastical orders and the disciplines of the canons, be so carefully observed by your affection that, if anyone should violate them, he must know that thereafter pardon will be denied him.”

Since, therefore, you cannot be ignorant of what Saint Celestine, the predecessor of blessed Leo, decreed—you inserted part of his decrees into your own collection, where he says:

> “Let no priest be permitted to be ignorant of his canons, nor to do anything that could oppose the rules of the Fathers. For what worthy thing shall be preserved by us if the standard of the decretal constitutions is broken at the pleasure of certain people, with license granted to the populace?”

[Col. 0414A] I cannot sufficiently marvel at how you were able to be ignorant of yourself and forget so great a matter, although you acted against Celestine’s decrees; and yet, among other things, you dared to place the words of that same Pope Celestine in your little memorandum. Although you prescribed this decretal judgment of blessed Celestine in the profession-decree subscribed by you, you deprived yourself of honor—not only by his judgment but also by your own—according to the sacred Carthaginian canons, which say (canon 13):

> “If anyone in any respect acts against his own profession or subscription, he himself shall deprive himself of honor.”

For you did what opposes the rules of the Fathers when, contrary to the decrees of Celestine and of the other Roman pontiffs, and contrary to the sacred canons, you prohibited penitents from being received into penance and prohibited the dying from being assisted with the viaticum [Col. 0414B]. By a judgment usurped according to your own pleasure, you broke the standard of the decretal constitutions.

Perhaps you did not wish to understand that those constitutions are your canons, and for that reason you put in your memorandum:

> “Let no priest be permitted to be ignorant of canons,”

omitting the word “his,” which is found there. The pronoun “his” must not therefore be erased or omitted from Celestine’s words, since the canons and rules of the Fathers are the canons and rules of priests—just as the Law of Moses is called the law of the Jews. The Lord says to the Jews: “In your law it is written” (John 8), and again concerning them: “In their law it is written” (John 15). Either someone is not a priest, and the canons are not his; or whoever is a priest has canons that are his.

This does not mean that, like the Jews with the law, they may bend those same canons to their own interpretation according to their pleasure. Rather, they must conform their understanding to their precepts by obeying them, so that, following their commands, they may make their steps straight and set up in their actions the lamp proclaimed by the light of the Scriptures, so that they may say with the Psalmist:

> “Your word, O Lord, is a lamp for my feet and a light for my paths” (Psalm 118).

If any crookedness appears in their understanding, precepts, or actions, it must be corrected by their rules and directed toward those things that are to be understood, held, and followed.

Read, then, the decrees of Siricius and of that same Celestine, and the sacred canons. You will find that, with criminal audacity, you prohibited such things against their decrees—indeed, against evangelical truth and apostolic authority—as I have already written to you once and again [Col. 0414D].

Perhaps, however, you do not wish to regard these things, which we call canons, as canons, but instead those things about which you have fabricated your own inventions. For that reason you inserted Celestine’s words with a foreign interpretation. Nevertheless, recall what you placed in that same memorandum from Celestine’s words:

> “Those things which we do not correct by the authority of admonition alone, we must punish with severity suited to the rules. Therefore we wish this to be made known throughout all the churches that lack their own rulers, so that no one, perhaps flattering himself with some hope, may deceive himself.”

Therefore you must henceforth take care that you are not judged by the very rules that you inserted into your collections from the words of Saint Celestine, just as I have endeavored to preserve what he commanded [Col. 0415A], namely, by making known what the Church of Laon ought to observe.

And since, as I showed above, you alienated the words of blessed Gregory from their proper meaning as far as lay within your power, falsified and mutilated them, so that you might turn the anathema which he had placed in that chapter with its appropriate meaning against those to whom it did not apply, I considered it worthwhile to write to you what he wrote concerning anathema in the synodical letter that, according to custom, he sent at the beginning of his ordination to the patriarchs—namely, to the patriarchs of Alexandria, Antioch, Jerusalem, and Constantinople (Book 1, Epistle 24):

> “Furthermore, since one believes in the heart unto righteousness, but confession is made with the mouth unto salvation, I profess that I receive and venerate four councils, just as I do the four books of the holy Gospel: namely, the Council of Nicaea, in which the perverse doctrine of Arius was destroyed; likewise the Council of Constantinople, in which the error of Eunomius and Macedonius was refuted; also the First Council of Ephesus, in which the impiety of Nestorius was judged; and the Council of Chalcedon, in which the depravity of Eutyches and Dioscorus was rejected. I embrace them with complete devotion and preserve them with unimpaired approval, because in them, as in a four-sided stone, the structure of holy faith rises.

> “Whoever does not hold their solidity, whatever kind of life or action he may have, even if he is seen to be a stone, nevertheless lies outside the building. I also venerate the Fifth Council, in which the letter called the letter of Ibas was rejected as full of error; in which Theodore was convicted of having fallen into impious unbelief by separating the person of the Mediator between God and human beings into two subsistences; and in which the writings of Theodoret, through which the faith of blessed Cyril was attacked, were refuted as having been produced with deranged audacity.

> “I reject all those whom the aforesaid venerable councils reject, and I embrace those whom they venerate, with total devotion. Since these councils were established by universal agreement, whoever presumes either to loose those whom they bind or to bind those whom they loose destroys himself, not them. Therefore, let whoever thinks otherwise be anathema. But let peace from God the Father through Jesus Christ, his Son, be with whoever holds the faith of the aforesaid synods—he who, being God consubstantial with the Father, lives and reigns with him in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.”

The sacred Council of Nicaea also says (canon 13):

> “Concerning those who are departing this life, the ancient law and rule shall still be maintained, so that, if anyone is departing from the body, he shall in no way be deprived of the final and necessary viaticum. But if someone who was considered hopeless and received communion and became a participant in the offering should subsequently recover, he shall stand among those who receive only the communion of prayer. In general, however, the bishop ought reasonably to give communion from the offering to anyone at all who is placed at the point of death and asks that the grace of communion be granted to him.”

Behold, brother, you have heard that the sacred Nicene canons command that communion not be denied generally to anyone placed at the point of death who asks for the grace of communion, but that the dying person should be absolved through that same communion.

And behold, you have heard blessed Gregory declaring:

> “Whoever presumes either to loose those whom the aforesaid councils bind—the first of which is Nicaea—or to bind those whom they loose, let whoever thinks otherwise be anathema.”

Imitate, then, Saint David, who, when he heard from the prophet Nathan about the sin he had committed, said from the depths of his heart:

> “I have sinned against the Lord” (2 Samuel 12);

and again: because he struck his heart, since he had defiled the garment of the Lord’s anointed (1 Samuel 24). The Lord’s garment is the Church, concerning which it is written:

> “As I live, says the Lord, you shall be clothed with all these as with an ornament” (Isaiah 49:18).

And the Apostle says:

> “All of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ” (Galatians 3:27).

Strike your breast, because striking the breast displays contrition of heart, and say with abundant tears:

> “I have sinned against the Lord,”

so that you may deserve to hear:

> “The Lord has taken away your sin; you shall not die” (2 Samuel 12).

## CHAPTER XXXIII. That he ordered burial to be denied to the dead in their own parish

[Col. 0416B]

In the chapter in which, as is contained in the petition presented to me by the Church of Laon, you ordered burial to be denied to the dead, you did not shrink from acting with excessive inhumanity against sacred histories and sacred canons. For, as we read in the venerable history of the Book of Kings, even the bodies of those who, because of Saul’s sin—which had caused famine continuously in David’s days for three years—had been crucified at the Lord’s command, were laudably guarded by Saul’s concubine, so that the birds would not tear them apart by day, nor the beasts by night, “until water dripped upon them from heaven” (2 Samuel 21) [Col. 0416C]. And thus they were buried together with the bones of Saul and Jonathan.

We read in the Gospel that, when Joseph requested it, Pilate ordered the Lord’s body to be returned (Matthew 27:58)—the body of the one whom, at the request of the Jews, he had adjudged worthy of crucifixion as though he were a criminal. Thus, according to Scripture, he was “numbered with the wicked” (Isaiah 53:12). And the Jews, so that even the bodies of criminals would not remain unburied on the cross on the Sabbath day, obtained from Pilate that their legs be broken and that they be taken away (Luke 21:38).

The rules of the ancient Fathers likewise command that the bodies even of those who have brought death upon themselves in any manner, or who are punished for their crimes, be carried to burial, although without hymns and psalms. They did not command that even such corpses be deprived of burial in the womb of the mother of all, that is, the earth [Col. 0416D].

If indeed you speak justice, then judge justly, son of man, and see whether, according to the rules and laws mentioned above, I have possessed the episcopal authority, as metropolitan, to correct these things that you have presumptuously done against the sacred rules.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. That, in matters certain and definitively settled, neither a synod is to be convened nor the apostolic see troubled, but what has been established is to be observed

But if you choose to remain in your obstinacy and contempt for me, and refuse to acknowledge what is true in this matter, then, since these are certain and manifest causes, in no respect doubtful or obscure to us, concerning which we possess definitive judgments promulgated by the holy Fathers that cannot be overturned by any reasoning [Col. 0417A], I ought not to await synodal deliberation or the counsel or consent of the co-bishops of our province. Nor ought I to depart from the rules already established through negligence or presumption, nor trouble the apostolic see by seeking a further decision from it.

Let Saint Innocent, writing to the archbishops and bishops of Macedonia, say what he thinks about this (Epistle 27):

> “When the letters had been delivered, I immediately ordered the archdeacon Vitalis, the bearer of your letter, to read them. In them I perceived many things that would cause astonishment in our minds and make us doubt considerably whether we should think otherwise, or whether those things had been written as they sounded. When I had them read repeatedly, I realized that an injury was being done to the apostolic see, to which the report had been sent and was running as to the head of the churches, since its judgment was still being led into uncertainty. Therefore, concerning matters about which I remember having written long ago, the repeated inquiry contained in your report now compels me to reiterate the matter with clearer arguments.”

And to Felix, bishop of Nuceria (Epistle 3):

> “We were astonished that a prudent man should have wished to consult about matters that are known with certainty to everyone.”

And Saint Zosimus says to Hesychius:

> “Whoever, setting aside the authority of the Fathers and of the apostolic see, neglects this shall know that it must be punished by us with the greatest severity. He must have no doubt that the standing of his office will not remain secure if he thinks that, after so many prohibitions, this can be attempted with impunity. For whatever is repeatedly usurped despite being forbidden is done out of a desire to insult.”

And Saint Celestine, whose words you too placed in your collections, as we have said above, writes (Epistle 11, to the bishops of Apulia and Calabria):

> “Let no priest be permitted to be ignorant of his canons, nor to do anything that could oppose the rules of the Fathers. For what worthy thing shall be preserved by us if the standard of the decretal constitutions is broken at the pleasure of certain people, with license granted to the populace?”

And a little later:

> “Those things which we do not correct by the authority of admonition alone, we must punish with severity suited to the rules.”

And Leo (Epistle 1, to the bishops)—whose words I do not hesitate to repeat—says:

> “We command that all the decretal constitutions both of Innocent, of blessed memory, and of all our predecessors, which have been promulgated concerning ecclesiastical orders and the disciplines of the canons, be so carefully observed by your affection that, if anyone should violate them, he must know that thereafter pardon will be denied him.”

The same Leo also says to Leo Augustus:

> “To seek what has been disclosed, to reconsider what has been completed, and to overturn what has been definitively settled—what else is this than failing to give thanks for the grace received and extending the wicked desires of deadly greed toward the food of the forbidden tree?”

The same holy Leo also says to that same Leo Augustus (Epistle 84):

> “Since we dare to undertake no discussion concerning matters defined at Nicaea and Chalcedon, as God willed, as though those things were doubtful or weak which such authority through the Holy Spirit established so firmly.”

Pope Hilary says (Epistle 11, to Veranus):

> “For one does not offend against the sanctions of sacred traditions less than one rushes forward in insult against the Lord himself.”

And Gelasius says:

> “It is exceedingly unworthy for anyone, whether among pontiffs or among the subordinate orders, to reject this observance, which he sees the see of blessed Peter both follow and teach. It is entirely fitting that the whole body of the Church should agree among itself in this observance, which it sees prevailing where the Lord placed the primacy of the entire Church.”

The same Gelasius also says to all the bishops established throughout Dardania:

> “Our Fathers,” he says (Epistle 11, at the beginning), “namely, the Catholic and learned pontiffs, whenever any heresy arose, at whatever time, wished whatever they had once decreed, after a congregation had been held according to the course of the Scriptures and the preaching of their predecessors, for the sake of the faith, the truth, and Catholic and apostolic communion, to remain thereafter firm and unshaken. They did not permit what had been established in the same matter to be reconsidered through any recent presumption.

> “They saw with the greatest wisdom that, if anyone were permitted to repeat decrees once salutarily made, no ecclesiastical settlement would remain stable against every individual error, and every complete definition would continually be disturbed by the return of the same frenzies.

> “For if, even when the boundaries of synodal rules have once been established, destructive forces do not cease to rise up again in renewed conflicts against the foundation of truth and to strike simple hearts, what would happen if it were continually permissible for the faithless to convene a council? However manifest the truth might be, pernicious falsehood would never lack something to bring forward; and, even if deficient in reason or authority, it would nevertheless refuse to yield in mere contention.

> “Our predecessors, seeing these things by divine inspiration, took necessary precautions: against every heresy, they did not permit what a synod once assembled had promulgated for the faith, communion, and Catholic and apostolic truth to be mutilated thereafter by new reconsiderations, lest the wicked be given an opportunity to attack what had been established as a remedy. Once the author of any madness and the error itself had been condemned, they judged it sufficient that anyone who at any time became a participant in that error should be bound by the principal sentence of its condemnation, since anyone could plainly be recognized either by his profession or by his communion.”

And if you wish to understand this only of heresies that have arisen, understand likewise what he says:

> “Once the author of any madness and the error itself had been condemned, they judged it sufficient that anyone who at any time became a participant in that error should be bound by the principal sentence of its condemnation.”

For what greater madness can there be, or what worse error, or what more serious schism against the Catholic Church, than to despise the decrees of holy councils and of the apostolic see; to trample upon the laws approved by the Church; to reject Christian piety; to deprive innocent people of rank and communion contrary to every divine and human law; to refuse to assist the innocent, on account of your own crime, in the urgent danger of death through the grace of baptism; to deny communion to those who are dying and ask for the grace of communion [Col. 0419A]; and to refuse the dead the kindness of burial?

“Whatever,” says Gelasius, “our predecessors promulgated for the faith, communion, and Catholic and apostolic truth, they did not permit to be mutilated thereafter by new reconsiderations, lest the wicked be given an opportunity to attack what had been established as a remedy. Once the author of any madness and the error itself had been condemned, they judged it sufficient that anyone who at any time became a participant in that error should be bound by the principal sentence of its condemnation, since anyone could plainly be recognized either by his profession or by his communion.”

The same Gelasius also says in his memorandum:

> “My predecessor,” he says, “was the executor of an ancient constitution, not the author of a new constitution—a role that is permitted not only to an apostolic bishop but to any pontiff.”

For it is not permitted to reconsider or oppose ancient constitutions; rather, new constitutions must be required for newly arising matters, provided that they are not contrary to evangelical truth or opposed to the decrees of the saints. The same holy Gelasius demonstrates this in his decrees, after listing those who, by established definition and at different times, were individually condemned (Epistle 11, near the beginning):

> “A synod, once held and condemning the aforesaid persons, did not permit them thereafter to come to new councils. Rather, the Church rejected all who in any manner fell back into these blasphemies, according to the synodal limit entrusted to it. Nor has it ever been shown right, however compelling the necessity, rashly to tamper anew with what had been salutarily established.”

And a little later:

> “Since the very error which was once condemned together with its author carries its own execration and punishment in every participant who becomes involved in an evil communion.”

And again:

> “Since a new cause had arisen in both pontiffs, it consequently required a new investigation, so that, as had always been the practice, judgments concerning priests might proceed from a priestly council.”

And again:

> “Since the causes were new, a new ecclesiastical investigation ought to follow.”

And again:

> “The causes were certainly new, and consequently a new synod was owed to them.”

And again:

> “Was it permitted for secular power, with Acacius consenting to such acts, to complete this without any synod—which the novelty of the circumstances themselves required—and without consultation of the apostolic see, while it was not permitted to the apostolic see, according to the tenor of the Council of Chalcedon, to expel from its communion Acacius, who communicated with the enemies of the Council of Chalcedon, in a matter already condemned by a just definition as an old cause and an old constitution?”

And again:

> “There was no need for a new synod, since the form prescribed by the ancient constitution was sufficient for this.”

And again:

> “The assembly of pontiffs was not held against Chalcedon, nor did it convene as a new synod against the ancient and first one. Rather, according to the tenor of the ancient constitution, it became a participant in the execution of the apostolic authority.”

And again:

> “There is no doubt that, just as in every heresy—which must be repeated without ceasing, because no Christian doubts that it is firm—all accomplices, followers, and participants in a perversity once condemned are judged to share the same fate.”

And again:

> “Those who had not been heard, examined, or convicted ought not to be struck down, especially when new causes and a new state of affairs appeared, so that these rulers of the peoples might be deprived of their sacred dignities by sudden attacks and at the will of worldly power, though they could not be shown or convicted to be associates through any old cause, any association in guilt, or participation in any error previously condemned, as though they were bound by a definition made in the past.”

Nor has the worthy rebuke of blessed Gregory to Vitalian, bishop of Sipontum, escaped my memory, when I dissolved your binding sentence—indeed, your detestable curse—with which that blessed man says (Book 8, Epistle 9):

> “If you knew how to be the guardian of religious discipline, or if you knew how to be a bishop, you would not have permitted the daughter of Tullianus, the glorious military master, while you were stationed there, either to abandon her religious clothing and return to secular dress or to send us a perverse letter. For, as we have said, if you had been vigilant, the punishment of the most wicked woman ought to have reached us before her fault.”

And from there, to Sergius the defender (the same book, Epistle 10):

> “If you were a human being, or possessed any discernment, you ought to have been such a guardian of regular discipline that the unlawful acts committed there would have been corrected by punishment before news of them reached us.”

And shortly afterward:

> “For if in any way you should prove negligent or slow in this matter, know that you will be punished with such severity that, when punishment reveals to you what you do not know about yourself, you may come to understand it. For, as we have said, if you had possessed human understanding, we ought to have learned from you, together with punishment, that the things you now order to be done had already been done by you.”

To avoid prolixity, and because the matter is very well known, I omit here the individual decrees of the sacred canons in their several councils. I shall set down only one testimony from the Council of Carthage, which I also cited above. Gratus, the bishop, said (First Council, canon 13):

> “New suggestions, whether obscure or concealed under a general category, will receive a determination after they have been examined by us. But concerning matters that divine Scripture has sanctioned most openly, judgment is not to be delayed; rather, it must be carried out.”

Read the *Summary of the Canons of the Province of Africa*, sent to the apostolic see and confirmed by that same see, and you will find these words at the beginning of the canons themselves.

## CHAPTER XXXV. That the apostolic see judges together with bishops who judge according to the canons, and that a metropolitan should not hear cases without the insistence of the provincials
Whoever, therefore, the primates of the provinces established by the Lord and confirmed by apostolic authority may be, and likewise whatever Catholic bishops may be, when dealing with definite and manifest matters for which we possess explicit judgments and definitive sentences that must be preserved irrefragably and unshakably, whatever we decree and judge according to the sacred canons and the decrees of the pontiffs of the Roman See [Col. 0421A], the apostolic See and the Catholic Church—founded upon the foundation of the apostles and built upon the cornerstone, Christ Jesus, in whom every structure rises into a holy temple in the Lord—in us, sons born in place of our fathers, that is, bishops created in place of the apostles, just as it coordinates in ordaining, so also canonically decrees jointly with us in decreeing and judges jointly with us in judging.

We, however, who carry out the sacred canons and the decrees of the pontiffs of the Roman See under the judgment of that apostolic rock, are nothing other than supporters of those who judge justly and executors of righteous judgments. We exist in dependence upon the Holy Spirit, who spoke through them, and upon the apostolic See, from which the stream of religion, ecclesiastical ordering, and canonical judgment [Col. 0421B] flowed forth. For whoever is baptized with Catholic baptism—as it was said to John the Baptist, “He,” namely Christ Jesus, “is the one who baptizes”—and whoever offers sacrifice, he is the priest according to the order of Melchizedek, possessing an eternal priesthood, who sanctifies (John I). For, as Saint Leo says (letter 91):

> “If anything is accomplished through our ministry in good order and with a gratifying result, we do not doubt that it has been granted to us through the Holy Spirit, and the Savior himself intervenes in our work. He is never absent from those things which he entrusted to his ministers to carry out, saying: ‘Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age’ (Matthew XXVIII).”

And Leo likewise says:

> “Concerning those who, at the Council of Nicaea, with the Holy Spirit [Col. 0421C] suggesting to them—for otherwise it must not be believed—established laws of the ecclesiastical canons that would remain until the end of the world, and which among us throughout the whole world live on in their constitutions: if anything is presumed anywhere contrary to what they decreed, it is annulled without hesitation.”

And Saint Augustine says (*On True Religion*, chap. 31):

> “It is lawful for pure minds to know the eternal law; it is not lawful for them to judge it. In the case of these temporal laws, although human beings judge them when they establish them, nevertheless, once they have been established and confirmed, it is not permissible for a judge to judge them, but only to judge according to them.”

[Col. 0421D] Therefore you cannot, by any subscription, however great or of whatever kind, of yourself and your accomplices, bind those things which, through me—however unworthy a metropolitan and primate of the province of Rheims, to whose care, according to the sacred canons and decrees of the pontiffs of the Roman See, solicitude for the entire province pertains—the apostolic See and our holy fathers, who reign with God in heaven and shine forth by miracles on earth, indeed, as I stated earlier, our Savior himself, have loosed among the things which you, a provincial bishop, bound contrary to the definitive judgments of the holy rules. Nor can you loose what I bind according to the rules previously established by the holy Fathers. For, as Gelasius says in his decrees—as you can reread in the book which I entrusted to you before the altar of Saint Mary on the day of your ordination:

> “An inferior cannot absolve a superior; but a superior consequently absolves an inferior.”

Accordingly, [Col. 0422A] the pontiffs of an inferior rank, who knew perfectly well that they could not release from their obligation a superior without the First See, especially one whom they knew to have been bound by its sentence, did not completely strip him of his bonds by their transgressive absolution; rather, by their transgression they bound themselves more tightly.

Moreover, since the Lord says to someone, “By your words I judge you” (Luke XXIV), although in your compilations you chose not to include, but rather to omit, certain words of those from whom you collected testimonies—words which you knew would bite you—I shall set before you, as though it were one definitive edict in place of all the rest, the following. When you included certain material collected by Pope Lucius from various statements of his predecessors and earlier forebears, you inserted:

> “Likewise, relying upon apostolic authority, we command that no metropolitan hear the cases of anyone without the insistence of all the other [Col. 0422B] bishops of his province, because such proceedings will be invalid and he himself will be liable for the act.”

You thought that you were binding upon metropolitans a heavy and unbearable burden, and imposing it upon their shoulders, but you were unwilling to move with your finger what the same Lucius wrote to you immediately afterward. For he says, without any intervening words:

> “Let the bishops in each province take care that those who came later do not place themselves before their predecessors, nor do anything without consulting them, except insofar as it concerns their own parish. Rather, let all of them pronounce and determine a harmonious judgment concerning matters common to them; for proceedings conducted otherwise will have no force and will not be regarded as ecclesiastical.”

Since, therefore, Lucius in part, and after him the canons of Antioch more fully, decreed (canon 9):

> “That a bishop [Col. 0422C] should do nothing apart from the metropolitan, except only those things which concern his own parish and the possessions subject to him, so that he may govern them according to the reverence due to each, and exercise care over every possession under his authority, ordaining priests and deacons and dealing with individual matters according to his own judgment,”

you must attend carefully to what follows: “Let him ordain priests and deacons,” it says, “and not unordain them.” For those whom you as bishop alone can ordain, you may by no means alone remove or suspend from sacred offices, except as the venerable canons prescribe. And it says, “Let him deal with individual matters,” not general ones, according to his judgment. You must know that the metropolitan bishop is responsible for the care of the whole province; for this reason all those from every direction who appear to have business [Col. 0422D] come together at the metropolis.

And Leo says to you in the same place:

> “Since in cases that concern the general observance of all the Lord’s priests, nothing ought to be carried out without the primates.”

Before Leo, Lucius had already declared to you what the canons of the province of Africa also say:

> “Do not do anything without consulting your predecessors, except insofar as it concerns your own parish; for otherwise the proceedings will have no force and will not be regarded as ecclesiastical.”

[Col. 0423A] Since, therefore, the things which you improperly bound—against evangelical truth, apostolic authority, the sacred canons, and the constitutions of the apostolic See—without the council of the metropolitan, who ought not to have consented to you and did not do so, have no force according to Lucius’s words and are not regarded as ecclesiastical, I was freely able to loose what you were not permitted to bind.

You also clearly did not understand this properly, and it is certain that you did not state correctly what Lucius said:

> “That no metropolitan may hear the cases of anyone without the insistence of all the other bishops of his province.”

For all the reprehensible things that, so to speak, fly from every mouth about you and cannot fail to reach me, whenever I hear those same accusations against you, I cannot always gather all the provincial bishops so that they may hear them with me. If you had correctly understood the Carthaginian canons, which say (Council of Carthage IV, canon 23):

> “That a bishop should hear no one’s case without the presence of his clergy,”

you would not have erred in this judgment concerning a hearing [Col. 0423B]. For what James said to Paul must be understood in another sense: “They will hear that you have come” (Acts XXI); and what Paul says about himself: “Let all the nations hear, and I was delivered from the mouth of the lion” (II Timothy IV); and what he says to the Corinthians: “I hear that there are divisions among you,” that is, schisms, “and I believe it in part” (I Corinthians I).

There is another sense in what he likewise says to them: “Fornication is heard of among you” (I Corinthians V); and in what Eli says to his sons: “The report which I hear about you is not good” (I Kings II). Thus you must understand that there is a distinction between one kind of hearing and another, or between hearing and a formal hearing, as the Scriptures also demonstrate.

Regarding a formal hearing, Felix says to Paul: “I will hear you when your accusers arrive” (Acts XXIII); and the canons say: “One must not deny a hearing to anyone who asks for it.” But “hearing” must be understood differently where it says: “Lord, I heard your report [Col. 0423C] and was afraid” (Habakkuk III); and differently where it says: “The righteous person will not fear an evil report” (Psalm III).

Similarly, you must understand the difference between one kind of naming and another, and between naming and recognition, as Paul also says: “If any brother is named as a fornicator” (I Corinthians V); and: “Behold, I, Paul, say to you: I will come to you shortly, if the Lord wills, and I will recognize not the speech of those who are puffed up, but their power” (I Corinthians IV).

From this, just as it is found in the laws and in the canons, you must also understand that there is a difference between investigation (*cognitio*) and acknowledgment (*agnitio*), as is shown in the canons of the province of Africa, in which it is written (canon 71):

> “Whoever has sought from the emperor an investigation into public judgments shall be deprived of his own rank [Col. 0423D].”

Elsewhere, the same canons and the canons of Sardica also explain the meaning of *cognitio*. And Saint Gregory, in a homily on the Gospel, demonstrates the difference between acknowledgment, which is perceived through indications or report—as in Paul’s words, “It has been reported to me concerning you by those of Chloe” (I Corinthians I), and so forth—and investigation, which is established by legal and canonical judgment. He speaks to bishops about the Simoniac heresy, which, if he had found it established in particular persons through formal investigation, he would not have dismissed without ecclesiastical judgment.

> “To you, priests,” he says (Gregory, *Homily 17 on the Gospels), “I speak with mourning, because we have learned that some of you perform ordinations for payment, sell spiritual grace, and, at the cost of sin, heap up temporal profits from the iniquities of others [Col. 0424A]. Why, then, does the divine voice’s command not return to your memory: ‘You have received freely; give freely’ (Matthew X)? Why do you not recall before the eyes of your mind that, when our Redeemer entered the temple, he overturned the seats of those selling doves and poured out the money-changers’ coins? Who are those in the temple of God today who sell doves, except those who in the Church receive a price for the laying on of hands, through which, plainly, the Holy Spirit is given from heaven? The dove is therefore sold because the laying on of hands, through which the Holy Spirit is received, is offered for a price. But our Redeemer overturns the seats of those selling doves because he destroys the priesthood of such traders. Hence the sacred canons condemn the Simoniac heresy [Col. 0424B] and command that those who seek a price for conferring orders be deprived of the priesthood. The seat of those selling doves is therefore overturned when those who sell spiritual grace are deprived of the priesthood, either in the eyes of human beings or before the eyes of God.”

Concerning this acknowledgment, Saint Augustine also says in his book *On Penance* (chap. 3):

> “Many good Christians,” he says, “are silent and endure the sins of others which they know, because they are often left without evidence, so that they cannot prove before ecclesiastical judges the things which they themselves know. For although certain things may be true, a judge cannot easily believe them unless they are demonstrated by certain proofs. We, however, cannot exclude anyone from communion—even though this exclusion is not yet mortal but medicinal—unless that person has either confessed voluntarily or has been accused and convicted by some secular or [Col. 0424C] ecclesiastical judgment. For who would dare to assume both roles for himself, so as to be someone’s accuser and judge? The wicked must not be separated from the Church’s communion rashly or arbitrarily, but through judgment. If they cannot be removed through judgment, they should rather be tolerated like chaff among the wheat until the final winnowing, or like bad fish among the good until the separation that will take place on the shore, that is, at the end of the age.”

Regarding this acknowledgment that has reached me [Col. 0424D], you can well remember that I have already admonished you, since I heard it from many people—and it even reached the ears of the lord king—that you accepted gifts even for the laying on of hands in the ordination of ecclesiastical ranks; that for the granting of churches, you demanded rewards amounting to no more than their endowment, that is, the *mansus* which they possess under immunity, as is contained in the ecclesiastical capitularies, together with the tithes of the faithful; and that you accepted payment from disreputable priests so that they would not be investigated.

For this reason the same lord king sought to hear the truth from the sons of your church; and, because a matter known to all intervened, he ceased pursuing the inquiry. I warned you as terribly as I could that you must in no way participate in these crimes.

You also heard me speak before the altar of Saint Mary, before which you were ordained bishop, and you accepted—if perhaps you obeyed and stored it in your mind—that what you received freely, you should also give freely to others according to the Lord’s command (Matthew X). For the right hand extended toward the price of ordainers is the right hand of iniquity.

And when I heard these things about you, and learned that the lord king had inquired into them [Col. 0425A], I repeated to you the words of blessed Gregory already cited, and took care to impress upon you what follows. In his thirty-ninth homily on the Gospel he says:

> “The Lord Jesus entered the temple and began to drive out those who sold and bought in it (Luke XIX). Just as the temple of God is in a city, so the life of religious people is in the faithful populace. Often certain people assume the religious habit, and when they receive a place among the sacred orders, they turn the office of holy religion into a business transaction. Those who sell in the temple are people who grant for a reward what is lawfully due to certain persons. To sell justice is to preserve it in exchange for receiving a reward. Those who buy [Col. 0425B] in the temple are people who refuse to render to their neighbor what is just, and, when they disdain to do what is legally owed, purchase sin by giving a reward to their patrons. To them it is rightly said: ‘My house is a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of thieves’ (Isaiah LVI). For when perverse people sometimes hold a place of religion, they kill there with the swords of their wickedness, where they ought to have brought life to their neighbors through the intercession of their prayer.”

And again, in his fourth homily:

> “The Lord says: ‘You have received freely; give freely’ (Matthew X). For he knew that some people would turn this very gift of the Spirit they had received into a means of commerce and direct the signs of miracles toward the service of greed. Hence Simon, desiring the miracles performed through the laying on of hands, wished to receive [Col. 0425C] the gift of the Holy Spirit for money, so that he might sell more wickedly what he had acquired wickedly. Hence our Redeemer drove the crowds from the temple with a whip made of cords and overturned the seats of those selling doves. To sell doves is to give the laying on of hands, through which the Holy Spirit is received, not for the merit of life but for a reward.

> “There are also some who do not receive monetary rewards for ordination, yet confer sacred orders for human favor and seek from that generosity nothing but the repayment of praise. These people do not give freely what was received freely, because they seek a coin of favor for the office of holiness they have bestowed. Therefore, when the Prophet described a just man, he rightly said: ‘He shakes his hands free from every gift [Col. 0425D]’ (Isaiah XXXIII). He does not say merely, ‘who shakes his hands free from a gift,’ but adds, ‘from every gift,’ because a gift from service is one thing, a gift from the hand another, and a gift from the tongue another. A gift from service is an improperly rendered submission; a gift from the hand is money; a gift from the tongue is favor. Whoever confers sacred orders therefore shakes his hands free from every gift when, in divine matters, he seeks not only no money but also no human favor.”

And in his letter to John, bishop of the Corinthians, he says (book IV, letter 55):

> “It has reached us that in those regions no one attains sacred orders without the payment of a fee. If this is so, I say with tears and announce with groaning that, when the priestly order has fallen within, [Col. 0426A] it will not be able to stand long outside either. We know from the Gospel what our Redeemer himself did, for when he entered the temple he overturned the seats of those selling doves. To sell doves is to receive temporal profit from the Holy Spirit, whom almighty God, consubstantial with himself, grants to human beings through the laying on of hands.

> “From this evil, as I have said, it is already indicated what will follow: because those who presumed to sell doves in the temple of God have had their seats overthrown by God’s judgment. This error spreads among their subjects with increase. For the person who is advanced to sacred honor through a reward, already corrupted at the very root of his advancement, is more ready to sell to others what he bought. And where is the saying: ‘You have received freely; give freely [Col. 0426B]’ (Matthew X)? When the Simoniac heresy first arose against the holy Church, why is it not considered, why is it not seen, that the person whom someone ordains for a price is, by advancing him, made to become a heretic?

> “Since the universal Church condemns this most wicked depravity, we exhort your Fraternity to restrain by every effort of its vigilance so detestable and monstrous a sin from all the places subject to you. For if we should thereafter learn that anything of this kind has occurred, we shall correct it no longer by words but by canonical punishment, and we shall begin to hold a different judgment of you—one which ought not to be necessary.””

On this subject he also wrote terrifying and weighty things in many letters to many bishops, which you can read in their proper places and must take care to avoid.

I also told you that the words of God, spoken by Saint Peter, chief of the apostles, who condemned this heresy in Simon Magus, remain truthful and effective against everyone from that time onward, now, and until the end of the age [Col. 0426C]. Just as Simon’s money was for him a cause of perdition, so all who give or receive gifts for this purpose remain in perdition and will remain there without end, unless they perform worthy repentance for it.

Although both are heretics—both the person who gives a price for the laying on of hands and the person who receives the gift—the one who enjoys the higher office commits the graver offense, because the eminence of dignities makes the vices of sinners more serious.

May God grant that the things I hear about you from many people are not true. I adjure you by the holy and inseparable Trinity; by the cross and blood of Jesus [Col. 0426D] Christ, the Son of the living God, from whom, by whom, and through whom every ecclesiastical episcopate began; by that Holy Spirit who works especially in ordinations; by the entire army of the holy angels; by the holy Church of all the elect written in heaven; and by the future judgment, when Christ will come to judge the living and the dead, the age by fire, and to repay each person according to his works: do not involve yourself in any way, through any means or device you may devise, in this commerce opposed to God and contrary to the divine and canonical constitutions; nor, insofar as it lies with you and concerns you, consent to anyone else’s involvement. Rather, strive to forbid it to your own people with every possible adjuration [Col. 0427A].

I do not make this adjuration through some novel presumption, but follow, according to my ability, the example of blessed Paul, who wrote to Timothy, whom he ordained bishop. Although he did not make the adjuration concerning this matter but concerning other matters which he deemed necessary, he employed an adjuration of this kind. I impress his words upon you as well—his words, through whom Christ spoke:

> “I testify before God, and Christ Jesus, and the elect angels, that you observe these things without prejudice, doing nothing by inclining toward either side” (I Timothy V);

and:

> “I charge you before God, who gives life to all things, and Christ Jesus, who gave the good confession under Pontius Pilate, that you keep the commandment without stain and irreproachably until the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ” (I Timothy VI).

I did not write to you about Lucius’s letter, which was composed before the Council of Nicaea, as though the authority expressed by the canons of the sacred councils and by the decrees promulgated from them, or by the other statements of the apostolic See, were insufficient. Rather, I wrote it to demonstrate that your knowledge, which puffs up without the charity that builds up, is swollen with wind.

Receive these words, brother, patiently and kindly, and learn wisdom from experienced physicians, because at their direction a madman often carries the rope with which he will be bound.

And understand carefully the matters by which you think you can catch me. There are certain things which a metropolitan must not do without the counsel and consent of all the co-bishops of the province: for example, bringing before examination cases concerning one who accuses a bishop, canonically judging that bishop himself, deciding whether he is guilty or cleared, ordaining someone in the place of a deceased bishop [Col. 0427C], and dealing with newly arising, doubtful, or obscure cases of any kind.

There are other matters for which we possess certain and explicit judgments in the sacred rules. These may not be opposed or overturned, but authority and reason themselves compel their execution without reconsideration.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Concerning the Irregular Subscription He Appended to His Compilation

From these most certain proofs it is evident—indeed, necessity itself compels me to repeat it—that if I had refused to correct, in your parish, which was entrusted to me together with the care of the entire province of Rheims according to the privilege granted to me, what you had wrongly permitted, I would have departed through negligence from the rules previously established, whereas you departed from them through presumption [Col. 0427D].

I therefore acted according to the right of metropolitan authority. In that right of metropolitan dignity, Saint Leo’s chapter distinguished me from you, the bishop of a subordinate city who is subject to me whether you wish it or not. It ordered the metropolitans of each province to preserve inviolate the right of the dignity anciently entrusted to them, so that they might depart from the established rules through neither negligence nor presumption.

Another chapter of the same blessed Leo joined me to you in fellowship of rank, in his letter to all the bishops established throughout the various provinces, concerning sacred orders and the discipline promulgated by the canons, when he says (letter 1):

> “Our admonition declares that if any of the brethren attempts to act contrary to these constitutions and dares to admit what has been forbidden, he must know that he is to be removed from his office and will not be a participant in our communion, since he refused to be a partner in discipline.”

Let us therefore consider, not with a deceitful but with a straight balance, which of us is more closely affected by this chapter: me, who resolved by metropolitan authority to preserve in the parish of the province entrusted to me the things established as irrefragably binding; or you, who both violated and caused to be overturned the things established as inviolably binding, and who, apart from me, your primate, subscribed and caused others to subscribe contrary to the ecclesiastical statutes.

For, as the ecclesiastical statutes teach, you have no power to determine without me matters that concern the general observance of all the Lord’s priests [Col. 0428B], just as the African council decreed, saying (African Council, canon 53):

> “That those who came later should defer to those who came before, and should not presume to do anything without consulting them. On this matter,” Aurelius says, “I speak as far as my understanding retains it: those who think that, having disregarded their superiors, something may be presumed should properly be restrained by every council.”

And on this point Leo says to Theodore, bishop of Fréjus (Leo, letter 59):

> “Since in cases that concern the general observance of all the Lord’s priests, nothing ought to be carried out without the primates.”

You therefore acted contrary to the constitutions when you ordered that things which those very constitutions command to be denied to no one who asks should be denied to everyone in your parish.

You dared to admit what had been forbidden when, setting me aside, you subscribed and caused others to subscribe against these provisions—something you ought not to have done even in matters that were correct. For your subscription, as many people report, is as follows:

> “Hincmarus, by the mercy of God bishop of the Church of Laon, have subscribed to these decrees of the holy Fathers of the apostolic See, which must be obeyed. May those also whom, by the same God as author, have been entrusted to me, and who likewise hold these views, being solicitous to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, share this peace with me. But if any take a different course, unwilling to become partners in this discipline, let them not be considered participants in our communion. Done at Laon, on the eighth day before the Ides of July.”

By your subscription it is made perfectly clear that, if in any respect you hold opinions contrary to the Council of Nicaea and the other general catholic synods, and to their fixed and immutable decrees, you have separated yourself and your accomplices from catholic communion, saying: “I have subscribed that these decrees must be obeyed.”

Therefore, in the words of blessed Gregory addressing Serenus, bishop of Marseille, I address you, saying (Book IX, Letter 9):

> “Tell me, brother: from what priest has it ever been heard that what you have done was done? If nothing else, at least this ought to have recalled you: that, scorning the other brothers, you should think yourself alone holy and wise. Especially since the prohibition of the sacred canons recalls you by every means from such presumption.

“As for what you say—that by the mercy of God you are bishop of the Church of Laon—we pray that this may be true. Yet we read that the Lord says of certain men: ‘They have reigned, but not from me; they have become princes, and I did not acknowledge them’ (Hos. VIII); and: ‘I have given them a king in my anger, and a prince in my fury’ (Hos. XIII); and: ‘He makes the hypocrite reign because of the sins of the people’ (Job XXXIV).

“In the words that you subscribed, ‘Done at Laon, on the eighth day before the Ides of July,’ we understand, according to the laws approved by the Church and according to the sacred canons, that this judgment pronounced without a consul is invalid. For some subscriptions are made to record a matter or a date; others, when a judgment has been issued in writing, bind it by subscription for observance of a constitution, profession, accusation, or petition.

“‘A judgment,’ say the laws (Theod. Code, Law 1, *De constitutionibus principum*, canon 56), ‘if pronounced without writing, does not even deserve to bear the name of a judgment’; and again: ‘If after these edicts or constitutions anything is found without a date and consul, it shall lack authority.’ Hence the canons of the province of Africa order bishops to receive from their ordainers letters written in the ordainers’ own hand, containing the consul and the date.”

Regarding what you added—“May those who have also been entrusted to me, and who think likewise in these matters, share this peace with me”—you seem not to have written the words “may they share this peace with me” with a simple meaning. For there is no true peace except in catholic unanimity; otherwise they say, as it is written: “Peace, peace, when there was no peace” (Jer. VIII). “There is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord” (Isa. XLVIII).

The wicked are called those who either are not incorporated into the catholic Church through right faith, or who withdraw from that faith in belief or practice through heresies or schisms. [Col. 0429C] And you did not subscribe in catholic unanimity, nor did you make those entrusted to you subscribe, if—as I have said—you hold or have held opinions contrary to the Nicene canons, the other general councils, and their fixed decrees. Consequently, you were in no way concerned in this subscription to preserve “the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.”

For, as it is written in the edict of the Fifth Synod:

> “Those who hold perverse opinions often use expressions that are piously spoken by the orthodox, in order to deceive the simpler; but they transfer the correct meaning and exposition of those expressions to their own impiety. For sometimes the same expressions, when rightly expounded and understood, are expressions of piety; but when they are wrongly interpreted and uttered by those who hold perverse opinions, they contain impiety.”

And Saint Gregory says in Homily 10 on Ezekiel:

> “For whoever, in explaining sacred speech, composes something by lying, perhaps to please his hearers, speaks his own words and not God’s—if, that is, he lies out of a desire to please or to seduce.”

And if you inserted this apostolic sentence into your own words so that you might more easily seduce your fellow ministers into subscribing to what is not permitted, then from God’s gold and silver—that is, from divine meaning and speech—as the Lord says through the prophet to the idolatrous people, you fashioned an idol for yourself and for them out of your own interpretation.

For it is evident that the apostolic sentence which you perversely inserted in that same subscription to confirm your judgment was not spoken by blessed Paul the Apostle with the meaning in which you placed it there. [Col. 0430A] When you confirmed that subscription—or rather weakened yourself and those who subscribed with you—you were not concerned to preserve “the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace”; rather, you were concerned to dissolve the unity of the Spirit against the bond of peace.

Therefore you must take care lest you be counted among the adulterators of God’s word, whom, as I stated above, the Apostle Paul rebukes. Concerning this same sentence—“Being concerned to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace: one body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling” (Eph. IV)—he also says:

> “One does not reach the one hope of calling unless one hastens toward it with a mind united to one’s neighbors.”

The Lord says to Moses: “There is a place beside me, and you shall stand upon the rock” (Exod. XXXIII). The place with the Lord is the unity of the holy Church, upon which one stands on the rock when the solidity of its confession is rightly maintained. Those stand in the place that is with the Lord and upon the rock who do not divide themselves from the unity of the Church through heresies or schisms.

For, as Saint Hilary the pope says (Letter 2), as I quoted above:

> “One sins no less against the ordinances of the sacred traditions than one rushes into an injury against the Lord himself.”

We believe, and with the catholic Church confess, that the sacred canons were established by the Spirit of God. Therefore those who stubbornly deviate from the sacred canons through contempt sin against the Holy Spirit by whom they were established.

I added “stubbornly” because the Lord says (Matt. XII) that those who sin against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven either in this age or in the age to come. Yet we read and believe that many heretics, returning to the catholic faith, received forgiveness here for their blasphemy and gained hope of obtaining mercy in the future. Nevertheless, this does not contradict the sentence spoken elsewhere: “Turn the wicked, and they will no longer be” (Prov. XII). This does not mean that they cease to exist in essence, but that they are no longer what they had been through the guilt of impiety. Thus Paul says of himself: “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. II). That savage persecutor had been extinguished, and the devout preacher had begun to live.

Here too I continue to say what I believe and confess with the catholic Church: that the sacred canons were established by the Spirit of God, as Leo affirms with the other orthodox. That Spirit is the Spirit of the Father and the Spirit of the Son; and the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, whose substance, will, and operation are one, are one Lord. Consequently, the sacred canons were established by the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—that is, by the entire Trinity, one God and Lord. Those who stubbornly deviate from them through contempt therefore sin against the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, that is, against God and the Lord.

It is therefore established that, as Pope Hilary writes, one sins no less against the ordinances of the sacred traditions than one rushes into an injury against the Lord himself—that is, against the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

And again I added “stubbornly,” that is, “perseveringly,” because blessed John the Apostle says:

> “There is sin unto death; I do not say that one should pray for it; and there is sin not unto death; I do say that one should pray for it” (1 John V, 16).

There is sin unto death for those who remain in the same sin; there is sin not unto death for those who withdraw from that sin.
