For there is no sin for which the Church either does not pray that it be forgiven, or which, by the divinely granted power given to her, she cannot absolve those who depart from it or release those who repent. To her it is said: “Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven” (Matt. XVIII, 18).

When it is said, “Whatever you loose,” all things whatsoever they may be, however great they may be, and of whatever kind they may be, are included, whatever their condition or whatever their fall. Nevertheless, the truth of those sentences remains which declare that certain things can never be loosed, so long as those who remain in the same condition continue in them; this does not apply to those who afterward withdraw from that same sin. [Col. 0431B]

From all this it is perfectly clear concerning your same subscription, in which you say: “I have subscribed that these decrees of the holy Fathers of the apostolic see—especially those selected by you—must be obeyed.”

For if, as I said above and now say again, you hold any opinion contrary to the Council of Nicaea and the other general and catholic synods, and to their fixed and irreformable decrees, which the apostolic see and the entire catholic Church receive, venerate, and observe—or if you decree that anything contrary to them should be held and observed—you have separated yourself and your accomplices from catholic communion. And when you subscribed to what is contrary to catholic observance, you were in no way concerned in that subscription to preserve “the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.”

Nor were you a partner in the discipline of blessed Leo, who decreed (Letter 59):

> “In matters that pertain to the general observance of all the Lord’s priests, nothing ought to be carried out without the primates.”

Therefore it must be feared that you are not even a sharer in his communion. If, God forbid, you are alienated from that communion, then, together with those whose decrees you caused to be overturned—as I sent to you in writing from the sacred canons and the decrees of the Roman pontiffs—you will not be able to have communion with the catholic Church.

Nor should what I quoted above from the words of the same blessed Leo seem in any way a light matter to you. He says (Letter 84, to Leo Augustus):

> “To seek what has been revealed, to reconsider what has been completed, and to overturn what has been defined—what else is this than to fail to give thanks for the grace received, and to extend the wicked desires of deadly greed toward the food of the forbidden tree?”

But consider with great attention of heart with which sin the sin you committed by overturning what had been defined should be compared: namely, the sin that cannot be cleansed except by the blood of the Son of God, the sin committed by our first parent and transmitted to all his descendants, as the Apostle says:

> “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. V, 12).

So too, through you, sin passed to all who subscribed with you against what had been defined by the holy Fathers. They sinned in this because, under your direction, they did so in that subscription. You did not entirely free yourself from it; rather, by transgression you bound them to yourself. You wished to show me, as though I were acting against the canons, as a transgressor of the canons because in your diocese I released what you had bound. You strove to brand me with the mark of condemnation from which your conscience could not escape. And therefore, fearing human shame more than guilt before the divine eyes—lest you become contemptible to your subjects because of the wrongs you had committed, which you could have corrected by humble repentance—you resorted to that argument and devised this irregular, indeed theatrical, subscription. By this invention you provoked the Lord still further to anger and bound others together with yourself.

Read, therefore, in the decrees of Gelasius the judgment concerning Acacius and concerning the bishops who argued that he could regularly be absolved. Apply it to yourself and to those whom you caused to subscribe with you, and recognize what you have done. And wherever you read there of the apostolic see, understand it as said of your metropolitan see, which carried out the commands of the apostolic see.

For he says (Gelasius, Letter 11, at the end):

> “For this reason they were in no way in agreement with the apostolic see, because they had fallen into the lot of the transgressor Acacius, and they clearly saw that they were consequently bound by his sentence. For this reason they did not want him to be regarded as condemned, because they recognized that they themselves had been condemned in the same transgression, in which they still persist to this day.
>
> “But just as those bound by a similar condition cannot judge their accomplice not rightly condemned, nor can the guilty properly absolve the guilty, so, when that transgressor has been justly condemned, they too lie prostrate under an equal condemnation and cannot be completely absolved from it unless they repent. For just as, through one person who wrote, the transgression of all who had fallen into the same act of treachery became public, so, when the transgression was punished in the one person who had written for all or, by writing, had betrayed the will of all, the transgression of all the accomplices was likewise punished together with him or in him.”

And Saint Hilary says in the letter on the synods which he sent from exile to the Gallican bishops:

> “Nothing should seem astonishing to you, dearest brothers, about the fact that the faith has so often begun to be expounded. Heretical fury imposed this necessity, and necessity introduced the practice of expounding the faith and subscribing to what had been expounded. For where the sense of conscience is endangered, there the written word is required; nor does it hinder subscription to confess what is salutary.”

Turn, therefore, the eyes of your mind toward your action: what you did irrationally, against authority, and without any necessity in this presumptuous subscription, and what you compelled your subjects to do. Take care lest your fury in this deed, although in a different manner, equal the fury of the heretics through the same deceit. There you demanded the written word where the sense of conscience was not endangered, and you caused people to subscribe to what it is not salutary to confess—if, that is, what was subscribed by you and your accomplices is in any respect contrary to the sacred Council of Nicaea, to the decrees of the pontiffs of the Roman see issued after the Council of Nicaea, and to the sacred canons. [Col. 0432D]

In this pernicious action you have seriously erred. Blessed Gelasius shows that the transgression of all is punished in the person who prescribed it to everyone and caused all his fellow ministers to subscribe to it. Hence Gelasius says:

> “Since the same error, once condemned together with its author, carries its own execration and punishment in any participant who becomes involved in wicked communion.”

And in his letter to Anastasius (Letter 10, near the middle):

> “Since the Apostle says (Rom. I) that not only those who do what ought not to be done are considered guilty, but also those who consent to those who do it, it follows that just as perversity cannot fail to be approved when a communicator in perversity is accepted, so perversity cannot be rejected when an accomplice and follower of perversity is admitted. Certainly, according to your laws, the same judicial penalty binds those conscious of crimes and those who receive robbers; nor is he considered free of the crime who, although he did not commit it himself, nevertheless receives those who committed it into familiarity and alliance.”

And it is written in the edict of the Fifth Council:

> “We marvel at the madness of those who do what is contrary to divine Scripture, which plainly says (Wis. XIV): ‘The ungodly person and his ungodliness are equally hateful to God.’ For the action will be punished together with its agent.”

But if impiety is likewise hateful to God, then the person who acts impiously is certainly separated from God and is justly subjected to anathema. For anathema signifies nothing other than separation from God, just as in the Old and New Testaments a judgment concerning anathema signifies.

Keep in mind, therefore, what was written by blessed Paul:

> “By sinning in this way against the brothers and wounding their weak conscience, you sin against Christ” (1 Cor. VIII).

Those sin gravely against Christ who, by the most dangerous and utterly detestable lie, lie in matters of religion and wound the consciences of the weak. Of such people it is specifically written: “You will destroy all who speak lies” (Ps. V).

And it is written in the decrees of the apostolic see:

> “For whoever agrees with a schismatic cannot be denied to be a schismatic.”

Schism, as the catholic teachers say, is so called from the division of minds. A schismatic believes with the same worship and the same rite as the others, but delights only in the division of the congregation. Even if he believes as the catholic Church believes, he is a schismatic if he cuts himself off from the catholic Church in ecclesiastical doctrines. Whoever agrees with such a person cannot be denied to be a schismatic. Even if all the priests and the whole world consent, condemnation involves those who consent; the consent does not absolve them from transgression. The crime is not diminished but increased when what was private becomes general.

This is what God demonstrated in the case of all humanity when he destroyed the sinful world by the universal flood. The catholic Church clearly demonstrates their destruction: just as she prays for heretics, so she prays jointly for schismatics, that they may return to the unity of faith and peace. She knows that heretics and schismatics who remain in heresy and schism will not enter the kingdom of God, because, except in judgment, God is not in the division of minds, as blessed Gregory says.

God is in unity, and those deserve to possess his grace who do not divide themselves from one another through the scandals of sects. Hence Truth itself admonishes us, saying:

> “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark IX).

Whoever strives to possess the salt of wisdom must necessarily take care diligently never to depart from the peace of concord. Yet there are some who, while striving to know more than is necessary, recoil from the peace of their neighbors, despising them as dull and foolish. This is what you did: together with your accomplices and those who subscribed with you, you divided yourself from the bond and unity of ecclesiastical peace, scorning the authority of your metropolitan see and contradicting and resisting what, out of concern, I wrote to you and to the metropolitan Church of Laon on the basis of evangelical truth and apostolic and ecclesiastical authority. By that same authority of the catholic Church, in view of the impending danger, I dissolved what you had wrongly bound in accordance with the duty of my office.

## CHAPTER XXXVII  
### That one should not be wise in one’s own eyes, and concerning discernment in maintaining peace

Therefore, brother, I admonish both you and myself to heed what the Lord says through the prophet: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent in your own sight” (Isa. V); and what he says through the Apostle: “Do not be wise in your own estimation” (Rom. XII); and: “If anyone thinks that he knows something, he has not yet known how he ought to know” (1 Cor. VIII); and: “If anyone among you wishes to be wise, let him become foolish so that he may be wise, for the wisdom of this world is an enemy of God” (1 Cor. III).

And through the Apostle James he shows that “the wisdom that is earthly, proud, and contentious is animal and demonic; but the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, moderate, compliant, and consenting to what is good” (Jas. III).

Knowledge is indeed a virtue, and humility is the guardian of virtue. A remarkable action accompanied by pride does not exalt but burdens. For whoever gathers virtues without humility carries dust into the wind, and by the very thing in which he is seen to bear something, he is blinded more severely.

Hence it is also written: “He sends forth springs in the valleys” (Ps. CIII); and: “The valleys will abound in grain” (Ps. LXIV). Water flows down from the mountains, because the truth of doctrine abandons proud minds; but springs rise in the valleys, because humble hearts receive the word of preaching.

Hence Truth itself admonishes us, saying: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark IX). Whoever possesses the salt of wisdom must earnestly take care never to depart from the peace of concord.

And so that no one may err in maintaining peace, Truth itself, distinguishing earthly peace from heavenly peace and urging the disciples from the present toward what was to come, says: “I leave you my peace; I give you my peace” (John XIV)—that is, “I leave you a passing peace; I give you one that endures.”

Therefore, if the heart is fixed upon the peace that has been left, it never reaches the peace that is to be given. Present peace must therefore be held in such a way that it is both loved and despised. If it is loved immoderately, the mind of the one who loves it is caught in guilt. While desiring human peace too greatly, it does not rebuke the wicked practices of human beings; by consenting to the perverse, it separates itself from the peace of its author; and while fearing outward human quarrels, it is struck by the examination of the inward covenant.

Hence David, binding his whole self to the covenant of inward peace, testifies that he did not maintain harmony with the wicked, saying:

> “Do I not hate those who hate you, Lord, and waste away because of your enemies? I hate them with perfect hatred; they have become enemies to me” (Ps. CXXXVIII).

To hate the enemies of God with perfect hatred means to love what they were made for, rebuke what they do, restrain the conduct of the wicked, and benefit their lives. It must therefore be considered what guilt is incurred when rebuke is withheld and peace is maintained with the worst of people, if the Prophet even offered to God as a sacrifice the fact that, for the Lord’s sake, he had stirred up the hostility of the wicked against himself.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII  
### That he should rightly understand the words of Holy Scripture and the sacred rules

I also admonish your affection to understand the sacred rules together with the words of Holy Scripture, just as they were established by the Holy Spirit, by whom Holy Scripture too was established. For those who do not rightly understand the words of the sacred law turn the most wholesome drink of wine into a cup of poison for themselves, and strike themselves with a mortal wound by means of the medicinal knife. Through the very means by which they ought beneficially to cut away what is injured, they destroy what is sound within themselves.

Perverse intention would not drag them toward a distorted understanding if pride had not first inflated them. For while they consider themselves wiser than others, they disdain to follow others toward a better understanding. And, in order to force the name of learning from the unlearned crowd, they strive with all their might both to destroy what others have rightly understood and to strengthen their own perverse opinions.

Their wisdom “makes deceit like a sharp razor” (Ps. LI). For just as a sharp razor often pretends to produce a clean appearance on the face, while wounding the cheeks with its cut, so deceitful cunning wounds those whom it pretends to heal with sound understanding, using the deceit of a perverse interpretation.

Hence it is rightly said through the prophet: “They cut open the pregnant women of Gilead in order to enlarge their border” (Amos I). For those who perversely understand what has been well said destroy by perverse teaching the minds of the faithful that had already conceived something of the understanding of truth. While they extend the name of learning for themselves, they cut the hearts of the little ones—already pregnant with the conception of the word—with the sword of error, and thus create for themselves a reputation for teaching.

Their first necessity is not to seek empty glory. For if the root of pride is cut away, the branches of perverse assertion consequently wither. The catholic teachers and rectors of the holy Church who have written against heresies count and record among those holding perverse opinions as heretics those who do not rightly understand or rightly interpret the words of divine speech, but allegorize them according to their own opinions.

## CHAPTER XXXIX  
### That he should remove grief from the author, danger from himself, and reproach from them both

[Col. 0436A]

I admonish you with paternal and fraternal affection to remove grief from me, danger from yourself, and the reproach inflicted upon us both by many. From me, indeed, grief; for, as Saint Gregory says: “Evils inflicted by strangers cause lesser grief, but those which we suffer from persons in whose dispositions we had confidence rage within us with greater torments, because, together with bodily harm, the evils of lost charity torture us.”

For this reason the Lord says through the Psalmist concerning Judas, his betrayer: “And indeed, if my enemy had cursed me, I would surely have endured it; and if he who hated me had spoken great things against me, I would surely have hidden myself from him. But you, a man of one mind with me, my leader and my acquaintance, who together with me took sweet food, we walked in the house of God in concord” (Ps. LIV). And again: “The man of my peace, in whom I hoped, who ate my bread, has multiplied treachery against me” (Ps. XL). It is as though he were openly saying of his betrayer: “I bore his transgression all the more grievously because I felt it from one who seemed to be mine.”

Therefore all the elect, because they are members of the supreme Head, also follow their Head in sufferings, so that in their death they experience as adversaries those in whose life they had trusted; and the reward of their work increases for them in proportion as their gain in virtue advances even through another’s loss of charity. And because missiles that are foreseen strike less, and we bear the evils of the world more tolerably if we are fortified against them by the shield of foreknowledge, I bear these things from you more tolerably because I read that the Lord long ago said through the prophet: “Let each one beware of his neighbor, and let him have no confidence in any brother; for every brother will utterly supplant, and every friend will walk deceitfully, and a man will mock his brother and will not speak the truth” (Jer. IX). And a little later: “With his mouth he will speak peace with his friend, and secretly he will lay snares for him. Shall I not visit for these things, says the Lord?” (Matt. X). And Truth itself says: “A man’s enemies are those of his household” (Mal. II).

And although it is written: “The lips of the priest shall keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth,” which among other things says, “Honor your father and your mother,” “because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Exod. XX), you, on the contrary, lest the greatness of the Lord’s mercies—which I received from his hand by gratuitous grace without any merit—should exalt me, have been given to me as a thorn for recognizing my weakness, an angel of Satan, to buffet me and your mother, the metropolitan see of Rheims that nourished you, by your haughty conduct and disobediences. But, knowing that strength is made perfect in weakness, I will gladly glory in the things inflicted upon my weaknesses, whether by God through bodily afflictions, by the devil through temptations, or by man through whatever assaults, so that the strength of Christ, who perfects strength in weakness, may dwell in me who am weak.

Remove from yourself as swiftly as possible also the danger of the discord which you seem to entertain against me contrary to authority, reason, and your own salvation; knowing most certainly that, however great the virtues in which you excel, you can in no way become spiritual if you neglect to be united with me and your other brothers through concord. For it is written: “The fruit of the Spirit is charity, joy, peace” (Gal. V); and whoever does not take care to preserve peace refuses to bear the fruit of the Spirit. For, if you have sound understanding, you are certain that for as long as you are at discord with the charity of your neighbors, you offer God no sacrifice of a good work; much less if you are at discord with my love—I who received you kindly to be nourished, nourished you as an orphan with tender affection, tonsured you into the clergy, instructed you in letters through myself and through all whom I could, advanced you through each rank to the order of bishop, and obtained for you the familiarity and sweet affection of our lord king.

You must consider with great fear what is written: “If you offer your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go first to be reconciled to your brother; then, when you return, offer your gift” (Matt. V, 23). From this command you should consider how intolerable is shown to be the fault of the person whose offering is rejected. For although all evils are washed away by the good things that follow them, we must consider how great are the evils of discord, which, unless they are utterly extinguished, do not permit good to follow; because, whatever good works may be in us, if charity is absent, through the evil of discord an opening is made in the battle-line by which the enemy can enter to strike us.

Believe me: I have discord not with you, but with your blameworthy habits and movements of conduct, for which I have often reproved and chastised you both by word and letter, and have grieved, as I still grieve. Do what I beneficially desire for you and what suits your ministry, and you will find me conciliatory and helpful in all things. Otherwise I shall wait, in the hope that through God’s grace the word of the Lord, which still labors between you and me, may at last be able to rest: “If your brother sins against you,” he says, “rebuke him; if he repents, forgive him” (Matt. XVIII).

Meanwhile, while this word of the Lord labors between you and me, I shall continually use the medicine of the healthful antidote against the deadly cup of discord offered me by you, which the Lord and our Savior, mindful of our weakness, deigned to bestow, saying: “When you stand to pray, forgive, if you have anything against anyone in your hearts, so that your heavenly Father also may forgive you your sins” (Mark XI). And assuredly, when our Creator sees such a pleasing disposition in our mind, he will release us from sin, because he will receive a gift in place of fault. This gift will also become a whole burnt offering by the grace of merciful God if it is fine flour mixed with oil and fried in the pan of zeal: namely, when we mercifully love, and pray for amid sacred rites, the one whom we seem to pursue with the ardor of salutary zeal, or by whom we are pursued with the pallor of envy—imitating him who had come even to die for his enemies and yet said that he would lay down his life for his friends, so that he might surely show us that, when by loving we can gain profit from enemies, even those who persecute us are friends.

I say this not because I fear or greatly feel your persecution in temporal losses or insults; even if you wish to harm me, you cannot. Rather, though I am unjust—for I truly and from my heart confess myself a sinner—I speak of that persecution of which blessed Peter says: “Those among whom Lot dwelt tormented his soul day by day by their lawless deeds” (2 Pet. II); and of which the Apostle, recalling the ancient history, says: “Just as then he who was according to the flesh persecuted him who was according to the Spirit, so also now” (Gal. IV). For, so to speak, the iron of our soul is not brought to the fineness of a sharp edge unless the file of another’s wickedness has rubbed it.

## CHAPTER XL  
### That what he was accustomed to say—that the king had opposed him at Hincmar’s counsel—was not true

And because I have been told that you are accustomed to tell many people that whatever our lord king has done against you concerning your men, concerning his men sent to Laon, and concerning his having commended you to Conrad, he did at my prompting, counsel, and consent, I tell you that this is untrue. I can show this from writings sent at that time to the same our lord king and also to others concerning this matter. And before many bishops at Pîtres I told our lord king that I had heard you say this; and before those same bishops our lord king replied—as he certainly spoke the truth—that he had done this neither at my prompting, nor by my counsel, nor with my consent, although there were and are certain matters for which you ought to have been, and ought still to be, corrected by metropolitan authority, synodal assembly, and royal power.

I say this not because I think it worthwhile to excuse myself before you, since our elders show it to be foolish if we seek to please, or fear to displease, those whom we know do not please good judges; but so that, in matters in which I can do so truthfully, as far as it lies in me and as far as I am able, I may make good the good name which the Apostle commands a bishop to have even from those who are outside. But because we are commanded by divine authority to obey the king, I do not deny that at his command I replied from the Scriptures, sacred laws, and sayings of the saints to your letters sent to him. If in that reply you have found that I said or did anything wrongly, show it; and I shall either defend it reasonably without contention or acknowledge it humbly without dispute.

## CHAPTER XLI  
### That, if he recognized his fault, he should seek forgiveness out of fear of God
Moreover, if I were to acknowledge that I had acted against the authority and the due unanimity of fraternal love which, as I said above, I heard that you had attributed to me, then, since the blessed apostle John says, “If we confess our sins, the Lord is faithful and just, so that he may forgive us our sins” (1 John 1), and since confession is the first hope of salvation, followed by love—for “love covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4)—I would not fail to seek from that source the healing medicine of pardon, not out of human fear, but out of fear of God, fraternal love, and concern for my own salvation.

For we priests must not read and heed perfunctorily what the Holy Spirit says even to laymen and women through the blessed Gregory (Homily 32 on the Gospels):

> There is a point at which each person should question himself and prove himself truthfully in the confession of Christ. We are often afraid of being despised by those close to us, and we disdain to endure insults in speech. If perhaps a quarrel occurs with a neighbor, we are ashamed to be the first to make satisfaction. For the carnal heart, while it seeks the glory of this life, rejects humility; and often the very person who is angry desires that the one at odds with him be reconciled, but he is ashamed to go first to make satisfaction. Let us consider the deeds of Truth, so that we may see where the actions of our perversity lie. For if we are members of the supreme Head, we ought to imitate the one to whom we are joined. What, then, does Paul, that outstanding preacher, say as an example for our instruction? “We are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us; we beseech you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God” (2 Corinthians 5). Behold, by sinning we have created discord between ourselves and God, and yet God first sent his ambassadors to us, so that we who sinned might come, when entreated, to God’s peace. Therefore let human pride be ashamed, and let anyone be confounded if he does not first make satisfaction to his neighbor, when, after our fault, God himself—so that we may be reconciled to him—also entreats us through intervening ambassadors, though he is the one who has been offended.

## CHAPTER XLII. On removing from both of us the reproach inflicted by many

Remove, then, by doing what you ought and what I desire and ask—and would that I had been worthy to be heard—the reproach from you and me which many attribute to me: namely, that I ordained as bishop one who has become such a man, acting contrary to the disposition of divine ordering, against the king, against me, against the Church entrusted to you, and against very many others.

But those who attribute these things to me do not consider that God, who knows all things, ordained Judas as an apostle, chosen not for present righteousness but so that the divine dispensation might be fulfilled through him; likewise Saul as king, though later rejected, of whom it is written: “He was a chosen and good man, and there was no man among the children of Israel better than he” (1 Samuel 9). God, who knows all things, ordered everything through his providence and incurred no guilt, since he could not sin. But I, as a human being ignorant of what was to come, ordained you through lack of foresight and became the instrument of a divine judgment that was not unjust, because, as I fear, I deserved this through my other sins.

Although the holy apostles, together with the blessed Stephen and the other deacons, also ordained Nicolas, they nevertheless did not share, through the laying on of their hands, in his words and deeds, which were later shown to be blameworthy. When they ordained him, they believed him good and hoped that he would remain good forever. Nor did Samuel incur guilt in the ordination of Saul, whom he ordained at the Lord’s command and whom the Lord later rejected; as the sacred history relates, he mourned him for a very long time, just as I grieve over you.

It is also attributed to me that I ordained you, my nephew, bishop because of our kinship. As though other bishops had not also been ordained by me who are not related to me by blood! Those who make this accusation refuse to consider that blood relationship does not prevent anyone from being ordained, provided that the person to be ordained has been chosen and requested according to ecclesiastical rules. Do we not read that the Lord, from whom and through whom the episcopate began, ordained apostles who were related to him by blood?

Yet although, in the case of you, my nephew, I did what causes me to groan—for I do not know how he who is terrible in his counsels toward the children of men, who has made darkness his hiding place, arranges this and my other deeds in his hidden judgment—I nevertheless know my almighty advocate and merciful judge, before whom is all my desire and from whom my groaning is not hidden.

For if you heed the admonitions that the blessed Paul addressed to Timothy, whom he had ordained bishop while still young, and if you remove from me and from yourself the reproach of your ordination, among other things he says: “Let no one despise your youth” (1 Timothy 4); that is, present yourself in such a way that no one regards you as contemptible because of the youthfulness of your age, since when a person’s life is despised, his preaching too is bound to be despised.

If these words, brother, seem in any respect harsh to you—though they were not spoken with the intention, God forbid, of bringing about your condemnation or dishonor in any way, but rather your salvation and correction—consider that, as the blessed Gregory says, through the bitter drink of a remedy one reaches the outcome of the salvation one desires. And Solomon says: “The wounds of a friend are better than the kisses of an enemy who hates” (Proverbs 27). And the Lord says: “Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline” (Revelation 3); and, “The Lord chastises the one whom he loves, and scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12).

## CHAPTER XLIII. On the falsification of the sacred Scriptures and his response to the letter concerning Nivinus; which canons are to be accepted, and on his ignorance and boastfulness; likewise concerning Bertricus, and the fact that he often admonished him

[Col. 0440D]

Finally, I hear that you defame me before many people because I am accustomed to mutilating the sacred Scriptures and twisting them to suit my own meaning. Although I still firmly believe that I have not done this in even one place, nevertheless, if you can prove what you say—and if you wish to bring this forward as proof—produce it before as many people and before whomever you please. I will either openly show that you do not understand my words correctly, or that they have been falsified by someone else. And if I should discover that I have done what you say, if indeed you say that I have, I will hasten to correct it.

For what you are said to claim about me, Gothescalcus was accustomed to do concerning the Scriptures: namely, to mutilate them and violently twist them to suit his own meaning; and also to utter to his hearers things that are not contained in the canonical books. I showed above that the ancient heretics likewise used to do this, because, as the blessed Gregory says:

> Heretics often, while striving to establish their own perverse doctrines, bring forward things that are certainly not held in the pages of the sacred books.

For this reason the outstanding preacher admonishes his disciple, saying: “O Timothy, guard the deposit, avoiding profane novelties of words” (1 Timothy 6). For when heretics desire to be praised as possessing exceptional intellect, they bring forward certain new things that are not found in the old books of the ancient Fathers. Thus it happens that, while they desire to appear wise, they sow seeds of folly in their wretched hearers.

And because Gothescalcus was convicted of having done these things in the episcopal assembly, that same council, as it is written, “He who imposes silence on a fool appeases anger” (Proverbs 26), imposed silence upon him and entrusted him to my custody. In this way the anger of some of his accomplices—who were already boiling over like worms swarming in corruption—was partly appeased, and they were gathered by the Lord as though into a waterskin, like the waters of the sea, while the bitterness of their perverse minds concerning what Gothescalcus had taught them has not yet burst forth among us into the voice of depraved license.

What Gothescalcus did concerning the sacred Scriptures, and what you accuse me of doing, you yourself, if I may say so with your permission, are accustomed to do concerning the sacred canons, ecclesiastical rules, and laws; and I can show that you have done so already four times.

First, there is the little scroll sent to me through Hadulphus, your archpriest, in which, by mutilating certain canons and laws, expelling certain passages from their context, and perversely interpreting them according to your own meaning, you composed several accusations against me concerning the chapel of my parish situated in the village of Attola.

Likewise, there is the little scroll that you gave me, in which, weaving together a story about Amalbert and his wife, you directed many attacks against him.

There are also the scrolls sent to the lord king and to me through your fellow ministers, in which you described the histories of the disputes between you and that same lord king, and likewise between you and Normannus, and explained the novelties of your words and deeds. In them you twisted against others, according to your own interpretation, the sentences of Scripture, the canons, and the laws that struck at you. I can demonstrate this individually and one by one from your speech and conduct and from those same sentences, with the teaching of our predecessors supporting me.

Likewise, in the small booklets sent to me by you through the venerable archbishop Wenilo, you collected many things that differed among themselves, which you judged to support your position, failing to see—or rather, being unable or unwilling to see—that they disagreed with one another. From the very letters out of which you compiled that collection, you deliberately omitted the passages that followed in conjunction with them. You also omitted those things which the entire Catholic Church receives, holds, follows, venerates, honors, and embraces, and which I returned to you in a document through the aforesaid venerable archbishop Wenilo—a small body, but of the greatest merit—and you did not wish to call them back to mind.

What I am saying would be excessive if the very writings of yours that I possess did not testify that these things are so; and the law that the Catholic Church receives expressly decrees, saying:

> A person may make confession in judgment not only by his own voice, but also by writings and by whatever means he can; but he can be convicted only by documentary evidence or witnesses.

And if, in these writings, you deny the things I mention, you will be able, if necessary, to be refuted in judgment.

Gelasius also says in his decrees to the bishops established throughout Dardania: “Since anyone can plainly be recognized either by his own profession or by his communion.”

Furthermore, most recently you sent me, through Heddon, the head of your clergy, a little scroll written in your customary manner, in response to the letters that I sent you concerning those who were offending in my parish. They read as follows:

**Hincmarus, bishop of Reims, to Hincmarus, our fellow bishop, greetings.**

**Nivinus, etc. The remainder of this letter: see above, column 224.**
You did not receive this letter as you ought to have done. Instead, finding in it an opportunity, you breathed out in words the bitterness that you harbor in your heart against me, wishing to display your wisdom and my folly, and to show that I had acted unjustly toward Nivinus and contrary to authority, and to silence me, so that I would not dare to rebuke you concerning what I had heard from you—so that, if those things should perhaps be true, you might correct yourself, and, if not, might take precautions lest you fall into them. For just as, so far as depends on us, we ought not through our own fault to sharpen the tongues of detractors for disparagement, so we ought, as reasonably as we can, to restrain the slanders of detractors.

But your mind is not such that you can hear kindly and patiently what is said or written to you in kindness, unless it is of the kind that occupies your own heart. Hence Solomon says: “Vinegar upon nitre is he who sings songs to a very evil heart” (Proverbs 25). “Vinegar,” says Gregory, “if it is poured upon nitre, immediately makes the nitre seethe and boil over; and a perverse mind, when it is corrected by rebuke or urged toward good by the sweetness of preaching, becomes worse through the correction, and is inflamed into the wickedness of murmuring by that through which it ought to have been restrained from wickedness.”

Yet to my letters, which you wished to dissect paragraph by paragraph, you replied without authorities appropriate to them, and in this you did not imitate, with right understanding, the man who is accustomed to answer your writings with authorities supported by truth and composed in this manner. For in this matter you do not strive to attend to reason according to the law, but to confirm your own intention by whatever means you can.

The man who is accustomed to answer your writings in this way did not learn this manner of response from those from whom he undertook to learn these things. As for Nivinus, I took care, as was my duty, to make known to you what had happened. I do not think it is appropriate for you to undertake his defense. But if you wish to undertake it against me, and reason and authority agree, I do not, so far as depends on me, refuse to answer you about it. Furthermore, he is of age; let him speak for himself. And if he wishes to accuse me lawfully and according to the rule—whether concerning excommunication, collaboration, or any other matter of prejudice—I do not refuse to give him an account of it.

No one, however, can accuse me before you according to canonical procedure, nor appeal from my judgment to your judgment. Nor has the care of the whole province of Rheims, together with my parish, been entrusted to you, so that I should be obliged to give you any further account of it than I have endeavored to give you in writing.

Examine the letter of blessed Augustine to his own primate Xantippus, which you are able to read above, and you will find that you owe me an account of your judgments. If anyone has appealed from your judgment to mine, I ought to investigate the truth of the matter and settle each point canonically.

When you heard these things, concerning which you wrote back to me after my letters had been sent to you, you ought humbly to have reported to me what you had heard about the matter, so that, if I had acted improperly, I might take care to correct it; or else I might have written back the truth to your filial affection with fraternal and paternal kindness. You would do this if you were humble and had charity toward me.

Nevertheless, following to the best of my ability the example of blessed Peter the apostle, who, when those lesser than himself asked why he had entered among the Gentiles, gave an orderly account and produced witnesses for his explanation, I think it good, in whatever way you have entrusted to me the matters about which you wrote, to write back to you again what is true about them.

Namely: as you wrote, I did not attribute to him the matters of which he had been accused on the basis of anyone’s wicked or false suggestion, nor did the case require witnesses to establish his crime, because, as you yourself wrote, the nature of the case either excuses or accuses each person.

Thus the Lord, concerning the matter in which a certain householder was told that someone had been accused before him of wasting his goods, said: “What is this that I hear about you? Give an account of your stewardship” (Luke 16). And above you have sufficient information about the cases in which witnesses examined lawfully and regularly must be sought, and about those cases that do not require witnesses.

It is manifest to the priests and to the other clerics, to the laymen and women, to the noblemen and peasants in our city that Nivinus first secretly stole from that monastery the nun about whom I wrote to you—who had been consecrated to God from childhood in a monastery and veiled by a priest. Nivinus kept her for many nights in the residence where he stayed near the gardens, with the consent of the gatekeeper, through whose complicity she left the monastery and was taken away by Nivinus’s men. In that monastery the nun had been disciplined according to the rule.

Therefore, when the rumor began to grow and I began to return to the city, he sent his men, namely Walchanus and Lupus, who at night led her out of that monastery by ladders hired for a price. They took her to the benefice that I had given him in our parish, and there Nivinus kept the same nun for several days, as the priests, the people living nearby, and the peasants know most clearly.

When our officials began to seek the nun, he had her taken by those same men to Calmont. As for the hearings granted him by me, the canons, monks, faithful and noble laymen, and parish priests know how many there were and how long they lasted. In their presence and with their counsel I dealt with the matter according to what I found in the sacred rules.

Regarding your statement that I asked him how he would clear his reputation: I did not ask him this because I did not know that he could not do it, but so that I might thereby compel him to confession and penitence and afterward to pardon, since I could not induce him voluntarily to undertake these things. I brought him to the point that, if the men mentioned above, since they are not of free condition, should undergo the judgment of God by means of hot water or cold water, whatever God might show me would be sufficient.

When he saw that he had been convicted and constrained by reason, he burst into defiance and insults. I told him that, unless he either confessed or made satisfaction to my parish for that of which he was being defamed, neither he nor those of his men who had stolen the same nun with him could remain in my parish. As he continued in insults and accusations—and since he was not of my parish or my province, and possessed neither property nor slaves in the kingdom of our lord by which I could constrain him to give an account, and he refused to submit to coercion through a benefice or private property—I excommunicated him from my parish.

What you say—that a bishop ought to do good to everyone and receive all the faithful—is true, and would that you acted accordingly. But your neighbors and parishioners say otherwise about you, and those specially entrusted to you think otherwise.

As for your saying that I had heard from you the things I reported to you: if I had reported such things to someone else, I know that he would have thanked me for them. You too would do so, as I understand it, if the bitterness of your mind allowed it and you did not wish to find an opportunity to compile again, in writings that were not relevant to the matter, what you gathered in the little booklets sent by you through the venerable Archbishop Wenilo, and to provoke me into saying something from which you could seize upon a phrase.

You clearly demonstrate this yourself in the writing mentioned above. After recalling the statements of Anacletus, Victor, Callistus, and Eleutherus—who, as Gelasius says, sent their letters to various persons before the Council of Nicaea for the consolation of certain people—you add:

“Behold, father, which canons are to be received, venerated, and observed.”

Because, as is evident, you called me “father” more in mockery than in veneration, I say to you: “And if I am a father, where is my honor?” (Malachi 1).

I will nevertheless say to you: Son, whether by your own authority or by that of another, if these are the canons to be received, venerated, and observed that you have recalled, which are those that both the apostolic see and all bishops throughout the world—from the pontiff of the first apostolic see even to the bishop most recently ordained after you, and indeed the whole Catholic Church—call canons?

Which are those that the Church retains for reception, veneration, and observance, from the Council of Nicaea—the first in our books, which our predecessors received from the apostolic see to be followed in order—through the African Council? Which are those that Innocent, Zosimus, Boniface, Celestine, Leo, Hilary, Symmachus, Gelasius, Hormisdas, Gregory, and all the others call canons to be observed?

Among these writings are the letters of the pontiffs of the apostolic see, which you call canons. Yet Gelasius, as I stated above, distinguishes between them: he decreed that those councils were to be observed as canons, while he says that those letters, sent for the consolation of certain persons, are to be received with veneration.

Likewise, in his decrees, among other things, Gelasius says in his memorandum to Faustus:

“They set the canons against us, although the Eastern bishops do not know what they are saying; and they themselves reveal that they are acting against those canons when they refuse to obey the first see, which gives sound and upright counsel. These are the canons that wished appeals from the whole Church to be brought before the examination of this see.”

It is clear that he is speaking of the Sardican canons. Innocent, in his letter to Victricius, and Gregory, in his letter to Vincentius, say similar things, as does also the work that you are reading here.

And in the same place, after a little further discussion, he says:

“Let them see, then, whether they have other canons by which they may carry out their absurdities. But these, which are celebrated as sacred, ecclesiastical, and legitimate—could they not only fail to summon the apostolic see for judgment, but should the bishop of the city of Constantinople, which certainly has received no name among the sees according to the canons, not have been removed from communion when he joined the faithless?”

For, as he himself shows, Heraclea was a suffragan see.

It is evident that Gelasius is speaking here of the sacred Nicene canons, which established the privileges of the sees, as is plainly shown in their sixth chapter. Hence Boniface says in his third letter to Hilary of Narbonne:

“No one, I think, is unaware of the decree of the Nicene synod, which commands—and let us set down its very words—that each province ought to have one metropolitan, and that no one province can be subject to two. Since it is not permissible to believe otherwise, they judged, with the prompting of the Holy Spirit, that this must be observed among themselves.”

And a little later:

“We say this so that your charity may understand that we preserve the prescriptions of the canons so carefully that our own decree also establishes that each province must always await the direction of its metropolitan in all matters.”

And Leo says to Anastasius (Letter 88, chapter 1):

“According to the canons of the holy Fathers, established by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, we decree that the bishops who are metropolitans of the individual provinces retain inviolate the right of the dignity anciently entrusted to them.”

Likewise Gelasius, as I showed above, after listing the authoritative Scriptures and the synods of Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus, and Chalcedon, added:

“And if there are any councils established by the holy Fathers after the authority of these four, we have decreed that they too are both to be guarded and to be received.”

As I said before—and necessity itself often compels me to repeat it—he says that those very letters, issued at different times by the apostolic see for the consolation of various Fathers, are to be received with veneration, just as we do.

I will add this also: if, as you say, the letters of the aforementioned pontiffs of the apostolic see are canons to be received and venerated—so that whatever you wish you call holy and lawful, and whatever you do not wish you call unholy and unlawful, as though everything depended upon your will and no one could resist your will—tell us, please, what you think of the decrees of those who, after the Council of Nicaea and the other Catholic councils, enacted and confirmed decretal constitutions concerning those same sacred canons for observance: Siricius, Innocent, Zosimus, Boniface, Celestine, Leo, Hilary, Symmachus, Gelasius, Hormisdas, Gregory, and all the others whose decrees the Catholic Church, and our Fathers and predecessors, held and venerated as things to be observed.

Since in some matters these decrees differ from those whom you call canons, decide with your magisterial authority which of them we ought to follow and which to reject. For unless you drive these things out of our custom with the rod of your singular authority—things that, like our Fathers, we have absorbed into our minds as matters to be held and observed—I do not think you can easily remove from ecclesiastical usage in general those things that we hold. You can read enough and more than enough about them above; and if that is not sufficient for you, nothing more will be sufficient.

I will add only one point: when you say, “Behold which canons are to be received, venerated, and observed,” you have not sufficiently examined those same canons. For in them, as you wrote, it is stated that whoever chooses to accuse another must accuse him in person and not through another, with a written indictment first presented.

Because you tried to turn this to your own defense, you ought to have read further. That very sentence was taken from the ancient Roman laws. In those laws, in the interpretation of Valentinian’s edict concerning episcopal judgment—namely, in the later constitution—it is written as follows (Interpretation of the Novels of Valentinian):

“This law establishes many things concerning various matters; but first, concerning clerics, it states that they must not approach episcopal judgment unless bound by a compromise. This was abolished by the later law of Majorian.”

The Church has preserved that constitution from then until now, just as it requested and obtained it.

But, as you read in my letters, you ought also to have understood the difference between an admonition and a judgment concerning an accusation, and between what I said—“if it is as it is widely spread by many, even publicly in public assemblies”—and what I did not say, namely, “that it is so.” Hence you are accused by many, even publicly in public assemblies or before public assemblies, of what is unlawful.

When you confusedly said that you were surprised if some people had made a petition to you from those hearings concerning this case, adding the words of Callistus, “Let no teacher be accused through writings,” you did not make the distinction correctly, because you did not properly understand from the laws and canons the difference between a petition and an accusation.

Turn over the laws and the decrees of the apostolic see, and learn what you do not know.

So once again, as though tracking you, I shall follow you through winding byways and tell you a little of many things—enough, however, to enable me to overtake you.

Innocent wrote to Bishops Maximus and Severus (Letter 4):

“Recently, our son Maximilianus, an official, brought forward a complaint of what kind, as the attached text of his petition makes clear.”

And Gregory wrote to the subdeacon Sabinus (Book 7, Indiction 11, Letter 46):

“The clergy of the church of Regium has complained to us, by submitting a petition, about our most reverend brother Boniface, its bishop, asking that it be permitted to come to us, so that the cases themselves might be carefully examined here. But since in the meantime we have not foreseen that our aforesaid brother should be brought here, it has seemed good to us to appoint someone there to investigate the same case.

“Therefore, with the holy Gospels present, let your Experience, together with Paulinus, Proculus, Palumbus, Venerius, and Martianus, our most reverend brothers and fellow bishops, with no regard for anyone’s person, examine with all equity and care both the complaint of the clergy against their bishop, as we have said, and any complaint he may perhaps have against them. Whatever you discover to be true, report to us carefully and diligently together with our aforesaid brothers, so that, having been made more certain by your report, we may decide what ought to be done.”

And to the aforesaid bishops he wrote:

“The clergy of the church of Regium has complained to us, by submitting a petition, about our most reverend brother Boniface, its bishop,” and so forth.

But concerning an inquiry without a petition or accusation, blessed Gregory likewise wrote to Sabinus (Book 11, Letter 28):

“It has come to our attention,” he says, “that our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Palumbus is neglecting the causes and interests of his church or parishes—something painful to say.”

And after a little further discussion:

“Therefore let your Experience take care to admonish our aforesaid brother to vindicate and defend reasonably the property and interests of his church or parishes, as well as their ministries,” and so forth.

Concerning the accusation of a bishop or of a cleric of any order, you can read sufficient material above from the sacred canons.

Nevertheless, you must understand carefully what the laws say about accusation:

“In criminal cases or charges,” they say, “no one may accuse by mandate, nor may he obtain this through an imperial rescript. Rather, the person who brings the charge must accuse in person and while present.”

Thus you may understand in what sense they say this concerning accusation.

And the canons say (Council of Carthage, canon 19):

“Whoever of the bishops is accused, let the accuser bring the case before the primate of that province; and let the person against whom the crime is brought not be suspended from communion unless, summoned by letter to state his case on the appointed day before the chosen judges, he fails to appear.”

It is clear that the accused bishop is shown not to be present before the primate, since he is ordered to be summoned by letter.

And Boniface says concerning Maximus (Letter 2):

“If he wishes to be present, let him answer the charges in person, if he has confidence—that is, before the accuser who is present. If he neglects to appear, let him not gain a postponement of the sentence by reason of his absence.”

Therefore adapt your understanding to well-spoken statements, and do not hand over good statements to be misunderstood by twisting them to your own meaning.

Whether you wish it or not, those will be the canons that the Catholic Church calls canons; they will not be the canons that, in your negligence, you invoke as canons for the license of your unrestrained conduct.

The letters issued by the apostolic see for the consolation of various Fathers will be letters to be received with veneration; these you call canons. And the councils established by the holy Fathers will be matters to be guarded and received for their authority, as Gelasius and the other pontiffs of the Roman see decreed, together with those who, under the prompting of the Holy Spirit within them, established sacred canons in those same councils—those whom the apostolic see and the Catholic Church call canons.

The obscure words, gathered from everywhere through little glosses and set down without reason, which you have placed in this writing—as you also collected them in others formerly sent to the lord king and to me—reprove you for the vanity of ostentation. The Apostle says: “Avoid novel expressions” (1 Timothy 6); and: “I would rather speak five words in the Church for edification than ten thousand words in a tongue” (1 Corinthians 14).

You cannot speak, or even understand without an interpreter, the language in which you were born, although sufficient Latin words were available for you to use in the places where you inserted Greek, obscure, and sometimes Scottish and other barbarous expressions, as you thought fit, marked and corrupted. It is therefore clear that you did not insert those Greek words, which you yourself do not understand, so improperly out of humility or for the sake of making your meaning clear. Rather, you inserted them most foolishly for ostentation, so that all who read them might understand that you wished to vomit up what you had not swallowed.

You had this habit even from childhood in the things that I asked you to dictate, especially in verses, and particularly in Porphyrian figures. In them you deliberately placed foreign and obscure words, inappropriate words devoid of useful meaning, which you yourself did not understand.

I perceived this inwardly, and it greatly displeased me. But when I saw that you were burning with vanity and love of praise, and realized that, in the immaturity of adolescence, I could not kindle in you such strength of mind as would draw you toward the study of learning and versification and erase from you the perversity of vanity, lest you be broken by a sharper correction and called back from your studies, I allowed you for the time being to devote yourself to literary study and to boast of your knowledge, until, at a more mature age, I might restrain you from that vice as well.

In this I followed, to the best of my ability, the Apostle, who, perceiving that his hearer was weak—either still wishing to act wrongly or rejoicing in the reward of human praise for right action—said: “Do you wish not to fear the authority? Do what is good, and you will have praise from it” (Romans 12).

Meanwhile, because the time before the time at which I had intended to address this matter passed away, you ought, in accordance with the Apostle’s command to avoid novel expressions, to have restrained yourself from this vanity and ostentation as a teacher and bishop. For holy, wise, and highly authoritative men, even those skilled in both languages, Greek and Latin, did not wish to insert Greek words ostentatiously into their writings unless they were words placed without interpretation in the Scriptures, canons, or laws and treated as though they were Latin in ordinary use.

As for the Hebrew language, they used “Alleluia,” “Hosanna,” and “Amen” without interpretation because of the authority of the original language and the reverence owed to their meaning.

We modern men too possess Greek glossaries, which we have heard are called *lexica*—“Lexicons”—as well as the writings of wise men concerning obscure names. We are clever enough to lengthen and extend our little compositions to such a point that we can produce Greek words or obscure words taken from glossaries to inspire admiration or bewilderment in those who do not know them, or in those who have itching ears. Scripture opposes this vanity, saying: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Ecclesiastes 1).

I fear that, just as you act concerning words and the meanings of canons and laws, delighting in seeking novelties of expression in them, the arrogance of your heart and the ostentation of inflated and empty knowledge may lead you so far that you will act and go astray in the meanings of Scripture as well. For Scripture says: “Whoever despises small things will gradually fall” (Ecclesiasticus 19).

Whoever neglects to correct and avoid lesser faults falls headlong into greater ones and, departing from the state of justice, falls entirely—not suddenly, but by degrees.

Therefore attend to what the Apostle says:

“If anyone thinks that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know” (1 Corinthians 8);

“If anyone wishes to be wise among you, let him become a fool, so that he may be wise” (1 Corinthians 3);

“Do not be wise in your own eyes” (Romans 12);

“Do not set your mind on high things, but associate with the lowly” (ibid.).

Blessed Gregory likewise says in his letter that, when sending greetings to the lady Dominica, he did not write back because, although she was Latin, she wished to write to him in Greek. He considered it of little importance to write back to her, since he weighed in his heart what she had received through speech in writing.

Regarding your request that I instruct you about how I would proceed against Bertricus if he belonged to my province but not to my own parish, I answer you under the inspiration of the one who, when those who spoke to him said, “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth, and that you do not care about anyone, for you do not regard the person of men; tell us, is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar or not?” (Matthew 22), replied:

“I will ask you one question.”

Write back to me fully and in order concerning what I did and said, and what you did and said, in the hearing concerning the boundary of our parishes. In that matter you stopped the agreement concerning Amalbert, my parishioner, who had lawfully taken a wife in your parish and my province and brought her into my parish. You irregularly excommunicated him, and you requested that his lawfully taken wife—who had reported to you by your command that the same man, her husband, was unable to have intercourse with her—be brought from my parish at Laon to your judgment.

Then I will tell you how I would act regarding Bertricus if he belonged to my province but not to my own parish.

Concerning your statement, “The manner of correction must be known”—namely, whether the correction of the aforementioned Bertricus was secret or public, whether he had been separated from the fellowship of Christians or from the body and blood of the Lord, since you say that you had not heard him placed under public penance, and since it is appropriate for us to know the manner of his expulsion from my parish—I answer you as follows.

If you had examined the sacred canons with sufficient zeal to conduct yourself with measured discernment in the actions of those subject to you, so that you would not offend against the authority of the sacred Scriptures and the preaching of your elders, and if among those subject to you you observed what is written, “Know well the face of your flock, and consider all your herds” (Proverbs 27), and, “Dig through the wall and see the abominations that these people are committing here” (Ezekiel 8); if you read with such attention the things from which you strive to compile your commentaries, so that you might be able to run along the path of your desires without restraint or anyone’s correction and pass over into the inclination of your heart, you could understand well the manner in which he was tolerated, corrected, and long awaited.

You could have heard this, just as you say that you did not hear him placed under public penance, and you could know why that same Bertricus—who is neither of my parish nor of my province—is regularly ordered, on this condition, to depart with his own people.

Since it cannot be hidden from me with what intention you ask this, I am ready, according to Peter’s words, to answer everyone who asks for a defense, insofar as God grants, concerning the hope that is in me (1 Peter 3). I answer you from this question as follows.

Pilate asked, “What is truth?” (John 18)—truth that he had before the eyes of his body, but not before the eyes of his mind—and he did not deserve to hear the answer. For, as Saint Gregory says, truth flees a mind that it does not find humble.

Again: “Those who seek the Lord deceitfully never deserve to find him” (1 Corinthians 1).

And again: “He is the power of God and the wisdom of God, from whose face come wisdom and understanding” (Psalm 93).

And: “He who teaches a man knowledge—against whom there is neither wisdom, nor prudence, nor counsel” (Proverbs 21).

He who is “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14)—the way, namely, of holy conduct; the truth of divine teaching; and the life of eternal blessedness—confesses, that is, praises the Father, because he has hidden these things from the wise and prudent (Isaiah 5). Of them it is written: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent in your own sight,” while he has revealed these things to little ones (Luke 10), that is, to the humble, because “he resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (James 4).

And: “The valleys”—that is, the humble—“will abound in grain” (Psalm 64), that is, in the nourishment of divine speech.

So much concerning those who are not of my parish, and indeed not even of my province.

But when you ask me about your parishioners, I trust in the most merciful grace of God, who says, “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Psalm 80), because he who has given me the governance of discipline will also give me the spirit of wisdom, by which I may be able to answer you with what is salutary.

Finally, concerning your accusation that you knew and believed that I had heard similar things about you many times, had accepted and retained as true things that I had heard falsely, and that I willingly listened to words of falsehood and gladly lent an ear to your detractors: I am not provoked to anger.

For many more and greater things were falsely brought against our Head as well: namely, that he had a demon and was a friend of tax collectors and sinners (Matthew 11), along with many other charges.

In these matters I recognize the title of my Lord. And you have done, said, and entrusted to me so many things of such a kind that I cannot be provoked by them. But the remedy that you have devised for yourself I accept as spoken remedially.

For just as Elihu, the guide of the arrogant—who did not deserve, through blessed Job, to be purified from his foolishness by sacrifices as his other friends were—says of himself, “Your belly is like new wine without a vent, which bursts new wineskins” (Job 32), unless your anger, swollen against me, vents itself in words, or bursts the wineskin of your swollen belly, or otherwise, according to the ancient poet,
It sounds as loudly as a burst bladder would sound. I have become foolish; you compelled me. Yet even if you had compelled me, I would not have answered you in this way, unless I had read that blessed Augustine responded in a similar sense, and partly even in these words, to Julian, an arrogant young man of hardened mind and an ex-bishop. Paul teaches, and Gregory explains, how one should answer those who have the mentality of the Galatians.

Nevertheless, because I am a debtor to the wise and to the foolish, especially to all who dwell [Col. 0451C] in the province of Rheims, whose care God has entrusted to my unworthiness, and to each person according to his rank, character, and condition—and you are numbered among them—woe to me if, according to my strength and understanding, I do not evangelize you with the others by teaching, guarding, advising, reproving, soothing, and frightening; sometimes acting gently, sometimes more severely; concerning those matters that pertain to right faith, good morals, and good works; so that in the holy Scriptures and sacred canons you may possess right understanding, continual observance, humility, and obedience toward your superiors, as required by the holy Scriptures and the same sacred canons, and may show your subjects the necessary care, kindness, and moderation, [Col. 0451D] persevering continually in these things.

For when it is said to whatever watchmen we may be: “If we do not announce it to them, their blood will be required at our hands” (Ezek. III), our fear is increased. For if the one appointed as a watchman over his subjects is held so gravely guilty even of the bodily death of those who will at some time die, with what guilt is he bound concerning the death of the souls of his subjects, who might have lived forever if they had heard words of correction? The blood, therefore, of the dying is required from the watchman’s hands, because the subject’s sin is reckoned to the superior’s fault if he has kept silent.

[Col. 0452A] And because, in accordance with the Lord’s command, I have frequently reproved you by word and letter, privately and together with others, but have not seen my correction benefit you as I wished, I dare not remain silent about the things for which I hear you reproached, nor about the schemes you undertake against me—contrary to reason, authority, and your own salvation—and against others who have not deserved ill from you. Through these actions you acquire among men a name unbecoming to a bishop and place yourself in danger before the Lord. I recall these matters not from resentment but from devoted sorrow of heart, and I must not keep them silent before you, since the Lord says: “You shall not hate your brother in your heart, but openly rebuke him, lest you bear sin because of him” (Lev. XIX); and again: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him” (Luke XVII).

[Col. 0452B] We must not, therefore, keep silent about those things that need to be said, whether to those who honor us or to those who despise us, since the Lord says to each of us: “Behold, I have made your face stronger than their faces, and your forehead harder than their foreheads; I have made your face like adamant and flint” (Ezek. III), so that we should neither blush before the humility of our subjects nor fear their pride.

Nor should we be ashamed to admonish those who honor or despise us, since the Truth says: “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him the Son of Man will be ashamed when he comes in his majesty” (Luke IX). Yet when we see someone weakened in his conduct or persisting in defiance, we must not show ourselves toward him to be too lax or lenient until he is strengthened and corrected. Hence it is written: “You have daughters; preserve their bodies, and do not show them a cheerful face” (Ecclus. VII).

[Col. 0452C] Weak souls, devoted to worldly desire, are sometimes better preserved by severity, so that a stern face—that is, through the guardianship of severity, closed against every hope of frivolous leniency—may frighten the unstable soul and restrain it from the pleasure of vices by the force of discipline. When a teacher does this, it is always necessary that sweetness and humility be retained in his heart, so that he may love greatly and never grow proud through elation against the person whom he corrects, while nevertheless refusing, for that person’s benefit, to display his love and humility toward him.

Therefore, my son—and my despiser—if you recover from the defiance of your heart, from disorderly habits, and from unbecoming actions, you will spare both me and yourself. I shall spare both you and myself when I do not remain silent about what I hear concerning you that is displeasing, or what I see or learn in you that requires correction.

[Col. 0452D] Thus, so that I may not remain silent and you may willingly hear and obey, let us consider together how free from the blood entrusted to him was that outstanding preacher who said: “I am clean from the blood of you all, for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God” (Acts XX). If he had not proclaimed it, he would not have been clean from their blood; but because he strove to declare to them the whole counsel of God, he was clean from their blood.

[Col. 0453A] By these words we are challenged, we are bound, and we are shown to be guilty—we who are called priests and superiors—because, in addition to the evils that are our own, we add the deaths of others. We kill as many as we see daily proceeding toward death while we remain sluggish and silent. We must pay the most careful attention to this: it is not enough merely to preach by word without a good example, for when a person’s life is despised, his preaching too will necessarily be despised. And: “Whoever breaks the commandment and teaches shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven; but whoever does and teaches shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V), that is, in the Church of the righteous.

[Col. 0453B] Correct, then, these things that you have done, and from now on diligently strive not to incur such reproaches by corrupting either the authoritative Scriptures or what the Lord has spoken through his saints, for it is written: “Do not add anything to his words, lest you be reproved and found a liar” (Prov. XXX). Catholic teachers explain this as follows: “Do not corrupt the utterances of the holy Scriptures”—something that certain heretics are known to have done so that they would not be convicted by them.

## CHAPTER XLIV. How he may return to the sweetness of paternal charity

Therefore, brother and once most beloved son, who, because of sins demanding it, flew away from your paternal nest like a fledgling, sooner than was necessary, and before you had become protected by the solidity of your feathers—that is, by the garment of humility—you settled, as though naked, among the thorns and briars of passions and worldly desires by which you are torn. But if you wish to be reconciled to the sacred rules and to religion, you will be able, by God’s grace, to return without difficulty to the resting place of paternal sweetness. Place yourself before yourself, remember from where you have fallen, and do penance.

[Col. 0453C] If you wish to do this, you must understand how great and how many are the offenses you commit: puffed up within yourself, you wish to be subject to no one, yet you cannot rule over everyone. For this reason you strive to tear down the sacred rules by interpreting them perversely, and by deliberately omitting from your collections those which you cannot interpret wrongly, as though they did not exist. You also insert certain things of your own against the truth; and while desiring to be unconquered, you defend outwardly what you ought not, while inwardly losing true love and cutting yourself off from the bond of fraternal unity.

[Col. 0453D] This has undoubtedly descended to you from the teaching of the one who, as it is written, “sees every high thing and is king over all the sons of pride,” and was made to fear no one (Job XLI), and who said: “I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV). Because Lucifer, who rose at dawn, did not wish to preserve the arrangement of the divine order and maintain social life in heaven, he fell from heaven. Losing true blessedness, he incurred everlasting misery; he made those who consented, obeyed, and joined themselves to him miserable instead of blessed; and he grew so deeply into misery that he could neither recognize nor humble himself.

He implanted this vice in our first parents, so that, when they sinned, they would not acknowledge their own fault but would strive to shift it onto another—namely, onto the author of their condition, though not of their iniquity. The human race still suffers from this vice to no small degree, and I fear and grieve that you and I are not wholly free from it.

[Col. 0454A] Attend, therefore, with the full attention of your mind to the words of blessed Leo, in which he says (Epistle 15, to Pulcheria): “The moderation of the apostolic see observes this restraint: that it act more severely with the hardened and desire to grant forgiveness to those who have been corrected.” The apostolic see received this moderation from divine teaching and proposed it for imitation by all sees, because confessed and corrected error is now without guilt, since it has forgiveness; but error that has been exposed and yet not corrected retains its guilt and lacks forgiveness.

“And, as Augustine says, humble confession in evil deeds is better than proud boasting in good ones.” Blessed John also says in the Apocalypse, by divine command to the angel—that is, the bishop—of Ephesus: “Remember from where you have fallen, and do penance, and perform your first works; otherwise I am coming to you and will move your lampstand from its place, unless you repent” (Rev. II).

[Col. 0454B] And to the angel—that is, the bishop—of the church of Laodicea he says: “Anoint your eyes with eye-salve, so that you may see” (Rev. III). We anoint our eyes with eye-salve so that we may see when we assist the sharpness of our understanding with the medicine of action, enabling us to behold the splendor of the true light.

Thus we shall be able to return to mutual grace if you wish to do and follow these and other things beneficial to you and appropriate to our ministry. For, as blessed Leo also says: “The gifts of divine grace come more sweetly whenever they are acquired not without great sweat, and peace continued through idleness usually seems less good than peace restored through labor. Truth itself also shines more clearly and is held more firmly when examination afterward confirms what faith had previously taught.”
