[Col. 0454C] Do not, therefore, continue to fight against us as though in a civil war, with our own banners and weapons raised against us; do not, through a renewed frenzy of defiance, revive for your own destruction and for the disturbance of the Catholic Church the seditions that have been suppressed by many and through many against many.

Return humbly to paternal charity, which you rejected defiantly. Let there be peace, as blessed Augustine says concerning the Donatists who rose against the Church, “in the strength of Jerusalem”—and that strength is charity. To this holy city it was said: “Let peace be in your strength and abundance in your towers” (Ps. CXXI).

[Col. 0454D] Do not exalt yourself against the maternal concern of your metropolitan see for the whole province, nor against the paternal kindness of your nourisher and ordainer. They desire to show you, together with the others and without any detriment, both the privilege of the metropolitan see and the affection of the metropolitan, provided only that you recognize yourself; and they wish to do so without difficulty.

For the authority of the metropolitan see and the metropolitan know that the truly great person is one who is entirely free from ambition, since the Lord says: “Whoever wishes to become great among you shall be your servant; and whoever wishes to be first among you shall be your slave, just as the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve” (Matt. XX). “And yet,” says Leo, “these things were then being explained to those who wished to grow from a small position and to pass from lowly things to the highest.”

[Col. 0455A] But you, as it is written, having already become “a teacher of infants and instructor of the foolish,” must recognize your own measure and demonstrate to your subjects—those from whom you demand obedience—the humility of obedience by rendering it to your superiors. This is especially so since the sacred canons, the decrees of the pontiffs of the Roman see, and the laws that the Church approves and observes sufficiently demonstrate the orders and distinctions of bishops and decree that they be preserved inviolably.

If anyone presumes to tear these down, what else is he doing but cutting himself off from the universal Church—which is partly already reigning with God in heaven and partly still traveling as a pilgrim on earth, longing for the heavenly homeland?

Therefore, brother, struck by the greatest sorrow of heart, I am compelled to say to you what Moses and Aaron said to the rebellious people who resisted them: “Your murmuring is not against us, but against the Lord. For what are we?” (Exod. XVI). And although I know myself to be nothing, I nevertheless know that I must preserve humility in my heart and, when the case requires it, mingle gentleness with severity in the exercise of discipline. A certain balance must be made from both, so that subjects are neither embittered by excessive harshness nor released from the laws of government through excessive kindness.

[Col. 0455B] According to Paul’s statement (Heb. IX), the ark of the tabernacle aptly signifies this: in it were the tablets, the rod, and the manna together. For just as the knowledge of sacred Scripture must be in the ruler’s breast, so must the rod of strictness be present along with the manna of sweetness. Yet there must not be such an excess of sweetness that someone perishes by forgetting his proper place through this loosening. For Eli, overcome by false piety because he did not wish to strike his delinquent sons, struck himself together with them by a cruel condemnation before the strict Judge.

[Col. 0455C] But if, because some obstacle blocks the way, I lack the opportunity and ability to carry out what I ought, I will place a frying pan between myself and the one resisting me—an iron wall—so that I may be defended by the fortification of zeal and not, through neglect, be condemned when I am abandoned.

## CHAPTER XLV. That he should remember how sweetly he lived at the beginning of his episcopate and lay aside his animosity

Finally, brother and son, I urge you: bring back to memory how peacefully you lived in the first days after you came to the episcopate, although now you are everyone’s proverb, the subject of head-shaking, a tale and a song throughout the day. Recall how free you then were from the tumult of the thoughts by which you are now pulled in different directions; how kindly you were received by our lord the king; how much sweetness you enjoyed from me; how united you were with our brothers and [Col. 0455D] fellow bishops; with how much love you were honored by the Palatines and by the other people of this land; and with how much reverent affection you were venerated by those entrusted to you, as well as by our own people—by whom, and among whom, and with whom you were raised.

This was before an immoderate love of the world crept into you and, through certain persons, stole you away and carried you off to itself. Once it had seized you, the world did what the unclean world is accustomed to do: it deceived all whom it received, mocked all to whom it smiled, and, as many say, led you to offer yourself willingly to the performance of acts—provided only that I did not know it, with no one compelling you unless perhaps desire or an improper fear compelled you—a fear you would not have if you lived episcopally—which you once detested so greatly that you would sooner have had [Col. 0456A] your neck cut off than been led to perform them. Many say that you have even repeated them.

And just as you did not preserve those true things which you took such pains, so often and for so long, to bind upon others—though you used to say and write that a priest’s words are either true or sacrilegious—so the things you are said to disseminate through many people are likewise false: namely, that I have nothing against you except that you do not wish to agree that the apostolic see should possess its authority.

You say these things on your own, not because others told you about me; you did not learn them from me, nor did you see them in me or hear them from me. Rather, you, an unrequested human helper, assist that supreme see in a way from which it does not feel itself assisted by you.

The first see, which had already been the head of the world for thousands of years even in pagan times, and which, after it deserved to receive Peter—[Col. 0456B] Cephas, indeed the head and prince of the apostles—to whom the Lord said, “You are Peter, and upon this rock”—that is, upon this firm and solid confession of faith which you have confessed—“I will build my Church” (Matt. XVI); and, “When you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke XXII); and, “If you love me, feed my sheep” (John XX)—namely, those throughout the whole world, wherever the Catholic Church extends itself, scattered through the regions of the earth yet enclosed under one shepherd and prince of shepherds, Christ, in the unity of faith and in one fold—has remained and remains the first see, the mother and teacher of all the churches throughout the entire world, since long before yesterday evening or the day before yesterday, before the earth brought you forth and your mother’s womb produced you into this light.

[Col. 0456C] For it is not I but you who seem to derogate from its authority and privilege, as you labor with all your strength to resist the order of God, which he established through that see, so that you might be subject to no one.

Yet you do not appeal in the manner or for the reasons prescribed by the sacred canons, which that see itself venerates and observes. Instead, driven by the agitations of your disordered mind, you appeal from every direction and through side passages from hour to hour, and, after being summoned by letters from that see once and even twice, you refuse to go to it. Meanwhile, whatever you wish and whatever matters for which you pretend to approach it by appealing, you obtain from our lord the king by whatever means you can. You know perfectly well that you are not yet being summoned in the regular order for those cases in which, by appealing at a synod, you should, together with your appeal, take care to approach that see, as it itself prescribes through the canons.

[Col. 0456D] Although, as far as can be established from your conduct, you obtained letters of summons without reasonable necessity in order to approach that first and holy see, nevertheless it itself replies according to the grounds on which, and the manner in which, it hears the case.

Believe me, brother and son: if there are people encouraging you to persist in this obstinacy, which you have assumed improperly and without any necessity and in which you remain, they are not doing so for your salvation or your honor. And when you come to sound judgment, you will not find a single bishop, or any sound and wise person, who agrees that the sacred rules should be understood as you interpret them and wish others to understand them—as though you ought to be subject to no one. I shall demonstrate this to you more fully if, God forbid, necessity compels me to do so against my will.

[Col. 0457A] Accept, then, the wholesome and honorable counsel offered to you. Lay aside the harmful animosity that affects you, and show me those vain songs—or rather, tragedies—that you go about interpreting through your collections and subscriptions. At a suitable time, let us read them familiarly with whichever and however many of our brothers and fellow bishops you wish, as well as with our common faithful, and let us find counsel there concerning how they may be silenced without danger to you and without disgrace.

For your subscription is a contradiction of the divine authority which, through blessed Leo, says that in matters pertaining to the general observance of all the Lord’s priests nothing ought to be carried out without the chief bishops. And if your mockery is brought to the knowledge of many wise people, “they will begin,” says the Lord, “all to mock him, saying: ‘This man began to build and was not able to finish’” (Luke XIV).

[Col. 0457B] For since nothing happens except what the Lord either does by his will or justly permits to happen at times against his will—and since it happens in a wondrous manner that even those things which oppose his counsel serve his counsel—if certain things are sometimes perversely obtained or vindicated by the perverse, the Lord justly permits this to occur either for their condemnation, for the purification of the elect, or for both. In his own time he will mock them, because, as it is also written: “He himself will mock them with mockeries” (Prov. III).

For this reason the Psalmist, filled with the Holy Spirit, admonishes every faithful person, saying: “Do not be envious of the one who prospers in his way, of the man who commits injustices, for those who do evil will be destroyed.” And: “I saw the wicked man highly exalted and [Col. 0457C] raised above the cedars of Lebanon. I passed by, and behold, he was not; I sought him, and his place was not found. Preserve innocence and observe equity, for there is a remnant for the peaceful man” (Ps. XXXVI).

## CHAPTER XLVI. Concerning his boasting that he has been and will always be victorious in everything he has undertaken against anyone whatsoever
For this reason I say this: as I hear from many people, you boast vainly that whatever you have undertaken—whether against the king, against me, or against any of your own people, clerics or laymen, who have acted against your will, or against your neighbors who have risen up against you—you have always overcome for the most part, and that you will overcome what still remains. Therefore you may glory in the Lord as a victor if you conquer error through rectitude; but if you conquer error through error, [Col. 0457D] or conquer rectitude through error, you cannot glory as a victor. Rather, you ought to weep miserably because you have been defeated by error. And if you do not understand this, you are foolishly senseless, because you boast about the very thing over which you ought to grieve and weep.

For those who rejoice even in their offenses, who delight when they have done evil, and exult in the worst things, are to be punished with a heavier vengeance. And a certain wise man says: “He who always wins does not always win well.”

Whenever the devil suggests to us the lust for victory, we ought to remember the sentence of blessed Gregory set forth above in chapter ten of this work. There he says that he had often seen how, when the rhinoceros—that is, one supported by temporal power—had become fiercely inflamed to strike and, as though with horn raised, [Col. 0458A] threatened his subjects with condemnation, suddenly, when the sign of the cross had been impressed upon his forehead, he extinguished within himself the whole fire of fury and laid aside his threats.

And if a man endowed with secular power must act in this way, what shall we wretched priests say at God’s judgment? Bound to the priestly office, we must avenge not our own injuries in any way, but divine injuries: with mercy and discernment toward others, and with severity toward ourselves. if we are always prepared to exact vengeance, though it is said to us: “Do good to those who hate you, not repaying evil for evil” (Matt. V). For it is written: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay,” says the Lord; “but if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink” (I Pet. III; Rom. XII).

And Solomon says: “The patient man is better than the strong, and he who rules his own spirit is better than one who captures cities” (Prov. XVI). [Col. 0458B] The victory by which cities are captured is therefore the lesser, because what is conquered lies outside us. Greater, however, is what is conquered through patience, because the spirit itself is overcome by itself and subjects itself to itself when patience lays it low in humble endurance.

The Apostle says: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Gal. V), so that, crucified not only away from evil deeds but also away from the desire for evil deeds, we may not follow—even in deliberation, much less in action—what is wrongly desired by us or suggested to the mind. Let us constantly ask the Lord’s mercy, so that he who commanded us to watch and pray lest we enter into temptation may protect us by his grace, so that we may not be led into temptation. And if, as human beings, [Col. 0458C] we stumble, may we return more quickly to repentance, so that sin may not reign in our mortal body by making us obey its desires. If we cannot remove that sin altogether so that it is not within us, let us nevertheless, with God’s help, take away its rule, so that it does not dominate us.

For the greatest unhappiness of a human being is to prosper happily in his own evil. For it is written: “There are three things that proceed well, and a fourth that walks prosperously” (Prov. XXXVIII). Not everything that proceeds prosperously proceeds well, nor does everything that proceeds well proceed prosperously. To walk prosperously at all times is characteristic of the son of perdition.

“Indeed,” says Jerome, “it is a great offense, after you have sinned, not to deserve the wrath of God.” [Col. 0458D] And Saint Gregory says: “We must consider sinners all the more wretched when we see them abandoned in their guilt without punishment.”

Hence Solomon says: “The turning away of the little ones will kill them, and the prosperity of fools will destroy them” (Prov. I). For whoever turns away from God and prospers comes that much nearer to destruction, the more he is found estranged from the zeal of discipline. In contrast, the Psalmist says of Moses, Aaron, and Samuel: “They called upon the Lord, and he answered them; he spoke to them in the pillar of cloud. They kept his testimonies and the commandment that he gave them” (Ps. XCVIII). Then, turning prophetically at once to the Lord, he says: “Lord our God, you answered them; O God, you were gracious to them, yet you took vengeance upon all their inventions.”

[Col. 0459A] God’s graciousness consists in correcting the sinner. “When we are judged,” he says, “we are corrected by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with the world” (I Cor. XI). And: “They spend their days in prosperity; in a moment they descend to the underworld,” as it is written (Job XXI).

For this reason the Psalmist says of the Lord: “He made a way for his anger through the sending of evil angels” (Ps. LXXVII). The Lord justly permits a heart already weighed down by its former merits to be deceived even by the subsequent persuasions of wicked spirits. When it is thereby deservedly drawn into guilt, its liability is increased in punishment.

Thus it is to make a way for the Lord’s anger when he extends his strict judgment against those who rightly refused to punish the causes of their own punishment: so that those who, having been enlightened, refused to do what was right may, having been justly blinded, continue to do what will make them deserving of even greater punishment. [Col. 0459B] Of such people the Apostle says: “That they may always fill up their sins” (I Thess. II).

Hence the angel’s voice says to John: “Let the one who does harm continue to do harm, and let the one who is filthy continue to be filthy” (Rev. XXII). Hence David says: “Add iniquity upon their iniquity, and let them not enter into your righteousness” (Ps. LXVIII). Hence it is said through Moses: “The sins of the Amorites are not yet complete” (Gen. XV). Hence the Lord says through the same Moses: “Are these things not stored up with me and sealed in my treasuries? On the day of vengeance I will repay them” (Deut. XXXII).

And because he had recounted their evils, he immediately added: “At the time when their foot shall slip.” Behold, their most atrocious sins are described, yet a subsequent fall is still awaited until the day of vengeance, by which their guilt may be increased. [Col. 0459C] They already have enough for which they deserve to be struck, but sin is nevertheless allowed to grow further, so that a more severe guilt may torment the sinners.

Sin and the cause of sin already deserve punishment, but it is still awaited that sin and the punishment of sin may supply an increase of punishment. [Col. 0459D] “Sin,” says Gregory (*Homily 11 on Ezekiel*), “which is not quickly erased through repentance is either sin and the cause of sin, or sin and the punishment of sin, or simultaneously the cause and punishment of sin. Everything we first commit is sin; but if it is not quickly cleansed through repentance, almighty God, in his just judgment, binds the mind burdened with sins and permits it to fall into another guilt, so that what it was unwilling to cleanse by weeping and correction, it may begin to heap up sin upon sin.

“Sin, therefore, which is not dissolved by the lament of repentance, is simultaneously sin and the cause of sin, because from it arises that by which the sinner’s spirit is bound still more deeply. But the sin that follows from sin is simultaneously sin and the punishment of sin, because, as blindness increases, it is generated as retribution for the earlier guilt, so that the very increase of vices may already be, as it were, punishments in the sinner.”

Your sin was the insolence of your defiance when, without cause—if indeed there was no cause—you irrationally rose up against the lord king. Because you were unwilling to turn back from that sin through the due and reasonable satisfaction demanded by humility, you brought it about that he acted and ordered action to be taken against you, so that, driven still more violently by fury, you would turn against him.

[Col. 0460A] Defeated by that agitation, you fell into the subsequent sin of unleashing the destructive curses of excommunication even against those who had not sinned against you in that matter—as though the dangers threatened by those same curses would rebound not upon you but upon him.

Who provoked you to curse the innocent in such a way, when the Apostle says of those who curse not by the judgment of justice but out of the spite of vengeance: “Nor will the cursers possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. VI).

This sin was also the punishment of the preceding contumacious and insolent sin, and the cause of a further sin. For when you wished to display that you had done nothing contrary to reason in that excommunication of your parish, to drive away from yourself the shame of an irrational act, and to show that you were not so subject to metropolitan authority that [Col. 0460B] you could freely do whatever you wished in your parish without consulting me; when you wished to show that I was a transgressor of the canons because I had presumed to absolve in your parish what you had bound; and when you wished to show that those whom I had absolved were not absolved—or rather, that the Apostolic See and all those through whom God, by his Spirit, established the sacred canons, and thus God himself, had not absolved them, if they did not agree with you against what I had written to you and your parish and did not subscribe to that interpretation—

you fell into this madness as a retribution of justice: just as it is written of the offending ruler, “He sinned and made Israel sin” (III Kings XIV). Against evangelical truth, apostolic authority, and the constitution of the sacred canons—concerning which those writings were promulgated, writings that I collected into one body and that plainly were sent to you and your parish—[Col. 0460C] you yourself subscribed and made others subscribe, despite the sacred rules protesting against you.

These rules say that you must presume to do nothing new without your superior, since matters belonging to the general observance of all the Lord’s priests ought not to be carried out without the primates.

[Col. 0460D] But because the sinews of Behemoth’s testicles are tangled, when you pretended to disentangle yourself from these things, you bound yourself more harshly and with more knots. Adding to the pain of your wounds, you yourself bound others together with you who had been free. Moreover, contrary to the canons and the decrees of the pontiffs of the Roman See, you gathered fabrications for the purpose of displaying yourself as a free wild ass, independent of the metropolitan see, and of showing me, bound by the same chains of your inventions, as a transgressor of the canons inextricably bound by those same chains of your inventions.

And you have continued to advance from bad to worse and from worse to worst, so that you displayed those compiled fabrications not only to the clerics entrusted to you but also to bishops, and as material to be given to the king; and you had them given to me so that through them I might entrust myself [the reading is uncertain] and subject myself so completely to you that, as you commanded, I would burn the evangelical, apostolic, and canonical words that I had sent to you and to the Church entrusted to you; strip myself not only of my rank but even of Christianity; and, drinking the cup of death that you had served me, become, like Judas, the murderer of myself through repentance—and in this differ from Judas even more gravely, in that I would repent of a good deed.

[Col. 0461A] For this cup, which you concocted from the names of the holy pontiffs of the Apostolic See, as though smeared with honey around the rim and indiscriminately mixed together, which you made the clerics entrusted to you drink and which you offered to certain bishops, is like the cup that Satan offered our first parents in paradise when he showed them an apple good for food, beautiful to the eyes, and delightful to behold. He said to them: “On whatever day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. III). To those to whom he promised divinity, he took away immortality; and while promising a free and subject-to-none equality with God, he brought upon them the wretched slavery of captivity, after making them his accomplices in iniquity.

“And let your clerics, who, as you say, were entrusted to me by the same God who commissioned me, and who [Col. 0461B] think similarly, being anxious to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, share in this peace with me”—as though you were plainly adding: “Let them walk into transgression of the sacred rules brought forth by the truly holy Spirit.” And then you continued:

“If,” you said, “any, unwilling to do otherwise, refuse to become partners in this discipline, let them not be considered participants in our communion.”

That is nothing other than saying: “Let them remain in communion with the Catholic Church, and, if not perhaps by words, then by persuading certain bishops through certain actions: ‘Hold fast to this compilation and uphold it with me; you will owe subjection to no one except the Roman pontiff; and with me you will scatter the divine ordinance by which the dignity of the common episcopal order has been distinguished among its sees.’”

[Col. 0461C] But let us grant that some arrogant and boastful person might say and do such things. I cannot imagine how it could have entered your mind that you wished to display that compilation to the king in inverted verses—that is, in language filled with flattering meanings—when you knew that he could not fail to understand for what purpose you had wanted to collect it.

How, moreover, could you command me not only to destroy what I had built, but also to subject to you both the privilege of the metropolitan see and myself; and, by burning the Gospels, the apostles, the prophets, and the canons, to deny them, so that I would become like a pagan and a publican to everyone? Yet, although weak and frail, I sing very frequently together with the holy Church that he is a holy man who contended unto death for the law of his God.

At this point, as I anxiously hesitated, [Col. 0461D] Paul’s words concerning such matters came to mind: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools” (Rom. I).

Of such people the Lord says to the prophet Ezekiel: “Their fathers,” he says, “transgressed my covenant up to this day, and their sons are hard of neck and unyielding of heart; to them I am sending you” (Ezek. II).

But first, from the words of blessed Gregory, we must explain what a covenant is:

“In a covenant,” he says (*Homily 9 on Ezekiel*), “the will of the parties in conflict is fulfilled, so that each may reach its own desire and bring its quarrels to the end it longs for. [Col. 0462A] God complains that this covenant between God and human beings has been transgressed.

“Behold one fault of pride: they have transgressed the covenant. Behold another, that of obstinacy: ‘up to this day.’ Behold the grave fault of shamelessness: ‘with a hard face,’ because they no longer blush at the evils they commit and never, even after their offenses, return to repentance, because they are unyielding in heart.

“When those to whom the prophet is sent are guilty of such great wickedness and such great obstinacy, who would not see that the prophet’s person could be despised by such perverse people? Yet the authority of his person is granted when it is added: ‘And you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord: If perhaps they themselves will hear, and if perhaps they will cease, for they are a provoking house’ (Ezek. XII).

[Col. 0462B] “And you, son of man, do not fear them, nor be afraid of their words, for they are a provoking house” (ibid.). It is exceedingly foolish if we seek to please those whom we know do not please the Lord.

“We ought, however, to hold in fear and reverence the judgments of the just, because they are members of almighty God. On earth they condemn what the Lord rebukes from heaven. For the disparagement of the wicked is approval of our life, since it is already shown that we possess something of justice if we begin to displease those who do not please God.

“Therefore the good must be feared, lest they be offended, lest perhaps through them he be provoked to anger who always dwells in their hearts. For this reason it is also added: ‘But you, son of man, hear whatever I speak to you, and do not be a provoking person, as the provoking house is.’

[Col. 0462C] “For unless, when he was sent to speak, he had obeyed the words, the prophet—that is, the preacher—would have provoked almighty God by his silence just as his hearers provoked him by their wicked deed.”

**CHAPTER XLVII. That he never acknowledges himself defeated; concerning his rebellion against the metropolitan; and that he sought to have the sacred words burned, and created a schism by his subscription; and concerning his unjust bonds.**
Therefore, since you are recognized as belonging to my pastoral concern, I must not remain silent to you. And because I have begun to struggle by admonishing, while you struggle by resisting, I think that in this present contest you will not allow yourself to be overcome before the sixth, or seventh, or even the tenth round. Indeed, as I fear, even when defeated most justly by the sharper duel of Dares and Entellus—with reason, truth, authority, and a cloud of witnesses—and already lying beneath your opponent, you will not deign to say that you have been defeated. What has been written for your instruction and correction you will not receive for edification, but will strive to magnify it into an occasion for contention. Following, as is your habitual custom, Heliu, the forerunner of the arrogant and himself most invincible in his arrogance, who said, “I am full of words, and the spirit of my womb constrains me; I will speak and breathe a little; I will open my lips and answer” (Job 32), you will not be able to restrain yourself within yourself, but will carelessly pour forth into the air, as you are accustomed to do, your knowledge without reason or authority. In order to compel me to write back to you, so that I may spend on uselessness and excess hours that ought to be devoted to usefulness and necessity, you will struggle to answer with frivolous, useless, and unreasonable arguments. You will demand that what I have already written to you—and also your own absurdities—be brought by me before the examination of bishops and learned men, to my grief on your behalf and to your ruin.

And there will come upon you, as I fear, that sentence which is written: “It is necessary that scandals come, but woe to that man through whom the scandal comes” (Matthew 18). Just as you abandoned me and those who together with me had nurtured you, and then one person after another, including many of those who had been entrusted to you, and indeed those whom you had received into friendship and intimacy, while in turn receiving others and still others into your friendship and intimacy; and just as you chose rather to follow the destructive obstinacy of those who, boasting themselves in various ways, cut themselves off from the unity of Catholic brotherhood, or demanded to be cut off because of their irrevocable stubbornness—such men as in our time Gothescalcus and Guntarius—than ecclesiastical gentleness and pious fatherhood: may it happen to you—God forbid—that you share their lot, since you have chosen to imitate their perverse intention.

Therefore, if—as I do not desire but fear—you wish to persist in this madness as you have begun, lest I continue to contend in words against one who is devoted to verbosity, let these things either suffice for your correction or, through the judgment of others, for your conviction. May I then suffer continual pain and perpetual mourning over the tearing out of my right eye or the cutting off of my right hand. As I have proposed to you from the words of blessed Gregory, there are three things: sin, the cause of sin, and the punishment of sin. Even if you wish to deny that you have committed these things, you will be proved guilty. I shall then propose to you three other things from the words of blessed Augustine, so that, as it is written, “you may see, and know, and consider, and understand together” (Isaiah 41).

The first is the advancement of avarice, concerning which the Apostle says, “and avarice, which is the service of idols” (Colossians 3). For, as Gregory demonstrates, avarice concerns not only money but also elevation. It is rightly called avarice when exaltation is sought beyond measure. You appear to have fallen into this, since, contrary to the decree ordained by God—that you should become subject, according to the canons, to your metropolitan, as I have shown above—you attempt to rebel.

If you choose to persist in this, I have judged it necessary to show you, from the words of that same blessed Augustine, which he drew from the sayings of Saint Cyprian, how greatly you are sinning when you are refuted by such powerful authorities. Saint Cyprian says (Letter 65, to Antonianus):

> “After the inspiration and revelation had been given, whoever knowingly and deliberately persists in what he had done wrongly sins without the excuse of ignorance; for he relies upon a certain presumption and obstinacy when he has been overcome by reason.”

Hence Augustine says (Book 4, On Baptism, against the Donatists, chapter 5):

> “This is most true: the sin of one who sins knowingly is far more serious than that of one who sins unknowingly.”

And therefore the holy man Cyprian was not only learned but also teachable. He understood this in the praise of the bishop whom the Apostle describes, so that he said that this too should be valued in a bishop: not only that he teach knowingly, but also that he learn patiently. I have no doubt that, if he had discussed this question—which had long and extensively been debated in the Church—with the holiest and most learned men, through whom it later came about that that ancient custom was confirmed by a plenary council, he would have demonstrated without hesitation not only how devoted he was to what he had grasped with the firmest truth, but also how teachable he was in matters to which he had paid less attention.

Yet since it is most evident that one who sins knowingly sins much more seriously than one who sins unknowingly, I would like someone to tell me this: If one person falls into heresy without knowing how great an evil it is, while another does not withdraw from avarice despite knowing how great an evil it is, which of them is worse? I can also put it this way: if one person unknowingly falls into heresy, while another knowingly does not withdraw from idolatry—for the Apostle also says, “Avarice, which is the service of idols” (Colossians 3)—and Cyprian himself understood the same judgment in no other way, as he writes to Antonianus (Letter 52):

> “Let the new heretics not flatter themselves in this respect, saying that they do not associate with idolaters, when among them too there are adulterers and fraudsters who are held under the charge of idolatry, according to the Apostle who says (Ephesians 5): ‘For know this with understanding, that no fornicator, or unclean person, or fraudster—which is idolatry—has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God’; and again: ‘Therefore put to death your members which are upon the earth, fornication, uncleanness, and evil desire, and avarice, which is the service of idols’ (Colossians 3).”

I therefore ask which person sins more seriously: one who has fallen unknowingly into heresy, or one who knowingly has not withdrawn from avarice, that is, from idolatry? According to that rule by which the sins of those who know are placed before the sins of ignorance, the avaricious person, because of his knowledge, surpasses the ignorant heretic in wickedness. But lest this be the case, the magnitude of the crime in heresy does what the conscious consent of the avaricious person does in avarice, so that the ignorant heretic is made equal to the knowingly avaricious person.

You also attempted to bring about the burning of the divine Scriptures—a thing that you tried to persuade me to do under the pretext of securing peace with you—just as under the same pretext you bound the clerics of your parish to yourself by an irregular subscription. We read that there is a mouth of the heart, just as there is a mouth of the body. Concerning the mouth of the heart it is written: “Deceitful lips are in the heart, and with the heart they have spoken” (Psalm 11); and according to evangelical truth: “From the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, perjuries, false testimonies” (Matthew 15), and the other things that proceed from the mouth of the heart into the knowledge of others through the mouth of the body.

We also read that the deliberation of the will is the completion of the deed, since the Lord says: “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5); and to his disciples: “I have appointed you to go and bear fruit” (John 15). “Go,” says Gregory, “by willing; bear fruit by doing. I said, ‘Go by willing,’ because to will to do something is already to go there in the mind.”

And you have advanced from the deliberation of your will to the performance of your words, so that you offered me something deadly to drink—namely, that I should burn the sacred Scriptures for your sake—unless the one who made this promise to those who believe in him had been present for me: “If they drink any deadly thing, it will not harm them” (Mark 16). “When they hear,” says blessed Gregory, “pestilential persuasions, but are not at all drawn into evil action, what they drink is indeed deadly, but it will not harm them.”

Although God has preserved me from this by his grace, you, unless you repent, will suffer the judgment of your enterprise. Blessed Gregory says (Pastoral Rule 3, admonition 33):

> “Sin is dissolved more slowly when it is also strengthened by counsel; for unless the mind utterly despised eternal things, it would not perish through judgment in guilt. Hence the Lord, through the prophet, reproves not so much the evil of rash actions as the deliberate pursuit of crimes, saying: ‘Lest my indignation go forth like fire, and burn, with no one to extinguish it, because of the wickedness of your enterprises’ (Jeremiah 4). Again, in anger he says: ‘I will visit you according to the fruit of your enterprises’ (Jeremiah 21). Since, therefore, sins committed by counsel differ from other sins, the Lord pursues not so much the evil deeds as the deliberate pursuit of evil. In deeds one often sins through weakness, often through negligence; but in deliberate pursuits one always sins through a malicious intention.”

From this, therefore, let those who bind themselves in guilt even through counsel infer with what vengeance they will eventually be struck—those who now become not merely companions but leaders of wickedness.

You likewise demonstrated that you would separate yourself from those entrusted to you unless they subscribed; and you separated from us those who subscribed together with you—although we preserve what I directed to you and to the church entrusted to you from evangelical truth, apostolic authority, and canonical institution, indeed from the Catholic Church, which preserves these things and teaches all people without possibility of refutation to preserve them.

Since you despise me because of what you suppose to be my deserts, recognize from the words of blessed Augustine, who teaches concerning the authority of Holy Scripture, how grave a sin idolatry is—the sin that you appear to have committed through your desire for exaltation. And because the burning of the divine Scriptures is more serious, to which you led me insofar as it depended on you; and because schism is the most serious sin, by which you separated yourself from our fraternal unanimity through your destructive subscription—if, God forbid, you choose to persist in it; and if perhaps you subscribed to things that are found to be contrary to evangelical truth and apostolic authority, opposed to the decrees of the holy councils approved by the assent of the universal Church and confirmed by the authority of the apostolic see—then hear what that same blessed Augustine says.

He speaks to the Donatists, or rather against the schismatic Donatists, as he is believed now to speak to you through the teaching of his writings and through that charity which could never die. As he himself says concerning Cyprian (Book 5, On Baptism, chapter 17):

> “He is present,” he says, “not only through his letters but also through that charity which especially flourished in him and could never die.”

Addressing you and those mentioned above, he says (Book 2, On Baptism, chapter 6):

> “Why did you separate yourselves—not, I do not say, from the innocent, which is proved, but from the very traditors, which is not proved? Or, as I had begun to say, are the crimes of the traditors more serious than those of schismatics? Let us not bring deceptive scales on which we may weigh whatever we wish and as we wish, saying according to our own judgment, ‘This is serious; this is light.’ Rather, let us bring the divine scale from the Holy Scriptures, as from the Lord’s treasuries, and weigh in it what is more serious—or rather, let us not weigh it ourselves, but recognize what has been weighed by the Lord.

> “At that time when the Lord (Exodus 32) showed, by the recent examples of punishments, that earlier sins were to be avoided; when an idol was fashioned and worshiped; when the prophetic book was burned in the anger of the contemptuous king (Jeremiah 36); and when schism was attempted, idolatry was punished by the sword, the burning of the book by war and foreign captivity, and schism by the earth’s opening, with its authors buried alive and the rest consumed by heavenly fire. Who, then, would doubt that the deed which was more severely punished was the more wicked?”

Concerning what you put into your subscription, namely, that those subscribing with you should “carefully preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” and enjoy that peace with you (Numbers 16), he says to the Donatists in the same book (Book 2, On Baptism, chapter 6):

> “Why do you not communicate with the churches to which you hold and read the apostolic letters sent, and according to those letters claim to live?”

After a few words, which I omit for the sake of brevity and which the reader can find there in order, he says:

> “Catholic unity embraces all these in its maternal bosom, bearing one another’s burdens and striving to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, until the Lord should reveal to some of them, if they thought differently in any matter.”

Regarding what you added, as though from the words of Leo (Ephesians 4), “If some do not wish to become partners in this discipline, neither are they to be considered participants in our communion,” compare your words with Leo’s words in the chapter where he says this, and read them together as they stand there (Letter 1, chapter 5):

> “Therefore our admonition declares that if any of the brethren attempts to act against these decrees and dares to admit what has been prohibited, he should know that he must be removed from his office, and that he will not be a participant in our communion, since he did not wish to be a partner in discipline. But lest anything that we may have omitted be thought to have been overlooked by us, we command that all decretal enactments—both those of blessed memory, Innocent, and those of all our predecessors—which have been promulgated concerning ecclesiastical orders and the discipline of the canons, be so carefully observed by your devotion that, if anyone violates them, he should know that forgiveness will henceforth be denied him.”

This is the complete chapter of blessed Leo. Let us therefore consider whether the discipline that you have proposed for your people is fairly compatible with the discipline that Leo taught must be followed; or whether your teaching disagrees with his teaching. Let heaven and earth judge which ought rather to be followed: your discipline or Leo’s doctrine.

Since Leo himself says, “He will not be a participant in our communion who did not wish to be a partner in discipline,” it must be discerned whose communion every Catholic ought to choose: Leo’s communion with the universal Church, or that of a local bishop with his accomplices—especially since Leo also says:

> “If anyone violates the decretal enactments both of blessed memory, Innocent, and of all his predecessors, which were promulgated concerning ecclesiastical orders and the discipline of the canons, he should know that forgiveness will henceforth be denied him.”

It is manifest that you have violated these decretal enactments, as is shown in the writings I have sent to you once and twice, and now demonstrated above for the third time in this writing. By this subscription of yours you have separated yourself from their discipline—or rather, from the Catholic Church of which they were rulers—if, as has been said and must always be said, the things you subscribed to are found to be contrary to those same enactments.

Therefore I have decided to propose to you three further passages from the words of blessed Augustine, the eminent doctor of the Catholic Church, prefacing them with these three words of blessed Cyprian, favorably praised by blessed Augustine (Letter 73, to Jubajanus, at the end) and to be accepted by all Catholics and those who live piously:

> “Charity of spirit,” says blessed Cyprian (Book 4, On Baptism, chapter 7), “the honor of the college, the bond of faith, and the harmony of the priesthood are preserved by us patiently and gently.”

“These are Cyprian’s words,” says Augustine. “Or perhaps envy and malicious dissension are a small evil? How, then, were these people in unity when they were not at peace? For the voice was not mine or that of any human being, but the voice of the Lord himself, sounding not through human beings but through angels at the birth of Christ: ‘Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will’ (Luke 2).

“This would certainly not have sounded from an angelic mouth at Christ’s birth on earth unless God wished it understood that those are in the unity of Christ’s body who are in the peace of Christ, and that those are in the peace of Christ who are people of good will. Just as good will is found in benevolence, so evil will is found in malevolence. But envy itself, which can be nothing other than malevolent, how great an evil is it? Let us not seek other witnesses; Cyprian himself is sufficient for us, through whom the Lord thundered so many completely truthful things about zeal and jealousy and gave such salutary commands.

“Let us therefore read Cyprian’s Letter on Zeal and Jealousy, and see how great an evil it is to envy those who are better—a sin whose origin, he memorably teaches, came from the devil himself:

> “‘To be jealous of the good that you see and to envy those who are better seems to some, dearest brothers, a slight and minor crime.’

Then, a little later, when he was seeking the head and origin of that evil:

> “‘From this,’ he says, ‘the devil, at the very beginning of the world, both perished first and caused the first ruin.’

And shortly afterward:

> “‘What an evil it is, brothers, by which an angel fell; by which that lofty and splendid eminence could be ensnared and overthrown; by which the deceiver himself was deceived? From that time envy rages on earth, while the one destined to perish through jealousy obeys the teacher of perdition, while he imitates the jealous devil, as it is written: “Through the envy of the devil death entered the world” (Wisdom 2). Therefore those who belong to his side imitate him.’”

I have placed these words before the three passages from blessed Augustine that I promised to propose to you because we truly believe that you acted through zeal and fury in creating those destructive bonds of which we are speaking, and that you devised this subscription against the sacred canons.

Therefore I judged it necessary first to show you that true bonds exist only in the Catholic unity that has not been divided by heresies or schisms, just as true sacraments exist only there. Blessed Augustine says (Book 7, On Baptism, chapter 51):

> “I think I am not speaking rashly when I say that some are in the house of God in such a way that they themselves are also that same house of God, which is said to be built upon a rock; which is called the one dove; which is the beautiful bride without spot or wrinkle; the enclosed garden, the sealed fountain, the well of living water, the paradise with the fruit of trees. This house also received the keys and the power of binding and loosing. If anyone despises this house when it rebukes and corrects him, ‘let him be to you,’ he says, ‘as a gentile and a tax collector.’”

We must also understand that when the rule of correction given to this house of God, namely the Catholic Church, is despised, this sentence follows:

> “Let him be to you as a gentile and a tax collector” (Matthew 18).

As a second chapter, directed against the unjust binding of innocent people that you perpetrated, I propose to you the words of that same illustrious teacher, as though he were speaking specifically about this act and counting you together with those whom he addressed. He says (Augustine, Book 2, On Baptism, chapter 6):

> “If you were then speaking truthfully against those whom you accused, you would have commended your cause to the unity of the whole world, so that, while you were retained, they might be excluded. But if you attempted to do this and did not succeed, the whole world is innocent, since it believed the ecclesiastical judges rather than defeated litigants. If, however, you were unwilling to plead your cause, the whole world is innocent, since it could not condemn people who had not been heard. Why, then, did you separate yourselves from the innocent? You cannot defend the sacrilege of your schism.”

But spiritual people, or those who are advancing toward this very condition through pious devotion, do not go outside. Even when they seem to be expelled through some perversity or necessity of human beings, they prove there all the more that they would remain within, since they do not in any way rise up against the Church, but are firmly rooted upon the solid rock of unity by the strongest strength of charity.

This is the meaning of what is said concerning Abraham’s sacrifice: “But he did not divide the birds” (Genesis 15), namely because spiritual people do not cut themselves off from unity.

By contrast, the Council of Antioch, concerning those who withdraw themselves from ecclesiastical ministry, gather separately, and divide themselves from unity, says (Council of Antioch, canon 5):

> “If any presbyter or deacon, despising his own bishop, separates himself from the Church, establishes an altar after gathering separately, and does not heed the bishop who admonishes him, nor consent or obey when summoned once and again, let him be condemned in every way and receive no further remedy, since he will not be able to recover his dignity. But if he persists in disturbing and troubling the Church, let him be suppressed by external authorities as a seditious person.”

The Council of Carthage likewise says (canon 11):

> “If any presbyter has been corrected by his superior, he ought certainly to bring his complaint before neighboring bishops, so that his case may be heard by them and through them he may be reconciled to his bishop. But if he does not do this, and, inflated with pride—God forbid—he judges that he must separate himself from communion with his bishop, or, making schism separately with certain others, offers sacrifice to God, let him be anathema and lose his position. If he has no just complaint against the bishop, an inquiry must be made.”

According to this chapter, together with the ninth chapter of the Council of Antioch, the fellow ministers of the Church of Laon, without schism or rebellion, in view of the pressure of time and the imminent danger, innocently suffering injury, approached their metropolitan bishop. Therefore, as I showed above, they ought to have been restored to and have remained in ecclesiastical communion.

Hence the Council of Carthage, concerning those who judge irregularly, those who are judged unjustly, and judges of greater authority, says (canon 15):

> “It has been decided that when an appeal has been made from any ecclesiastical judges to other ecclesiastical judges of greater authority, this must not prejudice those whose sentence has been set aside, unless they can be proved either to have judged with an inimical spirit or to have been corrupted by some desire or favor.”

Concerning a bishop who might perhaps have created schism in the Church against the sacred canons, the African Council says (canon 20):

> “Regarding those who are harmonious, not only concerning the Church of Carthage, namely the metropolitan church, but also concerning the entire fellowship of priests…”

And shortly afterward:

> “It is necessary that whoever has adhered to all the brethren and to the entire council should possess not only his own rights intact but also the dioceses. But those who think their own congregations sufficient for themselves, despising fraternal love, should lose not only the dioceses but, as I have said, also be deprived of public authority over their own people, as rebels.”

Concerning those whom you have separated from Catholic communion, as is contained in the petition given to me by the Church of Laon—namely, the little children in your parish whom, because of your injustices, you ordered not to be baptized, and the dying whom you did not reconcile through communion in the provision for the journey—hear what that same most Catholic teacher, investigator of the most subtle matters, and most discerning discoverer through the grace of God, says concerning the remedy (Augustine, Book 4, On Baptism, chapter 22):

> “That passion can sometimes take the place of baptism is shown by the robber to whom, though he had not been baptized, it was said: ‘Today you will be with me in paradise’ (Luke 23). Blessed Cyprian rightly takes this as no slight proof. Considering the matter again and again, I find that not only can suffering for the name of Christ supply what was lacking from baptism, but faith and conversion of heart can also do so if, in the crisis of circumstances, the celebration of the mystery of baptism cannot be reached.

> “For that robber was not crucified for the name of Christ, but for the merits of his crimes; nor did he suffer because he believed, but while he was suffering he believed. How powerful, even without the visible sacrament of baptism, is what the Apostle says—‘With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation’ (Romans 10)—was demonstrated in that robber.

> “But this is fulfilled invisibly when the ministry of baptism is excluded not by contempt for religion but by the crisis of necessity. For it might seem even more superfluous that Cornelius and his companions (Acts 10) should be washed with water, since they had already received the gift of the Holy Spirit—a gift which Holy Scripture testifies that no others received unless they had been baptized—and this was demonstrated by a clear sign appropriate to those times, when they had spoken in tongues. Nevertheless, they were baptized, and in this deed apostolic authority stands.

> “So far must no one, whatever progress he may have made in the inner person, if before baptism he has perhaps advanced through a pious heart even to spiritual understanding, despise the sacrament that is bodily administered through the work of ministers. Through it God spiritually effects the consecration of the human being.

> “I think that the office of baptizing was assigned to John, so that it might be called John’s baptism, for no other reason than that the Lord himself, who had given it, should consecrate the way of humility by not disdaining to receive the baptism of a servant, and should make completely clear by that act how highly his own baptism, with which he was to baptize, ought to be esteemed.

> “For he saw, as the most powerful physician of eternal salvation, that the pride of certain people would not be absent—people who, having advanced so far in understanding the truth and in commendable conduct that they did not hesitate to place themselves before many baptized people in life and teaching, would think it superfluous for them to be baptized once they felt that they had reached that condition of mind which many baptized people were still trying to attain.” (Ibid., chapter 23.)

But what the sanctification of the sacrament, bodily administered to a person, accomplishes and signifies—without which the robber nevertheless was not deprived, since he lacked not the will to receive it but the necessity of receiving it was present—is difficult to say. Yet if it had not possessed great power, the Lord would not have received the baptism of a servant.

Because it must be considered in itself, apart from the salvation of the person for whose perfection it is administered, it sufficiently indicates that it remains whole both in the wicked and in those who renounce the world in words but not in deeds, although those people cannot possess salvation unless they are corrected.

Just as in the robber, because the sacrament was bodily absent through necessity, salvation was nevertheless perfect because it was spiritually present through piety, so also, when the sacrament itself is present, salvation is perfected if what was present in the robber is absent through necessity.

The whole Church preserves this tradition when infants are baptized. They certainly cannot yet believe with the heart unto righteousness or confess with the mouth unto salvation, as the robber could. Indeed, while the mystery is celebrated in them, they interrupt the sacred words by crying and wailing; nevertheless, no Christian would say that they are baptized in vain. (Ibid., chapter 24.)

And if anyone should seek divine authority in this matter, although what the whole Church preserves—not having been instituted by councils but always retained—is rightly believed to have been handed down only by apostolic authority, we can nevertheless infer truthfully what power the sacrament of baptism has in infants from the circumcision of the flesh, which the former people received, although Abraham was justified before he received it (Genesis 17), just as Cornelius was enriched with the gift of the Holy Spirit before he was baptized (Acts 10).

Yet the Apostle says of Abraham himself (Romans 4): “Abraham received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of faith,” which he had already believed in his heart and which had been reckoned to him as righteousness.

Why, then, was he commanded to circumcise every male infant on the eighth day (Genesis 17), who could not yet believe with the heart so that it might be reckoned to him as righteousness, unless the sacrament itself was also powerful in its own right? This was manifested in the son of Moses through the angel (Exodus 4). While he was still being carried uncircumcised by his mother, circumcision was demanded in the face of an immediate and evident danger; and when it had been performed, the peril was removed.

Therefore, just as in Abraham righteousness by faith came first and circumcision was added as the seal of the righteousness of faith, so in Cornelius spiritual sanctification through the gift of the Holy Spirit came first, and the sacrament of regeneration in the washing of baptism was added.

And just as in Isaac (Genesis 21), who was circumcised on the eighth day of his birth, the seal of the righteousness of faith came first—and because he imitated his father’s faith, that same righteousness followed as he grew, whose seal had preceded him in infancy—so in baptized infants the sacrament of regeneration comes first. If they preserve Christian devotion, conversion of heart also follows, the mystery of which had preceded in the body.

And just as in the robber what was lacking from the sacrament of baptism was supplied by the kindness of the Almighty, because it was lacking not through pride or contempt but through necessity, so we must believe that in infants who die after being baptized the same grace of the Almighty supplies what is lacking. They cannot believe with the heart unto righteousness or confess with the mouth unto salvation, not through impious will but through the incapacity of their age.

Therefore, when others answer on their behalf so that the celebration of the sacrament may be completed for them, it certainly contributes to their consecration, because they themselves cannot answer. But if someone else answers on behalf of one who can answer for himself, it does not have the same effect. From this rule comes that saying in the Gospel which naturally moves everyone when it is read: “He is of age; let him speak for himself” (John 9). (Chapter 25.)

All these things demonstrate that the sacrament of baptism is one thing and conversion of heart another, but that the salvation of a person is completed through both. Nor, if one of these is lacking, should we therefore think that the other must also be absent, because the one can exist without the other in an infant, and the other could exist without it in the robber, God completing in either the one or the other what was absent not through the will.

But when one of these is absent through the will, the person becomes entangled in guilt. Baptism can indeed be present where conversion of heart is absent; conversion of heart can indeed be present without baptism having been received, but it cannot be present when baptism has been despised. For conversion of heart toward God cannot in any way be said to exist when God’s sacrament is despised.

And just as the saying of our Savior is truthful—“Unless a person has been born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3)—that is, unless he has been reborn either by invisible grace together with the visible sacrament, or by invisible grace without the visible sacrament, so the saying of that same Savior is truthful: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6).

Hence blessed Augustine, in a sermon concerning the sacrament addressed to infants approaching the altar, says:

> “The Lord Jesus Christ signified us; he wished us to belong to him; he consecrated the mystery of our peace and unity upon his table. Whoever receives the mystery of unity but does not hold the bond of peace receives not the mystery for himself, but a testimony against himself.

> “No believer should have any doubt that each person becomes a participant in the body and blood of the Lord when, in baptism, he is made a member of Christ’s body. Nor is he alienated from participation in that bread and cup even if, before eating that bread and drinking that cup, he departs from this world established in the unity of Christ’s body. He is not deprived of participation in and the benefit of that sacrament when he is found to possess what that sacrament signifies.”

For those who, while dying, sought to be reconciled through communion in the provision for the journey but could not obtain it, the remedial judgment of that same blessed Augustine seems applicable. Praising Cyprian’s view concerning those who died in the unity of the Church and were therefore believed not to have been separated from the Church’s gifts, he says:

> “He rightly presumed that the charity of unity could cover a multitude of sins.”

In harmony with this, blessed Ambrose, in his book On the Death of Valentinian, says among other things (after the middle, toward the end):

> “Does he not have the grace that he requested? Because he requested it, he received it. And where is that saying: ‘The just person, by whatever death he is overtaken, will be at rest in soul’ (Wisdom 4)? Therefore, holy Father, grant your servant the gift that Moses received when he saw it in the Spirit, the gift that David, because he knew it by revelation, merited (Wisdom 4). Grant, I say, to your servant Valentinian the gift that he desired, the gift that he requested while healthy, strong, and unharmed.

> “If illness had delayed him, he would nevertheless not have been wholly alienated from your mercy, since he was deprived by the speed of time, not by his will. Therefore grant your servant the gift of your grace, which he never denied, since before the day of his death he denied the privileges of the temples to those who rose up and whom he could have revered.

> “A crowd of gentiles stood by; the senate pleaded. He did not fear displeasing human beings in order to please you alone in Christ. Since he possessed your Spirit, how could he not receive your grace? Or does it trouble us that the sacred rites were not solemnly celebrated? Then martyrs who were catechumens should not be crowned either, for they are not crowned if they are not initiated. But if they are washed in their own blood, his piety and will also wash him.”

Again, in the same book, not far from the beginning, he says:

> “Clearly blessed is the person who corrects his error even in old age; blessed is the person who, even at the moment of death, turns his mind away from vices. For blessed are those whose sins are covered (Psalm 32), because it is written: ‘Turn away from evil and do good, and dwell for ever and ever’ (Psalm 36).

> “Therefore whoever turns away from sins and is converted to better things at whatever age will obtain forgiveness for his earlier sins, whether he has confessed them through the disposition to repent or has turned away from them through the understanding that corrects.”

## CHAPTER XLVIII. Concerning those who love their own opinion excessively, even to schism or heresy

From these things, brother, carefully attend and perceptively understand that, just as in the case of that thief (Luke 23)—in whom what had been lacking from the sacrament of baptism and from participation in the body and blood of Christ (which sacraments, before the Lord ascended onto the cross, he entrusted to all the faithful as things to be celebrated and received) was completed by the goodness of the Almighty, because it had been lacking not through pride or contempt but through necessity—and just as, in the case of infants who are naturally subject to another’s sin, the faith of others—that is, of sponsors answering for them at baptism—becomes their means of salvation, so in the case of the infants for whom you ordered baptism to be denied, the faith of parents or sponsors believing in their hearts and faithfully seeking baptism for their infants, but not obtaining it, together with their faithful petition, may have been beneficial, by the gift of him whose Spirit, through whom regeneration occurs, breathes where he wills. For he has power over whose heart he may enlighten by the visitation of his grace, just as with those two who were enrolled by Moses among the seventy (Numbers 11) so that they might go to the Lord’s tabernacle and be counted among the elders when his spirit had been extended, but who remained in the camp and prophesied.

And just as, before baptism, the Spirit came upon Cornelius and his friends, and just as, according to the African Council and the decrees of Leo, it is read that even the signs of those seeking and the testimony of those requesting communion ought to contribute to salvation, so, for those same persons who requested communion, although they did not obtain it, and for whom you ordered it to be denied, their faithful petition may have been beneficial through the mercies of our God, who made darkness his hiding place, and whose mercy we can neither measure nor define in time. The Spirit of God says through the prophet: “When you groan, then you shall be saved” (Isaiah 30). For “with the Lord there is mercy, and with him abundant redemption” (Psalm 130). This very petition, arising from faithful desire, may have been beneficial to them, if they were not, through God’s foreknowledge and the retribution of justice, left for punishment in the mass of perdition of the human race, but through God’s grace predestined from that same mass for glory.

Nevertheless, you cannot be secure if some have died without these same sacraments at your command, so that your wickedness will not be strictly judged on that account, unless true humility obtains forgiveness for you before God through worthy fruits of repentance and abundant tears. Leo says (Letter 59, to Theodore), and through him the catholic and apostolic Church:

> “To those who, in a time of necessity and under the pressure of imminent danger, implore the help of repentance and immediate reconciliation, neither satisfaction is to be prohibited nor reconciliation denied, because we can neither set measures nor define times for the mercy of God, with whom true confession suffers no delay in forgiveness. The Spirit of God says through the prophet (Isaiah 30): ‘When you groan, then you shall be saved’; and elsewhere: ‘You first declare your iniquities, that you may be justified’ (Isaiah 43); and again: ‘For with the Lord there is mercy, and with God there is abundant redemption’ (Psalm 130). In administering God’s gifts, therefore, we must not be difficult, nor neglect the groans and tears of those who accuse themselves, since we believe that the very disposition to repent has been conceived through God’s inspiration. The Apostle says (2 Timothy 2): ‘Lest perhaps God may give them repentance, that they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive for his will.’”

And shortly afterward:

> “But, as I said, the necessity of such persons must be assisted in such a way that the practice of repentance is not denied them, nor the grace of communion, if they request it even after losing the power of speech, by indications of an unimpaired understanding. But if they are so weakened by the force of illness that they cannot signify, in the presence of a priest, what they had shortly before requested, the testimony of the faithful standing around them ought to benefit them, so that they may obtain together the benefit both of repentance and of reconciliation.”

And Gregory says:

> “The pastors of the Church ought to remove from him the penalty he deserved, since he was not ashamed to confess what he had done.”

The sacred Nicene canons likewise plainly command that communion be granted to anyone at the point of death who requests the grace of communion (canon 13).

The third section concerns those who, by loving their own opinion excessively or envying those who are better, proceed as far as the sacrilege of cutting off communion and establishing schism or heresy. Accordingly, that same catholic and most diligent teacher says (Augustine, *On Baptism*, book II, chapters 4–5):

> “The health of peace brings this about: when obscure matters are sought for a long time, and their difficulty in being discovered gives rise to differing opinions in fraternal debate, the bond of unity should remain until the truth becomes clear, lest an incurable wound of error remain in the severed part. Therefore, often something is revealed less fully to the more learned, so that their patient and humble charity—in which the greater fruit lies—may be proved: either how they preserve unity while holding different opinions about obscure matters, or how they accept the truth when they recognize that what they had thought has been shown to be otherwise.
>
> “Of these two matters, one has been made manifest to us in blessed Cyprian: namely, how he preserved unity with those from whom he differed. For he says: ‘Judging no one, nor removing from the right of communion anyone who thinks differently.’ But the other matter—how he could accept a truth discovered contrary to what he had thought—even if the letters are silent, his merits cry out; if the letter is not found, the crown bears witness; if the council of bishops does not judge, the fellowship of angels indicates it. For it is no small testimony to a most peaceful soul that he deserved martyrdom in that unity from which, although he thought differently, he refused to separate.
>
> “For we are human beings. Hence, to think otherwise than the matter really is is a human temptation. But to love one’s own opinion excessively, or to envy those who are better [the printed text reads *mulieribus*, ‘women’; the context evidently requires *melioribus*, ‘those who are better’], even to the sacrilege of cutting off communion and establishing schism or heresy, is diabolical presumption. To think in no respect otherwise than the matter really is, however, is angelic perfection.
>
> “Since, therefore, we are human beings, but in hope we are angels, for we shall be equal to the angels in the resurrection (Matthew 22), as long as we do not possess angelic perfection, let us not possess the devil’s presumption. Therefore the Apostle says: ‘Let no temptation seize you except what is human’ (1 Corinthians 10). It is human, then, to think something otherwise. For this reason he says elsewhere: ‘Let us therefore, as many as are perfect, think this way. And if you think anything otherwise, God will reveal this also to you’ (Philippians 3).
>
> “But to whom does he reveal these things, whenever he wills—whether in this life or after this life—except to those walking in the way of peace and deviating into no separation? Not to people such as these, who have not recognized the way of peace and have broken the bond of unity for no other reason. Therefore, after the Apostle had said, ‘If you think anything otherwise, God will reveal this also to you’ (Ephesians 4), lest they suppose that what they thought otherwise could be revealed to them apart from the way of peace, he immediately added (1 Corinthians 13): ‘Nevertheless, let us walk in what we have attained.’
>
> “Walking in this way, Cyprian, through most persevering endurance—not by shedding blood, but by not shedding it within unity—for if he were to give his body so that it might be burned but did not have charity, it would profit him nothing—reached the light of the angels through his confession of martyrdom. Thus, if not earlier, then certainly there he would recognize as revealed what, although he thought otherwise, he had not placed an opinion differing from the truth above the bond of unity.”

But what Cyprian adds and says (*On Baptism*, book V, chapter 3) is also entirely true:

> “Yet because there was error at some time, it does not follow that there must always be error. Rather, it is more fitting for the wise and God-fearing to obey willingly and without hesitation the truth that has been disclosed and examined than stubbornly and obstinately to resist their brothers and fellow priests on behalf of heretics. He who resists the clearest truth is, most truly, opposed to no one more than to himself.
>
> “Primacy, however, exists only in holy conduct and a good life. All belong to that primacy who, as members, constitute that bride who has neither spot nor wrinkle, and that dove which groans amid the wickedness of many ravens. Unless perhaps those are to be considered holders of primacy who have lost the primacy with Esau because of their desire for a dish of lentils: defrauders, robbers, usurers, the envious, drunkards, and others of this kind, such as Cyprian lamented in writing were present in the Church of his time.
>
> “Therefore, either holding the Church is not the same as holding primacy in divine matters, or, if everyone who holds the Church also holds primacy, then all those wicked people do not hold the Church who nevertheless appear within it, and whom none of us denies either giving or possessing baptism. For who would say that they possess primacy in divine matters, unless he has no understanding of anything divine?
>
> “Outside, then—that is, in heresy or schism—nothing can be either bound or loosed, where there is no one who can bind or loose. But the person who makes peace with the dove is loosed, and the person who has no peace with the dove is bound, whether he is openly outside or appears to be within.
>
> “We know that Dathan and Abiram (Numbers 16), who tried to usurp for themselves the right to sacrifice against the unity of God’s people, and the sons of Aaron, who placed strange fire upon the altar, did not act with impunity. Nor do we say that other crimes remain unpunished, unless such people correct themselves, if God’s patience, leading them to repentance, grants time for correction.”

(Augustine, *On Baptism*, book III, chapter 16.)

> “The Holy Spirit, who is said to be given only in the catholic Church through the laying on of hands, was surely intended by our predecessors to be understood in accordance with what the Apostle says: ‘Because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us’ (Romans 5). For he himself is the love that those who have been cut off from communion with the catholic Church do not possess. Consequently, even if they speak with the tongues of human beings and angels, even if they know all sacraments [mysteries] and all knowledge, even if they possess all prophecy and all faith, so as to move mountains, and distribute all their possessions to the poor, and give their bodies so that they may be burned, it profits them nothing.
>
> “He does not possess the love of God who does not love the unity of the Church. Accordingly, it is rightly understood to be said that the Holy Spirit is received only in the catholic Church. For the Holy Spirit is not now given through the laying on of hands with temporal and perceptible miracles attesting it (Acts 8), as it was formerly given to commend the rudimentary faith and to extend the beginnings of the Church. Who now expects that those upon whom hands are laid for receiving the Holy Spirit will suddenly begin to speak in tongues?
>
> “Rather, invisibly and secretly, divine love is understood to be breathed into their hearts for the bond of peace, so that they may say: ‘Because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us’ (Romans 5).
>
> “There are many works of the Holy Spirit. When the same Apostle had mentioned as many of them as he thought sufficient in one passage, he concluded: ‘But all these things one and the same Spirit accomplishes, distributing to each one as he wills’ (1 Corinthians 12). Since, therefore, one thing is the sacrament, which even Simon Magus could possess (Acts 8), and another is the operation of the Spirit, which is often found even in wicked people, as Saul had prophecy (1 Samuel 10), and another is the operation of that same Spirit which only the good can possess, such as ‘the end of the commandment is love from a pure heart and a good conscience and an unfeigned faith’ (1 Timothy 1), whatever heretics and schismatics may receive, the love that ‘covers a multitude of sins’ (1 Peter 4) is the special gift of catholic unity and peace.
>
> “It is not in everyone, because not everyone belongs to it, as we shall see in its proper place. Nevertheless, that love cannot exist apart from it; without that love, the other gifts, even if they can be recognized and approved, cannot benefit or liberate.”
