And Saint Gregory, in the eighteenth book of the *Moralia* (chapter 14):

> “The fire of the furnace, which is tolerated outside the catholic Church, is shown by the Apostle Paul to be of no virtue whatsoever, when he says: ‘If I give my body so that it may be burned, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing’ (1 Corinthians 13). Some hold perverse opinions about God; others hold correct opinions about the Creator, but do not preserve unity with their brothers. The former are divided by error of faith, the latter by the commission of schism.
>
> “Thus, in the very first part of the Decalogue, the guilt of both parties is restrained, when the divine voice says: ‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength’ (Deuteronomy 6), and immediately adds: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ For whoever thinks perversely about God clearly does not love God. Whoever, while thinking correctly about God, is divided from the unity of the holy Church plainly does not love his neighbor, whom he refuses to have as a companion.
>
> “Whoever, therefore, is divided from this unity of Mother Church—whether by thinking perversely about God through heresy, or by failing to love his neighbor through the error of schism—is deprived of this grace of charity, concerning which Paul says what we quoted above: ‘If I give my body so that it may be burned, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing’ (1 Corinthians 13). It is as though he said openly: ‘Outside its proper place, the fire of my furnace torments me with punishment; it does not purify me by cleansing.’
>
> “All lovers of holy peace seek this place with the greatest diligence; seeking it, they find it; finding it, they hold it, knowing where, when, and to whom the remission of sins is given. Where, indeed, if not in the bosom of the catholic mother? When, if not before the day of the coming departure? For ‘behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation’; and: ‘Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near.’
>
> “To whom, if not to those who have been converted, who are formed in the imitation of little children by the instruction of profound humility, to whom it is said: ‘Let the little children come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven’ (2 Corinthians 6); and: ‘Unless you are converted and become like little children, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven’ (Isaiah 55).”

And in the decrees of the Apostolic See, when Vigilius, having taken many terrible oaths, had fallen into heresy and was being detained at Constantinople, a letter sent by the catholic clergy of the Roman Church to John, a schismatic priest, contains the following among the rules that the holy Roman Church itself preserves among the catholic regulations:

> “This has always been the position of every Church: those who agree in one communion are held together by one doctrine, one charity, and one consent. For just as one communion is formed from all who offer and returns as one in all—not by bodily division but by divine power—so unanimity extends through all who communicate there.
>
> “For if one communion is not the sign of one consent, what is mystically celebrated throughout the harmony of the whole Church for the purpose of confessing the faith? Do not now say to us (Matthew 19): ‘Therefore, if the priest is criminal, the crime passes over to the people.’ One thing is what is committed, another what is also preached. What each individual commits privately is private; but what is publicly preached and subscribed by the hands of so many priests becomes common to the Church.
>
> “And just as you cannot be absolved if you preach contrary things with your mouth and subscribe to contrary things with your hand at one and the same time, so the whole assembly of all of you cannot be absolved if it says and does contrary things—that is, if it communicates with a priest whose preaching and subscription it rejects. For just as your mouth and hand are members of one and the same body, so priests and people are members of one and the same Church, whether catholic with Catholics or unbelieving with unbelievers.
>
> “This is why the tares are commanded by the Lord to be gathered at the end of the age and bound into bundles for burning (Matthew 13). This is why, as the holy prophet Ezekiel testifies: ‘If the priest does not distinguish for the people, the people themselves will die in their sin, but I will require their soul from the hand of the priest’ (Ezekiel 3). He does not say that the people will not die because they are outside sin, but that they will die in their own sin: the people for themselves alone, but the priest also for the people.
>
> “This is why, if the blind lead the blind, not only the one who gives the guidance but both fall into the pit (Matthew 15).”

And again in those same decrees:

> “A schismatic or heretical people communicating with a schismatic or heretical priest cannot enter the kingdom of God, as the whole Church of God has always held and still holds; their portion is in Gehenna.
>
> “Therefore cease preaching such things, which it is a crime even to contemplate. Cease laying waste Christ’s flock, lest—as you yourself cannot deny—the destruction of that entire people fall upon your head. This is indeed a cause of perfect damnation for you, but it will not be able to absolve them entirely.
>
> “And again there, as I have also set down elsewhere in this same little work: Whoever assents to the leader of a schism cannot deny that he is a schismatic. Even if all the priests and the whole world give their assent, condemnation envelops those who consent; consent does not absolve the transgression. The crime is not diminished but increased when what was private becomes general.
>
> “God has shown this in the case of everyone, for he destroyed the sinful world by a universal flood. But what will you wretched people do? He who both foretold and brought about that flood now threatens a flood of fire; he himself threatens the unending torments of Gehenna. For just as he foretold that the righteous would enter eternal life, so he foretold that the ungodly would be condemned to eternal destruction, so that just as the blessedness of the righteous cannot end, neither can the torments of the ungodly end.
>
> “These things concern heretics and schismatics. And because whatever the Church now does is mystically a type of future things, if they taste the heavenly bread—that is, divine sweetness—the communion of Christ’s body is condemnation for schismatics and heretics, who thereby become participants in Gehenna.”

And Saint Augustine, in the letter of the African Council to the Donatists:

> “Whoever is separated from the catholic Church, however laudably he may think he lives, will not have life, but the wrath of God remains upon him, because of this one crime alone: that he has been separated from the unity of Christ.
>
> “But whoever has lived well in this Church is not harmed by the sins of others, because each person will bear his own burden in it, as the Apostle says: ‘Whoever eats the body of Christ unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself’ (1 Corinthians 11). When he says ‘eats judgment upon himself,’ he sufficiently shows that he does not eat judgment upon another but upon himself. For participation in the sacraments does not stain anyone through communion with the wicked, but through consent to their deeds.
>
> “If someone does not consent to them in their evil deeds, the wicked person bears his own cause and his own person, and does not prejudice another whom he does not have as a partner in the consent to the evil deed.”

(Augustine, Letter 152.)

And Prosper, in the *Book of Sentences*:

> “He receives the food of life and drinks the cup of eternity who remains in Christ and in whom Christ dwells. For whoever disagrees with Christ neither eats Christ’s flesh nor drinks his blood, even if he daily receives, without distinction, the sacrament of so great a reality to the judgment of his presumption.”

You hear, brother, that by loving his own opinion excessively, or by envying those who are better, a person proceeds to the sacrilege of schism. You hear that primacy is not in schism, nor anywhere except in the unity of the Church. You hear that the true bonds are not in schism, but only in the unity of the Church, in which the sacraments that are true and directed toward salvation are found. You hear that the Holy Spirit is not given or received in schism, but only in the unity of the Church, through whom charity is poured into our hearts. You hear that, for those who are not in the unity of ecclesiastical peace, if they taste the heavenly bread, communion in Christ’s body is perfect condemnation.

Therefore lay aside the swelling of your heart and the stubbornness of your obstinate mind. By loving your own opinion excessively, do not cut yourself off from that bond of charity in which you received all the ecclesiastical sacraments in catholic fashion, and in which you were therefore ordained bishop, so that you might remain in it and teach others to remain in it by faith and works, by example and by words.

Finally, concerning the origin of schisms, the same catholic teacher says (Augustine, *On Baptism*, book I, chapters 11 and 15):

> “The origin and persistence of schism has no other cause than hatred of a brother. The Church did not first have carnal or natural people and afterward spiritual people; rather, in the very condition of our mortality, from the time we are born from Adam, ‘the natural comes first, and afterward the spiritual.’
>
> “From this natural way of thinking, because the natural person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God, all dissensions and schisms arise. Those who persist in this way of thinking, the Apostle says, belong to the Old Testament—that is, to the desire for earthly promises. Spiritual realities are indeed represented in those promises, but the natural person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God.
>
> “Whenever, therefore, such people begin to exist in this life, although they have already been imbued with the divine sacraments according to the distribution of the ages, they nevertheless still think carnally and hope for and desire carnal things from God, whether in this life or after this life; they are natural people.”

And again, from the words of blessed Cyprian, as I have partly written above and as it is necessary to repeat for you, he says (Cyprian, Letter 65, to Antonianus):

> “Forgiveness can be granted to one who simply errs, as the Apostle Paul says of himself: ‘I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man; but I received mercy because I acted ignorantly’ (1 Timothy 1). But after inspiration and revelation have been given, whoever persists in the error in which he had been mistaken sins knowingly and deliberately, without the excuse of ignorance. For he relies upon a certain presumption and obstinacy when he is overcome by reason.”

Hence Augustine (*On Baptism*, book IV, chapter 5):

> “This is most certainly true: the sin of one who sins knowingly is far more serious than that of one who sins unknowingly. Therefore the holy Cyprian—learned not only in teaching but also teachable, which the Apostle nevertheless identifies as praise in a bishop—understood the matter in such a way that he said this too ought to be valued in a bishop: not only that he should teach knowingly, but also that he should learn patiently.
>
> “A teachable person is one who is gentle and mild in the patience required for learning. Bishops ought not only to teach but also to learn, because the person who grows and progresses daily by learning better things teaches better.
>
> “By these words the holy man, endowed with devout charity, sufficiently indicates that there is no need to fear reading his letters in such a way that, if the Church later confirmed something through more numerous and longer inquiries, we should hesitate. For just as there were many things that the learned Cyprian could teach, so there was also something that the teachable Cyprian could learn.”

Receive these things, brother, with your ears and understand them with your mind. Do not disdain to be a teachable bishop together with Cyprian and Augustine, as the Apostle commands. For if you choose to persevere in your obstinacy and presumption after being overcome by reason, you will sin knowingly and deliberately, without the excuse of ignorance.

For this reason the psalm says: “Let them descend alive into hell” (Psalm 55)—that is, let them fall knowingly into sin.

Accordingly, Leo writes to the Constantinopolitans (Letter 25):

> “For if ignorance seems scarcely tolerable in laypeople, then in those who preside it is even less worthy of excuse or pardon—especially when they presume to defend the inventions of perverse opinions and, by terror or favor, lead the most incurable people into their own agreement. Let such persons be separated from the healthy members of Christ’s body, and let catholic freedom not permit the yoke of unbelievers to be imposed upon it.”

Therefore withdraw from your obstinacy. Those whom you enticed or compelled in your assemblies to subscribe with you do indeed have an excuse, because either they surrendered captive hands to fear without the consent of their hearts, or, ignorant of what they were doing, they transgressed through your disguised persuasion against the bond of peace and through consent to your communion of peace, or perhaps both they and the others who knew what was happening did not dare to suggest anything to you about it.

Hence blessed Gregory says:

> “No one does greater harm in the Church than one who acts perversely while possessing the name or rank of holiness. No one dares to rebuke such a delinquent, and the fault is greatly extended as an example when, out of reverence for his rank, a sinner is honored. For them pardon is easier, because their guilt is also lighter.”

Concerning those who sinned after being led astray through ignorance, Saint Augustine says in the work mentioned above (book I of *On Baptism*, chapter 2):

> “If extreme necessity should compel someone, so that he cannot find a catholic person through whom he may receive it, and, while preserving catholic peace in his heart, he receives through someone situated outside catholic unity what he would have received within that catholic unity, and if he immediately departs from this life, we count him as nothing other than a catholic.
>
> “But if he is delivered from bodily death and returns even in bodily presence to the catholic congregation from which he had never departed in his heart, we not only do not disapprove what he did, but we praise it most confidently and truly, because he believed that God was present to his heart, where he preserved unity.”

Concerning those who knowingly entered this transgression through fear or favor, Leo writes to Pulcheria Augusta (Letter 53):

> “We exercise the justice of indignation in such a way that we do not lose the remedies of charity. As your piety recognizes, this is promised not only in words but also demonstrated by deeds. Indeed, nearly all those who had been led or compelled into agreement with the presiding authorities at that Ephesian gathering—which was not a judgment but a bandit raid—obtained perpetual abolition of their guilt and the grace of apostolic peace by rescinding what they had decided and condemning what they had written.”

And in his letter to Anatolius (Letter 42):

> “Nor can our kindness be criticized in any respect when we receive those who make satisfaction, whom we have grieved to see deceived. The grace of our communion, therefore, must neither be harshly denied nor recklessly granted. For just as it is full of piety to restore the Lord’s charity to those who have been oppressed, so it is just that everything be charged to the authors of the disturbance.”

Hear, then, both you and those whom you led astray or compelled to subscribe with you, the admonition of blessed Augustine. Addressing those who had separated themselves from fraternal unanimity, he warned them as follows (*On Baptism*, book II, chapters 10–11):

> “Let them see that nothing remains for them to say; nevertheless, let them also see that something remains for them to do, so that, for their past deeds, the sacrifice of love may be offered to the God who can be appeased—he whose unity they severed by their wicked crime, and whose sacraments they insulted for so long. For the Lord is merciful and compassionate, patient and greatly merciful, and true.
>
> “Let them embrace in the present life the merciful and patient Lord, and fear in the future the Lord who is true. For he does not desire the death of the wicked, but rather that he should return and live, because he bends his sentence against the injuries inflicted.
>
> “This is our exhortation. For this reason they regard us as enemies: because we speak the truth, because we fear to remain silent, because we fear to cease from pressing the matter as much as we can, because we obey the Apostle who says: ‘Preach the word; be urgent in season and out of season; reprove, exhort, rebuke’ (2 Timothy 4). But, as the Gospel says: ‘They love the glory of human beings more than the glory of God’ (John 12); they fear being reproved for a time but do not fear being condemned forever.
>
> “They themselves see what evil they are doing; they see that they have absolutely nothing to answer, but they display clouds to the inexperienced while they themselves are swallowed alive—that is, they perish knowingly and consciously. They see that people shudder at and intensely detest the fact that they themselves have been divided into many schisms, and especially that, in the capital of Africa and the most renowned city of Carthage, they attempted to repair the disgrace of their rags, thinking that they could remove the Maximianists.”

And after some intervening material (the same work, chapters 12–13):

> “Truth presses them from every side. They see that they have nothing to answer, and they suppose that they have nothing to do. They cannot find what to say; they are not permitted to remain silent; they prefer to resist the truth with perverse voices rather than be restored to peace after acknowledging their errors.
>
> “Who does not understand what they may say in their hearts? ‘What, then, shall we do about those whom we have already rebaptized?’ And you: ‘What, then, shall we do about those whom we have already led astray, or what shall we do—we who have been led astray?’ The answer is: ‘Return with them to the Church, namely, to fraternal unanimity. Offer the medicine of peace for the healing of those whom you wounded; offer the charity of life for the raising up of those whom you killed.
>
> “‘Fraternal harmony has great power to make God propitious. “If two of you,” says the Lord, “agree on earth about anything they ask, it will be done for them” (Matthew 18). If this is true of two people, how much more of two peoples? Let us prostrate ourselves together before the Lord; share with us in unanimity; let us share with you in sorrow; and charity will cover a multitude of sins.’”

And blessed Gregory says in his homily on Ezekiel (Homily 7, at the end):

> “Let us always place before the eyes of our mind both the virtues and the tears of the perfect. Let us imitate what we behold in them, so that, when we begin to grow through successive advances, we may be able to conceal from that distinct judgment the evils we have committed.
>
> “For in continual weeping and in our daily repentance, we have a priest in heaven who intercedes for us. Of him it is also said through John: ‘If anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and he is the propitiation for our sins’ (1 John 2).
>
> “Behold, the spirit rejoices when we hear of the power of our advocate; but fear again wounds our joy, because the one who is our advocate is said to be righteous. We have causes of injustice. But the righteous advocate in no way undertakes unjust causes, nor does he agree to speak in defense of injustice.
>
> “What, then, shall we do, my dearest brothers? But behold, what we should do comes to mind. Let us both abandon and accuse the evils we have committed. It is written: ‘The righteous person is first an accuser of himself’ (Proverbs 18). For every sinner who is converted in tears begins already to be righteous when he begins to accuse what he has done. Why should one not be righteous who already rages through tears against his own unrighteousness?
>
> “Our righteous advocate therefore defends us as righteous in judgment, because we both recognize and accuse ourselves as unrighteous. Let us not trust in our tears or our deeds, therefore, but in the pleading of our advocate.”

Let us fear what is written: “A wicked son declares himself righteous, but he does not cleanse his end”—that is, as Augustine says, he does not excuse it, wipe it away, or defend it.

Therefore, brother, after hearing so many sacred authorities, admonitions, and salutary counsels offered to you, do not turn to “excuses for sins” and obstinate defense, when no one seeks your condemnation but your correction and salvation before God and human beings.

As you read these things that I write to you with paternal devotion, store also in the secret place of your mind this saying of blessed Gregory—not long in number of words, but possessing immense and precious meaning:

> “In the words of sacred eloquence, this order of our study ought to be preserved: we should learn these things so that, being pierced with compunction over our iniquity, we may recognize the evils we have done and avoid doing others; and when, through long practice in tears, confidence in the forgiveness of sins has begun to arise, we may also draw others toward life through the words of God that we understand. For this purpose they are to be understood: so that they may benefit us and, through spiritual intention, be conferred upon others.”

## CHAPTER XLIX. He is admonished not to neglect the talent of understanding that the Lord freely gave him
Let us hear and obey the blessed Apostle, who admonishes us together with himself: “Let us not become desirous of empty glory, envying one another and provoking one another” (Gal. V). And again he says to us: “See carefully how you walk, not as fools but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (Eph. V); and: “Be subject to one another in the fear of Christ” (ibid.); and: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. VI); and: “In honor, anticipating one another” (Rom. XII).

Tell me, brother and son, what else have I required of you, after you became a bishop and acquired earthly riches, except that you should have God favorable to you, and, living as a bishop and conducting yourself with episcopal bearing, make yourself venerable to human beings? And for what reason have I been moved against you, except that I wished and admonished you to be such before God for salvation and before the world for the honor due to episcopal gravity and order? I saw that this was burdensome to you; and indeed it could have been burdensome to you until now, both because of your age and because you had not yet come to know the instability of this world and how changeable and fragile it is.

But now it is time for us to rise from sleep (Rom. XIII). We ought not always to remain young, just as a bad ox is always a calf. We must bring neglected matters back before the eyes of our mind and blush for our former conduct, as the outstanding preacher admonishes us, saying: “What fruit did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. VI). And we must strive to have our fruit in sanctification, and its end eternal life.

And if, brother and son, you do not wish or deign to hear me, hear and obey the blessed Apostle Paul himself, who admonished Timothy, his spiritual son, whom he had ordained as a young bishop: “Exercise yourself,” he says, “unto godliness. For bodily exercise is profitable for a little, but godliness is profitable for all things, having the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come” (I Tim. IV, 7). “Let no one despise your youth, but be an example to the faithful in word, in conduct, in charity, in faith, and in chastity. Do not neglect the grace that is in you, which was given to you through prophecy and the laying on of the hands of the presbytery. For by doing this you will save yourself and those who hear you.”

But if not, brother and son, fear what the Lord says with terrifying force to the one who had received a single talent, went away, dug in the ground, and hid his master’s money: “Wicked and lazy servant, you knew that I reap where I did not sow and gather where I did not scatter” (Matt. XXV), and what follows. To hide a talent in the ground is to entangle one’s received natural ability in earthly activities, not to seek spiritual gain, and never to lift the heart from earthly desires.

“For there are,” as the blessed Gregory says (Gregory, *Homilies on the Gospels*), “some who have received the gift of understanding, yet understand only the things of the flesh. Of them it is said through the prophet (Jer. IV): ‘They are wise to do evil, but they do not know how to do good.’ But the Lord who bestowed the talents returns to demand an account, because he who now distributes spiritual gifts will strictly investigate merits at the judgment. He considers what each person has received and weighs what profit each has brought back from what was received.”

Consider, therefore, what you have received without any merit of your own in the talent of understanding, and take care lest you hide it in the ground, and—God forbid—be condemned by him because of it.

## CHAPTER L. On what is said to be unbearable: that someone should be said to have shown him some good without his own merit

Finally, some say that you cannot patiently endure anyone’s saying to you that someone has shown you some good without your own merit. This disposition of mind plainly proceeds not from humility but from pride.

For the Apostle says: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (I Cor. IV).

It is read in Scripture that this is both the Lord’s custom and that of his saints: when we do not acknowledge from whom we have received good things, and either answer good deeds with evil works or prove ungrateful, the good things bestowed upon us are brought to light, so that, recognizing them, we may blush for our evils and for our ingratitude toward good things, and turn back both to restore what is good and to offer thanks.

Thus the Lord is very frequently read as acting in Scripture: from many examples, few in number but not in importance, are brought forward. For he says to his own peculiar people: “My people, what have I done to you? Show me. I led you through the wilderness for forty years; your garments were not worn out; I rained manna upon you from heaven—and have you forgotten me?” (Mic. VI).

And to David, his beloved servant, of whom he says, “I found David my servant, who does all my will,” he says: “I took you from your father’s house and appointed you to pasture my people’s flock, and I was with you wherever you went, establishing your kingdom forever” (II Reg. VII). And he reproaches him with many other things, because, after receiving manifold gifts, he had sinned grievously against him without regard.

Read Paul’s letters to the Corinthians and to the Galatians, and you will find sufficient evidence there. For we read of four kinds of arrogant people: those who think they possess by themselves the good things they have; those who think they possess them because of their merits; those who think they alone possess them; and those who think they possess them more than others.

Guard your heart against all these, according to what is written: “Guard your heart with all vigilance, for from it life proceeds” (Prov. IV).

## CHAPTER LI. On the gifts which he was said to demand from clergy and laity

Many also say that you burden the clergy and laity entrusted to you with numerous gifts on various pretexts. Showing that this is entirely inconsistent with Christian devotion, and least of all with episcopal religion, holy Pope Leo says:

“Just as,” he says (Epistle 84, to Anastasius), “a prelate does not wish to bear the burden of a heavy load, so he should not dare to impose an unbearable weight upon others. For we are disciples of the humble and gentle teacher who says: ‘Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls’ (Matt. XI). This humble and gentle teacher again speaks concerning a harsh and unbearable prelate: ‘If that wicked servant says in his heart, “My master delays his coming,” and begins to strike his fellow servants, while eating and drinking with drunkards, the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him asunder and appoint his portion with the hypocrites’ (Matt. XXIV).”

The blessed Gregory says from this point (Pastoral Rule II, chap. 6): “He is rightly numbered among hypocrites who, under the pretense of discipline, turns the ministry of governance into an exercise of domination.”

And the blessed Apostle Paul forbids a bishop to be a striker (I Tim. III; Tit. I). This does not mean merely one who does not strike subordinates with his fists, but one who does not strike the conscience of his subjects by his actions and words. The Lord rebukes such people through the prophet: “Those who strike with the fist wickedly” (Isa. LVIII).

We must therefore listen to what is said to prelates by a certain wise man: “They have appointed you leader; do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of them” (Eccli. XXXII); and: “If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. LXI).

We must also fear lest the pre-eminence and honors that we possess in this world, if we are in any respect good, become our recompense and make us strangers to the recompense of the just. Hence, in Abraham’s words, it is said to the rich man consumed by flame: “Remember, son, that you received good things during your life” (Luke XVI). The wicked man received good things here precisely so that he might receive more fully the evil things there, because here he had not been converted even by good things. For when the human mind does not follow God, who gives generously, with a response of good works, it is more justly condemned by the very means through which it is believed to have been piously nourished.

Hence the Psalmist says: “You cast them down when they were lifted up” (Ps. LXXII). For the reprobate, when they do not repay divine gifts with righteous works, when they abandon themselves entirely here and give themselves over to abundant prosperity, fall inwardly through the very things by which they prosper outwardly.

Many say that scarcely anyone, or rather no one, can obtain from you some benefit unless by giving a reward. This is utterly contrary to the authority of the sacred Scriptures and opposed to the decrees of the holy canons: that you should give as a reward for shameful profit the ecclesiastical possessions and resources which, at your episcopal ordination, you received without payment for governing and regularly dispensing.

When the Apostle Paul describes to Titus what a bishop ought to be, he says among other things: “A bishop must be blameless, as God’s steward; not proud, not angry, not given to wine, not a striker, not greedy for shameful profit” (Tit. I). And again he says: “Avarice, which is the service of idols” (Eph. V, 5); and: “The desire for money is the root of all evils” (I Tim. VI, 10).

The sacred Carthaginian canons say (canon 5): “It is altogether forbidden for any cleric to receive interest on any matter”; and shortly afterward: “Therefore, what is condemned in the laity ought much more to be condemned beforehand in the clergy. The entire council said: No one acts against the prophets or against the Gospels without danger.”

The Council of Nicaea, which is likewise found in many other canons, customarily gathers several matters into one chapter and says here, together with other provisions (canon 17):

“Since many who have been placed under the rule pursue avarice and shameful profits, the holy and great synod has rightly decreed that if anyone is found transacting business by any contrivance or in any manner whatsoever, or devising anything of this kind entirely for the sake of shameful profit, he shall be removed from the clergy and shall be a stranger to the rule.”

And Leo, in a letter to all the bishops established throughout the various provinces, says (Epistle 1):

“We have judged it necessary to give this warning beforehand: just as no cleric may attempt to practice usury in his own name, so neither may he do so in another’s name. For it is disgraceful to devote one’s own crime to another’s profit. The only interest which we ought to regard and pursue is that we may receive from the Lord, who will repay abundantly and eternally, what we mercifully give here. Our warning therefore declares that if any of the brethren attempts to act contrary to these constitutions, and dares to commit what has been forbidden, he must know that he is to be removed from his office and will not be a participant in our communion—he who was unwilling to be a partner in discipline.”

And the Lord says in the Gospel: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink; I was a stranger, and you did not welcome me; naked, and you did not clothe me; sick and in prison, and you did not visit me” (Matt. XXV, 42). He also prefaces these words by saying: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid., 41).

See: they are not accused of having committed robberies or any other acts of violence, yet they are handed over to the eternal fires of Gehenna. From this, then, we must infer with what condemnation those who seize what belongs to others must be punished, if those who indiscriminately kept what was their own are struck with such severity.

Let them consider by what guilt stolen property binds them, if property not given subjects a person to such punishment. Let them consider what the injustice inflicted deserves, if mercy not shown is worthy of such a blow.

When they intend to seize what belongs to others, let them hear what is written: “Woe to him who multiplies what is not his own and heaps thick clay upon himself” (Hab. II, 6). For the greedy person to heap thick clay upon himself is to accumulate earthly profits together with the weight of sin.

When they desire to multiply the spaces of their spacious dwellings, let them hear what is written: “Woe to you who join house to house and add field to field, until there is no more room: will you alone dwell in the midst of the earth?” (Isa. V, 8). It is as though he were saying openly: How far do you extend yourselves, since you cannot bear to have any companions in the common world? You oppress those who have been joined to you, but you always find others against whom you can extend yourselves.

When they pant after increasing their money, let them hear what is written: “The greedy person will not be filled with money, and whoever loves riches will gain no fruit from them” (Eccl. V). He would gain fruit from them if, without loving them, he wished to distribute them well; but because he holds them fast by loving them, he will certainly leave this life without fruit.

When they burn with eagerness to be filled with all riches at once, let them hear what is written: “Whoever hastens to become rich will not be innocent” (Prov. XXVIII). Indeed, because he strives to increase his wealth, he neglects to avoid sin; and, like a bird caught in a snare, when he greedily sees the bait of earthly things, he does not recognize the noose of sin by which he will be strangled.

When they desire whatever profits belong to the present world and are ignorant of the losses they will suffer in the future, let them hear what is written: “An inheritance to which one hastens at the beginning will lack blessing at the end” (Prov. XX). For from this life we begin our journey so that at the end we may come to the portion of blessing. Therefore those who hasten to inherit at the beginning cut themselves off from the portion of blessing at the end; while they desire to multiply here through the wickedness of avarice, there they become disinherited from the eternal patrimony.

When they either desire more or are able to obtain everything they have desired, let them hear what is written: “What does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” (Luke VIII). It is as though Truth were saying openly: What does it profit a person if he gathers everything outside himself, if he condemns only that which he himself is?

I have frequently warned you about this and rebuked you so severely that you took offense at it against me and against those loyal to me, and strove to devise whatever and however many snares you could.

But our lord the king also warned you about this in a letter given to you, as follows:

“Indeed,” he says, “I first consider it worthy to warn you that you should show due episcopal and pastoral kindness to the clergy and people entrusted to you. They chose you and earnestly requested that you be ordained their pastor, not under compulsion but led by hope: because, out of love for your uncle, who benefited both us and the kingdom and the Church of our kingdom in many ways, they saw that I loved you; because they thought you would follow in his footsteps and obey his counsels; and because the municipality of Laon had formerly been united to the Church of Reims, in which you had been raised. Therefore do not treat or afflict them so harshly, nor place over them others whom you previously did not know; and do not cast out from the bosom of the Church entrusted to you those who had been nourished and educated there, as you have already expelled some or compelled them to depart, nor force them to remain there amid groaning.”

Read intelligently and retain firmly this letter of the blessed Gregory to Constantius, bishop of Milan:

“On receiving,” he says (Book III, Epistle 1), “the letter of your Fraternity, I gave great thanks to almighty God, because I deserved to be relieved by the celebration of your ordination. But since, by heavenly grace, the unanimous consent of all converged upon your election, your Fraternity must consider this with the greatest care: after God, you are greatly indebted to those who, with such a submissive spirit, wished to have you preferred to themselves.

“It is therefore fitting that you should answer their conduct in all things with priestly kindness and meet their needs with compassionate piety. If perhaps they have faults, rebuke them with mature corrections, so that even priestly indignation may be mingled with the virtue of gentleness, so that your subjects ought to love you even when they fear you greatly.

“This also brings your person into great reverence in their judgment. For just as sudden and habitual anger is despised, so, in contrast, measured indignation against faults is often more greatly feared the longer it is delayed.”

You must also carefully consider that what I say for your benefit is not said for my praise but for the praise of God, whose gift it is. I, your fosterer, with whom you spent your years from childhood through youth, as you saw and heard, did not demand or seek in any way from clergy, laity, or parish priests any payments, gifts, or profits: not for the distribution of benefices, not for the appointment of ministries, not for receiving those same ministries, not for returning my favor to those who had offended me, not through any request for assistance, and not through any contrived pretext. In all things I considered their advancement and the usefulness of the place entrusted to me.

You should therefore remember that I frequently admonished you to be not burdensome but gracious to those entrusted to you, who willingly chose you.

And if my admonitions do not please you, read, together with other works, the homily of the blessed Gregory on the Gospel, “I am the good shepherd” (John X), and store it in your mind. Among other things, he says concerning the supreme and essential good shepherd, whose pattern we must follow:

“I know my sheep,” he says (Homily 14 on the Gospels), “that is, I love them; and my sheep know me, that is, loving me, they obey me. For those entrusted to us ought to obey us in Christ through love rather than, compelled by servile fear, serve us with groaning.”

To receive rewards or gifts from such pre-eminences, from the transactions mentioned above, or from any contrivances is simoniacal and contrary to the sacred Scriptures and, as I have shown above, contrary to the holy canons.

Therefore even the laws to which holy Church gives the reverence due to lawful observance say, in Constitution 117, chapter 352 of Justinian’s constitution:

“Let the administrators of venerable institutions be appointed without money. No administrator of a hospice, orphanage, hospital, or any religious house, nor any person responsible for ecclesiastical care, may give anything to the person by whom he is appointed or to any other person in exchange for the administration entrusted to him.

“Whoever, contrary to these provisions, gives or receives anything, or acts as an intermediary, shall be stripped of his priesthood, clergy, or entrusted administration. Whatever has been given shall be reclaimed for the religious institution whose consecration, care, or administration that person received. If the recipient or intermediary is a layman, double shall be exacted from him and paid to the religious institution in which that person received administration, consecration, or care.”

The laws therefore decreed these things justly and reasonably, in agreement with the sacred Scriptures and canons. For, as Saint Leo says (Sermon 9 on the Passion of the Lord):

“The Apostle rightly defined avarice as the root of all evils. No sin is committed without desire, and every unlawful appetite is a disease of this greed. Every affection is cheap in comparison with the love of money, and the soul greedy for profit does not fear perishing even for a small gain. There is no trace of justice in that heart in which avarice has made its dwelling. Thus faithless Judas, intoxicated with poison, reached the noose while thirsting for profit.”

## CHAPTER LII. On his pride, arrogance, and foolish and unbecoming boasting

Many also reproach you for being inflated with pride, boastful with empty glory, and overcome by arrogance. Let you and I therefore see ourselves and our minds, as in a mirror, in the words of the blessed Gregory, and compose ourselves before the divine eyes.

He says (Book XXXIV of the *Moralia*, chap. 18):

“Pride, which we have called the root of vices, is by no means content with extinguishing a single virtue. It rises against all the members of the soul and, like a general and destructive disease, corrupts the entire body, so that whatever is done when it invades—even if it appears to be virtue—is done not for God but solely for empty glory.

“It is as though a tyrant captures an occupied city when pride bursts into the mind. The richer the person it captures, the harsher it becomes in its domination, because the more extensively a virtue is practiced without humility, the more widely pride rules.

“Whoever receives its tyranny within himself with a captive mind first suffers this harm: with the eye of the heart closed, he loses equity of judgment. For everything that others do well displeases him, while he is pleased only with what he himself has done badly. He always despises the works of others and always marvels at what he himself does, because whatever he has done, he believes he has done uniquely. In what he displays, through desire for glory, he favors himself in his own thoughts.

“He does not consider what good another has more than he does, but what good he himself has more than another. He does not weigh what good the other spirit has received and he lacks, but what good he has and what evils belong to the other. And when he judges himself superior to all, he walks about with himself through the broad spaces of his thoughts and silently proclaims his own praises.

“Sometimes the mind is led to such great exaltation that, in what makes it swell, it is also unrestrained by ostentatious speech. Ruin follows all the more easily the more shamelessly each person exalts himself in his own eyes. Hence it is written: ‘The heart is exalted before ruin’ (Prov. XVI).

“This exaltation possesses some through secular things and others through spiritual things. One swells with gold, another with eloquence; one with the lowest and earthly things, another with the highest and heavenly virtues. Yet the same pride is acted out before God’s eyes, although, when it comes into human hearts, it disguises itself before them in different clothing.

“It attacks superiors and subordinates differently. To a prelate it suggests in his thoughts that he has grown above others solely through the merit of his life. If he has ever done anything well, it thrusts this insistently into his mind; and when it implies that he has pleased God in a singular way, in order more easily to persuade him of what it has suggested, it summons the very recompense of the authority entrusted to him as evidence, saying: ‘Unless almighty God had seen you to be better than all these, he would not have placed them all under your rule.’

“Then it immediately lifts his mind up and shows him that his subjects are worthless and useless, so that he now regards no one as worthy to whom he can speak with equanimity. Hence the tranquility of his mind is quickly turned into anger. While he despises everyone and reproves everyone’s understanding and life without moderation, he expands into anger all the more uncontrollably because he thinks those entrusted to him unworthy of himself.

“If they themselves are subject to others, pride urges their hearts to neglect entirely the consideration of their own actions and always to become, in silent thoughts, judges of their ruler. While they insistently look at what they ought to criticize in him, they never see what they ought to correct in themselves. Thus they perish all the more terribly because they turn their eyes away from themselves.

“Sometimes such subjects do not reveal at all the insolence they feel. Those whose talkativeness can scarcely be restrained sometimes fall silent solely from the bitterness of inward resentment. Withdrawing the words of their insolence out of mental anguish, although they are accustomed to speak evilly, they are worse when silent. For when, as sinners, they hear something about correction, they suspend even the words of a reply in indignation.

“When they are dealt with harshly, they often burst into complaints about that very harshness. But when their masters gently anticipate them, they are more deeply indignant at the very humility with which they were anticipated. Their minds are kindled all the more broadly the more carefully their weakness is judged.

“In all who swell with proud thoughts there is shouting in speech, bitterness in silence, dissipation in cheerfulness, rage in sadness, dishonor in action, a semblance of honor, haughtiness in walking, and rancor in reply.

“Their minds are always strong for inflicting insults but weak for enduring them; sluggish in obeying but troublesome in provoking others; cowardly in doing what they both ought and are able to do, but ready to do what they neither ought nor are able to do. They are moved by no exhortations toward what they do not freely desire, but toward what they secretly desire they seek to be compelled. Since they fear becoming contemptible through their desire, they wish to endure force against their very will.

“Therefore the Lord says to those afflicted by this vice: ‘God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble’ (James IV); and again: ‘Everyone who exalts his heart is unclean before God’ (Eccli. XVII); and again: ‘Why are earth and ashes proud?’ (Eccli. X).

“Since our Redeemer rules the hearts of the humble, while Leviathan is called the king of the proud, we clearly understand that pride is the most evident sign of the reprobate, whereas humility is the sign of the elect. When one recognizes what each person possesses, one discovers under which king he serves. For each person carries, as it were, a title of his work by which he readily shows under whose ruler’s power he serves.”

From this vice of pride also comes what many say about you before many people: that you boast of the strength and agility of your body, and frequently and willingly speak of battles and, as our people call them, vassal affairs; that you irreverently recount what you would do if you had been a layman; and that you say and do many other things unsuitable for you, without informing me.

You must consider what is written: “A man shall not be strengthened by his own strength” (I Reg. II); and: “A king is not saved by great power, nor shall a giant be saved by the abundance of his strength” (Ps. XXXII).

Thus David, strong of hand in his own eyes but humbly weak—and therefore truly strong—killed the giant of great strength and freed the king and the strength of his army from reproach. He says to the Lord: “I will keep my strength for you” (Ps. LVIII).

And Paul, who heard from the Lord, “Power is made perfect in weakness” (II Cor. XII), glories in his weaknesses, saying: “When I am weak, then I am stronger and powerful” (II Cor. XII); and: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should become reprobate” (I Cor. IX).

And when we have fought tirelessly in those struggles—not beating the air, but contending against aerial powers, the enticements of the flesh, and the desires of the world—we must say from the deepest affection of our hearts what the Lord commands us: “We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we were obliged to do” (Luke XVII).

For we are not sufficient of ourselves, as though our sufficiency came from us; our sufficiency is from God, who gives both the will and the accomplishment according to his good pleasure (II Cor. III); and who said to his own: “Without me you can do nothing” (Phil. II).

As for the vanity in which you boast about what you would do if you were a layman, I can answer you briefly: you would certainly do what your fellow-countrymen and lay relatives do—namely, live willingly and peacefully among your countrymen and neighbors. For if you presumed to act otherwise, you would find stronger and more powerful people who would resist and restrain you.

## CHAPTER LIII. On disorderly bodily movements and how he ought to avoid them

Since you are also reproached for disorderly bodily movements, you and I must attend to what the blessed Gregory says: that there is an inner discipline which keeps the outward limbs orderly.

Saint Gregory of Nazianzus describes the bearing of Julian the Apostate, saying (Oration 1 against Julian):

“His instability of character and excessive outburst made me extremely cautious. He is an excellent prophet who observes well. No useful sign appeared to me in him: an inflexible neck, shoulders that tossed about, darting eyes directed here and there and looking about wildly, restless feet, nostrils breathing out insults and contempt, laughable gestures—and gestures always of that kind—an uncontrolled and almost bubbling laugh, assent and denial at once, reasoning that held together with no reason, disordered questioning, and an answer that agreed with nothing.”

And the holy Pope Gregory, describing and rather painting the portrait of a certain young man, says of him:

“He was proud and slippery, light in words, unstable in gestures, swollen in mind, carefully arranged in dress, and disorderly in action.”

We must therefore consider this: if such faults are censured in laymen endowed with whatever powers, how condemnable must they be in us bishops, who seem to be the light of the world and a lamp placed upon a lampstand, so that we may shine for all who are placed in the house of God, that is, in the Church?

I write these things to you, brother and son, pierced with great grief and shame, urging you to see yourself with me in the basin which Moses made from the mirrors of the women who kept watch before the tabernacle of the Lord, in which the priests who were to minister in that same house of the Lord washed their hands and feet (Exod. XXXVIII). There let us wash away what is blameworthy in us, inwardly and outwardly: that is, in the precepts of sacred Scripture explained to us through the saints of God, and in the examples of those same saints. Let us present ourselves worthy of tears and holy works, so that we may be able to minister to him worthily.

Hence the Psalmist says to almighty God: “I will never forget your ordinances, because by them you have given me life” (Ps. CXVIII). The ordinances are called God’s commandments, in which he justifies us by correcting us. Concerning them the same Psalmist says more plainly: “I will meditate on your ordinances; I will not forget your words” (Ps. XVIII). In them, therefore, he gives us life, because through them he shows us spiritual life and pours it into our minds through the breathing of the Spirit.

## CHAPTER LIV. That he should not allow himself to be deceived by the flower of youth, bodily health, and the enticements of the world

Finally, I exhort and admonish you, brother and son, not to allow yourself to be deceived by the flower of youth, bodily health, and the enticements of the world. Always keep before the eyes of your mind what the Holy Spirit says here through blessed Job:

“Man born of woman lives for a short time and is filled with many miseries. He comes forth like a flower and is cut down; he flees like a shadow and never remains in the same condition. The days of man are short; the number of his months is with you. You have appointed his limits, which cannot be passed” (Job XIV).

And through the Psalmist:

“Nevertheless, a person passes away like an image, and is troubled in vain. He stores up treasure and does not know for whom he gathers it” (Ps. XXXVIII).

Always keep before the eyes of your mind how terrifying our judge will be in his counsels concerning the children of human beings, and how strict he will come to judge, with heavens and earth burning, all the powers of heaven and every creature moved to serve his terror.

When fire will go before him and burn his enemies round about; when he calls heaven from above and the earth to distinguish his people; when he comes to judge us concerning our thoughts, words, and deeds—we must anticipate him in confession and weep before him who made us (Ps. XCIV).

We must also consider what shame we shall then experience before the sight of the entire human race and all the heavenly powers; what confusion will seize us, and what punishment will follow our confusion, when guilt envelops the soul in immortal death and Gehenna consumes the flesh that perishes without end, if we have kept the roots of our hearts persistently fixed in this world.

For, as it is written, no one can rejoice here with the world and reign there with the Lord.

Let us therefore be, as the Apostle teaches, “as dying, and behold, we live; as chastised, and not killed; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as needy, yet enriching many; as having nothing, yet possessing all things” (II Cor. VI).

The hours flee in their moments, and time slips away. Let us therefore strive to keep them occupied with good and continual works, because it is written: “Blessed are those who keep judgment and do justice at all times” (Ps. CV).

And after the continual good works of the holy man have been described, it is written: “Thus Job did all his days” (Job I).

Therefore, just as we render daily and necessary payments to the body, so let us strive to pour out and render before the Lord daily and continual payments of good works to our souls: continence, reading, vigils, prayers, tears, almsgiving, offerings of the sacred sacrifice, groans arising from repentance for past deeds, and holy desire for things to come. Let us remain most watchful in these things with right faith, firm hope, and perfect charity.

We know that Joseph alone among his brothers is read to have been clothed in a long tunic (Gen. XXXVII), and that the tail of a sheep is commanded to be offered to the Lord in sacrifice, because “whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X).

And let us obey what Wisdom exhorts each of us through Solomon:

“Whatever your hand is able to do, do it diligently, because there is neither work, nor reason, nor knowledge, nor wisdom in the underworld to which you are hastening” (Eccl. IX).

## CHAPTER LV. Conclusion of the letter with the words of Elijah: “What was mine I have done for you”

In conclusion of all these matters, I write to you what blessed Elijah, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to Elisha, who was to be filled with the same Holy Spirit: “What was mine I have done for you” (3 Kings 19). For I believe that [Col. 0494B] even if—which God forbid—you do not heed me, my labor in you will not be vain and empty before God. For although a black Ethiopian enters the bath and emerges black from the bath, the bath attendant nevertheless does not lose the denarius—that is, the price of his bath. We and our words, however, are in the hand of God, who says: “I will rain upon one city, and upon another I will not rain” (Amos 4). To some he speaks by his voice, while, because their guilt requires it, by a hidden and just judgment he does not speak through anointing; to others, however, he speaks by the anointing of grace—that is, by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit together with his voice. May the Lord grant me both to will, to know, to say, and to do what he has commanded; and may he grant you to hear and to heed what is expedient, and to grant that both of us may will and do these things, and persevere in what he commands, so that we may be worthy to receive the gifts [Col. 0494C] that he promises.

# LETTER OF HINCMAR OF RHEIMS TO HINCMAR OF LAON

Received through Heddo, provost of the church of Laon.

(From Sirmond, based on an old manuscript of the Thuani Library.)

HINCMAR, bishop of Rheims, to his beloved brother Hincmar, bishop of the Church of Laon: greetings.

On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August of the present third indiction, our common brother and fellow minister Heddo, provost of the church entrusted to you, came to me in the evening. He delivered to me a message on your behalf, [Col. 0494D] as follows:

“I. My lord sends you greetings and faithful prayers.

“II. He sends you word that you know what was now done to him at Attigny, on account of which he departed from there, as he informed you through Teutland; and you know how it was done to him on the other occasion, when the king detained him.

“III. He sends you word that possessions belonging to his church were taken from him, and that Flothar, the king’s envoy, handed them over to a man of Nortmann. My lord already knew this when he departed from Attigny, because he knew that matters would come to this point: Herimund, a man of Nortmann, told my lord so when the king returned from Senlis.

[Col. 0495A] “IV. He also sends you word that his men hold other possessions belonging to his church by the authority and command of the king. He summoned his men to come to him on the previous Saturday, and wished to examine the king’s service and the work owed to his church; but they did not come. The king then sent him word through Bertharius that he should return Eligius’s benefice to him. Eligius brought from there a royal writ ordering that he return the benefice to him. My lord replied that he should return on Monday, and that he would then examine the matter with his faithful men and give him an answer. But he said that he should not have had to wait for this, because the king had returned that benefice to him; so he entered there and now holds it.

“V. Since you are his uncle and his archbishop, if you can obtain from the king [Col. 0495B] permission for him to administer the possessions belonging to his church, and to dispose of and govern them as he sees fit—for whatever he does, another undoes; whatever he arranges, another overturns—then he wishes to obey you, come to you, and act according to your counsel. For whatever he has done and arranged concerning the possessions of his church, he did not do so for money or a bribe (*scaz*), or through any relationship or friendship, but according to what he understood to be best, if indeed he did anything in that regard.

“And if you cannot accomplish this with the king, then he cannot obey the king, serve him, render him any temporal service, or come to him. Nor can he abandon the matter, but will appeal from it as high as he can, [Col. 0495C] that is, to the Apostolic See. Nor will he refrain from carrying out his ministry in this matter—that is, he will excommunicate them, as he has here what those bishops decreed. He cannot refrain from excommunicating them, because on the previous occasion, when he sent word to the lord apostolic about Nortmann, the lord apostolic sent him this reply: that he should first carry out his ministry in that matter, and then lodge his appeal. He has therefore postponed this until now, until he could inform you, so that you would know that he will now carry out his ministry in the matter.”

For this reason, together with the venerable bishops and our beloved brothers who were present—namely Remigius, Harduic, Franco, Hodo, and Willebert—I took care to present a petition to the glorious lord King Charles. He replied [Col. 0495D] that he had thought what he had already said to you at Attigny before the bishops, with a kindly disposition and calm address, ought to have been sufficient for you. He had told you that it had come to his attention that you had presumed to claim more of the possessions which you now report that his envoy Flothar handed over to Nortmann than was owed to the church entrusted to you, and more than was contained in the royal writ by which he restored to you possessions long withheld from the church of Laon, or granted them in response to your request without compensation.

This was most clearly evident in the possessions that you had unlawfully and irregularly usurped contrary to reason and justice, which were not contained in the writ and which his man had justly and reasonably recovered according to law. Therefore, he said, you were to receive immediately the estate—namely the villa of Pauliacum—which had long been [Col. 0496A] withheld from the church of Laon. As for the other possessions concerning which a complaint had reached him, you were meanwhile not to receive them, but merely to await the arrival of the writ. His envoy and mine were then to go into that district and investigate the truth of the matter; and whatever was found among those possessions to belong justly and reasonably to the church of Laon, he would not only not begrudge, but would willingly grant to that church. At that time you contradicted none of this.

Concerning the benefices of your men about which you sent word, I reply that your men appealed to him, alleging that you had unjustly and unreasonably taken from them their benefices, which they had held under your predecessors and under you. Accordingly, in keeping with the sacred [Col. 0496B] canons and with the decrees of the pontiffs of the Holy Roman See promulgated from those sacred canons, you requested from me bishops as chosen judges. By the judgment of those bishops and of other God-fearing men, it was decreed concerning some of them that they ought to recover their benefices, which they had lost unreasonably.

The case of others, however, because of certain intervening circumstances, remained undecided and still pending until another hearing. Yet, before a decision had been reached, you fled contrary to the sacred canons, without any necessity or reason, and scorned to await a regular judgment. Therefore you know very well what the sacred canons decree.

Now, however, since he is already on the move, going to meet his brother for the sake of peace and concord in charity, and to obtain [Col. 0496C] tranquility for the Holy Church and the Christian people, when he has returned from there with the Lord’s favor, come to him and bring the writ by which he restored or granted the aforementioned possessions to the church of Laon. He will see to it that action is taken concerning those possessions you claim, according to whatever is found to be just.

As for your men, whose case, because you withdrew irregularly and unlawfully, has still remained undecided and pending, let it be examined justly and reasonably and decided according to the sacred laws.

Furthermore, dearest brother, I was greatly astonished by the document purporting to contain the decision of the bishops at the synod held at Tusiacum—where and how you found it. Before I received it through your cleric Heddo, I had never seen it, and I had never heard of it anywhere. [Col. 0496D] Nor did the bishops who are now present say that they had seen or heard of it.

I possess the authentic decision that was decreed at that synod according to the sacred laws, at which you were present with me. I cannot imagine where this fabrication arose. As you can clearly recognize from what I have taken pains to write to you against your presumptions, it conflicts in certain respects with the sacred rules; and you could very easily have recognized it as false, if you had possessed those eyes in your head of which Scripture says: “The eyes of the wise man are in his head” (Ecclesiastes 2:14).

Your prudence is therefore astonishing: why did you prefer to possess and send me this false compilation, which—as I have said—conflicts in certain respects with the sacred rules, rather than [Col. 0497A] possess the true decision of the synod, consistent with the sacred rules, and receive it from me, your primate, whatever I may be, to be held and followed according to the sacred rules? For, according to the decrees of the pontiffs of the Holy Roman See promulgated from the sacred canons, you must always await my direction in such matters.

Even if the document you sent me appears to contain some reason or authority, you must nevertheless discern this: just as, when a definite complaint is received, a case is examined, the reason is sought, presumption or the rashness of usurpation is not found, justice follows, equity is preserved, and the severity of canonical discipline has no place, so, against those who deviate from reason, authority, and equity and who have hardened themselves in obstinacy and contempt, [Col. 0497B] the rigor of discipline intensifies its action.

“Blessed Leo says that the moderation of the Apostolic See maintains this restraint: that it acts more severely with the hardened, while desiring to grant pardon to those who have been corrected.”

Therefore, since—as Leo likewise says—we desire the counsels of priests to be mature, and since Holy Scripture says, “He who is hasty stumbles with his feet” (Proverbs 19), I exhort and admonish you, dearest brother, by paternal and metropolitan authority according to the sacred rules, not to rush, as you instructed me to report, into pronouncing a sentence on the basis of these arguments that you sent me, especially since I have already admonished you sufficiently, reproved you, and instructed you even from divine authorities.

Meanwhile, patiently endure what appears contrary to your authority. You ought to say with the Psalmist: “Sinners have built upon my back; [Col. 0497C] they have prolonged their iniquity” (Psalm 128). “By your patience,” says the Lord, “you will possess your souls” (Luke 21); and it is also written: “The instruction of a man is known through patience” (Proverbs 19). For the less patient someone is, the less learned he is proved to be.

The patient man is better than the strong man, and he who rules his spirit is better than one who captures cities. For he who subdues cities conquers something outside himself, whereas the patient man subjects himself to himself.

Therefore endure with equanimity those whom you consider opposed to you, and love those whom you endure. Let your goodwill accomplish more toward those who need correction than severity; let exhortation accomplish more than agitation; let charity accomplish more than power. You will not depart from this rule if you seek not your own interests [Col. 0497D] but those of Jesus Christ.

But if you wish to rule your subjects rather than advise them, honor will inflate pride, and what was provided in your ordination for the sake of concord will tend toward harm.

Therefore, dearest brother, act as befits episcopal dignity, and wait until we meet in the provincial synod, whose time is now near. In that synod, with the Lord’s favor and cooperation, according to the decrees of blessed Gregory, there will be both discussion of the cases that have arisen and a beneficial conference concerning ecclesiastical observance. Thus, while past matters are corrected through this process and future matters receive their proper rule, the almighty Lord may everywhere be praised through the concord of the brethren.

If we observe these things, we must believe with certainty that his presence will be with us, for it is written: “Where two or three are gathered [Col. 0498A] in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matthew 18). If he deigns to be present where two or three are gathered, he will much more certainly not be absent where a larger number of priests have assembled.

As for what you sent me word: that you cannot refrain from excommunicating those men who hold possessions belonging to your church against your will, because on the previous occasion, when you sent word to the lord apostolic about Nortmann, he sent you this reply—that you should first carry out your ministry in that matter and then lodge your appeal—we have neither found nor heard this in his letters.

Therefore, brother, beware lest, persuaded by someone’s word—perhaps by flattery offered to win your favor, but not spoken on the authority of the lord apostolic—you should rashly, imprudently, [Col. 0498B] and precipitately pronounce a sentence of excommunication contrary to the sacred rules. Instead, wait, as I said, until we bishops of the province of Rheims assemble in the provincial synod. If anything should prevent us from carrying out justly and reasonably, according to the sacred rules, what must be done—which, God forbid, we do not think will happen at all—then, if necessary and according to the sacred rules, let your complaint, if it is found to be just, reach the Apostolic See through a letter from us.

# HINCMAR OF RHEIMS TO THE SAME

He recalls to his mind how he had raised him as an orphan with tender affection under religious discipline, instructed him through letters, and advanced him through each ecclesiastical rank up to the summit of the episcopate.

[Col. 0498C]

Now, he says, “How long shall I endure one who repays me evil for good and hates me without cause, because I do not favor your fruitless works, while I am afflicted by you with so many injuries? For from the very day of your ordination, by your words as well as your writings, and by your disorderly actions and movements, I have been so burdened with repeated lacerations and bruises that I am weary of my life. For, because of the duty of my position, I have been so bound to your insolence that I have been unable to avoid admonishing you—not only after the first and second correction, according to the Apostle, but even after very many corrections, privately and before our common familiars, and also before the king, the bishops, [Col. 0498D] and many others, in words and in writing.

“And although I desire that wings might be given me like a dove’s, so that I might fly away and rest, removed from you in some solitude, I cannot escape anywhere without being distressed by reports about you: whether by the obstinate presence of your stubbornness, by the harsh words of your messengers, by the disparagements and useless dirges—or rather tragedies—of your writings, or by such things as are unbecoming to a bishop. And at last I thought you had become ashamed of carrying on such things, when behold, on the ides of November of the fourth indiction, you sent me an exceedingly long roll filled with lies, irrational claims, and reproaches against truth and authority.

“And I wonder why, having become so shameless [Col. 0499A] that, as the Lord complains of Judah (Jer. 6:15; 8:12), you do not know how to blush and are not nauseated by writing such great and such things—unless it is because you are no longer intent upon useful matters, nor occupied with necessary ones. And, to say nothing of other matters—for if I wished to recount them in order, daylight would fail before the page ceased to have things worth reading—I shall recount to you certain matters that I can neither can nor ought to pass over in silence.

“Namely, as soon as you, having been made a bishop, flew out from the nest of your paternal education, you abandoned me and those who had raised you, and sought and acquired secular friendships and intimacies. Then, abandoning and acquiring one person after another in this way, you rose up—not only against your peers but also against those entrusted to you—to the point that, contrary to the sacred Antiochene canons, which prescribe that you should do nothing without me [Col. 0499B] according to the rule established by our Fathers, except only those things that pertain to your parish and its subject possessions, you obtained an administration in the palace of our lord the king without the knowledge of myself or of our fellow bishops. I prohibited you from that administration in the presence of the same lord king and of the others who were present, on the basis of the sacred canons, and for some time you ceased from the administration.

“Afterward, however, through external—that is, secular—powers, contrary to the Sardican canons, you obtained the same administration together with an abbey in a third province, beyond the province of Rheims, without my knowledge. To that abbey you went, without my permission, as often as you wished, and you remained there as long as you wished, contrary to the decrees of Pope Hilary [Col. 0499C] who says (Letter 8 to the bishops of Gaul): ‘We could not pass over that matter which must be guarded with the greatest care: that no bishops should dare to proceed to any province without the letters of their metropolitans. This too must be observed in every kind of clerical office throughout the individual churches.’ Thus Zosimus had earlier decreed, and later Saint Gregory.

“Moreover, summoned once and again by canonical letters to the ordination of a bishop in the church of Cambrai, in the province of Rheims, which had been left without a pastor—and concerning which the Apostolic See, at my prompting, labored not a little—you neither came yourself nor sent me a representative in your place or letters expressing your consent, as the sacred rules prescribe. Hence Pope Symmachus promulgated from the sacred rules to Aeonius (Letter 11 to [Col. 0499D] Caesarius): ‘If any bishop, summoned according to canonical definition by the metropolitan pontiff, should refuse to obey, let him know that he is to be cut down—which we do not desire—by ecclesiastical discipline.’ But when I summoned you on this matter, you offered no satisfaction, nor even a humble reply, either to me or to our fellow bishops.

“After this, following the custom of your instability and inconstancy, you rose up against our lord the king so irrationally and obstinately that he removed from you both the palatine administration and the abbey itself, and, provoked by you, proposed to impose harsher measures upon you. Therefore, by words and writings, working on your behalf, I reconciled him to you.

“Then, as very many know, you rose up against him again and, despising his commands that you should come to him, provoked him to such anger—as everyone in these regions knows—that, [Col. 0500A] compelled by you, he attacked you through his faithful men as though you were unfaithful.

“You, however, before any unheard-of excommunication, without my knowledge and contrary to the sacred rules, hurled excommunication against the parishioners of myself and of many archbishops and bishops, and also against the king himself. Thus you scandalized many people and brought the greatest scandal not only upon the Church but also upon the king and the kingdom, although the law forbids that, when passing through another person’s harvest, one should put in the sickle; rather, one must crush the ears with the hand and eat them (Deut. 23:25).

“‘You cannot,’ says blessed Gregory, ‘put the sickle of judgment into a harvest that appears to have been entrusted to another. But through the effect of a good work, strip the Lord’s wheat of the chaff of its vices, [Col. 0500B] and by admonishing and persuading, as though by chewing it, convert it into the body of the Church.’

“After this presumption, bringing our fellow brothers together with me, I made peace between you and him, and I persuaded the bishops whose parishioners you had excommunicated not to bring you into a synodal judgment. I also, although not without labor and with the assistance of our lord the king, caused those same persons excommunicated by you to cease from acting against you.

“But you, adding worse things to those that came before, again provoked our lord the king—as it would take me too long to recount, and as many know—so greatly that, for the sake of correcting you, he ordered you to be detained for a while without my will and without my consent.

“You, however, on account of this alleged injury, without consulting me and without the consent of the fellow bishops of the province of Rheims—as the petition presented to me by the clergy of the church of Laon [Col. 0500C] demonstrates—excommunicated the priests and fellow ministers of the church and parish entrusted to you. You decreed that no one in that parish should celebrate the offices of Mass, that no one should baptize even an infant placed in imminent danger of death, that no one should receive anyone to penance, nor even assist a dying person with the provision of viaticum, and that no one should provide any deceased person with the service of burial, until either you yourself should come to them or they should receive a report concerning the matter from the Apostolic See.

“When I heard this, I confess, I was exceedingly horrified. Therefore, out of metropolitan concern, I sent letters to you, warning and urging you to dissolve as quickly as possible so destructive an excommunication and bond of impiety, undertaken at the peril of yourself and of many others.
