[Col. 0500D] I also sent to the ministers of the church of Laon, fearing the immense destruction of many people, the most certain and irrefutable definitions of evangelical truth, apostolic authority, the sacred canons, and the Apostolic See, so that, according to those same definitions, which cannot in any respect be divided, they too might act sufficiently against that dangerous and irregular excommunication.

“But because you did not wish to obey my admonition, I sent you letters about it again, and also sent clergy of the parish of Laon; yet even so I was unable to induce you to obey.

“After this, seeking devices by which you might cast off metropolitan subjection, you collected a booklet from the writings of the ancient Fathers, composed before the canons of the sacred Council of Nicaea [Col. 0501A] and of the holy synods. Into these you inserted mutually discordant opinions, contrary to evangelical, apostolic, and canonical authority and to the authority of the Apostolic See. Without the knowledge or consent of the metropolitan and of the fellow bishops of the province of Rheims, you subscribed that same booklet, and caused it to be subscribed by the clergy of your church and by the parish priests, wishing to display yourself as freed from subjection to your metropolis and to annul the privilege of the metropolitan see.

“As though I could not, by canonical authority and without your consent or a synodal assembly, dissolve the bonds of your impiety in your parish, when, concerning certain and manifest matters—matters that are in no way doubtful or obscure to us—and concerning which we possess definitive judgments promulgated by the holy Fathers, judgments that cannot be overturned by any reasoning, [Col. 0501B] I need not await synodal deliberation, or the counsel or consent of the fellow bishops of our province. Nor should I depart from the established rules, as Saint Leo says: ‘Neither through negligence nor through presumption should one depart from them, nor should one trouble the Apostolic See on this matter, as the blessed pontiffs of that holy See—Innocent, Zosimus, Celestine, Leo, Hilary, Gelasius, Gregory, and many other rulers of that same holy See—show in their decrees,’ and so forth.

“Likewise, after authorities of Pope Gelasius had been given:

“‘Afterward, finally, concerning the aforesaid monstrous booklet, monstrously collected by you, and concerning your subscription and that of your supporters, I admonished you again by a letter, a copy of which I possess, to take care to correct what you had done in your parish contrary to reason and authority. [Col. 0501C] But you did not obey my admonition.

“‘Then, from the aforesaid letters of the pontiffs of the Roman See, written before the Council of Nicaea, you sent me the booklet collected by you and entitled with verses in the name of our lord King Charles, through the venerable former archbishop Wanilo, at Gundulf’s estate, before the bishops who were present. I replied to you in writing concerning it; I possess a copy of that reply. I admonished you to place your faith in the sacred canons that had been promulgated and to render them their due obedience.

“‘Thereafter, at Attigny in the parish of Rheims, in your presence and before the bishops, I gave you a booklet in fifty-five chapters containing ecclesiastical authorities, contrary to what you had collected in your two aforementioned booklets. I admonished you to restrain yourself from such and similar objections, and, submitting yourself to the sacred rules, to strive, according to the Apostle, after peace and holiness.

“‘But you offered no satisfaction to my admonition. On the contrary, you presented in the same synod a very long roll composed against truth, authority, and reason, and you produced in that same synod the aforementioned monstrous booklet, subscribed by yourself and your supporters. I accepted it there, and have kept it ever since.

“‘When I saw that, after so many admonitions, I was accomplishing nothing with you, I presented a written statement at a synod of bishops from ten provinces. I asked those same venerable bishops for advice concerning what I could do against your obstinate disobedience, [Col. 0502A] and I had read before them the things I had sent to you and to your parish against the bonds of your impiety.

“‘Accordingly, by the authorities of the sacred assembly and of the bishops mentioned above, because you had presumptuously carried out so many and such excommunications unjustly and irregularly; because you had been accused by our lord the king of not observing the oaths you had sworn to him over the sacred objects; because you had seized his property contrary to divine and human laws; and because you had been accused in a synod by Nortmannus of having, without royal authority, with an armed military force and a crowd of common people gathered with swords and clubs, first driven away his wife, who was there alone, and afterward driven away Nortmannus himself, contrary to laws and rules, [Col. 0502B] from the things that had been granted to him by lord Charles with your permission and consent, and of having taken away everything of his that was there; and because you had been accused by your own men of having taken away from them their benefices contrary to divine and human laws—so that you might escape synodal censure, you gave to the king and to me in the same synod a booklet containing your profession of regular obedience. I possess it, and you cannot deny it, since you received its copy from my hand in that same synod, as I shall show in the course of this work. [Col. 0501D]

“‘But, being a man double-minded and inconstant in all your ways, on the following day you sent me through Arduicus, the venerable bishop of Besançon, a brief for you to profess and subscribe, as follows: [Col. 0502C]

“‘“I also, Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, shall preserve for you, Hincmar, bishop of Laon, your privilege due according to the sacred canons; and in whatever ecclesiastical matters you may have need, I shall provide you, according to the sacred rules, with the assistance due to you by right, by archiepiscopal authority.”

“‘This request proceeded not only from no humility but not even from sound sense. For it appears unjust and irrational that an archbishop, not deviating from the sacred canons, should satisfy a suffragan bishop ordained by him with a document of profession and subscription, as you had requested.

“‘For just as, according to Scripture, the lesser is blessed by the greater, so entirely is the lesser—not the greater by the lesser—judged, bound, or released by the greater, as is also demonstrated in the decrees of Gelasius.

“‘Accordingly, your answer is given justly and reasonably from James (chapter 4): “You asked and did not receive, [Col. 0502D] because you asked wrongly” [Jas. 4:3].

“‘Moreover, when you asked me to subscribe that I would preserve your privilege due according to the sacred canons, you asked for what you wanted, but you did not know what you were saying. For, as Saint Jerome says, “the privileges of individuals cannot become the common law.” And the sacred canons did not generally grant provincial bishops and their churches or sees privileges—that is, private laws or private rights—because what all generally possess cannot be a special right or a private law of dignity. But they granted privileges to metropolitan bishops and metropolitan sees,’ and so forth, as appended from the sacred canons and the decrees of Pope Leo.

“‘After these things he adds: [Col. 0503A]

“‘“Therefore, when you sent me such things for me to profess and subscribe, you ought to have known that in these regions hardly anyone is unaware that the municipality of Laon, in which you were ordained bishop, from its beginning—after it was founded by the praetor Marcobrius, as the histories report—never held a name or place among the provincial sees of the province of Rheims, whether in paganism or in Christianity, until Saint Remigius, the fifteenth archbishop of Rheims, for certain particular accidental reasons, first ordained a bishop there. To that municipality, which had been sufficiently and abundantly endowed from the possessions of the metropolitan see of Rheims, he assigned the county in which it lies, a part, namely, of the parish of Rheims.

“‘“But it was always a municipality of the province of Rheims, [Col. 0503B] just as even today there are other municipalities in the parish of Rheims that remain in the place and under the name of subjection.

“‘“Therefore, what you ought to have asked to be preserved for you was not a privilege but municipal status. For, as our fathers and teachers of the Church transmit, the Apostle Paul does not call himself a citizen but a municipal resident when he says: “I am indeed a Jewish man from Tarsus of Cilicia, a municipal resident of no obscure city” (Acts 22:3).

“‘“The Apostle was born in the town of Giscala in Galilee. When it was captured by the Romans, he migrated with his parents to Tarsus of Cilicia. They sent him to Jerusalem because of his zeal for the Law, and there he was educated by the very learned man Gamaliel, as he himself recalls later. Therefore he calls himself not a citizen but a municipal resident, from the municipality—that is, from the territory of the same city in which he was raised. [Col. 0503C]

“‘“That municipality is so called because it renders only its duties—namely, due tributes or services. For free and renowned causes, and those proceeding from the prince, belong to the dignity of cities.

“‘“Nor is it surprising that he calls himself a Tarsian and not a Giscalite, since the Lord himself, although born in Bethlehem, was called not a Bethlehemite but a Nazarene, from the place where he was raised.

“‘“Therefore you, born in the diocese of Rheims, raised in the metropolis of Rheims, and ordained in the municipality of Laon, ought to recognize yourself not as a civil or civic bishop, but as a municipal bishop—that is, a tributary or service-rendering bishop, if only of spiritual gifts—and, except insofar as you were ordained by several bishops, almost a vicarious bishop, whom the Greeks call a chorepiscopus. Accordingly, [Col. 0503D] what ought to be assigned to you is not a privilege but municipal status.

“‘“Nor should you have rebelled against the privilege of your metropolis. You would not have done so if you were in spirit like Paul—small and humble.

“‘“Hence it must be feared that in this too you imitate the son of perdition, who opposes and exalts himself above everything called God or worshiped as God. For, as far as it depended upon you, you handed over those whom you had irregularly excommunicated, as I said above, not so that their spirit might be saved according to the Apostle, but, as far as your fury and indignation could prevail, so that they might perish on the day of the Lord.

“‘“Against these bonds of impiety, as has often been said and must always be said, because I dissolved them regularly against your will, you rose up against me.”’

“Likewise, afterward, following authorities concerning the unlawful excommunication: [Col. 0504A]

“‘Concerning the oaths you gave to the king, I do not need to write anything, since almost everyone knows what the Lord says in the Law and the Prophets, in the Gospel, through the Apostles, and through the teachers and masters of the Church concerning perjury, if perhaps you committed it.

“‘And because, as it is said in the decrees of the Apostolic See, we did not wish to aggravate what had been done, lest we be compelled to judge what is just—for what was charged against you in the synod was not established in judicial order but was suspended through royal clemency—I omitted placing a regular judgment here, so as to send you back to your conscience.

“‘Your seizure of the king’s property, however, was made perfectly clear, because those things were never legally proved to have belonged to the rights of the church of Laon, [Col. 0504B] nor was it shown that they had been possessed by that church through its own donation or concession, or through anyone else’s. Hence a legal inquiry was made concerning your man Teduinus, to whom you had granted those seized possessions as a benefice.

“‘The accusation of Nortmannus against you also proved to be true and needed no witnesses, because what you had done against laws and rules in that matter was so manifestly evident to everyone in these regions that the deed could not be concealed or excused by any evasion.

“‘For it is well known to many, and you confess this in your writings sent to the lord king and to me: at the entreaty of Rodulfus and Conradus, after our lord the king had long before removed those possessions from the church of Laon and, in his piety, restored them to that church, you granted them as a benefice to the lord king himself, [Col. 0504C] without the knowledge and consent of myself, of our fellow bishops, and of your fellow ministers, so that he might grant them as a benefice to Nortmannus.’

“Likewise, after certain authorities had been given:

“‘You dissolved this act, which you had committed so irrationally, even more irrationally. With an armed military force, and with a mixed multitude of common people carrying arms and clubs and making a great tumult, as those who saw and heard the deed report, you violently expelled the same Nortmannus—who held those possessions, granted to you by the king, through the king’s benefice—without the king’s authority, word, or letters. After expelling him, you seized those possessions, entered them, and took possession of them.

“‘Yet there are laws and rules; there is also the king, who bears the sword for the punishment of wrongdoers; and there are bishops and canons for judging [Col. 0504D] sacrilegious crimes. Thus, if Nortmannus himself had been a seizer of ecclesiastical possessions, he would have been punished by the sword—that is, by royal vengeance; if he had been proved sacrilegious, he would have been judged by episcopal and canonical judgment.

“‘There are also judges and laws, by whose judgment, if anything had perhaps been unjustly done to you and to the church entrusted to you, it could have been corrected legally and regularly.’

“Likewise, after certain passages, especially decrees of the instructions of blessed Gregory:

“‘Finally, because your men complained to the king that you had unjustly and irrationally taken away from them the benefices they had held from your predecessors, after you had given the king and me in the synod a booklet concerning your regular obedience according to the sacred canons and the decrees of the pontiffs of the holy Roman See promulgated from the sacred canons, [Col. 0505A] you requested from me bishops chosen as judges, and you accepted the three whom I designated for you according to the African Council: Actardus, Ragenelmus, and John.

“‘By the judgment of these and of other God-fearing men, in the presence of our lord the king, as you requested, it was decreed concerning certain matters that they ought to recover their benefices, which they had irrationally lost. The case of some others, however, because certain reasons intervened, was not settled until another hearing but was left to be decided on another day. Before that decision, contrary to the sacred canons and without any necessity or reason, you fled and refused to await the regular judgment.’

“Likewise, after some discussion of the canons:

“‘As I said, you imprudently and dishonorably fled from the judgment of the chosen [Col. 0505B] judges. Departing, you sent me through your deacon Ermenoldus, on the sixth day before the Nones of July of the third indiction, a little document irrationally composed and subscribed by your own hand, entirely contrary to your aforesaid profession. It reads as follows:

“‘“To the most reverend Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, Hincmar, by God’s mercy bishop of the holy church of Laon, offers due devotion in Christ.

“‘“You know that I have twice been summoned by the universal pope of the holy Roman Church, our father and teacher, Hadrian. You yourselves, in the booklets given by you to me at the palace of Attigny, before the archbishops and bishops who were present, reproached me because I was unwilling to come to that same See after having been summoned an equal number of times. If, through a scribal error, the word is [Col. 0505C] detrectem, meaning ‘I decline’ or ‘I delay,’ rather than detractem, which may reasonably be understood as ‘I make a great issue of it,’ the correction was not marked in the text.

“‘“Therefore, for the love of almighty God and out of reverence for Saint Peter, I now earnestly ask you—as I asked you in the same synod, convened by you at Attigny, although I was unable to obtain it, and as I have now implored you for a full year, especially at the synod formerly held at the palace of Verberie, where I pleaded and cried out—I now also ask and again cry out, as I have done until now, that by your archiepiscopal authority you obtain from the clemency of our most glorious lord King Charles permission for me to obey the commands and ecclesiastical institutions of the lord and universal Pope Hadrian, as is fitting for everyone, since he has the right to judge concerning the whole Church. [Col. 0505D] In particular, may I deserve, as I have vowed, to enter the thresholds of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, since I have also been summoned there by him.

“‘“Otherwise, know that from now on I cannot canonically obey you as a fellow bishop ought to obey an archbishop. For, as blessed Pope Gelasius decrees, those who set the decrees of the bishops of the holy Roman Church against them as though against canons do not know what they are saying; to oppose those decrees is to rise up against the canons themselves.”’

“This venerable and holy Pope Gelasius sanctioned that all decretal letters should be received with reverence. Nor does the person receive them reverently who, although he bows his head toward the volume, does not obey them but rather rejects them, stretching out hands directly against them—something that cannot be done without danger—as one [Col. 0506A] who does not foresee that he himself is being judged.

“For whether we wish it or not, we shall either obey them or be struck down by their judgment; and no one among them can we reject at will.

“Concerning the archbishops Remigius and Arduicus, what you sent me through the deacon Teutlandus does not prejudice the privilege of the holy Roman Church; rather, the same holy See committed to them what it wished and determined to entrust concerning me. You, for your part, do what belongs to you. Farewell in the Lord Jesus Christ.

“‘I, Hincmar, bishop of the holy church of Laon, have willingly subscribed.’

“Concerning this little document I delayed replying to you, thinking that you would reconsider and recover from your contumacy. But you did not cease, as I omit the matter for the sake of brevity.

“After this, through your cleric Bertharius, [Col. 0506B] you sent your letters to the lord king, excusing yourself on the grounds that you could not come to him as he had commanded, because, being feverish, you could not bear the sun to touch you. But you asked him to give you permission to go to Rome, according to the vow you had made when you had a fever for the second time, so that, coming to the thresholds of the holy Apostles as you had vowed, you might there be freed from that fever.

“Our lord the king, however, through that same cleric of yours, replied to you in the presence of the bishops and of his other faithful men who were present that what you said was strange and untrue: you claimed that you could not come to him, yet you were able to go to Rome. You should come to him; and if he could ascertain that you wished to go there for a reasonable cause, he would not deny you permission.

“You refused to come to him until, around the Kalends of September [Col. 0506C] of the third indiction, he returned to Silvacus from a conference with his brother Louis. When you came to meet him there, you said nothing to him—and neither through yourself nor through your messengers did you say anything to me—about permission to go to Rome.

“Moreover, when the messengers of the lord Apostolic were at Rheims, you spoke every day for seven days with the king and with me, yet you said nothing about this. All the bishops who were present at those synods know clearly that, when you were reproved for your insolence, you asked for permission to go to Rome because you feared regular judgment or the king’s correction. But when you saw that both the king and the bishops were favorably disposed toward you, you said nothing about that permission, just as you do now, until you once again commit some new act, as is your custom and as I always fear. When summoned concerning it, you then bring out your customary song about permission.

“Your petition to our lord the king, when you came to him, was of this sort [Col. 0506D]—as many, indeed almost everyone, in these provinces are said to know, and as is evident. Adding grave matters to graver ones, as the judgments of the sacred canons themselves show, by I know what devices contrived by you, you extracted a royal order that those matters concerning which you had requested chosen judges according to the sacred canons should be reopened.

“Not only was this to happen with respect to the complaint of those whose case had been left for decision at another hearing; even those matters that, as I said, had been settled in the presence of the lord king by the sentence of the chosen judges [Col. 0507A] were to be reopened without the knowledge of the metropolitan and without canonical and episcopal judgment, through secular judges—namely, Helmigarius, the toll collector of the palace market, and Flotharius and Ursio, officials of the royal estates.

“This was contrary to the canons, which permit appeals from ecclesiastical judges to ecclesiastical judges of greater authority—not from greater to lesser, not from ecclesiastical to secular judges, and not to judges chosen without the consent of the parties.

“From these secular judges, whom you yourself requested, some matters already decided were reopened and changed, while certain matters still awaiting decision were decided. According to the contrived account reported by those who were present at that hearing, these judgments were based on unnecessary and inappropriate oaths, which you brought forward before the aforesaid judges and before those same accusers of yours, [Col. 0507B] whom you had accepted against the chosen judges, as you had requested.

“The purpose was that the man concerning whom it had been legally and regularly decided that he should possess his benefice, which he had lost contrary to reason and equity, should now abandon it because of the same contrivance; and that those whom it had been judged should retain their benefices until a lawful decision—because you had evaded the judgment of the chosen judges after requesting it—should abandon those benefices, so that you might carry through what you had begun.

“For just as you may not, whether in a criminal or a civil case, abandon ecclesiastical judgment and seek purification through a public judgment, so you may not, after setting aside or despising ecclesiastical judgment, flee to secular tribunals, nor drag anyone—even a lay person—to them, [Col. 0507C] nor follow him to his own forum if that lay person has consented to undergo ecclesiastical judgment, as the law of Valentinian, approved by the Church, demonstrates.”

Likewise, after the authorities had been displayed:

“‘Nor should you fail to consider why our lord the king agreed to your petition, so that, although you had received chosen bishops as judges from him in his presence according to the sacred canons, he nevertheless consented, without the knowledge of the metropolitan and without ecclesiastical judgment, that you should afterward receive secular judges to reopen matters that had been decided, or to decide matters for which you had received judges.

“‘I know and am certain that he knows the canonical judgment in this matter. I wonder and grieve that you did not wish to see it, or, blinded by arrogance—as God is judge, perhaps you were unable to see it.

“‘Therefore, according to the counsel [Col. 0507D] of the Apocalypse of John (chapter 3:18), anoint your eyes with eye-salve, so that you may see and be able to remove the cataract of arrogance from the eye of your mind, that is, from your understanding.

“‘And consider whether perhaps our lord the king, whom you have so often embittered, knowing the divine judgments and words, thought in granting your requests to bring upon yourself the divine sentences concerning those who are stiff-necked and untameable in heart:

“‘“Let the one who does harm continue to do harm, and let the filthy continue to be filthy” (Rev. 22:11);

“‘“So that they may always complete their sins” (1 Thess. 2:16);

“‘“I gave them over to the desires of their heart; they shall go on in their own devices” (Ps. 80:13);

“‘“Are these things not stored up with me and sealed in my treasuries? Vengeance is mine, and I shall repay them in due time, so that their foot may slip; the day of their destruction is near, and the appointed times hasten” [Col. 0508A] (Deut. 32:34).’

“And although you are found guilty of so many transgressions, you do not cease provoking me, so that I may write about the promised little document of your profession and subscription, concerning which, as I said, I have until now delayed replying to you, and also about your other professions and subscriptions, whether provoked or not. Thus, if many readers—and perhaps some who still do not know them—should read the histories of your professions and subscriptions, they may learn their diligence, their caution, and their usefulness.

“First, I shall reply to you concerning the aforesaid document subscribed by you, in which you write that you were reproved by me as an aid to yourself, and display me as blameworthy. But I disregard your reproof, [Col. 0508B] by which, as though under a kind of veil of excuse, you conspicuously strive, in your customary manner, to reprove me for a scribal error: either because I did not know the difference between the word detractem, which I placed in the writings given to you, and another form, or because I did not know how to correct the scribal error in them, or neglected to amend it.

“And from my reproof you wished to display your own learning in the manner of Cham, the son of Noah—not only concerning the difference between that word but also concerning another word, which I found repeated in your inventions for the sake of displaying yourself. When you wished by this means to show my ignorance, you endeavored to reveal your own folly among scholars.

“I care nothing about saying anything on my own behalf. It is a very small matter to me to be judged by you or to be reproved by your learning without affection.

“But so that you may not boast among those who exchange gossip with you, [Col. 0508C] as though you had made me mute and speechless, and as though you alone in our times had entered into the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, I shall show, when I have time, what the authorities of the art of grammar, the teachers of orthography, and the interpreters of sacred Scripture think and say about this matter. For the sake of brevity I omit it here.”

Likewise, after some further material:

“‘There are other matters from the sacred canons and the decrees of the Apostolic See that it would be lengthy for me to set down here. You can read them again in the little work of fifty-five chapters that I gave you for your admonition, correction, and instruction, as well as in the letters mentioned above that I sent you to rebuke your rashness, undertaken against evangelical truth, apostolic and canonical authority, and the decrees of the Apostolic See, [Col. 0508D] to your own destruction and that of many others, as was established in a synod of very many bishops.

“‘You can also read them in addition to the other letters and writings that I sent or gave you to restrain your insolence and to admonish and instruct your devotion, so that you might act according to the Lord’s command (Deut. 26:27): “What does the Lord your God ask of you, except that you fear the Lord your God, do his will, and obey his command?”

“‘Turn these matters over, brother, with attentive intention of heart, and consider what it means that you said: [Col. 0509A] “From the time when you sent me those letters, I knew that, as a fellow bishop ought canonically to obey an archbishop, you could not obey me.”

“‘Recall before your eyes what you professed before the bishops of ten provinces and subscribed with your own hand: namely, that you professed that, according to the privilege of the metropolitan church of the province of Rheims, according to the sacred canons and the decrees of the Apostolic See promulgated through the sacred canons, you would obey insofar as you knew and were able, and you subscribed to this.

“‘Tell me, brother: when, where, or in what matters did I ask or attempt to force you to obey me in any way contrary to this? I have never sought what belongs to you, but, according to the Apostle, I have sought you; and who
my injuries—that is, injuries to my person—I can readily, thanks be to God, forgive, as I do daily while devoutly imploring the Lord’s omnipotence on your behalf. But I can neither patiently endure nor ought I endure the injuries to the divine institution which your insolence seeks to inflict by refusing canonical subjection to metropolitan authority, injuries that rebound upon him who, through his Holy Spirit, from whom the canons are recorded and believed to have been promulgated, instituted them; [Col. 0509B] rather, I must strive with all the strength I can. For just as the care and primacy of the whole Catholic Church have been divinely entrusted to the pontiff of the holy Roman See, so also the care of the province entrusted to each metropolitan and primate of a province is known to have been committed to him through the sacred canons, composed by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world,” and so forth.

Finally, several further passages concerning the professions and subscriptions of the same Hincmar, and his rebukes, follow, up to the end of the work.

# Letter of Hincmar of Laon to Hincmar of Reims

He replies to the little work of fifty-five chapters and to other matters written or done against him.

[Col. 0509C]

(See *Patrologia*, vol. CXXIV, col. 1027.)

## Hincmar of Laon to the Same

On agreement concerning the excommunication imposed by him, which he demanded.

(See above, col. 1069.)

## Letter of Hincmar of Reims to Hincmar of Laon

(In Sirmond, from Flodoard, Book III, chapter 22.)

Hincmar, bishop of Reims, to Hincmar, bishop of Laon.

A man worn down by various scourges inflicted by various persons says: “Those who devour me do not sleep”—as though he were saying, “They do not rest.” And you, brother, do not cease to wear me down with the scourges of your tongue, nor to infect me by provoking me to anger with your poisonous writings. But he who guarded his servant from murmuring can guard me, a sinner and a frail man who trusts in him, from resentment and malice against your false accusations.

After adding much else concerning the pain of my wounds, you say: “As I find in your perverse writings, you detract from the authority of the apostolic see.” Therefore, no one of sound judgment has ever believed or will believe you; for both the writings that I have very often sent to the apostolic see and those that I have repeatedly sent to you in reply will convict you, both in this world and at the future judgment. [Col. 0510A] You will never be able to prove, anywhere or at any time, that what you say about me is true: namely, that “it is preached and taught by those who were bound to fight to the death for the privileges of the apostolic see, which belong to Christ, that the things established by that same see should be rejected or proved worthy of rejection.”

Rather, you are shown to resist the privilege of that see. According to the canons of the holy councils set out above, approved by that first see and by the whole Catholic Church as truly established by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the entire world, and according to the decrees of that holy see promulgated from those same sacred canons, you refused to obey the metropolitan privilege after being admonished once, twice, and three times. You were ordered to dissolve the bonds of impiety that you had ruinously bound, to your own danger and that of many others, against evangelical truth, apostolic and prophetic authority, and the sacred canons and decrees of that venerable see. [Col. 0510B]

Moreover, you perniciously signed, and caused to be signed, a document against the sacred rules and against the metropolitan privilege. Hence, when summoned to the synod by bishops of ten provinces, you presented a written declaration of your future obedience, signed in your own hand—which I possess—and then you signed again against it.

For my part, I both receive and affirm that the decretal letters of the apostolic see, issued at different times by the pontiffs of that same see for the consolation or consultation of various fathers, are to be received with reverence; and I profess, as I have shown above, that the canons of the holy councils, together with the decrees of the apostolic see promulgated from those same sacred canons, must be received, guarded, and observed. [Col. 0510C]

As for what you say you hear people saying against the judgment of Lord Pope Nicholas: if you mean me, you are lying. I did not oppose what he judged concerning Rothad or Wulfad; rather, I took care to obey as he commanded. In what you say concerning Rothad—that you did not consent to his deposition—your own handwritten signatures convict you. I did nothing concerning it that you did not do with me; I signed nothing that you did not sign. For I possess those very signatures of your hand.

And toward the end of this work:

As for the other matters that you falsely and reproachfully mention in the document delivered to me at Attigny, I do not care to answer you. But know that I have not forgotten what is written in the prophet Isaiah: when holy Hezekiah was pressed by distress, he spread out before the Lord in the temple the blasphemous letter directed to him, cried out to him, and was heard. [Col. 0510D]

I too shall stretch out my hands to the Lord with your blasphemous and most arrogant writings directed to me by you, praying that, when he knows, when he wills, and as he knows and wills, he may turn you toward love of true peace, charity, and due obedience, and free me from lying lips and a deceitful tongue.

Through the merits of my blessed and glorious Lady, Mary, Mother of God, and through the prayers of Saint Remigius, whose privilege you disparage, my Helper will hear me in times of need and in tribulation.

And because blessed Jerome says concerning those whose office you have gratuitously undertaken against me:

“Let my dogs hear this: you who grew from son into brother, and from there into a fellow bishop, and afterward progressed so far that you grew into my dog, accept this lengthy reply, demanded by the occasion of your perverse obstinacy. When I have leisure, I shall write more briefly concerning your other perverse and disordered writings, in which, while criticizing me, you have written some things falsely, some reprehensibly, and some with feigned humility but genuine arrogance. In that reply, since I read that the Lord said, ‘I shall no longer be angry with you,’ I shall, as far as I can yet see, put an end to writing to you about such quarrels.”

As for what you say—that people say of me, “What sort of uncle is he, to write such things to his nephew?”—let those same people also say of you: “What sort of nephew is he, who, having been taken up by such an uncle as he then was, and having become such as he now is in spiritual and temporal honor, demands such things from an unwilling uncle, lest he be judged by others as he is portrayed by his nephew, and lest through him the name of the Lord be blasphemed and his ministry dishonored?” In this I have followed the Apostle, who wrote to the Corinthians against those who blasphemed him and labored to have him despised by others. [Col. 0511B]

That excellent teacher acted so that, when his character was recognized, the life and tongue of those who preached evil were made worthless by their own preaching. He would have commended them if he had concealed himself; and by not showing himself, he would have given room to error.

Those same people also say of you: “What sort of nephew is he, who plots such things against his uncle, nourisher, and ordainer, and does as much evil as he can, while desiring to do more than he can?” You will clearly see this on the day of the great judgment, unless beforehand you recognize it and correct yourself through worthy fruits of repentance.

You weary me greatly, and rightly so; let it not be counted against you. But my weariness is consoled by what Gregory says, as I wrote to you:

“Even if an Ethiopian enters the bath black and comes out of the bath black, nevertheless the bath attendant does not lose the coin for his bath.”

I fear concerning you, my Alexander, what Paul said concerning his Alexander: “Alexander the coppersmith showed me many evils; the Lord will repay him.”

## Hincmar of Reims to the Same

(From Labbe’s Councils, as are the following letters.)

[Col. 0511D]

Hincmar, bishop of Reims and servant of the people of God, sends greetings to the priests, deacons, and the rest of the ecclesiastical order, and to all residing in the parish of Laon.

Our fellow priests and co-presbyters Hetto, Ermino, Hadulfus, and Clarentius, priests of your church, delivered to me on the day before the Kalends of June of the present second indiction, in place of all of you, a petition whose text follows in part, insofar as I judged sufficient. They consulted me concerning certain matters affecting your common necessity, as follows:

“On the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May, while our pastor was discussing on Mount Laon, in his synod, various matters concerning the welfare of his holy church, arranging and improving certain things in it, a part of that discussion arose from the circumstances of the times. Since the power of arranging ecclesiastical affairs was being taken away from him, although right and canon law command that a bishop should dispose of and administer the property of his church according to his will and as he wills, our pastor recited, by reading them aloud in the presence of the entire synod, very many authorities of Saint Peter and his successors, showing how and in what manner the power of binding and loosing had been given.

“After these had been recited, remembering the injuries recently inflicted upon him, he added that the time was approaching for the provincial synod held by you and your suffragans at the royal palace of Vermeria on the eighth day before the Kalends of May. Summoned to it by your letters, he willingly professed before everyone that he would proceed without delay. But because he believed that at that synod someone might unlawfully and contrary to the laws of the canons inflict some violence upon him, contrary to canonical custom, he declared under oath and by the authority of Saint Peter that, if permission to go to Rome were denied him or he were held captive, he had bound all the priests of his entire parish, so that none of them would exercise the priestly ministry there until he himself had spoken with us again in person or letters from the holy see of blessed Peter the Apostle had been sent to us.

“What did not happen then was carried out now at the royal palace of Silvacum, on the fifth day before the Kalends of June. Before he reached Silvacum on that day, however, foreseeing the violence that was to be inflicted upon him, he instructed our priest Clarentius and the deacon Teutlandus to inform us that we would observe in every respect what he himself had ordered all the priests of his parish to observe, by the authority of Saint Peter, in the aforesaid synod on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May, for the sake of his injuries—or, more properly speaking, for the welfare of the holy churches.”

And somewhat later:

“Therefore, since we could not approach our same lord, who was being held and confined by royal power, in person, and did not dare to enjoy the priestly ministry because he had forbidden it, we assembled at our capitol on the third day before the Kalends of June. There, after reconsidering the matter in common discussion, we judged it appropriate to ask humbly from your sacred fatherhood and benevolence advice for our salvation: whether we ought to exercise the office of the priestly ministry by celebrating Masses and offering sacrifices to the Lord for the restoration of our pastor and for the common welfare of the entire holy Church; by baptizing children; visiting the sick; reconciling those seeking penance with the provision of viaticum; and burying the dead, when we are completely forbidden to do all these things.”

And shortly afterward:

“Whether it ought to be exercised in our parish or not, and so forth.”

As I reread this, I confess that I grieved deeply and excessively, because our beloved brother and fellow bishop Hincmar has presumed, contrary to episcopal dignity, evangelical truth, and apostolic and canonical authority, to undertake such measures on account of his injuries—measures such as no bishop before him has undertaken. They are not only contrary to the path of the sacred Scriptures and opposed to the decrees of the saints; they are also hostile to human salvation and to the whole of Christianity.

For, as Pope Hilary says, one sins no less against the sanctions of sacred traditions than one attacks the Lord himself in an injury.

I commend your diligence, beloved sons and brothers, for I recognize that you have not read the precepts of the sacred canons superficially. The sacred and mystical Council of Nicaea says:

“Let the ancient custom be preserved throughout Egypt, Libya, and Pentapolis, so that the bishop of Alexandria has authority over all these places, since a similar custom belongs to the bishop of the city of Rome. Likewise, in Antioch and in the other provinces, let the privileges belonging to their churches be preserved.”

Pope Boniface, writing to Hilary, bishop of Narbonne, explains this canon as follows:

“It is fitting that we be careful guardians of the sanctions of our fathers. No one can be unaware of the constitution of the Council of Nicaea, which commands as follows, using its very words: throughout each province, each metropolitan is to possess his proper jurisdiction, and no one is to have two provinces subject to him. Since it is not otherwise to be believed, they judged that this must be observed, with the Holy Spirit suggesting it to them.”

And somewhat later:

“We say this so that your Charity may recognize how carefully we preserve the precepts of the canons: our own constitution likewise determines that each province must always await the direction of its metropolitan in all matters.”

Again, writing to Pope Celestine according to the African Council, he says:

“The decrees of Nicaea most clearly entrusted both clergy of the lower orders and the bishops themselves to their metropolitans.”

The venerable Council of Antioch likewise says:

“In each region, it is fitting that the bishops know that the metropolitan bishop has charge of the whole province. Therefore, all who appear to have business should come from everywhere to the metropolis. Hence it has pleased us that he should excel in honor, and that the other bishops should do nothing beyond him, according to the ancient rule established by our fathers, except only those things that concern their own diocese and the possessions subject to them. For each bishop is to have authority over his own parish, so that he may govern it according to the reverence due to each person, and administer every possession under his authority; he is to ordain priests and deacons and determine individual matters by his own judgment. But he must not attempt to do anything more without the metropolitan bishop.”

The bishop, it says, is to ordain the priests and deacons of his parish, not to depose them. For those whom the bishop alone can ordain, he alone cannot remove or suspend from sacred offices, except as the venerable canons prescribe.

And it says that he is to determine individual matters, not general ones, by his own judgment. The metropolitan bishop must be understood to have charge of the whole province. Therefore, all who appear to have business should come from everywhere to the metropolis.

Accordingly, beloved brothers, since blessed Gregory teaches us and says, “He who does not correct what must be cut away is an accomplice,” I have judged it necessary to direct the following letter, by metropolitan authority, to the aforementioned brother and fellow bishop Hincmar. I admonish him with paternal and fraternal love that, according to the decrees of blessed Pope Hilary, he should dissolve his wrongful act as quickly as possible.

If he refuses to do so and, obstinately—which God forbid—chooses to delay rather than obey, let the whole body of your fraternity know, by the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, who, as he himself says, came to save souls, not to destroy them, and came to seek and save what was lost; who, as he himself declares, is the way, the truth, and the life (John 14): the way, namely, of holy conduct; the truth, of divine doctrine; and the life, of eternal blessedness (John 4).

From him and through him the episcopal order received its origin for edification, not destruction. By the judgment of the Holy Spirit, through whom the sacred canons were promulgated, and by the instruction of the holy prophets and apostles, their successors, and the pontiffs of the apostolic see of blessed Peter, documents of salvation, wholesome rules, and beneficial decrees have been issued to us and handed down for inviolable observance.

Therefore, as you will read below, I declare and decree that everything contained in the chapters written in your petition which is contrary to divine authority—whether that authority binds subordinates, commands by word, or decrees in writing—is null, void, and without any force or authority. [Col. 0514C]

And I command you, ministers of the church in the parish of Laon, by the authority already mentioned, that in the celebration of Masses and in all other offices, both by day and by night, and in distributing, according to the Lord’s tradition, the heavenly sacraments for the benefit of brothers and peoples; in baptizing infants; in receiving those in need of penance; in assisting with viaticum those who are dying, according to the sacred canons; and in burying the dead, you diligently care for brothers and peoples, without hesitation or negligence, insofar as human frailty permits, carrying out the divine duties according to the path of the sacred Scriptures and the tradition of our ancestors.

Know that you will suffer the loss of your orders if you confess, or are regularly convicted, of having through your negligence—God forbid—exposed your neighbors to danger.

If, however, which must not be believed, our brother and fellow bishop Hincmar at any time does anything against the rules to any one or to any of you because you did not observe his unlawful command, let those who consider themselves injured hasten, according to the sacred canons, to your metropolitan or to the provincial council, so that whatever has been wrongly inflicted upon them—God avert it—may, after examination by the synod, receive the proper and necessary correction.

## Hincmar of Reims to the Same

[Col. 0515A]

Hincmar, bishop of Reims, sends greetings to his beloved brother and fellow bishop Hincmar, bishop of Laon.

On the day before the Kalends of June of the present second indiction, the flock of the church of Laon sent to me through its representatives—whose names we have recorded—a petition that had been presented. Among other matters, it contains the following:

“On the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May, while our same pastor was discussing on Mount Laon, in his synod, various matters concerning the welfare of his holy church, arranging and improving certain things in it, a part of that discussion arose from the circumstances of the times. Since the power of arranging ecclesiastical affairs was being taken away from him, although right and canon law command that a bishop should dispose of and administer the property of his church according to his will and as he wills, very many authorities of Saint Peter and his successors, showing how and in what manner the power of binding and loosing had been given, were recited by our same pastor, who read them aloud in the presence of the entire synod.

“After these had been recited, he remembered the injuries recently inflicted upon him and added that the time was approaching for the provincial synod held by you and your suffragans at the royal palace of Vermeria on the eighth day before the Kalends of May. Summoned to it by your letters, he willingly professed before everyone that he would proceed without delay. But because he believed that at that synod someone might unlawfully and contrary to the laws of the canons inflict some violence upon him, contrary to canonical custom, he declared under oath and by the authority of Saint Peter that, if permission to go to Rome were denied him or he were held captive, he had bound all the priests of his entire parish, so that none of them would exercise the priestly ministry there until he himself had spoken with us again in person or letters from the holy see of blessed Peter the Apostle had been sent to us.

“What did not happen then was carried out now at the royal palace of Silvacum, on the fifth day before the Kalends of June. Before he reached Silvacum on that day, however, foreseeing the violence that was to be inflicted upon him, he instructed our priest Clarentius and the deacon Teutlandus to inform us that we would observe in every respect what he himself had ordered all the priests of his parish to observe, by the authority of Saint Peter, in the aforesaid synod on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May, for the sake of his injuries—or, more properly speaking, for the welfare of the holy churches.”

And somewhat later:

“Therefore, since we could not approach our same lord, who was being held and confined by royal power, in person, and did not dare to enjoy the priestly ministry because he had forbidden it, we assembled at our capitol on the third day before the Kalends of June. There, after reconsidering the matter in common discussion, we judged it appropriate to ask humbly from your sacred fatherhood and benevolence advice for our salvation: whether we ought to exercise the office of the priestly ministry by celebrating Masses and offering sacrifices to the Lord for the restoration of our pastor and for the common welfare of the entire holy Church; by baptizing children; visiting the sick; reconciling those seeking penance with the provision of viaticum; and burying the dead, when we are completely forbidden to do all these things.”

And shortly afterward:

“Whether it ought to be exercised in our parish or not, and so forth.”

I trembled and was horrified sufficiently and more than sufficiently at this novelty, unheard of in the world until now, beloved brother, and I grieved deeply and excessively. Hence my tears increase; my groans cannot be contained within my heart. From the innermost pain of my being I attribute it to my sins that you, my son, are doing such things at this time, in the presumption of novelty—which is known to descend from pride—as no bishop is ever read to have presumed to do.

For, as we read in sacred History: “Peter was kept in prison, but prayer was being made without interruption by the Church to God for him” (Acts 12).

Pope Liberius, Pope Vigilius, Pope John, and the pontiffs of the holy Roman Church were sent into exile, and some of them were confined in prison. Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, the second see; Saint Meletius, bishop of Antioch, the third see; Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem; John, bishop of Constantinople; Paulinus, bishop of Trier; Saint Hilary, bishop of Poitiers; and Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, were removed from their parishes and sent into exile; yet they did not presume to do what you have done.

Blessed Ambrose, shut up in the church of Milan at the command of the heretical empress Justina, with armed men keeping watch around the church and a wagon placed before the door to drag him into exile, holding his life in his hands, did not do anything of the sort.

Rigobert, bishop of Reims, expelled from his see by cruel violence and living for many years in great want on his own property not far from that city, did not do anything of the sort with his fellow bishops.

Others also in our own age and time were temporarily expelled from their sees for various reasons; some were even cast out irrecoverably, yet they did not do anything of the sort. They remembered that the Apostle had said, confirming it by prophetic testimony: “Do not defend yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath. For it is written: ‘Vengeance is mine; I will repay,’ says the Lord” (Romans 12; Hebrews 10; Deuteronomy 32).

Even if this consideration alone—or any other—should have restrained you from such presumption, so that you would not be the only one to do what no one else had done, blessed Peter the Apostle says: “Let none of you suffer as a murderer, or a thief, or a reviler” (1 Peter 4).

Catholic teachers say that one suffers as a reviler who, during the time of his persecution, becomes unrestrained even in insulting his persecutor.

Again, the same prince of the apostles says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, so that you should follow in his footsteps. He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but entrusted himself to the one who judged him unjustly” (1 Peter 2). He entrusted himself, but he did not excommunicate or curse.

The Apostle Paul says: “Giving no offense in anything, so that our ministry may not be blamed; but in everything let us show ourselves as God’s ministers, in great patience. And be patient toward all” (2 Corinthians 6; 1 Thessalonians 5).

Saint Gregory, writing to Januarius, says:

“Among many complaints, the distinguished man Isidore has complained to your Fraternity that he was unjustly excommunicated and anathematized. When we wished to learn from your cleric, who was present, why this had been done, it became clear that it had been done for no other reason than that he had injured you. This greatly distressed us. For if this is so, you show that you think nothing of heavenly things but demonstrate that your way of life is earthly, since, in revenge for a personal injury, you have brought upon him the curse of an anathema, which the sacred rules prohibit.

“Therefore, henceforth be entirely circumspect and careful, and do not again presume to inflict such things upon anyone in defense of your injury. For if you do anything of the sort, know that afterward it will be avenged upon you.

“The petition presented to me by the church of Laon also demonstrates that this previously unheard-of excommunication was drawn out by you on account of your injury before that injury had been inflicted upon you. Moreover, last Sunday, namely on the fourth day before the Kalends of June of the present second indiction, it was carried out in the parish of Laon by omitting the celebration of Masses—alas!”

Saint Gregory likewise says in Homily 26:

“Those who follow either their hatred or their favor in the cases of their subjects cannot judge their subjects rightly. Hence it comes about that the one who exercises this power of binding and loosing according to his own desires, and not according to the character of his subjects, deprives himself of that very power. Therefore it is rightly said through the prophet: ‘They magnify souls that shall not die and give life to souls that shall not live’ (Ezekiel 13). He kills one who will not die when he condemns the just; and he attempts to give life to one who will not live when he strives to absolve the guilty from punishment. Causes must therefore be weighed, and then the power of binding and loosing must be exercised.”

Saint Augustine agrees with this, earlier in time but later in place, in his book *On Penance*:

“He did not wish a person to be judged by another according to the arbitrary judgment of suspicion or according to an extraordinary usurped judgment, but rather according to the law of God and the order of the Church, whether the person confessed voluntarily or was accused and convicted.”

Therefore, on account of your injuries, you ought not to have excommunicated priests from the office of celebrating the holy sacrifice. Although, according to the sacred canons, only a bishop can ordain priests, he alone cannot remove them from office unless they have confessed or been convicted of a crime, except as the venerable canons prescribe.

Still less, then, ought you to have deprived any priest—and least of all all the priests of your parish—of the priestly office on account of your injury.

For Saint Gregory, writing to Euphemius, says:

“The humility of God’s servants ought to appear in a time of affliction. Those who rise up against their superiors clearly show that they disdain to be God’s servants. For it is not a great thing for us to be humble toward those by whom we are honored; even worldly people do that. But we ought especially to be humble toward those from whom we suffer anything.”

The Psalmist says: “See my humility because of my enemies” (Psalm 9).

And he writes to Bishop Maximian:

“I remember that I have often admonished you that you should never be hasty in pronouncing a judgment.”

And to Marcian he says that no one is to be condemned without an examination.

The petition presented to my lowliness by the church of Laon also states that you forbade communion from being given to anyone in your parish, even to one dying and seeking final penance or viaticum; that no infant was to be baptized and no dead person buried in the same parish, if permission for you to go to Rome were denied or you were held captive, until you yourself had spoken with them in person or letters from the apostolic see had been sent to the church of Laon.

And how do you know, brother, whether you will live even until tomorrow? Will those whom you have decided to bind always remain bound?

To this blessed Gregory says:

“It is harsh that one who does not know how to govern his own life should become the judge of another’s life. It often happens that someone occupies the place of judgment whose life is wholly unsuited to that place; and it frequently occurs that he either condemns the innocent or, himself bound, absolves others.”

Therefore, insofar as it depends upon you, this cruelty of yours surpasses all the cruelty of all pagans and all the persecutions inflicted upon Christians by all persecutors, since the Lord says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew 10).

But you, brother, insofar as it depends upon you, send both soul and body into Gehenna. You not only kill all those whom, by your command, you cause to leave this world without baptism or penance and communion; you also make all the priests guilty of their deaths, and you render them deprived of their rank in the judgment of those who now reign with God in heaven and shine with miracles on earth. For so many deaths you will render an account, not only in the synod but also at the divine judgment.

For just as we read that Paul had Saint Stephen stoned by the hands of so many people as he equipped for the stoning, so you kill as many as, through your cruelty and unjust and wrongful command, you cause to leave the body without baptism and communion.

How has it escaped your mind, brother, that through the prophet the Lord says to each one of us: “I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel. If you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked person, and the impious person does not turn from his impiety, he will indeed die in his sin, but I will require his blood from your hand” (Ezekiel 33)?

And if God will require from your hand the blood of those to whom you did not announce their iniquity so that they might turn from their impiety, what will you say to him at his judgment, brother, who, as he himself says, did not come to destroy souls but to save them?

When those souls come before God—those who faithfully carried and presented their newborn children for the grace of baptism so that they might be freed from the power of the devil, or sent them through patrons [read: godfathers (*patrinos*)]—will they not cry out against you? And what of those little souls of infants, no less than the souls of adults, who could have been freed from bondage to another’s sin, not their own, had they not been destroyed by your cruelty, fury, and indignation?

For all these deaths, together with your own sins, you deserve as many deaths as the number of those whom you have killed by the sword of your sentence, crueler than a material blade.

Therefore, without doubt you will suffer the deserved penalties of vengeance. Why did you not fear, and why did the Lord’s promise not recall you from issuing this perverse sentence—a promise by which, through the prophet Isaiah, he made to his universal Church, saying: “I will bring your offspring from the east, and from the west I will gather you. I will say to the North, ‘Give’; and to the South, ‘Do not forbid’” (Isa. 43:5–6). Yet you forbid the Church to bear children to the Lord from the immaculate womb of the divine font—he who did not come to destroy souls but to save them.

[Col. 0519B] How could you have overlooked what you read in the Gospel: “They were bringing little children to him so that he might touch them. But the disciples rebuked those bringing them. When Jesus saw this, he was indignant and said to them: ‘Let the little children come to me, and do not forbid them’” (Matt. 19; Mark 10). And you forbid little children to be offered to the Lord?

And if the terrifying judgment of God did not frighten you, and could not recall you from the fury of your mind so that you would issue such commands—since never and nowhere, after the sacred Council of Nicaea was celebrated, had you heard that such a thing had been done, as you ordered it to be done—you ought to have feared lest you alone do what no Christian had ever dared to do. For concerning infants whose baptism is not yet known, the ecclesiastical rule issued through the blessed [Col. 0519C] Siricius demonstrates, whenever necessity demands it, saying as follows:

“We wish that infants who, because of their age, have not yet been able to speak should be assisted with all speed, so that, for those who need it in any kind of necessity, the water of sacred baptism may be provided; lest it tend to the destruction of our souls if, when those who desire it are denied the saving font, each one departing from this world should lose both the kingdom and life. Moreover, whoever has fallen into the danger of shipwreck, the attack of enemies, the uncertainty of a siege, or any bodily illness accompanied by despair, and has asked to be helped by the sole aid of faith, let that person, at the very moment when he asks, obtain the rewards of the regeneration he seeks.”

Let error on this matter suffice thus far. Now let all priests observe the aforesaid rule, if they do not wish to be torn away from the firmness of the apostolic rock upon which Christ built the universal Church.

And blessed Leo says:

“We must preserve the mystical and rational pattern of the principal and greatest sacrament, without an unauthorized license by which assistance is granted in baptism to those in danger. Thus we defer the free vows of those who are safe and living in security and peace to those two connected and kindred festivals—namely, Easter and Pentecost—so that in danger of death, in the peril of siege, in the distress of persecution, or in fear of shipwreck, we may at no time deny anyone this singular safeguard of true salvation.”

And the African Council also ordered that even those infants concerning whom no absolutely reliable witnesses are found who can testify without doubt that they were baptized, and who themselves, because of their age, are not competent to answer concerning the sacraments entrusted to them, must be baptized without any scruple, lest this hesitation cause them to be deprived of the cleansing of the sacraments.

And Saint Leo says on this matter:

“If no indications exist among relatives or household members, among clergy or neighbors, by which those whose baptism is in question can be shown to have been baptized, action must be taken so that they may be reborn, lest they plainly perish. In those cases, what is not shown to have been done reason does not permit us to regard as repeated. Those, however, who can remember that they came to church with their parents may recall whether they received what was given to their parents. But if even this is absent from their memory, what is not known to have been conferred appears to be something that should be conferred upon them; for presumption’s rashness does not intervene where the diligence of piety is present.”

And Saint Gelasius says:

“Let no one at any time suppose that there is confidence for baptism outside the paschal festival and the venerable sacrament of Pentecost, except only in the event of a serious attack of illness, when one must fear that, as the danger of the disease increases, the sick person may perhaps depart, overtaken by death without the saving remedy. Deacons must not dare to baptize without a bishop or priest, unless extreme necessity compels them to do so when the aforementioned ministers are situated at a considerable distance; and Christians who are laypeople are likewise often permitted to do this.”

And Saint Gregory, writing to John, bishop of Larissa, says:

“The second chapter concerning criminal matters appears to have been proposed against Bishop Adrian, concerning infants who were prohibited by his command from receiving sacred baptism and thus died unwashed in the filth of sin, in darkness.”

See, brother, that Saint Gregory shows this to be a criminal charge.

But his statement concerning final penance and the provision of the viaticum should have been sufficient for you: “The Son of Man came to seek and to save what had been lost” (Luke 19). And although the Lord’s mercy, with which the earth is full, can assist those who ask that final penance and the viaticum be given to them—if these are denied them—those who believe in their heart for righteousness and confess with their mouth for salvation, pierced with heartfelt sorrow and with a conscience baptized by their tears, may receive God’s grace in an incomprehensible manner, just as the omnipotent goodness completed in the case of that thief what, as blessed Augustine says, was lacking from the sacrament of baptism, because it had been lacking from him not through pride or contempt but through necessity. Nevertheless, you will plainly be guilty of all those souls if, by your command, they depart from human affairs without penance and the provision of the viaticum.

Concerning the viaticum of holy communion, the sacred Council of Nicaea says:

“Because, in general, the bishop ought reasonably to give communion from the offering to anyone at all who is placed at the point of death and asks that the grace of communion be granted to him.”

Concerning this holy and mystical synod, blessed Pope Leo writes to Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, saying:

“That provision of the Nicene canons, ordered by the truly Holy Spirit, is in no respect dissoluble. Let no synodal councils flatter themselves because of the increase of their assemblies, nor let any number of priests, however much greater, dare to compare or prefer itself to those three hundred and eighteen bishops, since that council was consecrated with so great a divine privilege that, whether ecclesiastical judgments are celebrated by fewer or by more, whatever differs from their constitution is entirely void of authority.”

And Saint Siricius also decreed concerning apostates and those profaned by the worship of idols and the pollution of sacrifices that the grace of reconciliation must not be denied them at the end of their lives, because the Lord says: “We do not desire the death of the sinner, but only that he turn and live.”

And Saint Innocent says that it was decided that communion should be given to the dying, as a kind of viaticum for those departing because of the Lord’s mercy, and lest we appear to follow the harshness and severity of the Novatian heretics, who deny pardon. Therefore, communion is given together with final penance, so that people of this kind, with the permission of our Savior, may even at the end of their lives be rescued from everlasting destruction.

And Saint Celestine says:

“We have learned that penance is being denied to the dying, and that the desires of those who, at the time of their death, wish this remedy for their souls to assist them are not being granted. I confess that we shudder to find anyone guilty of such great impiety as to despair of God’s mercy, as though he could not at any time assist one who hastens to him, and free a person endangered under the burden of sins from the weight by which he desires to be released. What else, I ask, is this than to add death to one who is dying, and by one’s cruelty to kill his soul so that it cannot be set free? For God is entirely ready to help, and he invites people to penance, promising through the prophet: ‘On whatever day the sinner turns, his sins will not be counted against him’ (Ezek. 33). And again: ‘I do not desire the death of the sinner, but only that he turn and live’ (ibid.). Whoever has denied penance to a person at the time of death therefore takes away his salvation and despairs of the clemency of God, because he does not believe that God can suffice to help the dying even in a single moment.

“The thief hanging at Christ’s right hand would have lost his reward if the penance of a single hour had not helped him. While he was undergoing punishment, he repented, and through the promise contained in a single utterance he obtained, by the Lord’s promise, the dwelling-place of paradise. True conversion to the Lord among those placed at the end of life must therefore be judged by the mind rather than by time, as the prophet asserts: ‘When you have turned and groaned, then you will be saved’ (ibid.). Since, then, the Lord is the examiner of the heart, penance must not be denied at any time to one who asks for it, since that person binds himself to the Judge to whom he knows that all hidden things are revealed.”

And Saint Leo says:

“Penance that has been deferred must not be denied when it is sought with greater earnestness, so that the wounded soul may somehow reach the remedy of pardon.”

And again:

“To those who, in a time of necessity and under the pressure of impending danger, implore the assistance of penance and immediate reconciliation, neither satisfaction must be forbidden nor reconciliation denied. For we can impose neither measures nor times upon God’s mercy, with whom true confession suffers no delay of pardon, since the Spirit of God says through the prophet: ‘When you have turned and groaned, then you will be saved’ (ibid.).”

And elsewhere:

“First declare your iniquities, so that you may be justified” (Prov. 18).

Again:

“For with the Lord there is mercy, and with him there is abundant redemption” (Ps. 129).

In dispensing God’s gifts, therefore, we must not be difficult, nor neglect the groans and tears of those who accuse themselves, since we believe that the very disposition to repent is conceived through God’s inspiration, as the Apostle says: “Lest perhaps God grant them repentance, so that they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive for his will” (2 Tim. 2).

Indeed, as we have said, assistance must be given to the necessity of such people in such a way that the act of their penance, and also the grace of communion—if they request it through signs of sound understanding even after losing the use of speech—must not be denied them. But if they have been so weakened by the force of illness that they cannot indicate, in the presence of a priest, what they had asked for shortly before, the testimony of the faithful standing around them must benefit them, so that they may obtain together both the benefit of penance and of reconciliation.

And again the same Saint Leo says:

“Our admonition therefore declares that if any of the brethren attempts to act against these decrees, and dares to commit what has been forbidden, he must know that he is to be removed from his office and will not be a participant in our communion, since he refused to be a companion in discipline. But lest anything be thought to have been omitted by us, we order that all the decretal letters both of blessed memory, Innocent, and of all our predecessors, which have been promulgated concerning ecclesiastical orders and the disciplines of the canons, be so carefully observed by your affection that, if anyone violates them, he must know that pardon will thereafter be denied him.”

Likewise, the same [authority speaks] concerning the condemnation of one who violates the sacred decrees established in such a matter.

And because, brother, you cannot be ignorant of these things, and you are not unaware that this judgment has been rightly derived—especially since this is not the position of Catholic bishops but of the Novatian heretics, as blessed Innocent, Saint Ambrose, and all the other orthodox teachers demonstrate, an exceedingly pernicious, destructive, and detestable [Col. 0522D] sect—you ought to have taken care not to issue such commands thoughtlessly, as the petition submitted to me by the Church entrusted to you shows.

For I think you have read Saint Augustine’s letter to Bishop Honoratus, in which you could have found that you ought rather to die with the people entrusted to you than allow them to lack the heavenly sacraments without which they cannot live and be saved. Therefore, brother, see to it that you are not a murderer—and even a murderer of murderers—because you cause the heavenly sacraments to be withdrawn from the people, without which they cannot live, although there are those who are able lawfully to administer those same sacraments to the people.

[Col. 0523A] “Fear, moreover, what our predecessors said concerning the sentence of the holy Gospel in which the Lord says: ‘If anyone says anything to you, say, “The Lord has need of them,” and immediately he will let them go’” (Matt. 21). Speaking in them through the Holy Spirit, our elders said:

“Teachers are instructed that, if anything adverse should obstruct them, if anyone should contradict the truth by word, if anyone should prevent sinners from being loosed from the snares of the devil and brought to the Lord through confession of faith, they must nevertheless not cease preaching. Rather, they must confidently make clear that the Lord needs such people for the building of his Church.”

And alas! Although no one contradicts them, you, by contrast, contradict those who implore you, binding them so that they cannot perform the divine offices for the people. Their responsibility is to celebrate the sacred offices of the Mass, distribute to the faithful the mystical nourishment of the spiritual food—that is, the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ—for the remission of sins, transfer the unbaptized from the power of the devil into the kingdom of Christ through the bath of regeneration, and free souls from eternal destruction through the door of reconciliation and the sanctification of the viaticum. The Lord cries to you from heaven that “the good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep” (John 10).

He did what he taught and showed what he commanded. When the cohort and the servants of the Jews, led by Judas, came to seize him and his followers, he said: “If you seek me, let these go” (John 18). Thus he allowed himself to be seized and permitted those who would convert the peoples to the faith and celebrate the sacred mysteries for the converted to depart unharmed.

For if, because you provoked it, anything adverse happened to you, you ought to have endured it patiently until I, however unworthy a metropolitan, together with my fellow bishops and our brethren, approached the clemency of our lord the king on your behalf. And, as we have already done, we would certainly have obtained from him what we requested justly and reasonably.

Therefore, we have no doubt that, with the Lord’s cooperation, we shall obtain what we request justly and reasonably—provided only that your insolence does not obstruct our petitions. For, since in this command of your presumption you have acted against the course of Scripture and against the sacred rules, I have judged it necessary, by virtue of our office and position, to show this to you.

For it is written: “Ask your father, and he will declare it to you; your elders, and they will tell you” (Deut. 32); and: “Let your eyelids precede your steps” (Prov. 4); and: “Do everything with counsel, and afterward you will not regret it” (Ecclus. 32).”

[Col. 0523D] And the sacred Council of Nicaea says:

“Let the ancient custom be observed throughout Egypt, Libya, and Pentapolis, so that the bishop of Alexandria has authority over all these regions, since the same custom also belongs to the bishop of the city of Rome. Likewise, in Antioch and in the other provinces, let the privileges belonging to their churches be preserved.”

Pope Saint Boniface explains this chapter in a letter to Hilary, bishop of Narbonne, as follows:

“It is fitting that we be careful guardians of our fathers’ decrees. For no one can be unaware of the constitution of the Nicene synod, which commands as follows, to repeat its very words: each province ought to have its own metropolitan jurisdiction, and no province is to be subject to two metropolitans. Since this must be believed in no other way, they judged, at the prompting of the Holy Spirit, that it should be observed.”

And after some further remarks:

“We say this so that your charity may understand how carefully we observe the precepts of the canons, so that our own constitution likewise determines that each province must always await the direction of its metropolitan in all matters.”

And the African Council, writing to Pope Celestine, says:

“The decrees of Nicaea entrusted both clergy of lower rank and the bishops themselves to their metropolitans.”

And Saint Leo, writing to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica, says:
