“According to the canons of the holy Fathers, established by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, we decree that the bishops who are metropolitans of their respective provinces, whose care is extended to your fraternity by delegation from us, retain inviolate the right of the dignity entrusted to them from ancient times, so that they depart from the established rules neither through negligence nor presumption.”

And again, writing to Theodore, bishop of Fréjus, he says:

“The proper order of your concern ought to have been that you confer with your metropolitan concerning what appeared to require inquiry; for in cases that pertain to the general observance of all the Lord’s priests, nothing ought to be accomplished without the primates. It is certain that the matters concerning the baptism of infants, final penance, and the denial of the viaticum to no one, which I have set forth from the sacred rules, pertain to the general observance of the Lord’s priests. Against these you ought not to have issued commands thoughtlessly.”

And the Council of Antioch says:

“It is fitting that the bishops of each region know that the metropolitan bishop has charge of the whole province. For this reason, all who appear to have business should come from every direction to the metropolis. It was therefore decided that he should excel in honor, and that the other bishops should do nothing beyond him, according to the ancient rule established by our Fathers, except only those things that pertain to their own diocese and to the possessions subject to them.

“For each bishop is to have authority over his own parish, so that he may govern according to the respect due to each person and exercise oversight over every possession under his authority; he is to ordain priests and deacons and handle each matter by his own judgment. But they must not attempt to do anything beyond this without the metropolitan bishop.”

[Col. 0524D] Pay close attention to what is said: “The bishop is to ordain the priests and deacons of his parish.” He is to ordain, not depose; nor is he to remove or suspend them from office contrary to the rules. And immediately afterward it says: “He shall handle each matter by his own judgment.” It says “each matter,” so that he may handle it by his own judgment—not matters that pertain to the general observance of all the Lord’s priests, which, as Leo says, must not be carried out without the primates.

And do not close the ears of your heart to what is said there most carefully: “Each bishop,” it says, “is to have authority over his own parish, so that he may govern according to the respect due to each person.”

Therefore, you ought to have taken care not to abuse the authority over your parish granted to you, contrary to these sacred canons. They say that a bishop is to govern his parish according to the respect due to each person, not *subrigat* (“raise it up”) [read *subruat*, “overthrow it”], as you have done, insofar as it depended upon you, bringing destruction according to a disrespect unsuitable to everyone.

For everyone recognizes that the disrespect you displayed in your parish is unsuitable, and it is shown to pertain to the destruction of all. Since the Lord says that, regarding individuals in individual cases—and all the more regarding many—one must be fearful: “Whoever scandalizes one of these little ones who believe in me, it would be better for him that an ass’s millstone be hung around his neck and he be drowned in the depth of the sea” (Matt. 18; Mark 9; Luke 17).

For, as blessed Gregory demonstrates, when someone has been elevated to the appearance of holiness but destroys others by word or example, it would plainly have been better for earthly actions to bind him to death under an external appearance than for him, placed in sacred office, to bring death to others by word and deed. For surely, if he alone fell, the punishment of hell would torment him in a manner at least more bearable.

Therefore, dearest brother, I ask, exhort, and implore you, and with all the gentleness and humility I can summon I beg you, and by metropolitan authority I admonish you: as the Lord commands through the prophet, “Hasten to loose the bonds of wickedness, undo the oppressive burdens” (Isa. 58); set free those whom you have bound, and break every such burden.

Paying attention to what Pope Hilary says in his decrees:

“Whoever,” he says, “has transgressed in God’s affairs through obstinacy or contempt, or has been unwilling to abolish what he wrongly did, will find in himself whatever evil he has not cut away.

“Therefore, since you know that you have been placed over certain people, as Saint Leo says in his decrees to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica: do not take it badly that someone has been placed over you; rather, render yourself the obedience that you demand. And just as you do not wish to bear a heavy burden imposed upon you by me, so do not dare to impose an unbearable weight upon others.

“For we are disciples of the humble and gentle Teacher who says: ‘Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls; for my yoke is easy and my burden is light’” (Matt. 11).

And if—which God forbid—you refuse to obey these sacred and canonical admonitions, know, by metropolitan authority supported by the Apostolic See and by the judgment of the sacred canons, as we have stated above, that this pestilential and deadly excommunication of yours is to be dissolved.

For if any person belonging to your parish had been excommunicated by you, and it could be doubted whether, as the sacred canons of Nicaea say, that person appeared to have been excluded from the congregation through your faintheartedness, contentiousness, or some other fault of yours, I would certainly have waited until the matter had been examined by all the bishops of the province assembled together and until it pleased either you or the common body to issue a more humane judgment in such a case.

But now, because the matter is so plainly evident, and what you commanded is found to be execrable and destructive, contrary to the evangelical commands and opposed to the decrees of the saints—something which, as Saint Leo writes, you ought to have avoided even in doubtful and obscure matters, and which permits no delay—I shall declare, by the authority stated above, that whatever you commanded from the aforesaid chapters, insofar as it differs from their constitution, is entirely void of force.

In annulling this presumption of yours, I am acting partly in the words and partly in the meaning of blessed Gelasius—not as the author of a new constitution, but as the executor of an old decree. This is permitted not only to a metropolitan prelate but to any pontiff, since an error once condemned together with its author carries with it its own execration and punishment for anyone who, in any way, becomes a participant in its wicked communion.”

## HINCMAR OF RHEIMS TO THE SAME MAN

[Col. 0526B] HINCMAR, bishop of Rheims, sends greetings to his beloved brother HINCMAR, our fellow bishop of Laon.

Not long ago, in precipitous anger and in disturbance contrary to the sacred rules, you hurled inappropriate and unlawful excommunications even against those who did not belong to you. As a result, you stirred up a very great scandal in this kingdom and in that church. Concerning these excommunications, I recently met with you and our brethren and fellow bishops at Verberie, and, although not without your slanderous hostility toward us, you dissolved them for those upon whom you had inflicted those curses, after being admonished by us not thereafter to be rash in pronouncing judgment.

But you have added worse things to the former ones. As the petition delivered to me by the Church of Laon shows, in revenge for your injuries you ordered that, in the parish entrusted to you, no one should sing Mass and no one should receive holy communion, although the Lord, when he handed over the sacred mysteries of his body and blood to be celebrated by his disciples and through them by all priests, said: “Whenever you do this, you shall do it in remembrance of me” (Luke 22). And concerning his body and blood he said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6).

You also ordered that no one should baptize infants in your parish, even when the danger of death was pressing, although the Lord says: “Teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Mark 16); and: “Unless someone is reborn from water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3).

You likewise forbade anyone to receive final penance or reconciliation, or to assist someone asking for the viaticum of holy communion at the point of death, although the Lord preaches to all: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near” (Matt. 3).

And the Apostle James says: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him bring in the priests of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord. And the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up; and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him. Therefore confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, so that you may be saved” (James 5).

And Saint Gregory, speaking of the resurrection of the dead man of four days, says that we must, through pastoral authority, loose those whom we know our Creator brings to life through his life-giving grace. This life-giving act is already recognized, before the work of righteousness, in the very confession of sin.

Therefore let the dead man come forth—that is, let the sinner confess his fault—and let the disciples, that is, the pastors of the Church, loose the one who comes forth, so that they may remove the punishment he deserved, since he was not ashamed to confess what he had done.

And concerning his body and blood, in which the salvation of our souls and bodies consists, the Lord says: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day” (John 6). This resurrection will be distinct from the resurrection of those who do not eat the flesh of the Son of Man and do not drink his blood, and therefore will not have life.

You also issued the most inhuman order that no one should bury the dead in your parish, although the Lord commands through the prophet that the poor and wanderers be brought into their own house, and at the judgment the Lord will say: “I was a stranger, and you welcomed me” (Matt. 25). Yet you ordered that hospitality in the womb of the mother of all—that is, the earth—be denied to the dead.

Concerning these matters I sent you evangelical and apostolic commands and the decrees of the saints. As I have been reliably informed, you did receive them, but you did not wish to read them, although the Apostle says: “Whatever was written was written for our instruction, so that through the consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope” (Rom. 15). For whoever rejects the instruction and consolation of the Scriptures shows that he has no hope of salvation.

The blessed Apostle John, exiled by the emperor Domitian to the island of Patmos and deprived of human consolation, wrote with his own hand, in that same exile and banishment, the consolation of the revelation he had received divinely, and sent it to the Churches to which he had been commissioned to preach.

And the holy Apostle Paul, writing to Timothy, says: “Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead, of the seed of David, according to my Gospel, in which I suffer hardship even to chains as though I were doing evil; but the word of God is not bound. Therefore I endure everything for the sake of the elect, so that they too may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus, with heavenly glory” (2 Tim. 2).

And you, dearest brother, ought not merely to have read the things I sent you and replied to me when you were able; you ought also to have treated the ministers of the Church entrusted to you—not by binding them with excommunication, but by consoling and exhorting them—in whatever ways you could, so that they might strive to labor in divine service, continual prayer, and the salvation of the people entrusted to you.

And if, because of my unworthiness, you despise me deservedly, nevertheless, remembering your profession and subscription, you ought not to have denied the obedience due to your metropolitan, whatever sort of metropolitan I may be—an obedience that you yourself demand from your subjects even in these pernicious commands of yours.

Therefore, by a repeated admonition, I have judged it appropriate, by virtue of my office and position, to summon you and urge you to dissolve what you wrongly bound.

Our Lord and Creator, Redeemer, and Savior says: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me” (John 12)—that is, let him imitate me. Concerning him it is written: “The things that Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1). He both did and taught what you ought to have done and commanded amid the tribulation of your injuries.

For when the moment of his passion was approaching, he prayed to the Father, both for himself and for his own, and also for those who were to believe in him through their word, according to his humanity—he who, equal with the Father in divinity, bestows all the gifts of grace.

And he who commanded his disciples: “Pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5; Luke 6), prayed on the cross not only for his persecutors but also for those who killed him; and now, seated at the right hand of the Father, he intercedes for us.

He also commanded his disciples, before he suffered, when he was weary and sorrowful even unto death, to pray so that they would not enter into temptation.

And, as we read, “Prayer was being made by the Church” (Acts 12) for Peter, who was shut up in prison and bound with two chains. Peter also prayed, as we read, for the Church.

Paul likewise, placed amid persecutions, prisons, bonds, and chains, often asked, as we read, that the Church pray for him to be delivered from unbelieving, troublesome, and evil people; and he himself also prayed for the Church.

The Apostle James, thrown down from the pinnacle of the Temple, prayed on bended knees for those who killed him. And blessed Stephen, kneeling, prayed for those who were stoning him.

Speaking of such people, the Apostle says to us: “Considering the outcome of their way of life, imitate their faith” (Heb. 13).

And again the Apostle James says: “Is anyone among you sad? Let him pray with an even spirit and sing psalms”; and: “Pray for one another, so that you may be saved” (James 5). For it is a form of no small effectiveness in being heard to cry out to the Lord in tribulation with contrition of heart, as it is written: “To the Lord, when I was in tribulation, I cried, and he heard me” (Ps. 119).

But you, as a new teacher—or rather, a new presumptuous man who has taken offense—have, as I have heard, refused to celebrate Mass or even to hear it; and, as though you needed no one else’s prayer, you have forbidden the Church entrusted to you to pray both for you and for itself. Because of your offense, you have ordered injuries and death to be inflicted upon Christ in his members—Christ who sits at the right hand of the Father and said to Paul, “Why are you persecuting me?” (Acts IX and XXVI).

[Col. 0528D] Paul and Silas, whose place you ought to occupy, were beaten with rods in the church and sent into the inner prison, their feet fastened in the stocks. At midnight they were praying and praising God, and those who were in custody were listening to them. Suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken; immediately all the doors were opened and everyone’s chains were loosed. When the jailer awoke and saw the prison doors open, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped. But Paul cried out in a loud voice, saying, “Do yourself no harm, for we are all here” (Acts XVI).

[Col. 0529A] Yet you have not allowed your Church’s children, entrusted to you, to receive as much kindness as that same Paul showed to the jailer who was about to die. Therefore, brother, I urge you again, with paternal and fraternal affection and with metropolitan authority: turn back from this perverse intention. Agreeing with the evangelical and apostolic precepts and with the decrees of the saints, which I sent you long ago on another roll, do not disdain to say, together with them and with your patron Saint Remigius—in whose seat, though unworthy, I sit—what the holy Apostle Paul also said to his inferiors: “If you have forgiven anything to anyone, I too forgive it” (2 Cor. II).

Obey, I beg you, the salutary decrees of those through whom Christ has spoken, lest—God forbid—he say to you: “Whoever is of God hears the words of God; therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God” (John VIII). Be afraid, I beg you, because Saint Innocent, Blessed Ambrose, and the other Catholic teachers declare that what you have ordered concerning not receiving penitents into penance is the heresy of the heretic Novatian. And refusing to baptize infants who are in danger of death is a very great schism from the universal Church.

[Col. 0529B] In the decrees of the apostolic see we read that, as the universal Church of God has always held and still holds, a schismatic or heretic cannot enter the kingdom of God unless converted to the holy mother, the Catholic and apostolic Church; their portion is in Gehenna. And if they taste the heavenly bread—that is, the sweetness of God—they become participants in Gehenna and incur judgment upon themselves.

Therefore, brother, call your mind back from this sect and from this schism, and follow what Saint Celestine wrote in his decrees to the bishops of Gaul, saying:

[Col. 0529C] “Let us consider,” he says, “the sacramental rites of priestly supplications, which, handed down from the apostles, are celebrated uniformly throughout the world and in the whole Catholic Church. Let the law of praying establish the law of believing. For when the shepherds of the holy peoples act as ambassadors before divine mercy with a mandate entrusted to them, they plead the cause of the human race; and, with the whole Church groaning together with them, they ask and pray that faith may be granted to unbelievers; that idolaters may be freed from the errors of their impiety; that, when the veil of their hearts has been removed, the light of truth may appear to the Jews; that heretics may return to the perfection of the Catholic faith; that schismatics may receive the spirit of renewed charity; that remedies of penance may be provided for the fallen; and finally, that, when catechumens have been led to the sacraments of regeneration, the hall of heavenly mercy may be opened to them.”

[Col. 0529D] While bringing these things to mind, do not close the bowels of compassion in your heart against those who seek salvation. Rather, ask almighty God to fulfill in you what he once promised through the prophet, saying: “I will take away from you your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh, and I will make you walk in my commandments and perform them” (Ezek. XXXVI).

Moreover, our brothers whom I sent to you reported to me that you instructed them to beg me, for reverence for God, for his saints, and for the authority of the apostolic see, not to compel you to answer while you remained in such confinement and in the absence of your clergy, and not to bring either judgment or prejudice against you or your parish.

That request is partly neither just nor reasonable. Your request that I not bring prejudice against you or your parish—I obey. Your request that I not bring judgment against you or your parish—I do not obey. For the Lord says through the prophet: “If you render judgment between a man and his neighbor” (Jer. VII), and so forth. And Wisdom says through Solomon: “Rescue those who are being led to death, and do not cease to free those who are being dragged to destruction” (Prov. XXIV).

[Col. 0530A] I obey the command which I have received from the Lord—who by his judgment willed to establish me in the metropolitan see of the province of Rheims—concerning those whom your command is leading to death and dragging to destruction. And the decrees of Nicaea, as the African synod demonstrates in its letter to Pope Celestine, entrusted both clergy of lower rank and the bishops themselves most explicitly to their metropolitans.

[Col. 0530B] Saint Boniface, explaining a chapter of the Council of Nicaea, determined, among other things, that each province should always await the direction of its metropolitan in all matters. And the Council of Antioch says:

“In each region, it is fitting that the bishops know that the metropolitan bishop has charge of the whole province. For this reason, all who appear to have business should come from every direction to the metropolis.”

And it has been established by the sacred canons that no one may hold councils in his own territory except those to whom metropolitan rights appear to have been entrusted. In those councils, presbyters and deacons should be present, together with all who consider themselves injured, and they should submit themselves to the examination of the synod.

[Col. 0530C] Therefore, in requesting that I not bring judgment against your parish, you have made a request contrary to the sacred rules; and the Apostle’s words must be said to you, as to such petitioners: “You ask, and do not receive, because you ask wrongly” (James IV).

“For,” says the Council of Antioch, “each bishop is to have authority over his parish, so that he may govern according to the reverence appropriate to each person, and may exercise care over every possession that is under his authority; so that he may ordain presbyters and deacons and include each matter within his own judgment, but may attempt nothing more without the metropolitan bishop.”

From this chapter I dictated certain things for you to be written in the tablet mentioned above, but the notary, constrained by lack of time and writing quickly, omitted them. I therefore ordered that what I had written for you should be copied from the tablets and written out more carefully for my use.

[Col. 0530D] Pay close attention to what is said: “The bishop is to ordain the presbyters and deacons of his parish.” He is to ordain them, not unordain them; nor, contrary to the rules, is he to remove them from office or suspend them. It follows in the same passage: “Let him include each matter within his own judgment.” By “each matter,” it means that he should include those matters within his own judgment, but not matters belonging to the general observance required of all the Lord’s priests—matters which, as Leo says, ought not to be carried out without the primates.

And do not close the ears of your heart to what is said there with the greatest care: “Each bishop,” it says, “is to have authority over his parish, so that he may govern according to the reverence appropriate to each person.”

Therefore you ought to have taken care not to abuse the authority granted to you over your parish, contrary to these sacred canons, which say that a bishop should govern his parish [Col. 0531A] according to the reverence appropriate to each person, and should not, as you have done insofar as lay in your power, overthrow it to destruction through an irreverence inappropriate to everyone. For the irreverence that you have displayed in your parish is known to be inappropriate to all and is shown to pertain to the ruin of everyone, since the Lord says that we must fear this concerning individuals, and all the more concerning many:

“Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him to have a millstone hung around his neck and to be drowned in the depth of the sea” (Matt. XVII; Mark IX).

For, as Blessed Gregory shows, when someone has been raised to the appearance of holiness and destroys the others by word or example, it would certainly have been better if earthly deeds, under an external form, had bound him to death than that, placed in sacred office, he should offer death to others by word or deed. For assuredly, if he alone had fallen, the punishment of hell would have tormented him somewhat more tolerably.

[Col. 0531B] Your command that I should not compel you to answer in the absence of your clergy demonstrates that you do not correctly understand the sentence of the Council of Carthage, which says that a bishop should hear no one’s case without the presence of his clergy—although I have already told you how it is to be understood and for what reason it was established.

As for your command that I obtain permission for you to go to Rome, as the apostolic lord had instructed me in writing: the apostolic lord did not instruct me to do this. I have his letter safe and intact, and it contains nothing of what you commanded.

[Col. 0531C] As for your claim that you appealed to the apostolic see at the synod recently held at Vermeria, all those more than twenty bishops who were present at the synod know very clearly that you did not regularly appeal to the apostolic see.

As for your claim that you appeal to the apostolic see, when in our judgment—that is, in an episcopal judgment according to the sacred canons—you appealed to the apostolic see, we have the established procedure for how we must proceed in that matter.

For the rest, as far as depends on me, I forbid neither you nor anyone else to go to Rome.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, in the present second indiction.

## HINCMAR OF RHEIMS TO THE PRESBYTERS AND DEACONS OF THE CHURCH OF LAON

Hincmarus, bishop of Rheims and servant of God’s people, sends greetings to the presbyters, deacons, and the other ecclesiastical orders residing in the Church of Laon.

As the petition submitted to me by some of your fellow ministers on behalf of all of you states, our brother and fellow bishop Hincmar, on account of his injuries, has excommunicated you from ecclesiastical office and the whole parish entrusted to him from receiving and sharing in the life-giving mysteries of our redemption.

[Col. 0532A] Concerning this, as some say, many died without the regeneration of holy baptism, without the final penance which they had sought but had not obtained, and without the gift of viaticum.

The prophet Daniel bears witness from the words of the Lord against those who judge unjustly, saying: “You shall not kill the innocent and the just” (Dan. VIII). That is, those to whom God has granted the power of binding and loosing must not assume, out of Pharisaical arrogance, that they may either condemn the innocent or consider themselves able to loose the guilty, since before God it is not the priests’ sentence but the life of those concerned that is examined.

We read in Leviticus (chapter XIV) about lepers, where they are commanded to show themselves to the priests; and if they have leprosy, then they are to be declared unclean by the priest. This does not mean that the priests make them lepers and unclean, but that they have knowledge of who is leprous and who is not, and can discern who is clean and who is unclean.

[Col. 0532B] Therefore, just as there the priest makes the leper unclean, so here the one to whom the Lord has given the power of binding and loosing binds and looses—namely, the bishop and the presbyter. That is, he does not bind those who are innocent or loose those who are guilty; rather, in accordance with his office, when he has learned the varieties of sinners according to the truth, he knows who should be bound and who should be loosed according to authority.

Saint Gregory also says of a bishop of the city of Nicotera, who had been assigned to penance for certain faults, that it is very harsh for that Church not to have a presbyter capable of celebrating the sacred work there until the bishop’s case has been carefully investigated.

And he writes to Maximinian, archbishop of Syracuse, instructing him to receive the offerings of the patrician Venantius—whose men had invaded his episcopal residence and committed various wrongs in a hostile manner, and for that reason Venantius and his household had been excommunicated by him—and to permit Masses to be celebrated for Venantius and his household, saying:

[Col. 0532C] “Earthly utility must be managed in such a way that no quarrel can separate us from the bond of charity; and we priests must show priestly affection toward our sons in such a way that, in causes, insofar as reason supports it, we must in no way neglect the jurisdiction of our Church.”

The same blessed Gregory also absolved those who communicated with Maximus, a bishop excommunicated by him, even though they had not requested it, in these words:

“Some people,” he says, “were violently compelled to communicate with that transgressor; others among you, I have heard, fell through ignorance. I beseech almighty God to guard with the perpetual protection of his grace those who in no way consented to this wickedness, and to answer them with the abundance they desire. And may he absolve from every guilt of sin and from every bond of another’s obligation those whom zeal, ignorance, or any other cause drew into guilt; may he grant to all, in the present life, the grace of his protection; and may he allow us to rejoice over you in the eternal homeland.”

[Col. 0532D] Since our same brother and fellow bishop, after what he himself had stirred up had been settled—through the kindness of the sovereign and through the intervention of myself, my brothers and fellow bishops, and certain other faithful of God, insofar as we saw it to be more reasonable and conducive to peace and concord—though not without great labor, has, as I have learned, been separated from his church for a time by command of our lord the king, because of certain causes and renewed disputes unbecoming episcopal modesty and because his obstinacy demanded it, until the bishops’ counsel considers how his province may be corrected, I admonish your affection with metropolitan concern.

Since that wicked bond, contrary to the evangelical and apostolic precepts and opposed to the decrees of the saints, which he appeared to have bound—as I have already informed you in another letter—has been recognized as dissolved according to the path of Scripture and the tradition of our elders, by the authority of the metropolitan see, devote yourselves to the diligent observance of holy religion. Give yourselves earnestly to prayer, sacred offerings, and the other practices of divine appeasement.

[Col. 0533A] The provost and dean should also diligently care for the brothers entrusted to their oversight, both in spiritual concern and in temporal administration. [Col. 0533B] The treasurer should provide for the lights and for everything else pertaining to the dignity, usefulness, and salvation of the Church, as well as to his own ministry.

The archpresbyters of the whole parish should show the greatest diligence toward the presbyters entrusted to them, and should carefully admonish the male and female superiors of the monasteries of that parish to provide the necessities entrusted to them, both in spiritual and in temporal matters.

They should urge the presbyters, and see to it, that they continually strive not to neglect watching over the flocks entrusted to them, lest scandals be perpetrated by them or those that have been perpetrated remain without ecclesiastical correction. Let no little ones die without the sacrament of regeneration. Let no healthy people remain without preaching and ecclesiastical ministry.

[Col. 0533C] Let no sick people depart from this world without penance and reconciliation, the anointing with holy oil, and the gift of viaticum. Let no dead person in any way lack the office of burial and pious commendation according to ecclesiastical tradition.

And let all, both subjects and prelates, make humility known to one another. Let the prelates love their subjects, serve one another through charity, instruct them beneficially by word and example, and direct them toward the way of salvation by teaching and correcting them. Let the subjects strive to obey their prelates in the Lord with sincere affection of love and humility, until either our aforesaid brother—your pastor, through divine regard and the prince’s understanding—is restored to you, or, with the counsel and agreement of our brothers and fellow bishops and after salutary deliberation, I discover [Col. 0533D] and announce to your unanimity in the Lord how the matter should be handled for you according to the sacred rules.”

## THE SAME HINCMAR TO HINCMAR OF LAON

Hincmarus, bishop of Rheims, sends greetings to Hincmar, his beloved brother and venerable fellow bishop.

As I have already commanded you, not once but twice, through letters sent by our fellow ministers, after receiving the petition submitted to me by your clergy: on account of your injury, you have exceeded the path of Scripture and the tradition of our elders in your parish. When admonished to correct these matters, you did not send me an appropriate reply.

[Col. 0534A] Indeed, when I admonished you in the presence of our lord the king and certain brothers and fellow bishops, using the Apostle’s words (2 Tim. I), not to neglect the grace of God given to you through the laying on of my hands, you did not answer me with anything relevant to the matter.

Thinking that you intended to answer me after more mature deliberation concerning how you had corrected the matters about which I had admonished you, I remained for more than ten days near your parish and in the vicinity of the church entrusted to you, yet you gave me no reply.

Now, because, as our lord the king has instructed me by his letters—and I believe you have already heard this—for the benefit of the holy Church and the peace of the Christian people we are going to travel with him into more distant regions, I considered it right, out of concern for my place, to admonish you to provide due satisfaction, in agreement with the sacred rules, concerning both the matters about which I wrote to you and any other matters that may have continued to be carried out improperly in your parish, and to strive to restore them to a path pleasing to God.

[Col. 0534B] Take care, by whatever means you can, that no disorderly practices remain there and that nothing contrary to ecclesiastical discipline be done there in the future. Consider what the Apostle warns us all: “Let no temptation seize you except what is human” (2 Cor. X). To be tempted is human; to be overcome by temptation is demonic, as is failing to bring your step back to the work of correction and satisfaction.

Therefore, in accordance with the admonitions of the same blessed Apostle, diligently take care to present yourself to God as an approved, unashamed workman, rightly handling the word of truth. [Col. 0534C] Keep watch; labor in all things; do the work of an evangelist; fulfill your ministry; pursue justice, piety, faith, charity, patience, and gentleness. Fight the good fight of faith. Take hold of eternal life, to which you were called and for which you confessed the good confession before many witnesses (2 Tim. II).

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of September, in the present second indiction.

## THE SAME HINCMAR TO THE SAME

Hincmarus, bishop of Rheims, to Hincmar, bishop of Laon, his beloved brother and fellow bishop.

What I recently learned through the hands of the venerable archbishop Wanilo, from letters of the pontiffs of the apostolic see—leaving aside others—concerning the sacred rules by which the holy Church is governed, I learned from the integrity of those same letters, which I possess, even before you were formed in the womb and before you came forth from it.

[Col. 0534D] I did not learn it, as is said, by using myself as a very bad teacher, but from the tradition of those who, illumined by the grace of the Holy Spirit, shone forth. Just as many things are found in the authentic Scriptures that appear to some people to be discordant, yet are not mutually contradictory, so I could demonstrate—if there were time and leisure, and if you would deign to listen—how these and other sacred rules agree.

I could show you a few of these, small in number but great in importance and weight of authority, which you entirely omitted, although you saw them—but did not clearly perceive what you wished to see—and did not see what you did not wish to see, or perhaps did not see what you ought to have seen.

[Col. 0535A] Since they do not support your intention, you did not endure even to move a finger toward them. I shall therefore set them before you, so that you may know from the materials you have assembled that you cannot bring the inclination of your intention to its desired result.

For the mystical and holy Council of Nicaea decides against your intention that the care of all the churches belongs to the pontiff of the first and holy Roman see, while the bishop of Alexandria is to have authority over all those entrusted to him. Likewise, at Antioch and in the other provinces, their privileges are preserved for those churches.

The Council of Antioch demonstrates which churches are meant and what privileges are to be preserved for them, and in what manner:

“In each region,” it says, “it is fitting that the bishops know that the metropolitan bishop has charge of the whole province. For this reason, all who appear to have business should come from every direction to the metropolis.”

And, with certain passages inserted between, it adds:

“Moreover, no provincial bishop is to attempt anything without the metropolitan prelate; nor is the metropolitan to act without the counsel of the other priests.”

[Col. 0535B] And the African council says:

“The decrees of Nicaea entrusted both clergy of lower rank and the bishops themselves most explicitly to their metropolitans,”

and so forth.

Saint Innocent says:

“If any disputes or contentions arise among clergy, whether of higher or lower rank, then, in accordance with the Council of Nicaea, the bishops of that province should be assembled so that the quarrel may be settled,”

and so forth.

Saint Boniface writes:

“It is fitting that we be careful guardians of our fathers’ sanctions. For no one can be unaware of the constitution of the Nicene synod, which commands as follows—we shall set down its very words: in each province, each metropolitan is to possess his own jurisdiction, and no one is to have two provinces subject to him. Since it is not permissible to believe otherwise, they judged, at the prompting of the Holy Spirit, that this must be observed.”

[Col. 0535C] And shortly afterward:

“We say this so that your charity may understand that we preserve the precepts of the canons so carefully that our own constitution likewise determines that each province should always await the direction of its metropolitan in all matters.”

Saint Celestine says:

“According to the decrees of the canons, let each province be content with its own metropolitan, as the decrees contained in the letter of our predecessor to the bishop of Narbonne establish. Let no place be granted to usurpation by any priest through injury to another. Let each person be content with the boundaries granted to him; let no one presume to do anything in another’s province.”

And Leo says:

“According to the canons of the holy Fathers, established by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, we decree that the bishops who are metropolitans of the individual provinces shall possess unimpaired the right of the dignity entrusted to them from ancient times.”

[Col. 0535D] The same holy Leo, pontiff of the apostolic see, knowing what his predecessors and earlier predecessors had written concerning these canons, says to Anatolius:

“That ordinance of the Nicene canons, established truly by the Holy Spirit, is in no respect dissoluble. Let no synodal councils flatter themselves by multiplying their assemblies. Nor should any number of priests, however much greater, dare to compare itself with or place itself above those three hundred and eighteen bishops, since the Council of Nicaea was constituted with such a divinely given privilege that, whether ecclesiastical judgments are celebrated by fewer or by more, whatever differs from the constitution of those bishops is entirely devoid of authority.”

[Col. 0536A] And to Maximus, bishop of Antioch:

“Although the merits of prelates are sometimes different, the rights of the sees over which they preside remain. Rivals may perhaps cause some disturbance, but they cannot diminish the dignity. For however large a number of priests may decree something through the subterfuge of certain persons, if it is found to be contrary to the constitutions of those three hundred and eighteen bishops, it is annulled by consideration of justice.”

[Col. 0536B] And to Theodore, bishop of Fréjus, he says:

“The proper order of your concern should have been that you confer with your metropolitan about what appeared to require investigation; and, if your affection itself did not know what he did not know, you should have asked that both of you be instructed together, because in matters belonging to the general observance of all the Lord’s priests, nothing ought to be carried out without the primates.”

[Col. 0536C] Pope Hilarus says:

“We could not pass over this matter either, which must be cared for with especially diligent concern: that no bishops should dare to depart for any province without the letters of their metropolitans. This must likewise be observed in every kind of clerical office throughout the individual churches.”

And Saint Gregory says to Innocent and the other bishops:

“We exhort your fraternity that, if necessity should compel any of you to travel somewhere farther for your own affairs, you should ask permission from your metropolitan according to the illustrious rule of the holy Fathers, and presume in no way to set him aside, except if—as we do not wish—some case should arise in which you have a matter against that same metropolitan, so that those who hasten to seek the judgment of the apostolic see may have permission to do so. You know that this was also permitted by the canons through the institution of the ancient Fathers.”

[Col. 0536D] It is clear which canons these are: those of the Council of Sardica, as Innocent likewise says to Victoricius, bishop of Rouen.

And Gelasius, agreeing with the foregoing, explains a verse of the psalm by saying:

“God will be known in her strongholds” (Ps. XLVII).

And again:

“Distribute her houses” (ibid.).

For without doubt this ecclesiastical order, described in the loftiness of ecclesiastical dignities, makes God known to us through ranks duly distributed and establishes him as ruler.

Leo clearly explains this to Anastasius:

“Although the order is general among all priests,” he says, “the dignity is not common to all. For even among the most blessed apostles, although there was a certain distinction of authority within their likeness of honor, and although the election of all was equal, nevertheless one was given precedence over the others. From this pattern the distinction among bishops also arose, and provision was made by a great ordering that they should not all claim everything for themselves, but that in each province there should be one whose judgment would hold first place among the brothers.”

[Col. 0537A] And shortly afterward:

“Therefore, whoever knows that he has been placed over certain people should not resent having someone placed over him; rather, he himself should render the obedience that he requires.”

The African council also decreed that a bishop summoned by his primate to a synod should attend at the proper time. If he cannot attend, he must first give an account of the reason for his impediment to his primate and remain content with communion in his own church.

But if someone is not in agreement with the metropolitan church and with the priestly fellowship, and, puffed up, separates himself from that fellowship, thinking that he ought to dominate his own people, and sometimes, when summoned, refuses to come to the council, then not only is the diocese not to be preserved for him; efforts must also be made in every way to have his own church, which has wrongly supported him, rejected by public authority and to remove him from that principal seat.

[Col. 0537B] If, when accused, he refuses to come to give an account, in accordance with the Council of Carthage, and is excommunicated by his primate, then, during the time in which he does not communicate, he is not to communicate in his own church or parish either.

Read through, brother, the sacred councils of the canons and the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, beginning with Siricius and continuing onward. You will find that this was decreed and preserved as has been stated. [Col. 0537C] Correct your understanding according to their judgments, and direct your intention toward their teaching and command.

Understand the sacred rules as they understood them. For it may happen that you and I are mistaken in many matters; but it must not be believed—or even suspected—that they were mistaken.

Therefore, whether you wish it or not, these statutes will remain unshaken. If anyone—God forbid—departs from them obstinately, he will not be counted among Catholics but will be condemned with the schismatics. For, as Pope Hilarus says, one sins no less against the sanctions of the holy traditions than one rushes into an offense against the Lord himself.

[Col. 0537D] And as it is written in the decrees of the apostolic see, whoever assents to a schismatic cannot deny that he is a schismatic. Even if every priest and the whole world should assent, condemnation envelops those who consent; consent does not absolve the transgression. The crime is not diminished but increased when a private matter becomes general. God demonstrated this with respect to all who sin when he destroyed the sinful world by a universal flood.

## HINCMAR OF RHEIMS TO THE SAME

Hincmarus, bishop of Rheims, sends greetings to Hincmar, his beloved brother and fellow bishop.

The people of a village called Follanaebrayus, belonging to the metropolis of the Church of Rheims committed to my unworthiness and situated in your parish, have appealed to me because, in the church to which [Col. 0538A] they and their predecessors had long contributed their vows and tithes, and in which they had received the service of the priestly office until the day before the Nones of February of the present year 860, the third indiction, they could neither hear Mass nor, in time of necessity, have their infants receive baptism as the sacred rules prescribe; nor could those who were dying be saved through confession and reconciliation with the gift of viaticum.

They say that, for as long as it can be remembered by those who are alive, that church has always existed on its own and has never been subject to any other church.

For in the time of Tilpin, archbishop of Rheims, when Rodulfus, the grandfather of Pardulus, bishop of Laon, held that village as a benefice, Ferterus was a presbyter in the aforesaid church.

After Ferterus’s death, Dodo was presbyter in that church, when Odelherus, the son of Rodulfus and father of Bishop Pardulus, held that village as a benefice.

After the death of the presbyter Dodo, Agmeradus was presbyter in that church, when Odelgisus, the brother of Bishop Pardulus, held that village as a benefice.

These three presbyters served in that church successively during the episcopates of the bishops of the Church of Laon: the younger Genebaudus, Bernico, and Gaufredus.

[Col. 0538B] After Agmeradus’s death, Ottericus was ordained presbyter there by Wenilo, bishop of Laon. While Ottericus held that church, he sang at Noviante, at the estate of Landrica, and at Broerae; but his title—and the place where he also resided—was at Follanaebrayus.

At that time Nodalbertus was presbyter at Codiciacum for twenty years. Wenilo died, and Ostroldus succeeded him as bishop in the Church of Laon. Nodalbertus, the presbyter of Codiciacum, died, and Gozmarus the presbyter succeeded him. Gozmarus had been sent from the canonry of Rheims to the Church at Codiciacum and remained there for approximately thirty years.

Ostroldus died, and the episcopate at Follanaebrayus was vacant for some time, while Odelharius held that benefice, until my time, when I was ordained bishop several years after the ordination of Bishop Simeon.

[Col. 0538C] Since Gozmarus could no longer perform the priestly office, he consented that another presbyter should succeed him in the same church. Thus, with the consent of Bishop Simeon, the cleric Haimeradus was sent to Bishop Simeon to be ordained at Codiciacum.

After the death of Bishop Simeon, Bishop Pardulus succeeded him in the Church of Laon. During Pardulus’s time, Ottericus, the presbyter of Follanaebrayus, died; he had lived as presbyter in that same church for approximately sixty years.

After Ottericus’s death, the people of that village came before Bishop Pardulus to appeal because they did not have a presbyter in their church. Bishop Pardulus, with my consent—and at the suggestion of Osverus, to whom I had entrusted the benefice of Odelharius, the son of Odelgisus and nephew by his brother of Bishop Pardulus—accepted the cleric Wlfegerus to be ordained in that church.

Before Wlfegerus could be ordained, however, Bishop Pardulus died.

[Col. 0539A] In the meantime, before your ordination, the presbyter Haimeradus, ordained at Codiciacum by Bishop Simeon, served there. Haimeradus himself appealed to me and before you, arguing that that Church ought to be subject to the Church of Codiciacum.

With my consent you sent your deputies—namely, Ivo, Luidon the archdeacon, Hedenulfus, and Angelrannus the dean and presbyter—to investigate the truth of the matter. They reported to you what is well known to you, and, as we have in our records, they found through reliable witnesses and clear documents that the Church of Follanaebrayus had never been subject to the Church at Codiciacum but had always had its own presbyter.

Then, as the people themselves say, with your consent, the presbyter Bertfridus sang in that church and in your church at Broerae for five years. Bertfridus appealed to you, saying that Haimeradus had left that chapel in ruins and had taken from it one pallium, one chasuble, one bell, and one book.

[Col. 0539B] And, as the people themselves say, you sent your deputies to investigate this matter—namely, Hadulfus the archdeacon, Fainulfus, and Angelrannus the presbyters—and they found the matter as Bertfridus had stated.

Therefore, Haimeradus restored before your envoys to that same church the things that had been reclaimed. In that church, as I said above, the same Bertfridus ministered for five years with your permission, until he withdrew after a report about him had become public. Then Sigebertus, to whom I had granted that benefice according to the ancient custom [the reading is uncertain: “de drame”; f., “given by me”], requested a cleric who might be ordained by you for that church. In accordance with the custom of my predecessors, and with ecclesiastical rules and synodal capitularies, I granted him a cleric from the authority of our church on this condition: that, if you judged him suitable, I would give him ecclesiastical freedom; and only then would you ordain him regularly.

That cleric, named Seminatus, held that church for four years with your knowledge and, according to his poverty, worked well in it, as we often saw together and as is still evident. In his place, until he came to ordination, Grimo, a priest of your diocese, ministered in that church for a year and a half on the recommendation of your ministers, namely Hadulfus the archdeacon and Angelrannus the priest-dean. Then, with their agreement, Heimericus, a priest of your diocese, performed the priestly office there for two and a half years, until, as I said above, the day before the Nones of the preceding February, when that church was forbidden to the aforesaid cleric.

Now, however, the matter is being reopened, as though the antiquity of the arrangement, such a long passage of time, and the number of bishops and priests under whom that church remained independent and subject to no other church ought not to suffice to put an end to the entire dispute. Yet public laws, both among the Romans and among our own people, as well as the canons and decrees of the Roman pontiffs, establish that no one may appeal after thirty years concerning something that the passage of time under the law excludes. Nor ought your inquiries and determinations, made through your ministers, to be insufficient, since public and ecclesiastical laws decree that what has been distinguished lawfully and regularly must not be uprooted or removed. Public and ecclesiastical laws have also been enacted against those who presume to remove what has been determined.

After that church was forbidden to the same cleric, as some have said, without your commendation, Mass was not celebrated there, nor did anyone from that village receive priestly service in confession, communion, or baptism. On this account, as the matter came to me, two men there died without confession and reconciliation through communion: one was called Erleherus and the other Gislehardus. The church itself possesses enough by which it can subsist independently; this too is shown among other indications by the fact that it has long existed on its own. It also possesses lands which Ottericus, the priest ordained there, purchased and, dying, left there according to ecclesiastical rules. The priests who served there for so long supported themselves adequately from it.

Therefore, brother, I admonish your affection: lay aside every irrational hostility contrary to the rules, and do not act against your salvation and ministry concerning that church on the ground that it is shown to exist from the church entrusted to me and from the benefice of Sigebertus, the faithful man who is your sister’s husband, against whom you have been unjustly angered. Above all, no one who performs the office of shepherd ought to be unaware that, in carrying out the divine mystery, just as he must not be drawn to what is unjust through anyone’s favor, so what is due must not be delayed or perverted through hatred of anyone or through the zeal of private interest.

For we know that the rules of the Council of Orléans, which were enacted in the time of King Louis, whom Saint Remigius baptized with the thousands of the Franks, say that all basilicas constructed in various places, or being constructed daily, are to remain under the authority of the bishop in whose territory they are situated, according to the rule of the earlier canons. The Council of Toledo also says that the endowments of churches and everything else, according to the ancient constitution, belong to the bishop’s ordinance and authority—namely, as the Council of Antioch says, that he should govern according to the reverence due to each person and exercise prudent care over every possession under his authority, so that he ordains priests and deacons and comprehends each matter by his own judgment.

But before these rules were established in the time of King Louis at the Synod of Orléans, the older rules of the Council of Orange, which did not contradict them, decreed that, if any bishop should intend to build a church in the territory of another city—whether because of his own estate, an ecclesiastical property, or any other convenience of his people—and permission to build had been granted, since it would be impious to prevent such a request, he must not presume to perform the dedication, which is reserved in every respect to the bishop in whose territory the church arises. This privilege is reserved for the builder in such a way that, if he wishes to see particular clerics on his property, the bishop in whose territory it lies should ordain them; or, if they have already been ordained, should consent to his having them. The entire governance of that church, moreover, belongs to the bishop in whose city’s territory the church has arisen.

By this authority, from the time of Saint Remigius, my predecessors, during the times of your predecessors, sent priests ordained with the consent of the bishops of those cities to the churches at the village of Codiciacum in the diocese of Laon, and also to the village of Juliacum in the diocese of Soissons. Thus I too found this arrangement at Codiciacum and Juliacum.

But because, out of respect for our fellow bishops, I was pleased that, when they died, I should send clerics to be ordained in those churches by the bishops of the respective dioceses, I sent to the aforesaid churches priests to be ordained, with ecclesiastical freedom and my letters. Simeon, as I said, ordained Haimeradus, whom I had sent to him, as a priest. Lord Rothadus, not resisting my commission, has already ordained at Juliacum as priests two clerics whom I sent to him. I preserve this same honor for him and for our other fellow bishops who possess churches in our diocese, just as my predecessors did for their predecessors.

It is right, therefore, that you should not derogate from the ancient authority and custom of your metropolitan see, preserved by your predecessors—especially since it was established in the first book of synodal capitularies, preserved by our elders in the time of our emperors, that priests must not be installed in any churches without the authority or consent of the bishops, nor expelled; and that, if laymen offer bishops clerics of reputable life and teaching for consecration and installation in their churches, the bishops must not reject them on any pretext.

Moreover, recently at the assembly of our lord King Charles at Pistes, a capitulary was established and confirmed with your consent, which says that, if abbots or abbesses, counts, our vassals, or other laymen offer bishops clerics of reputable life and teaching to be canonically consecrated and installed in their churches, the bishops or their ministers must not reject them on any pretext.

Therefore, if that cleric is not criminal and is teachable—qualities which the sacred canons also require in a bishop—then, since he is offered to you by us for ordination, you ought not to reject him from ordination in that very church, whose possession by him you consented to for so long.

Saint Innocent, in his decretal to Martianus, bishop of Naissus, concerning certain priests who for some time held churches in his diocese but, for a particular reason, could not obtain his communion, says:

> “Brother, most beloved, if their assertion receives the credit of truth, you ought not to hesitate to receive them, since you allowed them for so long to retain the churches entrusted to them.”

If you wish to ordain that same cleric in that same church, write to me according to custom, and I shall give him ecclesiastical freedom. But if you do not approve of that cleric—whom you consented for so long to have and labor in that church at Follanaebrayo—and if you reject him on reasonable grounds, either because of a crime or because he is unteachable, although you ordained him contrary to the rules, without my permission and without canonical freedom, show this to us, and we shall find another. Only let the aforesaid authority of the rules and the ancient custom concerning that church be preserved for us by you, as it was preserved in the times of your predecessors and predecessors in office: Genebaudus, Bernico, Gairfredus, Wenilo, and Ostroldus; when the bishopric was vacant at the time of Ailemarus; in the time of Simeon and Pardulus; and in your own time until now. It was preserved for my predecessors and predecessors in office: Tilpinus; when the bishopric was vacant after him; Wlfarius; Ebo; for as long as Fulco held that bishopric; and after him Noto. It has also been preserved for me, now ministering in the see of Rheims for twenty-five years, for more than one hundred years, as I have reckoned from truthful chronicles—and I can show this to you.

The laws and sacred rules establish that, just as we may not arbitrarily divide rural parishes established in ancient times without reason, so neither may we confuse them. But since you ordained that cleric contrary to the rules, the sacred rules demonstrate the matter by saying:

> “Those are admitted indiscriminately to the sacred order,” Leo says in his letter to all the bishops established throughout the provinces, “for whom neither nobility of birth nor dignity of character provides support. Since they have been unable to obtain freedom from their masters, they are advanced to the dignity of the priesthood, as though servile baseness ought to receive this honor; and one is believed capable of pleasing God who has not yet been able to prove himself to his own master. There is therefore a double guilt in this matter: the sacred ministry is polluted by the baseness of such an association, and the rights of masters are dissolved insofar as concerns the rashness of unlawful usurpation.
>
> “Therefore, most beloved brothers, let all the priests of your provinces abstain from such persons—not only from them, but also from others who are bound by an original or any other status—unless perhaps the request or will of those who claim some authority over them should intervene. For the person who is to be enrolled in the divine service must be free from others, so that he may not be drawn away by any bonds of necessity from the lord’s camp in which his name is enrolled.”

After setting forth the required nobility of birth and the character of those to be ordained, he adds this conclusion:

> “Our admonition therefore declares that, if any of the brothers attempts to act against these decrees and dares to admit what has been prohibited, he must know that he is to be removed from his office and will not be a participant in our communion—he who refused to be a companion in discipline.”

It must be understood that there is no lack of discrimination here in the use of this plural pronoun, when he says, “if any of the brothers attempts to act against these decrees,” and so forth, just as, according to the Lord’s saying, “Not one iota or one dot will pass from the law” (Matthew 5).

Let us return to what was said earlier in this letter: “Those are admitted indiscriminately to the sacred order for whom no nobility of birth provides support.” If the order of acolyte is not counted among the sacred orders, I make no further point here concerning our cleric named Senatus, whom you ordained as an acolyte without our permission or ecclesiastical freedom.

And because, as Innocent says, “the earlier observance is more severe, while the later, with mercy intervening, is more lenient,” later canons state that no one bound by servile or colonate status is to be admitted to ecclesiastical honors according to the statutes of the Apostolic See, unless it has first been established that he was lawfully freed either by testament or by written document. If any bishop, knowing the status of the person being ordained, should nevertheless wish to transgress this rule by an unlawful ordination, he must not presume to celebrate Mass for a year.

I know that you will not reject these Gallican canons, which you often use in your writings and by which you make your own appeal, since the Council of Antioch, which the Apostolic See and the universal Church accept, says: “A council is complete when the metropolitan bishop has been present.”

And Leo writes to Maximus, bishop of Antioch:

> “Whatever, on account of particular cases, is brought before the episcopal judgment of synodal councils may have some basis for adjudication, provided that nothing concerning it has been determined by the holy Fathers at Nicaea. Finally, the sacred canons requested from the emperors that manumissions be performed in the Church; this was granted by them, and from the time of that grant the rules—and soon thereafter the Church—have preserved and continue to preserve them.”

Thus it is written in the first book of the synodal capitularies, the fifty-five capitularies enacted in the time of our emperors Charles and Louis:

> “No bishop,” they say, “shall presume to promote another person’s slave to the clerical office without the will of his master.”

The Council of Gangra also prohibits this, in chapter 82, at the relevant place. Concerning the slaves of churches, moreover, it was decreed by common agreement that the archbishops established throughout the individual provinces should possess our authority, while their suffragans should keep with them a copy of it. Whenever someone useful from the household of a church is found who is to be ordained, that authority must be read to the people from the ambo, and before the priests or before the faithful laymen at the horn of the altar, as is contained in our authority. With every form of deceit removed, he must obtain freedom; only then may he be advanced to the ecclesiastical orders.

The same procedure must be followed concerning those whom laymen from the households of churches wish to promote to the sacred orders. The same form must also be observed concerning those whom the superiors of canons and monks request for ordination.

Therefore, show us this ecclesiastical manumission concerning the aforesaid cleric whom you ordained as an acolyte, and I shall make no further objection.

It has also been reported to me that you ordered this cleric to be summoned three times, by three priests, to your synod, so that he might give an account in your synod of the authority by which he received a church in your diocese. For this reason, I think I have already given you an account above of the authority by which, and the reason for which, he received the aforesaid church in your diocese—a church which you consented for so long that he should hold, as is evident to many.

He himself, having been deprived contrary to reason, ought to give you no account of the matter in your synod, since such a demand is contrary to reason and authority. But if you want him to come to your synod because the canons of Chalcedon say that no priest or deacon, nor anyone in an ecclesiastical rank, ought to be ordained absolutely, and so forth—perhaps so that, having forgotten, you may learn from him at whose persuasion you ordained him contrary to the rules—then, if you are challenged about this in a synod of bishops, you will have something to answer.

Send word to me, and, since he is a dependent of our church and has been granted no freedom, I shall send him to your synod through my envoys, so that you may say what blessed Leo wrote to Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople: “Just as wrongdoing is committed through evil persuasion, so sin is committed through evil consent.”

You should also reconsider the matter because, as I showed above, what had been established in the time of your predecessors, and what had been presumptuously undertaken after Ottericus’s death concerning the church at Follanaebrayo, was destroyed through your ministers Ivon, Luidon, and Angelrannus, and likewise through Hadulfus, Famulfus, and the same Angelrannus; what had been established in the time of your predecessors was rebuilt; and what has now again been destroyed concerning that church, as well as what I noted above from the ecclesiastical rules and synodal capitularies, you have transgressed.

You must in no way disregard the judgment of blessed Leo addressed to the Emperor Leo, which you heard at the synod held at Soissons; you can also read it yourself in the book that I gave you:

> “If I rebuild the things that I destroyed,” he says, “I make myself a transgressor and subject myself to the conditions of punishment which not only the authority of the blessed Emperor Marcian, but I also by my consent, confirmed.”

And just as you replied to our priest of the diocese whom we sent to you—“Just as you acted toward us in our diocese concerning your church, so you too will act toward us concerning our church in your diocese”—I not only do not consent to this, but I urge you to do it: namely, investigate carefully, under testimony to the truth, through the priests Angelrannus, Grimo, and Fraumarus, and also through Haimeradus himself, what your predecessor Pardulus testified concerning that church before them before his death.

Also investigate it lawfully through other priests, and through suitable laymen who live in that village and in the surrounding area, concerning what they know from the truth about the matters I have set forth. When you have found the truth, judge a just judgment concerning it as a bishop, just as I lawfully and regularly investigated before your envoys the matter of the chapel of your bishopric in our diocese and determined it according to the laws, the sacred canons, and the decrees of the Roman pontiffs. If necessity requires, I shall show you this at the proper place and time in a written document supported by truth and authority.

For there are several churches in my diocese belonging to the bishopric of Laon concerning which I have inflicted no prejudice upon you or upon any of your people, nor do I wish to do so, because I ought not. And because I did not agree with your intention concerning the chapel about which you sent instructions, reason and authority opposed me.

As for what some of your people say—that this chapel is older than the church in the village of Viviniacum—even if it were true, its antiquity would help it only if it had persisted in its antiquity until the present time, as the church at Follanaebrayo has. For Atrebates, Viromandui, and Bononia, from whose territory you are native, existed as older sees with their own bishops in the province of Rheims before the fortress of Mount Laon, among whose sees you were counted when you were ordained bishop.

But because, over a long period, through the occurrence of definite events and necessities, those sees became subject to other cities and lost their privilege, which they have not recovered, while the fortress of Mount Laon grew strong, the laws, the sacred canons, and the decrees of the Roman pontiffs establish that it is not permitted to appeal or resist on this account, since the passage of time under the law excludes such a claim.

Concerning the tithes of the church of the bishopric of Laon—and of my own diocese at Antenac, entrusted to my administration in the royal demesne by the lord king’s arrangement—not only to me and to the priest whom I appointed to administer it, but also to the lord king, your ministers have inflicted, during your time, a grave prejudice contrary to the laws and canons, something that had not previously been done. I have patiently endured this until now for the sake of preserving peace and charity. From this you can understand that I would not deny you justice concerning that chapel if justice itself supported your wishes.

Therefore, brother, in accordance with the duty of my office, I admonish you to carry out regularly what concerns the aforesaid church, as I have stated, supported by ancient custom, reason, truth, and authority. I desire that you receive and fulfill this with a kindly disposition.

What will you do if you choose to hear with the ear of your heart the command of blessed Leo? He says: “He who knows that he has been placed over certain people should not be troubled that someone has been placed over him, but should himself also render the obedience that he demands.”

And since no one can depart from the sacred rules or oppose the obedience that is due with impunity, add to your knowledge the words of blessed Gregory, in which he says to Peter, subdeacon of the Roman Church and keeper of the great patrimony of Peter in Sicily:

> “Concerning the things I write to you for the preservation of justice, I am absolved. But if you neglect them, you are bound. Consider the terrible Judge who is coming, and let your reflection on his coming now tremble, lest then you fear without remedy, when heaven and earth will have trembled before him.”

You have heard what I want. Consider what you are doing.

Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of May, in the present third indiction.

## HINCMAR OF RHEIMS TO THE SAME PERSON

Hincmar, bishop of the Rhemi, to Hincmar, bishop of Laon: greeting, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

By writing back, item by item—but not answering every individual point—you seek, in your wish to undo what I write to you, to dismiss it as boasting. For reasons not unknown to me, I shall answer certain matters, passing over others, in discharge of my office; lest you seem wise in your own eyes, you demand that I answer each point of your stubborn disobedience and disobedient obstinacy. You strive to appear superior and victorious in all things; with the privilege of the metropolitan see you greet me only nominally, ironically and by antiphrasis dishonouring it; and, disobeying with insulting dishonour, you oppose me. You so stop my mouth that I should not dare to warn you concerning matters for which those who seem to have business resort to me—me to whom, by the sacred canons and divine judgment, the care of the whole province in which you were ordained bishop has been entrusted—nor presume to reprove the blameworthy things concerning you that come to my notice; indeed, that I should not answer you in any respect, either in writing or in speech. To put the whole matter in a brief compass, I should fear even to utter a word displeasing to you.

But you are not such a bishop in wisdom, knowledge, religious devotion, or rank as to be able to obtain this. Had you truly been wise and devout, you would not attempt to obtain such things. And because you cannot prevail by truth, reason, and authority, you are distressed, aflame, and panting to resist, suppress, and refute me somehow, by plausible arguments and by things seemingly consonant with authority and reason. Thus you take pains to bend well-spoken things perversely to your own meaning and, so far as lies in you, compel them to wander from their proper meaning.

You have undertaken this ruinous contest against me without any necessity and toil at it without any benefit, though I ask nothing else of you than what is written (Deut. XXVI): “Fear the Lord your God with all your heart, and obey his command”; and that, as a bishop—as indeed befits every Christian—you “pursue peace and holiness, without which no one will see God” (Heb. XII), be content with the moderation proper to your rank, and act as a most dear brother and son, so that we may acknowledge one another, lest the ancient enemy, setting two persons in motion through scandal, make many utter things that ought not to be said through his most wicked victory. For, to state openly that I ask nothing from you out of arrogance, I could have kept silent about the provisions available to me from the canons—about which I have already written to you often for your recognition and amendment—if you had received with charity and humility what I would admonish in familiar speech.

Otherwise, as blessed Gregory says to John, bishop of Constantinople, “I do not wish to introduce a quarrel, but I do not avoid one coming from you, because I cannot, nor indeed dare I, in discharge of my office.” For, as though urging me on, the outstanding preacher says: “Reprove, entreat, rebuke in all patience and doctrine” (II Tim. III).

For if, to confess the truth—would that it were not to my condemnation—I were not your metropolitan by God’s judgment, and you were not a bishop of the province subject to the metropolitan see which, by God’s ordering, I serve and ordained by me, but had been ordained in another province by another bishop, and I heard such things concerning you as I began to hear when you began to follow the desires of the world and the exaltation of your heart, I would admonish you by speech and writing with charitable affection; and, if I were not obeyed, following the apostolic command concerning one who, warned once and twice, neither reforms nor obeys, I would avoid you.

But now, because I am debtor not only to the wise and the foolish, but also to the bishops of my province of Rheims—namely, to those better, wiser, and more devout than I—I can find no way of escape from warning you in season and out of season. For the most mighty preacher says: “I am clean from the blood of all; for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God” (Acts XX). Had he not proclaimed it, he would not have been clean from blood; but because he strove to declare to them the whole counsel of God, he was clean from their blood. By these words I too, a sinner and a fool, am compelled to warn and reprove you and, when necessity requires, rebuke you. I am sorely constrained; I who am called a metropolitan bishop am shown to be guilty, since, beyond the evils that are my own, I add also the deaths of others, killing, as I fear, as many as I daily see going to death while I am lukewarm and silent. The Lord says through the prophet concerning one who perishes: “I will require his blood at your hand” (Ezek. XXXIII); how much more concerning many?

This terrible denunciation is also directed at me concerning those through whom many ought to be saved—at me who, to keep watch and even to be set over bishops, have been raised by God’s judgment because my sins required it. For this reason I have been called archbishop, not to my joy but to my dread, since I am bound by guilt for the death of the souls subject to me, who perhaps might always have lived had they heard the words of my correction. Therefore the blood of one dying is required from the hand of the watchman, because, if he is silent, the sin of the subordinate is reckoned as the fault of the superior.

There is therefore, as blessed Gregory says, something for me to do, that even if the subordinate dies I may render myself free: I must rise, keep watch, oppose evil deeds, as it is written: “Run about, make haste, rouse your friend; give no sleep to your eyes, nor let your eyelids slumber” (Prov. XXVIII). And if you still persist, as you have begun, in resistance, I shall hear what the Lord God says in me and to me concerning those who resist: “Behold, I have made your face stronger than their faces, and your forehead harder than their foreheads; like adamant and like flint I have made your face” (Ezek. III): that is, so that, whether I am trampled upon and despised by hearers, my tongue may neither be restrained from shame by honour paid to me nor fall silent from weakness through contempt. Hence I hear again these words addressed to me: “Do not fear them or be dismayed at their face, for they are a provoking house” (Ezek. II). Thus a brother who is a provoking house must be rebuked and never feared.

Therefore, concerning the fact that, now for the third time, in the preface of your letter you have sent me the phrase “the due devotion in the Lord,” which in what follows you do not pursue as due devotion, I write back to you “the due devotion in the Lord.” For, insofar as concerns the human eyes of the flesh, you show me no due devotion; insofar as concerns the human eyes of the mind, you show no devotion in the Lord.
