Yet, insofar as I fear that this is weighed in the divine eyes by heavenly judgment, you render me due devotion: you ceaselessly torment me by deeds not so praiseworthy as I had desired, by your objections, and by your harshest answers and improper attacks against charity, which is God.

But would that what we hear in the Gospel (Luke XVI), in Abraham’s reply to the burning rich man concerning Lazarus, purified from his evils through sufferings, might happen to me: “Lazarus likewise received evils for evils in his life, just as the rich man received goods for goods in his life.” So I wish it to be done to me through you: if through lack of foresight I have offended God in anything concerning you—though with humble and contrite heart I confess that in many things I have offended and do offend him—may I receive from you, through you, purification in my present life, lest I be tormented for this in the life to come. For, as I said, through lack of foresight, not through a consciousness of ill will, I stirred up in your advancement the groans of so many who, as many say, groan under your hand as truly under a most grievous sickle. These groans, I believe, are daily sent forth to the Lord. Therefore, bound by daily—indeed continual—fear and pain, I not only groan, but groaning with them, scandalized by you and tortured in mind by the judgment of God whose permission it is, I say with the man worn down by the scourges of words and with a contrite heart:

> “Let him that began to crush me crush me; let him loose his hand and bring me to my end; and let this be my consolation, that, afflicting me with sorrow, he spare me not, and that I not contradict the words of the Holy One” (Job VI).

For I would wish, if it pleased him, that he should scourge me as one worthy of scourging through someone other than you. But because it so pleases him to whom all good things please, I will address him in his own words—the one who, from affection for our humanity, deigned to say to the Father: “Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matt. XXVI).

And again, by his Spirit he foretold concerning one who seemed to be his own: “If my enemy had cursed me, I would surely have borne it; but you, a man of one mind with me, my guide and my acquaintance, who together with me took sweet food; we walked in the house of God in concord” (Ps. LIV). “The man of my peace, in whom I hoped, who ate my bread, lifted up his heel against me” (John XIII). As though he plainly said: I endured it all the more grievously because I experienced these things from one who seemed to be mine.

But even if compassion for me does not thereby touch your heart, fear ought nevertheless to pierce it, because your contumacy and disobedience, inflicted by you upon me, whatever successor of blessed Remigius I may be in his metropolitan see, rebounds upon him who, in me his sinful vicar, bears the burdens of the whole province of Rheims. Indeed, O Christ our God, while that same most holy predecessor of ours prays with you for us, you deigned to take upon yourself my disgraceful calumnies and the persecutions caused by your disparagements. Trusting in the Father, above all the heavens and above the summit of all the angels, you said to Saul, as we read and believe: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts IX).

For it is not to be disbelieved that among the great multitude of believers persecuted by Saul there was someone imperfect, though not imperfect in the manner in which I am, in whom—as in the rest, who were plainly his body—the Lord said that he was being persecuted. And therefore I believe that, when I, though imperfect, am persecuted in any manner, he is persecuted, because in the voice of holy Church, of which I am the last member, it is said through the Psalmist: “Your eyes saw my imperfection, and all shall be written in your book” (Ps. CXXXVIII).

And again the Psalmist says: “The Lord blessed all who fear him, the small with the great” (Ps. CXIII); and he who at the judgment will say to benefactors concerning their good deeds: “As long as you did it to one of these least of mine, you did it to me” (Matt. XXV).

I truly believe that whatever kindness or malice is shown to me for his name is without doubt bestowed upon him. And because blessed John the Baptist undoubtedly died for truth, that is, for Christ, as Christ himself declares when he says, “I am the truth” (John XIV), I too, to use the Apostle’s words, have become your enemy by telling and urging you what is true, though unable to persuade you: that, as Truth itself says through blessed Leo, you should render to your superiors the obedience that you demand from your subjects, and remain in the calling in which you were called.

Because you do not endure this, you cause scandal not only to me but to many; and Truth says: “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it is better for him that a millstone be hung about his neck and that he be drowned in the depth of the sea” (Matt. XVIII).

Again, Christ, the power of God and wisdom of God, says: “For a man who despises one correcting him with a stiff neck, destruction will suddenly come upon him, and health will not follow him” (Prov. XXIX). And Moses and Aaron say to the people who resisted them with a stiff neck: “Your murmuring is not against us, but against God” (Exod. XVI).

Therefore I neither fear your enmities nor shall cease to warn you in necessary matters which I cannot omit without sin, knowing that I must keep peace in undivided love within myself, a peace which I do not fear to disturb outwardly by the force of my voice.

David declares that he observed both things when he says: “With those who hated peace I was peaceful; when I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause” (Ps. CXIX). Behold, he was attacked while speaking, and yet, though attacked, he was peaceful: for he neither ceased to rebuke those who raged nor neglected to love those whom he rebuked.

Paul likewise says: “If it be possible, as far as depends on you, having peace with all people” (Rom. XII). For when the Apostle exhorted them to have peace with everyone, he first said, “If it be possible,” and added, “as far as depends on you.” It was indeed difficult for them to have peace with everyone if they reproved evil deeds; but when temporal peace is disturbed in wicked hearts by our rebuke, it is necessary that it remain inviolate in our own heart.

Hence David again, when he bound himself wholly to the covenants of inward peace, testifies that he did not maintain concord with the wicked, saying: “Do I not hate those who hate you, O God, and waste away because of your enemies? With perfect hatred I hate them; they have become my enemies” (Psalm 138). To hate enemies with perfect hatred means to love what they were made for and to rebuke what they do; to restrain the conduct of the wicked and to benefit their life.

Therefore, when rebuke is withheld, one must consider how great the guilt is if peace is maintained with those who ought to be rebuked, but without rebuke. Thus the great prophet presented to the Lord, as it were, a historical account of having aroused the hostility of the wicked against himself. Hence Paul admonishes the disciples, saying: “If anyone does not obey our word through this letter, take note of him, and do not associate with him, so that he may be put to shame” (2 Thessalonians 3). And immediately he added: “Do not regard him as an enemy, but rebuke him as a brother” (ibid.); as though he were saying: “Break outward peace with him, but inwardly guard it thoroughly toward him.”

And because, out of affection for you, I believe that you flee to your customary refuges—to excuses for sins—in order to say that I judge even your thoughts, since the Apostle says: “Who knows what is in a human being except the human spirit that is within him?” (1 Corinthians 2), I anticipate this objection of yours by saying that one person’s spirit is unknown to another when it is not demonstrated by words or deeds. For since it is written, “You will know them by their fruits” (Matthew 7), whatever lies hidden within is disclosed by what is done outwardly. Hence it is rightly said through Solomon: “As faces are reflected in water for those who look upon them, so the hearts of human beings are manifest to the prudent” (Proverbs 27).

When you say that you wrote to remove the ambiguity of your tradition arising from the primitive genitive between the one who hands over and the one handed over, you spit in my face the grammar which I myself sufficiently pointed out to you. I can patiently bear this as a thanksgiving to Him who endured for me, a sinner, what He foretold concerning Himself: “I did not turn my face away from those who rebuked and spat upon me” (Isaiah 50).

But since, by the noun, you designate yourself as the one handed over and not the one handing over, I do not concern myself with this statement of yours, since my conscience bears witness to me that I owe you nothing in this matter. Hence it is of little importance whether I am judged by you or by a human day; indeed, I do not even judge myself in this matter (1 Corinthians 4).

Nevertheless, if I knew that you were so eager to be rebuked that this could contribute to your benefit and to the healing of your mind, or if I recognized that some necessity in this matter lay upon me, then, by my letters to the king and to the bishops, by their testimony, and through other suitable witnesses, I could show you that, as I said, I do not owe you anything in this matter: “For the day of the Lord will disclose the nature of each person’s work” (1 Corinthians 3).

But since you complain about your being handed over, and since nothing happens on earth without cause—and nothing happens unless God either mercifully brings it about or, in anger, permits it to happen—and since we read that acts of handing over occur in the plural and that different people are handed over in different ways and for different causes, you must scrutinize your mind carefully. Meditating with your heart, and weighing your character, thoughts, words, and deeds on a straight—not deceitful—scale, you should discover within yourself where this handing over of yours originated, from whom it proceeded, what course it has taken, and toward what end it is directed.

For we read that some people hand themselves over. Thus Paul says of certain persons to the Ephesians: “Those who, having lost all hope, handed themselves over to impurity for the practice of every kind of uncleanness in greed” (Ephesians 4). “For,” blessed Gregory says, “the more widely someone gives himself over to present evils, the more he despairs of attaining eternal goods after this life.” The apostle James also says: “Each person is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire” (James 1)—that is, drawn away from the right path and enticed into evil.

Again, Paul writes to the Romans concerning certain people: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts, and their senseless heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools” (Romans 1). And shortly afterward: “Therefore he handed them over.” By “handed them over” he means that grace did not liberate them, just as God hardened Pharaoh’s heart because grace did not soften it.

And the Psalm says: “He handed over their strength into captivity, and their beauty into the hand of the enemy” (Psalm 77). The strength and beauty of certain people are handed over into captivity and into the enemy’s hand when the ancient adversary, through the pride of a good work, gains dominion over a deceived mind.

Satan also demanded the apostles, in order to sift them like wheat (Luke 22); they were commanded to pray that they might not enter into temptation. Paul handed someone over to Satan so that his spirit might be saved on the day of the Lord (1 Corinthians 5). Again: “He handed certain people over to Satan so that they might learn not to blaspheme.” And we read that the daughter of Abraham was bent over by Satan. We also read that many, on account of sins deserving punishment and torture, were handed over, as it were, to certain inquisitors and executioners—to renegade spirits—because not only human beings are ministers and avengers of God’s wrath against those who do evil, and do not carry the sword without cause, but also hostile powers, which are called the fury and wrath of God (Romans 13).

Therefore, if, because your conduct and deeds required it, by the just judgment of God permitting it, you have been handed over—whether by yourself, through a renegade spirit into sin, since we read of “sending through evil angels” (Psalm 77), or through a human being, a minister of God, for the punishment of sin—then, if you do not recognize this and do not come to your senses by correcting yourself, you have no grounds for complaint, but you do have grounds for affliction. For the Lord does not say, “Blessed are those who suffer persecution because of injustice,” but “because of justice” (Matthew 5).

And the Apostle says: “Blessed is the one who endures temptation, for when he has been tested he will receive the crown of life” (James 1), because, as blessed Cyprian says, it is not punishment but the cause that makes a martyr. For the thief who was destined to perish also took up the cross with Christ, but the same crucifixion did not absolve the one whom his own guilt held bound.

Persecution or handing over, when it is not endured rationally, contributes nothing to salvation, as blessed Gregory shows. For no one has the right to expect the reward of merits through guilt; blessed Peter the Apostle also demonstrates this when he says: “What credit is there if, when you sin and are beaten, you endure it?” (1 Peter 2).

Against such people the prophet complains to the Lord, saying: “You struck them, and they refused to accept discipline” (Jeremiah 3). Hence the Lord says: “I killed and destroyed this people, and yet they did not turn back from their ways” (Jeremiah 15). Again he says: “The people did not return to the one who struck them” (Isaiah 9).

In the voice of those who scourge, the prophet complains, saying: “We treated Babylon, but she was not healed” (Jeremiah 51). Babylon is treated but is not restored to health when a mind confused by evil action hears words of correction and experiences the scourges of correction, yet refuses to return to the straight paths of salvation.

To the Israelite people, captive but still not converted from iniquity, the Lord reproaches them, saying: “The house of Israel has become dross to me; all of them are bronze, tin, iron, and lead within the furnace” (Ezekiel 22). As though he were saying openly: “I wished to purify them through the fire of tribulation, and I sought to make them silver or gold; but in the furnace they became bronze, tin, iron, and lead to me, because even in tribulation they burst forth not into virtue but into vices.” For either they erupted into the sound of murmuring, or they resolved not to be free from the vice of hypocrisy, or they persisted in the malice of harming their neighbors, or, weighed down by earthly desires, they could not be purified in tribulation.

Again it is written: “With much labor it was sweated, yet its rust did not come out of the soul, not even through fire” (Ezekiel 24). The Lord applies to us the fire of tribulation in order to purge from us the rust of vices; but we do not lose our rust even through fire when, amid the scourges or through the scourges, we do not cease from vice.

Again the prophet says: “The refiner has refined in vain; their wickednesses have not been consumed” (Jeremiah 6). Gregory says: “Present punishment, if it turns the afflicted soul, is the end of preceding guilt; but if it does not turn it toward the fear of the Lord, it is the beginning of the punishment that follows.”

Therefore we must be on our guard and watch with the utmost care, turning our whole mind toward tears, lest we pass from torments to torments. Thus the just person who suffers, if he patiently endures what he suffers, imitates Christ. The person corrected by scourges imitates the thief who recognized Christ on the cross and entered paradise with Christ after the cross. But the person who does not cease from his faults even amid scourges imitates the thief on the left, who went up onto the cross because of his sins and, after the cross, fell into hell.

If, therefore, you have been handed over in any way or by anyone on account of sin, and have been corrected through the persecution involved in that handing over, so that you might deserve to hear from the Lord—even if not with the ears of the body, then with those ears of which the Psalmist says, “I will hear what the Lord God speaks within me” (Psalm 84)—what the one who was scourged on account of sin and purified through the scourge heard, when the Lord said, “See, you have been made well; do not sin any more, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5), then you have grounds for rejoicing and something that you must preserve through vigilance.

But if you were handed over and scourged through that handing over not because you had sinned, but so that you would not sin—as Paul, who said, “To keep me from being exalted by the greatness of the revelations, a thorn in my flesh was given to me, an angel of Satan, to strike me” (2 Corinthians 12)—then gladly glory in your weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in you.

Finally, if you have been handed over by anyone or in any way, either not because of a preceding sin or so that you would not incur a sin that might befall you, but so that, as a just person, you might be further justified, as in the case of Tobit and Job, concerning whom the Lord said to Satan, “Behold, he is in your hand; only spare his life” (Job 1), you must take care not to murmur because of the scourge and, by murmuring, hand over to his power the soul which the Lord had commanded Satan to spare in Job.

“Do not murmur,” the Apostle says, “as some of them murmured, and were destroyed by serpents” (1 Corinthians 10). You must also be extremely careful not to defile through subsequent sin the merits increased by the scourge, but, retaining his word and purification with a good and excellent heart, according to the Lord’s saying, to bear fruit with perseverance (Luke 8). For those who humbly receive scourges even for their sins are exalted after the scourges and received into rest.

Thus grapes are beaten underfoot and dissolved into the flavor of wine; thus the olive, pressed by crushing, abandons its dregs and grows rich in the liquid of oil; thus, through threshing on the threshing floor, the grains are separated from the chaff and, purified, reach the granary.

Therefore, whoever desires fully to conquer vices should strive humbly to endure the scourges of his purification, so that he may come cleaner before the Judge hereafter, the more thoroughly the fire of tribulation now purges away his rust.

When you say that you are customarily bitten by my letters but have not felt yourself injured, if you understand what you say in the way it should be understood, I do not object. There was indeed something by which you should be bitten, but for the sake of health; and therefore you ought not to feel yourself injured. Let it be as we read in the Gospel: a wound was healed—namely, by the sharp bite of wine and by the soothing application of oil. When I showed you what had been done, you rightly understood it as pertaining to the bite; and when I showed you what ought to be done, if you act correctly you understand it as pertaining to the soothing application of oil.

But if you involve your attention so excessively in transient matters that you do not recognize by which arrows of negligence you are pierced or by which medicines of admonition you ought to be healed, then I rightly condemn you for not considering yourself either injured or capable of healing.

Hence, through Solomon, the voice of one who has been struck and is sleeping is expressed when he says: “They struck me, but I did not hurt; they dragged me, but I did not feel it” (Proverbs 23). For a mind sleeping through neglect of its own care is struck and does not feel pain. Just as it does not foresee impending evils, so it does not fear those already committed. It is dragged and feels nothing, because it is led through the allurements of vices, yet is not roused to guard itself.

When you say that you have been attacked by my arrows and marked with a blemish, do not act in such a way that it becomes necessary for me to do this; then you will feel me cease from these things.

When you say that you have been driven away for an entire year but do not say by whom you were driven away, I do not know what to answer you except what Scripture says—which may the Lord not allow to fall upon you: “The wicked flee when no one pursues” (Proverbs 28).

When you say that you were driven away like Abner (2 Kings 4), worn down by saws, and therefore not permitted to remain silent, you have not appropriately applied the judgment of blessed Gregory concerning Abner’s persecution by Asahel. You ought to have understood me not as your raging persecutor, but, in accordance with the office of my position, as one admonishing you in order to correct your excesses.

You do not strike me with averted spear, as Asahel pursued Abner; nor do you touch me calmly in certain matters and, as though sparing me, overcome me. Rather, by attacking and resisting me to my face, as far as you can, and by provoking me to fury through your obstinate contempt, you never cease to magnify the matter. Therefore, by the force of my replies, while I touch you inwardly with tranquillity, I do not fall or yield from what I had raised up on account of the necessity of my position. Rather, I always cry out more powerfully: I have cried out, I shall cry out forever, and “I will raise my voice like a trumpet” (Isaiah 58). I will announce your excesses to you and strive with all my strength to recall you from your obstinate arrogance.

When you say that you have been worn down by saws, your grammar, as boldly as I dare say, has produced this improperly. No one is worn down by saws; one is cut by them. Paul understood this well when, writing to the Hebrews and describing the sufferings of the saints, he said: “The saints experienced mockeries and scourging, and moreover chains and imprisonment; they were stoned, they were sawn apart” (Hebrews 11). He did not say, “They were worn down.”

For we read that a saw is made with teeth, and I, as far as I can, strive to cut you with toothed saws away from accidents that are not proper to a bishop. I will not cease to bite you with spiritual teeth, to prick you with the goads of admonishing words, and to fasten you with the nails of rebukes, because, as Scripture says, “the words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven deeply” (Ecclesiastes 12). For, as blessed Gregory explains, the words of the wise do not know how to flatter the faults of sinners, but to prick them.

Since you have improperly arranged the past tense of the verb *teror*—“I am worn down”—with *saw*, you can find this not only in your grammar but also in many passages of Scripture, including the place where the Lord commanded Moses how to make the incense which in our language is called *incensum*, saying: “When you have pounded everything into the finest powder” (Exodus 30).

Hence Saint Gregory says: “We crush all the spices into the finest powder.” Again, “to reduce spices to powder” means to wear down virtues by reflecting upon them. The passive form of this active verb is, as you know better, *teror*, whose past participle is *tritus*. This should properly be applied not to saws but rather to a mortar and pestle, as Solomon demonstrates when he says: “Even if you grind a fool in a mortar, like grain crushed from above with a pestle, his folly will not depart from him” (Proverbs 27).

And the incense which the Lord commanded through Moses to be made, we who are devoted to the ministry of the sacred altar must prepare daily, so that we may rightly say to the Lord: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your presence” (Psalm 141).

Concerning your statement that you are surprised that I do not send Hadulf back, although you had rightly agreed to my intervention on his behalf, I do not give a full answer because your command is not grounded in the sincere solidity of truth, charity, and peace. I write back only this: whenever you sent him to me, I always sent him back to you. Yet, unlike what you received in other letters sent to me about him, you did not receive him from me as a rebellious man—as though he had proved rebellious toward you.

It was not my persuasion but, as I think, your action that compelled this from him, because, as I suppose, he too was made to drink by you from the Babylonian cup from which, as we read, the nations were given drink in turn and one by one, up to the final Sesag [perhaps Sesach]. Many others also have been made to drink from it by you.

For, as it is written, “Begin from my sanctuary” (Jeremiah 25)—from me, your nourisher, and from those who nourished you together with me, or among whom you were nourished. You first began by abandoning us and beginning to hate us, while seeking the companionship of others. Then, through one person and another—both friends and subordinates, both clerics and laymen—you continued to wander about until now. Your course reached this man, who was most familiar to you, leaving behind those who preceded him one by one. He too fell from the glass ladder of your familiarity with the same kind of favor by which we earlier fell, as did his predecessors among your subordinates—if indeed such a fall ought not rather to be called an ascent.

Yet Solomon says to you: “Do not abandon your friend or your father’s friend” (Proverbs 27). And Saint Jerome says: “There is a proverb that no one can be served who has served no one; just as you cannot be served, since you have served no one, and since you obtained what you have not by labor but by indulging yourself and sleeping, through another’s labor.” Simonides also plainly demonstrated the answer when he was asked what grows old most quickly among human beings: “A benefaction,” he said. And Solomon says: “Evil will not depart from the house of one who repays good with evil, and one who is hard of heart will fall into evil” (Proverbs 28).

Concerning your statement that you do not know how I know that you consented to Sanatus, our cleric, holding the church at Follanaebrayo, since the matter is neither known nor altered by cases or even by plausible grammatical forms, I write back to you that it should have been unworthy of you—for it is certainly unbecoming that, in order to mock me, a bishop should return to the cradle of childish grammar.

This is what you used to write back to me at school when, at my command, you were being instructed to decline nouns, pronouns, or verbs. When your fellow student, a little boy, asked you, “What part of speech is this or that?” you used to answer as the part seemed to you to be. When he then asked how you knew this, you would say, “If I remember correctly”—something that has not come to my mind for many years—“because the matter is known and is inflected by cases, moods, or forms.”

And you, my brother and son, spew such things into my face for mockery, like phlegm—that is, coagulated, aged, and foul mucus—and you do not consider how greatly you offend God, whatever I may be, by showing no reverence for the sacred ministry.

Now, as the ancient proverb says, “A tired ox plants its foot more firmly.” Since you were unwilling—or rather, since you disdained—to understand this in my earlier letters, or, if you did understand it, refuse to say so, it is not burdensome for me, though it is unnecessary for you, to repeat how I know it: the matter is known, and for a long time it has been shown by humanly occurring cases and by forms that are not merely plausible but true.

As I wrote to you in order, this is demonstrated in the time of Tilpin; when, after him, the metropolitan see of Rheims was vacant for about nine years; in the time of Wulfarius; in the time of Ebo; when Folco held that bishopric; after him, when Nottho held it; and also in my own time.

It is likewise demonstrated through the bishops of the church of Laon: Genebaud the younger, Berneco, Gairfred, Wanilo, and Ostrold; during the vacancy of the episcopate under Ailemar; in the time of Simeon; under Pardulus; and also in your time.

It is further demonstrated by the successive holders of Follanaebrayo: when, in the time of Tilpin, Rodulfus held the estate of Follanaebrayo in benefice; after him Odelharius; then Odalgisus; then Odelharius again; and afterward, when the same benefice was entrusted to Osvero. That church at Follanaebrayo always had priests, for as long as memory reaches: Ferherus, then Dodo, then Haimbradus, then Ottericus, and afterward Bertfridus for approximately five years. It was never subject to the church at Codiciacum.

When Ottericus, a priest ordained by Wanilo, bishop of Laon, was residing in the church at Follanaebrayo, Nodalbertus was priest at Codiciacum for approximately twenty years. After Nodalbertus, Gozmarus was priest there for approximately thirty years.

After Gozmarus, as I previously wrote there, I sent this Haimradus, who now resides at Codiciacum, to Simeon for ordination. Simeon ordained him in the church at Codiciacum. Throughout the time of Simeon, Ottericus remained priest at Follanaebrayo, just as he had been ordained there.

[Column 0556C] Also during the time of Pardulus, until approximately the end of his episcopate, Wlfegerus the cleric held that church with Pardulus’s consent, until Pardulus’s death. After Pardulus’s death, and after your ordination, the priest Bertfridus performed the priestly ministry for approximately five years both in your church near Cadomum and in our church at Follanaebrayo.

Whether you consented to his holding your church—the one near which you went and returned when you went to the palace or returned from it—while he held the church at Follanaebrayo, you yourself must consider.

When Bertfridus departed from your parish because of the reputation concerning him that had become public, I granted Sigebert, to whom I had given that benefice, in the customary manner of my predecessors, permission to present our cleric Sanatus to you for ordination in that same church. If you judged him suitable, I would grant him ecclesiastical freedom, and then you would regularly ordain him.

That cleric held the church for four years and, according to his poverty, worked well in it, as we often saw together and as is still evident. When we were riding together past that church in which the same cleric was laboring, on our way to the king, the people themselves complained to me, in your hearing, about the delay in the ordination of that cleric, because they had no priest.

You replied, in my hearing and in the hearing of many others, both mine and yours, that they were not speaking truthfully, because they had no need of priestly ministry. In response to your words, and in your hearing, I said to those same people that you had arranged for them to have no need of priestly ministry until that cleric was ordained. You contradicted nothing.

For a year and a half, while that cleric held the same church, Grimmo, a priest of your parish, sang the office there. For two and a half years afterward, Haimericus the priest performed the priestly ministry there, up to the day before the most recent Nones of February.

And since you ask how I know this, the matter is known to me from what I learned about antiquity through truthful men, from what I heard from the mouth of Pardulus, and afterward from your own mouth, as I have said, and from what I saw with my own eyes. These true forms make it evident to me.

But if you deny what I know through you yourself, in the presence of many hearers, I will be less able to believe you if you excuse yourself on the basis of what I hear about you from others. Nevertheless, neither you nor I can escape the fact—and I wish this to be reckoned according to truth—that it is written: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wisdom 1). Also: “What proceeds from the mouth, namely what is contrary to truth, defiles a person” (Matthew 15). And Solomon says: “A false witness will not go unpunished” (Proverbs 19).

The authorities say that a person becomes a false witness in two ways: either by saying what is false or by concealing what is true. “Nothing,” says blessed Gregory, “is safer for defense than purity, and nothing is easier for speaking than truth. For when someone is compelled to defend his deceit, his heart is wearied by arduous labor.”

Hence it is written: “The labor of their lips will cover them.” What someone now fills, he will then cover, because the thing by which he currently expresses his mind through flattering unrest will then weigh him down through harsh retribution.

Hence Jeremiah says: “They have taught their tongue to speak lies; they have labored to act wickedly” (Jeremiah 9). As though it were said openly: Those who could have been friends of truth without labor labor in order to sin; and when they refuse to live simply, they impose labor upon themselves in order to die.

For often, when caught in guilt, people refuse to be recognized for what they are and hide themselves beneath a deceptive covering. They attempt to excuse what they do, although it is already plainly visible, so that the person who strives to rebuke their faults is often misled by clouds of falsehood that have been cast over him and seems almost to have lost what he had already held as certain about them.

Hence it is rightly said through the prophet, under the figure of Judea, against the sinful soul that excuses itself: “There the hedgehog had its den” (Isaiah 34). The name “hedgehog” signifies the duplicity of an impure mind that cleverly defends itself.

For when a hedgehog is caught, its head is seen, its feet are visible, and its entire body is plainly observed. But as soon as it is seized, it gathers itself into a sphere, withdraws its feet inward, hides its head, and within the hands of the person holding it everything that had previously been visible all at once disappears.

So indeed are impure minds when they are caught in their excesses. The hedgehog’s head is seen because the beginning from which the sinner approached his guilt is visible. The hedgehog’s feet are observed because the tracks by which the wickedness was committed are recognized. Yet, when excuses are suddenly produced, the impure mind draws its feet inward, because it hides all the traces of its iniquity.

It withdraws its head because, through remarkable defenses, it does not even show that it began some evil. And it remains like a sphere in the hand of the person holding it, because the one who rebukes it, suddenly losing everything he had already understood, holds the sinner wrapped up within his conscience. The one who had already seen everything by detecting it comes, through the wicked evasion of its defense, to know nothing of it at all.

The hedgehog therefore has its den among the reprobate, because the duplicity of a malicious mind, gathering itself together, hides in the darkness of defense.

Let the impure hear what is written: “The one who walks simply walks confidently” (Romans 10 and 23). Simplicity of action is indeed the great confidence of security. Let them hear what is said by the mouth of the wise: “The holy spirit of discipline will flee from deceit” (Wisdom 1). Let them hear what Scripture again testifies: “With the simple is his conversation” (Proverbs 3).

For God’s conversation is the revelation of hidden things to human minds through the illumination of his presence. He is said to converse with the simple because, through the ray of his visitation, he illuminates the minds of those concerning heavenly mysteries whom no shadow of duplicity darkens.

There is a particular evil in the double-minded: while they deceive others through perverse and double-dealing action, they boast that they are wiser than everyone else. And because they do not consider the strictness of retribution, these wretched people rejoice in their own losses. You can read the rest in order in the *Pastoral Rule* of blessed Gregory, which, together with the book of the sacred canons, I placed in your hands before the altar of Saint Mary on the day of your ordination, adjuring you concerning matters that you cannot ignore and must not forget.

Nevertheless, I will not consider this denial of yours, which you have undertaken without any necessity, to be an injury to me; nor will I reckon it as a crime; nor, on account of this denial alone, will I separate myself from communion with you, following the chapter of the African council which you sent me in truncated form and expounded contrary to its meaning, attempting to impose it on me by bending its final part toward your own interpretation.

For I do not think it should be considered a crime if you consented to a cleric who was to be ordained working, until the time of his ordination, in the church in which he was to be ordained, so that, if he were found worthy and suitable, he might be ordained. Nor did Saint Innocent, as I previously wrote to you, consider it a crime for a bishop to consent to certain priests retaining churches in his parish for a longer time, although they were not able during that period to merit his communion. Rather, he decreed that a bishop should in no way deny his communion to those whom he had permitted to retain those churches for a long time in his parish.

The complete text of that chapter of the African council, part of whose conclusion you inserted into your letter, is as follows:

“Likewise it was decided that, whenever a bishop says that someone confessed to him alone a crime committed by that person, and that person denies it, the bishop should not consider it an injury to himself that he alone is not believed. And if, because of a scruple in his own conscience, he says that he does not wish to communicate with the one who denies it until his bishop has communicated with the excommunicated person, then the other bishops should not communicate with that bishop, so that the bishop may be more careful not to say about anyone what he cannot prove by other evidence.”

These documents, which I have written to you both earlier and now, show how I learned the matter; you can recognize this from both the preceding and the present subsequent reading. To confirm them and convict you, I shall produce no witnesses, because I ought not to do so; nor do I wish to disclose your secret confession concerning this matter, which I have not received, since Scripture says: “He who reveals secrets and walks deceitfully, and widens his lips, do not associate with him” (Prov. 20). Catholic teachers explain this as follows: “Do not associate with the friendship of one who exposes the secrets of a former friend; beware of such a man as faithless” [Col. 0559B].

I must nevertheless show and admonish you, so that you may carry out what is just according to the laws and regulations. As for what you deny through many implausible circumlocutions—namely, that you did not consent to the cleric’s retaining that church—if you decide to persist in your defiance and denial, regard him as the judge of your conscience and denial, and you will also have him as your witness. Since you wrote to me that you ought to investigate the matter, which you do not know, and report it back to me, I fear for you lest, as you have already done, you should suffer shipwreck in the matter of this church, appearing victorious in a dispute when you subscribed to a pernicious decree, as it is said, against sacred authority, and compelled the clerics and priests of your parish to subscribe; and lest, binding others irregularly to yourself in order to prevail, you should lead them with yourself into shipwreck [Col. 0559C].

Therefore I adjure and admonish you by the holy and inseparable Trinity of the one divinity, by Christ Jesus our Redeemer, and by the grace of the Holy Spirit, who operates especially in ordinations and whom you received through the laying on of my hands; by the glory of holy Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin; by God’s elect angels; by the merits of blessed Remigius; and by the metropolitan authority divinely bestowed upon that same predecessor of mine and, in succession to him, upon me: do nothing in this matter of the church contrary to the laws that the Catholic and Apostolic Church accepted from ancient times as binding, nor contrary to the sacred canons of the holy councils, the decrees of the Roman pontiffs concerning sacred orders, or the disciplinary regulations promulgated by the canons. Rather, without any prejudice, carry out what you see to be just and reasonable, to the extent that God has given you the knowledge and ability to do so. I ask you not to neglect or despise this admonition, which is full of justice, reason, and authority. For if, through the ministry entrusted to me, I was able, in humility, to entreat God that you should become an ordained bishop through the laying on of my hands, I can and must also, through that same ministry and by its authority, adjure you to do what a bishop ought to do—just as Paul adjured Timothy, whom he had ordained bishop, not to turn aside in another direction but, without prejudice, to keep the commandment (1 Tim. 5) [Col. 0559D–0560A].

And know with absolute certainty that, if you act otherwise, then, with God’s assent and my life permitting, I shall not let the matter pass at a suitable time without regular examination—not for my own sake, God forbid, but because of contempt for the sacred regulations.

Concerning what you added in that same foolish letter of yours—“The canon says: He who cannot prove one crime must not be admitted to the others”—I write back to you: You do not know what you are saying. Filled with indignation and defiance, you cannot see with the eyes of your mind what you ought to express in words or what you ought to keep silent. If you followed blessed David, you would beseech the Lord to set a guard over your mouth and a door around your lips (Ps. 38).

The canon says: “Whenever many crimes are brought against clerics by their accusers, and the accuser is unable to prove one of those charges about which he first proceeded, he must not thereafter be admitted to the others.” Say who that accuser is. Say before whom the accuser accuses you. Say in what regular judgment he accuses you. Say of what crimes the accuser accuses you. Say what crime the accuser pursued but could not prove, so that he might not thereafter be admitted to the others. For whenever, by metropolitan authority—for the care of the whole province has been entrusted to me through the sacred canons—I admonish you concerning those matters for which people who appear to have business in your parish come to me, I shall always be your accuser. Even when I am physically separated from you and admonish you by words or letters, I shall be held to be your accuser of crimes in a regular judgment [Col. 0560B].

For the regulations state before whom and in what manner a bishop must be accused, and where, how, and by whom he must be judged. Whenever I show you, through the path of the holy Scriptures and the authority of the sacred regulations, the matters in which you transgress, you will complain that you have been judged by me irregularly—that is, without a regular synodal judgment. For the Lord says in the Gospel: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not kill’; and whoever kills shall be liable to judgment. But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother without cause shall be liable to judgment” (Matt. 5), and so forth [Col. 0560C].

The sacred canons also say repeatedly: “If anyone acts contrary to these provisions, raising himself up as though against the great council, he shall himself endanger his clerical dignity.” The decrees of the holy Roman See express the same sense: “If any of the brethren attempts to act contrary to these constitutions and dares to undertake what has been forbidden, let him know that he is to be removed from his office.”

When it is shown to you in what ways you act contrary to these provisions, you cannot endure it; instead, you always complain that you have been judged irregularly, and you labor to seek a knot in a rush. In the very matter on which you boast of your wisdom, you display your folly all the more, since the Apostle says: “If anyone among you wishes to become wise, let him become a fool, so that he may be wise” (1 Cor. 3). Solomon says: “He who is impatient exalts his folly, and he who hates reproof will die” (Prov. 14); and: “The pestilent man does not love the one who reproves him, nor does he walk with the wise” (Prov. 15); and: “A wise son is instructed by his father, but a mocker does not listen when he is reproved” (Prov. 13); and: “The ear that hears the reproofs of life will dwell in the midst of the wise. He who rejects discipline despises his own soul, but he who submits to reproof possesses a heart” (Prov. 15); and: “He who meditates discord loves quarrels, and he who provokes anger produces discord” (Prov. 30); and: “He who exalts his mouth seeks ruin” (Prov. 17); and: “A fool does not receive words of wisdom unless you say what is already in his heart” (Prov. 18); and: “Have you seen a man who seems wise to himself? A fool will have more hope than he” (Prov. 26); and: “It is better to meet a bear robbed of her cubs than a fool confident in his folly” (Prov. 17); and: “A fool mocks his father’s discipline, but he who keeps reproofs will become wiser” (Prov. 15) [Col. 0561A].

After a long interval, you proceeded to say not only useless but also foolish things: namely, that the chapter I wrote against you from the First Book of Synodal Chapters worked in your favor, since priests are not to be appointed or expelled in any churches without the authority or consent of bishops. You deliberately refused to mention the preceding material, as well as what is joined together in that same chapter and what I wrote to you, because they would have shown the chapter in its entirety: namely, that if laymen offer bishops clerics of commendable life and learning to be ordained and appointed in their churches, the bishops must not reject them for any reason whatsoever.

Tell me: who appointed anyone at Follanaebray without authority or your consent? As I said, I granted Sigebert, our cleric, permission to offer him to you for ordination; and if you wished to ordain him, I would grant him ecclesiastical liberty. How, then, did Sigebert appoint a priest there without your authority? And where is that priest? [Col. 0561B–C]

Thanks be to God that, as you said in the subsequent royal chapter inserted into your letter, you do not yet possess that power over Sigebert which would allow you to force him, by royal ban, to produce sureties and come to the royal palace. For he is neither your parishioner nor subject to your divine or human *missaticum*, nor did he appoint a priest in that church contrary to episcopal authority. But perhaps what is written is being fulfilled in you: “Every arrogant person is an abomination to the Lord; even though he join hand to hand, he will not be innocent” (Prov. 16). For if he ceases from the perversity that he cannot complete in action, he is not free from the malicious will that he desires to fulfill if he could accomplish it in practice.

You then return to me to gnaw at me, saying: “I inquire why, for so long a time, you did not investigate the irregular ordination of your—rather, my—cleric.” I answer you: Certainly because I did not previously hear that he had been ordained by you, until the people of the aforesaid village complained to me. Nor did I ever intend to bring a charge against you, anywhere or at any time, concerning an unlawful ordination performed by you [Col. 0561D–0562A].

Finally, you say: “First, the manner of the ordination ought to have been investigated; then either the ordainer or the ordained, or both, ought to be judged according to law or struck with the canonical cautery.” Tell me, brother: Who judged you? In what regular judgment were you judged or summoned concerning this matter? But it is not surprising that you act as you do; you do what you are accustomed to do, what you love. Scripture says: “Ephraim is a heifer trained to love threshing” (Hos. 10). And again: “Ephraim is a cake not turned” (Hos. 7).

Then you say: “Therefore, take up again in full the chapter from the book of our Augusti which you mutilated and inserted as though it were against me, although it acts in my favor.” This is untrue. I did not send you that royal chapter in mutilated form. For that cleric is not my slave, nor yours, nor the slave of any free man; therefore I did not include what that chapter says about slaves belonging to anyone, because it did not concern this cleric. But because he is a slave of the church entrusted to me and not to you, I wrote to you what that chapter says about ecclesiastical slaves, since I knew that this did concern the case of that cleric [Col. 0562B].

After this you continue: “Once the substance of this chapter has been considered, await my response concerning the ordination of your cleric, if it was carried out by me at the proper time and place and with the appropriate canonical procedure then in force; meanwhile cease judging my irregular ordination, since you cannot be both accuser and judge. After the chapter of the canons concerning knowledge of this cleric’s condition and concerning transgression through a forbidden ordination, it is clear what should be decreed. These matters should first, if you please, be brought forward, and judgment should be imposed upon either a confession or a conviction. Yet although I have neither been convicted nor confessed, you have acted without any synod, without any such examination, inquiry, or present summons, exercising the office of both accuser and judge, judging in writing both concerning the absent man and against the absent man, and pronouncing as follows: ‘Because you ordained that cleric contrary to the regulations, the sacred regulations demonstrate this by saying—’”

Then you set down the chapter of blessed Leo that I wrote to you. At its conclusion, in your customary manner, you display your learning. I do not care to speak about that displayed learning of yours, since it is neither useful nor necessary to do so. For just as we read about the chameleon, which changes into whatever color it sees, so you, leaping about, continually proceed in contradiction to your own statements [Col. 0562C].

Since I cannot be both accuser and judge, you say that when I judge you in your absence I sometimes assume the role of accuser and then accuse you. At one time you say that I judge you without a synod; at another, that I cannot judge you without a synod. You also fail to understand—and have failed to understand—that those subject to servitude may not be admitted to sacred orders. In many ways you wander and fluctuate back and forth like a reed shaken by the wind, with a wavering mind, because you are not established by the weight of any seriousness [Col. 0562D].

You also say that I expound Leo’s chapter as I wish, but not as you do. In this you speak truly: I expound it as I wish because I expound it as I ought; and I understand it as those who decreed in the synodal chapters concerning the slaves of churches understood it, as I wrote to you and you wrote back to me. I understand it also as it is demonstrated in the very manumission of an ecclesiastical slave.

For the sacred canons did not demand that manumission be performed in the church for people free by birth who were petitioned from the emperors. Nor does anyone free by birth become a Roman citizen through manumission; rather, those manumitted are slaves—whether ecclesiastical, royal, or belonging to any free men. Therefore holy Leo, in the chapter of his decree promulgated from the canons, established that no one bound to a condition of servitude is to be ordained unless, perhaps, the petition or consent of those who claim some power over him has been given [Col. 0563A].

As long as I am bishop of Rheims, I shall claim the authority properly belonging to me over the slaves of this church, and none of them ought to be ordained without the ecclesiastical liberty granted by me. Therefore I say to you briefly what the Lord said to the Jews: “I am not the one who accuses you; Moses, in whom you hope, is the one who accuses you” (John 5)—that is, the law against which you act.

Again the Lord says: “I judge no one; there is one who seeks and judges” (John 8). That is, if you ordained this cleric contrary to Leo’s decrees, it is not I, a sinner on earth, who judge you concerning it, but that holy man in heaven, through his decree. If you wish to confess that you ordained him irregularly, then, just as I do not seek condemnation concerning the others, so I neither seek nor desire your condemnation concerning this man, nor any human disgrace before the eyes of men. But if you deny that you ordained him, as I have already stated, regard him as the judge of your conscience and denial, and you will also have him as your witness [Col. 0563B].

The sacred canons further state that a bishop must not ordain clerics without the council of his own clerics, and that he must seek the agreement and testimony of the citizens. According to the sacred canons and the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, it is my responsibility—if the matter requires it and I compel you—to have you come to judgment concerning the ordination of this cleric, which you deny. Once the truth has been established through the holy Gospels, with both clerics and citizens participating—those whose consent and presence are required when ordinations are performed—whatever is found shall be established [Col. 0563C].

But if you fear God, the most equitable judge, to whom we shall render an account of all our deeds and judgments, there will be no need for this. Nor do I wish to exaggerate this or any other matter, since I do not wish to cause scandal to anyone in matters where I can avoid scandal without sinning against my own conscience.

If the cleric himself—which I neither hope nor seek—lodges a complaint in a provincial synod, whether concerning the ordination performed upon him by you or concerning any prejudice, then the sacred canons state that, after setting forth the judgment concerning priests and deacons, the bishop of the place alone is to hear and conclude the cases of the remaining clerics. If priests, deacons, or other clerics of lower rank complain in cases they have brought concerning the judgments of their bishops, neighboring bishops are to hear them with the consent of their own bishop and, having been called in by them, settle the matter between them. If they think they ought to appeal from these bishops to the primates of their provinces, let them appeal, as has often been established concerning bishops. All who consider themselves injured are to attend councils and undergo the examination of a synod. The canons say much more on this subject, but it would be lengthy for me to write it all [Col. 0563D–0564A].

Whatever we find by the consent and judgment of our brethren and fellow bishops, we shall strive to carry out in accordance with sacred authority, preserving peace and charity.

Concerning your statement that, once you have answered point by point concerning everything else, you will then respond fully concerning the reception of the Gallican canons, I write back to you that the Lord, who promised those who believe in him, “Open your mouth, and I will fill it,” and, “I will give you wisdom which all your adversaries will be unable to resist or contradict,” who also formed the braying of a dumb ass into human speech and commanded water to flow from a dry rock, will be able to give me what I should answer you.

After you had set forth many matters, which I passed over as useless—matters containing at one moment a denial and at another a demonstration of what you had denied—you proceeded, wishing to bind me, to speak of the judgments of the apostolic see written to you in my earlier letters [Col. 0564B].

Behold: in evil persuasion an offence, and in evil consent a sin, is brought forth. And you deign to concur with the opinions that I was ill-advised and understood the matter wrongly, when you say what I have already set forth: that I should write to you whether I wished to ordain him according to custom, and that you would grant ecclesiastical liberty to him whom you proclaim to have attained ecclesiastical orders in this manner.

Therefore I write to you what Solomon says: “He who instructs a mocker does himself an injury” (Prov. 9). You do not understand correctly because you do not want what I wrote to you well and rightly: namely, that if you had transgressed in this matter through anyone’s persuasion or through any deception, and if you had otherwise found that cleric useful in ecclesiastical service, I would supply what was lacking both to you and to him in his ordination, insofar as it pertained to me [Col. 0564C].

Read the decrees of the Roman pontiffs beginning with blessed Siricius and those who followed him, and you will find how many who were ordained irregularly were healed by ecclesiastical medicine, authority supplying during the process what had been lacking at the beginning of the ordination. “The experience of many illnesses,” says blessed Augustine, “compels us to discover many remedies.”

Then, wishing to show that I had written these things concerning the aforesaid cleric out of hatred for you and favor toward Sigebert, you compose harmful nonsense and lamentations—not things to be laughed at by a well-disposed and knowledgeable person, but things to be mourned.

As far as Sigebert himself and his interest are concerned, he has no concern that a priest should ever be ordained in that church, since he has no need of it. If a priest is ordained there, he will gain no earthly profit from it. If no priest is ordained in that church, he will suffer no spiritual or temporal loss or inconvenience from it [Col. 0564D].

Nor do I have any other concern in the matter except that ecclesiastical laws should not lose their force because of your insolence, that people should not lose the benefit which they and their predecessors have long enjoyed, and that you should not offend God in this matter.

Then there are the threats you direct against the aforesaid cleric. If you inflict prejudice upon him, there is a just judge who will judge between you and him. If he comes to the synod, we shall, as I said, strive to carry out whatever is ours to do.

As for what you add concerning sending my envoys to your synod, you do not accurately describe the office of my envoys to your synod. I myself, or my vicars, must review the acts of your synod according to the sacred canons if something contrary comes from there to me. I do not therefore send my envoys to your synod so that they may prove that a slave of our church, who is standing in no rebellion, is subject to servitude [Col. 0565A].

Although I am sufficiently foolish, I know how and where a rebellious ecclesiastical slave ought to be sought, and I ought to inquire into his profession of servitude elsewhere than in the synod of you, a provincial bishop.

Finally, concerning what you wrote—“Would that I were preserving you as a bishop, having been handed over, as I know, to prison custody, so that I might not inflict prejudice upon you and your parish, contrary to the decrees of all the apostles, even though you had been summoned by the apostolic see and appealed to it, and might not demand an answer from you until at least the synodal assembly”—and concerning the judgments of the pontiffs of the apostolic see gathered together in that same letter of yours: this requires a response for another time, and a longer one than this letter can bear [Col. 0565B].

At the close of this letter I thought it appropriate to set down the words of blessed Gregory addressed to a certain subordinate bishop, because in your letters directed to me I have often found things contrary to these admonitions. Henceforth, warned by me in my insufficiency, beware of inserting such things in letters that you send to me or to others possessing knowledge and authority.

“First,” he says, “this grieves me: your fraternity writes to me with a double heart, displaying one kind of flattery in its letters and another, worldly kind, on its tongue. Then it is grievous to me that my brother still retains on his tongue those mockeries which young notaries are accustomed to use: he speaks biting words and seems to rejoice in such a practice; in the presence of friends he flatters, while he speaks ill of the absent” [Col. 0565C].

Describing the vice of pride, he says: “Whoever has received its tyranny over himself with a captive mind suffers this first damage: with the eye of his heart closed, he loses equity of judgment. For everything that others do well displeases him, while only what he himself does wrongly pleases him. He always despises the works of others and always marvels at what he does, because whatever he has done he believes that he alone has done it; and in what he displays, through his desire for glory, he favors himself inwardly in his thoughts. He does not consider that another may possess more good than he does, but only that he himself possesses more good than another. He does not weigh what good the other’s spirit has received and what may be lacking to himself, but only what good he has and what evil the other has.

“When he thinks that he surpasses everyone in all things, he walks about with himself through the broad spaces of his thoughts and silently cries out his own praises. Sometimes the mind is led to such great exaltation that, in what makes it swell with pride, it is also unrestrained in the display of speech. The fall follows all the more easily the more shamelessly someone exalts himself; hence it is written: ‘The heart is exalted before ruin’ (Prov. 18)” [Col. 0565D].

And Saint Gregory of Nazianzus, describing the conduct of Julian—which I find in your letters—says: “Agreement and denial at once, reasoning sustained by no reasoning, disordered questioning, and an answer agreeing with nothing that agreed with itself” [Col. 0566A].

After all this, I admonish both myself and you to keep continually in mind what the Lord says: “Upon whom does my Spirit rest, if not upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66). For, as it is written: “The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit, withdraw from thoughts without understanding, and will not dwell in a body subject to sins” (Wis. 1); and: “The Lord is near to those who are brokenhearted, and he will save the humble in spirit; but the face of the Lord is against those who persistently do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth.”

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of May, in the present third indiction.

# Memorandum or Petition of Hincmar, Metropolitan of Rheims, Against Hincmar, Bishop of Laon

*Read at the Synod of Douzy.*

*(From volume VIII of Labbe’s Councils.)*

## Preface

Saint Celestine wrote to the synod at Ephesus: “The assembly of priests bears witness to the presence of the Holy Spirit. For it is certain what we read: our Truth cannot lie, and this is his sentence in the Gospel: ‘Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them’” (Matt. 18) [Col. 0566B–C].

Holding this with complete certainty, I seek counsel and assistance from your holy assembly, just as I have already done before those who attended the assemblies at Vermeria, then at Gundulf’s estate, and afterward at Attigny. I have submitted a memorandum in the synod concerning our brother and fellow bishop Hincmar, whom I rebuked in many letters, copies of which I possess, so that he might turn back from his persistent defiance of the privilege of his metropolitan see; but I was unable to correct him.

After many admonitions, through which I achieved nothing with him, I recently wrote to him on the fourth day before the Ides of June in the present fourth indiction concerning the matters briefly collected below in this memorandum, as well as concerning the petition of Bertharius, deacon of Laon, addressed against him, a copy of which I have here. In accordance with the office of my position, I invited him in writing to the next synod and admonished him, wishing to set his offenses before his face, so that he might read, bound into a letter and recalled to his memory, those things which I had earnestly wished to remain concealed before God and utterly forgotten before men, and might understand himself before a regular judgment seized him—one from which he could not escape [Col. 0566D].

In the schedule by which I summoned him to this synod, as I also summoned the other bishops of the province of Rheims, I added the following:

“Let your fraternity also know that those who last year laid their complaints against you before me, and against whom you were summoned at the synod at Attigny, are now again submitting their complaints, since you have not regularly pursued the matters that had been brought there. Therefore I admonish your fraternity to come to the announced synod having considered and prepared yourself in such a way that the complaints unbecoming to a bishop may be brought to an end, lest the good name which the apostolic rule commands a bishop to possess be stained in your reputation; and, as the same Apostle says, lest our ministry be blasphemed. Given on the day before the Ides of May in the present fourth indiction” [Col. 0567A].

Thereupon, blazing like fire among thorns, he sent me, in his customary manner, an extremely long roll on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July of the present fourth indiction, through his man named Chunibert. It was filled with reproaches and sprinkled with calumnies.

I sent him this reply through our fellow priest:

“Lord Pope Adrian has sent me letters concerning the affairs of our diocese, which ought to be read in the synod. Therefore, by the authority of that lord pope, I admonish you to come to the next synod at Douzy, in the parish of Rheims, on the Nones of August of the present fourth indiction. Given on the third day before the Nones of July of the present fourth indiction” [Col. 0567B].

Since I cannot correct him myself, I likewise seek your counsel and consolation in the matter, in the hope that the Holy Spirit, who breathes where he wills and whose presence your holy assembly attests, may at last correct him through your salutary admonitions and God-worthy prayers, or restrain his insolence through the regular remedy. For I do not dare to endure him any longer without correction, both for God’s sake and because of the metropolitan responsibility undeservedly entrusted to me.

This is especially so because the lord Pope Adrian recently admonished me concerning this matter in his apostolic letters. They are as follows:

“Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend brother Hincmar, archbishop. We have learned through the report of the faithful, and so forth. For the remainder, see among the letters of Adrian II, volume CXXII, column 70 of Migne’s *Patrologia*.”

I insist upon these matters, and upon the others that follow, not as an accuser concerned with my own personal and particular injuries, but out of concern for the privilege of the metropolitan see of Rheims—a decree established through the sacred canons, composed by the Spirit of God, consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, and confirmed by the authority of the apostolic see. I seek to vindicate that privilege against one who attempts to tear it down, to expose his contempt for his profession and subscription regarding the sacred canons of the holy councils and the decrees of the apostolic see promulgated from those canons, as well as regarding the sacred laws by which the Church is governed together with the canons; and I refute the false accusations that he has brought against me in writing [Col. 0567C–D].

For, as blessed Celestine says (Letters 1 and 3): “The matter rightly concerns us if we favor error by our silence. For what worthy cause will be preserved by us if the rule of established decrees is broken and license is permitted to the people according to the will of some? This is not the concern of the agents alone: the universal Church is shaken by every novelty.”

It is indeed something new that a provincial bishop who is not in a city that has from ancient times been counted among the provincial sees, but in the township of Laon—founded by the praetor Marcobrius, as the histories report—which from its beginning never possessed a name or place among the provincial sees of the province of Rheims, whether in pagan or Christian times, until Saint Remigius, the fifteenth archbishop of Rheims, for certain accidental reasons appointed a bishop there for the first time, and assigned to that township, already abundantly endowed with property belonging to the metropolitan church of Rheims, the county in which it stands, namely a portion of the parish of Rheims—that such a bishop should arrogate to himself a privilege [Col. 0568A].

It has always been a township of the parish of Rheims, just as today there are other townships in the parish of Rheims that remain in the position and under the name of subjection. He rebels against the privilege of his metropolitan see, although Saint Leo, writing to Maximus, bishop of Antioch, defines the matter as follows (Letter 66): “Although the merits of prelates are sometimes different, the rights of the sees nevertheless remain. Rivals may perhaps inflict some disturbance upon them, but they cannot diminish their dignity.”

Therefore I do not complain against this brother on account of a personal matter involving my injuries, but because of the contempt shown for the privilege of the metropolitan see of Rheims, which the sacred canons of the mystical Council of Nicaea irrefragably decreed should be preserved for the sees of each province.

Concerning these matters Leo likewise defined in his letter to Anatolius (Letter 53; see also Letter 55 to the Empress Pulcheria): “Whatever differs from their constitution is to be entirely devoid of authority” [Col. 0568B].

## Chapter One: That He Obtained the Administration of the Royal Palace and an Abbey Contrary to the Canons

*(Hincmar, Book 55 of the Chapters, chapter 2; Council of Antioch, canon 9.)*

Since the sacred canons of Antioch prescribe that no one is to do anything apart from the metropolitan, according to the ancient rule established by our Fathers, except only those things that concern his own parish and the possessions subject to it, he obtained the administration of the lord king’s palace without my knowledge or that of my fellow bishops. I prohibited him from that administration in the presence of the same lord king and of the others who were present, on the basis of the sacred regulations.

Afterward, again through outside powers—that is, through the intervention of secular persons—he obtained the same administration in the palace, together with an abbey in a third province beyond the province of Rheims, contrary to the canons of Sardica, without my knowledge, and held it for several years. This continued until he rose up against the lord king with such unreasonable defiance that the king took both the palace administration and the abbey away from him [Col. 0568C–D].

Against these actions the canons of Sardica say:

“For we ourselves know that, very often, because of the shamelessness of a few, the honorable name of the priesthood has been reproached.”

After some further provisions, those canons forbid subscribing to writings of this kind and receiving such a person into communion.

## Chapter Two: That He Went to the Same Abbey Without the Metropolitan’s Permission, Contrary to the Canons

*(Book 55 of the Chapters, chapter 2.)*

Whenever he wished, he went to that abbey without my permission, and he remained there for as long as he wished. This was contrary to the decrees of Pope Hilary, who says (Letter 8, to various bishops of Gaul):

“We could not pass over the matter that must be guarded with the greatest care: no bishops should dare to travel to any province without the letters of their metropolitans. This must also be observed in every kind of clerical office throughout the individual churches” [Col. 0569A].

Zosimus had previously decreed the same (Letters 5, 9, and 11), and afterward Saint Gregory likewise decreed it (Book 7, indiction 2, Letter 8), writing to Vincent [or Innocent] and the other bishops:

“We exhort your fraternity that, if necessity should compel any of you to travel anywhere farther away for your own affairs, you must request permission from your metropolitan, according to the rule handed down by the holy Fathers, and you must not in any way set him aside.”

And so forth [Col. 0569B].

## Chapter Three: That He Scorned Coming When Summoned to the Ordination of the Bishop of Cambrai or Sending a Vicar
(Lib. LV, Chapter 2.) Moreover, summoned to the ordination of a bishop in the church of Camaracum in our province, which had been deprived of its pastor, by canonical letters designating a fixed day and place and customarily sent to his church—of which I possess a copy—and for which the apostolic see, at my urging, labored not a little, he neither came himself nor sent in his place a representative or letters of his consent to me, as the sacred rules prescribe. For this reason the ordination of the elected man was postponed.

I therefore again sent such a letter to his church in the customary manner:

“Hincmar, bishop of Rheims, to his beloved brother Hincmar and our venerable fellow bishop, greeting. As I have already instructed your affection by letter on another occasion, the clergy and people of the church of Camaracum, with a canonical decree, have asked that John the presbyter, a man of good reputation, be ordained their bishop. We gathered for his ordination on the Nones of July near Beauvais. But because your fraternity did not come there, nor send in your place either a representative or letters of your consent, we postponed his ordination.

Therefore, since, as you yourself know, that see has long remained without a pastor, to the danger of many, I gathered with the other brethren on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August at the monastery called Isla, in the parish of Beauvais, in order customarily to ordain our same brother bishop. Given on the third day before the Ides of July.”

When we had gathered at the aforesaid place on the aforesaid Kalends, he neither came himself nor sent to me in his place a representative or letters of his consent, as the sacred rules prescribe. We, however, who had assembled, by the authority of the Council of Nicaea, which decrees (canon 6) that, in the ordination of a bishop, if two or three oppose a reasonable decision approved according to ecclesiastical rule by the common decree of all, on account of their own disputes, the judgment of the majority shall prevail, ordained the same venerable brother John bishop.

Concerning the contempt shown by brother Hincmarus, who had been summoned to come for the ordination of our fellow bishop but, after being warned a second time by letter, scorned to come, Pope Symmachus thus promulgated the rule from the sacred canons to Aeonius (Letter 10, to Caesarius, not to Aeonius):

“If any bishop, having been summoned by the metropolitan pontiff according to canonical definition, refuses to obey, let him know that he is to be cut down by ecclesiastical discipline—which we do not desire.”

Afterward, when I summoned him, he gave neither satisfaction nor even a humble reply to me or to our fellow bishops.

## CHAPTER IV. How he offended the king without reason or necessity and excommunicated the parishioners of other bishops

[Col. 0570B]

Afterward a prolonged scandal arose between our lord the king and his stubborn defiance, because his men complained to our lord the king that he had unjustly taken their benefices away from them. Therefore our lord the king ordered that I, together with our fellow bishops and his other envoys, should hold a hearing between them once and again; but we could not bend him toward reason and due obedience.

For this reason our lord the king ordered that he either come to his palace at Pontigon, in the province of Rheims, where several bishops and other faithful men were to assemble, or send representatives instructed in such a way that the complaints themselves might be brought to an end. He neither came there himself nor sent representatives so instructed that they could impose a lawful conclusion upon those complaints. Accordingly, our lord the king instructed him to allow those men to retain their benefices until the cases about which they had complained to him had been determined justly and reasonably.

Yet, in the absence of both the king’s envoy and the metropolitan, and while those who were bringing charges against him were absent, he interrogated seven men according to his own judgment, contrary to public and ecclesiastical laws, and did not obey what our lord the king had commanded him. Finally, when he came to our lord the king, he provoked him so greatly that the king took away from him both the aforesaid abbey and the administration of the palace.

After this, because he was unwilling to come to our lord the king as he had ordered him, sent no advocate on his behalf who could answer him against the complainants concerning their financial matters, refused to seek the judgment of chosen judges according to the laws and rules, and sent no message to me, his metropolitan, asking that he be assigned ecclesiastical judges, by whose judgment cases are brought to an end as the laws and rules command, he greatly increased our lord the king’s anger against him (Lib. LV, Chapter 21).

When I came to him with our fellow bishops, as before and afterward many times, I pleaded his case with the king’s kindness and made the king favorably disposed toward him. But brother Hincmarus, in his customary manner, again and again stubbornly rekindled our lord the king’s anger without any reason or necessity. Leaving him without his permission, he fled by night to Laon.

Our lord the king repeatedly summoned him to come to him by letters and envoys, both ecclesiastical and secular, but he scorned to come. And it came to our lord the king’s attention that he had made an agreement with Lothair to abandon the church and people entrusted to him and to receive honors in Lothair’s kingdom. In a letter sent to our lord the king he wrote:

“With God as my witness I speak to you: I would rather live outside your kingdom than appear as such in yours, as I know that some people whisper.”

Then our lord the king, compelled by necessity, ordered that, since he himself was unwilling to come, the free men of the bishopric of Laon should come promptly to him at the palace. Some of them came; but Hincmarus did not allow certain others to come to the king.
