Therefore our lord the king sent two bishops of the province of Rheims, namely Odo and Willebert, to him, ordering him at last to come to the king. He also sent ministers of the public authority to compel the free men who had not come to him as he had commanded, and who were living with Hincmarus, to come to him, willingly or unwillingly.

(Ibid., Chapter 3.) When Hincmarus heard of their arrival—as he himself also demonstrates in his written account—before the ministers of the public authority sent to him had reached Laon, he hurled an excommunication, previously unheard of in our times, against my parishioners and those of many archbishops and bishops: men who had not been accused of, confessed to, or convicted of any crimes, nor even admonished evangelically or according to the rules for acts committed in his parish, and this without my knowledge and contrary to the sacred rules.

By this he inflicted the greatest scandal upon both the king and the kingdom and upon these churches on this side of the Alps. The excommunication—or rather the curse—which, driven by madness, he pronounced, was as follows:

“By apostolic, indeed divine, authority, through the power of this wood”—that is, of the holy cross—“with the merits of this holy mother Mary cooperating, and with the authority of the most blessed prince of the apostles, Peter, we condemn with anathema all invaders both of this place and of my parish, all contaminators of this kind, and all who consent to them; and by the power of the Holy Spirit we decree them exiles from the thresholds of the holy Church of God and judge them alienated from all fellowship with Christians.”

Immediately afterward his written account continues:

“And all the clergy replied: ‘Let them be anathema,’ while the presbyters held the holy Gospels and the wood of the holy cross in their hands.”

The aforesaid bishops, when they came to him, obtained nothing concerning obedience to the king, which he had sworn to him upon the holy sacraments. The ministers of the public authority, sent by the king, inflicted violence on neither him nor anyone else; they confirmed the free men of the bishopric of Laon in fidelity to the king by oath, and thus returned to the king.

He, however, setting me aside, indulged his own whims in such an excommunication, although the sacred canons of the province of Africa command (canon 86) that later bishops defer to earlier ones and presume to do nothing without consulting them.

The law also forbids a person passing through another’s harvest to put in a sickle; rather, he is to crush the ears with his hand and eat them (Deut. XXIII). “You cannot,” says blessed Gregory to Augustine (Book XII, Letter 31, to Augustine), “put the sickle of judgment into a harvest that appears to have been entrusted to another. But by the effect of good works strip the Lord’s grain of the chaff of its vices, and by admonishing and persuading, as though by chewing it, convert it into the body of the Church.”

Likewise Saint Gregory wrote to Bishop Januarius, who had excommunicated Isidorus, an illustrious man, on account of an injury done to him, saying (Book II, indiction 10, Letter 34):

“For if this is so, you show that you think of nothing heavenly, but signify that your conduct is earthly, since, in revenge for your own injury, you have brought upon him the curse of anathema, which the sacred rules forbid. Therefore, from now on, be wholly watchful and careful, lest you again presume to inflict such a thing upon anyone in defense of your own injury. For if you do anything of this kind, know that afterward it will be avenged upon you.”

And Saint Augustine, in his book *On Penance*:

“Take the evil person away from among yourselves.” By these words he sufficiently shows that the wicked are not to be removed from the communion of the Church rashly or arbitrarily, but through judgment. For the Apostle did not wish a man to be judged by another according to the choice of suspicion or by an extraordinary judgment usurped at will, but rather according to God’s law and the order of the Church, whether he had confessed voluntarily or had been accused and convicted.

Otherwise, why did he say, “If anyone is named a brother who is a fornicator or an idolater,” and so forth, unless he intended “being named” to mean that which occurs when a sentence is pronounced against someone in judicial order and with integrity? For if merely naming someone were sufficient, many innocent people would have to be condemned, since a crime is often falsely alleged against someone.”

## CHAPTER V. How he unlawfully excommunicated the presbyters and ministers of his church

(Lib. LV, Chapter 28.) I rebuked him for this presumption before our fellow bishops, because he had committed it publicly; but he did not consent in any way to be corrected.

Therefore, again on account of his own injury, without consulting me and without the consent of the fellow bishops of the province of Rheims—as the petition presented to me by the clergy of the church of Laon demonstrates, and as I demonstrated at the synod held at Attigny—he excommunicated the presbyters and ministers of the church, so that no one in that same parish would celebrate the offices of the Mass.

Accordingly, Saint Augustine, the most renowned doctor and one most fully received by the apostolic see, who took part in the Council of Carthage and knew its constitutions most thoroughly (Council of Carthage, chapters 19–20), says among other things in his letter to the clergy and people of Hippo (Augustine, Letter 137):

“It was recently established in a council of bishops that no cleric who has not yet been convicted should be suspended from communion, unless he has failed to appear for the examination of his case.”

And Saint Gregory, later than Augustine in time but earlier in rank, promulgated from the sacred laws to Martin and to the bishops of Sicily (Book VII, indiction 2, Letter 61): “Let no one be condemned without an examination.”

Concerning the unlawful practice of excommunication, the law of the Catholic emperor Justinian, approved and observed by the Catholic Church, decreed in Constitution 118, chapter 441, that no bishop and no presbyter should excommunicate anyone before the case had been proved for which the ecclesiastical canons command this to be done.

If anyone, contrary to these provisions, excommunicates someone, the person who has been excommunicated is to return to the grace of holy communion by the authority of the greater priest; but the person who has excommunicated unlawfully is to abstain from holy communion for as long a period as the greater priest judges appropriate, so that he himself may justly suffer what he unjustly did.

For this reason Saint Gregory also wrote, among other things, to John, a bishop who had excommunicated unjustly, saying (Book II, indiction 11, Letter 6):

“After first annulling and reducing to nothing the decrees of your aforesaid sentence, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we decree that you are to be deprived of holy communion for a period of thirty days and are to implore from our almighty God, with the greatest penitence and tears, pardon for so great an offense. But if we learn that you have fulfilled this sentence of ours too laxly, you will know that not only your injustice but also the contumacy of your fraternity will, with the Lord’s help, be punished more severely.”

Likewise, after investigating whether the excess of certain bishops deserved exile or deposition, he decreed that those who had transgressed should do penance in a monastery, deprived for six months of communion in the body and blood of the Lord, with this condition: if the danger of death should threaten those deprived of communion, the blessing of the viaticum was not to be denied them.

“Concerning this matter,” he says elsewhere and in another place, “the anger that we are to follow has been shown to us, and a pattern has been set to which we must conform.”

## CHAPTER VI. How he prohibited infants from being baptized in his parish

(Lib. LV, Chapters 31, 47.) He also prohibited anyone from baptizing children in his parish, even when they were facing imminent danger of death, as the aforesaid petition states, although the Truth says:

“Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John V);

and:

“The Son of man did not come to destroy souls but to save them” (Luke IX);

and likewise:

“Let the little children come to me, and do not prevent them” (Matthew XIX).

He also acted contrary to the decrees of Siricius, Leo, Gelasius, and the African council. For concerning the baptism of infants known not yet to have been baptized, whenever necessity demands it, an ecclesiastical rule was issued through blessed Siricius; the conclusion of that rule reads as follows (Siricius, Letter 1, to Himerius):

“Now let all priests observe the aforesaid rule who do not wish to be torn away from the solidity of the apostolic rock upon which Christ built the universal Church.”

And Saint Leo decreed that this singular means of salvation should never at any time be denied (Saint Leo, Letter 92, to Rusticus).

## CHAPTER VII. How he prohibited penance and the viaticum from being given to the dying

[Col. 0574A]

(Lib. LV, Chapter 32.) He prohibited anyone from being received even for final penance and anyone from being aided by the gift of the viaticum, contrary to the canons of Nicaea and Africa and the decrees of Siricius, Innocent, Celestine, and also Leo, as is stated in the frequently mentioned petition.

Yet the Truth itself says:

“The Son of man came to seek and save what had perished” (Luke XIX);

and he came “not to call the righteous but sinners to repentance” (Matthew IX).

Many voices of the Lord and doctors of the Catholic Church cry out that the aid of regeneration and penance, and of holy communion, must in no way be denied to those placed in danger of death and requesting it.

The sacred Council of Nicaea also decreed (canon 13):

“Generally, the bishop ought reasonably to give the grace of communion from the offering to anyone at the point of death who asks that the favor of communion be granted to him.”

Concerning the decrees issued for this reason by the aforesaid apostolic pontiffs, Saint Leo the pope gave judgment (Letter 1, to the bishops): “If anyone has committed such a thing, let him know that afterward pardon will be denied him.”

## CHAPTER VIII. How he ordered burial to be denied to the dead in his parish

(Lib. LV, Chapter 33.) He also ordered that burial be denied to the dead, as the aforementioned petition states, with excessive inhumanity and contrary to the sacred Scriptures and sacred canons.

For, as we read in the venerable history of the Book of Kings (2 Kings XXI), even the bodies of those who, because of Saul’s sin—which caused famine in David’s days for three successive years—had been crucified after the Lord’s counsel was sought, were commendably guarded by Saul’s concubine so that birds would not tear them apart by day or beasts by night, until water dripped upon them from heaven. Thus they were buried with the bones of Saul and Jonathan.

And in the Gospel we read that, when Joseph made his request, Pilate ordered the body of the Lord Jesus to be returned—the one whom, at the Jews’ request, he had condemned to be crucified as though he were a wicked man (Matthew XXVII). Therefore, according to Scripture, he was reckoned among the wicked (Isaiah LIII).

And the Jews, so that even the bodies of criminals would not remain unburied on the cross on the Sabbath day, obtained from Pilate that their legs be broken and that they be taken away (Luke XXI).

The rules of the ancient Fathers likewise prescribe that even the bodies of those who in any way caused their own deaths, or who are punished for their crimes, be taken to burial, although without hymns and psalms. They did not command that even such corpses be deprived of burial in the womb of the mother of all, that is, the earth.

## CHAPTER IX. How he neglected to obey his metropolitan when admonished concerning these excesses

(Hincmarus, Letter 35.) When I heard these things, I was greatly horrified. Accordingly, out of metropolitan concern, I sent him letters once and again, warning and urging him to dissolve as quickly as possible the ruinous excommunication and bond of impiety imposed to the danger of himself and many others.

But I could not induce him to obey. Saint Boniface, explaining a chapter of the Council of Nicaea (canon 13), says to Hilary, bishop of Narbonne (Letter 3):

“Let your charity observe how carefully we preserve the precepts of the canons, so that our own constitution also defines that each province must always seek the direction of its metropolitan in all matters.”

And Leo said to Theodore, bishop of Fréjus:

“It ought to have been the order of your concern that you confer with your metropolitan concerning the matter that appeared to require inquiry, because in cases pertaining to general observance nothing ought to be accomplished without the primates by any of the Lord’s priests.”

For it is certain that the matters about which I had written to him from the sacred rules—concerning the baptism of infants, final penance, the gift of the viaticum, and the burial of the dead, which must be denied to no one—pertain to the general observance of the Lord’s priests.

He ought not to have presumed against these provisions. And when he had presumed to do so, he ought also, at the first admonition issued from evangelical truth and apostolic and canonical authority, and from the decrees of the pontiffs of the apostolic see, to have obeyed me, however unworthy a metropolitan I may be, when I urged him to dissolve those same bonds of impiety.

Saint Leo decrees:

“He who knows that he has been placed over certain people should not resent having someone placed over him; rather, let him himself render the obedience that he demands. And just as he does not wish to bear the burden of a heavy load, so he must not dare to impose an unbearable weight upon another.”

Nor ought he to have forgotten his profession and subscription before his episcopal ordination. Before the altar of Saint Mary and all who were present, according to the custom of the church of Rheims, just as bishops being ordained were accustomed to subscribe after professing the Catholic faith, he subscribed in his own hand to his obedience, according to the sacred rules, toward the metropolitan church of Rheims—not only before the church of Rheims and the parish of Laon, but also before the bishops of the province of Rheims and men of various ranks.

Therefore the sacred canons say:

“If anyone in any matter acts contrary to his profession and subscription, he himself will deprive himself of his honor.”

## CHAPTER X. How he subscribed to a certain profession with the consent of bishops of other provinces, setting aside his metropolitan

Afterward, without my knowledge or that of the fellow bishops of the province of Rheims, in another province and with the consent of bishops from other provinces, he subscribed to a profession and gave it to the king. It reads as follows:

“I, Hincmarus, bishop of Laon, from this hour forward will be faithful to my lord Charles, as a man by right ought to be faithful to his lord, and a bishop to his king; and I will be obedient in the way that a man by right ought to be obedient to his lord, and a bishop to Christ, according to my understanding and ability, for God’s will, for the king’s welfare, and for the stability . . . . . for my own welfare. H.”

The canons of the province of Africa say (canon 86):

“Later bishops are to defer to earlier bishops and presume to do nothing without consulting them.”

The canons of Antioch decree that the metropolitan should excel in honor, and that the other bishops should do nothing beyond him, according to the ancient rule established by our Fathers, except only those things pertaining to their own diocese and the possessions subject to it.

And if he subscribed to this profession in order to settle some matter or dispute directed against him, he nevertheless ought not to have done so without the knowledge of the metropolitan and of the fellow bishops of the province of Rheims.

Therefore Saint Innocent decreed to Bishop Victricius, saying (Letter 1):

“If any cases or disputes arise among clerics, whether of higher or lower rank, the dispute is to be settled according to the Council of Nicaea, when the bishops of the same province have been assembled. No one is permitted—without prejudice, however, to the Roman Church, to which reverence must be preserved in every case [alternative reading: ‘whose reverence must be preserved in every case’]—to abandon those priests who by divine will govern the Church of God in the same province and rush to other provinces.

If anyone should presume to do this, let everyone judge him both removed from the clerical order and guilty of injury.”

What it means to be judged guilty of injury is shown in Book V of Paul’s *Sentences*:

“He who institutes an action for injury through calumny is to be punished extraordinarily. For it has been decided that all calumniators are to be punished by exile, relegation to an island, or loss of rank.”

And in Book I of the *Sentences* of the same Paul:

“A calumniator is one who knowingly and deliberately contrives a case against someone by fraud. In both the aforesaid [read perhaps *privatis*, ‘private’] and public trials, all persons guilty of calumny are to be punished according to the character of the offense.”

Interpretation:

“Anyone who has been convicted of making a calumnious accusation either before *cinctos* [read perhaps *civicos*, ‘civic’] or before private judges is to be subjected to punishment, according to the nature of the case, without awaiting the judgment of his rank.”

And in the chapter cited above blessed Innocent says:

“But if greater cases have been brought forward, they are to be referred to the apostolic see, as the synod decreed and ancient custom demands, after the episcopal judgment.”

And Saint Gregory says to Vincent [variant: Innocent] and the other bishops (Book VII, indiction 2, Letter 8):

“No fellow bishop should presume in any way to set aside his metropolitan, except if it should happen that they have some case against that same metropolitan; so that, for this reason, if they hasten to seek the judgment of the apostolic see, they have permission to do so, as was also permitted by the canons through the institution of the ancient Fathers.”

It is perfectly clear which canons Innocent and Gregory mean: namely, the Sardican canons, concerning which Gelasius also says (*Commonitorium* to Faustus):

“These are the canons that wished appeals from the whole Church to be brought before the judgment of this see; but they judged that no appeal whatsoever should be made from it.”

It is therefore clear from these judgments of the holy pontiffs that, setting me aside, and acting on the judgment or advice of other bishops and of bishops from other provinces—Wenilo, archbishop of Rouen, and Aeneas, bishop of Paris—he ought not to have subscribed to the aforesaid profession and given it to the king without my knowledge or that of the fellow bishops of the province of Rheims.

For even if he had some grievance against me, he ought either to have approached the apostolic see or to have sent a petition supported by truth [reading uncertain: *sub . . . .*, apparently *subnixam*]. He ought not, setting me aside, to have presented a profession and subscription to the king in another province, on the judgment or advice of bishops from other provinces.

## CHAPTER XI. How he composed an inept collection of decrees and improperly subscribed to it

[Col. 0577B]

After this, seeking devices by which he might free himself from metropolitan subjection, he assembled a booklet from the writings of the ancient Fathers issued before the sacred Council of Nicaea and the canons of the other saints. In it he mixed together opinions discordant with one another and contrary to evangelical, apostolic, and Catholic teaching and to the authority of the apostolic see.

He subscribed to this booklet without the knowledge or consent of the metropolitan and of the fellow bishops of the province of Rheims. He also caused it to be signed by the clerics of his church and by the presbyters of the parishes.

Yet the canons of the province of Africa say (Council of Africa, chapter 53; Council of Milevis, chapter 13; *Code of the Canons of the African Church*, canon 86):

“Later bishops are to defer to earlier bishops and presume to do nothing without consulting them; and anyone who thinks that, disregarding his superiors, something may be presumed is rightly to be restrained by the whole council.”

The Council of Antioch decrees (canon 9):

“The metropolitan is to excel in honor, and the other bishops are to do nothing beyond him, according to the ancient rule established by the Fathers, except only those things pertaining to their own diocese and the possessions subject to it.”

And Saint Leo decreed to Theodore, bishop of Fréjus (Letter 91):

“Because in cases pertaining to the general observance of all the Lord’s priests, nothing ought to be accomplished without the primates.”

In this booklet he subscribed to various other opinions opposed to one another and caused the clergy of the parish to subscribe to them, because bishops cannot be condemned by human examination, since God has reserved them for his own judgment.

He also subscribed, and caused the clergy of the parish to subscribe, to the provision that:

“When a bishop has been canonically summoned to a place suitable for all, at the synodal time, he is to be heard by all the bishops of his province. They must pronounce a concordant judgment concerning him.”

The canons of Antioch also decreed this most explicitly (canon 14).

He also subscribed, and caused his clergy to subscribe, to the provision that:

“Either the accuser’s tongue is to be cut out, or, once convicted, his head is to be cut off.”

He then added Leo’s judgment, in which he says (Letter 1, to the bishops):

“Our admonition therefore declares that if any of the brethren attempts to act contrary to these provisions and dares to commit what is forbidden, he is to know that he must be removed from his office; nor will he be a companion of our communion who has refused to be a partner in discipline.

So that nothing may appear to have been omitted by us, we command that all the decretal constitutions both of blessed memory Innocent and of all our predecessors, which have been promulgated concerning ecclesiastical orders and the disciplines of the canons, be guarded by your affection in such a way that, if anyone has transgressed against them, he may know that pardon will afterward be denied him.”

He subscribed in these words:

“Hincmarus, by the mercy of God bishop of the church of Laon, have subscribed that the decrees of these holy Fathers of the apostolic see must be obeyed. May those also who have been entrusted to me by the authority of God, and who likewise hold these opinions, anxiously preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace and share this peace with me. But if some hold otherwise, unwilling to become partners in this discipline, let them not be regarded as participants in our communion.”

No one can doubt how contrary to one another the definitions subscribed by him above are, and how opposed they are to evangelical truth and apostolic authority, since the sacred rules contain definite and manifest judgments concerning bishops.

He subscribed, as you can see here, that either the accuser’s tongue should be cut out or the convicted person’s head should be cut off. And let those among his own people who hold otherwise and are unwilling to become partners in this discipline not be regarded as participants in his communion.

Yet Cyprian, in the *Degrees of Abuses*, and Innocent, in his decrees, teach from the apostolic judgment that the sword, as a lawful instrument of vengeance, has been entrusted to judicial authority. We read, however, that our predecessors did not permit ecclesiastical ministers to seize or carry it, whether in war or in sedition (see Antonius Augustinus, *Juris Canonici*, part III, title 20).

The Lord says:

“Bless those who curse you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Luke VI).

And Peter says:

“Not returning evil for evil or abuse for abuse, but, on the contrary, blessing” (1 Peter III).

And Paul says:

“Do not defend yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath” (Romans XII).

And Saint Gregory, in a letter to Sabinianus, deacon of Constantinople (Book VII, Letter 1):

“Briefly suggest to our most serene lords that, if I had wished to involve myself in the death of the Lombards, today the Lombard people would have neither king nor dukes nor counts and would be in utter confusion. But because I fear God, I am afraid to involve myself in the death of any person.”

And Saint Augustine to Boniface, proconsul of Africa:

“It is not lawful for an accused person to be killed at the suggestion of a bishop, since he is reserved for pardon if he should repent.”

If it is not lawful for an accused person to be killed at a bishop’s suggestion, since he is reserved for pardon if he should repent, then it is unlawful for an accused person, who is reserved for pardon if he should repent, to be sentenced to death by a bishop and for the bishop to subscribe to the judgment of his death.

And the bishop who, contrary to ecclesiastical order and regular discipline, subscribed that the ministers of the sacred altar who were unwilling to become partners in this discipline of death should not be regarded as participants in his communion appears, by subscribing to this judgment, to have separated himself from ecclesiastical communion. If the ministers of the altar had separated themselves from his communion by subscribing to a judgment of death, they would have remained more firmly in the communion of ecclesiastical discipline.

Therefore blessed Ambrose, in a letter to the emperor Valentinian, who was being pressed to subscribe to a law against the Christian religion, says:

“I appeal again to your faith; I appeal to your mind. Do not think that you ought to answer according to this request of the pagans, nor add the sacrilege of a subscription to such replies. For your voice, your hand, and your subscription are your deed.”

The canons of the ancient Fathers also decreed, saying:

“Often princes entrust their affairs concerning those liable to majesty to priests. And because the priests of Christ have been chosen for the ministry of salvation, let judges agree with kings where indulgence of punishment is entrusted by oath, not where a sentence of death is being prepared.

If any priest, contrary to the common decision, should become an examiner in dangers belonging to others, let him lose his own rank before Christ and the Church as guilty of shed blood.”

Here, however, with no one threatening or ordering him, he freely subscribed that either the accuser’s tongue should be cut out or his head cut off, and that anyone unwilling to become a partner in this discipline should not be regarded as a participant in his communion.

Nor was it enough for him to subscribe that the convicted accuser’s head should be cut off; he also caused the ecclesiastical ministers of his parish to subscribe to this perverse judgment.

Gelasius protests in his letter to the emperor Anastasius (Letter 10):

“The Apostle says that not only those who do what ought not to be done are considered guilty, but also those who consent to the doers. Certainly your laws bind accomplices in crimes and receivers of robbers to the same judicial penalty; nor is someone considered free of the crime who, although he himself did not commit it, has nevertheless received the perpetrators into intimacy and alliance.”

Here he both acted himself and urged some to act against the rules, persuading others to do so.

Hence the Apostle says:

“By sinning in this way against the brethren and striking their weak conscience, you sin against Christ. And the weak brother, for whom Christ died, will perish because of your knowledge” (1 Corinthians VIII).

And blessed Gregory, in the *Pastoral Rule*:

“The prelate must know that, if they ever commit perverse acts, they deserve as many deaths as they transmit examples of perdition to their subjects. Therefore they must guard themselves from fault all the more carefully, since through the evil things they do they do not die alone.”

And likewise Gelasius, in his decrees to the bishops established throughout Dardania, as though he were speaking of those whom he caused to subscribe with him, says (Gelasius, Letter 11, near the end):

“Just as those bound together in a similar condition cannot judge their accomplice to have been condemned unjustly, nor can defendants (*rei*; alternatively omitting *rei*) properly absolve an accused person (*reum*), so, once that transgressor has been justly condemned, these too lie prostrate under an equal condemnation. They cannot be completely absolved from it except by repenting.

For just as, through one person writing, the transgression of all who had fallen into the same act of perfidy was made public, so, in that one person who had written on behalf of all, or who by writing had disclosed the will of all, the transgression of all was punished.”

And because the sacred Council of Nicaea decreed that the bishops of the individual provinces should possess the privilege of metropolitan authority, Leo says to Anatolius (Epistle 55): “That provision of the Nicene canons, ordered truly through the Holy Spirit, is in no respect subject to dissolution.” Other catholic councils likewise defined that this should be observed by all, because by subscribing to things contrary to their immutable decrees, he appears to have separated himself and his accomplices from catholic communion.

Leo also clearly demonstrates this in his letter to the empress Pulcheria (Epistle 55), saying: “Against the statutes of the Fathers’ canons, which many ages ago were founded in the city of Nicaea by spiritual decrees, no one is permitted to venture anything: so that if anyone wishes to decree something different, he diminishes himself rather than corrupting them.” And because, as the blessed Leo himself, and before him Damasus and Boniface, and after him the other pontiffs of the apostolic see, wrote, these same sacred canons—laws destined to remain until the end of the age—were established by the Spirit of God.

That Spirit, according to evangelical and apostolic truth, is the Spirit of the Father and the Spirit of the Son, because he proceeds equally from the Father and the Son, and is wholly the Spirit of the Father and wholly the Spirit of the Son. The Father, the Son, and the same Holy Spirit, whose substance, will, and operation are one—that is, the Holy Trinity—is one God and Lord.

It is certain that these canons were established by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, that is, by the whole Trinity, the one God and Lord. Whoever obstinately departs from them through contempt sins against the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the one God and Lord.

And in this subscription of Hincmar there is the Apostle’s sentence, in which he was not concerned to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, but was concerned to dissolve the unity of the Spirit against the bond of peace. For the Apostle says—and he inserted this sentence into his perverse subscription—“being careful to preserve the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace; one body and one spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling” (Ephesians 4).

Hence the blessed Gregory says: “One does not reach the single hope of calling unless one runs toward it with a mind united to one’s neighbors. ‘The Lord said to Moses: There is a place beside me, and you shall stand upon the rock.’ The place beside the Lord is indeed the unity of the holy Church, in which one stands upon the rock when the solidity of its confession is profitably maintained. Those stand in the place beside the Lord and upon the rock who do not divide themselves from the unity of the Church through heresies and schisms.”

For, as Pope Hilary says (Epistle 4): “One commits no less an offense against the sanctions of the sacred traditions than when one rushes forward to insult the Lord himself.” And since the blessed Leo decreed (St. Leo, cited above) that, in matters pertaining to the general observance of all the Lord’s priests, nothing ought to be carried out without the primates, Hincmar was not a partner in this discipline. Therefore it must be feared that he is not also a participant in that communion. If he is alienated from it, he will not be able to have communion with those who took part in the aforementioned synods and whose decrees he caused to be overthrown, and consequently he will not be able to have communion with the catholic Church.

It is also written in the edict of the Fifth Council: “We marvel at the madness of those who act contrary to divine Scripture, which plainly says that before God the impious person and his impiety are equally abhorrent. For the deed will be punished together with its doer.” But if impiety is likewise abhorrent to God, then the one who acts impiously is certainly separated from God and is justly subjected to anathema. For “anathema” signifies nothing other than separation from God, just as in both the Old and the New Testament judgment concerning anathema signifies this.

## CHAPTER XII. How, in that collection, he corrupted the statements and meanings of the holy Fathers

And in the booklet under discussion, as well as in the one which he sent me through Wenilo, formerly archbishop, whom I shall mention shortly—for I have it before me—he altered the words of the blessed Gregory concerning the four chapters of error about which Gregory wrote to the patrician Theoctista (Book IX, Epistle 39, at the end). Gregory says: “But if there are some who say that, if someone anathematized himself under compulsion of necessity, he is not held by the bond of anathema,” and Hincmar imposed his own words upon them, inserting and adding: “or if he should presume against those things which have been forbidden under anathema.”

In the same passage, where Gregory said: “If, therefore, there are some who, under the Christian name, dare either to preach these chapters of error which we have mentioned, or silently to retain them within themselves,” Hincmar mutilated and distorted the text according to his own meaning, saying: “If, therefore, there are some who, under the Christian name, dare to preach these things.”

He did not fear the sentence pronounced by the holy Sixth Synod in its twelfth session, in these words:

“Macarius, inveterate in the dogmas of impiety, who not only was intoxicating with turbulent ruin the whole Christ-loving people inhabiting this God-preserved imperial city, but also falsified the testimonies of holy and approved Fathers, cutting out some things, adding others, and turning them aside according to his own judgment; who disturbed the most pious and God-crowned ruler by petitions which he presented, and from the rising of the sun to its setting, through his letters and the men he sent, disturbed everyone and separated them from the true faith—having been justly and reasonably stripped of pontifical dress, was in no way thereafter permitted by the divine rule to sit in a teacher’s seat, lest he should thereby make the understanding of his own heresy ferment anew and, as it is written, the last state of that man become worse than the first.”

Macedonius, bishop of Constantinople, is likewise recorded to have been expelled by the emperor Anastasius because he had falsified the Gospels, especially the Apostle’s statement: “He was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit” (1 Timothy 3). He perverted it so that it would read: “God was manifested through the flesh.”

The Apostle Paul rebukes such people, speaking of himself and his companions: “For we are not,” he says, “like many, adulterating the word of God” (2 Corinthians 2). “To adulterate the word of God,” says the blessed Gregory, “is either to think differently about it than one ought, or to seek from it not spiritual fruits but adulterous offspring of human praise.”

Hence Gelasius wrote to the bishops established throughout Dardania concerning those who held such perverse opinions (Epistle 13):

“Because our predecessors [variant: ‘Which our predecessors, discerning by divine inspiration’] necessarily took precautions that, against each heresy, whatever a synod once held [variant: ‘a synod convened’] had promulgated for the communion of the faith and for catholic, apostolic truth should not afterwards be clouded by fresh reconsiderations [variant: ‘mutilated’], lest an opportunity be afforded to the wicked to assail what had been medicinally established. Rather, when the author of any madness and the error alike had been condemned, they judged it sufficient that whoever [variant: ‘each person who’] at any time became a participant in that error should be bound by the principal sentence of its condemnation, since anyone could plainly be recognized either by his profession or by his communion.”

And a little later:

“Because that same error, once condemned together with its author, carries its own execration and punishment in anyone who becomes a participant in wicked communion.”

After this monstrous booklet, monstrously compiled by him, had finally been subscribed by himself and his followers, I again admonished him by letter—of which I possess a copy—to take care to correct the things he had done contrary to reason and authority in his own parish. But he did not obey my admonition, although the Apostle says: “Obey your superiors in the Lord” (Hebrews 13). And Saint Leo decrees that “he who knows that he has been placed over certain people should not take it badly that someone has been placed over him.”

## CHAPTER XIII. How, after being frequently admonished, he preferred to excuse his faults rather than correct them, and, when accused in a synod, took flight without awaiting the conclusion of the judgment

*(Book 55, chapter preface.)* Then, through Wenilo, formerly venerable archbishop, at the villa of Gundulf and in the presence of the archbishops who were present, he sent me a booklet compiled by himself from letters of the pontiffs of the Roman see written before the Nicene Synod, entitled in the name of our lord King Charles in twenty little verses. I replied to him in writing concerning it, and I have a copy here, admonishing him to place his faith in the sacred canons and in the decrees of the apostolic see promulgated from those same sacred canons, and to render them the obedience that was their due.

Thereafter, at Attigny in the parish of Rheims, in the presence of the bishops who were present, I gave him a booklet in fifty-five chapters, entitled in forty-four verses, containing ecclesiastical authorities against the things he had collected in his aforementioned two booklets. I admonished him to restrain himself from such criticisms and, submitting himself to the sacred rules, to strive, according to the Apostle, to pursue peace and holiness.

He, however, gave no sign of satisfaction in response to my admonition. Rather, he presented to me at the same council a very long scroll concerning a certain chapel, about which I had often admonished him by letter because of the complaints to me of people from his parish; but I achieved nothing. The scroll also contained fabrications concerning Fimo, a priest of his diocese, and an estate of our church, as well as other matters falsely composed—matters about which that priest himself had made no complaint to me and had raised no case at any provincial synod. *(It does not survive.)*

I judged it better to postpone speaking of this scroll to another time, lest his ravings cause you weariness and prevent you from deliberating on more necessary matters. He also brought forth at the same synod the aforementioned monstrous booklet, subscribed by himself and his followers; I received it there and have kept it to this day.

When I saw that, after so many admonitions, I could achieve nothing with him, I presented a document at the synod of the ten provinces *(this document does not survive)*, asking those venerable bishops for advice concerning what I could do against his obstinate contumacy. I also made known to them, in opposition, the matters which I had sent to him [lacuna] against the bonds of his impiety. Therefore, when he was summoned by that same synod because he had presumed to impose so many and such serious excommunications unjustly and irregularly, he gave me at that synod a booklet containing his profession of canonical obedience. I possess it, and it reads as follows:

“I profess and subscribe that, according to the sacred canons and the decrees of the apostolic see promulgated from the sacred canons, I shall obey, to the best of my knowledge and ability, the metropolitan privilege of Hincmar, archbishop of the province of Rheims.”

And because his own people had complained to the king that he had unjustly and irrationally taken away from them the benefices which they had held under his predecessors and under him, after giving me the booklet concerning his canonical obedience at the synod, he requested from me chosen episcopal judges. He accepted the three whom I designated for him according to the African Council: Actard, Ragenelmus, and John. At the judgment of these men and of other God-fearing persons, in the presence of our lord the king, as he had requested, it was decreed concerning certain matters that they ought to recover their benefices, which they had lost irrationally.

Their entire case, however, remained undecided until another hearing because of certain intervening circumstances; it was to be decided on another day. Before the decision, against the sacred canons, without any necessity or reason, he slipped away by night and took flight, refusing to await the canonical judgment.

Hence the sacred canons of the African Council, concerning Quodvultdeus, who, before either requesting chosen judges or even entering into the proceedings against his accuser, evaded the proceedings and departed, decreed as follows (African Council, canon 54; Code of the Canons of the African Church, canon 87):

“Concerning Quodvultdeus, bishop of Centuriae: because, when his adversary had requested that he be brought before our council, he was asked whether he was willing to have the matter tried with him before the bishops, and at first he promised that he was; but on the following day he replied that this did not please him and departed. It pleased all the bishops that no one should communicate with Quodvultdeus until his case had reached whatever conclusion it could reach. For no Christian could rightly think [variant: could have thought] that his episcopate should be taken away before the outcome of his case became clear.”

It also says (Council of Milevis, canon 21; African Council, canon 87; Code of the Canons of the African Church, canons 121 and 22):

“The case is to be concluded by episcopal judges, whether they are appointed for the disputing parties by the primates or chosen by the parties themselves, with mutual consent, from among their neighbors. If they choose neighboring judges by common agreement, either one or three may be chosen. If they choose three, they shall follow either the judgment of all or that of two. No appeal is permitted from judges chosen by common consent. Whoever is proved unwilling to obey the judges in a dispute, once this has been demonstrated to the bishop of the principal see, shall receive letters ordering that no bishop communicate with him until he obeys.”

The Council of Carthage also says (Carthaginian Council III, canon 7; Code of the Canons of the African Church, canon 19):

“Whenever a bishop is accused, the accuser shall bring the case before the primates of his province.”

And a little later:

“After the second month, he shall not communicate until he has cleared himself. If he refuses to attend the annual universal council, so that his case may be settled there, he shall be judged to have pronounced the sentence of condemnation upon himself. During the time when he does not communicate, he shall not communicate even in his own church or parish.”

A year has now passed since he requested and received the judges mentioned above from me, his metropolitan, and he has not regularly prosecuted the case of his accusation. Until now the sentence promulgated by the African Council concerning Maximinus the bishop has been deferred (African Council, canon 55; Code of the Canons of the African Church, canon 88):

“Concerning Maximinus,” it says, “of Bagai [variant: Maximianus of Bagai], it was decided that letters should be sent from the council to him and to that people, so that he himself should withdraw from the episcopate and they should seek another for themselves.”

## CHAPTER XIV. How he attempts to excuse that flight with weak arguments

Although these matters stand as described, the same brother, Hincmar, writing back to me, asserts through many arguments that he was compelled by necessity and fled in order to avoid persecution, as his letter, which I possess here, reveals.

He says, namely, that all his men were summoned to judicial proceedings, so that not even one was permitted to follow him while returning to his dwelling. Nortmann was responsible for this concerning the villa of Paillart, because, having received it by royal concession and also, as I understand, by apostolic authority, his men followed him into that same villa.

In the same arguments he cites testimonies from a letter of Pope Julius defending Athanasius’s flight (Epistle 2, to the Easterners):

“When the Pharisees took counsel against the Lord in order to kill him, Jesus, knowing this, departed from there. And the disciples, because of fear of the Jews, withdrew, hiding themselves.”

Paul likewise, when sought by the governor of Damascus, was lowered from the wall in a basket and escaped the hands of the one seeking him (2 Corinthians 11).

But whether, because the Frankish men were summoned to judicial proceedings according to their laws—so that they might either make amends according to law for what they were accused of having done contrary to the law, or defend themselves legally—Hincmar ought to have fled or not is readily apparent.

Whether the testimonies cited above apply to the persecution which he claims, to his own case and person, and to the person of his persecutor whom he specifically identifies, as well as to the other persons whom he names as persecuting him, reason plainly demonstrates.

Concerning the flight of Athanasius, and when, how, and for whose sake bishops or ecclesiastical ministers ought to flee, the blessed Augustine says among other things in his letter to Bishop Honoratus:

“Perhaps someone may say that, when such evils threaten, the ministers of God ought to flee in order to preserve themselves for the usefulness of the Church in more peaceful times. This may rightly be done by some when others are not lacking through whom ecclesiastical ministry may be supplied, lest it be abandoned by everyone. We have said above that Athanasius did this. For how necessary he was to the Church, and how much it benefited from that man remaining in the flesh, the catholic faith knows; it was defended against the Arian heretics by his voice and devotion.

“But when the danger is common, one must fear all the more that someone may be thought to do this not out of a concern for the common good but from fear of dying; and that his example may obstruct flight more than his ministry benefits continued life. In no way should he flee.”

And a little later:

“Therefore, whoever flees in such a way that the necessary ministry of the Church is not lacking does what the Lord commanded or permitted (Matthew 10). But whoever flees in such a way that the nourishment by which Christ’s flock lives spiritually is taken away is that hired man who sees the wolf coming and flees, because he has no concern for the sheep (John 10).”

## CHAPTER XV. How he granted the disputed possessions of the Church to be handed over to Nortmann

Concerning what he wrote—that I knew the same villa had been restored to him by royal concession and also by apostolic authority, as I read in his letter—I do not deny that I knew this. For he says there that, at the request of the men of venerable memory, Conrad and Rudolf, he granted the same villa to the king, so that the king might give it as a benefice to Nortmann, who had previously held it.

In his response he adds that, if he possessed the villa as an allod, he would gladly allow the king to do with it whatever the king wished, because this did not oppose the king’s desire and no danger to his soul threatened him on that account.

But when he made that grant from the possessions of his church, he did so neither with my knowledge nor with that of my fellow bishops of the province of Rheims, and not with the consent of the presbyters and deacons of the Church of Laon, as the canons require. I know this also from what I read about it in the letter of our lord the pope.

When I showed that letter to Nortmann and said to him that, unless he immediately divested himself of the possessions of the Church of Laon which he had invaded, I would excommunicate him according to the command of our lord the pope, he replied to me in the presence of many bishops that, for the love and honor of God and Saint Peter and our lord the pope, I should not excommunicate him, because he was not my parishioner, had not invaded those possessions, and had an authority who had granted them to him as a benefice. If that authority of his should later contradict the grant, he would presume nothing further concerning them.

## CHAPTER XVI. How he falsely says that he was detained from going to Rome, where he had appealed

Hincmar also says in that same writing that he fled from Attigny for this reason:

“At Silvacum he had remembered”—where I too was present—“that this had benefited him nothing but harmed him, because he was detained for the sole reason that he might not go to Rome in obedience to the commands of our lord the pope; something which has never been heard from bishops concerning a bishop.”

I replied that neither then, as I know for certain and those who were present know together with me, nor at any other time, as far as I can recall, had I heard him appeal to Rome for any cause whatsoever. At that time, however, I heard that he had been invited to the synod which was soon to take place.

It was also widely reported by many voices that he was negotiating with Lothair so that he might abandon the Church entrusted to him and the sheep committed to his care, go to Lothair, and obtain honors in his kingdom. Nevertheless, on this matter I had no discussion with our lord the king at that time, nor did the king say anything to me about it.

## CHAPTER XVII. How, after his flight, he informed Hincmar of Rheims by letter that he had been summoned to Rome by the pontiff, and how the latter replied to him; and how he acted against his own profession

After this brother Hincmar had accepted the judges regularly appointed for him by me, as I have written, and had imprudently and dishonorably slipped away by night and taken flight, he sent me through his deacon Ermenold, on the sixth day before the Nones of July, in the third indiction, a little document irrationally composed and subscribed by his own hand, wholly contrary to his aforementioned profession. It reads as follows:

“To the most reverend Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, Hincmar, by the mercy of God bishop of the holy Church of Laon, sends due devotion in Christ.

“You know that I have twice been summoned by the universal pope of the holy Roman Church, our father and teacher Adrian. You yourselves reproached me in the booklets given to me by you at the palace of Attigny, in the presence of the archbishops and bishops who were present, because I had delayed going to that same see after being summoned so many times.

“If *detractem* is written through a scribal error instead of *detrectem*, which has a different meaning, or *differam*—‘I delay’—then *detractem*, which can be understood as ‘I greatly deliberate,’ may not be inappropriate; the word was not marked with an interlinear sign. Therefore I now beg you, for the love of almighty God and reverence for Saint Peter, as I also requested from you at the same synod convened by you at Attigny, which I was unable to obtain, and as I have already implored for a full year; especially at the synod formerly held at the palace of Verberie *ab horno* [the transmitted reading is uncertain], where I pleaded and entreated.”

And so on.

“I, Hincmar, bishop of the holy Church of Laon, have willingly subscribed.”

Concerning this little document I replied to him at greater length in the little booklets given to him, as I said above. I also replied that I had never forbidden him, either at any time or in any place, to go to the apostolic see. Indeed, as he himself wrote, I reproved him for not having followed the command and invitation of our lord the pope.

Whenever he is rebuked for his insolence, he asks for permission to go to Rome or appeals to the apostolic see, wherever it seems good to him. But whenever the king and the bishops are favorably disposed toward him, he says nothing about that permission and does not appeal to the apostolic see, although the sacred canons prescribe how, from where, and where a bishop ought to appeal to the apostolic see.

Last year, after he had presented me at the synod at Attigny with a booklet concerning his canonical obedience, he did not appeal to the apostolic see and said nothing about permission to go there. But when he departed from there in an agitated and dishonorable manner, he sent me the aforementioned little document concerning permission to go to Rome around the Kalends of July.

Afterward he sent me no further message about it, nor did he say anything about it when he spoke with me. He also said nothing when he was with our lord the king in the following month of September at Silvacum, and in October at Rheims, where I too was present and where the envoys of our lord the pope were also present.

Then in February he was with our lord the king for several days at Compiègne, and I too was there. Afterward, in April, he was with our lord the king at Senlis. Finally, he was with our lord the king for several days at Silvacum, where I too was present, and he said nothing about it.

Several Kalends of August have now passed beyond the date set by our lord the pope, who sent him instructions that he should not delay beyond those Kalends but should proceed to Rome.

I also wrote to him that he had written foolishly when he said that, if I did not obtain permission from the king for him to go to Rome, he could not canonically obey me as a fellow bishop ought to obey an archbishop. Because he said this contrary to reason, I showed him from the letters of the blessed Leo that he was wrong. I urged him to receive reverently, according to the statement of the blessed Gelasius, the decretal letters which the most blessed popes had issued from the city of Rome at different times for the consolation of different Fathers—letters by which, in his obstinate contumacy, he seeks to strip himself of the metropolitan privilege established by the canons and by the decrees of the apostolic see promulgated from those sacred canons. I also urged him to preserve inviolably the sacred councils, as Gelasius and the other catholic and learned pontiffs had decreed.

As for what he wrote—that “what the apostolic see wished and arranged concerning him, it entrusted to the archbishops Remigius and Arduicus”—namely, that through them the letter of our lord the pope, about which I had instructed him, should reach our lord the king, and that they themselves should conduct his case—I do not believe him.

For the letter of our lord the pope addressed to me plainly demonstrates that he sent me the letter about which Hincmar spoke obliquely, so that I might conduct the case of that man, namely my suffragan, before the king, in order that the apostolic see might retain its proper authority and not diminish the rights it had granted to others.

By subscribing to these things, as I have said, Hincmar professed and subscribed contrary to the profession and subscription which he had made before the bishops of ten provinces at the synod at Attigny and had subscribed with his own hand: namely, that he would obey, to the best of his knowledge and ability, the metropolitan privilege of the Church of the province of Rheims according to the sacred canons and the decrees of the apostolic see promulgated from the sacred canons.

Concerning that profession and subscription given to me at the same synod, Saint Leo says in his letter to Bishop Septimus (Epistle 85):

“It is most salutary and completely filled with the benefit of spiritual medicine that presbyters, deacons, or clerics of any other order [variant: ‘or others’] who wish to appear corrected should acknowledge without ambiguity that they condemn their own error and the very authors of the error; so that, with no one lending support [variant: ‘with no hope remaining’], no opportunity may remain for perverse opinions long since destroyed, and no member of the Church may be violated by association with such people, once their own profession has begun to oppose them in every respect.”

In that profession and subscription, our fellow brothers and venerable fellow bishops, taking account of the hardness of his heart and supporting him in charity, did not wish to press him concerning the past. They wished only that he promise, by professing and subscribing, future correction.

They considered what the blessed Gregory says in the Pastoral Rule:

“Often those whom a strong potion of medicines could not cure have been restored to their former health by warm water; and some wounds which cannot be healed by the incision of iron are cured by applications of oil; and hard adamant does not at all admit the cutting of iron, but is softened by the gentle blood of goats.”

By this profession which he subscribed—saying that, if I did not obtain permission from our lord King Charles for him to go to Rome, although I had never at any time or in any place prevented either him or anyone else who wished to go there, he would henceforth know that he could not canonically obey me as a fellow bishop ought to obey an archbishop—and by adding, “I, Hincmar, bishop of the holy Church of Laon, have willingly subscribed,” he destroyed, insofar as he could, the profession which he had given me at the synod held at Attigny for the ten provinces.

The blessed Leo demonstrates this in his letter to the emperor Leo (Epistle 78), even speaking of himself as such a great pontiff:

“According to the Apostle (Galatians 2), if I rebuild the things which I destroyed, I make myself a transgressor, and I subject myself to the conditions of punishment which not only the authority of the emperor Marcian, of blessed memory, but also I, by my agreement, confirmed.”

At the aforementioned synod he had destroyed the insolence of his past disobedience, building up future obedience toward the privilege of his metropolitan see by professing and subscribing according to the sacred canons. By this profession and subscription of his transgression he again attempted to destroy and annul that obedience, revived his former insolence with renewed fury, and thereby made himself a transgressor.

Let your wisdom compare all his professions and subscriptions together and carefully consider and judge what the Holy Spirit has decreed through those in whom he has spoken—those who reign with God in heaven and shine forth through miracles on earth—concerning one who subscribes and professes, yet neglects and resists.

For the sacred Council of Carthage says (Carthaginian Council II, canon 13):

“If anyone in any respect acts against his own profession or subscription, he shall deprive himself of his honor.”

What could more appropriately be applied to this latest subscription of his, contrary to the sacred canons and to his professions and subscriptions written above, than the words: “I, Hincmar, acting against my profession or subscription, have willingly deprived myself of my honor”?

But perhaps he will say that he made his other subscriptions unwillingly and under compulsion. What will he say about that subscription by which, when no one requested or expected it, he subscribed to his booklet of compilations and caused certain others to subscribe unwillingly?

Those who speak about distinctions between words—such as the Peripatetic Nonius Marcellus in his booklet *On Concise Learning* (chapter 5)—say: “They maintain that *confiteri* and *profiteri* differ in this respect: to confess (*confiteri*) belongs to the will, whereas to profess (*profiteri*) belongs to necessity and compulsion.”

But this does not come to his aid, since he has acted against his profession and subscription. Saint Leo, as is found repeatedly in his letters, commands those who deviate from the unanimity of catholic peace to give a profession with a completely explicit subscription before all the clergy and the entire people.

And Saint Gregory, in his letter to the patrician Theoctista (Book IX, Epistle 39), speaks of those who said that if certain people, compelled by force, were to anathematize themselves concerning things for which they were rightly reproved, they would in no way be held by the bond of anathema. Gregory says most plainly:

“If there are any who certainly think or hold such things, there is no doubt that they are not Christians. I, together with all catholic bishops and the universal Church, anathematize them, because they think and speak things contrary to the truth.”

## CHAPTER XVIII. How he presented a fabricated document as though it had been written by the bishops of the Council of Toul, and how the bishop of Rheims replied to him, exhorting him to patience and a mature understanding of the facts

Finally, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the third indiction, he sent to me at Pontigon Heddon, the provost of his church, and through him sent me a certain document which I possess under his autograph. I gave him part of it to be read before the bishops who were present—namely Remigius, Harduicus, Franco, Odo, and Willebert—and before other ecclesiastical men, so that he would not afterward be able, if he wished, to deny that he had sent me that document.

It was composed as though in the name of the synod at Tusiacum. Before I received it through Heddon, his cleric, I had never seen it, nor had I ever heard of it anywhere or at any time. Nor did the bishops who were present say that they had seen or heard of it.

In that document, he claims that the bishops who had taken part in the aforementioned synod had subscribed in many ways and by many means, and that he himself had subscribed to it. Some of its provisions are contrary to the sacred rules and agree with the excommunication which he had imposed in his own parish.

For it says concerning a condemned person:

“While he lives, let him be removed from the assembly and fellowship of the faithful and separated from the body and blood of the Lord, so that he neither receives communion at the end of his life nor is his body led to burial in the manner of the faithful, with offerings, psalms, and hymns.”

A little farther below:

“And let princes and judges show this diligence among the people of God: whenever such persons have been requested from them by the bishops, wherever they may be within their jurisdiction, let them produce them without delay, lest, if they dissemble or despise the bishop’s command, they be cast out from the Church of God and not receive burial with the faithful.”

A little above this sentence it says:

“If a cleric corrupted by such a desire for sacrilege, or any layman deceived by this iniquity, should be involved in it, and, recognizing his condemnation, should submit himself to the remedies of penance according to the order and disposition of his bishop, we wish him first to restore to the church which suffered the loss what he seized and presumed upon, according to its character, either onefold, twofold, threefold, or fourfold. Then, for the sacrilege, let him receive from his bishop a counsel of salvation and a measure of penance.”

This regulation concerning restitution is known to be contrary, without prejudice to the force of the laws, to the decrees of the blessed Gregory addressed to Augustine, bishop of the English, in response to his question (Epistle 12, final letter, to Augustine, Question 4):

“I ask what punishment should be imposed if someone has stolen something from the church?”

The response of the blessed Gregory continues after a little:

“You also ask how those who have stolen things from churches ought to return them. But may it be far from the Church to receive with increase what it appears to have lost from earthly possessions, and to seek profit from vain things.”

This document, as I have shown, is contrary to ecclesiastical ordinances; and it is plainly shown to be false for this further reason: the names of bishops who were not yet bishops are written there as subscribers. Moreover, the names of two bishops from the same city and of the same period are placed there; and the names of bishops who succeeded others are placed before the names of their predecessors.

Thus the name of Christian of Auxerre appears there, and much later that of Abbo, also of Auxerre, whom Christian succeeded. The name of Rainelmus of Noyon is likewise entered there, although he was not yet a bishop; then, much later, the name of Immo of Noyon is entered, whom Rainelmus succeeded. The names of other bishops who were not present at that same synod are also found there. And as for us who were present, it falsely says that we subscribed with the others to documents to which we did not subscribe.

It must therefore be considered whether what the African Council decreed concerning a bishop who falsely claimed to have communicated with the Donatists applies to him (Code of the Canons of the African Church, canon 124):

> “If it should be proved that he lied concerning communion with them, saying that those had communicated with him whom, to his knowledge, it was established had not communicated with him, let him also lose his episcopate.”

After the same provost Heddo had given me the aforementioned document, he said, among other things, that his superior had instructed him that he could not refrain from excommunicating his men who, by the authority and command of the king, held property belonging to his church. For when he had previously sent word to the apostolic lord concerning Nortmannus, the apostolic lord had sent him this reply: that he should first perform his ministry in that matter and then lodge his complaint. For this reason he had until then left the matter unresolved, until he should give me this instruction, so that I might know that he would now perform his ministry in the matter. Accordingly, among other things, I wrote to him:

> “Do, dearest brother, what befits episcopal dignity, waiting until we meet in the provincial synod, whose time is now near. There, with the Lord’s favor and cooperation, in accordance with the decrees of blessed Gregory, there may be discussion of unsuitable [another reading: incidental] cases and a salutary conference concerning ecclesiastical observance, so that through this both past matters may be corrected…”

And what follows in Hincmar’s letter to Heddo, to the end.

## CHAPTER XIX. How, after fleeing from Attigny, he sought secular judges from the king, abandoning ecclesiastical judgment, and caused judgments already rendered to be reopened

After approximately two months had elapsed since he fled by night from Attigny, before the cases concerning which he had sought elected judges before metropolitan authority had been decided, he obtained by various contrivances an imperial order that the matters for which he had received elected judges according to the sacred canons should be reopened by secular judges—Helmigarius, market and palace toll-collector, and Flotarius and Ursio, administrators of the royal estates.

This was to apply not only to the complaint of those whose case had remained for decision at a later hearing, but also to those matters which, as I have said, had been decided in the presence of the lord king by the judgment of the elected judges. The reopening was to occur without the knowledge of the metropolitan and without canonical or episcopal judgment. This was contrary to the canons, which permit appeals from ecclesiastical judges to ecclesiastical judges of greater authority—not from superiors to inferiors, nor from ecclesiastical to secular judges—and do not permit appeals except to judges chosen with the consent of the parties.

Before these secular judges, whom he himself had requested, some matters already decided were reopened and altered, while others that were still awaiting decision were decided, on the basis of an invented charge, as was said by those who were present at that hearing: namely, that certain unnecessary and inappropriate oaths had been discovered. These accusations were brought before the judges themselves and before the accusers whom he had accepted against the elected judges, as he had requested.

The purpose was that the man concerning whom it had been legally and regularly decided that he should retain his benefice—which he had lost contrary to reason and equity—might be forced by this same contrivance to surrender it; and that those who had been judged entitled to retain their benefices until a lawful judgment, because he had evaded that judgment after requesting it, might abandon those benefices, while he himself secured what he had begun.

For just as he is not permitted, after abandoning ecclesiastical judgment, to clear himself before a public court of an accusation, whether in a criminal or civil case, so he is not permitted, after setting aside or despising ecclesiastical judgment, to rush to secular courts, or to drag anyone else—even a layperson—before them. Nor may he follow such a person to his own forum if the layperson has consented to submit to ecclesiastical judgment.

This is shown by the law of Valentinian, which the Church approves:

> “If a cleric brings an action against someone, let him be heard in the forum of the person whom he summons to judgment—unless the person summoned refuses to come to the judgment of the presbyter and bishop.”

And Saint Leo [rather, Leo of Bourges; A.] and the Roman synod, in the letter addressed to Sarmatio, Carato, and Desiderius, bishops and presbyters of all the churches established within the Third Province [another reading: Thrace], say:

> “If a cleric brings an action against a layperson, let him first ask to be heard by the bishops. Then, if he sees the layperson resisting his petition, let him, with the permission of his bishop, contend before the secular governor.”

That is, not personally, but through an advocate, as the laws and sacred regulations decree.

What is not permitted to any cleric is least of all permitted to a bishop. For, as Pope Saint Hilary says in his decrees, in the Roman synod cited above:

> “The person who enjoys the higher honor commits the greater offense; and the eminence of dignities makes the vices of sinners more serious.”

The African Council also decreed (African Council, canon 71; Code of the Canons of the African Church, canon 104):

> “It has been decided that whoever”—namely, among the clergy, including the episcopal order—“asks the emperor for a hearing by public judges shall be deprived of his own rank. But if he asks the emperor for an episcopal judgment, this shall not harm him.”

And the Carthaginian canons in the Third Council say (canon 9):

> “He to whom the authority of the Church everywhere stands open for choosing judges judges himself unworthy of the fellowship of the Church if, by thinking wrongly about the whole Church, he seeks help from a secular tribunal, since the Apostle commands that even the cases of private Christians be brought before the Church and settled there.”

The Carthaginian canons likewise command:

> “If any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or cleric, when a criminal charge has been brought against him in the Church, or a civil action has been instituted, wishes, after abandoning ecclesiastical judgment, to clear himself before public tribunals—even if a judgment has been pronounced in his favor—let him lose his position. This applies in a criminal case; in a civil case, let him lose what he has won if he prefers to retain his position.”

For this reason Saint Leo, together with the synod held at Rome, sent the following under its subscriptions to the aforementioned bishops Sarmatio, Carato, and Desiderius, and to the presbyters of all the churches established within the Third Province [Thrace]:

> “The secular powers have wished such reverence to prevail toward the priestly order—even those whom divine power has commanded to rule the lands under the imperial name—that, in accordance with the Imperial Constitutions, they have permitted holy bishops the right to decide disputes. Although this has frequently been confirmed by the edicts of ancient law and by unimpaired legislation, we find that in the present time it has been trampled upon by many. For, leaving aside priestly judgment, they have everywhere passed over to the examination of secular judges.  
>
> “Therefore it has seemed good to us that this insult to the sacred laws and to our order should both be punished for the present by full enforcement and that a rule for future observance should be established. We decree, therefore, that whoever, neglecting the priest of his church, goes before secular judges for a dispute shall be expelled from the sacred precincts and excluded from the heavenly altar. After this decision, which has been established by common agreement, let no one attempt to claim anything beyond what has been prescribed for him.  
>
> “Thus those who have previously gone astray may correct themselves by suitable amendment, while anyone who, under clerical discipline, is proved to be serving the heavenly office, if he has approached secular authority after neglecting the judgment of priests, is to be treated as an ex-cleric [another reading: cast out from the clergy]. We wish all and each to recognize this, so that what has been established with the full order of justice and law may receive complete and firm effect in all the affairs of clerics.”

A little later:

> “I, Leo, bishop, have subscribed.  
> I, Victorius, bishop, have subscribed.  
> I, Eustachius, bishop, have subscribed.”

[Another reading: “Leo, bishop, writes. Victorius, bishop, writes. Eustachius, bishop, writes.”] The other bishops who were present likewise subscribed.

Concerning the matters which, as I stated earlier, had been decided and were irregularly reopened, Saint Leo says in his letter addressed to Leo Augustus through Philoxenus, an imperial agent (letter 78):

> “To seek what has been exposed, to reopen what has been completed, and to tear down what has been decided—what else is this than failing to give thanks for the grace that has been obtained, and stretching criminal desires of deadly greed toward the food of the forbidden tree?”

We must therefore consider, in view of so great an amplification, how serious was the offense he committed: seeking what had been exposed, reopening what had been completed, and tearing down what had been decided. The pontiff of the Apostolic See, a man of such wisdom, holiness, and authority, compared this offense to the guilt which, as the Apostle teaches, passed into all humanity (Romans 5) and could be expiated only by the death of the Son of God. It must be considered whether such an act can pass without punishment and without danger to those whom the matter concerns.

## CHAPTER XX. How, after the fourth admonition, he did not subscribe to the excommunication of Carloman’s associates

(Aimoinus, Book V of the History, chapters 24 and following.)

Finally, after Carloman had improperly and disastrously withdrawn from our lord, the glorious King Charles, and had ravaged the kingdom of that same lord with many sons of Belial associated with him, we, the faithful who were living in that kingdom, exerted ourselves as much as we could. Our lord the king, after he returned here, also labored greatly through paternal promises and entreaties, as well as through generous pardons, so that he might restore this son of his to God and to himself and save his associates.

But when we bishops of his kingdom who were present saw that neither the terrors of divine judgment nor the promises of the eternal kingdom and temporal honors had any effect upon him or his associates, we exercised our episcopal ministry. He did not belong to the diocese of Rheims, but was a deacon of the province of Sens; therefore we pronounced the sentence of ecclesiastical excommunication against his associates who belonged to our parishes (Flodoard, Book III, chapter 26), and also against those who had committed many crimes in those same parishes, until they should repent.

We decided that this sentence should be sent to the archbishops of the various provinces. It reads as follows:

> “Hincmar, bishop of Rheims, etc. Carloman, the bodily son of our lord Charles, the glorious king, regenerated by water and the Holy Spirit in the diocese of Rheims, etc.”

See above among the letters of Hincmar of Rheims.

Since Brother Hincmar was at Compiègne when negotiations were still being conducted concerning the conversion of Carloman and his associates, and since he departed from there without my knowledge, I sent him, with the advice and consent of our fellow bishops who were there with me, a letter of this kind. I also sent it to the other bishops of the province of Rheims who were not physically present with us at that time:

> “Hincmar, etc. It cannot be unknown to you how many evils the associates of Carloman have committed in the territory of Rheims…”

See the letters of Hincmar.

I also sent him the aforementioned letter, appended to this one (Flodoard, Book III, chapter 21). Then, on the fifth day before the Nones of February, his provost Heddo came to me. Since, as I had instructed him, he had not sent his written consent concerning this canonical excommunication, I ordered him by word through Heddo to send me that same letter.

More than thirty days after he had received my letter, I wrote to him again, instructing him that, just as his predecessors and successors in office, and even those from more distant regions, had obediently sent letters of their consent, he should not delay any longer in sending his own; or else he should write back to me with a definite and regular explanation of why, although already admonished for the third time, he refused to send them.

He replied to me in this manner:

> “To the venerable Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, etc. Since you so insist upon my letter of consent concerning the excommunication carried out by you…”
