The rest is found among the letters of Hincmar of Laon, volume 124.

I therefore wrote back to him, among other things, in this manner:

> “Brother Heddo, etc.”

See the letters of Hincmar of Rheims.

## CHAPTER XXI. How thereafter, although admonished once and again concerning the same matter, he contemptuously refused to obey, and gives an indiscreet interpretation of the canon of the Council of Antioch

Afterward, on the third day before the Nones of May, his cleric, named Teutlandus, came to me, reporting certain matters to me on his behalf, which I omit here for the sake of brevity. I told him to say to his bishop that, just as I had already instructed him by letter and in person, he should no longer delay sending me his letter of consent concerning the excommunication of Carloman’s associates. Thus I admonished him for the fifth time.

Afterward, in a sixth letter, a copy of which I possess but which is no longer extant, I admonished him to send me without further delay his letter of consent concerning the canonical excommunication of Carloman’s associates. He had the customary disdain for obeying me.

Moreover, in his aforementioned document, among other things, he replied to me:

> “It is not worthwhile for you to seek the consent of the council whose counsel you disdain. And I wonder why you demand my consent in this matter, when you did not seek it—or rather, rejected my advice. For the Council of Antioch decrees: ‘Nor shall an archbishop act without the counsel of the other priests’; this excludes no fellow bishop.”

He did not consider how indiscreetly he was interpreting the council’s sentence, or how wisely that same council decreed when it said (canon 9):

> “It has been decided, in accordance with the ancient rule established by our fathers, that the other bishops, apart from the metropolitan, shall do nothing further…”

and so forth.

The holy Council of Nicaea plainly shows what the ancient rule established by our fathers was (canon 6, or 8 in another numbering). It decreed that, since the primacy and care of all the churches, received from the mouth of the Lord in the principate of blessed Peter, belongs to the pontiff of the first and holy Roman See, the bishop of Alexandria should have authority over all those entrusted to him (see Book 55, chapter 4). Likewise, at Antioch and in the other provinces, their privileges should be preserved for the churches.

The Council of Antioch cited above shows which churches are meant, what privileges they possess, and how those privileges are to be preserved (canon 9):

> “In each region, it is fitting that the bishops know that the metropolitan bishop has care of the whole province. Therefore all those from every direction who appear to have business should come together at the metropolis.”

The African Council likewise says (African Council, canon 105; Code of the Canons of the African Church, canon 138):

> “The decrees of Nicaea have most plainly entrusted both clerics of lower rank and the bishops themselves to their metropolitans…”

and so forth.

Saint Boniface writes (letter 3):

> “It is fitting that we be diligent guardians of our ancestral enactments. No one, surely, is unaware of the constitution of the Council of Nicaea, which begins—or, in another reading, commands—as follows: Each province must have one metropolitan with jurisdiction; no one province is to be subject to two. They judged that this must be observed by them, as it cannot otherwise be believed, at the prompting of the Holy Spirit.”

A little later:

> “We say this so that your Charity may understand that we observe the precepts of the canons so carefully that our own constitution likewise determines that every province should always await the direction of its metropolitan in all matters.”

The Council of Antioch therefore decreed distinctly that:

> “Apart from the metropolitan, the other bishops shall do nothing further except those things that pertain to their own diocese and to the possessions subject to them.”

Here “diocese” is used for “parish,” as elsewhere.

A little later it says:

> “Nor shall the metropolitan act without the advice of the other priests.”

But in this sentence it did not add what it had placed in the preceding one: “The metropolitan shall do nothing further without the advice of the other priests.” For the holy Council of Nicaea knew that it had decreed (canon 6) that if two or three provincial bishops oppose something because of their own disputes, the judgment of the majority should prevail.

It is therefore clear that Brother Hincmar bent the sentence of the Council of Antioch to his own interpretation in a manner different from what was proper. The same council, as well as Pope Saint Boniface, understood it in accordance with the sentence of the holy Council of Nicaea, since Saint Boniface himself promulgated in that same council:

> “Every province shall always await the direction of its metropolitan in all matters.”

He did not decree—and he ought not to have decreed anything contrary to the Councils of Nicaea and Antioch—that in all matters the metropolitan must always await the advice of all the fellow bishops of the province. For, concerning all the affairs of those who come from every direction of the province to the metropolitan, the metropolitan can neither seek nor await the advice of all the fellow bishops at all times, nor ought he to do so.

Rather, as Saint Leo writes to Anastasius of Thessalonica (letter 85):

> “According to the canons of the holy Fathers, established by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, it has been decreed that the metropolitans of the individual provinces should retain inviolate the right of the dignity anciently entrusted to them, so that they depart from the rules laid down neither through negligence nor through presumption.”

The metropolitan must exercise the privilege of his see in such a way that he orders these things to be preserved for each person. Likewise Leo writes to Hilary, bishop of Narbonne (letter 92, to Rusticus of Narbonne):

> “Things that are found to be neither contrary to the evangelical commands nor opposed to the decrees of the saints.”

This means departing from the established rules neither through negligence nor through presumption: namely, metropolitans must not neglect to carry out the rules established, insofar as they are able, nor overturn them presumptuously.

When, in accordance with the established rules, he issues appropriate commands to individuals concerning their affairs, and is unable to correct the rebellion or presumption of any person, he must correct it either by his own command, through judges appointed by him or chosen with the consent of the parties, or in a provincial synod, according to the sacred regulations, by correcting with the advice of the bishops of the province whatever has been neglected or presumptuously undertaken.

Keeping these sentences of the sacred canons before my mind—sentences observed by all the bishops of all the provinces in these regions, except by him—I did not pronounce the often-mentioned canonical excommunication against Carloman’s associates without the advice or consent of the other bishops who were present, who wished or were able to be present. I sought also the consent and advice of those who could not be present at that time, and I received it obediently given and sent by them.

From the man who could have been present but did not wish to be present, and who had departed from the proceedings concerning Carloman and his associates without my knowledge, I requested his consent. Just as I obtained consent from his predecessors and successors in office, I have thus far been unable to obtain it because of his contumacy.

## CHAPTER XXII. How in certain matters he wrongly reproved Hincmar himself, and concerning the punishment to be inflicted on the disobedient

He also wrote to me that he was very surprised that I could admonish him through his cleric. He did not consider that if he is the metropolitan who sits in the metropolitan city of Rheims, then he is also the metropolitan of his cleric, to whom, according to the sacred canons, all those throughout the province who appear to have business must come.

He himself must issue to each person, and to all collectively, commands that are found to be neither contrary to the evangelical commands nor opposed to the decrees of the saints; and he must correct in each person whatever may perhaps have arisen.

It is therefore established that a metropolitan may admonish him even through his cleric, and that, according to the Carthaginian canons, the provincial bishop may and ought, when useful, to be accused before him. Presbyters, deacons, and other lower clerics may likewise, in matters that concern them, if they have complained about the judgments of their bishops and have appealed from them and from neighboring bishops to the primate of the province, regularly admonish their own bishops by the authority of the primate.

Indeed, even the fellow bishops of the province of Rheims who live in distant regions have, from ancient times, regularly and lawfully been summoned to synods or ordinations by metropolitan letters sent through neighboring bishops; and they are likewise admonished concerning other matters.

The letter of Hincmar of Laon continues as follows—this letter is not extant:

> “What ought to have been done at the time of the synod and by judgment, if there were a legitimate reason for him to admonish me. For these commands of yours are not such admonitions. Nor am I, or any bishop, obliged to answer you when attacked in various places which you visit for your own convenience, but only in a synod.”

He did not see—or rather, blinded by arrogance, was unable to see—that it is one thing if someone attacks or accuses a person, and another if a metropolitan admonishes a person on behalf of someone from his own parish, urging a provincial bishop to amend something he has done rashly [the reading *perpere*, “wrongly,” seems preferable], or requiring his consent for necessary matters.

A metropolitan neither ought nor is able to summon a synod in order to admonish him concerning every matter of everyone who, from every direction, comes to his metropolis according to the canons.

He also reproved me because I gave a blessing publicly in his parish, without his consent, to Carloman and his followers, against whom he had threatened excommunication but had not yet pronounced it—as he himself also writes—and who professed their desire to correct themselves, when they asked for the blessing.

He quotes the following concerning certain people from Scripture:

> “They have taught their tongue to speak falsehood; they have labored to act wickedly” (Jeremiah 9:5);

and:

> “The labor of their lips shall cover them” (Psalm 139:10).

When we, the faithful of our lord—bishops, abbots, counts, and his other faithful who had gathered for a conference with Carloman and his followers—persuaded them that, after hostages had been exchanged on both sides, they should cease from the evils they were committing in our lord’s kingdom and live there peacefully until they could obtain our lord’s pardon, the conference was brought to an end.

As each of us prepared to return to his own place, both our lord’s faithful and Carloman and his followers, professing their intention to correct themselves, asked that a blessing be given to them by me and by the other bishops who were present.

After first recalling the Lord’s sentence in which he commanded his disciples:

> “Into whatever house you enter, say, ‘Peace be to this house.’ And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him; but if not, your peace will return to you” (Luke 10),

I prayed that God would confirm what he had worked in us and through us in them. I gave them a blessing as faithful people who professed that they possessed the will and devotion of fidelity.

Saint Gregory teaches, on the basis of a legal ruling (Book 12, final letter, question 9), that one may:

> “Pass through another man’s harvest, crush the ears with one’s hand, and eat them; so that from the crop which appears to be entrusted to another, through the effect of a good work the Lord’s grain may be stripped of the chaff of its vices” (Deuteronomy 23), “and may be converted into the body of the Church, as though by chewing it, through admonition and persuasion.”

The sacred canons say likewise (Council of Antioch, canon 22; see Antonius Augustinus, Book IV of *Pontifical Law*, title 50) that a bishop must not enter a city that is not subject to him, nor approach an estate that does not belong to him, concerning the ordination of anyone.

I understand that I did not do this, since the same sacred canons say:

> “In each region it is fitting that the bishops know that the metropolitan bishop has care of the whole province.”

Therefore, in whatever parish throughout the province it may seem appropriate to me, just as I have often done in the parish of Laon, I can freely summon a synod and correct individual matters if anything should perhaps have arisen, in accordance with the canons of Chalcedon and the decrees of the pontiffs of the Roman See.

I did not therefore enter a city that was not subject to me, nor did I approach an estate that did not belong to me concerning anyone’s ordination. Even if the parish of Laon were not subject to me by the privilege of the metropolitan see, I could freely strip the Lord’s grain of the chaff of its vices, through the effect of a good work, from a crop that appeared to have been entrusted to another, and convert it into the body of the Church, as though by chewing it, through admonition and persuasion.

We also wrote in the letter concerning the excommunication of Carloman’s associates, which was to be sent through various archbishops:

> “With this condition, namely, that, in accordance with the form of the mystical Council of Nicaea and the canons of the province of Africa, and likewise the decrees of the pontiffs of the Apostolic See—Siricius, Innocent, Celestine, and Leo—wherever they may be, the final penance and communion of the necessary viaticum shall not be denied to those who ask for them.”

According to his singular wisdom, he corrects this in his own document, writing:

> “As for granting them the viaticum, it is to be granted only after a profession—even if they are already at the point of death—namely, that if any of them should afterward recover, whoever has asked for the viaticum while lying ill must profess that he will no longer do such things or participate with those who do them. For holy Pope Gelasius established this in his constitutions: a sentence is, or has always been, prescribed for every error. The sentence prescribed for this error will never be entirely rescinded.”

What are we to do concerning this matter except enter his school and let him teach us with a master’s rod what the Fathers who assembled at the Council of Nicaea knew, and what the canons established by the Spirit of God and the laws destined to remain until the end of the age prescribed?

Did the bishops of the province of Africa, among whom the renowned Augustine—no small portion of Christ and an institution and defense of the Catholic Church—was prominent, not know this or forget it? Were Siricius, Innocent, Celestine, and Leo also unable to understand it?

Nevertheless, concerning this matter the Catholic and salutary teaching of so many authorities, whose example we have set forth, is sufficient for us. To it he wished, or rather presumed, to add something superfluous—or rather something arising from constraint—as though in concealment; yet that teaching rebuked him, against which he had not feared to act in his pernicious excommunication.

For this reason he did not dare send me a letter of his consent to the definitions of the canons and of the decrees of the pontiffs of the Apostolic See.

And what is written happened:

> “He who flees the iron weapons will fall upon the bronze bow.”

For while he wished to avoid writing, in the consent I had demanded from him, against the presumption of his pernicious excommunication, he rushed into judgment under the sacred laws, canons, and decrees of the pontiffs of the Apostolic See concerning that same presumption of an unlawful excommunication, his despised privilege as metropolitan, and his disobedience contrary to his own profession and subscription.

In order to establish his own sentence, he included in the same writing a testimony against himself from blessed Augustine’s book *On Faith and Works*, concerning the distinction between correction and excommunication. Like one fleeing from the face of a lion, he rushed upon a bear; and, leaning against the wall of a house, he was bitten by a serpent.

That is, he himself placed in his own writing a testimony against himself, drawn from the writings of the one who was lifted up on the cross, just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness.

> “Augustine says”—in the testimony placed by Hincmar (the book *On Faith and Works*)—“that the Apostle is not opposed to the Lord because he said, ‘Reprove sinners in the presence of all, so that the others may have fear,’ while the Lord says, ‘Reprove him between yourself and him alone.’ Both things must be done, as the differing weakness of those whom we have undertaken—not to destroy, but to correct and heal—requires.”

If he had paid attention to these words of the testimony he himself placed in his writing, he would never have presumed to threaten that pernicious excommunication for the destruction of many whom he had undertaken not to destroy, but to correct and heal.

Against this Solomon says:

> “Like a thorn in the hand of a drunkard, so is a parable in the mouth of a fool” (Proverbs 26:9).

For just as a drunkard carrying a thorn in his hand wounds himself, so a person careless in speaking strikes himself with his own sentence.

Again, in the same testimony blessed Augustine says:

> “There is likewise a reason for concealing and tolerating the wicked in the Church; and there is again a reason for chastising, correcting, not admitting, or removing them from communion. People go astray when they do not observe the proper measure. When they begin to incline excessively toward one side, they do not consider the other testimonies of divine authority by which they could be recalled from that purpose and made to stand in the truth and moderation tempered from both sides.”

If Brother Hincmar had paid attention to this distinction between correcting and excommunicating, or concealing and tolerating the wicked in the Church—a distinction which blessed Augustine expressed and demonstrated to be firmly grounded in the words of sacred Scripture—then, after being admonished by his metropolitan once and again from evangelical truth, apostolic and canonical authority, and the decrees of the Apostolic See, to rescind that pernicious excommunication, he would not have persisted in his obstinate contumacy to his own peril.

Against whose disobedience—since he stubbornly refused to send me, his metropolitan, a letter expressing his consent in this matter—I shall append what the sacred laws and rules say. Honorius and Theodosius, Augusti, in their legal enactment addressed to Aurelius, archbishop of Carthage, decreed as follows:

> “Therefore let Your Religiousness have all the bishops written to and admonished in due form, so that they may know that, by the decision of your holiness, this determination has been prescribed for them: whoever, through impious obstinacy, neglects to subscribe to the condemnation of those mentioned above, thereby showing that his mind is pure, shall be punished by the loss of his episcopate, expelled from the cities, and deprived of communion forever.”

[Col. 0600D] A little later:

> “For there is one and the same guilt in those who either restrain discipline by concealing it or, by failing to condemn, have offered harmful support.”

And for this reason Saint Gregory, writing to Bishop Felix at Sardica (Book IV, Letter 7), says:

> “You yourself do not doubt, from your own subjects also, how obedience and reverence ought to be shown to superiors. In this matter it is very useful if humility, without being compelled by anyone, has commendably preserved what the rigor of discipline imposes. It has therefore come to our attention that Your Fraternity disdains to obey our brother John, bishop of Justiniana Prima, according to the established custom [alternative: *the established custom* absent], and that you were unwilling to subscribe, in accordance with custom, either to his decree or to the report [alternative: *to the report that he sent to us*]. If this is so, we are saddened, because you plainly provide evidence of pride in yourself; how blameworthy this is, especially in a priest, is declared by the words of divine mercy [alternative: *the words of divine admonition cry out*]. Therefore we exhort you, having laid aside the swelling of your mind, to show yourself humble toward the aforesaid brother and our fellow bishop, and do not cease to obey, so that God may rejoice in the concord of your fraternities and others may take from you an example of goodness. For if—which we do not believe—it should happen that you remain in pride, know that the sacred canons impose upon your contumacy a strict and canonical correction of discipline [alternative: *know that we impose it strictly*]. You do well, therefore, to present yourself voluntarily, through salutary reflection, as the kind of person whom canonical coercion [alternative: *coercion*] would compel you to be. For after this admonition of ours you will not again be permitted, at your own will, contrary to custom, to remain disobedient to your superiors; nor should you think that we shall conceal or defer the ecclesiastical punishment of such great indiscipline.”

[Col. 0601A] Accordingly, let us consider the threat of judgment made by blessed Gregory against the disobedience of an archbishop toward his superior, where he says:

> “After this admonition of ours, you will not again be permitted, at your own will, contrary to custom, to remain disobedient to your superiors; nor should you think that we shall conceal or defer the ecclesiastical punishment of such great indiscipline.”

Discern, then, whether we—who remain on earth while living our manner of life in heaven, and who, though still living with you in our constitutions, are believed to threaten such things from heaven—ought, after so many admonitions, to conceal or defer any longer the punishment of such great indiscipline in this contemner of the rules, we who, by God’s grace, aspire to heavenly things.

## CHAPTER XXIII. How he falsely imposes upon that same Hincmar of Reims the charge of betrayal.

Finally, after so many other admonitions—which, to avoid prolixity, I pass over—and after I had brought forward sacred authorities to him, it happened to me, as the Lord complains concerning a people rebelling against Him: “We healed Babylon, and she was not healed.” And: “The house of Israel has become dross to me” (Jer. LI). What Solomon says happened to me from him: “Vinegar on nitre is he who sings songs with a most evil heart” (Prov. V).

> “When vinegar,” Gregory says, “is poured onto nitre, the nitre immediately seethes and boils over. Likewise, when a perverse mind is rebuked by correction, and is not persuaded to good through the sweetness of preaching, it becomes worse through the rebuke; and from the very thing by which it ought to have been restrained from iniquity, it is inflamed into the iniquity of murmuring.”

Hence the following appears in the memorandum recently sent to me, on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, in the present fourth indiction:

> “Not restrained by any affection of kinship, nor held back by any superiority or integrity of archiepiscopal office, from wrath (*orgē*, Greek: ὀργῇ), which does not practice justice, you have advised—indeed, compelled—me by betraying me, so that I might be handed over by royal power into custody, writing to him in your letters as follows: ‘And when he comes to Silvanectum, have such strong and experienced men ready as are needed to capture such a beast.’ And to Odo, your accomplice, you wrote in this way: ‘When we come to the synod, God may give us what we should say, until He frees us from this untamable unicorn and restless animal.’ You have not ceased striving to accomplish these things from the time when you held the synod in the city of Soissons for the deposition of Rothad, because I resisted the installation of a bishop in his place, contrary to the sacred rules, before the universal pope had been consulted about so important a matter, as authority requires. Since you could not accomplish this earlier, because my hour had not yet come, at Silvacum you obtained what you desired. And you denied at Reims that you had done this; yet at that time I did not wish to say this openly to you.”

[Col. 0602A]

Concerning these matters I write as follows. Justinian’s law says that:

> “The metropolitan or the primate of the province shall hear, according to ecclesiastical law, matters concerning ecclesiastical rights or other business between the parties; and he shall determine what accords with the ecclesiastical canons and our laws, and neither party shall be able to oppose his decision.”

For this reason blessed Gregory very frequently commands in his decrees from the *Register* that “ecclesiastical judgments be brought to an end according to the laws and canons.”

The sacred laws received by the Catholic Church say:

> “Since anyone may confess in judgment not only by his own voice but also in writing and in any manner he can, no one may be convicted except by written evidence or by witnesses.”

And concerning clerics, they demonstrate in the later law of Majorian that clerics are not to approach episcopal judgment through the bond of a compromise.

The sacred laws likewise say that in criminal cases neither the accuser nor the accused may defend himself through an agent or another person, unless a patron accuses an ungrateful freedman. In a capital case no one is condemned, nor may an absent person accuse or be accused through another, unless the accused, having been summoned legally and according to the rules—for, as Gelasius writes, “a person is summoned to judgment in such a way that he may either confess what is alleged or be convicted by the allegations”—delays coming to clear himself, contrary to the rule of summons. In that event, according to the laws and the decrees of Gregory, a sentence may be pronounced against him as against a contumacious person.

And according to the laws and canons, as Felix says, “he who distrusts answering confirms the charges”; so that, as Pope Boniface decreed, “he may not gain the postponement of judgment by his absence.”

The accuser too shall be subject to such a judgment according to the laws and canons if he does not pursue his accusation legally and according to the rules, so that he must either prove lawfully and regularly what he has alleged or be subjected, in a lawful and regular judgment, to the charge of falsehood. This is clearly shown in Book IX, chapters 26 and 27, of the Theodosian Code, in chapter 19 of the Council of Carthage, and in chapter 27 of the African Council.

Moreover, one who conspires with his own people and sometimes, when summoned, refuses to come to the council, thinking that his own people can suffice for him, and neglecting fraternal love, is commanded not only to lose his diocese but also to be removed by public authority from that principal see and deprived of his possessions, as a rebel, just as is contained in chapter 20 of the African Council.

Since, however, the most serious judgments concerning this crime are demonstrated both in the sacred laws and in the ecclesiastical rules, applying both to the accused and to the one who accuses through calumny without proving his charge—whether Hincmar, present at the judgment, pursues the charges he has made against me or answers the charges made against him, or whether, having been summoned regularly many times, he neglects to appear—it will be necessary to investigate the truth on both sides and to determine justly and reasonably whatever is discovered.

For he calls me his betrayer, that is, his traitor—namely, the accuser of a bishop by a bishop. Ecclesiastical histories and chronicles, especially the chronicle of Prosper, assert that the crimes brought against Caecilian, bishop of the Church of Carthage, were not proved, particularly the charge that he had been ordained by traditors of the divine Scriptures.

And it is no slight crime if I, an archbishop of whatever standing, betrayed a bishop whom I had consecrated to the Lord. Therefore that same brother of ours, Hincmar, ought to produce as proof the signs of my letters by which I would acknowledge myself to be his betrayer [the text has *deest*, “missing”; *debet*, “ought to be,” is required].

As it is written concerning the betrayer of our Lord: “The betrayer gave them a sign, saying that whoever he kissed was the one they should seize” (Matt. XXVI). Concerning him the same Lord says to Pilate: “He who handed me over to you has the greater sin” (John XIX).

He has also brought forward the words of two of my letters falsely, as though they were two witnesses against me [Col. 0603C], just as we read that this was done in the accusation of our supreme Head.

> “All the elect,” Gregory says, “because they are members of the supreme Head, also follow their Head in His passion, so that in their death they may experience those adversaries whose lives they had presumed upon; and the reward of their work increases for them in proportion as the gain of virtue advances through the loss of another’s charity.”

Saint Pope Zosimus, writing to Aurelius and to all the bishops established throughout the various provinces (Letter 6), shows how great the crime of betrayal is, saying:

> “Lazarus, formerly condemned as a calumniator by the judgments of the bishops mentioned above [alternative: *of the most serious bishops*] in the Council of Turin, after he had attacked the life of Briccius, an innocent bishop, with false allegations [Col. 0603D], later obtained the priesthood improperly [alternative: *an improper priesthood*] from that same Proculus, who, among the others, had agreed in the synod to his condemnation [alternative: *had joined in the synod of his condemnation*]. He then voluntarily removed himself from office by letters in which the awareness of his own life caused him to renounce it [alternative: *from his renunciation*].”

And in Book VIII, chapter 29, of the Theodosian law, it is written concerning calumniators:

> “Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius, Augusti, to Hellibicus, count and commander of both military services. There is no reason for the punishment of a manifest calumniator to be delayed. For we do not permit matters that could not stand at the first accusation to be repeatedly revived, nor innocent persons, secure from guilt, to be terrified by a condemnable attack. Given on the third day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of Merobaudes and Saturninus.”

The same Augusti to Menander, vicar of Asia:

> “It is contained in our constitutions and those of our parents that persons who presume to make accusations in the names of others are to be counted among informers. Therefore deportation shall follow upon the most calumnious head and the person made infamous by an invalid denunciation, so that from now on everyone, individually and collectively, may know that the minds of the emperors may not be stirred by something that cannot be demonstrated. Given on the Ides of May, in the consulship of Arcadius and Bauto.”

Likewise Arcadius and Honorius, Augusti, to Victurus, proconsul of Africa:

> “We do not permit innocent persons to be overthrown under the appearance of a false accusation by the attacks of cunning men. If such men attempt this, let them understand that the severity of the laws will weigh upon them for the crimes committed. Given on the fourth day before the Ides of March, at Milan, in the third consulship of Honorius Augustus and the consulship of Eutychianus.”

And there, after other material:

> “Calumniators also include those who, bringing false charges against the person of an innocent individual, presume to stir the minds of the emperors to anger. All such persons, having been made infamous, shall be thrust into exile.”

And in Book X, chapter 5, a law is issued concerning informers, which that same brother subscribed in his little compilations presented to the synod at Attigny, and which he caused his clerics to subscribe. Since it does not apply to ecclesiastical judgments concerning ecclesiastical ministers, I have refrained from inserting it here.

## CHAPTER XXIV. The calumny is dispelled by documents and witnesses produced by the man of Reims.

[Col. 0604C]

(Book LV, chapter 40.) Since he said, “by advising, indeed compelling me, you betrayed me so that I might be handed over by royal power into custody,” the lord king, if he deigns to do so, can speak the truth about this before you. No one knows better than he whether I betrayed that brother of ours, advised him, gave him counsel, or offered him consent that royal power should hand him over into custody.

For when Hincmar resisted the king’s commands and rebelled against him, he sent his letters to the lord king, and His Lordship forwarded them to me, ordering me to come to him at Silvacum and, before I came there, to send back a written response to Hincmar’s letters.

Since he commanded me nothing contrary to faith or good morals [Col. 0604D], and since apostolic rule commands us to “be subject to the king as to one who is pre-eminent,” I carried out his command as best I could, and consequently sent him a letter of this kind:

> “To the glorious lord, etc. Your most dear and most reverend Lordship,” etc.

You also have this among the letters of our Hincmar.

I do not deny that I wrote as I have set it out here. On the other hand, he himself writes that I wrote to the lord king: “When he comes to Silvanectum, have such strong and experienced men ready as are needed to capture such a beast.”

Judge how my letter agrees with betraying him, when it sought his salvation and not his betrayal.

I also sent the lord king another lengthy letter [Col. 0605A], of which I have a copy here. It contains the following passage:

> “For my part, I fear to proceed with these events as they stand, and I grieve in this way, although the same Hincmar, as I have learned with certainty from those who heard him and saw his gnashing movements when he speaks about me, attributes the whole matter to me, saying that, provoked by me, you have done and are doing whatever you have done against him. You know better than anyone himself that this is not true.”

And elsewhere in the same letter:

> “As for your command that I should arrange to send back advice about how you ought to act against Hincmar’s contumacy, I answer, with your lordship’s permission, that this seems to me not only difficult but even impossible.”

[Col. 0605B] A little later:

> “As you know sufficiently, the sacred canons prescribe what is to be done in the case of a bishop, especially when your royal power complains that it has been injured; and since, as I have been told, the authority of the apostolic see is being contentiously brought into the matter, I cannot give advice about a judgment or determine anything without the discussion and consent of my fellow bishops.”

I sent Odo a letter on his behalf, when he asked what I wanted him to advise Hincmar. I therefore sent him a lengthy letter (it is not extant), of which I have a copy here.

I sent another letter to the same brother Odo on Hincmar’s behalf, of which I also have a copy here. It contains the following:

> “Moderate the mind of the lord king as much as you can,” etc.

The rest you have among the same letters [Col. 0605C].

I also sent a third letter to the same brother on his behalf, of which I have a copy here. It contains the following:

> “I greatly fear and grieve,” etc.

See above.

This is what I wrote. Hincmar, however, says that I wrote to my accomplice Odo:

> “When we come to the synod, God may give us what we should say, until He frees us from this untamable unicorn and restless animal.”

The manifest difference between the two writings shows how far apart they are. For even if I had written to Odo as Hincmar says, he still could not infer from this that I intended to be his betrayer, since in his own letter he says that I declared: “When we come to the synod, God may give us what we should say” [Col. 0605D].

I searched among the copies of my letters for the letter containing these words that he alleges, but I could not find it.

And even if I had called him a unicorn—that is, an untamable beast—in my letters, I would not thereby have committed a criminal offense. For blessed Gregory, explaining the Lord’s statement to Job, “Will you bind the rhinoceros to plow with your harness?” (Job XXXIX), says concerning his emperor:

> “I remember that I have often seen that when this rhinoceros here had become fiercely aroused to strike, as though raising its horn, it threatened the smallest beasts with the exile of death and threatened its subjects with condemnation through immense terrors. Suddenly, however, when the sign of the cross was impressed upon its forehead, it extinguished within itself the whole blaze of fury.”

And would that this rhinoceros of ours would impress the sign of the cross upon his forehead and heart, extinguish himself from the ferocity of his own contumacy, and make himself another person, so that he could say with the Apostle:

> “I live, yet it is no longer I; Christ lives in me” (Gal. II).

Hence Gregory says:

> “That savage persecutor had indeed been extinguished, and the devout preacher had begun to live.”

Let him produce the letters about which he has written here, and let him bring forward the person who gave them to him; then the truth will be known.

As for his claim that I opposed him concerning Rothad, the subscriptions of his own hand, which I possess, refute him as a liar. They show that I decided nothing concerning Rothad and did nothing about appointing another in his place that he himself did not do with me. The synodal acts sent to the apostolic see, to which he himself subscribed, plainly show the same thing [Col. 0606B].

Moreover, I came to the lord king at Solarium in Cippidum (Suippes), and brought him a written response to his letters and Hincmar’s. In my presence, in the presence of Bishop Odo, Ottulfus and Hildeboldus, who were then priests, and also in the presence of Count Eiricus—and I do not remember the names of the others who were there—he gave that response to Hincmar and granted him the night for reading it [alternative: *granted him time during the night to read it*].

The next day I returned to the king, because Hincmar persisted stubbornly in his customary contumacy, so that neither I, nor brother Odo, nor any of the others who were present could obtain from him anything reasonable, humble, or worthy of episcopal gravity. I asked the lord king for permission [Col. 0606C], and because I was quite ill, I withdrew to my lodging.

If I spoke with the lord king about betraying him or handing him over into custody, the lord king not only knows this better than anyone; these religious bishops, Odo, Ottulfus, and Hildeboldus, can also declare the truth to us for the love of truth itself and pronounce me either guilty or innocent of this calumny.

For it is written: “By the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand” (Matt. XVI; 1 Tim. 5). The Apostle also shows that an accusation against presbyters may be received on the testimony of two or three witnesses.

The Council of Nicaea (canon 2) likewise commands that a neophyte bishop who has been reproved by two or three witnesses must abstain from the clergy if some offense affecting the soul is found in such a person [Col. 0606D].

And since, as I stated above, the sacred laws say that no one can be convicted except by writing or by witnesses, you have heard both his writings and mine. With the testimony of the lord king and these bishops, you can legally and regularly discern and decide whether the judgments of the laws and of Zosimus mentioned above ought to fall upon the man who has falsely calumniated me—judgments that would proceed against me if he could prove by calumny that I was his informer.

I say these things, and other matters inflicted upon me by him, not because of my personal injuries, but out of zeal for God, for the ecclesiastical rules, and for the divine ordinance, according to the constitutions of the Fathers [Col. 0607A]. I do so lest, through negligence, I should be condemned because of the office of my position; rather, as blessed Gregory demonstrates in the *Pastoral Rule*, I may afterward have this same zeal as a strong defense between myself and him, so that I will not then be deprived of recourse to punishment if I am now lax in correction.

I also do this so that the truth about me and the falsity of his letters may become clear to all who read his accusations and my defenses.

And if perhaps that same brother Hincmar subscribed, and caused the ecclesiastical ministers of his Church to subscribe, so that an informer, according to secular laws, might either have his tongue cut out or his head severed, intending this punishment to proceed against me, whom he later described as his informer, he acted rashly and contrary to ecclesiastical discipline. Before he had seen me confess or had seen me convicted according to the regular procedure, he condemned me by a judicial sentence—especially by a censure which ecclesiastical discipline does not accept [Col. 0607B].

## CHAPTER XXV. The uncle dispels another calumny of the nephew concerning contempt for pontifical excommunication.

Last year, on the Ides of November, in the fourth indiction, he also sent through his presbyter Clarentius an excessively lengthy memorandum in which the following was written against me:

> “It did not seem worthy of Your Excellence,” Hincmar says, “to tell Bertharius what he reported that you had said to me: ‘If I had excommunicated those aforementioned men of mine who did such things and are still doing them, they would not be held by excommunication—that is, they would not be bound by the bond of anathema.’ But it is no wonder if you make light of the excommunication of my insignificance and perhaps judge it unreasonable, when you both treat the excommunication of the apostolic see as nothing and declare that it ought to be treated as nothing, considering it absurd.”

Concerning this calumny brought against me, since Saint Gregory very frequently says in the book from the *Register* that cases must be investigated and judgments concluded according to the laws and canons, let the laws and canons be read.

The rules of our ancient Fathers say (Council of Toledo III, chapter 9, question “It is fitting”):

> “It is fitting that the life of an innocent person not be stained by the ruin of an accuser. Therefore, whoever is accused by anyone must not be handed over to punishment before the accuser is presented and the judgments of the laws and canons have been sought. If the person is found unworthy to accuse, he must not be admitted to the accusation. And if a bishop thinks that someone ought to be condemned for a crime, he must understand that he is to examine the matter in the place of the accuser. For what is proved to one ought to be proved to all.”

If he wishes to reject these canons, as he customarily rejects whatever is opposed to him, let him hear what Pope Leo says about this to Maximus, bishop of Antioch (Letter 62):

> “Whatever, on account of [alternative: *apart from*] special cases of synodal councils, is brought before episcopal examination may have some basis for judgment if nothing concerning it has been determined by the holy Fathers at Nicaea. For what disagrees with their rules and constitutions [alternative: *and constitution*] will never be able to obtain the consent of the apostolic see [alternative: *will obtain it*].”

The Synod of Antioch (canon 20) says that a council is complete when the metropolitan bishop is present.

Pope Zosimus, in his letter to all the bishops established throughout the various provinces, approves the provincial synod of the Gallican bishops, saying:

> “Lazarus, formerly condemned as a calumniator by the judgments of the most serious bishops in the Council of Turin, when he had attacked the life of Briccius, an innocent bishop, with false allegations.”

The canons of the province of Africa state (African Council, chapter 97; *African Church Canons*, canon 130):

> “Cases that are not common are to be judged in their own provinces.”

The African Council decreed:

> “Whenever many crimes are brought by accusers against clerics, among whom bishops are also counted, and they have been unable to prove one of the charges—the one with which they began—they are not to be admitted to the remaining charges.”

The sacred laws say that no one can be convicted except by writing or by witnesses.

And Gelasius, in the *Memorandum* given to Faustus while he was serving as legate, says concerning prevaricating bishops:

> “What, however, would they say if they were not defeated in every respect by their own documents?”

The African Council says (canon 131):

> “Witnesses are not to be admitted for testimony if they have been ordered not to be admitted for the accusation; nor are those whom the accuser himself has produced from his own household.”

The sacred laws likewise say:

> “The testimony of a single person, however distinguished and suitable that person may appear, is in no way to be heard.”

Since, therefore, the writing that brother Hincmar has calumniated is presently available [Col. 0608C], let the accuser produce either lawful and regular witnesses against me or the document by which he can prove this calumny: that I allegedly declare the excommunication of the apostolic see to be nothing and to be something that ought to be treated as nothing, as though it were absurd.

If he or anyone else cannot proceed with this, the laws and rules will pronounce judgment concerning the calumniator.

Brother Bertharius the deacon will come into your presence, the man whom Hincmar said had reported to him that I told him that, if he had excommunicated his aforementioned men who had acted—and were still acting—in such matters against the ecclesiastical laws, they would not be held by excommunication, that is, would not be bound by the bond of anathema.

Since Hincmar’s statement in his writing is distinct, because he complains to Bertharius about the annulment by me of his excommunication (Book LV, chapter 29), let me legally and regularly contest the matter with that same Bertharius in your presence.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Hincmar publicly professes his Catholic understanding concerning the supreme power of the apostolic see to bind and loose.

As for what that same Hincmar says:

> “It is no wonder if you make light of the excommunication of my insignificance and perhaps judge it unreasonable, when you declare the excommunication of the apostolic see to be nothing and to be something that ought to be treated as nothing, as though it were absurd,”

I must deal with him legally and regularly, with your counsel and assistance [Col. 0609A].

So that you may know what I think and maintain concerning the binding and loosing power of the apostolic see—which is the mother and teacher of all the Churches throughout the whole world, and whose pontiff is the patriarch of patriarchs and the first among the primates of all provinces—and may know that Hincmar has falsely calumniated me in this matter, although the African Council decrees:

> “Whenever many crimes are brought by accusers against clerics, and they have been unable to prove one of the charges with which they began, they are no longer to be admitted to the remaining charges,”

I set forth before you what I believe in my heart unto justice and confess with my mouth unto salvation.

I learned this from the teaching of blessed Leo, pontiff of that same holy and principal see. In a sermon on his anniversary (Sermon 3), among other things he says:

> “What is said to blessed Peter—‘I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven’—the right of this power certainly passed also to the other apostles, and the ordinance of this decree spread to all the leaders of the Church. Yet it is not without reason that what is entrusted to all is commended to one. For this is entrusted uniquely to Peter because Peter’s form is set before all the rulers of the Church.”

The privilege of Peter therefore remains wherever judgment is rendered according to his equity. There is neither excessive severity nor excessive leniency where nothing is bound and nothing loosed except what blessed Peter has bound or loosed. Since, as Augustine and the other teachers explain, Peter confessed the King of heaven with greater devotion than the others, he was deservedly endowed above the others with the gift of the keys of the heavenly kingdom, so that it might be clear to all that no one can enter the kingdom of heaven without that confession and faith.

The keys of the kingdom of heaven signify the knowledge and power of discernment belonging to judicial authority, by which it must receive the worthy into the kingdom and exclude the unworthy from the kingdom.

Hence the Lord clearly added:

> “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven” (Matt. XVI).

Although this power of loosing and binding appears to have been given by the Lord to Peter alone, it must nevertheless be known without any doubt that it is also given to the other apostles, as He Himself testifies. After the triumph of His passion and resurrection, He appeared to them, breathed upon them, and said to all:

> “Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them; whose sins you retain are retained” (John XX).

For just as, when all were questioned generally, Peter answered as one for all, so also what the Lord answered to Peter He answered in Peter to all.

Even now the same office is entrusted to bishops and priests throughout the whole Church: once the causes of sinners have been recognized, they are to absolve, moved by compassion, those whom they see to be humble and truly penitent and already freed from fear of eternal death; but those whom they recognize as persisting in the sins they have committed, they are to indicate as bound by every punishment [the text has *deest eam*, “it is missing”].

Therefore elsewhere the Lord commanded concerning a brother who had been corrected once, twice, and a third time, but had not repented:

> “If he does not listen even to the Church, let him be to you as a pagan and a publican” (Matt. XVIII).

And lest anyone should think it a small matter to be condemned by the judgment of the Church, He immediately added with terrifying force:

> “Amen, I say to you: Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven” (Matt. XVIII).

Authority to bind and loose is therefore given to the entire Church of the elect, according to the measure of sins or repentance.

That same blessed Peter, however, who confessed Christ with true faith and followed Him with true love, specially received the keys of the kingdom of heaven, the primacy of judicial power, and the care of feeding the sheep of the Lord’s fold. In his primacy, his successors on his see received these things [Col. 0610B], so that all believers throughout the world may understand that whoever in any way separates himself from the unity of his faith or fellowship cannot be absolved from the bonds of sins or enter through the gate of the heavenly kingdom.

Concerning this episcopal binding and loosing, which we, the sons and disciples of the apostolic see, must regard with sufficient fear, caution, and observance, Saint Gregory says in a homily on the Gospel:

> “Often, in binding and loosing their subjects, a pastor follows the impulses of his own will rather than the merits of the cases. It follows that the one who exercises this power of binding and loosing according to his own wishes and not according to the conduct of his subjects deprives himself of that very power. Hence it is rightly said through the prophet: ‘They put to death souls that do not die, and they give life to souls that do not live’ (Ezek. XIII).”

He puts to death one who does not die when he condemns the just; he tries to give life to one who will not live when he attempts to absolve the guilty from punishment. It often happens that he either condemns those who do not deserve it or himself looses others who have been bound. The cases must therefore be weighed, and only then should the power of binding and loosing be exercised.

Moreover, as blessed Augustine and the other Catholic teachers say, the bindings and loosings of the holy Church are not those performed against the holy Church or performed by those who, thinking contrary to the teachings of the Catholic Church, bind or loose things opposed to that Church.

For the holy Church says:

> “I have not sat with the council of vanity, and with those who do evil I shall not enter. I have hated the church of the malicious, and with the impious I shall not sit. I shall wash my hands among the innocent” (Ps. XXV).

Only in the unity of this Catholic Church—which has not been divided by heresies and schisms—are the bindings and loosings true, just as its sacraments are true. This Church was built upon the rock; it is called the one dove; it is the beautiful bride without spot or wrinkle; the enclosed garden, the sealed fountain, the well of living water, the paradise bearing the fruit of trees; the place beside God where one stands firmly; the place of gold where one is refined; and the house of God, which received the keys of the kingdom of heaven and the power of binding and loosing.

If anyone despises this house when it corrects and rebukes him, the Lord commands that he be as a pagan and a publican (Matt. XVIII).

[Col. 0611A] This is what I have received from the teaching of the apostolic see concerning the binding and loosing of the holy Catholic Church, of the pontiff of the apostolic see, and also of the bishops subject to him: this is what must be believed, held, and followed. And this is what I believe, hold, and follow.

Whoever has said or says otherwise about me will show himself malicious, and he will not be able to prove that I am not Catholic. He will instead prove himself a lying accuser and will show that I am not guilty of the charge.

As for what I must learn, I am prepared to learn, hold, and profess it willingly and obediently from the Catholic teaching of that supreme see—the see which, in the primacy of blessed Peter, to whom the Lord entrusted His sheep to be fed by a threefold repetition (John XXI) and commanded him to strengthen his brethren (Luke XXII), received the privilege of primacy over all the Churches throughout the whole world [Col. 0611B].

## CHAPTER XXVII. How he falsely reports many things concerning apostolic letters not shared with him.

Our brother Hincmar likewise fastened upon me a serious accusation in his letter—if what he said were true—that I had committed an offense against that same holy and apostolic see. He wrote:

“You summoned me by a letter bearing your authority to Attigny, to a synod, informing me that letters of the apostolic lord had been sent to the lord king Charles and to the bishops of his kingdom, letters to which no response could be given without synodal consultation. Although you had received these letters at Gundulf’s estate (Houdilcourt), where I was also present, you did not show them to me there in any way. When I came to Attigny, you gave me what was supposedly a copy of them, asking me to read it, and immediately to respond to you on the basis of it; you ordered me, after reading it through, to return that same copy to you at once. Later, however, I learned from another copy that several things were missing from the memorandum you had shown me.”

These statements of his are untrue. For on the very day when the apostolic lord’s envoys gave me his letters at Gundulf’s estate, in the presence of the king, the bishops, and the other faithful who were there—as the lord king, the bishops, and the others in whose presence I received those letters know—I reread them before leaving that house, with the king, the bishops, and all the others who were there listening. If Hincmar was present and wished to hear them, he could certainly have heard them, just as the others did.

What he says—that when he came to Attigny I gave him what was supposedly a copy of those letters, asked him to read it, and then required him to respond immediately—is not true. I gave him a copy for reading according to the authentic wording of the letter, just as I sent the complete letter to Erard [of Tours], Wanilo [of Rouen], Vulfad [of Bourges], and the other archbishops of the lord Charles. I also reread that same letter at the synod held at Attigny.

What he says—that I ordered him to respond immediately—I did not say. I told him to read that copy and see what response he would make to it.

As for what he says—that he learned from another copy that several things were missing from the memorandum shown to him by me—I gave him a complete copy of the letter to read. In the memorandum that I had compiled, reread and distributed to the kings and bishops, I included whatever I considered necessary from that letter and from the letter sent by the apostolic lord [nothing of these matters appears here], and I sent the apostolic lord a copy of that memorandum together with my letter. I have here both the apostolic lord’s letter, the memorandum just mentioned, and the writings of our brother Hincmar. By these it can be proved that I speak the truth and that he deviates from the truth.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. That he boasts vainly that the excommunication imposed by him will be approved by the apostolic see

He also wrote in the memorandum that he sent me through his presbyter Clarentius:

“I was questioned at Attigny so insistently about the excommunication imposed by me in my parish. For the present I disclose only this: you assert that the excommunication was imposed without a hearing, contrary to apostolic teaching, and contrary to ecclesiastical truth. I imposed no excommunication other than the one I learned from your oral teaching ought to be imposed; and you ought not irrationally to rebuild what you have rightly destroyed. Indeed, I have learned that the excommunication was previously imposed with the authority of the apostolic see at Rome, and I declare that same see to be its author. It is in its interest both to judge the excommunication imposed by me and to decide concerning your absolution.”

To this I reply. Our earlier teachers said that there are certain nouns which cannot be declined in the feminine, such as *auctor* (“author”) and *cursor* (“runner”). This new teacher, who has recently devised what to say about the excommunication itself, declares that the apostolic see is its author. But he will not have me as the author of what he says against me: “that he imposed no other excommunication in his parish than the one he learned from my oral teaching ought to be imposed.”

And what follows immediately—“since I ought not irrationally to rebuild what I have rightly destroyed”—I affirm to be true. For by evangelical truth, by apostolic and canonical authority, and also by the teaching and decrees of the apostolic see, I destroyed his pernicious excommunication. I ought not, do not wish, and am not able to rebuild it irrationally.

But in saying that he imposed no other excommunication than one which he had learned was previously imposed “with the authority of the apostolic see at Rome”—that is, previously inserted, previously imposed, previously introduced—he has spoken far too boldly against heaven. It is therefore no wonder that his tongue has passed over into earthly matters, so that he could say of me, a sinner: “I imposed no other excommunication than the one I learned from your oral teaching ought to be imposed.”

Yet just as the apostolic see ought not, and cannot, be accused by us, so it does not need the excuse of our humility. Nevertheless, what we have heard from reliable informants concerning this matter, we may freely say with the permission of that see.

We have heard that Pope Nicholas, of holy memory, when the holy Roman Church was afflicted, ordered litanies to be held by the authority of the Old and New Testaments, with fasting, weeping, mourning, ashes, and sackcloth. But we have heard from no one that, because of the injuries inflicted upon him and upon that apostolic see, he ordered that infants placed in danger of death be denied baptism; that those who were dying and asking for final penance be denied penance; that communion of the viaticum be denied to those requesting it; or that burial be denied to the dead.

Nor do we believe that he is telling the truth when, in faulty and slanderous language, he says that the same see is the author of the pernicious excommunication he imposed. Far be it from us to believe that the apostolic see consented to the bonds of his impiety, as our brother Hincmarus improperly proclaims in his pernicious writing; still less that it was their author.

Through blessed Celestine it thunders apostolically throughout the whole world:

“Let us consider the sacramental prayers of priests, which, handed down from the apostles, are celebrated uniformly throughout the world and in every Catholic Church, so that the law of prayer may establish the law of belief. For when the bishops of holy peoples fulfill the embassy entrusted to them, they plead the cause of the human race before the divine mercy; and, with the whole Church groaning together with them, they ask and pray that faith may be granted to unbelievers.”

Thus he demonstrates that the Catholic Church ought to intercede with the Lord for all, so that he may transfer those rescued from the power of darkness into the kingdom of the Son of his love (Col. I), and make them from vessels of wrath vessels of mercy (Rom. IX); he who does not desire the death of a sinner, but that he be converted and live (Ezek. XXXIII); he who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, and desires no one to perish (II Tim. II).

Far be it from me, I say, that the holy apostolic see should be the author of such stubborn cruelty toward so many people, who could have been saved through baptism or reconciliation by the ministry of priests, and could have been freed from eternal destruction through communion of the viaticum, *mortibus reo* [text defective]. For it could not have happened that, in so extensive a parish as that one, which is especially subject to the municipality of Laon, during the approximately five days in which it had been bound in that manner, as I have explained—because I did not hasten to absolve it earlier through metropolitan solicitude and by evangelical, apostolic, canonical, and apostolic-see authority—many did not die without baptism and without the grace of communion. Whoever among them was saved owes it to the gift of the one who saves; whoever perished did so through the fault of the one who destroyed and of those who perished.

Nevertheless, although, as Saint Ambrose shows in his devotion to the faith of Valentinian (Book *On the Death of Valentinian*), and blessed Augustine demonstrates in his discussion, just as omnipotent goodness completed in the case of the thief crucified and believing and confessing together with the Lord what was lacking to him from the sacrament of baptism, so perhaps the faith of parents or sponsors who believed in their hearts, and even the faithful words of confession of infants seeking baptism but not obtaining it, together with the faithful petition, may have benefited those infants—through the gift of him whose Spirit, by which regeneration takes place, breathes where he wills; and who even before baptism infused himself into those about to be baptized, as is read in sacred history.

Likewise, concerning those who sought final penance and communion of the viaticum but could not obtain them because of his prohibition, his grace may have assisted them toward salvation—the grace of him to whom every believer says, “My groaning is not hidden from you” (Ps. XXXVII), and who says individually to them, “As soon as you groan, you will be saved.”

Yet he cannot be secure concerning their destruction if some departed without those sacraments by his order, so that he may not be strictly judged on that account.

And if he wishes to speak of the excommunication of Nortmannus, which he deceitfully elicited from the apostolic see by concealment, suggesting that Nortmannus had invaded property belonging to his church—property which, as his own writings show, he himself had granted either to the king or to Nortmannus as a benefice, or had bestowed as a benefice upon Nortmannus’s son—we believe that the same holy and most discerning see would answer: “Let it be done to you according to your faith” (Matt. IX); and, “By your words you will be condemned” (Matt. XII).

And blessed Augustine says in Sermon 7 on the Gospel of John:

“It is a rule of forensic law that whoever has lied in his petitions should not benefit from what he has obtained. For you said what you wished, and the one to whom you said it did not know whether it was true. He left you to be convicted by your adversary, so that if you were convicted of lying before the judge—since he could only grant the request, not knowing whether you had lied—you would there be deprived of the benefit of the rescript by which you had secured that rescript.”

We read that this rule is also found in the body of the Theodosian law.

Moreover, just as the Apostle rightly says concerning almighty God, who can do all things—namely, those things compatible with his omnipotence—“He cannot deny himself” (II Tim. II), so we say concerning that holy see: it cannot in any way contradict itself, especially in such manifest and important matters and in the unique remedies of human redemption and salvation. What it established irrefragably through Siricius, Innocent, Celestine, and Leo, in accordance with evangelical truth, apostolic tradition, and canonical authority, it will in no way allow anyone to oppose with impunity.

It is, as this same brother Hincmarus writes, in the interest of that see “to judge the excommunication imposed by me and to decide concerning your absolution.”

Nevertheless, as Saints Innocent, Boniface, and Leo promulgated from the canons of the Council of Sardica, major cases that concern the condition of the Churches and the concord of priests ought first to be examined among us in the fear of the Lord; matters that perhaps cannot be settled by our judgment should be referred for resolution; and, after our judgment, a full account of matters settled by our decision ought to be sent to the apostolic see, so that what has been decided among us justly and reasonably, according to ecclesiastical custom, may be strengthened by the judgment of that apostolic see.

Saint Ambrose likewise shows in his letter to Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, that he understood the sacred laws and canons to require that a report be sent to the apostolic see after judgment, and that one who has been legally summoned but has neglected to appear for judgment should not profit by the postponement of the sentence to be pronounced against him as a contumacious person because of his absence. He says:

“When the holy synod has entrusted the right of judgment to your unanimity and to our fellow priests from Egypt, you must again summon our brother Flavian, so that, if he persists in believing that he ought not to come, you may proceed—while preserving the statutes of the Council of Nicaea and also those of the Council of Capua—in such undisturbed peace for all that we may not appear to destroy what has been built. For if I destroy what I have built, I make myself a transgressor; and likewise if I build again what I destroyed.

“Let the grace of the peace granted among all be preserved, and nevertheless let the withdrawal of the other party be unable to frustrate the outcome. We think it proper to refer the matter to our holy brother, the priest of the Roman Church, since we presume that you will judge matters which cannot displease him either. Such a consultation will be useful for the sentence, and security for peace and quiet, if your council establishes what does not bring disagreement to our communion. Thus, when we too have received the series of your decisions and learn that what has been done has unquestionably been approved by the Roman Church, we may rejoice to obtain the fruit of such an examination.”

## CHAPTER XXIX. That he falsely accuses the archbishop of Rheims of having imposed a similar excommunication

Concerning this excommunication also, at Gundulf’s estate he sent me word through the venerable former archbishop Wenilo—as the lord Adventius and the other bishops who were present know—that I had informed him about what he had done in that excommunication: namely, saying that he possessed a certain estate in my parish and that, because he had asked the people of that estate to give their tithe to the church to which they ought to give it, I had excommunicated them. He had recorded how many infants had died there without baptism and how many people without communion, matters which he would not bring openly against me, lest I later reproach him with them. If he knew other evils concerning me, he would mention those also.

I therefore immediately sent word to him through that same Wenilo that he should bring against me these matters, and anything else he wished, whatever seemed appropriate to him. But in this matter he would not speak the truth, and he confessed that he had acted contrary to the canons, since, disregarding me, he had usurped the administration of the tithe in my parish.

Afterward I answered him in writing, a copy of which I have here. In it I stated that I had considered three things in what he said: that I had informed him of the excommunication he had imposed.

First, if a dispute between him and the clergy of the Church of Laon were to be examined—namely, whether the petition presented to me by those clergy, with the reasons contained in it, was or was not based on truth—it ought to admit no question once it had been confirmed by the testimony of his own confession.

Second, by suppressing in silence the good matters that I had pointed out to him and had caused to be pointed out, while charging me with having falsely informed him concerning the excommunication he had perpetrated, he confessed himself guilty, because he had knowingly acted wrongly. Accordingly, according to the decrees of Pope Hilary, he himself ought to dissolve his action, which was contrary to the rules. If he did not wish to do so, metropolitan authority ought to destroy it by the judgments of the canons and the decrees of the apostolic see, which cannot be overturned by any means.

Third, so that he might entangle me together with himself—if, as can happen to an unprepared mind, I had immediately failed to answer these false charges against me because I was unprepared and angered, and he could then boast that I had admitted something in the matter—he deliberately tried to throw a noose around himself through such a confession.

Returning evil for good, he did not, like the chief of the traitors of old, pretend to peace with a kiss that he did not possess in his heart. Instead, with the sword of his tongue drawn, he resolved to attack me openly and shamelessly, and, as though he had betrayed me, his patron, benefactor, and ordainer, he tried to hang himself in the noose of such a confession concerning such impieties.

But blessed is the Lord, who, according to his promise—“You will be hidden from the scourge of the tongue” (Job V)—helped and comforted me by delivering my soul from lying lips and a deceitful tongue. I immediately rejected the weapon of falsehood by answering it with the shield of truth.

I said these things, pierced by sorrow of heart, not driven by malice of spirit, knowing that many false charges had been brought against our Head and Savior, and that false witnesses had been produced against him.

For we read that mortal and criminal accusations were falsely brought against the pontiffs of the Roman see—Damasus, Sixtus, and Leo III—and against the pontiffs of other distinguished Churches, namely Athanasius of Alexandria, John of Constantinople, and Caecilian of Carthage, men distinguished by the holiness of their faith, their works, and the teaching of their knowledge. Similar accusations were brought against many other venerable bishops by envious men who wished to obtain their positions and the reputation of their good name, though they strove to possess none of their merit. These accusations were even carried as far as ecclesiastical tribunals and public hearings.

There are indeed people of this viperous wickedness who, although their own envy first gnaws at their minds, nevertheless think that they can conceal their iniquities if they take care to stain others with infamy by any means. Those holy men bore their accusations with the greatest patience and, with the Lord’s help, defeated them with the greatest steadfastness.

As Scripture says, I must imitate the faithfulness of their conduct by considering their end. I have discovered this and experienced it fully in his case: a madman often strikes no one harder than the physician who wishes to cure him.

I also wrote to him that I was greatly astonished where he had his senses when, before a man of such authority, wisdom, and religion as the lord Wenilo was, he spoke against me and caused this to come to the knowledge of many bishops—something which, if he had said it in a regular court, he could not have proved. In particular, since he had confessed himself guilty of this very matter, and by confessing that he had done such things—which, even if he had not confessed to having perpetrated them, he could not deny—he was unable to see that he had entangled himself.

Since it was false that he had said I excommunicated the people of the estate from that rural parish, and that infants without baptism and people without communion had died there during that excommunication, I immediately sent him word that, since I had been ordained bishop, baptism or communion of the viaticum had never been denied by me or by any of my fellow ministers to anyone in my parish. Everyone in my parish knows this, both clergy and laity, men and women.

## CHAPTER XXX. That he asked his uncle to burn the writings composed against him; again concerning the preceding slander, because of which he ought not to be admitted to accusation

[Col. 0617B]

(Book LV, chapter, c. 4.) Through the aforementioned venerable former archbishop Wenilo, he also sent me word that, if I would burn before others the writings that I had sent to him and to the church entrusted to him concerning the excommunication imposed by him upon his parish—the writings that he had with him there—and declare them null, confessing that I had acted contrary to reason and authority, he would be willing to make peace with me.

At that time I sent him an answer through the same archbishop and through the glorious bishop Adventius, together with other matters that occurred to me. Later, in writing—copies of which I have here—I repeated those matters and others, because he was unwilling to approach me at any gathering, or to give me the kiss of peace, as the lord king, the bishops, and the other distinguished and ordinary people who gathered there did; nor did he deign to address me with a single word. I have thought it worthwhile to repeat some of these matters here.

Among other things, I wrote to him asking how such a proposal could have entered his mind. (This letter is not extant.) For the devil, when speaking to our first parents, and also to our Redeemer and Savior, tempted them not by humiliation but by advancement and by the greed for elevation.

He, however, surpassing—in a manner of speaking—even the devil’s wickedness, and forgetting that it is written, “The wickednesses will be exterminated” (Ps. XXXVI), most foolishly tempted me by humiliation. He knew that what I had sent to him and to the church entrusted to him in those writings had been composed from evangelical truth and apostolic and prophetic authority, as well as canonical authority and the constitution of the apostolic see, just as that holy see had received it through the tradition of the most blessed apostles.

We read that those who betray and burn the holy Scriptures are counted among sacrilegious persons. Therefore, if I were to burn what I had written from the Gospel, the apostles, and the prophets, as well as from the sacred rules composed by the Spirit of God—namely, the measure of wheat purified from the chaff and weeds to be burned—what had been brought forth from the Lord’s granary at the proper time for him, for the church entrusted to him, and through the care subject to me; and if I were to deny the truth, then without doubt I would deny that I knew Christ, believed in him, and was a Christian—for Christ was foretold and revealed in those writings, and through them we came to know him, and he himself spoke them.

And if I were to burn and repudiate the sacred canons and the decrees of the Catholic Church, I would undoubtedly not only cast myself out of the episcopate, but would also make myself separated and alienated from the Catholic Church—that is, a schismatic and anathematized person—by public and ecclesiastical laws.

As Saint Leo the pope says in a letter to the emperor Leo, speaking also of himself (Letter 78):

“If, according to the Apostle, I build again the things that I destroyed, I make myself a transgressor, and subject myself to those punishments imposed by law, which not only the authority of the emperor Marcian, of blessed memory, but also I myself confirmed by my consent.”

[Col. 0618B]

Therefore, although he regarded me as weak, fragile, and feeble—as I truly am—to such an extent that he thought I could be dragged or enticed into doing these things by threats or the blandishments of promises, a bishop nevertheless ought not to have doubted the truth promised by the mouth of him who perfects strength in weakness:

“The Lord,” he says, “will give great strength to those who proclaim the word” (Ps. LXVII).

Nor ought a bishop to have offered a deadly drink to another bishop, however insignificant—namely, that I should burn the sacred utterances for his sake.

Although God in his grace preserved me from this, he who promised protection to those who believe in him, saying, “If they drink anything deadly, it will not harm them” (Mark XVI), blessed Gregory says:

“When they hear poisonous suggestions and are nevertheless not at all drawn into evil action, what they drink is indeed deadly, but it will not harm them” (Blessed Gregory, Homily 29 on the Gospels).
