Nevertheless, unless he repents of this most pernicious suggestion, he will suffer judgment for his undertaking.

“Sin,” says blessed Gregory, “is dissolved more slowly when it is strengthened by counsel. For unless the mind utterly despised eternal things, it would not perish through judgment in guilt” (Pastoral Rule, Book III, admonition 33).

Since the Apostle says, “Greed, which is the service of idols” (Col. III), and blessed Gregory demonstrates that our first parents were tempted and overcome through the advancement of greed, showing that greed concerns not only money but also elevation; and since greed is rightly so called when exalted status is sought beyond measure, I wrote to him, drawing on the words of blessed Augustine concerning the authority of sacred Scripture.

Augustine was speaking against the schismatic Donatists, who had separated themselves without cause from the structure of Catholic unity, asserting what they could not prove: that Caecilian had been ordained by traditors of the sacred Scriptures. I wrote so that he might recognize how grave a sin idolatry is, a sin which he appears to have committed through his ambition for elevation, since he wishes to be subject to no one while being unable to preside over everyone.

And since the burning of the divine utterances, to which he wished to lead me, is a still graver sin; and since schism is a most serious sin, by which he separated himself from our fraternal unanimity through his pernicious subscription, as I showed in his monstrous libel subscribed by himself and by the clergy of his parish—where certain subscribed statements are found to be contrary to evangelical truth, apostolic authority, and the decrees of the holy councils, approved by the assent of the universal Church and confirmed by the authority of the apostolic see—blessed Augustine says to the Donatists concerning these three matters (Augustine, *On Baptism*, Book II, chapter 6):

“Let us not bring forward a fraudulent balance on which we weigh whatever we wish and, according to our own judgment, say, ‘This is heavy; this is light.’ Rather, let us bring the divine balance from the holy Scriptures, as from divine treasures, and weigh in it what is heavier—or rather, let us not ourselves weigh, but recognize what has been weighed by the Lord who weighs.

“In that earlier time, when the Lord showed through fresh examples of punishment what former sins were to be avoided, idolatry was punished by the sword; the burning of the prophetic book by the slaughter of war and foreign captivity; and schism by the earth’s opening and burying its authors alive, while the rest were consumed by heavenly fire. Who, then, would doubt that the more serious crime was the one punished more severely?”

Since it was not enough for him to slander me by claiming that I had taught him by example to carry out such a wicked and destructive excommunication, unless he also now slandered me in writing by saying that he imposed no other excommunication than the one he had learned from my oral teaching ought to be imposed, I see that I must answer his false accusation from sacred authorities, lest, by remaining silent and seeming to consent, I be judged guilty together with him.

As is contained in the petition that the clergy of the Church of Laon presented to me, and as I demonstrated at the synod held before him at Attigny, he bound all the priests of his entire parish, so that none of them might exercise the priestly ministry there until he himself had again spoken with them orally or letters had been sent to them from the see of blessed Peter the apostle. He completely prohibited all of them from baptizing children, visiting the sick, reconciling with the viaticum those who sought penance, and burying the dead.

In his memorandum to me he wrote that he had imposed no other excommunication than the one he had learned from my oral teaching ought to be imposed. I declare this to be a lie.

Since it is clear that he committed those bonds of impiety, and since, if such acts can be crimes—as Saint Gregory shows that they can—they were committed by him criminally, it must be shown from sacred authorities whether a criminal person can accuse another and make him guilty of a crime.

The sacred laws received by the Catholic Church state that it has been established by right and law (Julian, Letter II, chapter 28):

“By a voluntary confession, a guilty person must not make another guilty, nor should credit be given against another to one who has confessed himself a criminal.”

Likewise:

“Credence must not be given against others to the confession of those accused of crimes, unless they have first proved themselves innocent; for the confession of an accused person against anyone whatsoever is dangerous and must not be admitted” (3, q. 5, chapter *Accusatores*).

The sacred canons also state (Council of Africa, chapter 130) that:

“Those whom the public laws do not admit to accuse public crimes must not be admitted to accusation.”

Whenever many crimes are brought against clergy by accusers, and they are unable to prove one of the charges with which they first proceeded, they must not be admitted to the others.

The sacred Theodosian laws likewise state (2, q. 7, chapter *Si quis episcopus*):

“If a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or any other minister of the Christian law in an inferior position is accused before bishops—if the matter ought not to be heard elsewhere—by any person, whether that person is a man of distinguished rank or of any other dignity who has undertaken this kind of blameworthy accusation, let him know that he must bring forward documentary proof. If anyone brings an unprovable charge against such persons, let him understand by the authority of this enactment that he will suffer damage to his own reputation, so that, through the loss of honor and diminished standing, he may learn that he may not with impunity plot against another’s shame, or even speak such charges” (2, q. 7, chapter *Si quis episcopus*).

The African council says (Council of Africa, chapter 129):

“All who are stained by marks of infamy must not be admitted to accusation, except in their own cases.”

Concerning a bishop who had falsely claimed that he had communicated with the Donatists, the same council also decreed (ibid., chapter 124):

“If it is proved that he lied about having shared in their communion, saying that he had communicated with those with whom it is established, while he knew that he had not communicated, he shall also lose the episcopate.”

[Col. 0620C]

Therefore let your fraternity distinguish and decide between me and him as follows: if I, although falsely, were to confess that I had taught or urged him to do such things, as he says, I ought to lose the episcopate as guilty of the crime; what does he deserve who falsely slanders me as not merely a participant but even the author of these impious excommunications?

For this reason the canons of the ancient Fathers also enacted, writing to bishops established throughout Gaul and in every province, as follows:

“Nor have we judged this matter, brothers, to be foreign to the usefulness of the Church: that you might know that whoever, under the rank of deacon, presbyter, or bishop, says that he has been polluted by a mortal crime must be removed from the aforesaid orders—guilty either by a true confession or by a false lie. For he cannot be absolved who has said of himself that he is the cause of death, when the same statement made about another would be punished; since anyone who is the cause of his own death is a greater murderer.”

No sound-minded person understands the statement in this canonical judgment—“Whoever under the rank of deacon, presbyter, or bishop says that he has been polluted by a mortal crime must be removed from the aforesaid orders”—as referring only to sexual immorality, impurity, or pollution of the flesh, since it is written:

“He has scattered the proud in the imagination of their hearts” (Luke I).

“God resists the proud” (I Peter V).

And the Gospel says:

“The things that come out of the heart defile a person” (Matt. XV).

Saint Gregory says:

“Through the guardianship of humility, the purity of chastity must always be preserved.”

He also says:

“Sometimes it is less serious to fall into bodily corruption than to sin in silent thought through deliberate pride. For the king of Babylon did not first become guilty of pride when he reached words of pride. Indeed, even earlier, when he remained silent concerning his pride, he heard the sentence of reproach from the prophetic mouth. For the strict Judge first saw invisibly what he later condemned by striking publicly. Therefore he transformed him into an irrational animal, separated him from human society, and joined him, with an altered mind, to the beasts of the field (Dan. IV), so that by a strict and just judgment the man who had thought himself greater than other humans might cease even to be a human being.”

Scripture also says:

“The beginning of every sin is pride” (Ecclus. X).

Pride is the mother of disobedience and the queen of all vices. Through it the archangel fell from heaven and became the devil, who is king over all the children of pride (Job XLI).

No one who understands the matter is unaware that pride is a mortal sin. We also know that disobedience is a mortal sin—the disobedience because of which humanity was expelled from paradise and of which this brother is accused.

Scripture says of it:

“To resist is like the sin of divination, and to refuse to obey is like the crime of idolatry” (I Kings XV).

Therefore Saint Gregory says:

“Obedience alone possesses the merit of faith; without it, anyone is proved to be an unbeliever, even if he appears to be faithful.”

## CHAPTER XXXI. That he tries in vain to excuse the excommunication imposed by him

[Col. 0621C]

Brother Hincmarus confesses in his memoranda that he imposed the excommunication in question. He cannot deny that it was deadly, directed toward the destruction of many and the salvation of no one, and imposed by him without any discernment.

He dealt with it sufficiently to enable himself to conceal both his slander against the apostolic see—by saying that the same holy see had previously imposed that excommunication and was its author—and his false accusations against me, as though I had shown him by example that it ought to be imposed and taught him verbally to carry it out, so that he could not be reproved for having imposed it destructively.

But the purpose and reward for which he imposed it he clearly reveals in the memorandum sent to me through Clarentius, “to excuse his excuses in sins, so that he might always complete his sins.” He says:

“Pope Alexander teaches at the end of his letter that one must consider not so much what is done as the spirit in which it is done. Indeed, when this has been examined with the greatest precision both in you and in me, the benefit of justice will immediately become clear.”

He continues until this statement:

“Do not think that I speak on my own behalf as though I had been provoked by a personal injury. For, with God as my witness, I write to you rather to prevent harm to the ecclesiastical order, as it is written: ‘Do not give place to the devil’” (Eph. IV).

By these words he plainly shows that he does not wish the metropolitan authority to have any power, in accordance with the canons, to correct that man’s excesses. Anyone who reads or hears them should understand whom he identifies as a violator of the decrees of the apostolic see and as an offender against all laws, both divine and human; and against whom the prophetic “woe” hangs, because he teaches things by which such actions might in any way be presumed by anyone. He also plainly demonstrated in the preceding chapter whom he declares to have transgressed the sacred religion itself, when he called me his betrayer.

He also gave a corrupt interpretation of the words of Saint Alexander. For immediately after the same saint says, “Not so much what is done must be considered as the spirit in which it is done,” he continues:

“Thus also it is said that the Lord looked upon Abel’s offering, and not upon Cain’s, because he paid more attention to the spirit of the one offering than to the things offered.”

Hence Blessed Gregory says:

“God Almighty does not accept a gift that is offered with a heart bound in wickedness, because everything given to God is weighed according to the mind of the giver, since what spirit motivates such actions is unknown to those nearby. Thus, before God, a pure intention commends true goodness, for a bad tree does not produce good fruit. The tree is the human being, and the fruit is his works.”

In manifest evils, however, there is no need to investigate the intention of the heart, because it is not a good tree that produces bad fruit. The Apostle says: “The works of the flesh are manifest” (Gal. 5); after listing them, he adds the fruit of the Spirit.

Brother Hincmarus therefore, in excusing himself for his harmful excommunication, displayed an inappropriate interpretation of the Lord’s command concerning our first parents—not humility contrived by any sort of feigning, but naked pride. For, as blessed Gregory says (*On the Penitential Psalm*, Psalm 3):

“The marks of true humility are that each person recognizes his own iniquity and makes known what he has recognized by a confession of the mouth [variant: and erases what he has confessed by the satisfaction of penance]. By contrast, it is a common vice of the human race both to commit sin by falling and to defend the sin committed by denying it, and to multiply the sin once convicted of it by defending it [variant: and to multiply what has been publicly proclaimed by defending it].”

Similarly, violently twisting the Apostle’s statement to suit his own meaning, he says: “The law was established for transgressors” [Col. 0622D]. According to the meaning he imposed upon it, this could be expounded as though he were saying:

“I transgressed without fear; I set up a law against the law, the law of excommunication, which the king would fear and would not dare apply to me. While preaching that one must not steal, I was not afraid to steal; while condemning idols, I committed sacrilege.”

Then he cites Gregory’s words (*Book 7, Letter 6*): “He who does not correct what must be cut away commits it.” As though he were openly saying:

“I committed in many people the things that had to be cut away in me, by excommunicating them, so that by this act no one would dare correct what had to be cut away in me.”

Finally he adds: “With God as my witness, I write to you rather to guard against harm to the ecclesiastical order.” By these words he clearly reveals with what intention [Col. 0623A] he carried out that excommunication: namely, he called the correction of his own irrationality “harm to the ecclesiastical order,” so that the king would fear the excommunication and would not dare approach him while he was rebelling against the king; and so that he himself, who did not restrain himself out of fear of God and did not fear being constrained by any human being, might carry out the impulses of his own will as freely as he wished.

Finally he added: “I write to you to guard against harm to the ecclesiastical order, as it is written: ‘Do not give place to the devil.’” When he wished to hurl this testimony of the Apostle at another person with not an apostolic but an apostate meaning, he turned it back upon himself. The Apostle himself plainly demonstrates this in his Letter to the Ephesians, saying: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ps. 4). “Let not the sun go down upon your anger. Do not give place to the devil” (Eph. 4).

“Through anger,” says Gregory, “the light of truth is lost, because when anger brings the darkness of confusion upon the mind, God hides from it the ray of his knowledge.”

Thus he gave place within himself to the devil, the prince of darkness—that is, of iniquities—when, through anger, he brought the darkness of confusion upon his mind and thereby concealed from himself the ray of the knowledge of God, which is light. He could no longer see how great an evil he was not afraid to perpetrate in his harmful excommunication, for which, while excusing himself, he accuses himself. He transgressed ecclesiastical, indeed divine, laws and gave place to the devil, so that he might seize dead men without baptism and communion, lest anyone dare to have the opportunity to approach him against his will.

Nevertheless, according to his own understanding, he placed the same saying of the Apostle here with an adulterated meaning. For this reason, many are recorded as having been condemned in synods.

## CHAPTER XXXII. A large part of the letter of Hincmarus of Laon concerning the subscription he made at the synod at Attigny is reported.

And in the memorandum that he sent me on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July, he writes as follows:

“Because you have often reproached me concerning the subscription,”

and the rest, which may be found among the letters of Hincmarus of Laon, volume 124, up to the words, “By God’s favor I shall never do this.”

Hincmarus of Reims continues:

Against this it is written: “A foolish son says that he is just, but he does not cleanse his conduct.” After other intervening material, he returned to this subscription of his, saying:

“And even if there were something in that subscription that might perhaps be intolerable …”

The reader will find the rest in the place cited above.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Archbishop Hincmarus’s preceding objections are dispelled by a true account of what happened.

Let us examine his words one by one. He says that at that synod the subscription itself was first extorted from him by royal authority and afterward fraudulently by me. By God’s grace, the lord king has age, wisdom, power, and position with which to answer for himself; and concerning this action he has many truthful witnesses, both archbishops and bishops.

What he says afterward—that it was fraudulently extorted from him by me—is untrue. For when the synod had been adjourned that day, to convene again on the following day, after the lord king had left that house, and while certain bishops in the same house were speaking with their respective brothers as circumstances required, I was standing beside a certain window and speaking with Brother Odo. Archbishop Frotarius and Bishop Aeneas came to me and said in Odo’s presence that Brother Hincmarus wished to subscribe to a written declaration concerning his obedience to the lord king, and that we should be at peace with one another, as father and son, and archbishop and bishop, ought to be.

I received this gladly. They brought him to me from another window, beside which Hincmarus was standing with other bishops. Hincmarus himself asked that he be allowed to speak with me privately, alone. I withdrew with him beside the wall of the house, and he said to me that he had no hesitation about the subscription as far as I was concerned, but that he was concerned about the man who would succeed me in that metropolitan see.

I replied that he himself should dictate the written declaration as he wished. He asked me to dictate it. We returned together to the window beside which Aeneas and Odo were standing. I told Odo to take his tablets and record in them the written declaration to which Hincmarus was to subscribe. Odo recorded it as we dictated it together at that time.

I told him that he should change, remove, or add anything he wished there; and that is what was done. I told Odo to bring the written document on the following day, so that Hincmarus could subscribe to it in the synod.

Hincmarus replied that he was suffering from a fever and wished to leave at once in order to have blood removed. I ordered Odo to go to the king’s chancellor, obtain parchment and an inkpot from him, and write it quickly.

Meanwhile I told Aeneas, whom Hincmarus was then obeying, that it would be better for Hincmarus to wait until the following day. At Aeneas’s persuasion Hincmarus agreed. On the following day he came to the synod and made his declaration according to what was contained in the document. When Odo offered him the pen, he freely subscribed to that same document before everyone present, as was then evident, and handed it with his own hand to the king and to me.

At that point the lord king gave him the kiss of peace, and I did so after him.

On the following day, before I entered the house in which the bishops were to assemble, Bishop Harduicus, speaking with me in another house, told me in the strictest confidence that Hincmarus was sending me a small document and asking me to subscribe to it. He secretly gave it to me, and I received it and put it in my bosom. I did not read it until afterward, when I was on the road returning to my lodging.

In the presence of Bishop Odulfus, who was traveling with me, I read that document for the first time. After that neither Hincmarus nor anyone else had any discussion with me about it. Indeed, Fredericus, the priest of Harduicus, never had any discussion with me at all concerning that document.

And by such fraud, as you have heard, I extorted that same subscription from him.

[Col. 0625A] What he says—that he carried that declaration to his house before subscribing to it—is untrue. For after Bishop Odo had recorded it on his tablets, Hincmarus did not see it in written form until the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the third indiction, when he subscribed to that declaration in the synod before all the bishops who were present and before the lord king; he handed it to the lord king and to me, and in the synod I gave him a copy of it.

On the following day, that is, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, Archbishop Harduicus gave me the document sent to me by Hincmarus in the manner I have already described. Afterward, for as long as we remained at Attigny, Hincmarus said nothing to me about it, either orally or in writing.

Even if he had said something to me about it, I would have answered him from James: “You ask, and you do not receive, because you ask wrongly” (Jas. 4). For it is unjust and irrational that an archbishop who has departed from the sacred canons should satisfy, by a written declaration and subscription, a suffragan bishop who has exceeded his authority and who was ordained by him. For just as, according to Scripture, the lesser is blessed by the greater, so plainly the lesser, not the greater, is judged, bound, and released by the greater, as is also demonstrated in the decrees of Blessed Gelasius.

Concerning what follows there:

“For, as I have already written to you, you summoned me to that synod to answer the letters of the lord apostolic. When I came to it, you did not allow me to enter it; instead, outside the doors, you ordered me to subscribe to the privilege of your see.”

Let him say through whom I ordered this outside the doors; and let him show how it can be true that, when he came to the synod, I did not allow him to enter it. For after he came to Attigny, whenever we were in synod, he himself was present. In his presence, the matters that I had once and again decreed against him, from evangelical truth and from the decrees of the apostolic see, for dissolving his impious bonds, were read aloud.

And in the synod, in his presence and in the hearing of all, Bishop Otulfus said that he often declared—as did the other bishops who heard him with him—that the things being read were not worth a full mouthful of water.

He says that he replied that he had never done anything against my privilege, which I had received in the dignity of the metropolitan city. You judge whether, in the matters you have heard, he did in any way act against metropolitan privilege.

He says that he appealed to the apostolic see. Let him say who contradicted him so that he did not pursue his appeal.

He says that the lord king was incited by my contrivance—although on the previous day he had said that, for his part, he distrusted nothing in him—and afterward threatened him. The lord king’s reply will suffice.

He says that his men were compelled to give surety because they had followed him to the village of Pauliacum. If they gave surety because they had followed him irrationally to Pauliacum, he cannot deny that he was the author of their irrational conduct.

He says that, even if there were something in that subscription that might perhaps be intolerable, Blessed Pope Alexander would extend his hand to him. Let us see how the decree of Saint Alexander agrees with this and how it extends a hand to him. For in his letter to all the orthodox serving the Lord throughout the various provinces (Letter 1), he says:

“Something else has also been brought to this holy see, something shameful to say and hostile not only to the priestly name but to every Christian name. Namely, certain bishops or priests are compelled by fear, or forced by violence, or deceived by fraud to write and strengthen with their own hands, and to recite and confess before the people, declarations of their confession in a direction contrary to what they ought, or concerning matters that they have not demanded for themselves, or—what is worse—concerning the sects of another’s error [variant: concerning a sect of another’s error].

Some are said to be shut up in prisons and workhouses, so that, terrified by these snares, the priests of the Lord may at least deviate and favor the wishes of others.”

After inserting many chapters, he returns to this matter and says the following, which Hincmarus placed in his memorandum in a corrupt manner:

“Likewise, if any writings of this kind have in any way been extorted from such persons through fear, fraud, or violence, or if they have been written or confirmed by them through whatever ingenuity so that they might free themselves, we decree that this shall bring them no prejudice or harm whatsoever. Nor shall we ever, with the authority of the lord and of the holy apostles and their successors, permit them to suffer any disgrace, accusation, or separation from their possessions.

But confession in such matters must be made not under compulsion but voluntarily, as he himself testifies who says: ‘For out of the heart proceed murders, adulteries, fornications, blasphemies’ (Matt. 15), and the rest that pertain to these things. Nor must one consider only what is done, but the spirit in which it is done.”

And shortly afterward:

“Thus also it is said that the Lord looked upon Abel’s offerings, and not upon Cain’s, because he paid more attention to the spirit of the one offering than to the things offered.”

Let us compare Blessed Alexander’s words with Hincmarus’s declaration and subscription. Alexander says that certain bishops or priests are compelled by fear, forced by violence, or deceived by fraud to write and strengthen with their own hands, and recite and confess before the people, declarations of their confession in a direction contrary to what they ought, or concerning matters that they have not demanded for themselves, or—what is worse—the sects of another’s error.

Hincmarus made his declaration and subscription in this form:

“I, Hincmarus, bishop of the Church of Laon, from now and henceforth shall be faithful and obedient to my lord and senior, King Charles, according to my ministry, just as a man ought to be to his senior and a bishop rightly ought to be to his king. And, according to the privilege of Hincmarus, metropolitan of the province of the Church of Reims, in accordance with the sacred canons and the decrees of the apostolic see promulgated from the sacred canons, I profess that I will obey, to the best of my knowledge and ability, and I subscribe.”

Nothing is contained in this declaration and subscription concerning things that ought not to be observed. Nor does anything there refer to a confession in a direction contrary to what he ought, or to matters not demanded for himself, or to the sects of another’s error. Nor did anyone shut him up in prison or a workhouse so that, terrified by these snares, the priest of the Lord might deviate and favor alien wishes.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Continuation of the same refutation.

Concerning what follows in the same place:

“If one must not consider only what is done, but the spirit in which it is done, no one who knows even a little can be unaware of the spirit in which I did that. Indeed, at that time I would have done much more so that I might free my men, who were innocent and were being oppressed on my account.”

The Apostle Paul says: “The law was not established for the just, but for the unjust” (1 Tim. 1). Hence Saint Leo, writing to Ravennius (Letter 90), says:

“The law is said not to have been established for the just because he fulfills the rule of its command by the judgment of his will.”

If his men who followed him to Pauliacum gave surety according to law for what they had committed against the law, they were not innocent; and if the lord king ordered them to be punished as guilty, we dare say that he acted against the royal ministry.

If royal judges punished innocent persons as though they were guilty, contrary to the law, they were transgressors of the law. If arbiters [printed: arbitros] judged innocent persons as though they were guilty, they deserved to lose the authority and office of judgment.

Since neither he nor any of his men then protested that they were suffering prejudice in judgment; and since Saint Gregory often decreed that judgments should be settled according to the laws and canons; and since, according to the interpretation of the law of Honorius and Theodosius, it is said:

“Whoever did not raise an objection in court while his adversary was present cannot afterward initiate another action concerning the same matter. He tramples upon the law who, against the law and against what has been legally adjudicated—even in writing—revives the litigation and condemns anew,”

and since Hincmarus cannot prove that private individuals punished or judged his men contrary to the law, it is clear that, if his men legally gave surety, they had committed an offense against the law and were not innocent.

And he who [supply: says that he] brought them along so that they would follow him in committing the act for which they gave surety—men who were proved guilty—cannot rightly be called innocent; nor can a guilty man, by his testimony, make guilty men innocent.

[Col. 0627D] Concerning his statement that Saint Gregory wrote that a confession had been extorted from Bishop Pompeius “by torture and starvation”: in that synod we saw him sufficiently and more than sufficiently corpulent and confessing; we neither saw nor heard that he had been tortured or killed by starvation in order to make him declare and subscribe.

Concerning his statement, “Certainly, if an extorted confession does no harm, an extorted subscription does no harm,” I think that two hundred and fourteen holy bishops of the Council of Carthage are now crying out against him from heaven, and will cry out in the divine judgment. They decreed that “if anyone in any matter acts against his own declaration or subscription, he shall deprive himself of his office.”

And if he says in his own person, “Certainly, if an extorted confession does no harm, an extorted subscription does no harm,” then, unless he does penance, I believe that among other matters he will be judged by those same holy bishops for this lie.

He will also be condemned by blessed Gregory, who wrote to the patrician Theoctista (Book 3, Letter 39):

“If there are those who say that, when someone has anathematized himself under compulsion, he is not held by the bond of the anathema, they themselves testify that they are not Christians. For they think that they can dissolve the bonds of the holy Church by empty efforts; and consequently they do not regard as true the absolution of the holy Church, which she grants to the faithful, if they do not consider her bonds effective.

It is not necessary to dispute with them at length, because they must be despised and anathematized in every respect; and by the very means through which they think they deceive the truth, they are bound more truly in their sins.”

And somewhat earlier:

“If some, under compulsion, were to say that they anathematized themselves concerning the matters of which they were accused, they would in no way be held by the bond of the anathema. If there are those who most certainly think or maintain such things, there is no doubt that they are not Christians. I, together with all Catholic bishops and the universal Church, anathematize them, because they think and speak contrary to the truth.”

He also falsely attributes other lies to me; and concerning the writing itself he says certain things against which it would take too long for me to write and for you to hear.

## CHAPTER XXXV. He did not answer when summoned a third time to the synod, and therefore must be treated as contumacious.

Behold, your Fraternity has heard how false the writing of Brother Hincmarus is, and in how many matters. As the sacred laws say—and as has been established in every case—the person who produces a document must affirm it; for if the one who produced the document does not establish its truth, he must be held liable for falsification.

In the Council of Ephesus, the Council of Chalcedon, and also the Fifth and Sixth Councils, we read that persons convicted by their own writings and subscriptions, without any accusation or testimony from others being required, were condemned according to the sacred laws. For the sacred laws say that anyone may be convicted by written documents or witnesses.

We also find that those summoned a third time who refused to come—how much more so after so many and such serious admonitions—were deprived of every priestly office even in their absence.

We also read that John, bishop of Antioch, the bishop of the third see, because he sent writings containing blasphemies against Cyril, archbishop of the second see, was summoned a third time and, because he did not attend the Council of Ephesus, excommunicated there.

Likewise Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria of the second see, was deprived of every priestly ministry by the most blessed Leo himself through his representatives at the same great Synod of Chalcedon. Among other charges, he had acted against canonical order and ecclesiastical discipline, and had repeatedly presented at the council many writings full of iniquities against his own archbishop, the most holy and wise Leo of the first see, great Rome, repeatedly trampling upon the ecclesiastical canons. He was also summoned a third time, and because he scorned to present himself at the synod, we read that he was condemned in his absence.

Concerning the threefold admonition, the sacred laws say that anyone who has been summoned before a judge by three authoritative citations, or has been called to the judge by three edicts—or by one peremptory edict in place of all three, that is, one that extinguishes the case—and who refuses to present himself before the judge by whom he was notified, may be judged as contumacious.

Indeed, proceedings cannot be reopened by appeal whenever judgment has been given against a contumacious person; against a sentence issued against the contumacious, one may neither appeal nor bring the matter back for rehearing.

Hence Saint Gregory writes to Maximus, bishop of Salona (Book 5, Letter 103):

“Act in such a way that you no longer introduce delays in coming, lest your very absence make you more liable to the things being alleged. In the meantime, because of the crimes alleged—which you avoid purging—and also because of the fault of disobedience, may it compel us, as a council, to render a harsher judgment against you as a contumacious person [variant: lest this matter compel us to render a judgment against you as contumacious].”

And Saint Coelestine wrote to Nestorius concerning the threefold summons (Letter 5):

“Therefore, although Brother Cyril asserts that you have already been summoned by his second letters [variant: by his letters], I want you to understand that after his first and second letters, and after this correction of ours, which is evidently now the third, you have been completely separated from the whole body and assembly of Christians—unless the things wrongly said are corrected, unless you return to that path which Christ testifies to be his own [variant: which testifies that Christ is himself].”

And again in the same letter:

“I shall certainly pursue the enemies of my Lord as his faithful servant, since the Prophet declares that he hates them with a perfect hatred (Ps. 138). I am warned again by another speaker not to spare them. Whom, then, should I regard, to whom should I preserve any honor, when the matter concerns the removal of the very cause of all my hope? [variant: whom should I regard here?]”

These are the words of the Lord himself in the Gospel, in which he says that one must not place before him father, mother, children, or any other relationship (Matt. 10). For there is often a kind of piety from which impiety is born, when, because the affection of the flesh prevails, bodily love is placed before that love which is God.

And Saint Ambrose, on Psalm 118, says:

“There is a just mercy, and there is also an unjust mercy. Thus it is written in the law concerning a certain person: ‘He shall not show him mercy.’ And in the Book of Kings you read that Saul incurred offense because he showed mercy to Agag, king of the enemies, whom the divine sentence had forbidden to be spared (1 Kings 15).

If someone, moved by the pleas of a robber’s children and softened by the tears of his wife, thinks that a man whose desire is robbery ought to be released, does he not hand over the innocent to destruction when he frees one who is plotting the destruction of many? If he restrains the sword, he dissolves the bonds. Why does he loosen the exile? Why does he not, by whatever more merciful means he can, take away the robber’s opportunity for robbery, when he could not extort his will?

Again, between two persons—namely, an accuser and a defendant—whose lives are at equal risk, the one if he proves his case and the other if he is not convicted by the accuser: if the judge does not follow what justice requires, but, while pitying the defendant, condemns the one who proves his case, or, while favoring an accuser who cannot prove his case, condemns the innocent, this cannot be called just mercy.

Even in the Church, where mercy is especially appropriate, the rule of justice must be observed with the greatest care, lest someone excluded from communion, by a brief and temporary tear—or even by more abundant weeping—extort from the priest, through his leniency, the communion that he ought to seek for a very long time.

When he pardons one who is unworthy, does he not provoke many others to the contagion of falling? For ease in granting pardon gives an incentive to sin.

This has been said so that we may know that, according to the word of God and according to reason, mercy must be distributed to those who owe a debt.

If a physician finds an internal wound covered by a scab and, although he ought to cut out the disease of the ulcer lest it spread farther, is moved by the patient’s tears to cover with medicines what ought to be opened with the knife, is this not useless mercy, if, because of the brief pain of cutting or burning, the whole body wastes away and the use of life perishes?

Therefore the priest too must rightly cut away a wound from the whole body of the Church, like a good physician, lest it spread farther, and must expose the poison of the hidden crime, not nourish it. Otherwise, while he refuses to exclude one person, he may make many worthy of exclusion from the Church.

The Apostle therefore rightly exhorts us by the divine example, saying: ‘Consider therefore the goodness and severity of God: severity toward those who have fallen, but goodness toward you, if you remain in goodness’ (Rom. 11).”

And Saint Gregory, in the *Pastoral Rule* (Part 3, chapter 1, admonition 23), says:

“When we imprudently surround ourselves with the friendships of the wicked, we are bound by their faults. Thus Jehoshaphat, who is praised with so many commendations for his former life, is rebuked because, through friendship with King Ahab, he nearly perished. The Lord says to him through the prophet: ‘You give help to the impious and join yourself in friendship to those who hate the Lord; therefore you deserved the wrath of the Lord. But good works were found in you, because you removed the sacred groves from the land of Judah’ (2 Chron. 19).”

And in a homily on the Gospel:

“It is a serious matter when carnal affections strike at the mind’s intention and obscure its vision. Yet those who carry the ark of God in their mind do not turn aside from the straight path.”

And lest anyone say that Blessed Coelestine wrote to the heretic Nestorius concerning a third admonition, one must consider what Pope Hilarus says (Letter 2):

“For one does not offend less against the sanctions of the holy traditions than one rushes into an injury against the Lord himself.”

Such a presumptuous person, who stubbornly offends against the sanctions of holy traditions, must not be counted among Catholics but must be condemned with the schismatics. For, as it is written in the decrees of the apostolic see, whoever gives assent to a schismatic cannot deny that he himself is a schismatic.

Even if all the priests and the whole world should give their assent, condemnation involves those who consent; the consent does not absolve the transgression. The crime is not diminished but strengthened when what was private becomes general. God judged this in the case of everyone when he destroyed the sinful world by a universal flood.

Blessed Gelasius agrees with this in his decrees, as I could plainly demonstrate from his words here if I were not avoiding excessive length.

## Conclusion, showing that judgment may be rendered notwithstanding an appeal.

All the matters written above, as I have often stated, I have assembled not on account of injuries done to me, but in defense of the dignity of the metropolitan see entrusted to me, against Brother Hincmarus. I have not collected the sacred laws and canons in order to seek judgment against him in matters of my own, but to show the character and magnitude of his excesses and of my admonitions, and the constitutions—both numerous and weighty—against which he obstinately displayed contempt.

Let your unanimity, pleasing to God, discern all this, read aloud before it, with vigilant judgment. Although priests may not be ignorant of the canons, his error would nevertheless have been lighter if he had transgressed through ignorance than it is now, since knowingly and deliberately, with counsel and intent, he has become a transgressor through contumacy of the sacred rules whose protection and observance he confirmed by his declaration and subscription.

He is therefore bound by a double guilt: he is plainly shown to have acted not only against the decrees of the venerable Fathers but also against his own decrees.

Whether, then, the sentence pronounced with God as mediator ought to strike him, or whether it ought to absolve him if he truthfully acknowledges his fault and humbly begs for mercy—while the statutes of the holy councils and the decrees of the pontiffs of the apostolic see promulgated from those same sacred canons remain intact, and while in every respect the privilege of the first and apostolic see and the right of the metropolitan see of Reims are preserved—I commit this, as far as I am concerned, to the counsel and judgment of your unanimity.

For my part, I follow the words of Blessed Coelestine to Bishop Cyril concerning Nestorius (Coelestine, Letter 10, in Baronius, year 431):

“I strive for the peace of the Catholic Church; I strive for the salvation of the one who is perishing, if only he wishes to acknowledge his sickness. We say this so that we may not perhaps seem to fail the one who wishes to correct himself [variant: wishes to be corrected].

For if, while we wait, he adds thorns to himself, then, while the previous statutes remain in force, let him receive the fruit of his own judgment; let him gather what he has sown in the devil’s furrow, not through our counsel, but with himself as the author of his own destruction. He proves [variant: Let him prove] that we are not swift-footed to shed blood, since he recognizes that a remedy has also been offered to him.”

I say this without prejudging your deliberation: whether, in accordance with these words of Blessed Coelestine, he should be absolved if he truthfully acknowledges his fault and humbly begs for mercy, or whether he ought to be struck down because he has remained for so long obstinately contemptuous of the sacred rules.

For just as we must not depart, through negligence or presumption, from rules established concerning certain and manifest matters in which nothing is doubtful or obscure to us, as Leo decreed when writing to Anastasius (Letter 84), so, concerning matters for which we possess definitive sentences promulgated by the holy Fathers—sentences that cannot be overturned by any reasoning—we must not undertake a new discussion or await a new counsel.

*(Book LV, chapter 34.)*

Nor should the apostolic see be troubled by inquiries, as Saint Innocent writes to the bishops of Macedonia (Letter 27):

> “When I had repeatedly caused [the matter] to be brought forward again,” he says, “I perceived that an injury was being done to the apostolic see, to which the report had been sent as to the head of the Churches, since its judgment was still being called into question.”

And to Felix, bishop of Nuceria (Letter 3):

> “We were astonished that a prudent man wished to seek counsel about matters that are known to all by certain reasoning.”

And Saint Zosimus (Letter 1):

> “Let anyone who, setting aside the authority of the Fathers and of the apostolic see, has neglected this know that he must be judged more strictly by us; and let him have no doubt that the standing of his office will not remain secure if he thinks that, after so many prohibitions, this may be attempted with impunity. For whatever is repeatedly usurped after being forbidden is done out of a desire to insult.”

And Saint Celestine (Letter 11):

> “For what matter worthy of preservation will remain with us if the rule of the decretal constitutions is broken, at the pleasure of certain persons, by permitting license to the people?”

And again:

> “What we do not correct by the authority of admonition alone, we must necessarily punish with a severity appropriate to the rules.”

And Leo (Letter 1):

> “Therefore we command that all the decretal constitutions, both of blessed memory Innocent and of all our predecessors, which have been promulgated concerning ecclesiastical orders and the disciplines of the canons, be so carefully observed by Your Dilection that, if anyone violates them, he should know that pardon will henceforth be denied him.”

And Gelasius (Letter 11):

> “It is sufficiently unworthy for anyone, whether a pontiff or one of the subsequent orders, to reject this observance, which he sees the See of Blessed Peter teaching; and it is entirely fitting that the whole body of the Church should agree with itself in observing what it sees prevailing there, where the Lord established the primacy of the entire Church.”

And again:

> “There was no need for a new synod, since the constitution of old sufficiently prescribed this form.”

And again:

> “It is manifest that he never yielded, whatever necessity compelled him, but rashly violated anew what had been salutarily established.”

And Saint Gregory to Sergius the defensor (Letter 10):

> “If you were a human being, or possessed any discernment [variant: discretion], you ought to have been such a guardian of regular discipline that you would correct by punishment, before their report reached us, the things that are unlawfully committed there.”

And shortly afterward:

> “For if in this matter you should in any way prove negligent or slow, know that you will be punished with the utmost severity, so that by the punishment cutting through [variant: revealing] the matter, you may come to know what you do not know through yourself.”

And Lord Pope Adrian, in the letter most recently sent, as you have heard, says:

> “We have learned from the report of the faithful that Your Fraternity, not exercising the requisite vigor in the province of Rheims, allows many matters most deserving of correction to grow strong among your comprovincials. For this reason we rouse your negligence by these apostolic words, so that, according to the rules of the venerable canons, you may synodically cut away the vices of all your comprovincials—while preserving the privilege of the holy Roman Church—in such a way that you may not deserve to suffer, before God and our judgment, the loss of your privilege.”

And since Brother Hincmar has often appealed to the apostolic see irregularly—not in a canonical judgment, nor for certain causes, but because of the impulses of his own mind—and has neglected to pursue his appeal, even though it was irregular: if he now wishes to appeal regularly, the judgments of the laws and canons must be carried out humbly and moderately, so that he may both eat the fruit of his own way and be filled with his own counsels, while the apostolic see is honored according to the sacred canons, as is fitting, and we do not deserve to be reproached for dissolving regular discipline.

For Constantine Augustus decreed the following concerning appeals to Catulinus:

> “Protracted delays and appeals that are rather evasions than appeals should not be admitted. For just as assistance ought not to be denied to those who appeal properly, so it is not right that properly conducted proceedings should be delayed for those who appeal frivolously against persons who have been justly judged.”

And according to the interpretation of the law of Valentinian, Valens, and Gratian Augustus addressed to Claudius, the law says this: Bishop Cronopius had been condemned by many bishops, and had attempted, before judgment, to suspend by an appeal the sentence that was being pronounced; since that sentence had been justly delivered, he ought not to have appealed from it. It says that he was condemned in that matter to a heavy fine, namely fifty pounds of silver. Nevertheless, that amount of the fine was ordered not to benefit the treasury but to be distributed to the poor.

Thus the apostolic see will determine whether the appealing bishop has a good cause, as the Council of Sardica decreed (canon 3):

> “If any bishop has been judged in any case and thinks that he has a good cause, so that the council may be renewed, if it pleases you, let us honor the memory of the holy apostle Peter, so that those who examined the case may write to Julius, the Roman bishop. If he judges that the judgment should be renewed, let it be renewed, and let him appoint judges. But if he determines that the case is such that what has been done should not be reopened, whatever he decrees shall be confirmed.”

And in canons 4 and 7 the procedure for a bishop’s appeal, after episcopal judgment, to the apostolic see is set forth. Innocent, Boniface, and Leo promulgated this same procedure most explicitly in their decretals, on the basis of those same sacred canons.

Therefore Gelasius also writes (Letter 11):

> “We are confident that no one who is truly a Christian now remains ignorant that, for every synodical constitution approved by the consent of the universal Church, no see ought to carry it out more than the first see, which both confirms every synod by its authority and preserves it by continual moderation—on account, namely, of the primacy which the blessed apostle Peter received from the Lord’s own voice and which, with the Church following, he has always held and still holds.”

The apostolic see confirmed this Sardican synod through Hosius of Corduba, Gentius of Capua, and Calepodius of Naples, its vicars; and, with the Church following, it has always held and still holds it confirmed.

## Sentence of Deposition of Hincmar of Laon

Pronounced by Hincmar, metropolitan bishop of Rheims, in the Council of Douzy.

*(In Labbe, Councils, volume VIII.)*

Hincmar, bishop of Rheims, said:

> “I would never have wished to be obliged to judge him; and would that I had not been involved in ordaining him, since I always feared what I now see, after the world had seized him for itself. I frequently wrote this to him in advance: ‘He who is hard of mind will fall into evil’ (Proverbs 28).
>
> “But since he himself has demanded that judgment be rendered against him, let your unanimity state whether, if I judge him for the causes set forth above, you will judge him together with me unanimously or not.”

When the bishops answered individually that they would judge him together with him, Hincmar, bishop of Rheims, said:

> “And after I have judged him and subscribed the judgment according to ecclesiastical custom, will you subscribe the same judgment with me?”

They replied that whatever they had judged together with him, they would subscribe according to ecclesiastical custom.

Then the canons’ sentences were read in the synod by the deacon Adalgar, who spoke as follows:

The Sardican canons decreed (canon 3):

> “If any bishop has been judged in any case and thinks that he has a good cause, so that the council may be renewed, if it pleases you, let us honor the memory of the holy apostle Peter, so that those who examined the case may write to Julius, the Roman bishop. If he judges that the judgment should be renewed, let it be renewed, and let him appoint judges; but if he determines that the case is such that what has been done should not be reopened, whatever he decrees shall be confirmed.”

Pope Innocent decreed (Letter 1):

> “If greater cases have been brought forward, they are to be referred to the apostolic see, as the synod has established and ancient custom [variant: blessed custom] requires, after episcopal judgment.”

Pope Boniface says (Letter 2):

> “We shall send letters throughout all the provinces, so that Maximus may not lawfully plead ignorance as an excuse, but may be compelled to come to the province and there present himself for established judgment. Whatever Your Charity decides should be decreed in this case, once it has been reported to us, must necessarily be confirmed by our authority, as is fitting.”

And Saint Pope Leo decreed (Letter 87):

> “If any other cases should arise,” he says, “which concern the condition of the Churches and the harmony of the priests, we wish them to be examined there under the fear of the Lord, and a full report concerning all matters settled and concluded is to be sent to us, so that whatever has been defined justly and reasonably according to the custom of the Churches may also be strengthened by our [variant: my] judgment.”

Then Hincmar, metropolitan and bishop of Rheims, reading, said:

> “I, Hincmar, bishop of Rheims, declare Hincmar, hitherto bishop of the Church of Laon, to be a resister of evangelical truth and apostolic authority through the obstinacy of an unlawful presumption and excommunication; a transgressor of the sacred canons, of the venerable councils, and of the decrees of the apostolic see promulgated on the basis of those same sacred canons; and a new opponent of ecclesiastical order and regular discipline, in contempt of the privilege of his metropolis, against the sacred Council of Nicaea, against the other holy councils, and against the decrees of the apostolic see.
>
> “He is corrupted by inveterate dregs—namely, by the sedition of Korah—and, after the constitution of the Council of Nicaea, a reviver of the rebellion of certain subjects against their superiors; a professor and subscriber against ecclesiastical order and regular discipline; likewise a violator of his canonical profession and subscription; an adulterator of Holy Scripture, a perverter of Catholic words, and a falsifier.
>
> “He is also a resister of royal subjection and honor against the apostolic rule; likewise perjured, seditious, an appropriator of the property and resources of others, a calumniator, and guilty of injuries. After being summoned by his metropolitan to the synod on a third summons, and then summoned again by the synod three times—by three bishops, three priests, and three deacons—he persisted stubbornly in his prolonged contumacy and did not repent; he despised answering the charges brought against him in accordance with the rules.
>
> “By our Lord Jesus Christ, whose evangelical truth he resisted through the obstinate presumption of pernicious excommunication; by the judgment of the Holy Spirit, who spoke through the blessed apostles and the pontiffs of the apostolic see, whose teaching and decrees he cruelly and contumaciously opposed because of his own wrong; according to the sacred canons of the holy councils, established by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, against which he repeatedly rebelled after often being reproved but not corrected—therefore he himself has drawn forth against himself the canonical sentence of condemnation.
>
> “I decree that he is deprived of episcopal honor and dignity by judgment, and stripped of every priestly office, while in all respects reserving the legal privilege of our lord and father Adrian, pope of the apostolic and first see, just as the sacred Sardican canons decreed, and the pontiffs of that same apostolic see, Innocent, Boniface, and Leo, promulgated on the basis of those same sacred canons.”

## Synodal Letter to Pope Adrian

Written in the name of the Council of Douzy by Hincmar of Rheims.

*(In Labbe, same place.)*

To the most holy and most reverend Lord Father Adrian, pope of the holy Catholic and apostolic Roman first see: Hincmar, Harduic, Remigius, Frotarius, Wlfadus, Bertulfus, Adalardus, Ansegisus, Franco, Hildegarius, Adventius, Gislebertus, Hodo, Rainelmus, Engenoldus, John, Waltharius, Willebertus, Hildeboldus, Berardus, and Ingilwinus, bishops, who together with legates of various Churches assembled in synod at Douzy, in the territory of Rheims, in the name of Christ.

Worn out by the long-standing, numerous, most serious, and repeated outrages of the insolent Hincmar of Laon, whom his metropolitan—who had kindly brought him up as an orphan, tonsured him as a cleric, educated him through letters, and, through the successive degrees and by election of the clergy and people of the Church of Laon, with the favor of Lord King Charles, raised him to the summit of the episcopate—was unable to correct, despite admonishing him in many ways, by many means, in words and in writing.

The kindness of our lord King Charles, through the lavish granting of many benefices and through chastisements, was unable to draw him toward episcopal gentleness and gravity. Neither he himself nor his metropolitan could compel him to restore to the clerics and laymen whom he had unjustly treated what law and justice required. Rather, whoever complained against him to the king or to his metropolitan, he never ceased until he had completely expelled them.

Nor could synodal denunciations persuade him to abandon his contumacy and frivolity, to obtain by moral integrity and reverence for his order the good name which apostolic rule commands a bishop to possess even among those outside the Church (1 Timothy 3), or to display an example of good works. Nor could human shame draw him away from his reprehensible and disreputable actions, so that our ministry would not be brought into disrepute. Finally, your apostolic letters, appeals, and admonitions were unable to correct him or bend him toward the obedience he owed.

At last—and we say this not without groaning and pain of heart, since we could find no other medicine by which he might be healed—we removed him from the priestly order, as Your Holiness will find in the record of proceedings that we are sending to your authority through this brother and our venerable fellow bishop Actard, who sat with us in the synod.

For neither could the Church entrusted to him, which groaned under him as under an exceedingly heavy burden, bear him any longer; nor could the rulers of other Churches endure his insolence without reproach; nor could the power of royal dignity or the unity of the kingdom endure his disturbances and dishonor.

Of these matters you will find some, and only a few in proportion to his other excesses, in the aforementioned record of proceedings. This is because of the shortness of time: Hincmar himself refused to come to the synod on the appointed day, while our lord the king was hastening, together with certain bishops, to a conference with his brother, for the reconciliation of his sons, with their father and his brother. They feared that, once sedition had been stirred up, Christian blood might be shed through kinsmen fighting one another like parricides [reading: “might be shed”], and that, for this reason, the property of the Churches of God might be divided, the resources of priests and servants of God seized, and the poor despoiled.

Although we worked hard to bring Hincmar himself to give an account of the charges brought against him according to reason and authority, we could not do so. By interrupting with shouting and disorderly utterances, he again denied what he confessed in words and had professed in his writings, and again confessed what he had denied.

Therefore, setting aside [variant: passing over] the other matters which you will find in the record of proceedings, and which are contained in many letters of his metropolitan as well as in Hincmar’s own writings; and leaving aside also the many complaints of numerous persons who submitted petitions against him in the synod, concerning both the clerics and laymen of his own Church and the parish priests and free men—not only of his own diocese but also of other dioceses; and likewise leaving aside the matter of the great quantity of gold and many precious gems, and the many varied ornaments made of gold and gems, with which Pardulus, his predecessor, handsomely adorned the altar of Saint Mary in the Church of Laon, but which this man dismantled—and, as the officials of that Church say, ordered to be made into mountings for swords, belts, spurs, and fastenings for hose, called *hosobindae*, and gave them to his brother and to whomever he pleased.

We also leave aside the purest gold from a chalice which his aforesaid predecessor donated to that same Church; likewise other gold, and also the silver belonging to that Church; as well as precious vestments, which he gave to whomever he wished; and also a very fine consecrated cloth from the altar of Saint Mary, which he gave for secular uses; together with many other matters which we have not undertaken to submit for accounting and judgment.

Nor do we address the other seditions, apart from the one concerning which the king accused him in writing, in his presence before the synod. In one of these he himself was involved: arriving with many armed men and a mixed crowd of common people, with swords and clubs, at the estate where the wife of the king’s count, named Nortmann, lay in childbirth in the customary manner of women, he expelled her from the place and violently took away, without any royal envoy, letter, or word, everything she had there—gold, silver, clothing, many fabrics, grain, wine, and livestock of diverse kinds and both sexes—within his diocese and jurisdiction, as is contained in Nortmann’s own petition presented to us in the synod.

In another sedition, which was stirred up at his command, as those who took part in it say, one man was killed. For when our lord the king ordered his men and the household of the bishopric of Laon to go there with weapons and clubs and expel a vassal of the Laon bishopric named Amalbert, to whom he had ordered the return of a benefice that he had unjustly taken from him—and this was done—one man was killed there after Amalbert had been put to flight.

There are also many other matters which it would take too long to write. We have brought to judgment only those matters contained in our lord the king’s petition against him, submitted in the synod, while reserving in every respect the legal privilege of the apostolic see and your judgment, as the sacred Sardican canons and the decrees of the pontiffs of the apostolic see—Innocent, Boniface, and Leo—promulgated on the basis of those same sacred canons, decree.

The matters which his metropolitan had previously offered for reading at another synod—no document survives as having been submitted at the synod at Attigny—and recently offered at this synod for his correction, whom he could not correct by himself, we are for that reason sending to your authority, so that you may recognize more distinctly, certainly, and fully his arrogance, the hardness of his mind, and the irrevocable obstinacy of Hincmar himself; and so that you may understand that we did not issue the sentence of condemnation against him rashly, or by changing our decision inconsiderately, but under considerable compulsion, since he himself forced us to do so.

Accordingly, we earnestly beseech your authority to free us from the weariness caused by this incurable pest, whom we were unable to endure any longer, by your own judgment, confirming by your sentence what we have defined justly and reasonably according to ecclesiastical custom, as we understand it, without being corrupted by an inimical spirit, by any desire, or by favor, in accordance with the decrees of Boniface and Leo.

And if, contrary to our expectation, it should seem necessary to you that you renew the judgment according to the Sardican canons and appoint judges, by writing to the bishops who are in the neighboring and bordering provinces, so that they too may investigate everything diligently and define the matter according to the truth, we do not refuse. Nor do we refuse if you decide to send from your side men possessing your authority to judge together with the bishops, without restoring him meanwhile to his former rank, as the sacred Sardican canons prescribe.

Although, insofar as we can, we desire to avoid returning to the labor by which we have long been harassed, and in every way resist having widely publicized matters which, out of reverence for the priesthood, we would rather conceal than make public, nevertheless we earnestly ask with all the humility of devotion of which we are capable that, in this case also, you preserve for us the canonical definition.

Namely, if—and we do not believe this will happen—you should not presently be willing to confirm by your judgment what we have defined regularly, insofar as we understood the sacred rules, then let him not be restored to priestly communion, from which he has been separated, before the matters are investigated according to the rules and laws in the province where they were conducted and judged.

For up to our own time this has not been derogated from the Gallic and Belgic Churches by any definition of the Fathers, especially since the decrees of Nicaea most appropriately entrusted both lower-ranking clerics and the bishops themselves, as the African council writes, to their metropolitans.

Saint Boniface likewise explains this when writing to Hilary, bishop of Narbonne (Letter 3):

> “It is fitting,” he says, “that we be diligent guardians of the sanctions of the Fathers. No one can be unaware of the constitution of the Council of Nicaea, which commands as follows—let us set down its very words:
>
> “‘In each province the individual metropolitans are to have their proper authority, and no one province is to be subject to two [variant: may be subject to two].’
>
> “They judged this concerning themselves because nothing else ought to be believed, with the Holy Spirit suggesting it to them.”

And shortly afterward:

> “We say this so that Your Charity may understand that we observe the precepts of the canons so carefully that our own constitution also determines that each province must always await the direction of its metropolitan in all matters. For our most prudent and most just holy Fathers rightly understood this…”

As the African council wrote to Pope Celestine:

> “Each matter should be settled in the place where it arose, and no province should lack the grace of the Holy Spirit by which equity may be discerned wisely by the priests of Christ and held with the utmost firmness.”

Moreover, with the definition and protection of the holy and apostolic see, and according to the laws and canons of the province of Africa, it is shown that the judgment can be regarded as valid in the place “where the necessary persons among the witnesses can be produced, without impediment from sex, old age, illness, or many other excuses based on obstacles.”

For no one can be legally and regularly convicted except by writing or by witnesses, just as Hincmar has been convicted in the synod before us by his writings, subscriptions, and suitable witnesses.

Therefore, since we desire and strive, insofar as we know and can, both to preserve, obey, and exalt the privilege of the holy and first Roman see—

> “on account, namely, of the primacy which the blessed apostle Peter received from the Lord’s own voice and which, with the Church following, he has always held and still holds”—

let Your Paternity and the authority established by God in the first see preserve for us, his sons and subject bishops, the ecclesiastical privileges preserved by the sacred canons, by your predecessors, and by those who preceded them. Let the apostolic see retain its proper vigor and not diminish the rights it has granted to others.

As Blessed Gregory writes to Dominicus, bishop of Carthage (Letter 39):

> “Concerning the ecclesiastical privileges about which Your Fraternity writes, let it hold this without hesitation: just as we defend our own, so we preserve the rights of each individual Church. I do not grant to anyone, with favor assisting, more than he deserves; nor will I take away from anyone what belongs to his jurisdiction, prompted by ambition [variant: nor do I take away]. Rather, I desire to honor my brothers in every respect, and strive to raise each of them to honors, provided that there is nothing which one may lawfully oppose to another.”

And to Natalis, bishop of Salona (indiction 10, Letter 37):

> “As for what you say must be preserved in your times [variant: in our times], although it was handed down and preserved by your predecessors [variant: by my predecessors also], far be it from me to violate in any Church the statutes of my elders toward my fellow priests; for I do myself an injury if I disturb the rights of my brothers.”

And if, God forbid, through anyone’s suggestion or request something should be secretly obtained from the apostolic see—that this same despiser and trampler of the sacred canons be restored to his rank, or be sent back to our provinces for a hearing, or be ordered to remain restored without a hearing—then, if we may say so with your permission, he would once more obtain what he has sought from the very beginnings of his ordination: the freedom to do whatever he wished licitly in our provinces, without regard for any coercion, knowing that we cannot send reports to Rome about every individual matter.

Until those same holy Fathers of ours, who still live with us through their constitutions, and who, instructed and inspired by the grace of the Holy Spirit according to the path of the sacred Scriptures and the tradition of the apostles, have established definite judgments concerning such actions as Hincmar of Laon, known to be insolent and a transgressor of sacred laws and rules, has committed, come with the Lord to judge the excesses that he has committed and will commit in his episcopal [lacuna: *cum ma . . . ordine*] order; just as up to now we have not participated in curbing his acts, so thereafter we will issue no judgments concerning him, nor bring any complaint about him before anyone.

Let him live as he wishes, while the Apostle consoles and advises us:

> “Do not participate in the unfruitful works of darkness; rather, reprove them” (Ephesians 5).

For we have dealt with him to the best of our ability. As Blessed Augustine explains:

> “The evil man does not defile us in two ways: if we do not consent to his evil works, and if we reprove them.”

We certainly did not consent; indeed, we reproved his works. Since we could not correct him, and since he has been judged by us through the judgment of God, we have reserved him for your definition and judgment. We are sending to Your Paternity the record of the proceedings through our venerable fellow bishop Actard, who took part in our synodal definitions. [The passage is corrupt.]

We would have done the same concerning Rothad, if our envoys had been granted the opportunity to cross the Alps at that time.

Believe, therefore, in our good faith: we judged him neither with an inimical spirit nor out of any desire or favor, but because his many, great, and long-standing excesses compelled us. Therefore believe that, according to the Sardican canons, it can be sufficient, since we have regularly brought the matter to an end, with our judgment confirmed by your sentence.

*(Flodoard, Book III, chapter 21.)*

Finally, we entrust to your authority our venerable brother and fellow bishop Actard, whom the clergy and people of the metropolitan Church of Tours request to be incardinated in that same Church. He was baptized, tonsured, and brought up in that Church, and was advanced through each degree to the episcopal order. Your Paternity also commended him to us for incardination, even if a place should arise for him in our regions, in a metropolitan see.

Accordingly, if it pleases you, incardinate him as archbishop in the aforesaid metropolis on these terms: after his death, a bishop is to be ordained for that metropolitan Church, by the election of its clergy and people, as the sacred rules prescribe and ancient custom requires, by the suffragan and provincial bishops there. (Adrian, Letter 2 to the bishops of the synod of Soissons.)

Although, after the Council of Antioch had been duly completed and according to your apostolic letters, we could have incardinated him in a vacant Church, nevertheless, since the Church of Tours has from ancient times been a metropolitan Church, always most renowned and honorable through the merits of blessed Martin, and since our aforesaid brother Actard, the venerable bishop, has been honored by your kindness with the *genius of the pallium* [Note: Gregory called the *genius of the pallium* its gifts and significations (Book VII, Letter 131)], we have judged it more reasonable that, at the request of the clergy and people of that Church, with the agreement of our unanimity, the favor of our lord the glorious King Charles, and your authority, he should be incardinated in that Church. (Adrian, Letter 28 to Charles.)

May our God preserve Your Holiness, praying for us through a long life, most reverend Lord Father in the Lord. Given on the eighth day before the Ides of September, in the present fourth indiction.

## Letter of Hincmar of Rheims to Pope Adrian

*(In Labbe, at the place cited above.)*

To the most holy and most reverend Father among Fathers, Adrian, pope of the first apostolic see and of the universal Church: Hincmar, bishop of Rheims in name but not in merit, and servant of God’s people.

As Your Dignity instructed my insignificance by its letter (Adrian, Letter 4 to Hincmar), I received our venerable brother and fellow bishop Actard into the embrace of my affection. Expelled from his see by pagan Northmen and by the pseudo-Christian Britons, with the consent of the fellow bishops of the province of Rheims and with the favor of our lord the glorious King Charles, I granted him in the vacant Church of [Morin] in our diocese a place in which to celebrate and exercise episcopal ministry. According to the Sardican canons (canons 3, 13, and 21), I granted him permission to remain there, and I ordered that generous benevolence be shown him from the property and resources of that Church, until a suitable and fitting place should arise where he could be incardinated according to your instruction.

He could not be incardinated in that vacant Church of our diocese according to your apostolic letters, because the remnants of the property of the Church of Nantes left by the pagans lie far from the Church of Morin in the province of Rheims, and he could not regularly be enrolled in two provinces.

But now, since the clergy and people of the metropolitan Church of Tours request that he, who was baptized, tonsured, and brought up in that same Church and advanced through each degree to the episcopal order, be incardinated among them—and since Your Paternity commended him to us for incardination, even if a place should arise for him in our regions, in a metropolitan see—we refer him to your authority, so that, if it pleases you, you may incardinate him as archbishop in the aforesaid metropolis on these terms: after his death, the metropolitan bishop of that Church is to be ordained there by the suffragan and provincial bishops, through the election of the clergy and people of the metropolitan Church, as the sacred rules prescribe and ancient custom requires.

Although, after the Council of Antioch had been duly completed and according to your apostolic letters, we could have incardinated him in a vacant Church, nevertheless, since the Church of Tours has from ancient times been a metropolitan Church, always most renowned and honorable through the merits of blessed Martin, and since our aforesaid brother Actard, the venerable bishop, has been honored by your kindness with the *genius of the pallium*, we have judged it more reasonable that, at the request of the clergy and people of that Church, with the agreement of our unanimity and the favor of our lord the glorious King Charles, he should be incardinated in that Church by your authority.

As for the case of Brother Hincmar, the record of proceedings which the synod recently held in the territory of Rheims is sending to your authority through this venerable brother and our fellow bishop Actard will give you full information after all that had to be done concerning him.

After all the proceedings concerning him, I appear to have obtained from our lord the king, together with the other bishops and our fellow brothers, that anyone from the clergy or household of the Church of Laon who wished to depart with him should have permission to do so.

Would that I had never seen him, and would that I had not been involved in ordaining him bishop: through him such a scandal has been stirred up without any necessity in the Churches of our provinces and in the kingdom in which we live, and has continued for so long. So much so that I could not inappropriately say of him:

> “It would have been better for that man if he had not been born.”
