For instead of progressing in religious life after being raised to the episcopal rank, in the discipline in which he had been brought up, he began to follow the pomps and enticements of the world; he took pleasure in the companionship and associations of secular people; he frequently engaged in conversations about secular affairs; he pursued greed and avarice, not only for money but also for elevation and the profits of shameful gain; he received my corrections, and those of anyone else, with contempt and indignation; and he trusted in his own understanding and wisdom—as many, alas, in our regions know.

To omit counting many other matters individually, which for many years I endured with fear and pain of heart concerning his character and disreputable actions, and even, out of human shame, concerning his insolence—although I very often reproved him both verbally and in writing, privately, both by myself and through our mutual friends, and could not bring him to recognition or correction—I shall mention a few matters from four years ago, when, advancing and growing worse, he began to strive mightily toward his fall.

For he began to afflict the clergy and laity who had elected him through various pretexts; and, by various devices, to steal from them—or, to put it more plainly, to rob them—what they possessed or were able to acquire [Col. 0643A]; and then to drive them from the place where they had been raised, while receiving others from different provinces who held corrupt opinions. Consequently, both the clergy and the laity, distressed over the church entrusted to them, began to appeal to the lord king and to my unworthiness. I labored sufficiently and more than sufficiently on their behalf, but accomplished little or nothing.

Now, being stirred up because his own people had appealed against him to the lord king, on account of the properties seized by Nortmann—properties which he himself had granted to the king without the consent of myself and my fellow bishops, so that the king might bestow them as benefices upon Nortmann, as he himself also admits in his writings—he sent Nortmann, without my knowledge and without any necessity, to accuse me before your authority through his messenger Celsanus. And he informed me [Col. 0643B] that the lord king had proscribed and confiscated him and the entire bishopric of the Church of Laon, except the principal church, the episcopal residence, and the brothers’ cloister, because he himself had refused to appear before a secular tribunal.

But, believing him as a bishop, I wrote several letters about this to the lord king, and wrote with insufficient caution, reproving him for an unjust judgment. Since the matter was not as Hincmar had informed me, and as he himself later stated, I took him with me and came to the lord king; and, as I had done before and often did afterward together with my fellow bishops, I made the lord king favorable toward him. Later, however, without my knowledge or consent, he sent again to your authority to accuse not only the king but also me, as I discovered in the letters of your holiness. Among other things they contain the following:

“Why should I abuse the ministry of episcopal jurisdiction in these regions, while Hincmar, my nephew and namesake, a venerable bishop—as you have heard—suffers no small losses in his church, if, while I am lukewarm, he has been unable to find any consolation?”

Therefore I rightly sent a reply to your authority concerning this matter (this letter is not extant), which it is not now necessary to repeat.

But Hincmar himself, from the very matters by which he ought to have become more cautious and humble—namely, my intercession and the kindness of the lord king—was lifted up into pride and became bitter in spirit. He not only failed to correct himself but continually added worse things to his evil deeds. And because I was unwilling to agree with his wicked actions and reprehensible conduct, and avoided imprudently putting faith in his lies [Col. 0643D], indeed, because I began to rebuke him, he became irredeemably hostile even toward me; and he continually heaped up more and greater scandals against the king, the kingdom, myself, my fellow bishops, and his own church, both its clergy and its laity.

Although those scandalized by him did not openly say so, I learned that they called me the cause of these scandals, because I had ordained him—my nephew—as bishop. They did not consider that God, who knows all things, ordained Judas as an apostle in his present righteousness, and Saul as king, although Saul was later rejected, of whom it is written: “He was an elect and good man, and there was no man among the children of Israel better than he” (1 Samuel IX). God contracted no guilt, because he could not sin [Col. 0644A]. But I, as a man ignorant of what would happen, ordained this man through lack of foresight, and became the minister of a divine judgment that was not unjust; for, as I fear, I deserved this through my other sins.

Moreover, the holy apostles, together with blessed Stephen and the other deacons, ordained Nicolaus; yet, when his reprehensible words and deeds later became manifest, they did not thereby participate in them through the laying on of their hands (Acts VI). Nor did Samuel incur guilt in the ordination of Saul, whom he had ordained at divine command and whom the Lord afterward rejected; he mourned him for a very long time, as sacred history relates (1 Samuel XV). Since they said that I had ordained my nephew as bishop, they did not consider that other bishops had also been ordained by me who were not related to me by blood; nor does kinship prevent anyone from being ordained if the person to be ordained has been elected and requested according to ecclesiastical rules. For we read that the Lord himself, from whom and through whom the episcopate began, ordained as bishops men related to him by the flesh.

Although in the case of this nephew of mine I acted in a way over which I groan—for I do not know how, concerning this and my other deeds, he will arrange matters in his terrible counsels over the children of men (Psalm LXV), in his hidden judgment, he who made darkness his hiding place (Psalm XVII)—I nevertheless know an almighty advocate and merciful judge, “before whom is all my desire, and my groaning is not hidden” (Psalm XXXVII). He consoles me because I have received double for and through him. For, as Saint Gregory says:

“Those whom we love more than others cause us greater pain when we suffer adversity from them than do the evils inflicted by outsiders; and those torments we suffer from people whose minds we trusted rage more fiercely within us, because, while bodily loss afflicts us, the loss of charity also torments us. Hence the Lord says through the Psalmist concerning Judas, his betrayer: ‘Indeed, if my enemy had cursed me, I would surely have endured it; and if the one who hated me had spoken great things against me, I might perhaps have hidden myself from him. But you, a man of one mind with me, my leader and my acquaintance, who together with me used to take sweet food: we walked in agreement in the house of God’ (Psalm LIV). And again: ‘The man of my peace, in whom I trusted, and who ate my bread, has magnified his treachery against me’ (Psalm XL).”

As though he were saying openly concerning his betrayer: “I endured his transgression so much more grievously because I experienced it from one who seemed to be mine.”

I wrote to him many things, in many ways, so that he might correct himself. If they were gathered into one body, I do not think the volume would be smaller than the five books of Moses. I therefore turned to writing to him because he could not endure what was said to him by me. Nor can he patiently hear anything from any person unless that person says to him what is already occupying his own heart. Against these writings he himself also sent me many replies, in many ways, irrationally; unwilling to understand what I wrote to him as it had been written, he labored instead to criticize, accuse, and refute both me and the writings themselves [Col. 0645A].

By this I understood that he was incorrigible, and resolved in my heart that I would no longer labor fruitlessly with him. I saw being fulfilled in him what the Psalmist says concerning the Lord: “He made a path for his anger by the sending of evil angels” (Psalm LXXVII). Gregory says:

“The Lord rightly permits a heart weighed down by its former merits to be deceived also by the subsequent persuasions of evil spirits; and while it is deservedly drawn into guilt, its liability is already increased for punishment. Hence for the Lord to make a path for his anger means that, by strict judgment, he prolongs punishment against those who rightly refused to punish the causes of their own wrongdoing: so that those who, having been enlightened, refused to do what was right may, having been justly blinded, continue to do what they deserve to be punished for even more severely. Concerning them the Apostle says: ‘That they may always fill up their sins’ (1 Thessalonians II). And therefore the angel’s voice says to John: ‘Let the one who harms continue to harm, and let the one who is filthy continue to be filthy’ (Revelation XXII). Hence David says: ‘Add iniquity upon their iniquity, and let them not enter into your righteousness’ (Psalm LXVIII). Hence it is said through Moses: ‘The sins of the Amorites are not yet complete’ (Genesis XV).

“Through the same Moses the Lord says: ‘For their vine is from the vine of Sodom, and their branch from Gomorrah. Their grape is a grape of gall, and their cluster is bitterness to them. The wine of dragons is their wine, and the incurable venom of asps. Are these things not stored up with me and sealed in my treasures? On the day of vengeance I will repay them’ (Deuteronomy XXXII). And although he had recounted many of their evils, he immediately added: ‘At the time when their foot shall slip’ (ibid.). Their most atrocious sins are described, yet a later fall still reaches the day of vengeance, by which their guilt is accumulated. They already have grounds for deserving to be struck, but the growing sin is nevertheless endured, so that the more severe guilt may further burden the sinners. Sin and the cause of sin already deserve punishment, but it is still awaited that the sin and punishment of the sin may bring an increase of punishment.

“Seeing these things being fulfilled in him, I resolved, as far as I was able, to follow what the Lord says: ‘My people did not hear my voice, and Israel did not heed me; so I let them go according to the desires of their hearts: they shall walk in their own inventions’ (Psalm LXXX). And again: ‘I called, and you refused; you despised all my counsel and neglected my reproofs. Therefore such people shall eat the fruit of their way and be filled with their own counsels’ (Proverbs I).”

Since the Lord himself also says, “If your right eye or your right hand causes you to stumble, cast it away from you” (Matthew V), and commands us to hate our neighbors and even our own soul (Luke XIV), blessed Gregory says (Homily 37 on the Gospels) that anyone who is our adversary in this world is to be loved by us, but one who is opposed to us on the way of God is not to be loved by us, even if he is our neighbor. For although our neighbors are to be loved, and charity is to be shown to everyone, both relatives [Col. 0646A] and strangers, we must not, on account of that same charity, be turned away from the love of God. For the sake of carnal affection, those who carry the ark of God in their minds must not turn aside from the straight path, just as the cows that once carried the ark at Beth-shemesh did not turn aside from the right road (1 Samuel VI). We must recognize that compassion is owed to our neighbors, but uprightness to their vices.

I write this to your most holy authority, constrained by grief of heart, and give voice to my lament concerning him, so that you may know how much not only I, but also the churches of the cisalpine regions, and the king and kingdom of our lands, have endured through him until now. I inform your fatherhood that, as long as I live in this mortal flesh, as a metropolitan ought to render an account together with a bishop, so far as depends on me I shall have no further dealings with him concerning either the parish or any other matter of metropolitan concern. I can no longer endure his insolence.

It is more tolerable for me, even bodily, to lose an eye, a hand, or a foot by amputation than to engage in fruitless disputes over his insolence with one whom I loved with joyful hope and still love with grief for the sake of God. Having already been harassed by him in many ways and through many people, I must now seek not quarrels but peace. Thus, as I already await my end, or at that end, I may by God’s mercy say: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace” (Luke I).

Moreover, your fatherly authority recently sent me a letter concerning a priest of our parish named [Col. 0646C] Trisingus, ordering me to send you a full written account of his case. I now reply to your authority as the truth of the matter stands.

A certain free woman, the sister of a man named Livulf, from the very village in which the aforesaid Trisingus had been ordained priest, took as her husband the brother of that priest. Through this relationship Trisingus began frequently visiting his brother’s house. And, as the same Livulf—who lived in that village—as well as the parishioners and neighbors of the priest said, Trisingus began to have intercourse with the daughter of his brother’s wife, whom she had borne by another husband.

One day the priest and the aforesaid Livulf went to the fortress called Mouzon, and became drunk in a tavern, contrary to our episcopal prohibition. At every synod we prohibit our priests from doing this, in accordance with the definition of the African canons (African Council, canon 40): “Clerics are not to enter taverns for the sake of eating or drinking, unless compelled by the necessity of travel.” This priest entered the tavern to make himself drunk, not from the necessity of travel but from gluttony, since that fortress is no more than four miles from the priest’s residence.

As the priest and Livulf returned drunk from the aforesaid fortress, they began to quarrel with one another [Note: *Se prendre de paroles*, “to fall into a dispute.” Augustine said to Julian: “You quarrel idly,” that is, “you speak many foolish things,” book III against Julian, no. 46], as drunkards are accustomed to do. Their quarrel proceeded so far that Livulf reproached the priest concerning his own niece; and the priest, in turn, repeated to Livulf whatever insults he could find.

Livulf then struck the priest Trisingus twice with a staff that he was carrying in his hand. The priest thereupon rushed upon Livulf’s son, who was carrying a sword at his neck, drew that sword, and, wishing to strike him through the middle of the head so as to kill him, raised it. Livulf raised his hand against the sword and received the sword-blow, and two fingers were cut off that hand. When he fell from his horse, the priest thought him dead, mounted Livulf’s horse, and went to his own home.

When I heard this from many people, I summoned him before me in the presence of our clergy and assistants and questioned him concerning the truth [the transmitted text is syntactically defective]. Concerning the woman with whom he was accused of having intercourse, he denied that he had slept with her. But concerning his intention, namely, that he had wished to kill the man in the manner I have described, he confessed. By the testimony of the Apostle John he was thereby convicted as a murderer.

As blessed Augustine wrote to Xantippus, the primate, concerning a priest of his own parish: what the priest denied I left to God; what he was not permitted to conceal I judged. I removed him from the priestly office until he should come to a provincial synod, where, together with a definite number of bishops, his case would receive a settled conclusion, as the Carthaginian canons prescribe (African canon 95; Carthage III, canon 8) [Col. 0647C].

Although we held several synods in our province, he afterward came to no synod. I waited for him for a year and six months, and he made no effort to defend himself at a synod. The sacred canons decree (Carthage V, canon 12) that whenever clerics have been convicted of and confessed some crime, if they should wish to appear in the case and assert their innocence, they must do so within a year of excommunication. But if they neglect to clear themselves within a year, their voice is afterward to be heard not at all.

After a year and six months, when the parishioners of the church in which that priest had been ordained complained that they had no priest [something is missing here for the sense], I did not know that he had gone to Rome until, three months after another priest had been ordained in his place, he returned from Rome and brought me a letter from your holiness.

In chapter 67 of the fourth council of the province of Africa, it is written concerning seditionists and usurers, so that they may not become clerics (Carthage IV, canon 66): “Seditionists are never to be ordained [alternative: ‘ordained as clerics’], nor those who avenge their own injuries.” If such people are not to be ordained, it must be inferred what those deserve who, after ordination, do not fear committing such acts.

The ancient canons of the Fathers, in a synod attended by many metropolitans together with their suffragans, and with the Council of Antioch decreeing that a council is complete when a metropolitan bishop is present, expressly decreed (Toledo IV, canon 45; found also in Gratian, 23, q. 8, *Clerici qui*): “Clerics who are found to have voluntarily taken up arms in any sedition are to lose the rank of their order and be confined in a monastery for penance.”

Pope Zacharias also wrote to Boniface, bishop of Mainz, instructing him to remove from their ecclesiastical orders bishops, priests, or deacons found to have shed Christian or pagan blood. More than two years have now passed since the aforesaid Trisingus, wishing to kill the above-mentioned Livulf, mutilated him. At your command I now send this report to your authority.

Your wisdom knows very well that the people cannot safely be left without a priest for so long. May almighty God preserve your holiness for many years in the service you have begun, for the instruction and correction of his holy Church, most holy lord and most reverend Father of the Fathers in the Lord.

## In the Year of Our Lord 882. John VIII, Roman Pontiff

### Historical Notice concerning John VIII

By Pandulf of Pisa, as is believed.

(From Muratori, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, volume III, from a Vatican manuscript.)

[Col. 0647D] John VIII, a Roman by nationality, son of Gundo, occupied the see for ten years and two months. This most blessed man, for the benefit of all the churches of God, and especially of the Gallican Church, was taken by the coastal route to Arles. There Leo, the abbot, came into his presence and lodged a complaint against Gisbertus [Baluz., volume VII of the *Miscellanies*, Gilbertus here and below], bishop of Nîmes [Col. 0648D].

The monastery of Saint Peter, where the body of blessed Giles rests, was situated in the borders of Gothia, in the Flavian Valley. The former king Flavius had granted this valley to blessed Giles, and Saint Giles had thereafter made a complete donation of it to the Roman Church and to Pope Benedict. There he had built a monastery in honor of the chief apostles Peter and Paul [Col. 0649A]. The aforesaid Gisbertus, bishop of Nîmes, rashly invading that monastery, had taken it away from Leo, its abbot.

He then obtained a precept from the king of the Franks. Not trusting even in its validity, he approached the Roman pontiff and secretly sought apostolic authority concerning the matter, as though from his own possessions. But Pope Nicholas, of holy memory, although unaware of this fraud, nevertheless, filled with the divine Spirit, took pains to excuse all those who were seeking the law in the matter.

When Pope John, however, requested the documentary safeguards of the monastery, the privilege which the venerable Pope Benedict had physically handed over in Rome to Saint Giles was produced. Then Pope John, through Deusdedit, duke of Ravenna and his advocate, sought the monastery from Gisbertus, bishop of Nîmes.

After advocates had been appointed for both parties through sureties, with Gregory the notary as executor and Deusdedit acting, the bishop Gisbertus wished to defend the monastery by means of the precept of the lord Nicholas, of pious memory, which he had secretly obtained by fraud from the apostolic see as though it were his own, and by means of a precept he had obtained from a certain Frankish king—a false document in which no validity at all remained.

But the lord pope warned all the bishops and judges of Rome and the provinces, under threat of excommunication and anathema, to pronounce and execute the law rightly in this matter. Then Rostagnus, archbishop of Arles; Aribertus [Note: The name of Aribertus, bishop of Embrun, is absent in Baluz.], archbishop of Embrun; Waldbertus, bishop of Porto; Paschalis, bishop of Amelia; Radbertus, bishop of Valence; Litiduinus [Baluz., Lituinus], bishop of Marseille; Ictarius, bishop of Viviers [Col. 0650A]; and the other bishops and judges of the province, together with John, duke, and Dativus [Baluz., Daturus] of Ravenna, Ardus, Adbertus, Guisalfredus, Arderardus, Godulfus [Baluz., Gondalfus], and several other provincial judges, immediately recognized, when they heard the precept read, the apostolic censure of the lord Nicholas and excused those who had sought the law in the matter.

They declared that the monastery could not be defended by that precept, and judged that Gisbertus, the bishop, should immediately return the monastery to the lord pope and pay him the penalty for its seizure. The lord pope then sent there his advocate, Deusdedit, duke of Ravenna, who received from Gisbertus, the bishop, the formal physical surrender of all the property of the aforesaid monastery, both inside and outside.

Afterward, crossing into Gaul in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 879, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September [Note: Baluz. has “the year 878, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September.” He adds: “In the old manuscript it is read that these things took place in the year 879, in the ninth indiction, and that the Council of Troyes was celebrated in April. Since this cannot agree with the truth of the history, we have corrected those notes, as the matter is certain.”], in the eleventh indiction, in the sixth year of his pontificate on the most holy [Baluz., most sacred] see of blessed Peter the apostle [Baluz.: “in the sixth year, in the month of August, at the city of Troyes”], he celebrated at the city of Troyes, in the presence of the lord Louis, most serene king, a very large council [Note: The remaining material is absent in Baluz.].

During his time Anastasius, librarian of the Roman Church, also flourished. Skilled in both Greek and Latin eloquence, he translated the seventh universal synod from Greek into Latin. He also translated from Greek into Latin the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy* of Dionysius the Areopagite, bishop of Athens, written to Timothy, bishop of Ephesus, and sent it to Emperor Charles, son of Louis. He also translated from Greek into Latin the Passion of Saint Peter, archbishop of Alexandria; the Passion of Saint Acacius and his companions; and the Life of Saint John the Almsgiver.

### Another Notice concerning John VIII

(From the Councils of Mansi.)

[Col. 0649C] John [Note: John. In the year of the Redeemer 872, on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of January, according to Aimoinus, John, Roman by homeland and nationality, was made pontiff, the eighth of that name, from the archdeaconate. He became famous through the election, anointing, and coronation of the three emperors Charles the Bald, Louis the Stammerer, and Charles the Fat, who succeeded one another in the stated order after the death of Louis II.

When the Saracens were laying waste almost all Italy, he was entirely deprived of the aid of the men in whom he had placed hope of expelling the Saracens, and was forced to purchase peace and security from the barbarians and unbelievers by an annual census and tribute. This seems to have happened by God’s just permission, so that, instructed by this example, he might recognize that after the death of Emperor Louis II, persuaded by the evil counsel of carnal prudence, he had wrongly chosen, created, and crowned Charles emperor, expecting greater aid against the Saracens from him than from his brother Louis. Because of Charles’s invasion of another kingdom, John ought rightly to have harassed him with ecclesiastical censures, following the example of his predecessor Adrian II.

After the death of Ignatius, Pope John received Photius back into communion with the Church at the request of the legates of Emperor Basil and the patriarch of Jerusalem. Photius had obtained this through an astonishing fraud and imposture, which Nicetas recounts at greater length, and Ignatius, while still alive, had justly denied him a return to the Church, as had been established by the eighth synod. John approved Photius’s return to the patriarchal see, not without serious damage to his own reputation and the most shameful stain upon the pontifical chair.

The eighth ecumenical council had established, and had further confirmed by the oath of each individual, that Photius was not to be received into penance before the end of his life. The pontiff, who was not ignorant of this most sacred decree and perhaps was not forgetful of his own oath, ought in no way to have received the contumacious heretic into penance, still less into patriarchal dignity, but rather ought to have struck him with a sentence of anathema.

Photius undoubtedly obtained these things through Basil’s intercession, by promising ecclesiastical union, peace, and concord, and assistance against the Saracens, and by recounting numerous falsehoods—as though all the orthodox were interceding for his restoration. Yet this reasoning excuses John less than it disgraces him, making him one who, enervated by a eunuch and emasculated man, declared himself to be a woman rather than a man. If anyone were to believe with Baronius that from this deed the story of John VIII, not a pope but a *papess*, took its origin, he might perhaps not be judging badly. These matters are from Nicetas and Aimoinus, Baronius, volume X, in the Life of John. Severinus. Binius.]

He occupied the see for ten years and two days. By his decree he established that no duke should be permitted to bring any bishop into the presence of the Roman pontiff, or to demand from him a census for public expenses or any gifts whatsoever; nor did he permit a bishop to be summoned before laymen [Col. 0650C]. He decreed that clerics and nuns, orphans and widows, should be under the protection of bishops, and forbade in every way that they be dragged before secular courts. He decreed that any duke or other person acting contrary to these provisions should be excommunicated; and that one who persisted should be bound by the chain of anathema.

Among other matters, he gave the following instruction concerning tithes given to priests:

“We have judged that each believer should give those tithes to the priest in whose parish he is unquestionably known to remain under the jurisdiction of his own bishop [Note: The passage is corrupt.], since he has been appointed by his bishop to receive them; and therefore no priest or Levite of another diocese may insolently or rashly entertain, seek, or accept such dues owed by right to another [Note: the text reads *ea novum*, perhaps *canonum*, “of the canons”] as a condemnation or donation [Note: Perhaps simply ‘donation’]. But we judge that anyone who presumes to give or receive them otherwise should remain deprived of ecclesiastical communion until he has endeavored to act according to this chapter of our apostolic authority.”

During his time Emperor Louis, compelled by Adalgisus, duke of Benevento, and fearing for his life, confirmed by oath that he would never again enter the territory of Benevento and would never exact vengeance for the injury then inflicted upon him. Later, in Rome, the aforesaid pope absolved him from this oath by the authority of God and Saint Peter, affirming that it did not harm him that he had been compelled to make it in order to escape the danger of death, and that it should not be called an oath which had been uttered, even with many curses, against the safety of the commonwealth.

## The Letters and Decrees of Pope John VIII Arranged in Chronological Order

(For the letters or decrees whose source is not identified, attribute them to the Councils of Mansi.)

### Notice by Philipp Jaffé

(*Regesta Pontificum Romanorum*)

However great and extensive it is rightly considered, the surviving fragment of John VIII’s Register, containing 308 letters, must nevertheless be lamented for having reached us in poor condition. Through the carelessness either of the notary himself or, more probably, of those who copied it, many letters are not only badly corrupted and truncated, but even in arranging them no consistent attention was everywhere paid to their dates. Indeed, chronological disregard was carried so far that in very many consecutive letters, which internal evidence clearly shows to have been written at different times, the chronological headings were entirely discarded and the same formula was substituted throughout: “Given as above.”

I believe these words were added by some inept later-period copyist in place of “Given, and so forth,” especially since Pertz testifies in *Archiv für ältere deutsche Geschichtskunde* V, 32, that the manuscript from which the Register was copied was not produced until the eleventh century. Whatever the truth of the matter may be, no information about the dates of the letters could ever be extracted from that defective formula.

### I. To Anno, Bishop of the Church of Freising

Fragment—(Year 873). That he should transmit the revenues owed to the Roman Church.

[Col. 0651B]

We have gladly and gratefully received your most devout promise that you wished to prove by deeds the effectiveness of your loyalty toward the apostolic see, which you had certainly exalted in your letters; and we have received it as a commendation of the affairs of the Roman Church which, as you state, have been entrusted to your care.

Know, therefore, that very recently we sent letters to our beloved son King Louis, and also to the bishops and counts of the Italian kingdom, so that they might ensure that those revenues be safely brought to us. We recognize that nothing else remains except for you to bring or send us the gold and other commodities [Col. 0651C] which you admit you have collected, together with the arrears of the previous indiction, in their full amount, by the whole of September of the coming seventh indiction [Col. 0652B]. You should know that if these revenues do not reach us at the agreed time, this must be attributed specifically to no one other than your deliberate negligence.

We ask you also to bring or send with those revenues an excellent organ together with a craftsman able to tune and operate it with every musical effectiveness, so that, while you hasten to offer base metal to blessed Peter, you may receive from him the golden gifts of the heavenly kingdom.

### II. To Wilibertus, Archbishop of Cologne

Fragment—(Year 873). The pallium must not be given except after the customary profession of faith.

We have been unable to confer upon you the pallium you desired, [Col. 0652C] because we found that your statement of faith contained less than it ought to. In it, namely, you had mentioned neither any of the holy universal synods in which the symbol of our faith is contained, nor the decretal constitutions of the Roman pontiffs, as custom requires. Nor had you secured it with your own subscription, nor sent anyone to confirm it by oath.

### III. To Emperor Louis II

Fragment—(Year 874). Certain estates of the Church of Ravenna are asserted.

For we have not taken away from the archbishop of Ravenna the monastery of Saint Mary in Comacchio, called Pomposa; the monastery of Saint Saviour on Mount Feretrus; another monastery called Saint Probus; or the tenants in the territories of Ferrara, Adria, Gallicata, and Faventilla. Rather, finding those monasteries and places in the possession of our predecessors, we have possessed them and have retained them lawfully as our own until now.

There are also other places, villages, and estates from which the Church of Ravenna has received some payment for five hundred years. We wish that henceforth that Church should receive the former payment and contribution. Since we have neither taken away from that Church nor caused to be occupied any other places, let it retain what it has possessed until now, apart from the aforesaid places—that is, Gallicata and the estate of Faventilla—and apart from the aforesaid monasteries, until you recognize in our presence that even the places which it considers its own belong rather, in every respect, to our Church by law and right.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of February, in the seventh indiction [Col. 0653C].

### IV. To Ansbertus, Archbishop of Milan

Fragment—(Year 874).

A distinguished man named Rudolphus, an imperial official, recently came to us, complaining and affirming that, inflamed by zeal for chastity, he had marked his wife, named Bava, with the stain of an obscene suspicion and, as sinister rumor spread, had attacked her with a carnal accusation of crime.

When he had handed her over to her parents and relatives for purification according to the terms of his own law, she was detained for more than a year under the charge of criminal accusations. Therefore, kindled by love of equity, we command her parents by apostolic authority that, by the middle of August of the preceding seventh indiction, they should return this woman to her own husband, whether purified or otherwise, with no doubt that she would then undergo, if not the remedy of secular law, at least that of ecclesiastical mercy.

Otherwise, they should know that they would be deprived, together with her, of communion in the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, because they had shown reverence neither for the judgment of worldly or divine laws nor for the decree of the apostolic see. They did none of this, as the aforesaid man reported when he came to us again and as the outcome of the matter indicated.

For this reason we would rightly deprive them of the sacred gift of communion, as we had threatened them when bringing charges against them, unless we judged that the other party ought to be heard. Since it is said that mediators ought not to be just, whereas a mediator is not of one [the transmitted wording is problematic], we do not wish to trouble them further by traveling there. We therefore entrust this controversy to your holiness in our place and urge you, at the appointed and prescribed time, to summon the venerable bishops Lintfridus of Fiesole and Paulus of Piacenza; and, after having summoned the wife of the aforementioned Radulfus through your messengers and letters, exercise without delay whatever belongs to the law, whether worldly or divine, concerning both spouses, but only according to the measure of priestly office prescribed for you.

If, after your summons—which is unquestionably the third after our second summons—she should choose not to return to her own husband after being granted the lawful and indisputable freedom to clear herself, and if she should evade and avoid the inquiry of your holiness, then, agreeing in this with my spirit, you are to exclude from the communion of the sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ both her and the relatives who wickedly protect and defend her, indeed all her supporters and accomplices, until they obey.

### V. To Louis, King of Germany

(Year 874.) The privileges of the Roman Church are extinguished only by prescriptions of one hundred years.

(From Gratian, *Decretum*, causa 16, question 3, canon 17.)

No one should derive a pretext for delay from the number of years, because the privileges of the holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve, and which it received upon the firm rock of Peter’s stability, are restricted by no period of time and prejudiced by no division of kingdoms. Rather, the venerable Roman laws, promulgated by God through the mouths of pious princes, admit prescription concerning its possessions only after one hundred years.

## VI. TO PAUL, BISHOP. (Year 874.) A memorandum to Bishop Paul, serving as legate in Germany and Pannonia.

For the Apostolic See has from ancient times been accustomed to perform consecrations, ordinations, and dispositions not only between Italy and the other provinces of Hesperia, but also within the whole territory of Illyricum. But if he should perhaps raise an objection concerning the number of years, let him know that among Christians and those who are of one faith a fixed period has been established. Yet where the fury of pagans and unbelievers is involved, however much time may pass, it does not prejudice the rights of the Churches, which, knowing nothing of bodily weapons, await the Lord alone as their defender, patiently awaiting his mercy according to his will. But if the length of time impedes matters of this kind, then God himself would have to be blamed: he who, after four hundred and thirty years, freed the children of Israel from Pharaoh’s slavery and from the iron furnace, and who, after long ages, rescued the human race from the prisons of hell and the power of demons.

## VII. TO LOUIS THE EMPEROR. Fragment—(Year 875.) Rainaldus, bishop of Castrum Felicitatis, is excommunicated.

We believe that it is known to Your Serenity how Rainaldus, bishop of Castrum Felicitatis, was publicly denounced for homicide both before the Apostolic See and before the imperial court; how, when Gregory, our beloved son, nomenclator and apocrisiarius of our holy see, together with Gregory the illustrious master of soldiers and vestiarian of our sacred patriarchate, was residing with our most beloved daughter the empress Augusta, he was accused by the mother and other relatives of the slain young man; and how, compelled by our frequent letters of excommunication to come to Rome and clear himself, he did so.

But because, on coming to Rome, he forestalled the time appointed for his purgation, and, fraudulently leaving the place assigned to him by us at the synod convened on his behalf, threw himself down over the city walls like a thief, thereby evading judgment and revealing that the crimes charged against him were true, we therefore, by the authority of almighty God, of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and of our own unworthiness, completely exclude him from all ecclesiastical and Christian communion.

## VIII. TO LOUIS II THE EMPEROR. (Fragment—Year 875.) What is done contrary to the law is dissolved by the authority of the law.

*(In Gratian, Decree, Part I, Distinction 10, chapter 9.)*

[Col. 0655C]

You see, dearest son, that what is accepted contrary to the laws deserves to be dissolved by the laws.

## IX. TO THE NEAPOLITANS, SALERNITANS, AND AMALFITANS. Fragment—(Year 875.)

Let your conscience, rightly judging your love in Christ, determine how far removed from Christ are those who, contrary to the prohibition of the great apostle Paul, enter into a defiled union of alliance with his unbelievers. For whenever they are joined by any participation to the rebellions of the king, they are likewise judged liable to the crimes of treason and condemned by the same sentence. How evidently are they strangers to the body of Christ who, allied with his enemies, rend his members all the more perniciously because they draw nearer to the Church of God? Again:

How detestable it is to God to make treaties with an impious person is clearly understood from the following: King Jehoshaphat of Judah, although exalted by so many praises for his earlier life, is reproved for his friendship with Ahab when Jehu the prophet says to him: “Do you give help to the impious, and join friendship with those who hate the Lord? Therefore you deserved the Lord’s wrath; but good works were found in you, because you removed the sacred groves from the land of Judah” (2 Chronicles 19).

Moreover, how pleasing to God it is to withdraw from peace with the enemies of God, our Psalmist declares when he says: “Do I not hate those who hate you, O Lord, and do I not waste away over your enemies? With perfect hatred I hate them; they have become enemies to me” (Psalm 137).

From this, dearest sons, it is plainly shown with what guilt peace is maintained with the worst of men, if so great a prophet offered this as a sacrifice to God: that, for God’s sake, he aroused enmity against the wicked. Hence the tribe of Levi, taking up swords and passing through the middle of the camp because it refused to spare the sinners who deserved to be struck down, is said to have consecrated its hands to God. Hence Phinehas, spurning the favor of his sinful fellow citizens, struck down those who were coupling with the Midianites and, in his anger, appeased God’s anger.

[Col. 0656B]

Because we believe that we are speaking to the faithful who understand the mystery of Christianity, we avoid extending our discourse through further testimonies of the sacred Scriptures. Behold, we are sending to you Donatus, the venerable bishop whose praise is found in the holy eighth synod, and Eugenius, the religious presbyter, our beloved sons and counselors.

## X. TO THE SALERNITAN CLERGY. (Year 875.)

John, bishop, to the clergy and order of Salerno.

Those priests who, after being excommunicated during the time of our most holy predecessor, the lord Pope Nicholas, presumed to touch the sacred ministry incurred upon themselves the sentence of condemnation, as the holy canons establish. Nevertheless, because apostolic mercy customarily grants pardon to those who have corrected themselves, out of the abundance of mercy we grant them this indulgence: that, nourished by holy communion, they should strive for three continuous years to fast completely every Monday and Friday, either from wine or from cooked food [as it is read elsewhere], and that they should never again commit such grievous offenses.

## XI. Those suspected of the death of a Roman cleric are excommunicated. Fragment—(Year 875.)

Those who were suspected of the homicide of a religious Roman cleric, and whom we summoned to come in June of the present eighth indiction for the purpose of imposing their canonical excommunication, refused to come; and who, for this reason, were summoned a second and third time by our letters, and finally, through John and Leo, bishops, deprived of all communion—since they are shown thus far to have evaded the judgment of the Apostolic See and neither to have come nor sent anyone—we decree, by the authority of the Holy Spirit, that they are anathematized until the coming Kalends of October of the coming ninth indiction, when they may deserve to be canonically purified.

But if even then they do not show us the fullest satisfaction, let them remain bound by perpetual anathema, so that whoever henceforth shares food, drink, or prayer with them shall be bound by the same sentence of anathema as they are.

## XII. PRIVILEGE FOR THE FULDENSE MONASTERY (Year 875.)

He again declares the monastery of Fulda, with all its cells, churches, tithes, estates, and other possessions belonging to it, exempt and free.

*(In Schannat, History of the Diocese of Fulda, p. 238.)*

[Col. 0657A]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Sigahard, religious abbot of the venerable monastery of the Lord Savior, and through you to your successors, the abbots of the same venerable monastery, forever.

Since those things that accord with reasonable desires must always be granted, the authority of pious construction ought by no means to be denied to the devotion of its founder when privileges are being bestowed. Therefore, because you asked us that the monastery of the Savior, built by Saint Boniface the archbishop in the place called Boconia, beside the bank of the river Fuldaha, should be adorned with the support of a privilege from the Apostolic See, so that, established under the jurisdiction of our holy Church, which by God’s authority we serve, it might not be subjected to the jurisdiction of any other Church: favoring your pious desires, by this authority of ours we commit to effect what is requested. Accordingly, we prohibit every priest of any Church from exercising any dominion or authority in the aforesaid monastery, except the Apostolic See.

Moreover, by the provision of our privilege we confirm the place of Fulda, with all its cells, churches, tithes, estates, and all its possessions, both those which it presently holds or possesses and those which divine piety may wish to add to the rights of that place in future times. We decree, however, that it be reported to our ecclesiastical concern at suitable times how the monastic order is being directed in regular observance and devoted to appropriate ecclesiastical harmony, lest—God forbid—under cover of this privilege the mind and conduct of your rectitude be in any way turned aside from the rule of justice.

We also establish by this page of our decree that if any prelate of any Church, or any person of whatever dignity, should attempt to violate this charter of our privilege, which we confirm by the authority of the prince of the apostles, let him be anathema; let him incur the wrath of God and be an exile from the assembly of all the saints. Nevertheless, the dignity of the aforesaid monastery, granted by us and supported by apostolic authority, shall remain perpetually inviolate.

Written by the hand of Paul, notary and archivist of the holy Roman Church, in the month of October, in the sixth indiction. Farewell. Given on the fifth day before the Nones of October, by the hand of Gregory, nomenclator and apocrisiarius of the holy Apostolic See; while the Lord Jesus Christ reigns as emperor, in the first year of the pontificate of the lord John, supreme pontiff, universal pope, and bishop, in the sixth indiction.

## XIII. TO THE MONKS OF SAINT VAAST OF ARRAS. (Year 875.) He confirms everything contained in the charter of the Emperor Charles.

[Col. 0658A]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the brothers of the monastery of Blessed Vaast, which is called Nobiliacus or Atrebas, where Saint Vaast, confessor of Christ, himself rests bodily, forever.

If we have piously provided for the interests of the servants of God and fortified places dedicated to Christ with apostolic sanctions, so that the ministers of divine worship, devoting themselves to God there, may be protected from the assaults of worldly storms and varied disturbances, we believe that nothing more pleasing than this holocaust can be offered to our Redeemer.

[Col. 0658B]

It is therefore clearer than daylight to all the sons of the Church that our most beloved son, King Charles, visiting the thresholds of the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul and honorably received by us, after solemnly paying his royal vows at the tomb of Blessed Peter on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, received imperial dignity in the church of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, through the laying on of our hands.

Thereafter, no less sincerely than devoutly, he requested us to decree, by the authority of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of our apostolate, a privilege strengthened by the agreement of the Roman and Apostolic See for the brothers of the aforesaid monastery of the confessor of Christ, Vaast. By this privilege they were to possess securely and without disturbance the cloister and aforesaid monastery, together with everything which he had granted to them by his charter and caused to be fortified by the decree of the Gallican bishops.

For this reason, since we perceived that the same Augustus had done this after being touched by divine love, we gladly granted his petitions, decreeing by apostolic authority that the things inserted here should remain unshaken:

For the endowment of the church: Maisbodvillum, Bais, Senous, Herbodcisternam, Pomerias, Herlincurtem, and manses at Boninicurtem, together with Longobragium, Manium, Morsele, and Sceldogotheim, Juventiacum, one mansus in the estate called Dominica, and one mansus at Farreolo.

For the necessities of the brothers, namely food and drink: half of the village called Hovavilla, one tavern, the royal estate of Filciacum, Theuludum, Bigartium, Hecnam-curtem, Bernevilla, Mediolanas, Puteas Aquas, Angeli-curtem, a valley with one brewery and two mills, Stagras, Saltiacum, Atiamentarius, Mast, Marcheim, Seringe-him, Emmo’s precaria, and Tangigarii.

For the chamber: estates situated in the district of Batua, through which the two-branched river Rhine flows, namely Rehxnam and Wulfrum, together with the chapel situated there; and Rotheim, situated upon the river Versia. Likewise, in the other Rotheim, six manses; and, beyond the aforesaid Rhine, thirty-six manses, together with their appurtenant woods.

Then, in the district of Arras: Athejas, Saltiacum, Liniacum, Campanias, three manses at Fontanido, one mansus at Lambras, another at Hadas, and one tavern in the village of the monastery.

For the gatekeeper: the estate of Berneja; one mansus at Anzinio, with a mill; and five manses at Enez, with a mill, together with the tithe of the whole abbey.

For the hospital of the poor: seven manses at Daginvilla, the estate of Boneja, three manses at Lentsales, and a fifth part of the entire tithe.

For the house of the sick: all tolls from the market, and these estates which Saint Vaast gave or restored for the remedy of his soul: Frontellicurte, Cilliacum, Lutosus Mons, and Tilgidum.

Therefore, with all their appurtenances, revenues, and dependents, just as these estates have been arranged and handed over in the text of the charter, we sanction by the authority of our apostolate that no mortal may arrange, change, or in any way do anything else concerning them, whether much or little, except what has been established by our aforesaid most pious son, the Augustus. Rather, every arrangement shall depend upon the judgment of the abbot.

Whoever, therefore, treats as worthless what the holy Apostolic See has established, and attempts in any way to violate it through reckless audacity, prompted by avarice and diabolical greed, if he appears to be a transgressor in whole or in part, shall, by the authority of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of our apostolate, be bound by the bonds of anathema as a thief and sacrilegious person; excluded from the unity of Mother Church and from participation in the body and blood of Christ, he shall receive the sentence of condemnation with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, and with the devil and his most terrible pomp, on the dreadful day of the great judgment.

But whoever sincerely observes these apostolic constitutions shall receive blessing and mercy from the Lord Jesus Christ and shall have a portion and fellowship with those whose names are written in the Lamb’s book of life from the foundation of the world. Amen.

Given by the hands of Anastasius, chief archivist, in the first year of the empire of the most serene Augustus Charles, and in the first year after his consulship, in the eighth indiction.

## XIV. TO CARLOMANN [elsewhere, LOUIS THE KING]. (Year 875.) That the Pannonian diocese has been assigned to the privileges of the Apostolic See.

*(In Timon, Ancient Image of Hungary, p. 164.)*

[Col. 0659D]

John, bishop, to his beloved son Carlomann, glorious king.

Your prudence will be able to discern by many, varied, and evident indications that the Pannonian diocese was formerly assigned to the privileges of the Apostolic See, if the justice of God finds in Your Excellence the place it ought to find. For the synodal acts indicate this, and written histories demonstrate it. But because, owing to certain hostile disturbances and conflicts, a bishop was not sent there by the Apostolic See for a long time, this has come into doubt among the uninformed [lacuna].

## XV. TO THE BISHOPS OF GAUL AND GERMANY. (Year 876.) He entrusts his authority in Gaul and Germany to Ansegisus, archbishop of Sens.

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the most holy bishops established throughout Gaul and Germany.

[Col. 0660B]

We make known to Your Holiness that, in order to lighten the many ecclesiastical burdens by which we are daily weighed down sufficiently and abundantly—and especially the matters from the regions of Gaul and Germany with which we are continually constrained—we have appointed our brother [Note: Ansegisus, our brother. We have learned that he was raised in 871 from being abbot of Saint Michael’s in the bishopric of Beauvais to the see of Sens. Aimoin, Book V, chapter 27, mentions his Roman legation while he was still abbot. Those who confuse him with another, earlier Ansegisus, abbot of Lobbes, who compiled the capitularies of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious into four books in 827, are mistaken. SIRM. (Cols. 0659D, 0660D)] and fellow bishop Ansegisus, prelate of the Church of Sens, to exercise our authority whenever ecclesiastical usefulness requires it, whether in summoning a synod or in conducting other business throughout Gaul and Germany.

We wish the decrees of the Apostolic See to be made known to you through him, and, in turn, that whatever has been done should, when necessary, be disclosed to us through his report, so that greater and more difficult matters may be referred to us for arrangement and clarification on his recommendation.

Therefore, giving every attention to this pious sanction, unanimously accept what we decree concerning it by apostolic authority. We have recognized him, and have found him so devoted to the Apostolic See and so faithful in what has been entrusted to him, that we rightly judge that such matters can be committed to him. Indeed, we confidently believe that even greater responsibilities ought to be conferred upon him, on account of his holiness, the merit of his faith, and the gift of wisdom granted to him by God.

We wish you good health in Christ. Given on the fourth day before the Nones of January, in the ninth indiction. Read publicly in the synod of Pontigon.

## XVI. BULL OF POPE JOHN TO THE CONGREGATION OF SAINT MEDARD OF SOISSONS. (Year 876.) The division of the monks of Saint Medard of Soissons is confirmed.

[Col. 0660D]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable congregation of religious monks of the venerable monastery of Saint Medard, saint and confessor of Christ, and also of Blessed Sebastian, martyr of Christ, forever.

Whenever those things are requested of us by a petitioner’s desire which unquestionably accord with all reason, it is fitting that we grant them with willing mind and extend our assistance to pious petitioners. Therefore, let all the faithful of Christ know that our most beloved son, Charles the emperor Augustus, visiting the thresholds of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, devoutly represented to us that, for the benefit and use of the aforesaid venerable monastery and of the monks named above who serve the Lord there, we should confirm by the privilege of our apostolate the immovable properties which that most Christian Caesar is known to have bestowed by royal charter, both in honor of those same saints and for the increase of his reward. Their names are written below:

Berneium, Croviacum, Domno Regium, Sodoleum, Berziacum together with a mill, Berziso, two marisci, a granary, and, on account of these, Murocinetum, Cerniacum-vadum, as Hilduinus, the former abbot, held them as his demesne; adding at Murocinctum one mansus, as well as Malcas and fishponds by the sea, twenty-four bonaria of cultivated land at Cubonimaci, five manses at Ruminiacum, part of the meadow at Geigium, and two manses in the village called Lentegere-vicinium.

He decreed that the monks’ clothing chamber should have three estates, Capra, Albiacum, and Solma; that the hospital for nobles should receive a ninth from the estates of the abbey according to ancient custom and should have Cauciacum together with the timber lands of Pivone; and that the hospital for pilgrims should receive a tenth and have Hatoniscurtem.

The treasurer, gatekeeper, hospitaller, and chamberlain shall have a full provision twice a year, during the eight-day periods of the Nativity of the Lord and the Lord’s Resurrection. In addition, from the other aforesaid estates they shall have a full provision on the feast of the Nativity of his beloved son Carlomannus; after his death, they shall transfer that day to the day of his deposition. Likewise, from the estate of Bernoilo he decreed that an abundant provision should be made for the same monks on the anniversary of his aunt Berta, and that lights should be supplied to the lower church of Saint Sophia and the upper church of the Holy Trinity, as is contained in the privilege made by that pious Augustus concerning all these matters.

Thus, whatever the same illustrious Caesar has bestowed, or shall hereafter bestow, of movable and immovable property and of treasure, for the remedy of his soul, shall remain altogether firm and inviolate forever.

For this reason, since we trust that the same exalted emperor, touched by divine love, acted piously, and since we wish to favor his suitable requests, we decree, establish, and confirm in every way by apostolic authority all the immovable properties mentioned above, together with nobles and servants of either sex, and together with the treasure, for the use and benefit of the monks named above, just as that most excellent emperor has granted, or shall grant, them to the same monastery by imperial charter for the salvation of his soul.

We establish, under the invocation of divine judgment and the prohibition of anathema, that no mortal may in any way give away, remove from the rights of our venerable monastery or from the benefit of the monks, alienate, steal, or withdraw by any method or device any of all these things. Rather, all these possessions, and whatever shall further be brought into the rights, dominion, or benefit of our venerable monastery and of the monks living there, whether by the pious Caesar himself or by others who fear God, shall remain forever.

If anyone, which we never wish, should not fear to act otherwise against this decree of our confirmation, and should presume to alienate, diminish, withdraw, or rashly change anything belonging to it, or attempt to arrange it otherwise than has already been arranged, or should appear to be a transgressor in whole or in part, let him know that by the judgment of almighty God he is bound by the chains of anathema. Let him have his portion with the devil and his most terrible pomp, with Judas the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, and with all the impious, and let him be alien from the kingdom of God.

But whoever proves to be a true observer and guardian of these things in every respect, with a pious intention, may deserve to obtain blessing, grace, heavenly mercy, and forgiveness of his sins from the just judge, the Lord our God.

Written by the hand of Benedict, regional notary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of January, in the ninth indiction. Farewell. On the fourth day before the Nones of January, by the hand of Anastasius, librarian of the holy Apostolic See, in the fourth year, God favoring, of the pontificate of the lord John; while the lord Charles, the most pious emperor, crowned by God, reigns perpetually as Augustus, in the first year of his empire and the first year after his consulship, in the ninth indiction.

## XVII. TO HINCMAR, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS. (Year 876.) That a bishop should be ordained in the Church of Laon in place of Hincmar.

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims.

Although [Note: Although, etc. While Hincmar of Laon was still alive, he orders another to be installed in his place, agreeing with Emperor Charles concerning his deposition, which Adrian had disapproved. Thus Hedenulfus was elected three months later. SIRM. (Cols. 0661D, 0662D)] we had never doubted the judgment of Your Holiness, nevertheless, because our most beloved son Charles, the invincible emperor, questioned with the greatest care by us, reported to our Apostolate the circumstances of the judgment pronounced by Your Blessedness and your fellow bishops against Hincmar, formerly bishop of Laon, we have recognized that the judgment was entirely just. For so great a prince could affirm nothing unless it were supported by truth. Therefore we considered it wrong not to give his report an unhesitating hearing.

Do not now leave the Church of Laon widowed and without pastoral government; rather, select without partiality a suitable man from the clergy of the Church of Laon, one in whom the votes of all agree, and appoint him bishop over that Church without delay. We also wish an envoy of the aforesaid most pious emperor to be present at the election, so that, without worldly agitation, a man may be chosen from every side who is shown in all respects to be suitable according to the sacred canons.

We wish Your Holiness good health in Christ. Given at Rome to Theodoric, by command of Pope John and of the lord Charles, the new emperor, through the hands of Anastasius, librarian, in the secretariat of the church of Saint Peter, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 876, on the Nones of January, in the ninth indiction. It was carried by the same Theodoric to Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, in the city of Rheims, in the same year and indiction, on the fifth day before the Ides of March.

## XVIII. TO KING ALDEFONSUS. (Year 876.) The Church of Oviedo is made metropolitan for Galicia.

[Col. 0663B]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Aldefonsus, most Christian king, and to all venerable bishops, abbots, and orthodox Christians.

Since the eternal providence of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, makes us his successors in the care of all Christianity, we are bound by that exhortation of our Lord Jesus Christ with which he admonished the blessed apostle Peter, saying in a certain utterance [in place of a privilege]: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven,” and so forth (Matthew 16).

Again, when the hour of our Lord’s glorious passion was approaching, he said: “I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and you, once converted, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22).

Therefore, because the report of your renown has been wonderfully revealed to us through these brothers visiting the thresholds of the apostles, namely the presbyters Severus and Desiderius [elsewhere: the presbyter and Synderedus], with the sweet fragrance of goodness, I admonish you with paternal exhortation to persevere, with grace as your guide, in the good works you have begun, so that the abundant blessing of blessed Peter, your protector, and of ourselves may protect you.

And whenever any of you, dearest sons, wishes to come to us or send someone, from the remotest regions of Galicia—to which, apart from me, the Lord has appointed you as rulers—we embrace you with all the exultation of our heart and joy of spirit as our sons by right. We command all of you to be subject to the Church of Oviedo, which by your agreement and continual petition we have established as metropolitan.

We also grant to the aforesaid see that whatever kings or faithful people have justly offered, or shall in the future, with the Lord’s help, contribute, shall remain ratified, firm, and unshaken forever. I exhort you all to have these bearers of our letters commended to you. Farewell.

## XIX. [Note: This and the preceding letter are found in the History of Sampiro.] TO THE SAME. (Year 876.) He urges that the church of Saint James be consecrated.

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Aldefonsus, glorious king of Galicia.

Having received the letters of Your Devotion, and knowing you to be devoted to your holy Church, we offer you many thanks, praying the Lord that the strength of your kingdom may abound [elsewhere: abound abundantly] and that he may grant you victory over your enemies.

For we, dearest son, as you requested, pour forth continual prayers to the Lord, that he may govern your kingdom, keep you safe, guard and protect you, and raise you above your enemies. Have the church of Blessed James consecrated by the bishops of Spain, and celebrate a council with them.

We also, glorious king, are already constrained, as you are, by the pagans; day and night we engage them in war. But almighty God grants [elsewhere: may grant] us triumph over them.

For this reason we ask Your Devotion, and earnestly entreat you, that, since, as we have said, we are greatly oppressed by the pagans, you do not fail to send us some useful and excellent Moorish horses (*Mauriscos*) with trappings (*armis*), which the Spaniards call *Alpharaces*. In receiving them, we shall praise the Lord, give thanks to you, and repay you through their bearer with blessings from Saint Peter.

Farewell, dearest son and most illustrious king.

## XX. TO THE BISHOPS AND COUNTS ESTABLISHED IN THE KINGDOM OF CHARLES. (Year 876.) He praises them for having remained steadfast in faith toward Charles and speaks of the envoys whom he was sending to Gaul to settle disagreements.

[Col. 0664C]

Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has until now caused the constancy of your sincerity and faith—so to speak, harder than diamond—in loyalty to the invincible prince, the lord Charles, our spiritual son and ever Augustus, to persist not undeservedly; and who has more clearly demonstrated, by the gift of his generous grace, how great a warmth of charity flourishes in you, so that he might make known to the nations the power of his glory and reveal to all the riches of his goodness for the advancement of the faithful and the correction of unbelievers.

For you have shown, dearest ones, how benevolently your goodwill is disposed toward the cultivation of peace and harmony, and you have fulfilled in deed what Christ himself demands of you in the Gospel: “Whatever you wish people to do for you, do also for them” (Matthew 7). And the Apostle says: “Faith without works is dead” (James 2).

Therefore our apostolate, filled with the rejoicing of immense happiness, first rendered sufficient and due praise to almighty God, since we can do nothing without him; and it does not cease to give manifold thanks to you, who have diligently preserved unstained faith toward so great an emperor, and to raise you up with worthy praises.

Indeed, dearest ones, you acted with sufficient prudence when, although others—as we say with tears—were deceived either willingly or through cunning and fraud, you, using the warmth of faith and keeping God before your eyes, refused to be burdened or stained by the factions of the wicked or tyrants.

Rather, you resisted, did not consent to their wickedness, and did not participate in the sins of others. Therefore you will be able to say freely: “A perverse heart did not cling to me,” because “there is no faithful partnership between an unbeliever and a believer, between Christ and Belial, between justice and iniquity, or between light and darkness.”

Since this is so, stand firm in the faith and act manfully. Preserve unshaken, as you began, the allegiance specially promised to your elder, the lord emperor, and, strengthened for the better, provide for his honor and advancement. Strive with the utmost care lest, for temporal things, you lose eternal things; for bodily things, spiritual things; for earthly things, heavenly joys.

Know that, with the help of him who says, “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10), strength will be given you from heaven and perseverance granted. By the help of the supreme divinity your hearts will be strengthened; indeed, the Lord will strengthen your minds in charity and grace to repel all the snares of your enemies, and he will protect you forever and ever.

Thus the Lord and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ may again and again be blessed, and countless thanks may be returned to you by our pontificate—or rather, by all the faithful of Christ.

But if any among you should still be found to have suffered injury in some matter, which we by no means believe, we exhort them to come to their senses and to offer worthy correction by reforming themselves. For whoever he may be, of whatever rank, dignity, or order, who, together with our present envoys—namely John and John, venerable bishops, and also our beloved associates—whom we have sent in our name to those regions to examine and canonically or legally settle the matters that arose this year between the two brothers, refuses to meet them at the place they designate and humbly satisfy them, let such a person know that, by the authority of almighty God, of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, princes of the apostles, and of our unworthiness, pardon will henceforth be denied him, and that whoever refuses to be a companion in discipline will not thereafter be a companion of our communion.

We wish Your Holiness or Glory good health in Christ. Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the ninth indiction. Read publicly in the synod of Pontigon.

## XXI. TO THE BISHOPS WHO, DESERTING CHARLES, HAD ADHERED TO KING LOUIS. (Year 876.) He rebukes their disloyalty, urges them to repent, and instructs them to receive kindly the envoys sent by the Apostolic See.

[Col. 0665D]

By a true report [Note: [Col. 0665D] “By a true report.” The foremost of those who at that time deserted Charles was, according to Aimo, Ingelramnus, recently chamberlain and intimate of the king, now an adviser to Louis, king of Germany, in invading his brother’s kingdom. Concerning these matters, the same Aimo—or rather his Continuator, from the Annals of Saint-Bertin, under the year 875—says in Book V, chapter 32: [Col. 0666D] “To resist Louis, the leading men of Charles’s kingdom, at the command of Queen Richildis, bound themselves by oath; but they did not keep it. Instead, laying Charles’s kingdom waste from their own side, they devastated it in the manner of enemies. Likewise Louis, with his army, laid the same kingdom waste.” SIRM.] we have learned that, when our beloved and spiritual son, Charles, the most glorious Emperor Augustus, your elder, came to the thresholds of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, humbly paying everywhere to the Lord God the vows he had long before desired to offer, as befits the most Christian patron of Christ’s Church, and receiving through the ministry of our humility the imperial diadem undoubtedly bestowed upon him by God, his brother Louis—namely, the king, if indeed he ought rightly to be called a king, since he did not govern the impulses of his mind as they fell headlong into impiety—entered his kingdom with a gathered multitude of wicked people and, after the manner of pagans, disturbed the Church of God, that is, the people redeemed by Christ’s precious blood and dwelling in peace. Yet you presumed to abandon your fellow citizens and companions, who plainly appear to be faithful to God and their lord, and to cling to Louis; with him, against the Lord, your nation, and your people, you dared to take up arms against him along with his enemies, contrary to the state of your fidelity and to the promise of the divine sacraments, contrary to the duty of your sacred ministry and to the oath of your pledge and faith, and likewise to commit abominable and impious acts.

Alas, how grievous! Why did you not hesitate willingly to commit the crime of such great iniquity? Why did you not hesitate to display to the whole world, like Judas Iscariot, the evil of such great infidelity as an accursed example? What nation, on hearing this, will not hate you? What kingdom will not judge you hateful? Even among peoples who certainly do not know the true God, the commission of such wickedness appears improper. Yet for the sake of earthly gains or threats you did not disdain to attack those whom, by your fellowship and unanimity, you ought to have defended and saved as yourselves, and to persecute them together with their enemies.

For the Lord says: “No one has greater love than this, that he lay down his life for his friends” (John 15). It is therefore clear that you possessed none of that love which works through charity, without which it is impossible to please God, and upon which, as we know, the whole Law and the Prophets depend. Rather, you had long carried Cain the fratricide in your hearts.

Are you not, according to the testimony of Truth, the light of the world and the salt of the earth? By word and example alike, ought you not most earnestly to shine upon all as lamps in the world and season the foolish minds of human beings with the salt of heavenly wisdom? Did not the Holy Spirit appoint you bishops to govern the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood? Was it not rather your duty to teach the people, instead of lending your support to matters so perverse?

We therefore grieve over you as over members of Christ’s body, saying with the Prophet: “My belly, my belly, I suffer pain; the senses of my heart are troubled” (Jer. 4); and again: “Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, so that I may mourn for this people day and night?” (Jer. 9).

Accordingly, we admonish, exhort, and, desiring in our affection to care greatly for your salvation, earnestly urge you that, coming to your senses and abandoning the wicked author of such great iniquity, you should return with all your heart and faithful will to your elder, the emperor Augustus, beloved of God, and take every care thereafter to remain more faithful to him.

For it was your duty to announce peace to those who are near and to those who are far away, as the Lord says: “Climb upon a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion. Cry out, do not cease; lift up your voice like a trumpet” (Isa. 40). It was your duty to announce to the people their crimes and sins, lest their blood be required by the Lord from your hand—not, as has been said, to follow them. And therefore, according to the Prophet, you have been polluted, who says: “Woe, because I was silent, because I am a man polluted in lips, and I dwell among a people having polluted lips” (Isa. 6). By sharing in their evil crimes and fruitless works, you have shown yourselves blameworthy.

Nevertheless, because we know beyond doubt that the bowels of God’s mercy extend widely, return and do not hereafter bear the yoke with the unfaithful. No longer imitate those who violate the covenants of holy peace, divide unity, and presume to sow weeds in the Lord’s field to their own misery. Return and pursue the better gifts; do not again obey the deceits of the ancient enemy. Rather, as ministers of God, following the Lord’s commands, strive in every respect to stand perfectly with the aforesaid emperor, our most beloved son.

For if you attempt to remain with the aforementioned king Louis or with any of his sons for the purpose of causing scandal and disturbing the kingdom, or in any way to offer them assistance, and if you do not instead return with complete certainty to that same beloved son of ours, Caesar Augustus, and stand faithfully with all your strength beside him against his enemies, know that through the legates of our authority you will be subjected to anathema.

Receive kindly our present envoys, namely John and John, venerable bishops, and our beloved familiars. Listen intelligently to the mission entrusted to them and obey it effectively, so that all may understand how truly you are sons of peace and no mortal may remain unaware of it. For they serve as legates on behalf of Christ, who is our peace, since without doubt they have been sent by the apostolic see for the sake of peace.

We wish you now and always to prosper in Christ. Recited in the synod of Pontigon.

## XXII. To the Bishops Established in the Kingdom of Louis, King of Bavaria. (Year 876.)

He reproves them for not restraining King Louis from invading the kingdom of his absent brother Charles, and advises them to strive to satisfy the legates whom he is sending to examine the affairs that have arisen between the two brothers.

[Col. 0667D]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the most reverend and holy archbishops and bishops established in the kingdom of Louis, the glorious king of Bavaria.

We follow the order of apostolic moderation if, while retaining concern for the Churches of God, we set up a wall of correction for the house of spiritual Israel, and either embrace concordant minds within the unity of ecclesiastical peace, or recall the discordant to the grace of concord, or at least place an iron griddle between ourselves and those who, ensnared by the deceits of the apostate angel—that is, the sower of weeds—despise concord with the holy apostolic see, in accordance with the teaching of the prophet Ezekiel (Ezek. 4).

For the Lord of peace, about to return to the Father, earnestly commended the good of peace to his disciples and left it as an exceedingly firm testament to future heirs, saying: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14). And the blessed apostle Paul says: “Be diligent to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace: one body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling” (Eph. 4), since they can in no way reach the one hope of their calling unless they hasten toward it with united minds alongside their neighbors.

Therefore, just as those who preserve peace from the testament left to them through the apostles are sons of God, so plainly those who disturb peace are sons of the devil. For he was a liar from the beginning and did not stand in the truth; and through his envy, as it is written, death entered the world (Wis. 2). While envying our first parents, he—himself already deceived—prepared the snare of deception and offered mortals the cup of death. Those whom he knew would become immortal through the merit of obedience, he infected with the poison of disobedience; thus the enemy of life brought the sentence of death upon all human beings.

Finally, by the same snares with which he had deceived our first parents, he still slaughters the sons of Adam and, out of hatred born of his ambition, separates fraternal hearts. Thus those whom the one thigh of their father once held can no longer contain all Gaul; brother envies his brother’s advancement; and the one whom he had refused to follow despite repeated apostolic admonitions, even in the most difficult circumstances, he now grieves to see preferred by the apostolic see. Indeed, goaded like Cain by his brother’s sacrifice—that is, his obedience—he rushes against his brother, gnashing his teeth.
