He infects his faithful with various deceits, drives them to swear falsely by the terrible name of God, longs to corrupt the peace of the kingdom, rooted by his brother’s long labor, and, listening only to his sinful accomplices, causes his feet to run toward evil. Though the fields of Fontenay were still wet—fields he had stained with human blood in his youth—in his decrepit old age, breathing threats and slaughter, he hastens, for the sake of his singular ambition, to spill the blood of many Christians.

Though through his brother’s love he ought to have hoped, by the merit of his obedience, for the blessing of the apostolic see and to extend his own pious works, he desires stubbornly to subjugate another’s kingdom by his arms, so that he may possess by domination those whom he acquires by arms and force the necks of freeborn men, accustomed to ancient liberty, beneath a new servitude.

Who, most beloved, performs this deed among such brothers, whom we embrace with equal spiritual love, except the ancient adversary of the human race, acting through his agents? While he envies the advancement of the good, he always strives to sow weeds in the field of God’s holy Church.

Who, dearest ones, performs this deed except the devil? Envying Charles’s virtues from the beginning of his life and fearing that his religious purpose might spread farther, he first harassed him with light but frequent darts; then he goaded him with many adversities, like exceedingly hard battering rams. He persuaded his faithful to rebel repeatedly; while Charles was fighting on the front against the Northmen for the liberation of God’s Church and striving to force the enemies of Christ’s cross into final submission, he stirred up the mind of your elder to invade the abandoned empire. He incited his very familiars, and finally his own son, to attack Charles hostilely.

And lest Charles should ever be able to attain the empire, which it is clear was conferred upon him not by human favor, although through the ministry of our humility, but by God, the devil used all the power of his deceit and all the craft of his counsel to wage war against him.

But almighty God, by whose providence the expanse of the world is governed and ruled through princes of mutable affairs, wished to instruct Charles through scourges. He never permitted him to be utterly crushed, as you know. And, intending at last to reveal through him the afflictions of his holy Church, as had been divinely disclosed and as we now truly believe, God had Charles long desired by our predecessors, the pontiffs of venerable memory, Nicholas and Adrian. Finally, until these most dangerous times, when nearly all Italy is surrounded by the sons of Belial, he mercifully preserved him.

By angelic guidance he directed Charles’s paths through impassable places; he freed him after frustrating the ambushes prepared for him; he made slippery marshes passable on horseback; he showed that the fords of deep rivers, unknown for many centuries, could be crossed. When the elements yielded contrary to nature, he terrified the hearts of the doubting. He permitted Charles to enter Italy not only without bloodshed but with great honors, while the peoples on every side rejoiced; and, through the privilege of the apostolic see, approved by the favor of all, he raised him to imperial power.

Thus, although for so many years we have been afflicted in various ways for the defects of God’s holy Church, as our common sins deserve, we may be consoled through the prudent care he has shown. Through him the condition of the Gallican Churches and the vigor of the whole religion in those regions are known to have flourished again with general approval.

Therefore, foreseeing the future prosperity of the human race’s enemy, the devil stirred up the mind of our beloved son Louis, your glorious king—if indeed he deserves to be called a son, since he has always been most disobedient to the admonitions issued by our predecessors and by us; if he ought to be called glorious, although he approved wars against Christians that could win no triumphs; if he can be called a king, since he refused to govern himself—so that he might fight ingloriously against his absent brother.

Louis did not keep before his eyes the fear of God, nor recognize the judgment impending upon him in his advanced age, nor consider blood relationship and fraternal agreements; nor did he preserve the discipline of Christian religion. He disregarded both the writings of our predecessors and our recent admonitions to religious princes—and, what is more astonishing, contrary to the custom of ancient tyrants, he thought lightly of them. He anticipated the time imposed upon him by us, when he was to make a lawful peace agreement with his brother through our mediation, and, as far as lay within him, through your negligence or audacious compliance, invaded his absent brother’s kingdom. By this he stained the beauty of the whole Church of God, corrupted peace, banished religion, and—as Terence put it briefly—by appearing as an extortioner of another’s goods and a perverter of laws, he loosened the reins of every crime.

Although we do not deny that he is exceedingly blameworthy, whom meanwhile we embrace with the affection due to a son, we recognize that you are much more blameworthy. In those regions you have been endowed with priestly teaching and instructed by the recent admonitions of our apostolate. Since you never appear freely to have resisted in accordance with your office, you are plainly proved to have consented. You are called shepherds, yet because you did not pull back the flock entrusted to you, you certainly drove it toward the precipice.

And where, we ask, is the fact that we exercise Christ’s place in the Church, if we do not struggle on Christ’s behalf against the insolence of princes—especially since, according to the Apostle, “our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers” (Eph. 6)?

Where is the fact that we are called bishops, if from the lofty watchtowers of ecclesiastical discernment we do not see the sword approaching, or, seeing it, flee from announcing that it must be avoided? Indeed, we are rightly understood to be called priests not for honor but for display if we strive to follow those whom we ought to teach, and do not at least terrify with pastoral words those whom we ought to correct.

For this reason the Lord, through the prophet Isaiah, rebukes the silence of priests, saying: “Dumb dogs, unable to bark” (Isa. 56). Through Ezekiel he rebukes the negligence of priests, saying: “You did not go up to oppose them, nor set up a wall for the house of Israel, so that you might stand in battle on the day of the Lord” (Ezek. 13).

To go up to oppose them means to resist the powers of this world with a free voice in defense of the flock; and to stand in battle on the day of the Lord means to resist those fighting perversely out of love for justice.

Again, through the same prophet he terrifies us, saying: “If you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked man, I will require his blood from your hand” (Ezek. 33).

What shall we say to this, brothers? Perhaps you think yourselves excusable because you say that a king should not be rebuked but only admonished. The apostolic trumpet answers: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5). And Paul says to Timothy: “Reprove, entreat, rebuke, with all patience and teaching” (2 Tim. 4). Likewise he says to Titus: “Command the rich of this world not to be proud in mind, nor to hope in the uncertainty of their riches” (1 Tim. 6).

Perhaps you feared some persecution. But the Lord commanded as follows: “When they persecute you in one city, flee into another” (Matt. 10). Perhaps you feared death, which is the final punishment for all. But our same Redeemer exhorted us in the Gospel, saying: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (ibid.).

Since you feared none of these things, nor was any of them to be inflicted upon you, it undoubtedly remains that you not only failed, in accordance with the prohibition of the apostolic see, to restrain your countrymen as priests from invading another’s kingdom; rather, by joining your favorable complicity to their greed, you sewed cushions, as it were, beneath the elbows of their hands and hastened the prophetic “Woe” that says: “Woe to those who sew cushions beneath every elbow of the hands and make pillows beneath the head of people of every age, to capture souls” (Ezek. 13).

For just as an elbow is received by a cushion, or the head of one lying down by pillows, when the harshness of correction is removed from the sinner and the softness of favor is applied to him, so that he may lie comfortably in error, unstruck by any harshness of contradiction. Rulers who love themselves provide such things, as our blessed predecessor Gregory recalls, to those whom they fear they can influence less because of their zeal for temporal glory.

What, then, brothers—if indeed you still deserve to be called brothers—must you do? You have disregarded the salutary admonitions of the apostolic see and have not carried out Christ’s mission. Therefore, at last, agreeing in judgment with the holy see, you must admonish with a free voice both our beloved son Louis, your king, whom we still decide to embrace with paternal affection, and all the subjects of that kingdom, and completely restrain them from invading or oppressing the empire of our beloved son Charles, always Augustus.

Henceforth, whether through flatteries or threats, you must never give any consent or favor toward bringing about a fatal battle and shedding Christian blood—if you do not wish to be stripped of your priestly insignia, immediately separated from apostolic communion, and bound, which we never desire, by the chains of perpetual anathema.

For whoever he may be in rank, order, eminence, or profession, if he refuses humbly to meet our present legates, John the Sicilian and likewise John the Tuscan, venerable bishops, whom we have sent in our place [perhaps “we send” is missing; HARD.] to those regions to examine and at the same time canonically or legally determine the affairs that have arisen this year between the two brothers, at the place designated by them, and to satisfy them humbly, let him know that, by the authority of almighty God, of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and of our humility, pardon will henceforth be denied him. Nor shall he thereafter be a participant in our communion—whoever refuses to be a companion in discipline, to use the words of our most holy predecessor.

We wish your Holiness, obedient always to the admonitions of the apostolic see, to prosper in Christ. Recited in the synod of Pontigon.

## XXIII. To the Counts Established in the Kingdom of Louis, King of Bavaria. (Year 876.)

He reproves them for attempting to invade Charles’s kingdom, and advises them to recall King Louis from that intention and not to refuse to satisfy the legates whom he is sending.

[Col. 0672A]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the glorious counts established in the kingdom of Louis, king of Bavaria.

It is the duty of our ministry, according to the judgment of the blessed apostle Paul, to carry concern for the universal Church of God and to declare with censorial gravity what is suitable or unsuitable in every part of the world. Thus the Lord’s sheep, recognizing the voice of our pastoral concern and humbly listening to the prince of shepherds, may be placed, once recognized, in the fold of the Lord; while diseased sheep, which stubbornly neglect correction, may be driven away from the Lord’s fold through the ministry of apostolic authority, lest they injure the healthy sheep by contagion from the neighboring flock—since many things harm bodies through contact.

For it is written: “If you separate what is precious from what is vile, you will be like my mouth” (Jer. 15). Again: “Remove the evil from your midst.” And in the Gospel the Lord commands that if an eye, foot, or hand causes us scandal, it should be cut off and thrown away (Matt. 9). Elsewhere he says: “If he does not listen to the Church, let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector” (Matt. 18). The Apostle likewise says: “If anyone does not obey our word by letter, mark him, and do not associate with him” (2 Thess. 3).

These testimonies most clearly compel us to ensure that you—who, disregarding the letters of the apostolic see, attempted, as we have heard, to invade the kingdom of our beloved son Charles, the most Christian emperor, contrary to our prohibition and indeed contrary to fear of almighty God, and to corrupt the peace of God’s holy Church—should now be separated from the body of that same Church, which through our predecessors and through us has admonished you by its letters, though until now you have refused to listen.

But because the mercy of the holy apostolic see meanwhile embraces you with the love due to sons, and is known to prefer concealing your sins rather than punishing them, we again send these letters of God’s holy Church to your charity. We urge and insist that, mindful of divine judgment, remembering the fraternal covenant, and taking precautions against the final day of your calling, you flee the devil’s deceit through which death entered the world. Shun discord, the nurse of every crime, as a deadly poison, lest you become like the man of whom Solomon says: “An apostate man, a worthless man, walks with a perverse mouth; he winks with his eyes, shuffles with his foot, speaks with his finger, devises evil in his perverse heart, and continually sows quarrels” (Prov. 6).

Love peace and holiness, without which no one will see God. For just as peacemakers are called by the Lord not only blessed but also sons of God, so those who disturb peace are sons of Satan. The divided offer no sacrifice of good work to God so long as they are divided from the love of their neighbors.

Therefore Matthew gives this command: “If you offer your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, go first to be reconciled with your brother, and then come and offer your gift” (Matt. 5). In this command of the Lord we must consider whose offering is rejected and how intolerable the fault is shown to be. Since past evils are washed away by good works, you ought to consider, most prudent counts, how great are the evils of discord, which, unless extinguished, do not permit the good sacrifice to follow.

Who, then, most beloved, provoked you to crimes of such great discord except the ancient adversary of the human race? Having become an apostate from an angel, he continually strives to sow weeds over the good harvest. Of his greed the Apostle says: “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking someone to devour. Resist him, strong in faith” (1 Pet. 6). Certainly, “faith without works is dead” (James 2). And the blessed Paul, after listing many virtues, placed charity—which covers a multitude of sins—above them, saying: “Whether prophecies will be abolished, or tongues will cease, or knowledge will be destroyed” (1 Cor. 13); and below: “Now these three remain: faith, hope, and charity; but the greatest of these is charity” (ibid.).

Accordingly, John rightly says: “God is charity, and whoever remains in charity remains in God, and God in him” (2 John 4). It is therefore clear that whoever does not remain in God remains in the devil. His members are all who sow quarrels and reject ecclesiastical discipline. To them it is truly said: “You are of your father the devil” (John 8).

The devil, envying Charles’s virtues from the beginning of his life and fearing that his religious purpose might spread farther, harassed him with many adversities and frequently persuaded his faithful to rebel. While Charles was fighting against the Northmen for the liberation of God’s Church and striving to compel them into final submission, the devil stirred up the minds of your elder, your parents, and yourselves to invade his abandoned empire, just as he is known to have done now. He incited his very familiars, and finally his own son, to destroy him. And lest Charles should ever be able to reach the empire, which it is clear was conferred upon him not by human favor, although through the ministry of our humility, but by God, the devil fought against him with all the power of his deceit and all the craft of his counsel.

But almighty God, by whose providence the whole world is governed and ruled through princes of mutable affairs, wished to instruct Charles through frequent scourges. He never permitted him to be utterly crushed, as you have repeatedly observed, so that the future emperor, while exercising power in the kingdom, might learn how greatly he ought to fear the Lord in prosperity and how greatly to trust God in adversity.

Certainly Charles would be blameworthy if, entering the boundaries of his kingdom, he had usurped another’s territory; if, soliciting another’s faithful, he had compelled them to perjury, as you are proved to have done; or if he had violated the peace of the kingdom, as you are doing.

But now, since he came, divinely foreknown and predestined, not on his own initiative but invited by the sons of God’s Church; since by his goodwill alone, without bloodshed, he bound to himself the bravest leaders of this Italy; since he saw his paths directed by an angelic gift through impassable places; since, after the ambushes prepared for him had been frustrated, he recognized that he had been divinely delivered; since he found impassable marshes made passable for him; and since he found the fords of deep rivers almost dry for his armies, like another Israelite leader—we marvel and are astonished that you, who possess understanding, do not recognize that he was preferred by the Lord, whom the insensible elements appear to have recognized.

We marvel and are astonished that you raise murderous weapons against him, whom you saw wearied from infancy by many adversities but whom, under the protection of the Lord, you never saw overcome.

We marvel, I say, and are astonished that you do not follow as truly worthy of imitation the man whom you recognize to have been divinely preferred to you on account of his obedience, but strive, as far as lies within you, to persecute him as detestable. For if the holy see recognized you as more devoted to it on account of his example of obedience, it would pour out upon you the grace of its blessing in this world and obtain through its continual prayers that you be admitted in the future to the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom.

But when shall we think that you will preserve the obedience owed to the holy apostolic see, when we see you rebelling with such manifest signs against the ordinance of almighty God? Your murmuring is not against Charles but against the Lord, whose is the kingdom and who gives it to whomever he wishes. He also says through Solomon: “By me kings reign” (Prov. 8). Again, through the teacher of the nations he testifies: “There is no authority except from God” (Rom. 13); and again: “Whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance” (ibid.).

Return, therefore, to your hearts, transgressors, and, since death does not delay, do not put it off from day to day. Do not wage civil wars; do not raise murderous swords to your own destruction. Do not recall the detestable battle of Fontenay. For just as one who dies in defense of God’s Church is crowned by his own blood, so one who fights against God’s Church and is slain as a deserter from Christianity is undoubtedly condemned.

Do not, beloved, close the door of eternal reward to yourselves for the brief advantages of this life. Do not for passing things neglect the benefits of eternal goods. For, according to the saying of blessed Mark: “What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” (Matt. 8).

For this reason, through these letters of apostolic authority, we again exhort and entreat your entire community, whom we desire to embrace with paternal affection, that at last, agreeing in judgment with us, you admonish with a free voice both our beloved Louis, your glorious king—if indeed he deserves to be called a son, since he has always been most disobedient to the admonitions of the apostolic see; if he should be called glorious, since even in decrepit old age he desires the shedding of Christian blood; if he should be called a king, since he has been able to govern neither you nor himself so as to prevent him from corrupting the peace of his absent brother’s kingdom—and all the people of your kingdom.

You must utterly restrain them from invading or oppressing the empire of our beloved son Charles, always Augustus, and henceforth never, whether through flatteries or threats, give any consent or favor toward bringing about a fatal battle and shedding Christian blood, which may the Lord avert.

For whoever the person may be, of whatever eminence or dignity, who refuses humbly to meet our present legates, John the Sicilian and likewise John the Tuscan, venerable bishops, whom we have sent in our place [perhaps “we sent” is missing; HARD.] to those regions to examine and at the same time determine canonically or legally the affairs that have arisen this year between the two brothers, at the place designated by them, and to satisfy them humbly, let that person know that, by the authority of almighty God, of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and of our humility, pardon will henceforth be denied him. Nor thereafter shall he be a participant in our communion who refuses to be a companion in discipline.

We wish your Glory, ever obedient to the apostolic admonitions, to prosper in Christ.

## XXIV. To All the Gauls and Germans. (Year 876.)

Concerning the condemnation of Bishop Formosus, Gregory the nomenclator, and the others who had been excommunicated at Rome in the synod.

[Col. 0675C]

John, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and holy fellow bishops, the archbishops, bishops, abbots, priests, and all judges, and to the entire people established throughout Gaul and Germany.

The Church of God under our care, moved by zeal for the Christian religion and admonished by the impulse of our beloved son, the most serene emperor—or rather by the breath of the Holy Spirit—lodged two accusations concerning various injuries inflicted upon God’s Church against Gregory the nomenclator and his son-in-law George, two vessels of iniquity fighting against the worship of the Most High God. It did so both in the preceding month of February of the present ninth indiction, through Peter, the venerable bishop of Forum Sempronii, who made a tearful complaint before the aforesaid spiritual son of ours, and also through our own pontifical complaint, which it took care to present against the same men on the day before the Kalends of April.

Therefore, through Zacharias and Gaidericus, venerable bishops, and Christopher, primicerius of the apostolic see, we sent them a formal notification of the accusations, admonishing and ordering them that, if they had any confidence in the purity of their conscience, they should endeavor to come to the appointed hearing.

But they said, with smooth speeches and contrived inventions, that they would indeed come and would correct everything according to our will. Yet under the pretext of illness they postponed the day of judgment from one day to the next until they could either kill us together with the faithful of God’s Church or bring into the city of Rome the Saracens whom they had already invited through their closest associates, themselves likewise Saracens, for the destruction of all.

When they saw that, with the Lord’s help, we were prepared against both deceits, and learned that the appointed day of judgment was approaching, they—misled along with certain accomplices of theirs, namely Bishop Formosus, Stephen the secundicerius, Sergius the master of the soldiers, and Constantine, son of the nomenclator—whom not the judgment of our summons but the goad of their own guilty consciences was driving, conspired against the safety of the state and the kingdom of our beloved son Charles, the most serene prince, to whom they had always been unfaithful and whose advancement they had always hindered.

We do not know where they intended to go, but in the silence of night they opened with counterfeit keys the gates of the City called Saint Pancratius. Then, with their accomplices and all the treasures of God’s holy Church, they fled while the Saracens were ravaging everywhere. They left the gates open and, unless divine protection had guarded us, plainly left themselves a means of escape through “many pearls” (multis margaritis; reading uncertain) and the Saracens an entrance to enter.

Astonished at such deeds, we sent Dominicus and Grimoldus, venerable bishops, to summon them. When they returned, they reported that their agents had answered them that they did not know where the fugitives had gone.

When the judgment had been postponed to another day, and we again sought them synodically and legally but were entirely unable to find them, we summoned a synod with the whole Church of God in the basilica of the holy Mother of God, called the Church of the Martyrs. After the customary addresses, we pronounced sentences against them, copies of which, according to ecclesiastical custom, we shall communicate to all of you, so that no opportunity may be given you to share communion with them.

The sentence is as follows:

“Formosus, bishop of Porto, who, sent by our predecessor of blessed memory, Pope Nicholas, to the land of the Bulgarians, so corrupted by his deceits the mind of the king newly reborn in Christ that he testified that he had bound him to himself by terrible oaths, so that, while he lived, he would receive no bishop from the Apostolic See, and professed that he himself had likewise been bound to him by terrible oaths to return to him as quickly as possible; and who obtained from us permission, letters, and the necessary [Col. 0676D] assistance to depart thither: since long ago, driven by ambition, he had attempted to leap from a lesser Church to a greater one, namely the holy Apostolic See, had acquired many supporters for himself, and now, returning backward through a discovered hypocrisy, without our permission or knowledge, abandoned his own parish, left the city, and conspired with his supporters against the safety of the commonwealth and of our beloved son Charles, the prince whom we elected and appointed; unless from now, within the tenth day—that is, the third day before the Kalends of May of the present ninth indiction—he shows us his presence by making satisfaction, we decree, by the authority of Almighty God and of the holy chief apostles Peter and Paul, that he is deprived of all ecclesiastical communion.

“Do you also decree this?” They all answered: “We decree it.” “And unless, after the fifteenth day—that is, the fourth day before the Nones of May of the present ninth indiction—he comes to us, having come to his senses and ready to make satisfaction, we judge that, by the authority and judgment of the Holy Spirit, who always flees what is feigned, he shall be completely stripped of every priestly ministry. Do you also judge this?” They all answered: “We judge it.”

“If he is moved neither by compassion during this period of delay, and does not humbly restore himself to our presence after the twentieth day—that is, the seventh day before the Ides of that same month of May—or if he presumes in any way to disturb the Church of God, or attempts to act or rebel against this common sentence of all of us, let him be anathema from the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and let him know that no hope of restoration or avenue of satisfaction will ever be reserved for him in any synod.

“Gregory the nomenclator, son of the former nomenclator Theophylact, who, corrupting his oath of fidelity in various ways, stained the purity of the holy Church of God through his frauds, avarice, plunder, desires, and deceits for nearly eight years, and, when his accomplices had previously conspired with him, sought by faction to command the supreme pontiff of the Roman city; and who, openly charged with many publicly recited accusations, both first before our beloved son Charles, the most serene emperor, and afterward before us, before the generality of the holy Church of God, through various articles of accusation, and legally summoned by us through Zacharias and Gaudericus, venerable bishops, and Christopher, primicerius of the holy Apostolic See, together with his brother, his son-in-law, and his accomplices, promised that he would present himself for examination and, under oath, restore everything that he had taken from churches, pious places, and other people: afterward he deceitfully evaded our assembly from day to day, until he could either kill us or the faithful of this Church, or introduce into the Roman city the enemies of the Christian name, namely the Saracens, whom he had already invited through his closest Saracen associates; and, deceitfully seizing the appointed day on which he was to be heard canonically or legally, opened with George and Sergius, military commanders, and also Stephen, secundicerius, and his other accomplices, [Col. 0677D] in the silence of night the gates of this holy city, while Saracens threatened it on every side, using counterfeit keys; and, conspiring against the safety of the commonwealth and likewise against the peace of the empire of our aforesaid most serene son and Augustus, fraudulently escaped, and departed with almost all the treasures of the Roman Church, uncertain where he intended to go.

“Likewise, Stephen the secundicerius, who, despoiling various churches through avarice and disgraceful gains, multiplied ancient taxes, and who proved himself, in all the perversities named above, his brother’s associate and accomplice.

“Also George, son of Gregory the primicerius, who abducted his own brother’s concubine and killed him with poison; then, after execrable [Col. 0678A] incest against Christians, while the niece of Benedict, pope of holy memory—through whose resources he had risen from poverty—was still alive, joined himself in fornication to the daughter of the aforesaid nomenclator Gregory; on account of this he nearly openly killed the legitimate wife already mentioned. When, after extracting false envoys concerning this murder from the princes, his wicked son-in-law escaped punishment through the judgment of his accomplice and father-in-law.

“He, moreover, after various murders and kinds of plunder and wickedness, deprived both the patriarchium and the wardrobe of the Apostolic See entrusted to him not only of gold, silver, and cloaks, but also of bronze images and vessels; and, in all his impieties, speaking as his father-in-law’s equal—or rather preceding him—he, matching—or rather surpassing—his father-in-law in all impieties, fraudulently opened with him the city gates while the Saracens raged everywhere, and departed with him in conspiracies [Col. 0678B] against the safety of the commonwealth.

“Likewise Sergius, military commander, son of Theodore, military commander, who had received the niece of the lord Nicholas of revered memory in marriage, and had proved himself so ungrateful and inhuman that, while Nicholas was alive and lying at the point of death, he refused, together with his aforesaid accomplices, to surrender his treasures for almsgiving. He, having abandoned that same wife, through whom he had recovered from the greatest poverty, recently fled with his concubine Valuisindula, after giving an oath that he would take her in marriage, and conspired in all iniquities with his named accomplices.

“Also Constantina, daughter of the aforesaid nomenclator Gregory, who, first, with her father’s consent and under the condition of an oath, was lawfully joined to Cessarius, son of Pippin, the most powerful vestararius; then, after all the wealth of her father-in-law had been exhausted, abandoned her living and healthy betrothed without any legal inquiry and publicly hastened to the marriage of Gratian, son of Gregory, the military commander; and finally, desiring to flee with another man, committed incest. Found pregnant as a result, she abandoned the aforesaid Gratian, son of Gregory, her husband, and departed shamefully to fornicate with rapacious, perjured, sacrilegious, adulterous, and fornication-practicing men.

“Unless within the tenth day—that is, the third day before the Kalends of May of the present ninth indiction—the aforesaid Gregory, Stephen, George, and Sergius, together with Constantina, present themselves to us by making suitable satisfaction, we decree, by the authority of Almighty God and of the holy chief apostles [Col. 0678D] Peter and Paul, that they shall remain deprived of all Christian communion, together with all their communicants and supporters. And unless, after the fifteenth day—that is, the fourth day before the Nones of May of the present indiction—the aforesaid Gregory, Stephen, George, Sergius, and Constantina come to us simply and humbly, ready to be purified—or rather, to the Church of God—we condemn them, by the authority and judgment of the Holy Spirit, together with all who communicate with them, to perpetual anathema.

“But those who, removing themselves from every association with them, return to unity with the holy Apostolic See may trust that the grace of our communion and blessing will be restored to them.”

These things having thus been promulgated by the authority of the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0679A] we exhort all of you through this apostolic letter to read this letter publicly throughout all your dioceses and to send it to neighboring parishes, and to avoid the company of the aforesaid deposed, excommunicated, and anathematized persons as though it were deadly poison. Do not communicate in food, drink, or conversation with those who communicate with them, knowing that whoever mingles with them or with their communicants in prayer, food, drink, or conversation is in every way bound by the same censure of excommunication and anathema, according to the canonical provision, and that he will never be admitted by us to communion without worthy satisfaction and penance.

We desire that Your Holiness may prosper well in Christ, now and always.

Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May. Read out in the synod [Col. 0679B] of Pontigon.

## XXV. To Count Boson

(Year 876.) He gives thanks that, through his efforts, the envoys reached the emperor and completed what had been entrusted to them; and he asks him to arrange that assistance be sent to him against the Saracens as quickly as possible.

John, bishop, to the most illustrious count Boson.

Returning praises to Christ the Lord for your most dear nobility, we give thanks, and, extolling you with praises in the same Lord, rejoice that, supported by His grace and aided by our affection, you granted the envoys of our Apostolic See easy access to the presence of the most serene lord Charles, our spiritual son, ever Augustus, and took care to persuade him to heed with the ear of his piety what had been entrusted to them by us to say to him, and to bring it to a fitting outcome. Since Almighty God inspired the imperial greatness to accomplish this, we highly commend you, who have become a collaborator in our undertaking; and, as we have said, while returning thanks for your diligence, we shall not fail to repay you in return for these and other services. Moreover, whatever we recognize to be fitting for your honor or conducive to your advantage, we shall diligently carry out without delay, and, with the Lord’s help, labor with grateful affection until we complete it.

But you, dearest son, as you have begun, press on still more [Edit. Rom., “more and more”] [Col. 0679D] to eradicate completely the tyranny of our enemies and of those who oppose the holy Church of God, so that those who have not feared to injure the holy Roman Church in many ways may be struck by such a sentence—or rather, judgment—that thereafter, as you have promised, they may never find a place of restoration.

Furthermore, because we have heard that, owing to the extreme necessity of this region of ours, which the Saracens have almost entirely devastated, imperial assistance is to be sent to us, we earnestly beg Your Noble Magnificence not to allow that assistance—or an army of men, which would that it were already present—to linger in those regions in any way . . . by going there, exhort them to come, press them, and continue courageously, for God’s love and ours, until they arrive; for unless they come very quickly and bring us aid, we fear that matters will become worse than before. Through this, sin and loss may arise for the lord emperor, and, since the Church of God, or His pasture’s sheep, are being violently torn apart, the very name of Christ—God forbid—may be blasphemed among the nations.

Given on the Kalends of September, in the tenth indiction.

## XXVI. To King Louis

(Year 876.) He writes that he cannot settle the disagreements between Louis and the emperor unless he first hears the other party; meanwhile he advises him to preserve peace with everyone, especially with the emperor, and to restrain his subjects.

[Col. 0680B]

John, bishop, to his beloved son Louis, glorious king.

We have received letters from Your Belovedness—not, indeed, only one letter—and, on rereading them, we have found in them matters which, unless the prior complaint of our most beloved son, also the most serene emperor, Lord Charles, ever Augustus, had summoned us, we would not merely have admitted but would have investigated and examined before you expected it, and weighed in the balance of a right judgment—which, with God’s help, we trust we shall do.

But since one party ought not easily to be heard without the other, for the moment we do not write a deliberative judgment. Rather, we admonish Your Glory and, by apostolic authority, charge you to preserve peace with everyone, especially with the same emperor; to restrain those subject to you; and, until our examination, to keep yourself—as we hope you will—from every scandal and factional conspiracy. For we, who wish the judgments of the Lord’s priests to be mature, do not seek to favor either him or you against justice.

For this reason, by the grace of the Holy Spirit, through the effort of our humble office, we wish whatever the matter may be to be defined; and what we have decided must still be suspended we shall, with the Lord’s help, conclude by the judgment of our administration after due deliberation.

Given on the Kalends of September, in the tenth indiction.

## XXVII. To the Clergy, Order, and People of the Holy Church of Valva

(Year 876.) He attacks a certain invader of the Church of Valva while its lawful bishop is still alive; he praises them because they judged that the intruder should not be received, and at the same time commands that they never admit him, otherwise threatening the sentence of excommunication.

[Col. 0680D]

John, bishop, to the clergy, order, and people of the holy Church of Valva.

Because the greatest concern binds us to the vigilance which we have undertaken for the oversight of all the Churches of God, so that we may either cut away anticipated faults or watch lest faults learned of by report take root, we do not wish you to remain unaware that word has reached us that someone, trampling upon the reverence due to canonical discipline and acting against all right—indeed, against ecclesiastical law—wishes, while your shepherd is still alive, by rash audacity to corrupt your integrity, and—what is unspeakable—to invade the people themselves, tear apart the Lord’s flock, namely you yourselves, generate schisms, and provoke God to anger by this; claiming as though he had the authority of secular persons to do this and wickedly to exercise powers which cannot rightly be granted by them—or rather by us—while your bishop lives.

We prohibit and detest this so greatly because we know that such an attempt is contrary to the judgment of canonical authority, to the tradition of divine law, and to the examples of the ancient Fathers: while one bishop lives and remains in office, another—whether not requested, or one who cannot and ought not to be requested—invades the living bishop’s seat; either seeks it without our consultation, so to speak, or, because he survives, as we have said, allows such thoughts to enter his heart.

First, however, we give you thanks because, as we have learned, preserving the faith owed to your bishop, you proposed that the same intruder should not be received. Then, by the admonitions of our apostolate, we exhort, command, and advise the devotion of all of you that, while this same bishop of yours is alive, you never give assent to any mortal who attempts perhaps to deceive you, so that you may in any way depart, even slightly, from the fidelity owed to your present bishop, namely the venerable Arnulf. Rather, strive to show him every honor and reverence according to the sacred canons, so that we may have still more [Edit. Rom., “more and more”] [Col. 0681C] reason to give you thanks.

Know that we shall in no way consent to such a wicked deed, but rather shall punish both its perpetrators and those who agree with them. Nevertheless, if we learn that in any respect you have deviated from this legitimate charge of ours, and, despite possessing this authority of ours, we find that you have not resisted the factions of all ambitious persons; or if we learn that you have given your consent, even secretly—God forbid—to anyone attempting such things, know that we shall subject you also to anathema, and, condemning him by the same sentence, shall permanently deprive him of the entire ministry of priestly office, so that he may never preside over anyone.

[Col. 0681D]

Given, etc., in the tenth indiction.

## XXVIII. To a Certain Person

[Note: [Col. 0681D] Perhaps Athanasius, bishop of Naples, to whom several letters below are addressed; he is mentioned by Leo of Ostia, Book I of the *Chronicle of Cassino*, chapter 42. [Col. 0682D] He was the nephew and successor of Saint Athanasius, who is mentioned in the Roman Martyrology on 25 July.]

(Year 876.) He complains about the duke of Naples, the recipient’s brother, who did not obey his admonitions. Therefore he urges him to separate himself from him; otherwise he will be subjected to anathema together with him and his other supporters.

John, bishop . . .

Much has been said to the duke of the Neapolitans—or rather, to the duke of the blind—by us and by our revered predecessors, through envoys and circulating letters; but these words found no place at all in his heart. For his inward parts plainly refused to receive the words of eternal life. The Lord says to the Jews: “Whoever is of God hears the words of God; for this reason you do not hear, because you are not of God” (John 8). He says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word” (John 14). Therefore the proof of love is the exhibition of works.

Your brother is therefore proved not to love God, since he does not keep His commandments by associating with the faithless. For the apostle John says: “Whoever says that he loves God and does not keep His commandments is a liar” (1 John 2).

But even after being despised in this way, we did not neglect what concerned his salvation and that of all the others. Therefore it was not an angel, nor any envoy—as it was prophetically said of our Redeemer—but our own apostolate itself that came in person to save them. What ought it to have done and did it not do? Yet he, to speak with the prophet, “was turned into the bitterness of a foreign vine” (Isaiah 5), and, like deaf adders “stopping their ears” and refusing to hear the voice of the enchanters (Psalm 57)—that is, of preachers—he did not change the color or variety of his deceits, resembling the Ethiopian and the leopard, to which Jeremiah compared the hardness of faithless Israelites. Therefore they were deservedly cut off, as the Apostle wishes concerning such people: “Let those who trouble you be cut off from Christ” (Galatians 5)—that is, from the head and body, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of truth.

Since this is so, your prudence ought not to be disturbed if, among such people, the ministry of teachers ceases, whether because of the sluggish negligence of rulers or because the crime of their subjects requires it. Such things occur by divine judgment, although hidden, just as it is read in the book of blessed Job, where, among other things, it is said of God: “He leads priests away dishonored and overthrows the mighty, changing the speech of the truthful and taking away the teaching of the elders” (Job 12).

Having understood the marrow of this passage, know without doubt that we grant you the choice of one of two alternatives: either, according to what is written, “Go out, go out from their midst, and do not touch what is unclean” (Isaiah 52); or certainly, as long as you associate with such people, you will not be able to appear unlike them, but will surely be punishment for them, as one made like them by association.

For Lot, fleeing the chaos of Sodom, was saved alone when all the citizens had been killed (Genesis 19). Thus Peter, fleeing, was delivered from Herod’s chains and sent out to save the nations (Acts 12). Thus Paul, when the governor of Damascus was watching to seize him, refused to remain confined among the faithless and, lowered through the wall in a basket (Acts 9), hastened to the field of battle.

Nevertheless, lest their blood be required by God from your hands as from a sluggish and negligent watchman who sees the sword and the wolf coming and remains silent (Ezekiel 3), “press on,” as the Apostle urges, “in season and out of season; entreat, rebuke; let no one despise your youth” (2 Timothy 4; 1 Timothy 4). If they listen to you, you will gain your brothers; but if not, at least, by saving yourself, save your soul as quickly as possible, knowing without doubt that we shall soon assemble the bishops of the whole of Hesperia.

With these general threats hanging over them, we shall pronounce against your faithless brother and all his followers and supporters a perpetual anathema in every respect, never afterward to be dissolved. If you strive to escape this and to be found within the bounds of our affection, do not permit yourself in any way to depart from this command of ours or from our exhortation.

We also give thanks for those who through your diligence have been redeemed by the Lord, whom He redeemed from the hands of the enemy. Know that you will offer us nothing more acceptable than these people, for whom Christ’s blood was offered.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of September, in the tenth indiction.

## XXIX. To Bishops Leo and Peter

(Year 876.) He is surprised that, although he is afflicted by Saracen incursions, they have not returned to him; he charges them to return as quickly as possible. If they are subjected to violence by anyone, he commands them to act courageously and to report it to him.

To Leo and Peter, bishops.

Since the innumerable necessities of this Church of God are known to you no less than to us, and since you realized that you had been sent to the most pious Caesar to restrain them with great speed, we are astonished that, while we have been placed in such danger for so long and are being torn apart on every side by Saracen incursions, you have until now neglected to return to us.

For we believe that you have been delayed not so much by anyone’s violence as by your own negligence. We do not know under what ingenious pretexts—but by the counsels and deceits of those whom we have anathematized—you have, like the raven that did not return to the one who sent it during the time of the flood (Genesis 8), forgotten your mission until now, so that you did not trouble to return to Rome from Pavia for so many days.

For this reason we charge you, by the authority of Almighty God and of the holy chief apostles, to return in person as quickly as possible to the holy Apostolic See that sent you and to the seats of your bishoprics. But if, God forbid, [Col. 0683D] you are being held by the violence of certain people, as the satellites of those whom we have anathematized boast, and are not permitted to return to those who sent you, we command you, by the authority of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, remembering the ancient legates of the holy Roman Church, who never withdrew from their missions because of threats, terrors, or death, to strive, by the authority of this letter, to begin your return to us in person; and, if you are permitted, return to us immediately.

But if anyone obstructs you, let the violence you suffer be made known to all Christians and immediately revealed to us, so that, since the legation of the Apostolic See has now suffered shipwreck for the second time contrary to the custom of nations, we may, with the Lord strengthening us, prepare the speediest course of action.

## XXX. To Count Boson

(Year 876.) He grieves that Boson has not brought him aid despite his pleas for assistance against the Saracens. He indicates that the city is in great danger, since it is reported that a large army will soon come to attack it; therefore he asks him to send help as quickly as possible. He is surprised that Boson is detaining his envoys.

John, bishop, to John Boson, count.

We have often endeavored, through envoys and letters, to exhort and beg Your Glory to stretch out a hand of assistance and at last strive to confront the wicked Saracens as an enemy. But, alas, so far we have deserved to obtain no aid that we know we have not yet received from your nobility even an answer, just as we have received none concerning any of our other necessities.

Therefore, grieving and groaning deeply, we again and again admonish, exhort, and beseech Your Belovedness not to delay any longer, nor allow the Lord’s people to be torn apart by those divinely thunderstruck Hagarenes, who have covered the whole surface of the earth like locusts, so that, after almost all the inhabitants have been removed and handed over to plunder and the sword, the land has been reduced to a wilderness and to lairs of beasts.

What is even more to be feared and guarded against is that we have learned from a reliable report that a very large fleet will soon come to attack the city: one hundred ships, fifteen of them large, carrying horses [Col. 0684C]. If you consider attentively how great and incomparable an evil this is, you will understand; for the destruction of this city is the loss of the whole world, indeed the ruin of the Christian religion itself.

Therefore, in accordance with what our spiritual son, ever Augustus, has necessarily entrusted to your diligence, setting aside concern for all other matters, you must consider this with the full attention of your mind and send an army of no small size to our aid as quickly as possible.

For if you do not immediately extend to us strong and ample assistance, strengthened by God, know that nothing more remains except that, after abandoning us in despair of your aid, you too will have no further hope from this holy Church.

But if, in the present necessity, you provide us suitable and sufficient help, and without delay strive to aid the people of God, specially entrusted to blessed Peter by a prerogative, know that in every need of yours we shall be so much more ready to assist you as we shall have been made more secure from the enemy.

Furthermore, we are astonished that Your Belovedness has detained our envoys: Leo, the bishop, our dearest nephew, apocrisiarius and envoy of the Apostolic See, and Peter, likewise a bishop. When they were being sent through you in haste to the Augustus divinely protected, you detained them then and, without justification, continue to detain them now.

Since this is contrary to the dignity of the Apostolic See—and has never been done—we shall certainly not leave it unpunished once we are certain of the facts. For when we sent them with extreme urgency on account of the manifold necessities of our Church, you, who are not unaware of this, ought not to have obstructed them, but rather, as we believed, ought to have supported their accomplishing it more swiftly with your assistance.

Given as above.

## XXXI. To Landulf, Bishop of Capua

(Year 876.) He announces that the envoys have returned from the emperor; he writes that the emperor recognized the rights of the Roman Church in an assembly of bishops and nobles, and especially entrusted the pact concerning the land of Capua to his jurisdiction. Therefore he promises that he will come to Landulf’s region.

John, bishop, to Landulf, bishop of Capua.

The holy Roman Church, whose governance we preside over by God’s authority, is accustomed to repay all who have faithfully served it from the beginning with a worthy reward of good things in the present and future age. It will likewise soon favor you and its other faithful in every way, through maternal affection, because of the devotion of your fidelity, which we fully recognized while you were there.

We wish you to know the intention of Your Reverence: with the Lord cooperating, after Leo, our venerable nephew and distinguished apocrisiarius of the holy Roman Church, and our other envoys whom we had recently sent, returned from our dearest son Charles, the emperor Augustus, we consider it appropriate, as you are among our confidential counselors, to disclose to you his disposition—under God’s inspiration—toward the exaltation of the Churches, especially the Roman Church, which is the head of all.

He renewed by chapter the whole right of authority anciently assigned to it and, in an assembly of bishops and nobles [Note: [Col. 0685D] Aimoinus mentions this council and the envoys in Book V of *The Deeds of the Franks*, chapter 33.] granted it inviolably to be held. Among other matters, he entrusted to our right and authority the pacts concerning your land, so that we might establish them as we wished, with Christ as our guide, in order that we might show by the accomplishment of deeds what we have said in plain words with priestly speech, and so that, for the joy of your soul, the writing hand of the notarial fathers might speak [Note: [Col. 0685D] The passage appears to be corrupt. HARD.].

Prepare lodging, because by God’s grace we shall come into your region with a new company of guests. Impose the bridle of restraint upon the faithless as far as you can; promise the faithful the lifting of their future hope in the near term; and without interruption, I urge you, entreat the mercy of the Lord our God, and await our arrival with confidence.

## XXXII. To Guaifer, Prince of Salerno

(Year 876.) He shows himself ready to confirm the pact that Guaifer had made and asks him to prepare lodging for his arrival.

[Col. 0685D]

John, bishop, to his beloved son Guaifer [Note: [Col. 0686D] Leo, bishop of Ostia, mentions Guaifer, prince of Salerno, in Book I of the *Chronicle of Cassino*, chapters 42 and 44.], glorious prince.

Because we have learned not only from the reports of our envoys, among the faithful surrounding the governance of our Roman Church—which, by Christ’s authority, we preside over—that you are devoted, and that your most energetic son-in-law, the prefect Pulcar, is likewise devoted, but also found you certainly faithful when we came into your region for the liberation of the whole fatherland, which Christ has entrusted to our care, we are therefore prepared to establish that the pact you requested, as we had promised, is to be firmly secured for you by true pontifical declaration from our beloved son Charles, the emperor Augustus, with the authority duly and legally received through the venerable envoys of our Church who have returned.

At the same time, I wish you to prepare an escort and, as I have said, lodging for me and the new company; strengthen our faithful in the fidelity they have begun, impose upon the faithless, as far as you can, the bridle of correction, and await our arrival, with God as our guide.

## XXXIII. To Geilo, Abbot of Tournus, and His Monks

(Year 877.) By pontifical authority he confirms all their royal and episcopal privileges, in the year of Christ 876, adding exemption from the jurisdiction of every bishop.

[Col. 0686B]

From the original, written on philyra (bark-paper) in Gothic uncial letters, approximately twelve feet long and two feet wide.

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the illustrious abbot Geilo and our beloved sons in the monastery at Tournus, granted by our spiritual son, the glorious emperor Augustus Charles, to the holy, undefiled, and ever-virgin Mother of God Mary and to Christ’s precious confessor Philibert, and living now and in future times in religious observance under the rule of Saint Benedict.

When the hearts of Catholic emperors are to be stirred by pontifical admonitions toward those things which ought to be done, and are so inflamed by ardent desire, with divine grace going before, that they themselves voluntarily ask for them, they ought to be granted with an enthusiasm and joy proportionate to the fact that, if they were unwilling to do the things they desire, they would still have had to be asked.

Therefore, in accordance with the petition of our son, the most excellent emperor Charles, by a decree of our present authority we grant, concede, and confirm this privilege to the same venerable monastery for your time and for future times:

Just as that most glorious son of ours, led by divine love, confirmed by a command of his authority the privilege which he caused to be made and confirmed for our venerable brothers and sons, the bishops of those regions, concerning villages and resources, or provisions specially reserved for the use of the monks and for the ornaments of the church, lamps, matricularii, guests, and the poor, whether preserved, improved, or increased by arrangement; so, exactly as those privilege documents and commands made by our son Charles concerning these matters contain, all these things shall remain perpetually undisturbed.

Although it has been reported that this belonged to the bishopric of Mâcon, and although for a long intervening period no authority had been attached to it there by which it could be held, it seemed better—and far more holy—to our apostolic discretion that it be confirmed for the monastic uses of the aforesaid monastery than that it be surrendered to lay depredations without any acquisition for holy places.

By another authority of blessed Peter we establish that no king, no bishop or abbot, nor anyone endowed with any dignity, may, under any pretext or appearance of any cause, diminish or remove anything from the things contained in the aforesaid privilege or in the commands of that son of ours Charles concerning what we have mentioned, or from anything that in future shall have been lawfully granted by him or by anyone else from their own property for these special uses; nor may anyone apply such things to his own uses or presume to grant them to others under the guise of pious causes as an excuse for his avarice.

Rather, everything that has been offered, or may happen to be offered, for the aforesaid uses of the monks, the ornaments of the church, lamps, matricularii, guests, and the poor shall remain for all time untouched and undisturbed, without any disturbance, and shall in every way continue to serve the uses of those for whose support and administration they were granted.

Therefore, all these things contained in the page of this command and decree of ours we decree must be preserved perpetually both by you and by all who succeed you in the order and place in which you now are.

In all matters contained in the page of this decree, the authority and honor of the holy Roman Church and the privilege of the Apostolic See remain safeguarded.

[Col. 0687C] It is also pleasing that in future times the monks themselves shall have written permission to elect an abbot.

But if anyone, whether a person of high or low standing, presumes with reckless audacity to act against this apostolic decree of ours, let him know that he is bound by the bond of anathema, alien from the kingdom of God, and condemned, together with all the impious, to the punishment of eternal fire.

But whoever proves to be a true guardian and observer of this confirmation may deserve to obtain from the Lord blessing, grace, and heavenly mercy.

Written by the hand of Anastasius, regional notary and scriniarius of the holy Roman Church, in the month of October, in the tenth indiction.

Farewell.

Subscribed on the Ides of October, by the hand of Christopher, first secretary of the holy supreme apostolic see, [Col. 0687D] while the most pious lord Augustus, Prince Charles, crowned by God, ruled as great emperor, in the first year of his reign and the first year after his coronation, in the tenth indiction.

### XXXIV. TO THE ABBOT AND MONKS OF HERENSIS. (Year 876)

He approves the donation made to that monastery of Saint Porcianus.

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Geilo, religious abbot of the venerable monastery of the holy Mother of God, ever-virgin Mary, our Lady, and of Saint Philibert, and through you to that same venerable monastery in perpetuity.

It is fitting for apostolic governance to come to the aid of those endowed with pious religion through benevolent compassion, and to grant the petitions of their minds with eager devotion. For by this we earn above all the reward of profit from the Lord, creator of all things, when venerable places, suitably ordered, have without doubt been brought to a better condition.

Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to our own people, present and future, how your Reverence, through Adalgarius, most holy bishop of the holy Church of Autun, brought before our apostolate the request that we confirm by the authority of our apostolic privilege the little abbey called Saint Porcianus, which the emperor Charles, of blessed memory—namely, our spiritual son—granted and bestowed upon the same venerable monastery by the text of a charter for the sake of his perpetual remembrance. [Col. 0688B]

We, considering that this request would be beneficial and would provide stability to the same venerable monastery over which you are recognized as presiding, especially since we desire all pious places to possess what properly belongs to them, have yielded to your petitions. From the present ninth indiction, therefore, by this apostolic privilege we confirm and perpetually establish in the frequently mentioned venerable monastery the aforesaid little abbey, with all its movable and immovable possessions lawfully and legally belonging to it, just as it was granted by the aforesaid Augustus; and we strengthen it for our reward.

Likewise, investing it with apostolic authority, we decree [Col. 0688C] that no bishop shall attempt to go there for divine business or to conduct any other affair unless he has been invited by you or by your successors, the abbots. Indeed, we decree that no judicial authority shall dare to go there to inflict any injury or destruction whatsoever. This we establish for observance by all the faithful of Christ, in accordance with the custom of that venerable monastery, the grant of the aforesaid Augustus, and this apostolic grant and confirmation.

If, however, any person of whatever dignity should presume to act in whole or in part against this apostolic privilege of ours—which we do not believe will happen—or should dare in any respect to violate what has been salutarily decreed by us, let him know that by the authority of almighty God, blessed Peter the Apostle, and ourselves, he has been deprived of communion with the faithful; and unless he quickly repents and obeys canonical sanction, he has been condemned to perpetual anathema. But may whoever proves to be its guardian and observer deserve to obtain blessing and grace from the Lord our God.

Written by the hand of Anastasius, regional notary and scrivener of the holy Roman Church, in the month of October, in the ninth indiction. Farewell.

Given on the Ides of October by the hand of Christopher, first secretary of the holy supreme apostolic see. In the reign of the most pious lord Augustus Charles, crowned by God, great emperor, in the first year after his consulship, in the ninth indiction.

### XXXV. TO THE BISHOPS OF THE PROVINCE OF BOURGES. (Year 876)

That henceforth they should obey Frotarius as their metropolitan.

[Col. 0689A]

John to our most reverend and holy brothers, the bishops established throughout the province of Bourges.

Because we have learned from letters of some of you, as well as from the explicit report of Leo, the apocrisarius of the apostolic see [the Roman edition adds: “of our most holy men”], that the city of Bordeaux and nearly the whole province have been destroyed by various disasters, but especially by the attacks of the Northmen, and have been partly reduced to desolation by the sword and partly through captivity, we are compelled by the necessity of circumstances [Col. 0689B]—so that, grieving and lamenting, we may confess with Saint Pope Gelasius, our predecessor—and are constrained by the governance of the apostolic see to weigh the decrees of our fathers’ canons and measure them against the commands of our episcopal predecessors, so that, with careful consideration, we may moderate as far as possible whatever the necessity of the present times demands should be relaxed for the restoration of the churches.

Behold, the holy canons expressly provide that bishops should not migrate from one city to another [the Roman edition adds: “lest”]. But if we regard such decrees as requiring observance without any discernment or dispensation, we show no compassion toward brothers whom we see suffering the swords of pagans for the sake of preserving the Christian faith, needy, distressed, afflicted, and wandering here and there; especially since some of them have been so enlightened by the grace of God that they are able to instruct many not only by knowledge but also by their conduct, not only by word but also by example.

Since Frotarius, formerly bishop of Bordeaux, is one of their number, as your Fraternity attests, we necessarily judged that this man should be placed over and incardinated in another Church—namely, Bourges—which has been reported to us as vacant and worthy of the governance of so great a man. Otherwise, under a less suitable ruler, it would lack the salutary protection needed for the salvation of souls, and we would incur the burden of grave guilt if, in the face of so pressing a crisis, we failed to provide for so important a Church by entrusting it to an entirely unsuitable champion.

Therefore, while the earlier regulations remain undisturbed [Col. 0689D]—regulations which, where neither the circumstances nor the times impose necessity, ought rightly to be observed—we have ordered that, while the see is vacant, Frotarius, our brother and fellow bishop, be appointed and ordained priest at the see of Bourges. Thus, being incardinated there and, as it were, rooted by the privilege of apostolic authority, he shall possess, administer, and order the remaining rights of the metropolitan Church of Bourges and of its diocese as one who stands before God, with every subsequent complaint of the envious entirely removed.

It is fitting that you obey him as your own metropolitan and show him, according to ancient custom, the appropriate reverence and honor. We do not wish you to be unaware that, because of the considerable barbarian necessity intervening, we now grant this in such a way [Col. 0690A] that, once that necessity has been removed, it should no longer be demanded as a customary practice; and what necessity has obtained should itself also be removed.

We wish your holy Fraternity to prosper in Christ, now and forever. Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of November, in the tenth indiction.

### XXXVI. TO THE PEOPLE OF BOURGES

That all should obey Frotarius, archbishop of Bordeaux, to whom he entrusts the Church of Bourges for as long as the pagans possess the diocese of Bordeaux.

John, bishop, to the clergy, people, and order of the holy Church of Bourges.

Rereading your letter of petition, in which you request from the authority of our apostolate a decision concerning our brother Frotarius, the reverend archbishop, we have learned this from the testimony of others, and especially from the report of the most serene Augustus, also our spiritual son [Col. 0690B]. We have likewise learned from the returning legates of the apostolic see—namely, Leo, the venerable bishop, apocrisarius and envoy of the holy Roman Church, and Peter, likewise a venerable bishop—that almost the whole province belonging to the metropolitan see of Bordeaux has been so devastated by the persecutions of the pagans, as our legates were able to learn from those acquainted with the matter, that not only can our brother himself confer no benefit there upon his subjects, but even the habitation of the faithful has been removed from it.

Therefore, since we have discovered that the same man, Frotarius, the reverend archbishop, is distinguished by upright conduct and illustrious deeds and is capable of benefiting the souls of men [Col. 0690C], lest so great and worthy a man lack an opportunity for useful service, we entrust to him, by apostolic authority, the pastoral care of the same holy Church of Bourges, to which you are subject, and we judge that he must necessarily be incardinated in it.

Show him humble obedience and canonical submission appropriate to one who truly holds the rights of a metropolitan, as is fitting toward your own ruler and bishop; recognize that this has been defined by our apostolic authority, and behold, you have our command. Thus, while giving thanks to God for the goodness of your obedience, honor the aforesaid archbishop with the reverence due to him. And may he strive to preside over you with moderation, as one who will render an account to the Lord for you, and embrace you as beloved sons. [Col. 0690D]

Know, moreover, that because of the considerable barbarian necessity intervening, we grant this arrangement in such a way that, once that necessity has been removed, what necessity now demands should also be removed.

Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of November, in the tenth indiction.

### XXXVII. TO THE EMPEROR CHARLES THE BALD. (Year 876)

At the emperor’s request, while the province of Bordeaux was being devastated by pagans, he transfers Frotarius, archbishop of Bordeaux, to the Church of Bourges.

John, bishop, to the emperor Charles.

We rejoice that we have now brought your petition, dearest son, which we formerly delayed—not by denial but by prudent administration—to the fulfillment of our desire, especially because, with Christ leading us, we have recognized the perseverance of your glory as a witness, approved the concordant testimonies of the provincial bishops, and taken account of the most careful investigations of our legates.

Accordingly, although prompted by many canonical testimonies we were most eager to fulfill the petition of your devotion, and although we would not have hesitated to believe solely on the testimony of your Majesty concerning the destruction of the province of Bordeaux, nevertheless, since we recently learned that the letters of the bishops of the province agreed with the testimony of your piety, we have, in accordance with your most religious desire, decreed that Frotarius, the bishop of the diocese of Bordeaux, our brother, be made cardinal of the Church of Bourges [Col. 0691B], and we have taken care to invest him once again with the privilege of metropolitan dignity.

Admiring the diligence of your zeal, by which you always select suitable men for the Church through a certain nobility of natural intelligence, we have sent appropriate letters, by the authority of our see, to those concerned. And because we have recognized your magnanimity, which has inspired you to undertake this religious matter with regard to us, we rightly entrust to it also its execution.

For the sake of God, whose Son’s precious blood has redeemed the whole Church throughout the world, preserve the arrangements of this necessary dispensation in such a way that you never depart on the other side from the regulations established by the fathers in ancient times.

Moreover, since the diligence of your filial devotion requests that we disclose by whose suggestions your petition was formerly delayed, know fully that although we are unworthy, nevertheless, because the succession of our preceding pontiffs compels us to exercise mature judgment, we then did not readily consider so grave a matter ready for decision, lest, God forbid, by defining it we should appear to have acted without adequate order.

But after almighty God honored the petition of your Serenity through the testimony of the bishops of the province, or rather confirmed the bishops’ testimonies through the support of your piety, we fulfilled your religious request, extended our hands to the petitions of our brothers and fellow bishops, and, providing for the Church of God amid such great necessities, brought forth from the treasury of our pontifical heart [Col. 0691D] an answer in such a way that we cannot in any manner appear to have departed from the teachings of the ancients.

Given as above.

### XXXVIII. TO THE EMPEROR CHARLES THE BALD. (Year 876)

He praises him for the judgment pronounced against Emmenus and urges him to deal mercifully with him.

John, bishop, to the emperor Charles.

The whole earth rejoices with heaven over your judgment, most upright emperor, pronounced against Emmenus. For it is written: “The righteous man will rejoice when he sees vengeance” (Psalm 57). Why, however, do we say “rejoices,” when it is written concerning Solomon’s judgment: “All Israel heard the judgment which the king had judged, and they feared the king, for they saw that the wisdom of God was in him to administer judgment” (1 Kings 3)? Concerning this judgment, therefore, we rightly believe that the benevolent rejoiced, while the wicked were altogether saddened. Thus here also it is understood that the righteous rejoice over your judgment, while the unjust are terrified.

For almighty God, whose judgment you imitate, is terrifying to sinners and gracious to the righteous. Since, therefore, you have already displayed toward Emmenus the severity of judgment, we ask you henceforth to display the distinction of mercy. You have placed upon his shoulders the burden of severity; now apply the finger of gentleness to remove it. Remember that Paul sends this man back to you with Peter, his beloved ones, just as he once sent Onesimus to Philemon (Philemon 1), beseeching and entreating you to receive him as your own inward parts.

Even if perhaps at some time he appeared useless to you for a while, setting a bad example for others, he is now useful both to you, to us, and to many, showing all a model of endurance and patience. We therefore ask that, in your eyes, his offense not harm him so much as the affection of faith and love which he has shown toward you benefit him.

And because he does not refuse to confess his own offense and the penalty imposed upon him, once the punishment he deserved has been removed, let him recognize that he has successfully approached and greeted your patrons—the holy chief Apostles—and rejoice and be glad at so great a gift bestowed upon him, so that, according to the Apostle, “where sin abounded, grace might abound all the more” (Romans 5).

Given on the day before the Kalends of November, in the tenth indiction.

### XXXIX. TO THE EMPEROR AND EMPRESS. (Year 876)

On behalf of Madelgerus, who had killed Odelricus.

John, bishop, to the emperor and empress.

Since almighty God has desired to exalt the glory of your Serenity with imperial splendor by displaying no less regard for mercy toward offenders than severity of judgment against the wicked [Note: [Col. 0691] After the word “offenders,” the Roman edition adds: “your vassal”; the following corruptly transmitted words appear to mean, “having received him, show [mercy] rather than judgment,” etc. Mansi.], we, fulfilling pastoral care, have judged it fitting to intercede before the excellence of your Majesty for the salvation of many, or for the sparing of their lives, especially of those who, although committing abominable deeds at the devil’s instigation, nevertheless, moved by divine mercy, hasten to the thresholds of the chief Apostles Peter and Paul, your patrons, and humbly implore mercy.

With all the earnestness of our mind we intercede and, insofar as it is lawful, mercifully offer the aid of consolation to those who ask. Therefore, on behalf of this man, Madelgerus by name, who, urged on by the adversary, killed a certain man named Odelricus, we have petitioned your Majesty for the preservation of his life, the integrity of all his limbs, and the restoration of his possessions.

Dearest sons, for the love of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, and of the holy Apostles whose thresholds the aforesaid Madelgerus visited [Col. 0693A], and out of regard for the love of our fatherhood which you hold toward us most sincerely, we ask that you not disdain to restore your full favor to him. May he, accepted in consideration of your Serenity, be able to receive fruitful penance for his offenses, by which he may wash away the guilty stains of the crime he committed, so that his spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord, when he will render vengeance for all things.

For the sake of the exceedingly difficult journey which he endured in coming, we believe that he has earned some measure of indulgence for the crime he committed, aided by the intercession of him to whom the Lord is known to have said: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16).

Since this is so, we also ask that you order him to reach an agreement with the parents of the deceased man, lest some greater evil be committed thereafter, one that might harm the souls of many.

Given as above.

### XL. TO THE BISHOP OF CHARTRES. (Year 876)

On behalf of Madelgerus, who had killed Odelricus.

John, bishop, to Gislibertus, most reverend bishop of the holy Church of Chartres.

We have no doubt that your Reverence is endowed with spiritual virtues. Accordingly, by this letter of our apostolate we earnestly ask you, on behalf of the present man Madelgerus, who, persuaded by the adversary, killed with a sword a certain man named Odelricus, and who, moved by divine inspiration, took care to travel over long distances to the thresholds of the chief holy Apostles Peter and Paul for the abolition of that offense, that, for the love of God and of those to whose most sacred churches he came and before whom he prayed to God concerning his offenses, and also for love of our fatherhood, you not disdain to restore to him, with full favor, all his own possessions and the benefice together with the honors belonging to them which you took away.

Do this just as you sincerely desire to retain the fellowship and affection of our love toward you unblemished.

Given as above.
