[Note: [Col. 0693D] In the Roman edition, after this there is added a fragment that appears to belong to another letter: “Let your glorious greatness know that Roffredus, the glorious count, a monk of Saint Amantius, granted to blessed Peter, chief of the Apostles (something is missing here). Since Count Umfredus is said to have taken away certain possessions of his, we implore your pious glory, for the love of the holy chief Apostles, to have those same possessions restored immediately to the aforesaid monastery, so that the fruit of your reward may endure forever and ever. Given as above.” Mansi.]

### XLI. TO ADALARDUS, BISHOP OF VERONA. (Year 876)

He commends him for his distinguished virtues and orders him to come to Rome for the council.

[Col. 0693D]

John, bishop, to Adalardus, bishop of Verona.

Your prudence clearly perceives with what degree and quality of affection our apostolate burns toward you, since we have undertaken no small labor on behalf of your advancement, judging that you would rightly become a suitable priest of Christ and would pursue spiritual rather than worldly glory. The very marks of your nobility and the mirrors of your wisdom have given reason to hope such things of you.

Since we have learned that your Holiness vindicates those hopes by the efforts of virtue and integrity of conduct, we have returned countless thanks to God with great rejoicing. In this we have learned by experience that, according to the Apostle, “hope does not disappoint” (Romans 3).

Therefore, since we are soon to convene a council of certain bishops for both ecclesiastical and imperial convenience, we order your Dilection to be present at so great an assembly. Gird your loins, therefore, like a man; take wings for yourself like a dove, fly, come, and rest in the bosom of apostolic affection, so that on the day before the Kalends of December you may present yourself at the apostolic thresholds [Col. 0694B] and before our very eyes.

If you declare this impossible, then fulfill what we urge and command by the eighth day before the Kalends of January, provided only that you do not wish to be entirely barred from communion with the apostolic see. For it is not fitting that a man of such great wisdom should be absent from so great an assembly.

We wish your holiness to prosper in Christ. Given on the fourth day before the Nones of November, in the tenth indiction.

### XLII. TO THE EMPEROR CHARLES. (Year 876)

He praises him for receiving the legates of the apostolic see kindly and asks that he order the plunderers of the Roman Church, who had escaped while evading the judgment of his envoys, to be sought and restrained.

[Col. 0694C]

John, bishop, to the emperor Charles.

We offer innumerable thanks and praises to almighty God, who has deigned to fill the heart of your piety, which rests in his hand, with so great a grace of the Holy Spirit. You have inclined your sacred ears with such concern toward the advancement of the Church entrusted to us by God, and you have received the legates of the apostolic see—namely, Leo, apocrisarius and envoy of the holy Roman Church, and Peter, venerable bishops and our beloved men—with the kindness customary to you, and even more generously. You also ordered that what they proposed to you for the condition and exaltation of the holy Church of God should be brought to an effective conclusion.

Truly, dearest sons, your heart is in the hand of God, because at his counsel you arrange all things and wisely strive to govern the empire entrusted to you. Wisdom has grown with you from your mother’s womb, and righteousness has been your beloved companion.

Since no human tongue suffices to proclaim the multitude of your praises, let us turn in writing to what has been done concerning those who are faithless to us and to you.

When your men—most benevolent emperor—highly educated and fearing God, namely Ansegisus, the reverend archbishop, and Adalgarius, the venerable bishop [Note: [Col. 0695D] Ansegisus and Adalgarius. Both were sent to Rome by Charles with the apostolic legates after the synod of Pontigny. Aimoinus, Book V, chapter 33: “The synod was dissolved. Afterwards the emperor sent back to Rome the apostolic legates Leo and Peter, bearing gifts, and with them Ansegisus, bishop of Sens, and Adalgarius, bishop of Autun.” Sirm.], together with our common faithful, were sent by you to Rome, as we had requested, for the honor and advantage of your holy mother, the Roman Church, and arrived there, we recognized more clearly than daylight how much justice pleases you, and we rejoiced in the Lord over the affection of sons which you preserve toward us.

But concerning the faithless men and enemies of the holy Roman Church, whom the sheepfold of Christ does not receive because of their many crimes and wickedness, who hide here and there and try to conceal their abominable acts, the matter could not be completed as it ought, nor as your legates desired.

To speak plainly, they have been concealed and driven away by certain of your own faithless men and our enemies—namely, certain margraves, whom your legates will identify. They have neither returned to those who struck at them nor ceased to pollute others with the contamination of their wickedness. [Col. 0695B]

Therefore we implore the clemency of your Highness and adjure you by the future judgment of God to order that these enemies and plunderers of the holy Church of God, as well as sacrilegious men and tyrants, and therefore men synodically separated from the fellowship of Christ, be diligently sought out and, as you have already decreed, assigned to exile, there to lament the evils they have ceaselessly perpetrated until now.

For if those who have so stained the Church of God should now escape your decree with impunity, or if—which must not happen—they should roam so freely within your empire while receiving favor from certain persons, shameful though it is to say so, against your will, they will pollute your entire empire and bring ruin upon all Christendom. Since they are diseased sheep, they infect the whole flock, and “their last state will be worse than the first.”

Therefore, a greater illness must be treated with a greater remedy. If wounds emitting a great stench are not cut out at the root with the due severity and with the severity appropriate to the case, the whole body of the Church will waste away, and we, enduring these things, will be unable to exercise our ministry.

We did not refuse to receive Stephen and Sergius when they came deceitfully to us; rather, we ordered them to come to your Majesty. But, dearest son, know that the treasures of our Church, which those same most wicked men seized and stole, have been concealed by them in such a way that they cannot be found through those of their henchmen who remained here. Those who know where they hid them they cunningly keep with them, so that they cannot be exposed. Unless the men themselves are captured, the place where the treasures are hidden remains entirely unknown to us and our people.

Nevertheless, your aforesaid legates may, if it pleases you, tell you in writing and orally what was found with one man, what with another, and what was discovered in their houses.

Given on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the tenth indiction.

### XLIII. TO THE EMPEROR CHARLES. (Year 876)

He recounts the calamities inflicted upon the Church by the Saracens and asks the emperor to send aid against them.

[Col. 0696A]

John, bishop, to the emperor Charles.

What great and terrible things we suffer at the hands of the impious people of the Saracens—what can I say, since no pen is sufficient to write it, when all the trees of the forests, if turned into tongues, would not be able to recount it? Since your Excellence has already learned some part of these events, you determined to direct your army with a strong force to remove them.

When we heard this, we immediately raised our hands and praised the Lord, and, rejoicing in his clemency on behalf of your empire, at once implored him. But, dearest son, as greatly as we rejoiced at what was reported to us, so greatly, alas, were we saddened and embittered because what had been announced was not brought to completion in actual deeds.

For, as we have heard, they returned, leaving joy only to the pagans and nothing but indescribable tribulation to us. Behold, alas! While the enemies of the cross of Christ rejoice, the assembly of the faithful alone is consumed by great grief. The blood of Christians is poured out; the people devoted to God are devastated by continual slaughter.

Whoever escapes fire or sword becomes spoil, is dragged into captivity, and is made a perpetual exile. Behold, cities, fortresses, and villages have perished, abandoned by their inhabitants, and the bishops are scattered here and there. Only the thresholds of the chief Apostles remain for them as a refuge, while their episcopal residences have been turned into lairs for wild beasts, and they themselves are found wandering and without shelter. They are no longer permitted to preach but must beg.

Behold, dearest son, the sword has reached the soul. Behold the day of which we cry: “Blessed are the barren, and the wombs that never bore” (Luke 23). Behold those dangerous times foretold by the voice of Paul (2 Timothy 3).

Therefore I am moved to cry out with Jeremiah (chapter 9): “Who will give water to my head, or a fountain of tears to my eyes, that I may mourn such and so great a misery, such and so great a destruction of the homeland?” And this amid the grief—or rather the ruin—of the mistress of nations, the queen of cities, the mother of churches, the consolation of the sorrowful, the harbor of those in peril.

Behold, I say, truly the day of tribulation and distress, the day of calamity [Col. 0696D] and misery. Last year we indeed sowed, but we did not gather; this year, because we did not sow, there is no hope of gathering.

Why speak of pagans, when Christians are doing nothing better? I mean certain men from our borders and neighboring lands, whom you now customarily call margraves. To speak prophetically: “The locust’s remnant the caterpillar has eaten” (Joel 2).

And what, perhaps, is left for the unbelieving Saracens, who are sons of the slave woman, by those who ought through faith to be sons of the free woman? We are grazed down to the ground. For what do they do that these men do not do worse?

The former occupy the land; the latter, with Peter, leave nothing in the cities or countryside. The former kill with the sword; the latter, after taking everything away, slaughter people by hunger. The former lead people into captivity; the latter reduce them to slavery for themselves.

And when it is asked who will fight against the enemies, no one is found, since those held back by their oppression cannot be found at all to respond to our command. But when, distressed on every side, we cry out, there is no one who hears, no one who helps, no one who saves, except you, dearest son and most clement emperor, who after God have become for us refuge, consolation, and aid.

Therefore, moved with all our heart and all our inward parts, we entreat you, together with the bishops, priests, nobles, and all the remnants of the people once entrusted to us: command at last that your ears be opened; hear the groaning and sobs of us all; extend your hand; and give aid to the homeland in peril, to the city lying amid many miseries and hardships, and to this Church, your mother, from which you received the beginning not only of your reign but also of your belief in the one true Lord.

She it was who, at the end, setting aside a good and great brother, by the gratuitous will of God chose and preselected you, as another King David, and raised you to the imperial scepters. Consider, therefore, ever-Augustus, worshiper of God, warned by the prophet: if she is humbled, to whose aid will you flee? Or where will you leave your glory?

Reflect that, if she is humbled, not only will the glory of your empire be endangered, but the cultivation of the Christian religion itself will certainly perish in large part. Therefore, knowing these things, do not, I beg you, delay any longer; do not use postponements from day to day that will bring no benefit.

With the Preacher I cry out, and with Solomon I exclaim: “Do not say to your friend, ‘Go and return, tomorrow I will give you’” (Ecclesiasticus 9); and elsewhere: “Whatever your hand can do,” he says, “do it promptly” (Proverbs 3), etc.

For you do not know, if I may say so with your pardon, what the coming day may bring forth. Therefore, Christian son, consider and arrange swiftly and wisely what must be done for this Church and for the homeland, so that at least those very few remnants which remain may be saved—remnants that daily perish in masses by sword and plunder.

Come quickly to their aid; help without delay; and finally wipe away the tears from our eyes with the hand of your consolation, so that, by God’s favor, you may rejoice over them in the present and, leaving behind a widespread and praiseworthy fame that survives into the future, reign eternally with Christ in the heavens.

Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December, in the tenth indiction.

### XLIV. TO THE EMPEROR CHARLES THE BALD. (Year 876)

He writes that the emperor will learn from Bishop Adalgarius, to whom he grants the pallium, why the Church’s cause did not proceed according to their desire. He censures Ansegisus and commends Adalgarius’s fidelity.

John, bishop, to the emperor Charles.

Recognizing your praiseworthy intention and pious zeal, deeply and rightly directed toward the cause of our Church—namely, your mother, dearest son—we have offered innumerable thanks to God, who is the author and governor of every good thing and who teaches humanity justice.

But Satan hindered us, and our hope was frustrated, since the outcome of the matter did not proceed according to our desire and common purpose. How and through whose action the matter turned out this way, Adalgarius, most holy bishop, whom, moved not without reason by our love for you and by the integrity of his conduct, we have now sent to you wearing the pallium, will declare when questioned by your Majesty and adjured by the faith which he has promised to preserve inviolate toward you.

In the meantime, however, we recall to your memory what you formerly foretold to us about Ansegisus and Lantbertus by a certain prescience, as one truly foreseeing future events. For it happened just as you foresaw, and nothing escaped you beforehand that the eye of our understanding did not afterward perceive.

He did not walk rightly with him, as was fitting for a bishop; rather, proceeding through crooked and deceitful turns, he strayed far from the path of righteousness. When this has been brought to the light of truth, we do not believe that he will entirely escape punishment.

You will undoubtedly be able to discover the precise circumstances of the matter if, as we have said, that beneficent man, adjured under the testimony of the faith he promised you, is unwilling to keep them hidden from you.

We wish you to know that, since we had come to know that the aforementioned bishop was so faithful to you that we believed he could be drawn away from the sincerity of the faith he held toward you by neither gifts nor threats, he became attached to our soul as a son of salvation. For this reason we decided that he should be a mediator between our pontificate and your empire, so that he might be, as it were, the instrument of both voices: reporting your affairs to us and announcing our affairs to you, like the cornerstone established in Christ Jesus, who is our peace and has made the two one.

Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the tenth indiction.

### XLV. TO RICHILDIS, AUGUSTA. (Year 876)

He asks her to support the Roman Church.

John, bishop, to Richildis, Augusta.

How greatly our most devout spiritual son, the emperor, burns with love for this holy mother of his, the Church, is made abundantly clear by the fact that he has placed the conduct and arrangement of her cause especially in your own hands. For to whom, I ask, could he more suitably and honourably entrust her—whom he loves spiritually above all others—than to you, whom he commands to be loved by him as the Church is commanded to be loved by Christ? Therefore we rejoice greatly to hear so many praises of you, and we trust in the Lord that you will lighten upon the shoulders of your zeal the burdens which we bear, both from pagans and from the worst of Christians, and that you will act for the Church of Christ with your devout husband as that holy Esther did for the Israelite people with her husband (Esther 9).

Since we frequently send messengers or letters to your most Christian husband, ever Augustus, for various necessities, we now earnestly beseech and ask you: be for us the door, the tongue, and the hand; indeed, be everything for us, performing the duties of an advocate, and do everything for us in every matter. Thus, through you, the friends and faithful supporters of this Church may find a place with your husband and access to you, together with a wholly salutary remedy in their necessities; but, on the other hand, may her enemies and the faithless be put to shame and excluded through you. For we too shall be for you before all people and in every matter, especially before the most blessed princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul, your lovers and protectors. Thus, always striving to cherish you with paternal affection, and continually endeavouring to treat and shelter you in Christ as a spiritual daughter placed in the bosom of our love, we shall strive to commend you to them with unceasing prayers and shall continually endeavour to lay the remembrance of you before their sacred bodies.

We rejoice and are glad in the Lord, because all generations will call you blessed and happy: for, since your devout husband has entrusted you with so salutary a ministry, you thereby acquire in the present age a good name, which is better than many riches, and in heaven an imperishable kingdom among the angels. Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the tenth indiction.

### XLVI. TO CHARLES THE BALD, EMPEROR (Year 876)

He commends Wigbod, bishop of Parma.

**JOHN, bishop, to Charles the emperor.**

Because we cannot bear that you should be ignorant of anything—especially of those matters known to contribute to the increase of the glory of your exalted station—concerning your love, which we desire and embrace with the full strength of our inmost being, we have considered it worthwhile to make known that Wigbod, the venerable bishop of the Church of Parma, has approached the threshold and seat of the apostles, both out of a devotional vow of prayer and from a desire to find through us access to your glory.

Examining more closely the secrets of his mind, we frankly confess that it has by no means escaped us that he is now held by an affection of sincere faith toward your devout empire; and undoubtedly he would long ago have demonstrated this through the effects of his actions, had not a matter of such a kind been imposed upon him by the former prince of blessed memory—an obligation which he could not neglect without danger to himself.

Therefore, with your permission, we ask you to receive him now as my own inmost self. For even if perhaps he was once useless to you, he is now useful both to you and to us. Indeed, he should perhaps not be called useless, since, while keeping the faith formerly promised, he gave a similar indication of the faith that he was to preserve toward you—especially since, trusting in the Lord, he did not lose his courage when he changed sides. Now, as we instruct him, if he has in any way acted against you, he proposes to exercise all his strength on your behalf.

We therefore do not doubt that he will show himself more steadfast in his fidelity to you than he was when he was said to hold opinions against your empire. Therefore, most merciful emperor, since compassion has grown up with you from childhood, receive him as though from the very confession of the blessed apostle Peter, your patron, and strive to gain a reward through him, not holding against him that he came last. For that good householder is described as making the labourers of the eleventh hour equal to those who came at the third hour (Matthew 20).

You too love no less the soldier who first turned his back in battle but later returned and pressed the enemy vigorously than the one who never turned his back and never accomplished anything bravely. But why say more? Behold, dearest son, we pledge him to you before your devout imperial majesty. Behold, we offer ourselves as guarantor for him. Let your most merciful and serene piety act toward him in such a way that, once this is known, others may flock more eagerly beneath the shelter of your compassion and, through our intervention, make their way to you in eager competition as across an immovable bridge.

For he has been placed here as a kind of sign at the apostolic dwelling. He will either invite all earthly people to you, if they are well disposed, or frighten them away from you if they are badly treated. For we believe it difficult for anyone to obtain from your piety through others what he could not obtain through Peter and Paul, the eminent apostles. Given as above.

### XLVII. TO ADALGAR, BISHOP OF AUTUN (Year 876)

He decrees that the estate of Tilionacum be restored to him and confirms the other possessions of the see of Autun.

**JOHN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and holy ADALGAR, bishop of the holy Church of Autun, and through you to that Church in perpetuity.**

The words of divine command admonish everyone that whenever another’s property is detained by anyone contrary to the order of justice, it ought to be restored when equity demands it. It is established, therefore, that an estate called Tilionacum once belonged by right of ownership to the holy Leodegarius, bishop of Autun, and that this holy man bestowed it upon Nazarius, whose name the bishopric itself bears.

Afterward, when wicked men had retained it for a long time and had virtually converted it into their own property, our beloved son Charles, the most merciful emperor, having conducted a careful investigation into the matter, learned lawfully that it had belonged to the right of the Church of Autun and clearly discovered that it had first been possessed by that Church and afterward seized by violent men. By a command of his authority he restored it to that episcopate and recalled it to the right of that Church, to which the holy Leodegarius, mentioned above, had formerly given it.

Therefore, because your holiness requested that, in accordance with the imperial command, we confirm the aforementioned estate to the Church of Autun by the generosity or privilege of apostolic authority, we have inclined to your prayers, with the grace of heavenly compassion assisting us. We reconfirm to the aforesaid Church, over which your fraternity is known to preside, the aforementioned estate as it was in ancient times, so that what had been hers and has now been restored and is possessed by her may be possessed and retained without hesitation for all time.

By the authority of this privilege, we confirm and establish the aforesaid estate in the said episcopate, so that, now restored to the Church of that episcopate from which it had been taken, it may remain without ambiguity under its dominion. Moreover, we confirm not only the frequently mentioned estate but also all those possessions which now belong, or in future shall belong, to the same Church, to be held in that episcopate.

By pontifical censure, under threat of anathema and the judgment to come, we decree that no one may with any rashness violate, disturb, or reclaim anything promulgated by us concerning either the estate mentioned above or all the possessions held or to be held by that Church. Rather, we decree that these things shall remain unshaken in perpetual stability in that devout place.

If anyone, great or small, should attempt to act against this privilege fortified by the authority of the apostolic see, let him know that he will be condemned by an everlasting judgment and handed over to the unquenchable fire. But whoever proves its guardian and protector, may he enjoy eternal joys and obtain rewards with the angels in heaven.

Written by the hand of Gregory, regional notary and archivist of the holy Roman Church, in the month of November, in the tenth indiction. Farewell.

### XLVIII. TO URSUS, DUKE OF VENICE (Year 876)

He gives thanks because he has obeyed the admonitions of the apostolic see. He orders the bishops to come to the synod.

**JOHN to the glorious duke of Venice.**

We give thanks to your glory for your benevolent devotion, which you diligently declare and frequently display toward us not only in words but also in deeds. Therefore we cherish toward you a fatherly affection, and in matters which we recognize to concern and benefit you and your people, we shall always strive to be ready and kind.

We ask that you never consent to obstruct our intention and decree, which are based on the divine commands and sacred canons. Rather, whenever we enjoin anything upon you concerning ecclesiastical matters, obey us as a devoted son and always strive eagerly to fulfil what we direct. For you will find us more ready and more kind toward you in your affairs, and whenever an opportunity arises for you, the more clearly we see that you do not wish in any way to turn away from the commandments of God.

For, dearest son, we write to you familiarly as to one of our household, since we cannot place love for any mortal above the justice of God. We read in the Gospel: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10).

Let the bishops therefore come to our synod, so that, when they themselves inform us of the truth of the matter, we may more easily resolve in their presence the case of our brother and co-bishop Peter. Let the man who is weighed down by serious illness or old age, if he is in any way unable to come, send a capable representative in his place.

As for the one who is reported to be going to Constantinople, if he has not yet departed and is not expected to depart before the month of February, let him in no way withdraw from this common good; rather, let him come, so that, once every dispute has been settled, nothing but peace and tranquillity may endure in the Church of God. We wish your glory always good health. Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of December, in the tenth indiction.

### XLIX. TO FELIX AND PETER, BISHOPS (Year 876)

He forbids Felix and Peter sacred communion because they failed to show obedience to the archbishop of Grado; he orders them to come to Rome for the council under penalty of excommunication and, if prevented, to send representatives.

**JOHN to Felix and Peter, bishops of Mandanaucum and Equilium.**

How ungrateful and inhuman you have been toward our reverend brother Peter, bishop of the Church of Grado, is shown most clearly by this: when he undertook exile on behalf of the ancestral laws, he did not deserve to have any one of you as his companion in that pilgrimage—especially since he went to the threshold of the apostles and approached the see where Catholics are always aided, and where many saints who suffered injury found refuge in the rock from which Peter received his name.

To this was added, in order to demonstrate the full measure of your greater contumacy, that you not only failed, according to the prophet, to stand with him and “go up opposite” and “build a wall for the house of the Lord” (Ezekiel 13), but, like rebels, broke the bond of unity and crossed over to the enemies. Since you are not with him, you have certainly become against him, as the Lord says: “Whoever is not with me is against me” (Matthew 12). In this you have even surpassed the savagery of beasts, employing murderous counsels against him.

For all these things we have repeatedly admonished you by letters from our apostolate to come to Rome and satisfy us concerning these and other matters which we judged ought to be corrected. Yet until now you have contemptuously refused by every means to come.

Therefore, by the authority of the supreme shepherd, we temporarily exclude you from celebrating the sacred mysteries, ordering that on the Ides of February of this indiction—if you are present, or if you are not weighed down by the burden of serious illness—you hasten without excuse to attend our synod to be held at Rome. Thus you may be cleared of the charges brought against you and may in no respect be separated from the head, namely, either the apostolic see or your metropolitan.

Otherwise, God forbid, you may be ensnared by Satan, who always rejoices in dissension. Members that do not cling to the head are counted among the dead; and so, without doubt, are you, since you adhere neither to the decrees of the apostolic see, which is the head of all the Churches of Christ, nor to the affection of your own metropolitan, patron, and teacher.

If, however, you stubbornly disregard coming even on the Ides of February, then from that time onward remain excluded from the communion of the whole Church, together with those who support you, for as long as you do not care to come and satisfy us concerning the matters of which you are accused.

Behold, perhaps you have in your hands the venerable canons, which decree that such men are not to communicate until they have been cleared. If either of you claims that he is altogether unable to come, let him send his representative, who shall excuse the sender by oath and fulfil the sender’s place at the synod. Given on the Kalends of December, in the tenth indiction.

### L. TO DOMINIC, ELECTED BISHOP OF TORCELLO (Year 876)

He attacks Dominic, the elected bishop, because, having been summoned twice, he did not come to Rome; and he excommunicates him unless he comes on the appointed day.

**JOHN to DOMINIC, summoned and elected bishop of the Church of Torcello.**

Because, as rumour increasingly reported, you had invaded the Church of Torcello, we decreed once and twice that you should come to Rome. There, in the presence of our brother Peter, the holy metropolitan bishop of Grado, and together with the bishops who reside under him, an investigation concerning you would be conducted, so that the report spread far and wide might either be shown to be harmless and dismissed or, if proved culpable, condemned. We therefore determined by every means that you should come.

You would rightly have been condemned by us, had we not, at the request of our beloved Ursus, the glorious duke, dealt with you with less severity than patience. But because you have not come until now, know that you have rightly been excommunicated by us, while we stand ready, in accordance with the Apostle (2 Corinthians 10), to punish every disobedience.

Yet, although you have thus far despised us, we do not meanwhile despise your salvation. Therefore, behold, we summon you for a third time and command you to be present at our council at Rome on the Ides of February of the present tenth indiction. If you do not then appear, you shall thereafter remain alienated from us and from the whole body of Christ, together with those who support you, for as long as, failing to repent, you refuse to submit your neck to our commands in obedience.

If you persist in this indiscipline, know that forgiveness will thereafter be denied you; that, according to the holy canons, you will gain nothing at all from your absence; and that, struck by anathema, you will suffer without end the loss not only of communion but also of your honour. Given on the Kalends of December, in the tenth indiction.

### LI. TO URSUS, DUKE OF VENICE (Year 876)

He asks him to support at his own expense the bishops summoned to Rome for the synod; he threatens them with excommunication if they do not come.

**JOHN to Ursus, duke of Venice.**

We were greatly surprised that, although you had promised to send Dominic, the elected candidate, whom you were to associate with your son, to the apostolic see in order to settle the case of our venerable brother Peter, bishop of the holy Church of Grado, no truth followed your word. We clearly recognize that, as the Apostle teaches, we ought not to believe every spirit or trust every undertaking. For the performance of past deeds is evidence concerning the future.

Since this same brother and co-bishop of ours, following the custom of our ancestors, appealed to the apostolic see—in fact, he eagerly approached it—asking us to bring a lawful end to the controversy between him and the aforementioned Dominic, with both parties placed before us, we again command, as reason requires and canonical law dictates, that the aforementioned Dominic come to Rome on the Kalends of February at least, to satisfy us and clear himself.

For he is marked by the crime of ambition, and hence, according to the sacred canons, it is evident that the man who does not use the opportunity to clear himself confesses himself guilty.

If he should say that he cannot come unless the bishops come, let him know that we also order the bishops of that region to appear, and that the venerable priest of the Lord, Peter, is to be imitated. Although he was a metropolitan, he came to the memorial of the apostles without any bishops accompanying him, just as once the holy Athanasius honoured it.

Nevertheless, we decree that two of the bishops should come, namely Felix and Peter, so that so important a matter may not appear to be settled without the presence of bishops of the region who possess knowledge of it. If Felix claims that he is altogether unable to come, let him send his representative, who shall excuse the sender by oath and fulfil his place at the synod.

Peter, however, if he is present, must come by every means. For, as you report, we are not unaware either of your custom of sending him to Constantinople or of the timing. **Matarius**—perhaps **Maturius**, with the former word to be deleted [HARD.]—can come here and return to his own country before the customary time and season for the sea journey arrive.

Moreover, we order the archdeacon of the Church of Torcello to come to us, and likewise the abbot of the monastery of Altinum; and also the archpriest and archdeacon, together with their namesake and nephew Laurence, deacon of the Church of Grado, so that they may undergo there a suitable canonical examination concerning the charges brought against them and, if guilty, the punishment they deserve.

We wish all this to be made known to your glory so that those who are to come to the apostolic see and the holy synod may be supported by the assistance of your generosity and, supplied with expenses, bear the labour of the journey more easily and lightly, in accordance with devout princes who have always acted munificently in such matters.

As for those whom, by this authority of the apostolic see, we have decreed should be presented before us, since they have now been summoned for the third time and have so far contemptuously refused to appear, we have decreed that they are to come to Rome on the February days—**for “the Ides,” HARD.**—unless they choose to hasten here immediately.

After February—**perhaps “after the Ides of February,” HARD.**—each of them shall remain bound by the chains of excommunication, together with his supporters, for as long as he fails to appear before the apostolic see and regularly provide a suitable explanation concerning himself. Let him know that he will afterward be struck by a sentence of anathema. Given on the Kalends of December, in the tenth indiction.

### LII. TO DOMINIC AND LEO, BISHOPS (Year 876)

He announces that he has excommunicated certain men who neglected to come to Rome when summoned to the council, unless they come by the appointed day; he urges Dominic and Leo to perform their duties while those men are absent.

**JOHN, bishop, to DOMINIC of Olivolo and LEO of Capraria, bishops.**

We do not wish your holiness to be unaware that we have sent to Felix and Peter, the bishops; to Dominic, who is called the elected bishop of the Church of Torcello; to the abbot of the monastery of Altinum; to the archdeacon of the Church of Torcello; and also to the archpriest and archdeacon, together with their namesake and nephew Laurence, deacon of the Church of Grado, a future sentence of excommunication, because, having been summoned so many times by us to appear at the council in Rome, they contemptuously refused.

We have deprived any one of them who then delays coming even until after the Ides of February of all ecclesiastical communion for as long as, persisting in his obstinacy, he contemptuously refuses to approach the apostolic see.

We wish the others to take part in our council for the common interests of the Churches. We require certain of them to give satisfaction concerning certain excesses of which they are accused.

Therefore, dearest brothers, we command you to be on watch. If the aforesaid bishops, with the Right Hand of the Most High changing their hearts, appear at our council around the Ides of February, as stated above, remain in that region and carry out the works of true religion, so that no one departs without the complete sacraments of Christianity and no penitent fails without being sufficiently reconciled. Meanwhile, settle there the other matters belonging particularly to the office of bishops.

But if the father of disobedience has so occupied their minds that they utterly disdain obedience, it remains that you treat more kindly the one who obeys, while the one who is absent at the appointed time from all these men must know that after excommunication he will be punished by the sword of anathema.

For this reason we have taken care to make all these matters known to you, so that, knowing them, you may make them known to everyone and earnestly exhort them to do what we have decreed.

If they do not listen to you—for, to speak with the voice of God to Ezekiel, they do not wish to hear you because they do not wish to hear us (Ezekiel 3)—take them and proclaim everywhere, by every means, that they are to be treated as the Lord commanded the man who does not listen to the Church to be treated (Matthew 18). This is the same as saying, as we have indicated, that we have decreed they are to be treated in this way. **The Roman edition adds “above.”**

See to it that no person is able to impose silence upon you, lest, God forbid, you be judged idolaters. For, as Samuel teaches, refusing to obey is like the sin of idolatry (1 Kings 15).

Moreover, if Felix or Peter is prevented by an unavoidable obstacle and does not come, let him send a suitable man from the deacons of his Church, one who will fulfil his duties in every respect.

If, however, they are able to come in any way but refuse, then, since for that reason they are bound by the chains of excommunication together with the authors of so great an evil, not only keep entirely away from communion with them, but also from all who have communion with them—for all are bound by the same obligation. We wish your holiness well, and so forth. Given on the Kalends of December, in the tenth indiction.

### LIII. TO DELTUS, BISHOP (Year 876)

That, acting in the place of the apostolic see, he should go to Venice and cause the bishops of that region to come to Rome for the council, as he had ordered.

**JOHN to the most reverend bishop DELTUS.**

We make known to the sincerity of your love, joined to us by the concern of pastoral office—which we have decided to admit into partnership with our labour—that Peter, the most reverend bishop of the Venetian metropolitan see, burdened by many troubles caused by his suffragans and oppressed by evils contrary to canonical constitution, has chosen with devout heart to hasten to the thresholds of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and there receive help for his salvation and desired consolation, where Christ our God established the foundation of the whole Church and appointed the head of religion and justice.

Therefore, having lent the ears of our compassion to his complaints, we sent letters both to Ursus, duke of Venice, and to his suffragan bishops, whose disobedience and rashness have confused canonical authority, weakened the power of the Church of God, and corrupted metropolitan dignity. We wished to impose a proper end upon the case with even balance, in our presence and before the apostolic see, with both parties present and the dispute examined.

But the duke preferred to send words of excuse rather than the persons whom we had requested at the appointed time. Therefore, unwilling to leave the aforementioned brother and co-bishop without the consolation owed to him, we have judged it appropriate to send you there in our place, so that, relying on divine assistance, you may prudently carry out what is necessary for that brother and complete everything with the fear of the Lord.

Receive, then, these letters of our apostolate and strive to labour as a capable soldier of Christ for the benefit and salvation of the Church of God. For, as the Apostle says (1 Thessalonians 2), our labour will not be in vain in the Lord; and if we are companions in labour, we shall certainly also be companions in consolation.

With Christ as your guide, go to Venice, deliver the letter addressed to Duke Ursus, and earnestly admonish him to hear it with receptive ears, so that he may not resist the statutes of the apostolic see but rather take care to obey with a humble heart.

Deliver also a second letter to Felix, bishop of the holy Church of Equilium, whom we order to come to us. Give a third to Dominic, bishop of the Church of Olivolo, and Leo, bishop of the Church of Capraria, whom we wish to remain there and whom we have ordered faithfully to assist you in the things of God.

Take care to deliver a fourth letter to Dominic, elected bishop of the Church of Torcello. Earnestly adjure and command them to have these same letters read in the presence of the entire Church and people, with you present.

When they have been read, command the aforesaid bishops—that is, Felix of Matemautum and Peter of Aquileia [Note: Above, Epistle 50 has Mandanaucensis and Equilensis. HARD.]—as well as Laurence, archdeacon of the Church of Grado; the abbot of the monastery of Altinum; the archdeacon of Rosello; and the archpriest of Grado, together with his nephew Laurence, to come to Rome into our presence, by our apostolic authority, on the Ides of February, without putting off any delay or excuse, in accordance with the tenor of our letter.

For if they delay coming in any way on the aforesaid Ides, let them know that they are deprived of all ecclesiastical communion and bound by the chains of anathema until they take care to present themselves before our sight.

When you have completed everything according to the intention of our command with devout and faithful dedication, return to the bosom of your own Church, and do not delay reporting everything to us with certainty, so that, if anything further must be done concerning these matters, we may carry it out with prudent judgment and more diligent care, God being favourable.

### LIV. TO COUNT LAMBERT (Year 876)

That he restrain his subjects from the evils they were committing; if he cannot reform them, he threatens to excommunicate them. He indicates that he has entrusted his legates with many matters to report to him orally.

**JOHN, bishop, to Count LAMBERT.**

From long ago, if you remember, desiring your salvation and advancement, we have sought and wished both that your soul be saved and that you be heaped with bodily honours. And because now, dearest son, we desire this much more than before, know that we love you with paternal affection and embrace you altogether as a spiritual son. We regard your honour and advancement as our glory, and we rejoice in the Lord at the increase of your prosperity.

Therefore, mindful of us, we ask you never to neglect correcting both what we desire and those matters concerning your men which disturb our pontificate. For we do not suppose that you know what sorts of things are being perpetrated by these same men of yours in our territories.

It is necessary for your glory to investigate these matters carefully and, as is fitting, to correct them with every effort for the love of God and of us, because, as is reported, your men inflict countless evils and commit many acts of plunder both against the men of Saint Peter the apostle and against the men of your own Guido.

We ask you to have these matters corrected immediately and not permit those subject to you to do anything of this kind again. But if you confess that perhaps you are unable to correct it, then—with your peace, let us say so—we shall, with your consent, impose the sentence of our apostolate upon those wicked and unjust men out of love for you, and shall separate them from the thresholds of the holy Church until they repent.

As bearers of this letter, we have sent to your nobility the legates of the apostolic see, namely our beloved and venerable bishops Acimundus and Walpertus, so that they may orally declare what the letter has left unsaid and, on their return, make us more joyful concerning your goodwill. Given on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the tenth indiction.

### LV. TO GUAIFER, PRINCE OF SALERNO (Year 876)

He praises his steadfast faith toward the apostolic see; he detests the treacheries of Adelgisus and his accomplices, promises him his own assistance and that of other Churches against the Saracens, and urges him to persevere in the faith and send the bishop of Sorrento to him.

**JOHN, bishop, to Guaifer, prince of Salerno.**

We give worthy thanks to your glorious nobility, whom we embrace with spiritual arms and whom we ardently desire to cherish continually in the bosom of our affection, because, setting the feet of your steadfastness upon the rock of faith, you could be driven neither by floods nor by the violence of winds arising from various events to fall from your stability or to be removed in any degree from the promises we have made. For you are founded upon a rock.

As for what you reported concerning the former and recent fraudulent deeds of Adelgisus and his accomplices, we ourselves have truly perceived it, and we clearly recognize that your sagacity has perceived it as the matter stands. It shall be for them as it was for Saul and Ahab (1 Kings 20), and their life shall be given for the life of the enemies of God, because they were not at all afraid to release a man worthy of death.

With God favouring us, we shall sing and chant: “The sinner has been caught in the works of his hands” (Psalm 7); and again: “He opened a pit and dug it, and he fell into the pit which he made; his pain shall return upon his own head,” and so forth (Psalm 7).

Meanwhile, insofar as heavenly power deigns to assist us, we shall not fail to provide you with support both in counsel and in aid. We shall continually urge our most devout son, ever Augustus, to help you both personally and through his army as soon as possible. In the same way, we shall diligently endeavour to stir up and exhort all other faithful people and friends of the Church of Christ to do the same.

Whatever we ourselves may devise, or whatever you may promptly communicate to us as salutary discoveries, we shall hasten to undertake with great joy and gladness. Meanwhile, stand firm in the faith, act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened (Psalm 26)—not in **Insultam [“in Sultam”]**, which is more appropriately said to refer to Satan, but by hoping in the Lord.

Withdraw everyone from association with the pagans and bring yourselves into peace with one another and into the unity of concord in Christ Jesus our Lord. Whatever counsel may occur to you or appear salutary, do not be reluctant to make it known to us, so that by our judgment it may either be approved as salutary or, if something else has been revealed from heaven, be administered otherwise.

Indeed, we regard your losses as our own, just as, conversely, we certainly count your gains as ours.

Meanwhile, we were not a little displeased that the bishop of Sorrento, whether travelling by land or by sea, has not yet been sent to us; and unless he is sent more quickly, we shall rightly endure this with still greater displeasure. But if he is sent to us without delay, then we shall recognize great and customary indications of your devotion, and the marks of your love toward our pontificate will certainly shine more brightly than the sun. We wish your glory well, and so forth. Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the tenth indiction.

### LVI. TO LANDULF, BISHOP OF CAPUA (Year 876)

The same subject.

**To Landulf, bishop of Capua.**

Just as we rejoice in the devotion which your holiness has long held toward this holy Roman Church, so we are saddened by the hostility of the faithless and of our enemies, without in any way losing confidence in the mercy of almighty God—that a fitting recompense may be prepared for you and sudden confusion for them.

But, as is fitting, we honourably embrace the reverence of your fraternity, give you thanks, and, with apostolic gentleness, beg you to strive to persevere and advance in goodness. Since you are distinguished in those regions by holiness and placed over them in devotion, be also a rule against crookedness; as you are proved to have done until now, be happiness against the unhappy, equity against the unjust, and light against darkness.

Know that the consolation of the One who causes light to shine from darkness will soon come to us and to you, and that the almighty Lord will provide for the Church of Christ, afflicted for far too long.

Moreover, concerning the assistance which you request from us, as the immense necessity altogether demands, we are considering it, we desire it, and, with divine grace protecting us, we trust that we shall soon provide it. For we can no longer endure the calamity of the people entrusted to us; we are no longer able to behold the devastation of this land. We grieve so greatly that it could not be expressed even if all our limbs were turned into a tongue.

Therefore, with the counsel of your holiness brought in, we would wish to anticipate the matters necessary for our common security. Nevertheless, apart from what at present appears difficult to accomplish—as we may put it—when the first opportunity presents itself, although we hope soon to have an imperial army, we shall again report this very necessity to our spiritual son, the most serene, ever Augustus, and with the humblest prayers exhort him to come to our aid as quickly as possible with powerful strength.

Nevertheless, the Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth. “He will do the will of those who fear him; he will hear their prayers and save them” (Psalm 144). Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the tenth indiction.

### LVII. TO AJO, BISHOP OF BENEVENTO (Year 877)

He commends his zeal toward the apostolic see, advises him to assist in expelling the Saracens, and urges his brother to do the same.

**To the most reverend and holy AJO, bishop of Benevento.**
Having received and reread the letter of Your Holiness, we rendered thanks to almighty God, and greatly rejoiced in the Lord both for the affection of your devotion and for the concern you showed inquiring about our circumstances. For it is fitting, and wholly stands before the eyes of the divine majesty as appropriate, that those whom we perceive to be most faithful toward the holy mother of all, namely the Roman Church, should be embraced by our affections, if not bodily, then spiritually, and treated with fraternal love according to the merits of each.

As for your statement that you rejoice in our good health, just as you grieve, conversely, over the oppression of the Saracens: you touch very well, so to speak, upon what is outward; but you do not perceive what lies within, in keeping with the tribulation we suffer. Especially since, on account of the devastation of the people entrusted to us, only the grave remains for us, and since we are boiling with immeasurable anguish over those who ought to have fought alongside us but not only favor Christ’s enemies, but also obstruct our labor.

Yet in these matters we not only beseech you to aid us through your prayers, but also exhort you to recall by example in deed and by the word of preaching those whom you know to be turning aside from our common struggle. Although you did not attach yourself to our journey to Naples when we recently arrived there because of the greatest necessity of our Church, nevertheless what you did not accomplish by your presence you will certainly be able to accomplish by your absence, if that warmth of faith which we believe to be in you remains vigorous.

For you acquit yourself well in your ministry if you attentively consider both our labor, which, though very weak in body, we then undertook for the liberation of the Christian people, and if you always remember the tribulation that we now suffer. For never could the counsel of your brother be so overturned by anyone that, through the diligence of Your Holiness, it could not be turned by a change brought about by the right hand of the Most High [the text appears corrupt: *possit convertit*].

Come, therefore, dearest brother; gird your loins episcopally, and consider from the depths of your heart the killings and the captivity—horrible even to speak of—of our brothers, for whom Christ shed his blood. Press the matter at an opportune and inopportune time (II Tim. I), and exhort the aforesaid brother with admonitions, indeed with words of rebuke, so that he may follow our pious efforts, grant aid to us who are fighting for Christians, extend his goodwill, and, at your urging, display it in action. May God have mercy.

What benefit is the Christian name to us if we lack Christian action? What does it profit us to have known the way of justice when, after our knowledge, we turn backward and make alliances so freely with the enemies of the Christian name? Therefore, as we have said, may Your Holiness not prove ungrateful for the benefits of the holy Roman Church, but labor with us and become our fellow worker in those regions for the salvation of God’s people. Favoring our struggle, may you always show yourself devoted to the holy Roman Church in name and in deed.

For if you accomplish what you can, neither the deed of your brother nor that of any other man will be able, with Christ’s help, to destroy entirely our work and pious labor among your people; rather, it will increase and gain strength through Jesus Christ our Lord, and the labor will prove fruitful.

Given on the Kalends of February, in the tenth indiction.

## LVIII. To Charles the Bald, Emperor (877)

Because of the gravest dangers threatening from both the Saracens and certain Christians, he earnestly asks that the promised assistance be sent as soon as possible, and commends the envoys sent for this purpose.

[Col. 0711B]

**John, bishop, to Charles the emperor.**

When the daily pressure of ecclesiastical cares constrained us, and the continual grief of the people entrusted to us, which struck all our innermost being, disturbed us on every side, among other things we lamented this—as I may put it—that until now we had earnestly desired to send our messenger to you both by land and by sea, so that, since we desire and anxiously thirst for your prosperity, they might very quickly report your good health to us; but we were wholly unable to do so.

Hence I confess, dearest son, that we feared as many obstacles on both routes as we deplore the evils generated by pagans and wicked Christians without regard for the fear of God—evils such as our age does not remember. For they are so great that within the walls of the City the remnants of the people remain afflicted by countless poverty, while, with everything outside devastated and reduced to solitude, nothing now remains except, God forbid, the destruction of the City itself.

And just as the venerable bishop Leo, apocrisarius and envoy of the holy Roman Church, and also our common faithful servant, returning from your service, had made us glad by reporting that your army was to be sent against the Hagarenes, so, while we have continued to await it, a stronger grief and ineffable anguish have saddened us because what we hoped for has not followed.

For all Campania has been utterly devastated by those Saracens hateful to God; they now secretly cross the river that flows from the city of Tibur toward Rome, and plunder both the Sabines and the neighboring districts. They have also destroyed the basilicas and altars of the saints. Some priests and nuns they have led away captive; others they have killed by various deaths; and they have wiped out throughout the surrounding region the entire people redeemed by Christ’s blood.

And what shall I say? What shall I speak, when the sword has reached even to the soul, and the blood of all cries from the earth to God?

Therefore, most excellent of emperors, come at once to the aid of our calamity; now relieve the misery of our people; now extend the hand of your power; and liberate this land, whose necessities we made known to you from the very beginning of your calling, lest, if it is lost, your empire be cheapened and the whole of Christianity suffer loss.

Remember, therefore, for God’s sake; remember, because, relying on great hope and confidence, and striving by divine and human means to secure the imperial government for you, we undertook struggles and spared ourselves no labor. Therefore repay us in kind, so that our hope and labor may not be vain in the Lord. For since this has always been the chief object of our petition to you, if you continue to withhold your assistance from us, we shall collapse, falling into despair, and perhaps, having recovered a little strength, shall necessarily turn to another course.

For our whole Church does not suffer, as you perhaps suppose, a moderate evil, nor is the condition of the commonwealth afflicted by minor losses. Some parts have been destroyed by Saracen incursions, others by the tyranny of Christians, so completely that what was ours is no longer ours. Rather, we possess all those things in name alone, and never find support from anyone either for the defense of our country or for any use of our Church.

Moreover, many whom Your Majesty does not fail to know not only provide us with no assistance, but unremittingly seize whatever remains after the pagans, and trample by their violence upon all our administration in Roman territory. Thus no provisions, no four-footed animals of any kind remain anywhere for us, nor do our eyes see anyone who sympathizes with us or grieves over our sobs or groans.

But because little suffices for so great an emperor, and from these matters, dearest son, you will learn all the rest—things that we cannot utter because of groaning and the anguish of our heart—we beseech your magnificence as though prostrate upon the ground. Entreating you by the future judgment, we, together with our entire Church, earnestly commend to your divinely protected empire, and pour forth many prayers with humble petitions, that, without allowing any pretext and without omitting any delay, you provide every form of defense and due protection to your holy mother, the Roman Church, crushed and deprived of all human assistance.

For since we now stand beside the precipice, unless you hasten to aid us with the hand of your defense and with the necessary resources, as we have stated above and have repeatedly implored, once the hope of living among Christians has been removed, either we shall be subjected to the pagans themselves or—may divine power avert it—overcome by their multitude, we shall perish by a cruel death in the destruction of all Christianity. Consequently, the name of Christ will be blasphemed among the nations, and the achievements previously undertaken for your reputation will be consigned to oblivion.

For this reason, as we mentioned above, provide timely assistance and send us your army, fully prepared for a hostile expedition. Send also, with the utmost speed, other envoys who love God in all things, so that, following the path of justice, they may restrain the flames of vice. Thus may we, who are shaken and scorched by innumerable tribulations and tormented by the misery of the people entrusted to us, rejoice when refreshed by your consolations, and, having received tranquility through you, deserve, as is fitting, to attain the liberty we desire through so benevolent an emperor.

Finally, we ask Your Highness not to disdain to receive kindly and peacefully, according to custom, the bearers of this letter—namely the venerable bishops Peter and Peter, envoys of the apostolic see and our beloved ones—and to ensure, for the sake of your holy apostles as intercessors with God, that what they report in your presence for the welfare of the holy Roman Church may quickly reach a suitable and timely outcome.

Given on the fourth day before the Ides of February, in the tenth indiction.

## LIX. To Richildis Augusta (877)

That she may urge her husband, the emperor, to bring aid to the Church as soon as possible.

[Col. 0713B]

**John, bishop, to Richildis Augusta.**

For a long time now we have desired to send envoys of the apostolic see both to visit the clemency of our spiritual son the Augustus and to visit yours, so that we might become more joyful concerning the safety of you both and, recalling the calamities and oppressions of the Roman Church entrusted to us—your holy mother—which we continually suffer from Christians and wicked pagans, might at last deserve to obtain from that Augustus the consolation and desired assistance for which we hoped.

But with the entrances to all the roads occupied by evil men, grief compelled us to shed more tears than there was opportunity to send our envoys to you. For, as we have said, Christians on one side and pagans on the other persecute us so cruelly that, with only the walls of the City left, they have consumed everything far and wide around it and reduced it utterly to solitude.

We believed that we would already be relieved of these things by so great an emperor, and we were eagerly awaiting some recovery or remedy; but behold, entangled in other affairs because of our sins, he has until now delayed bringing us aid.

And since we can no longer endure it, we earnestly beseech Your Glory in many ways: relying on our authority, take on a manly heart despite your female sex, and, for the love of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, whose territory has been so devastated that it is more bearable to weep than to speak of it, persist with our most pious emperor until he both provides aid against the pagans and rejoices to restrain the Christians.

For this reason we took care to adorn him, long awaited and chosen by us, with the splendor of so great a diadem: so that the recovery and security of the holy Roman Church, whose loss we lamented, might return through his pious devotion, which he had always enjoyed.

Therefore, dearest daughter, we adjure you by God: press him at an opportune and inopportune time, so that, before another danger occurs in the city of Romulus—may God avert it—he may extend the hand of his defense and restore to liberty this land, which is the head of his empire, lest the nations one day say, “Where is its emperor?”

Thus may hope of escape and survival remain for us, and, before winter or spring passes, may his army and the promised assistance be prepared at Rome against those same pagans. Otherwise we shall either perish altogether or, compelled to redeem our lives alone, shall submit in whatever way we can to those who rule over us.

Given on the fourth day before the Ides of February, in the tenth indiction.

## LX. To Charles the Bald, Emperor (877)

He sends the emperor a palm branch and, after describing the evils by which he was oppressed by Saracens and wicked Christians, asks for assistance.

[Col. 0714B]

**John, bishop, to Charles the emperor.**

Among the other things that, as genuine devotion grows, we have long considered it necessary to make known to Your Piety as ecclesiastical matters, behold, we send you the prize of flourishing palms, which the Apostle declares is received not by all who run, but by one who competes lawfully for the sake of unity (I Cor. IX).

Therefore, dearest son, as though present, with bent knees and bowed head, we beseech and implore you to run and strive lawfully in the stadium of this age for the Church of Christ, so that your victorious right hand may be adorned not only with the prize, but your most sacred head also with a diadem of glory; indeed, that in place of these visible and corruptible things you may receive not merely a palm branch but also an incorruptible crown.

But alas, most merciful emperor, while you attend to other matters, your mother—the holy Church, which spiritually gave you birth—is in peril and has reached its final ruin. On every side, not only do the tents of these Idumeans, Ishmaelites, and Hagarenes drive her toward destruction by daily sword and captivity, but false sons of Sarah, whom you know very well, also miserably deliver her over to plunder and pillage.

Thus the former have often reached even the walls of the City, though at secret hours, and have crossed the Tiber River, once called the Albula, near the borders of the Sabines. The latter, who are our neighbors, rage and run wild on the other side, allowing no human being, field, beast of burden, animal, or anything belonging to the property of Saint Peter to remain. Everything their eyes see they seize with their hands, and they complete without delay the evils they devise.

These are, dearest son, a few of the countless afflictions that your mother, the Roman Church, alas, endures in your days—as though she had not specially and above all loved, invited, and exalted you; as though we had not, with God as author, crowned you emperor; as though we had not stood with you in all things, like the wisest Solomon, as once the faithful priest Zadok did (I Reg. I), against the other;  and as though we had not done everything that we ought to do for you; finally, as though even today we did not, by a special vow and privilege, send to your hand the palm of full blessing, as you see, triumphant over visible and invisible enemies.

For since we desire you to triumph over all adversaries, we considered nothing more suitable to offer you than palm branches, which the children also spread in the way before the Lord as he came to Jerusalem (Matt. XXII), when he was about to triumph over the ancient enemy and conquer the world.

But, they say, many concerns hinder you. We certainly do not fail to recognize this. Yet, to confess with the Lord (Luke XI), both these things ought to be done and those not omitted. For you, who contend in the contest so as to reach the prize of the heavenly calling and obtain the incorruptible crown, must abstain from all other things and strive lawfully, as we said above.

What is more lawful, however, than to care before and above all for the Roman Church, which is the teacher and mother of the other Churches, and which in your time is continually succumbing to dangers so great and so monstrous?

Finally, if this Church, which is the head, remains strong, the other members, though weak, do not lose hope of recovery. Yet they lack all strength if the head alone should happen to be weak—how much more if, may the Almighty avert it, it should happen to be extinguished?

Therefore, again and again, with all our sobs and with all our inmost being, we implore you and earnestly adjure you through Christ the Son of God, who raised you to so great a height and empire: now at last extend the swift arm of your clemency and stretch out your right hand of aid to your imperiled country—or rather, to the world.

Behold, Peter is drowning among the sheep entrusted to him. Raise them up, therefore, most merciful one, by your fruits. May he himself likewise raise you from the floods of your transgressions, unlock for you the halls of the heavenly kingdom by the keys of his intercession, and grant you, among the angels and without end, to find the pastures of eternal life, things which eye has not seen nor ear heard, and so forth (I Cor. II).

Given on the Ides of February, in the tenth indiction.

## LXI. To Anspert, Archbishop of Milan (877)

He replies that the abbot who had been removed from the administration of the royal monastery without any proven crime must be recalled, but that a murderer and his accomplice must be expelled from every administration.

[Col. 0715D]

**John, bishop, to Anspert, archbishop of Milan.**

We praise your holiness, dearest brother, burning with zeal for justice. But concerning the promotion either of a bishop or of an abbot, we can urge nothing other than what the sacred canons decree—canons which no priest is permitted to ignore or to do anything contrary to the rules of the Fathers.

Yet because the consent of our son the ever-August Emperor is said to have been involved in both matters, his arrival appears to be awaited concerning this. When Your Holiness approaches his piety, we believe that you will bring nothing upon the Church of God contrary to the rules of the Fathers.

For the moderation of the apostolic see and the administration of the universal Church compel nearly everything to be regulated provisionally in this perilous time. Although care must be taken for the present exile, nevertheless nothing should be done contrary to the canons of the Fathers when no necessity exists.

The abbot who was removed from the administration of the royal monastery without any proven crime must, with the permission of that most pious ruler and through our prayers joined to your diligence, be recalled. But we decree that not only a murderer, but also the accomplice of a murderer, must be expelled from every administration.

We have written these few things to your fraternity so that we might not appear to have entirely neglected to write back.

Furthermore, to speak with holy Pope Leo: “We who wish the judgments of the Lord’s priests to be mature can define nothing concerning unknown matters to the prejudice of either party before we truthfully hear everything that has been done.” For if, as the Apostle says (Gal. III), “the mediator of one” does not exist—[the wording is defective]—one who hears one party in such a way that he reserves nothing for the other party [Note: [Col. 0715D] Something appears to be missing.].

We wish, etc.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of March, in the tenth indiction.

## LXII. To the Bishops Established in the Kingdom of Emperor Charles (877)

He urges them to exhort the emperor to bring aid quickly to the Roman Church.

**John, bishop, to all archbishops and bishops established in the kingdom of Emperor Charles.**

Worn down by former miseries and oppressed by calamities, most beloved sons, we anxiously awaited the arrival of our great emperor Charles, as though it were the coming of the Lord and Savior himself, crying out to God from the depths; and, so to speak, we believed that his repeated descent for our salvation was at hand.

But alas! We are surrounded on every side by so many and such great dangers that even life has become wearisome to us. Behold, some of the Lord’s sheep are slaughtered by the Hagarenes, who are sons of fornication, and also by those who are Christians in name alone; some perish from hunger; others are led away for plunder and captivity.

Their shepherds too, the reverend bishops, flee, and wandering here and there, they waste away in utter poverty. The land has been reduced to solitude; when its people have been removed, it has become a haunt of wild beasts. Cities, fortresses, and villages have been overthrown, and not even traces indicate where their buildings once stood.

The destroyers have also demolished venerable places, dug up the Lord’s altars, and killed his ministers and servants. According to the Psalmist, we have become a mockery and contempt to those around us (Ps. XLIII), while they either obtain the assistance of their neighbors or at least, according to the Apostle, redeem the time, because the days are evil (Eph. III).

We sow little by little, though in tears, and do not gather in; indeed, the ability to sow is now no longer even available to us. The mistress of the world sits in sadness—the mother of the Churches, the teacher of the nations, the consolation of the sorrowful—and there is no one to help her, no one to comfort her, except you alone, O good God; and, if not in reality because of our sins, then in hope, which according to the Apostle does not disappoint (Rom. V).

We tell you these things in part, dear brothers—for if we had attempted to write them one by one, the paper would run out more readily than our speech—so that, just as we are one body in Christ the head, and members of one another, you may likewise grieve and suffer with us. For if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it, as the teacher of the nations says (I Cor. XII); and if we suffer together, we shall also reign together (II Tim. II).

Thus, grieving and suffering with us, approach our most Christian son and do not conceal from him the counsel of the Lord. Suggest and exhort him to consider who and how terrible is the one who before the ages predestined him to rule this region, and how strictly he will demand from him an account of what he entrusted to him—he who purchased by the outpouring of such precious blood that which he entrusted.

Let him also remember that we loved, chose, and preferred him above his other relatives and rivals. Therefore we determined that against all the enemies of the Church he should be not only its defender but also our patron and advocate, so that, just as we strive to be this for him before God, he might not refuse to become this for us among men—especially so that he may hasten to help us and without delay come to our aid against faithless Christians and unbelievers.

In this matter your holy fraternity must labor above all: on account of the priestly office entrusted to you, and because, as we must confess with the truthful prophet (Isa. X), if this is brought low, to whose aid will you flee, or where will you leave your glory?

Given on the third day before the Kalends of March, in the tenth indiction.

## LXIII. To Landulf, Bishop of Capua (877)

He sends envoys, as Docibilis the hypatus had requested; he urges him, together with the envoys, to work for the dissolution of the pact made with the Saracens; he will approve whatever Landulf determines.

**To Landulf, bishop of Capua.**

Let your diligence know that we have received the letters both of Sergius, master of the soldiers, and of Docibilis the hypatus. From them we learned that they attempted to render themselves excusable before us concerning the infamous treaty which they impiously made with the Saracens and have not dissolved. Indeed, the bearer of their letters reported that it had already been broken, had not your affection, out of reverence for us, judged that our decision in this matter ought to be awaited.

Although we have not wholly believed even this, since we have received no letter from you concerning these matters.

But because the aforesaid Docibilis the hypatus earnestly begged us to send our envoys to Gaeta to accomplish so great a good, beneficial to the whole Church, lest our negligence be accused of having set aside so great a salvation for the human race, we sent there Walbert of Porto and Eugenius of Ostia, most holy bishops, our beloved sons and counselors.

They are to speak either with the master of the soldiers or with his envoys and urge by every means that that pact, which is the cause of destruction, be dissolved. We send them in reliance upon your greatest wisdom.

Therefore we exhort you: let your skill labor in this matter with such zeal that you cannot doubt that you will receive not only a worthy return from us but also a crown in heaven from God and our Lord.

We admonish you: press the matter at an opportune and inopportune time (II Tim. IV), so that, once that impious pact has been broken, the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding (Phil. IV), may at last be restored to us from heaven.

If in the meantime any contention hateful to God intrudes, let it be wiped away by the hands of your wisdom. Let no rivalry, no desire for property or glory, withdraw you from so great a gain and benefit; for whatever it may be, it can shortly be settled peacefully and, with charity, defined with us as mediators.

Let your diligence therefore strive, labor, and take pains, and act in these matters on our behalf. Whatever must be done, whatever must be constructed by common agreement, let it do and establish in our stead.

For we shall gladly undertake and complete whatever your affection determines and fixes by unshakable decision. We strongly admonish your affection to have no hesitation in this matter.

See to it also that you send your envoys without distinction and without delay to Gaeta to join our aforesaid envoys, so that they may discuss all these matters profitably with them and accomplish what must be done.

We wish, etc.

Given on the Ides of March, in the tenth indiction.

## LXIV. To Frotarius, Archbishop (877)

He transfers Frotarius from the Church of Bordeaux, devastated by pagans, to that of Bourges.

To our most reverend and holy fellow-bishop Frotarius, formerly archbishop of Bordeaux, now archbishop of Bourges.

For this reason divine providence and heavenly governance wished us to preside over his Churches as rulers: so that we might diligently gather what has been scattered and preserve what has been gathered. We are to attend not only [perhaps: “and not only”; Hardouin] to the care of those Churches themselves but also to the welfare of their rulers and exercise our diligence on their behalf.

Thus, just as we provide for Churches deprived of their rulers by appointing others in their place, so, by entrusting the Churches of God to rulers who lack a see, we show that we exercise provident care for those Churches—especially for those who, although they are vigorous soldiers of the Lord, refuse to be confined within the narrow limits of idleness and therefore seek more freely opportunities for struggle against vices.

Therefore, since the Church of Bordeaux and nearly the whole diocese governed under it have been so consumed by the frequent incursions of pagan swords and continual plunder that almost every episcopal function there lies vacant, we have necessarily determined, by the authority of almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, the chief apostles, to place and establish your fraternity, whose lack of an office is a loss to the faith and a detriment to almost every virtue, over the Church of Bourges, which is known to be vacant of pastoral care, beginning with this present tenth indiction.

You are to be simultaneously placed in charge of it and incardinated there, with the whole right of the metropolitan see and diocese which was granted in former times by the sacred canons and preserved in that Church.
