Thus, from now on, you shall truly be called, held, and, Christ being favorable, honored as pastor, ruler, and bishop of that holy Church of Bourges, continually doing the things that belong to God and always attending to the usefulness of your neighbors.

Whoever should attempt to act contrary to the provisions of this apostolic privilege of ours—which we have issued under the compulsion of barbarian necessity and the circumstances of place and time, following also the example of our predecessors—shall be deprived of the divine mysteries for as long as he remains disobedient to the apostolic command without repentance.

Given, etc., in the tenth indiction.

## LXV. To Charles the King (877)

He urges him to arrange for the restoration of the goods taken from a monastery of nuns; if he does not do so within sixty days and report it to him through an envoy, or provide the reason why they have not been restored, he excommunicates him.

**John, bishop, to Charles, glorious king.**

[Note: [Col. 0719D] This Charles, who was called the Fat and was later made emperor, was the son of Louis, king of Germany; grandson of Louis the Pious; great-grandson of Charles the Great. Several letters below are addressed to him. Concerning him, see Ado of Vienne at the end of his *Chronicle*; Regino, Book II of the *Chronicle*; Aimoinus, Book V, chapter 40, and others.]

Since the nobility of your lineage is raised high by such brilliance of royal ancestry, we are amazed and astonished that a rumor, spreading so sinisterly far and wide, should overshadow it. The rumor asserts and affirms that, after entering Italy, you approached the monastery of the servants of God established at Brescia, and that, while you yourself were staying there, you tyrannically took away gold belonging both to that venerable monastery and to our beloved daughter Angelberga, worshiper of God, who had undoubtedly reserved it chiefly for the support of that monastery.

Therefore we are deeply afflicted with grief, lamenting that Your Glory has fallen into so monstrous a kind of sacrilege and has attempted, like some gentile king, to turn the vessels of the house of God to your own uses (Dan. I).

And so, desiring your affection to be in the inmost heart of Christ, we admonish you and address you in the words of Scripture, confessing with the Psalmist: “Do not place your hope in iniquity, and do not desire plunder” (Ps. LXI).

Therefore, if anything was taken from the aforesaid pious place, whether with or without the knowledge of Your Glory, let your diligence search for it most carefully, and let everything found be restored there without delay and in full. Otherwise, God forbid, if you act differently, you will both provoke God to anger against you, diminish the splendor of your royal nobility, and move us to punish these matters more severely according to our ministry.

Finally, unless, after this letter of our apostolate has been read, you resolve within the space of sixty days to restore that treasure without any reduction—so that your envoy, coming to Rome into our presence, may explain a true and adequate account of whether you have restored it or not, and of what course you have chosen to take—you shall from that time be excommunicated until you have made yourself wholly separate from every association with the robbery.

Know that thereafter you will be instructed by harsher blows if, touched in the meantime by these lighter ones, you should refuse to repent.

For we love you in a fatherly manner and wish to know you liberated and free from this second servitude to idols. For avarice, according to the Apostle, is the servitude of idols (Gal. V).

We wish, etc.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, in the tenth indiction.

## LXVI. To Engilberga (877)

He consoles her over the death of her husband and urges her to remain faithful to Emperor Charles, promising that he will act as her intercessor with that Augustus.

**John, bishop, to his beloved daughter Engilberga, dedicated to Christ.**

[Note: [Col. 0720D] Engilberga was the wife of Louis II, emperor. Several letters below are addressed to her. Aimoinus also mentions her, Book V, chapter 28, and Leo of Marsica, Book I, chapter 38.]

[Col. 0720C] We wish you to know, dearest daughter, that we burn toward your affection with no other feeling than that which we have had and which we also formerly resolved to maintain; for love knows no shadowing by changes and suffers no decline, since, according to the Apostle, it never fails (I Cor. XIII). For this reason we admonish your wisdom by these letters of consolation and exhortation not to grow faint in tribulations, knowing—as the Apostle teaches—that tribulation produces endurance, endurance probation, and probation hope; but hope does not disappoint (Rom. V). For all things that are seen are temporal, but those that are not seen are eternal (II Cor. IV).

You must therefore be fixed in these things and cling to them with all your roots, dearest daughter. Let your wisdom keep before her eyes the saints who, through endurance in this world, have shone forth in glory like luminaries, and let her proceed with unhindered steps toward the palm of the heavenly calling. This, indeed, will belong to those who, instructed by the Lord’s oracle, place their souls in their endurance (Luke XXI). [Col. 0720D] For hostile death or human agency has taken away nothing that Life—which is Christ—and his provident right hand have not transferred and restored for the better.

That death took away your mortal husband; but Life has bestowed upon you an eternal bridegroom. Thus you who were called the wife of an earthly ruler are now called, far more excellently, the spouse of the heavenly Father and King. The corruptible diadem has been removed, but an incorruptible crown is being prepared. [Col. 0721A] The ornaments that grow old have been taken away, but ornaments that do not wither have been stored up for you. And what more need be said? In place of an unhappy and illusory kingdom, you will receive a blessed and true sovereignty; and truly, this is the transformation wrought by the right hand of the Most High (Ps. LXXVI).

But since, as a wise woman, you know how to weigh much from little, these few words should suffice you. Having briefly set these matters before you, we rightly admonish your affection always to display to our spiritual son, the most devout Emperor Charles, the integrity of pure faith and sincere devotion; to draw everyone toward his gentleness; and by salutary admonitions to show that you preserve inviolable faith toward him. For there is no authority, as the Apostle says, except from God (Rom. XIII). And, “He who resists authority resists the ordinance of God” (ibid.).

Now, because we once chose him, as we believe, under divine prompting, we love him perpetually as our dearest son with every effort, so that we regard his friends and enemies as our own friends and enemies. If there are any requests that you wish to obtain from his clemency, you may be confident that, whenever you wish, you will easily obtain them through us. We shall most willingly undertake this for the sake of remembering your former kindness, and that devout Augustus, out of love for God and the holy apostles, as well as for us, will grant it with a grateful heart.

We wish your affection to fare well in Christ, dearest daughter. Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, in the tenth indiction.

## LXVII. TO WIGBOD, BISHOP OF PARMA (877)

He urges him to stir up as many people as he can to defend the holy Roman Church and to come to him with his companions, so that, by common counsel, the Saracens may be driven from Italy. He sends the requested letters and instructs him to have them delivered to those to whom they are addressed.

[Col. 0721C]

John, bishop, to Wigbod, bishop of Parma.

We return fitting thanks, being well aware of the devotion of your affection. But because we know that your holiness grieves that no task is imposed upon you by us, know that the only reason is that we recognize you as entangled in many waves of the storms of this present time. Yet, because great necessity presses upon us and your very ready zeal is evident, we exhort you to rouse, incite, and, as necessity demands, urge as many people as you can, in whatever way you can, to defend this holy principal Church and her sons. [Col. 0721D] Do not yourself hesitate to hasten to our conference with those who adhere to you, so that, by common counsel and with God’s help, the impious people may be expelled from our borders. This is what we require; this is what we previously demanded by special request.

As for what you wished to suggest concerning the dispatch of certain letters from us, we have gladly acceded to your requests insofar as the circumstances of the time and the administration of the matters permitted. Not only this, but we wish all the more willingly to show your holiness whatever we can, the more eagerly and urgently we observe you carrying out our affairs in those regions where you have previously been established. [Col. 0722A] The superscription of the letters themselves will show to whom they have been sent; without doubt, you will arrange for them to be carried to those to whom they are directed.

Be faithful, then, toward us; act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened; wait for the Lord; “gird up your loins like a man” (Job XL); and hasten, as we admonished your affection above.

We wish your holiness well, etc. Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, in the tenth indiction.

## LXVIII. TO DOCIBILIS AND JOHN (877)

He urges them to take care that Christians do not make a treaty with the Saracens.

[Col. 0722B]

John, bishop, to Docibilis [Note: [Col. 0721D] Leo, bishop of Ostia, mentions Docibilis, book II, chapter 14.] and to John, hypatus.

Having rendered thanks to your devotion for the labor of Christian faith that you cultivate, we exhort you again and again to strive and contend ever more earnestly, and to bring the work you have begun to perfect completion, so that men bearing the Christian name may shun treaties with pagans and learn to place their hope solely in God, who created them, and not in the members of the devil, who are the sons of fornication and vessels of wrath.

When you have done this, you will save your soul and cover a multitude of sins. For blessed James says: “He who converts a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins” (James V).

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of April, in the tenth indiction. [Col. 0722C]

## LXIX. TO PULCHAR, PREFECT OF AMALFI (877)

He advises him to arrange for the dissolution of the treaty made with the Saracens.

John, bishop, to Pulchar [Note: [Col. 0722D] Leo mentions Pulchar above.] prefect of Amalfi.

We admonish you to labor and contend with all your virtue and wisdom so that those men may arrange to break the pacts with the pagans. If they do so, we shall deny neither you nor them any of the things that we can rightly do, and for no cause or person shall we separate ourselves from your common salvation and assistance, or from theirs; nor shall we ever abandon them.

But if they refuse to do this, and you see that they merely wish to mock us from day to day, then at least act according to your own counsel—namely, according to what, with God’s inspiration, you have brought forth from a prudent heart as conducive to salvation. Whatever has been done or not done concerning these matters, or whatever ought to be done, report to us promptly through your messengers or letters, so that we may more easily and expeditiously undertake, prepare, and order whatever must thereafter be done by us.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of April, in the tenth indiction. [Col. 0722D]

## LXX. TO SERGIUS, MAGISTER OF NAPLES (877)

He grieves that, although often admonished, Sergius has refused to dissolve the treaty with the Saracens; he orders him finally to obey and threatens that otherwise he will excommunicate him again. He promises to receive him kindly if he sends faithful envoys.

[Col. 0723A]

John, bishop, to Sergius [Note: [Col. 0723D] Leo, book I, chapter 42, mentions Sergius.] magister of Naples.

When, after repeated messengers and letters, I had sown the seed of God’s word in your heart, even in person, I expected to gain not leaves of words but the fruit of deeds. But because our hope in this matter has been frustrated, I am compelled to break forth against the Israelite people in the voice of the Lord through the prophet Isaiah, crying: “What more ought I to have done for my vineyard that I have not done? Or what did I expect—that it would produce grapes, but it produced wild grapes?” (Isa. V).

Yet, to speak with the Apostle, “To write the same things to you is not burdensome for me, but necessary for you” (Phil. III). Therefore I do not refuse once more to admonish you and your people to withdraw from association with the faithless and at last to depart from so profane a treaty. If you heed us, you will not only have more abundantly from us the good things you desire, but you will also obtain great rewards from heaven.

If not, we shall not only strike you again with the spiritual sword, but those who carry material swords—not without reason, since they are powerful defenders and ardent champions of the holy Church—will, trampling all adversities and prosperities underfoot, immediately take up arms against you and hasten as avengers to attack you, her assailants. Knowing this, and wishing to preserve you safe in soul and body, we announce these things to you and command you to beware.

Moreover, we wonder how you attempt in your letters, which we received during the very celebration of Easter, to assert your innocence, when the whole world—which has been deserted—and the blood poured out upon the earth cry out against your sacrilege. Yet, with God’s grace going before us, we quickly believe that you too, coming to your senses, will be more fittingly released from the bond by which you are held, and that we ourselves, together with the heavenly choirs, will rejoice with equal joy over the salvation of you and your people.

Furthermore, if you send faithful envoys whom we can undoubtedly trust, we shall receive them with willing and kindly affection. Whatever accords with your desire or wish, we shall gladly arrange, confident that they will allege nothing impossible and nothing inappropriate. But if, on the contrary, you propose to carry the yoke of the treaty with the faithless to the very end, know for certain that, to confess with the Apostle, “I will come to you with a rod” (II Cor. IV).

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of April, in the tenth indiction.

## LXXI. TO THE BISHOP OF NAPLES (877)

He complains that the Neapolitans have made a treaty with the faithless and are not being recalled to the way of truth by their own bishop. He therefore urges both him and them to come to their senses. He further promises to receive kindly the envoys of the duke of Naples, should he send them, and declares himself ready for everything they report as needing to be accomplished for the benefit of the Church of God.

[Col. 0724A]

John, bishop, to the bishop of Naples.

After setting aside your letters, which we received on the great day, when the service of the paschal festival had already begun, we found nothing in them that could make us rejoice. Hence immense sadness and continual grief grew in our heart and, multiplied, afflict us greatly, because we see the people of your city—which was once God’s but has now become the possession of the prince of darkness—having wholly abandoned love for its Creator, carrying the yoke together with the faithless.

For this reason we see that you too are liable, since you dwell amid a people whose lips are defiled, yourself defiled and an accomplice; and we observe that you do not wish with all your strength to set yourself as a wall before the house of the Lord, as a worthy athlete of Christ ought to do. [Col. 0724B]

Yet for this very reason we had undoubtedly endeavored to raise you to so great an honor, so that, having you as our helper and faithful fellow worker, we might draw the Lord’s sheep from that dreadful abyss into which we saw them submerged and held by the enemy of the human race, and raise them to heavenly things, so that we might have an equal reward from God, the recompensor of all, for our common struggle.

But behold: neglecting the care of pastoral office and setting aside fear of divine judgment, you dwell with those whom you ought either to correct and recall to the way of truth, or, like a diseased flock chastised with so many blows of salutary discipline, to avoid when they refuse to accept their own salvation; and from whose midst, as we formerly commanded you by divine authority, you ought to have departed, no longer presuming to dwell with transgressors and those who maintain fellowship with the faithless. Thus, when the sincerity of your devotion became more clearly manifest, we might have you, whom we adorned with the insignia of the highest priesthood, joined with us in the fellowship of Christ’s body.

[Col. 0724C] Although we were then detained by continual bodily infirmity, we nevertheless wished with all devotion to save the city of Naples, as the Lord’s people and the sheep of his pasture entrusted to us in the very person of the prince of the apostles. We did not refuse the labor; rather, we placed our lives in our hands and, admonished by the Lord’s voice, came to strengthen them in God’s good pleasure as brothers and to assist them before the Lord as dearest sons. But with hearts hardened, they disdained to receive our prayers and admonitions and, like deaf vipers, to listen to them. Nevertheless, we did not fail to ordain you as their bishop, according to their wish and desire, although they did not deserve it, and we made many other good promises on this matter if they would fulfill the desire of our will with devoted minds.

Now, whether they remain uncorrected and refuse to return to the one who strikes them, or whether you dwell with them and are therefore, together with them, separated from all divine things, how can we spare you or release you from the bond of ecclesiastical judgment before you come to your senses and return to the way of salvation and justice?

First, therefore, release yourselves from the bonds of wickedness and from the impious treaty that you have made with the enemies of Christ; and once you have turned back, we shall not fail immediately to grant you the mercy that our God has given his Church in the Holy Spirit. For just as those who truly confess and make satisfaction ought to be spared, as the Lord says, “When you have turned and groaned, you will be saved, and while you are still speaking, I shall say, ‘Here I am’” (Ezek. XXXII), so there must be no mercy toward those who remain in impious crime. Before the worthy fruit of repentance, we can in no way show mercy toward you, since mercy must unquestionably be sought in such a way that salvation may be the result of discipline.

For, as Saint Gregory says (Book II on Ezekiel, homily 19): “Piety often goes astray through immoderate mercy, if it has perhaps spared what ought not to be spared. Sins that can be struck by the fires of Gehenna must be corrected by the rod of discipline. But disordered piety, when it spares temporarily, leads to eternal punishment.”

Therefore we wish to spare you when you come to your senses, so that you may not perish in the future. Moreover, if your brother—the duke of the Neapolitans—sends us through suitable envoys the requests and matters that ought to be carried out, conveyed by a truthful report, we shall receive them most gratefully and undoubtedly be ready to accomplish, for the benefit and salvation of the Church of God, whatever they report with sound judgment.

Act, therefore, and do not cease to toil for the common prosperity—indeed, for your own salvation and that of your fellow citizens—rebuking, beseeching, and reproving with all authority, so that your labor may bring forth in the house of the Lord a desired fruit for which you may be worthily rewarded.

Given as above.

## LXXII. TO AJOS, BISHOP OF BENEVENTO (877)

He praises his prompt zeal in defending the Church. He then urges him to provide aid against the Saracens and to arrange for the treaty made with them to be dissolved.

John, bishop, to Ajo, bishop of Benevento.

Having examined the letter of your holiness, we have recognized with the utmost clarity how fiercely the ardor of divine love burns within you. Observing no less how devoted you are toward the holy Roman Church, we give you manifold thanks for such kindness and ask the clemency of the Almighty that your holiness may be endowed with worthy successes for the advancement of our struggle. [Col. 0725D]

Indeed, dearest brother, you deserve to be praised, for you declare that, seeing as though present the tribulations that we endure for the people entrusted to us, and groaning and grieving with us, you wish to be, as is fitting, our prudent fellow soldier and fellow worker in removing them.

We therefore believe and suspect nothing else concerning your holiness except that, although absent in body, you are never absent in spirit from our sighs, and that you yourself clearly understand how grievous it is that the faithful are joined so destructively with the faithless. For this reason, since we should be careful not to multiply words rather than groans by dwelling on many speeches, [Col. 0726A] especially because your fraternity, as we see from your letters, is not unaware of our hidden sorrows, we adjure your reverence by him who appointed you his priest. Persuading and beseeching you in every way, and relying upon fraternal love, we command you, with all your strength and ability, to labor—both with your brother and with the other worshipers of Christ who can provide aid in this matter—so that, by Christ’s mercy, the impious treaties that the Neapolitans or their associates have made with the enemies of Christ’s name may be destroyed as quickly as possible.

May peace and concord among the faithful be restored through Christ the Lord, so that the body of the holy Church of God, for which Christ’s blood was shed, may not be torn among its members, and so that true religion and perfect charity may be recognized. For although you, or perhaps the whole world, may mourn the evils that threaten, we are afflicted and grieve more than all others to the extent that we understand that we have assumed, above all others, the solicitude and care of governing Christ’s sheep. Therefore, because we labor more than all, we specially beseech you that our labor may advance to its fulfillment through you.

Meanwhile, we ask you earnestly to exhort your dearest brother to send our letter promptly to the first of the Greeks who comes there and, with his own supplications, to urge him never to fail—once every obstacle has been removed—to send even ten dromons immediately to our aid. For, with Christ’s grace cooperating, we shall toil both with our dearest son Lambert, the glorious duke, who adheres to us in all things, and with other men who fear the Lord, so that the impious treaty made with the Agareni may be dissolved and freedom, or at least some security, may be restored to the Christian people.

Finally, since, as we have said, we necessarily labor more than all others, we shall refuse neither labor nor any bearable bodily hardship, so that, with the Lord’s help and with Christ going before us, we may vigorously persist in our work on behalf of such great necessities and for you. Perhaps Almighty God, when your labors have been added to ours, will have mercy on so many who are perishing, and, removing our sorrows, will dissolve the treaties that your people have made with wicked pagans. In this matter we ask you to toil with every effort. We hope to rejoice so greatly in the success of your struggle because we trust that we have you as our fellow worker in this undertaking.

Meanwhile, your holy fraternity should take the greatest care to inform us in writing, as quickly as possible, of whatever has been accomplished through your diligence or through your brother’s obedience, whether concerning the dispatch of dromons or the dissolution of the impious pacts. [Col. 0726D]

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the tenth indiction.

## LXXIII. TO GREGORY, IMPERIAL PAEDAGOGUS (877)

He rejoices that the emperor has sent a fleet against the Saracens for the defense of the Church and appointed Gregory as its commander. He then advises him to send ten *achelandia* [Note: [Col. 0727D] Alternatively, *chelandia*, which belong to the class of military ships.] to clear the coasts of Saracen pirates.

[Col. 0727A]

John, bishop, to Gregory, imperial paedagogus.

At the beginning of this letter from our apostolate, we first exhort your Magnificence to inform us of the health granted by God to our desirable son, Basil, the most tranquil emperor. We very greatly desire always to hear of the health of his soul and body, as befits the most devout champion of the orthodox faith.

We rejoice to hear that your Magnificence, accompanied by forces committed to God’s protection by the aforementioned emperor, divinely protected, has come into the territory of the Beneventans. We rejoice both because, thanks be to God, his divinely advanced empire, inflamed with pious zeal for the defense of Christendom, has arranged to send fleets and a strong military force against the enemies of Christ’s cross, and because he chose you above others, with God’s help, to carry out so great a task. We have heard that you are vigorous in all things and industrious in the worship of God.

For the rest, we believe that your Magnificence already knows how certain nets of bands of Agarenian brigands devastate our shores by secret incursions, and that, lacking the courage to act openly, they inflict many and manifold injuries upon this holy Roman Church of God through stealthy plundering. [Col. 0727B]

It therefore seemed good to us to send you this letter, so that you may send at least ten good and well-equipped *achelandia* to our port, to cleanse our shores of those Arab thieves and pirates. With the help of the right hand of the Most High, which, through the intercession of the princes of the apostles, will contend and assist on their behalf, they will be able to accomplish this quickly and without any impediment.

[Col. 0727C] Believe me, by heeding our admonitions in this matter you will win the favor of the most devout emperor. Since he is a most Christian man, a lover of God, and an ardent champion of the Lord’s churches, you will not be able to make yourself more pleasing to him than by striving through your own efforts to assist this holy Church, which is the first teacher and head of the churches. In this act, moreover, you will gain glory in the present age from that same Augustus, protected by God, and in the future an everlasting crown.

May Almighty God protect you and those who are with you, and defend you against the enemies of Christ with his powerful right hand.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the tenth indiction.

## LXXIV. TO EMPEROR CHARLES THE BALD (877)

He announces that he has excommunicated Adelard, bishop of Verona, because he had invaded the monastery of Nonantula.

[Col. 0727D]

John, bishop, to the emperor.

We have rightly and deservedly taken care, most glorious Emperor Augustus, to report in this present letter to the sacred ears of your imperial Clemency the disobedience and rash presumption of Adelard, bishop of Verona, which he committed not only in contempt of us but also as an injury to your Highness. [Col. 0728A] For the heavenly Majesty has granted you to us as the invincible patron, powerful defender, and energetic helper of his holy Church entrusted to us, so that in all ecclesiastical interests—through which you deserve to possess everlasting glory—we may have you as God’s avenging minister.

Accordingly, when we had discovered that the same Bishop Adelard had cunningly sought the venerable monastery situated at Nonantula—which, out of reverence for God and for so great a place, no bishop or judge had ever sought as a benefice—and had thereby presumed to undertake an unlawful act, disregarding divine fear and acting against the enactments of our predecessors and of our privilege, by which it is always ordered that an abbot be appointed from its own congregation, we made every effort to excommunicate him by apostolic authority. [Col. 0728B] [Note: [Col. 0728D] Something is missing.] We shall without doubt rebuke him by canonical corrections for retaining these things, insofar as apostolic authority supports us, so that, chastised with a fitting blow and bound by a canonical bond, he may learn to preserve obedience, since, when free, he refused to obey ecclesiastical and canonical commands. [The transmitted Latin is syntactically defective after the noted gap.]

Given as above.

## LXXV. TO JOHN, ANSPERT, AND WAIPERT, ARCHBISHOPS (877)

The same subject.

John, bishop, to John, archbishop of Ravenna; Anspert, archbishop of Milan; and Waipert [f. Valpert], archbishop of Aquileia.

[Col. 0728C] Following the decrees of the holy and great Council of Nicaea, which order (canon 12) that a regular letter be obtained in each province, lest those rejected by some be received by others, we wish your fraternity to know that Adelard, bishop of Verona, has been deprived of communion by the authority of the privilege of the apostolic see. For he seized the monastery of Nonantula, which had always been held secure by the privilege of the apostolic see and by that of our own authority, without any usurpation through invasion, and had been governed until now solely by the administration of an abbot elected and appointed from the company of the brothers. He applied it to his own uses, while reducing the monks to extreme poverty; and even now, after our frequent prohibition, he does not fear to oppress it and hand it over, divided among secular hands, contrary to the rules of the holy Fathers and also against the judgment of the apostolic see and of the entire holy synod, which we made known to all of you by letters sent through the several provinces.

[Col. 0728D] Even after our prohibition, frequently conveyed through our messengers and letters, he indiscriminately admits [an unspecified person] to communion and has appeared aware of and a supporter of all Adelard’s wickedness.

We have therefore excommunicated the aforesaid Adelard, bishop of Verona, until, coming into the presence of the apostolic see, he offers a suitable satisfaction before it concerning the nature of the aforesaid offenses. If, while remaining in this condition, he despises this, he shall by right remain wholly deprived of communion and shall bind with an equal bond all who communicate with him or rashly favor him against our prohibition. We therefore wish to make you cautious, if you do not wish yourselves to be subjected to judgment according to the sacred rules.

We wish your fraternity well, etc.

## LXXVI. TO THE CLERGY OF VERONA (877)

The same subject.

John, bishop, to all the clergy of the Church of Verona.

We wish your experience to know that Adelard, your bishop, has been deprived of communion by the authority of the apostolic see, because he seized the monastery of Nonantula, which had always been held secure by the privilege of the apostolic see and by that of our own authority, without any usurpation through invasion, and had been governed until now solely by the administration of an abbot elected and appointed from the company of the brothers.

[Col. 0729B] He applied it to his own uses, while reducing the monks to extreme poverty, and even now, after our frequent prohibition, does not fear to oppress it and hand it over, divided among secular hands, contrary to the rules of the holy Fathers and also against the judgment of the apostolic see and of the entire holy synod. Even after our prohibition, frequently conveyed through our messengers and letters, he indiscriminately admitted [an unspecified person] to communion and appeared aware of and a supporter of all Adelard’s wickedness. [Col. 0729C]

Know, therefore, that he has been excommunicated until, coming into the presence of the apostolic see, he offers a suitable satisfaction before it concerning the nature of the aforesaid offenses. If, while remaining in this condition, he despises this, he shall by right remain wholly deprived of communion and shall bind with an equal bond all who communicate with him or rashly favor him against our prohibition. We therefore wish to make you cautious, if you do not wish yourselves to be subjected to judgment according to the rules.

We wish you well, etc. Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of May, in the tenth indiction.

## LXXVII. TO LANDULF, BISHOP OF CAPUA (877)

He advises him to inform him whether the duke of Naples wishes to break the treaty made with the Saracens and to arrange that the same duke, Gauferius, and Pulchar come with him to Traiectum, where he is going. He declares himself ready to grant what he had promised and even more, if the duke persists in his resolve.

[Col. 0729D]

John, bishop, to Landulf, bishop of Capua.

Let your holiness take the greatest care to learn with certainty whether the duke of Naples now genuinely wishes to break the Saracen pact and henceforth truly to adhere, as is right, to the treaty of Christ that he made in the waters of regeneration. If you discover that he now has such an intention, inform us of it immediately.

Arrange that the duke of Naples, the glorious prince Gauferius, and Pulchar the prefect hasten together with you to Traiectum. When we arrive there as well, we shall determine what is pleasing to God. [Col. 0730A] We are ready to grant not only what has been stated but also greater things, provided that the word of the same *magister militum* is faithful and firm, and secured by every certainty, so that security may remain firm on both sides and persist without any doubt.

But if you discover that they either do not wish to fulfill what they promise or intend to delay it, you must not be permitted to conceal this from our knowledge; rather, you must report everything truthfully and without deceit. Take care, therefore, to inform us fully and as quickly as possible by letter concerning these matters, so that, with God’s help, we may begin and complete without delay whatever God thereafter dictates.

Take particular charge of these matters, since you are cherished above others with the special privilege of our heart.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of May, in the tenth indiction. [Col. 0730B]

## LXXVIII. TO PULCHAR, PREFECT (877)

The same subject.

John, bishop, to Pulchar, prefect.

If indeed the *magister militum* has proposed to break the Saracen pact, we exhort you to go to Traiectum with your illustrious father-in-law. When our presence is found there as well, we shall immediately and most gladly grant whatever is reasonably sought and whatever is requested as necessary or possible. Nor shall we in any way refuse to do greater things, so that, according to the Apostle, we may be able to gain all (II Cor. IX).

In this matter your diligence should labor all the more earnestly because you clearly understand that through it a heavenly reward from the Lord God will be bestowed upon you. [Col. 0730C] Otherwise, against him we shall, with Christ’s favor, unquestionably and without distinction carry out whatever we are rightly able to do; we shall in no way omit it.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of May, in the tenth indiction.

## LXXIX. TO EMPEROR CHARLES THE BALD (877)

He implores aid against the Saracens, who, after devastating Campania, were laying waste to everything around Rome.

John, bishop, to the emperor.

The divine Majesty chose your Excellency above others to raise you to the height of the Roman Empire and wished to crown you with the imperial diadem so that, with our God mercifully assisting, you might always protect the Church of Christ, founded by the word upon the rock of true faith, with the triumphal arm of your power, and defend her with devout concern from the savage and cruel attacks of the pagans, who, now surrounding us on every side like brigands, devastate all that is ours with fire and sword.

But since, while we are far away, we suffer daily so many harsh and unbearable things—for which we have already implored your imperial Majesty—especially since all Campania has now been laid waste and nothing remains for us, for the venerable monasteries, for the other holy places, or for the Roman senate from which we might be physically sustained, and since all the suburbs of Rome have been so thoroughly plundered that no inhabitant or person of any age seems now to remain there, [Col. 0731A] we are afflicted by immense grief and troubled by sorrow over these innumerable evils. We can take neither sleep with our eyes nor food with our bodies; instead of rest we suffer continual labor, and instead of the sweetness of bodily nourishment, bitterness of mind.

Therefore the holy Roman Church, which gave birth to you from her religious womb, through my speech but with her venerable affection, most humbly and earnestly beseeches your imperial Majesty, splendidly illumined by the light of all wisdom, that, removing every delay and undertaking her whole cause, you deign to come now as a merciful helper, powerful defender, and invincible savior, for her defense and the liberation of the entire country. For unless your most desired [Col. 0731B] presence comes to us, we shall be unable to obtain any defense or any remedy necessary for salvation.

We, together with the entire sacred order of the apostolic see and with religious men who fear God, shall with all our efforts implore Almighty God—for to him belong all salvation and life—for the prosperity of your glory and the continual health of your mind and body, so that neither the heat of the season, nor the unfamiliar nature of the place, nor any hardship may befall that could harm your distinguished body.

Therefore, doubting none of these things—which assuredly will not occur without God’s will—but rather trusting with all our strength in the Lord’s mercy, you will deserve to attain not only bodily safety but also the perpetual salvation and glory of your soul. [Col. 0731C]

May your most devout Serenity, most merciful Emperor Augustus, deign to hear our prayers and those of our Church for the liberation of so great a see and the salvation of so many people redeemed by Christ’s blood; may you look upon our sobs and attend to the tears of such great grief, continually poured forth. Thus, moved by compassion for us in the customary manner and with your customary tenderness, hasten to grant the aid of consolation to those who urgently seek it, and strive to assist us as opportunity requires, since, after God, you are unquestionably our one hope of salvation and our confidence of liberation.

Therefore do not delay in hastening in person to provide us with suitable and timely aid, so that the Lord, who chose you as the head and master of the world, may always deign to send you his help from the sanctuary, beloved son.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, in the tenth indiction. [Col. 0731D]

## LXXX. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF RAVENNA (877)

He orders him to attend the council with his suffragan bishops.

John, bishop, to the archbishop of Ravenna.

Because we have now reached the perilous times foretold by the Apostle (II Tim. 3)—or rather, alas, by the Lord: “Nation will rise against nation,” and among other things “a man’s enemies are those of his own household” (Luke 21; Mic. 7)—evil has grown beyond expectation. We are not only battered externally by the fury of unbelieving barbarians, but are also afflicted internally by the wickedness of depraved Christians. Yet the more the evils of the wicked multiply, the more the good deeds of rulers ought to increase. These cannot truly be accomplished except through the common college of brothers coming together in one body and mind. For the Church of God, because of its concord, is utterly terrifying to both visible and invisible enemies, “like an army drawn up in battle array” (Song 6).

Therefore, both for certain ecclesiastical necessities and for the welfare and correction of the commonwealth, by apostolic authority we have decreed to summon a universal council of our reverend brothers and fellow bishops of the Italian kingdom—that is, of the entire province. We have determined that no place could be found more suitable or convenient for holding it than Ravenna, accessible to those converging from every direction.

Let therefore your fraternity come eagerly with your suffragan bishops, whom you yourself should urge to assemble, to the designated city, and do not in any way tolerate being absent from the gathering which we shall celebrate there on the eighth day before the Kalends of July. Thus the tares springing up in the Lord’s field may be uprooted completely through common effort, and the shoots of wholesome virtues may be firmly planted in their place through shared struggle.

Moreover, we order that our brothers and fellow bishops who live under your beatitude come, at your urging, to the same universal synod. Whoever, however, should perhaps disdain to appear before your holiness must know that he will unquestionably be subjected to canonical reprimands, as the Apostle makes clear (II Cor. 10), while we stand ready to punish every disobedience.

Let your beatitude arrange for this letter of our apostolate, or copies of it, to be prepared throughout your diocese for all the bishops without distinction, lest anyone be able to put forward an inadmissible veil of excuse for disobedience.

### LXXXI. TO ANSPERT AND ANTONY, BISHOPS (877)

He orders them to come to Ravenna for the synod; if they do not obey, he threatens to excommunicate them.

John, bishop, to Anspert, archbishop of Milan, and Antony, bishop of Brescia.

Because we see the Churches of God entrusted to us disturbed by diverse and manifold troubles, deprived without delay of their own possessions, and the honor of their bishops diminished, compelled by daily concern for them, as the Apostle says (II Cor. 11), we have necessarily judged it appropriate, with God’s favor, to celebrate a general synod for their welfare and restoration to their former condition.

Although, following ancient custom, we ought to have held it at Rome and would not have refused the labor of so great a journey, nevertheless, out of consideration for our venerable fellow bishops whom we have summoned into our fellowship by letters, we shall certainly celebrate it at Ravenna on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, with the Lord’s help.

Accordingly, by these present letters we command your fraternity to come there, setting aside every excuse and putting away all delay, so that, through the common agreement and decree of many of our brothers, the Church of God entrusted to us may recover in full the rights of its proper dignity, which have been usurped by certain unjust men. Once we have finally been made secure from every evil, may we be able, as is fitting, to glorify the episcopal ministry which, by God’s gift, we have undertaken for the salvation of the Lord’s flock entrusted to us.

Therefore, we command you once again to come to the same synod, as stated. For if you should in any way disdain to hasten to that venerable council on the appointed day, and should refuse to share with us the labor required for the welfare of the Church of Christ our God—a matter urgently necessary at the present time—know for certain that henceforth you shall in no way be sharers in our communion. Rather, as wicked transgressors, you shall be struck and condemned by the judgment of canonical authority.

We wish your reverence good health in Christ.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, in the tenth indiction.

### LXXXII. TO URSUS, DUKE OF VENETIA (877)

He accuses him of disobedience and urges him to ensure that the bishops of Venetia come to the synod to be held at Ravenna; he himself too should either come or send legates.

John, bishop, to Ursus, duke of Venetia.

You would certainly deserve to be subjected to many reprimands from us for just correction, unless apostolic moderation dealt with you with less severity than patience. For, apart from those offenses which you had previously incurred through disobedience, you finally judged even the legation of blessed Peter unworthy of your attention, although it is clear that scarcely any pagan would have done such a thing—especially since what we sent to your affection consisted of paternal admonitions, not the blows of a hateful enemy.

Setting these matters aside, we inform your affection that on the eighth day before the Kalends of July we shall celebrate at Ravenna a synod of all the priests of Italy. We wish the bishops of maritime Venetia who are still known to survive to attend it, together with those persons elected to the episcopate and those whom we have already mentioned to you in various letters.

You will therefore act very well if you do not prevent them from coming to the aforesaid synod, but urge them by every means. We do not desire their ruin—far be it from us—but rather to restore the condition of that province and to settle canonically whatever dispute or controversy exists between them and their metropolitan.

Let them therefore come without hesitation, and do not allow them in any way to be absent from so holy and numerous a college of brothers. Believe me, they will not return to their own lands diminished in anything—may God avert that—but rather increased, with Christ’s favor. Otherwise, when it becomes clear that they have not obeyed the common decree of all, they will unquestionably be dealt with as the holy Gospel prescribes concerning such matters.

Know this for certain: we desire no diminution of your Church for the sake of any mortal. Rather, we wish and desire that your honor and reputation, as a distinguished and God-fearing man, be preserved.

Therefore we urge you not to hesitate to set out for us at Ravenna yourself. If not, at least do not refuse to send us some capable man who can discharge the embassy entrusted to him on behalf of your glory.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, in the tenth indiction.

### LXXXIII. TO PETER AND LEO, BISHOPS OF VENETIA (877)

He orders them to set out for Ravenna for the council, at which the controversies between them and their metropolitan are to be settled.

John, bishop, to Peter and Leo, bishops of Venetia.

The manifold and varied needs of the Churches at last compel us to celebrate a universal council. Therefore, to regulate and administer these matters, we have ordered the priests of all Italy to assemble at Ravenna on the eighth day before the Kalends of July of this indiction.

To that sacred college, through our pontifical authority, we urge your holiness also to attend, together with those who have been appointed in place of deceased bishops, and likewise those whom, in writing to the glorious duke Ursus and to you, we have repeatedly and explicitly named. To speak plainly and in due order, this includes all who consider themselves injured; your holiness will certainly have to summon them all to hasten there with you by apostolic authority.

Therefore, brothers, come without hesitation, so that, besides the common benefit which must unquestionably be arranged at the synod, whatever controversy exists between our brother and fellow bishop Peter, your metropolitan, and those men may receive a canonical conclusion, and peace and tranquility may be restored to your Churches as is fitting.

Do not, therefore, dearest brothers, allow yourselves to be absent from so holy and numerous a college. Believe me, we seek the downfall of none of you—far be it from us. Nevertheless, if you do not attend at least this previously announced universal synod, you will be subjected to the canonical laws by the common judgment of all and will rightly be punished for such great disobedience.

For, as holy Samuel teaches, to resist is like the sin of divination, and to refuse obedience is like the crime of idolatry (I Sam. 15).

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, in the tenth indiction.

### LXXXIV. TO AQUILEIEUS (877)

He indicates that the sinister reports circulated about him must be settled canonically in a general council.

To Aquileieus [editorial correction: Aquileiensem, “the bishop of Aquileia”].

We know that your beatitude is being defamed by certain people in connection with some matters, and that this must certainly be examined more fully [editorial correction: “more soundly”], inwardly, and perceptively in the synodal assembly and brought to an end in every respect by regular judgment, according to its nature.

But, with divine grace favoring us, we believe that when you are brought before the assembly you will be found so innocent that, once the truth has been stirred up, it will not emit filth from you—God forbid—but, like agitated ointment, will give forth a pleasing fragrance. Unless, perhaps, a deliberately arranged absence should confirm that what is said about you is true and should rightly impose punishment; had you been present, justice, acting as teacher, might perhaps have returned a different verdict.

Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, in the tenth indiction.

### LXXXV. TO GUAIFER, PRINCE OF SALERNO (877)

John, bishop, to Guaifer, prince of Salerno.

Because we awaited the legates of the duke of Naples according to his letters and yours, but have not seen them, we are compelled to write again to your excellence, so that we may restore him, separated from the treacherous, to the pious bosom of holy mother Church.

Since you have already labored greatly in this matter, we urge you again and again to continue your efforts diligently to the end. If he is preparing immediately to break the wicked alliance, once we know this for certain, we ourselves shall hasten to Traiectum and shall gladly grant more generously both what is being requested and what has already been promised, provided that a clearer certainty and the truth of faith are established between the two parties.

There we also desire the presence of yourself, the most holy bishop Landulf, the aforesaid duke, and the glorious prefect Pulcharis. We earnestly beg your diligence to see that this is accomplished.

But if that same duke, in accordance with his hardness and unrepentant heart, is storing up wrath for himself on the day of wrath (Rom. 2), so that he wishes either to prolong the matter or altogether to disregard the cause of his own salvation and that of many others, we also wish to learn this immediately. For no human or divine counsel or assistance will wholly fail us; let those who desire with all their heart to repay him according to his work and according to the fruit of his inventions [lacuna] rejoice at his coming, for almighty God will appear gentle to the just and terrifying to the unjust.

Therefore let your most beloved affection show itself to us in this matter with the greatest devotion, and, as long as your strength permits, do not cease to labor. Thus, when this petition of ours has been brought to completion through your exhortations, we may return worthy thanks to you and remember you in our prayers before the holy apostles.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of June, in the tenth indiction.

### LXXXVI. TO EMPEROR CHARLES, THE TORTUTIAN ABBOT GEILON, AND HIS MONKS (877)

He confirms the rights of the cell of Godith, founded by Prince Desiderius, and adds exemption from all episcopal jurisdiction in the year of Christ 877.

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our spiritual son, the glorious Emperor Charles Augustus; to the illustrious abbot Geilon; and to our beloved sons living now and in future under the rule of Saint Benedict at the monastery of Trenorchium, dedicated to holy, undefiled, and ever-virgin Mary, Mother of God, and to the precious confessor of Christ, Filibertus.

From the time when, with Christ’s help, the Church began, it has always been shaken by the blasts of the impious. But because in our times it is raised up on imperial wings, we must, insofar as we are able, confirm it by apostolic authority.

Therefore, at the petition of our most excellent son, the Emperor Charles, we grant, bestow, and confirm to this monastery, for your present and future times, a privilege of this authority of ours. Just as that most glorious son of ours, at the entreaty of Prince Desiderius, granted the cell called Godith in the district of Vallava, in the place called Vallis Angusta, together with the aforesaid place, the holy persons mentioned above, the villages, resources, and revenues; strengthened it by a document of his authority; and caused it to be confirmed by the privilege of our brothers and sons, the bishops of those regions, so, exactly as is contained in the noble charter which Desiderius made and in the decree of our son Charles, let these things remain undisturbed.

No king, bishop, abbot, or anyone endowed with any dignity whatsoever shall presume to diminish or remove anything from what is contained in this privilege or in the decrees of our son Charles. Rather, everything that has been offered or may be offered to the aforesaid church of Godith shall remain undisturbed and unimpaired.

By another authority of blessed Peter we establish that the church built in the aforesaid valley and dedicated in honor of the Savior and his Mother be immune from every earthly domination. For we judge it unjust that the glorious Queen of the world, who together with her Son has been exalted above the choirs of angels, should be subjected to human powers.

We therefore anathematize anyone who dares claim the place for himself, or who presumes to approach it on any pretext for absolution, excommunication, or sacred ordination, unless he has been invited by the abbot of the place or by the monks serving God there.

Moreover, as is contained in the decrees of our son Charles, we decree that it be free and undisturbed from every secular person. If anyone, whether of high or low rank, should presume by reckless boldness to act against this decree of ours, let him know that he is bound by the bond of anathema, alien from the kingdom of God, and condemned with the impious to eternal fire.

Written by the hand of Anastasius, regional notary and archivist of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of June, in the fifth indiction [editorial correction: “fifteenth”]. Farewell. On the lead seal of Pope John.

### LXXXVII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF RAVENNA (877)

He specifies the fixed day on which the archbishop must be present at Ravenna with all his suffragans; if anyone refuses obedience, he threatens him with excommunication.

John to the archbishop of Ravenna.

The journey which we undertook to Traiectum to dissolve the pact formerly made by the Neapolitans with the Saracens delayed us from the appointed day of the synod. But because, with God as author, that pact has now been broken and some measure of peace is evidently restored, behold, we write from the road that we shall certainly be at Ravenna on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August.

Your holiness must arrange to be present there in person, with all your suffragan bishops whom you ought to summon, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, with every excuse removed, so that through common deliberation the tares that have arisen among the Churches may be completely uprooted.

If anyone should think that your college ought to withdraw from this matter, let him know that he will in every way be deprived of participation in our communion. We unquestionably stand ready, according to the Apostle (II Cor. 10), to punish every disobedience.

Given as above, in the tenth indiction.

### LXXXVIII. TO THE SAME (877)

He writes that he has ordered all the bishops of Italy, especially those of Venetia, to come to the synod to be held at Ravenna.

To John [Note: “Perhaps John to Ursus, duke of Venetia, as the expression ‘your glory,’ which also occurs in the letter, indicates.” — Hardt] the archbishop of Ravenna.

We wish your glory to know that, because of the many needs of the holy Church of God, as you should already be aware, we have established that a synod must by all means be celebrated at Ravenna on the eleventh day before the Kalends of August of this tenth indiction, with the grace of the Holy Spirit assisting.

Just as we shall attend it, setting aside many other useful undertakings and refusing neither the labor of the journey nor the severity of the weather [Roman edition: “we are attending”], so we wish all bishops from every direction to come, so that whatever is recognized as having grown improperly in the holy Church of God through the sowers of tares may be uprooted completely through our common deliberation and common effort.

For this reason we do not allow your nobility to remain ignorant that we have summoned the bishops of Venetia, as well as the elected and appointed bishops of vacant sees, to the same synod, just as we have already summoned them, and have again decreed that they come. Thus every dispute between your reverend metropolitan and yourselves may be discussed, examined, and canonically settled before the holy synod.

Otherwise, if those who have already been summoned so many times by letter prove disobedient, they will deserve to incur the judgment of the synod as contemptuous persons, both from us and from the holy synod. Since the road from there to Ravenna is shorter, they will not be able to plead the labor of the journey as an excuse.

Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the tenth indiction.

### LXXXIX. PRIVILEGE GRANTED TO THE MONASTERY AND HOSPICE OF PIACENZA (877)

[In Campi, *Ecclesiastical History of Piacenza*, p. 463.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Angilberga, beloved daughter, empress Augusta, and through you to your venerable monastery newly built at Piacenza, in perpetuity.

By the Lord’s command we ought, with apostolic solicitude, to favor all who make just requests, but especially your devotion, our sweetest and spiritual daughter Angilberga, formerly Empress Augusta. The holy mother, the Roman Church, rightly embraces and continually cherishes you with honor and reverence as its dearest and principal offspring.

Therefore we embrace with commendable approval and paternal affection the monastery and hospice which, through prudent provision, you have recently wished to build from its foundations at Piacenza in honor of the Lord’s Resurrection, of the blessed apostles, and of the martyrs Bartholomew, Sixtus, and Fabian [lacuna].

By apostolic authority we establish it as ratified and permanently confirmed, so that, protected by blessed Peter and with the Lord’s protection, it may always remain unharmed and unshaken against every assault and disturbance by any hostile persons.

We also provide and firmly decree that everything which you have once distributed there to the Lord, in movable and immovable property, within and outside the monastery, in servants of either sex, in all ecclesiastical adornment, and in every kind of equipment, shall remain undisturbed in that consecrated place for future times. Every diminution or invasion of these things shall be completely suppressed.

We likewise favor, assist, and grant apostolic assent concerning those servants whom, for the redemption of your souls, you have prudently and deliberately granted freedom, or may hereafter grant it, so that they too, enjoying secure liberty and guided by God’s grace, may receive the everlasting joys of life.

As you, devoted daughter, requested, I appoint the consecration of the abbess of that place. We grant this to the archbishop of Milan, or to the bishop of Aquileia who, according to the Gospel’s expression, has entered through the door and has entered canonically; to him also we entrust the task of restoring peace with disciplined moderation if, God forbid, the evil of discord should arise there in human fashion.

If at any time the burden of hostile persons should compel some necessity, we command that the matter be freely referred to the apostolic see, so that it may determine and settle, by the balance of its judgment, whatever is more correct and excellent, and suppress the evil that threatens the aforesaid venerable place.

Meanwhile, with the consent of Paul, the venerable bishop who governs the see of Piacenza, we permit twelve clerics of any order to serve continually in that holy place and to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass, subject only to the regular oversight of their own bishop—namely, synodal summons and ordination for consecration.

Even so, neither in the said monastery and hospice nor in their possessions shall he henceforth claim any right of authority; nor shall he come to celebrate Mass, in accordance with the institutions of the Fathers, unless invited.

As for the tithes of your property which the aforesaid bishop has already devoutly and willingly granted to the venerable place mentioned above, out of love for God and in remembrance of your benefactions, we wish them to be held perpetually by the sacred hospice, without objection from him or from his successors, just as you yourself established.

Furthermore, we decree and establish by apostolic authority that, just as our predecessors appear to have granted and strengthened by their privileges, all the things which the late, divinely remembered Louis, most serene emperor, and your husband, while he lived, are known to have bestowed upon you through their munificence by imperial documents; and likewise whatever you yourself later acquired for your own use or for that of your aforesaid monastery through imperial gifts or through any lawful acquisitions, purchases, or exchanges; and also whatever is shown to have been added now or hereafter for the support of that consecrated place through the donation or generosity of kings or any other faithful persons—all these things shall remain unimpaired, inviolate, and unshaken, in the same terms and order in which they came to you or to your aforesaid monastery, and shall remain according to the statutes of your arrangement.

If anyone, which we do not wish, should attempt to act against these decrees concerning things offered or granted in the service of almighty God, or should recklessly wish to violate any of them, let him be subjected to excommunication and deprived of all ecclesiastical fellowship. Unless he immediately corrects and repents of such wickedness, let him remain guilty, bound by the bond of anathema through the authority of blessed Peter and our apostolate at the future judgment. For his great transgression, let him know that, together with Judas the betrayer, unrestrained and rebellious against the judgment of the Holy Spirit, who always flees what is false and deceitful, he will have his portion in the fire of eternal Gehenna.

Written by the hand of Leo, regional notary and archivist of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of August, in the tenth indiction.

Farewell. On the Kalends of August, by the hand of John, bishop, envoy and apocrisiary of the holy apostolic see, while our lord Charles, crowned by God, the great second emperor, was reigning; in the second year after his consulship, in the tenth indiction.

### XC. TO THE BISHOP OF TICINUM (877)

He grants permission to use archiepiscopal insignia, with authority to summon the archbishops of Ravenna and Milan to his synod.

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend John, bishop of the holy Church of Ticinus, etc., in perpetuity.

We have undertaken the care of this government and discharge the solicitude of apostolic mercy so that we may willingly receive the petitions of those who ask justly and, with the balance of equity, assist all who are placed in need. For, as bearers of the authority of the highest see, we must strive, insofar as divine assistance permits, for the stability of venerable places. Through this concern divine clemency is appeased, and the praise and usefulness of the Church of Christ are advanced.

Therefore, since your reverence has petitioned us concerning matters known to pertain to the stability and advancement of the honor of your holy Church, over which you are recognized as presiding by divine favor, and since we desire to accomplish these things with precision, we have inclined to your prayers and, through this privilege of apostolic authority, confirm to you and your successors all privileges and decrees both of holy pontiffs and of glorious emperors that have been granted for the honor of your holy Church and for the stability of all its movable and immovable property.

We also establish by apostolic judgment that, according to the sacred canons composed by the Spirit of God, clerics, religious women, and widows who stand under your care and that of your Church must remain there. No one, whether endowed with the honor of sacred office or holding secular administrative dignity, shall presume in any way to drag them or their property before a public court, or on that account to place their goods under ban. Rather, under your special presence, and that of your successors, they shall receive judgment and justice in every cause or matter that may arise according to the circumstances of the time.

We further decree that the monasteries situated within the boundaries of your diocese remain perpetually under your canonical authority and that of your successors, specifically with respect to the consecration of abbots and abbesses and the investigation of their offenses. No election shall be made in those venerable places whenever necessity arises without the provision and consent of you or your successors, as canonical authority commands, while the special privilege of the apostolic see remains secure in every respect.

By the tenor of this document we command that the monastery of Saint Donatus, founded by Bishop Luitprand, your predecessor, in the place called Scogialo, together with all movable and immovable property bestowed according to the terms of his testament, and the other monastery of Saint Mary situated at Cariata—which undoubtedly also appear to belong to the jurisdiction of your Church—we decree that you and your successors possess and retain in perpetuity.

Although they are situated in other parishes, by apostolic authority we order that you have free power, without anyone’s opposition, over everything that must be done or arranged there. We also decree that the priests and monks of all the aforesaid monasteries come without anyone’s opposition to your canonical council whenever ecclesiastical necessity requires.

If any enactments are found in those monasteries that seem in any respect contrary to canonical rules, we decree that the greater authority, canonically exercised, is to prevail over them [the wording is corrupt: “major hoc canonice factum ab illis habere auctoritatem”; Note: “The passage is corrupt.” — Col. 0739D].

We likewise command concerning the cemeteries situated within or outside the city of Ticinus that they remain under the care and power of the bishop of your Church, without anyone’s dispute.

We also establish, granting it by apostolic authority to you and your successors, that you may have and carry a cross wherever you wish. We likewise grant you the pallium, and permission to ride a white horse covered with a cloth on Palm Sunday and on the Monday after Easter.

We further establish that, according to the tenor of chapter ten which we decreed synodally at Ravenna in the tenth indiction, no person of whatever dignity or power shall ever presume, under the pretext of hospitality, to lodge in your venerable episcopal residence, or in the houses of your priests and all your clerics, without your will or that of your successors.

Having set forth these provisions, we decree that if the bishop of your see should depart this world through the human condition, the clergy and people shall have the power, according to the statutes of the venerable Fathers and the bishops of the Roman see, to elect as bishop someone from their own clergy whom the clergy and people find more suitable than others, without any secular power opposing them.

If perhaps no one should be found in that community—something we hardly believe—worthy of the honor of so great a see, then, if another is to be canonically provided from another Church, no bishop shall be ordained except one previously elected with the consent and will of that community.

We have also heard that in these regions, through a bad and troublesome custom, certain people ignorant of the sacred laws keep men of the clerical order under the yoke of servitude after their consecration and wish them to be called servants—a thing wicked to say.

We expressly wish and command that, just as one who has never belonged to any condition of servitude is free, so also the man whose dignity of character has recommended him for undertaking this office shall thereafter be bound by no man’s chain. For one whom divine grace has deemed worthy to raise to such dignity of sacred order ought not to be constrained by human law.

We further command that no one inflict any opposition, force, violence, or invasion upon any movable or immovable property belonging to your holy Church, or upon persons of either sex, whether free or enslaved, without a lawful judgment.

We also confirm the hospice of your holy Church founded within the city of Ticinus beside the church of Saint Mary called Minor. Our son, Lord Charles, the emperor Augustus, arranged by the document of his decree to restore it lawfully to that same Church, from which it had been unjustly taken. We decree that it remain perpetually under your right and authority and that of your successors, without any opposition.

We also establish the immunity of that church according to the imperial decrees and order by this apostolic privilege that it remain firm and unshaken.

If anyone should attempt by reckless boldness to act against the tenor of this apostolic command of ours, piously and canonically promulgated, and should fail to observe to the end all that has been established above for your holy Church, let him know that he is bound by the anathema of our lord, the chief of the apostles, Peter, and will be burned in eternal fire with the devil and his most dreadful pomp, and with Judas, the betrayer of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ.

But whoever, out of reverence, proves himself the guardian, obedient servant, and observer of this saving command of ours shall deserve to obtain from the just Judge, the Lord our God, the grace of blessing and the eternal joys of heavenly recompense.

Written by the hand of Leo, archivist of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of September.

Farewell. Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of September, by the hand of Leo, bishop, envoy and apocrisiary of the holy apostolic see, while our lord Charles, crowned and made great emperor, was reigning.

And so that this privilege of ours might appear more certain and remain unshaken, we ordered it to be marked with our seal.

In the second year; in the second year after his consulship; in the eleventh indiction.

Zacharias, humble bishop of the holy Church of Anagni, consented to and wrote this privilege.

Peter, bishop of the Church of Forosempronius, consented to and wrote this privilege.

Laurentius, humble bishop of the Church of Campania, consented to and wrote this privilege.

Leo, humble archivist and notary of the Holy Roman Church, wrote this with the command of the most reverend Lord Pope John, brought it forward to be confirmed by the others, and it is sealed with a large lead seal bearing the image of the most holy late Pope John, with the following similar inscription: “Pope John.”

### XCI. TO LAMBERT, THE GLORIOUS COUNT (877)

He explains that hostages from the Roman nobles cannot be given and advises him not to come to Rome, because he cannot receive him.

John, bishop, to Lambert, the glorious count.

When, with God leading us, we returned to Rome, we convened the whole Church and necessarily discussed in the assembly of the faithful of the holy Church of God what you had ordered concerning the giving of hostages from among the Roman nobles.

But—alas, what am I to say?—we so greatly stirred that entire Church against us that it seemed as though we had made it drink gall instead of honey. It is not recorded that the sons of Romans were ever given as hostages under this sky; how much less the sons of those who, with God’s help, preserve their imperial fidelity in both mind and deed?

Especially since we pity [editorial correction: “we doubt”] that this proceeded from an imperial order, and do not believe that the emperor himself wished to conceal his own secret from us. Such a plan could have been devised only by one who seeks to disturb this land and, through cunning frauds, plots to bring unspeakable harm upon the people of God—one who hates peace and quiet and certainly rejoices in dissensions.

Indeed, the Senate of the Roman fold would sooner choose death than consent in any way to this unheard-of and most evil affair.

Therefore, because the matter is entirely impossible, and because every illustrious person who heard it broke into the greatest suspicion and judged in every respect that it had not been said straightforwardly, we instruct your affection—which, though absent, we embrace as though present—not to trouble yourself to come here in any way. At present we cannot receive you at all, nor do we think that anything now needs to be undertaken under our roof.

When, with God’s help, the commonwealth returns to one agreement and one peace, and the fabrications of dispute—which we think have arisen like spiders’ webs against the imperial majesty—have been quieted, we shall receive both you and your nobility. We shall take care, with the greatest affection, to discuss with you what we recognize as pertaining to the common good and to bring it to completion with a man of such great prudence.

Before that time, however, you must not come in any way, because, as we have said, dearest son, we cannot receive you in any way.

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, in the eleventh indiction.

## XCII. TO WIDO, BISHOP OF INIVUM (877)

He entrusts to him the case of a certain Leontard, who had committed homicide with others; he urges him, since he had previously imposed a very severe penance upon him, now to impose a lighter one.

### To Wido, bishop of Inivum

A certain Leontard, a man of your diocese, worn down by sobs and groaning, approached the holy apostolic see and our humility. He reported that he had first incurred the guilt of homicide and had received penance from Your Holiness, which he had also completed; and that, after completing it, he had earned, by your judgment, mercy and ecclesiastical reconciliation.

Later, when he had been ordered by public decree to pursue certain robbers with some of his fellow townsmen, so that, if they could capture them, they should by every means prevent their being killed, he set out against them with the others. He asserts that, when one of them had been captured, those who seized him gouged out his eyes, and that, as a result, the wicked robber died.

After this had happened, the aforesaid Leontard came into your presence to receive penance and said that he had been judged by your decision as follows: that he would not receive holy communion until the end of his life; that he would not eat meat or drink wine except on Sundays and the feast days of the saints; that he would not shave his hair; that he would not take a wife; that he would not associate with people; that he would mourn in ashes and sackcloth; that he would not exercise authority over his servants or possessions; that he would not hold a lord’s benefice; and that he would not enjoy any of the other similar privileges that might otherwise be enjoyed.

When we heard all this and weighed it in our inmost heart, we found that, if this is so, you had judged him more severely than was expedient. For this reason we remit to you the whole of this judgment, and we urge you by every means to make use of our authority to pronounce a milder sentence upon him. Accordingly, considering altogether, for love of the apostles and of us, both the burden of the journey and the tearful intention of the aforesaid bearer, as well as the bitterness of his penance, do not refuse to deal more gently with him. Since he has fled for refuge to the holy apostles, do not ever fail to show him mercy in whatever matters may be appropriate, lest he fall into despair; for the Lord, as he speaks through the prophet, desires mercy and not sacrifice (Hos. 6).

Therefore we admonish and entreat you to extend mercy to him, so that, when we hear of the mercy you have shown, we may return manifold thanks to Your Holiness. We wish Your Holiness well-being in Christ.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of November, in the eleventh indiction.

## XCIII. TO KING CARLOMANNUS (877)

**[Note: [Col. 0743D] Carlomannus was the son of Louis, king of Germany, and grandson of Emperor Louis the Pious; several letters below are addressed to him [Col. 0744D]. Concerning him, see Ado, at the end of Book II of the *Chronicles*; “Chron. corum” [uncertain OCR]; Aimoinus, Book V, ch. 28; and Regino.]**

He grieves over the death of the emperor Charles and urges him to fulfill the promises made for the dignity of the Roman Church; he promises to send legates; at his request he sends the pallium to Archbishop Theotmar; and he orders him to transmit annually to Rome the revenues that the apostolic see possesses in Bavaria.

### To Carlomannus

Having received, therefore, the letters of Your Glory, together with their expression of congratulation on your safety and the success of your prosperity, I confess that, upon hearing of the death of Emperor Charles, we were struck to the side by excessive sorrow and grief. But suddenly raising, to some extent, the wave of our mind’s reflection toward divine judgment, we are compelled, astonished, to break forth in the words of the Apostle, saying: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and how inscrutable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?” (Rom. 11).

We say this so that diligent meditation of the heart may not cease to contemplate, upon this great sea, the course of unstable human life, and so that our activity, guided by Christ’s grace, may strive toward those joys which are fixed and immovable, never ceasing to be content with good works.

Concerning the reason for your coming to us, and your most exalted promise to exalt the Roman Church above all those who preceded you: when you have completed this work, he will be at hand as your rewarder—he who, by the contention of an oath, confirms the measures of human speech and says: “As I live, says the Lord, those who glorify me I will glorify” (1 Sam. 2).
