When, as you say, you have returned from your meeting with your brothers, we shall solemnly send legates from our side to you, together with a document containing, in chapters, what you and your protector, the blessed apostle Peter, owe perpetually to your mother, the Roman Church. When these matters have been completed, we shall then send others again, in due order and honor, who will endeavor to lead you, as befits so great a king, to the threshold of the apostles with every appropriate honor. There, meeting together, we shall be able, with God’s help, to deliberate usefully and establish arrangements concerning the condition of the state and the salvation of the entire Christian people.

Among these matters, I ask you, dearest son, that all our unbelievers and those lying in wait for our life whom you may come to know, by whatever means or indication [Rome ed.: “all who are”], should be unable to find any place or access with you or your faithful subjects, lest their unclean presence contaminate the royal height with some stain of association.

As for the pallium, yielding to your request, we have customarily sent it to Archbishop Theotmar. We desire that he shine inwardly in the eyes of the internal Judge with the same splendor with which he shines outwardly before human eyes. And, I ask you, entrust to him the possessions that the blessed apostle Peter holds in Bavaria, so that he may transmit their revenues to us annually at Rome.

Given in the month of November, in the fifteenth indiction.

## XCIV. TO THEOTMAR, ARCHBISHOP OF JUVAVUM (877)

He grants him the pallium and orders him to send to Rome the revenues that the Roman Church possesses in Bavaria.

### To Theotmar, archbishop of Juvavum

We have taken care to adorn your fraternity with the dignity of the pallium for this reason: so that, with Christ’s help, you may excel before the eyes of God in good and holy acts; so that you may always remain a devoted and faithful servant of the holy Roman Church, from which you drink the draught of an excellent cup; and so that in the future you may become a participant in its fruit, of that Church whose foundation, once laid, remains perpetual. We also urge you to act as a daily advocate for the Roman Church before King Carlomannus, our beloved son.

Among these matters, we entrust to your diligence and prudence the possessions which the blessed apostle Peter owns by right of property in the land of the Bavarians, so that from now on and thereafter you may send their annual revenues to Rome without delay.

Given in the month of November, in the eleventh indiction.

## XCV. TO EDERED, ARCHBISHOP OF THE ENGLISH (877)

He praises his pious disposition toward the apostolic see and grieves over his adversities; he urges him to act courageously for the Church; he shows that wives must not be abandoned; he announces that he has written to the king so that the king may treat him with due honor; finally, he confirms the privileges of his Church.

### To our most reverend and holy brother Edered, archbishop of the people of the English

Having reread your letters, we clearly perceive how great a faith of true love and sincerity resides in you—how you love Christ your God and your neighbor—and how fervently you are devoted to the apostolic see. In the manner of your predecessors, you have sought to refer to our episcopate, as to your teacher, the necessary concerns of your Church, and to receive from the apostolic see counsel concerning certain adversities that afflict you, as well as the protection of its authority; for in that see Almighty God placed the foundation of the entire Church.

And because, placed in the life of the present age—which truly is a temptation upon the earth—you endure certain hardships daily, we not only weep over our own troubles, which we likewise suffer, but also grieve with you, who endure such things. Since the whole world now lies in wickedness, with many adversaries everywhere existing against the servants of Christ, the greater and more frequent the temptations that daily threaten us, the stronger we ought to be, relying upon Christ’s consolation. For our sacred writings say: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested he will receive the crown of life, which God has promised to those who love him”; and the blessed God himself will not allow us to be tempted beyond what we can bear (Jas. 1), as the Apostle says: “but with the temptation he will also provide a way of escape, so that we may be able to endure it” (1 Cor. 10).

Nevertheless, because of the necessity of the present time, we exhort and admonish your fraternity that, putting aside every fear of the world, you oppose yourself as a wall for the house of the Lord, like a capable minister of God. Inflamed with zeal for him, do not cease to resist vigorously not only the king but all those within his realm who wish to do anything perversely. Honor your ministry for as long as you are permitted by the divine will to exercise the high priesthood; and make every effort to feed the people of the Lord entrusted to you with the nourishment of holy doctrine—namely, priests and ecclesiastical men and women, as well as widows and religious women—governing and protecting them according to their proper order and to the best of your ability, so that you may appear before the Lord as a capable shepherd, ready in mind.

For we have taken care, in letters of the apostolic see, to admonish and exhort your king that, for the love of Jesus Christ our Lord, he should not fail to be obedient and a devoted helper to you in all matters beneficial to the holy Church entrusted to you, just as history records that the most pious kings of the English, his predecessors, were. In this way he may retain securely the kingdom granted to him temporarily and afterward receive the life of the eternal kingdom.

Concerning those whom you say are abandoning their own wives contrary to the Lord’s command, we decree that neither a man may depart from his wife nor a wife from her husband, except on account of fornication. If one of them departs for that reason, he or she must remain unmarried, or they must be reconciled to one another, since the Lord says: “What God has joined together, let no man separate” (Matt. 19). Therefore, since no one may abandon a woman joined to him in a lawful marriage, it is in no way permitted to him to take another while the first is alive. If he does so and does not undertake to amend his fault through satisfaction, let him remain separated from the fellowship of the Church.

Nor may you permit anyone to marry from his own kindred, according to the decretal statute of our holy predecessor Gregory, teacher of your people (Book 22, Letter 31).

We undoubtedly wish to preserve intact for you the privilege of your see, which was sent there by the holy Gregory through the agency of the blessed Augustine for the salvation and conversion of many. And, according to the authority of that same holy predecessor of ours, Gregory [perhaps “a statute” or something similar is missing], whose ray of wisdom illumines the Church of Christ spread throughout the world, we establish and decree that it be guarded forever by all orders, both ecclesiastical and secular.

Whatever adverse report concerning you is brought to us by anyone, we do not believe it in any way before a true investigation. Rather, we have also admonished your king to show you the honor that is due, for the love of Jesus Christ our Lord, and to take care that all the rights of your privilege are preserved with perpetual stability and guarded undiminished—if he wishes to possess, in the same way, the grace and blessing of the apostolic see, which his predecessors merited by their good deeds.

Given as above.

## XCVI. TO ATHANASIUS, BISHOP OF NAPLES (877)

He commends the zeal for the faith that he displayed against Sergius, an enemy of the Church of God; he urges him to labor increasingly for the defense of the Church entrusted to him; and he commends to him the deacon Peter.

### To our most reverend and holy brother Athanasius, bishop of the holy Neapolitan Church

We offer countless thanks to your God-beloved goodness, and we rightly praise you above others with worthy apostolic commendations, because, in accordance with the Lord’s saying, “If your eye or your hand causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it from you” (Matt. 5), you took care to strike with the dart of divine vengeance your brother who was acting impiously toward the Church of God and walking upon an unrighteous path concerning the Lord, attacking Christ our holy God with rash audacity like another Holofernes, and sacrilegiously persecuting his ancestral inheritance. You judged him unworthy of the administration of so great an honor.

You did not spare your own flesh, because of the Lord’s saying: “Whoever loves father, or mother, or brother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10). In this we recognize that you are wholly worthy of God, because Your Holiness, with faithful devotion, willingly took care to cut off and cast far away a member of your body that stank with a great contagion.

**[Note: He is speaking of Sergius, as is clear from the following letter; Leo of Ostia mentions him in Book 1, chapter 42.]**

And because, until now, secular men who ruled in the city of Naples according to themselves and not according to God had committed many scandals and great disturbances, murders, and gougings out of eyes, within the city and beyond it, God has justly judged these deeds. It has therefore come to pass that the wicked domination has now ceased, sin has come to an end, and a man has arisen from the house of the Lord who, keeping the fear of God before his eyes, may rule Christ’s people in all justice and holiness, in all truth and gentleness, as a capable shepherd, and not abandon or destroy them like a hired servant.

Therefore we also confirm with perpetual stability all that is suitable and necessary to your dignity and honor. We exhort your prudence in these apostolic letters only to take care, with still greater zeal and multiplied concern, to stand and labor strenuously for the defense of the holy Church of God entrusted to you, so that it may remain safe and secure.

For, after all the other mancuses have been paid, we owe you 1,400, which we shall undoubtedly send to Your Love either at the beginning of Lent or on the day of the holy Resurrection.

Moreover, we commend to you in every respect this venerable deacon Peter, your deacon, because we know him to be faithful in all things to your Church and to the city of Naples. May you kindly deign always to retain him for love of us.

Given as above.

## XCVII. TO THE NEAPOLITANS (877)

He praises them because, inflamed with divine zeal, they cast Sergius out from among them and chose Bishop Athanasius as ruler of their commonwealth; he commands them to obey him and offers, together with him, to provide for their interests.

### To all the distinguished judges and to the entire people of the city of Naples

Behold, we recognize more clearly than light how fervently you are devoted in true faith toward God, the creator and savior of the world, and toward the Church of Christ. Filled with divine zeal, you endeavored to cast out from among you a man of such impiety—the son of perdition, the vessel of every iniquity—who was wickedly ruling over you, namely Sergius, the master of the soldiers, another Holofernes, and to cut him off and cast him far away from the body of Christ like a stinking member, in accordance with the Lord’s command: “If your eye or your hand causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it from you” (Matt. 5).

And because, after casting him out, you chose as judge the shepherd and bishop of your souls, namely Athanasius, our beloved brother and like-minded son, we offer countless thanks to your beloved prudence and unanimity. For, like ministers of God, you arranged that the wrath of the Lord of hosts, which was already threatening him according to his merits, should be avenged upon the one who did not hesitate to commit many unheard-of evils, more than all his fathers, in the city of Naples and throughout our territories, cruelly putting to death an innumerable multitude of men, as well as crowds of infants and women, by the sword, hunger, and captivity.

Therefore, in these apostolic letters we admonish and exhort you, my little sons, to treat our venerable brother Athanasius, your bishop, whom you chose, taught by divine inspiration, to serve as ruler, with faithful mind and devotion and with every honor. For we are ready, together with him, to assist you in all your needs and interests, and we desire to help you with equal purpose. Only stand courageously obedient to him in all things, like beloved sons.

Since, after all the other mancuses have been paid, we owe you 1,400, do not be troubled, for we shall undoubtedly send them to you either at the beginning of Lent or on the day of the holy Resurrection.

For your part, like beloved sons, labor with all your strength for the defense of the Church of God against unbelievers and common enemies, so that you may always possess both God’s grace and our blessing.

We wish you well in the Lord.

Given as above.

## XCVIII. TO COUNT LAMBERT (877)

He writes that he intends to travel to Gaul and therefore commands, under penalty of excommunication, that while he is absent Lambert inflict no harm upon the territory of the Roman Church or upon Rome.

### To the noble man Lambert, glorious count

We wish your sagacity and prudence to know that, not only because of the continual attacks of the pagans—which we have now endured for two years, with no one providing us the comfort of defense—but also because of the countless and exceedingly grave oppressions inflicted and daily inflicted by adversaries upon us and upon the flock of the Lord divinely entrusted to us, while we remain in the peace which Christ our God commands those who love him to possess, we are wholly unable to remain quietly and securely within the bosom of the apostolic see, which is the head of the world and the mother of all the faithful.

Therefore we desire to travel to Francia by sea and to visit the glorious King Carlomannus, and to behold his desired presence, humbly entreating him for the salvation and defense of the land of Saint Peter and of all Christendom. Thus, with the help of Almighty God and the power of the king, we may, as opportunity requires, direct and protect with healthy and prosperous success the territory and people of the Lord, redeemed by his precious blood, lest, because any of them perish through our negligence or carelessness, we be compelled to render a strict account to the Lord.

Therefore we admonish you and exhort Your Love with pious concern in these letters of our apostolate: as we depart for Francia for the defense of the holy Church of God and the stability of the commonwealth, do not exercise any opposition or hostility throughout the entire territory of the prince of the apostles. Nor should you prepare any adversities or ambushes against the city of Rome, which is a priestly and royal city through the holy see of the blessed Peter; nor should you do so, nor in any way consent to those who wish to do it.

For if, through you or through men subject to you, the same city of Rome suffers any disturbance or dishonor, or endures any adversity whatsoever, know for certain that we shall rebuke you in every way with canonical corrections and the victorious authority of the Holy Spirit, and shall deservedly separate you from communion with the apostolic see.

Given as above.

## XCIX. TO LANDULF, BISHOP OF CAPUA (877)

He urges him to agree with Athanasius, bishop of Naples, for the defense of the Roman Church, and to ensure that the pact made with the Amalfitans is observed by them.

### To our most reverend and holy brother Landulf, bishop of Capua

We undoubtedly remember with attentive recollection how diligently your Love and your benevolent fraternity have labored for the defense, liberation, and service of the holy Roman Church, over which, by God’s authority, we preside, and how with every effort of your heart you have labored in support of our work. For this reason your reward is certainly prepared and ready both with God and with us.

Therefore, because we have found you highly capable in such matters, we admonish and exhort you to be of one mind with Athanasius, bishop of Naples, in the present cause of the Roman Church. For we have clearly learned in Solomon [Rome ed.: “clearly and in writing”]: “A threefold cord is not quickly broken” (Ecclus. 4). At our urging and admonition, never cease to be his brotherly helper in all things.

Meanwhile, through the mediation of your benevolent fraternity and of our beloved son Guaifer, prince, we made a pact with the Amalfitans for 10,000 mancuses [*mancusorum*; variant *mancosorum*], namely that they should continually bring us assistance by naval effort from Traiectum to Centumcellae. But until now they have shown no such assistance at all. Moreover, by a certain exercise of cunning, they assert that both abbots—namely John and Anastasius, whom we sent there on our behalf—had agreed not merely to 10,000 mancuses but to 12,000. The same abbots deny under oath, in our presence, that they did so.

Therefore, may your prudence both restrain them from this unjust demand and confirm them in beneficial service through wholesome admonition, so that, having obtained our blessing, they may be safe in mind and body through Christ the Lord.

Given as above.

## C. TO GUAIFER, PRINCE OF SALERNO (877)

He urges him to persevere in his integrity and to rebuke the Amalfitans because they have not sent naval assistance and are using excessive cunning against him.

### To our most beloved son Guaifer, prince

I cannot explain in a few words the devotion of your heart from the day on which I came to know you. This, however, we truly know: [Rome ed.: “with God and with …”] all things concerning you are safely reserved with us for the appropriate time.

Therefore, admonishing you, we exhort you, and in asking we command you, to persevere in the goodness you have once displayed. For it is written: “The Lord is not slow concerning his promise, until what he has spoken is fulfilled” (2 Pet. 3).

We wish Your Glory to know that, on the part of the Amalfitans, they have not undertaken to provide us any assistance in naval warfare, as agreed, from Traiectum to Centumcellae. Moreover, by a certain cunning, they assert that our promise was not for 10,000 mancuses alone but for 12,000. This is in no way established as true, since the abbots whom we sent there on our behalf also admit under oath that they did not say this.

Concerning this and other similar matters, we hope, insofar as we are able, for correction and every improvement through the glory of your nobility. I ask you to hasten to do this promptly.

We wish you well.

Given as above.

## CI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF EMBRUN (877)

He reproves him because he consecrated another bishop in the Church of Vence, contrary to the one whom the clergy and people had elected; he commands him to come to Rome with both men.

### To our most reverend and holy brother Aribert, archbishop of Embrun

If you had observed the canonical statutes concerning the consecration of bishops, no controversy concerning the consecrated man would ever have arisen, as we have learned by report—especially since a certain deacon named Walden had lodged a complaint against Your Love—claiming that he had been canonically elected by the populace and people of Vence but rejected by your sagacity. Your fraternity would then rightly have escaped reproach.

But now, because, after the bishop of Vence had died, you consecrated not the aforesaid priest whom, as stated, the clergy and people of the city had elected and whom Emperor Charles of pious memory had confirmed by his assent, and because, after that Augustus had been removed from the present life, you are accused of having ordained, solely at your own pleasure, another man who came forward in opposition, was not elected according to the canonical rule, and entered neither through the door nor by the proper way, we see clearly that you have incurred no slight fault.

For, as our predecessor Pope Celestine says (Letter 1, to the bishops of Vienne and Narbonne): “Let no bishop be given against the will of the people.” You ought to have sought the consent and desire of the clergy, the people, and the order. By his authority clerics also have the power to resist if they see themselves oppressed, so that they need not fear rejecting those whom they recognize as thrust upon them from outside; for, even if they are not entitled to a reward, they ought to have free judgment concerning the one who will rule them.

For Saint Leo likewise says (Letter 95, to Rusticus of Narbonne): “No reason permits those to be counted among the bishops who have been elected neither by the clergy nor sought by the people.” Since a dispute often arises over an honor wrongly received, who could doubt that it must not be attributed to those whom it is not shown to have been conferred upon?

The same authority also commands in chapter 35 of his canons (Letter 88, to Anastasius of Thessalonica): “No bishop, as has been said, is to be ordained for those who do not ask for him, lest a city either despise or hate a bishop whom it did not desire; and thus it become less religious than is fitting, because it was not permitted to have the one it wanted.”

With these statutes established, and so that no scandal or schism may remain in the Church of God entrusted to you, we command Your Love to arrange to come to Rome at once with both the bishop consecrated by you and the man who asserts that he was canonically elected. Thus, in our presence and that of the apostolic see, the case of so important a matter may be carefully investigated and examined and, with God’s favor, receive a lawful conclusion.

You ought therefore to obey this command of ours, issued for the peace of the Church of God. For if you act otherwise, know that we shall in no way leave such an unlawful presumption unpunished.

Given as above.

## CII. TO COUNT CUNIPERT (877)

He commands him to restore the property of the Roman Church that he had seized.

### To our beloved son Cunipert, glorious count

We have learned by report, and also know truly, that you have invaded and seized, contrary to God and to our will, the estate of Saint Peter which is in Alviscutia. From that estate the Church of the prince of the apostles was accustomed to receive an annual census and payment for its lamps; but now, through your violence and greed, it can receive and possess nothing.

Therefore, by the authority of God, Saint Peter, and ourselves, we command you not to presume to retain that estate any longer, nor to interfere with its goods and appurtenances, if you desire to have God’s grace and the blessing of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and of ourselves. Allow the men of Saint Peter who are there to retain that estate securely.

For if you thereafter presume to hold that estate against our will, and inflict any violence or force there, know that we shall canonically separate you from all ecclesiastical communion and from the body and blood of our Lord, as an invader of ecclesiastical property.

Given as above.

## CIII. TO COUNT LAMBERT (878)

He warns him not to come to Rome for the purpose of bringing aid to the enemies of the apostolic see; if he comes for another reason, he promises to receive him honorably. He entrusts several matters to the legates and orders Lambert to believe them; he says that he cannot receive Adelbert, an enemy of the Roman Church, into communion.

### To our beloved son Lambert, glorious count

Holding the love and sincerity of your affection and friendship as a kind of indissoluble pledge of charity, we are as secure concerning the cunning devices of our enemies and the ambushes prepared against the apostolic see as we unquestionably believe the power of your nobility, joined to us with Christ’s help, to be present with us in all prosperity and adversity. For we too desire to be ready to assist you in everything suitable or necessary to Your Glory.

Therefore, not wishing to leave Your Eminence unaware of what we have learned from certain reports, we have taken care to inform you, as our spiritual son. We have heard that, at someone’s urging, you wish to bring assistance to our enemies and unbelievers, and that, by coming to Rome, you intend improperly to restore them to their possessions and benefices even against our will. No emperor, king, or count is remembered to have done this to our predecessors.

We are therefore greatly astonished, if this is true, that you have forgotten the great friendship so often established and promised between us, especially since, after God, we now regard you in all the needs and interests of the Church of Saint Peter as our sole helper and most faithful defender.

Although certain people advise you to do such things against the apostolic see and against us, we nevertheless place the greatest confidence in your devotion of faith toward the most blessed princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul, and toward our paternal authority. Therefore, as to a beloved son and like-minded friend, we command you that, for the love of God and of us, you do not now come to Rome in order to restore the cause of our enemies, since they have already been condemned twice and even three times by synodal judgment. We are deeply disturbed and saddened by this, and consequently cannot receive you honorably, as is proper and as we desire.

Accordingly, let your prudence destroy the plan of such perversity, and take care to rise against those enemies of ours with all your strength and, with a will united to ours, as is fitting, bring them to confusion. Thus, as we trust through you, we may remain secure and at peace, possessing God’s and your assistance.

If, however, you wish to come now or later to the threshold of Saint Peter and to our apostolic presence for another reason, we shall receive you honorably with ready and most grateful spirit, as is fitting, rejoicing and exulting together with you in the Lord.

We would indeed write you more concerning these matters, but because we have sent to you our capable and reverend faithful men, your devoted friends—namely the bishops Gauderic and Zacharias, our dear friends and counselors—who will be able to explain orally to Your Glory what is absent from the letters, we have omitted writing further. You should have no doubt that you may believe them concerning what they say to you orally as though you were hearing it from us.

Act, therefore, as we unquestionably believe you to be in all things: our helper and a like-minded friend in Christ.

As for Margrave Adelbert, if he comes to us, know for certain that we shall receive him in no way, because he has caused us many forms of opposition and has openly shown himself our enemy in all things.

Furthermore, as you have written to us, asking that, because of the present circumstances, we might leave the city of Rome and speak with you somewhere, we would gladly have done this if it had seemed useful and necessary. If you wish us to speak together, let it not be burdensome for you to come to us as a beloved son, so that together we may consider whatever appears appropriate.

Given as above.

## CIV. TO THE SAME (878)

He severely reproves him because, in the letters he wrote, he did not show the apostolic see the honor due to it and asked that legates not be sent without his consent.

### To the noble man Lambert, glorious count
The Apostolic See, which Almighty God deigned to establish upon the rock of his name, has been honored not only by the kings and princes of the earth, but also by the August emperors and the lords of the whole world in their written communications, as the head of all the Churches of God. They have praised its pontiffs—the vicars, namely, of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles—with worthy acclamations, and have earnestly sought to implore them with suppliant prayers; and, so long as Peter’s name and memory endure, they will not cease to make such supplication until the end of the age.

Therefore, when we heard the letter which you sent, we were greatly astonished at its inappropriate language. Those words neither resound with the praises due to blessed Peter nor agree with ecclesiastical rules or teachings. You sent us the expressions that you are accustomed to write to secular men and your equals: for example, when you say to us, “Your Nobility,” or when you say, “We admonish your Nobility.” By this we recognize more clearly than light that your mind toward us is by no means as devoted as we had supposed it to be. Thus you chose to write to our fatherhood in such base words and unsuitable expressions, with a mind more audacious than sincere. And it is no wonder, since sweet water is not drawn from a bitter spring.

Moreover, because you said that we ought nowhere to send our legations without your consent—and because this has never been customary, is found in no written document, and is not remembered by anyone now living as ever having been done—the Apostolic See, always existing in freedom, freely sends its legation everywhere, possessing the authority of the Lord who says: “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and you, once converted, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22).

As for the matters formerly spoken of between us, on account of the various and numerous oppositions and adversities, as well as the bodily ailments that we suffer daily, it is not permitted us to consider or discuss anything concerning them. Nevertheless, if we had known your prudence to be devoted to our advancement and to the interests of the Roman Church, and had known you promptly to fulfill our will, we would have desired to retain you as a beloved son and dear friend, and with grateful spirit we would have carried out whatever was useful for your salvation and prosperity. But since we see that, having abandoned us, you have inclined toward the opposing side, we are not only utterly astonished, but likewise withdraw ourselves from the fellowship of your friendship—a friendship which, for the love of God, we had greatly desired to preserve as dear.

Furthermore, we wished to send this letter to you, according to custom, through Longobard, your faithful servant and bearer of your letters. But he was unwilling to receive it from us and deliver it to your prudence, as both ancient custom requires [Note: [Col. 0753A] Something is missing] and manifest reason declares should be done.

Given as above.

### CV. TO ANGELBERGA AUGUSTA  
*(In the year 878.)* He grieves that Angelberga is afflicted by troubles and complains of the injuries which Lambert inflicted upon the Roman Church; he asks her to preserve the goodwill which she had been accustomed to show toward him.

To ANGELBERGA, our beloved spiritual daughter, formerly empress, consecrated to God [Col. 0754C].

Because we loved with great devotion and earnestness of mind the lord and master of blessed memory, formerly the most Christian emperor Louis, our spiritual son, we by no means fail daily to commemorate him before the Lord in our sacred prayers; and know that, for as long as we live, we shall continue to do so. We likewise remember you, dearest daughter.

For, God as our witness, we always desire that your prosperity and salvation may flourish unharmed, and we desire to hear of them. Concerning all the many and great adversities which, as we know, you have endured from the sons of this age, we sympathize and grieve with you in profound sorrow. Since we love you with paternal affection, we consider your grief our own, and rejoice that the tranquility [Col. 0754D] of your life is our own. For although no ancient writing celebrates and no history records such wicked and unheard-of evils as these, when we hear that you have endured at the hands of Lambert, count of Spoleto, what no emperor or king ever before made the vicar of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, endure, we readily recognize that you too are afflicted with a similar grief.

Therefore we exhort your affection, while preserving toward us a pious disposition of mind, not to neglect to do with all your strength whatever you see to be suitable or necessary for our interests. For we too, by God’s favor, eagerly desire, according to the power divinely granted to us, to confer upon you assistance and the consolation you seek in all things; and, if it should be necessary, we shall strive to protect you beneath the guardianship of blessed Peter the apostle [Col. 0755A] and preserve you unharmed, as our dearest daughter, if you should happen to come to the threshold of that prince of the apostles.

Meanwhile, take courage in the Lord, who consoles you in all things and will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation will provide a way of escape, so that you may be able to endure (1 Corinthians 10).

As for the rest, we have been unable to accomplish what you requested, being occupied by many impediments—those which the aforesaid count prepares for us with numerous plots and desires to inflict upon us every day. But if God grants tranquility and life, we shall gladly carry out everything useful to your wishes, so that your honor and the strength of your glory may plainly appear unimpaired.

May the right hand of the Lord deign to preserve you unharmed in all things. [Col. 0755B]

Given as above.

### CVI. TO COUNT BERENGAR  
*(In the year 878.)* He asks him to inform the emperor of what Lambert perpetrated at Rome and to work to restrain him.

To BERENGAR, our beloved son, glorious count, sprung from royal stock.

Having read the letters of your Nobility, we found that you possess great sincerity and devotion toward us, in the manner of your ancestors, for love of Jesus Christ the Lord and in reverence for blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. We have therefore been completely filled with the abundant sweetness of your honeyed speech, so that with the Psalmist we can say: “How sweet are your words to my throat!” (Psalm 118).

We undoubtedly recognize that you derive this outstanding ornament of goodness from the conduct of your noble father, of pious memory, who always strove with complete willingness of mind to show worthy honor and pious reverence to our predecessors, the holy pontiffs. Therefore the Lord of hosts, by his grace and mercy, will preserve unharmed the flower of your beautiful youth, springing from a righteous root; he will cause it to flourish prosperously in all things and bring it to a prosperous end.

For this reason, dearest son, we have often wished to write to your affection, not only to make our greeting known to you, but also because we desired to hear of your prosperity and safety. Yet, surrounded not only by the frequent incursions of pagans everywhere [Col. 0755D], but also by the plots of Christians, we were unable to do so.

But now, since by God’s ordering an opportune time has arrived, we report to your Excellence—like a dearest son and faithful friend—what things and what evils we, together with the whole Church and city of Rome, have suffered from Lambert the count.

Although we had daily done many good things for the aforesaid Lambert and had bestowed upon him an honor greater than our predecessors had bestowed upon his parents, he repaid good with evil. Gathering a multitude of the people, he invaded the entire territory of Saint Peter and tyrannically rules what he ought to defend from enemies, now that he has seized it. He came to Rome and, like an enemy, violently seized the gate of the Roman city; he caused his armed retainers to remain there for many days, and thus held the city, once invaded, in his possession. Indeed, while we were residing at blessed Peter’s, we had no authority whatsoever over the city of Rome—the authority which pious emperors had handed over to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and to his vicars.

When we were celebrating the sacred litanies according to custom, with bishops and priests and servants of God, and wished to come to the church of Saint Peter, he ordered us to be beaten and scattered with clubs. He inflicted upon us injuries such as had never been inflicted upon any of our predecessors, and he is ready to inflict still greater ones upon us again, for reasons we do not know.

Therefore, since it is our ministry continually to beseech the Lord for the salvation of all Christendom, so that by constant vows and prayers we may lead to the pastures of eternal life the sheep whom Christ our God entrusted to us in blessed Peter [Col. 0756B], we would have wished to possess the quiet due to us. But since he does not withdraw from his wicked thoughts and actions—in fact, since he wishes once again to trouble us by joining himself to our enemies and faithless opponents, whom we have already twice and three times excommunicated and anathematized—we ask your Nobility, for the love of God, blessed Peter, and ourselves, to make all these matters known to the glorious king and our spiritual son Carloman, so that by sending written communications of his own he may restrain him from such presumption; and likewise admonish and rebuke this same Lambert in your letters, so that hereafter he may not presume to inflict any opposition upon us, since the outcome of his rashness pleases neither God nor anyone who fears God.

But if Lambert does not cease persecuting us, how can we be faithful friends to the aforesaid king, since Lambert boasts that he is doing such things by the king’s will? Therefore arrange to help us, as stated above. For our part, we shall most gladly strive to accomplish whatever is agreeable to your will, since we wish to retain you as a most beloved son for as long as we live and desire, through you, to accomplish the necessary business of our Church.

Moreover, we kindly received your men, who came to the threshold of Saint Peter to pray to the merciful Lord for their sins, out of your great love; we strengthened them with our apostolic blessings and decided, through them, to make known to you the state of our safety, as you requested. We ask that you not fail to gladden us soon with your letters.

May Almighty God preserve your glory undefiled for long ages, dearest son.

### CVII. TO JOHN, ARCHBISHOP OF RAVENNA  
*(In the year 878.)* He explains the evils perpetrated at Rome by Count Lambert and indicates that he will go to Gaul to seek help against him.

To our most reverend and holy fellow-bishop JOHN, archbishop of Ravenna.

We do not allow the brotherhood of your unanimity to remain unaware of the evils and manifold injuries which, in these recent days, we have suffered from Lambert, count of Spoleto—injuries such as none of our pontifical predecessors is remembered to have endured from anyone who worshiped God.

Thus, while his men were tyrannically devastating nearly the whole territory of Saint Peter, he came to Rome with an immense multitude of people. We received him honorably at the shrine of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, as a beloved friend. But he, clothed as though in a sheep’s skin, filled with his customary wickedness and corrupted by a great bribe, did not hesitate to rise up against us (Aimoinus, Book V, chapter 37).

Forcibly, indeed fraudulently, he seized the gates of the Roman city and the whole city of Rome. He caused his men to remain there under such tight restraint for many days that neither the Roman nobles, nor the bishops and priests, nor even our own household could obtain leave to depart except after the most urgent supplication. They also most insistently prevented our provisions from reaching us.

Likewise, when venerable bishops, presbyters, deacons, and religious monks were coming to the church of the prince of the apostles with hymns, spiritual songs, and sacred litanies, alas, to our grief, they disturbed them in pagan fashion and wickedly scattered them by beating them with clubs, not allowing them to leave or offer to God the sacrifice that was due.

He also rashly brought against us the enemies and faithless opponents of the holy Roman Church and of ourselves, whom, with your consent and subscription, we have already twice and three times excommunicated, condemned, and anathematized; and he admitted them into the city of Rome without our consent.

Burdened by these wrongs and many injuries, we remained for many days so sorrowful, together with the entire Apostolic See, that we could scarcely do anything except weep. For during those days there was neither a vestment upon the altar of Saint Peter nor any nocturnal or diurnal office celebrated there according to custom.

Now he also threatens to inflict worse things upon us unless we humbly obey his will. Therefore we exhort your holiness, joined to us by the pious affection of fraternal love, to grieve together with us from the depths of your heart over such great afflictions and miseries inflicted upon our head, and to strive with all your strength to rise against our most evident and savage enemy.

For, unable to endure such great plots on his part, and unable to travel by land, we must, by God’s favor, depart for Francia by sea [Col. 0757D], to implore the glorious kings to free the Church of Saint Peter and the city of Rome—the head and mistress of the whole world—from such oppression and calamities; to allow it to remain safe and peaceful; and with powerful hand to protect it from the plots of the enemies which we suffer. Believe without doubt that we are going there for no other reason than the common salvation.

But, as we have learned from the truthful report of many, once we have departed from the city of Rome and begun our journey, we hear that this same Lambert intends to gather his armed retainers and approach Rome again to attack it. Knowing this, we have pronounced in the church of blessed Paul, teacher of the nations, a sentence of anathema against him and all his followers, should he presume to come again in any way against the city of Rome and the Roman Church and inflict opposition, trouble, or disturbance.

Therefore let none of you favor his wicked deeds. Rather, rebuke him freely, if you wish always to be supported by the aid of the Apostolic See. For this reason we earnestly exhort your holiness to make all these matters known to your suffragan bishops, so that they, who are members of the body of Christ, may strive and labor together with you for the exaltation of the Apostolic See.

### CVIII. TO MICHAEL, KING OF THE BULGARS  
*(In the year 878.)* Sent through the bishops Eugenius and Paul in April, on the sixteenth day, in the eleventh indiction. He grieves that Michael follows the Greeks and exhorts him to return to the embrace of the Roman Church; he then gives thanks for the gift sent to him; finally, he indicates that a certain Sergius, promoted by subreption to the priesthood and episcopate, has been deposed.

[Col. 0758B]

To MICHAEL, king of the Bulgars.

We rejoiced that you had been brought forth with spiritual affection, and we gave thanks for your salvation. But now that you have been deceived by the cunning of the wicked, we grieve and lament, fearing and dreading lest, if you should perhaps follow the Greeks, when they have fallen—as is their custom—into various heresies and schisms, you too should fall with them into the depths of error; and just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted and fall away from the simplicity and chastity that is in Christ Jesus.

For, my son, I entreat you in Mosaic words: “Ask your father, and he will declare it to you; your elders, and they will tell you” (Deuteronomy 32)—whether the Greeks have ever been free from this or that heresy. When you find that they have never at any time been free from some heresy, you ought to flee their deceptions and associations, lest, when they err, you also err; and when they turn to blasphemy, you too should be found blasphemers of the true faith. Nor will there be anyone afterward to correct you or lead you back from error.

Believe me, dearest son: this is what we grieve over; this is why we are anxious for you night and day. We seek neither glory nor honor nor revenue from you, but you yourselves rather than what belongs to you. For we do not desire to acquire the governance of your country or the administration of its commonwealth. Rather, we wish to resume, according to ancient custom, the care and administration of the diocese of that region, so that we may exercise with greater diligence the concern which we owe to all the Churches, insofar as we know that this diocese has anciently belonged more particularly to our ordering. Thus we may be able to watch more earnestly over the preservation of your salvation, since we know more clearly that God both desires us most fervently to confirm what he has worked in us and will demand it from us more strictly if, God forbid, we are found negligent in your instruction and defense.

Return, therefore, to blessed Peter, first of the apostles, whom you loved, whom you chose, whom you sought, and whose protection you received in your necessities; from whose streams of teaching you drank healthfully and fittingly; and to whose protection you commended and surrendered yourselves, together with all your subjects.

“You were running well,” we cry out with the Apostle; “who hindered you from obeying the truth?” (Galatians 3.) The Lord himself also says: “No one who puts his hand to the plough and turns back is fit for the kingdom of heaven” (Luke 9).

We do not say that there is not one faith, one baptism (Ephesians 4), one God belonging equally to us and to them. Rather, we say that among them, often through the agency of the bishop of Constantinople, or the emperor, or most frequently both, when heresy has been established, many of those subject to them become like them through flattery or, certainly, fear. And woe then to those who follow their association.

Tell me, I ask, dearest son: what would you or your people have done if, in the time of the Pneumatomachus Macedonius, bishop of Constantinople, when the impious Constantius was ruling there, you had been enjoying their association? Would you not have followed with them his dogma, blaspheming against the Holy Spirit? That sin, as the Lord testifies, is not forgiven either here or in the age to come (Matthew 12). If you had shared their polluted association, would you not likewise have possessed their perverse teaching? And consequently would you not, together with them, like bundles bound for burning, have been reserved for eternal fire, to be tormented on the day of judgment?

We believe that it is no longer hidden from you that the Apostolic See of blessed Peter has never been reproved for any other doctrine, while it has very frequently reproved all the others, and especially Constantinople. It has either freed them from error or, at least, condemned by its judgment those who refused to repent.

Therefore do not follow the Greeks, dearest son, because they are always devoted to deceptive arguments and always intent upon crafty stratagems. Take care lest what happened to the Gothic people happen to you. When that people wished to be freed from pagan error and joined to the faith of Christ, it fell upon a bishop who had the appearance of piety but denied its power; while freeing them from paganism, he entangled them in the blasphemies of Arius. Thus, while incautiously seeking to flee one error, they fell into another; and, following a blind guide, they became blind with him and descended into the precipices of Arian perversity [Note: [Col. 0759D] Socrates, Book V, chapter 27; Theodoret, Book VII, chapter 32; Sozomen, Book VII, chapter 37]. This is why we proclaim that the Greeks’ association must be avoided.

“For evil conversations corrupt good morals,” as the Apostle Paul says (1 Corinthians 15). Even if they sometimes say something good, do not be surprised, for the demons too confessed the Son of God (Matthew 18); but he himself rather ordered them to be silent, lest anyone hearing them proclaim the truth should follow them in their error.

Turn, therefore, to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, who first recognized and confessed the Son of God; who received the Lord’s sheep to govern; and who, so that he might lead them into the eternal pastures of life, earned here the power of binding and loosing and there the keys for opening to them the kingdom of heaven.

Know, therefore, dearest son, that if from this point your conversion should be toward the Greeks—which God forbid—your portion will divinely be placed with those who make the first faith void, and with those whose portion you willingly embrace.

But if you listen to us and return to the embrace of Saint Peter, we shall receive you as our most beloved sons with open bosoms, embrace you with outstretched arms, and always hold you within the heart of Christ’s love. If there are any holy, healthful, or suitable things, we shall not cease to offer and furnish them to you and on your behalf.

We received the gift sent to us from you, Urso, formerly of religious habit, carrying it. Giving thanks for your kindness, we praised God, who taught you to offer a gift to us devoutly; and, as we trust, who will soon cause you to give your whole and perfected self.

For the rest, let your Glory know that Sergius the eunuch, who was a Slav by birth and entangled in many wickednesses, obtained the priesthood by subreption. Later, after further offenses had been discovered and proved against him, he is known to have been deposed by his own bishop at that time. Subsequently, he was promoted, quite unworthily, to the episcopate of Belograd by George, who falsely usurps the name of bishop. By the authority of the princes of the apostles and of the holy canons, and also by the sentence of our decree, we have determined that he too is deposed. We make this canonically known both to you and to the whole community of your people, so that those who are rejected by others may not be received by them (Nicaea, canon 5), lest—something we do not desire—they be held bound with them by a similar penalty of judgment.

Given on the sixteenth day of April, in the eleventh indiction. [Col. 0760C]

### CIX. TO COUNT PETER  
*(In the year 878.)* Sent through the bishops Paul and Eugenius in April, on the sixteenth day, in the eleventh indiction. He exhorts him to recall King Michael to the embrace of the Roman Church.

To COUNT PETER.

Since we are sending a letter of our apostolate to our dearest son Michael, the most Christian king, we have judged it fitting to write also to your Glory and to disclose the groans of our heart, which we constantly endure, sighing and wondering with immense astonishment how that most wise king—and you yourselves—could have been turned away, could have departed from the straight path, and could have withdrawn from the see of blessed Peter, supreme among the apostles.

As the Gospel relates (Matthew 16), it was not flesh and blood—that is, human wisdom—but the Father himself who revealed to Peter the Son of God, while some considered him John, others Elijah, others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets.

We therefore write to you as one familiar and most dear to us. For, by God’s direction, you were the first precursor and guide to that king in this matter. You traveled between him and us as intermediary; and, thanks be to God, whatever was done for the salvation of that people was not done without your struggle. You yourself know what and how many labors we undertook for your instruction.

You formerly took pleasure in us and enjoyed spiritual joys and advances. But we do not know who has deceived you since then; who, having become an instrument of the devil—the devil who once deceived Eve through the serpent—has drawn you back from the right road by crafty persuasion. Hence we grieve greatly and are by no means lightly anxious.

Therefore, excellent among men, we exhort you: speak into the ears of that beloved son of ours, the king. May the Lord himself also speak into the ears of his heart, so that he may not make the first faith void; so that, walking before him, he may never look backward; so that he may not abandon the road on which he was walking; so that he may read the Gospel narrative and see there, above all, that Christ, the Son of the living God, was revealed to Peter alone, while the others held this or that opinion. “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22).

Therefore, if truth was revealed especially to Peter while these or those others held false opinions, and if the Son prayed especially for Peter’s faith, so that it might not fail, let the wise king consider how laudably he first sought the City to which this apostle, so great and so exalted, came and preached; to whom, through the Father’s revelation, the truth of the Son was disclosed; and whose faith did not fail because the Son prayed for it.

To this Roman city, after Antioch—which he visited in passing—and to the Church founded there, he hastened as to the mistress of the world. There he truthfully recognized and truthfully preached the Son of the living God, whom, as we have said, he recognized not through flesh and blood but through the Father’s revelation. Upon this solid rock of confession the Lord built his Church; and this is that rock upon which, as Solomon says, no trace of the serpent is found.

For this purest faith blessed Peter remained at Rome and established the Church there. After governing the Apostolic See for a long time, he accepted the glory of death for this faith. Thus, together with Paul—who filled the region from Jerusalem to Illyricum, the region in which you now live, with the Gospel—he consecrated and dedicated the holy Roman Church to the Lord God, founded upon this faith and established by his own blood.

By this faith the Romans grew and flourished so greatly within a short time that the eminent apostle, at the beginning of his epistles, seems to give thanks to God and proclaim its praises (Romans 1).

Therefore, dearest one, always flee this faith and persuade the pious king to thirst for it; urge him to seek it nowhere else above all but at Rome, where it was planted and rooted by blessed Peter, who, as we have shown, truthfully recognized and truthfully preached it.

For just as water can never be found elsewhere so pure or so clear as in the spring from which it draws its origin, so faith can never be found elsewhere altogether so pure or so bright as in the fishpond of our Church. It is not the leaking roofs—by which the contentious woman, that is, heretical perversity, is represented—that gathered it there, but the keeper of the keys of heaven, who gathered it abundantly and most purely from the living fountain itself, having drawn it from heaven and commanded that it be preserved clear.

Speak these things, dearest one, to the pious king, and exhort him in Christ Jesus, so that, in return for the talent of intimacy received and multiplied, you may deserve to enter into the joy of our Lord.

But if you listen to us—for we love you as brothers and sons with the greatest affection—we shall rejoice and exult exceedingly in your gain. Otherwise, we shall tell the whole Church and, as the Lord commanded (Matthew 18), regard you as heathens and publicans. Then you will see to yourselves when you have fallen into various temptations of error.

Sent through Paul and Eugenius, most reverend and holy bishops.

Given in April, on the sixteenth day, in the eleventh indiction.

### CX. TO A CERTAIN NOBLEMAN OF THE BULGARS  
[Note: [Col. 0761D] In Mansi this letter is incorrectly entitled “To Michael, glorious king of the Bulgars,” as is clear from the context.]  
*(In the year 878.)* It has the same subject, and nearly the same words, as the preceding letter.

[Col. 0762B]

Since we are sending a letter of our apostolate to the most Christian king, we have judged it fitting to write also to your Glory and to disclose the groans and sorrows of our heart, which we constantly endure, sighing, proceeding in deep sadness, and wondering with immense astonishment how that most wise king—and you yourselves—could have been turned away, could have departed from the straight path, and could have withdrawn altogether from the see of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.

As the Gospel relates (Matthew 16), it was not flesh and blood—that is, human wisdom—but the Father himself who revealed to Peter his own Son, while some considered him John, others Elijah, others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets.

We therefore write to you as the king’s brother and as one most dear to us. For you certainly know all that we did for the salvation of your people and what and how many labors we undertook for your instruction.

At first you took pleasure in us and enjoyed spiritual joys and advances. But we do not know who has since fascinated you, who has deceived you, or who, having become an instrument of the devil—the devil who once deceived Eve through the serpent—has drawn you back from the right road by crafty persuasion. Hence we grieve greatly and are by no means lightly anxious.

Therefore, excellent among men, we exhort you: speak into the ears of that beloved son of ours, the king. May the Lord himself rather speak into the ears of his heart, so that he may not make the first faith void; so that, walking before him, he may never look backward; so that he may not abandon the road on which he was walking; and so that he may read the Gospel narrative and see there, above all, that Christ, the Son of the living God, was revealed to Peter alone.

Let the most Christian king therefore return with eager heart to the see of this most blessed Peter. Just as a servant, when he has taken something harmful, desires the springs of water (Psalm 42), so may his soul desire and thirst for the health-giving streams of Peter’s teaching.

In this pious work, let your diligence labor before all others, so that you may not only win your dearest brother, but also obtain for yourself the rewards of recompense for the salvation of all your people. For nothing pleases God more than those who turn people from error or instruct many in righteousness.

Therefore, for such holy labor, with blessed Peter, keeper of the keys of the heavenly kingdom, interceding, you will “cover a multitude of sins,” as it is written (James 2), and you will be established like the firmament of heaven and like the days of eternity.

Meanwhile, we shall count you among our devoted sons, and we shall by no means cease continually to commend your memory at the confession-shrines of the princes of the apostles.

Given in April, in the eleventh indiction.

### CXI. TO IGNATIUS, PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE  
*(In the year 878.)* He now admonishes him for the third time not to usurp the region of the Bulgars, which has belonged to the Roman Church from ancient times, and to remove from that region within thirty days the bishops consecrated there either by him or by his suffragans; and, unless he obeys after two months, he deprives him of communion in the Lord’s body and blood and, if he persists in contumacy, even of the patriarchal dignity.

[Col. 0763B]

To our most reverend fellow-bishop IGNATIUS, patriarch of Constantinople.

Secondly, you have been admonished by letters from the Apostolic See and summoned by its envoys through formal exhortations, so that, content with the right of the Constantinopolitan diocese which, by the authority and favor of that same First See, with God’s assent, you had received, you would not extend the foot of presumption beyond the limits assigned to you by the canons, nor transfer by any usurpation the ancient boundaries established by your fathers. [Cols. 0763C–0764D]

No one is unaware that the region of the Bulgarians was governed, as far as the privilege of ecclesiastical provision is concerned, by Pope Damasus of holy memory and thereafter, until the irruption of the pagans, by the prelates of the Apostolic See. This is attested more clearly not only by various writings but especially by the deeds of different Roman pontiffs, which have long been preserved in the archives of our Church. Concerning what the devastation of war and the gravest incursions of hostility are known to have brought about, nothing ought to be judged more authoritative than what the most illustrious trumpet of the Church, namely Saint Leo, bishop of our See, taught and decreed when he said (Letter 85):

> “Care must be taken,” he said, “that the wounds inflicted by the assault of hostility may be healed especially through religious observance.”

When the condition of affairs had again, with the Lord’s help, been turned toward better things, he says once more:

> “When the evils inflicted by hostility have been removed, let what each person lawfully possessed be restored; and every effort must be made so that each person may recover what is his own.”

And again:

> “What has been disturbed by the necessity of war must be restored through the remedy of peace.”

But all these things, most reverend brother, you have read with closed eyes; you have trampled the decrees of the holy Fathers beneath a rash heel; and, forgetting the manifold benefits conferred upon you by the Apostolic See, you have risen against that same holy See, your benefactress. You have seized by unlawful invasion the ancient diocese established in the Bulgarian region, and have not hesitated, contrary to divine laws, to send the sickle into another’s harvest.

Therefore, after the first and second admonitions, we ought deservedly to have separated you from the fellowship of our communion, having at hand, according to the Apostle, the power “to punish every disobedience” (I Cor. X); and he also says: “If anyone does not obey our word through this letter, take note of that person, so that you do not associate with him” (II Tim. III). But because, making use of the moderation of the Apostolic See, we burn with a spirit of gentleness rather than severity in our desire to correct you, behold, for the third time we admonish, exhort, and formally protest to you, canonically through envoys and letters: without enduring any delay, send capable men into the Bulgarian region who, traversing the whole country, shall bring back without any delay all whom they find there who are said to have received from you or from your subordinates the gift of consecration.

Thus, within the space of thirty days, no bishop and absolutely no cleric who belongs to your ordination—or rather, your disorderly act—shall be found anywhere within the entire territory of the Bulgarians. For we do not permit those whom you unlawfully established there, and whom it is already established have been excommunicated by the Apostolic See for this very matter, to infect by the error of their transgression the hearts of the new servants of the Lord: those whom we planted in the faith by the hand of instruction, watered with the saving water of the fountain of teaching, and offered to God, their author, for the giving of spiritual growth, so that he himself might hold primacy in all things.

Moreover, if within the interval of thirty days you do not remove from the boundaries of the entire Bulgarian region all whom either you or your bishops are thought to have consecrated to any ecclesiastical rank, and if you do not withdraw yourself from every ecclesiastical right over that diocese, then, after two months counted from the day on which you receive the volume of this letter, you shall be deprived of the holy Body and precious Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ for as long as, obstinate in these decrees of ours, you refuse entirely to bow your neck in obedience.

But if you persist obstinately in this indiscipline and invasion, and do not drive out from there the bishops and all those whom either they or you appear to have consecrated there, then, by the judgment of Almighty God, by the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and by the sentence of our mediocrity, you shall be alienated and excluded from every dignity of the patriarchate which you received through our favor, possessing or enjoying no privilege whatsoever of the supreme priesthood.

Given in the month of April, in the eleventh indiction, sent through the bishops Paul and Eugenius.

## CXII. TO THE GREEK BISHOPS AND CLERICS [Cols. 0765A–C]

*(Year 878.) He declares them excommunicated because, invading the Bulgarian regions, they carried out unlawful ordinations there; he also declares that they are to be deprived of their dignity unless they withdraw from the whole Bulgarian region within thirty days. If anyone obeys, he decrees that the bishopric which he previously held in Greece is to be restored to him; and if he previously held none, he orders that a vacant one be conferred upon him, provided that he is worthy.*

To all the Greek bishops and other clerics who have invaded the Bulgarian diocese, and are therefore excommunicated.

We marvel and are exceedingly astonished that you have read the canons of the holy Fathers with your eyes closed, and, trampling upon your conscience, have transferred the eternal boundaries established by the Fathers and thrust the sickle of judgment into another’s harvest, entering the provinces of Illyricum which the Bulgarian nation now occupies and perpetrating unlawful ordinations there. Yet the sacred councils clearly indicate that these provinces once belonged to the See of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and the written records of the deeds of Saint Damasus, pope, expressly proclaim the same.

Since, with God’s help, the state of affairs had long ago been turned for the better, the Apostolic See had been acknowledged, sought out, and invited with many prayers by those who inhabit this region; and we had sent bishops and priests of lower rank there with mandates from the Apostolic See and undertaken many labors for the instruction of that region.

For if some of you came there secretly, we can aptly say of them, affirming that saying of the Lord: “All who came before me were thieves and robbers” (John X). The Lord himself says through the prophet: “They were coming, and I was not sending them.” Some of you, fleeing because of your crimes, and others departing to that place because of ambition and greed, went there neither called nor summoned; indeed, not even in such circumstances was it fitting for you to enter your own diocese in order to make any arrangement there.

Therefore, since we have found that you have acted in many ways against the sacred rules, we have excommunicated you, and you are excommunicated.

Whoever among you, after learning of this apostolic sanction, obstinately presumes, beyond the aforesaid period, to carry out any ordination or arrangement there without withdrawing from the entire Bulgarian region within the space of thirty days shall, by the authority of the holy Fathers and the sentence of our judgment, be deprived of his own office. He shall escape the penalty, or hope in any way for pardon, only after repenting.

But if anyone among you, humbly and obediently complying with these salutary admonitions of ours, yields the place to the Bulgarian diocese, let him know that we have decreed that the bishopric which he is known to have previously held in the Greek region shall be restored to him. If he never held one, a vacant bishopric shall be assigned to him, provided that he is such a person that no rule of the Fathers can stand in the way.

Sent through the bishops Paul and Eugenius. Given on the sixteenth day of April, in the eleventh indiction.

## CXIII. TO THE EMPEROR BASIL [Cols. 0765D–0767A]

*(Year 878.) Sent through the most reverend bishops Eugenius and Paul. He laments that the Church of Constantinople still suffers from schism and, for this reason, sends legates.*

To our most beloved and desired son, BASIL, most Christian and most tranquil emperor.

Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who has had mercy on us and consoled us in this present evil age (III Cor. I), visiting us and bringing about redemption by raising up the horn of salvation in the house of David (Luke II), namely Christ, his child.

For you, dearest son, not content with imperial dignity, according to the Apostle who says, “Strive for the better gifts” (I Cor. XII), have also imitated the ministry of the angels, desiring peace on earth for people of good will; and by this you plainly demonstrate that you will see heaven more clearly than daylight.

Both letters sent by your pontiff to our see plainly suggest that you burn with this desire, and they clearly indicate that you eagerly wish to restore the Church to the condition from which it was driven out by the dissension of the wicked.

For you consider your empire, advanced by God and adorned by you, through his agency, with justice and triumphs, to be less strong and less glorious unless you also strive to adorn it with supreme peace and concord.

But, dearest son, when we hear that the scandals of dissension still fluctuate within the Church of Constantinople, and that certain men of religious habit are scattered and cast down here and there and treated disgracefully, we rightly groan and are burdened with great sorrow. Above all, we perceive that peace there is continually disturbed by contention, although we had believed it built up through the many labors of the Apostolic See; and we have learned that certain consecrated persons have suffered various injuries, although we had hoped they had been rescued from every burden of oppression.

We bear the burdens of all who are weighed down—or rather, your beloved blessed apostle Peter bears them within us, for he protects and guards us as heirs of his solicitude in all things. But since, in accordance with the duty of our profession, we are also told with Jeremiah, “Behold, today I have appointed you over nations and over kingdoms, to uproot and to tear down, to destroy and to demolish, to build and to plant” (Jer. I), your piety likewise requests persons from our apostolate for this very purpose.

Behold, we are sending capable men from our side who, if they discover anything there requiring attention, may, after uprooting, destroying, scattering, and demolishing it from the roots according to the Lord’s command, likewise build and plant peace, unity, and charity in due measure.

For how can those who divide unity possess charity? We are unquestionably acting as ambassadors for Christ when we take pains to devote ourselves to the peace of the Church.

But because we cannot send the men beloved of God whom you request by name, since they are hindered by certain difficulties, we have sent Paul and Eugenius, most holy and reverend bishops and our beloved counselors, whose faith has been tested by us and whose knowledge is evident. We have given them written instructions that, with all hostilities quieted and calmed, they should construct with all their strength whatever pertains to peace, according to the holy rule of the Fathers, its teacher; and, with every contention removed, should, with God’s favor, award the palm to justice, doing only this for the praise of God and adding to the increase of your praises, as it is fitting for you to do from day to day.

Nevertheless, we do not wish your pious empire to be unaware that we have instructed the legates of the Apostolic See to visit, solely on the occasion of a visitation, the glorious prince of that province [Note: He perhaps means the king of the Bulgarians], and to announce to him, after completing the customary offices of greeting, the memory of the apostles which is desired of him.

Therefore we ask that, when you grant them access, you take pains to provide them with such an industrious man [something is missing: perhaps “hand over,” or something similar] as will lead them safely to the aforesaid prince and bring them safely back, after obtaining from him a written declaration that he will in no way again usurp that matter.

We desire that you remain well in Christ for many years and continually triumph over barbarian enemies, spiritual, desirable, and most Christian son, ever Augustus.

Given in the eleventh indiction.

## CXIV. TO THE SAME [Cols. 0767B–C]

*(Year 878.) He asks him to place faith in the legates sent by him and to bring aid to the Roman Church.*

To his beloved son, Basil, ever triumphant in the Lord, most pious emperor and Augustus.

We know, venerable emperor—we know and are entirely aware—that you excel in prudence, love equity, exalt piety, plant what is upright, and uproot vices. We also know and firmly believe that you wish to increase the strength and glory of the holy Roman Church, to groan over its tribulations, grieve over its distresses, and, insofar as it concerns you, remove its needs with pious regard.

For this reason, placing the greatest confidence in you, we entrust to you, with a singular hope, whatever grievously afflicts and tears apart this same holy mother of yours, the Roman Church, so that you may hear and correct it.

Nevertheless, so that you, whom we desire to be privy to our secrets, may not be unaware of what has been done in these days contrary to the will of God, contrary to the salvation of the whole Christian faith, and contrary to the privilege of the holy Roman Church, as well as contrary to the custom and political order of Rome, we have entrusted these matters to our envoys, the bishops Paul and Eugenius, to tell you orally.

We beg you to believe them as though we ourselves were speaking with you; and, believing them, we earnestly ask you to provide us with whatever aid or consolation you are able to offer, just as a beloved son is accustomed to offer it to his revered mother.

For through this you will have the holy apostles as your helpers, and you will possess us as your most devoted intercessors with the Lord.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of March [correction: May, as is clear from the preceding material], in the eleventh indiction.

## CXV. TO KING LOUIS THE STAMMERER [Cols. 0767D–0769C]

*(Year 878.) He laments the death of his father, Emperor Charles; exhorts him to maintain peace with his kinsman kings and to pursue the enemies of the Church, especially Duke Lambert, whose savage attacks he recounts; finally, he indicates that he will come to Gaul and celebrate a synod there.*

To Louis, glorious king, son of the emperor Augustus Charles II, of blessed memory.

With what love and affection, because of so many virtues and because of the daily worship offered to Almighty God, we loved your father, we cannot recall without shedding tears, Christ bearing witness to our conscience. And although we ought to rejoice that, after the successful course of his works, the rewards of eternal life received him among the company of the angels, nevertheless it is fitting to weep because, alas, in our bodily presence we have lost so great a helper of the Churches spread throughout the world.

Especially since at this time the holy Roman Church, mother of all, entrusted to my mediocrity by the disposition of the eternal counsels of Jesus—at a time when, as I might say with the Apostle, “the ends of the ages have come” (I Cor. X)—after being long harassed by so many persecutions and adversities, is worn down by the frenzy of its own household, so that I am forced to burst out with the prophet and exclaim: “I have come into the depths of the sea, and the storm has overwhelmed me” (Ps. LXIX); and again: “Lord, deliver my soul from lying lips and from a deceitful tongue” (Ps. CX).

But you, dearest son, I exhort and admonish with paternal affection to imitate his footsteps in the spiritual life by exalting the Churches. You were born in the beauty of whose flower and have attained royal dignity.

First, by maintaining the bond of peace and unity and of charity with your brothers, namely the sons of King Louis of Bavaria, and with faithful Christians; then, against the fury of the mad and against tyrants, stirred by your father’s example, may you be able, by the authority of Christ, to pour out from the depths, manfully and courageously, the strength of your power in defense of your mother, from whom you received both the drink of preaching through your forefathers and the imperial fillet.

For—and this cannot be said without a shower of tears—a root and fuel of the most wicked destruction has now arisen among us from the mass of sin: Lambert, the dreadful son of Wido, formerly duke of Spoleto. We confess him to be a member of Antichrist, who opposes and exalts himself by disparaging the origin of the royal lineage and, greedy for shameful gain, by secret plotting and the ardor of rapacity, now turning this way and that with his adulterous sister Rotilde and his accomplice, the faithless Marquis Adelbert—indeed, a plunderer of his country—impudently seeks, as true report spreads, to raise himself, as true report spreads, impudently—God forbid—to the “sickle” (*falcem*, reading uncertain) of the Roman Empire.

And now, as an abomination of desolation and son of perdition, the head of the scorpion and of the deaf asp, he destroys and squanders, and through his wicked plunderers disperses, the whole territory of Saint Peter and Paul, your protectors. For this reason nearly all our faithful appear to have been reduced to poverty and need, and he has not ceased to bind by oaths all the people of the territory of the holy apostles, so that they might conspire with him and not come at our command.

Now he has also sent an embassy to Tarentum among the pagans, sending gifts and receiving them from the pagans, and has humbly begged them that, once the message has been conveyed, they send him as quickly as possible a company of Saracens for the destruction of the Christian people.

Finally, how through wicked deceit and perjury he deceived us within the bosom of our Church and invaded the sacred city, we pass over in silence here because we have written certain things on the matter in another work for the knowledge of all Christians—those whom, for this reason, we have bound with the chains of anathema.

Therefore, dearest lord and son, wishing now, exhausted and wearied, to undertake a new labor of battle against these new and unheard-of evils among Christians—a danger by sea, namely the waves and perils of the sea—I desire to come to you, undertaking such dangers for the liberation of all the holy Churches, according to the Apostle, “not counting my life more precious than myself.” [The Roman edition reads: “I desire to undertake the journey, having crossed over from such dangers,” and so forth.]

And behold, insofar as concerns the governance of my ministry, I do not refuse, with his help, to die for the liberation of the sheep of Christ the Lord and to suffer loss.

I earnestly beg you, dearest son, look upon my tears and my arduous labor; prepare your mind, and that of your faithful, through continual exhortation for the defense of your holy mother; and, united with me in spirit, strive to hold the staffs of rebuke against ravening wolves. Thus, under the guidance of the grace of the Only-Begotten, after a long passage of time, having become fellow-workers in our struggle, may you be able to pass from the purple of earthly empire to an everlasting crown.
