We also ask your glory to deign without delay to send to your brothers—namely Carloman, Louis, and the younger Charles—the other letters which we are directing to them as exhortations on such matters. And I ask you, with paternal exhortation, to command that these matters be conveyed to all the most reverend archbishops and to the clergy of every rank throughout your kingdom, since, with the Lord’s mercy, we are about to celebrate among you a synod urgently necessary for all Christian peoples.

Whatever we wish you to know, we shall henceforth undertake concerning ecclesiastical affairs. You also, dearest son, by the authority of the Holy Spirit of our God, I appoint as my counselor in place of your father, Lord Charles, the perpetual emperor Augustus, who, as the saying goes, was a part of my soul. Gather and unite counsel concerning whatever must be done; for the pen must first be dipped in the fountain of your heart, and then our hand will form the strokes of the letters.

## CXVI. TO LOUIS, SON OF THE KING OF THE BAVARIANS [Cols. 0769D–0770C]

*(Year 878.) He exhorts him to preserve peace with his cousins; attacks Lambert, duke of Spoleto; asks him to inform the bishops that they should attend the synod.*

To Louis, son of the king of the Bavarians.

We read in Solomon: “A wise son makes his father glad, and is the joy of the mother who bore him” (Prov. X). Therefore, since Almighty God, by the counsel of his foreknowledge from eternity, has deigned to bring you, Louis, son of Charles, Louis, son of King Louis, forth from the lineage of kings and emperors, you strive to make him fully glad if with all your strength you hasten to assist your mother and her immaculate bride against the attacks of those lying in wait and her ravagers, and if, without respect of persons, you hasten as quickly as possible, in the manner of your parents and forebears, to offer the consolation of assistance.

The words of the Holy Spirit through Solomon testify: “A brother and a friend are proved in distress” (Prov. XVII). The sonship of your spiritual adoption will also be able to favor us well if, with Christ as its maker, you carefully strive to maintain in harmony with your brothers the bond of peace and unanimity; for, we confess, the salvation of the entire Christian people rests upon your peace.

For what necessity, and worn down by what distress, we were compelled to leave the seat of the apostolic summit and seek Gaul, and to ask you with paternal affection that, present there with us, you might deliberate concerning the common salvation of the holy Roman Church and the condition of the commonwealth, we now disclose in very few words, because in another work it has been written and preserved for the knowledge of all Christians how wickedly the matter was carried out. You perceive this more clearly than daylight.

Lambert, the faithless duke of Spoleto, offspring of Wido of old, son of perdition, rose to such pride through greed—as true report has it—you will undoubtedly recognize fully from our tribulations and distresses.

Feigning under secret deceit that he was coming to Rome as a devoted man, he was kindly received by us as a son of peace. But what poisonous counsel he was carrying in his heart he revealed at dawn on the following day. For, assigning guards and even armed retainers to the city gate that opens the way to those going to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, he prevented any of our faithful from coming out to us and restrained those bringing food, asserting that King Carloman had ordered him to do these dreadful things.

We cannot believe this, for no one from your lineage has ever raised his proud neck against this See; rather, for God’s sake, they have humbly bowed their necks.

We, dearest son, desiring to lay down our life for the Church of the Lord and its sheep, behold, have undertaken the difficult journey to you across the sea’s currents and salt waves, and, being present with you, intend, with the Lord’s mercy, to celebrate a universal synod for the whole holy Church. With your assistance, we shall strive to carry out its advancement and exaltation in its proper place.

Please deign to make this known to all the archbishops and our fellow bishops of your kingdom, and urge them to hasten with continual readiness to be present with us.

Given as above.

## CXVII. TO KING CARLOMAN [Cols. 0770D–0771C]

*(Year 878.) Nearly the same subject.*

To his beloved son Carloman, glorious king.

We fully remember, both from the text of your letters and from the envoys recently sent to us, with what exaltation of your pledge you strive to raise up the holy Roman Church, namely your mother and that of all Christians, which brought you forth nobly, nourishing you with the milk of her preaching from her breasts and bringing you by royal blood from your forefathers to the imperial scepters. We have also found that the fountain of your heart abounds, through the customary piety of your parents, in mercy toward the service of Almighty God.

We have therefore awaited your arrival to the aforesaid mother, as your imperial glory had promised, with all the greater eagerness and effort in our daily expectation, insofar as you promised to exalt and bless us and our Church, laboring amid so many adversities, above all emperors and kings who existed before you.

But alas, woe is me! Weary from the persecution and sword of the pagans, and from the annual levy of twenty-five thousand silver mancuses, indeed from the civic sword of distress added to your aforesaid mother, I would almost have been utterly destroyed, had we not been comforted by the sudden mercy of him who promises the faithful and says: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII).

Some went out from us, but they were not of us. We confess that they were not of us [perhaps better: “not of you,” HARD.]. They so dishonored the Roman Church and the sacred city, and so wearied and oppressed us, that nothing similar can be recalled as having been done even by Christian kings.

I speak of Lambert and Adelbert, the chosen marquises. In what manner they affected us by hostile force and secret deceit could not in any way remain hidden from your exalted glory; the matter has been written down in its own work for the knowledge of all of you.

For they closed the road to us when we desired to come to you, amid our other troubles. Compelled by this necessity, with our life in our hands, we laboriously undertook the danger of the sea; and we thought it worthwhile to go to Gaul, to strengthen your fraternal bond in the unity of peace, and to seek, as necessity demands, the liberation of your often-mentioned mother, the holy Roman Church.

We exhort you, and all the bishops of your kingdoms, to come there to celebrate a synod.

Given from the city of Genoa and sent to your glory through Anspert, our brother and fellow bishop of Milan.

We highly commend to your glory Peter, the presbyter of the cardinal church, the bearer of this letter. Please send him back to us quickly with your envoys and assistance.

## CXVIII. TO ANSPERT, ARCHBISHOP OF MILAN [Cols. 0771D–0772B]

*(Year 878.) He warns him to come as quickly as possible to the synod in Gaul with his suffragans; he complains of the treachery of Lambert, count of Spoleto.*

To Anspert, venerable archbishop of Milan.

Because of the countless and manifold distresses of oppression suffered by the entire holy Church spread throughout the world, we are going to celebrate, with Christ’s assistance, a universal synod in Francia (because in Italy, with the persecution of evil men raging [Note: These words do not fit what follows.]). We highly commend to your fraternity Peter, the presbyter of our cardinal church, whom we are sending to King Carloman [the text is corrupt: “we could not at all,” or similar]. We admonish your fraternity to hasten to it as quickly as possible, setting aside every delay, with all your fellow bishops and suffragans, except those whom the sacred canons permit to remain because of legitimate impediments.

For with Christ’s cooperation we hope there to raise up the condition and strength of all the Churches.

Again and again we admonish, exhort, and expressly command that no delay and no period of time impede you until you present your arrival to us in person; [Note: “So that together with me you may judge the cause of the common enemy.” Words of this kind or something similar seem to be missing here. Concerning Lambert and Adelbert, see Aimoin, Book V, chapter 37.] namely, the cause of Lambert, the faithless duke of Spoleto, son of Wido, and of his accomplice, Marquis Adelbert—or, more accurately, the traitor of his country—who, feigning under secret deceit that he was coming peacefully, treacherously stationed guards at the city gate, tyrannically invaded the sacred city, and, among his other crimes, attempted to confine us and our faithful within the church of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, in an unheard-of and dreadful manner [Note: “He attempted” or something similar seems to be missing here.].

Given as above [Note: In the Roman edition, the beginning of this letter reads: “To the archbishop of Milan; to the patriarch of Friuli; to John of Pavia.”].

## CXIX. TO ANGELBERGA, AUGUSTA [Col. 0772C]

*(Year 878.) That she should persevere in the faith of the Roman Church; he commends the bearer of the present letter.*

To his most beloved daughter Angelberga, empress and Augusta.

Remembering all your good deeds, we give thanks daily to our God, who from the beginning has so inflamed your mind with concern for devotion to the holy Roman Church, burning it with a spiritual flame.

But now, dearest daughter and devoted in Christ, I ask you to bring to bear the powers of your keenest intelligence and, in this untimely period, to come forward with your customary goodness, so that you may carry the good work you have begun through to its completion and receive the rewards of the eternal Recompenser.

I also ask you to hold in every respect commendable Peter, the presbyter of our cardinal church and bearer of this letter, and with your most prudent counsel, in your customary piety, arrange his journey so that, with God as his guide, he may return safely to us.

Given as above.

## CXX. PRIVILEGE FOR THE MONASTERY OF TORNUTIUM [Cols. 0772D–0774B]

*(Year 878.) The possessions formerly granted to the same monastery are confirmed.*

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 878, in the eleventh indiction, during the reign of the most pious and glorious King Louis, son of Charles, the most serene Augustus, with the assistance of our Lord, for the honor of that same God and our Lord Jesus Christ, I, John, bishop and servant of the servants of God, together with our aforesaid son, the glorious King Louis, convened an assembly of the venerable archbishops and bishops of the whole kingdom in the city of Troyes. The aforementioned most pious king was present.

After it had been completed, the aforesaid glorious emperor asked us, together with our sons and brothers, the bishops, to strengthen by a privilege of our authority the monastery of Tornutium, founded in the county of Chalon upon the river Saône, where the body of Christ’s martyr Valerian rests. His father, the emperor Charles, and afterward he himself, through a series of charters, had formerly granted it, with all the property belonging to that place, to the monks of Saint Mary, the holy Mother of God, and of the illustrious confessor Saint Philibert, present and future, in order to avoid the severity of the Marcomanni.

We yielded all the more willingly to his most pious command because we perceived that he was asking us to do the same with even greater insistence.

Therefore, by a privilege of our authority, we confirm to them everything contained in the charters of the most glorious emperors: namely, the aforesaid place and all its adjoining possessions, with complete liberty.

Also, in the county of Auvergne, the cell of Saint Portianus, with all its appurtenances.

In the district of Saintes, Asinarias, with all its property in its entirety.

In the territory of Poitiers, the cell of Saint Prudentius, with all the property adjoining it.

In the district of Angers, Cunaldus, with its entire property.

In the district of Le Mans, Bussiolium, with all its appurtenances.

In the district of Velay, the cell called Godditus, with all the property belonging to it.

And then in the parts of Burgundy, in the district of Lyon, the estate of Bisiacum, with its church.

In the district of Mâcon, the cell of Saint Romanus, and the estate of Olcasiacum, with its church and all its appurtenances.

But because, in order to avoid the persecution of the Northmen, the glorious king and likewise his father had granted the aforesaid place to the illustrious abbot Geilo and to the monks, present and future, and because pontifical cunning had subjected that same place excessively, the same king requested that so generous an almsgiving should, with our gracious assent, remain immune and free from every episcopal power.

The entire episcopal assembly, favoring his petitions, could not refuse what the most glorious emperor so piously requested.

Therefore, by the authority which we received in Christ Jesus our Lord, the supreme priest, in blessed Peter, we entrust the aforesaid monastery, with everything it possesses and shall possess, to Geilo, venerable abbot of the holy Mother of God, and to the aforesaid saints and to the abbots who shall succeed him, to be cultivated there according to the monastic order, with God’s help. At the command of our most pious son, the king, we confirm it perpetually, inviolably and inseparably, without division, alteration, or any diminution.

Therefore, by the authority of blessed Peter the apostle and our own, we anathematize anyone among the bishops of the present or the future who presumes to enter the place on any pretext for excommunication, absolution, or sacred ordination, unless he has been invited by the abbot or by the faithful monks of the place.

For we judge it unjust that the glorious queen of the world, who has been exalted above the choirs of angels, should be subjected to human powers.

Furthermore, we decree that the place shall be free and undisturbed from every secular power; and that it shall be regarded as the head of all things that have been offered, or shall henceforth, with God’s assent, be offered to the aforesaid saints or to the place, as is found in the charters of kings.

But if anyone, through rash presumption and blind greed, presumes in any respect to violate what we establish by the authority of God and of ourselves, let him know that he is to be punished with eternal damnation and burned forever in the fire with the devil and his angels. Let him also be regarded as an exile from the thresholds of the holy Church of God until, recovering from his unlawful presumption, he strives through fitting penance and correction to appease the anger of Almighty God, which he did not fear to incur.

I have therefore subscribed the clearest confirmation of these sanctions with the hands of the sacred bishops present; and we ask that they also be supported by no less valid guarantees from our absent fellow priests, through Christ and in Christ.

Hincmarus, bishop of Rheims, have confirmed this in the name of Christ.

Ansegisus, bishop of Sens.

Ottulfus, bishop. Gissibertus, bishop. Hildibaldus, bishop. Berno, bishop. Geraldus, bishop. Hincmarus, bishop of Laon. Edenulfus, bishop. Joannes, bishop. Raganulfus, bishop. Adalardus, archbishop. Alericus, bishop. Abbo, bishop. Agilmarus, bishop. Ingilwinus, bishop. Acfredus, bishop.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of May, by the hand of Christiforus, primicerius of the holy supreme Apostolic See, while the most pious Louis was emperor.

### CXXI. TO ANGELBERGA, THE AUGUSTA (878)

He reports that he has come to Arles and found everything prosperous there; he urges her to look after the interests of the Roman Church.

To his dearest daughter, the lady ANGELBERGA, empress, most serene Augusta, wife of the lord Louis, emperor of invincible and pious memory.

Since we have always striven, with immense desire and equally immense effort, to honor and bring to completion your imperial dignity in relation to the privileges of the Roman Church, and since we continue to love it—[reading uncertain: *adhaurimus*; perhaps *amaverimus* or *anhelaverimus*]—with Christ’s favor, we desire perpetually to know the greatness of so great a devotion of yours.

Behold, we have entered Arles, the delight of your kingdom, in good health, by the permission of the supreme Judge, through the intercession of the chief apostles. There, addressing the prince Boso, your son-in-law, and the lady Hermengarda, your daughter [Editorial note: Hermengarda, or Hermingardis, daughter of Emperor Louis II, is mentioned by Regino, *Chronicle*, Book II, and Aimoinus, Book V, ch. 32 (Col. 0773D)], [Col. 0774D] we found everything prosperous and continually desired. For love of you and of your recently deceased and most pious husband, we embraced them as sons; and for their advantage we shall do everything honorably, since through them, no less than through you, we seek consolation and protection for the holy Roman Church. With God’s permission, we likewise desire by every means to promote them to greater and higher positions, without prejudice to our honor.

Therefore we admonish and exhort you to support so great an undertaking and, enjoying your former counsel, not delay in informing both us and them of your decision by definite letters concerning each matter. [Col. 0775A]

Furthermore, we ask you to send letters from us to John, archbishop of Ravenna, expressing consolation and urging him to pray for us, not to fear in any way preparing himself against the enemies of God, and to send envoys to our faithful at Rome to console them. And, if it is lawful and if I have any power with you to obtain this, send your letters to Leo, our bishop-legatus and apocrisiarius, and to Peter and the other faithful concerning these matters, strengthening them as you know and desire.

### CXXII. TO THE BROTHERS MIRON AND HUNCFRID (878)

He orders Miron and Huncfrid, guilty of many crimes, to come to the synod.

To MIRON and HUNCFRID, his brother.

The grave and perverse acts arising from certain transgressions of yours, which have been reported to our apostolate—we confess that we name them tearfully—we order to be corrected most swiftly by apostolic authority, if you, Miron, do not wish, through the power of the Holy Spirit, deservedly because of your wickedness to be separated from all fellowship of Christianity and condemned forever to the flames of hell.

You have reduced the whole land of Septimania to desolation. You have stripped the churches, as they assert, of their ministers; you have craftily and deceitfully seized the castles of that land. Driven by what necessity, the men of the glorious margrave Bernard, confronting your rage with a multitude of men, committed certain wrongs in that same land, so that you may stand as the author of all sinners, like Jeroboam son of Nebat, who sinned and caused Israel to sin. [Col. 0775C]

Therefore, we wish you to come, setting aside every excuse, to our universal synod, which, God willing, we shall soon celebrate at Lyon, unless, as has been said, you wish to be punished utterly by the divine sword.

We also hear that the viscount Lindoinus, exercising your authority—as I dread to report—in the diocese of Sigebodus, archbishop of Narbonne, installs your priests in his churches. With prompt concern for your life, we command you to correct and amend this.

As for you, Huncfrid, we hear and grieve that you have apostatized from the office of the diaconate and from the venerable monastic habit. Therefore either free yourself, through the Lord’s mercy, by late repentance and flee to a monastery [Col. 0775D] as quickly as possible; or, if you trust your conscience, come to our synod to clear yourself of the charges brought and alleged against you. Otherwise, if you neglect this, you will be bound by the bond of anathema as an apostate and rebel.

Given as above.

### CXXIII. TO ROSTAGNUS, ARCHBISHOP OF ARLES (878)

He grants him his vicariate in Gaul and the use of the pallium.

**Editorial note:** In the Roman edition, and from it in the collection of the letters of John VIII, the portion of this letter beginning “Therefore to your fraternity,” and so forth, is presented as a new letter sent to the archbishop of Arles. We have omitted it from this collection as superfluous. —Mansi.

To the most reverend and holy brother ROSTAGNUS, archbishop of Arles.

[Col. 0776A] *(St. Gregory, Book IV, Letter 50.)* O how good is charity, which by love makes absent things present to one another through an image! It unites what is divided, orders what is confused, joins what is unequal, and completes what is imperfect. The distinguished preacher rightly calls it “the bond of perfection” (Colossians 3), because although the other virtues generate perfection, charity also binds them, so that they can no longer be dissolved from the mind of the one who loves.

Since, therefore, dearest brother, I find you full of this virtue, and since I had presented my bodily presence in the city of Arles for the restoration of the holy churches of God, as the true report of many testimonies concerning you proclaimed far and wide, and since you asked, according to ancient custom, for the use of the pallium and for the vicariate of the Apostolic See, let it be far from me to suspect that you sought either the height of passing power or the adornment of outward honor in our vicariate and pallium.

But since it is clear to all from where the holy faith arose in the regions of Gaul, when your fraternity renews the ancient custom of the Apostolic See, what else is happening than that a good offspring returns to its mother’s bosom? Therefore, with willing mind, we grant what you have requested, lest we seem either to take anything from your Church’s due honor or to have despised your worthy petition.

But now the matter requires greater diligence, so that as honor increases, concern may also advance and vigilance for the protection of others grow. The merits of your life must also become an example to those subject to you, and your fraternity must never seek its own interests through the favor of the honor it has received, but rather the gains of the heavenly homeland. [Col. 0776C]

For you know what the blessed Apostle says with a groan: “For all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1).

From the reports of certain persons I have learned that in the regions of Gaul or Germany no one attains the sacred order without payment. If this is so, I say with tears and declare with groaning that, when the priestly order has fallen inwardly, it will not be able to stand long outwardly either.

For we know from the Gospel what our Redeemer himself did: entering the temple, he overturned the seats of those selling doves (Matthew 21). To sell doves is to receive temporal profit from the Holy Spirit, whom almighty God, consubstantial with himself, grants to human beings through the laying on of hands. From this evil, as I have said, the consequence is indicated: because they presumed to sell doves in the temple of God, the seats of those who did so fell under God’s judgment; and this error spreads among their subjects with increase.

For the one who is advanced to the sacred order for a price, already corrupted at the very root of his advancement, is more ready to sell to others what he bought. Where is what is written: “Freely you have received; freely give” (Matthew 10)? And since the Simoniac heresy first arose against the holy Church of God, why is it not considered, why is it not seen, that the one whom someone ordains for a price, by promoting him, causes him to become a heretic? [Col. 0777A]

Therefore, with God as author, we entrust to your fraternity our vicariate in the churches under the kingdom of Gaul, according to ancient custom, while preserving to each metropolitan his proper honor according to the ancient practice. We have also granted the pallium for your fraternity to wear.

If any bishop should perhaps wish to travel farther away, however, he may not pass to other places without the authority of your holiness. If among the bishops any inquiry concerning the faith, or perhaps any other matter, should arise that is more difficult to decide, let it be debated and settled after twelve bishops have been assembled; but if it cannot be settled, let the truth be examined and the matter referred to our judgment. *(Up to this point, St. Gregory.)*

Alas! When we were in the regions of Gaul, among other things we found one practice that must be strongly prohibited: metropolitans presume to perform consecrations before receiving the pallium from the Apostolic See, although our predecessors and we have forbidden this by canonical decree.

Therefore we exhort your holy fraternity, which holds our vicariate throughout Gaul, to be concerned about this, to prohibit it by your authority lest it grow, and to admonish, urge, and command them to hasten to seek the pallium according to ancient custom. Whether they obey or not, report it above all to our apostolate. If possible, do not delay informing us by definite letters at the Nativity of the Apostles, either through yourselves or through one of our legates.

May almighty God protect you and grant that you preserve the honor you have received in your conduct.

Given as above.

### CXXIV. TO ALL THE BISHOPS OF GAUL (878)

That all should obey Rostagnus of Arles, to whom he has entrusted his vicariate in Gaul.

To all the most reverend and holy bishops and brothers established throughout Gaul.

*(St. Gregory, Book IV, Letter 52.)* Divine providence established ranks and various orders, distinct from one another, so that while inferiors show reverence to their superiors and superiors provide care for their inferiors, one structure of concord might be woven from diversity and the administration of each person’s duties properly carried out.

For the community as a whole could not subsist in any other way unless an order of such great distinction preserved it. Since creation cannot be governed or live in one identical equality, the examples of the heavenly armies instruct us: although there are angels and archangels, it is clear that they are not equal, but that one differs from another in power and order, as you know.

If, then, among those who are without sin this distinction is established, who among human beings would refuse willingly to submit to a disposition which he knows even the angels obey? From this, peace and mutual charity embrace one another in turn, and the sincerity of concord remains firm in an alternating and God-pleasing love.

Since every duty is then completed beneficially when there is one superior to whom recourse may be had, we have therefore judged it appropriate to grant our vicariate, according to ancient custom, to our brother Rostagnus, bishop of the city of Arles, in the churches under the kingdom of Gaul. Thus the integrity of the Catholic faith—that is, of the four holy synods—may, with God’s protection, be preserved in vigilant devotion; and if any dispute should arise among our brothers and fellow priests, he may restrain it with the strength of his authority and with prudent moderation, acting in the vicariate of the Apostolic See.

We have also instructed him that, if a dispute concerning certain matters should arise which requires the presence of others, he is to assemble a suitable number of our brothers and fellow bishops, examine the matter beneficially while preserving equity, and define it by canonical authority. If, however, a dispute concerning the faith should occur—which may divine power prevent—or a matter should arise involving a serious doubt and requiring, because of its importance, the judgment of the Apostolic See, let him examine the truth carefully and endeavor to bring it to our knowledge by his report, so that we may unquestionably settle it with an appropriate judgment.

We have also instructed him not to permit any archbishop in these regions to perform a consecration without the pallium sent by the Roman pontiff, and to rebuke those who do so by our authority.

Since it is necessary that bishops meet at suitable times with him to whom we have granted our vicariate whenever he judges this appropriate, in order to confer together, we exhort you that none of you presume to disobey his commands or postpone attending the common assembly, unless bodily illness should prevent someone or an excuse based on a just cause should not permit him to come.

Those who, because of some necessity, cannot assemble at the synod must send in their place a priest or deacon, so that whatever our vicar, with God’s help, has defined may reach the absent person through the one he sends by a faithful report, to be preserved with unshaken firmness, and so that they may not dare to violate it under any pretext whatsoever.

We have also judged that you should all be admonished that none of you attempt in any way to travel to more distant places without the authority of the aforesaid brother and our fellow bishop Rostagnus. Know that the commands of our predecessors, who granted their vicariate to his predecessors, unquestionably define the same thing.

Furthermore, we exhort each of you to be concerned for his office. Whoever desires to receive a share of the promised reward of the homeland should guard the flock entrusted to him with care and prayer, lest the lurking wolf tear apart the sheep entrusted to him by attacking them, and lest punishment be assigned in recompense for the gift.

Therefore, dearest brothers, we desire and entreat almighty God with all our prayers that he may cause your love to grow ever more fervent through the steadfastness of his good love, and grant that you remain in the peace of the Church and in one concord.

It has been reported to us that certain persons are brought to the sacred orders through the Simoniac heresy. We have commanded our holy brother and fellow bishop Rostagnus to prohibit this in every way. So that your fraternity may know and guard against it, this letter itself is to be read to you.

Given as above.

### CXXV. TO KING CHARLES (878)

He excuses himself for not sending an envoy to him, since the way was blocked by Lambert and his supporters, who were holding the city of Rome under siege.

To Charles, glorious king, beloved son.

Having received and read the series of your letters, we know that, in accordance with the custom of your predecessors, namely kings and emperors, and especially of your parents, toward the Roman Church, whose milk has until now nourished your offspring, you desire and seek everything in every respect. We therefore give thanks with paternal affection and understand fully what you have written.

Your affection also sought to ask our pontificate why we had not sent to you and why we had come in this manner. We wished to send to you and to your glorious royal brothers before we left the City, but because Lambert, Adelbert, and their supporters, who had been placed under anathema, obstructed us, we could not send anyone.

Nor is it surprising that they blocked our way, since they did not fear holding the Church of the blessed Peter, chief of the apostles—your mother, indeed, and the protectress of all the Churches of God—surrounded by armed men for thirty days, so that no one there was permitted even to light a lamp or offer praises to God until after we had left the City.

We made every effort to send to your glorious royal brothers, so that we might inform you of these matters; but since we now hear that you are nearer, we have decided to send this letter.

We came first for the cause of peace, unity, and tranquility of all the Churches of God, so that, with God’s consent, we might bring about one legitimate will among you four kings, as the Psalmist sang: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together,” and so forth (Psalm 132).

Next, we wish you, once assembled, to listen sympathetically to our oppressions. Therefore, dearest son, since it has greatly shone upon you… [the text breaks off; something is missing].

Given as above.

### CXXVI. TO ISAAC, BISHOP OF LANGRES (878)

That he should come to Troyes for the synod and send some men from Chalon to escort the pontiff there.

To the most reverend Isaac, venerable bishop of Langres.

We do not doubt that it is known to your holiness that we have come into the regions of Gaul for the condition of the holy churches. Therefore, with the Lord’s help, we shall celebrate a synod at Troyes, and we absolutely wish your holiness to be present.

Beforehand, however, let your venerability take care to send us men from Chalon who may guide our journey by the direct route to the aforesaid place. Also prepare suitable lodgings for us in your diocese, namely at the estate of Marmania, in the district of Alhense.

Given as above.

### CXXVII. TO ALL CHRISTIANS (878)

He excommunicates those who stole his horses and a silver vessel unless they return them within three days.

To all bishops, counts, and the entire Christian people.

Let it be known that, when we had come into Gaul for the peace and unity of the holy Churches of God, we suffered great dishonor at the city of Chalon, to the injury of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and of ourselves.

Among other things, our horses were stolen by robbery during the silence of night by fellow citizens of the aforesaid city, while our men were peacefully sleeping. Therefore we, who according to the duty of our ministry ought promptly to cut away growing vices with the spiritual sword, strike this evil with the heavenly blade.

Unless the aforesaid horses and the other stolen goods are returned to our men within three days, we shall excommunicate and subject to anathema the aforesaid thieves and all their accomplices, because they provide hiding places for robbers.

We also excommunicate the priest Aduvardus, who ministered to us at the monastery of Flavigny, because his men stole Saint Peter’s silver dish—whether with his consent or not, I do not know—on account of the sacrilegious theft. We bind them under the same sentence as above unless they return it.

Given as above.

### CXXVIII. TO THE SUFFRAGAN BISHOPS OF THE ARCHBISHOP OF ARLES (878)

He orders them to come with their archbishop to the synod at Troyes as soon as they are summoned.

To all the venerable suffragan bishops of our fellow bishop and brother Rostagnus of Arles.

Let it be known to all your holinesses that, with the Lord’s help, we shall celebrate a most necessary universal synod. As soon as your aforesaid archbishop summons you by letters from our apostolate, set aside every excuse and hasten to come in obedient and prompt steps.

For just as, at the common assembly, with Christ’s grace as guide, exaltation will follow from the paternal commands, so—God forbid—confusion will follow those who withdraw from this great college.

At the city of Langres, on the fourth day before the Nones of June.

Likewise to Otteramnus, archbishop of Vienne; Aurelianus, archbishop of Lyon; Rotbertus, archbishop of Aix; Teutrannus, archbishop of Tarentaise; Sigebodus, archbishop of Narbonne; and Aribertus, archbishop of Embrun.

### CXXIX. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS OF VARIOUS SEES (878)

To Hincmarus, archbishop of Reims; Ansegisus, archbishop of Sens; Frotarius, archbishop of Bourges; Joannes, archbishop of Rouen; Adelardus, archbishop of Tours—from their peers.

Observing the canonical institutions, whenever sufferings afflict the Church it is fitting for us to assemble colleges of priests, so that, when they meet together, they may impose upon the whole Church a beneficial counsel and the faith of all Christianity, and may have the measures of equity suitably *dilaniari* [reading uncertain; alternative reading: *moderamine queant congrue dilimari*, that is, “may be examined under a standard or moderation”].

Therefore we exhort your holiness that, when you hear of the arrival of Louis, the glorious king, and when he tries to come to us—we are not certain at which place we shall celebrate the council, but you will learn this when you hear it—as soon as you have received our apostolic letters in person, you should not delay coming to us after setting aside every postponement.

Thus the joy of your minds may be more richly multiplied through the harmony of your unanimity and peace, so that the assembly of all, and the response of your devotion, may benefit not only the favor of human beings but especially the Churches, to the praise of their Creator.

We desire that your fraternity prosper in Christ.

Given on the fourth day before the Ides of June, indiction 11.

### CXXX. TO HUGO, ABBOT (878)

He urges him to persuade King Louis to come to him; he also warns him to separate himself from the fellowship of certain persons.

To Hugo, vigorous, noble, born of royal stock, and most excellent abbot.

We cannot adequately express in words how much we love you, dearest son, since the celebrated report of your good works has kindled us everywhere. Therefore, so that we may obtain the fulfillment of our desire for your presence, we earnestly wish you to urge Louis, our son and king, and to hasten with him to us, so that, with Christ’s cooperation, we may work together for the exaltation of all Christianity.

Let your affection act so that you may moderate the sadness you recently caused me at Pavia by your absence.

Meanwhile, dearest son, we wish you to separate yourself from all fellowship with Formosus, who has been placed under anathema, and with John, archbishop of Rouen; Adelardus of Tours; and Frotarius of Bourges. [Alternative: *Rodonensis*, that is, of Rouen; nothing should be changed. Roman edition: *Beduriensis* for Frotarius.]

Given as above.

### CXXXI. TO TEUTRANNUS, ARCHBISHOP OF TARENTAISE (878)

He warns him to come to meet him with his suffragans and orders him to have Adalbert present at the synod to give an account of the matters about which Bishop Bernarius had complained.

To the venerable archbishop TEUTRANNUS.

We are surprised that, having heard of our arrival in these regions, you have not taken care, like the other venerable archbishops, to console us and come to meet us out of reverence for the blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, and for ourselves.

Long held in suspense by this astonishment, we admonish your fraternity not to delay coming to meet us as soon as possible with your suffragans, whom you can bring with you in person, so that together we may discuss the welfare of your Church.

Furthermore, we inform you that our venerable brother and fellow bishop Bernarius, having recently heard of our presence, lodged a complaint against your suffragan brother Adalbert, concerning whom he had already complained at Rome and had presented his written petition of complaint.

For this reason we sent letters to you and to the archbishop of Vienne, so that, after examining the complaints of both parties, you might judge what the canons prescribe. We also ordered the archbishop of Arles and the bishops of Valence and Viviers to be present as witnesses to this assertion.

But because, owing to various obstacles, their dispute has until now remained unexamined, we now command you, with admonitory authority, that wherever a synod is summoned by us, you order him to be present there canonically, prepared in every respect to render an account.

If he is absent, take care lest the judgment fall back upon you. Let him know that he will gain nothing from his absence.

Given as above.

### CXXXII. TO ROSTAGNUS, ARCHBISHOP OF ARLES (878)

That he should come to the synod with his suffragans as soon as possible.

To Rostagnus, venerable archbishop of Arles.

Since, through the mercy of almighty God, we shall soon celebrate a universal synod, we wish all your fellow bishops and suffragans and explicitly admonish and command you by apostolic authority to present yourselves at it as quickly as possible, setting aside every excuse, except for those obstacles to delay which the sacred canons permit.

Otherwise—God forbid—whoever withdraws himself on this occasion from so great a college will thereafter be wholly unable to be a participant in our communion.

Given as above.

### CXXXIII. TO HINCMARUS, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS (878)

That he should come without delay with his suffragan bishops to the synod at Troyes.

To Hincmarus, venerable bishop of Reims.

The good reputation of your fraternity, after a long passage of time, has brought us great joy through its widely known renown; and we cannot express in words how greatly we desire to behold you, especially since we have decided to come into these regions to pursue the cause of ecclesiastical welfare.

Therefore we are surprised that you have until now delayed your long-desired presence with us. Accordingly, by apostolic and paternal authority, we admonish you to come without delay with all the suffragans of your diocese to the present synod, which, God willing, we shall celebrate at Troyes.

Again and again we exhort you: set aside every delay and hasten to come as quickly and actively as possible, for we are postponing the handling of the affairs of the holy Churches of God until you, who are dearer and more useful to us than anyone, have come to us.

All we admonish is this: break your delays and strive to hasten with the utmost speed and energy.

Given as above.

### CXXXIV. TO FROTARIUS, ARCHBISHOP (878)

That he should come to Troyes with his suffragans for the synod.

To Frotarius, venerable archbishop of Bourges.

Having heard through the letters of your fraternity of the lamentation and distress inflicted upon you by the men of Count Bernard, our recent grief has been increased by the earlier one; and I consider the fact that the entrance to your see has been closed to you as an injury to myself.

Meanwhile, we exhort your affection to endure this patiently and to hasten as soon as possible to Troyes with the college of our brothers and fellow bishops of your diocese, for the synod which, with the Lord’s cooperation, is to be celebrated there.

We await daily, and eagerly desire, the arrival of Louis, our most beloved son and king.

We desire that your holiness prosper in Christ.

Given as above.

### CXXXV. TO BERNARD, MARGRAVE (878)

He warns him to make the way open for Frotarius to reach his see.

To our most beloved son, BERNARD, most noble of margraves.

Since at times we love certain persons more especially, we rebuke you with paternal affection in those matters by which we know your nobility offends God. This applies especially to the case of Frotarius, the venerable bishop, whose men, as we hear, rashly closed the road to his city so that he could not enter his see.

The Lord has reserved the judgment of bishops solely to his own decision, dearest son, and he does not wish laymen to judge bishops.

Therefore we admonish your loving affection to make haste lawfully to amend whatever wrong you have done in this matter against the aforesaid bishop. We shall in no way permit it to remain unpunished except through worthy correction, by virtue of our priestly office and ministry.

We desire that your nobility prosper.

Given as above.

### CXXXVI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ (878)

That he should exhort Louis, king of Germany, and his brothers to come to the synod or send envoys.

To the venerable archbishop LIUTBERTUS of Mainz.

Since ecclesiastical welfare demands it, and since, with God as guide, we have judged it useful to come into the regions of Gaul, we therefore necessarily urge your fraternity, according to the wisdom given you from heaven, to suggest repeatedly to King Louis and to his other brothers that they not fail to come, in accordance with Christ’s will, to a meeting with our humility and to the general synod assembled at Troyes.

Or, if the aforesaid king is prevented by some necessity and—God forbid—delays hastening to the aforesaid place, let him expressly send envoys there, where we shall speak with King Louis, so that, with the sons of the kings gathered as quickly as possible, we may, with God’s grace as guide, jointly consult for the welfare of all Christianity.

Likewise to Willibertus, archbishop of Cologne; Wittecherius, venerable bishop; and Bertulfus, archbishop of Trier.

Given as above.

### CXXXVII. TO ANGELBERGA, THE AUGUSTA (878)

He writes that on the anniversary of the day of her husband Louis he will perform sacred rites for him; he asks her to persevere in defending him; he announces that he will hold a synod at Troyes.

To his beloved daughter ANGELBERGA, empress, wife of the once most pious lord Louis, emperor, of divine memory.

Because you informed our pontificate that the anniversary of the greatly remembered lord Louis, emperor, was being observed, and asked us to celebrate our own prayers for him, we rejoice and shall gladly do everything appropriate for him according to his merits.

Furthermore, we ask you not to delay continuing now and forever, as we believe you have done until now, to be as concerned for our affairs as possible, so that through your labor and counsel we may soon, as is fitting, deserve to return with joy to our own see through the merits of the chief apostles.

Moreover, we wish you to know that at Troyes, on the Kalends of August, we shall celebrate a universal synod together with King Louis, son of the emperor Charles, and with all the bishops of Gaul. Then we shall address King Carloman and his brothers, so that by the equal counsel of all we may find consolation for our Church.

### CXXXVIII. TO SUPPO, COUNT (878)

He gives thanks for his fidelity toward the Roman Church and entrusts him with certain matters to be carried out with Carloman.

To his beloved son, SUPPO, glorious count.

First, we give great thanks to your devotion, because you do not cease, by your daily labor and activity, to demonstrate in what follows the former fidelity you had toward the holy Roman Church.

We too, loving you above all others, give preference to your counsels over all others. Take with you only the bishops Anspertus and Wibbodus, and present all our instructions properly to King Carloman.

Take the greatest care, however, that we not be deceived by any cunning fraud. Whatever you do in this matter, hasten to do it with all speed. Inform me of the place and time at which you should come to meet us and gather us again.

And lest any doubt perhaps remain in your mind, we are sending two letters to the aforesaid king. Read one of them so that you may know what it contains. We wish either you to carry it yourself or to send it through a suitable man of yours.

For we cannot remain in this land beyond the Kalends of August, since after coming into this land we must speak with King Louis. Hasten as quickly as you are accustomed to do to conduct the cause of our Church, so that your reward before the Lord may abound.

Given as above.

### CXXXIX. TO KING CARLOMAN (878)

He is surprised that he has not answered two letters. He laments his illness and adds that a synod will be held at Troyes.

**Editorial note:** Some material is missing.

Bishop Sabbatinus.

Bishop Sabbatinus first, and afterward through Anspertus of Milan—concerning which we are greatly surprised, since we have not yet received an answer or envoys from you.

At the first opportunity, we wished at least to speak with you through envoys, and afterward with your remaining brothers. Since this has been postponed because of your illness, which we deeply regret, we shall now, with Christ’s help, celebrate a synod at Troyes. We shall speak with Louis and your other brothers, and after the Kalends of August we shall return to you.

Only send us word in due time of a place where you should come to meet us, and do not refuse to undertake the labor for your mother, the holy Roman Church. For if you are partners in labor, you will likewise be partners in consolation (2 Corinthians 1). I ask you, therefore, not to delay in carrying this out.

Given as above.

### CXL. TO KING CHARLES (878)

He gives thanks for his observance toward the Roman Church; he is surprised that he has not sent envoys; he asks him either to come himself or to send envoys before the meeting he is to have with King Louis.

To his beloved son CHARLES, glorious king.

For what we stated concerning the peace and unity of the holy Churches of God and of all Christians in the earlier letter that we sent to your affection, we nevertheless return abundant praises of thanks to your glory. Your letter greatly rejoiced us, because it shows abundantly that you possess toward the Roman Church the affection of heart which your parents and forefathers had.

We are nevertheless greatly surprised that you have not sent your envoys to us, as we requested. Therefore, dearest son, we ask you, if it is possible, to hasten to the meeting that we shall have with Louis, king and son of Charles, emperor and king, at Troyes.

Or, if you are prevented by some obstacle—as we do not wish—and cannot come, send us vigorous envoys through whom we may confidently entrust to your glory everything secret that lies in our heart.

At the same time, explicitly designate a place to us where we may enjoy conversation with you and with your brother Louis, the glorious king, since we shall in no way return from this land before, with God’s help, we have held fully appropriate and mutual conversations with you.

We desire that your glory flourish through pious successes.

### CXLI. TO KING LOUIS (878)

The same subject as the preceding letter.

[Col. 0786A]

# To the Beloved Son, LOUIS, Glorious King

That we had come from the Roman See into the regions of Gaul for the peace and unity of all the holy Churches of God and of all Christians, we earnestly endeavored to make fully known in the letter that we sent to Your Glory. Yet we do not know when it reached you, nor why Your Affection has given us no reply concerning it. Therefore, dearest son, I ask you to hasten to come to us for the conference that we shall hold at Troyes with King Louis, son of the emperor Charles, if no difficulty prevents you; or, if you are hindered by some obstacle, as we do not wish, send us capable envoys through whom we may confidently entrust to Your Glory all the matters that lie in our mind. At the same time, specify to us a place where we may enjoy conversation with you and with your brother, the glorious King Charles. For we shall in no way return from this land before, with God’s help, we have held fully appropriate and mutual discussions with you. Given as above.

## CXLII. TO CHARLES, KING (878)

He reproves him because, though summoned to him, he did not come, as King Louis had done; and he warns him under penalty of excommunication to remain content with the boundaries of his kingdom and to offer no molestation to Boso.

[Col. 0786C]

To Charles, beloved and glorious king.

Keeping faith with the kings of the Franks, according to the pontificate of my predecessors, I have endured many harsh labors by sea and land. I came from the city and the Roman See into Francia. Through envoys, both by spoken message and by letters, I endeavored to summon all of you, so that you might strive to fulfill the pact that your grandfathers and fathers promised by oath to the holy Roman Church.

But alas, to our grief, through disobedience you all neglected to come, except King Louis, son of the emperor Charles of blessed memory. By his counsel and encouragement I made Boso, the glorious prince, my son through the grace of adoption, so that he might be free to attend to worldly affairs while we might freely devote ourselves to the things that pertain to God. Therefore, remain content with the boundary of your kingdom and strive to preserve peace and quiet, for now and henceforth we excommunicate all who attempt to rise against the aforesaid son of ours. Given as above.

## CXLIII. TO LIUTBERT, ARCHBISHOP (878)

He warns him to have the inheritance restored to Boso’s daughters.

To our most reverend and most holy brother, Liutbert, archbishop.

We wish your Fraternity to remember how we previously wrote to you concerning the properties of Boso and Engeltrude, warning you that you ought to return to their daughters the properties that you call allods, since they have repeatedly claimed them. For by the authority of all laws legitimate sons and daughters are the true heirs (*In Authentico, On Heirs Who Die Intestate*, §1), as your religiousness knows well. Again we exhort and warn you, and expressly command by apostolic authority: since you have delayed listening to our letters and have so far neglected to answer concerning these matters, we wish you, returning to your senses, to take care to invest those women who have repeatedly claimed them, or their representatives, with the aforesaid properties. You shall likewise admonish, by our authority and through excommunication, your own men and the other invaders to do the same. For the just Lord loved justice, and His countenance beheld equity.

[Note: [Col. 0787D] An accusation of adultery had been brought before the court, as appears from Letter 143.]

And if the bastard Godefredus, or Engeltrude herself, who is an adulteress, should wish to assert that she gave any of these things to someone in any manner without her husband’s consent, we judge, by our apostolic authority, until they have returned them—and because it is written under Pope John of Rome and the emperor Justinian (*In Authentico, On the Property of the Damned*, in the Code, *On Gifts Made by the Proscribed or Condemned*)—that bastards are exceedingly injurious, exceedingly bitter, and in our times always unworthy. Therefore it is fitting that Your Reverence continually admonish him concerning this.

Moreover, we exhort you to complete in every way what we have instructed. For if you act otherwise, know that you are to be condemned by canonical censure, so that you must excommunicate them. Given as above.

## CXLIV. TO MATFRED, COUNT (878)

He warns him to restore the inheritance to the daughters of Count Boso.

[Col. 0787C]

To Matfred, illustrious count.

At the complaint, namely, of the daughters of the late Boso and of Engeltrude, your relative by marriage, we have learned that you do not fear to hold their allods after invading them. Concerning this, we are astonished that a man of such wisdom is not ashamed to do so. Do you not know that, in receiving an inheritance, sons and daughters are to be preferred to all relatives? That adulterous woman could not, by the authority of any law, give any part of these things to anyone without her husband’s consent.

Therefore we admonish you, exhort you, and command by apostolic authority that, out of reverence for the princes of the apostles, from whom they have sought help through me, you do not delay returning those properties to their daughters. For if you act otherwise, know that you are to be struck by canonical censure. Given as above.

## CXLV. TO VALDERAM (878)

He warns him either to bring Valderam’s case to an end or to refer it to himself.

To the venerable Valderam.

The bearer of this letter, named Valderam, coming before us to your Fraternity, has tearfully complained that his father is being unjustly held in prison within your parish. Therefore, by the authority of our apostolate, we command your Fraternity, girded with priestly strength, to investigate the case of the aforesaid father with the greatest care and to give it a lawful conclusion and end, if the state of the matter appears sufficiently clear for the future. But if it seems doubtful to your judgment, we absolutely command you to order both parties, furnished with their allegations, to come promptly into our presence. Given as above.

## CXLVI. TO THEODORIC, ARCHBISHOP OF BESANÇON (878)

He orders him to come as soon as possible and forbids the ordination of a bishop in the Church of Lausanne, because of divisions among the electors, before they have conferred together.

To our most reverend and most holy brother Theodoric, archbishop and bishop of Besançon.

Since your Fraternity, hearing of the persecutions suffered by the apostolic and universal Church of God, has delayed showing compassion in every way, and since you have neglected to visit us, who are undertaking labor on behalf of him and of all the others, we are sufficiently astonished and in part troubled, recognizing that charity has grown so cold in you. Does not Truth say: “If brother helps brother, both will be exalted”? (*Proverbs* 18). And Wisdom says: “A brother and a friend are proved in troubles” (*Proverbs* 17). Our predecessor, Pope Gelasius, moreover, admonishing bishops who disregarded the afflictions of their brothers, writes in his decretal letters: “Why did you not have compassion?” and so forth.

Therefore we warn you to recognize that you have hitherto been negligent and nevertheless strive to restore the despised charity. Setting aside all other concerns, come in person with this envoy of ours to visit us. We have also heard—and we grieve to hear it—that contention has arisen in the Church of Lausanne, which is now seen to be without a father, and that its children are shamefully divided in the election of a bishop.

Therefore we warn you by God the Father, and adjure you by the Son and the Holy Spirit; and we expressly command by apostolic authority and forbid you: until you reach our common conference, do not presume to consecrate a bishop there, whether at the king’s command or at the request of the people. Thus, when we have conferred together, with God’s help and with common deliberation, we may permit the one whom we judge more useful to be consecrated according to custom.

What we have omitted writing here, we have instructed our envoy Deusdedit, glorious master of the soldiers, duke, and counselor, to communicate orally. Receive him kindly, and hear without resistance whatever he brings you on our behalf. Given as above.

## CXLVII. TO AMELIUS, PRIEST (878)

Privilege for the monastery of Saint Peter in the district of Nîmes.

[In D. Bouquet, *Collection of Historians*, vol. IX, p. 165.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend Amelius, priest, and Leo, abbot.

What you have requested from us, we grant to your religiousness: the monastery of Saint Peter, with all its cells and possessions belonging to it, where the body of blessed Aegidius rests, in the Flavian Valley, in the district of Nîmes, within the borders of Gothia. Flavius, once king, gave this valley to the aforesaid blessed Aegidius. That holy Aegidius thereafter made a complete donation of it to the Roman Church, and built there a monastery in honor of the princes of the apostles Peter and Paul.

But while the distance of that land separated the monastery from the Roman Church, because the Church had been unable to send an envoy there on account of other concerns, the bishop of Nîmes, invading it with a certain rashness, had taken it away. Then he had obtained a charter from a king of the Franks; and, trusting in neither its validity nor its firmness, he approached the Roman pontiff and secretly sought apostolic authority concerning this matter, as though the property were his own.

But the lord Nicholas, of holy memory, although unaware of this fraud, nevertheless, filled with the Holy Spirit, endeavored to excuse all those who were seeking judgment in the matter. When we searched for documentary records in our archive, however, we found there the charter that had been delivered to Saint Aegidius.

Afterward, when we were traveling to Arles by the coastal route on the business of all the Churches of God, remembering this, we claimed the monastery through Deusdedit, duke of Ravenna and our advocate, against Girbert, bishop of Nîmes. Indeed, after advocates of both parties had been appointed as guarantors, with only George the scriniary as executor and Deusdedit as agent, Bishop Girbert wished to defend himself by means of the charter of the lord Nicholas, of pious memory, which had been read there.

But Rostagnus, archbishop of Arles; Sigebodus, archbishop of Narbonne; Aribert, archbishop of Embrun; Walbert, bishop of Porto; Paschalis, bishop of Amelia; Ratbert, bishop of Valence; Litidumus, bishop of Marseille; Alictarius, bishop of Viviers; and the other bishops of the province; and the judges John, duke and prince of Ravenna, Ardus, Adbertus, Giselfredus, Alderadus, Godultius, and several other provincial judges, as soon as they heard the charter read, immediately recognized that the apostolic censure of the lord Nicholas excused those who were seeking judgment concerning the matter. They declared that the monastery could not be defended by that charter, and judged at once that Bishop Girbert should return the aforesaid monastery to Priest Amelius and Abbot Leo and should pay us the penalty for the invasion.

Because of his poverty, we remitted the penalty to him, provided that he did not sin further; and we received the monastery in its entirety. We sent our advocate, Duke Deusdedit, there, and he received from the aforesaid Bishop Girbert the formal physical delivery of all the possessions of the monastery:

The villa of Agarnella with the Church of Saint James and all its appurtenances; likewise the Church of Saint Andrew with its appurtenances; the Church of Saint Cecilia; the Church of Saint Saturninus with all its appurtenances; the Church of Saint Stephen with all its appurtenances; and the allods themselves that ought to belong to the monastery; the villa of Seura with its appurtenances and the slaves belonging there; Brasca with its appurtenances; Bionum with its appurtenances; gardens and fields at Brucianum; Luva with its appurtenances; the Gothic bank; Aspiranum with all its appurtenances; fields and vineyards at Generacum with their boundaries; vineyards at Costaballenis with their boundaries; fields and vineyards at Gurgis with their boundaries; fields and vineyards at Tovana; fields and vineyards at Aqua Viva; fields and vineyards at Alburnum with all their appurtenances; fields and vineyards at the place called Stacionensis with all their appurtenances; Coconum with all its customary dues.

[Col. 0790B]

Therefore we wish and command that all these aforesaid possessions, as well as whatever may subsequently be offered, be held inviolate and without disturbance for the use of the monastery and as the income of the blessed apostle Peter.

Nevertheless, since these things have been granted for the support and administration of whoever holds them, they shall in every way be preserved for the future, on this condition: that none of our successors in this holy See, which by the Lord’s authority we serve, shall ever or anywhere permit any of these possessions to be granted as a benefice, exchanged, or conceded under a rent in future times, except to Priest Amelius, who is entirely recognized as our own.

For this reason we entrust to you this charter for governing, protecting, and properly building up the monastery. Provided, however, that, receiving from you each year, in the name of a pension and according to ecclesiastical accounting, ten silver solidi and twelve denarii, they shall strive to extend to that monastery the support of pious fatherhood against all who attack it.

We likewise establish that, when the abbot of the aforesaid monastery dies, no other person shall be appointed there through any scheme of encroachment, except one whom the consensus of the monks, according to the fear of the Lord and the institution of the rule of Saint Benedict, has chosen, and whom the pontiff of this apostolic See has provided to be ordained—or whom the monks’ petition has agreed should be brought to Rome for ordination.

We add this clause to the present chapter in order to close the door to greed: no king, no priest, nor any of the faithful, through a substituted or interposed person, shall presume to receive anything in money, gold, or any other form of benefit or gift concerning the ordination of the same abbot, or of clerics or priests, or concerning the distribution of chrism, the consecration of a basilica, or any spiritual or temporal advantage, or concerning any matters belonging to the same monastery. Nor shall that same abbot presume to give anything on account of his ordination, lest on this occasion the things that the faithful offer, or have already offered, for the place be consumed.

Nor shall the bishop of the city in whose parish the monastery lies celebrate public Masses there or introduce stations into the monastery unless invited by the abbot of that monastery, lest the quiet of God’s servants be disturbed in any way by a popular gathering. Nor shall he presume to demand from it provisions or lodging dues.

As for the contributions of the faithful and religious persons and the benefactions that the Apostle commands all to provide according to the capacity and resources of the place, we not only do not forbid them from being given there freely, but also urge that they be given. Yet the proper number of the community shall be maintained so carefully that neither an excessive number, leading to poverty, nor too few inhabitants, leading to the abandonment of the place, may occur.

Therefore we decree that all these things contained in the page of this charter and decree of ours shall be observed perpetually by all who succeed us, who retain under usufruct the monastery acquired by us, and by those whom the matter may concern.

If any priest, judge, or secular person, recognizing this page of our constitution, should attempt to act against it, struck in his power, honor, and dignity by apostolic anathema, let him be deprived of them and acknowledge himself guilty before the divine judgment of the deed committed. And unless he either restores what he has wickedly taken, corrects what he has rashly presumed, or mourns his unlawful act with worthy repentance, let him be separated from the most sacred body of our Lord Jesus Christ and, with the devil and his most dreadful pomp, be subjected to strict punishment at the final judgment.

But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who observe the rights of this place and of our command, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find the rewards of eternal peace before the strict Judge. Farewell.

Written by the hand of George, scriniary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of August.

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, through the hand of Walbert, most humble bishop of the holy Church of Porto, in the sixth year, with the Lord’s favor, of the pontificate of our lord John, supreme pontiff and universal pope, in the most holy See of the blessed apostle Peter, in the eleventh indiction.

## CXLVIII. TO FROTARIUS, ARCHBISHOP OF BORDEAUX (878)

He orders him to come to the synod and to bring the privilege concerning the transfer of sees.

To Frotarius, venerable archbishop of Bordeaux.

For the synod that, with God’s authority, we are holding at Troyes with our brothers and fellow bishops from the other seven provinces of Gaul, we have endeavored, setting aside every pretext of whatever kind, both orally and in writing—and now for the third time—to admonish your Fraternity, together with your suffragan bishops, to come. We wished us to be assembled together so that emerging questions of cases might be settled by canonical statutes and a single concord of love might be established among the priests of the Lord.

But why you have delayed coming we all find grievous and are greatly astonished. Therefore, putting delay aside, present yourself as quickly as possible, together with the aforesaid suffragans, before us and the holy synod.

Come instructed in such a way that, if you are accused of transferring sees contrary to the canons, or of other offenses for which—something we do not wish—you might be struck according to the regulations of the Fathers, you may depart unharmed and innocent when the cause of justice has intervened.

In offering this advice to Your Reverence, we counsel you not to suppose that your absence will benefit you in any way; rather, according to the statutes of the Fathers, it will harm you more. If, as you admit, you have a privilege or documents concerning the transfer of sees from us or from our predecessors, make every effort to bring them with you without delay.

## CXLIX. PRIVILEGE FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT AEGIDIUS (878)

[In D. Bouquet, *Collection of Historians*, vol. IX, p. 167.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all bishops residing throughout the provinces of Gaul; to abbots, priests, and all orders devoted to the divine ministry; likewise to counts, viscounts, vicars, centenaries, judges, all persons established in positions of authority, all the people, and the entire universal Church.

With almighty God as author and mediator, in the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 878, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the eleventh indiction, by the Lord’s favor, in the presence of the lord Louis, most serene king, seated in the present council, and so forth.

Let it be known to all aforesaid that in former times, when we were coming to Arles by the coastal route on the business of all the Churches, we remembered the monastery of Saint Peter, where the body of blessed Aegidius rests, in the Flavian Valley, in the county of Nîmes, within the borders of Septimania. Flavius, once king of the Goths, gave this valley to the aforesaid blessed Aegidius, and Saint Aegidius again made a complete donation of it to the Roman apostolic See.

But while the remoteness of the land separated that monastery from our Church, because we had been unable to send an envoy there on account of other concerns, the bishop of Nîmes had presumed, with great rashness, to seize the monastery for himself.

When we searched for documentary safeguards in our archive, however, we found there the charter that had been delivered by Saint Aegidius. Then, through our advocate Deusdedit, duke of Ravenna, we claimed it against Girbert, bishop of Nîmes, who is seated in the present council.

That same Girbert wished to assert his claim by means of the charter of the lord Nicholas, which he had secretly and fraudulently obtained from the apostolic See as though it were his own, and by means of a charter that he had falsely obtained from a certain Frankish king, in which no validity remained.

But I admonished all the bishops and judges, Roman and provincial, under the anathema of excommunication, to pronounce and carry out a rightful judgment in this matter. Then Rostagnus, archbishop of Arles; Walbert, bishop of Porto; Paschalis, bishop of Amelia; Radbert, bishop of Valence; Litidumus, bishop of Marseille; Ictarius, bishop of Viviers; and the other bishops of Provence; and the judges John, duke, and Bativus of Ravenna, Ardus, Adbertus, Gisalfredus, Arderadus, Godulfus, and several other provincial judges, as soon as they heard the charter read, immediately recognized that the apostolic censure of the lord Nicholas excused those who were seeking the law. They declared that the monastery could not be defended by that charter and judged at once that Bishop Girbert should return the aforesaid monastery to us and should pay me the penalty for the invasion.

Because of his poverty, we remitted the penalty to him, provided that he did not sin further, and we received the monastery in its entirety. We sent our advocate Deusdedit, duke, there, and he received from the aforesaid Bishop Girbert the formal physical delivery of all the possessions of the monastery.

Therefore, relying also upon divine aid, I and all the bishops of this council, by the authority of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom, by whom, and in whom all things endure, detest, forbid, and excommunicate under the full force of anathema any attempt by any of our successors in this holy apostolic See, which by the Lord’s authority we serve, ever or anywhere, in the present or future times, to grant as a benefice, exchange, or concede under a rent any of these possessions. Neither emperor, king, nor any worldly power shall be able to do so in future times.

Nor shall the bishop of that diocese, to whose parish the place itself belongs, nor the count of that jurisdiction, dare to receive anything from the monastery on any pretext. Moreover, no one at all shall be permitted in any manner whatsoever to impose any diminution or force upon any of these things.

Rather, by the present council we confirm all these possessions to the aforesaid monastery, with all its appurtenances, its cathedra, and its other movable and immovable properties known to have been bestowed there through the generosity of those who fear God; and we confirm them to Amelius, priest and archdeacon of the Church of Uzès.

For this reason we entrust to you this charter for governing, protecting, and properly building up the monastery. Provided, however, that, receiving from you each year, in the name of a pension and according to ecclesiastical accounting, ten silver solidi and twelve denarii, they shall strive to extend to that monastery the support of pious fatherhood against all who attack it.

There is no doubt, brothers, that the apostolic Church is the mother of all churches, from whose regulations it is in no way fitting for us to deviate. And just as the Son of God came to do the will of the Father, so you must fulfill the will of your mother, which is the Church, whose head, as has been said, is the Roman Church.

Therefore our Father is undoubtedly God, who created us, and our mother is the Church, which spiritually regenerated us in baptism. Consequently, whoever takes away, defrauds, or steals the money of Christ and of the Church shall be judged a homicide in the sight of the just Judge.

Hence it is written: “He who steals his neighbor’s money commits iniquity; but he who takes the money or possessions of the Church commits sacrilege.” Thus Judas, who defrauded the money that, by the Savior’s command, was distributed for the uses of the Church—that is, for the poor whom the Church ought to feed, and whose place the bishops hold—became not only a thief but also a robber and sacrilegious.

Concerning such persons, that is, those who seize, defraud, or take away the resources of the Church, the Lord, threatening them, addresses all through the prophet, saying: “O God, do not keep silence; do not be silent, and do not remain at rest, O God,” and so forth.

In a letter of Pope Symmachus:

> “From this day forward, until, by the Lord’s arrangement, the teaching of the Catholic faith of the Savior endures, no prelate of the apostolic See shall be permitted to transfer an ecclesiastical estate, however great or small its extent, under perpetual alienation or exchange into the possession of anyone.”

And from a letter of Pope Simplicius:

> “It shall not be permitted for a bishop to alienate or exchange in any manner the estates of his titles, or anything that belongs to their rights. Whoever attempts to do this shall be punished by the loss of his rank.”

Likewise, in the same source:

> “Whoever asks for an ecclesiastical estate and receives it as his own property—or if any priest, deacon, or defender subscribes to such a transaction—shall be struck with anathema.”

Likewise, in the canons:

> “If a bishop has bequeathed anything from ecclesiastical property in a testament, it shall otherwise have no validity unless he supplies it entirely from the resources of his own rights.”

Therefore I, together with all the bishops of this council, separate, condemn, and excommunicate under the full force of anathema all plotters against this monastery of the apostolic See, and anyone who has acted against this priest, if they have committed such a crime, from communion in the body of Christ, from fellowship in brotherhood, and from the company of all Christians.

Let them be accursed in the city and accursed in the field; accursed be the fruit of their land. Accursed be their inward parts and their outward parts. Let the heaven above them be bronze, and the earth they tread iron. Let their prayer before God become sin. Let them go alive into hell like Dathan and Abiram.

All who have shared with them, or eaten food with them, or knowingly chosen to hear their accursed songs, shall share in Christ with Judas Iscariot, the betrayer. May their water rot; may their wine pour forth; may rust consume their bread; may moths eat their clothing.

And what more? May all the curses of the New and Old Testament come upon them until they come to worthy satisfaction and fitting repentance before Mother Church.

John, of the apostolic See of the apostle Peter, wishes good health in Christ to all the Churches that observe these provisions.

[Col. 0794D]

Hincmarus, archbishop of Reims, confirms. Ansigisus, archbishop of Sens, confirms. Aurelianus, archbishop of Lyon, confirms. Rostagnus, archbishop of Arles, confirms. Sigebodus, archbishop of Narbonne, confirms. Theodoricus, archbishop of Besançon, confirms. Auterannus, archbishop of Vienne, confirms. Frotharius, archbishop of Bourges, signs. Adalaldus, archbishop of Tours, confirms. Berno, bishop of Châlons, confirms. John, archbishop of Rouen, confirms. Aldebertus, bishop of Senlis, confirms. Isaac, bishop of Langres, confirms. Ingelvinus, bishop of Paris, confirms. Otulfus, bishop of Troyes, confirms. Ingomarus, bishop of Laon, confirms.

[Col. 0795A]

Eldeboldus, bishop of Soissons, confirms. Willelmus, bishop of Limoges, confirms. Gislabertus, bishop of Chartres, confirms. Rotbertus, bishop of Valence, confirms. Garbaldus, bishop of Cavaillon, confirms. Rainelmus, bishop of Noyon, confirms. Abo, bishop of Maguelonne, confirms. Oddo, bishop of Beauvais, confirms. Girbertus, bishop of Nîmes, confirms. Walterius, bishop of Orléans, confirms. Walafredus, bishop of Uzès, confirms. Macharius, bishop of Lodève, confirms. Rotfredus, bishop of Avignon, confirms. Alaricus, bishop of Béziers, confirms. Ictarius, bishop of Viviers, confirms. Teutarius, bishop of Girona, confirms. Abo, bishop of Nevers, confirms. Frodoinus, bishop of Barcelona, confirms. Lambertus, bishop of Mâcon, confirms. John, bishop of Cambrai, confirms. Adalgarius, bishop of Autun, confirms. Barnarius, bishop of Grenoble, confirms. Ademarus, bishop of Clermont, confirms. Arnulfus, bishop of Turin, confirms. Rainelmus, bishop of Meaux, confirms. Aigofredus, bishop of Poitiers, confirms. Ainulfus, bishop of Gévaudan, confirms. George, scriniary of the holy Roman Church, who completed and finished the written record of this judgment after the witnesses’ subscriptions and the delivery had been made, confirms. Raimundus, count, confirms. Berengarius, viscount, confirms. Aimaricus confirms. Olumbellus confirms. Teutrannus confirms. Gaucelinus confirms. Emenus, viscount, confirms. Oddo, viscount, confirms. Ugo, count, confirms.

## CL. TO ALL BISHOPS, COUNTS, VISCOUNTS, CENTENARIES, AND CATHOLIC JUDGES RESIDING IN HISPANIA AND GOTHIA (878)

Law concerning sacrilegious persons, added by Pope John to the Gothic laws in the Council of Troyes.

[Col. 0795C]
