John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all bishops, counts, viscounts, centenaries, and Catholic judges residing in the provinces of Hispania and Gothia, and to all the Catholic Western people: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Know, beloved sons, that for the condition of the holy Church of God we ordered a synodal council to assemble at the city of Troyes. While we were seated there in the assembly, our son Sigebodus, bishop of the principal see of Narbonne, came before us with his suffragan bishops and brought us a book of Gothic law. Nothing was found in it concerning sacrileges, and the same laws stated that judges of that country should not hear cases concerning which those laws contained no provision. Thus the law of the holy Church was suppressed by the inhabitants of the provinces of Gaul and Hispania.

Accordingly, our serenity, together with the aforesaid bishops, examined the Roman laws, in which provisions concerning sacrileges were found, and there discovered that the emperor Justinian had established a law setting the composition for sacrilege at five pounds of the finest gold.

But we command that the milder law be observed: the law established by the pious prince Charles concerning the composition for sacrilege, namely, thirty pounds of tested silver, that is, a sum of six hundred solidi in the purest silver.

Therefore, whoever is found guilty of sacrilege shall pay this milder composition to the bishops themselves, or to abbots, or to the persons to whom the complaint of sacrilege justly belongs. If the guilty person refuses to pay it, let him remain subject to excommunication until he pays the aforesaid composition of six hundred solidi. If he dies in this obstinacy, let his body not be carried to burial with psalms and hymns.

And we command that this law be written at the end of the code of secular law.

## CLI. TO ALL THE FAITHFUL (878)

Privilege of the Church of Poitiers, so that no one may invade its goods and so that what has been taken away may be restored.

[Col. 0796B]

To all the faithful of the holy Church of God, both present and future.

Since the Roman pontificate shines forth through divine generosity for all, it is clearer than daylight that it must defend what has been granted to all. For it is an unquestionable rule of law that what has once been granted must be retained in perpetual observance.

Moreover, let the religiousness and orthodox faithfulness of all recognize that, as we have learned from the report of certain persons, the Church of Poitiers, which has long been persecuted by the pagan enemy, suffers many hardships from unjust Christians. We ought to grieve deeply over these pressures and nevertheless lift the same Church from so great a burden.

Therefore we command, and expressly order by apostolic authority, that none of you—whether enjoying the priestly order or holding military office—presume to invade any church, monastery, or estate belonging in any way to the Church of Poitiers, or dare to take away any of its tenants, male slaves, or female slaves against the will of its bishop.

Rather, let Hecfridus, bishop of that Church, and his successors be permitted, under our protection, to hold what their predecessors possessed by the legitimate path of canonical authority, to possess it as they possessed it, and to administer it as they arranged it, according to their own judgment and with the considered consent of the canons of their Church, as ancient custom is known to require—without hindrance from you, your people, or any others who have hitherto presumed such acts.

Among these matters, we wish all cases brought against the aforesaid Bishop Hecfridus concerning this affair to be brought into our presence.

If any priest, judge, or secular person, recognizing this page of our constitution, attempts to act against it, struck in the power, honor, and dignity of his office by apostolic anathema, let him be deprived of them and acknowledge himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed. And unless he either restores what he has wickedly taken, corrects what he has rashly presumed, or mourns his unlawful act with worthy repentance, let him be separated from the most sacred body of God, our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ.

[Col. 0797A]

But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who observe the rights of the aforesaid Church, so that they may receive here the fruit of good works and find the rewards of eternal peace before the supreme Judge.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of September, in the eleventh indiction, at Troyes.

## CLII. TO THE BISHOPS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT GAUL (878)

A privilege is granted to the monastery of Floriacum by the Council of Troyes.

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all bishops and the other faithful of God established throughout Gaul.

Since by apostolic succession [read: “by apostolic prompting”] [Col. 0797B] we are obliged to extend our solicitude to all the Churches, we wish to provide for the general need in such a way that we may also examine without disdain the particular causes of each. Therefore, when, because of the manifold concerns of the Church of God, we had come into the region of Gaul and reached the city of Troyes in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 878, and were celebrating a general synod of many bishops in order to cut away whatever was useless or establish ecclesiastical rights, among other matters the venerable abbot of your region, named Theotbertus, brought to our authority the following petition.

He stated that there was a monastery called Floriacum, in the district of Orléans, which a certain devout abbot named Leodebodus, a monk, had built in honor of God, of holy Mary the Mother of God, and of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles [Col. 0797C]; that, by divine revelation, the body of Saint Benedict, formerly brought there from the province of Benevento by monks of that same place, had been reverently buried there, as is established by the clearest truth; and that, for the establishment of monastic religion, the glorious emperor Charles, of pious memory, had assigned by a command of his authority to that place the properties specified therein—some of them contributed there by religious persons for the love of God—so that the monks serving the Lord there might have food and clothing.

He also stated that the father of that emperor, the most serene Augustus, of blessed memory, had established in that place, for the almsgiving of himself and his parents, a hospice for nobles, called the Porta, according to regular institution, and likewise a hospice for the poor; and that he had ordered properties suitable for carrying this out [Col. 0797D], as well as other properties for maintaining the light of the Church, to be assigned. We have found that all these provisions have hitherto been observed there by the monks already mentioned.

Now he humbly requested, both for himself and for the unanimous congregation entrusted to him—although they had obtained the privileges of many bishops to restrain the unlawful greed of anyone—that they should also receive the privileges of our authority concerning the regular abbot to be elected from among them. Therefore, desiring to use for the benefit of all the power which we have freely received from Christ, in accordance with evangelical authority, we decree, in the place of blessed Peter the apostle, that at the frequently mentioned place the servants of God may perform the service required by their religion without disturbance [Col. 0798A], according to the Rule of Father Benedict, and that the monastery be governed perpetually by its own abbots, namely, monks regularly elected from that same monastery.

Nor shall they ever suffer from anyone any diminution of those properties which are specified by name in the aforesaid command, or which the venerable abbot Theotbertus, now abbot of that place, has assigned to the purposes of the aforesaid monastery, or of those properties which may henceforth be donated to the same place by any religious persons. If anyone should presume to violate this benefaction of ours and divert the stipends of the servants of God to other uses, we separate him from apostolic communion by the penalty of anathema, so that, unless he corrects himself immediately after being admonished, he may be excluded from the kingdom of God with the rapacious and suffer the torments he deserves. [Col. 0798B]

But so that this privilege may possess certain validity and confer security upon God’s servants in the aforesaid monastery of Floriacum for as long as God and our Lord shall have willed His Church to endure, we have strengthened it with our subscription. Written by the hand of George, notary of the holy apostolic see, in the month of August, in the eleventh indiction. Farewell in the Lord. Given on the Nones of September through the hand of Walbertus, most humble bishop of the holy Church of Porto, in the sixth year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of our lord John, supreme pontiff and universal pope, in the most holy see of blessed Peter the apostle, in the eleventh indiction.

### CLIII. TO WALA, OR WALON, BISHOP OF METZ. (Year 878.) He grants him the pallium to be worn on specified days.

[Col. 0798C]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Wala, venerable bishop of the Church of the Mediomatrici, which is also called Metz, in honor, namely, of Saint Stephen, the first martyr.

If shepherds of sheep, content to endure sun and frost day and night for the protection of their flock, constantly watch with vigilant eyes lest any of them perish by straying or be carried off, torn apart by the bites of wild beasts, with how much labor and care ought we to remain watchful, who are called shepherds of souls? Let us attend to the office we have undertaken and not cease to show ourselves diligent in guarding the Lord’s sheep, lest on the day of divine judgment the guilt of negligence on account of our laziness torment us before the supreme Shepherd—an office by which [Col. 0798D] we are now judged more exalted than others in the reverence of honor.

We have granted the pallium to your fraternity, according to custom, for celebrating the solemnities of Mass, for the days of your life alone. We grant you permission to use it—not your Church—while its privileges remain otherwise intact. Since the honor of the garment must be preserved by the modest vitality of one’s actions, we exhort you to make it correspond to the adornments of your character, so that, with God as author, you may be distinguished in both respects.

Therefore, let your life be a rule for your sons. By always considering themselves in it, may they advance, so that what they have lived well may appear, after the Lord, to be yours. Let them correct themselves, lest they be elated by the prosperity that temporally flatters, or cast down by adversity; but whatever it may be, let them overcome it by the virtue of patience. Let no place be found with you for hatred, nor any indiscriminate favor.

Accordingly, under this condition, we grant your fraternity permission to be vested from the secretarium to the holy altar, and from the altar to the secretarium, just as the ancient custom of being vested in the pallium [read: *palliatis*, “clothed,” HARD.] existed. By the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, you shall have this permission, as we have said, for the days of your life, under our jurisdiction and control.

We have not judged that this apostolic privilege granted to you gives your successors any right or custom. Nor shall any bishop or archbishop stir up a dispute or contention against you on this account. Thus, with the Lord guiding and directing your heart, strive to carry out the governance entrusted to you, so that, having obtained the office of this honor, you may take still greater care to adorn it with dignity and uprightness of character. [Col. 0799B]

Written by the hand of George, notary of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of September, in the twelfth indiction. Given on the eighth day before the Ides of September through the hand of Walpertus, most humble bishop of the holy Church of Porto, in the sixth year, by the Lord’s favor, of the pontificate of our lord John, supreme pontiff and universal pope, in the most holy see of blessed Peter the apostle, in the twelfth indiction.

This is the year 878. However, either September must be changed to October, or the twelfth indiction to the eleventh; as you will learn from the privileges of Floriacum, Chalon, and others, although we do not deny that in ancient charters careless notaries or scribes sometimes extended the indiction as far as Christmas Day or the day before the Kalends of January.

### CLIV. (Year 878.) The excommunication of Hugh and Emmo.

[Col. 0799C]

We deprive Hugh, formerly son of King Lothair—not legitimate, but natural, begotten through an adulterous union—who, after giving an oath, appears to have lied to our beloved son Louis, king of the Franks, and to be disturbing the peaceful kingdom of the aforesaid king; and Emmo, brother of Count Bernard and his accomplice in these excesses, of all Christian communion, unless within thirty days they return to the aforesaid senior lord and desist from disturbing the kingdom. If afterward they persist, let them know that they are to be bound by the chains of anathema. Given, etc.

### CLV. TO COUNT BERNARD. (Year 878.) He orders him to come with certain others to the synod at which Frotarius, bishop of Bourges, wished to clear himself of the charge of infidelity brought against him.

[Col. 0799D]

To Count Bernard.

It has been reported to our pontificate, through the account of a man, that Frotarius, venerable bishop, preferred to hand over the city of Bourges to the enemies of your senior lord, Louis, the glorious king, and that for this reason you had hastened there yourself. For the aforesaid bishop has now sought to lodge a complaint with us and with the aforementioned most glorious king, saying that he wished to submit himself and his people to justice concerning everything alleged against you [Col. 0800A] regarding disloyalty to your and his senior lord.

Therefore we send this exhortation and command by apostolic authority that you make every effort to come in person to this hearing and assembly, bringing with you Viscount Girard, Umbertus, Aguvarnus, and Ingelbertus, against whom he himself is making complaint, so that now, before us and before the frequently mentioned glorious king, whatever has been done contrary to divine and human right may nevertheless be brought to an end, both by canonical judgment and by the enactment of human law. Given as above.

### CLVI. (Year 878.) The excommunication of Count Bernard.

We declare Bernard, the sacrilegious son of Bernard and Belihildis, an invader of sacred ecclesiastical property and an opponent of the royal power ordained by God, to be alienated from the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ and separate him from all Christian fellowship until he approaches to make fitting satisfaction and amendment.

He had been summoned three times by his own archbishop Frotarius, from whom he took away both the city and everything he possessed; he had been recalled twice by our apostolic authority and once by the royal majesty, yet he refused to come and remained in his obstinacy. He also tyrannically extorted from his men, by flattery and threats, an oath that was damnable and to be condemned, against divine and human law. [Col. 0800B]

If he does not amend even now, and attempts to retain by force the things which, guilty as he is, he so grievously took away from the common possession of his faithful, and to oppose his faithful in this matter [Col. 0800C], we bind him with the bond of anathema by the authority of the Holy Spirit [addition: “by authority”]. Whoever communicates or agrees with him against this excommunication, we cannot prevent from being subjected to the same excommunication as those who communicate with excommunicated persons.

### CLVII. TO ADALARD, ARCHBISHOP OF TOURS. (Year 878.) He confirms the privileges granted to the Church of Tours.

To the most reverend and holy Adalard, venerable archbishop of Tours, and to your successors, as well as to all the faithful of the holy Church of God, present and future.

It is fitting that the Roman Church, which is the mother of all the Churches of God, should stand all the more firmly in pious mercy the more splendidly it flourishes in dignity, so that whatever the faithful rightly request may deservedly be granted by us with compassion and without delay.

We wish all your religiousness to know faithfully that the priests of the district of Tours came to our pontifical presence, petitioning us to confirm by apostolic authority for them both the royal capitulary and the document of the co-bishops, according to which every church ought to have its own holding with four dependents, three aripennia of vineyards, an equal amount of meadow, and a cemetery with dwellings, without any personal or civil exaction being demanded, except service to God alone in ecclesiastical matters, as the ancient authority of the canons and [Col. 0801A] modern practice grant; and that wherever the properties named above appear to have been donated in ancient times and taken away in the present, they should be restored without any delay or tardiness by pontifical authority and royal power.

Moved by their prayers, we wish and expressly command by apostolic authority that the aforesaid documents—delivered from our pontificate, confirmed by the co-bishops, and ordered by the kings—be valid and observed in every respect. If anyone should prove to be a violator of this apostolic decree through reckless presumption, then, if he is a priest, let him be deprived of his proper honor and, deprived of Christian communion, bound by the bond of anathema; if he is a layman, let him likewise be tormented with eternal damnation together with Judas the betrayer. But may the protector enjoy in every respect perpetual blessing from the princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul.

### CLVIII. TO VARIOUS BISHOPS. (Year 878.) That they compel the invaders of the property of the Church of Tours to restore it and to pay the ninths and tithes.

[Col. 0801B]

To the most reverend and holy Frotarius, archbishop of Bourges; Anselm, bishop of Limoges; Hecfridus, bishop of Poitiers; Dodo, bishop of Angers; Rotbertus, bishop of Le Mans; Hildeprandus, bishop of Sées; and likewise to all the other bishops and counts, and to other distinguished persons, faithful of the holy Church of God, in whose dioceses the estates of Saint Maurice of the Church of Tours [now Saint Gatianus, HARD.] appear to be situated.

Let the religiousness of all of you, or the faithfulness of all, know that, as the venerable archbishop Adalard related, our pontificate has learned that certain persons—both counts and their subjects—are holding, without the authority of any law, the property of Saint Maurice of the Church of Tours, which they have invaded by reckless presumption. Therefore we command and expressly order by our apostolic authority that you first admonish those invaders to make every effort to restore those properties to the aforesaid Church, setting aside every excuse.

If they should refuse to listen, then all of you, united and gathered together in one assembly as far as possible, must excommunicate them by our decree until they restore the properties unjustly retained by them. If—and this we do not believe—they prove disobedient to these censures, delay coming to make satisfaction, and refuse to render justice for what they have done, judge by our authority that they are excluded from all Christian communion. [Col. 0801D]

Meanwhile, also admonish them not to delay paying the ninths and tithes, according to ancient custom, to those to whom they ought to pay them, setting aside unlawful excuses. Finally, we declare that you must defend from all enemies all the properties of the aforesaid Church of Saint Maurice that exist in your dioceses; for if you act otherwise and do not obey our decree, you will be struck down by canonical sanction.

### CLIX. TO THE BISHOPS OF BRITANNIA. (Year 878.) He reproves them for withdrawing from the jurisdiction of the archbishop of Tours and invading his property; he orders them henceforth to obey him and seek his pardon for their offenses.

[Col. 0802A]

To Mahen, bishop of Dol, and to all the bishops of Britannia, or to all the faithful of the holy Church of God.

We wish to make known the sanctity or fidelity of all of you: while we were celebrating a synod at Troyes, at the petition of our fellow bishop, Archbishop Adalard, we heard that, despising your mother, the Church of Tours, you delay obeying it according to ancient custom; that you are attempting to break the privilege granted to it over you by blessed Peter the apostle; that you neglect to show your archbishop the honor due to him; and that, adding evil to evil, you do not fear to seize estates from the head mentioned above. [Col. 0802B]

We also heard, both from the aforesaid bishop and from other co-bishops who reported similarly, that you had not been consecrated by your metropolitan according to ancient custom, but that, after legitimate bishops had been expelled from their sees, one was consecrated by another solely through the power of your duke.

We were astonished at this; and, if it is so, we shall erase such great wickedness and, unless you make satisfaction, shall nevertheless impose punishment, because you appear to have been not shepherds but invaders. Therefore we admonish and expressly command by apostolic authority that, returning to your right mind, you return to your mother, the holy Church of Tours, strive to obey it according to ancient custom, and seek mercy from your archbishop Adalard for what you have committed up to now, so that you may be able to obtain forgiveness from the supreme Judge for all your negligences. [Col. 0802C]

For if you act otherwise, you will nevertheless be struck by canonical authority, alienated in every respect from our communion, and all your ordinations will have to be rejected by the supreme apostolic see. Given as above.

### CLX. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS OF ARLES AND NARBONNE. (Year 878.) That they canonically settle the case between the bishops of Uzès and Avignon.

To Rostagnus, venerable archbishop of Arles, and Sigebodus, archbishop of Narbonne.

It is known to your holiness how Walefredus, bishop of the Church of Uzès, presented to the synod which, with God’s help, we celebrated at Troyes a written complaint against Ractefredus, bishop of Avignon, alleging that he had taken away from him a certain estate belonging to his see, or diocese. But because Ractefredus, against whom the complaint had been made, was absent from the synod, we therefore command your fraternity by apostolic authority that, having assembled a number of bishops, you bring their case to an end by canonical judgment.

You must examine and determine the invasion arising from so great a presumption in such a way that none of your bishops may thereafter attempt to rise up against canonical precepts without danger to himself. You too must determine this judgment in person together with your bishops.

We are sending you certain chapters collected on the authority of the Fathers, according to which you must judge without delay, so that you do not take on unnecessary labor in such a case. We wish your fraternity good health in Christ.

### CLXI. PRIVILEGE FOR THE MONASTERY OF VÉZELAY. (Year 878.) The immunities formerly granted are confirmed.

[In Acherius, *Spicilegium*.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Eudo, venerable abbot of the monastery of Vézelay, and to the entire congregation of that monastery, forever.

Whenever things are requested from us that unquestionably conform to reason, we ought to grant them willingly and provide fitting assistance to the desires of those who ask. Therefore, because you requested from us [Col. 0803B] that we should establish a privilege of the apostolic see for the monastery of Vézelay, over which you are known to preside—a monastery which was formerly built by Gerard, a most noble and most Christian man, and by his wife Berta, in honor of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ and in veneration of the most blessed ever-virgin Mary, mother of that same Lord Jesus Christ, in the kingdom of Burgundy, in the district of Aval—

and which was bestowed by the aforesaid founders upon blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, through pious devotion and by a written testament [the source repeats: “which was bestowed ... by a written testament, we ought to make”]—we have been moved by your prayers and willingly decreed that this should be done.

By this privilege of the apostolic see we confirm and establish that no king, no bishop, no count, nor anyone else may disturb that monastery [Col. 0803C], or diminish, take away, or apply to his own uses, under any pretext or occasion whatsoever, those things which have been offered there by the founders already mentioned or by other faithful persons, or which may happen to be offered in the future. Rather, we wish and command that these things be possessed without disturbance for the support of that monastery and for the uses of the abbots and monks serving God there under the Rule of Saint Father Benedict.

This is on the following condition: no successor of ours as pontiff in this holy see, in which by God’s authority we serve, shall ever or anywhere allow any of those properties to be granted as a benefice to anyone, exchanged, or conceded under any form of rent in times to come. Instead, our successors, receiving only the rent assigned in the founders’ deed of gift by which they made this holy Roman Church heir of the same monastery—namely, one pound of silver each year—must strive, through the support of fatherly care and vigilant pastoral concern, to protect that monastery against all who attack it.

We also establish that, when the abbot of the aforesaid monastery dies, no other person shall be installed there through any artifice of concealment, except one whom the consent of the monks, in the fear of God and according to the institution of the Rule of Saint Benedict, has chosen and whom the pontiff of this apostolic see has judged should be ordained, or whom he has agreed to install at the monks’ petition.

We add this provision to the present chapter in order to exclude avarice: no king, no bishop or priest, nor any faithful person, either personally or through an intermediary, may dare to receive anything under any guise as a gift in connection with the appointment of that abbot or of clerics or priests, the distribution of chrism, the consecration of the basilica, or any matters whatsoever belonging to the same monastery. Nor may the abbot himself presume to give anything for his appointment, lest on this pretext the things offered by the faithful to the pious place be consumed.

Nor may the bishop of that city or diocese celebrate public Masses there unless invited by the abbot of that monastery; nor may he announce stations in the same monastery, lest the peace of God’s servants in any way be disturbed by a popular gathering; nor may he presume to demand provisions or lodging dues from it. [Col. 0804B]

As for receiving the faithful and religious men, and showing the hospitality which the Apostle commands to be offered to all according to the capacity of the place and its resources, we not only do not forbid this from taking place there, but also encourage it. Yet the size of the congregation must be maintained in such a way that neither an excessive number brings poverty upon the inhabitants nor too small a number brings desolation upon the place.

We also confirm by our authority the privilege granted to the same monastery by our predecessor, Pope Nicholas, of pious memory, except only that he granted it under the designation of the handmaids of God, who, because of the frequent assaults of the world, cannot now remain there in an orderly manner. We, however, for the sake of more suitable usefulness, decree that they should appropriately live under the monastic habit. [Col. 0804C]

If any king, bishop, priest, abbot, judge, count, or secular person should attempt to act against this document of our institution, struck by apostolic anathema, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power or honor and acknowledge himself guilty before the divine judgment; and unless he laments the things he has wrongly done, let him be separated from the most sacred body of our Lord Jesus Christ and subjected to the strict vengeance of eternal judgment.

But may there be peace from our Lord Jesus Christ for all who preserve the rights of that place, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and find with the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace.

Given through the hand of Walpertus, most humble bishop of the holy Church of Porto, on the third day before the Kalends of October [Col. 0804D], in the sixth year of that lord John, pope, in the twelfth indiction. Written through the hand of George, regional notary and notary of the holy Roman Church.

### CLXII. TO WIBBODUS, BISHOP. (Year 878.) He commends his faith, urges him to send a legate before coming to meet Carolomannus, and orders him also to attend the meeting.

To the most reverend and holy Wibbodus, venerable bishop.

From the reading of your letters and from the report of their bearer, your man, I have learned that you are most devoted and, as always, most faithful; for this we thank you and, with God’s help, shall repay you. Meanwhile, admonishing and exhorting you, we urge you to complete what you have begun and, before we speak with Carolomannus, to make every effort to send your legate with letters, and to strive to be present in the meeting, wherever it may take place. We wish your holiness good health in Christ, especially in this matter. Given as above.

### CLXIII–CLXIV. PRIVILEGE FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT MARCELLUS. (Year 878.)

[In Perry, *Histoire de Chalon-sur-Saône*, among the preliminary documents, p. 32.]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Deodatus, venerable levite and provost of the monastery of Saint Marcellus, situated in the territory of Chalon, at the places called Floriacum and Vallis Magnimontensis, and Gibriacum, with everything subject and belonging to them that pertains to the aforesaid place of Floriacum, and likewise at Boscrontum in the territory of Chalon.

Because your devotion, together with the entire congregation of Saint Marcellus, humbly requested that we confirm by apostolic authority, with kindly compassion, for that place a privilege concerning all the properties situated there, cultivated or uncultivated, with waters and watercourses, both in the territory of Chalon and in that of Beaune and Magnimont, as stated above, and also in the territories of Dijon and Lyon, we, moved by God and inclined toward your pious petitions, grant for you and your successors to the aforesaid place also the ninths and tithes, in the manner established by the ancient custom of preceding bishops or expected by those within whose dioceses the inhabitants of the aforesaid places appear to possess anything by their own right, according to the commands of kings and the donations of individual persons, which appear to have been legally granted by others before the donation or justly conceded afterward.

But so that they may remain more securely and peacefully in God’s service, we wish these brothers and spiritual co-inhabitants to remain free from every disturbance. Let no one of the kings, counts, or other leading men of the kingdom, powerful under any badge of dignity, dare or presume in any way or by any device to oppose these petitions which we have granted for God’s sake. What we indicate with the affection of fatherly compassion ought to be strengthened by the assent of our sons and must not, God forbid, be rashly violated in anything through rebellion against heaven or opposed by proud transgression.

Granted to Deodatus and to the entire congregation of the aforesaid place, while Lord John was seated in the apostolic see, in the sixth year, in the twelfth indiction. If anyone henceforth attempts to act against this privilege of ours, unless he comes to his senses within the appointed time, let him know that he is canonically to be bound by the chains of anathema.

+ Farewell. + On the Nones of October, through the hand of Walpertus, most humble bishop of the holy Church of Porto, in the year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of our lord John, supreme pontiff and universal pope, in the most holy see of blessed Peter the apostle, the sixth, in the twelfth indiction.

### CLXV. TO COUNT SUPPO. (Year 878.) He instructs him to come to meet him at Mount Cenis [Cinisium] and to urge the empress Angelberga and the bishops of Milan and Parma to do the same, so that together they may discuss matters relating to the Church’s welfare.

[Col. 0806A]

To his most beloved son, the glorious Count Suppo.

Because we, in whom, by God’s dispensation, the ends of the ages have arrived, are driven by various movements and pushed by storms of many waves on account of the condition of the holy Churches of God, yet are not abandoned because of Him who strengthens us, Christ Jesus, we have come hastening toward Gaul, preserving the faith of our predecessors toward the Frankish people, in order to bind the hearts of kings together by the bond of peace and unity.

But we see fulfilled what we read in the Gospel: “Because iniquity has abounded, the charity of many grows cold” (Matthew 24). Therefore, with the utmost confidence in your affection and proven faith, we command you to come as quickly as possible to meet us at Mount Cenis, with the service appropriate to your dignity, so that, meeting together, we may, with the Lord’s permission, discuss whatever is fitting for the common good. At the same time, entreat our beloved daughter Angelberga, the empress, and Anspertus, archbishop of Milan, Wibbodus, bishop of Parma, and the other faithful and friends to do likewise. Given as above.

### CLXVI. TO WIBBODUS, PAULUS, PAULUS, AND LUIDOINUS, BISHOPS. (Year 878.) He orders them to come to Pavia for the synod.

[Col. 0806C]

To the most reverend and holy Wibbodus, venerable bishop of Parma; Paulus, bishop of Piacenza; Paulus, bishop of Reggio; and Liudoinus, bishop of Modena.

We wish your holiness to know that we came to Turin on the eighth day before the Kalends of December; from there, God leading us, we shall come to Pavia, and there celebrate a synod concerning the condition of the Churches of God. Therefore we send this message and expressly command by apostolic authority that, on the fourth day before the Nones of December, you must be present there at the synod, setting aside every excuse. Whoever first carries this letter must transmit it to another with all haste. Take care not to act otherwise, for if you do, you will be struck by canonical force. Given as above.

### CLXVII. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF PAVIA. (Year 878.) That he come to meet him at Turin and send letters written by him to certain bishops so that they may come to the council.

[Col. 0807A]

To the most reverend and holy John, bishop of Pavia.

We wish it to be known to your holiness that we are now staying in the city of Turin. Furthermore, we direct you not to delay coming to meet us immediately, setting aside every excuse. Take care lest you perhaps be deceived by anyone’s prompting—something we scarcely believe—on behalf of the archbishop of Milan, since you are especially our own and directly attached to us. And because you depend on no one’s authority except ours [the source lacks *jubeo*, “I order,” or something similar], we direct you to ensure that you send as quickly as possible a letter to the suffragan bishops of the Church of Ravenna, to Paulus of Piacenza, and likewise to Paulus of Reggio and Liudoinus of Modena, so that they may come to Pavia on the appointed day, in order that we may discuss the condition of the holy Churches of God and their common and universal welfare. Given as above.

### CLXVIII. TO ANSPERTUS, ARCHBISHOP. (Year 878.) He recounts the labors undertaken for the Church and urges him to come to meet him at Pavia with all his bishops.

[Col. 0807B]

To the most reverend and holy fellow bishop Anspertus, venerable archbishop of Milan.

Your pious fraternity knows more clearly than light itself how much we ought always to labor and keep watch for the condition of the entire holy Church of God and for the whole flock of the Lord, for which almighty God did not spare His own Son but handed Him over for us all, and concerning which the apostle John exhorts us, saying: “Because He laid down His life for us, we also ought to lay down our lives for the brothers” (1 John 3).

Therefore, insofar as it has been and is within us by divine grace, from the time when His heavenly mercy placed us over His Church, we have never spared our life, nor have we ever avoided harsh dangers. Rather, night and day, scorched by heat [Col. 0807C] and frost, lest we present to the Lord anything that had been seized by a beast or torn apart, we have endured the waves of the sea for the liberation and salvation of all of you.

We also came to Francia and addressed the sons of the kings, some in person, some by letters and legates—all of them, namely, both Louises, Carolomannus, and Charles. After receiving their common counsel, we arranged that Boso, the glorious prince and count, should accompany us on our journey until, with Christ’s help, we returned to the City.

And because there are matters concerning the condition of the holy Church which we must discuss together, we command your holiness by apostolic authority to come to meet us at Pavia, together with all your suffragans and co-bishops, on the second day after the feast of Saint Andrew. Since the proven faith of all your predecessors toward the Roman pontiff was always steadfast, let your fraternity strive in every way to follow their footsteps in all things; for, God forbid, if it should be otherwise, canonical force cannot fail to remain against the disobedient. Given as above.

### CLXIX. TO COUNT SUPPO. (Year 878.) He is surprised that Suppo did not meet him as he should have; informs him about what he arranged with King Louis; and urges him to come to him.

To his beloved son, the illustrious Count Suppo.

Why, dearest son, your affection closed the road to us, and why, when you heard that we had come into your territories, you did not hasten to meet us [Col. 0808A], we wonder, since we have always known you to have shown such care in all our affairs; and whenever you had heard that we were nearby, you used to hasten to us, setting aside all your own important business.

Therefore we understand that you did this not from your heart but out of loyalty to your senior lord, and for that reason we spare you. For, as you have heard—and we too have already informed you by letter—we celebrated a synod in the regions of Gaul. We also spoke with Louis, the glorious king, who gave us Boso, a most prudent man and a prince closely connected with him in every respect, so that he might send us safely to the City without interference from the accursed Lambert; and with him we certainly came in peace.

We are sending this exhortation and, by our request, urge you to come in person to us, according to your custom, setting aside all other concerns and every excuse, and also to encourage the others to whom we are sending apostolic letters to do likewise. For, God knows, we wish to speak with you for no other reason than that we may consider together with you the condition of the holy Churches of God and the peace of the commonwealth. Nevertheless, make every effort to come before the others, so that whatever we do with them we may first settle familiarly with you. Given as above.

### CLXX. TO COUNT BERENGAR. (Year 878.) He commends Berengar’s affection toward the Roman Church, reports the synod held in Gaul and his safe return, and urges him to hasten to him.

[Col. 0808C]

To his beloved son, the illustrious Count Berengar.

From the report of certain persons, especially of this Count Wido, our counsellor, we have learned that your devotion may cause the charity which you have always shown toward us and toward our Church, your mother, to grow ever greater. For this we give thanks and urge you to advance. For you have heard on what account we celebrated a synod in the regions of Gaul and addressed the glorious King Louis, who gave us this Boson, a most prudent prince and in every respect closely allied to him, so that, with God’s help, he might send us safely to the city of Rome without hindrance from the accursed Lambert, anathematized by the holy Church of God. With him, certainly, we came peacefully.

Moreover, we send admonition and, in asking, exhort you: laying aside all other concerns, strive to come personally to us. For, God knows, we desire to address you for no other reason than that, together with you, we may discuss with honour the condition of the holy Churches of God and the peace of the commonwealth. Given as above.

## CLXXI. TO ANSPERT, ARCHBISHOP OF MILAN. (878)

He rebukes him because he did not bring him aid; and now for the third time he warns him to meet him at Pavia on a fixed day, with his suffragan bishops.

To our most reverend and most holy brother, ANSPERT, venerable archbishop of Milan.

How much your kindly fraternity ought to cooperate and agree with the holy Apostolic See, our predecessor, blessed Pope Gelasius, wrote to bishops who disregarded the affliction of their brethren, threatening them in these words:

“Why did you not have compassion on so many of your brothers? Why did you not approach the emperor? Why did you not lay down your life for your brothers, when you have been commanded to lay it down for the flock entrusted to you? Why did you not make yourselves a wall for the house of Israel, so that you might stand in battle on the day of the Lord?”

Therefore, having at last cast off negligence, return yourselves to the former struggle, hastening to bring aid to your brothers. These examples and others like them ought to have stirred your fraternity; and while we labour for the condition of the whole holy Church of God, you ought—and ought already—to have joined us not merely unwillingly, but willingly.

But now, after this third admonition, make every effort to meet us at Pavia on the coming Thursday, together with your brothers and fellow bishops, hearing the zeal for God that I endure on behalf of you all, and my grief, so that we may do whatever Almighty God shall hereafter decree through your common counsel.

Let no doubt dwell in your heart, dearest brother. Believe in my faith and in my priesthood: nothing contrary to your dignity and honour will in any way be brought against you. For, if—as we do not wish—you attempt to disregard these matters, after such great patience you will be [subject to canonical punishment]. [Note: Perhaps “to be corrected by canonical disciplinary action,” or something similar is missing.]

. . .

## CLXXII. TO COUNT BERENGAR. 

He recounts the labours undertaken for the Church.

To his beloved son BERENGAR, glorious count, and to all the nobles of the Lombard kingdom who are faithful to the holy Church of God.

How much and how greatly the Roman Church—your mother, that is—has thus far suffered at the hands of the most impious Christians, you have already heard both from our letters reporting it and from the report of the people. But, so that you may know more certainly, we report it again.

For this reason, and for the salvation of all of you, we have not spared our lives. Since, as circumstances required, we could not come to you by land, you being nearer to the aforementioned persecutors, we have taken the sea route and are going to Francia, seeking tranquillity and assistance, where our predecessors, the pontiffs, sought it.

For we sent to all the kings—that is, to Louis, son of the lord Emperor Charles, and to Carloman and Louis, and to Charles and Louis, the king’s sons—that they should come to us with their bishops and discuss these matters together with us. Of them, King Louis came; and, grieving deeply over such evils, he would have come with us himself had he not been ill. But since he could not on account of his illness, he gave us this Boson, closely allied to him in every respect, who would lead me safely through the enemies of the holy Church of God.

For, with God’s help, we have come to Pavia. Therefore we send admonition and, by apostolic authority, exhorting you, command you now for the third time, dearest ones, that you come personally to us as to a father; and that each of you urge the others to come, while the first who reads this letter should arrange for it to be sent on to the others.

Thus, when you have come, we may celebrate a synod together with you and discuss the condition of the holy Churches of God, the peace of the commonwealth, and the salvation of us all, yours and ours. In these matters, dearest sons, do not let your charity grow lukewarm, nor your religious devotion become disobedient; rather, show the compassion and grief that are required. For it is written how the lukewarm person is rightly to be vomited out, how through disobedience there can be guilt where none previously existed, and how one who does not show compassion is struck by pontifical decree. Given as above.

## CLXXIII. TO LOUIS THE STAMMERER, KING. (878)

He commends the devotion and service shown toward him by Count Boson and Bishop Agilmar, by whom he had been escorted into Italy.

To his most beloved son LOUIS, most glorious king, son of the Emperor Charles, of blessed memory.

We cannot explain in a few words how greatly we love you and how much affection of charity we hold toward you. Yet we wish your exalted glory to know this: just as we promised, we continually preserve toward you an unfailing devotion and ardour of charity.

Meanwhile, we offer a thousand thanks to your Serenity for Boson, our beloved and common son, and faithful servant. In obedience to our common commands, he acted so prudently and strove to obey us in everything that, as a true cultivator of the Christian religion, he did not spare his own life or soul, but willingly entrusted himself to death for the holy Church and the common fidelity, without hesitation; and, with God’s favour, he led us securely as far as Ticinum.

Therefore, dearest son and porphyry-clad king, we beseech the height of your excellence that, if circumstances require it, you provide him, as your Sublimity has deigned to promise us, with the assistance of fighting men for defeating our enemies. For it is right that all should provide aid to the one man who alone does not cease labouring for all.

We therefore most highly commend to your Excellence the bearer of this letter, Agilmar, venerable bishop, [Note: Agilmar. From the subscriptions of the Synod of Troyes and from a precept of Charles the Fat in the year 885, we understand that he was bishop of Clermont. Sirmond.] so that he and his Church may increase in the growth of perfection. In all our necessities he has been second to none, and we have found him most faithful to you in everything of which he has had knowledge.

Meanwhile, know that, apart from Agilmar, none of the bishops whom your Serenity ordered to come to our assistance has come. Therefore let the royal judgement of your exalted power compel them by its authority to come as quickly as possible to Rome in a hostile [perhaps: synodal] manner, so that henceforth they may learn to offer obedience fittingly to the Apostolic See and to royal Excellence.

## CLXXIV. TO KING LOUIS. (878)

He is astonished that he has not restored to Boson’s daughters the inheritance legally owed to them, for which he had previously petitioned; and he again warns him to restore the entire inheritance to them.

To the glorious King LOUIS, son of the glorious King Louis [the transmitted reading is corrupt].

We have already admonished your greatness, dearest son, by apostolic letters, exhorting you to take care to restore the properties to the daughters of Boson, formerly count, and of his wife Ingeltrudis, to whom the inheritance is granted by the authority of all laws as legally devolving upon them.

But, as we see, we have remained unheard—which astonishes us, and in our astonishment grieves us—although your offspring always obeys apostolic censures and, above all kings, renders judgement. As King David sang: “The king loves judgement” (Psalm 96).

Have you not read: “For the Lord loves justice, and his face beholds equity”? (Psalm 10.)

Moreover, we have heard the complaint of the daughters of the aforesaid Boson: that you retain some of the properties belonging to them and to their mother Ingeltrudis, while permitting others to be held by those to whom she herself, after the judgement pronounced against her and without her husband’s consent, gave them. This is wicked and wholly contrary to the authority of all laws.

For what can a wife do without her husband’s consent? How much more so a woman committing adultery, who, by divine judgement and on the sentence of our predecessor, the lord Pope Nicholas, perished (Nicholas, Letter 64; Regino, Book II of the Chronicle), and who ought also to have been punished under human law for the adultery committed?

Have not Pope John of Rome and the illustrious Emperor Justinian, when establishing Roman law, written as follows: “The property of those condemned for a capital crime ought not to be assigned for the profit of the governor, but returned to the relatives of the condemned”? And elsewhere: “In taking an inheritance, sons are to be preferred to relatives of every degree.”

Thus it is plainly evident, most glorious king, that neither you nor their relatives, but only the daughters themselves, who are legitimate, ought to possess those estates. Those, however, who were born after their crime are bastards and ought not to inherit, as the aforesaid pope and emperor wrote: “We judge bastards to be most injurious, most bitter, and always unworthy of our times.”

Therefore, as we asked, we ask again and again, and warning, we exhort your royal dignity to heed the complaints and groans of these women. For reverence toward the princes of the apostles, from whom they sought assistance, and for love of us, restore to them in full the properties that you call estates, and arrange for your men to restore them without any excuse. Given as above.

## CLXXV. TO HUGH. (878)

He warns him to settle the dispute that has arisen between Abbo and others.

To HUGH, noble abbot, born of an illustrious lineage.

Because we love you greatly, we rejoice with you and care for your soul; therefore we take pains to admonish you. [Perhaps: the dispute] . . . which has arisen between the parents of Bishop Abbo and Rotbert and Roclinus, should be corrected by royal [perhaps: with the addition “clemency”] rather than by vengeance. For an evil once committed under necessity ought not, in accordance with that necessity, to be expiated by further wrongdoing, but should be more mercifully remitted for pardon. Let your glorious nobility act as befits the dignity of so great a nature. Given as above.

## CLXXVI. TO ROMANUS, ELECTED ARCHBISHOP OF RAVENNA. (878)

He rejoices that he has been elected archbishop of Ravenna; orders him to promise nothing to anyone on account of the election; instructs him to arrange for his letter to Leo and the Romans to be delivered, and to send their reply to him; and orders that the property of the dukes John and Deusdedit be restored.

To ROMANUS, outstanding Levite, elected by the faithful of Ravenna, our people.

Having received and read your letter, beloved son, in which we learned that John, archbishop of Ravenna, had died, we grieved greatly, and we exhort you and your people to pray for him.

We rejoice, indeed, at your unanimous election; and because you sent us word by visiting us, reporting the health of our faithful and demonstrating your devotion, we give thanks.

Moreover, we admonish and expressly declare that, since by the favour of the supreme Shepherd you have now been elected for this task, so that you may become a shepherd, you must keep watch and labour in that Church. You must make no promise whatsoever, whether to great or small, whether to your fellow citizens or to any other persons, because that is simony, and this will in no way be hidden from us. If you do so, we adjure you by the apostles: we shall not bless you.

Meanwhile, we wish you to send this letter, addressed to Leo, the venerable bishop-envoy and apocrisiary, and transmitted to the other Romans, to them personally through your legate. When he returns, if possible—or another person with their letters—send him to us, beloved [perhaps: with the letters addressed to us]. He will then be able to announce to you with certainty our arrival.

Therefore we also wish you, for love of these faithful of ours and of our counsellors, namely the glorious dukes Deusdedit and John, to save and defend their property and persons to the best of your ability, and to restore in full whatever they have hitherto held under occupation. Since they serve him whose service they enjoy, it is fitting that they should also enjoy the aid of his protection. [Note: The passage is corrupt.]

Given as above.

## CLXXVII. TO THE PEOPLE OF RAVENNA. (878)

He grieves at the death of their bishop; he warns them to honour suitably the archbishop elected by them; and to defend the Church of Ravenna and the property of the dukes Deusdedit and John.

To the priests, senate, and people of Ravenna, our faithful.

Having heard of the death of the bishop of Ravenna, your father, that is, we grieve greatly; we exhort you to pray for him. Seeing your customary and great fidelity toward us flourishing in unity, we rejoice even more, and we shall strive with all our will that the Almighty, through the intercession of the princes of the apostles, may restore to you the father whom you desire.

Moreover, we admonish and exhort you, and expressly command that the man whom you have unanimously elected, as you have written, you should unanimously retain as your elected bishop, love him, and honour him according to your custom. Until, with God’s favour, the presence of our pontificate shines upon your desire, defend the Church of Ravenna against all enemies and, as far as you can, relieve it from plunder, so that the Church itself may suffer no depredation. We shall never leave this unpunished, and by every means we shall strike the plunderers and those who harbour plunderers with the force of law.

Moreover, we command you to preserve the movable and immovable property and the chattels of Deusdedit and John, our counsellors, the glorious dukes, and to defend their men, making no encroachment upon those possessions that they have hitherto held under occupation. Since they serve us, they ought by every means to enjoy our protection. As for the guardian of this command, the favour of the corrupter will be nothing to the one who carries it out. [Note: The passage is corrupt.]

## CLXXVIII. TO THE JUDGES AND DUKES OF RAVENNA. (878)

He orders them to defend the city courageously against Lambert.

To all the judges and dukes, and to the people dwelling at Ravenna, our faithful.

We wish to know your diligence and the fidelity of all of you. For we have heard from the report of certain persons that John the deacon and chartularius has gone astray and is recruiting Lambert’s Franks against our election. Therefore we send word and command by apostolic authority that all of you must stand together unanimously in fidelity and defend the city itself, so that no one who does not stand with you may allow Lambert’s Franks to be brought inside, nor may Lambert himself in any way gain access there, nor may any of his men enter.

Act in these matters as you wish to have the grace of God and of us. For whoever acts otherwise will have both our anger and will pay one thousand byzants to our palace. Given as above.

## CLXXIX. TO THE BISHOPS THEODORIC AND ISAAC. (879)

He orders them to excommunicate those who had abducted Count Wipert’s son and were ravaging that region.

To the most reverend and most holy THEODORIC, archbishop, and ISAAC, bishop.

Your religious devotion should know that Count Wipert, making complaint before our pontificate, reported that certain evil-doing men of his had seized his son and plundered the land with him.

Therefore we direct you, by our apostolic authority, to excommunicate them, so that, abandoning such plundering, they may return to their father and lord and live peacefully. Given as above.

## CLXXX. TO COUNT HUGH. (879)

He warns him to punish certain criminals.

To HUGH, glorious count.

A certain man named . . . . having reported this, we heard that your men, especially Conterius, had taken away his horses and plundered his dwellings. Therefore, warning you, we exhort you, for reverence toward the princes of the apostles and for love of us, to strive to render him the justice he has requested.

Let your nobility act in this matter as we believe you will, so that those evildoers may also be excommunicated by us, for we cannot permit such wickedness to be left unpunished. Given as above.

## CLXXXI. TO COUNTS HUGH, THEODERIC, AND BERNARD. (879)

He orders them to preserve the bond of friendship and charity made with Boson.

To HUGH, THEODERIC, and BERNARD, most illustrious men of the Frankish kingdom.

Relying upon your most noble birth and upon the obedience that, for God’s sake, you suitably owe us, I admonish and exhort you concerning our most beloved son Boson, your unanimous brother and close friend: let the indissoluble bond of charity and covenant of friendship that you have mutually formed before God never be severed in any way, whether by the tongue of any ill-speaking person or by any device of fraud.

Rather, with the Lord’s help, preserve the mind of our beloved son King Louis toward him always immovable and tranquil, and keep all his possessions safe and peaceful. For these things you will undoubtedly receive from Almighty God and the blessed apostle Peter the reward of the life to come, and from us and from him the most faithful recompense of friendship.

Given as above.

## CLXXXII. TO VULGARIUS, A MONK. (879)

He orders him to obey Bishop Wipert, who acquired him through a letter of release.

To VULGARIUS, monk.

Finally, when we ourselves were at Troyes, we learned that Bishop Wipert, our devoted son, had acquired you from your own bishop and abbot by a letter of release, at your own petition rather than otherwise.

Therefore, from that day forward it is fitting for you to obey him as your own bishop and not cease to follow him as your proper shepherd. For, if—as we do not wish—you act otherwise, we shall reasonably extend over you the bond of excommunication. Given as above.

## CLXXXIII. TO THE CLERGY OF MILAN. (879)

He orders that whenever the bishop of Pavia summons them to a synod, they should attend.

To all the most holy and reverend brothers and fellow bishops, both the archbishop of Milan with his suffragans and likewise the archbishop of Ravenna with his suffragans.

For it is written: “God, who is glorified in the council of the saints” (Psalm 88); and in the Gospel: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, I am in their midst” (Matthew 18); and again: “If brother helps brother, both will be comforted” (Proverbs 18).

Supported by these authorities, we command your collective holiness, and by apostolic authority order you, that whenever our brother and fellow bishop John of Pavia, and after him his successors, summon you to resolve emerging questions, you should immediately offer obedience to the blessed apostle Peter and not delay assembling together.

Thus, when the grace of our Redeemer has examined hostilities and purged vices, and the Church has been established in the tranquillity of peace, God may be glorified through Jesus Christ our Lord.

Whenever it is necessary, decide and determine, together with the aforesaid bishop as your own bishop, the judgements of priests and Levites, relying in every respect upon our apostolic authority. For by sharing our burdens with you, we shall be able to endure the remainder more easily.

We wish your holiness good health in Christ. Given as above.

## CLXXXIV. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF PAVIA. (879)

He orders the abductors of a certain man’s wife to be excommunicated.

To our most reverend and most holy brother JOHN, venerable bishop of Pavia.

A certain man named Ragibert, surnamed Judge, came before us and complained against Gotfred, son of John, count of the palace, and Iserbert the subdeacon, and Heribald the notary, son of Garibald. He alleged that they had forcibly and violently taken away Gausilda, lawfully married to his son, contrary to the authority of the canons and laws, trampling upon that command in which the Lord says: “What God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matthew 19).

Therefore let the zeal of your priesthood be kindled by the love of God through apostolic exhortation; raise your voice like a trumpet, and do not cease to announce their iniquity to the wicked, lest their blood be required from your hands.

Do not delay depriving the aforementioned transgressors of all Christian communion until they have legally made satisfaction for what they wickedly dared to perpetrate. If they neglect to hear you, we decree that they shall be perpetually anathematized. Given as above.

## CLXXXV. TO ALL THE FAITHFUL. (879)

He orders that no one inflict any harm upon the monastery of Saint Augentius.

To all the faithful of the Church.

We ought to have concern for all the Churches and to relieve the causes of individuals by a judgement of equity. Therefore, since it is fitting for us to deal with all matters alike, we command and establish by this present decree that, from the abbey of Saint Augentius—which the Emperor Charles, of divine memory, previously granted by right of benefice to his faithful servant and to the son of our Church—no one presume unjustly to take away anything from those possessions, nor to inflict any unlawful trouble upon the aforesaid bishop and the monks of that place in alienating them.

If anyone henceforth presumes to act in this way, let him be separated from communion with the faithful of the Church. If he persists stubbornly and refuses to make amends, let him be struck by the judgement of the Holy Spirit with the bond of anathema. Given as above.

## CLXXXVI. TO THE BISHOPS ESTABLISHED IN KING LOUIS’S REALM. (879)

He replies concerning the indulgence granted to those who had fallen while fighting against pagans.

To all the most reverend, most holy, and venerable fellow bishops throughout the entire kingdom of my beloved son Louis.

Since your venerable fraternity, asking with modest inquiry, has sought to know whether those who recently fell in battle for the defence of the holy Church of God, for the preservation of the Christian religion and the commonwealth, or who will hereafter fall for that cause, can obtain remission of sins, we confidently answer through the mercy of Christ our God:

Those who fall in battle with the piety of the Catholic religion shall be received into the rest of eternal life while bravely fighting against pagans and unbelievers. The Lord has deigned to say through the prophet: “At whatever hour the sinner is converted, I will remember none of all his iniquities any longer” (Ezekiel 18); and the venerable thief, by a single confession from the cross, deserved paradise (Luke 23).

Manasseh also, formerly a most impious king, after being captured and bound in a very strict prison, did penance there and, through the Lord’s mercy—which is immense toward the human race—obtained not only complete remission but also the restoration of his former kingdom and recovered the throne (2 Chronicles 33).

By our modest authority, through the intercession of the blessed apostle Peter, whose power of binding and loosing is in heaven and on earth, we absolve the aforesaid persons as far as is lawful, and commend them to the Lord in our prayers.

We wish your fraternity good health in Christ. Given as above.

## CLXXXVII. TO WIFRED, BISHOP OF VENCE. (879)

He prohibits a bishop who had communicated with excommunicated persons from celebrating Mass.

To WIFRED, venerable bishop of the holy Church of Vence.

By the authority of our Lord Jesus Christ, of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and of our apostolate, because you have communicated with excommunicated persons, as your letter makes clear, we deprive you of all celebration of Mass until you appear before us together with those same men. If—as we do not wish—you prove still more presumptuous, we declare that you are to be stripped of all priestly office. Given as above.

## CLXXXVIII. TO ODO, BISHOP OF BEAUVAIS. (879)

He determines that minors who had killed someone may be ordained after completing their penance.

To ODO, venerable bishop of Beauvais.

We learned from the report of certain monks of the monastery of Saint-Denis that, when certain boys still of immature age were quarrelling among themselves, one of them was killed at the instigation of those men.

Therefore we command that, if after completing their penance they are found, according to the canons, to be without guilt and of legitimate strength, you should not delay advancing them step by step to the ecclesiastical orders, while observing in everything the rules of the Fathers and the institutions of the canons. Given as above.

## CLXXXIX. TO THE BISHOPS AIMAR AND WIDO. (879)

He orders them to summon Rostagnus’s wife to him and to deprive her assistants of communion unless they repent.

To AIMAR and WIDO, most reverend bishops.

We exhort your holy fraternity and, by apostolic authority, stir up the priestly zeal of your vigorous office concerning Bertildis, wife of the illustrious man Rostagnus. She, having despised the fear of God and the law of the marriage bed, wanders as a fugitive through your parishes and, although repeatedly summoned by the bishops and by the synod, has delayed coming with deaf ears. Impose upon her every necessity of appearing before us, so that her case may receive a legal conclusion.

As for her assistants in so perverse an undertaking, bar them from access and from communion with the whole holy Church until they separate themselves entirely from association with the aforesaid Bertildis. [Note: The Roman edition does not contain the words “from association with Bertildis,” but instead gives, senselessly, “he swore spiritually”; then the text continues as here: “among whom,” etc. Mansi.]

Among them is Achetius, an adulterer; deprive him of communion on account of that association and strike him through your zeal.

I ask, admonish, and exhort you, dearest brothers, to present yourselves here most promptly. Again and again we order you, setting aside every summons [perhaps: every excuse], to hasten to us, so that, through the mercy of Christ the Lord, we may be able to bring a salutary conclusion to this and to other matters through common counsel. Given as above.

## CXC. TO WALAM, BISHOP OF METZ. (879)

He orders that a betrothed man not be compelled to marry a woman corrupted by another.

To the most reverend and most holy WALAM, venerable bishop of Metz.

The bearer of this letter, a man named Alpertus, came before us in tears and complained that his betrothed, named Walata, who was still living in her parents’ house, had been found pregnant through adulterous intercourse with a certain priest.

She has confessed the crime and willingly wishes to separate herself from him. But your fraternity, because of a certain affinity of kinship, is forcibly compelling him to take her in marriage, contrary to the rules of the Fathers and ecclesiastical institution.

Therefore, if this is so, having consulted the statutes of the laws and canons concerning the matter, promulgate without respect of persons what they prescribe concerning such cases. Given as above.

## CXCI. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF PAVIA. (879)

He orders him to deal more leniently with a certain man who had done penance for five years.

To JOHN, venerable bishop of Pavia.

The bearer of this letter, appearing before us, says that he was subjected to penance by your predecessor Liuttefred, venerable bishop, for five years now completed, on account of a certain matter: he had been involved when a thief was killed by a woman. Your fraternity should carefully consider this matter.

If the matter is as he asserts, then, because of the Lord’s mercy, which is great, deal with him more prudently and, as the order of the case requires, relax the restraint of canonical severity.

Or, if something has been judged impossible—which we do not wish—let your fraternity take care, in the gentleness of the spirit, to reserve it for our judgement. Given as above.

## CXCII. TO AGINULF, BISHOP OF GÉVAUDAN. (879)

He orders him to arrange for the return of what has been taken from the bearers of the letter.

JOHN to AGINULF, venerable bishop of Gévaudan.

The bearers of this letter have complained to this See that their people have been taken from them. Therefore, by apostolic authority, we command your fraternity, having investigated the truth of the matter, to seek with priestly diligence to restore to each person what is just; and whatever you are unable to determine yourself, do not fail by any means [to refer to us].

## CXCIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF BESANÇON. (879)

He announces that he has absolved Fulcard and his wife from excommunication.

To THEODORIC, venerable bishop of Besançon.

Let your holiness know that we have absolved Fulcard and Berelinda, his wife, from the bond of excommunication, until we have fully ascertained the judgement according to canonical rule. Therefore we order you to receive them into communion. We wish your fraternity good health. Given as above.

## CXCIV. TO GAIDER, PRINCE OF BENEVENTO. (879)

He consoles him concerning the damage inflicted by the Agarens, promises assistance, and declares that he will come to his region.

To his beloved son GAIDER, glorious prince of the Beneventans.

I confess that I received the letters sent by your affection with both a share of rejoicing and, nevertheless, of sorrow. As greatly as I exulted with joy on learning, with the deepest affection of my heart, of your devotion toward the service of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, so greatly did I grieve, with pastoral concern, when I heard of the pressures and depredations of the Agarens upon your land.

Therefore, with the chosen vessel, I am compelled to say and cry out tearfully: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not inflamed?” (2 Corinthians 11.)

Meanwhile, we must remember the one who says: “In the world you will have tribulation, but take courage, for I have overcome the world” (John 16); and the apostle: “Greater is the one who is in us than the one who is against us” (1 John 4).

Accordingly, dearest son, I exhort, admonish, and urge you by apostolic authority, meanwhile patiently to endure the burdens of these evils, continually beseeching the Lord’s mercy.

For, with Christ’s help, you will have in us, for the liberation of your homeland, an assistant more earnestly prepared than all other mortals, in proportion as we compassionately attend to your plight. We would demonstrate this by our actual presence [perhaps: “we would repay it in deeds”], if at this time the fodder for our horses had not completely run out on the journey, preventing us from immediately setting out on the road to come.

But, guided by the grace of our Redeemer, after the Easter solemnity has been completed, we shall hasten to come to your region. Once there with you, whatever counsel, comfort, and assistance we can devise for the liberation of the Christian people, we shall most willingly provide.

We wish the glory of your exalted office always good health in Christ. Given as above.

## CXCV. TO AJON, BISHOP. (879)

He commends his fidelity toward him; assures him of his own safety; and then consoles him concerning the death of his brother.

To our most reverend and most holy brother AJON, venerable bishop.

Because your venerable fraternity, out of kindly compassion of spirit, grieved for our absence for some time far from the City, on account of the relief of the holy Churches of God, you openly showed that the depths of your mind are filled with the charity of Christ. You strove worthily to preserve toward the holy apostles of God, through us, the proper—or rather mutual—love that you owe them, from whom without doubt you will receive the recompense of your merits at the end.

Your fraternity thirstily and ardently seeks to know whether we are safe. By the Lord’s gift, we seem to possess some measure of bodily health; but amid so many waves of the world and such storms of waters, what health of this life can remain tranquil even for a moment? Especially when we have heard of the death of your brother and of the frequent tribulations and afflictions of you and your dearest children.

Amid these things, however, it is fitting for us with every effort of the mind to raise our hearts toward the life of that heavenly homeland, in which peace and true security always dwell. For as long as we are in the body, according to the Apostle, we are exiles from the Lord.

According to the duty of the ministry entrusted to us by God, and to the limit of our strength, we eagerly desire to impart comfort to you and to your homeland. Given as above.

## CXCVI. TO COUNT DAFER. (879)

He consoles Dafer and promises him assistance.

To his beloved son, the illustrious and noble man, COUNT DAFER.

We greatly rejoice in the perfection of the heart of Gaider, your kinsman, and in your devotion toward God, beseeching him who began his work in you to carry it out and perfect the good work to the end.

We sympathize so deeply with your tribulations and distress that, by the hand of thought, we touch your pains in our own heart. But we trust in the mercy of the eternal Creator, because his help will soon be present. Through the prophet he admonishes us, saying: “Call upon me in the day of your tribulation; I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me” (Psalm 49).

For you should consider us so prepared to assist you that, when the suitable time comes, we shall not refuse to lay down our lives for our brothers.

I declare that I shall gladly give you the horse requested by your nobility when I reach your borders. Given as above.

## CXCVII. TO ROMANUS, ARCHBISHOP OF RAVENNA. (879)

He orders him to come to Rome to the synod with his suffragans.

To our most reverend and most holy brother ROMANUS, archbishop of the holy Church of Ravenna.

Canons of the holy Fathers command by their regulations that councils of bishops be held in every respect twice a year (Council of Nicaea, canon 5). For this reason, on account of the manifold benefits and necessities of the Churches of God, we desire, with the Lord’s assent, to celebrate a synod on the eighth day before the Kalends of May. Therefore we command your Dilection, setting aside every delay, to make every effort to come to Rome at the appointed time with all your suffragan bishops, so that you may celebrate that same synod equally with us and deliberate concerning the common salvation. Given on the third day before the Nones of March.

### CXCVIII. PRIVILEGE FOR THE MONASTERY OF PIACENZA. (Year 879.)

[From Campi, *Ecclesiastical History of Piacenza*, p. 464.]

[Col. 0821A]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter ANGILBERGA, empress and Augusta.

By the generosity of our Redeemer, those things that are recognized as pertaining to the protection of ecclesiastical possessions and holy places are always to be confirmed. Therefore, concerning the monastery of Caput Trebiae, which King Carolomannus, by a deed of donation and perpetual confirmation, granted with all its appurtenances to your monastery, which you built at Piacenza in honor of the holy Resurrection, for the remedy of his own soul and those of his predecessors: you ask, most beloved daughter, that we confirm this by a sanction of apostolic authority. Accordingly, by apostolic authority we grant effect to your just petitions to this extent: henceforth and thereafter, if any king or person of whatever power should presume, with rash audacity, to violate or alienate the aforesaid place’s complete and stable donation [the text reads *rotam*; perhaps *ratam*, “confirmed”], or to inflict any violence upon it, let him know that he will be separated from our communion and bound by the bond of anathema, and will nevertheless have his portion with Ananias, Sapphira, and Judas the betrayer. But if he obediently observes these commands of ours, may he deserve to receive the blessing of almighty God and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul in the fullest abundance.

Furthermore, as regards the order and administration of ecclesiastical affairs—that is, chrism or any priestly office—if the bishop of that place, moved by any cause, should presume to impose there any burden or exaction contrary to right and justice, let him thereby completely lose every right and power of ecclesiastical administration; and let the person presiding over the monastery be permitted to invite whomever he wishes for the ministry of the entire ecclesiastical office.

Written by the hand of Gregory, notary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of March, in the twelfth indiction, on the fourth day before the Kalends of April, by the hand of Zacharias, bishop of the holy Church of Anagni and librarian of the holy apostolic see, in the seventh year, by God’s favor, of the pontificate of our lord John, supreme pontiff and universal pope, in the month of March, in the twelfth indiction.

### CXCIX. TO ROMANUS, ARCHBISHOP. (Year 879.) That he ordain the priest Lupon as bishop of the Church of Sarcennum.

[Col. 0821D]

To our most reverend and holy fellow-bishop ROMANUS, archbishop of the holy Church of Ravenna.

From the report of certain persons we have learned that, although we commanded you to ordain as bishop of the holy Church of Sarcennum the man whom we designated for ordination—namely, the venerable priest Lupon [a leaf is missing: “we commanded”]—you are postponing his consecration, setting aside the mandate of our will and command, and nevertheless desire to ordain someone else in his place. If this is true, we are greatly astonished that you should wish, in any way or on any pretext, to withdraw from the promise that you made to us. Therefore, in the manner of a father, by these apostolic letters we admonish, exhort, and command your Dilection to remember your promise and immediately and in person ordain the aforesaid priest Lupon as bishop of the said Church, as we entrusted to you.

[For if you act otherwise, and if we discover that at the very beginning of your ordination [Note: [Col. 0821D] I supplied the words enclosed in parentheses from the Roman edition] you have so quickly withdrawn from the decree of our will, we will by no means fail to correct you with canonical penalties, as disobedient.]

### CC. TO ANSPERT, ARCHBISHOP OF MILAN. (Year 879.)
