That he come to Rome with his suffragans for the celebration of a synod, where the election of the emperor will be discussed; he orders him not to receive any king before he himself has elected the emperor; if he does not obey, he excommunicates him.

[Col. 0822B]

To the most reverend and holy ANSPERT, archbishop of the holy Church of Milan.

We know clearly, and do not fail to recognize, that your Fraternity is aware how many hardships of necessity we have continually endured, how much disturbance we have suffered until now, and what adversities we endure daily. You know equally well that, on account of these evils wickedly inflicted upon the apostolic see by its enemies, we have gone through storms and dangerous sea journeys in search of assistance for our defense. But since we have found no human aid at present, it is necessary, my brother, that we seek divine help instead and with common agreement beseech it from the Lord.

For this reason, by these apostolic letters, following the custom of our predecessors, we summon the fraternal college of your holiness and, solely by apostolic authority, associate it with our apostolic concern. Like a member clinging to its head, we command you to come to Rome with all your suffragan bishops by the Kalends of May of this twelfth indiction, so that, with the Lord’s help, you may celebrate a synod with us. Relying on the grace of the Most High, we may cut away with the ecclesiastical sword those things that must necessarily be removed, and by common decree, with God’s favor, establish those things that ought usefully to be established; lest through your absence and negligence this kingdom remain longer in confusion and a scandal worse than the former arise.

And because Carolomannus, as we have heard, is burdened by bodily illness and can no longer retain the kingdom, it is very necessary for you to be present at the appointed time, so that we may all deliberate concerning the election of a new king [a leaf is missing: “election”]. Therefore, before then, you must receive no king without our consent. For the one who is to be appointed emperor by us must first and above all be summoned and elected by us, since we wish, together with your Fraternity, to deliberate both on this matter and on the manner and order in which we should arrange and establish by canon law the common affairs and interests of the Churches of God entrusted to us. Thus may we cast far from us the burdens of such great evils that we endure and, as is fitting, bear Christ’s easy yoke upon joyful necks.

Therefore, do not offer any excuse for failing to come; make every effort to hasten eagerly and attend the said synod. The canonical rule of the holy Fathers commands that it be held twice a year, and the great necessity of the present time also compels it. We, loving you with fatherly affection, summon you for the common good, although your Dilection, already summoned to the synod for the third time some while ago, has disdained to come. For this you ought to have endured an appropriate sentence of correction, since assistance had always been granted you by the apostolic see, while you made no effort to offer us any support where it was required. But now, if you disdain to come to that same synod, know that we shall promulgate against you, as against the disobedient, a canonical sentence.

### CCI. TO ATHANASIUS, BISHOP OF NAPLES. (Year 879.) He commends his observance toward him; informs him of his safe return; exhorts him to persevere until they meet together.

To the most reverend and holy ATHANASIUS, bishop of Naples.

Because we have learned, not only from your notable actions—which have shown that your holiness’s devotion toward us is most faithful—but also from the report of our faithful people, how, while we remained far away for the sake of the Church’s condition, you preserved it unblemished in every respect, we therefore offer your Dilection worthy thanks. We also inform you that, with God’s favor, our return to our episcopate has been prosperous and safe, in accordance with your desire.

Therefore, in the manner of apostolic fatherhood, we admonish your Holiness, saying with the Apostle: “Be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might, for God is faithful; he will not allow those who hope in him to be tested beyond what they can bear, but with the temptation he will also provide a way through, so that you may be able to endure” (Ephesians 6; 1 Corinthians 10).

Let your Reverence, then, not be broken in any way by these circumstances of present adversity; rather, strengthened by confidence in God, let it remain steadfast until, with Christ’s help, we are joined to you by our personal presence and speak together. For then, God permitting, we believe that all the matters which must necessarily be established, having been discussed in common speech and agreement, will turn out for salvation. Nevertheless, we have commanded that the disposition of our will be made known to your Dilection through Peter, your venerable deacon and our common faithful servant, since, loving you as our own son, we wish to have you as a partner in all our affairs. Given as above.

### CCII. TO THE SAME. (Year 879.) On the same subject as the preceding letter.

To the most reverend and holy ATHANASIUS, bishop of the holy Church of Naples.

By these apostolic letters we offer many thanks and greetings to your Holiness, because, while we remain far away for the common good, you strive to display in every respect, as though we were present, the sincerity of your devotion and faith toward the holy Roman Church, your mother, toward our pontificate, and toward our faithful people. Therefore, let no trickery or cunning of the enemies incline you from your good-minded purpose toward any sinister path of thought or will; but, as you have begun, strive in every way to complete it, for, with Christ’s favor, both merit and worthy recompense will come to you.

For although, because of the deceitful wickedness of our enemies hindering us, we have not been able to complete everything we wished in full, nevertheless, with the Lord’s assent, we believe that we shall proceed without delay with what concerns the honor of the holy Church of God, the salvation of that land, and your defense, which we have already begun.

Accordingly, we exhort and admonish your Dilection that, just as you have stood until now, so henceforth you remain manfully and firmly established, until we are joined by our personal presence and speak together, laboring side by side for the common salvation and striving with all our strength. Since we desire to retain you as our most beloved son, we embrace you kindly and wish to rejoice with you in all things; for, as has been said, know for certain that you will undoubtedly receive from us a worthy recompense.

We commend to your Holiness in every respect this deacon of yours, who, out of love for you, has remained faithfully in our service for so long, so that he may receive from you the honor of recompense that he deserves. Given as above.

### CCIII. TO THE SAME. (Year 879.) That he inform him of a place where they can confer together concerning the salvation of their common homeland.

[Col. 0824C]

To our most reverend, holy, and beloved fellow-bishop and counselor, ATHANASIUS, bishop of the holy Church of Naples.

Knowing without doubt that you are faithful and devoted in every respect to our holy apostolic see and to our fatherhood, we love and cherish your Fraternity exceedingly, with all our heart. Therefore, on account of the manifold necessities of the present time and our common interests, we desire to speak with you in person, so that, with your counsel and by common deliberation, we may, with the Lord’s assent, arrange and establish wisely and beneficially those matters that must necessarily be considered and carefully discussed.

For we desire, in the pastoral manner, to accomplish the salvation of our land and yours—that is, of the entire people redeemed by Christ’s precious blood—and for this reason we wish to meet together with you, so that the stubborn boldness of the enemies may be restrained. Therefore, we wish you to communicate as quickly as possible to our episcopate, by your letters, a place for our conference that you recognize as suitable. For, with God’s favor, we shall not fail to hasten there without delay and speak eagerly with you. Given as above.

### CCIV. TO KING CHARLES. (Year 879.) He exhorts him to send envoys and come to the aid of the Roman Church.

[Col. 0825A]

To King CHARLES.

Having received and reread the letters of your Royal Excellency, we greatly desire not only—as we reported long ago—to enlarge ever more fully our disposition of affection toward you, so that we might remain in the love and devotion that you previously directed toward our episcopate, but also to retain you in every respect without doubt as our most beloved son, to the height of your rejoicing.

Only, do not in any way fail to send your suitable envoys to us as quickly as you have ordered. With them, we shall be able most firmly to investigate and deliberate concerning the exaltation of the holy apostolic see, the salvation of that land, and your honor [the manuscript has *profligare*; perhaps *investigare*, “to investigate”].

Therefore we exhort the glory of your greatness: girding your loins like a man and powerfully strengthened against the enemies by the arm of God’s power, do not hesitate to come in person. For if you had known the oppression of such great calamity that your holy Roman mother Church and that land suffer daily from their enemies, you would certainly grieve together with us.

Therefore, dearest son, before the enemies’ plots grow stronger and prevail, do not cease to attend with pious regard to our devotion and counsel; rather, following the custom of your parents, carry out with the greatest urgency those things that are necessary for us, since with outstretched arms of our apostolate we eagerly desire to embrace your royal presence. On the third day before the Nones of April, in the twelfth indiction.

### CCV. TO WIBERTUS, BISHOP. (Year 879.) He rebukes him because, summoned twice, he neglected to come to him; he commands him to come and answer the charges brought against him.

To the most reverend and holy Wibertus, venerable bishop.

We have already sent to your Holiness twice, asking you to come to us, but we do not know with what audacity you disobey. We send again, therefore, so that, setting aside all your other pressing business, you hasten to us in person, since many are bringing complaints against you, especially this old man, who has already come to Rome for this reason on behalf of his monastery. Moreover, know that if you delay coming, you are to be excommunicated; and if you persist in your [a leaf is missing: “obstinacy”], you are to be excluded even from communion. Given as above.

### CCVI. TO BERENGARIUS, COUNT. (Year 879.) He declares his goodwill toward him, commends his observance toward the Roman Church, and asks him to help Bishop Stephen defend the rights of his Church.

To his beloved son BERENGARIUS, glorious count.

Because, having reread the letters of your Nobility, we learned that you are safe and flourishing in the prosperity you desire, we became exceedingly glad. For, out of love for your Dilection, we always desire to remain devoted to you with apostolic benevolence and to carry out eagerly whatever appears useful or beneficial to you; nor would we abandon our beloved friendship with you for the sake of any person, but rather preserve it unharmed in every respect with pious regard.

You informed us through Demeus, the distinguished duke and our faithful servant, that you ought to be devoted and obedient in every respect toward the holy apostolic see and our fatherhood, and that you would fulfill all our will as our dearest son. We rejoiced greatly at this. But because we again instructed you through Peter, the venerable bishop, and John, the distinguished duke, to assist Stephen, the venerable bishop whom we appointed in advance at Comacchio, so that, supported by your help, he might securely retain the rights and possessions of his Church and the administration of his duchy, we are greatly astonished that we have not heard that he has been assisted by your aid.

Therefore we ask your Nobility to provide our aforesaid bishop with such assistance that he may securely retain and administer his Church and the ministry entrusted to him. And if, contrary to our belief, your disposition toward us has changed, so that you do not wish to listen to us about this matter, we ask you, for the love of God and of us, to forbid all your men to offer any opposition there to our people, so that, without their interference, we may be permitted, according to our ability, to punish them as rebels and disobedient to our apostolic command, lest we lose not only the tribute that we have lost from that place during the past two years [Col. 0826C], but also the tribute of this year. Given as above.

### CCVII. TO PANDENULFUS, COUNT. (Year 879.) He asks him to assist the emperor’s envoys as they pass through his region; expresses sorrow over the pagans’ attack upon him; excuses himself for not going to him; exhorts him to be courageous and promises assistance.

To his beloved man PANDENULFUS, glorious count.

[Note: [Col. 0825] Count of Capua, as is clear from letter 209. Leo mentions him in the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, book I, chapter 45.]

By these letters of our episcopate we offer many thanks to your Nobility. Since you have eagerly displayed your devotion and affection by obeying the commands of our will, we recognize without hesitation that you are sincere and obedient in every respect, especially since you sent before our presence this Greek, the man of the imperial official, to be presented to us safely.

But because the imperial envoys, as we have learned from the letters of that official himself, are to pass through your territory in order to come to our apostolic presence, we ask your Nobility, for love of us, to send them to us with your assistance and protection, with the Lord’s assent, on a prosperous journey.

As for your assertion that you are burdened by repeated attacks of the pagans, we grieve with you, especially because your fellow citizens, settled all around, are striving to make a pact with those sons of perdition. Therefore, await our necessary presence in your region.

As we instructed you some time ago, we greatly desire to come with every effort, solely for the common good and salvation, although we still remain exhausted both by continual bodily illness and by the journey through France, which has now been completed. For the present, therefore, we cannot hasten there before the arrival of the aforesaid imperial envoys. But when, with God’s favor, we have heard their embassy delivered to us and have made suitable replies, we shall then take every care to do what must most usefully be done, according to our strength.

You, however, trusting in the Lord, remain steadfast in spirit. He does not abandon those who trust in him. Thus may you appear in every respect more effective and stronger than your other neighbors and kinsmen; for, as opportunity requires, we shall assist you with our apostolic protection as our dearest son. Given as above.

### CCVIII. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS AND THEIR SUFFRAGANS. (Year 879.) That they not excommunicate Bicbertinus before the case has been examined.

To our most reverend and holy fellow-bishops, Aurelianus and Otteramnus, and also Theodoricus, and to all your fellow bishops.

We wish it to be known to the holiness of all of you that Bicbertinus has arrived, bringing an imperial decree and a document of exchange concerning the properties regarding which Charius and Archbishop Amulus formerly concluded an exchange. Moreover, he has informed our apostolate that you wish to excommunicate him without a proper examination.

Therefore, by apostolic authority we command that none of you excommunicate him before the matter has come to legal examination. Know that, as it is read in the hundredth chapter of the African Council, and likewise in the second book of Justinian’s Novels, no bishop or priest may excommunicate anyone before the case has been proved. Let the person who has been excommunicated approach a greater priest, and let the one who unjustly excommunicated him suffer a just penalty from that priest. Nor may any of you, or any of the aforesaid laymen, dare to seize the property before the sanction of the law.

For, contrary to what we believe, if anyone attempts to act against this apostolic authority of ours, let him know that he is bound by the bond of anathema. Given as above.

### CCIX. TO BOSO, COUNT. (Year 879.) He congratulates him on his safe and prosperous condition; shows that he regards both him and the empress Angelberga as dear; asks him to permit Adelbert and his wife Rotilda to retain the property they had possessed in the province.

To his beloved son BOSO, glorious prince.

Having reread the letters of your Nobility, we learned that you are safe and flourishing in the prosperity you desire, and we became exceedingly glad. For, out of love for your Dilection, we always desire to remain devoted to you with apostolic benevolence and to carry out eagerly whatever appears useful or beneficial to you. Nor would we abandon our friendship, which is dear to us, for the sake of any person; rather, with pious regard, we desire to preserve it unharmed in every respect.

Concerning our spiritual daughter Angelberga, empress and your most beloved mother, know for certain that we have always loved her with fatherly affection, and that, as long as we live with the Lord’s help, we greatly desire to love her and assist and protect her with our apostolic support, and to retain her with greater honor as our most beloved spiritual daughter.

As for the action of your will, which you say you are displaying, you will undoubtedly find us steadfast in your friendship. Concerning Adelbert, the glorious margrave, and his wife Rutilda [the heading has *Rotildae*], the countess, let your Nobility know that we recognize them as faithful and devoted friends toward you in every respect. Therefore we ask you to allow them henceforth to hold securely, for love of us, their county estates situated in the province, just as they have held them for a long time. We wish your glory to remain perpetual in Christ, now and always. Given as above.

### CCX. TO LIUDTEFRIDUS, COUNT, AND HIS WIFE. (Year 879.) He excommunicates them because they had abducted a nun from her monastery.

To Count LIUDTEFRIDUS and his wife.

Because you have not blushed to act rashly against the commands of God and the laws—indeed, trampling upon the fear of God, you dared, by the most deceitful persuasion, to remove Garelinda, clothed in the sacred veil and for a very long time living under a regular profession in the monastery of Angelberga, our beloved daughter, empress and Augusta, situated at Piacenza—we separate you and your wife, by the authority of the Holy Spirit of our Lord, from the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ and from the fellowship of Christianity until you restore the aforesaid woman Garelinda to the place from which you dragged her away. But if you neglect to do this, we bind you with the bonds of anathema. Given as above.

### CCXI. TO GREGORY, PRIMICERIUS. (Year 879.) He commends his zeal toward the Church and the emperors; declares himself prepared to settle the disturbances of the Church of Constantinople; indicates that he will receive the emperor’s envoys honorably, whom he had previously ordered to be received by the count of Capua and sent to him.

[Col. 0828D]

To his beloved man GREGORY, glorious primicerius and imperial official.

Having reread the letter that you sent us through Stephen, your faithful *candidatus*, and recognizing more clearly the sincerity and faith of your devotion toward the Church of God and toward the most glorious emperors and Augusti, we commend you exceedingly. Therefore, as you requested in humble prayer, we earnestly strive to commend you to the Lord in our sacred prayers, so that you may exist secure and victorious both against visible and invisible enemies.

And because you exhort us to favor your great emperor, who desires the Church of God to be pacified, we take care, aided by God, to do this readily, solely by the willing exercise of our office; for, as the Apostle says, concern for all the Churches of God rests upon us.

Therefore, following the custom of our predecessors, the pontiffs, we desire, insofar as is just and possible, to calm the Church of Constantinople, now disturbed by manifold scandals, and to establish perpetual peace.

Moreover, if the imperial envoys whom you say have been sent to our apostolic heights arrive, they will be received by us with appropriate honor, and we shall kindly accept the imperial embassy delivered to us through them. After learning the text and order of that embassy, we shall, together with the assent of the apostolic see entrusted to us, strive in every way, insofar as is lawful, to favor the imperial will for the peace of the Church of God.

For this reason we have also written to Pandenulfus, count of Capua, asking him to receive them when they come and, for love of us, endeavor, with the Lord’s assent, to send them to us on a prosperous journey. Therefore, let these same envoys now make every effort to come in person to Rome, since, being occupied with other matters, we cannot at present hasten to that region as we had arranged. Given as above.

### CCXII. (Year 879.) The excommunication of Anspertus because, having been summoned to the synod, he disdained to come.

Anspertus, archbishop of Milan, whom, while we were staying at Pavia and afterward, we summoned to the synod assembled at Rome for the many necessities of the Churches of God, was unwilling either to appear in person or to send us and the holy council his excuse in a written summons according to the sacred canons. Because of his audacity and disobedience, by the power of the Holy Spirit and of the chief apostles Peter and Paul, and by our authority, with the consent of the holy synod, we deprive him of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ until he makes every effort to present himself before us. Given as above.

### CCXIII. TO THEODOSIUS, PATRIARCH OF JERUSALEM. (Year 879.) He excuses the delayed return of his envoys, through whom he sends him certain gifts, asking him to pray to God continually on his behalf.

[Col. 0829D]

To our most reverend and holy fellow-bishop THEODOSIUS, patriarch of the holy Church of Jerusalem.

We wish it to be known to your Holiness that your monks presently here—namely, Theodosius, David, and Saba—came to Rome to the thresholds of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, but remained there because we had gone to France for the affairs and interests of our Church. When, however, by God’s will, we returned safely, we gave them permission to return to your fatherhood. Through them, for the sake of charity, we have sent your Fraternity a blessing of the blessed apostle Peter, though a modest one.

We ask you kindly to accept it for love of God and of that chief of the apostles, and for love of us, since, burdened by the excessive oppression of the pagans, we were unable to send more, as we wished. Moreover, we ask your holy Charity in the Lord, remembering us always in your holy prayers, to deign, dearest brother, to pour out prayers daily for us to Jesus Christ our Lord with eager heart. Given on the sixth day before the Nones of May.

### CCXIV. TO KING CAROLOMANNUS. (Year 879.) That the deacon Gospertus be appointed bishop in the Church of Vercelli.

[Col. 0830B]

To his beloved and spiritual son CAROLOMANNUS, glorious king.

From the report of many persons we have learned that the Church of Vercelli is now in great turmoil and subject to daily scandals. The people are divided into two parties over the election of a bishop: some contend and desire to elect and have one man, while others choose another, and each side strives to defend its candidate excessively.

But in accordance with the apostolic office and concern of our ministry, which has been entrusted to us in the chief of the apostles for all the Churches of God, and also in accordance with the canonical rule of the holy Fathers, which says: “If division has arisen among the clergy or people, and a dispute has broken out concerning the election of a future bishop, neither of the two is in any way to be consecrated to the episcopal throne, but another priest is to be elected for the Church deprived of its proper ruler and thereby disturbed”—we must come to its aid, bringing the rights of peace.

We ask your Royal Excellency, for love of God and Saint Peter and out of affection for our fatherhood, to grant the very bishopric of Vercelli at present, in a peaceful manner, to this most noble man, namely the venerable deacon Gospertus, well known to you and our common faithful servant, whom we sent into your service for ecclesiastical interests.

For we truly recognize that he will be energetic and highly useful in every respect, in civil as well as ecclesiastical affairs, and exceptionally faithful to us. Therefore, for the increase of your present and future glory, we ask you to grant this to us, and may your royal greatness eagerly fulfill this first just request of our pontificate. Thus we too may be able willingly to fulfill your desire, dearest son. For we shall appear to remain joined by the unity of true affection and the pious feeling of love if we accomplish by apostolic authority those things that you desire, and if you in turn, by your royal right, unquestionably strive with joy to heed the petitions of our desire.

We have learned that your forebears, the unconquered emperors and Augusti, showed such affection toward our predecessors, the holy bishops of the Roman see, that whatever was requested by either side was promptly and effectively fulfilled, with every pretext set aside. Thus, too, our pontifical majesty, preserved by God, and your royal greatness ought now to favor each other peacefully in turn. Given as above.

### CCXV. TO KING CHARLES. (Year 879.) He exhorts him to come as soon as possible with aid against the unbelievers and oppressors of the Church.

To his beloved and spiritual son CHARLES, glorious king.

We are astonished that, although we have repeatedly exhorted you and summoned you to come for the exaltation of the holy Church of God, for your honor, and for the defense of our entire land, you have delayed until now. You may believe us that, burdened everywhere by the excessive persecution of both pagans and wicked Christians and shaken on every side, we can no longer endure the things we have suffered for so long. Therefore, we admonish you again to attend without doubt, with every effort, as we have instructed you.

For you must know for certain that neither for anyone’s profit, nor through flattery or fear, will we separate ourselves from your fellowship or from the bond of your friendship. Therefore, do not hesitate in any way to act manfully in those matters that are profitable to us and to you.

But while awaiting your arrival, which we thought was being delayed for a long time, we supposed that perhaps you had been unable to come because of some impediment affecting your brother, the glorious King Carolomannus. For this reason we sent him our apostolic letter, admonishing him that if he continued to hold this kingdom in such occupation and disorder, without defense, it would certainly result in the loss of his soul; and that no one should presume to create any impediment for you when you came for the defense of the Church of God.

Therefore, let your Royal Excellency in no way cease to do what must be done. For if the holy Roman Church is exalted and defended through you, your honor and glory will unquestionably remain increased here and in the future before the Lord. Given as above.

### CCXVI. TO WIBBODUS, BISHOP. (Year 879.) That he go together with the envoys whom he is sending to Carolomannus, or send someone in his place; he rebukes him for not preventing the plundering of Angelberga’s property and exhorts him to recover it.

[Col. 0831D]

To Bishop WIBBODUS.

Since, above all those who appear to belong to these regions, we love you—God’s beloved priest—as our dearest son and like-minded brother with particular affection, and since we embrace with all the feeling of our heart the great devotion of your sincerity which you are known to hold toward us and the apostolic see, we therefore desire to foster your reverence, joined to us by holy love, with perpetual apostolic kindness and to strengthen it with our authority.

We therefore wish your affection to know that, because of the many and great calamities which, as you yourself know well, we continually endure, we have sent these present envoys of ours. They will enter, as it were through a certain door, to our spiritual son, the glorious king Carolomannus [Col. 0832A]. With them, either go yourself eagerly into the service of Saint Peter, and strive to accomplish before that king every matter and necessity of our will, or send from your side a most faithful and suitable man who can shrewdly fulfill your role in every respect.

For we urge you to equip these same envoys with your counsel and assistance, so that, by God’s favor, they may complete the mission of the apostolic see as is fitting and as the necessity of the present time requires. And because we command them to go and return without delay, do not arrange to keep them with you for more than three days; rather, having taken counsel immediately so that they may proceed safely and securely to the aforesaid king, let them not remain at all.

But if it should happen that they cannot go to Carolomannus because of his bodily illness [Col. 0832B], see to it that they proceed in whatever way possible to King Charles, his brother. Moreover, we have learned from the truthful report of many, resounding far and wide, that the property and possessions of our beloved spiritual daughter, the empress Angelberga, entrusted to Saint Peter, have been utterly plundered by certain evildoers—not only those situated outside, in fields and villages, but also those which had been stored inside venerable and inviolable places of the holy monasteries.

For this outrage, this monstrous crime and abominable sacrilege, we rightly rebuke your holiness. It is the duty of your priesthood to correct those who do evil by divine authority and restrain them with salutary words, lest, by remaining silent about such people, you appear, alas, rather to imitate than to prohibit them [Col. 0832C]. For from this there has spread throughout the whole world a very evil report: that you are treating badly your former lady and empress, to whom you gave your allegiance by oath, and to whom you ought always to have shown her former honor and the reverence due to her.

Therefore, for the love of Saint Peter, under whose special protection she remains, do not fail to assist her until she can recover all that she unjustly lost [folio missing here: *recuperare*, “to recover”]. Given as above.

## CCXVII. TO MICHAEL, KING OF THE BULGARIANS (879)

He urges him to return, together with his people, to obedience to the Roman Church, from which he had been led astray and had departed.

To his beloved son MICHAEL, king of the Bulgarians.

Since almighty God, by the gift of his freely given mercy, has deigned to call you and your people to knowledge of his name, you ought to have remembered what the Lord said to the blessed apostle Peter: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16). To Peter you entrusted yourselves at the beginning of your Christianity for governance, and to his successors for obedience.

But I do not know by what means you have been cunningly drawn away from his instruction by certain people, so that with the Apostle we must say: “Who has bewitched you, that you should not obey him to whom you formerly submitted your necks?” (Galatians 3). Or have you believed those who—if we may speak without offending the Greeks—are daily confused by new and varied disciplines and doctrines [Col. 0833A]?

But I beseech you, dearest son: abandon excesses and the scandals of seduction, and without delay bring yourself and your people back, with heartfelt love, to the embrace of your holy mother, the Roman Church, which, by God’s institution, is the head of all the Churches spread throughout the world. We love you with such paternal affection that we desire you to be in the very heart of Christ Jesus.

And behold, we are ready to win you over and to correct completely whatever was recently offended by the obscurity of our envoys, and to restore and repair everything with the greatest care. If need should arise, we shall not refuse not only to sympathize and grieve with you, but even to die for the salvation of your souls, as the apostle John says: “Since God laid down his life for us, we also ought to lay down our lives for our brothers” (1 John 3).

It is fitting, however, that your affection should always receive paternal admonitions with kindly love and lend an attentive ear to our warnings. For he to whom the Lord entrusted the keys of the kingdom of heaven, for binding and loosing, daily and without ceasing stretches out his arms and joyfully awaits you as you return to him, so that he may restore you to the eternal Shepherd as participants in eternal blessedness—the Shepherd from whom he received, through the ministry of his apostleship, the task of redeeming your souls. Given as above.

## CCXVIII. TO THE COUNSELORS OF MICHAEL, KING OF THE BULGARIANS (879)

The same subject.

To Peter, Cerbula, and Sundica, and the other nobles and counselors of our beloved son Michael, king of the Bulgarians.

Finally, I admonish all your affection to announce by continual exhortations and suggestions to our beloved son Michael, the glorious king and your superior, that he should return, and that you too should return with him, to the embrace of the holy Roman Church, which desires you to share in eternal blessedness. Do not continue any longer to suffer, God forbid, the ruin and loss of your souls through the persuasions of certain people’s perverse doctrines.

For we are moved toward you by such great love that you will be able to obtain from us whatever you ask justly and according to God’s will, and we earnestly desire to grant your petitions an unassailable fulfillment. We admonish you of this again and again, and declare it in Christ’s name: hasten without fail to return to us. For just as we fear that we would sin if we did not lead you back to the embrace of your holy mother, so you will sin against God if you neglect to hear our voice. Given as above.

## CCXIX. TO SEDESCLAVUS, COUNT (879)

He commands him to provide a safe journey and necessary supplies for the envoy whom he is sending to the king of the Bulgarians.

To his beloved son SEDESCLAVUS, glorious count of the Slavs [Note: [Col. 0833D] On the Slavs, see the *Historia Miscellanea*, book XVII, in Maurice, books XIX and 23.].

Since the reputation of your affection, goodness, and devotion toward God has reached us, we confidently command and instruct your glory, for love of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, your protectors, to ensure that this present envoy, whom we are sending to the Bulgarian people [Note: [Col. 0834D] Aimoinus, book IV, chapters 26 and 81. Cedrenus on Maurice; Nicephorus, book XVIII, chapter 28.], arrives safely and unharmed at our beloved son Michael, their glorious king.

Provide him, for the love of God, with whatever he needs for food and clothing, because the Lord says in the Gospel: “As long as you did it for one of the least of these, you did it for me” (Matthew 25); and the Apostle says: “Be hospitable to one another without grumbling” (1 Peter 4). “For through this some, unknowingly, received angels as guests” (Hebrews 13).

My dearest son, let your affection take care of this, so that he may be able to receive the rewards of eternal life. Given as above.

## CCXX. TO GREGORY, PRIMICERIUS (879)

He asks him to send the Constantinopolitan envoys to him; he promises that, when the king of the Franks comes to Rome, he will go to his aid.

To his beloved son GREGORY, primicerius and imperial official.

We warmly commend your devotion in Christ and in his Church, and we exhort you to advance more and more in good works. Send the envoys dispatched to us from the city of Constantinople through Benevento and then through Capua, for we have already arranged how, God willing, they may reach us safely and unharmed [Col. 0834C].

As for our coming to you, which your affection, dearest son, is investigating, we had certainly decided upon it. But the king of the Franks, hastening toward us, earnestly asks that we not depart from the City until he arrives. When he comes, with the Lord’s protection, we shall strive by every means to hasten there without delay with a strong force, as the necessity of the times dictates, for the salvation of the whole holy Church of God and of all Christians. Given on the sixth day of May, in the twelfth indiction.

## CCXXI. TO WIBBODO, BISHOP (879)

He urges him to act with Carolomannus or his brother Charles for the defense of the Church of God against pagan attacks; and, if Charles’s archchaplain comes to Rome, to come himself as well; otherwise, to disclose the will of those kings to him by letter.

To the most reverend WIBBODO, bishop and our beloved counselor.

Although we continually desire to have you, as our dearest son, in our service, we would now be pleased to benefit from your prudent counsel because of the many pressing matters of the present time. But because we undoubtedly believe that your diligence always wishes faithfully to undertake everywhere those things which concern the honor of the holy Church of God and our own, we do not now hesitate to summon you to our apostolic presence.

Therefore we inform your affection that, oppressed by the continual and exceedingly grave attacks of the pagans, we would already have wished to obtain the assistance of some king. Accordingly, if you know without doubt that Carolomannus is able to help, strive to conduct before him—or otherwise before his brother and namesake, namely the glorious King Charles—the affairs and interests of the holy apostolic see with prudent counsel alone and, with God’s help, bring them to completion, so that his royal majesty may preserve its former honor and strength in every respect, in the manner of his ancestors [Col. 0835A].

Moreover, if the archchaplain of the aforesaid King Charles has come, as you informed us, and wishes to hasten as one sent to our apostolic presence, we wish you to come to us together with him, so that by common deliberation we may consider together what must be done for the exaltation of the Church of God.

But if he has not come to Rome, after carefully inquiring into the matter, inform us personally by your letters, with complete certainty, of the affairs, wishes, and devotions of either Carolomannus or his aforesaid brother the king, so that we may know with the clearest understanding what ought advantageously to be done.

When you have read this letter, burn its text immediately in fire, so that no one may recognize it. Given as above.

## CCXXII. TO COUNT BOSO (879)

He writes that he is keeping silent about what he had secretly heard from him, and that he is altogether expecting the assistance he had promised; moreover, he says that he is well.

The secret which, with God’s help, we shared with you when we were at Troyes, we certainly retain unaltered and fixed in our apostolic breast, hidden away like a treasure. With all our strength, as long as life remains, we eagerly desire to carry it out insofar as it lies within our power.

Therefore, if it pleases your excellence, you ought now to bring this very matter to completion. For, in accordance with the holy Apostle’s admonition, “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 7) [Col. 0835D]—with the Lord’s favor, you can effectively fulfill your desires.

We are exceedingly distressed as we await your promise, which we have not yet seen fulfilled, because we are suffering in every way the continual and exceedingly grave attacks of the pagans. For this reason, in view of the present necessity, we have refrained from sending elsewhere and seeking suitable assistance.

Therefore, if you intend to act, do what must be done; otherwise, make haste to send us your reply without delay. Since you rejoice when concerned about our safety, we inform your greatness that, with Christ as our guide, we had a prosperous journey on our return and now enjoy good bodily health. Given as above.

## CCXXIII. TO ANSPERTUS, ARCHBISHOP OF MILAN (879)

He rebukes him for not having come when summoned to the council for the third time; he orders him to attend the synod with his bishops; and he forbids him to make any agreement with the Frankish kings who had entered Italy. Otherwise he threatens excommunication.

To the most reverend and most holy ANSPERTUS, archbishop of Milan.

You are plainly found guilty of great disobedience and dangerous presumption. While we were vigorously struggling, in this perilous time and under the pressure of extreme necessity, on behalf of all the Churches of God entrusted to us, in accordance with the Apostle, and for the salvation of the people, you offered no assent as was required and made no effort to provide assistance, as though out of compassion for your head [Col. 0836B].

Moreover, after letters from our apostolate had been sent to you a second and third time through our brothers and fellow bishops, we canonically summoned you, as a suitable fellow minister, to share in our solicitude, following the custom of our predecessors—first while we were in Gaul and afterward while we were staying at Pavia—but you did not wish to appear.

We also ordered by regular and apostolic summons that, because of so many matters requiring common discussion and synodal deliberation, you should make every effort to come to Rome without offering any excuse. Yet, contrary to canonical sanction, you neither took care to send us and the holy synod, in a letter of formal explanation, a suitable minister from your side to present your excuse, nor did you come yourself. You acted with nothing but reckless disregard, rather than striving with all your effort to bear together with us, who carry the burdens of you all, those burdens which the Apostle commands us to bear [Col. 0836C].

For all these manifest offenses and presumptuous acts committed by you, after deliberation with the venerable synod held before the most sacred body of the blessed apostle Peter, prince of the apostles, and in accordance with the unaltered rule of the African Council (African Council, chapter 42; Fifth Council of Carthage, chapter 10), we have deprived you, by the authority of the Holy Spirit, of all ecclesiastical communion. You failed to attend our council, failed to subscribe to your excuse in a letter of formal explanation, and failed to take care to give your rightful account of the reason for your impediment to us, the primate of you all [Col. 0836D]. This deprivation shall remain until you have taken care to present your personal presence to us and to the apostolic see.

Now, therefore, because while firmly upholding justice we must always offer mercy with kindness, we command your affection again by these apostolic letters: since you did not attend the aforesaid synod, attend devotedly, together with your suffragan bishops and setting aside every excuse, the synod which, with the Lord’s help, we shall celebrate on the fourth day before the Ides of October, in accordance with chapter 34 of the apostolic canon.

Or, if it becomes clear that some evident necessity prevents you from coming, send distinguished men from your side who can suitably inform us and the holy council of the reason for your inability, truthfully report it, and wisely deliberate with us concerning those things that must be undertaken for the benefit of the Churches of God [Col. 0837A].

For if, despising this fourth summons issued by our apostolic authority, you refuse either to come yourself to the synod already announced or to send your men, know for certain that we shall immediately bind you, as a disobedient person, with a greater ecclesiastical judgment.

Furthermore, we announce and command this also, by our admonition, to you and all your suffragans: when one of the kings of the Franks, with God’s favor, has entered Italy, do not presume to make any agreement without our consent and unanimity. The thirty-fifth chapter of the Apostolic Canon commands and says:

“It is fitting that the bishops of each people should know which one among them is to be regarded as first, whom they should consider as their head, and that they should undertake nothing beyond his knowledge except those matters alone which concern their own parish and the villages subject to it. Nor should he undertake anything without the knowledge of all. Thus there will be unanimity, and God will be glorified through Christ in the Holy Spirit” [Col. 0837B].

For this reason we too desire by your common deliberation and consent to undertake in every way those things which must be done for the common and necessary benefit of the Churches of God entrusted to us. For, as Saint Leo says, we are not otherwise one flock and one shepherd unless, as the Apostle teaches, we all say the same thing: “Let us be perfect in the same understanding and in the same knowledge” (1 Corinthians 1). Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the twelfth indiction.

## CCXXIV. TO THE SAME (879)

Nearly the same subject.

To ANSPERTUS, archbishop.

Since all who are counted by the Christian name, from the very beginning of the religion, have striven to follow the Roman Church, exalted by the faith and merits of Peter, with every veneration and to honor it with every reverence; and since no one has raised obstacles against it except one who wished to be judged by it, we are greatly astonished that you so exceed the duty of your order that, through the disguise of ignorance, you fail to notice what authority and what privilege belong to the same holy Roman Church, and that you do not strive, with any filial affection, to sympathize with her who gave you birth, grieving and suffering injuries [Col. 0837D].

Rather, in contempt of religion, you not only refuse to provide us with whatever assistance is possible, but, when we were recently returning from Gaul, you delayed meeting us at Pavia, even so that you might at least hear and grieve over our outcry and labor, which we were enduring on behalf of all. While we remained there for a longer time, we summoned you by our letters to come to the synod.

But, relying on the audacity of disobedience and presumption, you did not then take care to present yourself to us. Finally, after we had again summoned you to the general synod celebrated at Rome after the past Kalends of May, you entirely delayed attending.

For this reason, in accordance with the Apostle, we would have struck you with a fitting correction in canonical words, since we have ready at hand the means “to punish every disobedience,” had not the mercy of the apostolic see tempered our mind [Col. 0838A].

But you, dearest ones, do not abuse such great patience on our part. Come to your senses, lay aside all presumption, and adhere to us for the common salvation, peace, and security of the kingdom, so that you may accept what we accept and reject what we reject, in order that we may all say the same thing and hold the same understanding.

For I gladly hear that you are concerned for the common salvation, the condition of the kingdom, and peace; but, conversely, I do not willingly admit those who hold something other than what we hold.

Now, since you have repeatedly been summoned to the synod and have so far disdained to come, as we have stated, lay aside every presumption and unavoidable excuse and attend the other synod which, with the help of divine grace, we shall celebrate on the fourth day before the Ides of October of the coming thirteenth indiction [Col. 0838B].

Thus, with the Lord’s assistance, we may accomplish by common deliberation, common vote, and common agreement those things that concern the benefit of the holy Church of God. But if you then again disdain to come, know that you will be judged canonically both for your past and for your future negligences, so that, in accordance with the sacred canons, you may be content with the communion of your churches, since you do not wish to submit to ecclesiastical discipline (African Council, chapter 43; Fifth Council of Carthage, chapter 10). Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the twelfth indiction.

## CCXXV. TO THE ELECTED BISHOP THEODOSIUS OF NÔN (879)

He praises his observance toward the Roman Church and his distinguished virtues; he declares his goodwill toward him; he advises him to receive episcopal consecration from him.

To THEODOSIUS, venerable deacon and elected bishop of the holy Church of Nôn.

After receiving and reading your letter, we recognized with the clearest understanding the sincerity of your devotion and faith toward the Church of the blessed apostle Peter and toward our pontificate. We rejoiced greatly because you earnestly sought our grace and blessing with a wholly humble spirit.

For the venerable priest John, who came from your region, reported to us verbally many praises of your goodness and patience—qualities that must be possessed in great measure by a priest [Col. 0838D]. Therefore, as a beloved member of Christ’s body and our spiritual son, we embrace you with the outstretched arms of our apostolate, love you with paternal affection, and desire always to foster you with apostolic kindness.

For this reason we admonish your prudence not to turn aside in any other direction or seek to receive the grace of the episcopate contrary to the sacred institutions of the venerable Fathers. Listen to the desirable voice of the supreme Judge, who says: “Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many. Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matthew 25).

But return with all your heart and all your will to the bosom of the apostolic see, from which your predecessors received the honey-sweet teachings of divine law, together with the form of sacred instruction and the honor of the supreme priesthood [Col. 0839A]. Thus you too may receive episcopal consecration from the apostolic see, which is the head and teacher of all the Churches of God, through the laying on of our hands, with Christ’s approval.

Then, fortified according to the ancient custom by the authority and protection of Saint Peter and ourselves, you may govern vigorously and securely the people of the Lord entrusted to you. When you come into the presence of the Most High, may you come with rejoicing, carrying your sheaves, and be able to say joyfully to the Lord: “Behold, I and the children whom you have given me.” Through this may you be able to rejoice with God without end. Given on the fourth day of the month of June, in the twelfth indiction.

## CCXXVI. TO ANSELM, BISHOP OF LIMOGES (879)

A man who baptized his son under the pressure of necessity must not be separated from his wife.

To ANSELM, bishop of the Church of Limoges.

(30th question, 1, “Ad limina.”)

This man, named Stephen, came here to the thresholds of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, princes of the apostles, for the sake of prayer. By presenting his case to our episcopate, he informed us that, when his son was at the point of death and had not yet been washed in the waters of baptism, he had baptized him because the absence of priests compelled him to do so; that he himself had received the child by holding him in his own hands; and that, after the matter had been disclosed to your knowledge, your reverence, as though inflamed with zeal for righteousness, had judged that the aforesaid man ought to be separated from his wife [Col. 0839C].

This must not be done in any way, since Scripture says that a wife has been joined to a man by God, and: “What God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matthew 19). Hence the Lord also commands most clearly in the Gospel that no one may dismiss his wife except on account of fornication.

Therefore, relying especially on the command of such great authority, we say that what necessity imposed must be disregarded and judged blameless. For, according to canonical sanction, the act of baptizing may freely be performed by faithful laypeople as well, if necessity requires it.

Thus, if the aforesaid father, seeing his son dying in body, washed him in the water of sacred baptism so that he would not abandon a soul perishing in eternal death, but might snatch him from the power of the author of death and darkness and send him, indubitably regenerated, into the kingdom of Christ [Col. 0839D], he is rightly praised for having done well.

Accordingly, we judge that he may remain joined without penalty to his wife, to whom he was lawfully united long ago, for as long as they live, and that he must not on this account be separated in any way contrary to the divine authorities cited above. Given on the seventh day of the month of June, in the twelfth indiction.

## CCXXVII. TO KING CAROLOMANNUS (879)

He urges him to defend the Roman Church, which was suffering many losses from the Saracens; he asks him to receive the envoys kindly and to place confidence in them.

To our most beloved and spiritual son, CAROLOMANNUS, most glorious king.

Because, following the custom of our pontifical predecessors, we love your royal excellence, divinely exalted, with devoted affection of mind, we desire with a thirsting heart to see it devoted to the honor and exaltation of the holy Church of God. Thus, through the triumphal struggle of your greatness, the strength and honor of the apostolic see—which we remember it possessed in the time of your ancestors, the most glorious emperors—may remain undiminished and unimpaired while you reign; your royal glory may flourish without diminution, and the gift of eternal reward may be granted to you by heavenly grace.

Now, because of the many and great calamities and necessities which we continually suffer from pagans and evil Christians alike, although we cannot write about them in proportion to their number, and although we do not believe that your excellence is unaware of them, we have been moved by pastoral solicitude and, placing our lives in our own hands, have undertaken immense labors of every kind, both by sea and on land [Col. 0840B].

For we call God to witness—before whom the hidden things of all are manifest—that, in our eager desire for your wished-for honor, we sought the powerful assistance of no human being except you. But, obstructed by the plots of evil men whom you yourself know, we were unable to accomplish this.

Therefore, dearest son, by our apostolic exhortation we admonish your glory not to fail to undertake, for love of the holy Roman Church, your mother, the labor of its defense. From this, honor and salvation may increase for you both here and forever.

For this reason we ask you, for love of God and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, to heed our apostolic admonitions with all your strength, so that you may strive by every means to come to our aid, either personally or through your most salutary counsel. We are so heavily burdened and shaken on every side by the destruction of this land that we can no longer endure such things at all.

For if, God forbid, it should happen that through you the Church of God remains without defense in the present and continues in such turmoil, beware lest your souls suffer harm before Christ’s tribunal and in the presence of the princes of the apostles. Since we exhort you with paternal admonition, it is entirely fitting, according to the duty of our ministry, that we ourselves act without hesitation in matters that belong to God and are beneficial to your salvation.

We have sent to you our present envoys, John and Paschal, venerable bishops and our beloved faithful servants [Col. 0840D]. We ask you to receive them kindly for love of us, grant them a place of familiarity, and most willingly heed whatever they tell you on our behalf. Given on the seventh day of the month of June, in the twelfth indiction.

## CCXXVIII. TO THE SAME (879)

That Conspertus should be made bishop of the Church of Vercelli.

To his beloved and spiritual son, CAROLOMANNUS, glorious king.

Together with these present envoys of ours, we have sent this venerable deacon named Conspertus, known, as we believe, to you, into the service of your greatness [Col. 0841A]. We ask you to receive him kindly for love of us. Since he is faithful to both you and us, we ask your excellence to grant him the episcopate of the Church of Vercelli with a gracious spirit, so that, having obtained episcopal honor through our generosity and yours, with God’s help, he may prove more devoted and faithful to us all. Given on the seventh day of the month of June, in the twelfth indiction.

## CCXXIX. TO BRANIMIR (879)

He welcomes him as he returns to the embrace of the Roman Church; he urges him to persevere in the love of God; he imparts the apostolic blessing he had requested; and he urges him to allow his envoy to carry the letter to the Bulgarians.

To his beloved son BRANIMIR.

On rereading the letter of your nobility, which you entrusted to us through the venerable priest John, our mutual faithful servant, we have recognized with the clearest understanding how much faith and sincere devotion you hold toward the Church of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and toward us.

Since, with God’s favor, you profess that you wish to be faithful and obedient in all things as a beloved son to Saint Peter and to us, who by divine grace hold his place, we offer your nobility very worthy thanks through this letter of our apostolate. With paternal affection, as our dearest son, we receive you as you return to the embrace of the holy apostolic see, your mother, from whose purest fountain your fathers drank the honey-sweet streams of holy preaching [Col. 0841C]. We embrace you with spiritual arms and desire to foster you with apostolic kindness.

May the grace and blessing of God, of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, princes of the apostles, and of ourselves be poured out upon you, so that you may always remain safe and secure from visible and invisible enemies who never cease to plot against and obstruct human salvation, and so that you may more easily obtain victory over your enemies.

For the more humbly you strive to submit yourself to God, obey his commands, and show due honor to his priests and ministers for love of the Lord, the more certainly will you be victorious and powerful over all your enemies and rebellious adversaries.

Therefore we admonish your diligence always to keep God before your eyes in all your actions, to fear him and love him with your whole heart, for, as the Psalmist says: “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord; he greatly delights in his commandments. His offspring shall be mighty in the land” (Psalm 112 [111]). And he himself says in the Gospel: “Whoever loves me will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14).

Since this is so, if you glorify God by your good works, which shine in the present, you will undoubtedly be adorned with everlasting glory in the future, because he himself testifies through Moses that he will do this, saying: “Those who glorify me I will glorify” (1 Samuel 2).

As through the aforesaid priest you presented three requests to our episcopate, namely that we should bless you with our apostolic mouth for the increase of your salvation, we willingly did so. On the day of the Lord’s Ascension, while celebrating the solemnities of Mass at the sacred altar of the holy apostle Peter, we raised our hands upward and blessed you, all your people, and all your land, so that, saved here and forever in body and soul alike, you might govern prosperously and securely the earthly principality you possess and, after death, rejoice happily with God in the heavenly realm and reign forever [Col. 0842A].

Since we know that this same priest John is faithful in all things both to you and to us, we gave him our apostolic letter to carry to the king of the Bulgarians. Therefore, for love of Saint Peter and of us, we ask you to allow him, with your permission, to complete this mission of ours without delay, so that we may have abundant thanks for this also toward your affection. Given on the seventh day of the month of June, in the twelfth indiction.

## CCXXX. TO THE PRIESTS AND PEOPLES SUBJECT TO BRANIMIR (879)

He receives them as they return to the embrace of the Roman Church and urges them to persevere.

To all venerable priests and to the entire people.

When we read the letter of your prince Branimir, which he himself sent to us through the venerable priest John, we recognized not only his devotion but also the sincerity of your faith and the love which you hold toward Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and toward us [Col. 0842C].

Since, like dearest sons, you desire with all your mind and all your will to return to the holy Roman Church—from which you acknowledge that your ancestors received the honey-sweet teachings of holy preaching—and since you greatly desire to receive our apostolic grace and blessing, we have been filled with great joy.

Therefore, with outstretched arms we embrace you, receive you with paternal love, and desire always to foster you with apostolic kindness, provided that you sincerely retain this intention and promise of yours to the end and faithfully keep it. For the Lord says: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10); and the apostle Paul says the same: “You have become participants in Christ, if indeed you hold firm the beginning of your faith to the end” (Hebrews 3).

Therefore be faithful to God and to Saint Peter, as you have promised, until death, and you will receive the crown of life which God has promised to those who love him.

We continually make remembrance of you before the Lord in our sacred prayers, raising our hands upward to the Lord; we commend you, together with our beloved son, your prince, to almighty God, and bless you with every spiritual blessing in Christ Jesus our Lord, so that here and forever you may exist blessed in body and soul alike and rejoice in the Lord forever. Given on the seventh day of the month of June, in the twelfth indiction.

## CCXXXI. TO MICHAEL, KING OF THE BULGARIANS (879)

He gives thanks to God that Michael has sent envoys to him to receive ecclesiastical teaching and canonical institutions; he urges him to return to the Roman Church; and he promises that, if Michael wishes, he will send an envoy.

To his beloved and spiritual son MICHAEL, glorious king of the Bulgarians.

How great is the abundance of his goodness and compassion with which almighty God has loved you—who could adequately recount it, dearest son? When, through the infusion of his Holy Spirit into your heart, he graciously deemed it fitting to reveal to you his only-begotten Son, through whom he created all visible and invisible things; to illumine your mind with the light of his splendor; and to lead you from darkness [Col. 0843B] to the true light and instruct you in the doctrine of the true faith. Also, when his grace revealed this to you, you sent your legates—namely, Peter, your kinsman, and John and Martin—to the see of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, which exists as the head and teacher of all the Churches of God, and from which all kings and princes have received the word of truth, during the time of our lord Nicholas, most blessed bishop and predecessor. You sent them so that you too might receive ecclesiastical doctrine and canonical institutions from that place where Christ established the primacy of the whole Church; and this, in accordance with your will, you obtained from that same holy Roman Church.

Now, therefore, as though you were a sheep of the Lord’s flock entrusted to us in the person of that very prince of the apostles, we visit you, our dearest son, through these letters of our apostolate, and spiritually embrace you in our apostolic arms. We continually commend you, together with all your people, to the Lord in our sacred prayers, asking that he who granted you a glorious earthly principality may also grant you, after death, the heavenly kingdom and everlasting glory. Therefore we admonish your Glory to return with devoted mind and willing spirit to your holy mother, the Roman Church, so that, aided by the prayers of the holy apostles, you may easily overcome both visible enemies [f. lacking: and invisible ones]. And because, as has been said, we love you greatly, we wish to send to you a legate of ours together with a visitation from the apostolic see, and to visit you [Col. 0843D] as a shepherd visits the flock of his lord entrusted to him—provided, however, that we learn of your will, namely, that you desire to receive our legation and apostolic visitation. If you do desire this, take care to send word to us through this John, our faithful and venerable presbyter, with your written assurance, dearest and most beloved son.

May almighty God, who has shown you the way of truth and graciously illumined your heart with the light of his splendor, deign now and always to preserve you unharmed, together with every prosperity and [Col. 0844A] health. Given on the sixth day before the Ides of June, in the twelfth indiction.

### CCXXXII. TO AIRARD, ARCHBISHOP OF AUSCUM, AND HIS SUFFRAGANS. (Year 879.)

He urges the correction of the people’s corrupt morals, especially incestuous marriages: no one is to abandon his wife and marry another, or have a concubine together with his wife; no one is to appropriate the immovable property of the Church; and the clergy are to remain under the authority of the bishop.

To the most reverend and most holy Airard, archbishop, and to Involatus of Convenae, Wainard of Consoranni, and Sarsto, bishops of Bigorre [Note: [Col. 0843D] In the Roman edition the heading is corrupt; and since I have doubted whether Labbe corrected it here by his own conjecture rather than on the authority of any manuscript, I have thought it should be reproduced here as it stands in the Roman edition: “To the most reverend and most holy Airard, archbishop, and Involatus of Convenae, together with Ardo of Consoranni and Sarsto, our bishops of Ours.”].

We have learned through the truthful report of many people that, in your regions, many transgressions against the religion of all Christianity and the venerable decrees of the holy Fathers are being committed by wicked Christians. Yet you are in no way able to restrain or entirely suppress those whom neither the gentleness of your pious admonition, nor the bond of due excommunication, nor even the word of apostolic constitution can prevent from the assault and perpetration of such great evils. Therefore, my brothers, we grieve together with you over the rashness of the people who presume such things and are unwilling at present to undertake any fruitful penance for them, treating your salutary correction as worthless.

Since, therefore, you have humbly represented to our apostolate that, supported by apostolic authority, you might freely correct a people burdened and filled with iniquity, [Col. 0844C] we agree with the teacher of the nations, for we are taught by the divine word that we must sometimes strengthen our brothers, once converted, when they have been rendered ineffective by some worldly turmoil (Luke 22). We say with him: “Correct the unruly, console the fainthearted, rebuke sinners, entreat the insolent, and reprove those who act unjustly, with all authority” (1 Thess. 5).

For that people has been entrusted to you, just as a flock of sheep is entrusted to the shepherds of the Lord. Unless you correct them now through temporal reproof in such a way that they may be saved in spirit on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ, their blood will undoubtedly be demanded from your hands. But if they do not obey you when you proclaim these things, they themselves will perish in their iniquities, while you will have freed your own souls.

Moreover, we hear that they are committing a very unlawful and detestable evil against the venerable decrees of the holy Fathers—namely, that, observing no blood relationship and respecting no kinship of proximity, each man takes as his wife a female relative, whatever degree of relationship may exist, and joins himself to her in an incestuous and abominable marriage. It is not lawful for Christians to do this, so long as they recognize their descent.

Therefore our most holy predecessors, Stephen, Eugenius, and Leo, prohibited such an abominable marriage by synodal decree, saying: “No one shall presume to join in marriage with a cousin, niece, stepmother, brother’s wife, or any woman of his own kinship, because it is written in the law of the Lord: ‘You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s wife, or of your brother’s wife, or of your sister; for that is your own nakedness’” (Lev. 18).

If God commanded the Hebrew people to observe these things even before the incarnation of his only-begotten Son, how much more must we, who hold the teachings of the Christian religion, abstain from unlawful marriages, lest, plunged into the abyss of eternal fire, we be consumed in its flames? If anyone is found in such an abominable marriage and wishes to remain in it, or if, having now been separated from his wife, he attempts such a thing, let him know that by apostolic authority he is bound by the bond of anathema, and let no priest grant him communion. If, however, moved [to repentance], he separates himself from the unlawful union, let him be subjected to penance, as the priest of the place shall determine.

We also command them together with you that no one may abandon his own wife and, while she is alive, presume to take another; nor may anyone have two wives at the same time, or a wife and a concubine. We further command that no priest or layman may, under any pretext, remove immovable property from pious and venerable places and keep it for his own use. Whoever presumes to do so shall be subject to canonical corrections.

We also decree that all presbyters and clerics shall remain under the authority of their own bishop and do nothing without his knowledge, according to the rule established by the Fathers. If any priest or cleric presumes to act otherwise, let him be canonically rebuked by his bishop. A layman, moreover, who presumes to remove any cleric from the bishop’s authority shall be excommunicated.

These things, dearest brothers, we have written for you, at your request and for the sake of your honor, as authoritative instructions, so that, fortified by the commands of our constitution, you may confidently offer services worthy of our God and render the praises that are due. We wish your Holiness good health in Christ. Given on the Ides of June, in the twelfth indiction.

### CCXXXIII. TO ROSTAGNUS AND OTHERS. Fragment—(Year 879.)

To Rostagnus, archbishop of Arles; Sigibald, archbishop [Col. 0845D] of Narbonne; and Robert, archbishop of Aix, jointly.

We have learned from the report of trustworthy men that Gilbert, venerable bishop of Nîmes, rashly invaded a certain monastery of ours which we had acquired under the authority of that same bishop, distributed all the property of the monastery through his own men, and entirely expelled its monks from it, contrary to the sacred rules. This displeased us as greatly as—as you yourself recognize with us—you cannot doubt that, having trampled upon the reverence due to the venerable canons, he acted against the privilege of the apostolic see.

Therefore we send you, so that, acting in our place together with our brothers and fellow bishops, you may summon the same bishop of Nîmes to a common conference and admonish him by our authority to remove both himself and his men from every act of invasion of that monastery, and thereafter presume neither to molest its property nor the monks who serve the Lord there. If, however, God forbid, he should hear your admonitions with deaf ears, then, by the authority of blessed Peter the apostle, to whom that monastery belongs, and also by ours, suspend him from priestly ministry by excommunicating him, until either he withdraws from that invasion or comes to the apostolic see or to our presence to give us satisfaction. May your holiness act in this matter as is fitting, so that we may offer praise to God and return thanks to you. Given on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the twelfth indiction.

### CCXXXIV. TO THE CLERGY OF SALONA. (Year 879.)

He urges them to return to the bosom of the Roman Church; and that the archbishop elected by them receive consecration and the pallium from him, not from anyone else; and that they trust the legate who will report certain matters orally.

To the most reverend and holy bishops Vitalis of Adrana, Dominicus of Absarus, and the other Dalmatian bishops; also to John, archpresbyter of the holy see of Salona; and to all priests and elders of the people residing in the cities of Split, Zadar, and the other cities.

Moved by pastoral concern, we have undertaken through these letters of our apostolate to visit you, as though you were the Lord’s sheep entrusted to us in blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, the Lord saying: “If you love me, Simon Peter, feed my sheep” (John 21). Although until now we have been hindered by the continual persecution of the nations, we admonish your fraternity to strive, after the example of your predecessors, to return with all your heart and willing intention to the see of blessed Peter the apostle, which is the head and teacher of all the Churches of God, and to us, who by divine appointment preside over it. From that source you may receive the honor of the highest priesthood and the form of the entire ecclesiastical order—from the source, as you remember, from which your parents and predecessors drank the honey-sweet streams of holy preaching and apostolic teaching.

You ought to remember how clearly prosperity accompanied those same predecessors of yours when, with devoted hearts, they flocked to the threshold of Peter, the key-bearer of the heavenly kingdom, as his own sons; and how much adversity you have endured thereafter and until now, when you did not hesitate to separate yourselves from it as though you were strangers.

Therefore, because we love you greatly, seeking not what is yours but you yourselves, we admonish and exhort you with paternal kindness to hasten joyfully, as we have said, back to the bosom of the holy Roman Church, your mother. Thus the archbishop canonically elected by you, coming to us with the consent and will of you all, may without delay receive from us, according to ancient custom, the grace of episcopal consecration and the sacred pallium. Possessing the grace and blessing of Saint Peter and of us, you may be freed from every evil, filled with every good, rejoice in the present age, and undoubtedly exult without end with the Lord in the age to come.

Moreover, if you have any doubts, because of anything said by the Greeks or Slavs, concerning your return to us, your consecration, or the reception of the pallium, know for certain that we shall endeavor to assist you by our authority, according to the statutes of the holy Fathers and our predecessors, the pontiffs.

But if, perhaps treating this apostolic admonition—or rather, canonical command—as worthless, you disdain to return to the apostolic see of the Roman Church and there receive episcopal consecration and the sacred pallium according to the ancient norm, know that you are to be entirely excommunicated from all ecclesiastical communion. In the meantime, however, by the authority of God and Saint Peter, we command you not to have permission to receive consecration or the pallium from elsewhere. For if you do so, we shall undoubtedly judge you transgressors and disobedient.

We have sent this letter of our apostolate to your fraternity through this present John, a venerable presbyter, our faithful and intimate associate. We have entrusted him with certain matters to report to you orally; therefore do not hesitate to believe everything he says to you on our behalf. We have also ordered this letter to be sealed at the end with our bulla, so that it may be brought to the knowledge of all of you. Given on the tenth day of June, in the twelfth indiction.

### CCXXXV. TO THREE ARCHBISHOPS. (Year 879.)

That they remove the bishop of Nîmes from his unlawful invasion of a certain monastery and, if he does not obey, excommunicate him.

To Rostagnus, archbishop of Arles; Sigibald, archbishop of Narbonne; and Rotbert, archbishop of Aix, jointly.

We have learned from the report of trustworthy men that Gilbert, venerable bishop of Nîmes, rashly invaded a certain monastery of ours which we had acquired under the authority of that same bishop, and distributed all the property of the monastery through his own men, entirely expelling its monks from it contrary to the sacred rules. This displeased us as greatly as—as you yourself recognize with us—you cannot doubt that, having trampled upon the reverence due to the venerable canons, he acted against the privilege of the apostolic see.

Therefore we send you, so that, acting in our place together with our brothers and fellow bishops, you may summon the same bishop of Nîmes to a common conference and admonish him by our authority to remove both himself and his men from every act of invasion of that monastery, and thereafter presume neither to molest its property nor the monks who serve the Lord there. If, however, God forbid, he should hear your admonitions with deaf ears, then, by the authority of blessed Peter the apostle, to whom that monastery belongs, and also by ours, suspend him from priestly ministry by excommunicating him, until either he withdraws from that invasion or comes to the apostolic see or to our presence to give us satisfaction. May your holiness act in this matter as is fitting, so that we may offer praise to God and return thanks to you. Given on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the twelfth indiction.

### CCXXXVI. TO MICHAEL, KING OF THE BULGARIANS. (Year 879.)

He gives thanks for the legation and gifts sent; he grieves that Michael has defected from the Roman Church, to which he urges him to return; and he shows that the Greeks are unlawfully retaining the diocese of the Bulgarians, since it belongs to the Roman pontiff.

To his beloved and spiritual son Michael, glorious king of the Bulgarians.

We give many thanks to Your Royal Excellence because, like a dearest son filled with divine love, you took care to visit our fatherhood through Functicus, your distinguished and faithful servant, and to honor us with the gifts you sent. Through him we heard of your good health and that of all your faithful, and we rejoiced greatly.
