We, for our part, standing in our continual prayers before the most sacred body of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, strive always to commend you, all your princes, and all your people to Jesus Christ our Lord. We bless you, all your people, and your entire kingdom, praying that, freed from visible and invisible enemies and aided by God’s help, you may always be victorious over your enemies and gloriously attain the palm of the heavenly calling.

May he who, by the abundance of his grace, granted you an earthly kingdom, illumined the eyes of your mind, showed you the way of truth, and led you from darkness to the true light, deign to bring you safely and soundly, persevering in that same holy faith and in good works, to the end. Thus, after the end of this present life, through the intercessions of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, may you be worthy to receive the heavenly kingdom, where, together with all the saints, you may receive all those good things “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man,” which the almighty Lord prepared from the beginning of the world for those who love him (1 Cor. 2).

But you have filled us with no small sadness, dearest son, because you abandoned the see of blessed Peter, the key-bearer of the heavenly kingdom, who appeared to you in a manifest vision and offered you timely assistance. That see is the head and teacher of all the Churches of God. To its founder, blessed Peter, the Lord said: “Feed my sheep” (John 21); and to it the keys of the kingdom of heaven were entrusted, so that whatever it binds on earth may remain bound in heaven, and whatever it looses on earth may be loosed in heaven (Matt. 16).

Return now, most beloved son, to your holy mother, the Roman Church, which gave birth to you from her devout womb and through which, when our holy predecessor Nicholas was pontiff, you received the form of the whole religion and of justice. She holds the primacy of all nations, and to her, as to one mother and one head, the peoples of the whole world come together.

Do not abandon your mother any longer, for she does not forget you; rather, she loves you as her only child and continually makes remembrance of you before the Lord. It was not lawful for the Greeks to usurp another’s parish, since the holy Fathers expressly prohibited this. Therefore they retain our dioceses contrary to the canons established by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world. If our love for you did not restrain us, we would already compel them by apostolic judgment to withdraw from them. Given as above.

### CCXXXVII. TO ANASTASIUS, ABBOT. (Year 879.)

He commands him to return the cell to Bishop Gauderic.

To Anastasius, religious abbot.

We admonish your Religiousness and expressly command you that, setting aside every pretext and excuse for delay, you immediately restore to Gauderic, venerable bishop, the cell of Saint Valentine situated in the Sabine region, which you took from him. [The phrase “until our presence” is textually unclear.] Thus he may neither lose the fruit of his labor nor find that what he henceforth adds to us [reading uncertain] harms him; rather, let him recognize that it benefits him. We also command you through our present chamberlain to do this, and in no way to act otherwise.

When you have presented yourself to us, if perhaps he deservedly lost that cell because of his negligence, we do not wish to defend him against justice, just as we do not permit the innocent man to suffer losses. Given as above.

### CCXXXVIII. TO TUVENTARUS OF MARAUNA. (Year 879.)

He urges him, rejecting all false doctrine, to remain in the faith of the Roman Church; he expresses amazement that Methodius teaches otherwise than he had professed, and indicates that for this reason he has summoned him.

To Tuventarus of Marauna.

We wish you to know that we, who by God’s grace hold the place of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, embrace you as our dearest sons with devoted love and love you with paternal affection. In our continual prayers we commend all of you to Jesus Christ our Lord, always praying for you that almighty God, who has illumined your hearts and led you to the way of truth, may strengthen you in good works and deign to bring you safely and adorned with upright faith and good conduct to the end.

But since, as we have learned from the report of your presbyter John, whom you sent to us, you are uncertain in the true faith, we admonish your affection to hold and believe as the holy Roman Church learned from that prince of the apostles, has held, and will hold until the end of the age. Every day she sends throughout the world the words of the holy faith and the seeds of right preaching, just as you know that our predecessors—namely, the holy pontiffs of the apostolic see—taught your parents from the beginning.

If, however, any bishop of yours or any priest presumes to announce or preach something different to you, inflamed by zeal for God, reject the false doctrine with one mind and one will, standing firm in and holding to the tradition of the apostolic see.

Since we have heard that your archbishop Methodius, ordained by our predecessor, Pope Hadrian, and sent to you, teaches otherwise than he professed in words and writing before the apostolic see that he believed, we are greatly astonished. Nevertheless, for this reason we have sent word to him that he should take care to come to us without any excuse, so that we may hear from his own mouth whether he holds and believes as he promised, or not. Given as above.

### CCXXXIX. TO METHODIUS, ARCHBISHOP OF PANNONIA. (Year 879.)

He commands him to come to him so that he may learn about his doctrine. He prohibits Masses from being celebrated in the Slavic language.

To the most reverend Methodius, archbishop of the Church of Pannonia.

Although you ought, through the teachings of your preaching, to instruct and save the people of the Lord entrusted to you as to a spiritual shepherd, we have heard that you teach them things other than those which the holy Roman Church learned from the prince of the apostles and preaches daily, and that you are leading that people into error.

Therefore, through these letters of our apostolate, we command you to set aside every excuse and take care to come to us immediately, so that we may hear from your own mouth and learn whether you hold and preach as you promised in words and writing that you believed the holy [Col. 0850C] Roman Church, or not, and so that we may know the truth about your doctrine.

We have also heard that you sing Masses in a barbarian language—that is, in the Slavic language. Therefore, in letters already sent to you through Paul, bishop of Ancona, we prohibited you from celebrating the sacred solemnities of Mass in that language. Instead, you are to celebrate either in Latin or in Greek, just as the Church of God, spread throughout the whole world and extended among all peoples, celebrates.

You are permitted, however, to preach and address the people, since the Psalmist exhorts all nations to praise the Lord (Ps. 116), and the Apostle says: “Every tongue shall confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2). Given as above.

### CCXL. TO ANSPERT, ARCHBISHOP OF MILAN. (Year 879.)

He reproves him for not obeying the apostolic see, for treating its legates insultingly, and for celebrating Masses while excommunicated. He therefore urges him to come to the synod as soon as possible, either in person or through legates, to clear himself.

To Anspert, archbishop of Milan.

Alas, to our grief, you are found liable to such great transgressions as no one in the Church of Milan has ever been found liable to in any way. First, you were unwilling to be our associate and participant in our work and labor, but insolently, disobediently, and brazenly rebelled against the apostolic see. Then, when our legates, John, bishop of Ticinum, and Walpert, bishop of Porto, were sent to you from our side, you did not receive them. They stood for a long time before the gate, speaking to you the words of our admonition, so that you ought to have offered us, either personally or through your legate, the obedience appropriate to you according to the custom of your predecessors. Yet you made them stand there irreverently, and did not deign to grant them either reverence or a hearing. Rather, like a deaf asp, you firmly closed the inward chambers of your heart and your ears against the affection of charity.

For these and similar offenses we deprived you for so long of communion and of the celebration of Mass until you came to us and, either personally or through your representative, corrected all your errors, so that only then could we admit you personally into our fellowship.

But, in contempt and insult of the paternal canons, although excommunicated by us, you presumed to exercise the sacred ministry and celebrate Mass. We wished carefully to spare your old age and therefore investigated the matter; but we discovered that it was so true that the present presbyter-bearer of these letters, it seems, did not dare to provide this satisfaction on your behalf before the college of fellow bishops [Note: [Col. 0851D] It seems that the reading should be *praesentium*, namely, “the presbyter-bearer of these letters,” with *videlicet* understood; and that the word *videtur* should be deleted, since it arose from repetition of the following adverb, namely *videlicet*. HARD.].

Therefore, since, with the Lord’s help, we are going to celebrate a synod around the autumn season according to the statutes of the canons, we wish you, setting aside every excuse, to come without delay or send legates. When, with Christ’s assistance, you have cleared yourself of the transgression committed, we shall receive you fully into communion. Given as above.

### CCXLI. TO ANGELBERGA, AUGUSTA. (Year 879.)

He states that he does not wish to absolve Archbishop Anspert at present; but if Anspert clears himself at the synod of the crimes brought against him, then he will absolve him from excommunication. He says that he will offer sacrifice for Emperor Louis on the anniversary of his death.

To his beloved and spiritual daughter, the empress Angelberga.

With devoted affection, we would not fail to hear the prayers of your petition, by which you have asked us to absolve Anspert, archbishop of Milan, from excommunication, in accordance with the divinely granted power of binding and loosing entrusted to us—especially because the annual commemoration of the divine memory of our lord Louis, formerly emperor Augustus, is soon to be celebrated. But because we excommunicated him by synodal decree for his negligence and presumption, as you yourself know well, we do not now wish to absolve him without the consent and will of those same brothers and fellow bishops with whom we pronounced the sentence of excommunication against him. Otherwise, those who despise ecclesiastical discipline either through desire or negligence and presume many things that ought not to be presumed might make light of canonical judgment.

When he himself comes to the synod in question—which, according to the sacred canons established by the Spirit of God, we shall celebrate, with the Lord’s favor, on the fourth day before the Ides of October—or when he sends from his side venerable brothers and fellow bishops who can adequately satisfy us and the holy synod concerning the matters charged against him, then, after true satisfaction, we shall undoubtedly absolve him from every bond of excommunication and unhesitatingly receive him as a brother and fellow minister into the fellowship of our communion.

Therefore, concerning the aforementioned annual commemoration of that lord and your master, do not be troubled that we have not now heard you concerning the absolution of the aforesaid archbishop. For on the very day on which he departed from this world, we shall offer sacrifice to the Lord for the everlasting rest of his soul. We also pray almighty God, moved by fraternal compassion, for the soul of Suppo, that he may be worthy to receive the forgiveness of his sins.

### CCXLII. TO LOUIS, KING. (Year 879.)

He gives thanks for his favorable disposition toward the Roman Church; he urges him to come to defend it against pagan incursions, and tacitly promises him the empire.

To his beloved and spiritual son Louis, glorious king.

After rereading the honey-sweet letters of Your Royal Serenity, which you sent to us through your distinguished count Astald, we know more clearly than daylight how great is your devotion and most sincere desire to exalt and defend the Church of God, after the example of your most glorious parents, the emperors.

Therefore, greatly rejoicing, we give the greatest thanks to Your Excellence, because amid the many troubles and persecutions which we continually endure beyond measure from the pagans, you earnestly desire, with pious devotion of mind, to bring us the assistance and protection of your unconquered power.

Therefore, dearest son, we earnestly ask you to incline the ear of your clemency to our apostolic admonition and hasten to assist us with your powerful arm, so that you may effectively lead the holy Church of God, now placed amid great turmoil, to the harbor of salvation and tranquillity. Through you, with God’s favor, restore the ruined land to its former security, so that for this you may receive a worthy reward from almighty God and acquire an entirely praiseworthy name in the present age.

Therefore know for certain that none of your parents received from our predecessors as much glory and exaltation as we desire, with all our strength and in manifold ways, to bestow upon you if you come.

As for what you sent word about—that you are prevented by the affairs of the kingdom of Louis, your nephew of pious memory—we remain troubled by the great desire we have to see you. Yet, trusting in your kindness, we ask you to set aside every concern and, for the love of God and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, eagerly take to your pious heart the care requested in our petition. Thus, just as the apostolic see, which is the head of all the Churches of God, awaits you with great longing as its only and dearest son, so may it soon enjoy your personal presence.

For if, with God’s favor, you assume the Roman empire, all kingdoms will be subject to you. For if you fully knew how many evils on every side oppress and afflict us—evils which, because of their number, we have been unable to set down in writing—we recognize such wisdom in you that through your greatness we would already be defended. May God preserve you unharmed, dearest son. Given as above.

### CCXLIII. TO THE EMPERORS BASIL, CONSTANTINE, AND ALEXANDER. (Year 879.)

Moved by the emperors’ petitions that there might be peace for the Church of Constantinople, he makes a concession concerning Photius, allowing him to be substituted as patriarch of the Church of Constantinople in place of Ignatius, while decreeing that thereafter no one may ascend to patriarchal dignity except through the ecclesiastical grades. He commands the patriarch of Constantinople to leave the diocese of the Bulgarians under the jurisdiction of the Roman Church; he urges everyone to render the patriarch his due obedience; he commands that those who had been initiated by Methodius and Ignatius be admitted to communion with the Church; and he excommunicates those who refuse to communicate with Photius.

**[LETTER.]**

To our most beloved and excellent spiritual sons, Basil, Constantine, and Alexander, most glorious emperors, ever Augusti.

Among the distinguished praises of your wisdom and gentleness, most Christian princes, a certain light shines far and wide with a purer radiance: instructed in ecclesiastical disciplines, through your love of the faith and devotion to charity, you preserve reverence for the Roman see after the custom of your most pious predecessors, the emperors, and submit all things to its [Note: [Col. 0853D] Photius did not include this statement concerning the authority of the Roman Church in his translation.] authority. Concerning its founder—that is, the prince of all the apostles—the Lord commanded: “Feed my sheep” (John 21).

That it is truly the head of all the Churches of God is declared by the principal rule of the blessed Fathers and by the decrees of orthodox princes, and is attested by the most reverend writings of your Piety. For nothing shines forth with clearer light than pious devotion and right faith in a prince.

And because, with this ardor of mind and this devotion to religion, you earnestly request in your honey-sweet letters that reverence be shown to our pontificate, it is right that we should accomplish this, after due consideration of reason and the circumstances of the time, with the consent and will of the apostolic see entrusted to us.

You therefore asked us that, as the apostolic see opened the bowels of its compassion, we should receive the most reverend Photius into the honor of the patriarchate, the dignity of the highest priesthood, and the fellowship of the ecclesiastical college, and make him a participant in our communion, lest we allow the Church of God, already disturbed for so long, to remain divided and shaken by scandal.

Therefore, accepting the petitions of Your Serenity with appropriate consideration, and knowing that the patriarch Ignatius of pious memory has now departed from this present life, we have examined the circumstances of the time and determine that what was recently done concerning Photius may be granted pardon, although it is established that he usurped for himself an office forbidden to him without consulting our see [Note: [Col. 0853D] Photius removed the name of Ignatius and attached other material.]. [Note: [Col. 0853D] Photius changed this into the opposite sense, so that he might claim that this see had been received by him under compulsion from the emperors [Col. 0854D].]

We do not prejudice the apostolic constitutions, nor dissolve the regulations of the blessed Fathers; rather, relying upon their manifold authority, we note that the second canon of the Council of Nicaea says most plainly: “Since many things have been done against the ecclesiastical rule either through necessity or because men were otherwise compelled.” Hence Pope Gelasius also says that, where no necessity presses, the constitutions of the Fathers are to be preserved inviolate [Col. 0854B] [Note: [Col. 0854D] Gelasius, Letter 6: “At a time of necessity, dispensation has a place.”]. Saint Leo likewise, in the same spirit, commands that what necessity has imposed should be omitted and judged blameless. Felix, our predecessor, also says in his decretal letter, in words agreeing with this, that the matter of necessity must be handled in one way and that of free choice in another.

The holy council held in Africa likewise commands in its thirty-fifth chapter that, for the peace and benefit of the Church, if the clergy of the Donatists, after correction of the council, should wish to pass over to Catholic unity, and if this should appear beneficial to Christian peace, they should be received in their former honors—not so that the council held in the regions across the sea concerning this matter should be annulled, for in that council it was decreed that those ordained on the Donatist side, if they wished to pass to the Catholic side, should not be received in their honors [Col. 0854C]. The blessed Pope Innocent also says concerning this, in chapter fifty-five (Letter 27), that those who were ordained by the heretic Bonosus were received for this reason: so that scandal might not remain in the Church.

Now, therefore, since the other patriarchs—namely, those of Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem—as well as all the archbishops, metropolitans, bishops, and priests, and the entire clergy of the see of Constantinople who are concerned with the ordination of the patriarchs of blessed memory, Methodius and Ignatius, agree with one will and equal vote, we receive and recognize the same Photius, who, by way of satisfaction, seeks mercy before the synod according to custom [Note: [Col. 0854D] Photius deleted all this, concerning the mercy to be sought before the synod], as a brother in true love, as a fellow minister in the pontifical office [Col. 0854D] (and, by seeking mercy before the synod, as a fellow priest in pastoral teaching), for the peace and benefit of the Church of God, henceforth, with Christ’s favor.

For you, most Christian emperors Augustus, who govern the empire of the holy commonwealth with the most merciful devotion, appear to act as ambassadors for Christ (II Cor. V), since you plead for peace in the Church; and we, upon whom, according to the Apostle, rests concern for all the Churches of God [Col. 0855A] (II Cor. XI), wishing no further controversy to remain in the Church of God, release this same patriarch, together with all—whether bishops, priests, or other clergy, and all laymen—against whom the judgment of censure had been pronounced, from every bond of ecclesiastical sanction. We judge that he should recover the see of the holy Church of Constantinople and be pastor of the Lord’s flock, supported by that authority which the Church spread throughout the world believes was granted to us by Christ our God in the person of the prince of the apostles, blessed Peter, whom the same Savior specially appointed above the others:

> “To you I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew XVI).

For just as nothing is established as excepted in these words, so, through the office of apostolic dispensation, we can undoubtedly bind everything in general and consequently absolve everything, especially since an example of apostolic mercy ought thereby to be offered to all.

For the legates of the apostolic see, sent to Constantinople by our predecessor, the munificent bishop Hadrian, subscribed to the synod held there with vigilant zeal, up to the will of their pontiff. [Lacuna.] Nor should one remain apart from the apostolic see, because the see of blessed Peter, the keeper of the keys of the heavenly kingdom, has the power, after suitable judgment, to absolve whatever has been bound by pontiffs. Indeed, it is clear that many patriarchs—namely, Athanasius and Cyril of Alexandria, Flavian and John of Constantinople, and Polychronius of Jerusalem—although condemned synodally, were subsequently restored without hesitation through the absolution of the apostolic see [Col. 0855C].

Nevertheless, in establishing these provisions, solely by apostolic authority and by the venerable institutions of the holy Fathers, we decree that after the death of this patriarch no layman or court official may be elected or consecrated to the dignity of the patriarchate, except one of the cardinal priests or deacons of the see of Constantinople, in accordance with the sacred canons established by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world.

For no one should rashly act against the ecclesiastical canons and the decrees of the elders: a lector should not quickly become an acolyte, an acolyte a deacon, a deacon a priest, or a priest a bishop. Rather, they should remain for a long time in the lesser offices, and both their life and their service should be tested, so that, after the periods established by the elders have passed, and after their conduct has first been approved and the merits of a good life have shone forth, they may afterward attain the highest priesthood. For what a life tested over a long period deserves to receive must not be seized or usurped suddenly.

If, in every rank of the Church, care must prudently be taken that nothing disordered should exist in the Lord’s house, how much more must we labor to ensure that there be no error in the election of him who is placed above all the ranks? For the condition and order of the entire household of the Lord will waver if what is required in the body is not present in the head; and from this it will follow that all ecclesiastical discipline will be dissolved and every order disturbed. Therefore, although for the ecclesiastical unity and peace which Christ our Lord has given us we now tolerate this as, in some fashion, pardonable, it will not later be possible for it to remain unpunished [Note: [Col. 0855D] Here a period is missing, which I supply from the Roman edition: “If anyone should usurp what we absolutely forbid, since the remission of sin does not grant permission to sin again, nor will what could once be granted for some reason thereafter be lawfully committed with impunity. This also,” etc. [Col. 0856D]].

We further command that these provisions be made, moved by your excellencies’ prayers, provided that the patriarch himself does not henceforth presume in any way to claim or surrender to his own jurisdiction the diocese of the Bulgarians, which our predecessor Nicholas, of pious memory, instructed in apostolic teachings at the request of their king Michael, baptized through his venerable bishops, and trained in every ecclesiastical rule and discipline as was fitting; and provided that he makes no ordination there of anyone of whatever rank [Col. 0856B]. [Lacuna.] There are bishops or priests unlawfully ordained there [lacuna] to the archbishop, or to the bishops who appear to exist there [lacuna]. [Lacuna.] The patriarch himself should presume to send the sacred pallium, which pontiffs customarily use during the solemn celebration of Mass.

Furthermore, concerning the many disturbances by which your Church has now for a long time remained troubled, we earnestly advise your Augustal piety that, venerating the patriarch of Constantinople with due honor as a spiritual father and, as it were, the chief mediator between you and God, diligently proclaiming to you the divine things through which you may attain the eternal kingdom, you should always cherish him with devout affection and honor him in all things, as is fitting.

For in return for the temporal honor which you show him [Col. 0856C], you will receive temporal honor here, and without doubt you will receive manifold honor eternally from him who testifies that he glorifies those who glorify him (I Kings II). Nor should your imperial majesty deign to listen to the falsely spoken words of those who do not cease to sow the tares of scandals over the conspicuous field of the Lord. Nor, because of the whisperings of such men—who always strive to divide the unity of God, the Lord’s garment, the Church of Christ, and who never cease to act deceitfully with their tongues, bearing the venom of asps beneath their lips (Psalm XIII)—should you allow the disposition of your clemency to be moved in any degree against him, or so easily dishonor your supreme priest, established by God’s providence in the governance of the Church of Christ, in a manner which would plainly appear most dishonorable and unbecoming to your holy imperial authority [Col. 0856D].

Moreover, we also command that all bishops and priests, and clergy of whatever order, who adhere to the consecration of Ignatius, patriarch of good memory—whether they remain in the royal city itself or are hidden somewhere outside it, far away or near—be recalled with a merciful disposition to the bosom and unity of the holy Church, and that you receive and embrace them with extended arms and paternal affection. Command that each of them be restored to his own see, so that, just as there is one faith, one baptism among us, and we are all one in Christ [Col. 0857A], so also those who have returned to the unity and fellowship of the Church of God and the body of Christ, saying the same thing and being perfect in the same understanding and knowledge, may become one flock and one shepherd.

Let them no longer dare to say: “I belong to Cephas,” “I to Paul,” “I to Apollos” (I Cor. I), but let them belong to the one Christ, our true God, who is our peace and made both one, and who, coming, deigned to reconcile heavenly things with earthly things. For this reason he died once for our sins, so that he might gather into one the children of God who had been scattered (John XI, 52). Their bond of unity cannot be firm unless the tie of charity binds them into inseparable solidity, so that, with God’s favor, while you reign they may remain safe and secure without any disturbance and may always be able, with continual prayers, to entreat the Lord for your salvation and for the stability of the commonwealth [Col. 0857B].

But if some should perhaps arise who are unwilling to communicate with the same patriarch, let them be admonished a second and a third time to seek union with the holy Church. If they refuse to comply and wish to remain in their obstinacy, we have ordered, through these present envoys of ours together with the synod, that they be deprived of sacred communion until they return to their own patriarch and to the unity of the holy Church, especially since those bishops themselves have been canonically excommunicated by us.

Therefore, if he receives them into his fellowship or has any communion with them, we judge that the same patriarch, together with those bishops, is likewise deprived of ecclesiastical communion.

Issued in the month of August, on the sixteenth day [Col. 0857C] [Note: [Col. 0857D] “On the sixteenth day” is absent from the Roman edition], in the twelfth indiction.

Sent through Peter the priest.

## Annotation of Severinus Binius

### On Photius’s falsification of the preceding letter

We have explained above, in the notes to the Life of Pope John VIII, on what occasion the pontiff wrote this letter concerning Photius’s absolution and restoration. It was written in a Vatican manuscript in Lombard script, which was printed not long ago, though with some errors.

It was plainly by the great providence of God that letters of this kind from Pope John VIII were preserved intact down to our own time in his register—or, as people commonly say, his record—and were not lost like the letters of many other pontiffs, so that from these letters, as well as from those of Nicholas and Hadrian, Photius may a thousand times be convicted of imposture and falsehood.

He has returned to the impostor’s customary art of falsifying the letters of the Roman pontiffs and fabricating new writings. For, besides what has been said about him at sufficient length under the pontificates of Nicholas and Hadrian and proclaimed in the universal synod, new falsehoods have again emerged from the impostor. Thus what happened to these letters of Pope John is precisely what Nicholas exclaimed concerning his own letters, falsified by the same Photius, in his letter to the emperor Michael, when he said:

> “From what was read there from that letter, I find that some things have been added, many changed, and more removed; and in every respect it has been made such by you that we seem either to have ordered nothing, or scarcely anything, through it concerning the cause of our frequently mentioned fellow minister Ignatius.”

Such were Nicholas’s words then; and they would have had to be repeated now by John himself, if he had been able to live and see how Photius had treated the letters which Nicholas had sent to Constantinople—adding, removing, and changing them—most wickedly and disastrously.

“Why does he himself bring this forward?” you may ask. The criminal wished, as though from the letters of Pope John, not only to display his own restoration as firm and confirmed, but also, through those falsified letters, to prove that the eighth ecumenical synod had been condemned by the authority of that same pontiff; that the recent synod celebrated by him against it at Constantinople had been approved; and that this recent synod had likewise been called the eighth, in order to abolish the legitimate eighth ecumenical synod celebrated under Pope Hadrian.

From this arose that great evil whereby the Photian synod was accepted, especially by the Greeks, in place of the genuine eighth synod. This can be seen, among others, in Zonaras, who in his collection and interpretation of the canons placed the sacrilegious Photian synod in the place of the eighth ecumenical synod. Theodore Balsamon likewise calls it universal and cites three of its canons; so too does the rest of the Greek schismatic rabble.

You, therefore, reader, I ask you, sit here as judge of the truth. From the letters of Pope John which Photius rendered and recited in Greek [Col. 0858B] in the second session of his pseudo-synod, but which were restored to Latin by Frederick Metius—Greek by origin, but Catholic in devotion and Latin in faith, recently made bishop of Thermae because of the excellence of his virtue and learning—understand the evil arts of this trickster.

The entire Photian pseudo-synod exists in Greek in a manuscript of the Columnese library, formerly belonging to Cardinal Sirlet, marked number forty. In its second session the same letter of Pope John to the emperor is recited, altered so greatly that scarcely anyone would recognize it as the same letter of John which you have just heard recited. It runs as follows:

> “John, servant of the servants of God, to our most serene and beloved spiritual sons, beloved of God, Basil, Leo, and Alexander, victorious [for “victors,” HARD.] emperors and eternal Augusti.”

[Note: [Col. 0857D] Photius altered almost the entire beginning; [Col. 0858D] because he considered the emperor’s praise too meager, he wished it to be proclaimed more gloriously.]

> “The purity and splendor of your right faith, the integrity of your morals, and your perfect kindness, O most Christian and greatest emperors of the Romans, shine like lamps in the midst of the earth as far as all the ends to which the whole world extends and where it shines [Col. 0858C]. For you do not excel only in right faith while conducting yourselves carelessly in other matters; rather, upon your irreproachable faith you build not wood, grass, or straw, but precious stones, gold, and silver. In short, with eager zeal you accomplish everything by which you know that you can do what is pleasing to God.

> “Nothing is recognized as more pleasing to God than that all his Churches, wherever the sun looks, should live in right faith and mutual love and charity and give him thanks each day. Therefore, earnestly desiring to see this union also visible and flourishing in your Church of God, you have taken the holy Roman Church as your helper through your legates and sacred letters, confident that it would be ready to assist you in what you desired.

> “You were not the first to undertake this or to devise it, but, following in the footsteps of your predecessors, you have adhered to them. In what school? It is worthy even to ask: namely, in that of the prince of the apostles, Peter, whom the Lord established as head of all the Churches, saying to him: ‘Feed my sheep’ (John XXI); and likewise in the sacred and orthodox decrees and teachings of the holy Fathers, as your sacred and devout letters testify. You do this so that the firmness of your faith may shine forth with greater renown and so that your sincere and effective love toward God may be made manifest.

> “Nothing else can happen more suitably or worthily to those who are placed in the greatest dignities and principalities than that they should strive to excel in the splendor of right faith and the love of God, and take care that all who venerate God with the same faith should also be united and bound together by the bond of love.

> “Therefore, obeying your letters and captivated by your honey-sweet words, kindled like fire, we, together with our entire most holy Roman Church, have risen unanimously and harmoniously to carry out promptly and eagerly everything that you have written to us.

> “You wrote to us, our beloved son, asking that we mercifully open our apostolic heart and receive all those in your Church who, whether by their own written acknowledgments or by any other means, have transgressed and become subject to canonical censures, and that we take care for peace and union. Indeed, above all, you asked us to receive Photius, the most religious bishop, as heir and sharer in our communion and as our fellow minister, and to restore him again to the great height of the episcopate and the patriarchal dignity, lest the Church of God remain for a long time tossed about by the waves of schisms hateful to God and of evil scandals.

> “We, however, accepting the prayers of your serenity as rational, just, and pleasing to God, and judging that the time had now arrived which we had previously sought and for which we had prayed God to provide, and that it was also reasonable [Col. 0859B] to restore tranquility to the Church of God, therefore sent legates who would fulfill your will [Note: [Col. 0859D] Photius added this and changed into the opposite meaning what concerned himself].

> “And although your piety forestalled us by using force against Photius—namely, by restoring him before our legates had arrived there—we nevertheless supply what remains, not by our own authority, although we could also do this, but by bringing forward the testimony of the apostolic constitutions and the decrees of the holy Fathers. We do not dissolve the rules of the Church handed down long ago; rather, instructed by the Church itself, we draw them toward whatever serves the Church, since excessive and immutable observance of these rules in particular circumstances tears apart and destroys the entire structure of the Church’s body.

> “For the second canon of the Nicene synod says this: ‘Since men are frequently compelled by necessity or by any other means to transgress the ecclesiastical canons,’ and so forth.

> “Pope Gelasius also says of himself that, where force is not applied, the statutes of the holy Fathers should remain unshaken. Likewise, the most holy Pope Leo, in the same spirit, commands, saying: ‘Where force does not precede, let the statutes of the holy Fathers remain immovable; but where necessity and force are found, let him who has power dispense according to what is suitable for the Churches of God.’ For, according to the divine Apostle, a change is made in the law because of necessity.

> “Pope Felix likewise says in agreement: ‘For it is necessary to observe that, when necessity arises, it is often permissible even to transgress the constitutions of the Fathers.’

> “The holy synod of Carthage also says in its thirty-fifth chapter: ‘We command that the clergy of the Donatists return again to the churches, even though they have been condemned by a synod.’ A synod is also found to have annulled another synod for the sake of the unity and concord of the Church. Pope Innocent likewise says: ‘Let those ordained by the heretic Bonosus be received, lest scandals again arise in the Church of God.’

> “Nor has the apostolic see extended helping hands only to such men, even if they were of the kind that had been condemned as heretics. In its care for the peace of the Church, it has also aided orthodox bishops and patriarchs who fled to it and sought assistance, as the most religious Photius now does.

> “You certainly know the great Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, and Cyril and Polychronius of Jerusalem, and John whom your affection calls Chrysostom, and also Flavian of Constantinople. When these men, condemned and rejected by synods, fled to the holy Roman Church, this apostolic see of ours [Col. 0860A] confirmed them and restored them to their former dignity.

> “If, therefore, those who received ordination from the Donatists or from Bonosus and were expelled by a numerous synod from the boundaries of the Catholic Church are afterward received by another synod and placed among the priests, so that the Church of God may remain undivided, intact, and free from schisms—for nothing appears more detestable and abhorrent in God’s eyes than one who has become the author of schisms in the Churches, and nothing is more pleasing or dear to his goodness than preserving his Church in integrity, perfect love toward God, and love toward one’s neighbor—then much more should men distinguished by orthodox faith and renowned for the gravity of their life and their knowledge of affairs not be despised [Note: [Col. 0859D] Photius added these words himself] or burdened by the yoke of penance, but restored to their former dignity.

[Note: [Col. 0859D] Much is known to have been omitted here by Photius, including passages proclaiming the authority of the apostolic see and mentioning the legation of his predecessor Hadrian.]

> “Since this apostolic see once received the keys of the kingdom of heaven from the first and great high priest, Jesus Christ, through the prince of the apostles Peter, when he said to him: ‘To you I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven’ (Matthew XVI), it has the power to bind and loose all things and, according to the prophet Jeremiah, to uproot and to plant (Jeremiah I).

> “For this reason, exercising the authority of the prince of the apostles Peter, we affirm to you, and through you also to the most holy brothers and fellow ministers, the patriarchs of Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem, and to the remaining bishops and priests and to the entire Church of Constantinople, that we agree and consent with you—or rather, with God—in all the things which you have asked of us [Note: [Col. 0860D] All this was added by the impostor Photius].

> “First, we receive Photius, the most admirable and religious archbishop and patriarch, our brother, as a sharer and participant and heir of communion with the holy Roman Church—not only on account of the other virtues in which he excels, but also so that scandals may be removed, the peace of God established, and mutual love strengthened among us.

> “Receive him also yourselves with a sure and firm disposition, removing from your hearts every poison of iniquity and malice, every duplicity and ambiguity, just as the Roman Church has received him.”

[Note: [Col. 0860D] The entire following passage is likewise an addition by the impostor.]

> “For we have learned from nearly all those who come here from among those who are present there that Photius excels before God in every distinction, not only in wisdom and prudence concerning divine and human matters, but also in every moral virtue and in his observance of the divine commandments, and that he is celebrated as an irreproachable worker.

> “We did not consider it right that such a man should remain idle and useless, but that he should again be raised up on high and shine in your Church, exercising the works customary to him and beloved by God, both toward priests and toward bishops. Therefore, taking up our speech again, we say to you: Receive this man without any doubt.”

[Col. 0860D] [Note: [Col. 0860D] These are Photius’s additions against the synods held against him.]

> “Let no one, in excuse for himself, bring forward the unjust synods held against him, nor, as many more foolish people think, accuse the decrees of our blessed predecessors, the pontiffs Nicholas and Hadrian, issued against Photius. For the acts carried out against the most holy Photius were not accepted by them.

> “Let no one use your written acknowledgments as an occasion for fostering schisms with him or among yourselves. Everything has now been settled and annulled; everything done against Photius has been rendered void and null by us, the least of men, and placed in the hands of the prince of the apostles, and through him upon the shoulders of Jesus Christ, the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world [Col. 0861A].”

[Note: [Col. 0861D] These words were inserted by the same falsifier.]

> “Receive him, therefore, with open arms, our brother and fellow minister. Receive the bishop of God, irreproachable. Receive the patriarch of your Church. Confirm toward him love, faith, and obedient reverence, and through him confirm the same toward the holy Roman Church.

> “For whoever does not receive him does not receive what we and the holy Roman Church have decreed concerning him. Nor does such a person wage war against us, but against the holy apostle Peter, or rather against Christ himself, the Son of God, who so honored and glorified his apostle that he himself granted him the power to bind and loose.”

[Note: [Col. 0861D] The architect of falsehood, Photius, also added all that is contained under this heading, to secure his patriarchate.]

> “We also ask your piety to recall when scandals and schisms entered your Church and corrupted its integrity. These evils had no other cause than that you emperors admitted blasphemies and accusations against your pontiffs and patriarchs and the other priests of God, and that you regarded lightly the love, faith, honor, and reverence due to them.

> “We therefore ask your divine power to close the ears of your empire, chosen by God, from now on to accusations and slanders against pontiffs, which those evil men who rejoice only in wickedness are accustomed to suggest to you; and may you repel, as curses and abominations, the unjust arrows of their words.

> “Hold your patriarchs in honor and regard them as your own fathers; venerate them as mediators between God and men. They keep watch over your souls and continually pray to God for what contributes to your salvation. They also, as is fitting, offer sacrifices for those matters in which you have offended God by going astray, so that they may reconcile God to you and make him favorable toward you.

> “Nor is that all: they pray to our merciful God for the tranquility and continuance of your power and for victory over your enemies [Col. 0861C]. They are also your teachers and instructors, admonishing you to do those things by which you may obtain the kingdom of heaven.

> “Moreover, they are known to love you more than others. They do not know how to pursue the friendship of flatterers with you or love you in the manner of flatterers, but rather with the charity which Christ Jesus taught them through his holy apostles.

> “Your patriarchs therefore ought not to be despised by you, both because of all the matters we have mentioned and so that, according to the Lord’s commandment, you may love them. You should also know that, if you do this, you will obtain not only the honors of those whom you honor and venerate, but rather the honor of him who is ministered by their hands at the altar, namely Christ, who is offered to God for the sins of all.

> “For whoever honors them honors God; and whoever turns away from and rejects them rejects God himself. Let your empire therefore avoid false accusations and slanders, through which tares, schisms, and scandals arise in the Church of God and divide the seamless garment of Christ, as though they were the venom of asps. Rather, let it assist the most holy Photius, our brother and fellow minister, in everything that contributes to the good governance of the Church.”

[Note: [Col. 0861D] Photius judged these also to have been included for his own sake.]

> “Also rebuke those who do not treat him with the honor he deserves, so that they may be corrected. For often those whom fear of God, religious devotion toward divine things, and piety have not corrected are made more restrained when the indignation of emperors and rulers falls upon them [Col. 0862A].

> “If you do this, know for certain that you will obtain for yourself the kingdom of heaven, the everlasting continuance of your empire, and the confirmation of peace. But if you do not do this, be assured that schisms will never be lacking in the Church of Constantinople.”

[Note: [Col. 0861D] These words are from John’s letter, although Photius added some, such as: “After the death of the most holy Photius,” etc.]

> “We also advise your God-protected empire to enact a law concerning this: after the death of the most holy Photius, our fellow minister and brother, no one from the secular order should be elected or ordained to the pontifical dignity. Rather, the person should be chosen from the cardinal priests—that is, from those enrolled in the Catholic Church—or from its deacons or other priests who belong to the see of Constantinople, in accordance with the sacred canons, so that your affairs may not be conducted against ecclesiastical rule and the canons of the holy Fathers.

> “We wish him to proceed through each rank of the Church after sufficient testing [Note: [Col. 0862D] When you hear that the doorkeeper and exorcist have been omitted, although all Latins count them among the first four orders, know that the passage has been corrupted by the Greeks]: first lector, then [Col. 0862B] acolyte, afterward deacon, then priest, and finally bishop, provided that he has a good reputation for piety and knowledge.

> “For while he remains for some period in the lower ranks, his virtue and integrity are recognized. In this way your patriarchs ought to advance, not seize the individual ranks in haste, so that nothing disordered or ill-arranged may be found in the house of the Lord. For he who is placed above all the ranks ought to be found irreproachable in every respect.”

[Note: [Col. 0862D] The following material was added by Photius.]

> “Nor, because we, concerned for the peace and tranquility of your Church, receive Photius, our most religious brother, as Pope Hadrian received Tarasius, his uncle, should this now be usurped by you as a custom or rule. For things that are rarely good cannot become a law for many or be accepted as a law.

> “Taught by our Lord Jesus Christ, and receiving the bowels of mercy, we have granted your petition concerning Photius and have granted an indulgence concerning the other priests belonging to the other ordination [Col. 0862C]. But whoever in the future dares to commit this again shall, without any remission, receive from us the canonical penance and condemnation imposed upon him.”

[Note: [Col. 0862D] These words are John’s, but Photius mixed in some additions.]

> “We also ask your piety that neither our most holy brother and fellow minister Photius nor any other of his successors should henceforth perform ordinations in Bulgaria, whether through a pallium sent there or through a defensor serving that province of the Bulgarians as though it were his own.

> “It is not fitting for others to build on another’s soil. For our predecessor Nicholas, of blessed memory, at the prayers of the Bulgarian prince Michael, educated that people in apostolic teachings; and, having handed over to them through his religious bishops all ecclesiastical rules and canons and everything pertaining to the Christian religion, he brought them to completion.

> “Nevertheless, certain men audaciously seized the aforementioned province, which did not belong to them, and carried out ordinations and consecrations of churches and everything else which they ought not to have done [Col. 0862D].

> “Therefore, besides the matters already mentioned, we also make this known to you: if at any time we discover bishops residing there committing any offense against us, and we subject them to canonical penalties, they should not have you as a refuge to which they may flee. Rather, they should find you agreeing with us in this matter and not dissenting.”

[Note: [Col. 0862D] The impostor deleted the word *Mandamus* (“We command”) and the name Ignatius, and substituted *Oramus* (“We pray”), etc.]

“We further beseech your empire, beloved in Christ, [Col. 0863A] to assemble the bishops and presbyters of whatever ecclesiastical or civil rank who appear to dissent from us, wherever they may be within your territories; arrange that they be brought to you, and admonish them to unite themselves to the Church of God and to Photius, our most holy patriarch, brother and fellow minister, united with us. Restore to them their proper pontifical and sacred vestments, as well as their rank, and open toward them the depths of mercy, so that, just as there is one God, one baptism, and one faith, so we too may be one in Christ, and through your pious instruction they likewise may be one with us, coordinated and joined with us in the perfection of the Church of God and in the most holy body of Christ. Thus, remaining of one mind and one will, may we glorify the God of all.

“Let no one hereafter say, ‘I belong to Cephas,’ or ‘I to Paul’ (1 Cor. I); rather, let us all say that we belong to Christ, who was crucified and died for us, and who through his passion reconciled to one another the things on earth and the things [Col. 0863B] in heaven, and joined us to God and the Father through himself, by mutual love and communion.

“But if, after you have summoned, admonished, encouraged, and entreated them to assemble with you once, twice, and repeatedly for the unity of the Church, they refuse to obey, refuse to heed our letters and to gain their own salvation, and persist in their former obstinacy and rashness, we command that such men be excluded from participation in the immaculate body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ until they unite themselves to the holy Church of God and to Photius, our most holy patriarch, brother and fellow minister.

“And afterward: Since the matters that follow concern their just condemnation, we have not written them in these letters, lest the address be prolonged beyond measure; instead, we have set them down in the memorandum of our most religious legate, Peter the presbyter and cardinal, together with the most religious bishops Eugenius and Paul, so that, when he presides with them in the synod together with our most holy brother and fellow minister Photius, they may keep before their eyes the eye of God, which sees all things and is always watchful, as well as the unavoidable divine justice, and preserve their own consciences immaculate and blameless. They are to examine all matters concerning the Church of Constantinople, and everything requiring correction, as well as whatever ought properly to be avoided, so that what is better and more beneficial for the Church of God may be carried out. May the heavenly Emperor guard your pious power.”

Thus far from the Photian version of the letter of Pope John.

The reason why the name Constantine is absent from the title of John’s letter is that, as is reported by Nicetas, Constantine Augustus himself, the firstborn son of the emperor Basil, had died during these events.

You have seen, reader, lover and cultivator of truth, the impostures; you have undoubtedly execrated them—impostures that you could not fail to condemn even in a profane man, much less in a priest, bishop, and patriarch, or even in a pagan and barbarian ignorant of every divine and human law. So many falsehoods were inserted into letters issued not by some private [Col. 0863D] and unknown man, but by the apostolic see after a council of bishops; addressed not to some worthless son of the earth, but to the emperor of the East himself; and written not idly or lightly about matters of no importance, but about matters of the greatest possible weight. You ought therefore deservedly to condemn and execrate so great an author of crime, and to abominate and shudder at the deed itself, as at something fatal sent forth from the lowest regions of hell by the prince of darkness through the son of darkness, Photius, who falsely assumed in name the appearance of an angel of light.

## CCXLIV. TO THE CONSTANTINOPOLITANS

*(In the year 879.) He orders them, once the schism has been settled, to return to the unity of the Church and to communicate with Photius.*

To the distinguished men John, Leo, and Paul, patricians; and to Stilianus, John, and Metrophanes, most reverend metropolitans; and to the other priests, whether clerics or laymen of whatever rank.

Since, according to the Apostle, we have concern for all the Churches of God and bear the care of the flock of the Lord entrusted to us in the very person of the prince of the apostles, the Lord saying, “If you love me, Simon Peter, feed my sheep” (John XXI), we grieve with you, because for many years now, down to the present, we see you persist in the division of discord and the turmoil of scandals, without returning to the unity of the Church through the preservation of charity.

Whoever does not hold this unity does not hold the law of God, does not hold the faith of the Father and the Son, and possesses neither life nor salvation. This sacrament of unity, this bond of concord inseparably joined together, is shown when, in the Gospel, the tunic of our Lord Jesus Christ is not divided or torn at all. Rather, when lots are cast for Christ’s garment to determine who should put on Christ, the garment is received whole and uncorrupted, and the tunic is possessed undivided. For he cannot possess Christ’s garment who tears and divides the Church of Christ.

Who, then, is so criminal and faithless? Who is so deranged by the madness of discord? Who would either believe that God’s unity, the Lord’s garment, and the Church of Christ could be torn, or dare to tear them? He himself gives warning in his Gospel, saying: “There shall be one flock and one shepherd” (John XVI).

The Apostle Paul, likewise making this same unity known to us, exhorts us, saying: “I beseech you, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing and that there be no schisms among you; but that you be perfect in the same mind and in the same judgment” (1 Cor. I). And again he says: “Bearing with one another in love, taking care to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. IV), since he cannot have peace with God who, through zealous discord, has not had peace with his brothers.

What peace, then, do the enemies of their brothers promise themselves? What sacrifices do priests who are not clothed in the garment of God’s charity believe they celebrate? Christ gave us peace: “My peace,” he says, “I give you; my peace I leave you” (John XIV). He commanded us to be concordant and unanimous; he ordered the covenants of love and charity to remain uncorrupted and inviolate.

And [Col. 0864D] therefore, desiring your salvation, we admonish you and, with apostolic benevolence, command you all to unite yourselves to the holy Church, and to cleave to and communicate with your patriarch, namely Photius, whom we have received for the peace and unity of the Church of God. For if you disdain to hear these apostolic admonitions, confirmed by so many divine testimonies cited above, and wish to remain in your obstinacy, know that we command our envoys to deprive you of all ecclesiastical communion for as long as you refuse to return to the unity of the body of Christ and to your own pontiff.

Let none of you have this excuse when returning, on the basis of the writings composed concerning this matter, since by the divine power that the Church of Christ has received all bonds are loosed when, through pastoral [Col. 0865A] authority, what had been bound is loosed. For, as the holy Pope Gelasius says, no bond is insoluble except in the case of those who persist in error.

Given in the month of August, in the twelfth indiction, on the sixteenth day.

Sent through Peter the presbyter.

## CCXLV. TO THE CONSTANTINOPOLITAN CLERGY

[Note: [Col. 0865D] That this letter, like the others recited, suffered the imposture of the utterly depraved man Photius is clear from these words: “desiring that our venerable brother Photius seek mercy before the synod and exercise the honor of the patriarchate.” The proud and profane man plainly erased these words, which indicated a profession of humility, and substituted, as he had done in the other cases, the following: “Photius, our most holy and most religious brother, the patriarch, should not disdain our favor and attention in the presence of the synod, but rather proclaim the mercy of the Roman Church, by which he has been received.” SEV. BIN.]

*(In the year 879.) On the same subject as the preceding letter.*

To all the most reverend and most holy bishops, our fellow brothers, who look toward the see of the Church of Constantinople, and to the three other principal Churches of Jerusalem.

Receiving the writings of some among you, dearest brothers, we have found in them full unanimity and agreement with Photius. Therefore we earnestly desire that what has hitherto been done particularly may always and generally be done canonically, according to the things that belong to Jesus Christ and not to yourselves; that with pious devotion of mind you may seek, pursue, and find this same unity, so that there may be no schism among you.

As, through the moderation of the apostolic see, we grieve over division by contention and separation through error, so we rejoice that your brotherhood persists continually and inviolate in the bond and solid structure of peace and charity. According to the Apostle (1 Cor. XIII), “be of the same mind, and the God of peace will be with you.”

Your beloved community earnestly asks that, by the authority of the blessed prince of the apostles, Peter, we consent that Photius be patriarch in the imperial city of Constantinople. You retain this request in your mind more clearly than daylight: in the Gospel the Lord says to the first shepherd, “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and you, when once converted, strengthen your brothers” (Luke XII).

Inspired—indeed, strengthened—by these exhortations, insofar as we are able to offer assistance without grave offense, we never cease, following the examples of our predecessors, to assist both all the priests of the Lord and the Christian people throughout the world. Of these examples, we here reproduce the following words from the letter of Adrian, of holy memory, to the emperor Constantine and Empress Irene, concerning the recent confirmation of Tarasius as patriarch of the imperial city. Among other things he says:

“For Tarasius himself, the patriarch of the imperial city, sent us a synodical letter, fulfilling the ancient custom. [Col. 0865D] When we received it and examined it more closely, rejoicing both in his confession of the true faith and in the doctrines of the six holy synods and of the venerable images, we were nevertheless again greatly disturbed and grieved because he had been suddenly elected to the summit of the patriarchate from the lay order, having been assigned to imperial service, and had been made *apocaligus* [in Adrian’s letter, from *caliga militaris*, “military boot”] and patriarch contrary to the judgment of the sacred canons.

“And, though it is shameful to say and difficult to remain silent about, men who still ought to be governed and taught do not blush to appear as teachers, nor fear to assume the leadership of souls impudently, although every path of a teacher is unknown to them and they themselves are ignorant of the road by which they should walk. How perverse and rash this is is shown by secular order and discipline: since a military commander is chosen only after he has become experienced through labor and care, what sort of leaders of souls can those be who, with premature haste, desire to climb to the summit of the episcopate? Let them at least consider the matter by this comparison and refrain from suddenly undertaking labors for which they are inexperienced, since they have not learned what they are to teach. Hence canonical judgment has established that one must by no means pass suddenly from the lay state to the priesthood.

[Col. 0866B] “And unless, through his faithful cooperation, we had been able to give complete assent to his consecration for the erection of the holy images, we could not have assented to it at all.

“Moreover, we and you, dearest brothers, are bound by law never thereafter to promise that, through a similar transgression, you will violate the paternal regulations in the whole Church that is among you—that is, that a novice should not suddenly rise to honor [Note: [Col. 0866D] Something is missing.].

“And if you restore the parish of the Bulgarian people, which, by God’s authority, through the intercession of the blessed apostle Peter and through the labor of our predecessors, has been converted to Christ, once the unlawful ordination that you carried out there has been withdrawn; and if, through your labor and effort, you reconcile the rejected and dissident brothers [*f.* something is missing: ‘reconcile’] with the aforesaid Photius, whom you desire to have as patriarch in the imperial city; and if by other pious works you make reparation for the offense that you have incurred in this matter before God and the holy canons, then we wish our venerable brother Photius to seek mercy before the synod, to exercise the honor of the patriarchate, and, by the Lord’s mercy, to be a participant in our communion—indeed, in that of the blessed apostles and of the whole Church.

“We are especially strengthened by the example of our distinguished predecessor, the most holy Pope Innocent, who deigned to restore Photinus, saying (Letter 12, no. 7): ‘I shall now come to a great matter, almost a kind of theme: Photinus.’ And among other things: ‘Since the matter has returned to salvation through pardon, and since you press us to do so, we restore him after condemnation in the apostolic manner. Since you make such strong assertions, and since you are such good and beloved men, we judge that to refuse our consent would be harsher than all harsh circumstances. Therefore, for your approval, dearest brothers, and by your judgment and petition, accept the bishop Photinus. It is lawful to establish what you request; and, through your labor or testimony, receive our judgment, turned toward what is better, as the fulfillment of your desire. I gladly accept your concern for his salvation; to him to whom you extend your hand, I extend it with you; to him to whom I extend it, extend yours with me.’

“For this is the apostolic benevolence declared to the Corinthians: that in one spirit they should follow without distinction the judgment that has been brought forth and restored.”

Given in the month of August, in the twelfth indiction.

Sent through Peter the presbyter.

## CCXLVI. TO PAUL AND EUGENIUS, BISHOPS

*(In the year 879.) He appoints them, together with Peter the presbyter, as legates, so that, as he had instructed them, they might establish peace in the Church of Constantinople.*

To the most reverend bishops Paul of Ancona and Eugenius of Ostia.

Although you acted against our will, and, after coming to Constantinople to investigate the cause of the peace and unity of the Church, ought to have returned to Rome and reported everything to us in a definitive account, nevertheless, because you did not suitably carry out the first mission entrusted to you, we ought not therefore to entrust you with a second. Yet, using the benevolence of apostolic mercy, and so that you may faithfully complete this second mission, we associate you with this Peter, our religious presbyter, cardinal, and personal associate, so that you may act together in accordance with the matters that must be undertaken for the peace and unity of the Church of God, according to the apostolic directives of our authority and according to the contents, set out point by point, of our memorandum. Act and decide everything with very careful attention, so that by working with more faithful devotion you may obtain our favor, which you previously provoked by acting disobediently.

Given in the month of August, in the twelfth indiction.

## CCXLVII. TO PAUL AND EUGENIUS, BISHOPS, AND LIKEWISE TO PETER THE PRESBYTER

*(In the year 879.)*

[Col. 0867C]

### Mansi’s Notice Concerning the Following Letter

The Roman synod, convened by the authority of Pope John, furnished and fortified Peter and the other legates associated with him with authority only to absolve Photius from ecclesiastical censures and restore him to the see of Constantinople—not to condemn the true and genuine eighth synod held under Pope Adrian, nor to remove entirely from the Creed the phrase *Filioque*. They had been fortified with considerable authority for these purposes.

This is clear, first, from the letter of John written to the emperor Basil (Letter 243), in which he indicates that, in restoring Photius to his see, he is using not the dissolution or abolition of the council, but only a dispensation; second, from Letters 250 (now 297) and 251 (now 296), in which he states that he rejects everything done apart from the restoration of Photius; and third, from the memorandum itself, corrupted and falsified by Photius, in which the subscribing bishops declare that they are all subscribing to the memorandum for the restoration of Photius.

Since we lacked the genuine memorandum mentioned in Letters 203 and 250 (now 296 and 297), as well as in several other letters of Pope John, we thought that the memorandum corrupted by Photius and read in Act 3 of the Photian pseudo-eighth synod should be inserted here—both so that the acts of this council might thereby be confirmed, and so that the matters said to have been accomplished at Constantinople by the authority of the legates in the Photian pseudo-eighth synod might be clearly exposed as false and fraudulent.

The memorandum, written in Greek and rendered into Latin by Metius, is as follows:

### [LETTER]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God: a memorandum to the brothers Paul and Eugenius, bishops, and likewise to Peter, our cardinal presbyter, our legates at Constantinople.

When, by the favor of divine grace and through the intercession of the holy apostles, you have entered Constantinople, go to the place to which the emperor orders you; and before you visit the emperor, do not wish to deliver the apostolic letters to anyone else.

When you are in the emperor’s presence, you shall hand him the letters, addressing him in these words:

“Your kingdom, given by God, is greeted by your spiritual father, the lord John, the apostolic [Col. 0868B] pope, who commends your God-given power to the holy God every day in his prayers, so that he who has given you this desire for ecclesiastical peace may grant you his grace, console you with his blessed protection, and bring your desires for good to completion.”

If the emperor asks, before reading the letters or the chapters of our reply, answer him in these words:

“If your imperial power commands it, let it examine the letters.”

And if he says, “What do the letters contain?” answer him:

“They contain greetings, and they bring everything to a proper conclusion.”

On the following day go to greet Photius, the most holy man, and give him the letter, greeting him courteously in these words:

“Our lord John, the apostolic pope, greets you and wishes to have you as a brother and fellow minister, just as the emperor wrote, asking that, for the peace of the Church, we receive the most holy patriarch Photius, our brother and fellow minister; that we hear your petitions; and that we order him to come before us to the synod, so that the whole Church may receive him.”

According to the tenor of our letters, receive him as our fellow minister; and so that he may have the favor of the Roman Church, rise and say to him:

“Our lord, the most holy pope, commands that all those who have been outside your territories in various places—whether they are bishops, presbyters, or anyone else—and who until now have refused to communicate with you, be united through your work and labor to the Church of God and become one with you.

“If they come, receive them as a father receives his sons, and admonish them frequently to think, for the peace of the Church of God, the same things as the apostolic see, so that they may be of one will with it—namely, receiving Photius, the most holy patriarch, and communicating with him as one.”

If any of those who had previously been ordained should come, let them receive their sees; but those who were ordained afterward shall receive the necessary food and clothing from the bishops themselves.

[Note: [Col. 0868D] Here some material noted above concerning the requirement that Photius seek pardon before the synod has been removed, while other material has been added; from the letters quoted you can understand the matter.]

When you preside in the synod together with the aforesaid most holy patriarch and the Eastern legates, together with the remaining archbishops and metropolitans and all the priests of the Church of Constantinople, first let the letters sent to the emperor be read. Let the synod then be asked whether it accepts them and observes the testimonies contained in the letters themselves.

When they have assented, say the following:

“Our lord, the most holy pope, bearing the care of all the Churches and seeking your salvation, union, and peace, has sent us, his servants, to gather the scattered, reconcile the dissident, extend the hand of the Church’s mercy, and raise up the fallen, so that with one voice we may glorify the Father with the Son and the Holy Spirit.

“Following the canons of our Fathers, we declare that after the death of Photius, the most holy patriarch, no one from a civil dignity shall ascend to the see of Constantinople, as our letters also attest.

“We also wish you, before the synod, to ask Photius, the aforesaid most holy patriarch, neither to send the pallium to Bulgaria nor to ordain anyone in that province. For if he does these things, we shall accuse him according to the sacred canons.

[Note: [Col. 0869D] John’s letters concerning the Bulgarian matter contain not merely petitions but excommunication.]

“Furthermore, we wish it to be promulgated before the entire synod that the synod held against the aforesaid patriarch Photius in the time of Adrian, the most holy pope, both at Rome and at Constantinople, shall from now on be considered null and void and shall not be numbered among the other holy synods.

[Note: [Col. 0869D] You see here the same addition by the forger that was inserted above concerning the abolition of the eighth synod.]

“Take care to proceed according to our command. Do not allow yourselves to be corrupted by gifts, turned aside by flatteries, or diverted by threats and terrors, either to the right or to the left; walk instead along the royal road, as possessing our place and authority, which we have bestowed on you for the peace of the Church, so that through your labor and diligence you may worthily obtain our favor and that of the apostolic see, and become heirs of our communion.”

### Subscriptions of the Bishops Who Attended the Roman Synod, from Which the Memorandum Issued, and the Letter Was Given to the Legate Peter

Zacharias, bishop of the Church of Anagni and librarian of the apostolic see: “I have subscribed this memorandum for the reception of Photius, the most holy patriarch, with my own hand.”

Martinus, bishop of the Church of Narni: “I have subscribed this memorandum of the apostolic see for the restoration of Photius, the most holy patriarch, with my own hand.”

Likewise the following:

Dominicus, bishop of Trivento.

Florius, bishop of Matera.

Gaudericus, bishop of Velletri.

Stephanus, bishop of Ferentino.

Leo, bishop of Gabi [Sabina].

Petrus, bishop of Fossombrone.

Leo, bishop of Terracina.

Walpertus, bishop of Porto.

[Col. 0870A] Simeon, bishop of Fondi.

John, bishop of Sermoneta.

Benedict, bishop . . . .

Gregory, bishop of Silva Candida.

Boniface, bishop of Blera.

Theodorus, bishop of Gallese.

Stephanus, bishop of Nepi.

### Cardinal Presbyters

Germanus, presbyter of the title of Saints John and Paul.

Petrus, presbyter of the title of Saint Chrysogonus.

Benedict, presbyter of the title of Saint Balbina.

Adrianus, presbyter of the title of Saint Lawrence.

John, presbyter of the title of Saint Cecilia.

### Cardinal Deacons

[Col. 0870B] Paul the deacon: “I have subscribed.”

Leo the deacon: “I have subscribed.”

### Annotation of Severinus Binius

You have heard, reader, the addition by Photius concerning the abolition of the eighth ecumenical council celebrated under Pope Adrian, already most clearly refuted above by the quoted letters of Pope John VIII. But the same fraud is also exposed in this memorandum by the very subscription of the bishops, in which—as we have seen from what was set out above—they all declare that they are subscribing to the memorandum for the restoration of Photius.

If the condemnation of the eighth ecumenical synod had truly been defined by the judgment of the synod and entrusted to the legates in the memorandum given to them, it is surely more credible that they would have expressed it in their subscriptions than the restoration of Photius.

## CCXLVIII. TO PHOTIUS, PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE

*(In the year 879.) He establishes Photius as patriarch of Constantinople, provided that he seeks pardon in the synod; decrees that thereafter no layman is immediately to be ordained bishop in that Church; commands that the Bulgarian diocese be restored to the Roman Church.*

[Col. 0870C]

### [LETTER]

To Photius, patriarch of Constantinople.

[Note: [Col. 0870D] Photius corrupted this letter in the places noted below.]

Your prudent experience, abundantly revealed in the letters delivered to our pontificate, has become sufficiently known to us. We have praised the Most High Lord, giving him the most devout thanks, for he grants wisdom to all who ask him; he causes those who dwell in a house to live in unanimity; he saves all who hope in him; and he protects those who seek him in truth. He neither makes the upright guilty nor the pious tyrants; yet, judging justly, he reserves eternal rewards for the blessed and, after allowing the unhappy a period for repentance, bestows eternal punishments on those who do not repent.

Reading our praises in the letters mentioned above, we recognized your affection and found clearly enough how devoted you now are toward us. But in whatever respects our merits do not help us, we leave the matter to God; and when any mortal attempts to exalt us with human praise, we contemplate the frailty of our nature with the greatest fear, keeping that same God before our eyes. For we know that he himself says: “Whoever exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Matt. XXIII).

[Col. 0871A] As for the report that the holy Church of Constantinople has united itself with you, that you have received your own see, but that our envoys did not join with you in consecrating, we give thanks to God for the union of all. But we did not previously give our envoys instructions concerning this because we had not established with certainty how the see itself stood.

Now, however, just as we greatly rejoice over the peace and union of that Church, so we grieve over the dissent of those unwilling to submit, since, as Samuel testifies, “to resist is like the sin of divination, and not to submit is like the crime of idolatry” (1 Kings XV).

[Note: [Col. 0871D] Photius mutilated the passage here concerning the need to consult the apostolic see.]

But we ought first to have been consulted concerning the reception of the private see. Nevertheless, because we have heard that, after the death of our brother and fellow bishop Ignatius, you preside over the Constantinopolitan throne, we give manifold thanks to God, solely so that peace may increase and quarrels cease.
