You, however, soothing the minds of all, must not cease to embrace everyone with open arms and to gather all the scattered; diligently strive to collect everyone, because, as the holy Pope Leo the Great writes, “the moderation of the apostolic see preserves this balance: it deals more severely with the hardened and desires to grant pardon to those who have been corrected.”

And since no amount of mercy toward one who has been corrected is blameworthy, if, after making satisfaction, you seek mercy before the synod [Note: [Col. 0871D] Photius removed this passage about seeking mercy before the synod, here and elsewhere below] according to custom, and if you demonstrate evident correction, without forgetting your learning, and do not plot anyone’s destruction, but rather diligently dissolve the exiles of those who are said to be unwilling to consent to you, [Col. 0871C] restoring them to their churches and honors; and if, because our spiritual son Basil, the most Christian emperor, has intervened before us on your behalf with many petitions, all have come together with one vote, one agreement, and one concord for your restoration, then, for the peace of the holy Church of Constantinople, we grant you pardon, and we restore to you communion and rank as well, seeking mercy before the synod [Note: [Col. 0871D] Photius likewise shortened these four words]. We also consent that you should worthily preside over the holy Church of Constantinople, provided, however, that thereafter no one from the lay order be ordained bishop in that Church, contrary to the statutes of the holy Fathers, and that the whole of that evil practice be completely cut off, in accordance with the decree most suitably promulgated on this matter in the venerable synod held at Constantinople during the time of our predecessor, Adrian, the younger pope.

As for the remaining matters that your letter expects us to judge or settle, we have entrusted some in writing and others orally, through a memorandum, to our legates, our venerable cardinal presbyter Peter and our beloved counselors. Instructed according to the judgment of our apostolate concerning everything, they shall consider all matters with God before their eyes, diligently admitting what may lawfully be admitted and correcting what must be corrected according to the balance of equity.

Furthermore, just as your party seeks to strengthen its own wishes, so we wish our diocese of Bulgaria [Note: [Col. 0872D] Photius completely mutilated this passage concerning the Bulgarian diocese], which the apostolic see received through the struggle of our most holy lord Pope Nicholas of blessed memory and possessed likewise in the time of Adrian, that most blessed prelate, to be restored to us with the greatest speed. By apostolic authority we entirely prohibit all ecclesiastical ordination by the prelates of the Church of Constantinople in that Bulgarian diocese.

You must strive to ensure that the bishops ordained there, and all other clerics of lower rank, withdraw from there and refrain completely from invading our Bulgarian diocese. If you give any of them the pallium, carry out any ordination there, or communicate with them until they obey us, you shall be joined to them in equal excommunication and darkness.

### Annotation of Severinus Binius on the Adulteration of the Preceding Letter by Photius

This is the second letter that Photius received from Pope John VIII, himself translated into Greek, and caused to be read and promulgated in his pseudo-eighth synod after adding, mutilating, removing, and erasing passages in order to conceal his treachery.

Knowing how much authority the apostolic letters possessed, and intending to read them in the synod in order to persuade the assembly of whatever he wished, he added and removed whatever seemed suitable to him. What those alterations were, you will understand sufficiently from the recitation of the letter itself, extracted from its second session and rendered into Latin by the same Metius. It reads as follows:

“John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Photius, most holy brother and fellow minister, patriarch of the Church of Constantinople.

“When we perceived the wisdom and prudence of your brotherhood in the letter, resounding like thunder sent from heaven by God and filling all the ends of the earth with its roar [Note: [Col. 0872D] The deceitful Photius turns into praise of himself what John had said in praise of God, the Most High], we offered pious thanks and exalted praises to God, who grants wisdom to all who ask according to their request; who dwells in the house of concord; and who cherishes and protects all who place their hope in him through truth. For he neither finally rejects the wicked, nor permits the good to fall into any tyranny beyond their strength, but rather directs and happily governs all human affairs with equal justice and balanced judgments.

“And blessed is the one who, with an eager spirit, raises up through repentance those who have fallen in the present time; for in heaven he stores up treasures for himself. Remaining in this blessedness, he will enjoy everlasting future goods when the future glory is revealed.

“When we had therefore received your aforesaid most courteous letter, we recognized the excessive praises with which you adorn us and the eagerness of mind with which you regard us, and we understood how piously and soundly you conduct yourself. Yet the praises you bestow upon us are far from us. Since we have received a mortal and changeable nature, such praises are not entirely safe, and we are affected by great fear of him who sees and observes all things, both hidden and manifest: lest we be regarded one way by men and found another way in the sight of God, and gain everlasting disgrace in place of praise and the glory we desire.

“But let us meanwhile leave these matters to God, who knows all things and from whom nothing of ours is hidden. For we know that he says: ‘Whoever exalts himself shall be humbled’ (Matt. XXII).”

«You wrote to us that the most holy Church of Constantinople, in receiving you, became united and unanimous with you, and that you received the see which was yours and of which you had been deprived. [Note: Here Photius is silent about the private see—namely, the one he had established in the Magnaura while Ignatius was still alive.] For these matters—namely, concerning the Church and your restoration, by which you have been restored to your own see—we give thanks to God from our heart and to the best of our ability. Your Piety’s letter also stated that our legates were unwilling to join with you in ministry as soon as possible. We say that this happened because we had not yet permitted them to do what we had commanded. For if they had had our mandate, they would have had no doubt, nor would they have given your Piety cause for any sadness. Nor were we sufficiently certain concerning your fraternity that God had restored you to your see and that you had already obtained it. For if we had learned this, we should undoubtedly have sent to congratulate you, as was proper, on your recovery of the see. [Note: It adds some things and cuts out others that we noted above concerning consulting the apostolic see about other matters.] Do not, therefore, meanwhile take this amiss; for what was previously lacking has now been supplied in abundance.

«Moreover, we have learned that there are among you certain schismatics who do not remain quiet but labor in vain and wage a diabolical conflict, according to the prophet who says: “They are divided; they are crushed, so that they may tear away and overturn some of the simpler.” And just as we rejoiced over your restoration, which God brought about, and over the union effected in the Church, so we have been saddened by the destruction of those schismatics.

[Note: Photius added this concerning his own praises.] «But you, who excel in wisdom, prudence, and the grace bestowed on you by God—for what do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, we know that you do not boast as though you had not received it—should strive by your humanity to win over all those who have been separated and scattered far from you, opening to them the bowels of mercy and embracing them with kindness. Do not hesitate to gather them together, so that, as the most holy Pope Leo the Great writes, we may receive those who seek to be humbled in the sight of God and seek union with you. Conversely, against those who are hard of heart, let us overcome them by strength, constancy, and patience, and resist the hardness of their hearts. Likewise, let us extend helping hands to those who seek repentance, which raises up the fallen. For there is no despair for the penitent, and no shame for those who ask for mercy.

«Therefore we ask your Fraternity, by imitating Christ’s conduct, and especially his humility, which he endured for the salvation of our race, not to hesitate to proclaim in the synod God’s mercy and help toward you, [Note: John does not have this, but rather that he himself should ask for mercy before the synod; Photius very cunningly removed this here and below.] as well as the protection and defense of the most holy Roman Church and the labor which it endured for love of you, so that in this way you may build everyone up for our communion and the concord of our spirits. For whatever you asked of that Church, you obtained. And just as it is its custom to bring help to all who suffer unjustly, so you too were not deprived of its assistance, but by divine aid and through the labor and zeal of this holy see you were restored to your see.

«Therefore I consider it fitting that you not forget to make the sound of this customary assistance, and likewise of the kindness which you experience in its individual works each day, resound throughout the whole world; but also follow that Church, and, like it, inflict harm on no one, nor drive anyone away from the bowels of your mercy. If any up to now have been unwilling to embrace union with your Piety or to come to agreement with you, do not desist; rather, endure the labor and the struggle, both by teaching and by speaking, with patient admonition and also with a cheerful and benevolent countenance, so that, according to the Apostle, you may strive to win either all or most of them and reconcile them to yourself. Deign to receive them to yourself, and through yourself to God, as they approach God himself through you. Restore to them their priestly honors and their churches.

[Col. 0874B] «And just as we, in obedience to the reasonable, just, and pleasing petition of our spiritual son, the emperor Basil, did with your Piety what the emperor had asked, so we ask you also to forget the wrongs committed against you by those who had been alienated from you. [Note: Here again he cut out what John has in his letter concerning seeking mercy before the synod.] If they return from the heart, may your Piety deign to receive them with open arms, honored with distinction, so that all of us, happily agreeing to the conversion and restoration of your see, may celebrate a common joy, a feast, and a day of gladness.

«We also ask this of your Fraternity: join with us in decreeing that henceforth no secular person be raised to the pontifical see, but that each person, proceeding according to rank and order and showing the proper progress of virtue in his own rank, should thus attain the rank of the pontifical see. For whoever ascends otherwise acts contrary to our ecclesiastical canons. And we wish to abolish and invalidate for the future this custom—which is not to be approved—which was found at the beginning in your Church. [Col. 0874C] [Note: Here this falsifier and impostor most cunningly transferred to Adrian I what John said quite explicitly about Adrian II. He did this because, by those words, John indicated that he was proving the eighth synod to have been held under the younger Adrian.] We say this in accordance with the canon issued at the synod held in the time of Adrian, the most holy pope, and Tarasius, patriarch of Constantinople, of blessed memory.

[Note: There is absolutely nothing in John’s letters about the abolition of the synod held against Photius. This impostor added it so that, as though by the authority of the apostolic see, he might condemn what he later did to the eighth synod held under Adrian. Moreover, when this impostor added these things, he cut out what John has in the appended condition concerning the restoration of the diocese of the Bulgarians.] «But we have invalidated and annulled the synod held there against your Piety, indeed we reject it, both for other reasons and also because blessed Pope Adrian, our predecessor, did not subscribe to it. We omit writing the rest concerning ecclesiastical matters which your letter brought to our attention, because we wrote about them in the memorandum, which we all also signed for your restoration, and which we gave to Peter, the most religious cardinal-priest and our legate, whom we sent, [f. ut una, HARD.] so that, together with Eugene and Paul, our most religious bishops and legates, keeping the fear of God before their eyes and preserving their consciences undefiled, they might altogether do with you what they know to be beneficial to your Church. May God preserve you to the end, beloved brother, most reverend fellow-minister.»

You have now seen, reader, and by comparing the two copies have recognized how far the audacity of the impostor proceeded, and how boldly the shameless insolence of the falsifier dared to act: by adding these three lines to John’s letter at the very end, Photius, as far as lay in his power, demolished with his lying pen that great edifice—indeed, the ecumenical eighth synod—which West and East, pope and emperor together with bishops and magistrates, had striven with such great labor to raise up and establish. Thus we must once again, and indeed countless other times, give thanks to God, because, in order to avert so immense a danger and prevent so enormous a scandal, divine providence willed that copies of John’s letters should remain intact—the sole remedy for exposing the falsehood of that utterly corrupt man and revealing his imposture.

For this reason, as we have seen, Pope Nicholas himself, the subject of our discussion, likewise returned the greatest thanks to God because he had preserved copies of the letters in Rome, by which the falsehoods of the same Photius, shamelessly inserted into his own letters, could be convicted. Thus he says in his letter to the emperor Michael: [Col. 0875B] “Nevertheless, however that same letter may have been submitted to falsification or corruption, we give countless thanks to God, by whose inspiration we retained faithful copies of it among us, and by whose permission those who wrote these copies, or the authentic letter itself, are known to survive.” Thus he himself speaks.

But we are obliged to give thanks to God in two respects: both because John, like Nicholas, copied and retained copies of the letters he sent, and because those copies, together with the codex called the register, have survived intact to this day in the Vatican library, after so many shipwrecks of the Roman Church. Consequently, the translation made by Photius can be charged with fraudulent falsification in many places, especially in those passages by which he sought utterly to demolish the ecumenical eighth synod: first, because he completely erased and obliterated the citation of that eighth synod held under Adrian, a citation which proves that John received and approved it; and also because he expressly added that the same synod had already been condemned by Pope John himself and rendered, as he says, invalid and null.

For this was the entire aim of that profane man: to labor to abolish and extinguish utterly the ecumenical synod assembled against him, in which, so to speak, his crimes were marked in letters a cubit high in many ways, so that it might no longer even be named. But since it was known from the testimony of Greek and Latin historians that an eighth ecumenical synod had been celebrated at Constantinople, he wished his own false synod to be held in the same place and called by the same name, so that it might be substituted for the legitimate eighth ecumenical synod held under Adrian. To deceive everyone, he used the letters of Pope John quoted above, letters written to Photius but falsified by him; from these you may likewise detect other impostures of that most crafty scoundrel.

Although Pope John himself, both in the letter written to Photius and in the letter quoted above to the emperor, by citing the said ecumenical synod, appears, as has been said, to have approved it, yet in Photius’s additions that same John is asserted to have condemned it: this did not seem sufficient to him, and he also falsified the memorandum given by the same pontiff to Peter, the legate.

CCXLIX. TO LANDULF AND LANDON. (Year 879.) He writes that he will go to Traiectum and attend to what contributes to their peace; there he will also deal with other matters, including Landulf, elected bishop of the Capuan Church.

To the beloved men Landon, son of Landon, and his brothers, and to Landulf, son of Landenulf, and his brothers.

Having received and read your letters, which you sent to our pontificate, we know with complete clarity how, after the death of Landulf, bishop of Capua, of blessed memory, you had united with Pandenulf in peace and concord and had confirmed this by an oath sworn among you in a fraternal and indivisible bond. But, at the persuasion of the enemy of the human race, who has scattered among you the seeds of weeds, we see that all the concord and unanimity which had existed among you through divine regard has been corrupted and thrown into confusion.

Because of this evil of such great enmity, we already informed you in our letter delivered to you through Dominicus, our venerable bishop, that, by God’s favor, for the salvation and peace of you all, we wish to come to Traiectum on the Kalends of October. There we shall speak with you, with the glorious prince Guaifer, and with the Capuans and your other kinsmen, and first arrange what is necessary for us and for you and advantageous to your peace and welfare. Thus, once the scandal of all discord has been removed from your midst and God’s peace, which surpasses all understanding (Philippians IV), has been restored, you may all remain concordant and unanimous in fraternal love and your former devotion. Then, whether concerning Landulf, the venerable priest, whom you have elected by the vote and equal consent of all God’s priests and judges, or concerning other necessary matters, we shall fulfill your wishes according to the sacred canons. Therefore, let it not seem burdensome to your nobility to await our special arrival, as stated.

CCL. TO GUAIFER, PRINCE OF SALERNO. (Year 879.) The same matters as in the preceding letter; moreover, he reproves him for taking up arms against the Capuans and asks him to arrange for the Amalfitans to return the mancuses to him.

To his beloved son, Guaifer, the glorious prince.

Just as you informed us in your letters that you preserve devoted friendship and sincere affection toward us, so we recognize and hold this to be clearer than daylight, as many proofs have already shown. Hence our apostolic heart is kindly disposed toward your nobility, as toward a most beloved son, desiring always to see and hear of your honor and glory unimpaired.

As for Landulf, the venerable priest of the Capuan Church, concerning whom you have so often made petition to our pontificate, we have not until now neglected to hear you out of any disposition of ill will, but solely for the sake of true peace and the increase of affection among kinsmen. For, as we have now commanded you in our letter delivered through Bishop Dominicus, we wish, by God’s favor, for the salvation, concord, and unanimity of you all, to come to Traiectum on the Kalends of October. There we shall speak with you, with the Capuans, and with your other kinsmen, and first arrange what is necessary for us and for you and beneficial to your peace and welfare. [Col. 0877A] Then, whether concerning the aforesaid elected man or concerning other necessary matters, we shall fulfill your wishes, because, with your prudent counsel and common agreement, we desire to accomplish what must be considered and carried out for fraternal peace, for the defense of our land and yours, and for the destruction of the Saracens.

Therefore, just as we wish with eager minds to fulfill your desire and honor, so you too ought with devoted mind to carry out what is fitting for our apostolic dignity. Yet in this matter you seem deserving of no small reproach: having taken up arms against the Capuans, who are surrounded by the continual persecutions of pagans, you dared to pursue and attack them before you had made us truly acquainted with their faults.

As for the mancuses which, in your presence, we gave to the Amalfitans for the defense of the land of Saint Peter, we wish those same Amalfitans to carry those mancuses by ship with them as far as the port of the city of Rome, for there they will remain safe and secure. Then, after first receiving from us a pledge of security, let them arrange to return those mancuses to us, so that, once we have received what belongs to us, they may suffer no further accusation on account of it.

CCLI. TO LEO, BISHOP. (Year 879.) He laments that dissensions have been stirred up at Capua; he announces that he will go to Traiectum and there deal with Landulf, the elected bishop, whose confirmation he had requested.

[Col. 0877C]

To the most reverend and most holy Bishop Leo.

Having reread your letter, we know with shining clarity that you possess the priestly care and concern which the priests of the Lord undoubtedly ought to exercise for the benefit of God’s Church and for the concord and peace of the people. Concerned for the love of God and neighbor, you grieve that the Capuans—noble men, to be sure—have wickedly corrupted the fraternal bond established among them by oath and have reached genuine discord and enmity, and that they still remain in this reckless state of mind. You also petition our pontificate on behalf of Landulf, the venerable priest, elected by you, by the entire priestly body, by the company of the nobles, and by the whole people of the city of Capua, asking that we not delay ordaining him bishop for the sacred people of Capua.

Moved by pastoral concern, we likewise grieve with you over brothers and kinsmen who, through worldly greed, have been plunged into so great an abyss of discord and enmity. For their reconciliation, by God’s favor, we wish to come to Traiectum on the Kalends of October. There we shall speak with Prince Guaifer, with you, with the Capuans, and with your other kinsmen, and first arrange what is necessary for us and for you. Then, concerning the elected man himself, we shall fulfill your wishes according to the sacred canons. Therefore, let it not seem burdensome to your affection to await our special arrival, as stated.

One such letter to Bishop Adelchis; and another to Bishop Lupenus.

CCLII. TO LANDULF, THE PRIEST. (Year 879.) He praises him because he left Capua to avoid the plots of his relatives and is laboring to calm the dissensions; he announces that he will go to Traiectum and there deliberate concerning his election.

[Col. 0878A]

To Landulf, the venerable priest and elect.

Because you say that, by avoiding the plots of your discordant relatives and leaving the city of Capua, you now dwell in the ancient see of the holy Capuan Church, namely the radiant church of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, and that you are continually laboring together with the neighboring bishops so that, with God’s favor, you may unite those who are badly divided and reconcile those who are at odds, we have received this with approval.

Even before undertaking the office, you are carrying out what belongs to a good shepherd. We exhort you to persevere in this until our special arrival, for, by God’s favor, for the salvation, concord, and peace of you all, we wish to come to Traiectum on the Kalends of October. There we shall speak with the glorious prince Guaifer and with your other distinguished relatives, first arrange what is necessary for us and for you and beneficial to your peace and welfare, and then, once all have been reconciled, carry out your advancement according to the sacred canons.

CCLIII. TO PREFECT PULCAR. (Year 879.) He reproves him because he has neither broken the treaty made with the pagans nor defended the territory of Saint Peter as he had promised; he orders him to send back the money given for that purpose.

[Col. 0878C]

To the beloved man Pulcar, prefect.

For the salvation of your soul and for the defense of all Christendom—which, while you maintain a pact with the pagans, is daily plundered and led into dreadful captivity—we have done many good things for you and your people, which you requested. In addition, we gave you ten thousand mancuses of silver so that you might defend the land of Saint Peter after breaking the pagans’ treaty. You and your men promised under oath to do this, but, setting aside the fear of God’s judgment, you have been unwilling either to break the wicked pact or, on account of your oath, to defend our shores. Rather, already subjected to the devil’s authority, you permit them to be plundered and consent, to the destruction of your soul, to the sheep acquired by Christ’s precious blood being led into captivity.

Therefore it is right that we recover those mancuses which we gave you for the defense of our land. We wish you, accordingly, to send those same mancuses back to us by your faithful Amalfitans, who should come by ship as far as the port of the city of Rome. The Amalfitans themselves will remain safe and secure there; then, after first receiving from us a pledge of security, let them arrange to return the aforesaid mancuses to us, so that, once we have received what belongs to us, we may bring no accusation against you or your people. We have also instructed our dromons in no way to cause any injury to your people, provided that you return those mancuses safely to us.

CCLIV. TO THE MONKS OF THE MONASTERY OF PULTARIA. (Year 879.) He laments their troubles and announces that he has written on their behalf to Prince Boso and Abbot Hugh, asking them to protect them; he has also sent a copy of the testament of Gerard, the founder, to Archbishop Ansegisus and Count Conrad.

[Col. 0879A]

To the holy congregation of our monastery of Pultaria, belonging to the chief of the apostles, Saint Peter.

Let your Fraternity know for certain that, after rereading your letters, we are very sad over the many adversities which you daily endure from wicked men. For just as we rejoice in your prosperity, so we also grieve over your tribulation.

Therefore, wishing to keep your holy congregation—inasmuch as it is the Lord’s flock entrusted to us in the very chief of the apostles, Peter—safe and undisturbed, we sent, at your request, our apostolic letters to Boso, the glorious prince, and to Hugh, the most noble abbot. We asked that, for the love of God and of the chief of the holy apostles, Peter and Paul, and for love of us, they extend to you the help of their protection and stretch out the hand of their power against God’s adversaries and all your adversaries, so that, living quietly and securely, you may be able to offer the Lord your due praises, pray to almighty God for us and for all the Christian people, and peacefully administer, govern, and dispense according to the Lord the property of our holy monastery.

Moreover, by the present messenger of yours we have sent to Archbishop Ansegisus and to Count Conrad, in whose county those properties lie, a copy of the testament by which Gerard, the count of blessed memory, together with Berta, his late wife, transferred those properties to the chiefs of the apostles, Peter and Paul, secured by the seal of our name.

You should therefore see whether you have been aided in all these matters or not, and report to us, so that we may most willingly take care to help you as far as we can by better counsel. May the Lord deign to preserve your Fraternity, praying for us, safe and unharmed.

CCLV. TO HUGH, THE ABBOT. (Year 879.) That he should protect the monastery of Pultaria.

[Col. 0879D] To his beloved son Hugh, the most noble abbot.

How greatly we have loved you, and with what affection of our fatherhood—as though you were our only son—we have loved you since we came to know your exalted wisdom and glory, you yourselves remember well; for your Excellence has also taken care, with tranquil mind, to venerate and honor us in all things as a spiritual father.

Confiding in this unbroken bond of mutual love, we ask that the monastery of Saint Peter called Pultaria, which Gerard, the late count, completed and endowed from his own property and handed over to Saint Peter, be assisted in every way by your protection. The brothers who now dwell there and offer their continual praises to God, praying for the salvation of all who believe in Christ, are being harassed by hostile neighbors, and their entire household—indeed, ours—is continually cruelly troubled and oppressed, so that it is unable even to plow or to carry out the other tasks pertaining to the cultivation of the land.

Therefore extend your assistance to that holy place, and, for the love of God, of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and of us, stretch out the hand of your power against God’s adversaries and its own, so that, relying on your powerful arm, they may remain safe and secure in all things, and so that both in the present you may receive worthy rewards from us and in the future be able to receive multiplied recompense from the Lord with the saints.

CCLVI. TO HUGH AND RADULPH. (Year 879.) He says that he has granted the estate of Vendoara, belonging to Saint Peter of Pultaria, to no one, and has ordered Arembert, who received it from Boso, to be excommunicated unless he abstains from it.

[Col. 0880B]

To Hugh and Radulph, our beloved faithful men.

Let your Fidelity know for certain that we have neither given nor exchanged our estate of Vendoara—which, you say, was invaded by Count Boso, as though we had exchanged it with him and received another from him—whether in the manner of a benefice, by way of any exchange, or in any other manner whatsoever, with Boso himself or with any other person.

Therefore, remaining with devoted mind in the fidelity and service of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, hold that estate under our jurisdiction, defend it, and govern it with the Lord’s help. Do not believe any man who says that we shall ever give the aforesaid estate away in any manner.

We have sent our letter to the aforesaid Count Boso, asking him, for the love of God, Saint Peter, and us, to remove his men from it and not presume in any way to invade or retain the estate once invaded; rather, he should protect you with his arm and deign to defend you against all who act wickedly toward you, if he wishes to have the grace of God and of the chief of the apostles.

As for Arembert, his vassal, to whom he had given the estate as a benefice, we ordered through Isaac, the venerable bishop, that he be deprived of all ecclesiastical communion if he should thereafter rashly enter that estate or presume to cause any disturbance there.

CCLVII. TO COUNT BOSO. That he should remove Arembert and all others from the estate of Vendoara, restore it to the men of Pultaria, and protect the monastery itself.

To his beloved son Boso, the glorious prince.

How greatly we have loved you, and with what affection of our fatherhood we have loved you since we came to know your exalted glory, you yourselves remember well; for your Excellence has also taken care, with tranquil mind, to venerate and honor us in all things as a spiritual father.

Confiding in this bond of mutual love, we asked that the immovable properties situated throughout the provinces of Gaul under the jurisdiction of the holy apostles, the chiefs Peter and Paul, together with their men and everything belonging to them, should remain defended by your powerful arm and secure through your assistance. You readily promised to do this for the love of God, Saint Peter, and our honor.

Now, however, as we have heard, you have occupied our estate of Vendoara without our consent or will and given it as a benefice to one of your vassals, named Arembert. If this is true, you have not acted well, as was fitting for you.

Therefore we ask your Highness, dearest son, for the love of the Lord and Saint Peter, the key-bearer of the heavenly kingdom, to allow our men who reside there to possess that estate securely under our jurisdiction, as we have arranged it. Remove all your men and those of others from residence in or control of that estate, and do not permit us during your lifetime to suffer any disturbance from anyone.

In the same way we ask that the monastery of Saint Peter called Pultaria—which Gerard, the late count, completed and endowed from his own property and handed over to Saint Peter—be assisted in every way by your protection. The brothers who dwell there and offer their continual praises to God, praying for the salvation of all who believe in Christ, are harassed by hostile neighbors, and their entire household—indeed, ours—is continually cruelly troubled and oppressed, so that it cannot plow or carry out the other tasks pertaining to the cultivation of the land.

Therefore extend your assistance to that holy place, and, for the love of God, of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and of us, stretch out the hand of your power against God’s adversaries and its own, so that, relying on your powerful arm, they may remain safe and secure in all things, and so that both in the present you may receive worthy rewards from us and in the future be able to receive multiplied recompense from the Lord.

CCLVIII. TO GUAIFER, PRINCE OF SALERNO. He admonishes him to desist from the troubles he was inflicting on the Capuans; he announces that he will go into his territories and settle the dissensions.

To the most noble man, Guaifer, the glorious prince.

From the report of certain persons we have learned that, at the persuasion of the enemy of the human race, who is the author of all enmity and death, you wish to inflict manifold harms and adversities on the Capuans. Because of the evil of discord, daily generated by the envy of the world and increasing among relatives and friends, you are considering bringing about a general danger, from which considerable disturbance would arise in these parts of yours and a scandal of long duration remain.

Although foreign enemies are not lacking, with whom you must continually struggle, you wish to bring the dangers of conflict upon your relatives, whom you could have as supporters and helpers when you needed them. Therefore, in the manner of a father, we admonish you as a beloved son, and by the authority of almighty God and the power of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul we prohibit you from having permission to go against the aforesaid Capuans or to inflict any disturbance upon them until our special arrival.

For, with God’s help, when the heat of this summer season has passed, we shall come into these parts of yours for the salvation, concord, and unanimity of you all, so that, in our presence, every act of violence may be quieted and every scandal which has grown between you and them from a viper’s seed may be removed from your midst.

For we desire your salvation, lest you perish forever; therefore we wish you always to pursue the things that belong to peace. When we come, out of love for you, we shall, with the Lord’s favor, ordain as bishop for the people of Capua the very man whom you desire, so that your princely honor may remain undiminished. But if we should discover that you are acting otherwise, know that we shall not regard you as participants in our communion.

CCLIX. TO PANDENULF, THE CASTALD. (Year 879.) He announces that he has written to Guaifer to desist from inflicting harm on the Capuans.

To the noble man Pandenulf, the glorious castald.

Having reread the letter of your diligence, which you sent to us through such a faithful man of yours, we have heard, with apostolic kindness alone, the matters concerning which you strove to petition our pontificate, and, as reason required, we have partly fulfilled them.

For we sent a letter of our apostolate to Guaifer, admonishing, reproving, and excommunicating him, and declaring that by the authority of God, the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and ourselves, he had no permission to come against the city of Capua or to inflict any disturbance anywhere in its suburbs and borders, nor to devise any plots, until, with the Lord’s help, we should come into these parts after the heat of this summer season.

CCLX. TO KING CHARLES. (Year 879.) He writes that he summoned him by letter to advance to the imperial dignity, went as far as Ravenna to meet him, and hoped to receive his help against the enemies of the Roman Church; this hope disappointed him so completely that the enemies have never raged more fiercely. He asks him to aid the Church and, while preparing his journey, to send legates to him; he commends his own legates.

[Col. 0882D]

To his beloved and spiritual son, Charles, the glorious king.

Your royal Highness knows well that, for a long time now, desiring by God’s favor to lead you to the height of imperial power for the benefit and exaltation of the holy apostolic see, your mother, we summoned you by letters of our authority. Afterwards, because of the greatness of our love for you, leaving our Church amid the savage hands of enemies—not only pagans but also wicked Christians—we came to you at Ravenna. No one is remembered to have done this before us for your most glorious ancestors.

We hoped, of course, that through you the former honor and strength of the holy Roman Church would be brought to complete increase, and we thought that we should easily suppress and overcome in every way the fierce severity of the enemies of the holy Church of God. But because we accomplished none of these things with your Highness as we wished, on our return we found matters worse than before.

For our enemies, emboldened by greater audacity, do not hesitate not only to plunder the possessions of Saint Peter but also to gather and retain our men under their power. Therefore, dearest son, know for certain that we desire with all our strength to advance your honor and glory, and for that reason you ought, with pious regard and devoted mind, to carry out what is beneficial to the welfare and exaltation of the holy apostolic see.

Accordingly, we earnestly ask you to send us Luithbard, the venerable bishop; Manigold, son of Adelbert; and Adelbert, your chief cupbearer. Before you undertake the journey to come into these parts, let them assure us and your holy mother, the Roman Church, and make us favorably disposed and joyful with regard to your honor and glory, so that, with God’s help, when you come to Rome, you may strive, in the manner of your ancestors, to renew and confirm one of the pacts and the privileges of the holy Roman Church.

We ask you not to believe anything from our enemies concerning what we urge you to do for the honor of God and of the holy Church, or for your own honor; nor should you believe those who seek their own interests more than your glory. For the honor and exaltation of the holy Roman Church are your protection in all things, and its defense against all enemies is your own.

We have sent you these envoys of ours—namely, Marinus, the venerable bishop and treasurer of our see, and Peter, likewise bishop of Senigallia. We ask that you receive them kindly and not hesitate to believe what they tell you orally as though you were hearing it from us. Given as above.

CCLXI. TO THE SAME. (Year 879.) He laments that he cannot confer with him. He sends Arnulf as legate, asking him not to allow the Roman Church to be harmed by its enemies, and therefore orders that his legate be sent to him with Arnulf.

To his beloved and spiritual son, Charles, the glorious king.

We have heard that you are now to cross the Alps [Col. 0883D] and enjoy conversation with your beloved brother in common discourse. We are therefore greatly troubled, because, in accordance with our common agreement, we had hoped to meet with you in person and accomplish a great and beneficial work for the exaltation of the holy Roman Church, your mother, for your honor, and for the salvation of the whole land of Saint Peter.

For this reason we have sent you our beloved nephew Farulf, our cherished counsellor, through whom we suggest to your royal magnificence that you in no way neglect to arrange and order the land of Saint Peter so that it may remain secure and defended not only from pagans but also [Col. 0884A] from wicked Christians—as you undoubtedly know yourselves—until, with God’s help, you return and come to the embrace of your holy mother, the Roman Church. For if you neglect this, we can scarcely endure so many adversities on every side.

Therefore let your royal greatness take care that, in your days, this same Church suffer no diminution, but rather be increased through you, since its increase is your honor. We therefore ask that, together with the aforesaid nephew of ours, you send us from your side a suitable envoy who, for the safety and justice of the land, may meanwhile labor with us equally and most readily in every matter, as necessity requires; so that we too may most willingly accomplish all your honor requires. You should not disdain to believe whatever he tells you as though you were hearing it from ourselves. [Col. 0884B]

For this reason we ask that you strive with willing spirit to do this and to fulfill your promise in every respect. For we want you to be certain that with our whole heart we desire to promote your honor and glory.

## CCLXII. TO ROMANUS, ARCHBISHOP. (Year 879)

He wonders why, although provoked by injuries, he had not fled to him; he sends a messenger to Ravenna to investigate carefully everything done against him and compel those who had inflicted the injury to come to Rome, so that he himself may proceed with them to the synod, where his case will be heard; and he reproves him because he does not reside in his own Church.

[Col. 0884C]

To the most reverend and most holy ROMANUS, archbishop of the holy Church of Ravenna.

Having heard that you have suffered such plots and injuries from certain persons, we have wondered why you did not immediately come to the embrace of the Roman Church and to our apostolic presence. For if you had come, you may know for certain that, after diligently investigating everything, we would, with God’s favor, have brought your entire case to its desired and successful conclusion.

Now, for this matter, we are sending a prudent messenger to Ravenna, whom we order carefully to investigate what you have informed us was done against you, so that he may bind those who, as you assert, committed such acts by means of a guarantor and such an envoy that they may be compelled to come to Rome immediately. When they have come, [Col. 0884D] we wish you also to come on the Kalends of October, as has already been commanded you for the celebration of the synod, because we wish to deliberate on your case in our presence. For, in accordance with the power divinely granted to us, we shall take every care to assist you according to the custom of our predecessors. We desire that the honor of the holy Church of Ravenna always remain undiminished.

In this, however, you are to be reproved: having abandoned your Church at Ravenna, you travel about and reside in other Churches, contrary to your promise; for because of the things you say have happened to you [Note: [Col. 0883D] Something is missing.].

As above.

## CCLXIII. TO ALL THE FAITHFUL. (Year 879)

He commands them to obey the bishop of Ticinum, to whom he had granted the power of excommunication.

[Col. 0885A]

To all the most reverend and most holy bishops, and to the distinguished marquises and counts, and to all the faithful of the holy Church of God.

Since, according to the Apostle (II Corinthians 11:28), we have concern for all the Churches of God, we have judged it fitting to admonish your diligence by this letter of our apostolate and earnestly to exhort you with apostolic benevolence, so that the power which you possess by divine generosity may always serve the usefulness of the Church and the honor of the priesthood. [Col. 0885B]

Therefore we admonish you to show reverence and honor to the holy Church of Ticinum, which appears in a special way to belong to the apostolic see, and to its bishop, namely our brother John, to whom we have entrusted, in our place, the excommunication of transgressors—in such a way that those whom he excommunicates are themselves to be regarded as excommunicated—and to offer him your assistance readily. Permit no opposition or invasion of any kind against the property or people of that Church; rather, strive with the greatest diligence, for the love of God and of us, to protect them by your support. Nor should any of you presume to receive any of his clergy under commendation or under the pretext of any protection without the permission of the aforementioned bishop.

But if any of his clergy should attempt to act against this apostolic statute of ours, both the one who receives and the one who is received shall be deprived of ecclesiastical communion. [Col. 0885C]

As above.

## CCLXIV. TO ROMANUS, ARCHBISHOP OF RAVENNA. (Year 879)

He commands him to come to Rome for the synod.

To the most reverend and most holy archbishop of the holy Church of Ravenna.

Just as we formerly instructed Your Reverence that, because of the many needs of the Churches of God, you were to come to Rome on the fourth day before the Ides of October so that we might celebrate the synod together, so now, by this letter of our apostolate, we again command your fraternity [Col. 0885D] not to neglect, setting aside every delay or pretext, to attend the appointed synod with your suffragan bishops. With God as our guide, we shall celebrate it at the stated time in the church of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.

For we wish, as is fitting, to deliberate by common agreement and decree, according to the custom of our predecessors, concerning the usefulness and exaltation of all the Churches of God. Therefore, in accordance with the sacred canons, we desire your unanimity to be present, so that the vigor of the Church of God may, with Christ’s favor, remain unimpaired through synodal judgment.

Accordingly, if you now [Col. 0886A] permit any delay or negligence in coming, know that we shall rebuke you with canonical censure. We wish Your Holiness well, etc.

Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October, in the thirteenth indiction.

## CCLXV. TO THE CLERGY OF MILAN. (Year 879)

He commands them, in place of Archbishop Anspert, who had been deprived in the Roman synod, to provide another man to be consecrated by him; he sends legates to take part in the election with them and commands that they be obeyed in everything.

To all the bishops, priests, deacons, subdeacons, and all the clergy of the holy Church of Milan.

[Col. 0886B]

We wish it to be known to your God-beloved fraternity, dearest ones, that we, together with the holy synod held on the Ides of October in the church of blessed Peter the apostle, deprived Anspert, formerly your archbishop, of episcopal honor by the power of the Holy Spirit, the authority of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, princes of the apostles, and canonical and synodal sanction, because of his negligence and repeated presumptions. In the preceding synod, after a second and third summons and after canonical periods of grace had been granted to him for making satisfaction, he had refused to appear. For he had stubbornly presumed to communicate before his hearing and had not hesitated recklessly to perform the sacred ministry before the lawful examination of his purification, contrary to the statutes of the fathers. [Col. 0886C]

Therefore, by this present statute, we command you all, meeting and assembling with one mind and one will the pastors and people of the city, to promote to the honor of the archbishopric another man, whoever among the cardinal priests or deacons is found more worthy, with Christ’s assistance. Once this decree has been solemnly made and transmitted to this city, no bishop there is to presume to ordain anyone before everything has been reported to us, since, with God’s favor, we wish to consecrate the archbishop there according to the ancient custom and in accordance with the king’s grant.

For if you presume to act otherwise, we shall deprive you of ecclesiastical communion; and those who act against this statute of ours shall be entirely corrected by apostolic judgment. [Col. 0886D]

Indeed, we are sending there, in our place, our most reverend brothers and fellow bishops John of Ticinum and Welto of Rimini, who are to conduct this same election together with you. Let none of you presume in any way to impede them, since you understand that it is right for you to strive to obey us in everything. Whoever, in his arrogance, attempts to resist and act against this shall be separated from the fellowship of Christians [Note: [Col. 0885D] These words seem to belong earlier.].

And because he had not yet been released from the bonds of excommunication, he had presumed, outrageously and obstinately, to ordain a bishop in the Church of Vercelli, even against the king’s will.

As above.

## CCLXVI. TO KING CHARLES. (Year 879)

He announces that Anspert, formerly archbishop of Milan, had been deprived in the Roman synod, and that Joseph, whom Anspert had ordained bishop of Vercelli, had been deposed; he asks him to protect Conspert, whom he had consecrated bishop of Vercelli.

[Col. 0887A]

To his beloved and spiritual son CHARLES, glorious king.

We wish Your Royal Greatness to know, dearest son, that we had already canonically excommunicated Anspert, archbishop of Milan, in the first synod held in the church of blessed Peter the apostle, because of his evident negligence and presumptions, together with the most reverend assembly of bishops. But, lifting his mind into arrogance, [Col. 0887B] he not only did not humbly seek pardon for his offenses, but also, before his hearing and our apostolic absolution, presumed to celebrate the sacred ministry and, contrary to the sacred canons and to the royal and our apostolic will, outrageously presumed to consecrate a bishop in the Church of Vercelli.

Because of such great and reckless presumption, we deprived Anspert, formerly archbishop, of all episcopal honor in the synod recently held, and by synodal judgment decreed that the man whom he had illicitly ordained was deposed from the episcopal order. Out of consideration for mercy, however, we allowed him to return to the rank he had previously held.

Moreover, at the will and request of our beloved son Carolomannus, [Col. 0887C] the glorious king, we consecrated as bishop of that same Church of Vercelli the most reverend Conspert, about whom we formerly informed you through your faithful envoy, with the consent of all the bishops of the province. We earnestly ask you to protect him, for the love of God, blessed Peter, and ourselves, by the arm of your power, and always to provide him in every matter with worthy assistance, as his needs require.

May the Lord preserve Your Royal Excellence unharmed, dearest son.

As above.

## CCLXVII. TO THE PEOPLE OF VERCELLI. (Year 879)

He commands them to receive Conspert, whom he had appointed their bishop, and to honor him appropriately. He declares the acts of the usurper Joseph null.

[Col. 0887D]

To all the priests, deacons, subdeacons, and all the clergy and leading men, and to all the people of Vercelli.

By this apostolic letter we make known to you that we formerly deprived Anspert, formerly archbishop of Milan, of sacred communion, together with the holy synod, because of his many presumptions and negligences. But he acted contrary to the canonical statutes and to our apostolic and synodal judgment: before his hearing and absolution, he performed the sacred ministry and, while still excommunicated, rashly presumed to ordain in this Church of Vercelli a certain man named Joseph as bishop, as we hear, contrary to the royal and [Col. 0888A] our apostolic will.

Therefore, by the power of the Holy Spirit, the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, princes of the apostles, and our apostolic judgment, together with the synodal assembly of the most reverend bishops, we have decreed that both that archbishop and this Joseph himself, an invader and presumptuous man who did not enter through the door but entered the Lord’s sheepfold from elsewhere like a thief, are deprived of and excluded from all episcopal honor. Nevertheless, out of consideration for mercy, we established by synodal decree that the aforesaid Joseph, the invader of your Church, having been cast down from the episcopal order, should in every respect return to the rank and order in which he previously stood.

For since the aforementioned Anspert, formerly archbishop of Milan, had been regularly [Col. 0888B] excommunicated, he could in no way perform even the consecration of the lowest grades in the Church of God; for certainly he could not give what he did not possess.

Therefore let the discernment and praiseworthy fidelity of you all know that our beloved and spiritual son Carolomannus, glorious king of this Italian kingdom, granted the very bishopric of Vercelli to this most noble man Conspert, according to the custom of his royal and imperial predecessors. In the presence of our envoys, he petitioned our apostolic clemency by letter that we consecrate him bishop for you.

Moved by his petitions and unwilling to leave you for long without the care of your own legitimate shepherd, we consecrated this man, by apostolic authority alone, bishop of your holy Church of Vercelli, [Col. 0888C] and gave you, in place of that invader, this shepherd; in place of an idle mercenary, a sufficiently prudent rector. Instructed by our apostolic teachings, he is to strive with vigilant care and diligence to feed you, as the Lord’s people entrusted to him, with the nourishment of eternal life and salvation, like a true shepherd, and to govern you with the rod of equity and gentleness.

Therefore, by this present statute of ours, we command all of you, as our dearest sons, to receive him with one will and devout affection as the father and ruler of your souls; and, having rejected and repudiated the aforesaid invader, regard as your bishop this man whom we have ordained for you.

For you appear worthy of great praise because you have deserved to have as your bishop one consecrated by blessed Peter the apostle. [Col. 0888D] This will undoubtedly contribute to the increase of the honor of the Church of Vercelli if you obey our commands with devout minds.

We, desiring your salvation, therefore admonish you so that you may be safe in mind and body.

We also command that all documents or grants of whatever kind that he made concerning the parishes, estates, and villages of that Church of Vercelli have no validity; rather, we judge everything he did to be void and empty, because he himself was not the legitimate bishop and therefore could not grant anything. Whoever declares that anything among his acts is valid, we judge is to be struck with the anathema of Ananias and Sapphira.

But if, on anyone’s advice or urging, you should otherwise act, fail immediately to cast out that invader, and refuse willingly and eagerly to receive this man whom we have consecrated for you, we shall deprive you of all ecclesiastical communion and strike you with a fitting anathema. [Col. 0889A]

As above.

## CCLXVIII. TO NOTINGUS, BISHOP OF NOVARA. (Year 879)

He warns him to restore Angelberga’s property; otherwise he threatens him with excommunication unless he comes to Rome within two months to render an account concerning it.

To NOTINGUS, bishop of Novara.

We have heard that you are unjustly retaining the property of our spiritual daughter Angelberga Augusta. We wish you, and by apostolic authority command you, to hasten to restore it immediately. What no law permits you to retain, [Col. 0889B] release with all possible speed, so that she to whom it appears to belong may in every way be allowed to enjoy it.

For if you do not immediately restore the aforesaid property, we admonish you, and by apostolic authority command you, to come to Rome within two months to render an account concerning it and to offer suitable satisfaction before us. Otherwise, remain excommunicated for as long as, obeying this admonition of ours, you fail to carry out what we have established.

Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the thirteenth indiction.

## CCLXIX. TO THE PEOPLE OF AMALFI. (Year 879)

He announces that he has excommunicated them until they separate themselves from the pagans; he threatens them with further punishments unless they obey as soon as possible.

[Col. 0889C]

To the most reverend and most holy bishop PETER, and to PULCAR, the prefect, and to the entire people of Amalfi.

We wish it to be known to your love and unanimity that, contrary to the divine statutes and to our apostolic admonitions—which we have frequently addressed to you—and by the authority of God and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, we commanded you to maintain no pact with the impious Saracen people and to break entirely any pact already made. Yet you do not fear to remain in such a crime and in the company of the enemies of God.

Therefore, by the power of the Holy Spirit and the authority of blessed Peter, to whom the Lord granted the power of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth (Matthew 16), we have deprived you, together with the consent of the entire apostolic see, of all sacred communion—that is, of the holy body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ—and have separated you from the fellowship of the Church of God. We decree that you remain under this excommunication until, coming to your senses, you separate yourselves from the impious plunder of the pagans. Unless you are converted quickly, with pure heart and devout will, to the embrace of your holy mother, the Roman Church, we shall undoubtedly strike you with a sentence of greater condemnation. [Col. 0890A]

In the end, we seek your salvation; by apostolic benevolence we desire to save your souls in the sight of the Lord, and we long to lead you, like the Lord’s sheep, to the pastures of eternal salvation—provided that, devoting yourselves to good works, you strive to carry out our support, will, command, and admonition, and refuse to remain in such a pact of wickedness.

We wish you well in Christ.

On the twenty-fourth day of the month of October, in the thirteenth indiction.

## CCLXX. TO HELMOINUS, BISHOP OF PENNA. (Year 879)

He reproves him because he did not come to the synod; he orders him to come to him on the appointed day and meanwhile to absolve a man whom he had unjustly excommunicated.

To the most reverend and most holy HELMOINUS, bishop of Penna.

In accordance with the sacred canons of the venerable Fathers, composed by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, we determined in every respect that, for ecclesiastical needs and benefits alone, your fraternity was required to attend the synods which we recently celebrated on the appointed days, after letters of our authority had been sent according to custom. But since we have learned that, although the others came with great devotion, you did not come at all, and that you did not send us or the holy synod your excuse written in a regular form in a tractoria—plainly, as is evident, because of your presumption and disobedience—we do not wish to appear to have passed over your conduct without investigation. Therefore, by this statute of our apostolate, we command that within eight days of the month of December you come to us and present yourself before our sight, without any delay or uncertainty. [Col. 0890C]

For Oteramus, son of the late Corvinus, together with his fellow citizens, also brought a complaint against you before our apostolic presence and the venerable assembly of bishops. He stated that, when you had brought an ecclesiastical charge against him for contempt, and he had purged himself with his fellow swearers after taking an oath, your fraternity, as he declared, excommunicated him as though he were a perjurer. Yet canonical rule commands that a bishop should in no way claim this judgment for himself, and the Lord says to Moses that no one ought to be condemned on the testimony of a single person.

If this is so, since you ought not to have excommunicated him rashly, we command you to absolve him immediately and restore him to your communion. For if you act otherwise with reckless boldness, we command that he be considered undoubtedly absolved by apostolic authority.

And if, disregarding this command of ours, you presumptuously refuse to appear before us, [Col. 0890D] know that you are to be deprived of ecclesiastical communion as disobedient until you come and humbly offer us suitable satisfaction for your negligences.

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December.

## CCLXXI. TO PAUL, BISHOP. (Year 879)

He orders that the church situated in the village of Carpana be restored, that a priest be appointed there, and that sacred chrism be sent to it annually.

To the most reverend and most holy PAUL, bishop of the holy Church of Reggio.

[Col. 0891A]

To your love, instructed in the venerable rules of the holy Fathers, we command and by this letter of our episcopate order that you restore the Church of God situated in the village of Carpana, which was recently burned by fire, and do not neglect to restore it to its former beauty and order. Place it under the care of its own priest, who may daily offer diligent praise to the Lord there and pray to almighty God for the salvation of the faithful. With God’s favor, take care continually to send sacred chrism there annually, for it is the salvation and true perfection of all Christianity.

For if you act otherwise, we shall undoubtedly, by apostolic authority, entrust the aforesaid church to another bishop for restoration and canonical organization.

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December.

## CCLXXII. TO THEODORICUS, HEODICIUS, AND OTHERS. (Year 879)

He shows that a woman who had been compelled by force and threats to assume the religious habit is not bound to keep her vows; nevertheless, he entrusts her case to them for determination. If any difficulty arises, he orders them or their legates to come to him with the woman.

[Col. 0891B]

To THEODORICUS of Teate, HEODICIUS of Firmum, JOHN of Aprutium, and HELMOINUS of Penna, bishops.

A certain woman of your dioceses, named Theoderona of Vivelata, formerly the wife of Tresigius, approached the apostolic see and our pontifical office together, and complained to us that, after her husband’s death, the veil of the sacred habit had been placed upon her by that same husband’s own brother, acting not from love of the spiritual life but from ambition for property. She declared that, although she strongly resisted, she had received the same veil without a priest’s blessing, contrary to her own agreement, promise, request, choice, intention, vow, and spontaneous judgment.

We considered her profession before our fellow bishops and brothers and also questioned suitable men—Opteramus, Scattoimus, Erfemarius, Amedeus, and Cerisius—neighbors of the woman who happened to be present, asking whether the matter was so or not. They not only testified that it had indeed happened so, but also showed themselves ready to offer every satisfaction concerning this matter. [Col. 0891D]

We, therefore, possessing the same spirit of faith as our fathers and, through Christ’s grace, the same zeal for justice, hold and decree concerning those who have been lawfully veiled exactly as they did. We establish that what is admitted not by one’s own will, judgment, vow, request, or spontaneous decision, but rather under compulsion, must be annulled. This is especially so since the woman herself said that she had worn the veil for no more than approximately fifteen days, terrified by threats, and had received it forcibly, with no priest conferring a blessing.

Although we hope that this may suffice for her absolution—for if the matter is so, having been released from all bonds of force and necessity, she ought lawfully and without penalty to follow her own judgment, and she must not be compelled to endure what she did not choose—nevertheless we entrust her case to Your Holinesses. Assemble together, examine the woman’s case according to God, and, having discovered the complete truth of this complaint through careful investigation, bring it to a definite conclusion. [Col. 0892A]

We establish, however, that it is not right that she be compelled to bear a yoke to which she was subjected not by a movement of her own purpose but by ambition and the oppression of force. For the holy Pope Gregory also reports the following in his letter to Athanasius [elsewhere: Anastasius], priest of Isauria (Book V, Letter 67):

“Although things done under the impulse of force are not at all accepted by the judgment of the canons and are rightly considered invalid, since the one who compels a person to confess what is unjust dissolves them, that confession is rather to be received and embraced which is shown to proceed from spontaneous will.”

And again it is written: [Col. 0892B] “I will sacrifice to you voluntarily” (Psalm 53); and elsewhere: “Accept the free offerings of my mouth, O Lord” (Psalm 118).

Moreover, we have already instructed the aforementioned John, the reverend bishop of Aprutium, in words, ordering him, after summoning your fraternity, to discuss the entire matter together with you and strive to determine it canonically, as we have said. If any ambiguity should arise concerning this, we then order that either you or your legates, acting in your place, appear with the same woman before our presence, so that the truth of the entire matter may be investigated more carefully before us and settled according to the rule of equity. [Col. 0892C]

Finally, if any crime has in any way been maliciously charged against the aforesaid woman, do not admit it, keeping God before your eyes. If her accuser persists in his obstinacy, both the accused woman and the accuser are to hasten, together with your envoys, into our presence.

But if her accuser is absent, she is not to remain bound by that charge when she comes before us, according to the nineteenth chapter of the Council of Carthage, which says (Council of Carthage III, chapter 7):

“If her accuser has never been absent on the days appointed for the hearing of the case, he is not to be removed from communion; once the accused has been restored to communion, the accuser himself is to be removed from communion.”

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December, in the thirteenth indiction.

## CCLXXIII. TO ATHANASIUS, PULCAR, AND OTHERS. (Year 879)

He commands them to break the treaty made with the Saracens; unless they do so by the Kalends of December, he threatens them with excommunication. He warns Pulcar not to harass Pandenulf, the judge of Capua.

[Col. 0892D]

To ATHANASIUS, bishop of Naples; PETER, bishop, or PULCAR, prefect of Amalfi; the bishop of Gaeta, or DECIBILIS; and JOHN, the glorious hypati, from their peers.

I am ashamed, so to speak, that our pontificate must now admonish you concerning something about which we have admonished you so many times, yet you have refused to come to your senses and have until now scorned to dissolve the pact made with the Saracens, hateful to God.

But because we defer describing how many kinds of cruelty, desolation, and calamity of this land have arisen and continue to arise from this, [Col. 0893A] lest meanwhile we be compelled to pass the judgment that is deserved, we still beseech you, still exhort you as spiritual sons, and, striving to embrace you with paternal affection, command by the authority of God and of the chief apostles Peter and Paul that, now at last receiving discipline, you separate yourselves from those wicked sons of the slave-woman, the Saracens, and dissolve in every way the pact made with them, if you wish to share either in our communion or in Christianity itself. We would already have pronounced against them the sentence of the ecclesiastical sword, if apostolic patience did not restrain us.

Therefore we grant you a period of grace until the Kalends of December of this thirteenth indiction to break the pact with the Saracens. Desiring to win both you and the people of Gaeta and Amalfi, if, as is your custom, you refuse until that time to dissolve every friendship with the Saracens and every treaty as well, we shall strike both parties with the darts of ecclesiastical judgment and subject you to perpetual anathema, so that, since you do not wish to be partners in discipline, you may also not share in our communion. [Col. 0893B]

This is to be added in the letter to Pulcar.

Finally, we admonish Your Nobility not to be troublesome in any way to Pandenulf, the judge of Capua. Since he is devoted to us, be joined to him in devotion and friendship, and, insofar as you are able, set yourself as a wall against his adversities. Remembering his father, who suffered execution while saving his own parent, for the love of both men—if you have concern for us—attach yourself rather to Pandenulf’s advancement than appear in any way to oppose it. [Col. 0893C]

## CCLXXIV. TO ARPALDUS, BISHOP OF ASCOLI. (Year 879)

He reproves him because he did not come to the synod; he orders him to come to him so that he may answer the charges brought by his clergy.

To the most reverend and most holy ARPALDUS, bishop of Ascoli.

In accordance with the sacred canons of the venerable Fathers, composed by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, we determined in every respect that, for ecclesiastical needs alone, your fraternity was required to attend the synods which we recently celebrated on the appointed days, after letters of our authority had been sent according to custom. [Col. 0893D]

But since we have learned that, although the others came with great devotion, you did not come at all—even though you had also learned by report that we were celebrating the synod—and that you did not send us or the holy synod your excuse written in a regular form in a tractoria, plainly because of your presumption and disobedience, we do not wish to appear to have passed over your conduct without investigation. Therefore, by this statute of our authority, we command that you come to us immediately, without any delay or uncertainty, and present yourself before our sight.

For the clergy of your Church also approached us, complaining that they had suffered many grievous wrongs at the hands of your fraternity and had been unjustly oppressed contrary to ecclesiastical rule. You must undoubtedly answer these charges in the presence of our episcopate. [Col. 0894A]

Therefore, once you have received this command, strive to come before your Church suffers a greater schism or scandal. For if you now scorn to come, you shall certainly bear the fitting censure of excommunication pronounced by the apostolic see.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of December.

## CCLXXV. TO KING CHARLES. (Year 879)

He wonders why, although he had come to Pavia, where they were supposed to meet, he had not sent legates to him; he asks him to send them so that he may go to him.

[Col. 0894B]

To his beloved and spiritual son CHARLES, glorious king.

As you formerly informed our episcopal office by your royal letters that, after the Kalends of November had passed, we were to come to meet you at Pavia, so that by common deliberation we might together consider what was useful for the holy Church of God and beneficial for the stability of the kingdom, and secure it with perpetual firmness, we have since then been eagerly prepared to accomplish this.

But because we hear that you have entered Italy, we have been greatly surprised that you have not made your arrival known to us through the honeyed letters and suitable legates of Your Excellence. For, loving you with paternal affection, we especially desire to see Your Greatness, dearest son. [Col. 0894C]

Now, therefore, if it is entirely true that you have already come to Pavia, we wish you to send us distinguished legates from your side, bearing honorable letters to the apostolic see. After we have examined them, we shall undoubtedly be able to hasten to your serenity and hold a common conversation with you.

For when, with God’s favor, we have been joined with you, we shall easily be able to accomplish everything that appears to concern the exaltation of the holy apostolic see, your mother, and your honor and ours. For these things may the Lord multiply your glory in many ways in this age, and afterward undoubtedly grant you an eternal reward in the heavenly realm.

As above.

## CCLXXVI. TO THE SAME. (Year 879)

He gives thanks that, when Conspert had been ordained bishop of the Church of Vercelli by him, he had willingly accepted his ordination; he excuses himself for not absolving Anspert, archbishop of Milan, at his request.

[Col. 0894D]

To his beloved and spiritual son CHARLES, glorious and most excellent king.

We offer many thanks to Your Greatness because, concerning the bishopric of Vercelli, in which we ordained Conspert bishop together with the decree of the synod, you have willingly carried out our will.

As for the matter of the archbishopric of Milan, [Col. 0895A] dearest son, you have now instructed us that we ought to reconcile Anspert, the archbishop whom we judged in the synod because of certain negligences and presumptions of his. We would certainly have carried this out in every respect with eager spirit for love of you, if the sentence of condemnation that we pronounced against that archbishop had not been issued with a specific condition.

For it was stated that he was to remain suspended from honor and priestly ministry until, with God’s help, he presented himself personally to us to make satisfaction. Since it is our duty solemnly to preserve the privilege of the Church of God unimpaired, lest we appear in any way to overstep the boundaries of the Fathers, we could not act contrary to the statutes of our predecessors.

Therefore, with paternal affection, we admonish Your Benevolent Excellence not to be disturbed in any way because we cannot act otherwise without blame, since we desire in every respect to fulfill your will for your honor.

As above.

## CCLXXVII. TO KINGS LOUIS AND CAROLOMANNUS. (Year 879)

He gives thanks for their devotion toward the Roman Church and promises reciprocal diligence.

To his most beloved sons, LOUIS and Carolomannus, most glorious kings.

Having learned through the venerable bishop of your devotion, which you possess toward the holy Roman Church and which you strive to exercise with all your might, we give the greatest thanks to God and to you. Therefore, on our part, [Col. 0895C] we wish you to be assured that, just as the Emperor Charles, of blessed memory, your grandfather, and afterward your father, King Louis, commended you to the protection of the Roman Church and to our apostolic guardianship, so we are always prepared to show you our apostolic affection in all things and to assist and protect you with paternal devotion and love. Moreover, concerning the matters that you conveyed verbally through the aforementioned co-bishop, we have sent you our response through him. For whatever we have found upon our deliberation and have instructed you after making it known to you, believe without qualification to be beneficial to your honor.

## CCLXXVIII. TO HUGO AND THE OTHER COUNTS. (Year 879.) He gives thanks for the loyalty they maintained toward Kings Louis and Carolomannus.

[Col. 0895D]

To HUGO, distinguished abbot, and to BERNALD, GUITO, and the other glorious counts of the kingdom.

Having heard a good report about you—that you are in all things protectors, defenders, and faithful men of Louis and Carolomannus, the most excellent kings who have been entrusted to us by their forebears—we offer the greatest thanks. Therefore, by this apostolic letter we exhort your magnificence that, following the example of your faithful parents, you show toward them an ever greater and more sincere devotion, [Col. 0896A] because we also, by God’s favor, stand ready in every way to assist them together with you, so that you may deserve to receive a worthy recompense for this not only from God and from us, but also from them.

## CCLXXIX. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF PAVIA. (Year 879–880.) He orders him to restore the church situated in the village of Carpana, which Paul, bishop of Reggio, had neglected to repair, to establish a proper priest there, and to send the sacred chrism annually.

To the most reverend and holy JOHN, bishop of Pavia, and beloved fellow bishop.

Because Paul, bishop of the Church of Reggio, although admonished by canonical ordinances and exhorted by our apostolic [Col. 0896B] commands to restore the church of God situated in the village called Carpana, which had been burned by fire, and there to perform properly, according to ecclesiastical law, all its offices and ministry, rashly despised this obligation and refused to obey our salutary command, he does not appear to have rendered to our God the honor due in this matter. Therefore, commanding by apostolic authority, we order your devotion immediately and without any delay to restore that church to its former beauty and order, and to place it under the care of its own priest, who may daily offer continual praises there to the Lord and be able to entreat almighty God for the salvation of the faithful. You shall also diligently arrange that the sacred chrism be sent there every year, by God’s favor, without interruption, for it is the salvation and true perfection of all Christianity. [Col. 0896C] Issued as above.

## CCLXXX. TO TEUTMAR, ARCHBISHOP. (Year 879 or 880.) He is surprised that he delays and has not come to him; he urges him to come immediately.

To the most reverend and holy TEUTMAR, archbishop, our beloved fellow bishop.

As our beloved spiritual son, the glorious King Carolomannus, informed us in a royal letter that you ought to come into our apostolic presence, we, awaiting your arrival every day, wonder why you delay so long. For, filled with affection for your goodness and prudence, we already desire to behold your brotherhood with loving regard. Therefore, by this apostolic letter we admonish and exhort you to hasten to us with a willing mind in every way, so that together with you we may arrange, as necessity requires, those matters that are useful to the holy Church of God. [Col. 0896D] Issued as above.

## CCLXXXI. TO ANTONY, BISHOP, AND BERENGAR, COUNT. (Year 879–880.)
