He excommunicates Count Liutfred because he received a nun who had fled from a monastery and plundered the property of the Empress Angelberga, unless he makes satisfaction within the appointed time; he warns that no one is to associate with him.

To the most reverend ANTONY, bishop of Brescia, and to the most noble man and beloved son BERENGAR, glorious count.

Because our beloved spiritual son, the glorious King Carolomannus, entrusted to our episcopate, through his royal letters and through the word of our envoys, the care of this kingdom of Italy with pious affection, we wish with all our strength to restrain whatever we learn has been presumptuously committed anywhere against God and the rights of the law—both on account of the pastoral concern for all Christ’s sheep divinely entrusted to us and on account of the care granted to us in place of the aforesaid king—and to strike one sick sheep with the spiritual sword, so that the wounded soul may somehow reach salvation before the whole flock is stained by a single contagion.

Therefore, having heard and knowing for certain [Col. 0897B] that Count Liutfred received a certain consecrated woman named Gerlinda, who had fled from the monastery of Piacenza, and that, after our salutary admonition and prohibition concerning this matter, he detained her and shared fellowship with her together with his own wife; we command your nobility, with paternal affection alone, concerning both this consecrated woman [a passage is missing] and the possessions of our beloved daughter Angelberga Augusta, to whom he altogether ought to have kept due faith, which he secretly seized and whose return to her he has hitherto delayed despite our prohibition. Moreover, because he rashly presumed to plunder [the reading is corrupt; apparently: her property], which had been perpetually received under our apostolic protection and defense, we separate him from communion with the faithful, in such a way that, if he remains within the kingdom of Italy, he must have returned within thirty days, with true satisfaction, everything that he violently took away; and if he appears to be outside the kingdom of Italy, within sixty days.

Then, if he disregards all this and persists in his obstinacy, making no effort to amend his conduct, let him be bound by the bond of anathema until he comes into our apostolic presence and strives to make true satisfaction before us for all these unlawful acts. Therefore, we wish you not to associate with him in any way, if you wish, as beloved sons, to enjoy fellowship with us through our apostolic authority. Issued as above.

## CCLXXXII. TO EGILBERT, BISHOP. (Year 879–889.) He reproves him for associating with those excommunicated by the Apostolic See; he orders him not to associate with the excommunicated Liutfred and Odebric.

[Col. 0897D]

To the most reverend and holy EGILBERT, bishop.

By the command of the most blessed Apostle we are ordered to put off the old man with his deeds and to put on the new man, who has been created according to God in righteousness and the holiness of truth (Ephesians 4). For this reason, having heard that your devotion has associated, contrary to ecclesiastical law and before a hearing and true satisfaction has been rendered, with those who are rightly excommunicated by the Apostolic See—in which the authority of the blessed Peter and Paul always lives—we are deeply troubled with sorrow of heart. The distinguished teacher also says concerning avoiding such persons: “If anyone does not obey our word through this letter, take note of him, so that you do not associate with him” (2 Thessalonians 3).

Here also his fellow apostle John does not permit even a “Hail” to be spoken to such a person: “If anyone comes to you and does not bring this doctrine, do not receive him into the house, and do not say ‘Hail’ to him.” For whoever says ‘Hail’ to him shares in his evil works” (2 John 1). Likewise, blessed Clement, writing to James, the brother of the Lord, recalls that the apostle Peter thus instructed the people concerning himself: “If someone is an enemy on account of his deeds, do not wait for him himself to say to you, ‘Do not be friends with him.’”

Therefore, instructed by these salutary examples and also by canonical ordinances, lest you likewise be excommunicated together with them, we order you by apostolic authority not henceforth to presume to have any communion, even in ordinary conversation, with Liutfred and Odebric, who have been regularly excommunicated by us. If you do not wish the deserved sentence to fall upon you, take care that within thirty days after the announcement of this apostolic letter of ours they themselves return everything that they presumed to take away violently and fraudulently from that beloved daughter of ours, Angelberga Augusta.

## CCLXXXIII. TO EGIFRED AND THE OTHERS. (Year 879 or 880.) He asks them to take care of the property of the Empress Angelberga.

To the most noble men and beloved sons EGIFRED, SUPPO, [Col. 0898C] ERIPALD, BERARD, son of Boniface, and COTEPHRED, glorious counts.

Knowing assuredly that you will accomplish with devout affection, for the love of God, reverence for the holy princes, and our own love, the matters that we entrust to your prudence, we therefore earnestly beseech your glory, on behalf of our most beloved spiritual daughter Angelberga Augusta, by this letter of our apostolate, to exercise the greatest care and concern for all her possessions, wherever they may be located. Thus, through your prudent counsel and great assistance, all her property may remain safe, undiminished, secure, and defended, and you must not permit anyone to invade or plunder it.

For we shall undoubtedly strike with the spiritual sword anyone who presumes to do this or to favor one who does it, so that in consequence we may also, according to the apostolic authority divinely bestowed upon us, offer your nobility worthy and abundant thanks, blessing you with every spiritual blessing in Christ Jesus our Lord, and so that the laudable report of your faith may always resound everywhere through the mouths of the faithful, to the increase of your perpetual reward. Issued as above.

## CCLXXXIV. TO COUNT EUNIBER. (Year 879 or 880.) He threatens him with excommunication unless he restores the property of Saint Peter and of the Empress Angelberga.

To EUNIBER, glorious count.

[Col. 0899A] We have learned from a true report that you have invaded and retained unlawfully the property of the apostle Saint Peter, which we hold to have been granted to our spiritual daughter Angelberga Augusta, together with other possessions belonging to that same daughter of ours. Although you yourself were admonished concerning this invasion, you have not withdrawn from it; rather, you have continued without interruption in this same wickedness up to the present.

Therefore, we command you, putting aside every pretext and restraining yourself, to abandon these possessions completely and remove yourself and your men from them, so that our said daughter may lawfully reclaim and administer all of them as her own property and, as she wishes, retain them under our special protection. Otherwise, know that by our apostolic authority you are deprived of holy communion and separated from the fellowship of Christians until you restore, with appropriate satisfaction, what belongs to another. [Col. 0899B] Issued as above.

## CCLXXXV. TO GISULF, ABBOT. (Year 879–880.) He entrusts to his care the monastery of the Empress Angelberga.

To GISULF, venerable abbot of the monastery of Saint Christina.

By the authority of the holy Apostolic See, we entrust to your reverence the clear responsibility and care of the monastery of our beloved daughter Angelberga Augusta, situated in the city of Piacenza, as a capable minister of Christ and an outstanding shepherd of the Lord’s flock. In accordance with the rule of Saint Benedict, you are to arrange and regulate by the right of an abbot whatever must be arranged or regulated there, and whatever you discern must be corrected, you shall strive to correct by our authority, with careful investigation alone, so that you may please the Lord. [Col. 0899C] Issued as above.

## CCLXXXVI. TO GREGORY, THEOPHYLACT, AND DIOGENES, ETC. (Year 879 or 880.) He congratulates them on their victory over the Saracens; he is surprised that they did not come to Rome; he orders them to come to his aid against the Saracens.

To the beloved men GREGORY, imperial spatharius, THEOPHYLACT, [Col. 0899D] turmarch, and DIOGENES, imperial count.

Having heard that, with God’s help and according to the will of our spiritual son the emperor, you went to Naples and defeated with a powerful arm the multitude of Saracens stationed there, we rejoiced and immediately gave due thanks to almighty God for your victory and the destruction of your enemies.

But we were again surprised that you neglected to come to Rome and to see our apostolic presence, so that for the struggle of your labor you might receive from us and from the Apostolic See abundant grace and blessing poured out upon you. Thus, aided by the prayers of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and fortified with every spiritual blessing, you might be able to fight effectively against those sons of perdition with an ever-victorious right hand.

Nevertheless, so that you may be able to do this beneficially, and so that you may happily be victorious over your enemies and unbelievers on land and sea, we therefore order you to make every effort to come again to these regions with several dromons, for the honor of the aforementioned spiritual son of ours, the Augustus. In this way you will be able to provide us suitable assistance against those wicked Hagarenes, so that praise and reward may thereby increase for the emperor, and you may without doubt receive worthy recompense from us.

Therefore, we admonish and exhort you to attend willingly to our admonitions, and whatever you intend to do, let us learn of it quickly through you. [Col. 0900A] Issued as above.

## CCLXXXVII. TO ATHANASIUS, BISHOP OF NAPLES. (Year 879 or 880.) He commends his observance toward the Apostolic See; he urges him, as he had promised, to break the pact made with the Saracens. He indicates that the Amalfitans, admonished on this matter through his envoy, are to be excommunicated if they neglect to obey.

[Col. 0900B]

To the most reverend and holy ATHANASIUS, bishop of the Church of Naples.

We have always recognized that your holiness’s devotion toward the Apostolic See and toward our fatherhood is sincere and outstanding in every respect; this has also become even clearer to us upon examining the tenor of your present embassy. For this reason, by this letter of our apostolate we offer abundant thanks to your holiness, admonishing you with paternal affection not to cease laboring with all your strength, in accordance with the office granted to you, in matters belonging to God and useful to the Church of Christ.

And just as you informed us through your envoys that, whether the Amalfitans broke their pact with the Saracens or not, you would break it altogether, we wish you to strive continually to do so. We have also sent there our envoy, namely Dominicus, the venerable bishop, admonishing them patiently to fulfill our will in this matter. If they follow our will in this, we shall regard them as our associates and friends; but if not, we shall pursue them as foreign enemies with both the visible and the invisible sword, so that they may be held deserving of perpetual hatred by us and by all Christians. [Col. 0900D]

Through our aforementioned envoy, Bishop Dominicus, we have also ordered that those unwilling to obey him be excommunicated in person, and afterward we ourselves shall strike them with a deserved anathema. You, therefore, stand with us and break the unjust pact, because we too shall be with you in all things, and what we have already promised to give, with the Lord’s assistance, we shall undoubtedly grant you every year.

For if you do not maintain a treaty with the Saracens, then, with the Lord’s help, we shall have no concern for the treachery of the Amalfitans; we shall be able to pursue them with the spiritual sword and easily humble them. We wish your holiness well in Christ.

## CCLXXXVIII. TO THE AMALFITANS. (Year 879 or 880.) He warns them that, after breaking their treaty with the Saracens, they should return to the bosom of the Church, and for this reason promises to give them ten thousand mancuses each year and one thousand in the present year; if they do not obey, he threatens excommunication.

[Col. 0901A]

To the most reverend PETER, bishop, or PULCAR, prefect, and to all the priests and clerics, and to the entire people of the city of Amalfi.

We have often promised to do and bestow many good things upon you with a joyful mind, striving that you break in every way the pact that you maintain with the impious Saracen people, lest through you the Church of God be so cruelly afflicted by association with a wicked people, and lest you thereby acquire for your souls not only temporal danger but also eternal punishment. [Col. 0901B]

Now, wishing to save you in body and spirit as beloved sons, by this letter of our apostolate we admonish and exhort your community that, having now completely abandoned the fellowship of the Saracens and broken the treaty that you maintain with them to the destruction of your souls and of the land of Saint Peter, you should immediately return with a joyful mind and pious devotion to the bosom of the holy catholic and apostolic Church, your mother, and strive to return to our fellowship and communion.

We shall give you now and every year, as was established between us, ten thousand mancuses of silver. In this present year we give you, as a blessing, one thousand mancuses, and we grant you the toll that you ought to pay in our port. [Col. 0901C]

But if, persuaded by the devil, you presume to remain longer in such an impious crime and do not break that pact immediately, we order our bishop Dominicus to deprive you, in our place, of all ecclesiastical communion. When he returns, we ourselves shall bind you again with the bonds of perpetual anathema, and we shall close to you the entrances to all the lands in which you customarily conduct trade, so that you may conduct no business there.

If you doubt that the inhabitants of other cities will break their pacts, we believe that they will do our will; for at present they have an excuse through you. And if there is any among them that wishes to do as you have done, we shall arrange its destruction together with yours. [Col. 0901D] Moreover, know that we have retained in our presence Leo, your priest. Issued as above.

## CCLXXXIX. TO CHARLES THE FAT, KING OF ITALY. (Year 880.) He asks the king to allow Jerome to retain the bishopric of Lausanne peacefully and to order Hubo to return the property taken from the Church of Besançon.

To the beloved and spiritual son CHARLES, glorious king.

We wish your greatness to know that it is deeply beloved by us, because Jerome, bishop of the holy Church of Lausanne, having come to the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles and our pontifical see, has humbly asked that he be permitted, with your support, to continue to possess the Church of Lausanne, which he had formerly undertaken to govern. Moved by his prayers, in accordance with the charge entrusted to us for the care of all the Churches of God, and because we have recognized—at our exhortation—that he is faithful to you in all things and your own man, just as the other bishops of your kingdom are, we suggest to your excellence by this letter of our apostolate that, for the love of God, Saint Peter, and ourselves, you receive him kindly and permit him securely to receive and possess in its entirety the aforesaid bishopric of Lausanne, granted to him by God and also entrusted to him by our apostolic authority, lest that Church continue any longer without its own rector, contrary to the statutes of the Fathers. [Col. 0902B]

We unquestionably recognize that he was canonically elected bishop of the aforesaid Church, with his own archbishop giving consent on account of illness and the bishops who consecrated him requesting this in letters that he showed us. Therefore, we wish and ask that, without delay or any opposition, he possess and hold his bishopric, as we have said, and administer it with reverence for God. For while he is alive we shall in no way tolerate our consent to the election or consecration of another person, since the foremost authority of the holy Fathers commands that two bishops must not be in one city at the same time.

Therefore, dearest son, we nevertheless exhort and beseech your royal glory that, with God’s assistance, the Church itself, having now received its proper shepherd, may remain peaceful and tranquil under the protection of your clemency. Thus, aided by his prayers, after the earthly kingdom granted to you, may you deserve to receive the eternal one.

Moreover, Theodoric, archbishop of the holy see of Besançon, has sent many complaints to our apostolic ears concerning Hubo, your faithful man, because he invaded the property of that Church. For this reason also we ask that, for the love of God and of us, you have the same ecclesiastical property returned in its entirety to the aforesaid archbishop, and that you permit no further harm or opposition to be inflicted upon him. Issued on the twentieth day of June, in the thirteenth indiction.

## CCXC. TO LIUTWARD, BISHOP OF VERCELLI. (Year 880.) That he should advance the case of Bishop Jerome of Lausanne before King Charles.

[Col. 0902D]

To the most reverend and holy LIUTWARD, bishop of the holy Church of Vercelli.

With a familiar and pious affection, as toward one most faithful to us, we instruct and entrust your devotion, upon receiving this letter of our apostolate, to undertake our embassy to our beloved spiritual son, the most excellent King Charles, concerning Jerome, bishop of Lausanne. With great effort and prudent counsel, you should earnestly admonish and exhort the king’s greatness so that, for the love of God and of us, he may immediately return to him the bishopric of Lausanne, formerly granted to him by God, and permit him to hold it securely as his faithful servant. [Col. 0903A]

For while Jerome lives, we shall in no way give assent to the election or episcopal consecration of another; rather, by every means we shall prohibit this by apostolic authority, lest two bishops appear to be in one city contrary to the statutes of the Fathers.

Therefore, do not fail in any way to support our just commands with every effort and willingness, so that through your exertion our embassy may achieve an outcome of ecclesiastical salvation and peace before the most serene king, and so that the same Church of God, having received its own shepherd, may remain safe and tranquil in all respects. [Col. 0903B] Issued on the twentieth day of June, in the thirteenth indiction.

## CCXCI. TO THEODORIC, ARCHBISHOP OF BESANÇON. (Year 880.) He indicates that he has written to King Charles concerning his case; and concerning Bishop Jerome of Lausanne, he urges him to strive to assist him.

To the most reverend and holy THEODORIC, archbishop of the holy Church of Besançon.

We learn from your letters of the many and great disturbances and calamities that unjust men who do not fear God inflict daily upon the Church entrusted to you, and we deeply grieve over them. With God’s favor, we desire to provide you suitable consolation, so that you may happily retain the former strength of your see with its rights unimpaired. For, concerning your case and the salvation of your people, we have made a request to our beloved spiritual son, the glorious King Charles, that, for the love of God and of us, he protect you in every way with his aid and defense, deign to render justice against those who have presumed to invade the property of your Church, and order that the property itself be restored to you in its entirety. [Col. 0903C]

Nevertheless, as a good shepherd, be humble in prosperity and likewise courageous in adversity, so that you do not fail to govern steadfastly the people of the Lord entrusted to you despite the attack of the evils that you suffer.

We have also written to the same king concerning Jerome, the bishop, that he permit him securely from now on to retain the bishopric of Lausanne, granted to him by God and bestowed by our apostolic authority. Therefore, let your fraternity not fail to assist him in this to the best of your ability. [Col. 0903D] Issued on the twentieth day of June, in the thirteenth indiction.

## CCXCII. TO KING CHARLES. (Year 880.) He commends his observance toward the Roman Church; he asks him to send an envoy to assist him.

To the beloved and spiritual son CHARLES, glorious king.

By this apostolic letter we offer abundant thanks to your royal greatness for the great care and concern that you show toward the holy Roman Church, your mother, and for the sincerity of your devotion, by which you love us with a pure affection of mind, after the manner of your ancestors, and eagerly wish to assist us in all things. Since we know that you are willing to labor with a ready mind for the exaltation and benefit of the Apostolic See and for the defense of the whole land of Saint Peter, in this most pious desire of yours you will have the divine Majesty as helper and propitious toward your royal glory, and you will undoubtedly receive a worthy recompense for it not only in this age but afterward in the heavenly realm. [Col. 0904A]

As for what you commanded—that your margraves who are in our vicinity should strive together with us to carry out the necessary defense—this will in no way benefit us as it ought without your majesty’s presence or without a suitable nobleman of yours. The reason is that those margraves keep the men of our cities and our own territories, with whom we could adequately defend the territory of Saint Peter, in their continual service; they protect some of them by their own power and thus hinder them, so that they are entirely unable to perform our service according to our will.

Therefore, we beseech your excellence, for the love of God and the honor of the prince of the apostles, to send us immediately such an envoy that, through the power of your authority, we may unquestionably accomplish with him what belongs to the holy Church of God and to us. Thus we may recover by every means our own men who have been taken from us, so that the honor and strength of the holy Roman Church may in your days increase in all respects unimpaired and remain undiminished. For its honor and exaltation are your salvation and glory here and forever.

We too most willingly desire to accomplish whatever is beneficial to your glory, and we always strive to commend you to the Lord in our constant prayers, with the merits of the apostles assisting us. We therefore ask that these things now be done for the benefit of the holy Church, so that, when with the Lord’s favor we behold your glorious arrival, we may rejoice together in the joy we have desired and in the joy of our heart. Issued on the twenty-third day of June, in the thirteenth indiction.

## CCXCIII. TO COUNT SFENTOPULCRUS. (Year 880.) He congratulates him and his subjects on their observance toward the Apostolic See and receives them into his allegiance; he shows that Archbishop Methodius professed the orthodox faith, confirms his rights and privileges, and sends him to govern them. He announces that the bishop of the Church of Nitra has been consecrated and wishes another to be sent to him, whom he will place over another church; he orders everyone to obey that archbishop; he grants that the divine offices may be recited in the Slavonic language, provided that the Gospel is first recited in Latin.

[Col. 0904D]

To the beloved son SFENTOPULCRUS, glorious count.

We wish your diligence to know that, when our fellow bishop, the most reverend Archbishop Methodius [Col. 0905A] of the holy Church of Moravia, came to the threshold of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and into our pontifical presence together with Semisizus, your faithful man, and reported the matter in radiant speech, we learned of the sincerity of your devotion and of the desire of your entire people, which you hold toward the Apostolic See and toward our fatherhood.

For, inspired by divine grace and scorning the other princes of this age, you chose, together with the noble faithful men who belong to you and with the entire people of your land, to have the blessed Peter, prince of the apostolic order, and his vicar as your patron, helper, and defender in all things, out of a most faithful love. Submitting your neck beneath the protection of Peter and his vicar until the end, you desire, with the Lord’s assistance, to remain in this devotion as a most devoted son.

For this great faith and devotion of yours and of your people, with the arms of our apostolate extended, we embrace you as an only son with immense love. Together with all your faithful people, we receive you into the bosom of our fatherhood as sheep entrusted to us by the Lord; we desire mercifully to nourish you with the food of life and strive to commend you to almighty God in our constant prayers. Thus, through the support of the merits of the holy apostles, you may overcome every adversity in this age and afterward triumph with Christ our God in the heavenly realm. [Col. 0905B]

Therefore, in the presence of our fellow bishops, we questioned this venerable archbishop of yours, Methodius, whether he believed the creed of the orthodox faith and sang it during the solemn celebration of Mass in the way that the holy Roman Church is known to hold it and in which it was promulgated and handed down by the holy Fathers at the six universal synods, according to the evangelical authority of Christ our God. He professed that, in accordance with evangelical and apostolic teaching, as the holy Roman Church teaches and as it was handed down by the Fathers, he held and sang it.

Having found him orthodox and useful in all ecclesiastical teachings and matters, we have sent him back to you to govern the Church of God entrusted to him. We order you to receive him as your proper shepherd with fitting honor and reverence and with a joyful mind, because by a command of our apostolic authority we have confirmed his archbishopric and its privilege and have decreed that it remain firm forever, with God’s help, just as the rights and privileges of all the Churches of God stand established and confirmed by the authority of our predecessors. [Col. 0905D]

He is to have, in accordance with canonical tradition, responsibility for all ecclesiastical affairs and is to administer them as one watched by God. For the people of the Lord have been entrusted to him, and for their souls he will have to render an account here.

We have also consecrated the priest named Wichinus, whom you sent to us, as the elected bishop of the holy Church of Nitra. We order that he be obedient in all things to his archbishop, as the holy canons teach. We also wish you, together with the consent and foresight of that archbishop, to send us at a suitable time another useful priest or deacon, whom we shall likewise ordain bishop of another Church in which you know an episcopal see [or chair] to be necessary. Thus, with these two bishops ordained by us, your aforementioned archbishop may afterward, in accordance with the apostolic decree, ordain bishops in other places where bishops ought and can honorably exist.

As for the priests, deacons, and clerics of every order—whether Slavs or of any other people—who reside within the boundaries of your province, we order that they be subject and obedient in all things to the aforementioned fellow bishop of ours, your archbishop, and that they do absolutely nothing without his knowledge. If, however, in their contumacy and disobedience, they presume to cause some scandal or schism and do not correct themselves after a first and second admonition, we order by our authority that, as sowers of weeds, they be cast far away from your churches and territories, according to the authority of the capitularies that we gave him and sent to you.

Finally, we rightly praise the Slavonic letters, discovered by a certain philosopher named Constantine, through which due praises may resound to God; and we order that in the same language the proclamations and works of Christ our Lord be recited. For sacred authority admonishes us to praise the Lord not only in three languages but in all languages, commanding: “Praise the Lord, all nations, and praise him together, all peoples” (Psalm 116). The apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, spoke in all languages the mighty works of God (Acts 2). Hence Paul also sounds forth like a heavenly trumpet, admonishing: “Every tongue shall confess that our Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2). [Col. 0906C]

Concerning these languages, he also sufficiently and clearly admonishes us in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, so that by speaking in languages we may build up the Church of God (1 Corinthians 14). Indeed, it is no obstacle to faith or teaching either to sing Masses in the same Slavonic language, or to read the sacred Gospel, or the divine readings of the New and Old Testaments correctly translated and interpreted, or to sing all the other offices of the hours. For the one who made the three principal languages—Hebrew, Greek, and Latin—also created all the others for his praise and glory.

Nevertheless, we order that in all the churches of your land, for the sake of greater honor, the Gospel be read in Latin and afterward, translated into Slavonic, proclaimed to the ears of the people who do not understand Latin words, as appears to be done in certain churches. If it pleases you and your judges to hear Masses more in the Latin language, we order that the solemn celebrations of Mass be performed for you in Latin. [Col. 0906D] Issued in the month of June, in the thirteenth indiction.

## CCXCIV. TO LANDULF, BISHOP OF THE SURICI [Latin: Suricorum]. (Year 880.) He reproves him for violating what he himself had decreed between him and Landenulf, bishop of Capua, concerning the produce of that Church; he threatens him with the penalty of excommunication unless he obeys his decrees; he orders him, if he feels himself wronged, to come to him with the same bishop to plead his case.

[Col. 0906D]

[Col. 0907A] To the most reverend and holy LANDULF, bishop of the Surici [Latin: Suricorum].

By a report of ours (f. *Vera*) we have learned that whatever, at the time of your consecration, had been determined in our presence after due deliberation between you and Landenulf, bishop of Capua, concerning the produce of that church, you have violated with enormous presumption; and that what we had decided should be regulated according to the circumstances of the time, you have neglected to carry out. On hearing this, our spirit was greatly stirred, because you have so boldly treated our commands with contempt and exceeded the paternal boundaries. Therefore, wishing by the authority of our pontificate to restrain you from such conduct, [Col. 0907B] we command and in every way enjoin you that, laying aside all obstinacy, you take care without delay to carry out whatever we, when present there, decided between you and that same bishop—or between you and his brother Pandenulf, our faithful man—concerning the division or produce of that church. Know this: if you presume to act otherwise, we shall strike you, as an invader of sacred property, with canonical darts. But if you are confident that you have some complaint or just excuse, then we order you to come into our presence to plead your case together with that same bishop. Moreover, we instruct our present legate, Walpert, most reverend bishop and beloved counsellor, that, if you disdain to fulfil our salutary admonitions, he is to take care, by our authority, to excommunicate you, so that, [Col. 0907C] as we have said, you may come to Rome into our (f. added: presence). Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the thirteenth indiction.

## CCXCV. TO KING CHARLES (880)

He congratulates him on his observance toward the Roman Church, whose defender he chose him to be; warns him not to trust his adversaries; praises him for ordering that the territory of Saint Peter be defended against hostile attack. He declares that he will give no assistance to Boso as a tyrant; expresses his desire for Charles’s arrival and asks him to send legates.

To his beloved and spiritual son, the glorious King CHARLES.

Having received and carefully read the letters of Your Royal Greatness, we rejoice greatly and give immense thanks to the Lord, because we know that, in the manner of the most Christian princes, your parents, you wish to be filled with the teaching of our admonition and exhortation, and that, following our counsel, you gladly desire to accomplish whatever seems salutary and useful for the defence of your holy mother, the Roman Church, and of all Christendom. We wish that everything concerning you may always prosper by divine favour.

For matters concerning your affairs and your fortunes, which you did not report to us by letter, we have learned clearly through the trustworthy report of our common faithful man and most reverend bishop Wibod. We have granted him, with pious affection, every access to our intimacy and have learned the secrets of your will through him; through him, too, we sent certain matters to be conveyed orally to Your Highness. [Col. 0908A] (Aimoinus, book V, chapters 39–40; Regino, book II.)

As for the oppression by the Greeks—as some of our rivals have reported to you—we know absolutely nothing about it. If we knew it with certainty, we would immediately report it to Your Affection with every devotion, since, unquestionably by the inspiration and will of almighty God, we took every care to choose you above all others and to have you as the illustrious patron and defender in all affairs of the holy apostolic see and of our interests; and therefore, as long as life permits, we desire to possess you for a long time.

Accordingly, do not lend the ear of your clemency in any way to our enemies, whom you know to be our adversaries and sowers of tares. For an enemy always speaks contrary things. Nevertheless, we praise you for having acted well when, by your authority, you instructed and commanded all the bishops and counts who are stationed around us that, likewise equipped with our mandate, they should defend the territory of Saint Peter against hostile attack.

It is extremely necessary that they protect us not only from evil Christians but also from the Saracens, who are spread everywhere, continually plundering us on every side and robbing our possessions like thieves. Because of this necessity, which we suffer beyond measure, and at the urging of Bishop Wibod himself, we went out to one of our estates and wished to speak with Count Wido, son of Lambert, for this very reason; but he failed to appear, as our faithful man, already mentioned, and yours, will be able to tell you. [Col. 0908C]

Regarding Boso, we also wish you to be certain that he will neither have nor be able to find with us any place of intimacy or assistance through our reception, because, as we have already said, we have sought you as a friend and helper and desire with all the power of our mind to retain you in the place of a most beloved son. For nothing appears to us to concern his party, since he has dared to commit such tyranny.

We have also been greatly delighted by the news of your arrival, which you ordered to be announced as impending, God willing. Because of the many calamities by which we are surrounded and oppressed, we desire and earnestly ask to behold your special presence as soon as possible, with God’s favour.

As for the most reverend bishop John of Tritium, we have kept him with us on this occasion, so that, if anything new should happen to us, and it should be necessary to communicate anything through him to your faithful men, we may be able to inform them in due order of whatever is appropriate. [Col. 0908D]

For the administration of justice to the holy Roman Church, we urgently ask you to send us at once suitable and faithful men from your side. They are to proceed together with our envoys and render us full justice in every matter, correcting and amending wrongdoers by your royal authority. Moreover, as you promised us in person, dearest son, we ask that in this work alone we may recognize, as clearly as daylight, that your will and the affection of your heart toward us are entirely pure, so that we, too, may always be able to fulfil your desire with pious affection. Given as above.

## CCXCVI. TO THE AUGUST EMPERORS (880)

He commends their effort to establish harmony in the Church and urges them to persevere in it; gives thanks for the dromons sent as assistance; for the monastery of Saint Sergius and the Bulgarian diocese restored to the apostolic see; asks them to protect the Church of God; finally, he indicates that he approves what was done for Photius at the synod in Constantinople, provided that the legates did not act contrary to his commands.

[Col. 0909A]

To the August Emperors.

After the countless cares with which the imperial height is undoubtedly burdened, we recognize that Your Most Christian Clemency has formed the laudable purpose of wishing, once all the seeds of discord and tares that the enemy of the human race had scattered in the Lord’s field have been removed, to care for the holy catholic Church with the most devoted affection of your heart.

In this purpose and desire of your heart, your concern—stirred by the Spirit of God—shows how greatly divine providence deigns to favour human affairs. Through the authority and judgment of the apostolic see, which, by delegation from Christ the Lord, retains primacy over the whole Church, it has wished nothing unsettled and nothing discordant in the catholic Church. Rather, it has taken care, with merciful affection and zeal, to recall all those divided by schismatic depravity, or separated and scattered by any zeal whatsoever, to the firmness of true peace and the most sincere unanimity of concord, and to gather them into the one sheepfold of Christ with its own shepherd—namely, Photius, our fellow brother and fellow minister. [Col. 0909C]

For this reason, it is the duty of our pastoral office always to intercede before Your Serene Augustal Clemency with unceasing concern in every way, so that Your Piety’s Majesty may, in the manner of the most Christian emperors, be benevolent toward all; and, as though God were watching, may always rule and govern the people of the Lord entrusted to you with a fortunate regard, no longer allowing them to be dashed against the storms of this world or shaken by wicked disturbances. Thus, after the present life, may you be able to obtain the heavenly empire and retain it eternally with the Lord.

Therefore, for such devotion and sincerity of heart as you have shown not only in words but also in radiant deeds toward the Church of Saint Peter and toward our paternal office, we give Your Serenity immense thanks after God. First, because you sent us your dromons, which were to remain in our service for the defence of Saint Peter’s territory. Second, because, filled with divine inspiration, you restored to our episcopate, for the honour of the prince of the apostles, the monastery of Saint Sergius situated within your royal city, which the holy Roman Church once held by its own right. Third, we offer you many thanks because, out of love for us, you have permitted Saint Peter, with joyful heart, to possess the Bulgarian diocese, as was just. [Col. 0910A]

Accordingly, we earnestly ask that you not disdain to assist and defend the holy Roman Church in every way through your powerful support at this perilous time, so that thereby Your Imperial Glory, with the merits of the apostles supporting it, may increase more and more throughout all parts of the world and receive a worthy recompense from almighty God.

Again, we humbly ask you to remain steadfast in this good will and pious affection that you have toward the Church of Christ out of love for God. For we embrace Your Augustal Excellency with extended arms and paternal love, and we venerate you with due honour. We strive to commend you to almighty God in our constant prayers, poured out beside the most sacred bodies of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, so that, for the many benefits you bestow upon Saint Peter, he may preserve your holy empire here in the present age more and more safely, with every prosperity, and may always deign to adorn it everywhere with illustrious triumphs; and afterward may grant you eternal glory and blessedness with his saints and elect in the heavenly realm.

For we also accept what was mercifully done by synodal decree in Constantinople concerning the restoration of the most reverend patriarch Photius:

[Note: [Col. 0909D] The words “And if perhaps our legates...” indicate, among other things, that this synod was rejected as a pseudo-eighth synod by John VIII and his other pontifical successors, and by the Council of Florence. SEV. BIN.]

“And if perhaps our legates acted in that synod contrary to the apostolic command, we neither accept nor judge their actions to possess any validity.”

Given on the Ides of August, in the thirteenth indiction.

## CCXCVII. TO PHOTIUS (AS IT SEEMS) (880)

He congratulates him on the concord of the Church of Constantinople; wonders that many things he had decreed have been changed; approves what was done at Constantinople in the council concerning Photius, provided that the legates did not act contrary to his instructions.

[Col. 0910C]

This has always been the object of our struggle and labour; this is the object of our desire: that, for the integrity of the orthodox faith and for the condition and peace of all God’s Churches, whose care constrains us, we should labour so diligently that what is scattered may be gathered, what is gathered may be preserved, and whatever is dishonourable or otherwise than rectitude requires may, through God’s providence and with the merits of the holy apostles supporting us, be corrected. In accordance with the office entrusted to us, we strive with all our strength to watch over this.

For this reason, wishing in apostolic fashion to show mercy to the holy Church of Constantinople, we decreed that the increase of one should bring detriment to no one, but rather that the assistance of all should be manifest. Having convened our Church insofar as the necessity of the present time required, by apostolic authority and power we provided for the said Church of Constantinople, and, sending our legates, we instructed them to walk without stumbling. [Col. 0911A]

Accordingly, we rejoice in its unity of peace and concord. Although we cannot render fitting thanks to the all-powerful Lord, to whom we offer countless praises for this, we bless him who bestows such great blessings upon his servants and strive to glorify him with continual voices. Glory, praise, and power belong to him, by whose majesty and ever most praiseworthy grace things bent [f. *curvata*: “bowed”] are brought back to uprightness, crooked things are made straight, obstinacy is blunted, humility is exalted, tares are eventually pulled up, scandals are cut away, and every goodness is increased.

Therefore, let us glory, rejoice, and exult not in ourselves but in that same Lord, in his mercy, who says: “Take courage, because I have conquered the world” (John 16); and elsewhere: “Without me,” he says, “you can do nothing” (John 15).

But since we have mercifully decided, by letters and words, that we should deal with you personally, it is very astonishing why many things that we had decided are reported to have been treated otherwise or changed, and, we do not know through whose initiative or negligence, are shown to have been altered. Moreover, in writing you added that, as you implied, mercy must be sought only from those who do evil. We too, although we admit this administratively concerning those who do not confess that they know God, do not wish to exaggerate what has been read, lest we be compelled to pass the judgment that is deserved. Therefore let such an excuse be silent, lest the sentence apply to you which says: “You are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts, because what is exalted among men is an abomination before God” (Luke 16).

Accordingly, let your praiseworthy prudence, which is said to know humility, not take offence that it has been commanded by the Church of God to ask for mercy. Rather, let it humble itself so that it may be exalted, and learn to preserve a brotherly affection toward the one who shows mercy to it.

For if you strive to observe the devotion and growth in fidelity that you owe toward the holy Roman Church and toward our lowliness, we shall embrace you as a brother and retain you as a most beloved neighbour. We also accept what was mercifully done by synodal decree in Constantinople concerning your restoration. And if perhaps our legates acted in that synod contrary to the apostolic command, we neither accept nor judge their actions to possess any validity.

## CCXCVIII. TO KING CHARLES (880)

He gives thanks for his observance toward the apostolic see and testifies to his own goodwill toward him; awaits his arrival for the needs of the Church and urges him to send a legate. He complains about a certain excommunicated George who, supported by the emperor’s authority, had invaded the property of the Roman Church; he asks him to send the promised assistance.

[Col. 0911D]

To the most excellent and beloved son, the glorious King CHARLES.

Reading again the letters of Your Royal Excellence, we know as clearly as daylight your devotion toward the holy Church, your mother, and toward our pontificate. Therefore we offer Your Glory many thanks. We also always retain you as a beloved and spiritual son, desire to embrace you with pious affection of heart, and remain constantly and unhesitatingly concerned for the increase of your glory.

As for your instruction that we should await your desired arrival, so that we might correct the adversities of those who presume to inflict wrongs upon us and to withdraw our men from our jurisdiction: because of the many needs of the Church of God that must be remedied for the increase of your glory, we desire with our whole heart in every way to behold your arrival.

But, as we suggested to you some time ago in our apostolic letters, you should have sent us a suitable envoy with whom we might accomplish something for the benefit of the churches. We are astonished that you have not sent him for this purpose. Accordingly, we ask you not to fail to send that same envoy to us before you come, so that, when you arrive with God’s help and we meet together, true affection may exist between us, as between a spiritual father and a most beloved son. [Col. 0912B]

Moreover, after the excommunicated and anathematized George returned from you with Wido’s man, we have been disturbed by continual sorrow. For he came boldly, as though supported by your authority, and rashly entered, together with others, into properties that had once been his but had lawfully passed into the right of the holy Roman Church through the grant of the emperor Charles, your uncle of blessed memory, and that we have defended and held in our right until now. He does not cease to afflict and plunder our men who live in the surrounding area. [Col. 0912C]

Therefore, we earnestly ask Your Greatness to strive to fulfil in our presence what you promised us in person and commanded by your letter and through our legates, with Liutward, venerable bishop of the holy Church of Vercelli, acting as mediator. For we shall fulfil in every way what we promised you; or else drive those same faithless men of ours far from us, so that they may in no way be able to plot anything adverse or hostile against us until, with God’s favour, you arrive. On the fourth day before the Ides of September, in the fourteenth indiction.

## CCXCIX. TO ROMANUS, ARCHBISHOP OF RAVENNA (880)

He orders him to come to Rome for a synod in order to resolve certain questions.

[Col. 0912D]

To ROMANUS, archbishop of Ravenna.

Because, owing to the pressure of war—indeed, of the Saracens—we were unable to celebrate the synod as we had wished on the fourth day before the Ides of October, in accordance with the sacred canons, we have now judiciously and very necessarily foreseen that, with the Lord’s help, we should convene this same synod on the sixth day before the Ides of November of this fourteenth indiction.

Therefore, we urge Your Holiness to come to Rome at that same time without any delay, indeed setting aside every excuse, so that you may arrange and determine with us whatever concerns the honour or utility of the holy Church of God, and, with the grace of the Holy Spirit revealing it, decide by common vote. [Col. 0913A]

Meanwhile, the case of the illustrious man Deusdedit, glorious duke, who came to our pontificate saying that he had been deprived of communion by your prudence because of his marriage to his wife, whom you admit to be her relative, must certainly be examined, so that whatever the truth of the matter demonstrates may be carried out in every respect.

Because he has remained with us for so long and no one from your side has been found to give an account, it would have been reasonable for us to absolve him in the meantime. Nevertheless, since, as we have said, we must soon celebrate a synod at which this matter is to be examined, among other matters, with the agreement of our fellow priests and brothers and of yourself, we have judged it more fitting—and the matters themselves require this—to await your arrival, so that we may discuss it in the synodal assembly, rejoice in one another’s presence, and decide with a common judgment. At that synod we shall likewise order that whatever you may have against his son-in-law be determined.

Moreover, the wife of the aforesaid man, named Maria, has arranged through her legate Paul to send a written petition of complaint to our episcopate. She asserts that Your Holiness was aware of the marriage contracted with her by the consent of her father, and that, after her husband and she had become one flesh, you had often not only admitted but also invited both him and her to the spiritual, or Lord’s, table as well as to the common table.

She also made known through the same petition of complaint that Majoranus, also called the deacon Maginpertus, consented to the death of his own father. She asks us for fitting justice in this matter and earnestly requests that it not be left unexamined. The bishop of Bologna, for his part, has very frequently sought to claim this man as a servant of his Church. [Col. 0913C]

For this reason, we command that you bring that deacon with you to us in every way, so that, with the Lord’s help, we may examine whatever the order of reason requires canonically and establish it synodally. Given on the third day before the Kalends of October, in the fourteenth indiction.

## CCC. TO ALL BISHOPS (880)

That they should come to Rome for the synod.

To all bishops throughout the duchies of Spoleto and Camerino, and to all bishops established in the various provinces.

We do not wish your fraternity to be unaware that, because of the many needs of the holy Church of God, we shall celebrate, with the Lord’s help, a synodal assembly on the sixth day before the Ides of November of this fourteenth indiction.

Because we had been entangled in various impediments, especially those caused by the Saracens, and could not convene it at the proper time, we judged it fitting, for the increase and completion of ecclesiastical interests, not to omit it at the aforesaid time, lest such great necessity remain unresolved without the counsel of our other fellow bishops. Thus, supported by your salutary counsels, we might strive to accomplish together whatever pertains to the honour of God and the common good. [Col. 0914A]

Therefore, by the letters of this admonition we exhort Your Holiness not to delay coming to the same synod at Rome, laying aside your customary sluggishness, so that, as we have said, with Christ’s help we may accomplish together what must be done and prudently establish what ought to be established according to the duties of our ministry.

Take care, therefore, not to act with your customary negligence, lest, if matters beneficial to the honour and condition of the holy Church of God remain disordered through your fault, and you scorn to come when you ought, you justly be struck by canonical blows. Given on the day before the Kalends of October, in the fourteenth indiction.

## CCCI. TO KING CHARLES (880)

He rejoices in his safety and prays God that all things may turn out prosperously for him; announces that the Saracens have been defeated by the Greeks, while he himself is being severely oppressed by the Saracens and others as well; therefore he asks him to come to his aid as quickly as possible.

[Col. 0914B]

To the glorious King CHARLES.

Having received and reread the letters sent to us by Your Glory, our spiritual and desirable son, we learned that, thanks be to God, you are enjoying good health. We were refreshed by indescribable joy, beyond what can be expressed, and rejoiced in the Lord. With continual prayers we beseech that same Lord our God to grant you ever greater prosperity, give you triumph over your adversaries, and multiply your happy days so that you may govern the kingdom peacefully and with perfect justice. [Col. 0914C]

For nothing at all, dearest son, is sweeter or more beloved to us than to know that you are always most ready to defend and exalt your holy mother, the Roman Church, and to oppose those who attack her in various ways with the free judgment of correction and discipline.

Although we are placed amid countless infirmities and afflictions, thanks be to God, we endure as best we can. But our health will be greater when we know that you enjoy, as we have said, every prosperity and are hastening to come to our assistance, so that we may speak together face to face. We cannot bear to see delays.

As for your statement that you are sending Liutward, the venerable bishop and our common faithful man, ahead to us, we rejoice greatly in the Lord. Since we know that he always labours for the common good, his arrival will bring us great joy, because in his presence we shall behold Your Excellence. [Col. 0914D]

Finally, dearest son, you ask about the Greeks, the Ishmaelites, and all the other foreign peoples or our fellow citizens, and how matters are proceeding. We answer very briefly. But we exhort you with every effort of mind to consider all these things from the depth of your heart and with sorrow.

Nevertheless, thanks and praise be to God, because the Greek ships have most victoriously laid low the Israelite ranks at sea, and they were defeated, as the Lord willed. Yet the aforesaid Ishmaelites, as well as other fellow citizens of ours, attack and persecute us, so that outside the walls of the City no one at all can freely go out—neither those able to live by the labour of their hands nor, so to speak, those able to observe their Christianity as they should. [Col. 0915A]

Therefore, indeed because of all these things, if you do not come as quickly as possible, setting aside and rejecting every opportunity and every excuse, to bring assistance to us and to this severely afflicted region, you may know beyond doubt that this land will perish through your sin and to the harm of all.

Accordingly, for God’s sake, hasten to undertake the journey to us, and, under his command, come to the thresholds of the blessed apostles, so that you may fight the Lord’s battles in his place and hasten, with God leading you, to aid all Christians. Given on the third day before the Kalends of November, in the fourteenth indiction.

## CCCII. TO THE SAME (880)

He absolves Deusdedit of Ravenna, who had been unjustly excommunicated; confirms his marriage with his wife Maria; orders that he be defended.

[Col. 0915B]

To the most reverend and most holy Romanus, archbishop of Ravenna, concerning Deusdedit of Ravenna; and to Leo, venerable bishop, legate and *apocrisiarius* of our supreme apostolic see; likewise to any legates of the emperor, to all judges and peoples established in the Roman territory, and to all the faithful of the holy Church, present and future.

We exhort all of you to take note of this, with due reverence and diligence. Romanus, archbishop of Ravenna, declared both orally, when we were at Ravenna, and in writing that there had been, and daily continued to be, certain incestuous marriages in his diocese. Then, through his legate, namely the priest Dominic, he indicated that there were thirty-two of them, suggesting that by our authority he should be permitted to judge them all canonically.

After dismissing all the others whom he had also named, and, as we suppose, moved solely by envy—a fact that later became clear in the holy synod—he did not fear to excommunicate our faithful man Deusdedit, who, while we were at Ravenna, was with us every day and judged cases before me and the archbishop himself, as he ought to have done, after he had appealed to the apostolic see. [Col. 0915D]

Deusdedit himself, the duke, obeyed this out of fidelity to us and hastened in every way to come into the apostolic presence. When we heard his case and found no one from the archbishop’s side who ought to have accused him, we could have absolved him; but we were unwilling to do so until we had sent word to the archbishop—or rather, until we sent word to him—that the archbishop himself should come, for the statutes of the holy Churches of God, on the sixth day before the Ides of November, to celebrate a synod, bringing with him accusers and witnesses, so that, once these had been presented, we might conclude the case of Deusdedit canonically among the other matters.

He sent Dominic the priest, a member of his own household, and John the deacon in his place, transmitting written accusations with them. When these writings had been read before the holy synod, Deusdedit answered them and denied that he had committed incest or any abomination. Before everyone, he demonstrated his innocence and proved by the authority of divine and human law that he was married. [Col. 0916A]

Therefore, together with the holy synod, we absolved him, restored him to our communion, and confirmed that Maria, his wife, was his legitimate spouse, with the blessing of almighty God and of us. If the aforesaid archbishop or his ministers should wish to invade or forcibly seize his property or that of his men, you, the people of Ravenna, are to defend him in possession of his property. Given as above, in the fourteenth indiction.

## CCCIII. TO ANSPERTUS, ARCHBISHOP OF MILAN (880)

He accuses him of disobedience and orders him to return honourably to their monastery Rhodoaldus and Warlenus, monks whom he had unjustly thrown into prison.

[Col. 0916B]

To ANSPERTUS, archbishop of Milan.

It was fitting, dearest brother, that you should daily offer the holy apostolic see, over which by God’s authority we preside, with pure sincerity of heart the reverence and honour that all your predecessors, living laudably up to your time, offered to this Church with willing devotion of mind.

For this reason, having been received into its embrace, certain men were loved more than others. But behold—what cannot be said without sorrow—I do not know through what fraud of the ancient enemy, from the day of your ordination and during the time of your old age, you have not ceased to show yourself toward the holy Roman Church, your mother, now disobedient, now deceitful.

Compelled by this necessity, we judged it worthwhile to correct you with the apostolic scourge; yet again, out of paternal mercy, we did not fail to bring you back to us, hoping that thereafter no trace of fault toward us would in any way be found in you, since your profession had also pledged this before us by oath.

Behold, good man: you did not fear to commit something worse when you ordered certain monks of ours, named Rhodoaldus and Warlenus, who were travelling from Rome to their monastery of Pultaria, to be arrested and kept for a long time in the bonds of custody.

Consider with sound understanding how great a sacrilege this is, and how great a disgrace to the apostolic see, which, by Christ’s authority, has always appeared free to carry out its legation even among barbarian nations. [Col. 0916D]

We exhort you to correct this wicked offence with all possible speed and to allow the aforesaid servants of God, together with all their possessions, to depart unharmed to the place of their habitation, by God’s mercy. And just as we know with certainty that they were innocently committed to custody on your advice, so, through your action, let us know that they have been completely released and with suitable honour. Given in the month of November, in the fourteenth indiction.

## CCCIV. TO SOLOMON, PROCURATOR OF PAVIA (880)

The same subject.

To SOLOMON, procurator of Pavia.

By apostolic authority we command you to release our monks, namely Rhodoaldus and Warlenus, whom, disregarding the fear of God, you dared to arrest and keep in custody while they were returning from the thresholds of the holy apostles to their monastery and simply travelling along the road. Without any delay or postponement, let them return, healthy and unharmed, with all their possessions to their monastery.

For by this act you have committed such a great crime and injury against the apostolic see that you ought justly to have been deprived of the fellowship of all Christendom. We declare that, if you do not immediately correct this, we shall prohibit you from receiving the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ and from entering the church. Given in the month of November, in the fourteenth indiction.

## CCCV. TO ADELBERT, MARQUIS (880)

He absolves him from excommunication, and also his men, provided that within fifteen days during the month of March they make satisfaction to the Church.

[Col. 0917B]

To ADELBERT, marquis.

Because we have recognized you as converted and faithful toward the holy Roman Church and toward us, we absolve you unconditionally from all excommunication. We restore sacred communion to your men on this condition: they must hasten to make every required amendment within fifteen days during the month of March, as was promised.

If they neglect to do this, let them all remain under the same excommunication until they again make full satisfaction for the evils they have committed. Given as above, in the fourteenth indiction.

## CCCVI. TO OTERAMUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE (880)

He accuses him of favouring Boso’s associates and of claiming that he does so by the pope’s command; he orders him to come to Rome to clear himself of the crimes charged against him.

To OTERAMUS [Note: [Col. 0917D] Ottramnus, who will often occur later], bishop of Vienne.

We wish and entirely intend to count you among the distinguished priests of Christ our God. But because we hear that you are acting contrary to ecclesiastical peace and utility, we are greatly astonished and, at the same time, disturbed. For, as we have learned from the report of faithful men, you presume, with rash audacity, to favour those who, together with Boso, the usurper and disturber of the kingdom, do not cease to exercise tyranny, and to share in their evil works. As a follower of their arrogance, you do not hesitate, on the basis of a false opinion, to defame our holy Roman Church by claiming that you have its authority for carrying out such actions. You will not be able to show how true this is, since you ought to have opposed yourself, as a wall on behalf of the Roman Church, to all those acting wickedly.

For all these evils and such great acts of presumption, we command you by the authority of God, of the holy apostles, and of ourselves [Col. 0918A] to arrange to come immediately to Rome, to the thresholds of the holy apostles and into our presence, so that you may clear yourself of such charges by giving satisfaction before us and the apostolic see according to the authority of the holy Fathers, and so that we may be able to retain you among our brothers and fellow priests.

For—something we do not believe—if you act otherwise and delay coming, know that you are to be deprived of every episcopal office until you fulfil this command of ours.

## CCCVII. TO COUNT BARNIMERUS, THE PRIESTS, ETC. (880)

He declares that their observance toward the apostolic see was most pleasing to him and urges them to persevere. He orders them to send legates to him, promising that, when they return, he will send his own legate, to whom they are to promise fidelity according to the rite of the Church.

[Col. 0918B]

To the most excellent man BARNIMERUS, glorious count and our beloved son, and to all devout priests, honourable judges, and the entire people: peace and grace from the Lord Jesus Christ.

Having learned through your venerable bishop Theodosius of the faith and devotion which, as we understand, you bear toward the see of blessed Peter the apostle and toward our pontificate, we have been filled with great joy, giving immense thanks to God, who has now deigned to lead you to such grace and to number you among his sheep, according to what the Lord entrusted to that prince of the apostles when he said: “If you love me, Simon Peter, feed my sheep” (John 21).

Therefore, through this apostolic letter, we admonish and exhort your fidelity and most Christian devotion: just as you have begun to act through divine inspiration, do not fail to complete and observe it to the end. Thus, you who have undertaken with all your strength to submit yourselves under the protection, governance, and defense of blessed Peter the apostle and of us, and to persevere in his service as beloved sons, may show and fulfill this more openly, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Let your light so shine before men that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5).

And may this pledge of yours be proclaimed throughout the world, so that, with the Lord’s help and through the merits of the holy apostles’ intercession, we may without hesitation accomplish whatever is beneficial to the salvation and advantage of all of you, for the honor and exaltation of the holy apostolic see, just as you commanded us in writing in your name. May it likewise remain written in the heavenly book.

Therefore we command that, when your beloved bishop returns to you, you do not fail to send suitable envoys from your midst to us in person. On behalf of all of you, they are to consult us and the apostolic see about the matters you have entrusted to us, so that we too may send our envoy back to you with them. According to the custom and practice of our Church, your entire people is to promise him fidelity.

Meanwhile, we admonish you to remain steadfast, for it is written: “It is better not to make a vow than, after making a vow, not to fulfill one’s promises” (Ecclesiasticus 5). May the Spirit of the Lord, who has filled the world, fill your heart with all peace and joy in Christ Jesus our Lord.

### CCCVIII. TO MICHAEL, KING OF THE BULGARIANS (Year 880)

He wonders why he has not sent envoys, as he promised long ago, and urges him to do so as soon as possible.

To our beloved and spiritual son MICHAEL, glorious king of the Bulgarians: grace to you and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

We wonder why, after so much time has already passed, you have not sent your envoys to the holy Roman Church, your mother, and to us. But now, as the venerable bishop Theodosius has reported to us, you promised to send your envoys with him; we do not know, however, for what reason you failed to send them.

Therefore you ought now to have recognized that you must return with complete devotion even to the shepherd and pontiff of your souls. Hence, through this apostolic letter, we admonish and exhort you as our dearest sons not to hesitate to send us suitable envoys immediately, so that you may be nourished at the breasts of your mother, the holy Roman Church, and filled with every good.

For, in the manner of a father, we are ready to embrace you with outstretched arms and, as sheep entrusted to us by Christ, to feed and save you, according to what the Lord says to blessed Peter: “Feed my sheep.” Whatever we send to you, you may believe without reservation, because we always desire to act and accomplish everything unhesitatingly for your salvation.

We wish you good health in Christ, now and always.

### CCCIX. TO A CERTAIN PERSON (NAMELY, CHARLES THE FAT, KING) (Year 881)

He urges him to carry out what he conveyed through his envoys.

Having received a letter from Your Glory in which you show with full determination that you are hastening to the thresholds of the apostles—indeed, rather, that you wish to fly there with hurried and even headlong steps—we are astonished, or rather utterly amazed, that your dignity should overstep the boundaries of the Fathers, trample underfoot in a proud spirit the line of your ancestry, and come together wholly for the worse, not for the better.

And behold, sorrowfully, I am compelled to say with the Apostle: “In the last days perilous times will come, when men will be lovers of themselves and will seek what is their own, not what belongs to Jesus Christ” (2 Timothy 3).

But because we love you greatly, dearest son, in the bowels of Christ, we desire to urge you toward those things that contribute to the salvation of your soul. We have sent envoys fully instructed on our behalf; you should have no doubt that you are to believe everything they convey, both verbally and in writing, according to the capitular instructions we gave them.

Therefore, with paternal affection, we admonish you to take the utmost care to fulfill everything they have conveyed to you from us. Know, then, that if you do not fully carry out everything we have sent, we, inflamed with the zeal of God, will strive with all our power to increase whatever pertains to the honor of the holy Roman Church. No ferocity and no threat from evil men will be able to separate us from these things so long as the spirit governs our limbs.

By placing, with great presumption, an absurd obstacle against the command of our pontificate, you have struck yourself back with your own weapon; and, like a deaf asp, you have refused to lend an ear to what accords with your salvation.

But why say more? Again and again, by apostolic authority, we prohibit and command that you do not stir up in your mind any intention of entering the territory of Saint Peter until our aforesaid envoys have returned to us and reported everything, and until you take care to send others to us as well.

Issued on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, in the fourteenth indiction.

### CCCX. TO ANSPERT, ARCHBISHOP OF MILAN (Year 881)

He confirms the ordination of Joseph, bishop of Asti, who had previously been made bishop of the Church of Vercelli contrary to the canons.

To ANSPERT, archbishop of Milan.

Having examined your consultation, by which you wished to consult us concerning Joseph, recently ordained in the Church of Vercelli, regarding his new election or ordination in the Church of Asti, and having considered the representations by which you seek a decision from our authority on this matter, we judged it canonical and, with divine favor, responded to you consistently with our decrees.

A certain irregular arrangement had first been made concerning him, as you yourself remember with me. But, while we were seated with the holy synod before blessed Peter the apostle, having obtained sound counsel, we corrected his contentious attitude and immediately applied the remedies of mercy, with the grace of the Holy Spirit revealing the way—namely, that after he had been restored to his former order, if you wished to grant him another bishopric, and if the clergy and people should unanimously seek him as their bishop, then he could be elected and created bishop, as one who had previously received nothing from the ordaining bishop.

Meanwhile it happened that, when the proper ruler of the Church of Asti died, the same Joseph was to be ordained bishop in that church, with the permission of Charles, the glorious king, following the election of the clergy and the request of the people. Your fraternity, prompted both by our absolution and by the exhortations and admonitions of that king, willingly accepted this and endeavored to fulfill what had been canonically ordered.

Since you have now likewise followed our judgment and have devoutly embraced the royal permission, as is fitting, and since you have placed the aforementioned Joseph, priest of the holy Church, over the Church of Asti as bishop, we decree that his ordination be held valid, and by apostolic authority we silence all mouths that in any way murmur against it.

For just as the zeal of justice rouses us to correct whatever has been irregularly done, so divine grace makes us rejoice in the praiseworthy deeds of good men. The apostolic see, moreover, according to what Pope Saint Leo writes, preserves this moderation: that it acts more severely toward the hardened but desires to grant pardon to those who have been corrected.

Therefore, setting these matters aside, let your holiness have no hesitation whatsoever concerning Joseph’s second creation, since we accept it as approved and command that it be accepted by all. For where it is not shown that anything was done through the laying-on of hands of the one who, during his legation, seemed to give what he did not possess, reason does not permit it to be regarded as repeated.

Issued on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the fourteenth indiction.

### CCCXI. TO ATTO (Year 881)

He excommunicates him unless he restores to the Church of Milan the property he had taken and, together with his associates, returns to obedience to his archbishop.

To ATTO, excommunicated.

From the report and representation sent to our pontificate by Anspert, archbishop of the holy Church of Milan, we have learned that, through the shamelessness or audacity of dreadful presumption, you have committed many unlawful acts and, in contempt of blessed Ambrose and in opposition to that bishop himself, have committed with your sons every kind of evil and outrage you could in places and against property belonging to him.

The archbishop repeatedly took care to confront you and remove you from these acts, admonishing, beseeching, and rebuking you as a sheep of the Lord’s flock, so that he would not leave you, once deceived by the cunning persuasion of the ancient enemy, fallen and lying in the deep abyss of death.

But when he saw that you utterly refused to obey the wholesome words of sacred admonition with humble devotion, and that, like a deaf asp, you would neither incline nor yield the ear of your heart, after so many corrections he separated you, together with the assembly of venerable fellow bishops, from communion in the sacred body and blood of the Lord, according to the severity of the paternal ordinance, and rightly removed you from the fellowship of the Church of God.

He now grieves to see you still lying foul and wounded in the same filth of iniquity, and, seeing that with an unrepentant heart you refuse to return to the one who strikes you, he cries out so that he may heal the wounds of your soul through remedies leading to salvation.

Therefore, moved by pastoral concern and by the present affection of our brother the archbishop, we command by a decree of our authority that, casting far away such perversity and hardness of heart—for until now, setting aside the fear of God, you have polluted many with the leprosy of your iniquity and have not hesitated to become the author of so many evils—you return with all speed to make true satisfaction to the aforesaid bishop, together with your sons and all your accomplices, whose instigator in evil you have not feared to remain even after so many corrections.

You are to remain submissive and obedient to his wholesome admonitions, once all the Church’s plunder has been fully restored and all matters corrected and settled according to the privilege of that Church.

But if, after reading this letter of our command, you persist in your wicked obstinacy and, as stated, disdain to return to your bishop in order to make satisfaction, then, by the authority of God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, by the power of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and of all the holy Fathers, and by our apostolic sanction, in accordance with the sentence formerly pronounced against you by our beloved brother the archbishop and the bishops, we command that you, your sons, and your accomplices be deprived of all ecclesiastical communion and excluded and condemned from the assembly and fellowship of all most Christian people, as perpetrators of such great and unrepented evils.

This shall remain in force until, by correcting what you have done wrongly and making canonical satisfaction, you merit to receive fitting pardon.

Issued on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the fourteenth indiction.

### CCCXII. TO ANSELM, ARCHDEACON OF MILAN (Year 881)

He threatens him with excommunication unless he returns to obedience to his archbishop.

To ANSELM, archdeacon of Milan.

Anspert, the most reverend archbishop of the holy Church of Milan, whose minister you appear to be, sent a representation to our pontificate and complained about you. We have learned that, among the other disturbances you have rashly inflicted upon him, and after causing him no small losses, without abandoning your own Church, you have dared to separate yourself from his service and fellowship and, like a schismatic, to reside in other parishes contrary to canonical statutes.

You have also hurried to the ruling power and, through cunning persuasion, deliberately prepared harmful plots against him.

Therefore, through this apostolic letter, we confront your affection with paternal concern; nevertheless, with full authority we command you to hasten immediately, with great devotion, back to the bosom and embrace of the holy Church of Milan, your mother, which you abandoned in a furious spirit.

Strive with complete readiness of mind to be under the governance and in the presence of your own shepherd; and, as a suitable minister, offer with utter humility the service and obedience due according to your rank, so that, having obtained his favor, you may always be able to please the almighty Lord through the assiduity of your office.

But if you presume to act otherwise, contrary to the principal and inviolable institutions of the holy Fathers and contrary to this salutary command of ours, and if you disdain to return to your Church and your shepherd, as ecclesiastical discipline teaches, know that, by the power of almighty God, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and by ours, and by the canonical judgment of the Fathers, you will be deprived of all ecclesiastical communion.
