This shall remain so until, as stated above, you earnestly strive to return to your Church and submit your neck in humility to your shepherd. For wounds must be cut away with iron when, after the application of remedies, they have felt no healing.

### CCCXIII. TO JOHN, EGILULF, AND OTHERS (Year 881)

He entrusts to them the case pending between the bishops of Trent and Verona, admonishes them to decide it according to law, and to send him their judgment so that he may confirm it.

To JOHN of Bologna, EGILULF of Mantua, EICARD of Vicenza, and VIATOR of Ferrara, bishops.

We do not wish your holiness to be unaware that a dispute once arose between the holy Church of Verona and the Church of Trent concerning certain property of the village of Asiana. We established through a truthful report from our envoys, who at that time were carrying out our legation in the regions of Italy, that this property belonged to the Church of Verona.

We also saw the definition of their judgment and read through their subscriptions in their own hands. From these it is made even clearer that the property had justly belonged to the holy Church of Verona and that it had been determined that the Church should possess it in perpetuity.

But because contention often gives rise to discord, Adelchisius, the venerable bishop of Trent, is now said to be acting against that definition and to have presumed to stir up opposition against his own profession and handwritten subscription.

We entrust our role in this matter to your reverence, so that, going to that region and meeting with Adelard and Adelchisius, the venerable bishops, you may hear the dispute again and deliberate upon it—although, since it was considered with our envoys, we judge this unnecessary—and strive by every means to bring it to a lawful conclusion.

When this has been properly done, according to the wording of their documents, we wish you to inform our apostolate in writing of whatever the outcome may be, so that we may gladly accept it and not fail to establish it by our authority.

For this matter was first judged before apostolic envoys and other most reverend bishops in the synod of Pavia, and afterward in the church of Trent, likewise before our envoys and other imperial judges; it was legally defined there.

Issued on the fourth day before the Nones of March, in the fourteenth indiction.

### CCCXIV. TO ADELCHISIUS, BISHOP OF TRENT (Year 881)

He rebukes him for invading the property of the bishop of Verona; he states that he has entrusted his case to certain bishops and urges him to accept their judgment.

To ADELCHISIUS, bishop of Trent.

At the representation of our fellow bishop Adelard, bishop of Verona, we have learned that your holiness has acted otherwise than canonical—or rather Christian—observance appears to require.

For, having despised the judgment of the preceding Fathers, at which you yourself are recognized to have been present, you are said to have seized certain property belonging to the holy Church of Verona, and you are thought in some way to have acted against your own handwritten subscription.

If the legates of the apostolic see had not been present at the definition of these matters, we would still hope to be able to obtain information about them from the testimony of others. But since we have foreseen that this would not be appropriate, we have entrusted our role in this question to John of Bologna, Egilulf of Mantua, Eicard of Vicenza, and Viator of Ferrara, venerable bishops, so that, convening for this purpose according to God and defining the matter anew insofar as it concerns the contempt of the disobedient, they may meet together and determine this dispute with your holiness.

They are to strive to define it irreproachably, keeping God before their eyes.

Therefore, we admonish you with fraternal love to act in this matter in such a way that you cannot rightly be reproved by us and do not reject the canonical sentence. Nevertheless, do not fail to hasten to the place that the aforesaid venerable bishops indicate to you.

You are also to answer concerning the same property of the village of Asiana, so that from this point no question at all may remain or arise again.

Issued as above.

### CCCXV. TO THE KINGS LOUIS AND CARLOMANN (Year 881)

He asks them to agree with the emperor Charles to recall Angelberga and send her to Rome, where he promises to guard her so that she will be unable to plot anything against them.

To LOUIS and CARLOMANN, kings; and to HUGO, abbot.

We wish Your Affection to know that we asked our spiritual son, the most serene emperor Charles, who is residing with us in Rome, to bring back from exile our spiritual daughter Angelberga, devoted to God. She had commended herself and all her possessions to blessed Peter the apostle and to us; while still alive, her husband, Louis Augustus of blessed memory, had also specially entrusted her to our protection.

We asked Charles, for the love of God and Christ, the blessed apostle Peter who holds the keys, and ourselves, to send her to us in Rome, where no further unfavorable suspicion could arise concerning her.

He has willingly promised to do this and, as we understand, is awaiting your consent in the matter.

We rejoice, indeed, in your common affection, peace, and concord, and we render innumerable thanks to God for it. But we entreat you concerning the recovery and return of this spiritual daughter of ours with the same earnestness with which we assure you, by our testimony, that if she is brought back to us, she will be guarded so carefully that she will be entirely unable to act against that emperor or against you.

Therefore, joined with the obedience of that Augustus, do not fail, without any delay, to send back for the love of God and of us the woman devoted to God whom we have received for safekeeping at the thresholds of the apostles, under the protection of the confession of their altar.

For if she returns and lives here with us, believe us, she will be kept under such vigilant guard that she will in no way be able to provide Boso or any other person with help or assistance, whether by word or writing, for the disturbance of the empire or kingdom.

There is, however, one point that we truthfully propose to you, so that you may not take from it an occasion to despise us. If we learn through clear indications that Angelberga has attempted or wished to undertake even the slightest hostile action against the emperor’s or our will, we shall strive immediately to restore and send her back into the emperor’s presence. Thus, if she should delay receiving whatever discipline she may perhaps deserve—which we do not desire—she will not escape your secular judgments, nor will she find our mercy, which is accustomed to spare offenders.

Therefore, dearest sons, be our fellow workers and helpers in this matter. Let Your Excellency hear us continually, so that you may merit to be heard by the Lord; and, while guiding the reins of the kingdom through prosperous times, may you, through the intercession of the blessed apostles, receive with Christ the kingdom whose bounds no end confines.

Issued on the fourth day before the Ides of March, in the fourteenth indiction.

### CCCXVI. TO ALL THE ARCHBISHOPS, BISHOPS, AND COUNTS OF ITALY (Year 881)

He urges them to see to it that the emperor Charles allows Angelberga to come to Rome, promising that he will guard her so that she can plot nothing against Charles with Boso; and, if she attempts anything, he promises to send her back.

To all the most reverend and holy archbishops and bishops of this Italian kingdom, and to all the glorious counts of our son the emperor.

If, mindful of divine mercy, we strive to do what is necessary for the salvation and advantage of our neighbors, according to the concern and care for the Lord’s flock entrusted to us for proper governance, we shall certainly have almighty God propitious toward us in the matters of which we ourselves daily stand in need through human weakness, and without doubt we shall have his help in all good things.

Therefore we wish your holiness to know that, through envoys and letters of our apostolate, we have earnestly asked the clemency of our beloved spiritual son, the most glorious emperor Charles, to order that our daughter Angelberga be brought back in person from the place where she is now known to be and sent to us, for the love of Jesus Christ our Lord, for reverence toward the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and because of our paternal affection.

The late king Louis, father of the emperor, and Louis the emperor, her husband, entrusted her to us at Verona; afterward she herself handed herself over to blessed Peter, and we received her for safekeeping at the confession of his altar.

Therefore, brothers and fellow ministers, we appeal to you and exhort you with devoted affection of mind to cooperate and labor together with us for this woman’s return and safety. Through your counsel and urgent exhortation, may that Augustus, following the example of his parents, fulfill the desire of our request with willing good will.

For just as the kingdom in which she is now held in custody belongs to him, so does this one. And just as she is guarded there so that she cannot give Boso any assistance or counsel or take any action on his behalf, so we shall cause her to live in a place where she will be unable to plot or contrive anything adverse for the disturbance of this kingdom or empire.

And if we learn that she has acted or wished to act in any way against his will or ours, we shall immediately send her back to the emperor’s presence, and she will no longer have the benefit of our counsel.

To ensure that we are believed without any doubt, we have ordered one of these envoys of ours, the venerable bishops whom we sent to the emperor on her behalf, to return and confirm that we will unquestionably do this. For, as was promised together with his fellow bishops and leading men, she will provide Boso with no temporal assistance or counsel; and, as we have stated, being most carefully guarded, she will be unable to do anything in all these matters.

Therefore, by the Lord, we adjure you to labor with all your strength together with us in this work for the love of God and to strive to lend him your hand, so that we too may be ready to advance your useful interests and needs; and, with you, may we extend every possible help to the one to whom you lend your hand. May we be able to offer worthy thanks to your holiness, beloved of God, for your labor and devotion.

### CCCXVII. TO THE CLERGY OF MILAN (Year 881)

He receives Haderic under the protection of the apostolic see and excommunicates all who inflict harm upon him or his churches.

To all the most reverend bishops and priests, or clergy, and to the people of the holy Church of Milan.

Instructed by the example of the good householder, whom we know to have rewarded those who labored well and faithfully, and taught by the guidance and mercy of apostolic authority, as well as by benevolence, we ought to provide timely and necessary assistance to all whom we see laboring faithfully for the interests of the Church of God.

Therefore, because we have clearly and repeatedly learned that you, Hoderic, venerable priest and abbot of the sacred monasteries of the blessed Gervasius and Protasius and of Simplicianus, as well as of the hospice [lacuna] of the holy Cosmas and Damian, which is called the Roman one, together with your other benefices and patrimonies located within or outside the city of Milan, have remained and striven with faithful devotion and with the whole strength of your mind for the former state, vigor, and restoration of the holy Church of Milan, in obedience to Anspert, your most reverend archbishop and our brother, and that you have fulfilled the legation of the Ambrosian Church with Catholic faith and with the most ardent zeal, as far as your strength allowed, we have frequently recognized this.

For this reason, since certain people, moved by the spite of obstinacy against your affection or by other causes of envy, have become hostile to you—people who now, with deceitful lips, are stirred up against you under the pretense of zeal and afterward contrive to harm you by cunning devices—we decree by our statute and establish by the authority of almighty God, of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and by our sanction:

No archbishop, priest, or cleric of any order of that holy Church of Milan, nor of any other Church, nor any person, great or small, of whatever rank or dignity, may at any time, on account of the commendable devotion of your affection, the sincerity of your faith, or the struggle of your charity—which we know you have maintained in our days for the benefit of that Church—bring any accusation against you in any way or under any pretext involving ecclesiastical property, or deprive you of the benefices and patrimonies that you retain for the merit of your worthy labor, or of your own movable property.

Rather, throughout the days of your life, according to the decree of our authority, for the love of God, for the reward of our soul, and because of your fidelity—which we know you bear toward your Church—you shall be permitted, under the protection of the apostolic see and our successors, to remain peacefully and securely with your own benefices and with all your people of both orders.

Moreover, whoever presumes to act against this statute of ours with reckless audacity and to accuse you on such a matter, we judge to be deprived of all ecclesiastical communion until, through fitting satisfaction, in the presence of us or our successors, he takes care to correct what he wrongfully inflicted.

Therefore, by our apostolic authority we also command that you be subject to the judgment of no bishop or priest until you come freely and securely into the presence of us or our successors, without any obstacle or impediment.

Issued as above.

### CCCXVIII. TO ATHANASIUS, BISHOP OF NAPLES (Year 881)

He rebukes him for not breaking the treaty he had made with the Saracens, although he had promised to break it; he shows that many evils had been inflicted upon Christians because of him by the Saracens; he threatens him with excommunication unless he breaks that treaty.

To ATHANASIUS, bishop of Naples.

Since you have forgotten the breasts of your holy mother, the Roman Church, which nourished you and raised you from your very cradle, you should at least not have forgotten our benevolence, which we have shown to you in a fatherly manner. We have foreseen measures for your salvation and, according to the circumstances of the time, have provided you with every kind of support in temporal advantages.

Because we wish to have you as our fellow worker in the things of God, and because we love your holiness exceedingly, we admonish you even now to return to your senses, to cleanse whatever is wicked in accordance with your ministry, and to avoid, with abhorrence, the treaty with the enemies of the Christian name.

Thus you may gain profit for your soul, enjoy our affection more and more, and, with the favor of God, be spared the blasphemies and curses directed against the remnants of the Christian people.

Remember, I beg you, what you are; remember what you will be if you do not repent; and remember the judgments of the Lord, lest you be compelled to render an account to God for so many who have been killed through your negligence and for those who, led into captivity, have perished by various deaths.

What can we say about their cruelty? So many things here must be wept and mourned that, if we wished to write them down, streams of tears would flow and the paper would give out before the words.

When we were once necessarily staying at Gaeta, your envoys promised that within twenty days you would not only dissolve the pact made with the Agarenes, but would also capture the Saracens and send them to us. But behold, what was promised has until now lacked fidelity; the words of all your pledges have been annulled and, as it appears, frustrated.

Therefore, as we have said, let this most savage plague now cease—let it cease—so that what remains of the Christian people may not utterly perish and you may not incur loss to your soul. For if you show compassion to God’s people, you will make God favorable to you, receive our fatherly affection in the customary manner, and preserve your ministry.

Otherwise, we shall not only fail to forgive you our grievances, but shall also bring against you the canonical sentence according to our ministry.

By the authority of our apostolate we also admonish you and, under threat of excommunication, forbid you in every way: since “behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6), do not undertake any sedition, disturbance, danger, or injury with those who dwell in Berolassi, nor consent in any way to those who do so.

Thus, by pursuing peace and purified from every wickedness, you may offer God an unblemished gift and permit the love of God, poured into your vessel, to dwell with you.

For we, who are concerned for everything, will, with God’s help, hasten there suitably, and, with you above all cooperating, restore peace and friendship among you.

Issued on the day before the Ides of March, in the fourteenth indiction.

### CCCXIX. TO METHODIUS, ARCHBISHOP (Year 881)

He rejoices in his devotion to orthodox faith and in his zeal and care for religion; he prays that his spiritual progress may increase daily and consoles him.

To METHODIUS, archbishop, concerning the faith.

We approve the care of your pastoral solicitude, which you display before our God and Lord in winning the souls of the faithful. As we observe you to be an energetic champion of orthodox faith, we rejoice exceedingly in the same Lord and do not cease to offer him immense praise and thanks, because he kindles you more and more in his commandments and mercifully rescues you from every adversity for the advancement of the holy Church.

But, having learned through your letters of the various misfortunes and events that have befallen you, you will be able to perceive how deeply we have grieved with you in compassion. You may see this from the fact that, when you were present before us, we admonished you to follow the teaching of the holy Roman Church according to the trustworthy tradition of the holy Fathers, and entrusted to you the teaching and preaching of both the Creed and the right faith.

We also indicated this in our apostolic letter to the glorious prince Sfentopulcus, which you say was delivered to him. No other letter of ours was sent to him, nor did we enjoin upon that bishop, openly or secretly, anything else to be done, nor did we decree that you should undertake anything different.

How much less, then, should it be believed that we demanded an oath from that bishop, when we did not address him even with a passing word concerning this matter.

Therefore, let this doubt cease. With God cooperating, inculcate among all the faithful the observance of orthodox faith, as evangelical and apostolic teaching requires, so that through the labor of your struggle you may bring abundant fruit to the Lord Jesus Christ and, rewarded by his grace, receive a fitting recompense.

As for the other temptations that you have endured in various ways, do not grieve. Rather, according to the Apostle, consider this entirely as joy, because if God is for you, no one can be against you.

Nevertheless, when you return with God as your guide, whatever has been committed against you in an outrageous manner, and whatever the aforesaid bishop has exercised against you contrary to his ministry, we shall, with the Lord’s help, examine both hearings before us and bring them to a lawful conclusion. We shall not fail to correct his obstinacy by the sentence of our judgment.

Issued on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, in the fourteenth indiction.

### CCCXX. TO CHARLES, THE EMPEROR (Year 881)

He announces to the emperor that he is suffering such evils from the Saracens that he can no longer endure them; he asks him to send an army promptly to his aid and sends him the palm together with his blessing.

To CHARLES.

[Note: The third of that name, surnamed the Fat.]

My dearest son, you ought not to forget our many oppressions, nor should you fail to remember the calamities that your holy mother, the Roman Church, suffers; and then at last you ought to stretch forth the hand of your piety toward some consolation of ours and provide us aid as quickly as possible. For you know what evils, how many, and of what kind we suffer, especially from the pagans, and how great are the miseries we endure; you have also experienced how greatly we are daily afflicted by the wrongs committed against us, and we partly made this known to your clemency a little while ago.

And since we see these same evils daily not diminishing but rather increasing and spreading more and more, pain and groaning, and endless sadness, threaten us; and therefore, alas, we would rather die than continue to endure such things. Accordingly, our spiritual son and ever-Augustus, we earnestly beseech your Glory, for love of almighty God and in reverence for the princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul, not to permit your [perhaps: “hostile”] army, which you said would come to these regions, to suffer delay, but to send it with all speed to our aid. Thus, with the Lord’s help, it may defeat the Hagarenes for our relief and be able to bring us even a small measure of peace from those pagans.

Moreover, you must by every means provide from your side a man so energetic and suitable that he can command that army, foresee what defense or assistance they should provide for us, and accomplish in your place whatever must be done or lies within your authority. Otherwise, this will not only be the result of the greatest negligence and the whole of your advantage will perish, but our later circumstances will also be worse than the earlier; and it cannot be said how great a sin you will have incurred by this.

Therefore, for God’s sake, come to our aid—come to our aid—so that the nations round about may not say: “Where is their emperor?” Furthermore, behold, according to custom we have sent to your Honor, with an apostolic blessing, a palm, by which the sign of victory is given, wishing and praying almighty God that he may make and permit you to carry it with joy on the day of so great a solemnity. May he also graciously incline the ears of your hearts, by divine action, toward the benefit and advancement of us all.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of April, in the fourteenth indiction.

CCCXXI. TO VARIOUS BISHOPS. (Year 881.) He announces that he has excommunicated Athanasius, bishop of Naples, who, though often warned, never wished to break the treaty he had made with the Saracens, as he had promised, together with all who consented to him.

To all the bishops dwelling at Gaeta, Naples, Capua, Berolassim, Amalfi, Benevento, and Salerno, from their peers.

We would wish not to have to tell you what and how great are the adversities that the Church of Christ suffers from Athanasius, bishop of Naples, unless they were extraordinarily grave. For behold—as most of you already know in large part—for the destruction of all Christianity, he made a pact long ago with the sons of Ishmael, namely the Saracens, hateful to God, and reduced this entire land to such ruin that now no one remains who inhabits it at all.

Concerning this crime we admonished him very frequently, sparing our own body in no way. We hurried all the way to Naples, brought him a great amount of silver, and begged him to separate himself from their association, so that at last, coming to his senses, he might eradicate so great a plague. He, as I might put it, unable to endure our importunity, although deceitfully, promised that he would do so and dissolve the pact made with the Saracens, on this one condition: that if thereafter he became involved in this evil in any way, he would both be deprived of the priesthood and lie under anathema.

But alas! For the sake of the profit of shameful gain—which he received from the Saracens themselves by taking a share of their plunder—he forgot this promise and refused to fulfill what he had promised, in the presence of many witnesses, both in writing and by word.

Again, after we had increased the weight of the silver we brought, and had arrived at Gaeta, we commanded him through our legates that, if within thirty days he did not break the treaty made with the Saracens or send back what he had deceitfully taken from us, he should once more receive by our judgment the sentence which he had brought upon himself. But, putting aside both his many oaths and his unqualified promises, he deceived us from day to day; while everything outside was scattered and many of our possessions were taken within through his cunning, to this day he has neither dissolved the pact made with the Saracens nor been willing to show mercy to the remnant of God’s people.

Rather, by associating with them, he advanced from these evils to worse ones; despising God’s commandments and forgetting even his priesthood, he not only became like them but, in many respects, worse. For this reason, in synod at the church of the blessed apostle Peter, we pronounced sentence against him and, together with all who consented or gave support to him, deprived him of all ecclesiastical communion under the imposition of anathema.

The form of the excommunication is as follows:

We admonished Athanasius, bishop of Naples, very often and by giving him many weights of silver, to break the pact made with the Saracens. He promised, however, that he would dissolve that pact in every respect and separate himself from their association, on the condition that, if he again made a treaty with them in any way, he would be deprived of every priestly dignity and anathematized. But because he thought nothing of all this, continued to make a pact with them to the destruction of Christians, repeatedly deceived us, and received a share of their plunder, by the judgment and authority of almighty God, of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and of ourselves, we deprive him and all his followers of every ecclesiastical communion, and until he has completely separated himself from those Saracens, we anathematize him as an enemy of all Christianity.

Given in the month of April, in the fourteenth indiction.

CCCXXII. TO ROMANUS, ARCHBISHOP OF RAVENNA. (Year 881.) He reproves him for having admitted Count Alberic to Ravenna and harassed the noblemen of Ravenna contrary to the oath they had given him; he says that, once he has returned from Naples, he will attend to all these matters; he orders Dominicus, archdeacon of the Church of Faenza, to be consecrated bishop.

To Romanus, archbishop of Ravenna.

What you instructed us to accomplish for the benefit and necessary restoration of the holy Church of Ravenna, informed by the shining examples of our predecessors, we gladly wish, with God’s favor, to provide to that Church as suitable and timely consolation and assistance in its defense, especially since its governance has been entrusted to us.

But because many of the noblemen of Ravenna do not cease to strike the ears of our apostolate with repeated complaints alone, the benevolence of our clemency toward you is rightly regarded as disturbed. For, to omit other matters, because you rashly presumed, without consulting us, to summon Count Alberic to Ravenna as though on the imperial side and to coerce its noble citizens, we are astonished, since we know that you acted wholly contrary to your promise, given under oath before us and the apostolic see. Therefore you must take great care lest, on account of such actions, your own sentence punish you as a transgressor.

For we have determined that you should feed the Lord’s flock, not disturb it; save it, not destroy it. Nevertheless, when, God willing, we have returned from Naples, where we are now setting out—and either you have come to Rome according to the order sent to you, or we or our envoy have come to these regions—we shall in every respect administer full justice concerning everything that we learn to be necessary for your Church.

Moreover, after the bishop of the Church of Faenza had died, we judged that this venerable archdeacon Dominicus was worthy of the episcopal honor of that see. By this decree of our authority we command your affection to take care, without any delay or postponement, to consecrate that same archdeacon as bishop according to custom. For if, corrupted by any rashness, you presently refuse to do this contrary to the written oath of your pledge, know for certain that we, having the care and concern of that Church, shall immediately consecrate the aforesaid archdeacon as bishop when he returns to us at our command.

Given as above.

CCCXXIII. TO ROMANUS, ARCHBISHOP OF RAVENNA. (Year 881.) He reproves him for consenting that another man’s lawful wife be handed over to a ravisher and for daring to oppose the Roman Church; for these reasons he suspends him from conferring sacred orders until his case is examined by the synod to which he orders him to come.

To Romanus, archbishop of Ravenna, sent through the venerable bishop Delto.

Among the other things we have heard about you, the duke Deusdedit, on coming to us, reported that you had cunningly caused the wife of that man, concerning whom a lawful determination had been made, to come to you and had handed her over to another man, her ravisher, for sexual violation. This crime of such great wickedness you ought, in accordance with your ministry, to have prohibited and utterly cut off in every way; yet you unlawfully gave your consent.

We also know from many indications that you did not hesitate, with rash boldness, to rebel against the holy Roman Church, your mistress, and to act most plainly against the terms of your sworn pledge. Therefore, by the authority of God, blessed Peter, and ourselves, we instruct you and by this present decree command you not to presume in any way to perform any priestly ordination, on account of the crimes with which you are entangled, until you make every effort, setting aside every excuse, to come by the eighth day before the Kalends of October of the coming fifteenth indiction to the synod which, with God’s favor, we shall celebrate for ecclesiastical purposes according to the statutes of the holy Fathers. Thus, after the matters we have learned about you have been examined by synodal decree, they may receive a canonical conclusion.

Given as above.

CCCXXIV. TO THE SAME. (Year 881.) He orders the clerics of Piacenza, whom he had received when they fled to him without letters of commendation, to be sent back to their bishop; he also orders the clerics of that Church to be absolved until he comes with them to the synod.

To the most reverend and most holy Romanus, archbishop of Ravenna.

Among the other unsuitable pretexts of personal affection by which you do not hesitate daily, with an incautious mind, to entangle yourself, we have learned—when Paul, bishop of the most beloved Church of Piacenza, humbly complained to the ears of our apostolate—that you had received, contrary to the statutes of the holy Fathers, clerics of that Church who were unwilling to follow the norm of its rule and had therefore fled to you without letters of commendation, and that you had decreed that those whom you received should serve you.

Because we wish to cut this off, on the authority of the apostolic see and by the principal instruction of the holy Fathers, on account of the great disturbances and seditions that often arise, we command your Reverence to take care to return or send immediately to the bishop of the aforesaid Church of Faenza [Piacenza, as above] the clerics of that Church whom you appear to be improperly retaining, especially the deacon Gausus.

For it is not permitted for any cleric to be enrolled simultaneously in the Churches of two cities, nor, out of a desire for empty glory, to flee to another Church as though it were superior to the one in which he existed from the beginning. Therefore we decree that they be recalled to their own Church, and you are not to receive them again in any way.

You must take the greatest care not to do anything further, lest by the judgment of the holy Fathers, which has been pronounced against transgressors of this rule, you deserve to be condemned altogether. But if some dispute should arise among them, settle it canonically, with the honor and authority of the apostolic see preserved, and with the privilege of your Church likewise preserved.

Furthermore, absolve the priests and clerics of the Church of Piacenza whom you excommunicated from that excommunication, until at the proper time you come with them together to Rome for the synod.

Given in the month of July, in the fourteenth indiction.

CCCXXV. TO THE PRIEST CONSTANTINUS. (Year 881.) He excommunicates him because he was promoted by the archbishop of Ravenna to the episcopate of the Church of Faenza without his permission; he also forbids him to exercise the administration of that Church until he comes to the Roman synod.

To Constantinus, priest of the Church of Faenza, from the parish of Saint Peter Transilvanus.

We have learned that you were improperly promoted, as if to episcopal honor, by Romanus, archbishop of Ravenna, without the authority or permission of our pontificate and without observing the rule of canonical institution. Therefore, by these letters of our apostolate, on the authority of almighty God and of the chief apostles, Saints Peter and Paul, and by our apostolic right, we excommunicate you, so that you have no license whatsoever to perform anything belonging to episcopal office, or in any way to invade the Church of Faenza, or presume to exercise any dominion over the parishes, property, or people of that Church, until you make every effort to present yourself in person, together with your archbishop Romanus, [lacuna] on the eighth day before the Kalends of October.

For if, against this apostolic command of ours and after this sentence of our excommunication, you presume to perform anything belonging to that episcopal ministry, or attempt with rash boldness to interfere in anything pertaining to that episcopate, and if you postpone coming to the aforesaid synod, know for certain that we shall not only deprive you of all ecclesiastical communion, but by synodal decree shall also declare you alien from priestly honor.

Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the fourteenth indiction.

CCCXXVI. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF FICOCLE. (Year 881.) He entrusts him with the visitation and care of the Church of Faenza, which has been deprived of its shepherd, until a new shepherd is placed over it.

To John, bishop of Ficocle.

A report sent some time ago makes known the death of Romanus, bishop of the city of Faenza. Therefore we solemnly entrust to your fraternity the visitation of that Church, which has been deprived of its shepherd. You ought to carry this out in such a way that no one presumes to seize anything belonging to the Church—whether the clerics’ revenues, income, ornaments, ministries, or whatever else there may be in that administration. Therefore let your fraternity make every effort to go to the aforesaid Church, so that in the meantime you may provide with diligent care whatever is fitting for its welfare, until the election or ordination of the bishop who is to succeed him has been examined before us by synodal inquiry and, with God’s help, concluded by apostolic judgment.

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the fourteenth indiction.

CCCXXVII. TO ROMANUS, ARCHBISHOP. (Year 881.) He orders him to come to Rome for the synod under penalty of excommunication, so that he may answer the charges brought against him.

To our most reverend and most holy brother Romanus, archbishop.

Some time ago, by letters of our apostolate sent to you through John, the venerable bishop of Montefeltro, we ordered you to come to the synodal assembly which we were to celebrate together with you solely for ecclesiastical purposes; but you scorned to present yourself to us. Now, recognizing that you are entangled in many crimes, assailed by the dreadful accusations of many people, and especially stained by manifest perjury, by the authority of this second summons we order you to come, setting aside every excuse and delay, together with all your suffragan bishops, to the venerable synod which, with God’s favor, we shall celebrate on the eighth day before the Kalends of October of the coming fifteenth indiction.

There, before the brotherly and venerable gathering of bishops, you will be able to answer in person, as required, concerning everything brought against you after it has been examined, and demonstrate your innocence. For if, swollen with rashness or moved by the goad of disobedience, you scorn this apostolic and canonical summons of ours—which we first sent to you through Delto and now also through John, venerable bishops of Calla—and refuse to come to the aforesaid synod, know for certain that we shall deprive you of all ecclesiastical communion, and that by fleeing you will suffer the sentence of your condemnation and the loss of your honor.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of August, in the fourteenth indiction.

CCCXXVIII. TO THE EMPEROR CHARLES. (Year 881.) He sends Peter and Zacharias as legates to him, in order to correct the evils which he complains of having suffered during Charles’s reign.

To Charles, the emperor.

Because now, while all of you are reigning, by God’s favor, through the office of our humility, we suffer and endure everywhere the same adversities that we daily remember having endured before your imperial Glory’s advancement, we have judged it proper, by sending these letters of our apostolate, to bring to your Imperial Serenity’s attention, for the benefit and manifold necessity of the universal Church over which by God’s grace we preside, and to make it known in every respect, that, in accordance with the common agreement and decree, we have sent Peter, a distinguished official of our palace, our counselor in these matters [reading uncertain], and common faithful servant, together with Zacharias, the venerable bishop and librarian of our see, to receive justice and correction concerning everything that has hitherto been wrongly done, and for the safety and restoration of the entire land of Saint Peter.

Thus, in the presence of your envoys, whatever necessarily had to be amended and corrected might be corrected according to lawful justice, so that such a long-standing evil might come to an end.

CCCXXIX. TO THE PEOPLE OF RAVENNA. (Year 881.) He orders them to separate themselves from the communion of the archbishop of Ravenna, who has been excommunicated in synod, until they learn that he has been absolved.

To all the venerable priests and clergy, and to all the judges and people of Ravenna.

We wish your fidelity and unanimity to know that we deprived your archbishop Romanus, manifestly stained by the crime of perjury and assailed by other monstrous crimes, and therefore summoned to the synod for his purification but refusing to come, of all ecclesiastical communion, together with the decree of the holy synod, until he makes every effort to present himself to us in person.

Therefore, by these letters of our apostolate, we order you, and by the authority of God, the blessed prince of the apostles Peter, and ourselves, we command, that all of you separate yourselves in every way from his association and communion, until you learn that through the office of our apostolic mercy he has been absolved from the bond of this excommunication.

But whoever presumes to communicate with him in any way before our hearing and absolution shall remain entangled in the same snare of excommunication, according to the institution of the holy Fathers, until he has been mercifully absolved by us.

Given on the fourth day of the month of October, in the twelfth [fifteenth] indiction.

CCCXXX. TO THE EMPEROR CHARLES. (Year 881.) He congratulates him on his observance toward the Roman Church; he rejoices that Charles wishes to come to Ravenna in order to discuss the condition of the Church and the Empire; he asks him to come before the day he had appointed.

To the emperor.

After receiving and reading the letters of your Serenity, and in accordance with what you instructed us verbally through John, bishop of Ventimiglia, we learned that you wish with all your strength to secure the honor of the holy Roman Church, your mother, and the safety of its territory. We therefore rejoiced greatly in spirit.

Moreover, you instructed us that on the day of the Purification of blessed Mary, ever-virgin, we should come to Ravenna and meet together in order, with God’s help, to consider and accomplish the advancement of the holy Church of God and the condition of your Empire. We gladly accept this as well, and wish you to be there four days before the aforesaid feast, because we also most eagerly desire to meet with you and willingly fulfill your request, if, with the Lord’s favor, bodily health is divinely granted to us.

And since, as we have heard, you piously desire to complete the labor and struggle for the condition of the Churches of God, the security of your Empire, and the common salvation of Christians, by these letters of our apostolate we admonish and exhort you to advance more and more in this imperial concern of yours. We beseech your Glory and your Greatness that, when you begin to come to these regions, you order the illustrious Count Suppo, our common faithful servant, to come with you.

CCCXXXI. TO WILIBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF COLOGNE. (Year 882.) He commends his vigilance and, moved by his prayers, absolves a certain excommunicated priest who, according to Wilibert’s testimony, has now been purified by long penance, and restores him to priestly ministry; he entrusts him with the case of Gideon’s adultery, so that he may pronounce sentence canonically.

To the most reverend and most holy Wilibert, archbishop of Cologne.

Having examined your letters, we clearly recognize and praise the prudence of your Holiness, which is solicitous, with priestly vigilance, for the salvation of the Lord’s flock entrusted to you and for its liberation from the jaws of the evil enemy, who always eagerly strives to drag the unwary into the depths of eternal death, according to the pastoral instruction divinely entrusted to your Reverence.

Preserving the privilege of the apostolic see with discerning understanding, you found that this priest of your diocese, named Tal [some material is missing], had imprudently communicated with Ingeltrude, wife of the former Count Boso, when she had abandoned her marriage bed contrary to the precepts of divine law, although he had been lawfully excommunicated by our predecessor Pope Nicholas of blessed memory; you therefore deprived him of sacred communion long ago.

When you sent him to our pontificate with the attestation of your faithful devotion, you declared that he had humbly endured the sentence of excommunication imposed upon him for eleven years and had purified, by the long satisfaction of penance, the poison he had drawn from polluted intercourse with the woman. You asked us to absolve him from the bond of his obligation.

We, however, moved by consideration of mercy and inclined by your prayers, following the judgment of the inner Judge, absolve him—if the matter is indeed so—from the bond of that excommunication, and command him solemnly and freely to perform every priestly office or ministry, according to the preceding custom, always with fear of the Lord.

Furthermore, concerning Gideon, whose wife, you state, committed adultery with this man’s brother, we are uncertain whether what is said about this is true or not. We therefore entrust the matter to your affection, so that, having discovered the truth of the case in every respect with diligent care, you may reread what the most excellent teacher, blessed Augustine, said about this in his books *On Adulterous Marriages to Pollentius*, and what Pope Innocent established in chapter twenty-six [Epistle 2], and then strive to decide the matter according to their ruling.

Thus their souls may be aided by the remedies of penance, and their bodies may, in all things according to God, be directed through the providence of your Holiness.

CCCXXXII. TO LEO, LANDULF, AND LANDON. (Year 882.) He orders them to ensure that the son of Auxentius, captured by Attinulfus, is restored to his father.

To Leo, bishop of Teano; likewise to Landulf, bishop; and to Landon, gastald, his father.

We have learned with more reliable testimony that Attinulfus captured the son of Auxentius of Capua, who is specifically our own man, and, treating him badly, held him by force. We are greatly astonished at this and have taken it badly that he presumed to do such a thing.

Therefore, by letters of our apostolate, we have judged it proper to instruct you to make every effort and, on our behalf, press Attinulfus until he restores this son of Auxentius—namely, our man—safe to his father and returns him unharmed with his men. Otherwise he will not be able to escape our sentence, since he did not refrain from afflicting our man, who was proceeding so innocently.

We ask you, however, to act so energetically that we may give you thanks and be encouraged to entrust greater matters to you.

CCCXXXIII. TO MICHAEL, KING OF THE BULGARIANS. (Year 882.) He exhorts him to return to the faith and obedience of the Roman Church and to send legates.

To Michael, king of the Bulgarians.

Since it is not beginnings so much as endings that deserve praise in good things, we give thanks to almighty God, creator of all visible and invisible things, who has until now strengthened your good will in the firmness of true faith, and, making you a lover of himself, has caused light to shine from you as though truly from ancient darkness, and by the power of his grace has enlightened your most benevolent heart for the salvation of many.

We have also judged it fitting to offer your devotion suitable thanks for this reason: your conduct has partly shown how carefully you strive to observe fidelity toward the holy Roman Church, the mother and head of all lands. You sought this Church at the beginning of your conversion and have not ceased to show that you wish to have it as your helper for your perpetual salvation, namely by visiting the holy apostles and, as we have said, seeking their intercession.

It is therefore exceedingly absurd and inappropriate that your pious will should afterward have chosen to conduct itself otherwise than it did at first, as is known to all. For, divinely inspired, you rightly sought the mother of all religion, the holy Roman Church, as your guide and as the way by which you would be led to the pastures of eternity. And she, because she offers and has always offered maternal compassion to all the faithful, received you with arms outstretched toward God, giving thanks to Christ.

It followed that you should not turn aside from the straight path, nor, after placing your hand on the plow, attempt at anyone’s persuasion to look back. Do you not hear with deaf ears, dearest son, the holy Gospel, where it is written: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved”? (Matthew X.) Or, if you have heard and obeyed, “Return to your mind; return to your heart”? (Isaiah XLVI.) And remember your pledge.

For love and fear of God made you more trusting in the apostolic privilege than, so to speak, the examples of many. If everyone must indeed return what he has vowed to God, then you ought very greatly to strive to return to the end what you freely vowed to the holy Roman Church, not ignorant that the blessed apostle Peter received from the Lord Jesus Christ the keys of the heavenly kingdom and earned the power to open them to some of the faithful and close them to others.

Therefore, using this power, as did our predecessors, although unworthy, we are compelled—if you do not correct what you have done—to chastise you worthily in this world and, insofar as it lies within us, not to refrain from filling you with curses in the future.

For this reason, dearest son, hasten to correct what you have done wickedly; and, setting aside every excuse and delay, send us word through your legate of whatever you wish to amend in this matter. For, with God’s help, we shall fulfill every desire of your correction, and, wishing you to be safe in soul and body, we shall strive to order the matter according to God.

CCCXXXIV. TO THE EMPEROR AND EMPRESS. Fragment—(Year 882.)

When we had returned, we found all our shores plundered, and Saracens residing in Fundi and Terracina as though in their own home. Because of them, we remained in the City for no more than five days, although we were suffering considerable bodily illness; then we went out with our faithful men and, with the Lord’s help, captured eighteen ships. Many Saracens were killed, while we freed nearly six hundred captives.

Therefore, when you come, it is very necessary that such a force of men remain on the seacoasts, by whose valor all our possessions may remain safe and the places not yet plundered may not be plundered.

CCCXXXV. TO THE EMPRESS ANGELBERGA. Fragment—(Year unknown.)

The evil has grown and become so great that, through the faction of the archbishop of Ravenna, Maurinus, together with his accomplices—who have already been excommunicated and anathematized by us—entered Ravenna and utterly seized and devastated the possessions of our faithful together with them. He even violently took the keys of the city of Ravenna from our Vestararius and, according to his own will, by an authority whose source we do not know, granted them by force to that same archbishop—something which, as far as we remember, had never been done.

CCCXXXVI. TO THE SAME. Fragment—(Year unknown.)

Indeed, by God’s power we shall defend what belongs to us better than Naletus, and we have absolutely no need of them in anything, building dromons together with the other ships, as well as other war vessels and equipment; indeed, we are also preparing the courage of the men themselves and continually arming them against hostile attacks.

CCCXXXVII. TO THE SAME. Fragment. (Year unknown.) He excuses the removal of Bishop John from military service.

[In Gratian, *Decretum* II, distinction 23, question 8, chapter 1.]

He certainly fears excessively [or: “indeed”], and rightly fears, to practice secular warfare contrary to the profession of his order: to defend territory, deliberate about battles, and wield arms are matters of secular power.

CCCXXXVIII. TO DOMASOL, THE GLORIOUS DUKE. Fragment—(Year unknown.)

Moreover, we exhort the zeal of your devotion to burn all the more vehemently against the maritime brigands who, under cover of your name, rage against Christians, the more you recognize that the reputation of your name has been darkened by their wickedness. For although it may be believed that they lie in wait for sailors against your will, nevertheless, since they are said to be capable of being restrained by you, you will not be considered blameless unless you restrain them.

For it is written: “Whoever does not correct crimes when he can amend them, himself commits them.”

CCCXXXIX. TO ROSTAGNUS, ARCHBISHOP OF ARLES. Fragment—(Year unknown.) The betrothed woman is to be deprived of communion unless she wishes to abandon the ravisher and return to her betrothed.

Atho, the bearer of this letter, complains that, while he was faithfully keeping watch in our service, a certain man abducted the woman betrothed to him. Therefore, supported by our authority, let your fraternity summon his suffragan bishops in person; and by unanimous judgment let them deprive both the ravisher and the abducted woman of all communion, if the ravisher does not return the woman to this man and if she does not wish to return to her former betrothed.

CCCXL. TO SIGIBOD, ARCHBISHOP OF NARBONNE. Fragment—(Year unknown.) Concerning the examination of the case of a certain priest.

The bearer of this letter, presented to the apostolic see, declared in a plaintive and lamenting voice that he was a priest and that he had been suspended from the priestly office by the bishops of the diocese subject to your Holiness, and subjected to certain other penances until our special judgment, because, he says, during a disturbance he seized a certain man, lifted him from the ground by the arms, and hurled him with powerful force against his own brother, so that that brother, struck to the ground by the evil [read: “the evil weight”] of so great an impact, fell and, prostrated and crushed, violently lost the breath of life.

Finally, when, as this man reported, the revered bishops were uncertain whether he ought or ought not to be deprived of the office formerly entrusted to him, they did not wish to deliberate on this themselves, but wanted it to be decided and determined by our judgment. They would have acted properly in this only if they had first examined the matter fully and, according to the canons, through a judgment assigned for a priest’s case, with four persons appointed from among those versed in venerable decrees and laws present, and had discussed it by careful inquiry. Then, after making a written report, if anything seemed to them doubtful or difficult, they could have sought our decree on the matter according to ancient custom.

But since both the identity of the person making the report is unknown to us and his commendation has not been confirmed in writing by any bishop, and since there is no accusation from a prosecutor, no confession of guilt by the accused, and no corroboration by faithful witnesses, we can neither be credulous toward his sole account nor pronounce a definitive sentence of condemnation against him.

Therefore, at least now, let your fraternity, possessing metropolitan authority, associate with you six bishops from among those dwelling under you or in neighboring districts, together with the bishop to whose parish this man belongs; let them thoroughly examine the matter with the winnowing fan of careful investigation, and, having discovered what is just, let them decree it canonically and determine it by the common judgment of the brethren.

CCCXLI. TO CENNEMOCUS, BISHOP OF VENCE. Fragment—(Year unknown.) That a murderous priest cannot remain in the priesthood.

I am astonished that your insufficiently instructed judgment should think that a priest can minister in the priesthood after committing homicide; indeed, what is worse, you wish to persuade us to give our assent to such a presumption. For who, however foolish or perverse in understanding, would judge such a thing permissible, even after however great a penance, when it is wholly contrary to canonical discipline?

Therefore, deprived of the priesthood, he must wash away so monstrous a crime with a fountain of tears, so that, healed at least by such remedies, he may be able to find the assistance of salvation.

CCCXLII. TO THE BISHOPS OF BRITAIN. (Year unknown.) Concerning monks ordained by the abbot Heclocar.

[Martin, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. III, p. 867.]

JOHN, bishop of the Roman see, to Mainus, beloved and distinguished son, archbishop, and to the other bishops residing throughout Britain [or: dwelling there]: greetings and apostolic blessing.

[Note: The people of Tours rightly maintain, in their replies to the objections of the people of Dol, that through a copyist’s carelessness the title “archbishop” entered the heading of this letter; this is shown by the heading of the following letter, where only the bishop of Dol is named.]

Let it be known to you how Resgallon and Corvili [alternative: King Gallon and Gorvilli], together with other monks, visited the bodies of the apostles and came into our presence. Afterwards, concerning their ordination and that of the other monks received from Abbot Heclocar through ignorance, we judged that, if he usurped the office unworthily, since he had not received it from anyone who was properly an ordainer of that office, their ordination should nevertheless be regarded as complete, because wicked men can administer good things properly, although they themselves are evil. But let him ordain no one further until he has been released from the bonds of his own contagion.

We advise these men henceforth to attend to their rule, so that he may receive the brothers and sons [alternative: the sons] energetically in his monastery, putting every excuse aside, and thereafter show good zeal toward himself and his subjects, lest he become a sower and scatterer of tares among his flock; and lest complaints about him again reach our ears, let him deal with them as the rule shall rightly determine.

### CCCXLIII. TO BISHOP PETER. Fragment—(Date uncertain)

If Deodatus and Gregory refuse to come to us at the appointed time and to correct everything justly and canonically, we shall bind them with the heavier chains of perpetual anathema. We shall write out their crimes, excommunications, and anathemas and suspend them before the most holy image of the blessed Apostle Peter, so that their wickedness may be known to all who come from every part of the world to the apostolic threshold, and so that they may be regarded as strangers to communion with the holy Church.

### CCCXLIV. TO MARINUS AND PULCHER. Fragment—(Date uncertain)

Moreover, we charge the provinces entrusted to your fidelity that, with some ships, you send in person your strongest soldiers, who, together with our infantry, may capture the forty Saracens who recently fled to sea from our Greek ships and who later, after our infantry had stripped them by force of all their arms, escaped into the hiding places of Mount Circel. We do not wish to fatigue our dromons for so few Saracens, while we are prompted to trust you—and, as you are said to desire, are encouraged to do so—in every way, placing our confidence in you.

For if henceforth we find your constancy in obedience and purity of faith joined with effective courage toward the Holy Roman Church, we shall not only lighten, insofar as reason requires, the burden of the three matters about which you say that you have been excessively weighed down, but, with the Lord strengthening us, we shall also strive to protect you, as the household of Saint Peter, by land and sea.

### CCCXLV. TO COUNT COZIL. (Date uncertain)  
#### Concerning those who, having dismissed their wives, have entered into other marriages

As for those who have dismissed their wives, or, while their wives were still alive, have entered into other marriages, we excommunicate them, together with those who approve of them, until they remove the later wives and receive the former ones again in penitence. For, just as marriage is from God, so divorce is from the devil, as Saint Augustine bears witness. “What God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Matthew 19:6), especially since this very wicked custom has remained from the practice of the pagans, among whom, in such matters, no one other than the devil himself was teacher and author.

Most prudent man, take care and make provision that those two men who cast away the wives whom God prepared and joined to them may in no way be permitted to reject them. For it is impious that those who, by God’s authority, were united in a lawful bond should be separated at human pleasure—or rather, through diabolical fraud. The same warning was given to Bishop Paul.

Take care that you exercise the greatest diligence concerning the separation of married couples, so that those who have been separated after receiving the letters of the apostolic see may, without blame, take back their former wives, with an appropriate penance imposed, and dismiss those whom they subsequently took. If they are unwilling, put them outside the Church together with those who receive them into communion, until they amend what they have done.

### CCCXLVI. CONSTITUTION CONCERNING THE RIGHTS OF THE CARDINALS. (Date uncertain)

By this present constitution we likewise order you to assemble twice a month or more often, either at this or that titular church, or at this or that diaconia, or at any other churches. You are to examine the life, morals, character, and manner of dress of yourselves and of the lower clergy; how each superior behaves toward his subjects; whether subjects obey their superiors; and to cut off every illicit practice. You are also to settle, insofar as possible, the complaints of clergy and laity that belong to our judgment.

For we are certain that, just as Moses represented our gentleness, so your fraternity is to represent the seventy elders who, under him, judged the affairs of disputes in turn. We entrust to you the arrangement of monasteries deprived of their abbots, and the substitution of abbots—subject to our prior knowledge—with men who are or shall have been among us in the monastic profession.

For the care of the churches and the discipline of their clergy, and for settling the complaints of the laity, we order you to assemble twice a week at the sacred palace, in accordance with the decrees of our predecessor Leo IV.

We likewise decree that, concerning our parishes, you shall possess permanently, insofar as belongs to the pontiff, the pontifical benefice; that in the principal churches you shall perform the divine offices in turn according to the priority of your consecration; and that you shall share equally in their offerings, while the ancient custom of the cardinal deacons is always preserved, both for your use and for the furnishing of the lamps of your churches.

### CCCXLVII. Fragment—(Date uncertain)  
#### Against violators of the house of God

If anyone violates the house of God and removes anything from it without the permission of the person to whom it is known to have been entrusted, or commits an injury against ecclesiastical persons, let him know that he shall be deprived of communion until, having been lawfully admonished in an assembly, he makes satisfaction. If, after a second and third summons, he refuses to make satisfaction before the bishop, he shall be held liable before all for the danger of sacrilege, so that, according to the Apostle, he is to be joined to none of the faithful.

### CCCXLVIII. TO THEIBERGA AND ALDERIC. (Date uncertain)  
#### He urges them to restore his wife to Radulf

(At Ivo, Book VIII, chapter 118.)

Again and again we admonish you and, by these letters of our apostolate, exhort you to restore his wife to the nobleman Radulf as soon as possible, as we have already said, and to have her adhere to her husband and act according to the law of the Lord. For no law permits a person either not to confess a charge brought against her or, after a lawful preliminary purgation, not to be released from the charge brought against her.

If she chooses to do neither, but, relying solely upon obstinacy, fails to undertake any satisfaction, it is plainly evident that she undoubtedly confesses the crime which she does not purge away. For, as the holy Pope Hormisdas writes, only those who do not hold fast to what is right escape the examination of conscience.

Therefore, if he, or she, or you, Theiberga and Alderic, postponing obedience to the decrees of our apostolate, should attempt any longer, without any reasonable cause, to withdraw the woman mentioned above either from her husband’s authority or from the scrutiny of the law, then both she and you, until you obey our sanction, shall be excommunicated by the judgment of Almighty God and by the sentence of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, the chief apostles, and shall be excluded from the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, together with your supporters, those who approve of you, your followers, and your accomplices—as violators of divine and human laws, despisers of the decrees of the apostolic see, and offenders who have broken them so often and in so many ways.

### CCCXLIX. TO ABBOT BERRARIUS. Fragment—(Date uncertain)  
#### Concerning reverence toward the supreme pontiffs

(At Ivo, Book IV, chapter 102.)

Far be it from pious minds to think anything sinister concerning the pontiff of the Roman summit, since, as the blessed confessor Ennodius, bishop of the city of Ticinum, writes, we are taught that Almighty God either raises distinguished men to such heights or, at any rate, illumines those whom he has chosen.

### CCCL. TO PHOTIUS, PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE [Note: Among other calumnies that Photius falsely attributed to Pope John, he invented the charge that John held the same view as the Greeks concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit, and fabricated this letter under the name of Pope John VIII as though it had been written to Photius concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit. It must have been composed either by Photius himself or by someone else. That in these times it was unquestionably customary in the Roman Church to say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son is clearly proved, among other considerations, by the following fact. John, a deacon of the holy Roman Church, wrote to this same Pope John four books of the Life of Pope Saint Gregory that he had composed. When discussing the Dialogues written by Gregory and translated into Greek by Pope Zacharias, John rightly complains that, although Saint Gregory explicitly affirmed in them that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, they corrupted the text and removed the words “and the Son.” He severely rebukes them for corrupting Saint Gregory’s text so boldly and shamelessly, plainly indicating that the Roman Church held nothing different from Saint Gregory himself and that John, to whom he was writing, did not dissent from that judgment.] (Years 879–882.)  
#### Concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit

JOHN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Photius, most reverend and catholic brother, patriarch of Constantinople: grace from above for salutary works.

We are not unaware that some of those who are with you, having little zeal for peace, speak evil of our Church and of us ourselves, neglecting the truth. The matter has gone so far that your fraternity is almost led to think ill of us and of those subject to us. They have indeed found an opportunity—as I myself would affirm, one sufficiently suited to such a purpose—but the truth itself, as it stands, has in no way been adulterated or corrupted. What follows will make the matter clear, and God himself will confirm this to us from above by his testimony.

They, however, like those who mix wine with water and adulterate it, introduce various falsehoods fabricated and devised by themselves. For the devil, who from the beginning was the author of evil, who placed enmity between us and God, and thereafter separated our first parent from the love of God and made him an enemy of his Creator, must even now have certain ministers of his own and drive these very men to stir up some scandal between the Churches.

But I, directing my eyes rather toward God, the author and giver—who delivered enmity itself over to death on his cross—strive with all my strength to close the mouths of those men who delight in evil. For this reason, even before your fraternity communicated anything to me, I resolved to make these matters clear to you, so that, being sufficiently informed about our affairs, you may lend less ear to those who strive to argue and revile, but instead reject and spurn them; and moreover ensure that others do not believe their words.

Your fraternity also knows that when the man whom you recently sent to us came and consulted us concerning the holy Creed, he found us preserving it unshaken, exactly as it was handed down to us from the beginning, and that we had neither added nor taken anything away from it, since we rightly know that a grave condemnation awaits those who dare to do such things.

Therefore we again inform your Reverence that, concerning this addition to the Creed—namely, “from the Son”—we satisfy you by declaring that we not only do not say this, but also condemn as transgressors of the divine word those who, in their madness, first dared to say it: we condemn them as destroyers of the theology of Christ the Lord and of the holy Fathers who assembled synodically and handed down the holy Creed to us. We place them together with Judas, because they were not afraid to perpetrate the very same things that he did—not because they delivered the Lord’s body over to death, but because they separated and divided God’s faithful, who are his members, from one another through schism. Thus they cast themselves headlong into eternal fire, and all the more so they themselves, just as that aforesaid Judas, the unworthy disciple of Christ, strangled himself.

We suppose that your Reverence, since you are wise and endowed with learning, rightly understands that while we strive with all our strength to ensure that the rest of our bishops hold the same opinion as we do, this causes us no small distress. Indeed, no one could quickly alter so grave a matter, even if it had arisen only recently and had not been confirmed over the course of many years.

For this reason it seemed reasonable to us that no one among you should be violently compelled to abandon that addition which he knows himself to have added to the Creed. Rather, such men should be admonished with some gentleness and gradually recalled from blasphemy: “Feed,” says Peter, chief of the apostles, “the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight, not under compulsion but willingly, not as domineering over the clergy, but becoming examples to the flock” (1 Peter 5:2–3).

Those who therefore accuse us as though we held such opinions wrongly accuse us. It is fitting, then, that your fraternity neither suffer any scandal against us nor be cut off from the rest of the Church’s body, but rather endure with us the struggles of faith with prudence and patience, and recall to the embrace of the truth those who have departed from it, so that you may receive the same reward with us on their behalf.

Farewell in the Lord, most reverend and catholic brother.

### CCCLI. TO A CERTAIN [alternative: ROMAN ARCHBISHOP OF RAVENNA]. (Year 880.)

He praises his zeal toward the apostolic see and urges him to persevere; he promises to count him among his friends; he orders him to come to Rome.

As you stated to us by your letters and verbally through Deusdedit, your religious priest, that you wished to preserve undiminished, with all your strength, the faith and devotion which you ought to have toward the apostolic see, we have received this gladly.

Therefore we admonish you in every way and exhort you by these apostolic letters that no cunning or seduction by your enemies may in any way remove you from our fidelity; rather, in accordance with the tenor of your pledge, strive to remain in it with the utmost devotion.

Know, therefore, that, without any doubt, wishing to retain you among our beloved ones, we also wish and command you to come in person and without hesitation to our apostolic presence in Rome, both for the needs of the Church and for your own advantage. For, with the Lord’s help, we desire to preserve the status of the holy Church of Ravenna unharmed and to secure your advancement and honor.

### CCCLII. TO ATHANASIUS, BISHOP OF NAPLES. (Years 881–882.)

He absolves him from excommunication and restores him to the priestly ministry, provided that he breaks the pact made with the Saracens, as he had promised, and sends some of them captive after the others have been slaughtered, and thereafter makes no treaty with them.

To Athanasius, bishop of Naples.

Following the outstanding example of the Good Shepherd, who came to seek and save what was lost, we gladly receive you, who for so long wandered along byways, having cast aside Christ’s easy yoke and not hesitating, in disgraceful desire, to take up an obscure yoke with unbelievers, although at last you sent word that you wished to return to the one who struck you. We wish to retain you as especially honored among our fellow priests, just as you undoubtedly remember that we formerly did.

But because, at the prompting of your audacity in so great a crime, we justly removed you from our communion in the divine mystery by the judgment of the Holy Spirit, now, in accordance with your requests and the report of Peter, your venerable deacon, we absolve you from the bond of excommunication and restore to you the episcopal office according to the former custom, provided that you have openly broken the pact which you have hitherto maintained with the impious Hagarenes [Saracens] and have separated yourself by every effort from their most wicked association.

This is also conditional upon your capturing, together with all the others, as many of the Saracens as you can—especially the leading men whom we specifically seek—and sending them to us after the others have been slaughtered, with these envoys of ours present: namely, Marinus, most reverend bishop and treasurer of our holy see, and Sico, an outstanding man.

This absolution and restoration are granted on the express condition that, once the Saracens have been captured and handed over as stated, you presume thereafter to make no further treaty with them in any way. For if you again attempt to make any pact with them, we decree that you shall remain under the same excommunication and, by the authority of Almighty God, of the blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, and of ourselves, we decree that you are to be deprived of every episcopal honor and condemned by perpetual anathema.

### CCCLIII. TO THE GENEVESE. (Year 882.)

He orders them to obey Bishop Optandus, whom he consecrated.

To the clergy and people of Geneva.

Having learned from the report of our most beloved son, the Emperor Charles, and of his princes that your Church was without a shepherd, and that, because of the opposition of Boso, with whom the metropolitan of that same see appears to have allied himself, you were delaying the ordination of your elect, Optandus, we consecrated him by apostolic authority and power, in accordance with the petition of that most serene emperor—our spiritual son Charles—and his nobles. We had already learned of all your election of Optandus and of how that same most serene emperor had permanently granted the Church its election from its own clergy, lest the Church remain any longer without a shepherd.

With the grace of the Holy Spirit, we have therefore consecrated him and sent him to govern you pastorally. Receive him devoutly and unanimously, and obey him in all things as your own spiritual father. Nevertheless, the ancient privilege of that place’s own metropolitan see is to remain intact.

We decree that whoever attempts to oppose, resist, or disobey this authority of ours and this apostolic decision, or—God forbid—ever to pervert or violate the election of this Church, which, by God’s favor, has attained a just outcome, shall know that he is to be struck by the sword of canonical discipline and shall not escape the vengeance of Almighty God unless he is quickly healed by worthy satisfaction.

Finally, by the authority of our apostolate, we confirm that he is to possess all the property of that Church peacefully and quietly in perpetuity. Whoever dares to invade and disperse it, after having been canonically admonished by his own bishop, shall be condemned under anathema if he does not make amendment according to divine and human laws.

### CCCLIV. TO THE EMPEROR CHARLES. (Year 882.)

He complains that many possessions of the Roman Church have been seized by a certain Marquis Wido; he asks him to defend the Church and come in person as its helper.

To the Emperor Charles.

Both before you received the empire and after you assumed the imperial scepter, through the ministry of your humility divinely entrusted to you, we repeatedly cried out in great sorrow over the countless necessities and manifold oppressions that your holy mother, the Roman Church, suffers daily. Yet up to now we have been unable to obtain any help of the consolation we desired or any support for our defense.

For, concerning all the immovable properties of the territory of Saint Peter which, while we were staying at Ravenna, both Marquis Wido returned to us in your serene presence as restitution, we have not recovered even a single place. He and his men presume to retain everything against right and equity.

When we were staying in the Pentapolis, that is, in the city of Fano, Adelard, your most reverend bishop and your beloved and common faithful servant, came in accordance with the command of your delegation. There we awaited the presence of the aforesaid Wido and his followers, who had violently taken and retained our possessions, so that from there at least, with the beginning of every correction and justice, we might proceed through the other cities and receive everything according to your clemency’s decree, obtaining justice in the presence of your representative.

But since he was always fleeing judgment and craftily avoiding your most pious command, and since he did not come, it became clearly evident to us that it would be fruitless to travel through those cities, which were oppressed by their burden. We therefore sent, together with the same Adelard, your venerable bishop, your envoy Valpert, our most reverend bishop and faithful counselor, so that in our place he might receive the consolation of justice rendered to us in your presence and lawful restitution concerning all the other matters.

They departed, but received no fruit of justice and returned to us. Wishing entirely to remove every excuse from their defense, we decided to send them again, so that at least later we might receive justice. When they had again gone to the aforesaid Wido, they could obtain from him or his followers neither any correction nor any restitution, although it had been promised.

Thus he returned to us as before without any result, and your envoy returned to you entirely without justice, although our brother Adelard himself had struggled in many ways, with great and faithful devotion, to obtain justice.

Now, therefore, knowing for certain that we can obtain neither justice nor correction for such great evils through any envoy of your Highness, but only through your imperial presence, we earnestly ask and beseech Almighty God that you yourself, with God’s help, deign willingly to come to defend and free from the hands of the evildoers who savagely devour it the Church of the blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, entrusted to you. By divine providence she has chosen you to be her helper and defender in all things.

Thus, relying upon God’s and your support, she may securely retain what belongs to her together with the splendor of her former dignity, to the praise and everlasting reward of your soul.

### CCCLV. TO RICCARDIS, THE AUGUSTA. (Year 882.)

He complains that no help is being provided against the incursions of the Saracens; he asks her to request aid quickly from the emperor; he commends his envoy; he asks her to work for Angelberga’s recall from exile and her dispatch to Rome.

To Riccardis, the Augusta, or to Liutward, bishop of Vercelli, from his peers.
