Such anguish of heart, such pain and groaning, with streams of flowing tears on every side, shake and shatter our age; and such mourning for the devastation of this land—which we now see utterly plundered by the enemies of the Christian name, the Saracens hated by God—afflicts us and dissolves our inmost being, that sleep flees from our eyes and food from our taste.

With Jeremiah I am compelled to sing: “Who will give water to my head, or a fountain of tears to my eyes?” (Jeremiah 9:1), and the rest. Indeed, we expected light, and behold darkness; we sought help, and we do not dare to leave the walls of the City.

Before your arrival in Rome, we had at least some degree of tranquility; now, however, the storm of persecution is intolerable and unbearable, because neither our spiritual son, the Augustus, nor anyone from any other nation provides us assistance. Unless the supreme Divinity comes to our aid, we shall fall into despair; for we see an army coming against us not merely twice as large, as the Lord says, but even three or four times as large. We shall seek terms of peace; or else we shall not only be forced to submit to their yoke, but, once captured by them, shall also be wickedly slaughtered.

As you know, we have cried out very often, yet neither the Augustus himself, as we have said, has offered us any defense whatsoever, nor has he withdrawn from the yoke of those foreigners the men of our cities who are held by them against God and against all our privileges—as though they were not our men—in order to perform service for the holy Roman Church, as was customary.

Therefore, dearest daughter, having heard these cries and lamentations of ours—for we speak to wise people—immediately, for God’s sake and for the sake of his holy apostles, kneel before our aforesaid spiritual son, the Augustus, and urge him, setting aside or at least suspending every other necessity, to come to the aid of the calamity of his holy mother. Let him perceive her trampling and indeed her destruction and, before we perish, provide the swiftest assistance, or promptly give suitable counsel.

For our life is of no benefit to us; and, placed at the extremity, even if we did not desire it, death already presents itself openly to our view.

Also show the greatest goodwill to the venerable Bishop Peter, whom we trust greatly and who is our most beloved familiar, and, since he was sent from so great a see, grant him the most fitting place of familiarity with the lord Augustus. Trust him completely on our behalf, so that whatever he reports in words may, through your efforts, be fulfilled in deeds.

We also beg this of you: because the Augustus’s mind was angered against him at Ticinum when that same bishop explained to the Augustus the matters which we had entrusted to him, let whatever it may have been be entirely erased by your insistence. Let the imperial mind also be made agreeable in every respect toward treating this bishop kindly, since he had not spoken these things defiantly or against imperial dignity, but, moved by zeal for God, did not wish to return to us without effect.

Finally, daughter who worships Christ and is beloved of God, we are distressed that, although we have often entreated you, we have been unable through you to provide any remedy for our spiritual daughter Angelberga, so that, her exile being dissolved, we might have her brought back to the holy Apostle Peter.

Therefore we now earnestly beg that, for the love of God and of us, the holy apostolic see may be honored in this matter. As the aforesaid Augustus likewise promised you, may she be brought back safe and unharmed from the captivity in which she is being held without cause. For once she has been restored to us—having been entrusted to us and committed to the protection of her protector, the holy Apostle Peter—no one, believe us, will be able to harbor any sinister suspicion concerning her.

### CCCLVI. (Year 882.) Privilege for the monastery of Monte Cassino

(At Cocquilin, *Bullarium Diplomaticum*, etc., enlarged collection, vol. I, p. 881.)

JOHN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Bertharius, religious abbot of the venerable monastery of Blessed Benedict, confessor of Christ, situated at Cassino, and through him to that venerable monastery and to the entire congregation forever.

Since whatever accords with reasonable desires ought always to be granted, it is fitting that the devotion humbly acquired in me by the petitioner should not be denied by our clemency when privileges are being granted.

Therefore, because you asked us that the monastery of Blessed Benedict, confessor of Christ, and the monastery of Blessed Scholastica, together with the churches built in the several places and belonging to the aforesaid monasteries, should be adorned with the privileges of the apostolic see, so that, established under the jurisdiction of the holy Church which, by God’s authority, we serve, they might not be advanced or subjected to the power of any church or of any bishop, we favoring your pious desires, by this authority of ours commit to them what your petition requests.

Accordingly, we entirely prohibit any bishop of any church from exercising any jurisdiction whatsoever over the aforesaid venerable places. From now on and henceforth, let them look only to our apostolic see. We prohibit every innovation and violence against these monasteries, so that, unless invited by the abbot of the monastery, no one may presume to enter either to consecrate a church or to ordain a priest in the aforesaid monasteries or in any of the cells belonging to them; nor may any bishop presume in any way to celebrate the solemnity of Mass there.

For the consecration of a church in his monasteries or cells, we grant the abbot the power to invite whichever bishop he wishes, without anyone’s hindrance. Since they remain subject to apostolic privileges, what has been granted must remain steadfastly granted.

Together with our priestly college, we establish by this apostolic privilege all the places that those venerable monasteries have ever possessed, or that faithful people have now or later granted to them in different territories. No castald, bishop, or person of high or low status may, by any device or contrivance, invade those possessions in any way, exact tribute, or afflict the monks or servants. Rather, to the praise of Christ and the eternal memory of the donor, let them remain perpetually untouched by all and serve only the holy mother, the Roman Church.

Let no prelate henceforth dare to impose any excommunication upon the monks subject to our holy Church in these places. Let them be permitted to perform the divine offices in the manner prescribed to them by Blessed Benedict through his Rule.

We also establish that no prelate may presume to exclude from the churches belonging to the said monasteries the people who come there to hear the word of God and confess their sins, whether in the cities or outside the cities. Rather, the devout people shall enter and leave there canonically, and your churches subject to your jurisdiction shall be open to all.

But since pastoral care has been entrusted to us by God so that we may deserve to be courageous in all things, lest, God forbid, the Lord’s sheep be torn by the bites of wolves, therefore, under the solemn testimony of the blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, we command and order all venerable bishops, priests, abbots, deacons, dukes, tribunes, counts, castalds, administrators, and all who fear God, by the authority of our apostolate.

The blessed Peter received from the Lord our God the power to bind and loose human sins in heaven and on earth, and by God’s divine grace we exercise his office. Through the text of this decree of ours, we forbid all prelates of every Church, and all persons endowed with whatever dignity or power, under the prohibition of anathema and the obligation of eternal judgment, to presume in any way to violate this present constitution granted by us for the aforesaid monastery. Whoever dares to do so shall be condemned under anathema.

Written by the hand of Anastasius, regional notary and archivist of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of May, in the fifteenth indiction. Farewell.

On the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, through the hands of Walpert, bishop of the Holy Church of Porto, in the tenth year—by God’s favor—of the pontificate of our lord John, supreme pontiff and universal pope, in the most sacred see of the blessed Apostle Peter; in the second year of the reign of our most pious lord Charles Augustus, crowned by God as great emperor.

### CCCLVII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF VIENNE. (Year 882.)

He rebukes him for appointing another man in the Church of Geneva after having thrust Bishop Optandus into prison; he orders him to restore Optandus to his see and to come to the synod to clear himself of the charges brought against him.

To Oteramo, archbishop of Vienne.

We have learned through a truthful report that Your Holiness consecrated a bishop in the Church of Geneva, although we, having considered the exigencies of the times and acting first at the urging of the clergy of that same Church, had already appointed over it by apostolic authority a bishop named Optandus. [Col. 0952B] When we heard this, we were exceedingly astonished at your boldness and temerity and were especially disturbed because you not only laid hands upon our ordination, but also, in contempt of and insult to the Apostolic See, shamefully seized the aforesaid bishop and thrust him into close confinement; after plundering all his property and belongings, you—[f. adds: “against or through”]—through your ministry, which no Christian is permitted to do, torment the priest of God in a foul prison. You evidently did not keep before your eyes the fact that Holy Scripture sometimes calls the priests of God “gods” and sometimes “angels,” and that whoever touches them touches the apple of the Lord’s eye (Zech. II).

[Col. 0952C] Therefore, by the authority of almighty God and of the chief apostles Peter and Paul, and likewise by our own, we command you that, upon receiving this letter—or learning its contents in whatever manner—if within eight days you neglect to return and restore the aforesaid bishop to his own see and to his own honor and dignity, you, together with all who support you in this action, shall be wholly excluded from the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ until you have endeavored to carry out our disposition according to these instructions.

And because many other matters are brought against you by certain persons, matters that must be corrected through synodal examination, we decree that, with every excuse removed, you must not fail to come to Rome to the synod on the eighth day before the Kalends of October of the coming first indiction, so that you may then give an account both of the charges brought against you and, if you have any complaint against the same bishop consecrated by us, so that we may be able, with God’s help, to determine whatever it may be by canonical judgment. Know this also: if you delay coming to that synod at the appointed time, we shall pronounce against you the canonical sentence of censure.

### CCCLVIII. TO OTERAMUS, ARCHBISHOP OF VIENNA. (Year 882.)

He deals with Bishop Optandus, replying to his letters, and with the letter he is sending to the bishop of Maurienne so that he may come to Rome.

To Oteramus, archbishop of Vienna.

Having received the letter of Your Fraternity, we have learned quite fully that it was composed, so to speak, out of zeal for some measure of rectitude; [Col. 0953A] for you admit that, after many events in the Church of Geneva, you consecrated a bishop, and that a certain cleric named Optandus, who had never been baptized, made a cleric, ordained, acclaimed, or instructed in the Church of Geneva, invaded that Church. We are astonished in many ways that you claim not to know what, as we think, the whole West knows. Indeed, earlier we had been informed that you had refused to consecrate a bishop in that same Church; therefore, having considered the exigencies of the times and at the urging of the clergy of that Church, we consecrated there, by apostolic authority, a bishop named Optandus. For this reason we judge that you did not act rightly when you laid hands upon our ordination [Col. 0953B] and ordained another bishop there.

As for your statement that Optandus himself had never been baptized, made a cleric, ordained, acclaimed, or instructed in the Church of Geneva, this must for the moment be covered in silence, since, speaking with charity toward you, Your Holiness was consecrated in the Church of Vienna while possessing none of these qualifications. Nevertheless, leaving these matters aside for the moment as necessary, we warned Your Holiness some time ago by letter that, because certain charges are brought against you which must be corrected by synodal examination, you should, with every excuse removed, make every effort to come to Rome to the synod on the eighth day before the Kalends of October of the coming first indiction. Nonetheless, we decree again that at the same time you present yourself before our apostolic presence, [Col. 0953C] so that you may then give an account of the charges brought against you and, if you have any complaint against the same bishop consecrated by us, we may be able, with God’s help, to determine whatever it may be by canonical judgment.

Moreover, we have sent to Adalbert, bishop of the Church of Maurienne, a letter of our authority, which we order you to deliver to him, so that he may come to Rome with Barnerius, bishop of the see of Grenoble, on that same eighth day before the Kalends of October, in order that, before us, he may offer full satisfaction for the matters he irreverently brought forward with such rash audacity, forgetting his own rank.

### CCCLIX. TO ADALBERT, BISHOP OF MAURIENNE. (Year 882.)

He orders him to come to Rome with the bishop of Grenoble, whom he had treated disgracefully.

[Col. 0953D]

To Adalbert, bishop of Maurienne.

A sorrowful report struck us when we heard that you, forgetful of your rank, entered the church of Barnerius, bishop of the see of Grenoble, at the morning hour when he was publicly performing the office, with a crowd of people and an armed force, and, without reverence, carried him away with you and treated him disgracefully, although he had given you no cause for offense. This displeased us as greatly as we altogether judge that you acted rashly. Therefore, by a letter of our apostolate, we command you, with every excuse removed, to come with the same venerable bishop Barnerius to our synod at Rome on the eighth day before the Kalends of October of the coming first indiction, [Col. 0954A] so that, possessing the rule of equity and with God’s help, we may endeavor in some manner to examine and determine whatever dispute has arisen between you.

### CCCLX. TO ANSELM, ARCHBISHOP OF MILAN. (Year 882.)

He confirms the privileges of the Church of Milan; exhorts him to remain faithful to the Roman Church; recounts the injuries inflicted by the Saracens and wicked Christians; asks him to pour out prayers to the Lord for the Church.

To Anselm, archbishop of the holy Church of Milan.

We willingly confirm the authority of the privilege of your Church in the manner Your Fraternity requested, being necessarily supported by apostolic moderation and moved by charitable affection. At the same time, we desire that you never cease, through the infusion of the Holy Spirit, to ask, seek, and do whatever is suitable and beneficial for the salvation of your soul and the protection of your flock . . . so that, when you must give an account before the tribunal of the eternal Judge, with the grace of His mercy cooperating, you may receive the reward of everlasting life with the saints.

Meanwhile, we exhort Your Fraternity’s affection to strive with all the mind’s strength and every devotion to remain entirely faithful to the holy Roman Church, your mother, which does not cease to labor for all of you and for your salvation, as a head does for its members. For in her exaltation and safety, as from the beginning, there will be for all of you a sure salvation before God and in the present age. We suffer such great persecutions in this land, both from pagans and from malicious Christians, that we cannot express them in words. Amid countless robberies, plunderings, and very many evils, to increase our grief, a certain criminal Lombard named—an associate of the margrave Wido—captured eighty-three men; after their hands had each been severed, many of them were immediately killed in the city of Narni as a result of this mutilation.

Therefore, together we beseech the Lord in prayer that He rescue His holy Church from its present evils—the Church for which He did not spare His only-begotten Son. And we, holding the pastoral staff in our hands, shall not cease, with the Lord’s protection, to resist the ravenous wolves. Given in the month of August, indiction XII [f. XV].

### CCCLXI. TO ROMANUS, ARCHBISHOP OF RAVENNA. (Year 882.)

He orders him to receive Deacon John kindly and restore the property taken from him.

To the most reverend and holy Romanus, archbishop of Ravenna.

Because not only at the time of your ordination, by letters and words according to custom and canonical sanction, but afterward also, very often, we took care to admonish you to be a suitable pastor, always maintaining a peaceful mind and cheerful affection toward the sons and members of your holy Church, we are greatly astonished that, by disregarding our admonitions, you have not hesitated, as we have heard, to inflict injury and intolerable hardships upon them. Therefore, by this present decree of our apostolate, we again command Your Fraternity that you receive kindly within the bosom of your holy Church this John, a venerable deacon and our commendatory dependent, who, having fled to our apostolic see and being unable to endure the injury inflicted upon him by you, requested our apostolic protection and assistance. Moved therefore by our customary mercy, we command you with apostolic benevolence to restore immediately, willingly and for love of us, the monasteries or property which your ministers have seized from him. Whatever they have taken from his property, you must restore in every way.

Do this so that henceforth it will not be necessary for him to complain to our apostolic ears. In the same way we also command you to take care to return at once to John, the venerable deacon and chartulary of your Church, the monastery of Saint Martin, which he formerly obtained from you by his merit. We have sent our instruction to you in apostolic benevolence so that you may carry this out peacefully. But, although we do not believe it, if Your Fraternity acts otherwise, these our legates, supported by our apostolic authority, will undoubtedly endeavor to accomplish this. For we judge it right that, after the long services and enduring duties they have performed in the holy Church of Ravenna, they should not only not be deprived of worthy remuneration but should rather rejoice gladly in the benefits they have acquired. Let Your Fraternity act in this matter so that you may in every way obtain what you have requested from us for the benefit of your Church. Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, indiction XV.

### CCCLXII. TO THE CLERGY OF RAVENNA. (Year 882.)

He orders them to hand over to his legate and to Duke John a certain Maimbert, whom he had previously ordered expelled from the Church of Ravenna, after he has been captured, and to arrange for him to be sent to the pope.

To all the venerable priests and subdeacons, and to the entire clergy of the holy Church of Ravenna.

Having often heard of the affliction and misery you continually suffer because of Maimbert, a cleric of Bologna, we sent you long ago our apostolic authority through John, deacon and chartulary, ordering you all, with one mind and steadfast devotion, to expel the aforesaid Maimbert, a most notorious sower of weeds, from the archbishop and from your holy Church as though he were a diseased sheep. We are astonished that you have so far neglected this. Therefore, now moved again by your petition and inflamed by divine love, through this apostolic authority we command all of you, after rereading the earlier letter, to join together unanimously and faithfully unite yourselves with our present envoy. If the same Maimbert, your adversary, refuses to come to us of his own accord or wishes to go off in any direction, you must boldly endeavor to seize him; then hand him over to this envoy of ours and also to our faithful Duke John, so that, in accordance with our command, they may exact what is due from him and bring him to us, if you wish to have the grace of almighty God, the holy apostles, and ourselves.

For if any one of you withdraws from this in any way, on account of any matter whatsoever, and neglects to carry out gladly this command, issued for the welfare and peace of the holy Church of Ravenna, let him remain suspended, by the authority of almighty God, the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and our apostolic authority, from wine and cooked food and also from his own ministry until our presence. Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, indiction XV.

### CCCLXIII. TO JOHN, MARTIN, AND OTHERS. (Year 882.)

The same subject.

[Col. 0956B]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Martin, John, Demetrius, and Romanus, illustrious dukes, and also to our other faithful.

Let the fidelity of all of you know that we have very often admonished Romanus, archbishop, both through venerable bishops and also by our apostolic letters, to separate Maimbert, the cleric of Bologna, from his extremely superstitious intimacy and send him back to his own Church, as is canonical. Maimbert himself also repeatedly declared before us that he would withdraw; but they were wholly unwilling to comply with our [Col. 0956C] apostolic command. Therefore, commanding, we command, and expressly ordering, we order you to join together unanimously with this faithful envoy of ours, setting aside every pretext and removing every delay, seize the aforesaid Maimbert, forcibly separate him from the archbishop, and hand him over with all your strength to this envoy of ours and to Duke John, so that they may exact him according to our apostolic authority.

But if you, whose names are written above, are negligent in this, and he somehow escapes from you, know that each one of you shall pay one hundred gold pieces to our treasury. Moreover, by the authority of almighty God, the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and our apostolic authority, remain suspended from wine and cooked food [Col. 0956D] until our presence. As for the others, if they do not wish to accomplish what we command, or if by withdrawing they turn aside here or there in any way and do not persevere until the matter is completed, let them be subject to the foregoing excommunication. Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, indiction XV.

### CCCLXIV. TO DUKE JOHN. (Year 882.)

He orders him to bring the captured Maimbert to the pope, detain the women who are with him, and arrange for the letter to be delivered to Archbishop Romanus.

To John, beloved duke, our faithful man and envoy.

You should believe that we rejoice greatly because we have found your fidelity toward the holy Roman Church and our apostolate to be steadfastly vigilant [reperitur: “is found”]. Therefore, through these apostolic letters we command your fidelity to see to the matter of Maimbert in every way, as you have written, acting together with this envoy of ours, so that he cannot escape in any manner. After you have resolutely exacted all his possessions from him, separated him by force from the archbishop, and compelled him to submit, endeavor to bring him under guard to our presence. We also order you to retain in our administrative residence the women whom he now keeps gathered in his dwelling, until we are informed.

As for the letter that we are sending to Archbishop Romanus, ordering him to restore the property or monasteries which he has in any way seized from John, our faithful commendatory deacon, to invest him in possession of everything, and to have his servants return whatever they have taken from John’s property, deliver it to the archbishop and have it read before priests and judges. Likewise, according to our command, let him return the monastery of Saint Martin to John, the deacon and chartulary, for love of us. The dwelling which Maimbert fraudulently took from that same deacon you must likewise endeavor to restore to him, together with his nephew Peter, by investing them in possession. Given as above, indiction XV.

### CCCLXV. TO CHARLES, THE EMPEROR. (Year 882.)

He congratulates him on his safety; rejoices that he is about to come immediately to Italy; exhorts him to come promptly to the aid of the Roman Church and order the plunderer Wido to be driven from the Church’s territories.

[Col. 0957C]

To Charles, the emperor.

When we learned of your safety—which we had ardently desired—we gave thanks to God, and with suppliant prayers we earnestly implored the divine majesty to support you more and more with prosperity and countless joys, knowing and learning through many experiences that you desire the same things: for if our modest means should have strength and be effective, they will urge you to do this, whereby the defense of the holy Roman Church, your mother, will be increased and abundant reward will be stored up for you forever in heaven.

As for your statement that, setting aside your other concerns, you have arranged your journey to Italy by a direct route, we received it with grateful spirit; and, if only you were not merely at Pavia but even nearer, the greatest necessity demands it. Therefore let Your Sublimity, with God’s help, quickly complete what you have begun, and, as you have said, setting aside other concerns, come powerfully in mind and arm to the defense—or rather the security—of the holy Roman Church, for we can no longer express how greatly it is afflicted and trampled down.

Moreover, concerning Wido of Rabia, the invader and plunderer, let Your Glory come to our aid and order him by every means to be driven from our territories, so that our people may at least be somewhat relieved. Given on the third day before the Ides of November.

### CCCLXVI. TO LIUTWARD, BISHOP. (Year 882.)

He gives thanks because he took pains to bring the emperor to Italy for the defense of the Church.

[Col. 0958A]

To Liutward, bishop.

We give you thanks for your effort—which, as you assert, you made together with our spiritual daughter, the empress, so that the lord emperor might enter Italy for the defense of the holy Roman Church—and we strongly exhort you to complete, through your persistence, what remains to be done, as you well know. For we need this so greatly that we cannot explain it. Therefore act in such a way that we may give you greater and greater thanks and be encouraged to repay you in temporal benefits.

### CCCLXVII. TO ALL BISHOPS. (Years 879–882.)

He admonishes them to observe his ordinances and judge justly.

[Col. 0958B]

Address and exhortation of the pontiff to all the bishops.

Behold, most holy priests: after offering the preceding prayers, I address Your Fraternity with pious exhortation and beseech you by the divine name to receive with all piety whatever we have said concerning God, the sacred orders, or holy conduct, and to intend to carry it out with the greatest reverence. If perhaps any one of you has understood anything differently from what was said, let him, without any contentious scruple, bring back for discussion among the fellowship of us all the very matters about which he has doubted, so that, with God’s help, he may either be instructed or instruct others. [Col. 0958C]

Furthermore, together I earnestly charge, entreat, and beseech you that none of you, when judging, accept a person or knowingly turn aside or depart from a just judgment, impelled by any favor or gift. Rather, with complete piety, reconsider the case of anyone who has brought himself before our assembly to be judged. Thus neither contentious disagreement should find a place among us for the overthrow of justice, nor should the strength or diligence of your order grow lukewarm in seeking equity. Given as above.

### CCCLXVIII. TO CHARLES, THE KING. (Year uncertain.)

An insertion urging him to confirm King Carlomannus in love of the Roman Church.

[Col. 0958D]

Now, because we see you, dearest son, to be endowed with such great devotion and such great fidelity toward the pontificate of the Roman Church, your mother, we admonish you as one born from her womb, and ask and urge you, for the love of the chief apostles, as though it were your own concern and not through a representative, to send to the glorious King Carlomannus, giving him counsel that, honoring his old friends and enjoying their affection, he should return to the counsel of his parents and answer the letters which we sent him from the maritime journey. He should reverently love the Roman Church, which has brought royal and imperial honor to both of you, sending in person to the excommunicated Lambert and Adalbert. Given as above.

### CCCLXIX. TO MICHAEL, KING OF THE BULGARIANS.

[Col. 0959A]

John VIII to Michael, king of the Bulgarians.

If you receive any sacraments from those whom we held to be excommunicated, it is clear that you appear to have abandoned idolatry, not so that you might be Catholics, but so that you might become schismatics [*deliquisse* for *dereliquisse*, HARD.].

### CCCLXX. TO LUITBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ. Fragment—(Year uncertain.)

Know that Engeltrude, the wife of Boso, has been struck repeatedly not only by excommunication, which separates one from fraternal fellowship, but also by anathema, which cuts one off from the very body of Christ, which is the Church.

### CCCLXXI. TO LOUIS, THE EMPEROR. Fragment—(Year uncertain.)

[Col. 0959B]

You see, dearest son, that what is accepted contrary to the laws deserves to be dissolved through the laws. Likewise, without doubt, the one who does not correct what he can correct bears the guilt of the one who acts. For it is written: “Not only those who do these things, but also those who consent, are judged participants.” And he offers favorable things to the Lord who drives adversities away from the afflicted. To neglect, when one can overthrow the wicked, is nothing other than to encourage them; nor is he free from the scruple of secret consent who ceases to oppose an open crime. And he proves that he hates vices who condemns those who err; he leaves himself no opportunity to deviate who has not spared the transgressor. The first degree of innocence is to hate wicked things. He opens a broad entrance to delinquents who joins consent to depravity; and it is of no benefit to someone not to be punished for his own offense if he must be punished for another’s sin.

### CCCLXXII. TO THE BISHOPS OF BRITAIN. (Year uncertain.)

What should be done concerning monks ordained by their abbot.

John, servant of the servants of God, bishop of the Roman city, sends greeting in Christ and visitation to all the bishops of nearer Britain, brothers in Christ.

Because, by the place of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, and by the Lord God’s gracious will, we have undertaken the care of all the Churches, we must everywhere carefully ensure that the faith of each person is preserved intact in the same Lord, without which no one can please Him. Therefore let it be known to you that our dearest brother Arduinus, archbishop of the holy Church of Tours, came to Rome to pray at the threshold of the apostles and appealed to us because the rights of his archbishopric, which from ancient times had been granted and confirmed to his predecessors through the decrees of the holy pontiffs of the holy Roman mother Church, appear to have been taken away by your archbishop and his predecessors through violence and through the opposition of the pagan Northmen.

Therefore, by apostolic authority, know that you are forbidden henceforth in any way to resist his right concerning all the matters which the aforesaid archbishop confirms ought to belong to his archbishopric, until your archbishop—or someone among you together with Archbishop Arduinus, whether with his suffragan or another faithful envoy—comes to our holy mother Church, so that, after the cases between you and him have been examined there, whatever we establish as equitable may be determined, to the praise of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ. But if you act otherwise than we command, against his will, know that by the authority of God and of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, through the command of our humility, you yourselves are excommunicated from every ecclesiastical office.

If, however, you are willing to observe due reverence toward the aforesaid brother of ours, remain, according to the decree of justice established by the holy Roman Church, in the unity of our Catholic communion with God’s blessing. Meanwhile, let the people of your kingdom, especially the nobles—namely Berengarius, his son Conanus, and Hoel with his brother Guerech, together with the other leading men—know that if they are disobedient to this command of ours against justice and become opponents or rebels against our aforesaid brother, the bishop of Tours, they too shall be excommunicated and deprived of our apostolic blessing.

### CCCLXXIII. TO A CERTAIN PERSON.

The administrators of secular dignities, who have been appointed for the protection of churches and widows and the restraint of plunderers, whenever they are approached by ecclesiastical men, should listen attentively to their complaints and diligently and quickly carry out whatever is necessary for them. If they neglect to avenge or correct these matters, after a third admonition they shall be deprived of communion.

### CCCLXXIV. TO ANOTHER UNKNOWN PERSON.

When governors have been promoted to the governorship, they should receive ecclesiastical letters of communion, but in such a way that, wherever they exercise the governorship, the bishops of that place are to take responsibility for them, so that, if they begin to act against public discipline, they may exclude them from divine communion.

### CCCLXXV. Address of the pontiff to the bishops near the end of the Synod of Troyes.

[Col. 0960D]

I wish you, my brothers and fellow bishops, to join with me unanimously in the defense of the holy Roman Church, which is acknowledged to be the head of all the Churches, until, with God’s help, we return to the see of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, with the armed military force of all your people. Concerning this, I ask you to give me here, without any delay, an immediate answer—not by postponing it, but with complete speed and the certainty of a pledge.

### CCCLXXVI. Another address of the pontiff to the king.

[Col. 0961A]

You, dearest son, glorious King Louis, I beg you to hasten, without procrastination or any delay, to the defense, liberation, and exaltation of the holy Roman Church, as your predecessors did and commanded you under solemn attestation to do; for you are ministers of God, avengers in wrath against those who do evil, and you do not bear the sword without cause. Take care lest, God forbid, that guilt cover you or your kingdom which once damnably ensnared certain ancient kings who spared the enemies and unfaithful of God. Or, if you prefer otherwise, give me an answer here in person without delay; I adjure you by God and by blessed Peter.

### CCCLXXVII. Address of Pope John to the Fathers of the Second Synod of Troyes concerning the excommunication of Lambert, Adalbert, and their other followers.

[Col. 0961B]

Dearest brothers, grieve with me and with the Apostolic See, which is the head and teacher of all God’s Churches, and which gave birth to you from her religious womb: kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and all judges of the earth, sacred brothers and fellow priests of God, venerable rulers of Christ’s Churches, and all men of the sacred order. Weep together with me and seek relief for the great injuries inflicted upon the Church of Saint Peter, chief of the apostles and keeper of the heavenly kingdom, to whom the power of binding and loosing was given by God. Mourn with immense sorrow the many invasions and insults inflicted upon the city of Rome; [Col. 0961C] and stand courageously with me, who bear care and solicitude for all of you and, according to the Lord’s command, must, whenever the cause requires, turn to confirm you in every good work and provide the aid of necessary consolation. Together seek out and judge the perpetrators of such great iniquity and the perpetrators of such great presumption, so that, punished temporally with fitting vengeance, they may be saved in spirit on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.

For we excommunicated the aforesaid Lambert and Adalbert and their followers, on account of the great crimes and perjuries exposed against them, in the church of blessed Peter the apostle, together with our fellow bishops and Italian brothers; and because they persisted in these things, we decreed that they should be excluded from Christian communion. We placed that decree, written in the aforesaid church of blessed Peter, so that those entering and leaving might read it and grieve, and hold them anathematized. And you, dearest brothers, hold them alien from our communion, as we decreed, and together with me overthrow their supporters as anathematized persons.

### CCCLXXVIII. The bishops’ response.

[Col. 0961D]

Most holy and most reverend lord, Father of Fathers, John, pope of the Catholic and Apostolic Church, namely of the Roman first see: we, servants and disciples of Your Authority, the bishops of Gaul and Belgium, grieve with you over the things which malicious men and ministers of the devil have committed against our holy mother and teacher of all the Churches, adding them to the wounds of your sorrows. We share your grief, pouring out our lament with yours, and, by our vote, voice, and unanimity, and by the authority of the Holy Spirit, by whose grace we have been consecrated in the episcopal order, we pursue and destroy them with the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. [Col. 0962A]

Those whom you have excommunicated we hold excommunicated; those whom you have cast out from the Church we cast out; those whom you have anathematized we judge to be anathematized; and those whom Your Authority and the Apostolic See receive after they have made regular satisfaction, we shall receive.

But, as we read in the sacred history about the Egyptian plague justly inflicted by God (Exod. XII), because there was no house in which a dead person did not lie, and no one was able to console another, since each person had something in his own house to mourn, so we too mourn in our Churches the things that must be mourned. Therefore, with all humility of mind, we ask that your authority come to our aid, requesting that you promulgate a chapter of your authority instructing us how we ought to act toward those who invade our Churches, so that, strengthened by the censure of the Apostolic See, we and our successors may thereafter be able, with greater strength and readiness and with one judgment, to stand against the wicked plunderers and devastators of ecclesiastical property and resources and the despisers of the sacred episcopal ministry, with the Lord’s help. Thus, according to the word of the distinguished preacher and the promulgation of Your Authority, having been handed over to Satan, they may be saved in spirit on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.

### CCCLXXIX. Excommunication enacted at the same synod against those who seize ecclesiastical property.

Concerning those who seize ecclesiastical property, whom the sacred canons—composed by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world—and the decrees of the pontiffs of the Apostolic See have established to remain under anathema until regular satisfaction; and also concerning robbers, of whom the Apostle, with Christ speaking through him, testifies that they shall not possess the kingdom of God (I Cor. VI), and commands that no true Christian should even eat with such a person while he remains in that crime (I Cor. V): by the power of Christ and the judgment of the Holy Spirit we decree that, if before the coming Kalends of November the usurpers do not return to their respective Churches the same property which each unjustly seized, after making regular satisfaction, they shall be held excluded from communion of the body and blood of Christ until the ecclesiastical property has been restored and satisfaction made.

And those who despise the excommunication of the ecclesiastical episcopal ministry, according to evangelical and apostolic authority (Matt. XVIII), after being admonished by the bishops concerned, if they do not repent and make regular satisfaction, shall remain bound by the bond of anathema until satisfaction. If they die persisting in that obstinacy, no one shall bury their bodies with hymns and psalms, nor shall their memory be held at the sacred altar among the faithful dead, as the apostle and evangelist John teaches: “There is sin unto death; concerning that I do not say that anyone should pray” (I John V). For sin unto death is perseverance in sin until death. The sacred canons of the ancient Fathers, inspired by the Holy Spirit, have likewise decreed concerning those who voluntarily inflict death upon themselves and those who are punished for their crimes, that their bodies are not to be carried to burial with hymns and psalms.

Following their decrees, we too decree by the judgment of the Holy Spirit what we have set forth concerning those who seize and rob ecclesiastical property and resources, if they do not repent, just as blessed Gregory decreed, saying that such persons are not Christians, and whom I, all Catholic bishops, and indeed the universal Church anathematize.

### CCCLXXX. Pope John’s repeated excommunication against Bishop Formosus, Gregory the nomenclator, and George, master of soldiers.

By apostolic authority we again pronounce an equal sentence against Formosus, very recently bishop of Porto, and Gregory, master of soldiers: a sentence of anathema and perpetual obligation. And because they do not cease to trouble the ears of kings and princes, and, joining themselves with plunderers and subverters of Churches, daily strive to add new and recent evils to their former ones, we condemn them by the power of the Holy Spirit of our God with an indissoluble perpetual bond and without hope of recovery. We irrevocably exclude from them every presumption of obtaining pardon, and all who have communicated with them or provided them assistance—of whatever rank, whether episcopal or lay, powerful, middling, or poor—shall be involved in the curses pronounced against them if they do not fear to associate with them; and unless they repent, let them be anathema maranatha.

### CCCLXXXI. Decree of Pope John against laymen who, while their wives are living, take other wives, and against bishops who, for reasons of ambition, transfer from a lesser to a greater Church.

[Col. 0963D]

Among several matters brought before the holy synod, it was complained that certain laymen, after first lawfully contracting marriages, later, setting aside the fear of God, contracted the bond of a second or third marriage while their wife was still living. Among these, it is reported by the widespread testimony of many that a certain Otilo did so within the parish of Rostagnus, bishop of Arles, and Eooldus within that of Ottramnus, archbishop of Vienne.

As an increase to these transgressions, and something we grievously lament, it was also added that certain bishops within the seven provinces of Gaul, trampling upon the boundary established by the Fathers [Col. 0964A] and despising the enactment of canonical authority, move from a lesser to a greater episcopal see out of ambition. The canons, in harmony through the grace of the Holy Spirit, oppose them. We likewise, supported by the authority of those whom we reverently imitate and embrace, whose statutes we approve, and whose Churches we govern, forbid this by our authority and prohibit it with adherence to the law, so that no Catholic may henceforth dare to act in this way; and if, contrary to our wishes, anything of this kind has been done previously, let it be corrected by fitting ecclesiastical penance.

Finally, by this apostolic authority and through the power of our God, we intercede that the bishops return without delay to their former sees, because if they delay they will immediately be stripped of every priestly honor [Col. 0964B]; and let the laymen return to their first marriage. Otherwise, let them be bound by the bond of anathema.

## CCCLXXXII. TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF AUGUSTODUNUM

*(Date uncertain.) Privilege granting them the right to place over themselves one of their own whom the clergy and people have proclaimed, notwithstanding any contrary choice by kings or princes.*

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the sons of the holy Church of Autun, and through you to your successors forever.

It has been heard by our apostolic ears, and has often been repeatedly reported, that violence is inflicted upon the Churches of Gaul contrary to the decrees of the canons in the election of their bishops [Col. 0964C]. We, who—although unworthy—have been entrusted with the care of all the Churches, grieve over this from our inmost heart. Desiring to cut away this violence, introduced throughout all the Churches, by the authority of God and blessed Peter, we have especially decreed that this privilege of our present decree be written for you, namely for the holy Church of Autun, first exhorting the kings of the Franks to observe it.

In it we decree and regularly ordain that henceforth no king, prince, or any other person presume to place or appoint over you or your successors anyone except one from the sons of that very Church, in accordance with the provisions of the canons, whom the clergy shall have elected and the people proclaimed, if a worthy person can be found in it. But if—as we do not believe will happen—no such person is found in it, then, by the unanimous counsel of both clergy and people [Col. 0964D], let the worthiest person from elsewhere be sought.

Finally, with respect to the honor which you have obtained from your elder, we grant you permission, by the authority of this apostolic see, to establish and choose legitimate heirs from your own households, your canonries, the common resources of the brethren, and all your property, without anyone’s dispute or impediment. But if anyone, great or small, should presume in any respect to rise against this decree of ours and this grant of generosity, or to violate or weaken our apostolic authority, let him know that, by invocation of the Holy Trinity, by the power of the blessed apostle Peter, and by our authority, he is eternally [Col. 0965A] struck down and condemned forever, together with the enemies of God and those who oppose Him, until satisfaction has been made.

But may those who preserve this decree of ours obtain peace, joy, and blessing from God, the giver of all good things [Col. 0966A], and may they deserve to possess eternal life.

Written by the hand of Theodore, scriniarius of the holy Roman Church, in the month of March and the sixth indiction. Given … Farewell.

# In the Year of the Lord 884. Pope Marinus I

[Col. 0965]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

*(In Mansi, Expanded Collection of the Sacred Councils.)*

[Col. 0965B] Marinus, a native of the town of Gallese, was elected pope three days after the death of John VIII, on the Kalends of February, by the unanimous consent of the entire clergy—not from the rank of deacon, but as a bishop—in the year of the Lord 882, during the reign of Charles III and the rule of the emperor Basil. He occupied the see for one year and twenty-one days.

While he was cardinal-deacon of the holy Roman Church, he was sent with Donatus and Leo to Constantinople to announce to Photius the sentence of anathema with which he had been struck by Pope Nicholas. Together with Donatus and Stephen, during the time of Adrian II and on a renewed apostolic embassy, the holy man deposed Photius at Constantinople, restored Ignatius, and presided over the eighth holy ecumenical synod. The Bulgarians repeatedly asked Adrian II that he be given to them as their bishop, but they did not obtain this.

Having been made bishop by Pope John and being about to undertake a third embassy, he was sent for the third time to Constantinople, to repair the ruin which had been caused there when Peter, Paul, and Eugene—three envoys of the apostolic see—had been sent to the synod to restore Photius [Col. 0965C]. After he had there, with the greatest firmness of spirit, before the emperor Basil, rendered null everything that the aforesaid three legates had wrongly done, he was detained in prison for thirty days, as Stephen says in his letter to the emperor Basil.

Crowned with this glorious testimony of confession, he was sent by the same John VIII to Athanasius, bishop and prince of the city of Naples, so that, if Athanasius dissolved the treaty which he had made with the Saracens, Marinus might absolve him from the sentence of excommunication which had been imposed upon him by synodal judgment. John the pope’s Letter 294 indicates that Marinus had been treasurer of the apostolic see.

At the beginning of his pontificate he condemned Photius and all his acts relating to the episcopal office, and completely rejected the acts of the pseudo-eighth council. For this reason the emperor Basil, gravely offended and inflamed with great fury, wrote to Rome saying that Marinus was not pope, because he had previously been ordained bishop of another Church [Col. 0965D]. He also uttered many other accusations against that most holy pope and strove to cast him down from the papal throne. What Pope Stephen, Marinus’s successor, wrote back to Basil in his defense will be found below in Stephen’s letter.

Intending to rescind the wrongful actions of Pope John, Marinus, among other things, recalled Formosus, bishop of Porto, who had performed his apostolic office among the Bulgarians with distinction and had been adorned by the merits of other embassies. John had deposed Formosus from the episcopate and bound him by oath never to return to the episcopal see, but to remain thereafter content with lay communion. Marinus restored him to the city and episcopate and returned him to his former status.

For what reason he had been deposed by John, and in what manner he was restored by Marinus, is not certain. There is no doubt that Marinus could have absolved him from an oath unjustly exacted and retracted Pope John’s sentence as inequitable and perhaps issued out of private feeling. Which of these things occurred is uncertain; and therefore it is remarkable that people ignorant of what had happened should reproach Formosus because he resumed the pontificate.

These matters are taken by Baronius from various letters of the popes.

He granted the pallium to Fulco, archbishop of Reims, who had been substituted for Hincmar, after Fulco had professed the orthodox faith. Flodoard, *Life of Fulco*.

At the request of King Alfred he freed from tribute the School of the English that existed at Rome. Matthew of Westminster.

Since Marinus is named in all the places cited above, Onuphrius rightly reproves Platina’s error, namely, that Platina writes that those who call him something other than Martin were deceived by the similarity of the names.

During his time the Northmen devastated by fire and plunder the cities and strongholds of Trier, Tongeren, Cologne, and the other surrounding peoples. Baronius, from the *Acts of Saint Gudila* and the Frankish annals.

At this time the schismatic Photius, responding to an ignorant and schismatic archbishop of Aquileia concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit, gave occasion for the Roman Church—just as long before this the Churches of Spain and Gaul had done, and also in order to blunt the heresy of Photius and his followers concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit—to add the expression *Filioque* (“and from the Son”) to the Constantinopolitan Creed in later centuries and to sing it publicly in church. When, for what purpose, by whose authority, and in what manner this was done, Baronius reports from Aetherianus and the Council of Florence under the year 833, number 34 and following.

Marinus, having commendably fulfilled his apostolic office, departed this life on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February in the year of the Redeemer 884, after having occupied the pontificate for one year and twenty-one days. After his death the see was vacant for two days.

[Col. 0967]

# PRIVILEGES OF POPE MARINUS

## I. FOR THE MONASTERY OF SOLESMES

*(Year 883.)*

*(In Mansi, Collection of the Councils.)*

[Col. 0967A] Marinus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved abbot Daniel of the monastery of Saint Peter of Solemnes, formerly built by the blessed man Eligius, and to your successors and the monks nobly dwelling there forever.

It is fitting for our pontificate that, just as it rises above all others in dignity, so it should shine above all in the most serene piety. You therefore asked us to place the aforesaid monastery under the protection and guardianship of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and of ourselves [Col. 0967B], just as we read that this was done by our predecessor, the blessed pope, at the request of the most noble king of the Franks, Dagobert, and of the holy man Eligius, bishop of Noyon, the builder of that place, so that you may be able to remain peaceful and secure in time to come.

We, recognizing your holiness and granting assent to your religious devotion, concede this with as much eagerness and joyful mind as we recognize you to be closer to God in your sacred way of life. Therefore, in accordance with your petition, by a decree of our present authority we bestow, grant, and confirm this privilege upon the same venerable monastery, for your times and those of your successors.

Just as the most noble king of the Franks Dagobert, and the most glorious emperors Charles and his son [Col. 0967C] Louis, and their sons and grandsons, the emperor Charles and the same Charles’s son Louis, as well as Carloman, son of Louis, who now appears to govern the kingdom of the Franks successfully, moved by divine love, gave from their estates, resources, or revenues, or whatever goods were bestowed there in any manner by faithful men, and just as you have acquired them by whatever means, as is contained in the charters of the aforesaid kings or inserted in the charter of the founder of the same monastery, namely Bishop Eligius, so by the privilege of our authority we confirm all these things intact and undisturbed.

We also grant permission for a fortification to be constructed there on account of the persecution of the unbelievers who devastate Christendom. By another authority of blessed Peter we establish that no king, bishop, abbot, or anyone endowed with any dignity presume, under any pretext or appearance of a cause, to diminish or remove anything from what is contained in the aforementioned charters, or what in the future may lawfully be granted to these particular uses by them or by anyone from his own property; nor may anyone grant such things to others under the pretense of pious causes as an excuse for his own greed.

Rather, everything that has been offered, or may happen to be offered, for the use of the monks [Col. 0967D] or the Church [Col. 0968A] shall remain forever, without any disturbance, beneficial to those to whom it has been granted. It is also decreed that no bishop or count presume to demand or exact there *mansionaticum*, *paratae*, or lodging-stations. Instead, let the servants of God be permitted to serve God without disturbance and to extend the kindness of hospitality to all the faithful as they wish.

It has pleased us to insert into this document that, when the abbot of the aforesaid monastery dies, no one may presume, through any ambitious act of seizure, to install an abbot there except one whom the monks of that place, according to authentic and regular institution, have chosen from among themselves to be appointed.

But if anyone, recognizing this constitutional document, attempts to act against it [Col. 0968B], let him be excluded from the most sacred body of the Lord Jesus Christ; and unless he corrects what he has presumed or restores what he has wrongly taken, let him receive punishment with Judas the betrayer and experience blessed Peter as his enemy.

But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who observe what is just toward that place, so that they may find here the fruit of good action.

Written by the hand of Zachariah, scriniarius of the holy Roman Church, in the month of May, in the first indiction. Farewell. On the day before the Ides of June, by the hand of Valentine, bishop of the Church of Porto, while our Lord God reigns forever. In the first year of the pontificate of Lord Marinus, universal pope, in the first indiction.

## II. FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAVIGNY

*(Year 883.)*

*(From Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. IV, p. 657.)*

[Col. 0968C] Marinus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved, most reverend, and most holy Gerard, bishop of the holy Church of Lodi, and through you to the present and future members of that Church and monastery of Savigny forever.

From your account we have learned that, through the generosity of the emperors and kings who lived in our times, and through their diligent service toward them, the monastery of Savigny was granted to your Church and confirmed by their charters, in such a way and under such terms that regular discipline should always be observed in that monastery, while the right to the things granted to it for its own uses was preserved.

But you, taking precautions lest after your departure any of your successors, or any other secular power, be able to overturn that monastery from its proper condition and order by subverting or invading the property or households there, faithfully asked, by the authority and privilege of the apostolic see, that the things which had been assigned and granted by charter to the uses of the monks and the benefit of the whole monastery, by the most pious emperor Louis of blessed memory, and afterward carefully provided for, should be confirmed to it with equitable consideration.

These included: from the city of Tortona, whatever belongs to the little abbey itself as far as the monastery; in the counties of Tortona and Genoa; on the sea-coast and in Tuscany; also the village of Arderato and that of Pasqualino; and the house at Pavia with its steward at Aurello. The bishop of Lodi was to retain and possess the remainder of that little abbey for the benefit of his own Church, for the defense and protection of the same monks, namely for every watch and expedition, both palatine and military.

Therefore, through the grace and power which have been bestowed upon us by God through the merits of the apostles, as stated above [Col. 0969B], and in accordance with the common wish and equitable moderation of both parties, we confirm by apostolic authority and decree, with the Lord Jesus Christ as author, that this shall henceforth remain inviolable.

We also decree that when the present abbot of that place, Adalbert, or his successors, have been taken from this light by divine summons, another shall be appointed by common agreement, not from elsewhere but from that very community. If, however, because of the election itself, disagreement among the brethren, or any other necessity of that place, the bishop of Lodi—indeed, no one else—or his representatives should come when summoned to assist the monastery, its cells, or its estates, they shall bring no more than thirty men and forty horses. They shall be provided stipends from the monastery’s own resources and shall not remain there more than three days, unless the abbot and the brethren ask them to stay longer because of charity or necessity [Col. 0970A].

Three times each year, either the abbot or the monks from that place shall honorably visit the bishop of Lodi in his church and be received there.

Moreover, we decree that if the abbot of the same monastery should ever recognize that he is being unjustly burdened by that bishop or by others, he may freely appeal to our apostolic see and take refuge there, so that he may obtain without challenge the rights secured to him by apostolic mercy.

But if anyone, having learned these provisions, should attempt to corrupt them or disturb or harass the holy community itself, neglecting apostolic or regular judgment, and should in any way corrupt this privilege of ours, then, by the power of the Holy Spirit and of the blessed apostles [Col. 0970B], let him be separated from the fellowship of all the just until, humbled by fitting satisfaction, he strives to correct whatever he has committed against that venerable place to his own peril.

But whoever is the guardian and observer of this apostolic privilege of ours shall obtain blessing and grace from the Lord.

Written by the hand of George, scriniarius of the holy Roman Church, in the month of June, in the first indiction. Farewell.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, by the hand of Zachariah, bishop and librarian, and envoy of the holy apostolic see, while our most pious lord, the perpetual Augustus Charles, crowned by God, the great emperor, was reigning, in the third year of his reign and the third year after his consulship, in the first indiction.

[Col. 0969]

# LETTER OF POPE MARINUS I TO THE MONKS OF SAINT GILES

*(Year 883.) He appoints the presbyter Amelius.*

*(In the proofs of the new history of Nîmes, p. 15, in D. Bouquet, *Scriptors of the History of the Franks*, vol. IX.)*

[Col. 0969C] Marinus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all our faithful monks of the monastery called Vallis-Flaviana, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We make known to all of you that the present religious presbyter Amelius has been commended to us. Therefore, on account of his fidelity, we grant him—and also your monastery, with all its appurtenances—to hold and to rule and govern you, while preserving the annual pension to be paid to us.

Therefore we command you to receive him honorably and to regard him as your superior with all reverence, because we have appointed him over you for your salvation and governance. Farewell.

# In the Year of the Lord 885. Adrian III, Roman Pontiff

[Col. 0971]

## LIFE OF POPE ADRIAN III

[Col. 0971A] Adrian III, a Roman by nationality, was made pope on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the year of our Redeemer 884, during the reign of Charles III and the rule of the emperor Basil. He occupied the see for one year, three months, and nineteen days.

The emperor Basil urged him to communicate with Photius in matters of faith and religion. Adrian not only refused to yield to his request, but, following the example of his predecessor Marinus, attacked Photius most fiercely as though he were a layman. As a result, the emperor was exceedingly angered against him and sent him hostile letters full of insults.

Adrian died before receiving the emperor’s most threatening letters [Col. 0972A]. Stephen received them and replied to Basil with the letter that you will find printed above in the appendix to the eighth synod.

Concerning the election of the pope, Adrian decreed that the authority of the emperor should not be awaited in the creation of a pontiff, so that the suffrages of the clergy and people might be free.

During his time, the monastery of Cassino was burned by the Saracens, as Leo of Ostia writes in Book I, chapter 45. He died in the year of the Lord 885, amid the great mourning of the universal Church, and was buried in the basilica of Saint Peter. How long the apostolic see remained without a pastor after his death is not sufficiently clear, and so forth.

[Col. 0971]

# PRIVILEGE OF POPE ADRIAN III FOR THE MONASTERY OF PIACENZA

*(In Mansi, *The Most Extensive Collection of the Sacred Councils*, vol. XVIII.)*

[Col. 0971B] Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Angilberga, beloved daughter and imperial Augusta, and through you to your venerable monastery newly built at Piacenza, forever.

We ought, at the Lord’s command, to favor all who rightly ask with apostolic solicitude; but especially your devotion, our sweetest and spiritual daughter Angilberga, formerly empress Augusta, whom our holy mother, the Roman Church, rightly embraces and cherishes as her most beloved and principal offspring with honor and reverence.

Therefore, with fatherly affection we embrace the praiseworthy desire with which, through wise foresight, you recently wished to build from the foundations at Piacenza a monastery and hospice in honor of the Lord’s Resurrection and of the blessed apostles and martyrs Bartholomew, Sixtus, and Fabian [Col. 0971C] … Establishing it perpetually as confirmed and secure by apostolic authority, and providing in every way and decreeing firmly that, under the protection of blessed Peter, it may always remain unharmed and unshaken, with the Lord’s protection, from every attack and disturbance by any hostile persons, we further provide and firmly decree that everything which you have once distributed there to the Lord—whether movable or immovable property, inside or outside, households of either sex, all ecclesiastical ornament, and every kind of equipment—shall remain undisturbed in that consecrated place in future times, with every diminution or invasion entirely suppressed.

We likewise favor, assist, and grant apostolic assent concerning those households whom, with prudent regard for the redemption of your souls, you have set free, or may hereafter set free, so that they too, possessing secure freedom, may, under the guidance of God’s grace, receive the everlasting joys of life [Col. 0972B].

As you, devoted daughter, have asked, we entirely permit the consecration of the abbess of that place according to what is most prudently contained in your testament, which you drew up concerning that same monastery of yours. Namely, when an abbess is to be appointed there, the archbishop of Milan who is in office at that time, summoned by those persons of your lineage whom you have placed over that establishment and to whom you have entrusted its principal care, shall come there simply to elect and consecrate the abbess. He shall remain in the place no longer than you have prescribed, nor burden the monastery by demanding greater stipends than those fixed by you.

Likewise, if the evil of discord or any kind of disagreement should arise, he shall come to quell it and strive to establish peace with disciplined moderation. But if, for any reason or through violation of your institution, the archbishop of Milan should neglect to exercise this care and solicitude as we have prescribed, then the patriarch of Aquileia, summoned in the same manner as above, shall faithfully carry out all these duties.

And if at any time, whether on account of the matters prescribed above, some necessity of the time, or even the burden imposed by wicked people, it should be necessary to appeal to this apostolic see, we beseech and adjure all our successors, by the merits of the blessed apostles, to strive manfully to provide assistance and defense for that place until all its disputes have been put to rest [Col. 0973A].

Meanwhile, with the archbishop of Ravenna, the bishops of Pavia, Piacenza, and Reggio, the bishop of Modena with the bishop of Mantua, the bishop of Verona with the bishop of Lodi, and the bishop of Vercelli, together with the other co-bishops, celebrating a holy synod with us and giving assent to your will, we wish and establish that clerics of whatever order who serve in that consecrated place by celebrating the solemn rites of Mass, and those who continually perform the divine offices in the chapels of the same monastery wherever they may be, may be promoted and consecrated especially by the archbishop of Milan or the aforesaid patriarch, or by any other bishop whom the abbess of that place may choose to ask [Col. 0973B].

These and the other ministries of ecclesiastical office shall be at the abbess’s discretion, so that she may obtain chrism and the consecration of her churches, at any time, from whomever she wishes. Nevertheless, if the bishop of Piacenza should at any time be asked to perform these duties, let him know that henceforth and thereafter he has no right of authority over the aforesaid monastery, hospice, or their property; nor may he come to celebrate Mass there according to the institution of the Fathers unless he has been invited.

As for the tithes of the entire estate belonging to the monastery, which the bishops who … [lacuna] … and in whose neighboring parishes they have devotedly and willingly granted them to the aforesaid venerable place for the love of God and in memory of your benefactions: we wish and confirm by apostolic authority that, without opposition from those bishops or their successors, they shall belong perpetually to the sacred hospice and its chapels, just as you have established [Col. 0973C].

Moreover, we decree and establish by apostolic authority that, in accordance with what our predecessors, the bishops Adrian, John, and Marinus, are known to have granted and confirmed for you in their privileges, everything that the most serene emperor Louis of blessed memory, your lord and husband, is shown to have conferred upon you during his lifetime through his imperial generosity and august charters, as well as everything that you afterward acquired or may acquire for your own uses or for the uses of the monastery named above through imperial gifts or through any lawful acquisitions, purchases, or exchanges, and likewise everything that is shown to have been added or may later be added for the support of that consecrated place by the gift or generosity of kings or of any other faithful persons, shall remain intact [Col. 0974B], inviolate, and unshaken, in the same terms and order in which they came to you or to your aforesaid monastery, and shall remain according to the provisions of your institution.

If anyone—which we do not wish—should attempt to act against these statutes concerning offerings made or granted for the service of almighty God, or should rashly wish to violate any of these provisions, let him be subjected to excommunication and deprived of all ecclesiastical fellowship. Unless he immediately corrects and repents of such wickedness, let him remain guilty at the future judgment, bound by the bond of anathema through the authority of Saint Peter and of our apostolate; and for the excess of so great a transgression, let him know that he will share in hellfire with Judas the betrayer, unrestrained and rebellious against the sentence of the Holy Spirit, who always flees what is false and deceitful.

Written by the hand of Leo, scriniarius of the holy Roman Church [Col. 0974C], in the month of April, in the third indiction. Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, by the hand of Gregory, nomenclator, envoy and apocrisiarius of the holy apostolic see, while our most pious lord Augustus Charles, crowned by God, the great emperor, was reigning, in the fifth year of his reign, in the third indiction.

[Col. 0973]

# LETTER OF POPE ADRIAN III TO SIGIBODUS, ARCHBISHOP OF NARBONNE

*(In D. Bouquet, cited above.)*

He admonishes Girbertus, bishop of Nîmes, not to inflict any harm upon the monastery of Saint Giles.

[Col. 0973D] Adrian, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and most holy Sigibodus, archbishop of Narbonne.

We wish your holiness to know that the monastery of Saint Giles, with all its appurtenances, stands under our apostolic authority, together with Leo, its religious abbot, and the monks of that monastery. Therefore we admonish your fraternity to warn Girbertus, bishop of Nîmes, not to presume to inflict any force, opposition, or oppression upon that monastery, its monks, or its households, nor to leave to his followers any opportunity for their oppression [Col. 0974D], because that monastery, with all its property, most certainly stands under the dominion and authority of the blessed apostle Peter and of ourselves.

We wish you to tell the same bishop to strive to return everything that he has taken by force from the monastery. And know that we have already granted that monastery into the power of the presbyter Amelius, for its protection and defense. If Bishop Girbertus refuses to heed our admonitions and yours, know that he is excommunicated and irrecoverably condemned.

Act in this matter as we have good confidence that you will. Farewell.

# In the Year of the Lord 884. Saint Bertarius, Abbot of Cassino

[Col. 0975]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON BERTARIUS

*(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*.)*

[Col. 0975A] Bertharius, or Bertarius, descended from the stock of the Frankish kings. He was abbot of Cassino and was beheaded by the Saracens, becoming a martyr, in the year 883, on October 22. On the authority of the Old Codex, and according to Leo of Ostia, Book I, chapter 32, and Peter the Deacon, chapter 12, he wrote two books of the *Contrasting Sentences* (*αὐτικειμένων*) of the Old and New Testaments, published without the author’s name at Basel in 1530, in folio; at Paris in 1530, in octavo; at Cologne in 1533, in octavo; and at Paris in 1556, in duodecimo, together with the books of Junilius Africanus.

They are also found in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, where, on the authority of Felix of Toledo, they are attributed to Julian of Toledo; but they are no more his than they are those of Salvian of Marseille, with whom Johannes Alexander Brassicanus published them in 1530 [Col. 0976A]; or of Richard of Cluny, to whom Sixtus of Siena refers them in Book IV of the *Bibliotheca sacra*, p. 371.

I do not wish to repeat what has already been recorded about the rest of Bertarius’s writings by Peter the Deacon, in the notes of John Baptist Mari upon him, and by Cave, except that it is worth mentioning that verses on the life, death, and miracles of Saint Benedict were also published in the *Acta Sanctorum of Benedict*, vol. I, p. 29; by Trithemius, chapter 326; and in *Illustrated Benedictine History* II, 72. The latter merely mentions his elegant sermons.

[Col. 0975]

# SAINT BERTARIUS’S POEM ON SAINT BENEDICT

*(In Mabillon, vol. I of the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, from vol. III of Prosper Martinengo.)*

[Col. 0975B]

O Father Benedict, most celebrated throughout all lands,  
who possess the summit of honor among confessors,

God chose you from childhood from heaven  
and appointed you father of holy offspring.

You are the way, the guide, the shepherd, the teacher  
of those who, scorning earthly things, seek the heavenly kingdoms.

Scorning studies, you flee the city that rules the world,  
and submit your gentle neck to the yoke of the Lord.

By your prayers you restore the solid fragments of a shattered vessel,  
which the nurse had carried away in your service.

The envious enemy shattered with a thrown stone  
the bronze that gave signals for your table, Benedict.

But the Roman does not cease to provide you  
with your customary food, secretly committing a pious theft.

The priest had prepared for himself a great Paschal meal,  
but the Lord assigns it to you with its dishes [Col. 0975C].

A very foul bird thrusts itself upon your holy gaze  
and, in the form in which it had once appeared, burns you.

But, lying among thorns and pierced by their spines,  
you immediately overcome wound with wounds.

The vessel in which the poison lay hidden is broken by the power of the cross  
when the holy right hand of so great a Father makes the sign.

The boy whom a black one was drawing away from holy prayers  
is stopped by the Father’s rod, and the dark boy departs.

Receive, holy Father, the boys whom the glory of Rome  
in pious devotion sent to your threshold.

The mountain gave a stream to the brethren entrusted to you;  
water flowed from the rock when you asked the Lord.

While the Goth was cutting brambles, the iron leapt into the waters,  
but soon returned to the handle when you dipped it into the water.

[Col. 0976B]

While Placidus was drawing water regularly from the pool,  
the flowing water carried him away.

“Hurry, swift Maurus,” the provident Father says at once;  
“the current is already dragging the boy headlong into the lake.”

He hastens over the waters, carrying out the command, and returns,  
with the rescued boy, as though walking upon the ground.

The priest, ready for every evil in his dreadful heart,  
himself first suffered the poisons that he had sent.

Behold, the wretched man is struck down by the roof of the collapsing house;  
his body crushed, he goes to the cruel underworld.

While the disciple swiftly carries such news,  
he shakes the inmost heart of the holy Father.

The Father enjoined upon him, on account of the rejoicing at such a death,  
that he should bewail his own guilt with tears.

The bird carries away the bread with which he had concealed the poison,  
hiding it where no human being could see [Col. 0976C].

By your holy merits you turned the temples of false gods  
into praise and glory for God, holy man.

That treacherous dragon, hurled down from high heaven,  
spoke such words against Christ’s servant:

“Accursed one, what have you to do with me? Why, Benedict,  
do you persecute me? Why do you seize my rights?”

An immovable stone stands fixed beneath an enormous weight,  
and that impious enemy, sitting upon it, presses it down.

But suddenly, at the voice of blessed Benedict,  
the stone is lifted; the rider goes far away, and afterward consuming flame follows.

The brethren thought falsely that the kitchen was burning,  
but when the Father came, the false vision fled.

A boy is crushed and killed by the mass of a wall;  
the Father raises him and orders him to return to his work.

[Col. 0977A]

The brethren took their meals in unauthorized houses;  
though absent, he sees it and reproves them severely.

There is present an unassuming guest, a traveler encountered on the road,  
for whom they prepared a meal in the soft meadows.

The holy shepherd reproves him for this crime;  
at once he asks pardon for his fault.

Riggo comes resplendent in the garment of the deceitful tyrant:  
“Those garments that your back is wearing are not yours,” he says.

King Totila comes, humbly prostrate;  
you foretell all the fortunes of his life.

“For twice five years you shall retain the heights of kingship;  
death will follow them. Be righteous in your conduct.”

From that time he ceases to be savage in his deeds  
and lives more gently through the years allotted to him.

Honor, Rome, your prophet, learned in your doctrine,  
who sings that your walls will remain safe throughout the ages [Col. 0977B].

You will be shaken by many storms and flashes of lightning,  
but no enemy will exist who can overthrow your defenses.
