“Cleric, accept neither a meal of flesh nor ever profit from sacred office, and you will be safe.”

When he despised these things, that wicked man returned to him whom he had once abandoned,  
as the holy prophet had foretold.

All that I have heaped up for the monks through Christ’s gift  
has been handed over to the peoples at the Lord’s discretion.

I could scarcely prevail upon the heavenly Lord by my prayers

that he himself might yield to me even the souls of the brothers.

Afterward, when the Lombards came in the night,

they carried away everything else as well, laying all waste.

The brothers, saved by the gift of the eternal King,

none of that flock could be harmed by him.

[Col. 0977C] The serpent keeps the vessel hidden along the path, my son;

I warn you to take care promptly to turn away.

The little napkin is a witness, which you hold against your breast, brother:

why has wickedness entered your heart?

The things that his proud mind desired do not remain concealed from the Father,

as he offered the service of the light to the one dining.

“Brothers, behold, today there is no bread in the storerooms;

tomorrow, by God’s mercy, there will be an abundance of bread.”

To those who take pains to establish the sacred enclosure of the monastery,

standing by in a dream, he shows the work of building it.

Through him, the sisters who customarily spoke harmful words

against the servant of Christ are returned to their tombs.

For while the boy anxiously sought his native roof,

he went there without orders and died on the spot.

[Col. 0977D] The grave could not retain his body,

but the servant of the Lord united it with the earth.

A wicked serpent stands with open mouth in the middle of the road;

when the brother sees it, he returns to the holy enclosure.

A peasant who came suffering from leprosy, his body disfigured,

departed healed, glorifying God.

Golden gifts are poured down from heaven to the gracious Father,

so that the petitioner may receive it, with which to pay his debts.

A glass vessel, sunk among the exposed rocks of the mountain,

remains intact, still holding all the oil.

After praying to the Lord, he filled the jar with oil,

which before this had been entirely empty.

“Where are you hurrying, Satan, prepared in the manner of a physician?”

[Col. 0978A] “I am going to give drink to your brothers.”

The holy right hand immediately saved the old man seized by that demon,

and drove Satan away.

A peasant who came with his arms bound by cords

is released at the first sight of the saint.

The bereaved man asks that the pledge taken from him be restored;

when the saint prays, life returns to the boy.

The holy sister, pouring forth prayers, draws down rain from heaven;

she keeps the Father with her unwillingly through the night.

After three days, the brother, rejoicing over his sister’s death,

buries her immediately in his own tomb.

One tomb now holds the two pledges of the saints,

[Note: [Col. 0977D] Alternatively: “whom God joined to the earth and to heaven.”]

whom God joined to heaven and to the earth.

Here he sees the souls of the saints being carried through the air

in angelic arms toward the joys of heaven.

[Col. 0978B] The whole world is present, gathered like the sun’s radiance,

beneath the visions of the night, gracious Father, shown to you.

A witness to great merit is present, Servandus by name,

for he too sees a portion of the light.

Your rule, holy Father, sends many to heaven,

joining them above the stars to the choirs of the saints.

As the servant of the Lord breathes out his soul with holy praises,

he climbs by a wondrous ladder to the stars of heaven.

Garments are spread out, mingled with divine light,

by which the sacred Father ascends to the sacred kingdoms.

A woman remaining out of her mind, climbing through trackless places,

was saved when she entered his cave.

Christ’s grace granted you very many signs,

illustrious Father, which no one now knows.

But of the things known throughout the regions of the world,

who could suitably compose them, as your deeds deserve?

And what deeds of former signs shine forth today,

performed in our times through your merits?

For Andrew, born of German stock,

was never able to walk with straight steps;

as soon as he was deemed worthy to touch the threshold of your church,

he was immediately healed by the Lord’s gift.

Another, carrying a serpent hidden in his belly,

for whom medicine provided no help,

hastening here and climbing, seeking the gifts of mercy,

reached your holy threshold, Father.

After he vomited out the serpent, once he had climbed your threshold,

he remained unharmed here through the mercy of God.

David, whose contracted body the Cimbrian land produced,

is raised upright in your temple, in your church.

[Col. 0978D] Ah, blessed Father, who shine with such great light,

resplendent in the heavenly dwelling with such great mercy,

be a guardian and teacher to your servants forever,

so that no ambushing wolf, no pestilential enemy,

may ever take from the flock the sheep whom you retain by your own right.

Protect and preserve your servant Bertharius,

who, moved by love for you, brought forth these humble poems.

We ask this of almighty God, who wills all to be saved,

of Christ, who rules heaven and earth through the ages:

grant us, and grant us also the joys of paradise,

and bestow true crowns upon us all without end.

# APPENDIX TO THE WRITINGS OF SAINT BERTHARIUS

[Col. 0979]

# LIFE OF SAINT SCHOLASTICA, VIRGIN, SISTER OF SAINT BENEDICT

From a homily preached on her feast, commonly but improperly attributed to Bede the Venerable

[Col. 0979A] 1. Since, dearest brothers, we celebrate the feast of blessed Scholastica, it is fitting to introduce into this little work something about the merits of her life from the life of the most blessed Benedict, so that the excellence of her holiness may not be concealed in silence. But first let us send prayers to almighty God, who made all things in wisdom, so that he may himself deign to grant this, since he deigned to say: “Let the one who thirsts come and drink, and from his belly shall flow living waters” (John 7:37). Thus may we worthily continue what we have begun, so that it may belong to the honor of so great a feast and provide growth for your charity.

2. His sister Scholastica—[from Gregory the Great, Book II of the Dialogues, chapter 23]—dedicated to the almighty Lord from the very time of infancy, used to come to him once a year. First, let us examine the power of so great a name, so that the prayer may proceed with its own beauty. For Scholastica derives from *schola*, “school,” which is the nurse of wisdom. From it the standard of all virtues grows, and the whole virtue of the soul becomes eager to learn good and evil, so that it may run along the straight boundary on the way of salvation: so that it may despise the world destined to perish, lest, wandering, it regard good as evil, evil as good, darkness as light, light as darkness, bitter as sweet, and sweet as bitter; and so that it may discern which virtue belongs to the spirit and which to the flesh, lest, undertaking everything indiscriminately, it hope to choose the good where the whole standard is wickedness. As it is written: “Whoever has not been a disciple of truth will be a teacher of error.”

3. But let us see who Benedict could be, in every respect, the brother of such a great sister—not only in name, [Col. 0979C] but also in deed; not only on earth, but also in heaven. Scholastica was formed not in the school of the philosophers but in Christ’s school, fleeing the world’s mockeries from childhood and preparing a heavenly Bridegroom for herself. He, seeing from the time of his youth the broken studies of vices and worldly literature at Rome, withdrew his foot with an aged heart from the one whom he had set before himself at the entrance into the world. How fortunate the land of Nursia, which sends forth such pupils! For the golden realms of Canopus send tyrants; you send to Christ offspring worthy of the heavens. O happy womb of so great a mother, which gave such offspring to the world—namely, offspring of blessing and wisdom. Truly this is that fertile soil which, after receiving the seed, produced in one case a hundredfold fruit and in another sixtyfold.

4. But why did you, holy sister, come only once a year? [Col. 0979D] Perhaps you feared the length of the journey because of your tender feet? [Col. 0980A] Or were you preparing a gift to bring? Or perhaps the good brother made the heavenly dew of the word fruitful only once and once a year, so that it would suffice for the growth of the meadows of your minds once they had been moistened? Or did you have in mind that saying of Solomon: “Keep your foot from your neighbor’s house, lest, when he is satiated, he hate you” (Proverbs 27:6)? And this: “You have found honey, my son; eat what is sufficient for you, lest, when you are filled, you vomit it up” (Proverbs 25:16). Thus, thus, let all sisters act: let them not frequently visit the thresholds of their brothers; let them not seek carnal kisses; let them not utter foolish stories; let them not bring merely a gift that a textile depicts or a skilled hand adorns; let them bring neither perfumes nor cakes of varied flavors. Instead, together with Scholastica, seek the sacred school of your brother Benedict, so that, satisfied more with heavenly food [Col. 0980B] than with an earthly gift, you may be able to return to your own homes. It follows:

5. The man of God would descend to meet her not far outside the door, on the monastery’s estate. How holy, how modest, how discreet was his approach! So that the fragile sex might not be harassed, her brother came to meet her, lest the labor of the journey break the devotion of her mind. Did he regard it as unlawful that a woman’s foot should tread upon the threshold of so great a monastery? Or perhaps he avoided the barking of secular people, who, like dogs, ravage the good morals of monks, and who believe of them what they do not hesitate to do in their own evil actions; and if it were unlawful to expect this of so great a Father, would they, with inflated throats, shriek their laughter at his more tender disciples? For this reason the life-giving Father descended not onto the property of secular people, but onto his own estates. [Col. 0980C] It follows:

6. One day she came, as usual, and her venerable brother descended to her with his disciples. He came “as usual” because he approached out of a good habit of mind and with unfeigned faith. How holy the approach, how holy the arrival, how pious the journey! He ran more through the love of his mind toward Christ than through the devotion of his feet toward his brother—or rather toward Christ his brother. For he himself also says: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother, sister, and mother” (Matthew 12:50). But with what devotion she ran, the Psalmist says: “As the deer longs for the springs of waters, so my soul longs for you, O God” (Psalm 40:2). But why did the Psalmist mention the deer metaphorically, so that the soul should run to God as a deer to a spring? These things do not remain empty of mysteries. Does only the deer, and not the dove, the turtledove, and the sparrow, seek a spring? But the deer and the dove run back to the stream of the spring in different ways. The former descends by the course of its feet, the latter by aerial flight. The deer, pursued by the hunters’ devices, runs exhausted to the water; the dove approaches in its accustomed manner, without weariness. If we wish to consider this mystically, the invisible soul possesses the form of a visible animal: with one course of weariness, the former proceeds to an earthly spring, the latter to a heavenly spring. The former, wearied by the voices of dogs, the latter, pursued by evil spirits, must run to that spring which is the living fountain, the well of the house of Jacob, from which a bubbling stream of water springs up into eternal life.

Certainly such a sister came to such a brother with such faith. For the sick goes to the physician in one way, the healthy in another: the former so that the healthy person may visit the healthy, the latter so that the healthy person may care for the sick. The thirsty person also hastens to a spring in one way, the person drunk with wine in another. The former goes so that, after drinking, he may refresh his mind; the latter so that, not thirsting, he may proceed along the right path. But this sister, seeing both graces in so great a brother, came with a wise step and without weariness: first, so that, being healthy, she might visit the healthy; then, so that she might cure one sick not in body but in mind by instruction in salvation, since not even the stars are pure in God’s sight, and, according to the Apostle, neither is an infant of one day. It follows:

7. They spent the whole day in God’s praises and sacred conversations; when the darkness of night was already pressing upon them, they took food together. Blessed is such a sight of kindred, with the Lord’s command before their eyes: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matthew 6:33). Blessed are such dishes, where the bread of angels is placed before human bread, and where the mind is refreshed before the belly. For here food is stored up that can please the heavenly table; there remains food that the body’s indigestion sends forth. And blessed is the conversation extended through the whole day in divine praise, in which sacred praises alternate and respond from the first rising of the light until sunset. It follows:

8. While they were still sitting at table, and the hour grew later amid their sacred conversations, that holy woman, his sister, asked him, saying: “I beg you, do not leave me this night, so that until morning we may speak of something of the joys of heavenly life.” They sit at table and take food; with the single tooth of charity they chew the bread and sacred conversations, so that there might be one mouth with which they broke both earthly and heavenly bread. For while the belly was full of food, the mind was still fasting from the word of salvation. Therefore, like a hungry woman, she asks that she may satisfy her mind with divine nourishment, in heavenly delight, until daylight, so that he who had been a teacher in the light of day might also become a masterly teacher amid the darkness. It follows:

9. He replied to her: “What are you saying, sister? I cannot remain outside my cell in any way.” Behold, the brother questions his sister, the teacher his disciple, the holy man the holy woman, as though he did not know what she had said. But this inquiry belongs more to one who is angry than to one who is asking, since the Father had heard well what his sister requested. It was as though he were saying: “What you are asking is not right: that I should remain outside my cell contrary to custom; I cannot fulfill it.” O lover of holiness, why do you deny your sister what you offer even to strangers? But religion causes this, not a reason for grief. You know the Lord’s command: “Whoever loves father or mother or brother or sister more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10:37). Therefore you return to your accustomed place of prayer, where you are accustomed to cling more to God than to your sister.

But we say with presumptuous voice: Is God not here, where your good sister seeks the mysteries of God, when he himself says: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in their midst” (Matthew 18:20)? Behold, she does not ask to see you for a long time in the manner of parents; she asks for the space of one night, in which you may offer sacred conversation. How harshly you attend, holy brother, to your sister’s prayers, on account of your sacred religious observance. She rightly asks to receive from you; you likewise rightly seek to return. She acts in faith; you in faith. She acts out of love for God; you likewise act as she does. She asks to spend the night in preaching with your sister; you ask to offer the customary praises to the Lord with your brothers. But which of the two acted better, the following sentence shows.

The sky was so clear that no cloud appeared in the air. Truly no cloud could exist where there was the true light that enlightens every human being coming into this world. It follows:

10. When the holy woman heard her brother’s words of refusal, she placed her hands, with her fingers interlaced, upon the table and bowed her head into her hands to pray to almighty God. Tell us, blessed virgin, what school taught you, that you propose a judgment against your teacher? Does he not say: “Every disciple will be perfect if he is like his teacher” (Luke 6:40)? And in the Gospel he says: “Let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing” (Matthew 6:3); and you join both hands? And this: “Cast the net on the right side of the boat” (John 21:6); and you rightly immerse it on both sides? He places the sheep on his right, and you also on the left? The Psalmist places them on the right, saying: “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand” (Psalm 109:1); and also: “The right hand of the Lord has shown strength; the right hand of the Lord has exalted me” (Psalm 117:16); and in the Canticle: “Your right hand, O Lord, has been glorified in strength” (Exodus 15:6), and so forth. And you, disparaging these things, not only clasp your hands but also interlace your fingers?

The Lord says in the Gospel: “When you pray, enter your room and, having shut the door, pray to your Father” (Matthew 6:6); and you, sitting at supper, pour out prayers and tears before human eyes? But how worthy of praise are your deeds, O holiest of women! What do you do in a private chamber when you perform such things beneath an open sky? For this reason you have one part, right and left, because you contemplate the handiwork of the one who has no left hand, as it says: “God saw everything that he had made, and it was very good” (Genesis 1). And in the Song of Songs: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me” (Song of Songs 2:6). And in the Psalm: “Your hands, O Lord, made me and fashioned me” (Psalm 108). And this in the Canticle: “My hands dripped with myrrh” (Song of Songs 5:5).

By this authority, how beautifully your hands remain clasped, upon which, bowing your head, you poured out a heavenly rain of tears. But the Apostle says whose head it is: “The head of a woman is man, and the head of man is God” (1 Corinthians 11:3). For whose man except the one of whom the Prophet says: “Man is his name; Orient is his name”? (Zechariah 6:12.) Behold, the one who, for the salvation of all, gave up his spirit on the cross with bowed head has now bowed his head into your palms, so that from the stars there might flow to you the secret of his mystery that you sought in your mind. You performed such a miracle merely by interlacing your fingers; what would you have done if you had extended your palms in prayer?

When she lifted her head from the table, such was the force of the flashes of lightning and thunder and such the flood of rain that neither venerable Benedict nor the brothers who were with him could move their feet beyond the threshold of the place where they had been sitting. How new these miracles were to the world, how worthy of praise through all ages! Although there was no shadow of a cloud, the air thundered with clamorous sounds, and dense peals of thunder resounded where there had been no agitation of wind. For one fountain of eyes both drenched the table with tears and the fields with rain from the heavens.

Let holy charity now stand firm; let the brother’s feet remain motionless. Let the brother’s love not deny what the sister requests. Give, Father, whether willing or unwilling, the sacred conversation lasting through the night. Behold, she fulfills the Lord’s command: she asks that she may receive, seeks that she may find, knocks that it may be opened to her. Let her herself say what she asks: “So that until morning we may speak of something of the joys of heavenly life.” For this reason you descended to meet her, so that you might bring forth these gifts; complete what you began. For the reward does not appear at the beginning, but at the end of good works. Therefore the Lord poured rain from above, so that you would not deny the stream of praises. Truly she does not seek a perishable gift but desires the gain of the heavenly kingdom. It follows:

11. The holy woman, bowing her head into her hands, had poured rivers of tears upon the table, through which she drew the clear air toward rain. Nor did that flood follow long after her prayer; rather, the correspondence between the prayer and the flood was so great that, at the very moment when she lifted her head from the table amid the thunder, the rain began to fall. How good is the God of Israel to the upright in heart, how kind to the soul that seeks him! Behold, he who searches minds and sees the hearts of all, who says through the Psalmist: “He will call upon me, and I will answer him; I am with him in trouble” (Psalm 91:15)—behold, he did not delay, did not require many prayers, but in the blink of an eye and the instant of the heart granted the gift to the one who asked. For when she lifted her head from her hands, there was a single correspondence between prayer and flood.

Rejoice and be glad, holiest of men, for behold, you hold what you wished; behold, you have what you always sought. Behold, you see remarkable miracles, attested by heaven and earth. Truly, if you had not denied what you were seeking, the signs that sacred reading proclaims throughout the whole world would not have arisen before human eyes. Behold, Scholastica’s name now shines with the praise of virtues. Behold, the holy people rejoice with her because of her miracle. Behold, the fruit of signs is borne by the one whom you cultivated with the heavenly hoe. It follows:

12. Then the man of God, seeing that he could not return to the monastery amid flashing thunder and the flood of heavy rain, began to complain in sorrow, saying: “May almighty God forgive you, sister; what have you done?” Why do you ask, man of God, what your sister has done? Do you not see what she has done? Do you not see the drops of rain? Do you not hear the roaring crashes of the sky? Do you not feel the miracles flashing, the signs flowing, the foundations of the house trembling, and yet you say, “What have you done”? Did she herself do what your holy refusal did even more? For if you had not refused, the miracle would not have occurred.

Christ, the lover of mercy, did this. He delayed hearing the prayers of the Canaanite woman who asked him, so as to sharpen her faith, so that bread belonging to the children might be given to the little dog seeking crumbs. But although she came then as a stranger from the borders, she was no longer a stranger to Christ’s fellowship. This woman, however, dedicated to Christ from the cradle, deserved to hear, together with the glorious Virgin Mary: “She has chosen the better part” (Luke 10:42).

And why do you, Father, say sorrowfully: “May almighty God forgive you, sister; what have you done?” O man of God, minds are open to you; for you the air pours forth its coins; for you dry jars stream with oil; for you the heights of the deep lake return iron from below; the underworld itself gives back a soul. And now, as though sorrowful and ignorant, you say: “What have you done?” O blessed Father, if it is permissible to say so, how much more just would it have been to say: “May almighty God forgive me, because I do not hear your good prayers,” rather than: “May almighty God forgive you; what have you done?” This is that saying of Solomon: “Reprove the wise man, and he will love you” (Proverbs 9:8). It follows:

13. She replied to him: “Behold, I asked you, and you were unwilling to hear me; I asked my Lord, and he heard me.” The meaning is: “I asked you as a brother, but you were unwilling to hear me as your sister. I hoped that you would have in mind the womb of our mother, the pain of childbirth, the milk-filled breasts, the nurse’s cradle, the midwife’s baths, and the swaddling clothes by which infancy was once nourished. But you were unwilling to hear me, and you were hastening rather to the brothers whom only Christ’s charity makes your brothers, whom you do not even know from what region of the world he sends them to your cradles.

“Therefore I asked my Lord, and he heard me. You did not consider that one father fashioned the limbs of us both. You did not see that we have [alternatively, had] one dwelling [Note: [Col. 0983D] Thus Benedict and Scholastica were twins, born in one birth; for they do not have one dwelling in some place if they succeed one another there after intervals. Trithemius, in Book I of *On Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, chapter 1, speaking of their mother Abundantia, says: ‘She, having been in danger during childbirth, gave birth to twins, namely a son, Benedict, and a daughter named Scholastica.’] within the barriers of the womb. Therefore I ran to that Father who gave us our souls, who granted earthly things and did not deny heavenly ones.

“Now, then, if you can, go out, leave me, and return to the monastery. ‘Now’ concerns the present time: now, when almighty God has closed your roads; now, when he has denied you a way of departure; now, if you can, leave me and return to the monastery.

“And why, Father, are you weary? Is this not a monastery, where you are, since you are the head of all monasteries and the teacher of all monks, given that it is not the place that sanctifies the person but the person who sanctifies the place? Remain now, most holy Father, unwillingly, so that the sun of another day may offer you a path for your steps.” It follows:

He was unable to go outside the shelter; he who had not wished to remain there voluntarily remained unwillingly. To how many holy men have you, man of God, become comparable, who unwillingly performed good deeds! Jacob unwillingly fled from his brother and later returned with many things. Thus Joseph unwillingly went to that position so that he might become a teacher to God’s people. Thus Daniel went to the citadel of Babylon so that he might become first among all the wise. Thus Saul unwillingly became Paul so that he might become the preacher of the nations. Therefore, holy man, let your charity not refuse to remain unwillingly, so that you may offer Christ’s instruction of salvation. It follows:

14. And so it happened that they spent the whole night awake and satisfied one another in reciprocal conversation about the sacred things of spiritual life. Behold, new spiritual joys now arise, because the one who had first refused has now become the giver of heavenly things. They satisfy one another through reciprocal sacred conversation, though previously they had been at odds with concord.

How great are your wonders, almighty God! For you willed and made all things good, and no one can resist the power of your majesty. Therefore the heavens, the air, the earth, the sea, and all that is in them praise you, because you continually renew your signs and wonders, so that the whole world may recognize you as its Redeemer.

Now, mercifully grant pious Father Benedict a path by which he may return to his cell. Restrain the aerial stream; remove the drops of rain; grant the sun of clear weather, so that he who approached joyfully may depart rejoicing. Let his sister likewise bid her brother farewell and return to her own place; let them both, rejoicing and exulting, be carried by your gift to their homes. It follows:

“For this reason I said that he wished something but could not accomplish it. For if we examine the mind of the venerable man, there is no doubt that he wished the same clear weather in which he had descended to remain. But contrary to what he wished, through the power of almighty God he found a miracle arising from a woman’s breast. Nor is it surprising that the woman who had long desired to see her brother prevailed over him at that moment. For since, in John’s words, ‘God is love’ (1 John 4:16), by a very just judgment the one who loved more was able to do more.”

These matters should not be discussed at length. For according to the grammarians, *charitas*—“charity” or “love”—is a middle kind, since charity can exist between good and evil people, and between robbers and devout people. Thus it is written: “Perfect love casts out” (ibid., 17). Certainly, if this is the perfect love that casts fear out among good people, nevertheless that love is believed to be imperfect which provides an agreement in wickedness between evil and proud people.

Thus, during the Lord’s Passion, Pilate sent Jesus to Herod, by whom Jesus was sent back again to Pilate, and Herod and Pilate became friends on that very day; for previously they had been enemies of one another. But this is the perfect love that is God, by which one was able to do more than the other. Of this the Apostle says: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5). It follows:

15. On the following day, when the same venerable woman had returned to her own cell, the man of God returned to the monastery. And behold, after three days, while standing in his cell, he raised his eyes into the air and saw the soul of that same sister leaving her body and entering the hidden regions of heaven in the form of a dove.

How blessed are the eyes that can contemplate blessed souls, that can see spiritual things with bodily sight! These lights do not lie beside the foundation of the forehead, but shine within, toward the windows of the heart, of which it says: “Who are these who fly like clouds and like doves to their windows?” (Isaiah 60:8.) Behold now, Father Benedict, this dove flies to the windows of your heart, so that your sister’s soul, passing through them, may be carried to that heavenly gate. She became the guide of so great a soul, who was once the bird sent back to the ark bearing peace. How blessed is the bird adorned with such mysteries, which also deserved to carry the Holy Spirit above the Lord Christ! This bird busily attends upon the services of the eternal King; its back, shining with accustomed silvered wings, gleaming with gold, carries a message to paradise. Of it the Song of Songs says: “Rise, my beloved, my bride, and come: my dove in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the wall” (Song of Songs 2:14). It follows:

[Col. 0986C] 16. Rejoicing with her in such great glory, he gave thanks to almighty God in hymns and praises and announced her death to the brothers. The holy Father announced to the brothers what he had deserved to see with sacred sight in secret; and rejoicing in such wishes, he gave thanks to almighty God, because he saw the woman whom, three days earlier, he had drenched with the dew of heavenly speech climbing toward the heavenly kingdoms in the form of a dove. It follows:

17. He immediately sent them to carry her body to the monastery and place it in the tomb that he himself had prepared. When this had been done, it happened that, since their minds had always been one in the Lord, even burial did not separate their bodies.

Behold, brothers, the heavenly pearl, long ago bought by the merchant, is fitted into heavenly ornaments; now, feeding among the shining lilies, it follows the Lamb wherever he goes. Behold, she is placed by the angels in the Lord’s paradise. Behold, on earth she is fitted into her brother’s tomb by the hands of monks, so that neither heaven’s gate nor earthly burial might separate the gift bestowed by one mother, and so that those whose minds had always been one in Christ might have one tomb for their bodies.

Behold, your losses have been repaired, O paradise. Behold, the virgin fashioned by God’s hand, whom the pestilential enemy took away from your place, now returns to the heights of heaven; now she recognizes the palm of her creator; now, because she was conquered, she tramples victorious upon the neck of the wicked enemy.

Speak, speak, minister of hell; speak, soldier of Tartarus; speak, race of Orcus, filled with the deceit of every poison: what did God’s most holy creation do to you? What harm did the well-formed woman do to you? For what reason did you, as counselor, thrust yourself in voluntarily, so that she might eat what was not yours?

Speak, pestilential thief: because you could not seize a portion of God’s kingdom, you therefore wished to seize God’s creature through the serpent. Indeed, as the Lord is, so he sends such a servant. You are the slippery serpent; he is the twisting serpent. You are full of every grief; he is full of every poison. You give counsels of death; he hisses counsels of death through his organs and offers them.

Could you not find another animal in God’s paradise that would agree with your wishes, except a serpent? Truly, no. You were more cunning than the holy angels; he was more cunning than all living creatures. You were created good in heaven but became evil of your own will; he was created good in paradise but became guilty through you. The virgin of God, God’s creation, God’s good woman, was created good; through you and the serpent, by tasting what was unlawful, she became a sinner.

What did this madness profit you? You heaped up everlasting fires for yourself; he will eat earth all his days. You are bound with fiery chains; he is pressed down by the anger of all and battered by heels and scourged with blows. Woe, woe to you both in every respect.

Behold, the woman has been restored by Christ’s blood. In place of the loss of the earthly paradise, she now holds the heights of heaven, from which you fell headlong. Your gall has been changed into the sweetness of honey, your wicked deceit into the restoration and salvation of all. Your jaw has been pierced, so that you bite no one and devour no one unless God wills it. And if you devour someone, choked by God’s mercy, you will spew him out with blood, and God will draw him from your entrails.

[Col. 0987C] 18. Rejoice now, virgin of God, raised to such great triumphs; [Col. 0988A] exult, most holy Father Benedict, holiest of fathers, sweetest teacher of teachers, because, when your holy works have been completed, you rejoice together above the kingdoms of heaven.

Intercede for those entrusted to you; ask for us who are afflicted; pray for our sins; petition Christ not only for the monks entrusted to you but also for your maidservants, so that every age, every sex, and every order that bows its neck to your commands may despise the world destined to perish, desire eternal joys, seek the blessed kingdoms, and receive prosperity of soul and body.

May they suffer no distress through any diabolical deceit; may they be afflicted by no attacks of evil spirits; may they be destroyed by no calamities. Well done, blessed Father! Favor those who pray; incline your ears to the prayers of your servants; grant pardon to those who ask; grant gifts to those who seek; spare sinners. For you are the shepherd, while we are sheep. Hear the bleating of your sheep; draw us after you, so that we may come to you and there find true pastures, where true everlasting joys are.

Return to God talents multiplied from us; carry back with interest the entrusted gifts of teaching; and join me, an unworthy presumptuous author of this work, to your sacred little servants, so that together with the whole flock entrusted to us we may obtain the rewards of life. Then may God say to you: “Well done, good and faithful servant, because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much; enter with all those entrusted to you into the joy of your Lord”—through him who has deigned to promise worthy joys to his servants, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0987]

# HOW ONE SHOULD FAST THROUGHOUT THE YEAR

(From a manuscript of Cassino, cited in Mabillon, volume I of the *Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*, p. 704.)

[Col. 0987C] There are four seasons, that is, four prescribed fasts in the year: in the first week of the first month, on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday, one must fast until evening, with twelve lessons. In the second week of the fourth month, that is, June, on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday, one must fast until None, with twelve lessons. In September, that is, in the third week of the seventh month, on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday, one must fast until None, with twelve lessons. In the fourth week of the tenth month, on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday, one must fast until evening, with twelve lessons.

These twelve prescribed fasts throughout the year atone for one hundred solidi in refined gold on account of sins. And when these two have been diligently … [Col. 0987D] [lacuna] [uncertain reading: “no pellit,” ‘drives away’] [lacuna] will free [lacuna] the soul. In addition to those fasts that the Prior may prescribe for any tribulation.

## Concerning the remaining fasts
On the vigil of Saint Matthew, of the Nativity of the Lord, and of the Epiphany, one must fast until evening. On the vigil [Col. 0988C] of the Ascension of the Lord, Pentecost, Saint John the Baptist, Saint Peter, Saint Lawrence, and Saint Mary, one must always fast until the ninth hour on the vigils of these feasts, and, when Mass has been completed, they shall eat. If any of the aforementioned vigils falls on a Sunday, it is not permitted to fast.

The octave of the Nativity of the Lord, the octave of the Epiphany, the Purification of Saint Mary, as well as Saint Scholastica, Saints Faustinus and Jovita, Saint Germanus, the dedication of Saint Benedict above, and the dedication of the Lord Savior and of Saint Mary below: on all these feasts there is no fasting until evening, unless Saint Scholastica, Saints Faustinus and Jovita, or Saint Matthias the Apostle falls [Col. 0988D] during the fiftieth day, or during Lent. If this happens, it shall be done as on the other sacred days of fasting. For the offices, like everything else concerning the feasts written above, shall be performed as we have said, just as on Sunday.

On Saint Gregory, Saint Benedict, and the Annunciation of Saint Mary, twelve lessons are read, and the brothers do not kneel in prayer [Col. 0989A], but observe the fast until evening; nevertheless, after Vespers they take cooked food and wine. On Saint Stephen, Saint John the Evangelist, and on the Monday and Tuesday after Easter, they read nine lessons; but Mass is celebrated as on Sunday. On all the feasts written above, “The Lord reigns” is always sung at Matins, and they do not kneel; nor are the chapter and the reading read at the late hour.

On all the other saints’ days, they read nine lessons; Matins and Mass are conducted as on ordinary days, they kneel, and they observe the fast until the appointed hour. They shall not sing “Have mercy on me, O God” at Vespers, Matins, or Prime; it is sung at the other hours, except if the feast falls on a Sunday: if that occurs, it is celebrated as a Sunday.

The division of Matins and the night office is conducted as follows. From the Kalends of November until the vigil of the Lord’s Supper, it is done as Saint Benedict ordained. Moreover, on the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, and on all saints’ days and Sundays, it is not permitted to divide it [Col. 0990A].

From the Nativity of the Lord until the Epiphany, they do not kneel. They do not sing “Have mercy on me, O God” in the public prayer at any office until the octave of the Nativity of the Lord. Likewise, from Easter until the octave of Pentecost; afterward they shall sing it.

As for the refectory, everything must be carried out as Saint Benedict says—whether in summer, winter, or Lent, everything according to its proper season. Except that it is customary, both above and below, not to eat at the ninth hour until they have harvested the grapes. When they have been released from the grape harvest, they immediately eat at the ninth hour, and after Vespers they eat a snack and drink again, although this is not written in the Rule.

Likewise, during the fiftieth day, after the meal, according to custom, they drink throughout the whole week before the reading is read, although this too is not mentioned in the Rule. When they perform the mandatum, if the Lord has given an abundance of wine, they always drink; but if there is little, they abstain.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 884. HARMOTUS, ABBOT OF SAINT GALL

[Col. 0989]

INSCRIPTIONS IN THE CHURCH OF SAINT OTHMAR

(According to Canisius, *Ancient Readings*.)

Abbot Harmotus had the church of Saint Othmar painted, and on one wall Wisdom was depicted with this encomium of the Fathers:

O noble mother, most pleasing to all the learned;

O glory of the empire, most worthy ruler of the world;

Brighter than the sun and more precious than gleaming gold,

How splendidly you shine throughout the whole world, Wisdom.

See how beautifully the mother of daughters

Is adorned in due order, illustrious, rich, and radiant Wisdom.

On another wall were the Seven Wise Men.

This wall contains monuments of the ancient sages,

Who taught the whole world by a clear path.

On another side was a crowd of the blessed standing before God.

Bands of saints, praising with serene voice,

Stand before the Lord’s throne throughout all ages.

On the wall above the door:

Here God is present to those who ask with pure mouth,

Giving forgiveness to the wretched and healing to the contrite in heart.

[Col. 0991]

EPITAPH OF GRIMALD, BY HARMOTUS

(*Literary History of France*, vol. V, p. 404.)

Here within lies the lover of the divine law,

Grimald the humble, who ordered this temple to be built.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 888. SAINT REMBERT, BISHOP OF HAMBURG

[Col. 0991]

LIFE OF SAINT REMBERT, BY AN ANONYMOUS AUTHOR, HIS CONTEMPORARY

(According to Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*.)

PROLOGUE

[Col. 0991A]

In writing the Life of the bishop Rembert, who must always be remembered with the utmost veneration, we faithfully relate, insofar as we have learned these things, on what occasion his office first arose, who instructed him for it or advanced him in his way of life, and how, once chosen for it, he subsequently lived.

CHAPTER ONE

When the emperor Louis held the monarchy of the Frankish kingdom, he took care to render such a devoted return to God, the author of his elevation, that the churches of God established in his kingdom might advance with suitable strength, and that the condition of God’s male and female servants might expand more widely with an increase of honor.

Amid these constant meditations, by divine inspiration there also came to his mind how his most serene father, Charles, surnamed the Great, had converted the Saxon people, previously unbelieving, to the faith of Christ, having by that time established throughout the province a sufficient number of bishops and suitably distributed their sees. He had reserved the farthest part toward the northern edge of that same province for the establishment there of an archiepiscopal see, from which the word of God could be preached to the neighboring peoples: the Swedes, Danes ([Note: [Col. 0991C] The words enclosed in parentheses appear to have been inserted by later hands, as was noted in the *Life of Saint Anskar*:] Norwegians, Faroe Islanders, Greenlanders, Icelanders, Scridefinni), Slavs, and also all the northern and eastern nations called by whatever name, who were still entangled in pagan errors.

CHAPTER TWO

For this purpose the church of Hamburg was constructed and dedicated on the border of the Danes and [Col. 0991C] Slavs, namely, in the farthest parts of Saxony among those who are called the Nordalbingians. Together with the inhabitants of the region, that same church was entrusted by order of the glorious [Col. 0992A] emperor Charles to priests for its governance, until, at the appropriate time, after sufficient bishops had first been appointed to the place, he could have an archbishop consecrated there.

But when he was taken from this life before the fulfillment of his vow, his most devout son, the aforementioned Louis, reconsidering this intention of his with his faithful followers, had Anskar, a man of the highest holiness, elevated, as his father had decreed, both in the rank and in the name of an archbishop, and ordained as ruler of the aforementioned new church and of the peoples still inexperienced in the faith, as well as a dispenser of the divine word to the nations not yet believing, as has been said.

Whoever wishes to know about his conduct from childhood in the fear of God, the growth of his virtues with advancing age, the many signs by which his episcopal and preaching office was divinely foretold, how his entire cause was secured through the privileges of the Apostolic See, and his zeal and progress in winning souls for God—souls whom he daily strove either to strengthen in the faith or to lead from paganism to Christianity—should read the little book of his life and will appreciate how holy a man he was.

We shall now begin to relate what concerns Rembert, both imitator of his holiness and successor to his dignity: how he first became known to him and was subsequently chosen by him.

CHAPTER THREE

When the boundaries of the newly established church of Hamburg had become too narrow, and the revenues collected from its possessions did not suffice for the great office entrusted to its bishop, while even the income that might have been produced was carried off by frequent hostile [Col. 0992C] incursions, the emperor Louis, so that the man of God might not thereby be hindered in his work of preaching—which in his deeds is usually called his mission to the nations—gave to that mission, to serve it perpetually, a certain cell in Gaul called Torhout [Note: [Col. 0993] Torhout in Flanders near Bruges, Rembert’s birthplace, as is clear from this passage. Those who say that he was born in Frisia are therefore mistaken.]

At a certain time, while the lord bishop was staying there, he saw some boys hurrying to the church with playful and aimless running. Among them was one, almost the smallest of all, who walked gravely, carefully avoiding childish frivolity, performed his prayer with reverence and fear, and, rising, fortified his forehead with the sign of the cross. He displayed in every respect the self-control of someone of more mature age.

Thus the man of God observed that the sacred childhood of the devout boy was already burning with love for divine service. He summoned the boy’s parents, learned that the boy’s name was Rembert, and, having obtained their consent, gave him the tonsure and ecclesiastical clothing. Commending him there to paternal care [Col. 0993B], he ordered that he be diligently instructed. After spending a few days there, he departed and devoted himself earnestly to the pastoral office he had undertaken and to his mission among the nations.

CHAPTER FOUR

After this, the boy, already beloved by God, advanced more and more in seriousness, applied himself eagerly to learning the liberal disciplines, and, meanwhile accustomed to prayers and other occupations concerned with good things, in a few years shone forth perfected in every maturity of knowledge and virtue.

Even then, in accordance with the Psalmist, his heart grew hot within him, and in his meditation fire burned (Ps. 38:4), as he desired to discover what would be most beneficial for him to accomplish while remaining in this life. As he meditated on these matters, he recalled, according to a certain wise man, that the first definition of philosophy is meditation on death. He absorbed this with all his heart, so that throughout his life he might deserve to attain this highest wisdom: that at the time of his death he might not be grieved by neglect of this forethought, but rather, by observing the Scripture that admonishes and says, “In all your works remember your last end, and you will never sin” (Ecclus. 7:40), might, insofar as human nature allows, rejoice securely in either the guarding against or the remission of sins.

CHAPTER FIVE

The venerable bishop who had devoted him to divine service, as is read in the account of his life, was accustomed to foresee and arrange almost everything that was to happen to him or that he himself was to do, either in a dream or through an intimate revelation in his mind. The writers of his life judge that this intimate revelation in the mind was something like what is repeatedly found in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 8:10–11): “But the Spirit said to him,” or “to that disciple.”

Therefore, it should not be doubted that the man of God, not by observing an event but by the impulse of divine admonition—which, as a spiritual man, he used to perceive in his soul through a hidden sense—admitted this fortunate boy of whom we speak to divine ministries with such paternal affection. Rather, from the pattern of his conduct and the manner in which he was always thereafter treated and regarded by him [Col. 0994A], it seems likely that it had been clearly revealed to him by God that Rembert would become his successor in the episcopate.

For when, at the beginning of his study of the arts and scholastic disciplines, the strictness of his teachers was relaxed toward him—as we say in ordinary speech, when he had left school—the lord bishop immediately made him his inseparable companion in the mission. When he came from the aforementioned little monastery to which he had entrusted him for education, he received him joyfully and allowed him to be acquainted in every respect with his deeds, by which he served God with complete devotion, whether secretly or openly.

CHAPTER SIX

Finally, one day, when they were standing together for prayer according to custom, and, their supplication completed, were preparing to leave the church, the bishop, recognizing in his disciple the gift of a more secret grace, addressed him in these words:

“Rembert, my son, you ought always to give thanks to him who called you from the turbulent waves of the world to the harbor of quiet. Since I see that you have directed your heart to that harbor without hesitation, I confess that I burn with affection for you, and you should not doubt that this love on my part will endure toward you to the end.”

He replied: “I am unworthy, my lord, of such grace from you. Yet because you show me this clemency, I ask that through your merits it may be obtained for me from God that in the future life I may attain a share in your rewards.”

Then the holy bishop—whose mind, as we have said, was often illumined by God’s grace for foreknowing future events—gave no immediate answer to the words of the most worthy Rembert. But after three days had passed, when Rembert had already been wearied by anxious thoughts about why the bishop had remained silent regarding his request, he gave him this consolation:

“I have already obtained from the Lord that in the future age, as you asked, we shall not be separated from one another. There we shall share in eternal blessedness, though we must not presume that we can reach it by our own strength—for that is the guilt of pride, through which those who practice iniquity fell. Nor, again, must we become sluggish through laziness and forget what is said: ‘In God we shall perform strength’ (Ps. 59:14). Rather, let us strive daily that, as blessed Gregory advises, a good work may be held by us in our will; and thus let us confidently trust that, according to the same teacher, through divine assistance it will be brought to perfection.”

If anyone is troubled by the fact that the bishop delayed three days before giving this answer, let him remember that we previously said that his mind was often illumined by God’s grace for foreknowing the future. Concerning this, however, the following words are written in his Life:

“He therefore wished to have time for considering everything that he might perhaps have to determine as especially important, and he decided nothing rashly before, illumined by God’s grace, he himself perceived in his mind what would be better. Thus, having been assured in his mind by a heavenly visitation, he arranged without hesitation what had to be done.”

Let the reader understand that we have suitably inserted this passage from his Life so that this testimony might establish that he gave no answer to the request of this most holy disciple of his, Rembert, except what the Holy Spirit infused into his mind during those three days, in accordance with the statement from the Acts of the Apostles that we cited above.

CHAPTER SEVEN

A certain vision also contributes to the prophecy of the blessed man’s virtues. It was revealed to the bishop’s steward on the very first night of Rembert’s arrival at Hamburg, when Rembert himself was still in the first period of adolescence.

The steward seemed to see Rembert himself seated at the summit of the oratory, and one of the church’s signals, which we call a bell, appearing in the sky. From it a linen cord, as is customary, hung down in the manner of a rope all the way to Rembert himself. By means of it he appeared to draw the same signal joyfully and to take sweet delight in its sound.

We have found an appropriate interpretation of this dream in the divine Scriptures (Exod. 28). The Lord commands Moses that, among the other mystical garments of priestly clothing, the following also be made:

“Below, around the feet of the same robe, you shall make something like pomegranates, of violet, purple, and twice-dyed scarlet, and, as is found in what follows, of twisted byssus, with bells mixed among them.”

Why the bells are commanded to be attached is shown below:

“So that its sound may be heard when the high priest enters the sanctuary before the Lord, and he may not die.”

For the priest dies when entering or leaving if no sound is heard from him, because he provokes the anger of the hidden Judge if he proceeds without the sound of preaching.

Since, therefore, it was to happen that, having ascended to the highest rank of the Church, the man of God would shine with spiritual ornaments, and since he was also to be shown to have carried out the office of preaching with distinction, he was rightly seen seated at the summit of the temple—which signifies the height of the episcopate—with the sweetness of doctrine and a sound drawn from heaven, calling the sacred people of Christ to divine service.

The celestial signal, resounding in the showing of this vision and drawn by him, can signify this, which the bells on the high priest’s vestment are shown to represent. We have also judged it worthwhile to explain for the progress and imitation of readers how he always displayed spiritually in himself the other ornaments of priestly clothing that we have drawn from sacred Scripture.

He wore pomegranates, in which many seeds are covered within by a single outer rind, because he always carried within himself a manifold working of virtues, everywhere enclosed under the single protection of charity. These pomegranates were made of purple, violet, twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted byssus, all of which most suitably apply to him.

For he always sought heavenly things with every desire, signified by the violet; he was prepared even for martyrdom in the name of Christ, signified by the purple; and he burned with love of God and neighbor, expressed by the twice-dyed scarlet.

Just as byssus, extracted from the earth, customarily loses its grassy color through long labor—drying, beating, cleansing, boiling, and spinning—and takes on a white color, so he, with great labor of self-restraint, as though sweating out his natural moisture, attained the beauty of a purity worthy of God through the diligent practice of fasting, vigils, prayer, and reading, as well as perseverance in patience and humility.

With all these he had bells intermingled, because rarely was anything heard from him other than the most pleasing sound of the virtues mentioned above. That sound was in turn commended to the minds of his hearers by the sublimity of his works, as the subsequent narrative of this little work will show more clearly.

CHAPTER EIGHT

While he was still in the service of his predecessor, the lord Anskar, the priest Arnulf, who had long been dead, appeared to him. When Rembert asked about his condition in the life of the other age, Arnulf replied sorrowfully:

“While I was still in the flesh, I was negligent about the salvation of my soul. I did not maintain the seriousness appropriate to my position; I frequently devoted myself to idleness; and at times, even during an imposed fast, I ate meat and often made use of other forbidden foods and drinks as well.

“For such offenses I have until now been unworthy of coming into God’s presence. But if your fraternity, content with bread, salt, and water, were willing to abstain from all other food for forty days on my behalf, I would believe that, through God’s mercy, I might be freed from the sentence or punishment of this exclusion of mine.”

Rembert promised him, as it seemed to him, that he would do so. When he awoke from sleep, as soon as he was able to address the bishop, he related the entire vision to him. Having received his advice, he used no other food or drink throughout the whole forty-day period except bread and water.

At that time he was afflicted by such severe toothache that he could not bear to chew bread itself in order to eat. Therefore, by grinding the bread into small pieces or rubbing it apart with his hands, he mixed it into the water and softened it somewhat, like porridge, to relieve his teeth. This also increased the severity of his abstinence, since even what might have remained in a simple preparation of bread was largely absent—both the strength of the nourishment and the pleasantness and enjoyment of the taste.

When the days of this abstinence had been completed, the priest for whom these things had been done appeared in a vision to a certain woman named Helahvih, who had lain paralyzed for many days. A long illness had indeed weighed down her limbs; nevertheless, as blessed Gregory says concerning a certain man [Note: [Col. 0995D] Namely, concerning Servulus, in Homily 15 on the Gospels and in *Dialogues*, book IV, chapter 14], that very illness had not bound those limbs from good works.

For every day she had herself carried to the church, where she delighted to hear the word of life and, as far as she could, to devote herself day and night to hymns and praises.

The aforementioned priest appeared to her, as has been said, in a vision and asked that thanks be conveyed to the servant of God Rembert for the frugality undertaken for his salvation. He declared that it had benefited him so greatly that through it the access to God’s presence and entrance into the heavenly court previously denied him had evidently been granted.

“Rembert himself,” he said, “will be numbered among those of whom it is said: ‘The righteous shall shine, and as sparks they shall run through the stubble’ (Wis. 3:7); and among those of whom the Psalmist says: ‘They shall go from strength to strength’ (Ps. 83:8).”

The man of God was never accustomed to let his soul be elated by visions of this kind. Rather, always walking along the safest path of humility, he ascended the steps of virtue daily, so to speak, in such a way that he seemed constantly to heed what blessed Gregory said:

“Let each one of you, brothers, strive to be great, but nevertheless let him somehow not know himself to be great; lest, while he arrogantly attributes greatness to himself, he lose it.”

CHAPTER NINE

As long, therefore, as the man of God Anskar remained in the body, this servant of God, Rembert, was accustomed to be with him more familiarly than all the others in every matter. We have mentioned him several times in this work, and the little book of the deeds of the aforementioned bishop, edited by Rembert himself and another fellow disciple, bears witness to him.

In that book, wherever mention is made of a certain most faithful disciple of his—as the reader will often find there—he should know that this was Rembert. But since, as we have said, he was one of the two editors of those deeds, he wished to express the truth of the matter while suppressing his own name, lest he appear boastfully to claim for himself a more intimate favor.

Thus blessed John the Evangelist also acted in his Gospel, where he preferred always to indicate his own person by signs of what happened rather than identify himself by name.

How steadfastly the holy man Rembert persevered in this place of devotion in familiar association with the bishop is known from the words of the aforementioned little book, in which the death of the lord bishop is recalled as follows:

“Having received communion of the Lord’s body and blood, the holy bishop prayed to the Lord that, if anyone had in any way sinned against him, divine mercy might forgive him for it. Then he began to repeat these verses frequently:

‘According to your mercy, remember me, for your goodness’ sake, O Lord’ (Ps. 24:7);

and:

‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner’ (Luke 18:13);

and:

‘Into your hands, O Lord, I commend my spirit’ (Ps. 30; Luke 23).

“When he had repeated these things many times, and, already breathing heavily, could no longer continue repeating them, he ordered a certain brother to sing them repeatedly in his place. Thus, with his eyes fixed on heaven, he breathed out his spirit commended to the Lord’s grace.”

The one whom he ordered to repeat the words of prayer on his behalf was Rembert. To him, as his speech failed, the bishop entrusted the words of his prayerful wish, believing that through Rembert he could make up whatever he himself, now dying, was less able to accomplish in prayer. He did not doubt that, because of Rembert’s merit, he would be heard on his behalf, and he did not distinguish what Rembert did from what would have been done by himself, since they had always been one heart and one soul, one spirit and one faith.

CHAPTER TEN

Finally, when, during the illness by which he departed from this life, the lord Anskar was consulted about the choice of his successor, and some also asked what he thought about Rembert, he is reported to have replied that it was not his office to decide this. Perhaps, he said, he had offended the feelings of many while serving as bishop; he ought rather to correct this than, by naming such a person as his successor, increase the agitation of their minds—a person who might perhaps burden his subjects through his own shortcomings, causing bitter complaints against him.

“Let Rembert’s merits nevertheless be recognized,” he said, “for he himself is more worthy of the archiepiscopal office than I am of the office of subdeacon.”

His observer [Rembert] preserved these words about himself out of a profoundly humble intention. The bishop, as a true observer of the same humility—which he himself had once practiced in the monastic way of life (ch. 7)—said:

“The seventh degree of humility is that a monk not only declare with his tongue that he is lower than everyone else, but also believe it with the inmost affection of his heart, humbling himself and saying with the Prophet: ‘But I am a worm and not a man’ (Ps. 21:7).

“For holy men, when they perform mighty deeds, customarily think lowly of themselves, in accordance with what David said of himself while dancing before the ark of the Lord and despising the power of his kingdom: ‘I shall play, and I shall become even more contemptible than I have been, and I shall be humble in my own eyes’ (2 Sam. 6:22).

“Of this the Apostle also admonishes us, saying: ‘Complete my joy, that you may think the same thing, having the same charity, being of one mind and thinking the same thing, doing nothing through contention or empty glory, but in humility considering one another superior to yourselves’ (Phil. 2:2).”

The holy man Anskar was accustomed to observe the former of these testimonies—that is, the Prophet’s—in himself, so that, thinking humbly of himself inwardly, he did not seek honor outwardly, as though saying: “I shall play, and I shall become more contemptible.” Nor, again, because he displayed himself as contemptible outwardly, did he become inwardly puffed up; rather, he fulfilled what follows: “And I shall be humble in my own eyes”—that is, I consider myself inwardly to be as I display myself outwardly while despising myself.

By this intention of despising himself he also fulfilled what we cited from the Apostle: free from all contention and empty glory, through humility he considered others superior to himself. Hence it was written above that he gave such great testimony to the blessed Rembert, whose merit was greater than his own.

Yet although he said such things about himself for the sake of humility, it is not our place to place either of them above the other, but to believe that they were equal in merit—men whom both devotion to the same faith and the administration of the same office, though at different times, commend equally.

CHAPTER ELEVEN

Although, as we have just said, the holy bishop was unwilling to tell others anything about his future successor, in order to avoid offending them, he nevertheless did not wish to defraud at the end the man who was almost entirely his confidant in this matter. Three days before the day of his death, therefore, he disclosed his secret to the man of God Rembert: that after him Rembert was to be advanced to the summit of the episcopate.

Rembert then began to resist so great a ministry, declaring that he was suitable for it neither in strength nor in merit. The holy bishop, reminding him that what he had foretold was God’s disposition [Col. 0999B], added appropriate admonitions: he ought to bend his will to the judgment of divine providence, in accordance with the words of blessed Thomas addressed to the Lord: “You are my Lord, and I am your servant; your will be done.”

After this, the glorious Rembert lacked the firmness to resist or oppose the matter, since he knew that the bishop had received these things from God. Nor was there any disagreement among the clergy or people, amid several candidates, about the election. On the very day of the deposition of the lord Anskar, they all unanimously elected Rembert.

In accordance with this unanimous agreement, venerable men brought him to the glorious king Louis of that time: Thiadricus, bishop of the church of Minden, and Adalgarius, abbot of the monastery of New Corbie. He was honorably received by the king, and, according to custom, through the presentation of the pastoral staff [Col. 0999C] he obtained possession of the episcopate.

[Note: [Col. 0999D] Henschenius believes that these words were inserted in favor of imperial investiture during the time of Henry IV, chiefly because no trace of this matter appears in the primary privileges of the churches of Hamburg and Bremen. Yet Adam, a contemporary of Henry, praises these privileges as evidence of imperial investiture in the following words of chapter 28: “Rembert received the episcopal pallium from Pope Nicholas, the pastoral staff from Caesar (one should write: king) Louis, as can be recognized in the privileges.”]

In the documents of the Roman pontiffs of the Apostolic See, by whom the archiepiscopal privilege was sanctioned for the see that he then assumed, this too is contained [Note: [Col. 0999D] Namely, in the privilege of Pope Gregory IV, which contains the following words: “As for the consecration of succeeding priests, until the number of consecrators has increased from among the nations, we meanwhile entrust it to the sacred palatine authority.”]:

Because, on account of the new establishment of that see and the fact that the peoples had not yet been converted to the faith, it had no suffragan bishops by whom one archbishop could be consecrated upon the death of another, the consecration of succeeding bishops was meanwhile entrusted to the palatine authority, until the number of suffragan bishops from among the nations—who canonically ought to consecrate him—was completed.

With this statement concerning the manner of his ordination, the glorious king sent the venerable Rembert to Liudbert, archbishop of Mainz, by whose order he was consecrated. It was prudently arranged that, to assist at the consecration, suffragans should assemble not from one metropolitan church but from two: namely, Liudhard, bishop of Paderborn, belonging to Mainz, and the aforementioned Thiadricus, suffragan of the archbishop of Cologne.

It pleased them to be present together in this way so that both this consecration and the earlier ordination of the lord Anskar to that same see, carried out in a similar manner, might serve as a sign for future times: namely, that the consecration of a bishop for this see should not belong specifically to the diocesan bishops of any particular province, but should be entrusted, as we have said, solely to the palatine authority until the number of consecrators from among the nations was completed.

CHAPTER TWELVE

This most holy man had once made this vow concerning himself: that after the departure of the lord Anskar he would immediately assume both the monastic purpose and the monastic habit. Therefore, after his ordination, he hastened to the monastery of New Corbie with the counsel of the bishops who had consecrated him. He fully received the garment implied by that promise, and fulfilled the promise of that way of life by displaying his way of life, the stability of his conduct, and obedience according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, insofar as the labor and responsibilities of the episcopate he had undertaken permitted.

[Note: [Col. 0999D] This is how the printed books read in Philip Caesar and Bollandus. Perhaps someone may think that one should read “that he might display stability and the conversion of his conduct,” etc., in agreement with chapter 58 of our Rule, where these words occur: “The one to be received shall promise in the oratory before all concerning his stability, the conversion of his conduct, and obedience before God and his saints.” All Benedictines have followed this form of profession to the present day. Yet I think that Rembert’s profession was published in another form. Since his dignity did not allow him to remain in the monastery, he vowed to God only stability of conduct according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, not stability in the monastery. Consequently, I consider the correct reading of this passage to be the one given above. Moreover, in this matter it is worth observing that Rembert was admitted to the profession of monastic life without undergoing any probation. See the preface to the preceding volume.]

And, so that he might become more faithfully accustomed to fulfilling this promise, he asked that one of the brothers of the same monastery be assigned to him, with whom—since he was not permitted to remain in the monastery—he might have the support of continual meditation there and practice in restraining himself according to the regular discipline he had promised.

It pleased them to assign him a man distinguished in his way of life, a deacon named Adalgarius [Note: [Col. 1000D] From this it is evident that Adalgarius, who succeeded Rembert, was not abbot of Corbie, as Henschenius correctly observed against Letzner], namely, the brother and namesake of the abbot of that same monastery, whom we mentioned above.

This venerable man, both in imitation of Rembert’s way of life and in the dignity of his succession, still survives today, bearing witness, together with many others, that the holy bishop whose life we are writing lost nothing of monastic perfection on account of his pastoral care. Indeed, no one living even within the monasteries observed the instruments of good works mentioned by their Rule (ch. 4) as faithfully as he did.

His deeds can scarcely be explained by us; but the weakness of our knowledge is wholly unable even to express or adequately appreciate his daily fellowship with God and his soul always directed toward heaven.

He considered it a serious matter to pass any time empty and without the work of God. Prayer always followed reading, and reading followed prayer in his practice. If anything arose that seemed to prevent him from praying, he nevertheless always did what was right and must be understood to have prayed without interruption, as blessed Augustine teaches:

“For the one who is engaged in divine service, all his deeds and words are counted as prayer.”

CHAPTER THIRTEEN

[Col. 1001B]

He observed the vigils with moderation. He practiced abstinence so carefully that every day was a fasting day for him, while his meals avoided satiety. In this, he took care that, according to blessed Jerome, he should so subdue the appetite of the body that his strength would not fail for reading, psalmody, or the duties of his altar and episcopate. “For it is of no benefit,” says the same Jerome (*Letter 22 to Eustochium*), “to carry an empty stomach for two or three days if, at the same time, it is overwhelmed and the fast is compensated by satiety. The mind is immediately dulled when filled, and watered soil produces the thorns of lust.” Wishing, as we have said, to guard against this in himself, the man of God so maintained moderation in fasting [Col. 1001C] that, when condemning the Jews in the Gospel because they accepted neither John fasting nor himself eating and drinking, the Lord added: “And wisdom is justified by her children” (Matthew 11:19). By this he showed that the children of wisdom understand that righteousness consists neither in abstaining nor in eating, but in even-tempered endurance of want, in not allowing abundance to corrupt temperance, and in taking—or not taking—at the proper time those things whose use, rather than whose desire, is to be censured.

## CHAPTER XIV

Whatever his predecessor of blessed memory had established for the needs and support of the poor, he himself disturbed in no respect. Rather, he applied every care and diligence so that everything established for this purpose would suffer no loss in his time, but instead receive some daily addition through his own efforts. For a hospital had been established in his diocese for the relief of the needy, and such an abundance of assistance had been assigned to it that we know of no place where this provision was made more generously or wisely. Outside the diocese as well, wherever he might be, he always had men appointed to carry money in small bags for distribution to the poor. He himself [Col. 1001D] likewise always carried in his belt a purse with coins for this very purpose, so that, if the distributor of his alms happened to be absent when a needy person arrived, he would himself have something to give without delay. He was indeed concerned that no such person should leave him without relief. Frequently exhorting his attendants in similar words, he used to say: “We must not delay in helping all the poor, because we do not know who Christ is, or when he has come to us.”

## CHAPTER XV

Meanwhile, in accordance with the admonition of blessed Gregory, he also unceasingly practiced the almsgiving of the word and constantly devoted himself to the study of saving doctrine, remembering what the same teacher says (*Homily 6*): “It is more important that the mind, which will live forever, be nourished by the food of the word than that the belly of dying flesh be satisfied with earthly bread.” For this reason he made an excerpt useful to readers from the books of Saint Gregory, writing it out with his own hand. He also composed several edifying letters to various people. One was addressed to a certain handmaid of God in the monastery called Herisi [Note: [Col. 1001D] Now Nova Herisia, commonly Nienherse, a community of canonesses three hours’ journey from the city of Paderborn, according to Henschenius.] and to the other sisters living there in the service of God.

This servant of God, of whom we are speaking, was the niece of the venerable Bishop Liuthard, whom we mentioned above. He had bound himself to the holy man with such complete devotion that he was not merely a lover of his sanctity himself, but also strove to commend to him everyone in any way connected with him—especially this niece of his, of whom we are speaking, who had been offered to God from infancy [Col. 1002C] and remained in virginity. Through her own devotion she also merited that the holy man habitually call her his only beloved daughter.

Although, to avoid vainglory, she did not wish her name to be publicly announced, we have nevertheless decided to set down here, for the edification of sacred virgins, the letter written especially to her, though without naming her. It is as follows [Note: [Col. 1001D] From this point Philip Caesar begins Chapter 16; [Col. 1002D] but the following letter belongs to Chapter 15, as is clear from Adam, for whom Chapter 16 is what follows the letter, reproduced in full by him in Chapter 29.]:

> “To my dearest daughter and to the other virgins and brides of Christ, Rembert, the unworthy little servant of God’s flock, sends greetings in the Lord.
>
> “Brother Adalgarius, recently returning from you, told me that you were deeply distressed because you rarely received a letter from my unworthiness. Since I now wish to remedy this, nothing more suitable occurs to me to write than to stir you concerning the purpose of your sanctity. If, therefore, you wish to attain the highest glory, you must cultivate incorruptibility of body and spirit with every virtue. For the chastity of the outward person must necessarily be supplied by the inward nourishment and sustenance of purity, and must continually be encouraged to persevere in perpetual incorruption. Those are the true and incorrupt virgins of Christ—not those who fear to fornicate, but those who have no desire to fornicate.
>
> “If you recognize that you have attained this gift by God’s grace, then, the greater you are, the more you must humble yourselves in all things, as sacred Scripture urges, ‘and you will find grace before God’ (Sirach 3:20). For by this path you must come to Christ the Lord and your bridegroom, since he himself said: ‘Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart’ (Matthew 11:29).
>
> “Therefore you must take care that the mind be guarded with every vigilance from the swelling of pride. Your thoughts do not fly empty before the eyes of God. God sees within what raises the mind, and therefore permits without what will bring it down. Hence it is said through Hosea against the Israelites: ‘The spirit of fornication is among them, and they have not known the Lord’ (Hosea 5:4). To show, as blessed Gregory says, that the cause of lust bursts forth from the fault of pride, he immediately added [Col. 1003B]: ‘And the arrogance of Israel will answer to his face’; as if he were saying: The fault that lay hidden within through the elevation of the mind will answer openly through the wantonness of the flesh.
>
> “Purity of chastity must therefore be preserved by guarding humility. For if the spirit is held beneath God, the flesh is not unlawfully raised above the spirit. The spirit has been entrusted with dominion over the flesh, provided that it recognizes beneath the Lord the rightful laws of servitude. But if, through pride, it scorns its creator, it rightly receives warfare from the flesh subjected to it.
>
