> “This is why prolonged continence is suddenly broken; this is why virginity, often preserved even into old age, is violated. Because humility of heart is neglected, the righteous Judge also regards the integrity of the body. At times, through manifest evil, he declares reprobate those whom he had long tolerated as reprobate in secret. For whoever suddenly loses a good long preserved had another evil held within himself, from which the other suddenly burst forth. Thus he was already alien from almighty God even when, through bodily purity, he appeared to cling to him.
>
> “Daughters, I do not write these things because I have perceived in you anything characterized by pride or vainglory. Rather, I desire you to belong to the company of those of whom it is written that ‘they follow the Lamb wherever he goes’ (Revelation 14:4). I grieve that many have fallen there; I desire you to walk cautiously, and I wish your Lord and bridegroom to say to you: ‘You are altogether beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you’ (Song of Songs 4:7).
>
> “Follow the Lamb here, therefore, in his commandments, so that, with his help, you may be able to follow him in eternal life, singing the song that no one can utter except the choir of virgins. Blessed Augustine beautifully explained this when admonishing virgins (*On Holy Virginity*, chapter 27):
>
> “ ‘Go forward,’ he says, ‘holy boys and girls of God, men and women, celibates and unmarried women; go forward perseveringly to the end. Praise the Lord more sweetly, whom you have contemplated more abundantly; hope more happily in him whom you serve more earnestly; love more ardently him whom you please more attentively. With your loins girded and your lamps burning, await the Lord when he comes from the wedding feast. You will bring to the Lamb’s wedding a new song, which you will sing on your harps—a song of such a kind that no one will be able to utter it except you.
>
> “ ‘For someone especially beloved by the Lamb, who was accustomed to recline upon his breast, saw you in the Apocalypse: twelve times twelve thousand holy harpists, incorrupt in virginity of body and inviolate in truth of heart. Follow the Lamb, because the Lamb’s flesh too is virgin. Follow him in virginity of heart and flesh wherever he goes. What is it to follow him, if not to imitate him? Of him blessed Peter says: “Christ Jesus suffered for us, leaving you an example, so that you might follow his footsteps” ’ [Col. 1004B] (1 Peter 2:21).”

We have inserted this letter here so that readers may see how great, in accordance with the Apostle’s admonition, was his devotion to the doctrine that accords with godliness, and how powerful he was in that doctrine to exhort others as well.

## CHAPTER XVI

Moreover, he diligently carried out the office of his mission, which his predecessor had first undertaken for preaching the word of God to the pagans and which afterward came to him by right of succession as though by inheritance. Whenever his other occupations permitted, he himself personally devoted himself to this mission. He always had priests appointed, however, through whom the pagans might hear the word of God and Christian captives might receive consolation, for visits to churches established among the pagans far from the church of his see—visits that, most gravely, had to be undertaken amid the dangers of the sea.

He himself endured these dangers more frequently and more abundantly, so that he often seemed to testify of himself, like the Apostle, that he had suffered shipwreck, and was often close to saying with him: “Night and day I was in the deep sea” (2 Corinthians 11:25). But surely the Holy Spirit was with him, renewing the inner person day by day amid the corruption of the outward person, smoothing all the hardships of the present life through hope of future blessedness, and lightening its burdens. He was comforted by continual meditation on the apostolic saying: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Romans 8:18). Thus, whatever hardships befell him in his labor [Col. 1004D] were accustomed to grow mild because he endured them for Christ [Note: [Col. 1003D] Here the author omits a notable deed of Saint Rembert, reported in the Preliminary Observations: the victory won by the Frisians over the Northmen through the merits of Saint Rembert.].

## CHAPTER XVII

Since he was compelled to witness the misery of many still held among the pagans, he spent nearly everything he possessed on the redemption of captives. He did not hesitate even to devote the vessels of the altar to their redemption [Note: [Col. 1003D] Adam quotes these words from this Life in Chapter 32, mistakenly citing Chapter 20; after these words [Col. 1004D] he adds that Rembert said with blessed Ambrose: “It is better to preserve souls for the Lord than gold. Those vessels, therefore, are precious which redeem souls from death.” See Book I of the *Life of Saint Caesarius, Bishop of Arles*, paragraphs 17 and following.].

When some people of less elevated understanding thought that he had acted wrongly, as though he were diverting to other uses what had been assigned to sacred mysteries, and someone asked him why he did this, he satisfied the questioner with a sound explanation:

> “I do not fail to recognize,” he said, “that the things belonging to ecclesiastical service must be treated with due reverence and that they have been deposited for this purpose under a grave obligation. Nevertheless, in God’s sight it is more valuable that Christian captives in distress be helped through these things than that this deposit be preserved. If necessity imposes the choice between two goods, so that one must be chosen and the other abandoned, one ought to take what is better and leave what is considered inferior.
>
> “Therefore, he said, since I have no other course, I do not act impiously if I redeem a Christian, who is a child of God, with the treasures of the Church. We can always find something sufficient for the use of sacred ministry; but it is irreparable if a Christian perishes in the affliction of captivity.”

## CHAPTER XVIII

For the sake of example, we relate one of these deeds, in which he shone no less through the power of a miracle than through an act of mercy. On one occasion, when he had come to the territory of the Danes, where he had a church built for the newly Christian people, at a place called Sliaswich, he saw a multitude of Christians being dragged away in chains as captives. Among them was a religious woman. When she saw him from a distance, she appeared both to venerate him by kneeling and repeatedly bowing her head and to implore his mercy for her redemption.

To make it understood that she had been a Christian, she raised her voice and began to sing psalms. The bishop, moved by compassion, tearfully prayed that divine aid might be granted to her. At his prayers, the chain that bound her neck was immediately broken. Yet, lest she escape, the pagans who held her between their hands easily kept possession of her.

Then the holy bishop, moved by anxious concern for her, began offering the pagans who held her various sums of money and goods of different kinds. But they were unwilling to accept any arrangement unless he gave them his own horse, which he ordinarily used for his saddle. He did not refuse. He suddenly leapt [elsewhere, *desiluit*] from the horse and gave it, together with all the equipment he had on it, in exchange for the captive woman. Having redeemed her, he granted her freedom and allowed her to go wherever she wished.

As we have said, by this deed he left behind a twofold memorial of praise: he broke the chain by the power of his prayer and at the same time displayed this remarkable work of mercy.

## CHAPTER XIX

In accordance with the Apostle’s command that the servant of the Lord be gentle toward all (2 Timothy 2:24), he lived in such a way that in his time no one, like him, fulfilled that Mosaic description according to which the meekest man was described as being above all men [Col. 1006A] (Numbers 12:3). Yet on several occasions, without any impairment of this gentleness, he remained so firm and steadfast in his judgment when investigating or examining cases that no one could turn him to another position.

What we have said about this occurring without detriment to his gentleness was fulfilled in him so truly that he never displayed anger or agitation to those who opposed him, nor acted against them with harsh words. Rather, through familiar conversation and a pleasingly restrained manner, he carried out everything he intended with kindness toward all. When someone close to him asked more privately about the inflexibility of mind that existed in him, he explained as follows:

> “Whatever I ought to do or omit, and concerning all future events, I always take an omen from visions of the Lord and of my predecessor Ansgarius. For when he appears to me, he is accustomed, through the character of his face, to show me how I ought to involve myself in matters requiring action. Whatever I perceive from him, I cannot pretend otherwise in carrying it out.”

## CHAPTER XX

He is also said to have performed certain miracles in the manner of the ancient saints: frequently, while traveling to Sweden, he calmed storms at sea by his prayers; he restored sight to a certain blind man through confirmation, which he performed upon him in episcopal fashion with sacred chrism. He is also said to have freed a certain king’s son from a demon. This claim appears to be supported by the fact that, while many bishops were standing by, a cry repeatedly came from the afflicted man’s mouth, declaring that Rembert alone among them had properly performed the office entrusted to him, and that Rembert himself was the source of that voice, to his torment [Note: [Col. 1005D] Adam, in Chapter 34: “We believe this king’s son to have been Charles, who, in the final years of the archbishop’s life, was deposed from the kingdom and succeeded by Arnulf, the son of his brother. Indeed, in the Fulda and Bertinian Annals, under the year 873, it is reported that an evil spirit invaded Charles and grievously tormented him, because he had conspired against his father Louis.”].

But because in our times, as the Psalmist says, “the holy man has failed, and truths have diminished among the sons of men” (Psalm 11:2), and because it is not easy to accept that such things have been done by any men of our own age, let it suffice that we have thus far established that this man of God reached the summit of holiness through those forms of virtue that the Lord proposes in the Gospel for hastening toward blessedness: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matthew 5:3), and so forth, from the eightfold catalogue of virtues, by which is signified the perfection of our hope to be fulfilled through the grace of the resurrection.

Nor were spiritual miracles lacking to him. Blessed Gregory, explaining the Lord’s words, testifies that such miracles are still performed by the faithful in the Church (Homily 29 on the Gospels): “These signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues; they will take up serpents; and if they drink any deadly thing, it will not harm them; they will lay hands on the sick, and they will recover” (Mark 16:17–18). But it would be lengthy and unnecessary to review the exposition of that teacher concerning each of these matters, since the homily containing it is readily available. We therefore refer the reader to it and must bring to completion the work begun on the life of Lord Rembert [Col. 1007A].

## CHAPTER XXI

When old age had begun to weigh upon him, constant pain in his feet was also added to his distress. Therefore, first with the glorious King Louis, through whose recommendation he had received the bishopric, and afterward with his sons Louis and Charles, he obtained that the distinguished man Adalgarius—namely, the monk from the monastery of New Corbie, as we related above—should be assigned to him and confirmed as his assistant, so that whenever any illness hindered him, he would have in Adalgarius a companion for traveling through the diocese, attending legal proceedings, and, whenever required, going on campaign or to the palace with his retinue.

Not long afterward, he also obtained that Adalgarius’s succession to him should be confirmed by formal election, that he should be made the king’s man by the reception of hands, and that he should be placed among the king’s counselors, with the consent of the abbot and brothers of his monastery and with the holy synod confirming all these arrangements [Note: [Col. 1007D] Adam reads differently in Chapter 38: “He also obtained that he himself should be confirmed as his successor in the election and placed among the king’s counselors, with the consent of the brothers and the abbot of his monastery,” and so forth.].

After this, as though freed from secular affairs, he strove every day with complete earnestness to increase whatever good he had previously practiced. He did not remain long afterward in this life; his passage to the Lord is said to have occurred in the following manner.

## CHAPTER XXII

Almost a full year before the day of his death, he privately disclosed to some of his faithful that many signs had been shown to him by which he knew that he would not remain long in this life, and that he would not see again in this life those to whom he was speaking. “Certain portents of this matter,” he said, “have come to me, which I am not permitted to disclose to others. Yet I will relate to you a vision shown to me last night, in which I understand my departure to have been most clearly prefigured.

“For it seemed to me that I was in a certain church divided through the middle by a very strong wall: I was on one side of the wall, while on the other was the lord and my predecessor Ansgarius. I saw an innumerable crowd of both sexes, turning this way and that like people searching for something, but unable to find anything of what they were seeking. Lord Ansgarius said to them: ‘What are you seeking?’ They replied that they were seeking my ring. Then they heard the bishop say again that they should stop looking for it, since he himself would have it with him.”

When Lord Rembert related this to certain people, as we have said, he asserted from this and many other indications that he was assured he would depart from this life in that same year. And, because he knew that this too was loved by them, so that his memory might be more firmly impressed upon the minds of those listening through the words he would speak as he departed, he gave them salutary admonitions, his words flowing abundantly for their edification. After this he bade them farewell and departed from them. As he himself had foretold, they never saw him again.

How the dream just related was fulfilled with evident effect in his death and burial arrangements, as he himself had understood, we shall fittingly explain in the place where it will be necessary to recount how his soul was raised to heaven and how his body was committed to burial.

## CHAPTER XXIII

Twelve days before his death, therefore, he arrived at the church of Bremen, and on that very day was struck by illness. As the illness grew more severe with every hour [Col. 1008B], he remained constantly devoted to psalmody and sacred readings, carefully preparing himself for his future departure from this life. Although the severity of his illness brought weakness to his bodily powers, he remained undefeated in spirit and displayed apostolic strength, of which it is said: “For when I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Corinthians 12:10).

Seven days before his death, the ministry of holy anointing with sacred oil began to be performed for him. Together with communion of the Lord’s body and blood, he received this saving remedy every day until the day when his soul departed from the body [Note: [Col. 1007D] A custom formerly prevailed in the Church whereby the anointing of the sick, which preceded the viaticum, was repeated over several days by several priests. See Menard’s notes on the *Book of Sacraments*.].

When he was now about to depart from the world, he summoned the priests and all the brothers and asked forgiveness for anything in which he might perhaps have sinned against any of them. In turn, he reconciled himself with all Christians against whom anyone might have committed an offense, and he asked the Lord’s forgiveness for them. After receiving the Lord’s body and blood, he gave up his holy soul [Note: [Col. 1007D] Adam, in Chapter 37: “He died in the year of the Lord 888, in the sixth indiction, and his deposition is celebrated on the third day before the Ides of June.” That year and day appear to be certain. Trithemius is therefore mistaken in assigning Rembert only nine years of rule; he should have assigned him twenty-three years and five months.].

Then an unbelievable lamentation followed from everyone, especially the poor, who amid their tears uttered these words: “Woe to us, holy Father! How shall we live after you, having until now been sustained in food and clothing by your alms? From whom shall we henceforth obtain these things?” But to you, they said, “Christ, we pray that the soul of your servant may now discover that you remember your words, in which you deigned to promise that whoever gave some comfort in your name to one of your least would be rewarded by you.”

## CHAPTER XXIV

While he was still alive, the man of God, out of regard for humility, ordered that he not be buried in the church. Since the brothers of that church did not dare to violate this command, they buried him outside the basilica, near the tomb [Note: [Col. 1008D] With the church’s wall or partition intervening. For Saint Willehad, the first bishop of Bremen, was buried inside the Bremen basilica and was transferred to another one by his successor Willeric, as is clear from the Life reported in Part 2 of the third volume of the century.] of Saint Willehad, outside the eastern wall of the church [Col. 1009A]. Adalgarius, whom we mentioned above and who succeeded the holy man in the episcopate, afterward built over the tomb and adorned a small chapel dedicated in honor of Saint Michael and the holy martyrs Stephen and Vitus.

Thus the vision mentioned above was fulfilled: Rembert and Lord Ansgarius were confined in one church, but separated from one another by the intervening wall. The aforementioned chapel is contiguous with the ancient church, with only its eastern wall preventing passage from one to the other. In this new chapel, as we have said, Lord Rembert was buried; in the ancient church Lord Ansgarius rests.

This is what Ansgarius seemed to say in the vision: that he would have Lord Rembert’s ring with him. Lord Rembert, perfected through faith and good works, was soon to be joined with him—not only in the nearness of their tombs but also in the reception of blessed rest—just as he had formerly foretold through the revelation of the divine Spirit.

The ring signifies faith, through which the image of God is expressed in us. Since the hands are customarily adorned with it, and the hands signify action, it is rightly shown by this that good work must always be present as the adornment of faith. Because Lord Rembert always displayed this in his conduct toward those entrusted to him, it was rightly shown in the portent of his death that the multitude of the people sought his ring. This signified that, at the time of his death, those entrusted to him anxiously desired still to enjoy the examples they had observed in him.

But the time of his rest required that this could no longer happen; Bishop Ansgarius signified this by restraining the people from seeking the ring and saying that he would have it with him.

## CHAPTER XXV

A wooden lamp was also suspended above his tomb so that a perpetual light might be maintained there. Beneath it, spread out across the surface of the tomb, lay a covering. A remarkable miracle is said to have occurred there, which, insofar as we retain it from the report and recollection or understanding of those who tell it, is known to have happened as follows.

One night the same lamp caught fire. At first, glowing coals repeatedly fell from it onto the aforementioned cloth; immediately afterward the entire lamp also fell, and it was wholly consumed upon the same cloth, without any damage whatsoever to the cloth itself. No one should doubt that Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever, brought this about to make known the merits of his servant.

[Col. 1009]

# LIFE OF SAINT ANSCHARIUS, ARCHBISHOP OF HAMBURG, BY SAINT REMBERT

(See *Patrologia*, volume CXVIII, column 959.)

IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 888. AIMOIN, MONK OF SAINT-GERMAIN.

[Col. 1009]

# HISTORICAL NOTICE ON AIMOIN

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*)

[Col. 1009C] Aimoin, or Aymoin, was a notary and monk of Saint-Germain-des-Prés in the Parisian suburb. He subscribed a charter issued in the year of Christ 872, in the thirty-second year of Charles [the Bald]’s reign.

His two books addressed to Berno, abbot of Castres, concerning the discovery and translation of the body of Blessed Vincent, levite and martyr, from Valencia in Spain in the year 864 to the monastery of Castres in the diocese of Albi in Gaul, written in hexameter verse, together with a letter to the monk Theotger and a poem of sixty heroic verses on the same translation, are extant with Breul’s *Aimoin, Writer of Frankish History*, Paris, 1603, folio; in Bosc’s *Bibliotheca Floriacensis*, Lyon, 1605, octavo; in the *Acts of the Saints* for January, volume II, page 405; and in Mabillon’s *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, fourth century, part 1, page 652.

His book on the miracles of Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, from the year 846 to 874, written in 892, appears in Jacob Mosander’s appendix to Surius, under 25 July; in the *Acts of the Saints* for 6 May, page 801; and in Mabillon’s *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, third century, part II, page 104.

A book on the translation of Saints George, the monk, Aurelius, and Natalia, and two books on their miracles, are found in the same Mabillon, fourth century, volume II, page 45. Some also attribute to this Aimoin the books on the miracles of Blessed Maurus and the history of the discovery of the bodies of Abbot Placid and his companions.

[Col. 1011]

# HISTORY OF THE TRANSLATION OF SAINT VINCENT, LEVITE AND MARTYR, FROM SPAIN TO THE MONASTERY OF CASTRES IN GAUL

Written in two prose books by Aimoin, monk of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, and likewise in two books of verse.

(In Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*.)

# MABILLON’S PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS

[Col. 1011A] 1. I presented Aimoin’s two little books on the miracles of Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, in the second volume of the third century (see below, column 1027). Now it is appropriate to present his two books on the translation of Saint Vincent, written in prose, together with two others in verse.

He was a monk of the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés near Paris under Abbot Gozlin, who began to preside over that place around the year 850 and commissioned Aimoin to write down the miracles of Saint Germanus. Aimoin wrote these books from the account of Audald, the monk who assisted in the translation, receiving what is related from his own mouth, as is clear from Book I, chapter 2.

These four books were published by Jacob Brolius, a monk of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, in the *Supplement to the Antiquities of Paris*. Aimoin had as his pupil Abbo, a monk of the same place, who composed two books in verse on the siege of Paris, preceded by a dactylic poem addressed to Aimoin, his teacher. From this it is understood that Aimoin was still alive in 888, the year in which Abbo was writing. His death is recorded [Col. 1011B] in the very ancient necrology of Saint-Germain-des-Prés in these words: “On the fifth day before the Ides of June, the deposition of Lord Heimo, priest.”

He is distinct from Aimoin, the writer of Frankish history, who was a monk of Fleury under Abbot Abbo.

2. He dedicated the first two books on the translation of Saint Vincent to Berno, abbot of Castres, and to his brothers. This monastery was built “in the year of the Lord 647 by Robert, Anselin, and Daniel, three pious and noble men, in the district of Albi, beside the River Agout, under the rule of Saint Benedict,” with the help of Faustinus, a vigorous and very wealthy soldier, “who, having become a monk, built the church of Saint Benedict from its foundations at great expense and, after Robert’s death, became the monastery’s second abbot,” as is read in the chronicle of that monastery, printed in volume VII of the *Spicilegium*.

In the year 870, the eleventh abbot, Berno, presided over that place; Aimoin addresses the following books to him. The monastery was erected as a cathedral church by John XXII and is now occupied by secular canons.

3. In passing, I note that Guarnerius, abbot of Rebais, who is omitted from the printed indexes, wrote a hitherto unpublished metrical work on Saint Vincent the martyr. I read it in a manuscript from Gembloux, beginning as follows:

> Who would not wish, O Christ, to hand down in titles  
> the saving works that you, almighty, perform, and so forth?

Then, in what follows, he discusses the cell or monastery of Saint Vincent near Seville in these verses:

> A cell, two days’ journey away,  
> remains far from the dwelling of the people.  
> Holy monastic religion  
> dwells here as though in exile  
> and needs no one’s assistance.  
> This wilderness is devoted to God alone.  
> It bears cliffs and an arid grove.  
> A lofty mountain rises above the air;  
> below, it looks upon the ocean.  
> Nothing outward pleases the monks.
>
> The mountain also contains a church,  
> set midway between the two glories;  
> the cloisters have the appearance of beauty.  
> All things retain the form of goodness,  
> and, even in their outward appearance, gracious abundance.
>
> Here Vincent, mighty in arms,  
> to whom the almighty Lord God  
> granted victory over his executioners,  
> when he distributed his relics,  
> exposed his noble head.

It seems to me that Eugenius II, bishop of the see of Toledo, lived the monastic life in that place. For, fleeing with sagacious haste, he sought the city of Zaragoza, where he clung to the tombs of the martyrs and there fittingly cultivated the studies of wisdom and the monastic vocation, as Hildefonsus writes in chapter 13 of his *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.

# AIMOIN’S LETTER TO LORD BERNO, ABBOT, AND THE OTHER BROTHERS UNDER HIM

[Col. 1011C] To the worthy holy Fathers, Lord Abbot Berno and the other brothers under him, who in the district of Albi and in the monastery of blessed Benedict called Castres, under his governance, serve as fellow soldiers of God through disciplined observance: Aimoin, a sinner, the least of the monks of the gracious Germanus, bishop of Paris, wishes present prosperity and an eternal crown in Christ.

Having learned, most beloved Fathers, of your prudent and imitable simplicity, I am not surprised that your holiness has been pleased to entrust me with so small a task: namely, to commit to writing for posterity and future generations the arrival among you of the blessed levite and martyr of Christ, Vincent, and the cause of that arrival, prompted by heavenly admonition.

In this matter it is also appropriately required that I illuminate great things with few words, or, to avoid weariness, compress extensive material into a brief account, so that this work may, with Christ’s favor, be more acceptable to all who read it. I shall also touch upon the miracles of the same saint, displayed in great number during the journey and among you, only insofar as is needed to establish with certainty his discovery and his translation to you.

But since you have graciously applied to me about this matter, unworthy though I am, may the pious will of the Lord always be done, and may the prayer of this holy and outstanding witness, both continual and effective with him, follow on my behalf. [Col. 1014A] Nor is it right that I should be found disobedient to so many and such great teachers, who, though I am unworthy, ask this of me. May your holiness also entreat divine mercy for me, so that, supported by the help of holy prayers, I may accomplish what I do not presume upon the strength of my merits—not I, indeed, but the grace of God with me.

# HERE BEGINS BOOK ONE, ON THE DISCOVERY OR TRANSLATION OF BLESSED VINCENT, LEVITE AND MARTYR, CELEBRATED ON THE SIXTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF NOVEMBER

[Col. 1013]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 1013B]

In the year 855 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, while the orthodox Frankish ruler Charles, son of the Emperor Louis, was reigning in a certain part of his kingdoms—namely, in Aquitaine and at the monastery commonly called Conkittas—a vision was shown to a certain monk named Hildebert. The following account will make clear that it had been revealed from heaven.

This man was simple, and had passed beyond the age of youth; in character he was old, and trained in the disciplines of holy patience. Having also acquired the monastic habit—which he had especially and eagerly desired from the time of his priesthood—he had displayed himself in the practices of the whole religious life in such a way that, following the footsteps of the fathers who had gone before him in this life, he too became an example to many.

Once, after he had discharged the duty of keeping vigil, he gave himself over to sleep. Then a divine voice sounded in his ears, saying:

“Brother, are you awake?”

When he replied, “Lord, what do you wish me to do?” the voice said:

“Rise, go, and undertake the journey to Valencia of Hispania; and search outside that city’s walls for the burial place of Vincent, levite and martyr. The church that once stood over it was destroyed by the pagans because of the wicked conduct of the citizens and inhabitants of the surrounding area. There, without any religious honor and with no covering to protect it, his body is drenched by the heavenly rain. For know that it is worthy, and the Lord wills it, that this glorious friend of God, carefully dug up from there, be transferred to a place of peace and legitimate worship.”

After these words, that heavenly apparition, together with the voice, withdrew at once from the sight of the man who was seeing and recounting this vision. When sleep had been driven away, he recalled what he had seen with a wakeful mind and rose, humbly praying for God’s mercy, so that the maker of all things might deign to accomplish through him what He had shown.

## CHAPTER II

There was, in fact, another religious monk in the same monastery, likewise both priest and convert [Note: Among monks, “converts” were formerly called those who turned from secular life to the monastic life in mature age.], named Audaldus, bound to him by a special intimacy and nearly his equal in age and manner of life. From his own mouth, we confidently believe that we have received what is related here, and much more besides, in faith.

The first-mentioned priest, Hildebert, approached him. Revealing in a private conversation what had been disclosed to him, he asked him to become his companion in the undertaking, encouraging him in many ways. He urged his friend and entreated his beloved companion; he promised that God and the holy martyr would provide assistance, and he also pledged the reward of eternal recompense for the sweat of the labor.

The devout man received these words in the secret depths of an attentive heart. Immediately, approving his companion’s words, he gave his assent most willingly—especially since he had often heard from a certain noble Spaniard named Berta that the body of that same holy levite and martyr could easily be carried by anyone to any place from the deserted site where it lay.

The minds of both men became most eager to travel across so many intervening lands and most ready to endure whatever obstacles might arise. Accordingly, they disclosed their intention to Blandinus, the abbot of that place, and to the other brothers, from whom they needed to seek counsel about undertaking and completing the matter.

A common and powerful enthusiasm for this undertaking arose among all who had gathered. Their minds had been enlightened by heavenly virtue, and the joy of a shared hope had breathed upon them.

## CHAPTER III

Having received this divine command—with ardent minds, it must be admitted—they made all preparations and set out with only two servants, proceeding joyfully toward the place and task revealed to them from heaven.

As they traveled and hastened along the road at a rapid pace, Hildebert, overcome by bodily illness, reluctantly abandoned the journey he had undertaken. Audaldus, however, sorrowful and thereafter content with a single companion, passed boldly onward under Christ’s guidance, enduring many ambushes of the pagans and equally many pressures of varied tribulations, which it would take too long to recount. At last he reached the city of Valencia mentioned above.

There he remained for four days in its suburb, already completely abandoned by Christians, anxious and uncertain what to do. On the fifth day he approached a certain Moor named Zacharias, with whom he was staying. Privately he questioned him about the matter for which he had come, revealing his secrets and asking whether Zacharias could help him in it.

Zacharias replied that he could do so very well and that he knew precisely the place where the precious martyr of the Lord lay, as well as the tomb-chest of his monument, which was still intact.

“Let us go,” said Audaldus, “and see whether it is as you assert.”

Zacharias answered:

“What money will you give me if I show you what you seek?”

The monk replied:

“I have little indeed; but I will pay all of it, or certainly as much as you ask, without hesitation.”

Accordingly, the aforementioned Zacharias, restrained by heavenly prompting and, as we believe, through the favor of the holy martyr, asked for no more than forty silver pieces—that is, five solidi.

These were willingly paid, and they went together to the place. There they found only the ruins of the church’s walls still visible, and they discovered the position of the tomb itself, just as it had been, undefiled and marked with an inscription. Written above it was the statement that the holy levite and martyr Vincent rested there.

Among other things, the names of his distinguished parents also shone forth, inserted in the same epitaph: his father Euticius and his mother Enola, from whom this athlete, destined for such a struggle, had sprung.

Thus, after the location of the sarcophagus had been discovered and identified, they returned home while there was still much daylight. Audaldus glorified and blessed God, who had directed the beginning of his journey so favorably.

## CHAPTER IV

Then, when the rest of night was gently soothing human limbs, they rose at first light and returned alone and secretly to the tomb. They found a marble vessel of extraordinary beauty, carefully fortified on every side as was fitting. With unexpected ease, beyond what can be expressed, they both exerted their strength together and opened it.

What further wonder, on account of its incredible integrity, and what compunction or tears—arising, clearly, from joy and from the unprecedented fragrance of spices diffused there—the monk mentioned above, the discoverer of so great a treasure, experienced at that moment, is ineffable; he himself attests it under oath.

Yet this shines forth more clearly than daylight: by signs of this kind, as by certain voices, it was proclaimed that Vincent, the Martyr and Levite of God whom they sought, had been found.

Apart from the many and astonishing injuries inflicted upon him in his sufferings, he was found, as we have already indicated, so whole and free from the taint of decay that he could in no way be arranged in the sack prepared for carrying him, while his sinews were still rigid. Necessity itself compelled them to bend and loosen him by folding his limbs.

When this had been done with reverence and fear, he was carried to their lodging, where they awaited, day by day, the time and opportunity to leave and return to their homeland.

## CHAPTER V

Finally, they purchased palm branches and tied them around the body, as though a treasure acquired for this purpose were being concealed. Bearing such a great and venerable prize, laden with this gift and enriched by this pearl, that poor but exceedingly wealthy merchant resumed his desired journey when he saw that the time was right.

The Lord wished once again to show him that he had found the body of Vincent, levite and martyr. One night, when sleep—more powerful than usual—had fallen upon Audaldus and all the others, a sudden radiance, unquestionably fallen from heaven, filled the entire dwelling in which the saint was staying.

The host, lying apart, thought nothing other than that his own house was burning, consumed by the devouring force of fire. While he cried out in fear, asking who had kindled the fire, Audaldus, as though weary from the journey, scarcely rose after shaking off the stillness of sleep. Hearing the host’s shouts, he silently and fearfully observed the heavenly work, suffused with the radiance itself.

When he had gathered himself and recognized the power of the Most High, he soothed his host with gentle speech, since the man was fierce according to the custom of the gentiles, so that he would not be afraid. He declared that the fire had undoubtedly been kindled by him.

When the host heard this, he confined himself within the barriers of his own room. He was neither permitted nor deemed worthy to learn the mystery of the miraculous event.

## CHAPTER VI

At daybreak the monk rose quickly and hastened to complete the remainder of his journey. After several days he hurried to the city of Zaragoza. There, as a pilgrim, he was received for that night by a woman devoted to God who had a house near the walls of the city and, out of mercy, offered him lodging.

While she remained awake and silent in a more secluded part of her house, she noticed the monk mentioned above standing before the holy body, chanting among shining candles.

Accordingly, when the signal for the night had been sounded, she hurried to the church and reported what she had seen to the bishop of the city through an intermediary.

The bishop hastened there. He ordered the bundle, together with the palm branches, to be carried away without regard for modesty, and commanded that the monk be seized.

A short while earlier, however, Audaldus had been considering the expenses necessary for the road. He had left his servant at home, since the man was mute, and had gone to the marketplace to buy bread.

The bishop divided the bundle and exposed everything that it contained before all present. He found within it the sacred relic concealed and carefully sewn into the sack.

Greatly astonished and amazed, and judging plainly that it was certainly the body of some holy martyr, he ordered it to be taken away and reverently deposited in the church of blessed Mary, ever-virgin—the mother church of that city. In former times, under Bishop Valerius, that same vigorous martyr and athlete had prominently held the office of archdeacon there.

## CHAPTER VII

After these things had been carried out by deception, Audaldus, unaware of them, returned home with bread for his meal. When he learned—alas!—of this grievous deed, he was struck with anguish of heart and approached the same bishop, named Senior [Note: Saint Eulogius, priest of Córdoba, praises Senior, bishop of Zaragoza, as a man endowed with upright conduct of life in his letter to Wilesindus, bishop of Pamplona.], full of tears. He complained to him about the little body unjustly taken from him.

“That man,” he said, “was my relative—my own relative—who recently died and was buried in the regions of Hispania. Seeking to place his corpse among the lifeless bodies of my other relatives, I traversed these lands, enduring many hardships, by Christ’s favor. I redeemed it from the pagans’ hostility after giving a considerable gift.

“But alas for the sacrilege!” he continued. “I have encountered a bishop more cruel than the heathens. What their severity, softened by human compassion, granted to one who asked with devotion, your violence, wickedly stirred to every excess, seizes and arrogantly claims. Like a madman, you call the holy body the body of a sinful man.”

At these words and others, the bishop was inflamed by exceedingly violent anger. He ordered the monk to be held, promising him unspeakable kinds of torture and bruises from rods unless he disclosed from what city or place he had stolen the body, or by what name the saint was known.

When he began this interrogation and persisted in cruelly abusing Audaldus in a disgraceful manner, the monk, willing or unwilling, was beaten for a long time and finally hung by the testicles. He seemed to confess that he had brought the body from the regions of Hispania and that the saint’s name was Marinus—a name invented for the occasion.

Passing over the rest, the bishop, wickedly invading the sacred treasure and partly deceived, drove the monk away amid great lamentation of heart and abundant tears. Audaldus returned sadly to his own place, worn down by the blows.

When the brothers of his monastery heard this, they did not believe him and accused Audaldus of lying. Calling him a wandering monk, they excluded him from their company and, when he thereafter departed of his own accord, drove him away. They granted him permission—indeed, compelled him—to remain wherever he wished.

He eventually reached the monastery of blessed Benedict, called the Upper Castle. There he explained in order to the abbot of that congregation, the religious man Lord Gislebert, and to the other brothers living there, the entire course of his journey and actions, and how the body of the holy levite and martyr had been taken from him.

They were astonished and greatly rejoiced at what they heard. First, according to the rule, they received Audaldus; then they granted him a place to live among them for as long as he should live. Together they deliberated, awaiting a suitable time, so that with the assistance of heavenly grace they might one day strive to transfer so great an honor to themselves.

## CHAPTER VIII

When the appointed time had passed—namely, after eight and a half years had elapsed—they sent brothers to Zaragoza, at the command of Salomon, count of Cerdanya and Audaldus’s most intimate associate. These brothers were to receive the body of the holy levite and martyr and, with Salomon arranging it, bring it back with them, if Christ showed mercy.

Salomon had learned of the matter long before. As he was prudent and eager for what was good, he had gone to the king of Córdoba, Major, when an opportunity arose. Among other things, he pretended that a relative of his named Sugnarius, while being brought from the regions of Hispania through Zaragoza, had been violently seized and detained by Senior, the bishop of that city.

The king, besides other gifts voluntarily offered, demanded one hundred solidi in exchange for ordering the body to be returned. He instructed Abdilam, the local ruler of the aforesaid city, to issue a document commanding that, after receiving an equal sum of one hundred solidi, he should order the body of his relative Sugnarius to be restored to Count Salomon.

When these matters had been settled, and the minds of the rulers had been won over by the stipulated sum of money, the bishop was summoned. He was strictly questioned, as though guilty of treason, as to why he had committed such an injustice against a dead man, setting aside imperial reverence, and why he had shown no respect even for himself.

He denied everything, affirming with many oaths by God and the saints that he had not done it. But Audaldus came forward and prepared to convict the bishop firmly and with steadfast courage.

After they had disputed for a long time without result and, as the saying goes, like women, the bishop refused to confess the truth despite being invited with gentle words. Tortures were proposed for him: he would be tied by the feet or neck with a rope, dragged around the city, and finally, after being mocked, torn limb from limb.

Although the virtues of Saint Vincent—albeit under the name of Saint Marinus—had often been displayed there during the prescribed period and had drawn his mind toward love of the saint in a wondrous manner, he was nevertheless terrified by the horror of the threats. He confessed what had been done and, not without pain and groaning, revealed the place where the sacred body had been buried.

The monks who had come reached the place and found and lifted up so precious a talent of heavenly treasure.

One of them, named Radbertus, hesitated and wondered whether it was this body or another. He insisted that the matter should first be carefully verified by opening the little coffin and examining the certain signs known to Audaldus. Immediately, however, the foot that he had advanced for this purpose became infirm, and his knee and shin were afflicted with severe tingling.

At this sign, the others became sufficiently certain that the body had been restored and arranged it suitably for carrying.

Having obtained what they had desired, and after the monk shortly afterward fully recovered the strength of his foot, they set out with hymns and praises of thanksgiving, as the circumstances and character of the place required, intending under the Lord’s guidance to return to their own home.

To Him belong honor and power, might and dominion, forever and ever. Amen.

Thus far concerning the discovery, or recovery, of the holy body. Now let the following little book, together with the prologue attached to it, take up what remains concerning the translation and the miracles performed during it.

Since up to this point, under Christ’s guidance, we have set down in faithful writing what was done concerning the discovery or recovery of the body of this holy levite and martyr, let us now carefully examine, in the brief treatment with which we began, what remains concerning his translation and the miracles performed during it.

The reader ought not to be driven away; rather, he should be invited toward what is being related. Even if an uncultivated style is harsh, at least brevity may make it pleasing.

For this reason we have also wished to divide this entire work into two parts, though small in extent. We ask that whatever we have exceeded in these matters be forgiven us. Having read much only briefly, we have taken care, out of devoted labor, to write on the very spot those things that we found worthy of faith and report, with those who had witnessed them present and bearing testimony.

# BOOK TWO BEGINS

## CHAPTER I

When they had hastened to the town of Balagivum, beside the river Segre, they settled on an island adjoining the mainland.

Immediately it became known that the body of the noble levite and martyr was present. Some people then gathered, offering gifts and services according to their ability. Among them a woman who had long been blind was brought. Prostrate on the ground before the relics themselves, she asked that sight be granted to her.

After weeping for some time and persisting in prayer, she recovered her sight, as all those present witnessed. Astonished at herself—what she had been when she came and what she had become—she said:

“I give thanks to you, God, and to you, holy martyr, who have judged me worthy of the abundance of your power.”

## CHAPTER II

From there they departed and directed their journey at a rapid pace toward the fortress of Berga. There the Lord likewise displayed mercifully, through a miracle, how much merit and favor the holy levite and martyr possessed with Him.

Among the others seeking his most welcome gifts, there was a certain lame man who had been carried there and was ill throughout his body. Before the relics, as commonly happens in such circumstances, he first began to suffer intense pain and roll about on the pavement.

This seemed astonishing to those standing by. But shortly afterward, through God’s mercy and the intercession of blessed Vincent, the bases of his feet were strengthened and his steps straightened, so that, accompanied by the joy of restored health, he returned home sound on his own.

## CHAPTER III

Since a lamp must not be hidden but placed on a lampstand so that it may give light, they fitted that holy body, shining with so great a radiance of virtues, into a bier. With Count Salomon preceding them as a peaceful guide, they reached Cerdanya.

They had decided, with sound judgment, to remain there for a while because of those who would meet them and because the journey required rest.

Entering a village of that same region, which had received the name Albi from its ancient inhabitants, they placed the body upon the altar of the church of the blessed Virgin Mary.

An innumerable multitude of both sexes gathered there for two days. Among them were two whose knees were contracted, one weak woman, one blind man, and people suffering from fevers or possessed by demons. All were freed from the burden of their illnesses through the holy merits of the saint.

We have not heard that anyone afflicted by any disease of weakness, if he approached faithfully, regretted either coming there or departing without the medicine of healing.

## CHAPTER IV

Thus, after miracles had been performed at nearly every stopping place—for example, two lame men were raised upright at Livia, and at Carcassonne, outside the city, in a church consecrated to Christ in honor of the Levite and Martyr himself, many demoniacs and other sick people were healed—they now approached joyfully the Castle toward which they were traveling, the monastery of the principal Father Benedict.

But if one attempted to describe how splendid was the monastic procession worthy of so great a reception, with crosses, candles, and every fitting adornment, as well as the most devout gathering of the people, I think it would be superfluous.

Accordingly, they placed the body of the Martyr in the church of the gracious Mother of God, Mary, before the entrance of the monastery itself, chiefly because of the devout attendance of women, who, according to the ancient custom of the fathers of that place, were denied entrance to the monastery.

They nevertheless resolved to build a new basilica in his honor near the monastery, to which devoted persons of both sexes would have free access.

## CHAPTER V

Since there might perhaps be doubt about this discovery and its desired conveyance, almighty God wished to strengthen it, as an addition to His goodness, by the following miracle.

In the village of Vidcellas, only three miles from the monastery, a woman still living there named Aitrudis was admonished by a neighbor to set aside her wool-working and hurry with the others to welcome the martyr Saint Vincent.

She refused to do so and, with a burst of laughter, said that it was more likely the body of some Moorish or Spanish pagan than that of a martyr.

Immediately she was deprived of the functions of all her limbs and, falling miserably to the ground like a corpse, proclaimed in a terrifying voice that she would soon die. She begged her people to carry her to the saint’s church.

Carried there in a cart, she remained for nine days, enduring the same paralytic affliction while many looked on. After another nine days she was restored to health and went out strong, as she remains even now.

## CHAPTER VI

As crowds frequented the place, whether sick people afflicted with various illnesses seeking the remedy of healing or others, certain men came from the region of Cerdanya. Not far from the monastery they were stripped of their possessions and arrived naked, groaning and weeping, before the saint.

But, in a wondrous manifestation of heavenly justice, it happened that the plunderers, attempting to flee elsewhere, were miraculously forced by an opposing protection to hurry back to the same place with everything they had taken.

When the plunderers and the plundered looked at one another, the former began to fear, while the latter were astonished far more greatly. When the people wished to rise against the guilty men, they humbly begged that, for the love of Christ and the holy martyr, no harm should be done to them.

Having obtained this, they restored everything. Praising God and holy Vincent, each group returned home: the one joyful over what had been recovered, the other over the forgiveness freely obtained.

## CHAPTER VII

Nor should the following event, equally worthy of wonder, be passed over in silence.

A certain man from the district of Camers, arriving late in the day for the sake of prayer, left his lance leaning against one of the trees in front of the entrance to the aforementioned basilica, while preserving the honor due to the religious place.

After entering the church thus unarmed and devoting himself to prayer, a certain thief seized his lance and fled, making for his nearby home.

But, mentally disturbed, he reached the hut of the man whose spear it was, nearly thirty leagues away, exhausted by fasting and by traveling throughout the night. When he asked for a little water because he was thirsty, the woman recognized her husband’s spear, took it back, and, when the thief confessed his guilt, forgave him.

This was not without demonstrating the power of Saint Vincent, who had arranged for the injury done to his pilgrim to be repaired in this manner.

## CHAPTER VIII

Since we have mentioned the building of a new church for the holy levite and martyr Vincent, it is fitting to report a new miracle here.

More than two hundred men came together for this construction with gifts, apart from women, children, and the sick. Among them was a certain blind man who was also poor in possessions.

So that he would not appear empty-handed in the service of the saint, he asked the guide to give him a fairly large stone from the road, and immediately lifted it and placed it upon his neck.

The crowd accused him of foolishness, since he was attempting an impossible task because of the weight. But he declared that he would never rest from what he had begun until he had carried the gift of the stone he had taken to the construction of the new church of Saint Vincent.

Before he had finished speaking, his blindness was removed and he recovered his sight.

## CHAPTER IX

The venerable man Helisagar, bishop of the city of Toulouse, having heard these signs of power, used his pastoral authority to exhort the clergy and people to prepare to go with him, if they wished, to pray to the holy martyr.

When the appointed time arrived, the good shepherd came reverently, surrounded by crowds of his flock, and barefoot from the ninth milestone, having become an example to the flock.

One of those who accompanied him had, from birth, the fingers of both hands so contracted and attached to the palms that they could never be opened or extended. After prayers and tears had been poured out before the holy martyr, he felt them loosened, although living blood continued to flow from the places where they had previously been attached.

When the bishop and all who were with him saw this, they burst forth into divine praises, singing litanies, hymns, and the *Te Deum laudamus* in tearful voices. They also kissed with great joy the hands stained with blood.

## CHAPTER X

A certain man had hidden some silver in his bosom for a work that he needed to undertake. A shameless woman skilled in the art of theft drew it out.

But the hand that held the silver immediately became rigid, so that she could neither open it nor draw it back toward herself, as everyone watched.

She fled to the sacred relics of Saint Vincent and prayed there devoutly with the brothers and other faithful people. She was healed, her hand was released, and she returned the stolen silver.

## CHAPTER XI

Another man had a daughter blind from birth. Trusting in the hope of healing her, he decided to bring her to the widely proclaimed patronage of Saint Vincent.

When he reached the monastery, he learned that the sacred body itself had been moved to a more remote and safer place because of fear of the pagan Northmen. He repeatedly uttered groans, saying:

“Have mercy, Christ; have mercy, most blessed Vincent. Have mercy on me, miserable man; have mercy on this daughter of mine.”

At these tearful words, heavenly mercy—which does not sleep—was stirred to compassion. Immediately, through the prayers of the great athlete and the faith of the father, the girl received back her sight.

## CHAPTER XII

When the Northmen, who had come to besiege Toulouse, approached, the monks brought back the holy body and placed it once more in the place where it had previously been, to be venerated with fitting rites.

## CHAPTER XIII

Again, a certain girl blind from birth, firmly believing that through the intervention of so great a martyr she could recover her sight, asked her sister to take her to him as quickly as possible.

As they traveled together, they heard that he had been carried far away into the countryside. Since they were unable to reach the place because of the severity of winter and the rugged mountain ridges, the blind girl urged her sister to make candles from the wax they had brought with them and at least carry them to the place where the holy body had paused briefly during the journey.

She had heard that the place was famous for miracles, so much so that even animals without reason became weak when they touched it.

When they had done this and both had prostrated themselves there, groaning and pouring out their prayer, the woman who had arrived ignorant of the light began to say that she could clearly see everything around her.

## CHAPTER XIV

In the same district of Albi there was a fisherman named Ubidandus. When he saw his companions, as they were going fishing, lingering at the aforementioned place for the sake of veneration, he rebuked them, saying:

“I wish you would worship all the trees of this forest, since you consecrate every street and road indiscriminately with the observance due to an oratory.”

As soon as he had said these words, his insolent mouth was turned upward toward his ear and became monstrously deformed beyond what can be expressed.

Then he repented, ran to the place mentioned above, and, stretching his whole body out, confessed that he had been insulting and blasphemous.

Afterward he hurried to the church in which the body of the holy levite and martyr was being honored. He visited it at every hour of the day and night until he was healed.

## CHAPTER XV

With this light thus spreading far and wide, people blind from birth who were brought there were also illumined; the functions of their senses were restored to the deaf and mute; the lame were healed; those possessed by demons were cleansed when the demons were driven out; and those weighed down by any distress of other illnesses, whether present or absent, were made healthy.

Accordingly, a certain poor woman who had long been deprived of her sight was being led to the holy martyr. In the middle of the journey, her guides, exhausted by weariness and labor, abandoned her.

She asked one of the bystanders at least to offer before the altar of the holy martyr candles—small gifts expressive of her blindness—after lighting them.

As he extended his hand to receive them, the woman herself saw the candles. Drawing back her arm, she no longer sought either a guide or anyone to carry them. Joyful and seeing more clearly with each passing day, she completed the journey she had begun, overtaking even many others along the way, and finally reached the tomb of blessed Vincent.

There, with the candles burning, she offered them herself rather than through another, and recovered the full sharpness of her eyes.

## CHAPTER XVI

A similar miracle was performed in the district of Rodez, commonly called Rodinigus.

A certain man whose knees were contracted was being brought to Saint Vincent. In the middle of the journey his lazy, sluggish, and inhuman guides abandoned him alone and weeping.

But because the Lord never ceases mercifully to hear the prayers of those who cry out to Him from whatever strait of necessity, He immediately took pity on the wretched man. Suffused with heavenly medicine, He made the weak man who lay there rise upright.

He walked with great strides and soon caught up with those who had deserted him.

They, astonished at so great a miracle, began to accuse and sharply rebuke themselves because they had so lazily and mercilessly abandoned a man worthy of heavenly healing.

## CHAPTER XVII

As we have mentioned, it was the custom of the aforesaid congregation that all women be kept from entering the monastery.

For this reason the brothers of that monastery had wisely arranged that the body of blessed Vincent, levite and martyr, should be placed in the basilica of Mary, the Mother of God, to which women had free access.

In the course of time, however, when this gathering of people ceased for several days, they carried the body into the older church of the monastery and placed it behind the altar of Saint Benedict, until his church should be completed.

After this, a woman who had been blind for many years attempted to enter as far as the place where the saint lay. But someone who met her drove her back and forced her to depart sorrowfully.

She sighed, raised the eyes of her mind toward heaven, and humbly prayed that the holy martyr would grant her assistance.

Thus, amid streams of tears, she drove away her blindness.

## CHAPTER XVIII

In a certain place adjoining the same monastery, called Waldarius’s cell, the following memorable proclamation of power shone forth.

Military forces had been spread around the place. The monks approached Count Hermengaud of Albi and begged him to protect the crops and fields belonging to their obedience from the invasion of the enemy and the grazing of their horses.

For there are very few meadows in those regions.

Hermengaud ordered four cloths belonging to the church of Saint Vincent, which had been offered by poor women, to be taken and tied to an equal number of poles or staffs. He then ordered them to be fixed around the flowering field, so that by this sign the enemy might refrain from plundering the harvest.

But one of them, despising such a sign, knocked one of the cloths and its staff to the ground. When he attempted to drive his horse into the very crops, the horse struck him in the forehead with its heels, and he breathed out his spirit.

When this was heard and spread among the enemy, fear seized everyone. The evident judgment of God and the merit of the holy martyr were proclaimed everywhere by all.

## CHAPTER XIX

The following event is almost similar to this one.

Lord Alberic the monk had gone into the district of Empúries with his brother Helias and was staying in a village belonging to his obedience called Garriculas. The enemy arrived and devastated the district and the village, sparing no one.

They also carried off Alberic’s horses, and he could not obtain the return of even one, although he knew that one of them was stronger than the others.

But that very horse which he had requested, as though avenging a double injury—the theft, and the just demand for its return—struck the thief with its hooves on his bare head and handed him over to death.

Terrified by this deed, the accomplices in the crime fled, leaving behind not only the horses but also whatever else they had stolen in the same village.

## CHAPTER XX

The following example, concerning a mute and deaf man who was healed, will bring the account to an end.

A certain illustrious man named Georgius had a servant who was mute and deaf. When the servant was being led to the tomb of Saint Vincent, levite and martyr, and was about twelve miles from the monastery, he began to speak and to hear those who spoke without impediment.

Then he asked his companions to take him quickly to the place so that he could give thanks to the holy martyr.

They did so, to the glory and praise of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, who causes His saints to triumph everywhere by wondrous power. His honor and dominion remain without end, forever and ever. Amen.

# LETTER OF THE SAME AIMOINUS TO LORD THEOTGERUS, MONK OF THE SAME CONGREGATION

[Col. 1025]

To the distinguished among levites, Lord Theotgerus—who, in accordance with the concordant etymology of his name, bears God—Aimoinus, fellow minister, sends greetings.

To your praiseworthy charity, my sweetest Theotger, who diligently and constantly devotes yourself to caring for me, I, devoted to obeying you in everything, bow myself willingly as your camel, to bear the burden you have imposed upon me. Indeed, after completing a prose work, your affection compels me to produce two little books about the arrival of the blessed levite and martyr of Christ, Vincent—an unprecedented and, for its brevity, astonishing work. I shall close each of them with thirty verses, arranged in ten chapters each. Therefore I more prudently choose to seem like a recent writer than, under any pretext whatsoever, to absent myself from your love, which is sweeter to me than honey.

*The Letter ends.*

# BOOK ONE BEGINS, CONTAINING THIRTY VERSES

## Chapter I. How Audaldus, entering Spain, reached Valencia

When twice four hundred, ten times five, and four further cycles had rolled by

Since the birth from the virginal and ever-sacred seed of Christ,

Audaldus was known by such a name,

A monk at the common monastery, approved according to its rule,

And bearing the sacred honor of holy Aaron.

Taking one companion, he endured many bitter things;

But turning all of them into sweet flavors,

He boldly persisted until at some time he reached Valencia,

Where it might receive him, after he had completed his pilgrimage.

## Chapter II. How he revealed his secret to the Moor Zacharias, and how he found the saint’s tomb

He discloses to that guest of the Moorish prince Zacharias

The secrets already held within his heart:

That he had come down into the land of Spain

Out of love alone for the levite and martyr of God, Vincent.

Then, by flattering prayers, he caressed his mind and heart,

And bribed the Moorish merchant with the eager coins of silver.

Finally, rising, they searched for the enclosure of the monument,

Which shone clearly with this inscription:

“Here lies Vincent, the levite,

Established in the honor of martyrdom.”

For the written names indicated the lineage of his parents.

## Chapter III. How they returned together by night to the monument and raised the saint’s body

Having examined these signs by night,

They applied their strength, dug, and opened the tomb.

They brought out the sacred body with a lamp serving them,

A heavenly sign by which the sweetness of the truth was made manifest.

It rose above and pervaded all the spices.

And when it was necessary to complete the work with bindings,

Audaldus used a cuculla sewn from a linen cloth.

From there they returned home joyfully beneath the shining stars,

While Audaldus awaited the day on which he would return to his homeland;

And, once the favorable time had come, he did so cheerfully.

*The first book ends.*

# BOOK TWO BEGINS, CONTAINING THE SAME NUMBER OF VERSES

## Chapter I. How, when the sacred body reached Castrum, it was honorably received

The holy martyr and levite of Christ reached Castrum,

The beautiful father’s cell of Benedict,

Leaving behind the deceit of the Elder Caesar,

And omitting other matters, lest speaking of them should take too long.

No one bearing a human face could express in words

What joy there was at his arrival.

Only Jesus, who was present as witness, knows

What kind of splendid reception the monks provided,

With suitable golden ornaments poured forth everywhere,

And a jewel-bearing green radiance shining upward even to the heavens.

## Chapter II. How a woman, at first doubting him, became contracted, and afterward, believing, deserved to be healed

Then there was a woman who laughed,

Too proud to believe that the body was that of the holy levite,

Insisting, perhaps because she thought so, that it was rather the body of a Moor.

Immediately, her limbs collapsed as she was thrown to the ground;

She became contracted, her hope of escaping with her life taken away.

But when she was brought to the saint, faith arising, she was healed;

She arrived on a cart and departed cured on her feet.

After this first sign had been accomplished with such great power,

Many more followed, beyond what any number can count,

Some of them also recorded in prose.

## Chapter III. Where the sacred body was received and placed, and how it was afterward located behind the altar of Saint Benedict

These things were being performed before the gates of the monastery,

In the court of the Mother,

Under this immense gift of Christ,

While a sacred church was being built in his own honor,

Where at last he might peacefully pass over and be buried according to his right,

So that, coming thither, male and female alike might approach.

After the passage of time had flowed by,

It pleased them to lift the sacred body from there

And place it worthily behind the altar

Of the holy and devout Father Benedict.

There he is venerated with a full observance of merited honor,

Shining properly through continual signs of his powers.

By the aid of the King of kings and Lord of lords, Jesus Christ,

The good and gracious Savior of the world,

Who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God

For infinite ages of ages. Amen.

# On the Translation of the Holy Martyrs George the Monk, Aurelius, and Natalia from the City of Córdoba to Paris

See among the works of Saint Eulogius, *Patrologia*, volume CXV, column 939.

# Two Books on the Miracles of Saint Germanus, by the same author, the monk Aimoinus

(Printed in Mabillon, in the same place.)

# The Letter of the Monk Aimoinus Begins

Health and perpetual peace in Christ to devoted readers eager for learning,

From Jesus, ruler of all rulers.

Since the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear with hearing, and since many will pass through the world and knowledge will be multiplied, I have no doubt that this little book of the miracles of our lord Germanus, resplendent with shining distinctions, will be passed from hand to hand. These events, granted to the world by heavenly favor through the merits of that holy bishop during the time of the ancient Danes—namely Ragenarius and his companions—were spread abroad by worthy reports until they reached the ears of the most serene King Charles. He rejoiced in them and, as though the world under his reign might become more generous through the preciousness of these accounts, ordered them to be recorded with careful diligence and joined, according to ecclesiastical law, to the pages of Catholic writings.

At that time the venerable lord and abbot Ebroinus presided over the monastery of the aforesaid holy bishop. He was bishop of the see of the church of Poitiers.

**Note:** He was chief chaplain of King Charles, as Sirmondus noted in his commentary on the third capitulary of Charles the Bald, held at the palace of Verneuil under Ebroinus’s presidency.

Since Ebroinus, under royal authority, was occupied with carrying out the task entrusted to him, he delegated its execution to two brothers of our congregation, advanced alike in maturity and learning. Each wrote separately according to the abundance of his own understanding, and afterward each produced his own little work.

When both works had been read by the aforesaid lord bishop Ebroinus and by others, it was decided [perhaps: it was not decided] that one should in some manner be preferred to the other. For that reason the unusual labor of both remained unfinished until the time of the lord Gozlinus, the eminent Father of that place.

**Note:** He too was chancellor of Charles the Bald after Abbot Louis; later, after Charles’s death, he became bishop of Paris. He will be mentioned again below.

When this had become known to him after some years, he ordered me—not as a wiser brother, but rather as a manual laborer—to join the two works into a single little volume. He asked only that, if I found anything entirely superfluous, I should cut it out, and that I should polish whatever was less well adorned with the elegance of a more flourishing style, doing nothing beyond the truth.

I confess that I undertook this not through my own strength, unless strength had been given from heaven, nor out of confidence in my ability, but rather trusting in the obedience owed to so great a prelate. I would have deserved the guilt of wrongdoing if I had neglected to carry out the command of my commanding lord.

# The Prologue of the Monk Aimoinus Begins

Just as we believe those worthy of praise who take pains to write, for the edification of the faithful, the deeds or miracles that divine power deigns to perform through the saints, so without doubt we know that those are blameworthy who, through laziness and sluggishness of mind, neglect to commit such things to writing for the benefit of those to come.

Many people are daily awakened, as though from sleep, to the love of God and the practice of good living when they read in books the deeds of the holy Fathers and behold their sacred miracles as though they were present. Therefore, let everyone who possesses the gift of a talent fear lest he hear what that wicked servant heard—the servant who did not fear to return to his Lord the money he had received and wickedly buried in the earth, without profit from interest.

This must not only be undertaken voluntarily; whenever it is commanded, the command of the one giving the order must also be obeyed with the utmost diligence.

Almighty God has deigned to perform many astonishing deeds, worthy of being reported, through that same blessed bishop, both in past times and in our own. Through inertia they have been suppressed in silence and through the carelessness of writers left unrecorded.

Now, however, with the Lord’s help and with the merits of that saint assisting us, at the command of the lord king, and of Ebroinus, bishop and ruler of his monastery, we gladly strive—though in an unpolished and unlearned manner, yet with truthful and faithful speech—to touch upon the things that the grace of that most holy man has recently pleased the Creator of all things to perform, and to leave them for reading by both present and future generations, just as they truly occurred and as they have already been widely reported among the people of the Northmen.

# The First Book Begins

## Chapter I

In the year 846 of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the sixth year of the most eminent king Charles, when the kingdom of the Franks had been divided into various parts after the death of the lord Louis the emperor, and the sins of the people were increasing, blood touching blood, it came about—by God’s permission and because their crimes demanded it—that foreign peoples left their own settlements: namely, the nation of the Danes, whom common usage calls Northmen, that is, “Northern men.”

With proud and swollen hearts, and with a powerful fleet of ships, they entered the territories of Christians. Raging here and there, and roaming everywhere with great arrogance, they began to lay waste to various islands of the sea, until, with no one resisting them, they entered the Seine and, by an astonishing stroke of fortune, landed at Rouen.

After lingering for a while in that city, they observed that the leaders of the region—something we cannot mention without great anguish of heart—were sluggish and timid about fighting. They came out from their ships, spread far and wide, and began to slaughter and capture people of both sexes, burning villages, monasteries, and churches as they plundered them, and exercising the full extent of their lust with every cruelty as they raged against the people of God.

They continued until they came to the place called Caroli-venna, with winds and sails furthering their wickedness according to God’s just judgment, and sailed there in security beyond hope.

**Note:** *Caroli-venna*, that is, “Charles’s fishery.” Charles the Bald, in a charter for the monastery of Saint-Denis preserved by Sirmondus in his notes on the *Capitula*, mentions “the customary due from the fishery which is upon the River Loch in the district of Tellau,” and so forth. Caroli-venna was a place near Rueil, equipped as a fishery by Charles Martel, as is clear from a letter of Louis Augustus, which we shall quote later to illuminate this place. The cell of Saint Germanus was not far away, as appears from Chapter 6 below. We therefore conclude that this was the place which has retained, to the present day, the vernacular name Chalevanne, on the Seine, a little above the town of Saint-Germain, in the forest of Ledia. Not far from this place lies the village of Rotoialus, or Rueil, and the cell of Saint Germanus, La Celle. In one of our Germanensian cartularies there is an arbitration of Robert, Abbot of Saint-Victor, issued in 1253 for the benefit of the people of Saint-Germain against the Dionysians, concerning a mill at Caroli-venna that they had built two years earlier. In the Dionysian cartulary there is also a charter of Philip III, king of the Franks, by which he grants the Dionysian monks high and low justice at Caroli-venna.

Then the glorious prince King Charles, unable to arrive sooner because of their sudden advance, summoned part of his army and first came to the monastery of Macharius Dionysius,

**Note:** It is evident that even then it was customary for the king of the Franks, when undertaking a war or battle, to commend himself and his army before Saint Dionysius; later generations religiously observed this practice. Read Chapter 20 of Book II on the Miracles of Saint Dionysius below, under the year 784.

He came there to be strengthened by the saint’s prayers and thus proceed more securely against the enemies of God and of his own people. Then, being—as a young man—vigorous in spirit and arms, he approached the aforesaid place to fight, prepared not only to engage in battle but also to die honorably for the faith and for the defense of God’s holy Church.

When his enemies learned of his arrival, they crossed to the opposite bank of the aforesaid river, where only a small part of the population was present. After immediately putting these people to flight, they suspended approximately eleven captives on stakes on an island in that river, to the disgrace of Christians; they fastened many others through houses and trees; and, pursuing some wretchedly through villages and fields, they slaughtered and killed them.

Then, arriving at Paris on the very Saturday of the most sacred Paschal festival, they found the once-populous city completely empty and all the monasteries around it deserted by their inhabitants. Fear and terror had seized everyone, since they had deservedly been stripped of divine assistance by their iniquity and were therefore deprived of the support of worldly defense.
