Who, I ask, would not grieve to see an army put to flight before battle was joined, pierced before an arrow was shot, and shamefully subdued before the clash of shields? For the entire order of things in the Church had been utterly confused and turned away from the pursuit of goodness; by this very deprivation of good, it had deserved, with sufficient retribution, to reach the fuel of destruction.

But the merciful and just Father, always correcting those who sin and graciously receiving those who have been corrected, did not do this in order to condemn us cruelly under the weight of our countless offenses, but in order to amend the afflicted through the immense benevolence of his generosity.

Then, alas, the most sacred body of blessed Germanus was dug from its tomb and carried to a possession of that same Church called Cumbis.

**Note:** The estate of Cumbae, Combes-la-Ville, is a village in the district of Brie, six miles from Paris; formerly it belonged by right to the monastery of Saint Germanus, as recorded in the codex of Abbot Irmino.

But what eloquence or what speech could explain the kind of mourning and the magnitude of grief that arose in that Church while these things were being done? Old men and young men, boys and infants wept, since no one was able to restrain himself from tears.

Likewise, the bodies of other saints living in the same district were exhumed and carried to various places, with the sole exception of the remains of Macharius Dionysius and his companions, the martyrs. Although these too were removed from their own tombs, they were not then compelled to go elsewhere because of the king’s presence.

**Note:** Nevertheless, read the Translation of the Relics of Saint Dionysius in Book III of the Miracles of Saint Dionysius below, under the year 784.

For the king had determined that, while the people were slipping away from him, he would at least defend the monastery of the aforesaid holy martyr, because his father of blessed memory, when he was still a child, had commended him to that same saint by a special act of dedication.

## Chapter II

In the order of the narrative, we should insert what almighty God deigned to show while the saint’s body was being moved.

While we were all intent upon its excavation and upon determining how it should be carried, with candles lit out of reverence, it happened by chance that one candle, which a boy was holding carelessly, slipped from his hands, fell, and was entirely extinguished.

When the same boy quickly lifted it from the ground and wished to borrow its lost light from another candle, the merits of so great a patron brought it about that the extinguished candle was immediately lit again in his hands.

We consider this marvelous, though not inappropriate, if divine fire shone there, where, although amid mourning, a son of light was being venerated. Therefore all who were present gave thanks to God and praised the splendid merits of the bishop, and began to devote themselves more and more to psalmody and the praises of God, until the sad work was honorably completed.

## Chapter III

Should that vision which was shown to certain brothers of the monastery on the same night when the body of the most blessed man was exhumed, before the following day’s dawn appeared, be omitted from the account?

When, during the first watch of that night, some brothers had gone to the River Seine, each carrying his own belongings to the ships, and were returning from there to the monastery, an immense brilliance of light appeared to them, and to the servants who accompanied them. It shone over that part of the church where the body of the most holy man had been placed, so that its brightness equaled that of day; the church itself seemed to be burning, as though fire had been placed beneath it.

While they marveled greatly among themselves and their hearts remained stunned by such a sight, the vision gradually faded and disappeared. When they reached the monastery, they asked whether any of the brothers had been above that very church with a light at that hour.

Since no one who had done so was found, they understood that it had been an angelic vision, accomplished by divine power through the saint’s merits: by a grace granted to him, he had taken care to visit his bones, which were about to be moved, and his pious ashes, with such radiance.

## Chapter IV

Nor should we remain silent about that distinguished miracle which, two years before these events occurred, was shown to a monk of that monastery, advanced in age and character. If the examples and deeds of this exceptional man are followed, they may provide great benefit for salvation.

One night, while asleep, he saw blessed Germanus apparently leaving his tomb, unencumbered and prepared to undertake a journey. Since he seemed to recognize that this was the most blessed servant of God, he asked him in a humble voice where he intended to go forth in such a manner.

The saint replied that he was about to depart from that place.

Then the monk, questioning him with a fearful heart, said: “Lord, if you depart then, what shall we, such insignificant little servants of yours, do afterward?”

The saint, as the brother perceived, answered with a sorrowful expression and great grief: “You too shall depart from this place. Yet you will truly learn that I shall return, and by divine mercy you will return together with me at the appointed time.”

That this vision was entirely true was shown by the events that were completed afterward.

## Chapter V

Nor should we pass over in silence what was revealed to a certain man in that same church by Christ, since, when we preach such things, the hearts of those who hear are stirred to seek the honey-sweet assistance of the saints.

A certain devout brother of that monastery, while the others, after Compline had been completed, hurried to rest so that their weary bodies might recline on their beds after the day’s labor, threw himself before the tomb of blessed Germanus for the sake of private prayer.

For a long time he prayed to the Lord of heaven and of the whole world for his sins, and with attentive heart asked the help of blessed Germanus and the other saints for all the faithful. News of the pagans had by then certainly spread frequently to our ears.

Approximately fifteen days before their arrival, this marvelous vision was shown to him. Rising from the prayer in which he had been lying, he saw with open eyes—as once Father Benedict saw the whole world—the tomb of the most blessed Germanus as though it had been opened, and the most holy body itself clothed in undisturbed garments and arranged in the sarcophagus in the proper order, with the divine service exactly as it had been.

Shortly afterward, he himself and all of us who were present together saw this with grief.

Thus the Lord and holy Germanus wished to show his beloved servant what, because of our sins, was soon to be fulfilled. The vision was not disclosed until what followed the vision was revealed to everyone.

## Chapter VI

Finally, while the people of the Northmen remained at the aforementioned place of Caroli-venna, seeing themselves victorious and superior, they came out from their ships and hastened at a swift pace into our cell, which lies opposite or beside that same place.

We think it best to relate the miracle that we learned had occurred there.

**Note:** In Abbot Irmino’s codex it is called Cella Equilina, because it is not far from the forest of Equilina. This is the cell which Abbot Wandremarus is recorded to have given to Saint Germanus; it remains to this day under the right of our monastery, commonly called La Celle.

When they had tried three or four times to set fire to the churches of the apostle Peter and of the blessed Germanus, they failed. Unable to burn them through the merits of the two saints, they eventually came out from the enclosure of the cell and burned a granary that stood nearby.

From it such a great globe of flames rose high into the air that it set fire to certain trees growing even beyond the aforesaid cell, while it left the churches themselves untouched and whole, just as they had been.

Moreover, although a southern wind was blowing with great force and was driving almost the whole fire in that direction, at once a northern wind rose from the opposite quarter. With a marvelous reversal, it bent the southern wind back toward the other side and likewise turned all its force back upon itself.

Thus God is marvelous: he who, with his servants shining together with him in heaven, continually performs wondrous works on earth through the common grace of his mercy.

## Chapter VII

When, as stated above, the fleet of ships had reached Paris on Holy Saturday, then on the following day, when the sun was sending forth its light-bearing rays and illuminating the whole world with its own lamp, they burst from their ships and found the city itself and its neighboring suburbs without inhabitants, as we have already related.

They entered the monastery of the most blessed Germanus and began to defile God’s sanctuary and the remaining furnishings of the church, which had survived the destruction, and to demolish them with polluted hands.

But since, through the Lord’s mercy, the power of that most holy Father was not absent even there, the miracles that the Creator of the whole world deigned at that time to show there, through the grace of that bishop, to the praise of his name, must not be concealed.

Because none of us was present, we knew nothing at all about them. Later, however, we learned of them from faithful messengers of Louis, king of the Bavarians—namely Kobbo and others whom he had sent as envoys to the prince of the Northmen, Horich by name. They related the events faithfully to us, just as they themselves testified: they had seen some of them in the presence of Horich, and had heard the rest from the Christians who were present in that very church when these things occurred.

When that wretched people attempted to cut down the church’s beams, which were fir and therefore suitable for shipbuilding, three of their wicked number suddenly fell before the step of the altar of Saint Stephen, struck down and weakened in all the strength of their bodies. After their bodies were broken, they breathed out their unbelieving and God-hated souls, while the others were seized with fear, and descended to the everlasting shades, where their devouring worm shall not die and their immense fire shall not be extinguished.

## Chapter VIII

When they had thus been prevented from taking the beams of that temple of God and were plundering the whole monastery at once, it happened that one of them—among them the most impious—came to the shrine of Lord Germanus carrying a drawn sword in his polluted hand.

What I am about to say is astonishing.

He struck a marble column, which stood there on the right of those praying, thirteen times with the whole force of his body, as though he were chopping at an enemy. Immediately the strength of his right hand, with which he had cut into that column, vanished so completely that after that day it remained forever immobile, dry, and extended as it had been, until his wretched departure from this life.

Kobbo himself saw this; while we were unaware, he was present and showed us the cuts. The iron hilt also became so joined and fastened to his hand that it could never be torn away from it by any skill or art without taking part of the skin with it.

He was tormented for so long by extreme suffering in his afflicted body that he finally ended his wretched life, full of indignation and anger, carried by the hands of demons to the infernal regions, to the foul lake of Cocytus and the stinking pool of Avernus.

## Chapter IX

We believe it worthwhile to relate that great miracle as well.

While the most holy oratory itself was being criminally violated by that cruelest crowd, it was suddenly filled with such dense fog, and its obscene violators were so stricken with the blindness of divine judgment, that, frightened by great fear and trembling and wishing to leave, they could scarcely find the doors or entrances through which they had come.

After wandering about in confusion for a long time and becoming exhausted, they finally broke out and fled as quickly as possible. From that day onward they were so thoroughly overcome by such terror that they did not dare to defile that church any further by any kind of pollution.

Moreover, they were subsequently afflicted—so the report has spread—with dysentery to such a degree that, while they died day after day, none of so great a multitude expected to escape.

## Chapter X

Meanwhile, pretending to be ill, they sent an embassy to the most eminent King Charles, asking that he receive them peacefully as faithful subjects and permit them to return to their own country after paying tribute to the kingdom.

When these arrangements had been made, and although the king was unwilling, certain princes—who, as he admitted, had been corrupted by gifts—brought their duke Ragenarius and all their leaders before the king, who was then residing in the monastery of Macharius Dionysius.

They swore by the gods and by the divine powers or weapons in which they most believed themselves protected and saved that they would never again enter or touch the borders of his kingdom, except perhaps as auxiliaries.

They were dismissed in this manner, rejoiced at an escape they had scarcely hoped for, and returned happily by the route they had come, having received a fixed amount of gold and silver.

But as they returned, they were afflicted and tortured, growing weaker each day from the disease with which they had been struck in the aforesaid church. In torment they miserably breathed out their wicked souls, while none of the Christians who accompanied them felt such a plague.

In all these events we must contemplate God’s power and embrace his mercy: he saves the innocent so mercifully, and so terribly punishes the profane by working wonders through his saints.

## Chapter XI

We must not suppress what happened in that same church after most of the brothers had returned from exile.

The most sacred bones of the blessed man had not yet been carried back to their proper tomb. One night, while the guards of that church were sleeping and before the brothers were awakened, as was customary, to offer praises to God, they heard before the altar of Saint Stephen a great din of demons, as though a multitude of men were running about for some purpose.

They immediately rose and went around the whole church with a light, but found no one. They understood that it had been a trick and deception of demons. They were grieved to be expelled from the holy seats of the temple, into which, while it had been permitted by the faithless to be polluted, they had doubtless been granted some access, in accordance with the words: “And the hairy ones shall dance there” (Isaiah 13:21).

After his sacred ashes had been brought back and, with Christ’s favor, restored to their place, nothing of this kind was heard again in that basilica, through the merit of his holiness.

## Chapter XII

Ragenarius, the instigator and author of all the evil described above, came with immense arrogance before Horich, the impious prince of the Northmen. He showed him the great quantity of gold and silver that he had carried away from there, and said that he had captured the celebrated city of Paris; that he had entered the residence of the old Germanus, which was considered the finest in that land; and that he had subjected the whole kingdom of Charles to himself by right of tribute.

But Horich did not believe these things. He ordered the aforesaid Ragenarius to bring before him a section of a beam cut from the monastery of Lord Germanus, together with the lock of the gate of the city of Paris, as evidence.

Ragenarius also told him what a good and fertile land he had found, filled with every kind of resource; but that the people living there were fearful and trembling when it came to fighting. He reported that the dead had greater power there than the living, and that he had found no one who resisted him except the dead old man Germanus.

As he was saying these things, he suddenly fell trembling and terrified to the ground and began to cry out in a frightening voice that Germanus was standing before him and was severely beating him with the staff he held in his hand.

When Horich, all those standing beside him, and Kobbo himself—the envoy sent there by King Louis—saw this, they were greatly astonished and shaken with wonder.

Ragenarius, thus humbled and suddenly crushed, was quickly lifted up by the hands of others and carried away.

After being shamefully afflicted for three days by the greatest torments, he finally ordered a golden statue in his own likeness to be made and carried by that same Kobbo to the old Germanus. He promised that, if he escaped, he would thereafter become a Christian and would unquestionably believe in the God of the Christians.

But because he was not one of Christ’s sheep, he did not deserve to obtain what he requested.

He became so swollen and distended—just as that same Kobbo made clear to us—that his body could perceive neither hearing, sight, smell, nor taste.

At last, with his entrails bursting forth, he split open in the middle and the wretched man ended his life in the morning.

The statue, unworthy of sacred offerings, was retained by those to whom it had been assigned and remained rejected as utterly unclean by the purest examiner of hearts.

## Chapter XIII

But let us continue by relating how those who remained ended their lives.

From the day on which they entered the monastery of the blessed bishop Germanus until they all perished under punishment, they were struck—as we have said, according to Kobbo’s testimony—with such swelling of the bowels that their entire company died day after day, even in their own homeland, except for those whom Horich later ordered to be killed.

For he himself, his nobles, and the whole people alike feared being condemned to such a terrible death. He ordered all who remained—apart from a few who escaped by flight, though we do not believe that they escaped death’s destruction—to be beheaded. Their heads were then handed over to the Christian people who were held captive there, as though to make satisfaction for the disease.

For, with God permitting it, the plague had grown so fierce against many that almost anyone who touched a sick person was himself struck by the same disease and perished.

He also ordered all captives who were counted as Christians to be sought throughout his kingdom, and permitted them, without anyone’s opposition, to return to their homeland in freedom and honor.

Those who reported these events also said other things beyond what has been recorded here. We, however, have resolved to set down only what we learned from eyewitnesses. We consider it a sufficiently great thing that blessed Germanus, illustrious in merits and glorious in miracles, deserved to obtain from God such a triumph: the victory that the multitude of the people, because of their common guilt, had been unable to gain over their enemies.

## Chapter XIV

Since, with Christ as our leader, we have proceeded this far by following the sweetness of these signs, we shall now begin to relate the order in which the body of that most blessed man was brought back, after first recording the things we learned were granted through his patronage to the sick who came to the estate of Cumbis.

The more these things are narrated, the more they encourage us not to depart from the path of pious narration.

A boy named Dagenus, from the household of that same monastery, was deaf and mute and deprived of the use of all his limbs. When his relatives had carried him to the aforesaid estate, he was suddenly restored to his former health through the merits of that glorious bishop. He both spoke and heard; and although he had arrived paralyzed, carried by the hands of others, he began to walk on his own feet, exulting and rejoicing, after three wonders had been displayed in his case.

A little later, rising unharmed from the ground, he said with great joy of heart to those who were present: “Behold, behold, blessed Germanus is here; through him, thanks be to God, I know that I have been completely healed.”

## Chapter XV

Nor should we omit what Christ deigned to grant to the praise and glory of his servant, which we also believe will benefit those who hear it.

There were two girls in that same estate who had long been so severely afflicted by fevers that they could scarcely walk on their feet, and no medical skill had so far been able to help them.

With great confidence they went to the same church where his most sacred remains had been placed, and asked the custodians that they might at least pass beneath the venerable body of so great a bishop.

When the custodians observed the fullness of their faith, they promised that they would allow them to pass through, as they humbly requested.

Their faith did not delay receiving its reward. As soon as the bier bearing the saint’s body had passed over them, they were immediately cured of the same illness, so that thereafter they suffered no further discomfort from it during that period.

Truly, God is marvelous in his saints: he not only glorifies them in the present by gifts of grace, but after their death also glorifies them through signs of miracles, granting such benefits through their merits.

## Chapter XVI
After this, when his most sacred body was being carried back from the aforesaid village of Cumbis to the monastery, it is pleasing to make known to the people what happened on the journey. As the monks were bringing the most blessed remains of so great a bishop back to their proper place with praises and hymns, it happened that the candle carried before them, burning in a very powerful wind, was extinguished even inside the lantern in which it had been placed. When someone wished to go on horseback to the village for fire with which it might be relit, it shone forth from heaven, so that, appearing radiant in the same lantern to all who were present, it seemed as though it had never been extinguished. In testimony to this event, therefore, the faithful place a wooden cross at that spot [Note: This cross is said to have been placed between Quinciacum and Villeneuve-Saint-Grégoire], so that what happened there—and the doubled miracle that occurred before they reached the monastery—might not be unknown to passers-by or to future generations.

## CHAPTER XVII

After many sick people had been healed, they arrived with magnificence and reverent honor at Theodasius [Note: Theodasius, Thiais, a village until recently subject to the monastery of Prato, one mile beyond the city, not far from the Seine. It is called Theodaxium in Irmino’s register], the village of the same saint. On the following day, accompanied once more by signs of miracles, they gladly departed and came singing, proceeding by the direct route as far as the river commonly called the Biber [Note: The Biber River, commonly the Bièvre, joins the Seine at the city].

After they had crossed it, the venerable bishop and the abbot of that monastery, Lord Ebroinus, came to meet them, together with many men and women of different ranks and orders, bearing crosses, candles, and all the other sacred equipment. A considerable crowd also came from the city and the surrounding villages, all running with the greatest eagerness and devotion of heart. The clerics praised God in loud voices, sometimes singing while shaken by sobs; the people, at one moment shedding tears from immense joy, at another exulting from the rejoicing of their hearts, offered countless thanks to God. The weeping of sorrow during the departure was no greater than the joy at the return.

The aforesaid bishop, together with the other priests and noblemen chosen for this task, carried his most sacred body in turn upon their shoulders. All the others, singing praises and hymns before and behind the bier, hastened to touch the clothing of those who bore it, and they carried him back to his own church. When they reached the monastery’s first gate, they began to sing before him the hymn “We praise you, O God; we confess you, O Lord,” while the heavens resounded. They placed him upon the altar of Saint Stephen in the principal church. He remained there until the feast of his translation, celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of August [July 25], arrived. Then the aforesaid abbot, Lord Ebroinus, bishop, approached, took him, and placed him in his sarcophagus with reverence and the utmost care, while all who were present blessed him and praised God.

## CHAPTER XVIII

Finally, after his most sacred body had been placed in its tomb, we must not pass over in silence a vision revealed one night to a certain brother of ours in that same monastery. While he was asleep, he seemed to see all the brothers of the monastery standing in the choir, dressed in ceremonial vestments and speaking with one another about the evils that had occurred. Looking toward the eastern part of the church, they saw the blessed Germanus standing before the altar of Saint Stephen as though in military dress, helmeted and magnificently armored, like a warrior returning weary and armed from the field of battle.

Looking at them all, he asked, using the customary name of the people, where the Northmen were, or where they had gone—the violators of this church and devastators of the homeland, who had forced them to exhume the remains of himself and the other saints. They replied with a sufficiently humble answer, as was fitting, that the Northmen had departed. Then the venerable Father answered, “Good,” and added, “Thanks be to God.”

Next, as the brother understood, he sat upon a seat prepared before the aforementioned altar. He summoned the brothers and ordered them to help him lay down the military weapons that he was carrying. At this point, the apparition disappeared.

We understand that this appearance and this vision foreshadowed what we now know truly to have happened: the vengeance which the holy man obtained from heaven against his enemies. His question was a declaration of their destruction. From their assistance in laying down his weapons, we also infer that we ought to help him—or rather, to help ourselves—by helping him well, so that such things may never again happen to us or to him on our behalf.

## CHAPTER XIX

Now, therefore, let us consider briefly how greatly the judgments of almighty God are to be feared and guarded; how great is the patience and justice of our most merciful Creator, truly terrible in his counsels, patient and perfectly just in all his works. If he becomes angry with his negligent servants, yet, when they quickly repent, he is appeased and reconciled to them; and when visible or invisible enemies have been cast down, he grants peace with victory to those whose hearts are contrite.

We often read this concerning the people of Israel; we have frequently heard it in our own times; and we ourselves have experienced the grace of his mercy. For he is the God who repels and destroys, who grows angry and shows mercy, and who heals the wounds of the brokenhearted.

We must also consider how greatly the blessed Germanus is to be glorified and venerated. He mercifully helps those who flee to him with confidence, and, as must be acknowledged, he strikes those who oppose the just merits of his cause with terrible force. Since it would be long and difficult to recount his virtues one by one—especially since even before he was born he was so beloved and pleasing to God that, like John, he was found leaping in his mother’s womb, and the power of miracles became his servant—it is pleasing at this point to play briefly with verses in his praise. Let this be the end of the first book.

[Col. 1040A]

Here is Germanus, whom his mother wished in the womb  
To destroy by drinking deadly draughts.  
But because he had been sprinkled with life-giving oil,  
The evil could not stain the holy man.

For he was born from an illustrious line of parents,  
Who once shone upon earth and now shine above the stars.  
If anyone, while remaining in fragile flesh, desires  
To know what sort of man he was, let him read his deeds.

And after he ascended to heaven, what great things  
The Almighty accomplished through him, no tongue can utter.  
This is left to him who alone can drink up the sands  
And count the drops of the sea.

I urge all those whose conduct stains them  
Often to seek his aid in devout prayers.  
When the weak multitude came to his tomb,  
It returned from there healed, by God’s favor.

[Col. 1040B]

Let us now and always give thanks to him who, through the merits of this most faithful bishop of his, rescued us from so many and such great evils, and who every day, through his intercession, grants us the benefits of countless gifts, doing great and marvelous things without number. To him be honor and power, glory and dominion, for infinite ages of ages. Amen.

# THE PREFACE OF THE SECOND BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 1059]

[Col. 1039C]

Because, with Christ guiding the sails of our discourse, we have reached the limits of the first little book and are drawing near to the desired harbor, we consider it appropriate now to add the signs of those miracles which the Lord afterward deigned to reveal through the glorious merits of the same bishop. Those things also which happened again during the pilgrimage of the holy man and of ourselves might properly be added, unless perhaps they seem matters of shame.

For, having disregarded the lessons of divine chastisement and having thought little of the time for correction and the fruit of amendment, we have again fallen into such a state that we ultimately had to endure a longer exile through a most deserved expulsion. But far be it from us either to conceal by silence an iniquity of ours that ought not to remain unaccused, or to suppress the heavenly kindness mercifully applied to us for our healing, lest it be proclaimed, or to pass over without remembrance the grace of miracles granted by so great a bishop for human salvation.

# THE SECOND BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 1039]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 1039C]

When the holy body had been brought back and restored in due order to its proper place, as described above, a poor woman from the district of Oximus [d’Hyesme], named Hirmintrudis, came there. For nine years she had been afflicted by the calamity of paralysis, and she could not move from place to place unless carried by the hands of others.

When the Lord wished to heal her through the glorious bishop Germanus, one night she saw two holy virgins standing before her with radiant faces. They brought her bread and milk, signs of the health that was to come, and urged her to eat. She had fallen asleep, exhausted by the distress of her illness. After she had eaten what they had brought, they said to her:

“Rise, and, however you can, hasten to Paris, to the tomb of the blessed Germanus. You will learn through his gift that you are to be healed of your bodily weakness.”

Because of the long bondage of her illness, and despairing of her recovery, she thought she was being deceived by the empty phantom of a dream. Her parents, to whom she reported this, said the same. But on another night the aforesaid virgins appeared to her again and, with a certain indignation but in gentle speech, said:

“Rejoice, for it is near at hand that you will be healed. And why have you not gone where we commanded you? Go, then, at least now, and do not delay.”

The woman awoke, and at last, with the assistance of her brother, was lifted onto a little donkey. Thus she was carried and laid before the tomb of so great a patron. She was permitted to rest that night in the atrium of the same church. Before half the night had passed, however, she awoke as though an ointment had been applied to her and made her way into the church by herself, while the brothers were already celebrating the customary vigil service.

Meanwhile, the limbs that had been badly joined to one another began to loosen and soon returned to their former function. Because of the anguish and relaxation of her heart and body, she began to emit loud cries, so that all of us who were present heard her. When morning came, by the mercy of the Lord, through the prayers of the blessed Germanus, she was granted the use of her own feet. Returning by the road on which she had come, she told everyone of the good gift she had received.

## CHAPTER II

We must not pass over a miracle that occurred in a similar manner. Among the others who hastened from various places came a young man from the district of Bayeux [de Bayeux], named Hildemodus. For three continuous years his loins had been contracted, and because of that very pain he had been deprived of the use of his knees, shins, and feet. He visited many venerable holy places, seeking to recover his former health through their intercession, but nowhere was he destined to be healed.

As the feast of the most holy bishop approached, a certain venerable man admonished him in sleep to visit the bishop’s monastery in order to be healed. Without doubting the vision, on the day preceding the same solemnity, the ninth day before the Kalends of August [July 24], he came with axillary crutches before the tomb of the holy Father and threw himself face down upon the ground.

After he had prayed for a long time with the greatest intensity to blessed God and the bishop for his recovery, he suddenly began, groaning, to stretch out before the eyes of all who were standing there his limbs, which had been numb from prolonged illness. There was no delay. He immediately rose, blessing God and glorifying Saint Germanus. Not only he himself, but all of us who were present and the entire crowd that had gathered, likewise blessed the Lord, who had deigned to grant such things through the merits of his confessor.

## CHAPTER III

What divine goodness wished to show that same evening for the fame of so great a man’s name must not be omitted from the account of the notable miracles. There was a boy, thought to be twelve years old, from the district of Orléans and belonging to the household of the blessed Father Benedict. He had emerged from his mother’s womb contracted in his loins and knees. He could not move himself in any other way except by supporting himself with his hands and dragging forward his half-strengthened little body. Moreover, from the beginning of his life he had grown up deprived of the use of speech, so that, in the manner of his tongue, he expressed rather a noise than the meaning of words.

Someone, moved by pious kindness, carried him to the tomb of the blessed martyr Chéron [S. Chéron], situated near the town of Chartres [Karnotinum]. Through the intervention of Saint Chéron himself, the boy’s feet, while the contraction of his knees remained, were separated only from behind. From there he was eventually brought to the protection of our gracious patron and, through the mercy of the saint, was allowed to remain at the confession of the holy bishop.

While he lay there and the brothers were already singing the evening service in the church, the tendons and joints of his body, contracted from birth, immediately began to loosen. Through the mercy of God, by the intercession of the blessed man, they were fitted again for the use of walking. By coming in faith, he was able to obtain what his impaired nature had denied him.

## CHAPTER IV

For those things which Christ deigns to grant to his holy friends ought not to be a burden—far be such an attitude from the faithful. Whoever refuses to hear of the deeds and virtues of those who now reign with the Lord in the heavenly Jerusalem thereby proves that he does not yet wholly long for their fellowship. But whoever remembers, reads, or hears of them clearly demonstrates that, although still placed on earth, he is a fellow citizen of theirs in heaven.

Accordingly, from a certain estate of the blessed man, situated in the district of Poissy [Note: Pinciacum, Poissy, a place six miles below the city of Paris, made famous by the birth of King Saint Louis; not far from it is Prunay. The district of Pinciacum extended a long way. According to Irmino’s register, it included the village of Magedon, later Meudon, somewhat below the same city; and Surisnas, commonly Suresnes, according to a diploma of Charles called the Simple], a place called Prunidus, there was a man named Adoardus. He was so deprived of the light of his eyes that he lived in continual night and could draw in no light at all.

As a blind man, he was led there by the hands of others for the feast of the holy bishop. He stood devoutly among the others who had gathered for the sacred solemnity of Mass. Suddenly, before the Gospel began to be read, a great stream, as though of tears, began to flow in a marvelous manner from his eyes.

When this had continued for a long time, and he repeatedly wiped the source of the little streams from his cheeks with his hand, he began, by a heavenly act of attention, to perceive a small amount of brightness. Then, giving thanks with the whole devotion of his heart, he threw himself face down upon the ground and earnestly prayed that the light already partly opened to him might be restored more fully.

His prayers were not frustrated before the Most High, who examines the heart, nor before the holy man. He was immediately heard and recovered his former sight. After the solemnity of the Mass had been completed, he came, now seeing clearly, before the shrine [that is, the tomb] of the blessed confessor, glorifying God, who through the saint’s prayers had restored to him the faculty of sight that had been taken away for so many years.

## CHAPTER V

So that the immeasurable mercy of divine goodness, which chastises us, may be proclaimed more clearly, let us continue with the miracles that, as we remember, occurred again during the pilgrimage of the same saint and of ourselves, honoring them not with an abundance of ornate words but with the beauty of their virtues.

After not many years, following repeated misfortunes, God raised up against us the fiercest persecution of those same peoples, by which he justly afflicted us and, as a father in his mercy, compelled us in our affliction to amend. For just as prosperity sometimes turns away from the right path through the elation of the mind, so adversity, through the humility of a contrite heart, recalls us to our protection. “Only affliction will give understanding to hearing.”

When the scourge of this persecution arose, the bodies of saints lying throughout the region were not only dug from their tombs amid renewed sorrow, but were also carried here and there to their own estates. When preparations had been made to carry the most holy body of Germanus again to the aforesaid village of Cumbis, it is pleasing to recount the miracle that occurred there at that time.

One of us, named Adalarius, a monk and priest, had become so weakened by continual strain in his kidneys that for some time he could not walk even a little by himself unless supported by one, and especially by two, staffs. Supported by these, he came groaning to the church among the others. Approaching the body of the holy bishop, already placed in the bier for removal, he tried not to be slower than the bearers.

With divine assistance granted through the saint’s prayers, he was strengthened and abandoned—or, as he himself later said, forgot—the use of his staffs. He carried the body in turn until he reached the aforesaid village of Cumbis, freed from the bond of his illness. There, when the mass of the blessed body had been displayed upon the venerable altar, he gave thanks and became healthy in every respect.

## CHAPTER VI

After some time had passed, it happened that a man possessed by a demon was brought there, whom about four men could scarcely restrain. He was under the power of an evil force, belonged to the household of the same saint, and came from the village of Prunidus mentioned above.

He arrived, driven forward by the hands of violent men, while the enemy struggled and resisted, greatly fearing the presence of Justus. Some of our men therefore subjected him to many adjurations according to the custom of exorcism and also gave him a drink of blessed water.

But, so that the radiant merit of the apostolic man might be displayed more clearly in him, after everyone had at last ceased, the final and effective remedy of the same saint approached. When the diseased filth of the crafty invader had been driven out, all his soundness was restored, his senses recovering their vigor. After the most wicked inhabitant had been cast out, the captive came forth free from the serpent; and he remained capable not merely of the strength of four men, but of that of one less than four.

## CHAPTER VII

A woman was also brought who carried both her hands dried and useless. Long before, because of an illness that had clung to her, she had established an annual vow to the basilica of Saint Mary [Notre-Dame de Moussy], situated nearby, according to the measure of her poverty, in the amount of half a denarius.

But when the day of the Lord’s Resurrection arrived, she took advantage of the gentle opportunity offered by the day, bought some meat, and ate it, thinking little of the principle that it is better not to make a vow than, after making one, not to fulfill it. As soon as, with the sun having set, she withdrew to the privacy of her bed in search of sleep, her hands, which had violated the vow, were contracted that very night. The function of working having died in them, the extended nails seemed to penetrate into the innermost parts of her palms.

When morning came, she arrived and was placed before the altar where the holy body rested. After a short time, her fault corrected, she returned healthy, just as she had been before. The glorious lady did not disdain to have the glorious Germanus as the companion or restorer of her miracle.

## CHAPTER VIII

To say nothing of the remaining miracles performed by the same saint in that place at that time, let us now recount the case of a certain blind man who was marvelously healed. He had been led there with the assistance of another person’s steps and was awaiting his salvation there, praying for it day after day.

He was also accustomed, because of some other intervening illness of which I know not what kind, to utter frequent cries of pain, more often than sudden ones, accompanied by groaning. For this reason, some people rebuked him as though he were troublesome and disturbing the silence of the church. Deeply saddened, he withdrew, intending to go elsewhere, and resolved in his mind to turn aside to a certain church in the village of Ruoilo [Note: The French translator interprets this place as the village of Ruyau in the diocese of Sens, although the church of that village is dedicated to Saint Julian. Nor does this passage seem to be explained by the village of Rioilo in the district of Poissy, by the Seine, mentioned in a diploma of Louis the Pious; for the church of that place is said to be dedicated to Saint Peter], dedicated to the honor of the same saint, since it was nearby, and to remain there until the time of his mercy should come.

After he had done this, with someone leading him on the way, he recovered the light of his eyes before entering the door of the same basilica. Immediately, rejoicing at so great a heavenly visitation granted to him, he returned to Cumbis, now seeing and crying out praises to the same saint.

There was joy among the brothers and all who lived there, and throughout the surrounding region there was no small gladness of amazement. Those whom he had left in anger now repented and said that they and others had been admonished by this event that they ought to be patient with the importunities of the poor and the infirm.

## CHAPTER IX

Let us now see Helagia, a woman of noble blood, come there among the others to be healed and return healed at the same time. She had grown so weak from the distress of suffocation over a long period that she could not even remain standing to attend the divine offices, although she desired to do so, when only the reading of the Gospel was being performed.

The Lord did not wish her to be deprived of the holy man’s pious benefits. For many days she was carried by the aid of others. She repeatedly visited the church where his body was kept and venerated her most merciful patron from the depths of her heart, with candles and other offerings.

When the time appointed by God for the labor of her devotion to be rewarded had arrived, she was immediately filled with heavenly medicine and granted such strength of body before the presence of the same saint that, giving thanks to God and to the blessed man, she returned restored to health and exulting.

## CHAPTER X

We consider it worthy to insert among the following events, in the rhythm contained below, a miracle that ought to be remembered.

The Northmen, residing on a certain island of the Seine at the place called Oscellus [Note: Charles the Bald mentions this place in a proclamation against Wenilo, archbishop of Sens: “Then, against the pagans,” he says, “I proceeded to the island of the place called Oscellus”], often came by naval raids to Paris whenever it pleased them. All the monasteries nearby were therefore ransomed, so that they would not be burned by the Northmen’s violence after fires had been set. They also took to their horses in turn, so that they might capture certain noblemen for the sake of money.

Thus, from the ransom of the most gentle true lord, Abbot Luduwicus [Note: Some inexperienced person substituted Hilduinus in manuscript copies at this point, observing that no abbot named Ludovicus had presided over the monastery of Saint Germanus at that time. But the name Luduwicus, or Ludovicus, should be retained: he was abbot of the monastery of Saint-Denis, was captured by the Northmen, and was freed after a ransom was paid. See the Life of Saint Faro in volume II], they acquired a considerable and incomparable profit.

Whenever they planned to do something of this kind, they concealed themselves for many days beforehand, pretending that they were going nowhere, so that their secret arrival might not become known to anyone. They had therefore decided, by mutual and silent deliberation, to rush either to Paris or at some time to our place and unexpectedly deceive all who were staying there in false security.

Nearly twenty brothers had remained in the same monastery to guard it. While they were celebrating the service of the holy Paschal feast, at the first light of dawn, the Northmen appeared. They had mounted their horses and begun their journey on Good Friday. Some of our horsemen arrived shortly afterward and, though late, announced to the brothers their enemies’ malicious approach.

The brothers did not believe them, but continued more earnestly in the divine praises. Without delay the pagans pursued them, arrived, and surrounded everyone as they were singing in the church.

Then, in what proved a great means of escape, the church doors were closed before their eyes, and all the brothers hid themselves by plunging into various hiding places or wells. By the merits of so great a bishop interceding for them, the Northmen killed only one of all those who were there, a man who had trusted in his horse.

The fugitives went away before their eyes. Indeed, as I say with complete truth, some of our men passed through before their drawn swords in broad daylight unharmed. While they were thus saved by angelic protection, the heralds were killed, as were many others from the surrounding area and from the monastery’s household. The invaders, filthy as they were, plundered everything they found inside and outside the church, and then returned in triumph after setting fire to the brothers’ storehouse.

At that point, everyone emerged from whatever hiding places they had entered. With the people of the city also rushing together from every direction, they overturned the force of the fire by the grace of the Holy Spirit. The flames had already risen to greater heights, seeking to consume everything. Nor, as later happened to us again because of our sins, did the place then perish by being completely burned.

## CHAPTER XI

Moreover, so that Justus may remain in memory with praises, we have learned what happened at our village of Novigentum [Note: They call it Novigentum of Artaldus, in the vernacular Nogent-l’Artaud, in the district of Brie on the river Marne; it is recorded in Irmino’s register, having recently been exchanged for an estate commonly called Amblainvillers], situated on the river Marne, while he was staying there and while he was returning from there. But let us not turn our discourse to everything.

For if we went through each event, the abundance would exceed the limits of the page. It happened, then, that because of fear of the pagans, who had already advanced beyond Paris and the boundaries of the castle of Melun [Milidonis], the most holy body was transferred there from Esmant [Acmant], from which it had recently been carried away.

A man from the same village had been so ill for years that he could scarcely walk, and his whole body was weakened, with no medicine helping him. He came bringing a candle with him—a gift of faith and the price of health. Before he could finish what he had begun, trying to light it, he received, in the sight of everyone present, the gift granted by heaven’s regard.

If the immeasurable greatness of the kingdom of heaven can be bought for any price at all, then bodily health can be obtained even more by true faith. For a Christian receives as much as he believes. Immediately, after offering his gift, he was healed and joyfully returned to the threshold of his home.

## CHAPTER XII

There was indeed a very large gathering there of sick people flowing in from every direction. To summarize their cases briefly: the blind rejoiced, seeing; the lame walked; various fever sufferers were cured; and very many people, freed from different bodily afflictions, gave thanks with joy. The grace of healing was granted to each according to how worthy each was found of the physician’s mercy.

Thus, at least, someone who arrived weak in the evening very often went out unharmed when morning came. Among them a little boy from the district of Étampes [Stampensis] was brought, insane [or perhaps: gravely afflicted]. His limbs were disabled by contracted tendons.

His mother carried him there and earnestly begged that she might be allowed to remain with the boy that night in the same basilica where the body of the holy bishop was venerated. When the hour of that night arrived—by common opinion, about midnight—the boy, unknown to his mother, rose alone and tried to walk through the same church, with the stiffness of his feet somewhat loosened.

The woman awoke and rejoiced at seeing her son’s recovery. After she and the boy had spent that night and the following night in the same place, he departed after two days completely restored, with his mother rejoicing.

## CHAPTER XIII

In that same village of Novigentum, what and how many gifts of healing were displayed to those who came there through the gift of his goodness, as we related a little above, we confess without blame that we do not know. How countless they were, only Jesus, the most merciful helper who granted them, knows.

Therefore, turning to what our heart longs for, let us hasten to describe his return with joyful mind. The brothers who were there, guarding the most holy members of his body and eager at least to visit the ruins of the place with him, went out together. Since the Northmen had already been driven from the kingdom by a friendly treaty of peace, they gladly undertook the journey back. They had a suitable fleet for the return.

Sailing down the river Marne and then the Seine, they came to a harbor below the confluence of the Bièvre and the Seine. The most sacred body was brought out from the ship, and many people of both sexes and every rank gathered there to receive it, so that it was scarcely possible for the clerics to approach in order to lift it.

The canons from the house of his former bishopric, attending him as their bishop, first performed the duty of receiving him, singing with fitting jubilation the melody of this antiphon:

> O how venerable you are, illustrious Germanus, confessor,  
> Who despised earthly things and joyfully sought heaven’s gate!  
> Now you shine victorious in heavenly power;  
> Therefore we humbly beseech you to intercede for us  
> With the Lord our God.

After kneeling, and after the Lord’s Prayer and a Mass had been solemnly said for all, the clerics from the monastery of Saint Peter and from that of the blessed virgin Genevieve approached devoutly. Following the same order, they took the holy body upon their shoulders and began to sing this antiphon:

> This is Germanus, the greatest of bishops,  
> Who by heavenly grace gives divine miracles;  
> Receiving the promised gifts,  
> He lives in everlasting glory.

Then, as was fitting for us, his humble servants, we fell down and reverently approached with a new hymn of greeting. Rising from the ground where we had lain prostrate in the deepest reverence toward him, after prayer and the collect, and after the gift of healing had been granted to a certain contracted woman and two blind men, so that each reception might be adorned with its own miracle, we raised our voices and sang:

> Hail, blessed bishop; hail now, most merciful one,  
> O venerable Germanus, Father and eminent man,  
> With the faithful throng of people who accompany you.  
> Come now, come in kindness; return, excellent shepherd.  
> Seek out your own sheep and restore them to peace;  
> Do not allow them any longer to mourn the pledge that was taken away.  
>   
> Lutetia lamented that you, its lord, had departed;  
> It grieved and mourned that it had been deprived of its glory,  
> And now it rejoices to have received your presence.  
>   
> Alas, how your servant-monks wept and groaned,  
> And the whole multitude of the people, so wholly your own,  
> When you, most holy one, had been exiled from your place!  
> What speech can express the lament of their hearts  
> And at the same time set forth their bitterest tears,  
> Because the merciful priest had been impiously driven away?  
>   
> Even if he withdrew before the harshness of the pagans,  
> And before neither place nor avenging flame, yet he was present  
> In the dangers, serving the worthy prayers of his servants.  
> Therefore it pleases us to approach that noble event in speech,  
> Which brought about a wondrous and astonishing miracle,  
> For which fitting thanks should be offered to the confessor.  
>   
> Thus, when the bright day of Easter dawned,  
> And the monks celebrated the morning praises,  
> They mocked the surrounding pagans  
> In a marvelous manner.  
>   
> For while the wretched men boasted  
> That they had captured everyone,  
> And soon enclosed nearly all of them in a circle,  
> The humble servants, almost captured, were freed through your prayer.  
>   
> While no one thought that he would survive,  
> And one had escaped the sword-line of the Danes,  
> They all plunged unharmed into hidden places.  
>   
> Then you could see them weeping, unable to speak to one another,  
> As though they saw themselves rising from the jaws of death.  
> They offered only the silent vows of their hearts, most worthy one.  
>   
> Only one was hindered by the barrier of blind death,  
> And the enemy pierced him swiftly with a weapon,  
> So that the supreme bishop might not lack so great an offering.  
>   
> Hail, merciful one; from here we beseech you, hail, holy bishop.  
> Grant that we and all the clergy who honor you,  
> Together with your devoted people, may now  
> Make use of a favorable prayer;  
> Obtain for us from here the kingdom of lofty paradise,  
> So that together with you we may sing praises  
> To the Father and Lord,  
> And, joining our voices with the angels,  
> Sing to the whole Trinity:  
>   
> Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God of hosts;  
> Heaven and earth are full of your glory.  
> Hosanna to him who came blessed in the highest.  
> Glory to God the Father and praise to the Most High;  
> Honor, virtue, and power to Jesus Christ the Lord.

And let there also be one dignity and one summit for the Paraclete. Amen.

When this had thus been completed all the way to the end, although we were already close by on the opposite side of the city—partly scorched and also very extensively devastated—its ruined appearance, bringing us all into sorrow, appropriately compelled us to sing:

> Look, Lord, for the city has been laid waste, a city full of riches; the mistress of nations sits in sadness, and there is no one to comfort her except you, our God.

For while many were singing, still more could be seen weeping. Thus we proceeded as far as the meadow [Col. 1047] beneath the monastery.

[Note: Hence the monastery was called Saint-Germain-de-Prés, though not before the eleventh century; more recently, Saint-Germain-des-Prés.]

We were grieving because, after we had entered our own land, we had found none of the miracles displayed as before. But suddenly, from so great a multitude of people, one man ran forward and approached us. He had an iron ring, tightly wrapped around his arm as a penance, as is customary. A considerable period had now passed since this punishment had come upon him because he had accidentally killed his own mother.

Crying out and imploring the compassion of so great a man to help him, he stretched out his hand, wishing at least to touch the pall that covered the bier on which the sacred body of the saint was being carried. Immediately the iron sprang from his arm with a wondrous crack, so that many saw it fly upward into the air. This event made all of us more joyful and moved some even to tears of happiness. The flesh of the arm, moreover, eaten deeply away by the harshness of that ring, revealed the precious miracle that had occurred.

## CHAPTER XIV

A certain woman also arrived, accompanied by the aids of faith. From infancy she had been called Electa. She told us that, as though still suffering from the same affliction, her right hand had withered and wasted away for ten years, so that she had been entirely unable even to bring it to her mouth.

Approaching, therefore, she began to plead with prayers of great humility that she might be granted passage beneath the bier of that same holy body, as we were walking, solely for her own sake. But once she had scarcely been admitted and had passed through—for the crowd was very dense—the weakness of her withered hand was immediately healed, so completely that, having recovered all its strength, it resumed the ordinary function of its natural activity.

We saw her restored to health, and Meroldus, who had come blind, and Aldegundus, seeing.

## CHAPTER XV

We therefore reached the monastery gate, singing, but exhausted by excessive weariness and the heat of the sun, at about the sixth hour. The year of the cycle of Christ’s resurrection was 863; the day was reckoned as the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August.

Then, having begun the hymn *Te Deum laudamus*, we entered the church and placed the same most holy body upon the very tomb in which it had previously lain. Next, singing the antiphon:

> Give praise to our God, all his saints, and you who fear him, small and great, for the Lord our omnipotent God will reign. Let us rejoice and exult and give him glory,

and having offered a prayer and celebrated Mass for the entire assembled company, we carried it into the crypt of Saint Symphorian, where it had first rested after departing this life. Then we placed it, to be venerated, behind the altar of that same holy martyr, in the tomb prepared for it.

[Note: Thus what the anonymous author writes above in the book of the Translation—that the body of Saint Germanus was originally buried in the portico of the church of Saint Vincent—should be understood of the chapel of Saint Symphorian, which still exists in the atrium of the church.]

After a period of time had passed and the monastery had already been partly rebuilt, the ever-glorious and pious King Charles arrived, together with Richildis, queen and partner in his kingdom, and also our father and shepherd, the lord Gauzlinus, abbot, along with Ingelvinus, bishop, and other prelates or nobles of his kingdom. They carried those same most holy remains back with praises and hymns to the place of their proper tomb.

[Note: In the codex of Abbot Irmino there is a deed of donation written in a somewhat later hand. In it, a certain freeborn man named Brunardus gives two manses of his hereditary property to the most blessed Bishop Germanus, situated in the villa named Celciacum after that holy Pontiff, in the pagus of Stampense, on the condition that from the revenue and rent arising from it a lamp might be provided before his holy tomb. Done at Paris in the tenth year of King Charles, on the Kalends of April, under Abbot Gozlinus. From this it appears that Gozlinus was already presiding over the monastery in the year 850. Here should be added the diploma of Louis Augustus, surnamed the Pious, from which we learn the location of Karoli-venna, mentioned by Aimo above at the beginning of Book I on the miracles of Saint Germanus; it has been copied from the original parchment in the following words.]

There, with God and our Lord Jesus Christ assisting, and with the accompanying grace of the Holy Spirit, many sick people who come even to this day are healed through the merits of that same holy Bishop, to the glory and praise of the holy and undivided Trinity, forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1049]

# ACTS OF THE TRANSLATION OF SAINT SAVINUS THE MARTYR, BY AIMOINUS

*(In Martène, Old Writings and Monuments, enlarged collection, vol. VI, p. 806, from the manuscript of the most illustrious lord Chauvelin, keeper of the royal seals.)*

[Col. 1049]

## PRELIMINARY OBSERVATION

[Col. 1049D] The Acts of the translation of Saint Savinus the martyr were supplied to us by an ancient codex belonging to the most illustrious lord Chauvelin, keeper of the royal seals, written about 800 years ago. Aimoinus, their author, appears to us to be none other than that celebrated Aimoinus, a monk of the Parisian monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, who in the time of Charles the Bald composed a book on the discovery and translation of Saint Vincent, along with other works. Certainly, he hints at this clearly enough at the end of his preface, where he says that he asks to be assisted by the holiness of Saint Savinus and of “my lord Germanus.”

Two matters in this little work especially deserve notice. First, the distinguished man Baidulus, a cleric of the palace and abbot of the monastery of Marmoutier at Tours—until now unknown to scholars—transferred the body of Saint Savinus from a church once destroyed by the Vandals, which had been completely deserted for many years and overgrown with brambles and thorns, to his own estate at Cerisiacum. There he built a basilica in honor of Mary, the Mother of God, installed and endowed canons, and enriched them with various benefactions.

Second, after a monastic rule had been established there, that place became far more cultivated and venerable, since the entire complex, together with its church, rose in a nobler and more spacious form. They report that this was accomplished through the authority and piety of Charlemagne, who entrusted the monastery, constructed with royal magnificence, to Benedict of Aniane, the restorer of the monastic order in Gaul, to govern. After a very large company of monks had been gathered there, the Benedictine way of life flourished so greatly that it was later spread from there into various congregations.

For from the monastery of Saint Savinus, in order to restore discipline at the monastery of Saint Martin in Autun, that great Berno was chosen together with Saint Hugh and sixteen other monks. Berno later presided as abbot over the congregations of Gigny, Baume, and finally Cluny. This occurred at the request and through the efforts of Count Badilo, restorer of the monastery of Autun, whose relative, as we conjecture, Baidulus formerly constructed and endowed the basilica of Saint Savinus.

Moreover, Aimoinus composed these Acts at the request of Hucbertus, abbot of Saint Savinus, who has until now been absent from the published lists of this monastery and who appears to have held his place after Dodo, the disciple and successor of Benedict of Aniane.

# PREFACE OF AIMOINUS

[Col. 1051]

[Col. 1051A] **1.** I would truly believe that this mystery of the following work, both small and great, has been granted to me through the mercy of God and of Saint Savinus, that distinguished witness of Christ. I call it small in the extent of its volume, but great in the reverence due to the martyr. For works of this sort must be made known briefly, lest they become wearisome to the minds of readers and hearers.

And would that, although an unworthy priest, I might be found to be such a man as would pay due honor both to the saint and to the congregation that embraces him—namely, to Hucbertus, the abbot of that monastery, and to the Fathers who are piously to be honored under him—and leave something that would endure with honor, so that it might contribute to the praise of the holy martyr and to your delight.

I humbly implore the friends of God and Saint Savinus to help me through the holiness of that saint and of my lord Germanus, and through the comfort of your prayers.

# THE TRANSLATION BEGINS

[Col. 1051]

[Col. 1051B] **2.** At the time when the devastation of the Vandals, as antiquity has handed down to the present day, was raging far and wide against neighboring and foreign peoples, the church above the body of the most blessed martyr of Christ, Savinus, was destroyed. The place itself was so abandoned because of the absence of inhabitants that, covered by the desolation of a wilderness, it remained uninhabited and deserted for many years.

Although a few neighboring inhabitants had remained, their hands were entirely insufficient to repair it. Much time passed, but the memory of the place was not forgotten. Though uncultivated, it continued to be called sacred in the mouths of the ancient inhabitants and was known to have been dedicated to the body of the blessed Savinus.

When, after a still longer period had elapsed, the Almighty resolved both to restore the place and to cause the saint to be honored more openly, it is pleasing to relate briefly how this came about.

**3.** Once, then, a certain farmer’s animal had strayed from the herd. Since he did not find it among the pastures, he entered the more remote parts of the woods, despairing of the animal. Having found a trace beyond the herd, he began to follow it until the roughness of the thorns and brambles drove him farther from his undertaking.

But, as is customary with poor country people when something is lost, he persisted in overcoming the labor, however difficult. With a blade in his right hand, he cut down the brambles and every obstructing plant on either side, until at last, sweating with exertion, he broke through to a place where he saw the four-footed animal he was seeking lying on the ground.

He approached and tried to move it, but the animal could not rise in any way. For, as it entered, it had been caught within the enclosure of the former basilica and lay so weak that, with all its limbs contracted, it was completely unable either to stand or to walk. He nevertheless placed it upon his arms and carried it home, recounting the whole event to his neighbors.

**4.** The story therefore grew day by day and spread widely. As we have said, a living reputation of the saint and his church still remained; but, since those who had known it were now dead, it was not known where it had stood.

Nevertheless, there were some who declared with complete certainty that they had often previously heard from those who had seen the earlier condition of the basilica what was then being reported as though it were new.

**5.** Meanwhile, a certain priest named Bonitus, distinguished both by his name and by his merits, having carefully considered these matters, undertook—moved by divine love and love of the holy martyr—to rebuild the church of the martyrdom and to restore the site for habitation as it exists today.

Among other things, we learned from Bonimius, a priest and nephew of this Bonitus, of one miracle that occurred there, and we judged it sufficient to insert it here in connection with the present account.

He said that, among the things he frequently asserted had been related by that same uncle of his about the saint, there was this: Bonitus had once deserved to recover, through the intervention of Saint Savinus, a horse that had been secretly stolen from him.

When the horse was lost, he took its bridle and saddle and cast them before the saint’s tomb, saying in grief:

> Holy martyr, I can restore to your worship and veneration the church rebuilt for you, even if the labor is small; yet, shame upon it, you have not guarded my horse through your merits, though you were able to do so. I serve the church—am I to suffer this? If this seems right, let God judge, and you consider the matter and restore my horse to me.

After he had brought forward these and many other complaints as though he were justly arguing his case, he returned home. When night had come, he gave himself over to peaceful sleep. Then, awakening at the cockcrow that warned him to leave the torpor of sleep, he reverently completed the nocturnal and morning office before the saint’s tomb, as was customary.

When this was done, as he was returning from the church to his house, the horse that had recently been stolen was immediately present before him, without anyone guiding it. Recognizing its master’s manger, it entered the stable at a gallop. When the priest saw this, he gave thanks to the Lord and to his holy martyr Savinus and thereafter displayed even greater devotion in the worship of God’s martyr.

**6.** Finally, there was a man illustrious by lineage and distinguished by his possessions, Baïdilus, a cleric of the palace and abbot of the monastery of Marmoutier at Tours. By hereditary right and through kinship he possessed estates there, beside a villa called Cerisio.

When he arrived at this place and learned the circumstances, he began prudently to reflect upon what he had heard and to investigate carefully whether the reports could indeed be true. When, from the testimony of contemporaries and ancients, from the additional evidence of miracles, and from the testimony given by the place itself, he had concluded that the matter was entirely true, he began eagerly and diligently to devote himself to pious efforts, so that grace might accrue to him from the holy martyr and the dignity of the holy martyr might be increased by a portion of his possessions.

What more shall I say? On that same estate, where he had previously built nothing, he founded and consecrated a basilica in honor of the Virgin, the Mother of Christ, inspired by divine zeal. He built dwellings, installed clerics, and furnished everything necessary.

Finally, he approached the saint’s tomb with confidence and every diligence of service. After celebrating the offices and solemn Masses, he asked God and the holy martyr to grant him success in completing what he had undertaken. Singing with trembling, he took up so great and abundant a pledge from the place where the body lay.

He proceeded with the bier beneath which the body had been placed, rejoicing exultantly, with no difficulty obstructing him in the holy undertaking, until he reached the venerable urn that he had prepared for the distinguished martyr. There, giving thanks to God, he reverently placed the precious body, and donated to the church and to the martyr the endowment, the entire estate, and its household.

Thus, magnifying God because he had granted his prayers, and glorifying Saint Savinus, he left rejoicing and exultant.

**7.** Moreover, as long as he lived, he did not cease to give gifts and increase the benefactions by which the place might be enriched and enlarged. Many nobles also imitated his outstanding deeds, added treasures, and donated allodial properties. The place shone with many gifts, and when a monastic rule had been established there, it became all the more cultivated and therefore altogether more venerable.

It was and remains well situated: delightful in the beauty of its woods and fruitful trees, with meadows and vineyards, water and mills.

**8.** Thus, while the monks diligently devoted themselves after the performance of the divine office to the work of their hands, which is properly theirs, the entire house, together with its church, rose in a nobler and more spacious form.

The piety of their goodness and discipline, with God and the holy martyr assisting, became there such as gently to invite the minds of many, and especially of the great, to remember and enrich the place. Such it flourished; such, with the fruits of good works, it continues to blossom even now. May it, I ask and desire, remain such in Jesus Christ.

**9.** Nor do I think that the particular virtue recognized as having occurred after the venerable translation of his body should be passed over in silence. It most clearly demonstrates his holiness and shows that, although he had left the place from which he had been transferred bodily, he had not left it without his protection.

A priest, while driving a cart loaded with must along the same road by which the body of the holy martyr had been transported, had not yet reached home when the bung came out of the bottom of the cart and sprang onto the ground, without anyone noticing it.

Nevertheless, the must did not flow out any more than if the opening had been stopped; not a single drop escaped. When the cart had reached the storage place, the priest approached and looked around the cask to see whether anything had happened. He noticed that the bung was missing from the open hole and, fearing and supposing that no must remained in it, began to rebuke the servants in great anger and bitterly reproach them for having failed to prevent this.

While he was speaking in this very bitter mood, one of them ran back, picked up the bung lying not far away on the ground, and fitted it to the open hole in the cask. Once it had been fitted to the opening, before it was inserted, the force of the must shot directly outward and flew as far as the beard and chest of the man holding the bung.

The priest and those standing by were astonished and amazed at the spectacle of this wondrous event. Raising their hands to heaven, they joyfully sent hymnlike voices to the Creator of all and to his holy martyr Savinus.

The priest, having recovered the wine in the same quantity in which he had put it into the cask, joyfully offered thanks with an even greater vow and in fuller words. Bonimius admitted that he had learned this and other events from his aforementioned uncle Bonitus through frequent repetition.

**10.** But why should we contribute so many things by writing about the saint? Shall we make him appear to have greater merit because of this? For example, if we were to relate how Giboldus had crooked feet, turned inward and facing one another, and how they were immediately straightened through the saint’s prayer by heavenly mercy; or how, concerning that vineyard beside which his body had rested, he was not removed from there until that same vineyard was given to him; or how another man, stirred in his dreams, came from the regions of France, having long possessed a withered hand, and was immediately healed there through the martyr’s intervention; or how a blind man, deprived of the light of his eyes for thirty years, was given sight there after the passage of 360 months and departed cheerful and seeing—

if I were to begin carrying out these and similar matters at length, granted to the weak at the martyr’s threshold through his kindness, and if I decided to recite the names of those healed, their native countries, and the villages in which they were born or from which they came, I do not deny that I would impose weariness upon sober readers and eager hearers.

There is a measure of discretion to be observed in divine and hagiographical writings. If we report only a few things about him, shall we mutilate the grace of his merit and power by speaking of only a few?

Let this statement, reinforced by a few others, suffice: Blessed Savinus, thus decently translated, is held to be a precious and glorious martyr of Christ. He wished to show through a revelation of the spirit to a certain man from the same monastery, devoted to God and to himself, that he preferred to be called a martyr because of the shedding of his blood for Christ, rather than, like all who confess Christ, to be called properly a confessor.

**11.** He is rich in merits and powerful in prayers. Let us ask him; let us humbly implore him, that he may deign to intercede for the salvation of our soul and body with him who made him a martyr and crowned him in heaven with the reward of martyrdom. May that same Lord, through the prayers of him and of all the saints, absolve our crimes, forgive all our sins and offenses, and grant us everlasting glory and life, forever and ever. Amen.

# IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 890. RATPERTUS, MONK OF SAINT GALL

[Col. 1055]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON RATPERTUS

*(In Pertz, Monuments of German History, vol. II.)*

[Col. 1055B] Ratpertus undertook, toward the end of the ninth century, to describe the beginnings and vicissitudes of the celebrated abbey of Saint Gall in Switzerland. What he began was continued in the eleventh century by Ekkehard IV, in the twelfth by Burchardus, in the thirteenth by Conrad of Fabaria, and in the fourteenth by Christian Kuchimeister. Their work is especially well suited to learning about the character of the Middle Ages.

[Note: He drew his notices from the Lives of Saints Columbanus, Gallus, and Otmarus; from the traditions of the ancient Fathers; and from authentic books and charters preserved at Saint Gall. Finally, he himself had been a considerable part of the history of his own time. —PERTZ.]

Ratpertus was born at Zurich and embraced the monastic life at Saint Gall after the middle of the ninth century. His teachers were Marcellus and Iso, and his fellow students were Saint Notker the Stammerer, Tutilo, Hartmannus, Waltramus, and Salomon, later bishop of Constance—men of great renown in that age.

Afterward placed in charge of the schools, he devoted himself to letters with such indefatigable zeal that he would allow neither care for his body nor the common prayer to draw him away from them. He left the house so rarely that he would not wear out two pairs of shoes in an entire year. He did not regularly attend the daily recitation of the psalms, saying: “We celebrate good Masses if we teach others to celebrate them.”

When he was charged with flogging brothers who, for offenses committed, had been condemned by their superior according to the prescriptions of the Rule of Saint Benedict and bound to a column, he exercised that duty sharply upon such idle and useless men.
