At the end, while he lay dying, forty canons who had once been his students came to visit him. They had gathered there from many churches of Alamannia to celebrate the feast of Saint Gall, and each one promised to offer thirty Masses to God for him after his death.

He died on October 25, around the year 900. Of what he wrote, besides these *Casus*, there survive several charters of donations, numerous sacred hymns transmitted for publication by Jodocus Mezler Canisius, and a Latin translation of the Life of Saint Gall, composed by him for the use of the people in Teutonic verse.

His style, although polished and in most respects appropriate to his age, nevertheless contains Germanisms and expressions borrowed from the Bible, the liturgy, and the Rule of Saint Benedict. It also contains certain words of rustic Latin introduced into writing by authors of the sixth and seventh centuries.

As is customary with medieval authors, he sometimes errs in proper names or in certain circumstances while narrating true events. No one will be surprised that such lapses of unreliable memory occurred among those who reported what they had heard and lacked the assistance of books.

The earliest text of these *Casus* is contemporary with the author. It is found in codex no. 614, bound together with the canons of Bishop Remedius and the Roman orders. It is written elegantly and correctly, with the errors of the scribe corrected by a contemporary hand.

I have adhered to this codex with such fidelity that I have departed from it neither in a word, syllable, nor letter, except in capitalization and punctuation. These, being obsolete, do not appear to me suitable for retention in reprints, although they closely resemble those which fragments of our manuscripts more than seven centuries old show the Romans occasionally to have used.

For in these most ancient pages we see a point in the middle of the line used in place of a comma, a form resembling a question mark in place of a full stop, and a point before and after numbers.

Ratpertus’s *Casus* are also found in codex no. 615. But since that manuscript was copied from codex no. 614 and does not exceed the thirteenth century, I judged that it should be set aside.

Melchior Goldast first published Ratpertus’s *Casus* at Frankfurt in 1606, following the authority of six manuscripts, though more recent ones. This is why errors entered his edition; since later editors likewise failed to return to the original codex, we see those errors repeatedly reproduced.

At Saint Gall, 1824.

**ILDEPHONSUS VON ARX, Librarian**

[Col. 1057]

# BOOK OF RATPERTUS ON THE VICISSITUDES OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT GALL

## HERE BEGINS THE TEXT ON THE ORIGIN AND VARIOUS VICISSITUDES OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT GALL, PUBLISHED BY RATPERTUS

[Note: Ratpertus (Rathgeber) is consistently called by this name, not Ruhpertus (Ruhebringer) or Rudpertus (Larmmacher). He reveals that he was born at Zurich in the following verses, inscribed in a codex preserved at Zurich concerning Saints Felix and Regula:

> I beg you, grant me leave to return gradually to my homeland,
>
> which I hasten to see, wishing to behold Felix nearby,
>
> and his sister, who is rightly called Regula.]

[Col. 1057A] **1.** After the most blessed men—namely, the holy abbot Columbanus, together with the blessed Gallus and his other disciples—had been kindled by the fervor of divine love, left Ireland, rejected their parents and their paternal estates, crossed the various seas, and arrived in Gaul, they approached Sigibertus, the king of that province.

When he learned of their desire, he granted the servants of Christ with the greatest devotion that they might choose wherever they wished a place suitable for the service of God and inhabit it according to their pleasure. He also promised to be their supporter in all their needs, and he fulfilled this promise most generously.

They therefore entered the wilderness called the Vosges and found a place that had formerly been cultivated but had then completely collapsed through age and been utterly destroyed. It was nevertheless distinguished by its hot waters and was called Luxovium.

[Note: Luxeuil, in the county of Burgundy.]

[Col. 1057B] Building little cells there at once, they persevered in a blessed life and a manner of living pleasing to Christ until the time of Hiltibertus, son of Sigibertus the Younger and thus grandson of Sigibertus.

[Note: Sigibertus the Younger was the son of Theuderic II, grandson of Childebert II, and great-grandson of Sigibertus I.]

He too was most kindly disposed toward the saints. But his grandmother Brunnehildis, the wife of the earlier Sigibertus, was full of the devil, a companion of darkness, an enemy of light, and opposed to every good thing. She did not tolerate the saints’ remaining in that kingdom and did not rest until she had driven them from it.

They therefore left that land and rejected the daughter of the devil, making their way to King Lotharius. Received by him with the greatest kindness, they were brought with honor, as they desired, to Theodebertus, king of the Austrasians.

Having received from him permission to choose a place in Alamannia suitable for divine service, they came to Tuconia, which lies at the head of Lake Zurich.

[Note: Today Tuggen, at the mouth of the Linth.]

When they wished to settle there and recall the people from the error of demons—for they were still sacrificing to idols—Gallus broke the false idols and threw them into the neighboring lake.

[Note: Jonas, in the *Life of Saint Columbanus*, writes that these were idols of Wodan; Ratpertus, in his song of Saint Gall, says Jupiter; Ekkehard IV, Jupiter and Neptune.]

The people, enraged, drove the saints away, not without great and disgraceful loss to themselves and to their future offspring.

[Col. 1058A] Proceeding from there, they came to a fortress called Arbona, beside Lake Constance. There the priest Willimar received them honorably, and they remained joyfully for seven continuous days.

[Note: Today Arbon, called *Arbor felix* by the Romans, a town three hours distant from Saint Gall.]

When the saints asked him whether he knew of a place in the wilderness suitable for their purpose, he showed them a most pleasant place to inhabit, called Brigantium.

[Note: Today Bregenz, at the upper end of Lake Constance.]

There they found a temple once dedicated to the Christian religion but now polluted by images of demons. By cleansing and consecrating it, they restored it to its former condition, and in place of the statues they had cast out, they installed the relics of Saint Aurelia.

[Note: No sacred writers mention this saint, who was also venerated at Strasbourg (*Gallia Christiana*). She appears to have suffered martyrdom in these regions during Roman times.]

Building little cells there, they wished to remain and serve Christ in that place, but they were prevented by the people, most of whom were still deceived by diabolical errors.

Driven out from there at the instigation of Duke Cunzo, Saint Columbanus went with his companions to Agilolfus, king of the Lombards, while Saint Gall, detained by illness in those regions, was left behind.

Thinking that Gallus was pretending to be ill because of the hardship of the journey, Saint Columbanus forbade him the service of the altar for as long as Columbanus himself remained in this life.

[Note: After the word “illness,” the scribe omitted the following words; another contemporary hand added them, and, following the character of the Teutonic language, wrote *mansisset* instead of *maneret*.]

Whoever wishes to know these matters more fully, as well as certain things that follow in this work but which we have touched upon only in part, will find them fully set out in the books of the acts of these same saints.

[Note: This book is still present in the library of Saint Gall, no. 553.]

We, however, shall proceed as we began: let us touch briefly upon a few necessary points from the notes available to us and, with God’s gift, hasten more quickly to matters not yet treated.

Accordingly, after the departure of his blessed master, Gallus diligently began to seek a place in the wilderness, on the other side of the aforementioned fortress, suitable for divine service.

[Note: Namely, *Arbor felix*.]

When he found it, a place pleasant for its waters and level ground, he accepted it with no small joy, guided by a certain deacon of the priest Willimar [Col. 1059A]. He consecrated the place through fasts and prayers and quickly built there a cell in which he and those who would serve the Lord with him might live.

Meanwhile, the daughter of the aforementioned Duke Cunzo, namely the fiancée of King Sigibertus, was seized by an evil spirit.

[Note: This fiancée, whom the author of the Life of Saint Gall calls Frideburga, caused considerable difficulty for scholars who were unable to identify Sigibertus as the bridegroom.]

When the bishops sent by the king, whose holiness he also trusted, were unable to drive the spirit from her and were themselves driven out by it in disgrace, the blessed Gallus, after the same duke had summoned him a second time—not the first—and had made the request with the greatest humility, came to the place where the girl was being tormented, accompanied by a priest.

After prayer, he powerfully drove out the evil enemy from the possessed house with a commanding voice and restored the girl healthy to her father. He immediately returned to the dearer sanctuary of his beloved solitude.

[Col. 1059B] When the aforementioned king heard that the girl had been healed from so great an affliction, he ordered her to be brought before him. When the prince asked her about the cause of her recovery, she described the holy man and his deeds, and the benefits he had shown her through him, in due order. She added a request that the king deign to favor the holy man with the grace of his benevolence.

The king received this kindly and asked whose guest he had been in the wilderness. When, from the girl’s account and from that of other trustworthy men, he learned that the wilderness where the saint lived with his companions belonged partly to the royal authority and partly to the possessions of noblemen, he immediately transferred to the aforementioned saint, by his own authority, the portion belonging to the royal power.

[Note: That part of the forest which was lower and closer to the cultivated regions of Thurgau belonged to the Taltones. Since it also included the round mountain, it reached the cell of Saint Gall. Thus it is said to have lain, with uncertain and undefined boundaries, now on their estate and now on the king’s.]

He decreed that both the saint himself and his successors, who would serve the Lord there in imitation of him, should henceforth retain by royal authority [Col. 1059C] the aforesaid place together with the useful surrounding forests, with the greatest security.

And so that no one might later be able to overturn this arrangement, he resolved to protect it with a most firm written grant of his own authority, and, as he wisely intended, he carried it out perfectly.

He also ordered Duke Cunzo to be a diligent and devoted supporter of Saint Gall in all the needs of the wilderness and its neighbors, both in construction and in whatever matters required his assistance. He fulfilled this faithfully.

By this authority and by such a firm written grant, the place remained safe from its adversaries until the time of Pippin and Charles.

We have also taken care to record below [Col. 1060A] the names of the religious men who received that same saint on their own property and who, by the authority of their own hands, granted him the hereditary right to that wilderness. Their names are these: Willibertus the priest, and Talto, an illustrious man, namely the chamberlain of King Dagobertus and afterward count of that same county.

Saint Gall, while he lived in the body, was held by them in the greatest veneration, and they contributed substantially to the enlargement of this place.

## 2.

But after he had passed from the body and sent his spirit to the stars, this place was likewise enlarged by the successors of these men, out of love for the Saint, until the time of Charles [Note: [Col. 1059D] Namely, Charles Martel.].

Talto’s son was Thiotolt, whose son was Pollo; Pollō’s son was Waldpertus, who begot Waldrammus. This Waldrammus [Note: [Col. 1060D] Waltrammus, as a charter of the year 779 bears witness, was tribune of the neighboring territory. By his wife Waltrada he begot Waltbertus, who in the aforementioned year, with the consent of his mother and brothers, gave to Saint Gall vineyards, fields, and a church at Rumanishorn—now Romishorn—as well as the right to cut timber in the forest adjoining the monastery, to pasture pigs, and, by clearing, to bring new land under cultivation.] desiring to enlarge this place in every way for love of Saint Gall and wishing to establish a regular life there, obtained the holy man Otmar [Col. 1060B] from Victor, count of Chur in Rhaetia, entrusted to him the aforesaid cell with everything belonging to it, and appointed him abbot, as is fully contained in his Life.

Afterward, as time passed and the condition of the monastery improved, the aforementioned Waldrammus presented the same abbot Otmar to King Pippin and handed over to that king the monastery—which he still held in his power by hereditary right—together with the abbot himself. His purpose was that the abbot and his successors, retaining the same monastery by royal authority, should thereafter be oppressed by no one’s violence but should obey only the commands of kings.

The benevolent prince received this kindly and immediately ordered a charter to be drawn up concerning the matter; [Col. 1060C] namely, that the monks of that place should thereafter have the power to elect an abbot for themselves and should be subject solely to the kings. He confirmed this charter with the seal of his authority [Note: [Col. 1060D] Neither this document nor the donation charter mentioned above survives.] and sent the abbot himself back to his monastery. The latter ruled the monastery successfully for forty years, with the aforementioned Waldrammus supporting him for twenty years.

Afterward—anyone who wishes to know for what reason, when, and how this same abbot was condemned to exile by Warinus and Ruadhardus [Note: [Col. 1060D] Warinus was count of the three counties surrounding Lake Constance: Thurgau, Linzgau, and Hegau. *Codex Traditionum S. Galli*. Ruadhardus is recorded in 769 as count in Baar, in the same source. It is uncertain which of the two should be counted among the lineage of the Welfs.] and brought to the eternal crown will find the whole matter fully set forth in the books of his Life.

After this, Sydonius, bishop of Constance, who also held in his power the monastery called Auva [Note: [Col. 1060D] Rich Augia, situated on an island near Constance.], at the urging of the aforementioned counts, began to claim our monastery and to bring it under the authority [Col. 1061A] of the bishopric. To secure their assistance, he promised and granted them benefices [Note: [Col. 1061D] The charters by which the monastery of Saint Gall acquired these estates are still preserved: Vina, from the year 754; Duringa, near Buchhorn, from 752; and Uzinaha, at Lake Zurich, from 745.]. To Warinus he gave Vina, Turinga, and Engi; to Ruadhardus, Antolvinga and Uzinhaha; and to Milo, the advocate of that monastery, he granted a sixth estate, called Heimbach, so that he might withdraw his support from them [Note: [Col. 1061D] A Germanism for *subtraheret*, “might withdraw.”].

For this reason the aforementioned Sydonius, with the assistance of wicked princes, completed most disastrously for his own condemnation—as subsequent events showed—the evil undertaking he had begun, and brought the monastery itself under the jurisdiction of the bishopric.

Accordingly, the aforesaid bishop, continually inflicting many injuries on the brothers of the monastery of Saint Gall, entered the monastery in turmoil one day, intending to burden with even greater accusations those who might be opposed to him. When he had taken his stand before the confession [Note: [Col. 1061D] Today, the presbytery.] of Saint Gall, as though to pray, what he had in mind was revealed—as is written in the Life of Saint Gall—by a bodily affliction and the filth of his bowels. When this punishment overflowed, he was carried to Auva, where he breathed out a life full of miseries from the sewer of his body.

## 3.

After his death, John, a monk of Augia who had been ordained bishop of Constance, assumed the governance of both monasteries. He brought up three nephews and intended, after his departure, to distribute among them the position of authority that he held in those three places.

When the brothers of both monasteries learned of this, they approached the bishop together and asked him to obtain privileges for them from the prince, as well as the right to elect abbots. They promised that, if this were done, they themselves would elect his nephews as their abbots. He agreed and promised that he would do so. [Col. 1061C]

After some time had passed, King Charles, on his way to Rome with his wife Hildegard, arrived at Constance. Thinking that they had found a suitable opportunity, the brothers of both monasteries approached the prince concerning the necessity mentioned above and appealed to his clemency.

The king asked the bishop what he thought about the matter. The bishop replied that the king would thereafter obtain the joys of eternal blessedness if he granted the servants of Christ such great and secure protection that they could serve the Lord without any disturbance.

When he heard this, the king rejoiced and immediately granted the brothers of both monasteries—the monasteries of Saint Gall and Augia—a privilege with the firmest authority. He also ordered immunity charters to be drawn up for retaining these same rights and confirmed them with the seal of his authority [Note: [Col. 1061D] From this charter, issued at Worms on 8 March in the twelfth year of his reign, Ratpert is shown to be in error. The agreement was made not with John, but by John as pro-abbot, with Bishop Sidonius. [Col. 1062D]].

He decreed and ordered that, after the bishop’s death, the monks of the aforesaid monasteries should have the power to elect abbots for themselves and should thereafter be subject to no one except the kings.

The brothers therefore returned joyfully to [Col. 1062A] their monasteries. The bishop, however, retained with himself the charters of both, which the king had ordered to be made.

When the same bishop recognized that the end of his present life was approaching, he took the charter of the brothers of Augia and went to that monastery, but left the charter of the brothers of the monastery of Saint Gall in the archives of the Church of Constance, because they had refused to elect his nephew as their abbot, as they had earlier promised.

For they had perceived that the charter given by the king had been seriously corrupted and had been written in a form very different from what the king had ordered and what their situation required. For this reason they neglected to elect his nephew as their abbot. The brothers of the other monastery acted in the same way.

After the aforementioned bishop had died, the monks of Augia elected as their abbot an old priest and monk named Peter, with the advice of Queen Hildegard. Through her assistance their affairs there also remained in this condition, since the place was largely established and enlarged by Count Gerold, the queen’s brother.

Our brothers, however [Note: [Col. 1062D] Here the following is added in the margin of our manuscript in a thirteenth-century hand: “They appointed Rupert as their abbot; when he died after one year, Walton, etc.” Hermannus Contractus likewise, and three catalogues of abbots written in the eleventh, twelfth, and thirteenth centuries, count Rupert among the abbots of Saint Gall; conversely, they exclude the bishops of Constance John, Egino, and Wolfleoz.], with the king’s permission, appointed their fellow monk Walton, a wise man, as abbot. But matters did not remain in this state until the end, as we shall clearly explain below.

## 4.

After the death of Bishop John, Egino assumed the rights of the bishopric of Constance. Immediately he did not hesitate to employ every kind of intrigue against our monastery. Just as Sydonius had persecuted Saint Otmar, so Egino began to persecute Abbot Walton, in order once again, by the perverse custom of his predecessors, to subject the monastery to the bishopric. [Col. 1062C]

For this purpose he bestowed countless estates and sums of money on the king’s leading men, urging them to support his cause and, as it is written, blinding even the eyes of the wise with gifts. With their assistance he completed most wickedly what he had begun and again caused the monastery to be subjected to the bishopric without equitable observance.

But Charles, the serene Augustus, wishing to reconcile the aforesaid abbot with the bishop on the condition that, while obeying the bishop’s command, he should exercise the office of abbot in the monastery, the aforesaid Waldo—unable any longer to endure before his eyes such great humiliation of his own people—is said to have given the king this reply:

“When I had once entered the hands of your lordship and had deserved to be raised by your dominion to so exalted a dignity, I have decided never thereafter, while I retain the full strength of these three fingers”—for he was an outstanding scribe—“to subject myself to the hands of a person of lower rank.” [Col. 1062D]

Thus, with the emperor’s consent, he went to the neighboring monastery called Auva, intending to remain there. [Col. 1063A] There he was later elected and ordained abbot and ultimately undertook the governance of the monastery of Saint-Denis. [Note: [Col. 1063D] At Paris, in the year 796. Mabillon, *Annales*.]

## 5.

Then the aforementioned bishop took a certain foreign priest [Note: [Col. 1063D] That is, a secular priest.] named Werdon and presented him to our monastery, intending to appoint him abbot, lest, if he appointed one of the monks themselves, the affairs of the monastery seem in some measure to have been yielded by him.

The monks, however, did not accept him as abbot while he remained in such a condition. When Werdon realized this, he changed his manner of life and clothing; only then, after he had been received in monastic dress, was he ordained abbot, as the bishop had decided.

Then, after a pact of perverse faith had been made between the bishop and the abbot against the needs of the monks, our affairs began to decline more and more into desolation. Those who ought to have been protectors had afflicted us, and there was no one among our own people who could restrain them.

The brothers of our monastery still possessed the very firm immunity charter that Pippin, the king of blessed memory, had ordered to be written for them and had handed over, confirmed by his own hand. They placed great confidence in it. The same bishop repeatedly sought it out with the greatest diligence but could not find it.

The charter that, as we showed above, had been issued by the emperor Charles under Bishop John was still being kept in the archives at Constance. The monks did not accept it because, as we said above, it had been corrupted and had been written contrary to the emperor’s command and to their needs. [Col. 1063C]

It happened at a certain time that Wolfharius, bishop of Reims, having been sent by Lord Charles on an embassy to administer justice in Chur-Rhaetia [Note: [Col. 1063D] Marlot, in his *History of Reims*, bears witness that this Wolfharius acted as a royal envoy under Charles the Great.], came to that county and, returning from there, arrived at our monastery. There he was kindly received, insofar as their means allowed, and sustained by devoted service.

Since he was not unaware of the accusations and injustices suffered by the inhabitants of our monastery, he asked them to show him the aforesaid immunity charter. When he had seen and read it through, he urged them to send the charter of protection to the emperor through some trustworthy person. He promised that he would make their circumstances known to the emperor and would provide them assistance.

Accepting his advice, they entrusted the charter—or rather, the hope of complete security [Note: [Col. 1063D] That is, the right of free election of abbots.]—to a certain vassal of the emperor named Engilrammus, in whose loyalty they had great confidence.

He also swore on the altar of Saint Gall that he would carry the charter to the king and return it very carefully to the monks themselves. But, persuaded by the devil, he carried this out differently from what he had promised [Note: [Col. 1063D] By a Germanism, the pluperfect is used for the imperfect.].

Finally, when he departed from the monastery and carried the charter with him, the bishop learned of the matter. He immediately sent him substantial gifts and obtained the aforesaid charter, which he had long desired, bringing it under his own control.

At once, wishing to remove every hope of security from our people completely, he came to the monastery itself and searched with the greatest care to see whether a copy of the charter might be found anywhere [Note: [Col. 1064D] The same Germanism.]. When he found none at all, because none existed, he was informed that the monk and deacon Amalgarius [Note: [Col. 1064D] Charters of tradition testify that Amalger had held the offices of porter, cellarer, and provost. Ermenricus writes in Codex no. 265 that he was accustomed to pray diligently before the golden altar.] had wished to hand over a copy of it.

Although he had no reason to fear concerning this act, he could not otherwise excuse himself before the bishop than by affirming under oath at the altar of Saint Gall that he neither had it written in any form nor knew it to have been written anywhere.

Only then, secure in the accomplishment of his will, did the bishop return to his own residence. He sent the monks of our monastery who were accustomed to remain with him outside, as though for another reason, and handed the oft-mentioned charter over to the flames, reducing it to ashes, as we learned afterward. [Col. 1064B]

After some time had passed, Bishop Egino ended his present life in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 813, and in the forty-sixth year of the empire of Charles the serene Augustus. [Note: [Col. 1064D] More correctly, “of the Frankish reign.”] After his death, Wolfleoz, a fellow monk of the monastery of Saint Gall, obtained the bishopric of the Church of Constance.

## 6.

After Abbot Werdon had later ended his life, Cozbert, a monk of the same congregation, was elected and ordained abbot by the brothers. He was tall in stature [Col. 1064C] and outstanding in wisdom and dignity of conduct. This occurred in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 816, and in the third year of the reign of the emperor Hludowic, son of the aforementioned Augustus Charles. [Note: [Col. 1064D] Or fourth.]

Since Bishop Wolfleoz, following the custom of his predecessors, also subjected the affairs of the monastery to his own authority, the inhabitants of the monastery trusted that they could find consolation in him as in their own brother and fellow servant. But not only was he no milder than the others, nor did he spare in any respect those from whom he had come; rather, insofar as he could, he attempted, after the manner of Jeroboam, to display toward his subjects a finger thicker than the backs of his predecessors, and he did not cease to afflict the monks from whom he had sprung, now that the example of the earlier men had ceased.

It is not fitting to commit to memory all that these actions were, how great they were, and of what kind; nevertheless, we append to this text what is necessary—and even that only very briefly. The same bishop had ordered all the affairs of the monastery to be brought before him wherever he wished. No less frequently visiting the monastery according to his own desires, he had twisted all the customary functions there to serve his pleasures.

Finally, he appointed laypersons over the cellarer’s office and all the monastery’s similar workshops [Col. 1065A], people accustomed to serve him from outside. None of the monks who had been appointed to these same offices had any power either to enter or in any way to administer or possess them [Note: [Col. 1065D] Read: “to administer or possess.”].

As a result, not only other necessities but even food—the chief support of the body—completely failed the brothers.

Because of this great necessity, the brothers from the monastery of Saint Gall approached the most pious emperor Hludowic and asked that his clemency become a consolation for their misery.

The bishop was also present at that time, relying on the support of his fellow bishops and on other members of the king’s household, all of whom he knew to be supporters of his party and adversaries of the monks.

He placed his greatest confidence in his obstinacy in a certain charter which, written by the devil’s machinations by some servant of the devil, falsely declared that not only the same monastery but also many other places belonged to the bishopric as though by hereditary right [Note: [Col. 1065D] Read: *cavebat*, “declared” or “provided against.”].

At that time the monks, on the other hand, possessed no charter of their security: one, as we have said, had been burned, while the other, as we have also mentioned, was being held by the bishop because the monks had refused, for some reason, to accept it.

When a dispute arose between the bishop and the monks before the prince, the bishop asked that his charter be read before the emperor and that the matter be judged according to it. He intended to produce the very document mentioned above, one filled with errors [Note: [Col. 1065D] Read: *proferre*, “to produce,” in place of *praeferre*.].

But divine mercy, through the intercession of Saint Gall, deigned to provide heavenly assistance to his own servants, for whom human help was lacking. The bishop thought that he would receive from the hands of his own minister the charter he desired—or rather, an envious snare intended to destroy the servants of Saint Gall. But, through an error profitable to us, he presented before the emperor and all the princes, entirely unaware of the matter, not the charter he wanted but another one: the charter that, as we mentioned above, had been made for us by Emperor Charles under Bishop John, but had not been accepted by our predecessors because of the stain of some unspeakable addition.

When the most pious emperor received it and recognized the seal of his father, he kissed it reverently and handed it around to those standing by so that they too might kiss it as a mark of honor. Then the charter was handed over to be read.

When the bishop heard that the text of the charter was proceeding contrary to his decision, he immediately rejected it, asserting that it was corrupt and wishing to bring another document expressing his perversity before the emperor.

The benevolent emperor did not consent. Instead, he restored and handed over to the monks the protection of such firm authority that, returning freely to their own place, they would thereafter have the power to elect abbots for themselves, and the bishop would thereafter possess no authority over them except in matters of spiritual instruction.

There was one exception: a census which, according to the aforementioned charter, was to be paid annually from the monastery to the bishopric—namely, one horse and one ounce of gold. [Note: [Col. 1065D] This was the same census that free monasteries paid to the king.] [Note: [Col. 1065D] The words “adulterated by John” were added later by Ekkehard IV.]

Moreover, the aforesaid prince, to increase their security, handed over to them an immunity charter by his own authority [Note: [Col. 1065D] This document survives; it was issued at Aachen on 27 January, in the second year of the emperor’s reign, indiction 9.].

When these matters had been completed, the monks returned joyfully to the monastery with their abbot Gozpert, while the bishop nevertheless returned sadly to his own residence.

Abbot Gozpert, returning to the monastery together with his monks, diligently devoted all the skill of his labor to the common welfare of the brothers. Wherever he could, he increased the advantages of our congregation in every matter.

For the enlargement of our monastery, after destroying the old basilica, he began to build a new one for Saint Gall. It now stands before those who see it, constructed with a sound and lofty form of considerable size [Note: [Col. 1065D] Its ground plan, undoubtedly drawn by the king’s architect Gerungus and sent to the deacon Gozpertus, still survives; it is three and a half feet long and two and a half feet wide. The monks Winiharius and Isenricus supervised the work, and all the stone columns were transported with immense effort. Ermenricus, in his letter.].

This was in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 830, and in the seventeenth year of the emperor Hludowic [Col. 1066C]. He brought it to completion over a period of seven years and carried out the dedication of the basilica in the ninth year.

Wolfleoz, bishop of Constance, in whose diocese it lay, came to the monastery for this purpose, together with Oadalrichus, bishop of Basel, and Erlebaldo [Note: [Col. 1065D] Since Erlebaldo died in 838, some think that Ratpert should have named his successor.] also, abbot of the monastery of Augia [Note: [Col. 1066D] What follows up to the word “dedication” was written by a different but contemporary hand.], remaining there with some brothers of his congregation [Note: [Col. 1066D] The acts of this translation were written by a monk of Saint Gall who came from Scotland; it was easy for Ratpert to consult them in the library. See the catalogue of ninth-century books.], together with many other princes of Alamannia.

The dedication of the basilica thus having been gloriously begun and honorably completed, not without the splendor of miracles, the aforesaid Abbot Gozpert afterward continued without ceasing to devote himself to every advantage of our monastery.

For books, of which there had been the greatest scarcity [Note: [Col. 1066D] Nevertheless, there were books written in Roman script in the fifth, sixth, and seventh centuries, as is clear both from the surviving fragments—for example, of Virgil and the Gospel—and from nine palimpsest codices, as well as from the notes *ancient*, *most ancient*, *old*, *very old*, and *cannot be read*, which were added to many codices in the ninth-century library catalogue. It is also attested by many codices surviving from this period that in the eighth century the ascetics of Saint Gall were already laboring at the writing of books, especially Saint Paul’s Epistles, no. 70, and the Book of the Prophets, no. 44, as well as by what Ratpert says about the scribe Waldo.], had existed in our place until his time, he produced such an abundance that the place increased considerably through their multiplication. Whoever seeks more carefully will be able to discover who they were, what sort they were, and how many there were.

## 7.

As time proceeded, the same abbot, now believing that the gravity of age and the weakness of his body were insufficient for the pressing demands of his affairs, obtained from the most clement Augustus Hludowic that Bernwicus, our monk, should become his successor. This was immediately carried out as he had requested.

Bernwicus was ordained abbot while Gozpert was still alive, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 837 and in the twenty-fourth year of the emperor Hludowic.

After this, the emperor Hludowic departed from this light on 20 June, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 840. In the same year there was also an eclipse of the sun, on 5 May, on the vigil of the Lord’s Ascension. [Note: [Col. 1067D] Anyone who investigates will find that all these chronological indications are correct.]

After the emperor Hludowic’s death, the greatest discord arose among his sons: Lothar, who was the eldest in age, and Hludowic and Charles.

Since Lothar was the eldest in age, he surpassed the others in power and in the multitude of peoples inclining toward him. Since, as we have said, the greater part of the people followed Lothar, it happened that our abbot Bernwicus also supported that party.

Meanwhile, Hludowic entered Alamannia and subjected each place to his own authority and that of his people. From there he appointed Engelbertus, our monk, abbot in our monastery.

Thus it happened that, just as the kingdoms were shaken by various errors and hardships, so too were the monasteries.

The greater part of the people followed Lothar to such an extent that certain princes of Alamannia went to meet Hludowic with a large army, intending to prevent him from entering their territories. He immediately engaged them in a fierce battle, struck down the greater part of them, and put all the rest to flight. In this way he reached his brother Charles.

In those regions Lothar was present with a very large army against his brothers Hludowic and Charles, and they against him. On the appointed day a very fierce and miserable battle was joined, and, by the will of the Lord, the younger brothers were victorious in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 841.

After this miserable conclusion of the war, Hludowic immediately sent and handed over the abbacy of Saint Gall to Grimaldus [Note: [Col. 1067D] Grimaldus was brought up and well educated at the royal court (Ermenricus, *Letter*). His brothers were Wettinus, a monk of Augia, and Thietgaudus, archbishop of Trier (Mabillon). Made archchaplain and placed over three abbeys, he preferred Saint Gall above all of them. (Ermenricus of Augia, *Letter*).]. He immediately obtained it, insofar as he was able, by reason of royal authority.

## 8.

After the division of the kingdom had been carried out and peace had been firmly established between the royal brothers, Abbot Grimaldus came to the monastery of Saint Gall. He was received honorably by the brothers of that monastery, with every gracious expression of service, and was sustained by their devoted service.

The reason was one that I think no one will find surprising: our brothers were greatly troubled because the security of their election, which, as we said earlier, had been acquired only with very difficult labor and after so many struggles, was now being removed so easily from their power.

But, with the Lord’s help, a joyful remedy came for this sorrow. For the aforesaid Grimaldus had always been accustomed to protect the same monastery and to act mercifully toward it, even before [Note: [Col. 1067D] That is, before he had obtained the abbacy of Saint Gall.] he acquired the place and authority. Having received that position, he had not diminished this concern but rather increased his affection, thereby demonstrating the greatness of his authority.

With this confidence, the monks began to urge him that, just as they had lost the privilege of immunity in him, so through him they might recover an increase of their former security.

He received this request most graciously and diligently fulfilled it. Having obtained permission for them from King Hludowic, he granted that they should immediately elect someone who, after him, would govern them and all their possessions, so that afterward they would have no uncertainty concerning their security and their own election.

They immediately received this blessing [Note: [Col. 1067D] That is, gift.] with gratitude and elected Hartmotus, distinguished for learning, conduct, and nobility. Grimaldus brought him with him to the king.

When Grimaldus had handed him over into the king’s hands and the king had received him graciously, Hartmotus immediately received from the royal authority the place of Saint Gall with everything belonging to it, to govern after Grimaldus in the second place [Col. 1068C] [Note: [Col. 1068D] Namely, in the second position after the commendatory abbot.].

The arrangement was that, after Grimaldus’s death, this same stability of election, granted by the king and begun in Hartmotus, should thereafter be marked out and firmly established for the present occupants and for all future members of that place.

When this had been completed, Abbot Grimaldus returned to the monastery with Hartmotus, rejoicing, while the brothers likewise rejoiced.

After this, Grimaldus began to establish regular life in our monastery with every kind of prudence and mental energy. Since he himself was often occupied with royal duties, he entrusted this task to Hartmotus, so that he might lay the foundations of spiritual buildings in the brothers and also diligently construct the necessary external workshops.

[Col. 1068D] Hartmotus received this commission with a benevolent mind and diligently carried it out. Although the monks had previously occupied buildings unsuitable for their needs, before much time had passed he had brought all the dwellings of our cloister [Note: [Col. 1068D] Hartmotus built the monastery not like a palace, with long continuous stretches of buildings, but like a village, with separate houses, following for the most part the ground plan cited above. This plan of the monastery of Saint Gall was published in Mabillon’s *Annales Benedictini*, volume II, page 870. The Leonine verses explaining it are found in Canisius’s *Lectiones antiquae*.]—though begun earlier—to the most beautiful completion, as we see them now, and handed them over to the returning Grimaldus [Col. 1069A].

Likewise, too, for that same abbot, a separate residence with all the necessities belonging to it, most usefully and beautifully... [Note: [Col. 1069D] This palace, later called the *Pfalz*, was decorated with marble columns and gilded paintings, with royal architects and painters from Augia lending their assistance, as the contemporary codex no. 397 testifies:

> This splendid hall is adorned with marble columns,  
> which Grimaldus, triumphant, built upon a firm foundation.  
> He adorned and cultivated it in the times of the gracious prince Hludowic,  
> joyfully and successfully for many years.  
> This palace hall was completed by royal masters,
The illustrious island of Augia had sent painters. ] built. Since Grimald therefore often stayed among our people, it came about that our advancement grew considerably in prosperity. But just as night and day succeed one another by turns, so adversity was often mingled with prosperity, and such alternations varied our circumstances.

For the venerable bishop of the church of Constance, Salomon by name, wishing not merely to diminish but rather religiously to increase in every respect the dignity of his see, sent messengers to our monastery, seeking the restitution to the episcopal side of the census which, as we have often mentioned, had been imposed upon the monastery under an unholy condition.

[Col. 1069B] This disturbance unsettled the brothers to some degree, especially since that census had been granted by Emperor Louis under the following condition:

> [Note: [Col. 1070D] After Charlemagne and Louis the Pious, Louis his son confirmed this census by a charter issued at Frankfurt in the first year of his reign, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the twelfth indiction; the charter still survives. The confirmation of this agreement by Louis the Pious, which likewise still survives, was issued at Aachen on the third day before the Nones of June, in the fifth year of his imperial rule, in the eleventh indiction.]

The condition was that the monastery itself had been freed from the authority of bishops and of all secular powers, except the kings. Abbot Grimald, however, wishing everything on both sides to be brought to an end in peace and charity, entered the cloister of the monastery and summoned the leading brothers to him. He began to ask them why they did not pay the census to the bishopric, as their own document required.

Then Hartmot, speaking before the others, replied:

> “We are not obliged, rightly, to pay this census as we have hitherto done.”

Grimald said:

> “For what reason should the payment of this census to the bishopric cease?”

Hartmot replied:

> “Because the security and immunity which, through the gracious gift of the kings, this census has until now secured for us have been completely taken away from us.”

Grimald said:

> “For what reason, and by whom, has this liberty been taken away from you?”

Hartmot replied:

> “Certainly on your account. Since we have been handed over to you as a benefice, we ought not to pay the census to the bishop. For we believe that it is sufficient for us to remain in the service of your lordship, and therefore we cannot be divided between different authorities.”

After hearing this, Grimald from that time began, at the request of Hartmot and the other brothers, to consider and discuss with them how the monastery might be freed both from this census and from every troubling burden. By God’s mercy, we shall show below how this was accomplished.

From that time, therefore, the rulers of both places—the bishopric and the monastery—began, together with their subjects, to seek how the healthful peace between the two places might be established and confirmed in such a way that, without discord, both might at some time be permitted to devote themselves to the service of Christ.

[Col. 1069D] When this matter had repeatedly been discussed at length on both sides, a salutary plan was finally discovered. The aforementioned rulers, with the agreement of the households of both parties, found and decreed that certain possessions should be transferred from the monastery to the bishopric. By this donation the monastery would be separated from the episcopate and thereafter made secure against every burden of the census.

This decree, devised by the bishop and the abbot, pleased both parties—namely, the sons of the bishopric and the inhabitants of the monastery.

Meanwhile, it happened that the most devout King Louis held a public assembly in the estate called Ulm, in the presence of his sons and of the other leading men of his kingdom. The case concerning this agreement was brought before that assembly. From then on the king began carefully and prudently to deliberate and discuss it with his advisers.

[Col. 1070B] When the nobles [Note: [Col. 1070D] That is, the optimates.] who were present strove to turn [Note: [Col. 1070D] That is, to turn.] the matter toward a favorable outcome, the most devout ruler finally asked the bishop, the abbot, and the monks who were present whether both parties—namely, the monks and the clerics—consented to the arrangement.

The abbot and the monks who were present answered that they and their entire community remained steadfast in this intention. The bishop, likewise questioned, gave a similar answer on behalf of himself and his people.

When the king saw the unity of both parties, he placed himself between them as mediator. Taking the whole matter upon himself, he transferred the aforesaid properties to the bishopric by his own authoritative hand; and by that same authoritative hand he entirely withdrew and separated the monastery from the bishopric.

[Col. 1070C] Thus, thereafter, the bishops were to possess no authority over the property of that monastery, whether in respect of the census or of any other similar matter, except solely the spiritual dignity of episcopal office. From that time onward, therefore, the monks were to have permission, with a pure mind, to serve God there [Note: [Col. 1070D] Namely, in that same place.] and to be subject to no secular power except the kings alone.

When this confirmation had been established [Note: [Col. 1070D] Read: “had been established.”] by royal authority for both parties, the necessity of settling another similar matter arose, and this too was immediately brought to a complete conclusion in the same assembly. For since the two places had previously been joined in such unity that they always seemed to be subject to a single authority, certain people, on account of this communal arrangement, had transferred to the monastery their hereditary property at Constance, which paid the census due from it; conversely, the monastery’s tributaries had transferred that same tributary inheritance to the bishopric.

And so that every disagreement might be entirely removed in this matter as well, the same king, with the consent of the abbot and the brothers, granted certain properties belonging to the monastery to Constance. He did this on the condition that everything then under the authority of the monastery—whether transferred there by the aforementioned tributaries or confirmed there in any manner whatsoever—should thereafter, without contradiction from any person, be secured there to remain permanently.

When the merciful king had settled these matters with the full agreement of all, he ordered a charter of his authority to be written immediately for both parties, as a perpetual confirmation of this agreement. To make this written guarantee of security still more certain, he first ordered that the text, merely dictated and written down on some draft sheet, should be presented to him. When he had approved the matter, he then ordered the chancellor to write the confirmation of the aforesaid agreement on proper charters.

[Col. 1071B]

> [Note: [Col. 1071D] Issued at Ulm, in the royal palace, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of August, in the twenty-first year of his reign in East Francia, in the second indiction.]

When the documents had been written out, he confirmed them by the authority of his own hand and gave one to the bishop and his people, and another to the abbot and the monks, with instructions that they were to be retained forever as an unshakable confirmation, without any overturning.

Whoever wishes to know how great were the properties transferred for the redemption of the aforesaid census and the security of the monastery, and, moreover, for the reconciliation of the aforesaid tributaries to the bishopric, should read the charters mentioned above; there he will find what he seeks.

Furthermore, the most devout King Louis immediately ordered another charter of the strongest immunity to be made for the monks, so that after Grimald they would thereafter have perpetual authority to choose their own abbots and would be subject to no human beings except the kings alone. He also ordered that, in the same charter, the royal gifts that were to accrue to the monastery itself each year, according to the custom of other monasteries provided with security, should be recorded: namely, two horses and two shields with spears.

Having thus handed this charter to the monks, confirmed by his own hand and sealed with his own ring,

> [Note: [Col. 1071D] This diploma was issued at Ulm in the same year and on the same day as the preceding one; but through an obvious error it reads “the eleventh day before the Kalends” instead of “the second day before the Kalends.”]

he allowed them to return joyfully to their monastery.

### 9

When these matters had been accomplished by God’s providence, Abbot Grimald, entrusting all the affairs of the monastery to Hartmot, now confidently presented himself at the royal court. Hartmot, therefore, having at last obtained with the brothers the quiet of the desired security, devoted himself entirely to the necessary works. Above all, he began to adorn and exalt with various ornaments the temple of God constructed in honor of Saint Gall.

First, he caused the tomb of Saint Gall,[Note: [Col. 1071D] Here “tomb” denotes a silver shrine fashioned in the form of a small chapel, in which Saint Gall’s bones were carried in processions. Hymn of Ratpert concerning Saint Gall, in Canisius, *Lectiones antiquae*.] together with the other altars, the lectern,

> [Note: [Col. 1071D] This was a pulpit from which sermons were delivered and the Gospel was read at Mass.]

and the confessionary, to be renovated; for the most part he had the entire structure rebuilt from the ground up, just as it is seen and observed today. Moreover, he took great care to distinguish the basilica itself with silver crowns,

> [Note: [Col. 1071D] That is, a silver orb from which several lamps were suspended; hence the word *Kronleuchter*.]

with various other lights, and likewise with the splendor of many kinds of ornaments.

He also arranged, at that same time, for the apse [Note: [Col. 1071D] The vaults forming this apse of the choir were wound in spirals. Ground plan, ninth century.] behind the altar of Saint Gall to be honored with gilded painting, just as we see it at present.

Under the same abbot, Hartmot also produced a considerable number of books. Know that their titles were as follows:

> [Note: [Col. 1071D] Ratpert borrowed the following catalogue from manuscript no. 267, where it bears this title: “These books were produced by Abbot Grimold in the monastery of Saint Gall in the days of Louis, king of Germany, with the assistance of his provost Hartmot, over thirty-one years.” The codices marked with an asterisk still exist in our library.]

- The five books of Moses, Joshua, and Judges, in one volume.
- Three books of Kings, in one volume.
- The three books of Solomon, the Book of Wisdom or Jesus, Job, and Tobit, in one volume.
- Chronicles, Judith, Esther, Ezra, and the two books of Maccabees, in one volume.
- All the prophets, in one volume.
- The Epistles of Paul, the Acts of the Apostles, the seven canonical Epistles, and the Apocalypse of John, in one volume.
- Parts 2 and 3 of Saint Augustine on John.
- Twenty-two books of *The City of God*, in two volumes.
- Fifteen books of Augustine’s *City of God*, in one volume.
- Two books of *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, in one volume.
- Eighty-two Questions and *Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets*, in one volume.

  > [Note: [Col. 1072D] The aforementioned manuscript no. 267 has them in two volumes.]

- Six volumes of Augustine on the Psalms.
- Likewise, highly useful excerpts from the same books, in two volumes.
- The twelve books of Saint Augustine’s *Confessions*.
- Seven books of the same author on baptism.
- Twelve books *On Genesis Literally*.
- One book of Saint Ambrose *Against the Arians*, together with his Epistle and Saint Augustine’s work against the same people, in one small volume.
- Four books *On Christian Doctrine*, in one volume.
- Saint Augustine’s *Recapitulations*.
- A lectionary for the basilica.

  > [Note: [Col. 1072D] Ratpert’s manuscript no. 614 adds: “without the Gospels.”]

- Two volumes of the Epistles of Saint Jerome.
- The homilies of John Chrysostom, together with *On Compunction of the Heart* and *On the Restoration of the Fallen*, in one volume.
- One volume of Saint Hilary on Matthew.
- Two *Collectaries*, each in a separate volume, covering the period from Advent to Easter.

  > [Note: [Col. 1072D] That is, collections of sermons by the holy Fathers to be read in choir throughout the yearly cycle and during meals on Sundays, as is noted in manuscript 103, p. 253.]

- One volume of Saint Ambrose, bishop, on the Gospel according to Luke.
- Two volumes of the same author on the Epistles of Paul.
- One volume containing the same author’s *On the Good of Death* and Jerome’s work on the Apocalypse of John.
- Victorinus *On the Holy Trinity*.
- The book of Saint Clement.
- Two *Passionalia*, in two volumes.

  > [Note: [Col. 1072D] This was the name given to books recounting the sufferings of the holy martyrs.]

- Cassiodorus on all the Psalms, in three volumes.
- Bede on the *Song of Songs*.
- The third and fourth parts of the *Conferences of the Fathers*.
- The Rule of Saint Benedict and the works of the other Fathers, in one volume.
- An explanation of the readings, in one volume.
- Isidore’s books of *Etymologies*, in one volume.
- Josephus, *On the Antiquity of the Jews*, twelve books, in one volume.
- Likewise, four books, in one volume.
- Likewise, seven books of the same author *On the Jewish War*, in one volume.
- Excerpts from Pompeius, in one volume.
- The *Deeds of Alexander*, in one volume.
- An excellent book of hymns.
- Priscian’s grammar, in one volume.
- The book of canons.
- The Passion of the Apostles.
- The Passion of Saints Sergius and Bacchus.
- The chronicle of Eusebius and Jerome.

  > [Note: [Col. 1073D] In Ratpert’s manuscript 614 the title of the book has been erased. Manuscript 267 lists it in these words: “The Lives of the Fathers, which they call the Greater.”]

- Origen’s treatise on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans.
- One volume of Rabanus, bishop, on the latter part of the prophet Jeremiah.
- Likewise, the Epistles of the Apostle Paul and the seven canonical Epistles, in one volume.

  > [Note: [Col. 1073D] This book is not found in manuscript 267.]

- The Acts of the Apostles and the Apocalypse, in one volume.
- The Life of Saint Columba, in one volume.
- Likewise, Job, Tobit, Judith, and Esther, in one volume.
- The Visions of Wetti and Barontus.

Moreover, during Grimald’s tenure Hartmot also strove, as far as he could, to improve and increase the necessities of the brothers,

> [Note: [Col. 1073D] Namely, food and clothing.]

and what was then established has remained similarly secure to this day.

At that time also, because his merits required it, the body of Saint Otmar was solemnly lifted from the church of Saint Peter and carried to the basilica of Saint Gall with the due honor of praise. Grimald, abbot and archchaplain of King Louis, and Salomon, bishop of the church of Constance, were present, together with an innumerable multitude of people. This took place on the fourth day of the week, on the eighth day before the Kalends of November, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 864.

> [Note: [Col. 1073D] The year, weekday, and day of the month agree perfectly.]

The body of the holy man was placed in the church of Saint Gall beside the altar of Saint John the Baptist. There the renown of his merits shone forth in a great abundance of miracles, until a new basilica was built for him,

> [Note: [Col. 1073D] Small chapels are often called “basilicas.”]

which was completed immediately within a short time, and a tomb was prepared for him in silver and gold. The relics of the holy man were honorably carried into it. This basilica too, after Grimald’s time, was enlarged and constructed by Abbot Hartmot in the form in which it is seen today, with the tomb and altar more fully adorned.

After this, as the course of time passed, Abbot Grimald, now advanced in years, began to reside diligently in our monastery, wishing to spend the remainder of his life in quiet

[Col. 1074A]

and to lead it in the service of Christ. At Grimald’s command, Hartmot energetically completed in his place all the labors and journeys—whether to the royal court, on military expedition,

> [Note: [Col. 1073D] That is, whether to the king’s court or on military campaigns.]

or for any other necessity—and took upon himself the care of all affairs.

Grimald himself, since he had other places and monasteries subject to his authority, especially wished to await the end of his days in this monastery.

> [Note: [Col. 1073D] He also left his books to the monastery. Manuscript 267 lists thirty-three volumes under this title: “These books Lord Grimold gave from his own possessions to Saint Gall.” Of one of them the catalogue says: “A glossed Psalter, which Grimald first gave to Noting, bishop of Brescia, and later to Queen Engilberga, and through the master Rihbert received another in return.” Engilberga was the wife of Louis II, king of Italy; she was sent into exile in Alamannia—perhaps to Saint Gall—by Charles the Fat, according to the *Annals of Saint-Bertin* under the year 882. This seems to be the same Psalter celebrated in Italy under the name Engelberga.]

He began to exercise himself most zealously in monastic disciplines. Although he was not a monk in habit, he was nevertheless a monk in conduct and intention. He was frequently devoted to prayer and alone possessed a generosity in almsgiving surpassing that of the others, so much so that he was called—and truly was—the father of the poor.

Growing daily in these and similar advances in good virtues, he, an old man full of days, departed from this light, at the Lord’s call, in a confession of the true faith and ascended, as we believe, to the height of perpetual light. He was buried in the same monastery with every honor and due veneration, and rests in the Lord.

> [Note: [Col. 1074D] He received this epitaph:
>
> “Here within lies the lover of divine law,
>
> Grimald the humble, who ordered this temple to be built”—
>
> namely, the temple of Saint Otmar. Ninth-century manuscript no. 397, p. 52.]

His departure occurred on the sixth day before the Ides of June, on the sixth day of the week, at sunrise, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 872. He ruled our monastery successfully for thirty-one years.

> Bestow on him, O Christ, the rewards of such great labors,
>
> and grant him heaven, you who created the lofty stars.
>
> Let Matthew, Mark, Luke, and likewise John
>
> be his companions, whose honors he celebrated.

> [Note: [Col. 1074D] Manuscript no. 615, from the thirteenth century, and Goldast’s edition present these verses in another form, corrected by Ekkehard IV.]

After Grimald’s death, the brothers, in accordance with the permission promised to them, immediately elected Hartmot as their abbot with the greatest unanimous agreement. Certain senior brothers went with him to the most devout King Louis.

> [Note: [Col. 1074D] It was customary, when a newly elected abbot was chosen, for part of the electors to approach the king with the abbatial staff.]

When the king learned of their agreement and desire, he did as he had previously arranged: he entrusted the monastery to Hartmot with the full liberty of secure independence, adding or interposing no condition by which the integrity of that security could in any way thereafter be violated.

Hartmot returned to the monastery with the brothers and strove everywhere and in every respect to exercise the perfection of an excellent shepherd and father. Although he had been responsible for the greater part of the labors and achievements of the past, he now, as though beginning anew, desired to increase the accumulation and growth of his customary merits.

He caused the walls of the basilica of Saint Gall—in the choir, outside the choir, and behind the temple—to be adorned and beautified at that same time with gilded painting, as they are now seen.

> [Note: [Col. 1075D] Manuscript no. 615, from the thirteenth century, adds: “This Hartmot also donated an excellent veil, which still hangs before the cross outside the choir during Lent, woven by the hands of his sister Richlin.”]

Moreover, in other buildings he himself produced a great deal of beauty for our monastery during his tenure, as can be seen at present. To summarize briefly, wherever he was—inside or outside, among the wealthy or among people of moderate means—through God’s gift and the wisdom granted him by God, by providing for all our affairs with the greatest care, he always kept us secure.

The books which he produced in his own time for the common use of the monastery have the following titles:

> [Note: [Col. 1075D] Ratpert copied the following catalogue from the same manuscript, no. 267, omitting its title, which reads: “These books Hartmot himself, appointed abbot after Grimold under the aforesaid King Louis and his son Charles the Emperor, caused to be written during the days of his rule.”]

- The Gospel readings, a book which he adorned with gold, silver, and precious stones.
- A lectionary prepared with ivory

  > [Note: [Col. 1075D] A contemporary hand adds “ivory.” These two distinguished books were removed during the Reformation and later perished.]

  and gold.
- The thirty-five books of blessed Gregory on Job, in six volumes.
- Two collectaries, from Easter to Advent.
- Seven books of Saint Augustine on the Heptateuch.
- Three books of Saint Ambrose *On the Faith Against the Arians*, in one volume.
- Likewise, three books by the same author specifically *On the Holy Spirit*, one *On the Incarnation of the Lord*, and another *On the Praise of the Saints*, in one volume.
- The Life of Saint Martin, in one volume.
- The Lives of Saints Gall and Otmar, in one volume.
- The Life of Saint Silvester, in one volume.
- The Institutions of the Fathers, which they call the Lesser Lives of the Fathers, in one volume.
- Twenty-two homilies of Gregory on the prophet Ezekiel, in one volume.
- Three books of Ambrose *On Duties*, in one volume.
- Saint Augustine *On the Teacher*, together with his Epistles.
- Likewise, *On Grace and Free Will*.
- The collected works of Florus the presbyter, drawn from the volumes of Saint Augustine on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, in one volume.
- Saint Augustine *On the Usefulness of Believing* and *On the Good of Nature*, Cyril’s scholia on the incarnation of the Lord, and a few questions.
- Solinus’s *Polyhistor*, in one volume.
- The *Disputations of Atticus and Cretobulus* could not be found for a time. Before it was found, another work was written in its place, and to it were added Saint Augustine’s book *On the Christian Life* and the *Disputation of the Church and the Synagogue*.
- The collected works of Florus on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians and on the Epistle to the Hebrews.

  > [Note: [Col. 1075D] The catalogue in manuscript no. 267 adds: “They are now in our hands.” From these words it is clear that this catalogue is older than Ratpert’s copy of the book.]

- The Decrees of the Roman pontiffs, in one volume.
- The Rule of Saint Basil and the rules of the other Fathers.

He also produced other books in an attractive script for his own particular use. After the end of his days, he likewise permanently handed them over to the service of Saint Gall to be retained. He invoked upon anyone who might dare to remove any part of them from the monastery of Saint Gall and take them away from its service the disgrace of no small confusion.

> [Note: [Col. 1076D] Some of the imprecations read as follows: “If anyone takes them away, let him be condemned to a thousand lashes and, by God’s judgment, succumb in body to disease.” Manuscript no. 19. “And if anyone takes these away, may he be covered with scabs and the itch.” Manuscript no. 46.]

The titles of these books are as follows:

- The five books of Moses, Joshua, and Judges, in one volume.
- The four books of Kings, in one volume.
- A Psalter translated from the Hebrew.

  > [Note: [Col. 1076D] A very rare codex.]

- The Proverbs of Solomon, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs; likewise, the Book of Wisdom, Jesus son of Sirach, and the two books of Chronicles, in one volume.
- Job, Tobit, Judith, and Esther, in one volume.
- Ezra, Nehemiah, and the two books of Maccabees, in one volume.
- Isaiah and Jeremiah, in one volume.
- Ezekiel, the twelve prophets, and Daniel, in one volume.
- One volume of the Gospels.
- One volume of the remaining books of the New Testament.
- Two small books by Bede, *On the Nature of Things* and *On Times*.
- Likewise, one large book and other works on computation, in one volume.
- The Rule of Saint Benedict, Bede’s martyrology, a hymnary, and the homilies of Caesarius, in one volume.
- Two volumes of Isidore’s *Etymologies*.
- One medical book.
- A gloss on the Epistles of Paul.
- Two volumes on the readings.
- Two volumes on the Gospels.
- A volume of Orosius.
- Two books of Martianus on *The Marriage of Mercury and Philology*.
- Likewise, seven books on the seven liberal arts.
- Boethius’s five books of the *Philosophical Consolation*, in one volume.
- Another five books, in a second volume.

Among these books he also produced a world map in fine workmanship, which he likewise counted among the books.

> [Note: [Col. 1076D] These books are also listed in the library catalogue, which survives in a copy made in the ninth century.]

After the death of the most devout King Louis, when our monastery, together with the rest of the kingdom, fell to Charles, his son, Abbot Hartmot caused all the charters of immunity granted to us by his father Louis to be renewed for us by that most merciful son Charles and to be written out again by his authority.

> [Note: [Col. 1076D] This diploma was issued in the year 877, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the first year of Charles’s reign, in the tenth indiction, without a stated place.]

Nor should it be passed over in silence how much was granted to our monastery at that time from royal gifts. For the aforementioned King Louis, of most blessed memory, while Abbot Grimald was still alive, transferred by royal authority to the monastery of Saint Gall, in perpetuity as a reward, the place called Mecchinga.

> [Note: [Col. 1076D] Issued at Frankfurt, in the royal palace, on the Nones of October, in the twenty-ninth year of his reign, in the tenth indiction. The estates of Mechingen and Göttingen lie near the palace of Bodman.]

After his death, and after Grimald too had died, the most merciful King Charles, his son, at Hartmot’s intercession, granted to Saint Gall in perpetual possession a property belonging to royal authority in the district of Thurgau, situated in a place called Roholvesriuti,

[Col. 1077A]

and immediately confirmed the grant by a written instrument of his authority.

> [Note: [Col. 1077D] This estate, situated near Wil in Thurgau—Rossrüti—was granted in the year 878, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the eleventh indiction and the first year of Charles’s reign.]

He also transferred to the monastery of Saint Gall, at that same time, a certain mountain situated in Chur-Raetia, on which the basilica of Saint Victor the Martyr had been built and from whom the place itself was called Mount Victor. He ordered a charter of confirmation to be made for it by royal authority.

> [Note: [Col. 1077D] The diploma by which Charles the Fat gave Saint Gall the monastery of the Scots situated on Mount Saint Victor near Feldkirch was issued in the year 883, on the ninth day before the Kalends of October, in the first year of his imperial rule in Italy and in the … year in Francia. Two years later, at the same monastery of Saint Victor, Charles founded a hospice for twelve pilgrims traveling to Rome, from the property of the estate of Raitinis—Rötis. It was issued at Bodman on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, in the year 885, in the third indiction, the eighth year of his reign, and the fifth of his imperial rule.]

This was done at the request of Eusebius the Scot, who had voluntarily lived enclosed there in the service of the Lord for thirty years. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 884, on the day before the Kalends of February, he passed from this light to perpetual light.

> [Note: [Col. 1078D] The necrology in manuscript 915, from the tenth century, gives the same day as Eusebius’s day of death.]

After the same Charles had entered Italy and peacefully subjected it to his empire, he likewise transferred to Saint Otmar by imperial authority another property in the aforementioned district, subject to royal authority, called Stamheim, together with everything belonging to it. He most firmly reinforced the security of this donation by a charter of imperial authority.

> [Note: [Col. 1078D] This was written in the year 880, on the ninth day before the Kalends of December, in the twelfth indiction, in the fifth year of his reign in Francia and the first in Italy.]

He also ordered the imperial record of the donation mentioned above to be written out again; this was done as he commanded.

> [Note: [Col. 1078D] The second grant of Roholvesriuti was recorded at Pavia on the fifth day before the Nones of October, in the second indiction, in the third year of his imperial rule in Italy and the second in Francia.]

After the same most gentle Emperor Charles had ruled all the peoples of Italy and Germany in most gracious order, at Hartmot’s request and through the agency of Liutward, bishop and imperial archchancellor, he transferred by imperial authority to the monastery of Saint Gall a small abbey in Italy, fertile in olive trees and vineyards, which Liutward then held as a benefice and which was called Massin.

[Col. 1077C]

He did this on the condition that Liutward, during his lifetime, should possess the property in usufruct and pay each year to the aforesaid monastery the census agreed upon by him for that place: either six *laguenae* of oil or sixty silver solidi. After Liutward’s death, the property was to belong perpetually, without contradiction from anyone, to the rights of the monastery.

A charter of this transaction was immediately written and confirmed with the greatest firmness by his authority. At the emperor’s command it was placed upon the altar of Saint Gall, where, God willing, it is still held in peace today.

> [Note: [Col. 1078D] The original of this diploma has been missing for several centuries.]

Thus the venerable Abbot Hartmot, wishing, after completing so many labors as we have recounted above, to see with his own eyes the end of his distinguished administration, and now compelled by age to seek rest, began earnestly to ask the emperor and to confer with the brothers about how he might be released from these labors and another appointed in his place, one whose age and strength would be suitable for bearing the various trials which now arise in the world, even greater than those of former times.

He could not easily obtain consent to this matter either from the emperor or from the monks. But when he persisted in this request for a very long time and in every possible way, frequently pleading the burden of his age, he finally, with great difficulty, obtained from the emperor a promise concerning the request.

He therefore began joyfully to seek a suitable time for carrying out these affairs. After some time had passed, it happened that the lord emperor, returning from Italy, entered our monastery. He was received with the greatest honor of praise and with no small joy on the part of all.

> [Note: [Col. 1078D] Jodocus Mezler collected these royal receptions and published them in Canisius’s *Lectiones antiquae*.]

The emperor himself also remained there joyfully for three days.

Then the venerable Abbot Hartmot, believing that the opportune time for fulfilling his wish had arrived, began most earnestly to beseech the emperor’s clemency to remember his promise. The most devout ruler, not forgetful of any previous word or promise, wished both to grant the abbot’s request and to satisfy the monks in every respect. He therefore left it to their decision to choose for themselves as abbot, and as Hartmot’s successor, whichever one of their number they wished.

When the brothers heard this, it became the source of great sadness and tears, mingled equally with joy: sadness, because they refused in their hearts to withdraw from the authority of so great a father while he was still alive; but joy, because the most merciful emperor, when necessity required the matter to be settled, preferred to confirm and establish our affairs not in his absence through messengers, but by coming in person.

When this necessity—or rather this most worthy advantage—required the matter to be concluded, all alike, old and young, from first to last, by God’s gift and with common counsel and one voice, elected Bernard as their abbot: a man distinguished by nobility and youth, whose wisdom, character, and kindness gave them confidence that both royal services could be carried out and that he would protect them and all their possessions with complete faithfulness.

When news of this had been brought to the emperor, he immediately deigned to attend their assembly. There, first of all, he honorably and with great thanksgiving released Hartmot, as he had so often requested, from the burden of such great labors, but did not remove him from the direction of those dwelling there.

Afterward, when everyone requested Bernard as their abbot, the most gracious ruler immediately heard their desire, entrusted the monastery and its community to Bernard,

[Col. 1079A]

and appointed him abbot. Among many other words of consolation, he also made this promise: that he would never take this security away from us, provided that someone suitable for this office could be found among our own number.

When everything had been properly arranged, the lord emperor made all who were living there joyful and himself too departed joyfully from the monastery.

This appointment took place near the end of the year from the incarnation of the Lord 883: on the sixth day of the week, the eighth day before the Ides of December, in the first indiction, and in the third year of the emperor Charles.

> [Note: [Col. 1079] The attentive reader will discover that this chronological specification agrees perfectly with the facts.]

Above all, our Lord Jesus Christ was reigning, to whom belong honor and glory throughout the endless ages. Amen.

[Col. 1079]
