# The Minor Work of Fifty-Five Chapters Against Hincmar of Laon

Table of chapters. 282

Metrical title. 287

Reply. 287

Preface. 290

## Chapter One

—Concerning the chapel situated in the estate of Attola. 293

## Chapter II

—Concerning the administration of the palace and the acquisition of an abbacy contrary to the canons; concerning his failure to come when summoned to the council; and concerning the irregular excommunication of Amalbert. 295

## Chapter III

—Concerning the threatened excommunication of the parishioners of other bishops. 299

## Chapter IV

—Concerning his demand that the writings produced against him be burned. 299

## Chapter V

—Concerning the two judgments of Hincmar, which he claimed had been annulled by the Apostolic See. 302

## Chapter VI

—Concerning his claim that Hincmar ought to be degraded. 310

## Chapter VII

—Concerning his seeking to be cleared by secular counsel. 313

## Chapter VIII

—Concerning the letters written by the pope in support of his complaint. 315

## Chapter IX

—Concerning the monk excommunicated by the bishop of Laon. 315

## Chapter X

—Concerning the compilation from letters of the Apostolic See sent in small booklets; concerning the word *promulgo*; and concerning a chapter of Pope Leo. 316

## Chapter XI

—That a fuller account must be given of the sacred orders and the disciplines of the canons, from the words and meanings of orthodox writers. 324

## Chapter XII

—What the orders are in heaven, in the Church, and in the earthly commonwealth. 325

## Chapter XIII

—That although there is one general order for all bishops, dignity is not common to all. 326

## Chapter XIV

—That in the commonwealth also, after the pattern of the heavenly army, there are different orders. 327

## Chapter XV

—Concerning fatherhoods and dwelling places in heaven, in the Church, and in the commonwealth. 328

## Chapter XVI

—Concerning the metropolitan church of Reims and the fortress of Laon; and that the three primatial sees were one see of Peter. The letter of Hormisdas to Saint Remigius. 334

## Chapter XVII

—Concerning the rebellion of lesser priests against their superiors, and concerning the see of Constantinople resisting the Apostolic See. 340

## Chapter XVIII

—That people of unsound mind have erred through lack of discernment in the Holy Scriptures. 350

## Chapter XIX

—That they have erred by misunderstanding the sanctions of sacred traditions. 352

## Chapter XX

—That in the ancient letters of the Apostolic See, as in laws, certain provisions were later abrogated or altered. Concerning the six general councils, the seventh among the Greeks, the Frankish council, and the letters of Pope Julius and Felix. 353

## Chapter XXI

—That no more than twenty chapters were established at the Council of Nicaea. 365

[Col. 1083]

## Chapter XXII

—Concerning the four chapters mentioned by blessed Gregory in his letter to the patrician Theoctista. 366

## Chapter XXIII

—That the Apostolic See does not accept part of the ninth canon of Chalcedon, as Pope Saint Leo demonstrates. 368

## Chapter XXIV

—Concerning the same canon of Chalcedon; concerning the canons of the Apostles; concerning the judgments delivered to Angilram; and concerning the letters of pontiffs collected by Isidore. 373

## Chapter XXV

—Concerning the authority and distinction of councils and of the letters of the pontiffs of the Apostolic See. 384

## Chapter XXVI

—Concerning this same distinction again, and concerning plenary councils and the prerogative of the Council of Nicaea. 391

## Chapter XXVII

—Concerning the canons and judgments wrongly understood and usurped by him. 393

## Chapter XXVIII

—Concerning those unjustly excommunicated: who ought to be excommunicated and in what manner; and concerning the order to be observed in ecclesiastical judgments. 397

## Chapter XXIX

—What the canons decree concerning those irregularly excommunicated. 403

## Chapter XXX

—By what means unlawful excommunications can be lifted, and concerning those who excommunicate unjustly. 407

## Chapter XXXI

—Concerning his prohibition against baptizing infants who are often endangered by the peril of death. 412

## Chapter XXXII

—Concerning his prohibition against giving penance and viaticum to the dying. 413

## Chapter XXXIII

—Concerning his command that burial be denied to the dead in his parish. 416

## Chapter XXXIV

—That when matters are certain and settled, neither a council should be summoned nor the Apostolic See troubled, but the established decisions should be observed. 416

## Chapter XXXV

—That the Apostolic See judges together with bishops who judge according to the canons; and that he does not properly understand the rule that a metropolitan should not hear cases without the request of the provincial bishops. 420

## Chapter XXXVI

—Concerning the irregular subscription that he appended to his compilation. 427

## Chapter XXXVII

—That he should not be wise in his own eyes, and concerning the discernment to be maintained in peace. 434

## Chapter XXXVIII

—That he should understand correctly the words of Sacred Scripture and the sacred rules. 435

## Chapter XXXIX

—That he should remove grief from us, danger from himself, and reproach from both of us. 436

## Chapter XL

—That it is untrue that he used to say that the king had opposed him on Hincmar’s advice. 438

## Chapter XLI

—That if he acknowledged his fault, he would seek pardon out of fear of God. 438

## Chapter XLII

—Concerning the removal of the disgrace inflicted upon both of us by many people. 439

## Chapter XLIII

—Concerning the falsification of the Sacred Scriptures and his reply to the letters concerning Nevinus. Which canons ought to be accepted; and concerning his lack of learning and boastfulness. Concerning Bertricus as well, and concerning the fact that he often admonished him. 440

## Chapter XLIV

—How he may return to the sweetness of paternal charity. 453

## Chapter XLV

—That he should remember the great sweetness that prevailed at the beginning of his episcopate and lay aside his hostility. 455

## Chapter XLVI

—Concerning his boasting that in everything he undertook against anyone whatsoever he had been, and always would be, victorious. 457

## Chapter XLVII

—That he never acknowledges himself defeated. Concerning his rebellion against the metropolitan; his demand that the sacred writings be burned; his creation of a schism by his subscription; and his unjust bonds. 461

## Chapter XLVIII

—Concerning those who love their own opinion too much, even to the point of schism or heresy. 473

## Chapter XLIX

—He is admonished not to neglect the talent of understanding that the Lord freely gave him. 483

## Chapter L

—Concerning the claim that he cannot bear anyone’s being said to have offered him any good without his own merit. 484

## Chapter LI

—Concerning the gifts that he was said to demand from clerics and laypeople. 485

## Chapter LII

—Concerning his pride and arrogance, and his foolish and unbecoming boastfulness. 489

## Chapter LIII

—Concerning disordered bodily movements, and how he ought to guard against them. 492

## Chapter LIV

—That he should not allow himself to be deceived by the flower of youth, bodily health, and the allurements of the world. 493

## Chapter LV

—Conclusion of the letter in the words of Elijah: “What was mine to do, I have done for you.” 494

# John VIII, Roman Pontiff

Historical notice. 647

Second notice. 649

# Letters and Decrees
I. — To Anno, bishop of the church of Freising. 651

II. — To Wilibert, archbishop of Cologne. 652

III. — To Emperor Louis II. 653

IV. — To Ansbert, archbishop of Milan. 653

V. — To Louis, king of Germany. — The privileges of the Roman Church are annulled only by a prescription of one hundred years. 654

VI. — To Bishop Paul. — A memorandum to Paul, bishop serving as legate in Germany and Pannonia. 654

VII. — To Emperor Louis. — Rainaldus, bishop of Castro Felicitatis, is excommunicated. 655

VIII. — To Emperor Louis II. — By the authority of the law, whatever is done against it is dissolved. 655

IX. — To the Neapolitans, Salernitans, and Amalfitans. 655

X. — To the clergy of Salerno. 656

XI. — Those who were suspected of the death of a Roman cleric are excommunicated. 656

XII. — Privilege for the monastery of Fulda. 657

XIII. — To the monks of Saint Vedastus of Arras. — He confirms everything contained in the charter of Emperor Charles. 658

XIV. — To Carloman (alternatively, King Louis). — The diocese of Pannonia is assigned to the privileges of the apostolic see. 659

XV. — To the bishops of Gaul and Germany. — He entrusts his authority in Gaul and Germany to Ansegisus, archbishop of Sens. 660

XVI. — Pope John’s bull to the community of Saint Medard of Soissons. 660

XVII. — To Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims. — That a bishop be ordained in the church of Laon in place of Hincmar. 662

XVIII. — To King Aldefonsus. — The Church of Oviedo in Galicia is made a metropolitan church. 663

XIX. — To the same. — He advises that the church of Saint James be consecrated. 663

XX. — To the bishops and counts established in the kingdom of Charles. — He praises them for having remained steadfast in their loyalty to Charles, and speaks of the legates whom he was sending to Gaul to settle the disputes. 664

XXI. — To the bishops who, having defected from Charles, had attached themselves to King Louis. 665

XXII. — To the bishops established in the kingdom of Louis, king of Bavaria. — He rebukes them for not restraining King Louis from invading the kingdom of his absent brother Charles, and urges them to make every effort to satisfy the legates whom he is sending to investigate the matters at issue between the two parties. 667

XXIII. — To the counts established in the kingdom of Louis, king of Bavaria. — He rebukes them for having attempted to invade Charles’s kingdom; he urges them to turn King Louis away from that intention and not to refuse to satisfy the legates whom he is sending. 672

XXIV. — To all the Gauls and Germans. — Concerning the condemnation of Bishop Formosus, Gregory the nomenclator, and the others who had been excommunicated at the synod held in Rome. 675

XXV. — To Count Boso. — He gives thanks because, through Boso’s efforts, the legates reached the emperor and completed what had been entrusted to them; he asks him to arrange for aid against the Saracens to be sent to him as soon as possible. 679

XXVI. — To King Louis. — He writes that he cannot settle the disagreements between Louis and the emperor unless the latter hears the other party as well; meanwhile, he urges him to preserve peace with everyone, especially with the emperor, and to restrain his subjects. [Col. 1085] 680

XXVII. — To the clergy, the order, and the people of the holy church of Valva. — He inveighs against a certain invader of the Church of Valva, while its legitimate bishop is still alive; he praises them for judging that the man should by no means be received, while also commanding them never to admit him, otherwise threatening the sentence of excommunication. 680

XXVIII. — To a certain person. — He complains about the duke of the Neapolitans, the addressee’s brother, who did not obey his admonitions. Therefore he urges the addressee to separate himself from him; otherwise he will be subjected, together with that man and his other supporters, to anathema. 681

XXIX. — To Bishops Leo and Peter. — He is surprised that, although harassed by Saracen incursions, they have not returned to him; he earnestly begs them to come back as quickly as possible. If they suffer violence from anyone, he commands them to act courageously and to report it to him. 683

XXX. — To Count Boso. — He grieves that Boso did not bring him aid when he begged for help against the Saracens. He indicates that Rome is in great danger, since rumor has it that a large army is about to come to attack it; therefore he asks Boso to bring assistance as quickly as possible. He is surprised that Boso is detaining the legates. 684

XXXI. — To Landulf, bishop of Capua. — He announces that the legates have returned to the emperor, who, he writes, acknowledged the rights of the Roman Church before an assembly of bishops and leading men and, above all, entrusted the pact concerning the land of Capua to his jurisdiction; therefore he promises to come into his territory. 685

XXXII. — To Guaifer, prince of Salerno. — He shows himself prepared to confirm the pact that he had made, and asks that lodging be prepared for him as he travels to Guaifer. 685

XXXIII. — To Geilo, abbot of Tornus, and his monks. — By pontifical authority he sanctions all their privileges, whether royal or episcopal, in the year of Christ 876; to these he adds exemption from the jurisdiction of every prelate. 686

XXXIV. — To the abbot and monks of Xerres. — He approves the donation of the monastery of Saint Porcianus made to them. 687

XXXV. — To the bishops of the province of Bourges. — That henceforth they obey Frotarius as their metropolitan. 689

XXXVI. — To the people of Bourges. — That everyone obey Frotarius, archbishop of Bordeaux, to whom he entrusts the Church of Bourges for as long as the pagans possess the diocese of Bordeaux. 690

XXXVII. — To Emperor Charles the Bald. — At the emperor’s request, since the province of Bordeaux had been devastated by pagans, he transfers Frotarius, archbishop of Bordeaux, to the Church of Bourges. 690

XXXVIII. — To Emperor Charles the Bald. — He praises him for the judgment pronounced in the case of Emmenus and urges him to deal mercifully with that man. 691

XXXIX. — To the emperor and empress. — On behalf of Madelgerus, who had killed Odelricus. 692

XL. — To the bishop of Chartres. — On behalf of Madelgerus, who had killed Odelricus. 693

XLI. — To Adalard, bishop of Verona. — He commends him for his outstanding virtues and orders him to come to Rome for the council. 693

XLII. — To Emperor Charles. — He praises him for having kindly received the legates of the apostolic see and asks him to order that the plunderers of the Roman Church, who had escaped by hiding from the judgment of his envoys, be sought out and restrained. 694

XLIII. — To Emperor Charles. — He recounts the calamities inflicted upon the Church by the Saracens and begs the emperor to send aid against them. 696

XLIV. — To Emperor Charles the Bald. — He writes that the emperor will learn from Bishop Adalgarius, to whom he grants the pallium, why the Church’s cause did not proceed according to its wish. He censures Ansegisus and commends Adalgarius’s fidelity. 697

XLV. — To Empress Richildis. — He asks her to support the Roman Church. 698

XLVI. — To Emperor Charles the Bald. — He commends Wigbode, bishop of Parma. 699

XLVII. — To Adalgarius, bishop of Autun. — He decrees that the estate of Tilionacum be restored to him and confirms the other possessions of the see of Autun. 700

XLVIII. — To Ursus, duke of Venice. — He gives thanks because Ursus obeyed the admonitions of the apostolic see. He orders the bishops to come to the synod. 701

XLIX. — To Bishops Felix and Peter. — He forbids Felix and Peter the sacraments because they failed to show obedience to the archbishop of Grado; under penalty of excommunication he orders them to come to Rome for the council, and, if they are prevented, to send substitutes. [Col. 1086] 702

L. — To Dominicus, bishop-elect of Torcello. — He inveighs against Dominicus, the bishop-elect, because, having been summoned twice, he did not come to Rome; unless he comes on the appointed day, he excommunicates him. 703

LI. — To Ursus, duke of Venice. — He asks him to support at his own expense the bishops who are being summoned to Rome for the synod; if they do not come, he threatens them with the sentence of excommunication. 703

LII. — To Bishops Dominicus and Leo. — He informs them that he has excommunicated certain men who, having been summoned to Rome for the council, neglected to come, unless they appear by the fixed appointed day; he urges the bishops to perform their duties for as long as those men are absent. 705

LIII. — To Bishop Deltus. — That, acting in the name of the apostolic see, he go to Venice and ensure that the bishops of that region come to Rome for the council, as he had ordered. 706

LIV. — To Count Lambert. — That he restrain his subjects from the evils they were committing; if he cannot correct them, he threatens to excommunicate them. He indicates that he has entrusted the legates with many matters to report to Lambert orally. 707

LV. — To Guaifer, prince of Salerno. — He praises Guaifer’s steadfast loyalty toward the apostolic see; he detests the frauds of Adelgisus and his accomplices, promises him the aid of himself and of the other Churches against the Saracens, and urges him to remain faithful and to send the bishop of Sorrento to him. 708

LVI. — To Landulf, bishop of Capua. — On the same subject. 709

LVII. — To Aio, bishop of Benevento. — He commends his zeal for the apostolic see and urges him to aid in expelling the Saracens and to impel his brother to do the same. 710

LVIII. — To Emperor Charles the Bald. — Because of the gravest dangers threatening from both the Saracens and certain Christians, he earnestly asks him to send the promised aid as soon as possible and commends the legates designated for this purpose. 711

LIX. — To Empress Richildis. — That she urge her husband, the emperor, to bring aid to the Church as soon as possible. 713

LX. — To Emperor Charles the Bald. — He sends the emperor a palm and, after describing the evils with which he was being oppressed by the Saracens and wicked Christians, asks for aid. 714

LXI. — To Anspert, archbishop of Milan. — He replies that the abbot who, without any proven crime, had been removed from the administration of a royal monastery must be recalled; but that a murderer and his accomplice in the crime must be expelled from every administration. 715

LXII. — To the bishops established in the kingdom of Emperor Charles. — He urges them to encourage the emperor to bring swift aid to the Roman Church. 716

LXIII. — To Landulf, bishop of Capua. — He sends legates, as the hypatus Docibilis had requested; he urges Landulf to work with the legates to dissolve the pact made with the Saracens, promising to approve whatever Landulf decides. 717

LXIV. — To Frotarius, archbishop. — He transfers Frotarius from the Church of Bordeaux, devastated by the pagans, to the Church of Bourges. 718

LXV. — To King Charles. — He urges him to arrange for the goods taken from a monastery of nuns to be restored. If he does not do so within sixty days and report it to him through a legate, or does not provide the reason why they have not been restored, he will excommunicate him. 719

LXVI. — To Engilberga. — He consoles her over the death of her husband and urges her to remain faithful to Emperor Charles; he promises that he will act as her intercessor with that emperor. 720

LXVII. — To Wigbode, bishop of Parma. — He urges him to stir up as many people as he can to defend the holy Roman Church and to come to him with his followers, so that, by common counsel, the Saracens may be expelled from Italy. He sends the requested letters and asks him to ensure that they are delivered to those to whom they are addressed. 721

LXVIII. — To Docibilis and John. — He urges them to take care that Christians do not make a treaty with the Saracens. 722

LXIX. — To Pulchar, prefect of Amalfi. — He urges him to arrange for the treaty made with the Saracens to be dissolved. 722

LXX. — To Sergius, master of Naples. — He grieves that Sergius, although often warned, was unwilling to dissolve the treaty with the Saracens; he commands him finally to obey. Otherwise he threatens to excommunicate him again. He promises that, if Sergius sends faithful legates, he will receive them kindly. [Col. 1087] 723

LXXI. — To the bishop of Naples. — He complains that the Neapolitans have made a treaty with unbelievers and have not been recalled to the way of truth by their own bishop. Therefore he urges both the bishop and the Neapolitans to repent. He further promises that, if the duke of Naples sends legates, he will receive them kindly and will be ready to do whatever they report should be undertaken for the benefit of the Church of God. 724

LXXII. — To Aio, bishop of Benevento. — He praises his prompt zeal in defending the Church; then he urges him to bring aid against the Saracens and to arrange for the treaty made with them to be dissolved. 725

LXXIII. — To Gregory, imperial tutor. — He rejoices that the emperor has sent a fleet to defend the Church against the Saracens and appointed Gregory its commander; then he urges him to send ten *achelandia* to cleanse the shores of Saracen pirates. 726

LXXIV. — To Emperor Charles the Bald. — He announces that he has excommunicated Adalard, bishop of Verona, because he invaded the monastery of Nonantola. 727

LXXV. — To the archbishops John, Anspert, and Waipert. — On the same subject. 728

LXXVI. — To the clergy of Verona. — On the same subject. 729

LXXVII. — To Landulf, bishop of Capua. — He urges him to inform him whether the duke of Naples wishes to break the treaty made with the Saracens and to ensure that the same duke, Guaifer, and Pulchar come with him to Traiectum, where he is going. He declares himself ready to grant what he had promised and even more, if the duke persists in his decision. 729

LXXVIII. — To Pulchar, prefect. — On the same subject. 730

LXXIX. — To Emperor Charles the Bald. — He implores aid against the Saracens, who, after devastating Campania, were plundering everything around Rome. 730

LXXX. — To the archbishop of Ravenna. — He commands him to come to the council with his suffragans. 731

LXXXI. — To Bishops Anspert and Antonius. — That they come to Ravenna for the synod; if they do not obey, he threatens to excommunicate them. 732

LXXXII. — To Ursus, duke of Venice. — He accuses him of disobedience and urges him to ensure that the bishops of Venice come to the synod being held at Ravenna; he himself is likewise to come or send legates. 733

LXXXIII. — To Peter and Leo, bishops of Venice. — That they proceed to Ravenna for the council, at which the controversies between them and their metropolitan are to be settled. 734

LXXXIV. — To Aquileius. — He indicates that the matters being reported adversely concerning him must be canonically settled at a general council. 734

LXXXV. — To Guaifer, prince of Salerno. 735

LXXXVI. — To Emperor Charles, Geilo, abbot of Tornus, and his monks. — He confirms the rights of the cell of Godith, founded by Prince Desiderius; to these he adds immunity from every episcopal jurisdiction, in the year of Christ 877. 735

LXXXVII. — To the archbishop of Ravenna. — He fixes a definite day on which the archbishop is to be present at Ravenna with all his suffragans; if anyone refuses to obey, he threatens him with excommunication. 736

LXXXVIII. — To the same. — He writes that he has ordered all the bishops of Italy, especially those of Venice, to come to the synod being held at Ravenna. 737

LXXXIX. — Privilege granted to the monastery and hospice of Piacenza. 737

XC. — To the bishop of Pavia. — He grants permission to use the archiepiscopal insignia, with the authority to summon to his synod the archbishops of Ravenna and Milan. 739

XCI. — To the glorious Count Lambert. — He indicates that hostages of the Roman nobles cannot be given; he warns Lambert not to come to Rome, because he cannot receive him. 742

XCII. — To Wido, bishop of Ivrea. — He delegates to him the case of a certain Leontardus, who had committed homicide with others; because Wido had previously imposed a very severe penance on the man, he urges him now to impose a lighter one. 743

XCIII. — To King Carloman. — He grieves over the death of Emperor Charles and urges Carloman to fulfill the promises made for the dignity of the Roman Church. He promises to send legates. At Carloman’s request he sends the pallium to Archbishop Theotmar, whom he orders to transmit annually to Rome the revenues belonging to the apostolic see that he holds in Bavaria. 744 [Col. 1088]

XCIV. — To Theotmar, archbishop of Juvanum. — He grants him the pallium and orders him to send to Rome the revenues that the Roman Church possesses in Bavaria. 745

XCV. — To Edered, archbishop of the English. — He praises his devout attitude toward the apostolic see and grieves over his troubles. He urges him to act courageously on behalf of the Church; he declares that wives must not be dismissed. He announces that he has written to the king so that the king may treat Edered with the honor due to him. Finally, he confirms the privileges of Edered’s Church. 745

XCVI. — To Bishop Athanasius. — He commends the zeal for the faith that Athanasius had shown against Sergius, an enemy of the Church of God. He urges him to labor increasingly for the defense of the Church entrusted to him and commends the deacon Peter to him. 747

XCVII. — To the Neapolitans. — He praises them because, inflamed with divine zeal, they cast Sergius out from among them and elected Bishop Athanasius as governor of their commonwealth. He commands them to obey Athanasius and offers to consult, together with him, for their welfare. 748

XCVIII. — To Count Lambert. — He writes that he wishes to travel to Gaul; therefore, under penalty of excommunication, he commands Lambert not to inflict any harm, in his absence, on the territory of the Roman Church or on Rome. 749

XCIX. — To Landulf, bishop of Capua. — He urges him to cooperate with Athanasius, bishop of Naples, in defending the Roman Church and to ensure that the pact made with the Amalfitans is observed by them. 749

C. — To Guaifer, prince of Salerno. — He urges him to persevere in his integrity and to rebuke the Amalfitans because they had not sent naval aid and were dealing with him with excessive cunning. 750

CI. — To the archbishop of Embrun. — He rebukes him for having consecrated another bishop in the Church of Vence, apart from the one whom the clergy and people had chosen; he commands him to come to Rome with both men. 751

CII. — To Count Cunipert. — He commands him to restore the goods of the Roman Church that he had occupied. 752

CIII. — To Count Lambert. — He warns Lambert not to come to Rome for the purpose of bringing aid to the enemies of the apostolic see. If he comes for another reason, he promises to receive him honorably. He entrusts various matters to the legates and commands Lambert to believe them. He says that he cannot admit Adelbert, an enemy of the Roman Church, into communion. 752

CIV. — To the same. — He severely rebukes him because, in the letter he wrote, he failed to show the honor due to the apostolic see and requested that legates not be sent without his consent. 753

CV. — To Empress Angelberga. — He grieves that Angelberga is being afflicted by troubles and complains of the injuries that Lambert inflicted upon the Roman Church. He asks her to preserve the goodwill that she used to have toward him. 754

CVI. — To Count Berengar. — He asks him to inform the emperor of what Lambert has perpetrated at Rome and to take care that Lambert be restrained. 755

CVII. — To John, archbishop of Ravenna. — He sets out the evils perpetrated at Rome by Count Lambert and indicates that he is going to Gaul to seek aid against him. 756

CVIII. — To Michael, king of the Bulgarians. — He grieves that Michael follows the Greeks and urges him to return to the embrace of the Roman Church. He then gives thanks for the gift sent to him. Finally, he indicates that a certain Sergius, promoted by underhanded means to the priesthood and episcopate, has been deposed. 757

CIX. — To Count Peter. — He urges him to recall King Michael to the embrace of the Roman Church. 760

CX. — To a certain Bulgarian nobleman. — On the same subject, and containing almost the same words as the preceding letter. 761

CXI. — To Ignatius, patriarch of Constantinople. — For the third time he warns Ignatius not to usurp the Bulgarian region, which from ancient times belonged to the Roman Church, and to remove from it within thirty days the bishops whom Ignatius or his suffragans had consecrated there. If he does not obey after two months, he deprives him of communion in the body and blood of the Lord and, if he persists in his contumacy, also of his patriarchal dignity. 762

CXII. — To the Greek bishops and clerics. — He declares them excommunicated because, invading the Bulgarian regions, they performed illicit ordinations there. They are also to be deprived of their dignity unless they depart from the entire Bulgarian region within thirty days. If anyone obeys, he decrees that the episcopate he previously held in Greece is to be restored to him; if he previously held none, he orders that a vacant bishopric be conferred upon him, provided he is worthy. 764

CXIII. — To Emperor Basil. — He grieves that the Church of Constantinople still suffers from schism; for this reason he sends legates. [Col. 1089] 765

CXIV. — To the same. — That he place confidence in the legates sent by him and bring aid to the Roman Church. 766

CXV. — To King Louis the Stammerer. — He laments the death of Louis’s father, Emperor Charles; he urges him to maintain peace with his kinsmen who are kings and to pursue the enemies of the Church, especially Duke Lambert, whose terrible attacks he recounts. Finally, he announces that he will come to Gaul and hold a synod there. 767

CXVI. — To the son of Louis, king of the Bavarians. — He urges him to preserve peace with his cousins and inveighs against Lambert, duke of Spoleto. He asks him to inform the bishops that they are to come to the synod. 769

CXVII. — To King Carloman. — On almost the same subject. 770

CXVIII. — To Anspert, archbishop of Milan. — He urges him to come to the synod in Gaul as soon as possible with his suffragans and complains of the treachery of Lambert, count of Spoleto. 770

CXIX. — To Empress Angelberga. — That she persevere in faith in the Roman Church. He commends the bearer of the present letter. 771

CXX. — Privilege for the monastery of Tornus. — The goods formerly granted to the monastery are confirmed. 771

CXXI. — To Empress Angelberga. — He indicates that he has come to Arles and found everything prosperous there; he urges her to look after the interests of the Roman Church. 773

CXXII. — To the brothers Miro and Huncfrid. — He orders Miro and Huncfrid, guilty of many crimes, to come to the synod. 774

CXXIII. — To Rostagnus, archbishop of Arles. — He grants him his authority in Gaul and the use of the pallium. 775

CXXIV. — To all the bishops of Gaul. — That they all obey Rostagnus, bishop of Arles, to whom he has entrusted his authority in Gaul. 777

CXXV. — To King Charles. — He excuses himself for not having sent a legate to him, because the road was blocked by Lambert and his supporters, who were holding the city of Rome under siege. 779

CXXVI. — To Isaac, bishop of Langres. — That he come to Troyes for the synod and send some men from Chalon to escort the pontiff there. 779

CXXVII. — To all Christians. — He excommunicates those who had stolen his horse and a silver vessel, unless they restore them within three days. 780

CXXVIII. — To the suffragan bishops of the archbishop of Arles. — He orders them to come with their archbishop to the synod at Troyes as soon as they are summoned. 780

CXXIX. — To the archbishops of various sees. 780

CXXX. — To Abbot Hugh. — He urges Hugh to persuade King Louis to come to him and also warns him to separate himself from the communion of certain persons. 781

CXXXI. — To Teutranus, archbishop of Tarentaise. — He urges him to come to meet him with his suffragans and to order Adalbert to be present at the synod so that he may give an account of the matters about which Bishop Bernarius had complained. 781

CXXXII. — To Rostagnus, archbishop of Arles. — That he come as soon as possible to the synod with his suffragans. 782

CXXXIII. — To Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims. — That he come without delay to the synod at Troyes with his suffragan bishops. 782

CXXXIV. — To Frotarius, archbishop. — That he come to Troyes for the synod with his suffragans. 783

CXXXV. — To Bernard, marquis. — He urges him to leave the way open for Frotarius to reach his see. 783

CXXXVI. — To the archbishop of Mainz. — That he urge Louis, king of Germany, and his brothers to come to the synod or send legates. 783

CXXXVII. — To Empress Angelberga. — He writes that on the anniversary of the death of her husband Louis he will celebrate sacred rites for him. He asks her to persevere in defending him and announces that he will hold a synod at Troyes. 784

CXXXVIII. — To Count Suppo. — He gives thanks for Suppo’s fidelity toward the Roman Church and entrusts him with certain matters to be done with Carloman. 784

CXXXIX. — To King Carloman. — He is surprised that Carloman has not replied to two letters. He laments his illness and adds a note concerning the synod to be held at Troyes. 785

CXL. — To King Charles. — He gives thanks for Charles’s respect toward the Roman Church and is surprised that Charles has not sent legates to him. He asks him, before the meeting he is to have with King Louis, either to come himself or to send legates. 785

CXLI. — To King Louis. — On the same subject as the preceding letter. 786 [Col. 1090]

CXLII. — To King Charles. — He rebukes Charles because, although summoned to him, he did not come, as King Louis had done. Under penalty of excommunication, he warns him to remain content with the boundaries of his own kingdom and not to trouble Boso in any way. 786

CXLIII. — To Liutbert, archbishop. — He urges him to ensure that the inheritance be restored to the daughters of Boso. 786

CXLIV. — To Count Matfred. — He urges him to restore the inheritance to the daughters of Count Boso. 787

CXLV. — To Valderamus. — He urges him either to bring Valderamus’s case to a conclusion or to refer it back to him. 787

CXLVI. — To Theodoric, archbishop of Besançon. — He orders him to come as soon as possible and forbids a bishop to be ordained in the Church of Lausanne, on account of the divisions among the electors, before they have conferred together. 788

CXLVII. — To the priest Ametius. — Privilege for the monastery of Saint Peter in the district of Nîmes. 788

CXLVIII. — To Frotarius, archbishop of Bordeaux. — That he come to the synod and bring the privilege concerning the transfer of the sees. 789

CXLIX. — Privilege for the monastery of Saint Giles. 790

CL. — To all bishops, counts, viscounts, hundredmen (*centenarii*), judges, and Catholics living in Hispania and Gothia. — A law concerning sacrilegious persons, added by Pope John to the Gothic laws at the council of Troyes. 795

CLI. — To all the faithful. — Privilege of the Church of Poitiers, so that no one may invade its goods and so that what has been taken away may be restored. 796

CLII. — To the bishops established throughout Gaul. — A privilege is granted to the monastery of Fleury by the council of Troyes. 797

CLIII. — To Wala, or Walon, bishop of Metz. — He grants him permission to wear the pallium on specified days. 798

CLIV. — Excommunication of Hugh and Emmo. 799

CLV. — To Count Bernard. — He orders Bernard to come, together with certain others, to the synod at which Frotarius, bishop of Bourges, wished to purge himself of the charge of infidelity brought against him. 799

CLVI. — Excommunication of Count Bernard. 800

CLVII. — To Adalard, archbishop of Tours. — He confirms the privileges granted to the Church of Tours. 800

CLVIII. — To various bishops. — That they compel the invaders of the goods of the Church of Tours to restore them and to pay the ninths and tithes. 801

CLIX. — To the bishops of Brittany. — He rebukes them because they have withdrawn from the jurisdiction of the archbishop of Tours and invaded his goods. He commands them henceforth to obey him and to seek his forgiveness for their offenses. 802

CLX. — To the archbishops of Arles and Narbonne. — That they canonically settle the case between the bishops of Uzès and Avignon. 802

CLXI. — Privilege for the monastery of Vézelay. — The immunities formerly granted are confirmed. 803

CLXII. — To Bishop Wibode. — He commends Wibode’s faith and urges him to send a legate before coming to a conference with Carloman; he also orders Wibode to attend the conference. 804

CXLIII, CXLIV. — Privilege for the monastery of Saint Marcellus. 805

CLXV. — To Count Suppo. — He orders Suppo to come to meet him at Mount Cenis (*Cinisium*) and to urge Empress Angelberga and the prelates of Milan and Parma to do the same, so that together they may discuss matters concerning the Church’s welfare. 806

CLXVI. — To Wibode, Paul, and the bishops Paul and Luidoinus. — He orders them to come to Pavia for the synod. 806

CLXVII. — To John, bishop of Pavia. — That he come to meet him at Turin and send the letters written by him to certain bishops, so that they may come to the council. 806

CLXVIII. — To Anspert, archbishop. — He recounts the labors undertaken for the Church and urges Anspert to come to meet him at Pavia with all his bishops. 807

CLXIX. — To Count Suppo. — He is surprised that Suppo did not come to meet him as he should have; he informs him of what he had done with King Louis and urges him to come to him. 807

CLXX. — To Count Berengar. — He commends Berengar’s devotion toward the Roman Church and announces that the synod in Gaul has been held and that he has returned safely. He urges Berengar to hasten to come to him. 808

CLXXI. — To Anspert, archbishop of Milan. — He rebukes him because he did not bring him aid and now for the third time urges him to come to meet him at Pavia on a specified day with his suffragans. 808

CLXXII. — To Count Berengar. — He recounts the labors undertaken for the Church. 809

CLXXIII. — To King Louis the Stammerer. — He commends the devotion and service toward him of Count Boso and Bishop Agilmar, by whom he had been escorted into Italy. [Col. 1091] 810

CLXXIV. — To King Louis. — He is surprised that Louis did not restore to Boso’s daughters the inheritance legally due to them, for which he had previously asked, and again urges him to restore the inheritance to them intact. 811

CLXXV. — To Hugh. — He urges him to settle the dissension that had arisen between Abbo and the others. 811

CLXXVI. — To Romanus, archbishop-elect of Ravenna. — He rejoices that Romanus has been elected archbishop of Ravenna. He orders him not to promise anything to anyone on account of the election and to ensure that his letter to Leo and the Romans is delivered and that their reply is sent to him. He orders the goods of the dukes John and Deusdedit to be restored. 812

CLXXVII. — To the people of Ravenna. — He grieves over the death of their bishop and urges them to honor suitably the archbishop whom they have elected. He commands them to defend the Church of Ravenna and the goods of the dukes Deusdedit and John. 812

CLXXVIII. — To the judges and dukes of Ravenna. — He orders them to defend the city manfully against Lambert. 813

CLXXIX. — To Bishops Theodoric and Isaac. — He commands them to excommunicate those who had abducted the son of Count Wipert and were ravaging that region. 813

CLXXX. — To Count Hugh. — He urges him to punish certain criminals. 814

CLXXXI. — To Counts Hugh, Theodoric, and Bernard. — That they preserve the bond of friendship and charity made with Boso. 814

CLXXXII. — To the monk Vulgarius. — That he obey Bishop Wipert, who obtained him by a letter of release. 814

CLXXXIII. — To the clergy of Milan. — He commands that whenever the bishop of Pavia summons them to a synod, they come. 815

CLXXXIV. — To John, bishop of Pavia. — He orders that the men who abducted the wife of a certain Ragibertus be excommunicated. 815

CLXXXV. — To all the faithful. — He commands that no one inflict any harm upon the monastery of Saint Augentius. 816

CLXXXVI. — To the bishops established in the kingdom of Louis. — He replies concerning the indulgence granted to those who had fallen while fighting against the pagans. 816

CLXXXVII. — To Wifred, bishop of Vence. — He forbids a bishop who had communicated with excommunicated persons to celebrate Mass. 816

CLXXXVIII. — To Odo, bishop of Beauvais. — He decrees that minors who had killed another person may be ordained after completing their penance. 817

CLXXXIX. — To Bishops Aimar and Wido. — He orders them to command Rostagnus’s wife to come to him and to deprive her supporters of communion unless they repent. 817

CXC. — To Wala, bishop of Metz. — A betrothed man is not to be compelled to marry a woman who has been corrupted by another. 817

CXCI. — To John, bishop of Pavia. — That he deal more leniently with a certain man who had performed penance for five years. 818

CXCII. — To Aginulf, bishop of Gévaudan. — That he arrange for the goods taken from the bearers of the present letter to be restored. 818

CXCIII. — To the archbishop of Besançon. — He announces that he has absolved Fulcard and his wife from excommunication. 818

CXCIV. — To Gaideris, prince of Benevento. — He consoles him for the losses inflicted by the Hagarenes, promises aid, and says that he will come over to his side. 819

CXCV. — To Bishop Aio. — He commends his devotion toward him, informs him of his own safety, and then consoles him over the death of his brother. 819

CXCVI. — To Count Daferius. — He consoles Daferius and promises him assistance. 820

CXCVII. — To Romanus, archbishop of Ravenna. — He commands him to come to Rome for the synod with his suffragans. 820

CXCVIII. — Privilege for the monastery of Piacenza. 821

CXCIX. — To the archbishop Romanus. — That he ordain the priest Lupo bishop in the Church of Sarcena. 821

CC. — To Anspert, archbishop of Milan. — That he come to Rome with his suffragans for the synod to be held, at which the election of the emperor will be discussed. He commands him not to receive anyone as king before he himself has elected the emperor; if Anspert does not obey, he excommunicates him. 822

CCI. — To Athanasius, bishop of Naples. — He commends his devotion toward him, informs him of his safe return, and urges him to persevere until they meet together. 823

CCII. — To the same. — On the same subject as the preceding letter. 823

CCIII. — To the same. — That he indicate a place where they may meet and confer concerning the safety of their common homeland. [Col. 1092] 824

CCIV. — To King Charles. — He urges him to send legates and come to the aid of the Roman Church. 825

CCV. — To Bishop Wibert. — He rebukes him because, having been summoned twice, he neglected to come to him; he commands him to come and answer the charges brought against him. 825

CCVI. — To Count Berengar. — He declares his goodwill toward Berengar and commends his devotion toward the Roman Church. He asks him to assist Bishop Stephen in defending the rights of his Church. 825

CCVII. — To Count Pandenulf. — He asks him to provide assistance to the emperor’s legates as they pass through his territory. He expresses sympathy for the pagans’ incursion against him, excuses himself for not going to him, urges him to be courageous, and promises assistance. 826

CCVIII. — To the archbishops and their suffragans. — That they not excommunicate Bicbertus before the case has been examined. 827

CCIX. — To Count Boso. — He congratulates him on his safe and prosperous condition and shows that he holds both Boso and Empress Angelberga dear. He asks him to permit Adelbert and his wife Rotilda to retain the goods they possessed in the province. 827
CCX.—To Count Liudtefrid and his wife.—He excommunicates them because they had carried off a nun from her monastery. 828

CCXI.—To Gregory the primicerius.—He commends his zeal toward the Church and the emperors; he declares himself ready to settle the disturbances of the Church of Constantinople. He indicates that he will receive the emperor’s envoys honorably—envoys whom he had previously ordered to be received from the count of Capua and sent to him. 828

CCXII.—The excommunication of Anspertus because, summoned to the synod, he had disdainfully refused to come. 829

CCXIII.—To Theodosius, patriarch of Jerusalem.—He excuses the delayed return of his envoys, through whom he sends him certain gifts, asking him to pray continually to God on his behalf. 829

CCXIV.—To King Carloman.—That the deacon Gospertus be appointed bishop in the Church of Vercelli. 830

CCXV.—To King Charles.—He urges him to come as soon as possible with aid against the oppressors of the faithful and of the Church. 831

CCXVI.—To Bishop Wibbodus.—That he go together with the envoys whom he is sending to Carloman, or send someone in his place. He reproves him for not preventing Angelberga’s property from being plundered and urges him to arrange its recovery. 831

CCXVII.—To Michael, king of the Bulgarians.—He urges him to return, together with his people, to obedience to the Roman Church, from which he had withdrawn after being led astray. 832

CCXVIII.—To the counselors of Michael, king of the Bulgarians.—The same subject. 833

CCXIX.—To Count Sedesclavus.—He orders him to provide the envoy whom he is sending to the king of the Bulgarians with a safe journey and the necessary supplies. 833

CCXX.—To Gregory the primicerius.—He asks him to send the Constantinopolitan envoys to him; he promises that, when the king of the Franks comes to Rome, he will go to his aid. 834

CCXXI.—To Bishop Wibbodus.—That he act with Carloman, or with his brother Charles, concerning the defense of the Church of God against pagan attacks; and, if Charles’s archchaplain comes to Rome, that he himself also come. Otherwise, he is to disclose to him by letter the wishes of those kings. 834

CCXXII.—To Count Boso.—He writes that he is keeping secret what he had secretly heard from him, and that he altogether expects from him the aid he had promised; he also states that he is well. 835

CCXXIII.—To Anspertus, archbishop of Milan.—He reproves him for not coming to the council when summoned for the third time. He orders him to come with his bishops for the celebration of the synod and not to make an agreement with the Frankish kings who had entered Italy; otherwise he threatens him with excommunication. 836

CCXXIV.—To the same.—Nearly the same subject. 837

CCXXV.—To Theodosius, elected bishop of Nin.—He praises his devotion toward the Roman Church and his outstanding virtues; he attests his benevolence toward him and advises him to receive episcopal consecration from him. 838

CCXXVI.—To Anselm, bishop of Limoges.—A man who has baptized his son under urgent necessity is not to be separated from his wife. 839

CCXXVII.—To King Carloman.—He urges him to defend the Roman Church, which was suffering many injuries from the Saracens [Col. 1093]; he asks him to receive the envoys kindly and to place confidence in them. 839

CCXXVIII.—To the same.—That Conspertus be created bishop in the Church of Vercelli. 840

CCXXIX.—To Branimir.—He welcomes him as he returns to the embrace of the Roman Church and advises him to persevere in the love of God. He grants the apostolic blessing that Branimir had requested and urges him to allow his own envoy to carry the letter of the Bulgarians. 841

CCXXX.—To the priests and peoples subject to Branimir.—He welcomes them as they return to the embrace of the Roman Church and advises them to persevere. 842

CCXXXI.—To Michael, king of the Bulgarians.—He gives thanks to God that Michael has sent envoys to him to receive ecclesiastical teaching and canonical institutions. He urges him to return to the Roman Church and promises, if Michael wishes, to send an envoy. 843

CCXXXII.—To Airardus, archbishop of Auch, and his suffragans.—He urges them to correct the people’s depraved morals, especially incestuous marriages: no one is to abandon his wife and take another, or to keep a concubine together with his wife; no one is to appropriate the Church’s immovable property; and the clergy are to remain under the bishop’s authority. 844

CCXXXIII.—To Rostagnus and others. 845

CCXXXIV.—To the clergy of Salona.—He advises them to return to the embrace of the Roman Church, and that the archbishop elected by them receive consecration and the pallium from him, not from anyone else. He also instructs them to believe the envoy concerning what he will report orally. 846

CCXXXV.—To three archbishops.—That they remove the bishop of Nîmes from the unjust seizure of a certain monastery and, if he does not obey, excommunicate him. 847

CCXXXVI.—To Michael, king of the Bulgarians.—He gives thanks for the embassy and gifts sent; he grieves that Michael has defected from the Roman Church, to which he urges him to return. He points out that the Greeks are retaining the Bulgarian diocese, although it belongs to the Roman pontiff, contrary to the canons. 848

CCXXXVII.—To Abbot Anastasius.—He orders him to return the cell to Bishop Gaudericus. 849

CCXXXVIII.—To Tuventarus of Marauna.—He urges him, rejecting every false doctrine, to remain in the faith of the Roman Church. He expresses astonishment that Methodius teaches otherwise than he had professed and indicates that for this reason he had summoned him. 849

CCXXXIX.—To Methodius, archbishop of Pannonia.—He orders him to come to him so that he may learn about his teaching. He prohibits the celebration of Masses in the Slavonic language. 850

CCXL.—To Anspertus, archbishop of Milan.—He reproves him for not obeying the Apostolic See, for treating its envoys abusively, and for celebrating Masses while excommunicated. He therefore advises him to come as soon as possible, either in person or through envoys, to the synod to clear himself. 850

CCXLI.—To the Empress Angelberga.—He declares that he is unwilling for the moment to absolve Anspertus, archbishop of Milan; but if Anspertus clears himself at the synod of the crimes alleged against him, then he will release him from excommunication. He says that he will celebrate the sacred rites for Emperor Louis on the anniversary day. 851

CCXLII.—To King Louis.—He gives thanks for his favorable disposition toward the Roman Church. He urges him to come to defend it against pagan incursions and silently promises him the empire. 852

CCXLIII.—To the Emperors Basil, Constantine, and Alexander.—Moved by the emperors’ petitions that peace might exist in the Church of Constantinople, he makes a dispensation concerning Photius, allowing him to be substituted for Ignatius as patriarch of the Church of Constantinople. He decrees that henceforth no one may rise to patriarchal dignity unless he has ascended through the ecclesiastical grades. He orders the patriarch of Constantinople to leave the Bulgarian diocese under the jurisdiction of the Roman Church and advises everyone to render the patriarch his due obedience. He orders them to admit to communion those who had been initiated by Methodius and Ignatius and excommunicates those who refuse to communicate with Photius. 853

CCXLIV.—To the Constantinopolitans.—He orders them, with the schism settled, to return to the unity of the Church and to communicate with Photius. 863

CCXLV.—To the clergy of Constantinople.—The same subject as the preceding. 865

CCXLVI.—To Bishops Paul and Eugenius.—He appoints them, together with the priest Peter, as envoys, so that, as he had instructed them, they may establish peace in the Church of Constantinople. 867

CCXLVII.—To Bishops Paul and Eugenius, and likewise to the priest Peter.—Mansi’s notice concerning the following letter. 867

Notice of Severinus Binius. 870

CCXLVIII.—To Photius, patriarch of Constantinople.—He appoints Photius patriarch of Constantinople, provided that he seek pardon at the synod. He decrees that henceforth no layman in that Church may immediately be ordained bishop. He orders the Bulgarian diocese to be restored to the Roman Church. 870

Notice of Severinus Binius. 872

CCXLIX.—To Landulfus and Lando.—He writes that he will go to Traiectum and take care of whatever may contribute to their peace; there he will deal, among other matters, with Landulfus, the bishop-elect of the Church of Capua. 875

CCL.—To Guariferus, prince of Salerno.—The same as in the preceding letter; moreover, he reproves him for taking up arms against the Capuans and asks him to arrange for the mancosi owed to him by the Amalfitans to be restored. 876

CCLI.—To Bishop Leo.—He grieves that dissensions have arisen at Capua. He declares that he will go to Traiectum and there deal with Landulfus, the bishop-elect whose confirmation had been requested. 877

CCLII.—To the priest Landulfus.—He praises him for having left Capua to avoid the plots of his relatives and for laboring to settle the dissensions. He declares that he will go to Traiectum and there deliberate concerning his election. 878

CCLIII.—To the prefect Pulcher.—He reproves him for neither breaking the treaty made with the pagans nor defending the territory of Saint Peter as he had promised. He orders him to send back the money given for that purpose. 878

CCLIV.—To the monks of the monastery of Pultaria.—He grieves over their misfortunes and states that, on their behalf, he has written to Prince Boso and Abbot Hugh so that they might help them. He also states that he has sent a copy of the testament of Gerard, the founder, to Archbishop Ansegisus and Count Conrad. 879

CCLV.—To Abbot Hugh.—That he protect the monastery of Pultaria. 879

CCLVI.—To Hugh and Radulfus.—He states that he has granted the villa of Vendoara, belonging to Saint Peter of Pultaria, to no one, and has ordered Arembertus, who received it from Boso, to be excommunicated unless he withdraws from it. 880

CCLVII.—To Count Boso.—That he remove Arembertus and anyone else from the villa of Vendoara, restore it to the people of Pultaria, and protect the monastery itself. 880

CCLVIII.—To Guaiferus, prince of Salerno.—He advises him to desist from the harassment he was inflicting on the Capuans. He declares that he will go into his territory and settle the dissensions. 881

CCLIX.—To Pandenulfus, the castaldus.—He declares that he has written to Guaiferus to desist from inflicting harm on the Capuans. 882

CCLX.—To King Charles.—He writes that he had summoned Charles to Rome by letter so that he might promote him to the empire; that he had advanced as far as Ravenna to meet him; and that he had hoped to receive aid from him against the enemies of the Roman Church. This hope frustrated him so completely that the enemies had never raged more fiercely. He asks Charles to aid the Church and, while preparing his journey, to send envoys to him; he also commends his own envoys. 882

CCLXI.—To the same.—He grieves that he cannot confer with him. He sends the envoy Arnulfus to him, asking him not to permit the Roman Church to be harmed by its enemies; for that reason he orders Charles’s envoy to be sent to him together with Arnulfus. 883

CCLXII.—To Archbishop Romanus.—He expresses astonishment that, although harassed by injuries, Romanus had not fled to him. He sends a messenger to Ravenna to investigate carefully everything done against him and to compel those who had inflicted the injury to come to Rome, so that Romanus himself may proceed with them to the synod, where his case will be heard. He also reproves him for not residing in his own Church. 884

CCLXIII.—To all the faithful.—He orders them to obey the bishop of Pavia, to whom he had granted the power of excommunicating. 885

CCLXIV.—To Romanus, archbishop of Ravenna.—He orders him to come to Rome for the synod. 886

CCLXV.—To the Milanese clergy.—He orders them, in place of Anspertus, archbishop of Milan, who had been deposed in the Roman synod, to choose another whom he would consecrate. He sends envoys who are to attend the election with them and orders that they be obeyed in all matters. 886

CCLXVI.—To King Charles.—He declares that Anspertus, formerly archbishop of Milan, had been deposed in the Roman synod, and that Joseph, whom Anspertus had ordained bishop of Vercelli, had been deposed. He asks Charles to protect Conspertus, whom he himself had consecrated bishop of the Church of Vercelli. 887

CCLXVII.—To the people of Vercelli.—He orders them to receive Conspertus, whom he had appointed their bishop, and honor him suitably. He declares all the acts of Joseph, the usurper, null.

CCLXVIII.—To Notingus, bishop of Novara.—He advises him to restore Angelberga’s property; otherwise he threatens him with excommunication [Col. 1095] unless he comes to Rome within two months to render an account concerning these matters. 889

CCLXIX.—To the Amalfitans.—He declares that he has excommunicated them until they separate themselves from the pagans. He threatens them with other punishments unless they obey as soon as possible. 889

CCLXX.—To Helmoinus, bishop of Penne.—He reproves him for not attending the synod. He orders him to come to him on the appointed day and, in the meantime, to absolve someone whom he had unjustly excommunicated. 890

CCLXXI.—To Bishop Paul.—He orders the church situated in the villa of Carpana to be restored, a priest to be appointed there, and the sacred chrism to be sent to it annually. 890

CCLXXII.—To Theodoricus, Heodicus, and others.—He shows that a woman who had assumed the religious habit under compulsion by force and threats is not bound to keep her vows; nevertheless, he entrusts them with deciding her case. If any difficulty should arise, he orders them, or their envoys, to come to him with the woman herself. 891

CCLXXIII.—To Athanasius, Pulcher, and others.—He orders them to break the treaty made with the Saracens; unless they do so by the Kalends of December, he threatens them with excommunication. He advises Pulcher not to harass Pandenulfus, the Capuan judge. 892

CCLXXIV.—To Arpaldus, bishop of Ascoli.—He reproves him for not coming to the synod and orders him to come to him to answer the charges brought by his clergy. 893

CCLXXV.—To King Charles.—He expresses astonishment that, although Charles had come to Pavia, where they were both supposed to meet, he had not sent envoys to him. He asks him to appoint envoys so that he may go to him. 894

CCLXXVI.—To the same.—He gives thanks that, when Conspertus had been ordained bishop of the Church of Vercelli by him, Charles had willingly accepted his ordination. He excuses himself for not absolving Anspertus, archbishop of Milan, at Charles’s request. 894

CCLXXVII.—To Kings Louis and Carloman.—He gives thanks for their affection toward the Roman Church and promises reciprocal devotion. 895

CCLXXVIII.—To Hugh and the other counts.—He gives thanks for the loyalty they were showing to Kings Louis and Carloman. 895

CCLXXIX.—To John, bishop of Pavia.—He orders him to restore the church situated in the villa of Carpana, which Paul, bishop of Reggio, had neglected to repair, to appoint its own priest there, and to send sacred chrism annually. 896

CCLXXX.—To Archbishop Theutmar.—He expresses astonishment that he is delaying and not coming to him; he advises him to come immediately. 896

CCLXXXI.—To Bishop Antonius and Count Berengar.—He excommunicates Count Liutfredus because he had received a nun who had fled from her monastery and had plundered the property of the Empress Angelberga, unless he makes satisfaction at the appointed time. He advises no one to communicate with him. 896

CCLXXXII.—To Bishop Egilbertus.—He reproves him for communicating with persons excommunicated by the Apostolic See. He orders him not to communicate with the excommunicated Liutfredus and Odebricus. 897

CCLXXXIII.—To Egifridus and others.—He asks them to take care of the property of the Empress Angelberga. 898

CCLXXXIV.—To Count Eunibertus.—He threatens him with excommunication unless he restores the property of Saint Peter and of the Empress Angelberga. 898

CCLXXXV.—To Abbot Gisulfus.—He entrusts the monastery of the Empress Angelberga to his care. 899

CCLXXXVI.—To Gregory, Theophylact, Diogenes, and others.—He congratulates them on their victory over the Saracens and expresses astonishment that they had not come to Rome. He orders them to come to his aid against the Saracens. 899

CCLXXXVII.—To Athanasius, bishop of Naples.—He commends his devotion toward the Apostolic See and urges him, as he had promised, to break the treaty made with the Saracens. He declares that, if the Amalfitans, who had been admonished about this matter through his envoy, neglect to obey, they are to be excommunicated. 900

CCLXXXVIII.—To the Amalfitans.—He advises them, after breaking the treaty with the Saracens, to return to the embrace of the Church. For this reason he promises to give ten thousand mancosi each year and one thousand in that year. Unless they obey, he threatens them with excommunication. 901

CCLXXXIX.—To Charles the Fat, king of Italy.—He asks him to permit Jerome to retain the bishopric of Lausanne peacefully and to order Hugh to restore the property of the Church of Besançon that he had taken away. 901

CCXC.—That he pursue the case of Jerome, bishop of Lausanne, before King Charles. 902

CCXCI.—To Theodoricus, archbishop of Besançon.—He declares that he has written to King Charles concerning his case; concerning Jerome, bishop of Laon, he urges him to strive to help him [Col. 1096]. 903

CCXCII.—To King Charles.—He commends his devotion toward the Roman Church and asks him to send an envoy to him with assistance. 903

CCXCIII.—To Count Sfentopulcrus.—He congratulates him and his subjects on their devotion toward the Apostolic See and receives them into his protection. He shows that Archbishop Methodius had professed the orthodox faith; he confirms his rights and privileges and sends him to govern them. He declares that a bishop has been consecrated for the Church of Nitra and wishes another to be sent to him, whom he may place over another church. He orders everyone to obey that archbishop. He grants that the divine offices may be recited in the Slavonic language, provided that the Gospel is first recited in Latin. 904

CCXCIV.—To Landulfus, bishop of Sora.—He reproves him for violating what he himself had decreed between Landulfus and Landenulfus, bishop of Capua, concerning the produce of that Church. He threatens him with excommunication unless he obeys his decrees. He orders that, if he considers himself injured, he come to him with the same bishop to plead his case. 906

CCXCV.—To King Charles.—He congratulates him on his devotion toward the Roman Church, which had chosen him as its defender, and advises him not to trust its adversaries. He praises him for ordering the territory of Saint Peter to be defended against hostile attack. He declares that he will not give aid to Boso as a tyrant. He desires Charles’s arrival and asks him to send envoys. 907

CCXCVI.—To the august emperors.—He commends their zeal in establishing harmony in the Church and advises them to persevere in it. He gives thanks for the dromons sent as aid, for the monastery of Saint Sergius, and for the restoration of the Bulgarian diocese to the Apostolic See. He asks them to protect the Church of God. Finally, he declares that he approves what was done for Photius in the synod of Constantinople, provided that the envoys did not act contrary to his orders. 909

CCXCVII.—To Photius.—He congratulates him on the concord of the Church of Constantinople. He expresses astonishment that many things he had decreed had been changed. He approves what was done at Constantinople in the council concerning Photius’s case, provided that the envoys did not act contrary to his instructions. 910

CCXCVIII.—To King Charles.—He gives thanks for his devotion toward the Apostolic See and attests his own benevolence toward him. He awaits Charles’s arrival for the needs of the Church and advises him to send some envoy. He complains about a certain George, an excommunicated man who, relying on the emperor’s authority, had invaded the property of the Roman Church. He asks Charles to send the promised aid. 911

CCXCIX.—To Romanus, archbishop of Ravenna.—He orders him to come to Rome for the synod to resolve certain questions. 912

CCC.—To all the bishops.—That they come to Rome for the synod. 913

CCCI.—To King Charles.—He rejoices in Charles’s safety and prays God that all things may turn out favorably for him. He announces that the Saracens have been defeated by the Greeks and that he himself is being severely pressed by the Saracens and others as well. Therefore, he asks Charles to come to his aid as quickly as possible. 914

CCCII.—To the same.—He absolves Deusdedit of Ravenna, who had been unjustly excommunicated; he confirms his marriage with his wife Maria and orders him to be defended. 915

CCCIII.—To Anspertus, archbishop of Milan.—He reproves him for disobedience and orders him to return the monks Rhodoaldus and Warlenus, whom he had unjustly cast into prison, honorably to their monastery. 916

CCCIV.—To Solomon, procurator of Pavia.—The same subject. 916

CCCV.—To Marquis Adelbertus.—He absolves him from excommunication, and his men as well if, within fifteen days during the month of March, they make satisfaction to the Church. 917

CCCVI.—To Oteramus, bishop of Vienne.—He reproves him for favoring Boso’s associates and claiming that he was doing so by papal command. He orders him to come to Rome to clear himself of the crimes alleged against him. 917

CCCVII.—To Count Barnimerus, the priests, and others.—He shows that their devotion toward the Apostolic See has been most pleasing to him and urges them to persevere. He orders envoys to be sent to him and promises that, when they return, he will send his own envoy, to whom they are to promise fidelity according to the rite of the Church. 918

CCCVIII.—To Michael, king of the Bulgarians.—He expresses astonishment that Michael has not sent envoys, as he had long since promised, and advises him to do so with all possible haste. 919

CCCIX.—To a certain person, namely Charles the Fat, king.—He advises him to carry out what he had commanded through his envoys. 919

CCCX.—To Anspertus, archbishop of Milan.—He confirms the ordination of Joseph as bishop of Asti, although Joseph had previously been appointed bishop of the Church of Vercelli contrary to the canons. 920

CCCXI.—To Atto.—He excommunicates him unless he restores to the Church of Milan the property he had taken away and returns, with his associates, to obedience to his archbishop. 921

CCCXII.—To Anselm, archdeacon of Milan.—He threatens him with excommunication unless he returns to obedience to his archbishop. 922

CCCXIII.—To John, Egilulfus, and others.—He entrusts them with the case pending between the bishops of Trent and Verona. He advises them to decide it according to law and send their judgment to him so that he may confirm it. 923

CCCXIV.—To Adelchisius, bishop of Trent.—He reproves him for invading the property of the bishop of Verona. He declares that he has entrusted his case to certain bishops and advises him to accept their judgment. 923

CCCXV.—To Kings Louis and Carloman.—He asks them to agree with Emperor Charles concerning the recall and sending of Angelberga to Rome, where he promises to keep her under such guard that she will be unable to plot anything against them. 924

CCCXVI.—To all the archbishops, bishops, and counts of Italy.—He urges them to make every effort so that Emperor Charles will permit Angelberga to come to Rome. He promises to keep her under such guard that she will be unable to plot anything against Charles together with Boso; and, if she attempts anything, he promises to send her back. 925

CCCXVII.—To the Milanese clergy.—He receives Hadericus under the protection of the Apostolic See and excommunicates all who inflict any harm upon him or his churches. 926

CCCXVIII.—To Athanasius, bishop of Naples.—He reproves him for not breaking the treaty he had made with the Saracens, although he had promised to break it. He shows that, because of this, the Saracens had inflicted many evils upon Christians. He threatens him with excommunication unless he breaks that treaty. 927

CCCXIX.—To Archbishop Methodius.—He congratulates him on his cultivation of the orthodox faith and on his zeal and care for religion. He prays that he may make ever greater spiritual progress and consoles him. 928

CCCXX.—To Emperor Charles.—He announces to the emperor that he is suffering such evils at the hands of the Saracens that he can no longer endure them. He asks him to send an army promptly to his aid and sends him a palm together with a blessing. 929

CCCXXI.—To various bishops.—He declares that he has excommunicated Athanasius, bishop of Naples, together with all who agree with him, because, although often admonished, he never wished to break the treaty made with the Saracens as he had promised. 930

CCCXXII.—To Romanus, archbishop of Ravenna.—He reproves him for admitting Count Alberic into Ravenna and harassing the noblemen of Ravenna contrary to the oath they had sworn to him. He says that, when he returns from Naples, he will take care of all these matters. He orders Dominic, archdeacon of the Church of Faenza, to be consecrated bishop. 931

CCCXXIII.—To the same.—He reproves him for consenting that another man’s lawful wife be handed over to her abductor and for daring to oppose the Roman Church. For these reasons he suspends him from conferring sacred orders until his case has been examined by the synod, to which he orders him to come. 932

CCCXXIV.—To the same.—He orders the clergy of Piacenza, whom Romanus had received when they fled to him without letters of recommendation, to be sent back to their bishop. He also orders the clergy of that Church to be absolved until Romanus comes with them to the synod. 933

CCCXXV.—To the priest Constantine.—He excommunicates him because, without his permission, he had been promoted by the archbishop of Ravenna to the bishopric of the Church of Faenza. He also forbids him to exercise the administration of that Church until he comes to the Roman synod. 933

CCCXXVI.—To John, bishop of Ficoclensis.—He entrusts him with the visitation and care of the Church of Faenza, which is without a pastor, until a new pastor is appointed over it. 934

CCCXXVII.—To Archbishop Romanus.—He orders him to come to Rome for the synod under penalty of excommunication, to answer the charges brought against him. 934

CCCXXVIII.—To Emperor Charles.—He sends Peter and Zacharias as envoys to him, for the purpose of correcting the evils that he complains of having suffered during Charles’s reign. 935

CCCXXIX.—To the people of Ravenna.—He orders them to separate themselves from communion with the archbishop of Ravenna, who had been excommunicated in the synod, until they know that he has been absolved. 935

CCCXXX.—To Emperor Charles.—He congratulates him on his devotion toward the Roman Church. He rejoices that Charles wishes to come to Ravenna to discuss the condition of the Church and the empire [Col. 1098]. He asks him to come before the day he had appointed. 936

CCCXXXI.—To Wilibertus, archbishop of Cologne.—He commends his vigilance and, moved by his prayers, absolves a certain excommunicated priest who, according to Wilibertus’s testimony, had now been cleansed by a lengthy penance, and restores him to priestly ministry. He entrusts him with the case of the adulterer Gideon, so that he may pronounce a canonical judgment. 936

CCCXXXII.—To Leo, Landulfus, and Lando.—That they arrange for the son of Auxentius, who had been captured by Attinulfus, to be restored to his father. 937

CCCXXXIII.—To Michael, king of the Bulgarians.—He urges him to return to the faith and obedience of the Roman Church and to send envoys. 938

CCCXXXIV.—To the emperor and empress. 939

CCCXXXV.—To the Empress Angelberga. 939

CCCXXXVI.—To the same. 939

CCCXXXVII.—To the same. 939

CCCXXXVIII.—To the glorious duke Domasolus. 939

CCCXXXIX.—To Rostagnus, archbishop of Arles.—The bride is to be deprived of communion unless she wishes to abandon her abductor and return to her bridegroom. 940

CCCXL.—To Sigibodus, archbishop of Narbonne.—Concerning the examination of the case of a certain priest. 940

CCCXLI.—To Cennemocus, bishop of Vannes.—That a murderous priest cannot remain in the priesthood. 941

CCCXLII.—To the bishops of Britain.—Concerning monks ordained by Abbot Heclocarus. 941

CCCXLIII.—To Bishop Peter. 941

CCCXLIV.—To Marinus and Pulcher. 942

CCCXLV.—To Count Cozila.—Concerning those who, having dismissed their wives, have entered into other marriages. 942

CCCXLVI.—A constitution concerning the rights of cardinals. 942

CCCXLVII.—Against violators of the House of God. 943

CCCXLVIII.—To Theiberga and Aldericus.—He urges them to return Radulfus’s wife to him. 943

CCCXLIX.—To Abbot Berrarius.—Concerning reverence toward the supreme pontiffs. 944

CCCL.—To Photius, patriarch of Constantinople.—Concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit. 944

CCCLI.—To a certain person, perhaps the archbishop of Ravenna.—He praises his zeal toward the Apostolic See and advises him to persevere. He promises to count him among his friends and orders him to come to Rome. 946

CCCLII.—To Athanasius, bishop of Naples.—He absolves him from excommunication and restores him to priestly ministry, provided that he breaks the treaty made with the Saracens, as he had promised, sends some of them to him as captives after the rest have been slaughtered, and thereafter makes no treaty with them. 946

CCCLIII.—To the people of Geneva.—He orders them to obey Bishop Optandus, whom he himself had consecrated. 947

CCCLIV.—To Emperor Charles.—He complains that a certain Marquis Wido has seized much property of the Roman Church. He asks Charles to defend the Church and to come in person as its helper. 948

CCCLV.—To the Empress Riccarda.—He complains that no aid is being brought to him against the Saracen incursions. He asks her to seek assistance quickly from the emperor. He commends his envoy and asks her to work for Angelberga’s recall from exile and her being sent to Rome. 949

CCCLVI.—A privilege for the monastery of Monte Cassino. 950

CCCLVII.—To the archbishop of Vienne.—He reproves him for placing Bishop Optandus in prison and appointing another in the Church of Geneva. He orders him to restore Optandus to his see and to come to the synod to clear himself of the charges brought against him. 952

CCCLVIII.—To Oteramus, archbishop of Vienne.—He deals with Bishop Optandus in replying to his letters, and with the letters he writes to the bishop of Maurienne, that he may come to Rome. 952

CCCLIX.—To Adalbertus, bishop of Maurienne.—He orders him to come to Rome with the bishop of Grenoble, whom he had treated disgracefully. 953

CCCLX.—To Anselm, archbishop of Milan.—He confirms the privileges of the Milanese Church and urges him to remain faithful to the Roman Church. He recounts the injuries inflicted by the Saracens and wicked Christians and asks him to pour out prayers to the Lord for the Church. 954

CCCLXI.—To Romanus, archbishop of Ravenna.—He orders him to receive the deacon John kindly and restore to him the property that had been taken away. 954

CCCLXII.—To the clergy of Ravenna.—That they hand over to his envoy and to Duke John a certain Maimbertus, whom he had previously ordered to be expelled from the Church of Ravenna, after he has been captured, and arrange for him to be sent to the pope. 955

CCCLXIII.—To John Martinus.—The same subject. 956

CCCLXIV.—To Duke John.—That he bring the captured Maimbertus to him, detain the women who are with him, and arrange for the letter to the archbishop of Ravenna to be delivered. 956

CCCLXV.—To Emperor Charles.—He congratulates him on his safety and rejoices that he is about to come immediately to Italy. He urges him to come promptly to the aid of the Roman Church and to order the marauder Guido to be expelled from the Church’s territories. 957

CCCLXVI.—To Bishop Liutwardus.—He gives thanks that he had taken care that the emperor come to Italy for the defense of the Church. 958

CCCLXVII.—To all the bishops.—He advises them to observe his institutions and to judge justly. 958

CCCLXVIII.—To King Charles.—A supplementary clause: that he may strengthen King Carloman in love for the Roman Church. 958

CCCLXIX.—To Michael, king of the Bulgarians. 959

CCCLXX.—To Luitbertus, archbishop of Mainz. 959

CCCLXXI.—To Emperor Louis. 959

CCCLXXII.—To the bishops of Britain.—What is to be done concerning monks ordained by their abbot. 959

CCCLXXIII.—To a certain person. 960

CCCLXXIV.—To another unidentified person. 960

CCCLXXV.—The pope’s address to the bishops near the end of the Synod of Troyes. 960

CCCLXXVI.—Likewise, the pope’s address to the king. 961

CCCLXXVII.—Pope John’s address to the Fathers of the Second Synod of Troyes concerning the excommunication of Lambertus, Adalbertus, and their other followers. 961

CCCLXXVIII.—The bishops’ response. 961

CCCLXXIX.—Excommunication issued at the same synod against invaders of ecclesiastical property. 962

CCCLXXX.—Pope John’s repeated excommunication against Bishop Formosus, the *nomenclator* Gregory, and the *magister militum* George. 963

CCCLXXXI.—Pope John’s statute against laymen who, while their wives are living, take other wives, and against bishops who, for the sake of ambition, transfer from a lesser Church to a greater one. 963

CCCLXXXII.—He grants the privilege of appointing over himself one of his own number whom the clergy and people have acclaimed, notwithstanding a contrary choice by kings or princes. 964
